CVM Logices Commentarios nostros nuper editos, adeò vobis gratos extitisse viderem, Rector dignissime, Doctores, Magistríque grauissimi, & sapientissimi; celebris, multísque nominibus Academia illustris, vt inito consilio, omnium calculo, & sententia probatos, instituendæ iuuentutis gratia, Dialecticæ professoribus, & Magistris discipulis explicandos præscripseritis: cùm denique decretum hoc vestrum auctoritate regia firmatum, stabilitúmque sit, vtpotè Scholasticis omnibus perutile, qui germanum huius Academiæ, & Aristotelicæ disciplinæ consonam doctrinam, vestro iudicio in hisce Commentariis repertam imbibere possent: hoc sanè totum meum animum, huic vniuersitati iam dudum, nec immeritò, deditissimum, adeò necessitudinis amorísque vinculo adstrictum reddidit, vt nihil non aggrediendum, nihil non tentandum putarem: quod huic Academiæ vtile, vel certè gratum fore iudicarem. Cùm autem eiusdem Academiæ viri grauissimi, [PDF 8] pariter, & doctissimi, quibus me multis nominibus deuinctum fateor, Commentarios nostros vberiùs protractos, quàm in eadem vniuersitate inueteratus ferret vsus, viderent: gratum pariter, ac vtile fore arbitrabantur, si eosdem Commentarios in compendium redactos, non sine multorum id iam dudum expetentium acclamatione iterum proferrem. Cùm ergo communis boni studio tenerentur accensi, & id à me iterum, ac sæpius postularent: eorum præceptis parendum omnino fuit, quorum auctoritas apud me plurimùm valens, ad alia properantem animum, extemplo ad hunc laborem suscipiendum conuertit. Suscepi sanè, & qua potui diligentia perfeci. Habetis iam viri grauissimi compendium hoc, nihilo magis fermè nostrũ: omnino vestrum: re quidem exiguum: placendi studio maximum. Id certè, vel maximè in eo spectandum fuit vt liberalium artium attingentium limina, iuuarentur ingenia: ne rerum multitudine oppressi, vel certè deterriti, ab incepto desisterent, aut perfectè rem se assequi posse desperarent. Hunc ergo æquo certè animo laborem susceptum, grati erga vos animi monumentum, vestro maturiori prudentíque iudicio submitto, dignitatíque vestræ sacratum volo. Quòd si conatus nostros ea qua estis benignitate præditi, sensero probari: quæ supersunt omnia pari, & (si fieri poterit) maiore diligentia prosequar.

ince I saw that our Commentaries on Logic, S lately published, were so welcome to you, most worthy Rector, most grave and most wise Doctors and Masters, of an Academy famed and illustrious on many accounts, that by common counsel, approved by the vote and judgment of all, you prescribed that they be expounded to their pupils by the professors and Masters of Dialectic for the instruction of youth; since, finally, your decree was confirmed and established by royal authority, inasmuch as it would be useful to all Schoolmen, who might imbibe in these Commentaries a doctrine, approved by your judgment, genuine and consonant with that of this Academy and of the Aristotelian discipline: this, indeed, long since made my whole mind entirely devoted to this University, and not undeservedly; and it has bound me by so close a bond of attachment and love that I thought there was nothing I should not undertake, nothing I should not attempt, which I judged would be useful, or at least welcome, to this Academy. But when the most grave men of this same Academy, ã ij [PDF 8] as well as most learned, to whom I confess myself bound by many titles, saw that our Commentaries had been drawn out more fully than long-established usage in that same University would bear, they judged that it would be welcome and likewise useful if I were to bring out the same Commentaries again, reduced to a compendium— not without the acclaim of many who had long been asking for it. Since, therefore, they were fired with zeal for the common good, and asked this of me again and more often, I had to obey their precepts altogether: their authority, which weighs very much with me, at once turned my mind, hastening to other things, to undertaking this labor. I undertook it indeed, and completed it with what diligence I could. You now have, most grave men, this compendium—hardly more ours than wholly yours: small indeed in substance, very great in the desire to please. This, certainly, was to be kept in view above all, that the minds of those approaching the threshold of the liberal arts should be helped, lest, overwhelmed by the multitude of matters, or at least deterred, they should abandon what they had begun, or despair of being able to master the subject perfectly. This labor, then, undertaken with a truly willing mind, a monument of a mind grateful toward you, I submit to your more mature and prudent judgment, and I wish it dedicated to your dignity. But if I perceive that our efforts are approved by you, endowed as you are with such kindness, I shall pursue all that remains with equal and (if it can be done) greater diligence.

PDF 9

AD LIBERALIVM ARTIVM STVDIOSOS FLORENTISSIMÆ Complutensis Academiæ.

O F T H E L I B E R A L A RT S OF THE MOST FLOURISHING Academy of Alcalá.

VOS pariter, studiosi adolescentes, quæ vberiùs antea, & fusiùs disputauimus, ea nunc paucis cõtenta suscipite. Quod iam dudum petistis, imò expetistis: quod Academia vera Complutensis probauit: quod libens suscepit, & Aristotelicæ, ac diui Thomæ doctrinæ iudicauit consonum offerimus. Nostris vtinam cedat votis: quod susceptis iam suscipiendísque laboribus contendimus. Neque enim æquè aliud in animo est nostro: atque omnibus, qua fieri poßit maximè (vt profeßionis nostræ ratio institutúmque postulat) continuò prodesse. Hic nostrorum laborum scopus: hic finis. Nostra ergo diligentia, & opera (vtinam vtili) libentes fruimini. Omnia deinceps reliqua, modò diuinum adsit nomen, accepturi. Valete.

ou likewise, studious young men, receive now, contained in Ya few pages, the things we formerly disputed more fully and at greater length. What you have long asked for, nay demanded; what the Academy of Alcalá approved; what it gladly accepted and judged consonant with the true Aristotelian doctrine and that of St. Thomas: this we offer. Would that what we strive for in the labors already undertaken and yet to be undertaken may answer our wishes. For we have nothing else so much in mind as to be of continual benefit to all, as far as possible (as the character and institute of our profession demands). This is the aim of our labors, this their end. Enjoy, therefore, gladly our diligence and work (would that it be useful). All the rest hereafter, provided the divine name be with us, you shall receive. Farewell. ã iij

uan de Ribera, by the grace of God and of the J Apostolic See Patriarch of Antioch, Archbishop of Valencia, and Councillor to the King, etc. By the tenor of these presents we grant licence and faculty to print, in this city and diocese of Valencia, this book of Commentaries on the whole Dialectic of Aristotle, by Father Antonio Rubio, of the Society of J e s u s , Doctor of Sacred Theology. y order of the most Illustrious and most Reverend Lord B Don Juan de Ribera, Patriarch of Antioch and Archbishop of Valencia, I have read through these Commentaries of Father Doctor Antonio Rubio, of the Society of Jesus, on the whole Dialectic of Aristotle; in which not only have I found nothing contrary to Catholic doctrine, but I have also recognized them to be filled with doctrine most useful to Philosophers and Theologians; and I have judged that they will be very profitable not only to the pupils of the most flourishing Academy of Alcalá (at whose request the author now brings these Commentaries to light again), but also to all the most learned. QUESTIONS

QVAESTIONES PROOEMIALES DIALECTICÆ INTRODVCTIONE

ON DIALECTIC, B Y WA Y O F I N T R O D U C T I O N .

QUESTION ONE

QVÆSTIO PRIMA.

[…]

Vtrùm Dialectica sit necessaria.

Whether Dialectic is necessary.

DIALECTICAM, vt titulum quæstionis explicemus, in Naturalem & Acquisitam distinguunt quidam: Naturalem vocantes, discursus illos, quos solo naturali lumine efficere solent rustici etiam homines. Acquisitam verò eam, quam studio ac labore comparamus. Si tamen propriè loquendum est, non Dialecticam, sed quoddam eius initium à natura habemus, nempe naturale lumen intellectus, à quo discursus illi inordinati procedunt, qui satis impropriè Dialectica vocantur: propriè verò pro facultate acquisita solùm accipitur, de qua inquirimus, An sit necessaria. Sed Necessarium dupliciter accipi solet in schola; simpliciter quidem aut sine addito, vel secundùm quid, aut ex suppositione. Necessarium simpliciter illud vocatur, quod non per ordinem ad aliud, sed ex propria natura necessitatem habet: in qua acceptione solùm Deus dicitur ens necessarium, quia absque ordine vel dependentia ab alio habet, quòd non possit non esse. Necessarium verò ex suppositione vocamus illud, quod ex suppositione alicuius finis consequendi tale est, vt cibum capere necessarium dicimus ad sustentandam vitam. Ergo dum titulus quæstionis inquit. An facultas Dialecticæ sit necessaria, non de prioris necessitatis modo intelligitur, sed de posterioris: ita sensus sit, an sit necessaria ad alias scientias acquirendas. Prima opinio tenet, Dialecticam non esse necessariam ad alias scientias, sed posse sine illa acquiri, quamuis

o explain the title of the question, some divide T Dialectic into Natural and Acquired: calling Natural those discur‐ sive reasonings which even rustic men are accustomed to carry out by the natural light alone; and Acquired, that which we obtain by study and labor. If, however, we are to speak properly, what we have from nature is not Dialectic but a certain beginning of it, namely the natural light of the intellect, from which those disordered reasonings proceed that are quite improperly called Dialectic: properly, however, it is taken only for the acquired faculty, about which we are inquiring whether it is necessary. But “necessary” is customarily taken in the schools in two ways: either simply, that is, without qualification, or in a certain respect, that is, on a supposition. That is called necessary simply which has its necessity not through an order to something else but from its own nature: in which acceptation God alone is called a necessary being, because He has it without order to or dependence on another that He cannot not be. We call necessary on a supposition, on the other hand, that which is such on the supposition of some end to be attained, as we say that taking food is necessary for sustaining life. Therefore, when the title of the question asks whether the faculty of Dialectic is necessary, it is understood not of the former mode of necessity but of the latter, so that the sense is: whether it is necessary for acquiring the other sciences. The first opinion holds that Dialectic is not necessary for the other sciences, but that they can be acquired without it, although A

p. 2

non sine magno labore, nec sine errorum admixtione, esse verò vtilem, vt commodiùs ac faciliùs, & sine periculo errandi comparentur: ita tenet Iauellus in compendio suæ Logicæ, tractatu. 1. cap. 2. quem sequuntur pauci, & probatur duplici argumento. Primò, quia non est necessaria propter se, nec propter alias scientias, ergo nullo modo. Antecedens probatur, quòd nõ propter se: quia cùm Logica sit scientia simul & modus sciendi, si ad seipsam esset necessaria, simul acquirẽda esset scientia & modus sciendi, aduersus dictum illud Aristotel. 2. Meta. tex. 1. Scientiam simul & modum sciendi quærere absurdum est: quòd verò propter alias scientias non sit necessaria, probatur, quia quælibet scientia habet proprias definitiones, ac demonstrationes, ergo est sibi modus sciendi, quare non indiget Dialectica pro modo sciendi. Secundò, quia duo sunt necessaria, vt aliquis consequatur scientiam: Primum, vt principia cognoscat: Secundum, vt certò sciat, se aptis ratiocinationibus vti, & non fallacibus in colligendis conclusionibus ex eis. Sed vtrumque potest homo sine Dialectica, per lumen naturale intellectus, vt patet in rusticis, qui vnum ex altero euidenter colligunt in hac vel illa materia: & de aliis refertur, quod scientias sine Dialectica comparauerint, vt medicinam Hippocrates, & mathematicas disciplinas alij: ergo non erit Dialectica ad alias scientias acquirendas necessaria.

not without great labor nor without an admixture of errors; but that it is useful, so that they may be obtained more conveniently and easily and without danger of erring. So holds Javelli in the Compendium of his Logic, tract. 1, ch. 2, whom few follow; and it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because it is necessary neither for its own sake nor for the sake of the other sciences; therefore in no way. The antecedent is proved: that it is not necessary for its own sake, because, since Logic is at once a science and a mode of knowing, if it were necessary for itself, the science and the mode of knowing would have to be acquired at the same time, against that saying of Aristotle, Metaph. 2, text 1: It is absurd to seek at the same time a science and the mode of knowing. That it is not necessary for the sake of the other sciences is proved because every science has its own definitions and demonstrations, and is therefore its own mode of knowing, so that it does not need Dialectic as a mode of knowing. Second, because two things are necessary for someone to attain science: first, that he know the principles; second, that he know with certainty that he is using apt reasonings, and not fallacious ones, in drawing conclusions from them. But a man can do both without Dialectic, by the natural light of the intellect, as is plain in rustics, who evidently infer one thing from another in this or that matter; and it is related of others that they obtained sciences without Dialectic, as Hippocrates did medicine, and others the mathematical disciplines: therefore Dialectic will not be necessary for acquiring the other sciences.

Secunda opinio opposita est, quæ affirmat, non posse vllam scientiam vllo modo acquiri sine Logica, quam tenent plures quos idem Iauellus citat vbi suprà, & probant vnico arg. quia vt aliquis acquirat scientiam certò scire debet reducere conclusionem vsque ad prima principia, vt docet Arist. 1. lib. Posteriorum cap. 2. per euidentes consequentias, sed repugnat absque Dialectica talem reductionem posse efficere, cùm non possit certò cognosci, quòd tota conclusionum multitudo ex principiis deriuetur, nisi per artem, ergo non poterit nisi per Dialecticam.

The second opinion is the opposite one, which affirms that no science can in any way be acquired without Logic. It is held by many, whom the same Javelli cites in the place above, and they prove it by a single argument: because in order to acquire science one must know with certainty how to reduce the conclusion back to the first principles, as Aristotle teaches in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2, through evident consequences; but it is impossible to effect such a reduction without Dialectic, since one cannot know with certainty that the whole multitude of conclusions is derived from the principles except by art; therefore one cannot do so except by Dialectic.

Communis sententia media videtur inter has extremas, quam tenent Sotus & Cardinalis Toletus quæst. 1 proœmialis, quos sequuntur alij, nempe Dialecticam esse necessariam ad reliquas scientias perfectè acquirendas: sed ad comparandas modo imperfecto, non esse necessariam; sed vtilem, ita vt sine illa comparari imperfectè possint.

The common opinion seems to lie midway between these extremes. It is held by Soto and Cardinal Toledo, proem. q. 1, whom others follow: namely, that Dialectic is necessary for acquiring the remaining sciences perfectly, but that for obtaining them in an imperfect manner it is not necessary but useful, so that without it they can be obtained imperfectly.

2 Pro solutione quæstionis tria sunt breuiter notanda. Primum est, duo esse necessaria ad comparandam scientiam: Primum, quòd cõclusio per euidentem consequentiã, ex euidenti principio deducatur: Secundum, quòd vtrumque constet euidenter

2 For the solution of the question three things should briefly be noted. The first is that two things are necessary for obtaining science: first, that the conclusion be deduced through an evident consequence from an evident principle; second, that both be evidently

p. 3

ei qui scientiam acquirit: nam si non cognoscit euidenter principium, solùm erit ei creditum, vel opinatum: & si non cognoscat euidentem esse consequentiam, solùm erit respectu illius probabilis: & tam ex primo quàm ex secundo sequitur, quòd conclusio quam colligit, non sit euidens, sed probabilis, cùm non possit esse certior præmissis, aut consequentia; quare non erit scientifica. Secundò adnotandũ est, posse quidem hominem per lumen naturale intellectus, imperfecto quodam modo discurrere, vnumque ex alio deducere, inordinatè quidem, hoc est, non cognoscendo ordinem, ac dependentiam, quam habet conclusio ex principiis, quod docuit Arist. 1. Rheto. ad Theodoctem cap 1. illis verbis: Multi hæc temerè & casu, nonnulli exercitatione ac habitu factitant, &c. quia ordo ille nequit sine arte cognosci. Tertiò adnotandum est, habitum scientiæ per vnam demonstrationem generari, propter efficacitatem demõstrationis: sed dum generatur per vnum actum, imperfectam habet rationem habitus, aut scientiæ, quia nondum est radicatus in subiecto; quare nec ipsum denominat talem simpliciter: non enim dicitur acquisisse talem scientiam, quia vnam, aut alteram conclusionem eius acquisiuit; nisi secundùm quid, hoc est, secundùm vnam illam conclusionem.

evident to the one who acquires the science: for if he does not know the principle evidently, it will be only believed or opined; and if he does not know the consequence to be evident, it will be only probable with respect to him; and from both the first and the second it follows that the conclusion he gathers is not evident but probable, since it cannot be more certain than the premises or the consequence; wherefore it will not be scientific. Second, it should be noted that a man can indeed, by the natural light of the intellect, reason discursively in a certain imperfect manner and deduce one thing from another, though in a disordered way, that is, without knowing the order and dependence that the conclusion has on the principles. This Aristotle taught in Rhetoric to Theodectes 1, ch. 1, in these words: Many do these things at random, and some by practice and habit, etc., because that order cannot be known without art. Third, it should be noted that the habit of science generated through one demonstration, on account of the efficacy of the demonstration, while it is being generated through one act, has the ratio of a habit, or of science, imperfectly, because it is not yet rooted in the subject; wherefore it does not denominate its subject such simply: for a man is not said to have acquired such a science because he has acquired one or another conclusion of it, except in a certain respect, that is, according to that one conclusion.

Ex his duas conclusiones colligo, quibus meam scientiam explico. Prior est; Ad vnam, vel alteram conclusionem alterius scientiæ acquirendam, non est necessaria Logica, sed per solum naturale lumen acquiri potest. Probatur hæc: quia sicut naturale lumen se extendit ad cognoscenda principia; ita etiam ad vnam, aut alteram conclusionem principiis proximam: quia notissima est, per propriam industriam, & laborem hominis potest se extendere: & cùm per vnam conclusionem scientia acquiratur, saltem imperfecta, verum est in hoc sensu, quòd ad alias scientias imperfectè comparandas Dialectica non sit necessaria. Secunda conclusio. Integra scientia, non potest acquiri sine Dialectica, hoc est, secundũ omnes conclusiones eius; quàm sic probo. Non potest aliquis omnes conclusiones ex principiis colligere per euidentes demonstrationes nisi cognoscat euidenter ordinem, secundùm quem vna deriuatur ab altera vsque ad vltimam, quæ proximè colligitur ex principiis: Sed ordo omnium conclusionum inter sese, & cum principiis cognosci nequit sine arte reducendi, aut resoluendi eas in principia; Ergo non poterit integra scientia acquiri sine Dialectica: & hoc est non posse perfectè sine illa acquiri: & iuxta has duas conclusiones nostras, intelligenda est tertia opinio communis, quã sic intellectã veram esse dicimus.

From these I gather two conclusions, by which I explain my view. The first is: For acquiring one or another conclusion of another science Logic is not necessary, but it can be acquired by the natural light alone. This is proved: because just as the natural light extends itself to knowing the principles, so it can also extend itself, by a man’s own industry and labor, to one or another conclusion proximate to the principles, since it is very well known; and since through one conclusion science is acquired, at least imperfect science, it is true in this sense that Dialectic is not necessary for obtaining the other sciences imperfectly. Second conclusion: An entire science cannot be acquired without Dialectic, that is, according to all its conclusions; which I prove thus. No one can gather all the conclusions from the principles through evident demonstrations unless he knows evidently the order according to which one is derived from another, down to the last, which is gathered proximately from the principles. But the order of all the conclusions among themselves and with the principles cannot be known without the art of reducing or resolving them into the principles; therefore an entire science cannot be acquired without Dialectic: and this is what it means that it cannot be acquired perfectly without it. And in accordance with these two conclusions of ours the third, common, opinion is to be understood, which, understood thus, we say is true. A ij

p. 4

4 Ad primum argumentũ primę opinionis respondet Cardinalis Toletus: Logicam esse necessariam ad seipsam secundùm diuersas partes, quæ præsupponuntur aliis, vt secundùm partem prædicamentorum, ad partem enuntiationis, & secundùm hanc ad syllogismum: sed cùm prima pars non pręsupponat alteram, non explicat hæc solutio, quonam modo Logica secũdùm primam partem possit esse ad se necessaria. propterea alio modo respondeo: Logicam duo habere, nempe esse scientiam, in quantum suas conclusiones demonstrat, & esse modum sciendi, in quantum instrumenta conficit, per quæ scire possimus: & hæc ratio prior est illa secundùm nostram considerationem: quia priùs intelligimus instrumenta sciendi, vt definitionem, ac demonstrationem, quàm intelligamus conclusiones demonstratas in logica. Dicimus ergo, Logicam, vt modum sciendi, non solùm secundùm diuersas partes, sed etiã secundùm se totam esse necessariam ad seipsam, vt scientiam, ad quod satis est, quòd vt scientia præsupponat seipsam vt modum sciendi: dum autem Aristotel. docuit, absurdum esse simul quærere scientiam & modum sciendi, per modum sciendi Dialecticam intellexit, sed per scientiam, non eamdem Dialecticam sed quamlibet aliam scientiam, vt docuit D. Thom. in expositione eiusdem loci, quam absurdum esse simul cum Dialectica quærere: quasi dicat priùs esse addiscendam Dialecticam, tanquam necessariam ad alias. Ad secundum respondeo, non posse naturale lumen nisi perficiatur per artem Dialecticæ, cognoscere ordinem omnium conclusionum inter sese, & cum principiis, & ideo nec perfectè alias scientias acquirere, vt iam docuimus. Argumentum secundæ opinionis solùm probat, sine Dialectica non posse scientiam perfecto modo comparari. Ex dictis colligitur, quem locum Dialectica obtinere debeat in acquisitione scientiarum est enim prima, à qua incipiendum est: quia cùm sit modus sciendi, non possunt aliæ sine ea comparari, nec proinde simul cum ea acquiri, nisi absurdum illud sequatur, quod simul scientiam & modum sciendi quæramus.

4 To the first argument of the first opinion Cardinal Toledo replies that Logic is necessary for itself according to its different parts, which are presupposed by the others: as the part on the categories by the part on enunciation, and this latter by the syllogism. But since the first part does not presuppose another, this solution does not explain how Logic according to its first part can be necessary for itself. Therefore I reply in another way: Logic has two aspects, namely that it is a science, inasmuch as it demonstrates its conclusions, and that it is a mode of knowing, inasmuch as it produces the instruments by which we are able to know; and this latter ratio is prior to the former according to our way of considering, because we understand the instruments of knowing, such as definition and demonstration, before we understand the conclusions demonstrated in logic. We say, therefore, that Logic as a mode of knowing is necessary for itself as a science, not only according to its different parts but also according to its whole self; for which it is enough that as a science it presupposes itself as a mode of knowing. And when Aristotle taught that it is absurd to seek at the same time a science and the mode of knowing, by the mode of knowing he meant Dialectic, but by science not Dialectic itself but any other science whatever, as St. Thomas taught in his exposition of that same passage, which it is absurd to seek together with Dialectic: as if to say that Dialectic must be learned first, as necessary for the others. To the second I reply that the natural light, unless it is perfected by the art of Dialectic, cannot know the order of all the conclusions among themselves and with the principles, and therefore cannot acquire the other sciences perfectly either, as we have already taught. The argument of the second opinion proves only that without Dialectic science cannot be obtained in a perfect manner. From what has been said it is gathered what place Dialectic ought to hold in the acquisition of the sciences: for it is the first, with which one must begin; because, since it is the mode of knowing, the others cannot be obtained without it, nor, consequently, be acquired together with it, unless that absurdity follow, that we seek at the same time a science and the mode of knowing.

QUESTION II

Vtrùm Dialectica sit scientia

Whether Dialectic is a science.

3 Scientia hac in parte propriè accipitur, pro certa cognitione per demonstrationem comparata, vt docuit Arist. 1. lib. de posteriori resol. ca. 2. sed diuiditur in scientiam Actualem

3 Science is taken here in its proper sense, for certain cognition obtained through demonstration, as Aristotle taught in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2; but it is divided into Actual

p. 5

& Habitualem: Actualis scientia dicitur assensus conclusionis, quæ per demonstrationem probatur, vt assensus huius conclusionis, Homo est risibilis: Habitualis verò scientia est quæ generatur in intellectu ex multis conclusionibus demonstratis: & licèt vtraque sit propriè scientia, tamen in communi modo loquendi pro habituali accipitur. De hac loquitur titulus quæstionis dum quærimus, An Logica sit scientia.

and Habitual. Actual science is said to be the assent to a conclusion that is proved through demonstration, as the assent to this conclusion, Man is risible; habitual science, on the other hand, is that which is generated in the intellect from many demonstrated conclusions. And although each is properly science, yet in the common manner of speaking it is taken for the habitual. Of this the title of the question speaks when we ask whether Logic is a science.

Et prima opinio negat Dialecticam esse scientiam, sed asserit esse facultatem quandam, seu artem scientia inferiorem: & hanc tenuerunt, Ammonius in prologo prædicamentorum, Alexander in principio Topicorum, Ægidius 1. lib. Posteriorum, quæst. 1. Magnesius lib. 1. de interpretatione in principio: Petrus Niger quæst. 11. sui Clypei, & alij, quos secutus est Villapandus quæst. 26. proœmiali. Probatur primò duplici testimonio Aristotelis, qui 1. lib. Rhetoricorum ad Theodectem cap. 2. docet, Rhetoricam esse particulam quandam Dialecticæ, & neutram esse scientiam sed facultatem quandam inueniendarum rationum. & 1. lib. Topicorum cap. 1. Dialectici officium esse, inquit, ex probabilibus disserere. Secundò, probatur ratione, quia quælibet scientia debet habere materiam particularem ac determinatam, circa quam versetur, tanquam circa proprium obiectum, & per quam distinguatur ab aliis, sed Logica non habet materiam determinatam, sed versatur circa materiam omnium scientiarum, quia in omni materia conficit definitiones, ac syllogismos, ergo non erit scientia. Vnde Arist. 2. lib Meta. cap. 2 textu 5: & 1. lib. de posteriori resolut. cap. 8. tex. 27. docuit non habere certum genus subiecti, hoc est, certam materiam circa quam versetur.

And the first opinion denies that Dialectic is a science, but asserts that it is a certain faculty or art inferior to science. This was held by Ammonius in the prologue to the Categories, Alexander at the beginning of the Topics, Giles of Rome on the Posterior Analytics 1, q. 1, Magnesius on On Interpretation 1, at the beginning, Peter Nigri in q. 11 of his Clypeus, and others, whom Villalpando followed in proemial q. 16. It is proved, first, by a twofold testimony of Aristotle, who in Rhetoric to Theodectes 1, ch. 2, teaches that Rhetoric is a certain part of Dialectic, and that neither is a science, but a certain faculty of finding arguments; and in Topics 1, ch. 1, he says that the office of the Dialectician is to discourse from probable premises. Second, it is proved by reason: because every science must have a particular and determinate matter about which it is concerned, as about its proper object, and through which it is distinguished from the others; but Logic does not have a determinate matter, but is concerned with the matter of all the sciences, because in every matter it produces definitions and syllogisms; therefore it will not be a science. Whence Aristotle, Metaph. 2, ch. 2, text 5, and Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 8, text 27, taught that it does not have a definite genus of subject, that is, a definite matter about which it is concerned.

Secunda opinio est communis, & tenenda, Quòd Logica sit vera scientia, quã sequuntur D. Thom. 2. Meta 2. lect. 4. Scotus lib 1. Elenchorum, quæst 1. & in prædicabilibus, q. etiam 1. Niphus 4. Meta. textu 5. in fine. Scotus, & Card. Toletus, q. 2. proœmiali, Fonseca 2. lib. Meta. 3. qu. 1. sectio. 9 & alij omnes. Probatur vnico arg. ex definitione scientiæ tradita ab Arist. 1. lib. Poster. cap. 2. Scientia est habitus per demonstrationem acquisitus, sed Dialectica habet plures demonstrationes, ex euidentibus principiis procedentes, ergo ex eis generabitur scientia. Probatur minor. nam syllogismum primæ figuræ euidenter concludere, demonstratur ex illis principiis, Dici de omni & Dici de nullo, & in singulis partibus Dialecticæ fiunt aliæ demonstrationes similes.

The second opinion is the common one, and to be held: that Logic is a true science. It is followed by St. Thomas, Metaph. 2, 2, lect. 4; Scotus, on the Sophistical Refutations 1, q. 1, and on the Predicables, also q. 1; Nifo, Metaph. 4, text 5, at the end; Soto and Cardinal Toledo, proemial q. 2; Fonseca, Metaph. 2, 3, q. 1, sect. 9; and all the others. It is proved by a single argument, from the definition of science handed down by Aristotle in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2: Science is a habit acquired through demonstration; but Dialectic has many demonstrations proceeding from evident principles; therefore science will be generated from them. The minor is proved: for that a syllogism of the first figure concludes evidently is demonstrated from those principles, Said of all and Said of none; and in the individual parts of Dialectic other similar demonstrations are made.

4 Ad primum argu. dicimus, Rhetoricam particulam esse Dialecticæ, docuisse Aristo. quia sub parte Topica quodammodo

4 To the first argument we say that Aristotle taught that Rhetoric is a part of Dialectic because under the Topical part it is in a certain way A iij

p. 6

continetur, in quantum docet loca inuenire, ex quibus eruantur probabilia argum. & quantum ad hoc neutra est scientia: Dialectica verò non solùm docet loca inuenire, sed ea probat per demonstrationem, Præterea, quòd probabilia arg. generent opinionem, & ex hoc habet veram rationem scientiæ: nihil autem horum rhetorica facit, & propterea scientia non est, sed ars quædam scientia inferior Secundum testimonium Arist. eodem fere modo declaratur; quia officium Dialectici est, probabiliter disserere non quomodocumque sed ducendo per veram demonstrationem, ex quibus sit constituendus syllogismus probabilis, & quod probabilem solùm generet assensum, & hoc est esse veram scientiam.

contained, inasmuch as it teaches how to find the places from which probable arguments are drawn; and as regards this, neither is a science. But Dialectic not only teaches how to find the places, but proves them through demonstration; and further, that probable arguments generate opinion; and from this it has the true ratio of science. Rhetoric, however, does none of these things, and therefore it is not a science but a certain art inferior to science. The second testimony of Aristotle is explained in almost the same way: because the office of the Dialectician is to discourse probably, not in just any way, but by teaching through true demonstration from what premises a probable syllogism is to be constructed, and that it generates only a probable assent; and this is to be a true science.

Pro solutione secundi arg. distinguenda duplex materia Logicæ, Remota & Proxima: Remota sunt res omni mundi, nam circa omnes efficit syllogismos, & definitiones, Proxima verò materia sunt operationes intellectus, quas dirigit & ordinat, constituendo ex eis instrumenta. arg. ergo probat de materia remota, de qua etiam loquitur Aristot. in eo loco, scientia verò debet habere materiam proximam circa quam versetur, & per quam distinguatur ab aliis, & hæc sufficit, vt sit scientia determinata: quòd verò materia eius remota non sit determinata, nullum est inconueniens, quia ex materia remota non sumitur ratio scientiæ, sed ex proxima.

For the solution of the second argument a twofold matter of Logic must be distinguished, Remote and Proximate. The remote matter is the things of the whole world, for it produces syllogisms and definitions about all of them. The proximate matter, on the other hand, is the operations of the intellect, which it directs and orders, constructing instruments out of them. The argument, therefore, proves concerning the remote matter, of which Aristotle also speaks in that passage; but a science must have a proximate matter about which it is concerned and through which it is distinguished from the others, and this suffices for it to be a determinate science. That its remote matter is not determinate is no difficulty, because the ratio of a science is taken not from the remote matter but from the proximate.

QUESTION III

Quæst. 3. Vtrum Logica vtens sit scientia — Whether logica utens is a science.

Vtrùm Logica vtens sit scientia.

[…]

Præsupponit titulus quæstionis, quòd Logica diuidatur in Docentem, & Vtentem: quam diuisionem tradiderunt D. Tho. 4 Met. lect. 4. & Scotus qu. 1. Elench. & quæst. etiam prima prædicabilium, à quibus eam accepit schola: sed priusquam diuersas opiniones proponamus declarandum est, an sicut Logica docens, pro tota ipsa scientia accipitur, ita etiam Logica vtens pro tota accipiatur, vel solùm parte topica. Nam quidam dicunt, solam partem topicam esse vtentem, & non demonstratiuam nec reliquas: quorum fundamentum est authoritas D. Tho. qui id videtur asserere 4. Meta. lect. 4. & hoc arg. probare, quia Logica, vt est vsus definiendi, diuidendi, ac demonstrandi in aliis scientiis, non tam Dialectica appellanda est quàm Philosophia, aut quælibet altera scientia, circa cuius materiam talis vsus versatur.

The title of the question presupposes that Logic is divided into docens and utens: a division handed down by St. Thomas, Metaph. 4, lect. 4, and by Scotus, q. 1 on the Sophistical Refutations and also the first question on the Predicables, from whom the schools took it. But before we set out the different opinions, it must be explained whether, just as logica docens is taken for the whole science itself, so too logica utens is taken for the whole, or only for the Topical part. For some say that only the Topical part is utens, and not the demonstrative part nor the rest. Their foundation is the authority of St. Thomas, who seems to assert this in Metaph. 4, lect. 4, and they prove it by this argument: because Logic, as it is the use of defining, dividing and demonstrating in the other sciences, is to be called not so much Dialectic as Philosophy, or whatever other science it is about whose matter such use is concerned.

Communis tamen modus loquendi & sciendi Dialecticæ

The common manner, however, of speaking and thinking of the Dialectical

p. 7

scholæ, Logicam pro tota scientia diuidit in Docẽtem, & Vtentem: ita vt sicut tota ipsa docens est, in quantũ tradit præcepta conficiendi enunciationem, & syllogismum, ac reliqua instrumenta per demonstrationem: ita in quantum vtitur omnibus instrumentis in aliis scientiis dicatur vtens: & hoc est nobis tenendum tanquam verum & necessarium: & probatur primò quia tantùm se extendit Logica vtens, quantum vsus Logicæ docentis, sed Logica docens dicitur de tota scientia, & singulis partibus, & non de sola parte topica: ergo logica vtens de tota & singulis partibus etiam dicetur. Secunda pars topica dicitur Logica vtens, quia probabilibus argumentis vtitur in cæteris scientiis: sed etiam vtitur Logica definitionibus, ac demonstrationibus in cæteris scientiis; ergo dicetur vtens quantum ad reliquas partes præter topicam.

school divides Logic, taken for the whole science, into docens and utens, so that, just as the whole of it is docens inasmuch as it hands down through demonstration the precepts for producing the enunciation and the syllogism and the remaining instruments, so, inasmuch as it uses all the instruments in the other sciences, it is called utens. And this we must hold as true and necessary. And it is proved, first: because logica utens extends as far as the use of logica docens; but logica docens is said of the whole science and of its individual parts, and not of the Topical part alone; therefore logica utens will also be said of the whole and of the individual parts. Second, the Topical part is called logica utens because it uses probable arguments in the other sciences; but Logic also uses definitions and demonstrations in the other sciences; therefore it will be called utens as regards the remaining parts besides the Topical.

Ad D. Tho. respõdeo, hanc esse mentẽ eius, vt Logica quantum ad partem demonstratiuam & reliquas, (præter topicam) verè sit vtens, sed quia forma demonstrandi qua vtitur in aliis scientiis, vniuersalis & quasi generica est, determinatur per materiam earum, quasi per differentiam ac speciem: non tam Dialectica quàm Philosophia vocatur, eo modo quo genus cuiuscunque rei sub nomine specierum comprehenditur. v. g. animal, quod est in homine, non vocamus animal, sed hominẽ, sed de parte topica diuersa est ratio quia cum argumenta probabilia non generent scientiam sed opinionem: potiùs retinet nomen Dialecticæ, vsus huius partis quàm aliarum scientiarum: quia pars est Dialecticæ, quæ vera scientia est, & quia proprium Dialectici officium est, probabiliter disputare in qualibet scientia: & differentiam hanc inter partem Topicam, & reliquas partes Logicæ significauit D. Tho. eodem loco; ex quo colligo, hanc fuisse eius mentem, & non excludere vllam partem Logicæ à vera ratione vtentis.

To St. Thomas I reply that his mind is this: that Logic as regards the demonstrative part and the rest (besides the Topical) is truly utens; but because the form of demonstrating which it uses in the other sciences is universal and as it were generic, and is determined by their matter as by a difference and species, it is called not so much Dialectic as Philosophy, in the way in which the genus of any thing is comprehended under the name of the species: for example, the animal that is in man we do not call animal but man. But with the Topical part the ratio is different: because, since probable arguments generate not science but opinion, the use of this part retains the name of Dialectic rather than of the other sciences; because it is a part of Dialectic, which is a true science, and because it is the proper office of the Dialectician to dispute probably in any science whatever. And this difference between the Topical part and the remaining parts of Logic St. Thomas indicated in the same place; from which I gather that this was his mind, and that he does not exclude any part of Logic from the true ratio of utens.

5 Supposito ergo, quòd Logica vtens pro tota ipsa sciẽtia, & omnibus partibus sumi debeat: Quærimus, an sit scientia, aut saltem distinctus habitus à Logica docente: & prima opinio asserit esse veram scientiam, sed non esse habitum distinctũ à docente, sed eundẽ; ita vt scientia sit, in quantũ docens, & etiã in quantum vtens. Hanc videtur sequi Niphus 4. Meta. tex. 5. & probatur hoc argumento. Quando aliquis vtitur Logica in aliis scientiis efficiendo demonstrationes, acquirit facilitatem intellectu ad eas & alias iterum efficiendum, & hanc facilitatem acquirit per actus procedentes à Logica docente, quam præsupponit: ergo perficit eandem Logicam docentem: & ideo erit vera scientia; quia scientia non perficitur nisi per scientiam

5 Supposing, then, that logica utens ought to be taken for the whole science itself and all its parts, we ask whether it is a science, or at least a habit distinct from logica docens. And the first opinion asserts that it is a true science, but not a habit distinct from docens, rather the same one, so that it is science both inasmuch as it is docens and inasmuch as it is utens. Nifo seems to follow this, Metaph. 4, text 5, and it is proved by this argument. When someone uses Logic in the other sciences by producing demonstrations, he acquires a facility of the intellect for producing those and others again; and he acquires this facility through acts proceeding from logica docens, which they presuppose; therefore it perfects the same logica docens; and therefore it will be true science, because science is not perfected except by science A iiij

p. 8

, non tamen distincta, nec distinctus habitus, sed idem quasi seipsum perficiens.

yet not a distinct science, nor a distinct habit, but the same one, as it were perfecting itself.

Secunda opinio, quam sequuntur moderni quidam, asserit, Logicam vtentem esse veram scientiam, & distinctam à docente. Vt autem vtrumque probẽt, distinguunt duo officia vel actus Logicæ. Primum, quo docet conficere instrumenta, vt syllogismum, aut definitionem. Secundum, quo vtitur præceptis traditis, efficiendo eadem instrumenta in aliis scientiis, & cùm per multiplicationem actuum generetur facilitas in potentiis, quam facilitatem vocamus habitum, necesse est ex diuersis actibus diuersos quoque habitus generari in intellectu: ita vt primò reddatur facilis intellectus ad tradenda præcepta. deinde aliam facultatem diuersam acquirat per exercitium eorundem præceptorum efficiendo syllogismos Exemplum assignari potest in musica, in qua duplex facilitas acquiritur: prima, in intellectu tradente regulas cõsonantiarum, secunda, in manibus: & primam vocare solent Theoricam, postremam Practicam. Vnde sequitur duplicem etiam facilitatem ponendam esse in Logica, vnam, quæ sit Theorica, seu speculatiua, aliam, quæ sit Practica: & illa erit habitus Logicæ docentis, hæc verò Logicæ vtentis. Probant primò, quòd sint habitus distincti, quia syllogismus factus in Philosophia naturali non procedit ab habitu eiusdem Philosophiæ: quia nõ docet quomodo sit componendus syllogismus: sed nec procedit à Logica docente: nam hæc solùm habet tradere præcepta in communi efficiendi instrumenta, non ea efficere in particulari, ergo debet procedere ab alio habitu, qui sit Logicæ vtentis. Deinde probant secundò quòd vterque habitus sit scientia: & de docente manifestum est, sed de vtente probatur, quia vt actus efficiendi syllogismum perfectus sit, & sine errore procedat, præsupponere debet habitum Logicæ docentis, per quem docemur quomodo efficiendus sit: quòd si eum præsupponit, non poterit ab eodem procedere, ergo ab alio habitu distincto, qui etiam est scientia, cùm præsupponat habitum docentis, qui verè est scientia, & modo scientifica procedat in componendo syllogismo.

The second opinion, which certain moderns follow, asserts that logica utens is a true science and distinct from docens. And in order to prove both, they distinguish two offices or acts of Logic. The first, by which it teaches how to construct instruments, such as a syllogism or a definition; the second, by which it uses the precepts handed down, producing those same instruments in the other sciences. And since through the multiplication of acts a facility is generated in the powers, which facility we call a habit, it is necessary that from different acts different habits too are generated in the intellect: so that first the intellect is made apt for handing down precepts, and then it acquires another, different faculty through the exercise of the same precepts, by producing syllogisms. An example can be given in music, in which a twofold facility is acquired: the first in the intellect, which hands down the rules of consonances; the second in the hands; and the first they are accustomed to call Theoretical, the latter Practical. Whence it follows that a twofold facility must also be posited in Logic, one which is Theoretical, or speculative, the other which is Practical; and the former will be the habit of logica docens, the latter that of logica utens. They prove, first, that they are distinct habits: because a syllogism made in natural Philosophy does not proceed from the habit of that Philosophy, since it does not teach how a syllogism is to be composed; but neither does it proceed from logica docens, for this has only to hand down in general the precepts for producing instruments, not to produce them in particular; therefore it must proceed from another habit, which is that of logica utens. Next they prove, second, that each habit is a science. Of docens it is manifest; but of utens it is proved: because in order that the act of producing a syllogism be perfect and proceed without error, it must presuppose the habit of logica docens, through which we are taught how it is to be produced; but if it presupposes it, it cannot proceed from the same; therefore from another, distinct habit, which is also a science, since it presupposes the habit of docens, which is truly a science, and proceeds in a scientific manner in composing a syllogism.

Nostra sententia est, quòd Dialectica vtens, vt vtens est, non sit scientia, nec habitus distinctus à Logica docente: sed habitus idem prout ars est, singulares syllogismos efficiens: itaque idemmet habitus Logicę, prout tradit pręcepta in communi componendi syllogismum, & alia instrumenta per demonstrationem, est Logica docens: sed in quantum efficit syllogismos singulares, est ars, & Logica vtens vocatur. Hanc

Our view is that Dialectic utens, as utens, is not a science, nor a habit distinct from logica docens, but the same habit as it is an art producing singular syllogisms. And so the very same habit of Logic, as it hands down through demonstration the precepts in general for composing a syllogism and the other instruments, is logica docens; but inasmuch as it produces singular syllogisms it is an art, and is called logica utens. This

p. 9

sententiam sequitur D Tho Met. lect. 4. sed quia duplicem partem continet, primam, quòd Logica vtens non sit scientia, secundam, quòd sit ars, vtraque probanda est. Probatur ergo primò, quòd non sit scientia: quia cõclusio scientifica est actus, quem per demonstrationem colligimus ex principiis per se notis: sed actus logicæ vtentis non est assensus conclusionis, quem per demonstrationem colligimus: sed opus quod efficimus, nempe, syllogismum aut definitionem: ergo Logica vtens, non est scientia.

view St. Thomas follows, Metaph. lect. 4. But because it contains two parts, the first, that logica utens is not a science, the second, that it is an art, each must be proved. It is proved first, then, that it is not a science: because a scientific conclusion is an act which we gather through demonstration from principles known per se; but the act of logica utens is not the assent to a conclusion which we gather through demonstration, but a work that we produce, namely a syllogism or a definition; therefore logica utens is not a science.

Secundò, scientia proximè versatur circa vniuersalia, nec de singularibus est: sed Logica vtens non versatur circa vniuersalia, sed circa actus singulares quos exercet componendo syllogismos iuxta præcepta tradita à docente: ergo non est scientia, sed scientiam præsupponit.

Second, science is proximately concerned with universals, and is not of singulars; but logica utens is not concerned with universals but with the singular acts which it exercises in composing syllogisms according to the precepts handed down by docens; therefore it is not a science, but presupposes science.

6 Secunda pars nostræ sententiæ quòd Logica vtens, vt talis, non sit habitus distinctus à docente, sed idem prout est ars, præsupponit Logicam esse artem, non mechanicam quæ versatur circa opera externa, vt fabrilis est: sed liberalem, quæ versatur circa opera intellectus, ea dirigendo Hoc docet expressè D Th. 1 2. q. 57. art. 3. ad 3. & 1 lib. Posteriorum lect. 1. & colligitur euidenter ex doctrina Arist. 6, Eth. lib. cap 4. vbi definit artem. Quòd sit habitus cum ratione factiuus vel actiuus: per factiuum intelligens artes mechanicas, quibus efficiuntur opera externa, per actiuum verò liberales, quibus non efficitur externum opus: sed opera animæ interna diriguntur. Hoc supposito probatur primò, quia euidens est, habitum Logicæ esse scientiam, cùm procedat per demonstrationem: sed est etiam ars, quia est habitus cum ratione actiuus: nam opera intellectus dirigit, efficitque singulares syllogismos ex eis: ergo simul est scientia, & ars diuersa ratione, ita vt quatenus tradit præcepta efficiendi syllogismum, & alia instrumenta per demonstrationem, sit Logica docens, & vera scientia, vtens verò quatenus est ars efficiens singulares syllogismos iuxta præcepta à seipsa, vt docente, tradita.

6 The second part of our view, that logica utens as such is not a habit distinct from docens but the same as it is an art, presupposes that Logic is an art: not a mechanical one, which is concerned with external works, as the smith’s art is, but a liberal one, which is concerned with the works of the intellect, directing them. This St. Thomas teaches expressly, 1-2, q. 57, a. 3, ad 4, and Posterior Analytics 1, lect. 1; and it is gathered evidently from the doctrine of Aristotle, Ethics 6, ch. 4, where he defines art: That it is a habit, with reason, productive or active; by productive understanding the mechanical arts, by which external works are produced, but by active the liberal ones, by which no external work is produced, but the internal works of the soul are directed. This supposed, it is proved first: because it is evident that the habit of Logic is a science, since it proceeds through demonstration; but it is also an art, because it is a habit active with reason, for it directs the works of the intellect and produces singular syllogisms out of them; therefore it is at once a science and an art under different rationes, so that inasmuch as it hands down through demonstration the precepts for producing a syllogism and the other instruments, it is logica docens and a true science; but utens inasmuch as it is an art producing singular syllogisms according to the precepts handed down by itself as docens.

Secundò probatur: nam habitus Logicæ docentis per primam demonstrationem acquisitus habet pro obiecto modum sciendi, cuius naturam contemplatur, & opera rationis, ex quibus docet syllogismos conficere: sed eo ipso quòd docet efficere syllogismos, habet virtutem eosdem efficiendi, cùm non egeat alio instrumento, per quod eos efficiat: sed per eundem intellectum efficit, ergo eo ipso, quòd est Logica docens: est etiam habitus cum ratione actiuus, quod est esse artem liberalem: quare sequitur vtramque rationem habere

It is proved, second: for the habit of logica docens, acquired through the first demonstration, has for its object the mode of knowing, whose nature it contemplates, and the works of reason, out of which it teaches how to construct syllogisms; but by the very fact that it teaches how to produce syllogisms, it has the power of producing them, since it does not need another instrument through which to produce them, but produces them through the same intellect; therefore, by the very fact that it is logica docens, it is also a habit active with reason, which is to be a liberal art. Wherefore it follows that both rationes are possessed by

p. 10

eundem habitum Logicæ, nempe scientiæ, & artis, sed ratio scientiæ primaria est in eo, atque præcipua, ratio verò artis quasi secundaria, & rationẽ scientiæ pręsupponens. Nam priùs intelligimus, quòd præcepta per demõstrationẽ tradat, deinde quod iuxta præcepta tradita, singulares syllogismos efficiat.

the same habit of Logic, namely of science and of art; but the ratio of science is primary and principal in it, whereas the ratio of art is as it were secondary and presupposes the ratio of science. For we first understand that it delivers precepts through demonstration, and then that, according to the precepts delivered, it produces singular syllogisms.

Ad arg. primæ opinionis respondeo, Logicam perfici per exercitium efficiendi syllogismos, nõ vt scientiã, sed vt artem: sicut perficitur in ratione scientiæ per demonstrationes, quibus probat suas conclusiones: quare non sequitur, vt vtentem esse scientiam, sed artem.

To the argument of the first opinion I reply that Logic is perfected by the exercise of producing syllogisms not as a science but as an art, just as it is perfected in the ratio of science by the demonstrations by which it proves its conclusions. Wherefore what follows is not that, as using, it is a science, but that it is an art.

7 Pro solutione argumentorum secundæ opinionis, notanda est differentia inter artes quæ per membra corporis aliquo modo exercentur, quales sunt domificatoria, & musica ex vna parte, & cęteras, quæ circa actus purè internos versantur, vt Logica: quòd illæ duplicem facilitatem petunt. Vnam in intellectu, in quo sunt tanquam in subiecto, alteram in membro externo, per quod exercentur, vt musica, præter facilitatem intellectus, petit aliam in manu, vel lingua, & palato: & cùm facilitas sit habitus, includunt duos habitus, quamuis facilitas, quæ est in membris externis non sit propriè habitus. Aliæ verò artes, quæ solùm dirigunt operationes intellectus qualis est Dialectica, sicut non exercentur per membra externa: sed per solum intellectum: ita non petunt nisi facilitatem intellectus: quia habitus est: per quem singulares operationes efficiunt, ac dirigunt: & hæc est vna, & eadem in Logica, vt probatum est: per quam præcepta in communi, & per demonstrationem tradit, vt scientia: & per quam singulares efficit syllogismos, vt ars. Et ideo vnus est, atque idem habitus scientiæ, & artis: ex quibus sequitur negandum esse illam distinctionem de duplici facilitate in his artibus, quæ per membra externa non exercentur.

7 For the solution of the arguments of the second opinion, note the difference between the arts that are exercised in some way through the members of the body, such as house-building and music, on the one hand, and the others, which are concerned with purely internal acts, such as Logic: namely, that the former require a twofold facility. One in the intellect, in which they exist as in a subject; the other in the external member through which they are exercised: as music, besides the facility of the intellect, requires another in the hand, or in the tongue and palate. And since a facility is a habit, they include two habits, although the facility that is in the external members is not properly a habit. But the other arts, which only direct the operations of the intellect, such as Dialectic, just as they are not exercised through external members but through the intellect alone, so they require only a facility of the intellect: because this is the habit by which they produce and direct singular operations; and this is one and the same in Logic, as has been proved, by which it delivers precepts in general and through demonstration, as a science, and by which it produces singular syllogisms, as an art. And therefore the habit of the science and of the art is one and the same. From which it follows that the distinction of a twofold facility must be denied in those arts which are not exercised through external members.

Iam ergo ad primum arg. eiusdem sententiæ respondeo, syllogismum factum in Philosophia naturali, à duplici habitu procedere, nempe ab habitu eiusdem Philosophiæ, & simul ab habitu Logicæ, ab illo secundùm rationem particularem talis scientię, ab habitu verò Logicæ secundùm rationem communem formæ syllogisticæ, hoc est, modi & figuræ: præterea ab illo, vt scientia, ab habitu verò Logicæ, vt arte. Petit ergo talis syllogismus duplicem facilitatem, & duplicem habitum non Logicæ: sed vnum Logicæ, alterum Philosophiæ.

Now, then, to the first argument of the same opinion I reply that a syllogism made in natural Philosophy proceeds from a twofold habit, namely from the habit of that Philosophy and at the same time from the habit of Logic: from the former according to the particular ratio of such a science, but from the habit of Logic according to the common ratio of the syllogistic form, that is, of mood and figure; moreover from the former as a science, but from the habit of Logic as an art. Such a syllogism therefore requires a twofold facility and a twofold habit, not of Logic, but one of Logic, the other of Philosophy.

Ad secundum, concedo, actum efficiendi syllogismum, præsupponere habitum Logicæ docentis: sed ex hoc non sequitur quòd generet alterum habitum, sed quòd eundem sub

To the second, I grant that the act of producing a syllogism presupposes the habit of logica docens; but from this it does not follow that it generates another habit, but that it generates the same habit under

p. 11

ratione artis perficiat Falsum igitur est quòd ab eodem habitu docentis Logicæ non procedat.

the ratio of art. It is false, therefore, that it does not proceed from the same habit of logica docens.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Quæst. 4. Vtrum Logica sit vnus simplex habitus — Whether Logic is one simple habit, and one simple quality.

Vtrùm Logica sit vnus simplex habitus, vnáue simplex qualitas.

[…]

8 Triplicem possumus considerare vnitatem in scientia, sicut in aliis rebus, numericam, specificam, & quasi genericam: sed de vnitate numerica non procedit quæstio, quia certò constat, Dialecticam non esse vnam numero, sed tot esse quot sunt intellectus diuersi: vt alia numero est Dialectica, quam Petrus habet, ab ea quam habet Ioannes. In hoc ergo sensu manifestum est, non esse vnam simplicem qualitatem, sed multiplicem. De vnitate ergo specifica aut generica inquiritur, quamnam ex his habeat. nam si solùm habuerit genericam, non erit vna qualitas simplex, neque vnus habitus, sed plures sub se continebit: sicut animal continet plures species, quæ sub eo habent vnitatem genericam, si verò habeat vnitatem specificam, erit vna secundùm speciem, sicut albedo: quare nec ex multis habitibus, aut qualitatibus erit composita, sed qualitas simplex, simplexque habitus vocabitur.

8 We can consider a threefold unity in science, as in other things: numerical, specific, and as it were generic. But the question does not proceed concerning numerical unity, because it is certainly established that Dialectic is not one in number, but that there are as many as there are different intellects: as the Dialectic that Peter has is other in number from that which John has. In this sense, then, it is manifest that it is not one simple quality but manifold. It is asked, then, concerning specific or generic unity, which of these it has. For if it has only generic unity, it will not be one simple quality nor one habit, but will contain several under itself, just as animal contains several species, which have generic unity under it. But if it has specific unity, it will be one according to species, like whiteness; wherefore it will not be composed of many habits or qualities, but will be called a simple quality and a simple habit.

Iuxta has duas vnitates, genericam, & specificam, duæ sunt opiniones Prima asserit, Dialecticam non esse vnum habitum, nec simplicem qualitatem, sed compositam ex multis habitibus, & qualitatibus: ita vt tot sint habitus Logicæ distincti, quot sunt conclusiones diuersæ, nempe, alius habitus prædicabilium, alius prædicamentorum, sicque pro cæteris partibus distinctos habitus ponendos esse. imò & pro singulis conclusionibus eiusdem partis, si diuersæ sint, ex quibus quasi vnus habitus totalis, & quasi genericus componitur, & vna etiam scientia, in quantum obiecta omnium partium, sub ratione communissima entis rationis, aut modi sciendi continentur. Hanc sententiam tenet Scotus quęst. 3. prologi, dub 2. Ocham ibidem, dub. 8. Marsilius, qu. 2. art. 4. Greg. eadem q. 3. art. 3. Gabriel quæst. 8. Cardin. Toletus quæst. 3 proœmiali. Fonseca 5. Meta. cap. 7. quæst. 5. sect. 2. & probabilem reputat Sotus quæst. 3. proœmiali. Probatúrque duplici ratione. Prima, habitus, & scientiæ sumunt vnitatem, ac distinctionem specificam ex obiectis, atque etiam ex principiis, per quæ probant suas conclusiones, sed partes Dialecticæ habent diuersa obiecta, atque principia: ergo petunt distinctos habitus. Probatur

In accordance with these two unities, generic and specific, there are two opinions. The first asserts that Dialectic is not one habit nor a simple quality, but composed of many habits and qualities: so that there are as many distinct habits of Logic as there are different conclusions, namely one habit of the predicables, another of the categories, and that distinct habits are likewise to be posited for the other parts; indeed, even for the individual conclusions of the same part, if they are different; out of which one total and as it were generic habit is composed, and also one science, inasmuch as the objects of all the parts are contained under the most common ratio of being of reason, or of mode of knowing. This opinion is held by Scotus, q. 3 of the prologue, doubt 2; Ockham in the same place, doubt 8; Marsilius, q. 2, a. 4; Gregory, in the same q. 3, a. 3; Gabriel, q. 8; Cardinal Toledo, proemial q. 3; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 5, sect. 2; and Soto, proemial q. 3, considers it probable. And it is proved by a twofold reason. First, habits and sciences take their specific unity and distinction from their objects, and also from the principles through which they prove their conclusions; but the parts of Dialectic have different objects and principles; therefore they require distinct habits. The minor is proved

p. 12

minor: quia prædicabile, prædicamentum, enuntiatio, & syllogismus, quæ sunt obiecta diuersarum partium, specie diuersa sunt. Habent etiam diuersa principia quia definitiones horum obiectorum principia sunt, per quæ demonstrantur conclusiones in singulis partibus; & sunt valde diuersæ: ergo habebunt principia diuersa & conclusiones diuersas, per quas diuersi generabuntur habitus Logicæ.

because the predicable, the category, the enunciation and the syllogism, which are the objects of the different parts, are different in species. They also have different principles, because the definitions of these objects are the principles through which the conclusions in the individual parts are demonstrated; and they are very different; therefore they will have different principles and different conclusions, through which different habits of Logic will be generated.

Secunda ratio. Videmus sæpè intellectum esse faciliorem circa vnam partem Logicæ. propter frequentiorem vsum eius, quàm circa alteram; vt circa syllogismos probabiles efficiendos, quàm circa demonstrationes: ergo diuersos habet habitus earum. Probatur consequentia: quia non potest vnus habitus simul esse facilior, & minùs facilis; sicut nec potest idem homo velociter simul, & tardè currere.

The second reason. We often see that the intellect is more facile with one part of Logic, on account of more frequent use of it, than with another: as with producing probable syllogisms than with demonstrations; therefore it has different habits of them. The consequence is proved: because one habit cannot at the same time be more facile and less facile, just as the same man cannot run swiftly and slowly at the same time.

Secunda opinio maiorem vnitatem ponit in Logica; affirmans esse vnam specie; ita, vt nec plures habeat habitus, circa diuersas conclusiones eiusdem partis, nec circa diuersas partes: sed eundem habitum se extendere ad omnes partes, & ad omnes conclusiones earum. Hæc est expressa sententia D. Tho. 1. Posteriorum ca. 22. & 12. quæst. 54. art. 1. Eam sequuntur Caie. ibid. Ferra. 2. contra Gent. cap. 4. Sotus quæst. 3 proœmiali, & ex modernis plures; & nobis videtur probabilior. Sed vnde, aut ex quo hanc vnitatem accipiat; non est certùm apud omnes, qui eam sequũtur. Sed quidam asserunt a materia, aut materiali obiecto habere vnitatem: non ita vt obiectum materiale sit vnum specie, quia hoc non requiritur; sed satis est quomodocũque esse vnum; hoc est, vniuocum, vel analogum, genus, aut speciem, vel etiam vniuersalissimum, vt ens, quod est obiectum Meta. à quo etiam si sit analogum, & vniuersalissimum, vnitatem specificam sumit Meta. sic ergo Logica habet vnitatem specificam ab ente rationis aut modo sciendi vniuersalissimo.

The second opinion posits a greater unity in Logic, affirming that it is one in species: so that it does not have several habits, either concerning the different conclusions of the same part or concerning the different parts, but the same habit extends itself to all the parts and to all their conclusions. This is the express opinion of St. Thomas, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 22, and 1-2, q. 54, a. 1. It is followed by Cajetan in the same place; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 4; Soto, proemial q. 3; and many of the moderns; and to us it seems more probable. But whence, or from what, it receives this unity is not certain among all who follow it. Some assert that it has its unity from the matter, or material object: not in such a way that the material object is one in species, because this is not required; but it is enough that it be one in some way or other, that is, univocal or analogous, a genus or a species, or even most universal, like being, which is the object of Metaphysics; from which, even if it is analogous and most universal, Metaphysics takes its specific unity. Thus, then, Logic has its specific unity from being of reason, or from the most universal mode of knowing.

Alij verò ex obiecto etiam sumere vnitatem habitum inquiunt, non materiali, sed formali: distingunt enim duplicem vnitatem in obiecto cuiuscunque scientię, Potentię, aut Habitus; ita vt altera sit vnitas eius in esse rei, quam Materialem vocant, altera in esse scibilis, quam vocant Formalem, vt in colore, qui est obiectum visus, vnitas in esse rei est, esse qualitatem: quæ genus est ad albedinem, & nigredinem: vnitas in esse visibilis est, quam habet in quantum mouere potest visum: dicunt ergo, scientiam habere vnitatem ex obiecto, non in esse rei, quia sequeretur, tot esse scientias, quot sunt res specie, aut genere diuersæ, quod nullus dixit: sed ex eodem obiecto in esse

Others say that habits take their unity from the object too, but from the formal, not the material, object. For they distinguish a twofold unity in the object of any science, Power or Habit: so that one is its unity in its being as a thing, which they call Material; the other in its being as knowable, which they call Formal. Thus in color, which is the object of sight, the unity in its being as a thing is to be a quality, which is a genus with respect to whiteness and blackness; the unity in its being as visible is that which it has inasmuch as it can move sight. They say, therefore, that a science has its unity from its object, not in its being as a thing, because it would follow that there are as many sciences as there are things different in species or genus, which no one has said; but from the same object in its being

p. 13

scibili, hoc est, in quantum per scientiam cognoscibile est. Hęc tamen distinctio obiecti, falsa reputatur à quibusdam modernis, quod probant testimonio Arist. & ratione. Arist. enim 5. li. Meta. cap. 15. docet, neque scibile per scientiam neque scientiam per scibile definiendam esse, quia committeretur vitiosus quidam circulus, vnum per alterum vicissim explicando, & ex consequenti idem per seipsum: vt si definias visum per visibile, dicens, Visibile est, circa quod versatur visus, & rursus, Visum quòd sit id, quod versatur circa visibile, non est aliud, quàm visum per seipsum definire. Probatur: nam si visibile definitur per visum, ergo visus definit visibile: & si visibile rursus definitur per visum, ergo definitur per suam definitionem: quod idem est, ac definire per seipsum, nam definitio, & definitum idem sunt. Ratio eorum est, quia obiectum in esse scibilis, est posterius scientia: cùm ab ea dicatur scibile: ergo non sumit ab eo vnitatem specificam. Probatur consequentia: quia si scientia prior est, ergo priùs vna est quàm obiectum intelligatur: ab alio ergo, quod sit prius obiecto in esse scibilis, sumere debet vnitatem.

as knowable, that is, inasmuch as it is knowable through science. This distinction of the object, however, is reputed false by certain moderns, which they prove by the testimony of Aristotle and by reason. For Aristotle, Metaph. 4, ch. 15, teaches that neither is the knowable to be defined through science nor science through the knowable, because a vicious circle would be committed, explaining each in turn through the other, and consequently the same thing through itself: as if you were to define sight through the visible, saying, The visible is that with which sight is concerned, and again, Sight is that which is concerned with the visible, this is nothing other than to define sight through itself. This is proved: for if the visible is defined through sight, then sight defines the visible; and if the visible is in turn defined through sight, then it is defined through its own definition; which is the same as to define it through itself, for the definition and the defined are the same. Their reason is that the object in its being as knowable is posterior to the science, since it is called knowable from it; therefore the science does not take its specific unity from it. The consequence is proved: because if the science is prior, then it is one before the object is understood; therefore it must take its unity from something else, which is prior to the object in its being as knowable.

9 Nobis tamen, vera, ac necessaria videtur distinctio obiecti in esse rei, aut in esse scibilis, aque etiã, quod ab obiecto in esse scibilis sumat scientia vnitatem specificam, quia vtrumque colligitur ex doctrina D. Tho 1. part. q. 1. art. 4. & 2. 2. q. 1. art. 1. & est cõmunis sententia fere omnium. Quod probo primò, quia conclusio eadem in esse rei, pertinet ad duplicẽ sciẽtiam, quod non potest esse vero, nisi diuersam rationem scibilis in ea consideremus, hæc autem ratio scibilis diuersa, sumitur ex diuerso medio, per quod probatur, nempe ex diuersis principiis diuersaque demonstratione: ergo necessariò talis distinctio & vnitas specifica scientiæ, ex vnitate obiecti in esse scibilis & non in esse rei accipienda est. Exemplum sumere possumus in hac conclusione, Terra est rotunda, quæ ad Astrologiam pertinet, in quantum demonstratur ab ea, per medium Mathematicum, & ad Philosophiam naturalem, in quantum demonstratur per medium Philosophicum. Secundò probatur in potentia visiua, quæ colorem percipit, & lumen, adeò diuersa, & quæ non possunt conuenire ad constituendum vnum obiectum visus, sub ratione qualitatis: nam sequeretur quòd visus omnem qualitatem perciperet: neque etiam sub ratione qualitatis passibilis, quia sequeretur omnem qualitatem passibilitatem percipere: & vtrumque est falsum. Necessarium igitur est, quòd sub alia ratione magis particulari conueniant, vt vtrumque ab eadem potentia percipiatur: & hæc ratio

9 To us, however, the distinction of the object in its being as a thing or in its being as knowable seems true and necessary, and so too that science takes its specific unity from the object in its being as knowable; because both are gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 1, a. 4, and 2-2, q. 1, a. 1; and it is the common opinion of almost all. Which I prove first: because the same conclusion in its being as a thing pertains to two sciences, which cannot be true unless we consider a different ratio of knowability in it; but this different ratio of knowability is taken from the different middle through which it is proved, namely from different principles and a different demonstration; therefore such a distinction and specific unity of a science must necessarily be taken from the unity of the object in its being as knowable and not in its being as a thing. We can take an example in this conclusion, The earth is round, which pertains to Astrology inasmuch as it is demonstrated by it through a Mathematical middle, and to natural Philosophy inasmuch as it is demonstrated through a Philosophical middle. Second, it is proved in the visual power, which perceives color and light, things so different, and which cannot agree in constituting one object of sight under the ratio of quality, for it would follow that sight perceives every quality; nor yet under the ratio of passible quality, because it would follow that it perceives every passible quality; and both are false. It is necessary, therefore, that they agree under another, more particular ratio, so that both may be perceived by the same power; and this ratio

p. 14

non potest esse alia, nisi, quia vtrumque potest mouere visum, & hæc est ratio visibilis: Eadem ergo ratione, omnia obiecta materialia alicuius scientiæ, diuersa quidem in esse rei, cùm sint res diuersæ, sub aliqua ratione particulari conuenire debent; in quantum ab eadem scientia percipi possunt: & hanc vocat Caiet. rationem scibilis, per quam obiectum tribuit scientiæ vnitatem.

can be no other than that both can move sight; and this is the ratio of the visible. By the same reasoning, then, all the material objects of any science, which are indeed different in their being as things, since they are different things, must agree under some particular ratio, inasmuch as they can be perceived by the same science; and this Cajetan calls the ratio of knowability, through which the object confers unity on the science.

10 Ad argumentum modernorum hac distinctione respondendum est: Denominatio scibilis duplex est, Actualis, & Relatiua, & virtualis atque absoluta: & prima à scientia ipsa sumitur, & ideo posterior illa est, secunda verò ex natura, & essentia eiusdem obiecti: sicut etiam denominatio intelligibilis. v. g. homo dicitur intelligibilis denominatione actuali, & relatiua, ab intellectu, & intellectione, per quam intelligitur, aut intelligi potest: & ideo posterius est in esse intelligibilis, intellectu & intellectione, sed denominationem virtualem, & quasi radicalem, non ab intellectu, sed à propria natura sumit, quia ex propria natura, & entitate, res quælibet est intelligibilis: quare secundùm hanc denominationem, non dependet ab intellectu, sed prior est illo. Testimonium verò Arist. tangit modum definiendi vnum relatiuum per alterum, quare non potest commodè explicari, vsque ad prædicamentum ad aliquid.

10 To the argument of the moderns one must reply with this distinction: the denomination “knowable” is twofold, Actual and Relative, and virtual and absolute. And the first is taken from the science itself, and therefore it is posterior; the second, on the other hand, from the nature and essence of the object itself: just as is also the denomination “intelligible.” For example, man is called intelligible by an actual and relative denomination from the intellect and the intellection through which he is understood or can be understood; and therefore in his being as intelligible he is posterior to the intellect and the intellection. But the virtual and as it were radical denomination he takes not from the intellect but from his own nature, because by its own nature and entity anything whatever is intelligible; wherefore according to this denomination it does not depend on the intellect, but is prior to it. The testimony of Aristotle, on the other hand, touches on the manner of defining one relative through the other; wherefore it cannot be conveniently explained before we reach the category of relation.

Sed licèt distinctio obiecti in esse rei, & in esse scibilis à Caie. tradita necessaria sit, non est tamen sufficiens ad explicandam vnitatem specificam, quam in Logica ponimus, nisi ampliùs explicetur, & ostendatur, à quonam sit sumenda vnitas obiecti, in esse scibilis: nam illud tantùm erit ratio formalis à qua eandem vnitatem accipiet scientia. Explicandã verò est per aliam distinctionem, ita habentem. In quocumque obiecto scientiæ, potentiæ, vel habitus, duo reperimus, nempe rem, quã per scientiam, aut potentiam percipimus: & hæc vocatur ratio Quæ, hoc est ratio Quæ percipitur: reperitur etiam ratio Sub qua potentia versatur circa illam, aut eam percipit: & hæc dicitur ratio, Sub qua, obiecti, per quam determinatur: & ex vtraque ratione, Quæ, & Sub qua, constituitur vnum obiectum completum atque totale: ex ratione, Quæ, tanquam ex materiali, & ex ratione, Sub qua, tanquam ex formali: vnde contingere potest, quod eadem ratio. Quæ, sit obiectum diuersorum habituum, aut potentiarũ, propter diuersas rationes, sub quibus percipitur: & propterea verum est, à ratione, sub qua, tanquam à formali, & vltima, sumere suam vnitatem, potentias, habitus, & scientias Hoc exemplo fiet res manifesta. In obiecto visus, reperimus id, quod videtur, & hoc est color, aut lumen, & vocatur

But although the distinction of the object in its being as a thing and in its being as knowable, handed down by Cajetan, is necessary, it is not, however, sufficient to explain the specific unity that we posit in Logic, unless it is explained further and it is shown from what the unity of the object in its being as knowable is to be taken; for that alone will be the formal ratio from which the science will receive the same unity. It is to be explained, then, by another distinction, which runs thus. In any object of a science, power or habit we find two things: namely the thing which we perceive through the science or power, and this is called the ratio Quae, that is, the ratio Which is perceived; and there is also found the ratio Sub qua, under which the power is concerned with it or perceives it; and this is called the ratio Sub qua of the object, by which it is determined. And from both rationes, the Quae and the Sub qua, one complete and total object is constituted: from the ratio Quae as from the material, and from the ratio Sub qua as from the formal.
