The adequate object must contain proximately and adequately all the things that are treated in the science; but neither argumentation, nor syllogism, nor demonstration contains proximately and adequately the simples about which Dialectic disputes, but only remotely, insofar as they are parts of the enunciations of which they are proximately composed; and division or definition they contain in no way: therefore they cannot be adequate objects of Logic, though they can well be objects of some part of it; and perhaps one of them could be called the principal object, such as demonstration, which is the chief instrument for attaining science. Hence if they spoke of the principal object, at least the last could be admitted; but as for the adequate object, none of them is to be admitted.

21 Restant prima & secunda de quibus iudicandum est, vtra illarum sit probabilior: quod, vt meliùs fiat, illud tanquam certum supponendum est, propriã materiã Dialecticæ esse operationes intellectus: & ideo ad obiectũ eius pertinere nõ secundùm propriam naturã: nam hoc modo, ad Philosophiã potiùs pertinent, sicut anima, & intellectus, à quibus tanquã à principiis efficientibus procedunt: sed in quantum ab eo diriguntur.

21 There remain the first and the second, concerning which it must be judged which of them is the more probable; and for this to be done better, it must be supposed as certain that the proper matter of Dialectic is the operations of the intellect, and that therefore they pertain to its object not according to their own nature (for in this way they pertain rather to Philosophy, like the soul and the intellect, from which they proceed as from efficient principles), but insofar as they are directed by it.

22 Secundò supponendũ est, quid sit operationes has dirigi ab intellectu: non est enim aliud quàm fieri syllogismum, definitionem aut aliud instrumentum: vt tres propositiones ordinari non est aliud quàm vnam pro maiori sumere, pro minori aliam, & tertiam pro conclusione: ita vt in modo, & figura, cõstituatur

22 Second, it must be supposed what it is for these operations to be directed by the intellect: for it is nothing other than for a syllogism, a definition, or another instrument to be made: as for three propositions to be ordered is nothing other than to take one for the major, another for the minor, and the third for the conclusion, so that in mood and figure there is constituted

p. 30

ex eis syllogismus: & quod in eis resultat, est passiua ordinatio, id est, esse ordinatas ac syllogismum constituentes. Tria igitur possumus considerare in his operationibus, in quantum pertinent ad Dialecticam ordinabilitatem, seu dirigibilitatem, directionem actiuam intellectus, & passiuam, resultantem in eis ex actiua.

from them a syllogism; and what results in them is the passive ordering, that is, their being ordered and constituting a syllogism. We can therefore consider three things in these operations insofar as they pertain to Dialectic: ordinability or directibility, the active direction of the intellect, and the passive direction resulting in them from the active.

Et de dirigibilitate probatur, vel non pertinere operationes secundùm eam ad Logicam, vel non esse realem, sed ens rationis, hoc arg. Aut operationes esse dirigibiles, est potentia seu aptitudo naturalis, conueniens eis ex propria natura, vel solùm obedientialis in eo consistẽs, quòd sicut lignum subditur artifici, & quasi ei obedit, vt ex eo possit cathedram efficere, sic operationes istæ subduntur intellectui. vt ex eis possit facere syllogismũ: & si naturalis sit potentia, euidẽs est, non ad Dialecticam, sed ad naturalem Philosophiam pertinere: sicut quæcunque à natura habent operationes ipsæ, pertinent ad scientiam, quæ agit de natura earum, & hæc est Philosophia naturalis: si verò sit obedientialis, non potest esse realis. Nam potẽtia obediẽtialis ligni ideo est realis quia per eam subditur artifici, ad formam realem cathedræ suscipiẽdam: quare si forma cathedræ, nõ esset realis sed ens rationis, nec potentia illa esset realis: sed operationes subdũtur intellectui ad suscipiendi, formã syllogismi quæ nõ est realis, sed ens rationis: ergo talis potẽtia non est realis. Probatur minor. Ordinatio per quã efficiũt syllogismũ est relatio vnius ad alterã, non realis quia nõ ordinãtur ex natura rei sed ab intellectu: ergo est relatio rationis.

And concerning directibility, it is proved either that the operations do not pertain to Logic according to it, or that it is not real but a being of reason, by this argument. The operations’ being directible is either a natural potency or aptitude, belonging to them from their own nature, or else only an obediential one, consisting in this: that just as wood is subject to the craftsman, and as it were obeys him, so that he can make a chair from it, so these operations are subject to the intellect, so that it can make a syllogism from them. And if it is a natural potency, it is evident that it pertains not to Dialectic but to natural Philosophy: just as whatever the operations themselves have from nature pertains to the science that deals with their nature, and this is natural Philosophy. But if it is obediential, it cannot be real. For the obediential potency of wood is real for this reason, that through it the wood is subject to the craftsman for receiving the real form of a chair; wherefore if the form of the chair were not real but a being of reason, neither would that potency be real; but the operations are subject to the intellect for receiving the form of syllogism, which is not real but a being of reason: therefore such a potency is not real. The minor is proved. The ordering by which it makes a syllogism is a relation of one to another, and not a real one, because they are not ordered from the nature of the thing but by the intellect: therefore it is a relation of reason.

23 Secundum, quod in operationibus considerare possumus, est ordinatio actiua, quã intellectus facit per actũ reflexũ, quo supra eas reflectitur & eas ordinat, cõstituens syllogismum: & hæc ordinatio actiua, realis est cùm sit actus realis intellectus ordinantis: & per illa solùm dicuntur operationes ordinatæ, denominatione reali extrinseca v. g. syllogismus, aut demonstratio: sed esse syllogismum, aut demonstrationem, habent formaliter, per relationem ordinationis inter eas resultantem ex operatione intellectus ordinantis: & relatio ordinationis inter eas, non potest esse realis, quia non ordinantur ex sua natura, sed ab intellectu qui nihil reale in rebus per suam ordinationem ponere potest: ergo directio per quam formaliter sunt syllogismus, vel aliud instrumentum, & ad Logicam pertinent; non est aliquis modus realis, sed sola relatio rationis.

23 The second thing that we can consider in the operations is the active ordering, which the intellect makes by a reflex act by which it reflects upon them and orders them, constituting a syllogism; and this active ordering is real, since it is a real act of the intellect that orders; and by it alone the operations are called ordered by a real extrinsic denomination, e.g., syllogism or demonstration; but they have their being a syllogism or a demonstration formally through the relation of ordering that results between them from the operation of the ordering intellect; and the relation of ordering between them cannot be real, because they are not ordered from their own nature but by the intellect, which can posit nothing real in things through its ordering: therefore the direction through which they are formally a syllogism or another instrument, and pertain to Logic, is not some real mode, but only a relation of reason.

His explicatis, est prima conclusio huius quæstionis, Obiectum Logicæ aliquid dicit pro materiali, & aliquid pro formali: pro materiali quidem, reales operationes intellectus:

These things explained, the first conclusion of this question is: The object of Logic signifies something as material and something as formal: as material, indeed, the real operations of the intellect;

p. 31

pro formali verò relationem rationis, quæ dicitur ordinatio formalis earum, per quam efficiunt syllogismum, aut aliud instrumentum. Hæc probatur efficaciter ex doctrina tradita, hoc arg Logica habet pro obiecto operationes intellectus, quas dirigit, vt per directionem constituat ex eis syllogismum, aut aliud instrumentum: ergo materiale obiectum, sunt operationes reales, formale verò, directio aut ordinatio earum, per quam constituunt talia instrumenta: sed ordinatio est relatio rationis: ergo obiectum formale est ens rationis.

and as formal, the relation of reason which is called their formal ordering, through which they make a syllogism or another instrument. This is proved effectively from the doctrine delivered, by this argument. Logic has for its object the operations of the intellect which it directs, so that through direction it may constitute from them a syllogism or another instrument: therefore the material object is the real operations, while the formal object is their direction or ordering, through which they constitute such instruments; but the ordering is a relation of reason: therefore the formal object is a being of reason.

Secunda conclusio. Obiectum adæquatum Logicæ est modus sciendi communis omnibus instrumentis, qui ex ente reali, pro materiali constat, & ex ente rationis pro formali. hæc sequitur ex prima: quare non indiget noua probatione. His duabus conclusionibus continetur, & explicatur secunda opinio D. Th. & aliorum, quæ communis fuit semper in schola, & vt probabilior est amplectenda.

Second conclusion. The adequate object of Logic is the mode of knowing common to all the instruments, which consists of real being as material and of being of reason as formal. This follows from the first; wherefore it needs no new proof. In these two conclusions is contained and explained the second opinion, that of St. Thomas and others, which has always been the common one in the school and is to be embraced as the more probable.

25 Solum restat arg. primæ opinionis soluere: & ad primũ cõcessa maiori, neganda est minor, quòd ens rationis Logicũ nec naturã, nec proprietates habeat, nec per se cõsideretur in Dialectica: quamuis enim nõ habeat naturam realẽ, nec subiecto inhęreat, sed solùm sit obiectiuè in intellectu actu cõsiderãte: est tamẽ quędã denominatio rebus attributa ab intellectu, per modum, ac similitudinẽ formæ inhęrẽtis, vt esse genus aut speciem, attribuitur naturę ab intellectu: sicut albedo, aut alia forma inhærẽs attribuitur corpori. vnde nõ est omnino ens fictũ, sicut chimera, sed habet fundamentũ in eisdẽ naturis, quibus attribuitur, prout ab intellectu, hoc aut illo modo, cõcipiũtur: & hoc esse diminutum, considerari potest ab aliqua scientia.

25 It remains only to solve the arguments of the first opinion; and to the first, granting the major, the minor must be denied, namely that the logical being of reason has neither a nature nor properties, nor is considered per se in Dialectic: for although it does not have a real nature, nor inhere in a subject, but only exists objectively in the intellect actually considering it, it is nevertheless a certain denomination attributed to things by the intellect after the mode and likeness of an inhering form, as being a genus or a species is attributed to a nature by the intellect, just as whiteness or another inhering form is attributed to a body. Hence it is not altogether a fictitious being, like a chimera, but has a foundation in the very natures to which it is attributed, according as they are conceived by the intellect in this or that way; and this diminished being can be considered by some science.

26 Quòd verò ad proprietates eius pertinet, hac distinctione explicandum est: ens rationis dupliciter considerari potest: primò, in abstracto, hoc est, vt forma quædam sine ordine ad subiectum, cui attribuitur: quemadmodum consideratur albedo, sine ordine ad corpus, cui inhęreat. Alio modo, potest cõsiderari, in concreto, hoc est, vt forma applicata ad naturã, quã denominat. Et cõsiderata primo modo, habet passiones vniuersales iuxta similitudinem entis realis, vt verum, bonũ &c. cõsideratum verò secundo modo, non habet passiones adeò vniuersales: quia nõ applicatur, aut attribuitur naturis in cõmuni consideratum, sed in particulari, secundùm suas species: nõ enim denominatur natura aliqua ab ente rationis vniuersalissimo, sed à particularibus: vt à genere specie, subiecto, aut prædicato. quare sic sumptum, nõ habet passiones, nisi in suis speciebus, vt vniuersale in communi, habet prædicabilitatem pro

26 As regards its properties, the matter must be explained by this distinction: a being of reason can be considered in two ways: first, in the abstract, that is, as a certain form without order to the subject to which it is attributed, as whiteness is considered without order to the body in which it inheres. In another way it can be considered in the concrete, that is, as a form applied to the nature which it denominates. And considered in the first way, it has universal attributes after the likeness of real being, such as true, good, etc.; but considered in the second way, it does not have attributes so universal, because it is not applied or attributed to natures considered in common, but in particular, according to its species: for a nature is not denominated by the most universal being of reason, but by particular ones, as by genus, species, subject, or predicate. Wherefore, taken thus, it has no attributes except in its species: as the universal in common has predicability as

p. 32

passione, & prædicabilia, habent particulares passiones, vt genus, esse prædicabile de speciebus: sicque de cæteris: & quemadmodum ens rationis, consideratum in abstracto, non pertinet ad Logicam, sed ad Met. tanquam deficiens à perfectione entis realis, quod per se ab illa scientia consideratur: ita probare passiones vniuersales de illo, non ad Logicum sed ad Metaphysicum pertinet: sed passiones quas habet, vt applicatum naturis, aut eas denominans, in Logica probantur: & hoc sufficit, vt sit obiectum eius, de his verò passionibus, non prædicantur species entis rationis, quibus attribuuntur prædicatione formali: quia non est verum formaliter, quòd prædicabile sit vniuersale, sicut nec risibile formaliter est homo.

its attribute, and the predicables have particular attributes, as genus has that of being predicable of the species; and so of the rest. And just as the being of reason considered in the abstract does not pertain to Logic but to Metaphysics, as falling short of the perfection of real being, which is considered per se by that science, so to prove universal attributes of it pertains not to the logician but to the Metaphysician; but the attributes which it has as applied to natures, or as denominating them, are proved in Logic; and this suffices for it to be its object. Of these attributes, however, the species of being of reason to which they are attributed are not predicated by formal predication: because it is not formally true that the predicable is the universal, just as neither is the risible formally man.

Ad secundũ respõdeo, Ens rationis dũ fit ab intellectu, nõ esse directè, aut per se cognitum, sed indirectè, & quasi per accidẽs: sed postquã factũ est, bene potest intellectus illud pro obiecto quasi per reflexionem sumere, & cognitionẽ eius per se primò intẽdere: & hoc modo accipitur, dũ dicitur esse obiectũ Logicę.

To the second I reply that a being of reason, while it is being made by the intellect, is not known directly or per se, but indirectly and as it were per accidens; but after it has been made, the intellect can well take it for its object, as it were by reflection, and intend its cognition per se and primarily; and it is taken in this way when it is said to be the object of Logic.

Ad primũ aliud arg. quo probantur operationes reales esse obiectũ Dialecticæ, hac distinctione respõdendũ est. Demonstratio dupliciter consideratur, materialiter, pro operationibus ordinatis, aut formaliter, pro ordinatione, à qua habent vt sint syllogismus aut demonstratio: & in prima cõsideratione, admittendum est esse instrumentum reale, non in secunda: sed relatio rationis est. Et quod dicitur habere effectum realem, nempe scientiam, quam generat, etiam est admittendum, ratione operationum, quas pro materiali includit: non ratione significati formalis, in relatione rationis cõsistentis. Quòd denique Logica sit scientia practica, vt in eodem argumento dicitur, verum est, & habere praxim, aut operationem pro obiecto, ab intellectu directam: ex quo non sequitur directionem esse realem, neque id est necessarium, vt Logica sit scientia practica: sed satis est operationem vtcunque dirigere, siue directio passiua realis sit vel solùm relatio rationis.

To the first of the other arguments, by which the real operations are proved to be the object of Dialectic, one must reply with this distinction. Demonstration is considered in two ways: materially, for the ordered operations, or formally, for the ordering from which they have it that they are a syllogism or a demonstration; and in the first consideration it must be admitted that it is a real instrument, but not in the second: rather it is a relation of reason. And what is said, that it has a real effect, namely the science which it generates, must also be admitted, by reason of the operations which it includes as material; not by reason of the formal significate, which consists in a relation of reason. Finally, that Logic is a practical science, as is said in the same argument, is true, and that it has as its object a praxis, or operation, directed by the intellect; from which it does not follow that the direction is real, nor is that necessary for Logic to be a practical science; but it is enough that it direct operation in some way, whether the passive direction be real or only a relation of reason.

Ad secundum concedendum est, operationes, vt dirigibiles considerari posse ab aliqua scientia, & verè considerari à Dialectica, negandũ verò, quòd dirigibilitas sit realis: nõ est enim nisi ens rationis: sicut directio, per quam constituunt syllogismum, & ad quam ordinatur dirigibilitas, solùm est relatio rationis, vt probatum est. De intelligibilitate verò, & numerabilitate, diuersa est ratio: quia istæ conueniunt rebus, aut qualitatibus, ex propria natura: dirigibilitas verò, non nisi potentia obedientialis est, respectu formæ syllogisticæ, quæ solùm est relatio rationis: & ideo nõ est quid reale, sed ens rationis.

To the second, it must be granted that the operations as directible can be considered by some science, and are truly considered by Dialectic; but it must be denied that directibility is real: for it is nothing but a being of reason, just as the direction through which they constitute a syllogism, and to which directibility is ordered, is only a relation of reason, as has been proved. With intelligibility and numerability, however, the case is different: because these belong to things or qualities from their own nature, whereas directibility is nothing but an obediential potency with respect to the syllogistic form, which is only a relation of reason; and therefore it is not something real, but a being of reason. Commentaries

p. 33

COMMENTARIES ON THE PREDICABLES OF PORPHYRY, TOGETHER WITH THE DOUBTS AND QUESTIONS

COMMENTARII IN PRÆDICABILIA PORPHYRII, VNA CVM DVBIIS ET QVÆSTIONIbus hac tempestate agitari solitis, compositi.

customarily debated in our time, composed.

CAPVT I, PORPHYRII.

C H A P T E R I O F P O R P H Y R Y.

Cùm necessarium sit, Chrysaori, & ad eam, quæ est apud Aristotelem, Prædicamentorum doctrinam, &c.

Since it is necessary, Chrysaorius, both for the doctrine of the Categories which is found in Aristotle, etc.

BREVIS EXPOSITIO TEXTVS.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

HOc primum caput, quasi proœmium est totus libri Prædicabilium, & tria in eo agit Porphirius. Nam primò, docet necessariam esse cognitionem prædicabilium, ad prædicamenta Aristot. intelligenda: quia cùm prædicamentum sit prædicabilium ordinatio secundùm debitam subiectionem, & prædicationem: non potest ordinatio prædicamentalis cognosci, sine cognitione prædicabilium. Secundò, proponit materiam, de qua agendum est in toto libro, quæ sunt quinque vniuersalia, aut prædicabilia, nempe genus, species, differentia, proprium, & accidens. & tandem asserit, quæstiones, quæ de his prædicabilibus tractari possunt, esse in duplici differentia: nam, quædam faciles sunt: quia circa ea versantur quæ naturæ eorumdem prædicabilium proxima iudicantur. & ideo cognita eorum natura, facilem solutionem habent: vt An vniuersalia, hoc aut illo modo prædicentur de inferioribus: & similes. Aliæ verò sunt difficiles: quia altiora quædam inquirunt: vt An vniuersalia sint in rebus, vel obiectiuè solùm in nostra cognitione. & illas quidem proponendas, ac disputandas esse asserit: has verò vsque ad Philosophiam relinquendas: quia non facilè à Dialecticis intelligi possunt. Et his continetur litera Porphyrij.

his first chapter is as it were the proem of the whole book of T the Predicables, and in it Porphyry does three things. For first, he teaches that knowledge of the predicables is necessary for understanding Aristotle’s categories: because, since a category is an ordering of predicables according to due subjection and predication, the categorial ordering cannot be known without knowledge of the predicables. Second, he proposes the matter to be treated in the whole book, which is the five universals or predicables, namely genus, species, difference, property, and accident. And finally he asserts that the questions which can be treated concerning these predicables are of two kinds: for some are easy, because they concern matters judged to lie close to the nature of these same predicables, and therefore, once their nature is known, they admit of an easy solution, as: Whether universals are predicated of their inferiors in this or that way, and the like. Others are difficult, because they inquire into certain higher matters, as: Whether universals exist in things, or only objectively in our cognition. The former, he asserts, are to be proposed and disputed; the latter are to be left to Philosophy, because they cannot easily be understood by Dialecticians. In these words the letter of Porphyry is contained. C

p. 34

QUESTION I ON UNIVERSALS

Vtrùm Vniuersalia sint in rebus.

Whether universals exist in things.

29 QVæstio hęc quasi fundamentum est omnium aliarum, quæ de vniuersalibus disputari possunt. Vt autem titulus intelligatur, notandum est, Vniuersale duplex esse, Complexum, & Incomplexum. Vniuersale cõplexum, est propositio vniuersalis, & per se nota, quæ principium est vniuersale alicuius scientiæ: ex quo multæ inferuntur conclusiones: vt in scientia de homine, vniuersale principium est, quòd sit rationalis, ex quo colligitur, quòd sit admiratiuus & risibilis. Vniuersale incomplexum, est vox quædam simplex, significans aliquid multis commune, vt homo, & animal. Et de vniuersali complexo non procedit quæstio præsens: sed solùm de incomplexo: quod quadruplex est, in causando, in significando, in essendo, & in prædicando. Vniuersale in Causando, dicitur causa, quæ plures effectus producere potest, vt cœlum. Vniuersale in significando, est vox, vel conceptus communis, rem etiam communem multis significans, vt vox homo, & conceptus hominis, quem in mente formamus. Vniuersale in Essendo, esset res separata à singularibus, & in eis existens, si daretur, qualis esset idea illa, quàm dicunt aliqui posuisse Platonem, nempe homo separatus à Petro & Ioanne, à quo procederent. Vniuersale denique in prædicando, dicitur natura communis, quæ de multis prædicari potest, & quam significant voces communes: vt natura hominis signata per hanc vocem homo, quæ de Petro & Ioanne prædicari potest.

his question is as it were the foundation of all the others that can be 29 T disputed concerning universals. But in order that its title may be understood, it should be noted that the universal is twofold, Complex and Incomplex. The complex universal is a universal proposition, known per se, which is the principle of some science, from which many conclusions are inferred: as in the science of man the universal principle is that he is rational, from which it is gathered that he is capable of wonder and risible. The incomplex universal is a certain simple word signifying something common to many, as man and animal. Now the present question does not proceed concerning the complex universal, but only concerning the incomplex, which is fourfold: in causing, in signifying, in being, and in predicating. The universal in Causing is said of a cause that can produce several effects, as the heavens. The universal in signifying is a common word or concept signifying a common thing, as the word man and the concept of man which we form in the mind. The universal in Being would be a thing separated from singulars and existing in them, if such a thing were given, such as would be that idea which some say Plato posited, namely a man separated from Peter and John, from which these would proceed. Finally, the universal in predicating is said of the common nature which can be predicated of many and which common words signify: as the nature of man, signified by this word man, which is predicated of Peter and John.

Et vniuersale in Causando ad Physicum, aut Metaphysicum pertinet, qui de natura causarum agit: quare de illo non disputamus modò, nec de vniuersali Significando: quia Dialecticus non agit principaliter de vocibus, sed de rebus per eas significatis: sed nec de vniuersali in Essendo, quia iudicatur impossibile, vt videbimus inferiùs. Solùm ergo proponitur quæstio de vniuersali in Prædicando, an in rebus verè sit: vt an id, quod de Petro & Ioanne prædicatur in his propositionibus, Petrus est homo, Ioannes est homo, sit aliquid præter vocem, quod in eis existat.

And the universal in Causing pertains to the Physicist or the Metaphysician, who treats of the nature of causes; therefore we do not dispute of it now. Nor of the universal in Signifying, because the Dialectician does not deal principally with words but with the things signified by them. Nor of the universal in Being, because it is judged impossible, as we shall see below. Only the question of the universal in Predicating, therefore, is proposed: whether in these propositions, Peter is a man, John is a man, that which is predicated of Peter and John is truly something besides the word, which exists in them.

Circa quam fuit prima opinio Heracliti Ephesij, & Cratyli antiquorum Philosophorum, vt asserit Arist. 3. lib de cœlo, & mundo, tex 3. 1. lib. Me. cap. 5. tex. etiam 4. lib. 4. tex 22. qui omnino negabant aliquid vniuersale in rebus esse, propter hoc argumentum. Omnia quæ sunt in mundo, sunt singularia: ergo nihil est vniuersale. Antecedens probabant dupliciter

On this the first opinion was that of Heraclitus of Ephesus and Cratylus, ancient Philosophers, as Aristotle relates in On the Heavens 3, text 3; Metaph. 1, ch. 5, text; and also 4, text 22: who altogether denied that anything universal exists in things, on account of this argument: All things that are in the world are singular; therefore nothing is universal. They proved the antecedent in two ways:

p. 35

Primò ex sensibus: quia quæcunque per sensus cognoscimus, vt per visum, auditum, & reliquos, singularia sunt, & nihil commune multis, ergo non datur vniuersale in rebus. Secundò, omnia quæ fiunt in rerũ natura singularia sunt, cùm fiant per actiones causarum, quæ non nisi de singularibus sunt: ergo nihil fit vniuersale: sed nihil est in rebus, quod non sit factum: ergo omnia sunt singularia, & nihil est vniuersale, & cùm scientiæ non sint de singularibus, quæ passim corrumpuntur, negantes vniuersalia, consequenter negabant scientias, & videtur idem tenere Arist lib. de Anima, tex. 8. vbi ita ait. Animal vniuersale aut nihil est, aut posterius: similiter autem, & si quid commune aliud prædicetur.

First, from the senses: because whatever we know through the senses, as through sight, hearing, and the rest, is singular, and nothing is common to many; therefore there is no universal in things. Second, all things that come to be in the nature of things are singular, since they come to be through the actions of causes, which are only of singulars: therefore nothing that comes to be is universal; but there is nothing in things that has not been made: therefore all things are singular, and nothing is universal. And since the sciences are not of singulars, which perish on every side, those who denied universals consequently denied the sciences. And Aristotle seems to hold the same, On the Soul, text 8, where he speaks thus: The universal animal either is nothing, or is posterior; and similarly if anything else common is predicated.

Secunda opinio fuit Platonis, vt affirmat Arist. 1. lib. Meta. c. 3 tex. 12. & c. 5. tex. 5. & 6. qui ponebat naturas quasdam vniuersales separatas à singularibus, à quibus eadem singularia procedebant: vt pro hominibus naturam humanam separatam à Petro, & Ioanne & cæteris, à quibus singulares homines fiebant: quamuis D. August lib. 73. quæstionum, quæst. 46. & Seneca lib. 8. epistolarum, epist. 66. affirment, hanc non fuisse mentem Platonis, sed per ideas intellexisse quasdam similitudines rerum omnium, quas Deus intra se habet, & per quas eas producit. Omitto opinionem Nominalium, qui solùm posuisse videntur vniuersalia in vocibus de quibus scientias esse dicebant, & non de rebus.

The second opinion was that of Plato, as Aristotle affirms, Metaph. 1, ch. 3, text 12, and ch. 5, text 5 and 6, who posited certain universal natures separated from singulars, from which those same singulars proceeded: as for men, a human nature separated from Peter and John and the rest, from which singular men came to be; although St. Augustine, book of 83 Questions, q. 46, and Seneca, Letters bk. 8, letter 66, affirm that this was not Plato’s mind, but that by ideas he understood certain likenesses of all things, which God has within himself and through which he produces them. I omit the opinion of the Nominalists, who seem to have posited universals only in words, of which, they said, the sciences are, and not of things.

31 Vera sententia Arist. & communis iam in schola, ab omnibus tenenda, tribus conclusionibus explicanda est. Prima conclusio. Non solùm dantur voces vniuersales, sed etiam res de quibus sunt scientiæ. Probatur hæc aduersus Nominales autoritate Aristot. lib. de interpretatione cap. 5. vbi quasdam res vniuersales esse, ait, alias singulares: ergo sentit non solùm in vocibus, sed in rebus dari vniuersale. Deinde ratione, quia nomina vniuersalia, vt homo, aut equus, non sunt imposita ad significandum res singulares, vt Petrum, & Ioannem: nec aliquem eorum distinctè significant: sed propriis nominibus significantur: ergo aliquid datur, præter singularia, ad quod proximè atque distinctè significandum imponuntur. Quod cùm non sit singulare, erit vniuersale. Secundæ istæ propositiones sunt veræ, ac necessariæ, Petrus est homo, & homo est animal, & tamen si nihil præter voces prædicatur, erunt falsæ, cùm nec vna vox sit alia, nec in ea includatur: ergo necesse est præter voces, res vniuersales ponere.

31 The true opinion of Aristotle, now common in the school and to be held by all, must be explained in three conclusions. First conclusion. There are not only universal words but also universal things, of which the sciences are. This is proved against the Nominalists by the authority of Aristotle, On Interpretation, ch. 5, where he says that some things are universal, others singular: therefore he holds that the universal is found not only in words but in things. Next, by reason: because universal names, such as man or horse, are not imposed to signify singular things, such as Peter and John, nor do they signify any of them distinctly; rather these are signified by proper names: therefore something is given besides singulars, to signify which proximately and distinctly they are imposed; and since this is not singular, it will be universal. Second, these propositions are true and necessary, Peter is a man and Man is an animal; and yet, if nothing besides words is predicated, they will be false, since neither is one word the other, nor is it included in it: therefore it is necessary to posit universal things besides words.

Secunda conclusio. Non datur vniuersale separatum realiter à singularibus. Hæc est contra Platonem (si sententiam

Second conclusion. There is no universal really separated from singulars. This is against Plato (if the opinion C ij

p. 36

illam tenuit, de ideis, quam ei tribuit Aristoteles) & probatur ex Arist. 1 lib. Poster. c. 35. tex. 38. 3. Meta. tex. 10. 7. Meta. tex. 51. & 57. & 10. Met. tex. 6. quibus locis ostendit vniuersalia esse non posse separata à singularibus. Deinde probatur ratione, quia quidquid verè & realiter prædicatur de aliquo, debet esse in eo: sed vniuersalia verè prędicantur de singularibus in his propositionibus, Petrus est homo, & homo est animal: ergo verè & realiter in eis sunt. Probatur maior, quia ab eo, quod res est, vel non est, propositio dicitur vera, aut falsa: sed in his propositionibus prędicãtur vniuersalia de singularibus: ergo aut sunt in eis, aut propositiones sunt falsæ.

he held about ideas, which Aristotle attributes to him); and it is proved from Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 35, text 38; Metaph. 3, text 10; Metaph. 7, text 51 and 57; and Metaph. 10, text 6; in which places he shows that universals cannot be separated from singulars. Next it is proved by reason: because whatever is truly and really predicated of something must be in it; but universals are truly predicated of singulars in these propositions, Peter is a man and Man is an animal: therefore they are truly and really in them. The major is proved: because a proposition is called true or false from the fact that the thing is or is not; but in these propositions universals are predicated of singulars: therefore either they are in them, or the propositions are false.

Tertia conclusio. Licèt omnes res mundi sint singulares, in ipsismet singularibus dantur vniuersales naturæ, quæ de eisdem prædicantur. hæc est aduersus Heraclitum. & probatur simul ac declaratur hac ratione, Singularia naturæ humanæ, vt Petrus & Ioannes, magis similia sunt inter sese quàm singularia alterius naturæ: habent enim definitionem, & prædicata essentialia sibi communia. Nam vterque est homo, & animal rationale: ergo concipit intellectus naturam humanam in vtroque existentem, & vtrique communem: & ideo erit vna, & in multis, quod est esse vniuersalem.

Third conclusion. Although all the things of the world are singular, in the singulars themselves there are universal natures, which are predicated of them. This is against Heraclitus, and it is proved and at the same time declared by this argument. The singulars of human nature, such as Peter and John, are more like each other than the singulars of another nature; for they have a definition and essential predicates common to them: for each is a man and a rational animal: therefore the intellect conceives the human nature existing in both and common to both; and therefore it will be one and in many, which is to be universal.

32 Ad argumentum primæ opinionis, concesso antecedenti, quòd omnes res mundi sunt singulares: neganda est consequentia, quòd nihil sit vniuersale: nam licet nihil sit vniuersale, ab eisdem singularibus realiter separatum, (vt fortè asseruit Plato) nec in ipsismet singularibus realiter ab eis distinctum, natura tamen, in qua omnes conueniunt, vniuersalis est, solùm ab eis distincta per intellectum, eam concipientem, non conceptis singularibus, & de hac est scientia, etiam si non sit de singularibus. Ad testimonium autem Arist. respondet D. Tho. in commentariis eiusdem, per illa verba excludere voluisse errorem Platonis, de ideis separatis, & simul docere, quonam modo vniuersale in rebus reperiatur: ideo sensus verborum eius talis est: Animal vniuersale nihil est, separatum à speciebus hominis, & equi, vt fingebat Plato: est tamen in eis quasi quid posterius, quia in eisdem fundatur, & ex eorum conuenientia sumitur.

32 To the argument of the first opinion, granting the antecedent, that all the things of the world are singular, the consequence must be denied, that nothing is universal: for although there is nothing universal really separated from those singulars (as perhaps Plato asserted), nor anything in the singulars themselves really distinct from them, yet the nature in which they all agree is universal, being distinct from them only through the intellect, which conceives it without conceiving the singulars; and of this there is science, even if there is none of singulars. To the testimony of Aristotle, St. Thomas replies in his commentary on that work that by those words he wished to exclude Plato’s error about separated ideas, and at the same time to teach in what way the universal is found in things: therefore the sense of his words is this: The universal animal is nothing separated from the species of man and horse, as Plato imagined; but it is in them as something posterior, because it is founded in them and is taken from their agreement.

QUESTION II

Quænam sit essentia, & natura vniuersalium.

What the essence and nature of universals is.

33 NAtura, & essentia cuiuslibet rei, explicatur per definitionem eius: ideo solutio huius quæstionis ex definitione

33 The nature and essence of any thing whatever is explained by its definition: therefore the solution of this question from the definition

p. 37

vniuersalis dependet, qua adducta & explicata, soluta etiam erit quæstio. Duplicem definitionem vniuersalis tradit Arist. diuersis suæ doctrinæ locis: Primam 7. lib, Met. tex. 45. his verbis: Hoc enim dicitur vniuersale, quod pluribus natura aptum est inesse: Secundum verò 1. li. de interpretatione c. 5. vbi ita ait, Dico autem vniuersale, quod in pluribus prædicari natum est, vt homo quidem vniuersalium est. Vtraque verò simul posuit 1. lib. de posteriori resolutione, c. 10. tex. 25. dicens: Esse quidem igitur vnum de multis, verum dicere necesse est: non erit enim vniuersale, nisi hoc sit. oportet igitur aliquid vnum, idemque in pluribus esse, non æquiuocè: quibus vniuersale duo habere docet: Quòd sit vnum, hoc est vniuocum: quare excluduntur æquiuoca, & analoga à ratione vniuersalis: quia vel nullam habent vnitatem, vt æquiuoca: vel solùm vnitatem secundùm quid, hoc est secundùm proportionem, vel attributionem, vt analoga. Deinde in multis, & quòd de illis prædicetur, quæ licèt non distinguantur realiter in vniuersali, quia formaliter sumptum, non est quid reale, sunt tamen duæ rationes, ita se habentes, ac si realiter distinguerentur: ex quibus prior est, quòd in multis sit, posterior verò, quòd prædicetur de multis. Quod ita probo. Causa veritatis prædicationum est rem ita se habere extra, sicut per illas significatur, & enuntiatur, vt docet Arist. 1. lib de interpretatione, dicens: Ab eo quod res est, vel non est, propositio dicitur vera, vel falsa: ergo causalis ista propositio vera est: Quia vniuersale est in multis, prædicatur de multis: sed causa prior natura est suo effectu: ergo prius est, quod vniuersale sit in multis, quàm quod prædicetur de multis. Licèt autem prior sit ratio essendi in illis, quàm prædicandi, conuertuntur tamen: quia verùm est. quod est in multis, prædicari de multis: & contrà, quidquid prædicatur de multis, in eis esse, cùm nihil prædicetur de aliquo, nisi sit in eo.

of the universal depends; once it has been adduced and explained, the question too will be solved. Aristotle gives a twofold definition of the universal in different places of his doctrine: the first in Metaph. 7, text 45, in these words: For that is called universal which is apt by nature to be in several. The second in On Interpretation 1, ch. 5, where he speaks thus: Now I call universal that which is apt by nature to be predicated of several, as man is one of the universals. And he posited both together in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 10, text 25, saying: It is necessary, then, that there be one thing truly said of many: for there will not be a universal unless this is so. There must, therefore, be something one and the same in several, not equivocally: by which words he teaches that the universal has two things. That it be one, that is, univocal: wherefore equivocals and analogues are excluded from the ratio of the universal: because either they have no unity, like equivocals, or only a unity in a certain respect, that is, according to proportion or attribution, like analogues. Next, that it be in many, and that it be predicated of them; which, although they are not really distinguished in the universal (because, taken formally, it is not something real), are nevertheless two rationes, related as if they were really distinguished; of which the prior is that it be in many, the posterior that it be predicated of many. This I prove thus. The cause of the truth of predications is that the thing is outside just as it is signified and enunciated through them, as Aristotle teaches, On Interpretation 1, saying: From the fact that the thing is or is not, a proposition is called true or false: therefore this causal proposition is true: Because the universal is in many, it is predicated of many; but a cause is prior in nature to its effect: therefore its being in many is prior to its being predicated of many. Now, although the ratio of being in them is prior to that of predicating, they are nevertheless convertible: because it is true that what is in many is predicated of many; and conversely, that whatever is predicated of many is in them, since nothing is predicated of something unless it is in it.

34 Ex quibus sequitur primò essentiam vniuersalis esse, quòd in multis sit, & quasi propriam passionem eius, quòd de multis prædicetur. Probatur hoc argumento. Illud quod primò intelligimus de aliquo, dicimus esse essentiam illius: sed primum quod intelligimus de vniuersali, est, quòd sit in multis: ergo hoc erit de essentia eius. Illud etiam quod posterius intelligimus, si conuertatur cum priori, dicimus esse propriam passionem eius: sed prædicari de multis est quid posterius quàm esse in multis, & cum eo conuertitur, vt probauimus: ergo erit propria passio eius.

34 From which it follows, first, that the essence of the universal is to be in many, and as it were its proper attribute, to be predicated of many. This is proved by this argument. That which we first understand of something we call its essence; but the first thing that we understand of the universal is that it is in many; therefore this will be of its essence. That, too, which we understand posteriorly, if it is convertible with the prior, we call its proper attribute; but to be predicated of many is something posterior to being in many, and is convertible with it, as we have proved; therefore it will be its proper attribute.

Sed dum dicimus esse in multis, pertinere ad essentiam vniuersalis, & prædicari de multis, esse passionem: neutrum intelligendum

But when we say that being in many pertains to the essence of the universal, and that being predicated of many is its attribute, neither is to be understood C iij

p. 38

est secundùm actum: sed vtrumque secundùm aptitudinem, vt verba Arist. docent, & probat experientia: cùm videamus naturam Solis, & Lunæ esse vniuersalem, & nec esse actu in multis, nec actu de illis prædicari, sed vtrumque habere in potentia. Et hoc est, quod communiter dici solet, Verba in definitionibus non dicunt actum, sed aptitudinem: quare sensus primæ definitionis est, Vniuersale est, quod aptum est esse in multis, sensus verò secundæ, Vniuersale est, vnum prædicabile de multis.

according to act, but each according to aptitude, as the words of Aristotle teach and as experience proves: since we see that the nature of the Sun and of the Moon is universal, and that it neither is actually in many nor is actually predicated of them, but has each in potency. And this is what is commonly said: Words in definitions do not signify act, but aptitude: wherefore the sense of the first definition is: The universal is that which is apt to be in many; and the sense of the second: The universal is one thing predicable of many.

Secũdò sequitur, primam definitionem esse quidditatiuam, aut essentialem: quia continet essentiam vniuersalis. Secundam verò descriptiuam, quia datur per passionem.

It follows, second, that the first definition is quidditative or essential, because it contains the essence of the universal; but the second is descriptive, because it is given through an attribute.

35 Tertiò sequitur, falsum esse, quod à quibusdam modernis dicitur esse in multis & prædicari de multis, non esse rationes distinctas vniuersalis, sed eandem omnino: quia eo ipso, quòd intelligimus naturam in multis esse, intelligimus etiam esse prædicabilem. Hoc enim non est verum, nam si esse in multis est ratio prior, & causa prædicabilitatis de multis, vt probauimus, euidenter sequitur, quòd possit intelligi, non intellecta prædicabilitate de multis: cùm sit euidens, id quod prius est, posse intelligi sine posteriori.

35 It follows, third, that what is said by certain moderns is false, namely that being in many and being predicated of many are not distinct rationes of the universal, but altogether the same: because by the very fact that we understand a nature to be in many, we also understand it to be predicable. For this is not true: for if being in many is the prior ratio and the cause of predicability of many, as we have proved, it evidently follows that it can be understood without predicability of many being understood; since it is evident that what is prior can be understood without what is posterior.

Explicata essentia vniuersalis, respondendum est tribus quæstionibus, quas Porphyrius omisit, propter earum difficultatem: quia ex earum solutionibus, meliùs intelligetur eadem essentia vniuersalis. Prima quæstio erat, An vniuersalia sint in rebus. Secunda, An sint substantiæ vel accidentia. Tertia an sint æterna, vel temporanea. Pro quarum solutione, notanda est distinctio vniuersalis, quam tradit D. Tho. 7. Met. lect. 23. dupliciter enim sumi potest, nempe pro natura, quæ denominatur vniuersalis, qualis est homo, vel animal: & hoc modo sumitur materialiter, aut fundamentaliter: aut pro vniuersalitate, quæ est forma, à qua denominatur vniuersale: & hæc forma vocatur secunda intentio, aut relatio rationis, per quam refertur natura ad indiuidua. Et si Vniuersalia sumantur primo modo, in rebus esse dicuntur, & non ab eis separata: quia homo & animal, in rebus ipsis sunt: homo in singularibus hominibus: animal verò in suis speciebus, equo, & leone. Si verò sumatur secundo modo, non sunt in rebus; sed obiectiuè solũ in intellectu: quia secunda intentio, aut relatio rationis, non habet aliud esse, quàm cognosci ab intellectu: eam attribuente naturæ, quam cum indiuiduis comparat.

The essence of the universal having been explained, we must answer three questions which Porphyry omitted on account of their difficulty: because from their solutions that same essence of the universal will be better understood. The first question was: Whether universals are in things. The second: Whether they are substances or accidents. The third: Whether they are eternal or temporal. For their solution, the distinction of the universal which St. Thomas gives, Metaph. 7, lect. 13, must be noted: for it can be taken in two ways, namely for the nature which is denominated universal, such as man or animal, and in this way it is taken materially or fundamentally; or for universality, which is the form from which the universal is denominated; and this form is called second intention, or relation of reason, through which the nature is referred to the individuals. And if universals are taken in the first way, they are said to be in things, and not separated from them: because man and animal are in the things themselves; man in singular men, animal in its species, horse and lion. But if they are taken in the second way, they are not in things, but only objectively in the intellect: because the second intention, or relation of reason, has no other being than to be known by the intellect, which attributes it to the nature that it compares with the individuals.

36 Et eodem modo soluitur quæstio secunda: quia Vniuersalia materialiter, aut pro fundamento considerata: aut sunt

36 And in the same way the second question is solved: because universals, considered materially, or for the foundation, either are

p. 39

entia realia vt equus, aut leo: vel entia rationis, vt genus, aut species: vel sunt substantiæ, vt homo vel animal: aut accidentia vt albedo, & color. Si verò sumantur secundo modo, non sunt substantiæ, sed accidentia: non realia, sed rationis: quia solùm sunt denominationes quædam, quas intellectus attribuit naturis, eas vniuersales vocans. Ad tertiam tandem quæstionem sic respondendum est, si vniuersalia sumantur formaliter pro vniuersalitate, non sunt æterna, sed temporanea: quia vniuersalitas non est, nisi dum actu consideratur ab intellectu, sed non semper est intellectus in actuali consideratione: ergo nec semper vniuersalitas. Si verò accipiatur pro fundamentis, alia distinctio addenda est. Nam res vniuersales, dupliciter sumi possunt, nempe secundùm actualem existentiam, quam habent in inferioribus, hoc est in indiuiduis, aut speciebus: & hoc modo non sunt æterna, sed eis corruptis, ipsa quoque corrumpuntur. v. g. Flores diuersarum specierum, vniuersales sunt: & si sumantur secundùm actualem existẽtiam in indiuiduis, non sunt in hyeme: ergo nec sunt semper, nec æterna, sed temporanea: sicut indiuidua ipsa. Si verò considerentur secundùm essentiam, hoc est secundùm prædicata essentialia, æterna sunt: quia licèt actu non existant in singularibus, debita sunt eius eadem prædicata essentialia, non minùs quàm si actu in eis existerent, vt homo, & animal, secundùm essentiam æterna sunt: quia etiam si nullus sit homo, aut animal in rerum natura, verum est hominem esse animal rationale, & animal viuens sensibile: quia hæc prædicata essentialia eis debentur.

real beings, such as horse or lion, or beings of reason, such as genus or species; or they are substances, such as man or animal, or accidents, such as whiteness and color. But if they are taken in the second way, they are not substances but accidents: not real ones, but of reason: because they are only certain denominations which the intellect attributes to natures, calling them universal. To the third question, finally, one must reply thus: if universals are taken formally, for universality, they are not eternal but temporal: because universality exists only while it is actually considered by the intellect; but the intellect is not always in actual consideration: therefore neither is universality always. But if it is taken for the foundations, another distinction must be added. For universal things can be taken in two ways, namely according to the actual existence which they have in their inferiors, that is, in individuals or species; and in this way they are not eternal, but when these are corrupted, they too are corrupted. E.g., flowers of diverse species are universal; and if they are taken according to their actual existence in individuals, they do not exist in winter: therefore they neither always are nor are eternal, but temporal, like the individuals themselves. But if they are considered according to essence, that is, according to their essential predicates, they are eternal: because, although they do not actually exist in singulars, those same essential predicates are owed to them no less than if they actually existed in them; as man and animal are eternal according to essence: because, even if there were no man or animal in the nature of things, it is true that man is a rational animal, and animal a living sentient thing: because these essential predicates are owed to them.

37 Et si inquiras, vbi essent vniuersalia, si nullũ esset singulare (nam si perpetua sunt, alicubi permanere deberẽt.) Respõdeo nullibi esse actu, sed solùm obiectiuè in intellectu diuino, actu cognoscẽte eis esse debita essentialia prędicata atq; etiã virtualiter in diuina omnipotentia, à qua produci possunt in suis singularibus: & ecce quomodo essentialiter sumpta æterna sunt.

37 And if you ask where universals would be if there were no singular (for if they are perpetual, they would have to remain somewhere), I reply that they would be nowhere in act, but only objectively in the divine intellect, which actually knows that the essential predicates are owed to them, and also virtually in the divine omnipotence, by which they can be produced in their singulars: and behold how, taken essentially, they are eternal.

QUESTION III

Quæst. 3. An detur in rebus ante operationem intellectus vnitas formalis minor numerali — Whether there is in things, before the operation of the intellect, a formal unity less than numerical.

An detur in rebus ante operationem intellectus vnitas formalis minor numerali.

[…]

AGens Aristotel. de vnitate rerum, 5. lib. Meta. cap. 6. triplicem posuit vnitatem, Genericam, Specificam, & Numericam. Generica est, quam habent species in genere, vt equus, & leo in animali. Specifica quam habent indiuidua in specie, vt Petrus & Ioannes, in homine. Numerica quam habet quodcunque indiuiduum in seipso, in quantum non est

Aristotle, treating of the unity of things, Metaph. 5, ch. 6, posited a threefold unity: Generic, Specific, and Numerical. Generic is that which species have in the genus, as horse and lion in animal. Specific, that which individuals have in the species, as Peter and John in man. Numerical, that which any individual whatever has in itself, insofar as it is not C iiij

p. 40

distinctum à se, sed à quocunque alio: vt Petrus, dicitur vnus numero, quia est hoc indiuidium, hoc est, à seipso non distinctus, sed à Ioanne, & cæteris.

distinct from itself, but from anything else whatever: as Peter is called one in number because he is this individual, that is, not distinct from himself, but from John and the rest.

38 Ex his autem tribus vnitatibus, maior est numerica; minor specifica, & minima generica: cuius ratio est manifesta; quia illa est minor vnitas, quæ secum compatitur maiorem diuersitatem, sed vnitas generica maiorem compatitur secum diuersitatem, minorem verò vnitas specifica, & nullam numerica: ergo hæc maxima vnitas vocari potest; specifica minor, & generica minima. Probatur minor, quia quæ sunt vnum genere, differunt per differentias essentiales, & specificas, vt homo, & leo: quæ sunt vnum specie, non per differentias essentiales, sed per indiuiduales multò minores: at quod est vnum numero, neque habet in se diuersitatem specificã, nec indiuidualem, sed vtroque modo est in se vnum. Et de vnitate numerica, non potest esse dubium, quin & realis sit, & ante operationem intellectus detur: quare de hac non procedit quæstio, sed de specifica, aut generica, quæ formalis dicitur: quia est vnitas in essentia, & prædicatis essentialibus à forma substantiali rerum procedentibus, & est minor numerali: de qua ideo quærit titulus quæstionis, an detur ante operationem intellectus.

38 Of these three unities, the greatest is the numerical, the lesser the specific, and the least the generic: the reason for which is manifest: because that unity is lesser which is compatible with greater diversity; but generic unity is compatible with greater diversity, specific unity with lesser, and numerical with none: therefore the latter can be called the greatest unity, the specific lesser, and the generic least. The minor is proved: because things that are one in genus differ by essential and specific differences, as man and lion; things that are one in species differ not by essential differences but by individual ones, which are much less; but what is one in number has in itself neither specific nor individual diversity, but is one in itself in both ways. And concerning numerical unity there can be no doubt that it is both real and given before the operation of the intellect: wherefore the question does not proceed concerning it, but concerning the specific or the generic, which is called formal: because it is a unity in essence and in the essential predicates proceeding from the substantial form of things, and it is less than numerical; and of it, therefore, the title of the question asks whether it is given before the operation of the intellect.

39 Et est prima opinio Scoti 7. lib. Meta. quæst. 16. & in 2. dist. 3 quæst. 2. asserentis, dari vnitatem formalem, genericam, & specificam, ante operationem intellectus, esséque essentialem ipsis naturis, aut saltem eis conuenire tanquam propriam passionem. Et probatur 1. ex Aristotele in prædicamento ad aliquid, vbi docet, Primum genus relationis fundari in vnitate specifica, aut generica, quæ si sit inter substantias, erit relatio identitatis, vt identitas specifica inter Petrum & Paulum, in vnitate naturæ humanæ: si sit inter qualitates, erit relatio similitudinis, vt inter duo alba: si inter quantitates, relatio æqualitatis, aut inæqualitatis: vt inter duo corpora eiusdem longitudinis. Ex quo tale argumentum colligitur. Relatio huius generis est realis, & datur ante operationem intellectus, nam duo alba, etiam si non cognoscantur ab intellectu, erunt similia: ergo fundamentum eius, quod est vnitas formalis, erit etiã reale, & dabitur ante operationem intellectus. Probatur etiam ratione, quia vnitas est passio entis realis, ergo cuicunque gradui entis realis, correspondet sua vnitas realis: vt gradui entitatis realis, correspondet sua vnitas realis, vt gradui entitatis numericæ, vnitas numerica realis, & gradui entitatis specificæ, vnitas realis specifica, & hæc est formalis, ergo erit realis, sicut gradus entitatis specificæ realis est, dabiturque ante operationem intellectus.

39 And the first opinion is that of Scotus, Metaph. 7, q. 16, and on 2, d. 3, q. 2, who asserts that there is a formal unity, generic and specific, before the operation of the intellect, and that it is essential to the natures themselves, or at least belongs to them as a proper attribute. And it is proved, first, from Aristotle in the category of relatives, where he teaches that the first genus of relation is founded on specific or generic unity; which, if it is between substances, will be a relation of identity, as specific identity between Peter and Paul in the unity of human nature; if it is between qualities, it will be a relation of similarity, as between two white things; if between quantities, a relation of equality or of inequality, as between two bodies of the same length. From which such an argument is gathered. A relation of this genus is real and is given before the operation of the intellect: for two white things, even if they are not known by the intellect, will be similar: therefore its foundation, which is formal unity, will also be real and will be given before the operation of the intellect. It is also proved by reason: because unity is an attribute of real being; therefore to every grade of real being there corresponds its real unity: as to the grade of real entity there corresponds its real unity, as to the grade of numerical entity a real numerical unity, and to the grade of specific entity a real specific unity, and this is formal; therefore it will be real, just as the grade of specific entity is real, and it will be given before the operation of the intellect.

p. 41

Secunda opinio, negat omninò dari aliquam vnitatem formalem minorem numerali, ante operationem intellectus, quam sequitur S. Tho. opusc. 55. non longè à principio, & 1. p. quæst. 85. art. 2. ad 2. Albertus Magnus in lib. prædicabilium quæst. 6. Themistius paraphrasi super proœmium Arist. de Anima, cap. 4. Alexander Aphrodisius super 7. lib. Meta. post medium, fol. 131. pag. 1. & 2. Iauel. tract. 4. de quinque vniuersalibus in sua Dialectica. D. Ioannes Damascenus lib. de Dialectica cap. 64. Capreol. in 2. d. 8 quæst. 2. Venetus lib. 2. suæ Dialecticæ tract. 4. par. 4. cap. 4. & probatur. Quia quidquid conuenit naturæ specificæ essentialiter, aut tanquam propria passio, debet etiam conuenire cuicunque indiuiduo eiusdẽ: vt si naturæ humanæ conueniunt rationalitas & risibilitas, Petro & Ioanni cõuenire debent: ergo si vnitas formalis specifica conuenit ei essentialiter, aut tanquam propria passio, necesse cuicunque indiuiduo conuenire, & ita, Petrus erit vnus, vnitate formali specifica multis communi, quod euidenter falsum est.

The second opinion altogether denies that there is any formal unity less than numerical before the operation of the intellect. It is followed by St. Thomas, opusc. 55, not far from the beginning, and 1 p., q. 85, a. 2, ad 2; Albert the Great in the book of the Predicables, q. 6; Themistius in his paraphrase on the proem of Aristotle’s On the Soul, ch. 4; Alexander of Aphrodisias on Metaph. 7, after the middle, fol. 131, p. 1 and 2; Javelli, tract. 4, on the five universals, in his Dialectic; St. John Damascene in his book on Dialectic, ch. 64; Capreolus in 2, d. 8, q. 2; Venetus, bk. 2 of his Dialectic, tract. 4, part 4, ch. 4. And it is proved: because whatever belongs to the specific nature essentially, or as a proper attribute, must also belong to any individual of it: as, if rationality and risibility belong to human nature, they must belong to Peter and John; therefore, if specific formal unity belongs to it essentially, or as a proper attribute, it must belong to any individual whatever, and so Peter will be one by a specific formal unity common to many, which is evidently false.

Tertia opinio, distinguit vnitatem formalem, in Actualem, & Potẽtialem: Actualem vocat eam, per quam natura est actu, & formaliter vna multis communis; Potentialem verò, quam habere potest: & vtramque ait esse realem: sed potentialem tantùm conuenire naturæ ante operationem intellectus in illa proprietate naturæ, qua prior est suis indiuiduis; quam haberet (inquit) actualem, si ab eis realiter separetur, licet hoc sit impossibile: hanc verò vnitatem non communicare indiuiduis, quia ei conuenit, vt est prior natura eis. Hanc sententiam tenent Soncin. 7. Meta. quæst 40. Fonseca 5. Meta. cap. 18. quæst. 3. sect. 2. 3. & 4. probantque hoc argum. Natura specifica significatur communi, & vniuoco, vt natura humana, hoc nomine homo: sed vniuocum nomen significat aliquid vnum: ergo datur aliqua vnitas formalis in natura, ante operationem intellectus, ratione cuius significetur nomine communi: Quod si negaueris, sequitur nomen homo, & quodcunque aliud, significans naturam communem, esse æquiuocum: cùm non significet aliquid vnum, quod est falsum.

The third opinion distinguishes formal unity into Actual and Potential. It calls actual that by which the nature is actually and formally one common to many; potential, that which it can have. And it says that both are real, but that the potential belongs to the nature before the operation of the intellect only in that property of the nature by which it is prior to its individuals; which (it says) it would have as actual if it were really separated from them, although this is impossible; but that this unity is not communicated to the individuals, because it belongs to the nature inasmuch as it is prior in nature to them. This opinion is held by Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 40; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 18, q. 3, sect. 2, 3 and 4; and they prove it by this argument. The specific nature is signified by a common and univocal name, as human nature by this name man; but a univocal name signifies something one; therefore there is some formal unity in the nature before the operation of the intellect, by reason of which it is signified by a common name. If you deny this, it follows that the name man, and any other signifying a common nature, is equivocal, since it does not signify something one, which is false.

Postrema sententia est Caietani in opusculo de ente, & essentia, cap. 4. quæst. 6. Vbi alio modo distinguit vnitatem formalem, in positiuam & negatiuam. Positiua vnitas est, quam habent aliqua in forma, aut prædicato positiuo; vt Petrus & Ioannes, habent vnitatem formalem positiuam, in humanitate abstracta per intellectum ab indiuiduis, aut cum eis cõparata. Negatiua verò, non est aliud, quàm negatio diuisionis, & si sit

The last opinion is that of Cajetan in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4, q. 6, where he distinguishes formal unity in another way, into positive and negative. Positive unity is that which some things have in a form or positive predicate: as Peter and John have positive formal unity in humanity abstracted by the intellect from the individuals, or compared with them. Negative unity, however, is nothing other than the negation of division, and if

p. 42

negatio diuisionis materialis, erit vnitas numerica, quam habet Petrus per hanc materiã in se non diuisam, si verò sit negatio diuisionis formalis: erit vnitas formalis negatiua. Hac distinctione supposita, asserit, naturam non habere vnitatem formalem positiuam, ante operationem intellectus, quia diuisa est per differentias numericas in singularibus: quare nulla datur forma positiua communis, in qua singulariter homines cõueniant, quousque abstrahatur eadem natura humana per intellectũ ab eisdem singularibus, & cognoscatur eis non cognitis, tunc enim tamquam forma positiua eis communis cõcipietur: Sed habet, inquit, vnitatem formalem negatiuam à parte rei: quia licèt sit diuisa per differentias materiales, & numericas, non tamen per formales, & specificas: vnde Petrus & Ioannes, conueniunt & humanitate ante operationem intellectus negatiuè, ex eo solùm, quòd non distinguuntur in ea formaliter, aut essentialiter, licèt distinguantur per hanc, & illam humanitatem singularem indiuidualiter. Hanc sententiam Caietani sequuntur plures moderni, probántque hoc argumento.

it is the negation of material division, it will be numerical unity, which Peter has through this matter undivided in itself; but if it is the negation of formal division, it will be negative formal unity. Supposing this distinction, he asserts that the nature does not have positive formal unity before the operation of the intellect, because it is divided by the numerical differences in the singulars: wherefore no common positive form is given in which men agree singly, until the same human nature is abstracted by the intellect from those same singulars and is cognized without their being cognized; for then it will be conceived as a positive form common to them. But it has, he says, negative formal unity on the part of the thing; because although it is divided by material and numerical differences, it is not, however, divided by formal and specific ones: hence Peter and John agree in humanity before the operation of the intellect negatively, solely from the fact that they are not distinguished in it formally or essentially, although they are distinguished individually by this and that singular humanity. This opinion of Cajetan is followed by many moderns, and they prove it by this argument.

42 Vnitas numerica, est carentia diuisionis materialis, ergo vnitas formalis, & specifica, est carentia diuisionis formalis, & specificæ: sed Petrus & Ioannes ante operationem intellectus, carent diuisione formali, & specifica, cùm non distinguantur per differentias formales, aut essentiales, sed solùm per numericas, & quasi materiales: ergo habent vnitatem formalem in humanitate, saltem negatiuam.

41 Numerical unity is the lack of material division; therefore formal and specific unity is the lack of formal and specific division; but Peter and John before the operation of the intellect lack formal and specific division, since they are not distinguished by formal or essential differences, but only by numerical and as it were material ones; therefore they have formal unity in humanity, at least negative.

Et confirmari potest: quia quæcunque non sunt distincta in aliquo, dicuntur in eo conuenire, & esse vnũ, saltem negatiuè, sed Petrus, & Ioannes, ante operationẽ intellectus, non distinguuntur formaliter, aut specie in humanitate, ergo in ea cõueniũt, & sunt vnũ: quare dabitur vnitas negatiua vtriq; cõmunis.

And it can be confirmed: because whatever things are not distinct in something are said to agree in it and to be one, at least negatively; but Peter and John before the operation of the intellect are not distinguished formally or in species in humanity; therefore they agree in it and are one: wherefore there will be a negative unity common to both.

43 Pro solutione huius quęstionis notãdũ est primò. Vnitatem formalem duplicem esse: Nam quędam est, per quã aliquid dicitur in se vnum formaliter: quam habet Petrus per suam formam & essentiam, à qua dicitur vnus formaliter. Altera est, per quam aliquid dicitur vnum formaliter, multis commune, vt vnitas formalis, quam habet natura humana, dum consideratur ab intellectu abstracta à conditionibus singularium, per quas diuisa est in eis. Et de prima vnitate formali, duo sunt certa apud omnes. Primum, quod cuicunque naturæ conueniat ex se, realiter, & essentialiter, & ideo eam habeat ante operationem intellectus in suis indiuiduis: ita vt quodlibet dicatur per eandem naturam, quæ in eo est, vnum formaliter, & essentialiter, ita sentiunt D. Tho. Scotus, & alij vbi suprà.

43 For the solution of this question it should be noted first that formal unity is twofold. For one is that by which something is said to be formally one in itself: which Peter has through his form and essence, from which he is said to be formally one. The other is that by which something is said to be formally one, common to many, as the formal unity which human nature has while it is considered by the intellect as abstracted from the conditions of the singulars, by which it is divided in them. And concerning the first formal unity two things are certain among all. First, that it belongs to any nature of itself, really and essentially, and therefore the nature has it before the operation of the intellect in its individuals: so that each thing is said to be formally and essentially one through the same nature that is in it; so hold St. Thomas, Scotus and others in the places cited above.

p. 43

44 Secundò certũ est, hanc vnitatem formalem, aliquo modo distingui à numerica: cùm ex diuersa radice oriatur. Numerica enim oritur, ex materia, aut etiam ex forma, in quantum ex earum vnione resultat hæc entitas huius indiuidui: formalis verò ex sola forma, non vt causa huius entitatis, sed vt est radix omnium prædicatorum essentialium, quæ ei possunt conuenire. v. g. Vnitas formalis à qua Petrus est vnus homo, procedit ab eius anima, in quantum est principium ratiocinandi, ex quo habet idem Petrus vt sit rationalis, & eodẽ modo in cæteris naturis. Sed an distinguantur hæc vnitas formalis, & numerica, in eodem indiuiduo, ex natura rei, & ante operationem intellectus, vel sola ratione, & per intellectum, in hoc non conuenit Scotus cum D. Thom. asserit enim distinctas esse ex natura rei: sed D. Tho. quem omnes ferè sequuntur, tenet, non distingui ex natura rei, sed sola ratione per intellectum, præsupposito tamen fundamento in re, in quantum à diuersa radice procedunt, vt explicatum est. Et hoc videtur nobis non solùm probabilius, sed omnino verum, & tenendum: quod hac ratione efficaciter probatur. Idem est ex natura rei in Petro, esse hominem, & esse hunc hominem, quia non est nisi in quantum hęc humanitas veram habet humanitatis essentiam, sed per hanc humanitatem est vnus homo formaliter: ergo vtraque vnitas, formalitas & numerica est eadem res. Sed distinguuntur per intellectum, in quantum ex diuersa radice proueniunt.

44 Second, it is certain that this formal unity is in some way distinguished from the numerical, since it arises from a different root. For the numerical arises from matter, or also from form, inasmuch as from their union there results this entity of this individual; but the formal arises from the form alone, not as the cause of this entity, but as the root of all the essential predicates that can belong to it. For example, the formal unity by which Peter is one man proceeds from his soul inasmuch as it is the principle of reasoning, from which the same Peter has it that he is rational; and in the same way in other natures. But whether this formal and numerical unity are distinguished in the same individual from the nature of the thing and before the operation of the intellect, or by reason alone and through the intellect: on this Scotus does not agree with St. Thomas. For he asserts that they are distinct from the nature of the thing; but St. Thomas, whom almost all follow, holds that they are not distinguished from the nature of the thing, but by reason alone through the intellect, a foundation in the thing being presupposed, however, inasmuch as they proceed from a different root, as has been explained. And this seems to us not only more probable but altogether true and to be held, which is efficaciously proved by this argument. To be a man and to be this man are the same from the nature of the thing in Peter, because he is not a man except inasmuch as this humanity has the true essence of humanity, but through this humanity he is formally one man; therefore both unities, the formal and the numerical, are the same thing. But they are distinguished by the intellect, inasmuch as they come from a different root.

45 Certùm est tertiò, Vnitatem formalem cuiuscunque rei, determinari per differentiã indiuidualem, & per eam fieri hanc numero: quod probo primò. Petrus est vnus formaliter, per vnam formam & vnam essentiam quam habet, hoc est, per vnã humanitatem, sed humanitas eius est vna numero ratione differentiæ indiuidualis: ergo vnitas formalis, quam habet per eã, est vna numero ratione eiusdem differentiæ indiuidualis. Quod adeo verum est, ac necessarium, vt omnes gradus naturæ eius, omnia prædicata essentialia, quæ ratione eorum possunt ei conuenire, sint hæc, propter differẽtiam indiuidualem: est enim Petrus hæc substãtia, hoc corpus, hoc viuẽs, hoc animal, hoc rationale, & hic homo, imò repugnat aliquid esse in Petro, quod non sit hoc numero, ratione differẽtiæ indiuidualis, à qua natura eius, & essentia sit hæc distincta à quacũque alia. Vnde sequitur, quòd sicut tot sunt in Petro vnitates formales, ratione distinctæ, quot sunt gradus naturæ eius, ita omnes sunt indiuiduæ, quia coniunguntur differentiæ indiuiduali determinati omnes, & facienti eas has numero,

45 It is certain, third, that the formal unity of any thing whatever is determined by the individual difference, and becomes this in number through it: which I prove first. Peter is formally one through the one form and one essence that he has, that is, through one humanity; but his humanity is one in number by reason of the individual difference; therefore the formal unity which he has through it is one in number by reason of the same individual difference. Which is so true and necessary that all the grades of his nature, all the essential predicates that can belong to him by reason of them, are this, on account of the individual difference: for Peter is this substance, this body, this living thing, this animal, this rational thing, and this man; indeed, it is impossible that there be anything in Peter that is not this in number, by reason of the individual difference by which his nature and essence are this, distinct from any other whatever. Hence it follows that, just as there are in Peter as many formal unities, distinct in reason, as there are grades of his nature, so all are individual, because they are all joined to the individual difference, determined by it, and it makes them these in number.

p. 44

Quibus suppositis, nostra sententia tribus conclusionibus cõtinetur: Prima. Non datur aliqua vnitas formalis positiua & actualis, ante operationem intellectus, quæ conueniat naturæ realiter, & essentialiter, aut tanquam propria passio, per quam dicatur multis communis. Hæc est contra Scotum.

These things being supposed, our view is contained in three conclusions. First: There is not given, before the operation of the intellect, any positive and actual formal unity which belongs to the nature really and essentially, or as a proper attribute, through which it is said to be common to many. This is against Scotus.

46 Secunda cõclusio. Non datur ante operationẽ intellectus vnitas formalis in potentia, quæ conueniat naturæ in illa prioritate, quam habet respectu indiuiduorum, quibus non communicatur. Hæc est contra secundam opinionem Soncinatis.

46 Second conclusion: There is not given before the operation of the intellect a formal unity in potency which belongs to the nature in that priority which it has with respect to the individuals, to which it is not communicated. This is against the second opinion, that of Soncinas.

Tertia conclusio. Non datur vnitas formalis negatiua ante operationem intellectus. Hæc est contra Caiet. & probantur omnes simul ex doctrina tradita, hoc argum. Vnum, & indiuisum idem sunt, ergo diuisio opponitur vnitati, & eam tollit ac dissoluit: vt si diuidantur partes hominis, nempe brachium à capite, & caput à pedibus, eo ipso tollitur vnitas compositi, & earundem partium: sed omnis natura secundùm omnes gradus quas habet à parte rei, est diuisa per differentias indiuiduales, ergo nullam habet vnitatem formalem multis communem: Probatur minor. Natura humana, quæ est in Petro & Ioanne, est diuisa per differentias eorum indiuiduales: ita vt quidquid habet Petrus, sit hoc, atque distinctum ab aliis quæ habet Ioannes, nempe, hæc substantia, hoc corpus, hoc viuens, hoc animal, hic homo, & Paulus alia hæc substantia, aliud hoc corpus, aliud hoc viuens, aliud hoc animal, alius hic homo: ergo nec naturam, aut essentiam, neque vllum gradum naturæ possunt habere vnum aut communem, sed omnis vnitas formalis debet eis conuenire ratione naturæ, aut alicuius gradus eius, qui in eis sit vnus: ergo nullam habent vnitatem formalem communem.

Third conclusion: There is not given a negative formal unity before the operation of the intellect. This is against Cajetan. And all are proved together from the doctrine delivered, by this argument. One and undivided are the same; therefore division is opposed to unity, and takes it away and dissolves it: as, if the parts of a man are divided, namely the arm from the head and the head from the feet, by that very fact the unity of the composite and of those same parts is taken away; but every nature, according to all the grades which it has on the part of the thing, is divided by the individual differences; therefore it has no formal unity common to many. The minor is proved. The human nature that is in Peter and John is divided by their individual differences: so that whatever Peter has is this, and distinct from the others that John has, namely this substance, this body, this living thing, this animal, this man; and Paul has another this substance, another this body, another this living thing, another this animal, another this man: therefore they can have neither a nature or essence, nor any grade of the nature, that is one or common; but every formal unity must belong to them by reason of the nature, or of some grade of it, which is one in them; therefore they have no common formal unity.

Argumentum hoc concludit aduersus Scotum, quòd nullam habeant vtilitatem realem positiuam & actualem. Sed videtur posse respondere, Soncinas, & Caiet. quòd ille non ponit vnitatem actualem sed potentialem: & Caietan. non ponit vnitatem positiuam, sed negatiuam.
