Sed verè non minùs aduersus eosdem concludit, quàm aduersus Scotum. Probatur, aduersus Soncinatẽ concludere, quia si natura humana in Petro ante operationem intellectus est hæc, secundùm omnes gradus formales, & essentiales; & diuersa à natura Pauli, & gradibus eius: ergo repugnat, quòd à parte rei possit aliquam habere vnitatem in eis: quare nec habebunt vnitatem formalem in potentia, nam quibus repugnat actus, non potest conuenire potentia. Sed eadem secunda opinio probatur falsa, quia duo asserit impossibilia. Primum, quod natura, vt est prior

This argument concludes against Scotus that they have no positive and actual real unity. But it seems that Soncinas and Cajetan can reply that the former does not posit an actual unity but a potential one, and Cajetan does not posit a positive unity but a negative one. But in truth it concludes no less against these same than against Scotus. That it concludes against Soncinas is proved: because if the human nature in Peter before the operation of the intellect is this according to all its formal and essential grades, and diverse from the nature of Paul and its grades, then it is impossible that on the part of the thing it can have any unity in them; wherefore neither will they have formal unity in potency, for potency cannot belong to things to which the act is repugnant. But the same second opinion is proved false, because it asserts two impossible things. First, that the nature, as it is prior

p. 45

indiuiduis, habet vnitatem formalem realem: hoc autem impossibile est, quia natura non est prior indiuiduis aliqua prioritate reali, sed solùm per intellectum, considerantem illum, non consideratis indiuiduis, ergo si secundùm hanc prioritatem est vna formaliter, non conuenit ei talis vnitas à parte rei, sed per intellectum.

to the individuals, has real formal unity: but this is impossible, because the nature is not prior to the individuals by any real priority, but only through the intellect, which considers it without considering the individuals; therefore, if according to this priority it is formally one, such unity does not belong to it on the part of the thing, but through the intellect.

Secundum, quod asserit, est naturam non communicare illam vnitatem formalem indiuiduis, quod impossibile probatúr hac ratione. Natura communicatur indiuiduis, secundùm omnes gradus formales, & essentiales, quos habet: sed non potest habere vnitatem formalem actualem, aut potentialem à parte rei, nisi ratione alicuius gradus formalis, atque essentialis: ergo nec potest habere vnitatem, quę indiuiduis non communicetur.

The second thing it asserts is that the nature does not communicate that formal unity to the individuals, which is proved impossible by this argument. The nature is communicated to the individuals according to all the formal and essential grades which it has; but it cannot have actual or potential formal unity on the part of the thing except by reason of some formal and essential grade; therefore neither can it have a unity that is not communicated to the individuals.

48 Quòd verò aduersus Caie. concludat argumentũ nostrũ probatur: Quia solùm posset respõdere, naturam esse diuisam secundùm omnes gradus per differentias indiuiduales, non per essentiales, aut formales: quare cum tali diuisione bene potest esse non distinctio formalis, quæ vocatur vnitas formalis negatiua. Sed hoc non tollit difficultatem nostri argumenti. Nam licèt natura humana non sit diuisa per differentias formales, in Petro, & Ioanne: satis est esse diuisam per indiuiduales: vt verum sit, quòd diuersa est vnitas formalis eius in eis: ergo non potest habere aliquam vnitatem formalem etiam negatiuam, aut non distinctionem eis communem Probatur consequentia: quia cùm formæ, & essentiæ sint diuersæ, necesse est vnitates formales etiam negatiuas, aut non distinctiones esse diuersas: quare sicut non possunt habere aliquid positiuum commune ante operationem intellectus, sic non possunt habere aliquid commune negatiuum: ideo non dabitur vnitas negatiua à parte rei, quam ponit Caietanus.

48 That our argument concludes against Cajetan is proved: because he could only reply that the nature is divided according to all its grades by the individual differences, not by the essential or formal ones; wherefore with such a division there can well be a non-distinction in form, which is called negative formal unity. But this does not remove the difficulty of our argument. For although human nature is not divided by formal differences in Peter and John, it is enough that it is divided by individual ones, so that it is true that its formal unity in them is diverse; therefore it cannot have any formal unity, even negative, or a non-distinction common to them. The consequence is proved: because, since the forms and essences are diverse, the formal unities, even the negative ones, or the non-distinctions, must be diverse: wherefore, just as they cannot have anything positive in common before the operation of the intellect, so they cannot have anything negative in common; therefore the negative unity on the part of the thing which Cajetan posits will not be given.

49 Argumenta aliarum opinionum soluenda sunt, & pro solutione illius testimonij pro quod opinione Scoti adduximus ex Aristotele, in prędicamento ad aliquid, notandum est: quòd licèt vnitas formalis, qua aliquid est in se vnum, sit realiter coniuncta, & realiter eadem cum vnitate numerica, distinguitur tamen ab ea quasi virtualiter, ante operationem intellectus: quia ex diuersa radice prouenit, vt vidimus: & ratione huius distinctionis virtualis, potest intellectus eas distinguere, concipiendo vnitatem formalem, non concepta vnitate numerali, & dum sic eam concipit, dicitur eam abstrahere ab indiuiduis, & facere communem multis, & vniuersalem. Ex quo intelligitur, totum fundamentum vnitatis formalis,

49 The arguments of the other opinions must be solved. And for the solution of that testimony from Aristotle, in the category of relatives, which we adduced for the opinion of Scotus, it should be noted that, although the formal unity by which something is one in itself is really conjoined and really the same with the numerical unity, it is nevertheless distinguished from it as it were virtually before the operation of the intellect, because it comes from a different root, as we have seen; and by reason of this virtual distinction the intellect can distinguish them, conceiving the formal unity without conceiving the numerical unity; and while it conceives it thus, it is said to abstract it from the individuals and to make it common to many and universal. From which it is understood that the whole foundation of the formal unity,

p. 46

specificæ, aut genericę, per quam aliquid est multis commune, & vniuersale, esse vnitatem formalem, qua aliquid est in se vnum formaliter, in quantum virtualiter distinctam ab vnitate numerica, cui à parte rei coniuncta est: ideò talis vnitas formalis, vocari potest vnitas vniuersalis, specifica, aut generica, in fundamento saltem remoto: & fundamentum etiam remotum vniuersalis: sufficiens tamen pro relationibus primi generis, identitatis, similitudinis, & æqualitatis, & in ea fundari intelligit Arist. non in alia.

specific or generic, through which something is common to many and universal, is the formal unity by which something is formally one in itself, inasmuch as it is virtually distinct from the numerical unity, to which on the part of the thing it is conjoined: therefore such formal unity can be called universal, specific or generic unity, at least in its remote foundation; and also the remote foundation of the universal, sufficient, however, for the relations of the first kind, of identity, similarity and equality; and it is in this, not in another, that Aristotle understands them to be founded.

50 Ad argumentum Scoti respondeo singulis gradibus entitatis, correspondere suas vnitates, non tamen distinctas, nisi per intellectum: sicut nec gradus naturæ distinguntur, nisi ab intellectu: & ideo, nec conuenientes naturæ à parte rei, sed solùm per intellectum.

50 To the argument of Scotus I reply that to the single grades of entity there correspond their unities, which are not, however, distinct except through the intellect, just as the grades of the nature are not distinguished except by the intellect; and therefore they do not belong to the nature on the part of the thing either, but only through the intellect.

Ad argumentum Caietani neganda est maior, quòd vnitas numerica, sit carentia diuisionis materialis, aut specifica, carentia diuisionis formalis: Nam carentia negatio est, vnitas verò non dicit solam negationem, sed entitatem etiam pro fundamento: & cùm diuersæ sint entitates specificæ, diuersæque vnitates formales, ante operationem intellectus, etiam si diuisione careant formali, non possunt habere vnitatem formalem.

To the argument of Cajetan the major must be denied, namely that numerical unity is the lack of material division, or specific unity the lack of formal division. For a lack is a negation, whereas unity does not express a negation alone, but also an entity as its foundation; and since the specific entities are diverse, and the formal unities diverse, before the operation of the intellect, even if they lack formal division, they cannot have formal unity.

Et eodem modo respondeo ad confirmationem, antecedens esse falsum, quòd quęcunq; non sint distincta in aliquo, dicantur in eo conuenire: quia nõ distinctio solam negationem dicit: vnum verò, positiuam entitatem cum negatione adiuncta. Argumentum igitur procedit à pura negatione, ad positiuum habens negationem adiunctam, & ideo non est bonum.

And in the same way I reply to the confirmation that the antecedent is false, namely that whatever things are not distinct in something are said to agree in it: because non-distinction expresses a negation alone, whereas one expresses a positive entity with a negation adjoined. The argument therefore proceeds from a pure negation to a positive having a negation adjoined, and therefore it is not good.

Ad argumentum deniquè tertiæ opinionis respondendum est, nomina significare res, mediis cõceptibus, quos de illis formamus: vnde non significant eas, vt sunt à parte rei, sed vt à nobis cognoscuntur: & cùm vniuoca nomina sint communia, significant rem, vt à nobis conceptam, conceptu cõmuni: quare non sequitur ex eorum significatione, dari vnum multis commune à parte rei, sed solùm obiectiuè in intellectu, nec proinde vnitatem formalem inter multa, sed hanc fieri ab intellectu, naturam cognoscente, non cognitis inferioribus: siue positiua illa sit, vel negatiua.

Finally, to the argument of the third opinion it must be replied that names signify things by means of the concepts which we form of them; hence they do not signify them as they are on the part of the thing, but as they are cognized by us; and since univocal names are common, they signify the thing as conceived by us by a common concept: wherefore it does not follow from their signification that there is something one common to many on the part of the thing, but only objectively in the intellect; nor, consequently, a formal unity among many, but that this is made by the intellect cognizing the nature without the inferiors being cognized, whether that unity be positive or negative.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

An vniuersale sit in rebus ante operationem intellectus.

Whether the universal exists in things before the operation of the intellect.

51 CVm vniuersale sit vnum in multis, eodem ferè modo loquuntur authores de illo, & de vnitate, & ideo Scotus

51 Since the universal is one in many, authors speak in almost the same way of it and of unity; and therefore Scotus,

p. 47

qui docuit quæst. præcedenti: vnitati formalem minorem numerali ex se conuenire naturæ, & ideo ante operationem intellectus eam habere, consequenter docet, esse vniuersalem à parte rei. Et hæc est prima opinio circa hanc quæstionem, quam tenuit in 2. d. 3. quæst. 1. & 7. Meta. q. 18. Vbi eam defendit Antonius Andreas, atque etiam Ioannes Monlorius in disputatione quadam de vniuersali cap. 5. & 6. Probatúrque duplici argumento. Primò, quia vniuersalia sunt obiecta scientiarum, & etiam dicuntur ingenerabilia, & incorruptibilia, sed conditiones istæ sunt reales: ergo conueniunt naturis ante operationem intellectus: quare ante illam erunt realiter vniuersales. Probatur minor, Quia scientiæ sunt de naturis realibus, quæ non generantur, neque corrumpuntur, nisi secundùm esse reale, quod habent.

who taught in the preceding question that formal unity less than numerical belongs to the nature of itself, and that it therefore has it before the operation of the intellect, consistently teaches that the universal exists on the part of the thing. And this is the first opinion on this question, which he held in 2, d. 3, q. 1, and Metaph. 7, q. 18, where it is defended by Antonius Andreas, and also by Juan Monllor in a certain disputation on the universal, ch. 5 and 6. And it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because universals are the objects of the sciences, and they are also said to be ingenerable and incorruptible; but these conditions are real; therefore they belong to the natures before the operation of the intellect: wherefore before it they will really be universals. The minor is proved: because the sciences are about real natures, which are neither generated nor corrupted except according to the real being that they have.

52 Secundò, natura humana ex se non est incommunicabilis pluribus: ergo ex se est communicabilis, & ante operationem intellectus communicatur multis singularibus; sed esse vniuersalem idem est, quod esse communicabilem multis, ergo ex se, & ante operationem intellectus erit vniuersalis. Maiorem ita probo, Si natura ex se non est communicabilis multis, ergo de se est incommunicabilis: sed esse incommunicabilem, est esse singularem: ergo ex se erit singularis, quare nullo modo posset fieri vniuersalis: quod est falsum.

52 Second, human nature of itself is not incommunicable to several; therefore of itself it is communicable, and before the operation of the intellect it is communicated to many singulars; but to be universal is the same as to be communicable to many; therefore of itself and before the operation of the intellect it will be universal. The major I prove thus. If the nature of itself is not communicable to many, then of itself it is incommunicable; but to be incommunicable is to be singular; therefore of itself it will be singular, wherefore it could in no way become universal: which is false.

Secunda opinio est D. Thom. 7. Meta. lect. 13. opusculo de ente, & essentia cap. 4 1. p. q. 85. art. 1. & 12. quæst. 29. art. 6. quibus locis asserit naturam ex se, hoc est, ex propria essentia, non esse vniuersalem, nec singularem, sed per conditiones, indiuiduantes fieri singularem, & per intellectum vniuersalem: ideo ante operationem intellectus non dari vniuersale. D. Th. sequuntur Capreol. in 3 art. 3. d. 5. quæst 3. Soncinas 7. Meta. q. 40. Caietanus in opusculo de ente, & essentia, cap. 4. Sotus q. 2. vniuersalium. Durandus in 1. q. 2. prologi, & d. 14. p. 2. Toletus in quæstionibus vniuersalibus. P. Fran. Suarius tomo 1. disp. 6. sectio 5. Et est communis sententia scholæ à nobis tenenda.

The second opinion is that of St. Thomas, Metaph. 7, lect. 13; in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4; 1 p., q. 85, a. 1 and 12, q. 29, a. 6; in which places he asserts that the nature of itself, that is, from its own essence, is neither universal nor singular, but becomes singular through the individuating conditions, and universal through the intellect; and therefore that before the operation of the intellect the universal is not given. St. Thomas is followed by Capreolus in 3, a. 3, d. 5, q. 3; Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 40; Cajetan in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4; Soto, q. 2 on universals; Durandus in 1, q. 2 of the prologue, and d. 14, part 2; Toledo in his questions on universals; Fr. Francisco Suárez, tom. 1, disp. 6, lect. 5. And it is the common opinion of the school, to be held by us.

53 Sed vt eam probemus, notandum est, quòd cùm vniuersale sit vnum aptum prædicari de multis, secũdùm definitionem ab Arist. traditam, duo sunt necessariò requisita vt aliquid sit vniuersale: Primum, quòd sit vnum, non solùm vnitate formali, quia aliquid est in se vnum, sed vnitate formali, qua aliquid est multis commune. Quòd enim prima vnitas formalis requiratur, quæstione præcedenti probatum à nobis est: quia cùm vniuersale communicet suam essentiam singularibus, & per

53 But in order to prove it, it should be noted that, since the universal is one apt to be predicated of many, according to the definition delivered by Aristotle, two things are necessarily required for something to be universal. First, that it be one, not only by the formal unity by which something is one in itself, but by the formal unity by which something is common to many. For that the first formal unity is required was proved by us in the preceding question: because, since the universal communicates its essence to the singulars, and through

p. 48

suam essentiam sit aliquid vnum formaliter in se, necesse est, quòd vniuersale habeat vnitatem formalem, per quam sit vnum formaliter in se: & hanc vnitatem dicimus esse primum fundamentum atque remotum vniuersalis. Sed quòd hæc vnitas nõ sufficit ad rationem vniuersalis, probatur, quia vt etiam quæst. præcedenti diximus, vnitas formalis, qua aliquid est in se vnum, eadem est secundùm rem cum vnitate numerica, & ideo ei semper coniuncta à parte rei, ex quo sequitur esse diuisam in singularibus, ita vt tot sint vnitates formales, quot sunt indiuidua. Non ergo sufficit vt natura dicatur vniuersalis, sed requiritur, quòd ab intellectu consideretur eadem vnitas formalis, non consideratis singularitatibus, per quas diuisa est à parte rei: & ita considerata, vocatur vnitas formalis, per quam natura est vna formaliter multis communis, quod est esse vniuersalem.

its essence is something formally one in itself, it is necessary that the universal have the formal unity through which it is formally one in itself; and this unity we call the first and remote foundation of the universal. But that this unity does not suffice for the ratio of the universal is proved: because, as we also said in the preceding question, the formal unity by which something is one in itself is the same in reality with the numerical unity, and therefore always conjoined with it on the part of the thing; from which it follows that it is divided in the singulars, so that there are as many formal unities as there are individuals. It does not suffice, therefore, for the nature to be called universal; but it is required that the same formal unity be considered by the intellect without considering the singularities by which it is divided on the part of the thing; and so considered it is called the formal unity through which the nature is formally one common to many, which is to be universal.

54 Secundò requiritur, quòd sit apta esse in multis, hęc autem aptitudo secundùm Scotum, & alios, qui sequuntur eius sententiam, realis est in natura, & ante operationem intellectus, sed apud D. Tho. neutrum habet, sed per operationem intellectus ei conuenit. Duas igitur conditiones debet habere natura, vt dicatur apta esse in multis. Prima est, quasi remota, nempe, quòd ex suis principiis realibus multiplicari possit in multis indiuiduis: quod habent omnes naturę materiales, & corruptibiles: si verò in vna tantùm esse possit, ita, vt repugnet omnino habere multa, vt de naturis Angelorum tenent multi, non erit vniuersalis, vt videbimus in capite de specie. Alterum requiritur, tanquam proximum, nempe, quòd non sit determinata per singulares conditiones, sed quasi indifferens: ita vt non magis respiciat vnum singulare, quàm alterum: & cùm à parte rei sit determinata per conditiones singulares, non habet aptitudinem, vt in multis sit: quia singulare cùm sit incommunicabile, non potest communicari multis, necesse est ergo vt indifferens sit, quod per intellectum consideretur sine conditionibus singularibus: & ita considerata, non erit determinata ad aliquod singulare, sed æqualiter poterit determinari ad omnia: & hoc est esse indifferentem, & aptam communicari multis. Itaque aptitudo naturæ præsupponit tria, duo quidem quasi remota. Primum, quod ex suis principiis realibus possit multiplicari: Secundum, quod sit vna vnitate formali, per quam aliquid est in se vnum. Et pręterea, tertium, quasi proximum, quod sit vna vnitate formali, qua aliquid est commune multis. Et præter hæc tria, addit, quod sit indifferens ad multa: & licèt hanc indifferentiam habeat, eo ipso, quòd vna est vnitate vniuersali,

54 Second, it is required that it be apt to be in many. And this aptitude, according to Scotus and the others who follow his opinion, is real in the nature and before the operation of the intellect; but according to St. Thomas the nature has neither, but they belong to it through the operation of the intellect. The nature, then, must have two conditions in order to be said to be apt to be in many. The first is as it were remote, namely, that from its real principles it can be multiplied in many individuals: which all material and corruptible natures have; but if it can be in one only, so that it is altogether impossible for it to have many, as many hold of the natures of the angels, it will not be universal, as we shall see in the chapter on species. The other is required as proximate, namely, that it be not determined by singular conditions but as it were indifferent, so that it does not regard one singular more than another; and since on the part of the thing it is determined by singular conditions, it does not have the aptitude to be in many, because the singular, since it is incommunicable, cannot be communicated to many. It is necessary, therefore, in order that it be indifferent, that it be considered by the intellect without the singular conditions; and so considered it will not be determined to any singular, but will be able to be determined equally to all: and this is to be indifferent and apt to be communicated to many. And so the aptitude of the nature presupposes three things, two as it were remote. First, that it can be multiplied from its real principles; second, that it be one by the formal unity by which something is one in itself; and besides these, a third, as it were proximate, that it be one by the formal unity by which something is common to many. And besides these three it adds that it be indifferent to many; and although it has this indifference by the very fact that it is one by universal unity,

p. 49

tamen priùs hæc vnitas intelligitur in ea, quàm indifferentia, vel aptitudo, sicut dicebamus quæ. 1. priùs intelligi in natura, quòd sit vniuersalis, quàm quòd sit prædicabilis

nevertheless this unity is understood in it before the indifference or aptitude, just as we said in q. 1 that it is understood in the nature that it is universal before it is understood that it is predicable.

Ex tota hac doctrina, colligitur efficax argumentum ad probandã nostram sententiam, quòd non detur vniuersale à parte rei, sed solùm per operationem intellectus, contra Scotum. Vniuersale est vnum in multis, & aptum prædicari de multis sed natura ante operationem intellectus, nec est vna, neque habet aptitudinem prædicandi de multis: ergo non est vniuersalis. Probatur minor. Natura à parte rei, est diuisa per differentias indiuiduales: ita vt alia sit in Petro, & alia in Ioanne: ergo est plures, & non vna Sed si non sit vna, non potest habere aptitudinem prædicandi: quia aptitudo præsupponit vnitatem vt probatum est: ergo nec vna, nec in multis erit, quousque per intellectum abstrahatur à conditionibus, per quas diuidatur & fiat vna.

From this whole doctrine is gathered an efficacious argument for proving our view, that the universal is not given on the part of the thing but only through the operation of the intellect, against Scotus. The universal is one in many and apt to be predicated of many; but the nature before the operation of the intellect is neither one nor has the aptitude of being predicated of many; therefore it is not universal. The minor is proved. The nature on the part of the thing is divided by the individual differences, so that it is one in Peter and another in John; therefore it is many and not one. But if it is not one, it cannot have the aptitude of being predicated, because aptitude presupposes unity, as has been proved; therefore it will be neither one nor in many until it is abstracted by the intellect from the conditions by which it is divided, and becomes one.

Ad primũ argumentum Scoti, concedenda est maior, & minor neganda, quia sicut scientiæ habentur per operationes intellectus, & ante illas non dantur, eadem ratione non dantur obiecta scientiarum, nisi per intellectum abstrahentem naturam, & efficientem illam aliquo modo vniuersalem: & vt sic abstracta, ingenerabilis est, & incorruptibilis, & non vt est in indiuiduis, quæ passim corrumpuntur. Quare falsum est, quod in minori dicitur, naturam habere tales cõditiones à parte rei: neutram enim habet, nisi operatione intellectus præsupposita.

To the first argument of Scotus, the major must be granted and the minor denied: because, just as the sciences are had through operations of the intellect and are not given before them, by the same reasoning the objects of the sciences are not given except through the intellect abstracting the nature and making it in some way universal; and as so abstracted it is ingenerable and incorruptible, and not as it is in the individuals, which are corrupted everywhere. Wherefore what is said in the minor is false, that the nature has such conditions on the part of the thing: for it has neither except on the presupposition of the operation of the intellect.

Ad secundum concesso antecedenti, neganda est consequentia, dicendúmque naturam nec esse ex se proximè communicabilem multis, sed solùm remotè, nec ex se incommunicabilem, vt docuit D. Tho. vbi suprà: sed primum habere per intellectum, secundum à parte rei, per differentias indiuiduales, quibus coniũcta est, ex se autem solùm ei conuenire prædicata essentialia, vt naturæ humanæ rationalitatem, sicque de cæteris.

To the second, granting the antecedent, the consequence must be denied, and it must be said that the nature is of itself neither proximately communicable to many, but only remotely, nor of itself incommunicable, as St. Thomas taught in the place cited above; but that it has the first through the intellect, the second on the part of the thing, through the individual differences with which it is conjoined; while of itself only the essential predicates belong to it, as rationality to human nature, and so of the rest.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Quæst. 5. Per quam operationem intellectus fiat vniuersale — Through which operation of the intellect the universal is made.

Per quam operationem intellectus fiat vniuersale.

[…]

57 VT quęstio intelligatur, explicandus est modus, quo intellectus procedit, dũ intelligit, vt ex eo cognoscamus quonam modo efficiat vniuersale. Notandum est ergo, quòd cùm omnis nostra intellectio incipiat à sensibus, necesse est, vt id quod intelligendum est, priùs percipiatur à visu, vel alio sensu: quod fit per quandam similitudinem sui, quam ad

57 That the question may be understood, the mode must be explained in which the intellect proceeds when it understands, so that from it we may come to know in what way it makes the universal. It should be noted, therefore, that since all our understanding begins from the senses, it is necessary that what is to be understood be first perceived by sight or some other sense: which happens through a certain likeness of itself which, to D

p. 50

oculum mittit, & quæ vocatur species intentionalis eius rei, à qua repræsentatur: Per hanc ergo speciem vnitur obiectum potentiæ visiuæ, & fit visio rei. Virtute huius visionis, producitur alia species eiusdem rei visæ in alio sensu interiori, qui dicitur sensus communis, ex eo, quòd ad ipsum perueniunt species omnium, quę sentiuntur per sensus externos: & ipse discernit inter omnia, cognoscens esse diuersa. Deinde ab hoc sensu, emittitur alia species eiusdem obiecti in alium, qui vocari solet phantasia, & est veluti memoria quædam: non solùm sentiens ea, quæ per alios sensus percipiuntur, sed conseruans species omnium sensibilium: quæ species in ea conseruatæ solent vocari phantasmata.

it sends to the eye, and which is called the intentional species of the thing by which it is represented. Through this species, then, the object is united to the visual power, and the vision of the thing takes place. By virtue of this vision another species of the same thing seen is produced in another, interior sense, which is called the common sense, from the fact that the species of all the things that are sensed by the external senses reach it; and it discerns among them all, cognizing that they are diverse. Then from this sense another species of the same object is emitted into another, which is customarily called the phantasy, and is like a kind of memory: not only sensing the things that are perceived through the other senses, but preserving the species of all sensibles; and the species preserved in it are customarily called phantasms.

58 Notandum est secundò, quòd obiecto iam cognito per sensus vsque ad phantasiam: incipit operatio intellectus: qui duplex est: vnus qui dicitur Agens, & alter Possibilis: inter quos hæc est differentia, quòd intellectus agens non est virtus cognoscitiua, nec aliquid intelligit: possibilis verò est, qui cognoscit. Præterea intellectus agens, adiutus phantasmate, hoc est, specie sensibili conseruata in phantasia, producit aliam speciem eiusdem rei, repræsentatæ per idem phantasma in intellectu cognoscente, non iam sensibilem, & corpoream, sed spiritualem: sicut intellectus agens, à quo producitur: & possibilis, in quo recipitur, spirituales potentiæ sunt. Et agens dicitur ille: quia sua actione speciem producit: iste verò possibilis, quasi passibilis aut passiuus: quia recipit eandem speciem, per quam ei vnitur idem obiectum, quod à sensibus cognitum est: & informatus hac specie, seu similitudine obiecti, quæ intelligibilis dicitur: sicut species per quas cognoscunt sensus, dicuntur sensibiles, ipsum intelligit. Per hanc autem speciem intelligibilem (vt multi asserunt) repræsentatur natura sine conditionibus singularitatis, & ideo eam vocat abstractionem. Quia natura sine conditionibus repræsentata, quasi abstracta ab eis dicitur.

58 It should be noted second that, once the object has been cognized through the senses as far as the phantasy, the operation of the intellect begins. The intellect is twofold: one which is called Agent, and the other Possible; between which there is this difference, that the agent intellect is not a cognitive power, nor does it understand anything, whereas the possible is the one that cognizes. Moreover, the agent intellect, aided by the phantasm, that is, by the sensible species preserved in the phantasy, produces another species of the same thing represented through the same phantasm in the cognizing intellect, no longer sensible and corporeal, but spiritual, just as the agent intellect by which it is produced and the possible intellect in which it is received are spiritual powers. And the former is called agent because by its action it produces the species; the latter possible, as it were passible or passive, because it receives that same species, through which the same object which was cognized by the senses is united to it; and informed by this species, or likeness of the object, which is called intelligible (just as the species through which the senses cognize are called sensible), it understands the object. Through this intelligible species (as many assert) the nature is represented without the conditions of singularity, and therefore they call it abstraction, because the nature represented without the conditions is said to be as it were abstracted from them.

Sed tertiò est notandum, quòd intellectus possibilis duplicem habet operationem: Vnam per quam cognoscit obiectum, vt repræsentatum in specie, sine conditionibus: & hæc propriissimè dicitur abstractio, quia est cognitio naturæ, non cognitis indiuiduis: Alia est operatio intellectus, per quam eadem natura cognita, non cognitis singularibus, iterum cognoscitur eisdem simul cognitis, & ad ea comparatur: & ideo vocatur comparatio: & ecce tres operationes, vna intellectus agentis à quibusdam vocata abstractio, & duæ aliæ intellectus possibilis, vna quæ vocatur abstractio, & alia comparatio,

But it should be noted third that the possible intellect has a twofold operation: one through which it cognizes the object as represented in the species without the conditions; and this is most properly called abstraction, because it is the cognition of the nature without the individuals being cognized. The other is the operation of the intellect through which the same nature, cognized without the singulars being cognized, is cognized again with those same singulars cognized at the same time, and is compared to them; and therefore it is called comparison. And behold three operations: one of the agent intellect, called abstraction by some, and two others of the possible intellect, one which is called abstraction, and the other comparison.

p. 51

Iuxta has igitur tres operationes, sunt tres opiniones diuersæ. Prima, asserit vniuersale fieri per abstractionem intellectus agentis, quam sequitur Caie. in opusc. de ente, & essentia, cap. 4. quæstio. 6. ad finem. Sotus q. 3. vniuersalium Zumel. 1. p. quæst. 13. art. 7. conc. 3 Et probatur testimonio Aristotelis. 3. li. de anima, tex. 18. vbi comparans officium intellectus agentis, cum lumine corporeo, docet, quòd sicut lumen corporeum sua illustratione materiali, facit colores visibiles actu: qui in tenebris solùm erant visibiles in potentia, ita intellectus agens per actionem, qua producit speciem intelligibilem in intellectu possibili: facit naturam actu intelligibilem. Ex quo ita colligunt: Obiectum intellectus possibilis, est vniuersale, sed per intellectum agentem, fit natura actu intelligibilis, dum repræsentatur in specie intelligibili, sine conditionibus: ergo fit actu vniuersalis.

In accordance with these three operations, then, there are three different opinions. The first asserts that the universal is made through the abstraction of the agent intellect. It is followed by Cajetan in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 4, q. 6, toward the end; Soto, q. 3 on universals; Zumel, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, concl. 3. And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, On the Soul 3, text 18, where, comparing the office of the agent intellect with corporeal light, he teaches that just as corporeal light by its material illumination makes colors actually visible, which in the darkness were only potentially visible, so the agent intellect, through the action by which it produces the intelligible species in the possible intellect, makes the nature actually intelligible. From which they gather as follows. The object of the possible intellect is the universal; but through the agent intellect the nature becomes actually intelligible, while it is represented in the intelligible species without the conditions; therefore it becomes actually universal.

Deinde duplici argumento. Primum sumitur ex definitione vniuersalis, quod est vnum in multis, sed natura per abstractionem intellectus agentis, est vna in multis: ergo est vniuersalis. Probatur minor, quia in specie intelligibili repręsentatur, sine conditionibus, ergo vt sic repræsentata est vna, cùm solùm per conditiones sit à parte rei plures: & est etiam in multis, à quibus abstrahitur, ergo vniuersalis.

Then by a twofold argument. The first is taken from the definition of the universal, which is one in many; but the nature through the abstraction of the agent intellect is one in many; therefore it is universal. The minor is proved: because in the intelligible species it is represented without the conditions; therefore, as so represented, it is one, since it is many on the part of the thing only through the conditions; and it is also in the many from which it is abstracted; therefore it is universal.

Secundò, naturam esse vnam vnitate vniuersali, duo dicit, Vnum pro fundamento, nempe vnitatem formalem, qua est in se vna: & aliud quasi pro formali, nempe carentiam diuisionis quam habet à parte rei, per differentias indiuiduales: sed repræsentata in specie intelligibili, est vna formaliter: & caret diuisione, cùm repræsentetur sine conditionibus: ergo est vna vnitate vniuersali: & habet aptitudinem prædicandi de multis, quia repræsentata sine conditionibus, non est determinata ad aliquod indiuiduum, sed ind indifferens ad omnia, ergo est vniuersalis.

Second, for the nature to be one by universal unity expresses two things: one as foundation, namely the formal unity by which it is one in itself; and the other as it were as the formal element, namely the lack of the division which it has on the part of the thing through the individual differences; but represented in the intelligible species it is formally one, and it lacks division, since it is represented without the conditions; therefore it is one by universal unity; and it has the aptitude of being predicated of many, because, represented without the conditions, it is not determined to any individual, but is indifferent to all; therefore it is universal.

Secunda opinio tenet, per abstractionem intellectus agentis, nondum esse naturam vniuersalem, sed requiri abstractionem intellectus possibilis; per quam natura cognoscatur sine conditionibus, & per illam fieri vniuersalem. Hæc est sententia Duran. in 1. d. 2. q. 5. ad 2. & in 2. d. 3. q. 7. nu. 12. & Cardinalis Toleti q. 2. vniuersalium. Vnicum est argumentum huius sententiæ: Natura est vniuersalis à parte rei, ergo vniuersalitas eius non est realis, sed ab intellectu tribui debet: sed intellectus nihil potest tribuere naturæ, nisi eam cognoscat: ergo cum intellectus agens non cognoscat, non potest ei tribuere vniuersalitatem, sed cùm primùm cognoscitur ab intellectu, denominatur vniuersalis.

The second opinion holds that through the abstraction of the agent intellect the nature is not yet universal, but that the abstraction of the possible intellect is required, through which the nature is cognized without the conditions, and that through it it becomes universal. This is the opinion of Durandus in 1, d. 2, q. 5, ad 2, and in 2, d. 3, q. 7, no. 12, and of Cardinal Toledo, q. 2 on universals. There is a single argument for this opinion. The nature is not universal on the part of the thing; therefore its universality is not real, but must be attributed by the intellect; but the intellect can attribute nothing to the nature unless it cognizes it; therefore, since the agent intellect does not cognize, it cannot attribute universality to it; but when it is first cognized by the intellect, it is denominated universal. D ij

p. 52

61 Tertia sententia, neque vnam, neque aliam abstractionẽ sufficere docet, vt natura fiat vniuersalis, sed necessarium esse, vt comparetur ad indiuidua: quod cùm fiat per secundam operationem intellectus possibilis, quæ dicitur comparatio: per hanc fieri vniuersale: hanc sequuntur Soncin. Meta. quæst. 17. concl. 2. & 10. Meta. q. 15. Niphus, Meta. qu. 17 conc. 1. Deca Hispalensis in 1. d. quæ. 1. art. 4 ad 1. Canar. 1. par. quæ 28. art. 1. fol. 2. Probatur primò: Quia intellectus non potest tribuere naturæ denominationem vniuersalis, nisi eam cognoscat vt vniuersalem: Vniuersale dicit respectum ad multa, vt colligitur ex eius definitione, qua dicitur esse vnum in multis: ergo non cognoscitur natura vt vniuersalis, nisi cognoscatur per respectum ad multa, sed non potest cognosci per respectum ad multa, nisi eis cognitis: quia respectu non est cognoscibilis nisi cognito termino. At per abstractionem intellectus agentis nullo modo cognoscitur, & per abstractionem possibilis cognoscitur non cognitis indiuiduis: ergo non cognoscitur vt vniuersalis, nec tribui potest talis denominatio. sed per solam comparationem, per quam cognoscitur in ordine ad multa.

61 The third opinion teaches that neither the one nor the other abstraction suffices for the nature to become universal, but that it is necessary that it be compared to the individuals; and since this is done through the second operation of the possible intellect, which is called comparison, that the universal is made through this. It is followed by Soncinas, Metaph., q. 17, concl. 2, and Metaph. 10, q. 15; Niphus, Metaph., q. 17, concl. 1; Deza of Seville in 1, d., q. 1, a. 4, ad 1; Canar., 1 part, q. 28, a. 1, fol. 2. It is proved first: because the intellect cannot attribute to the nature the denomination of universal unless it cognizes it as universal. The universal expresses a respect to many, as is gathered from its definition, in which it is said to be one in many; therefore the nature is not cognized as universal unless it is cognized through its respect to many; but it cannot be cognized through its respect to many unless they are cognized, because a respect is not cognizable unless its term is cognized. But through the abstraction of the agent intellect it is in no way cognized, and through the abstraction of the possible intellect it is cognized without the individuals being cognized; therefore it is not cognized as universal, nor can such a denomination be attributed to it, except through comparison alone, through which it is cognized in order to many.

Secundò vniuersalitas est relatio vnius ad multa, non realis, cùm non conueniat naturæ à parte rei, ergo rationis: sed relatio rationis non potest fieri, nisi per notitiam comparatiuam, ergo solùm per hanc fit vniuersale Probatur minor, quia relatio est comparatio inter duo extrema: ergo non potest fieri, nisi ab intellectu vtrumque cognoscente, & comparante, solùm ergo fit vniuersalis per comparationem.

Second, universality is a relation of one to many, not real, since it does not belong to the nature on the part of the thing; therefore of reason; but a relation of reason cannot be made except through comparative cognition; therefore the universal is made through this alone. The minor is proved: because a relation is a comparison between two extremes; therefore it cannot be made except by the intellect cognizing and comparing both; therefore it becomes universal through comparison alone.

62 Præter has tres opiniones diuersas, inuenio quartam, per quam moderni quidam videntur ad concordiam reducere secundam & tertiam, hac distinctione. Vniuersale duobus modis sumi potest. Primò, per modum absoluti, non dicentis respectũ ad alterum, sed potentis fundare talem respectum, vt album, aut quantum: quæ absoluta sunt, & possunt fundare relationẽ similitudinis, aut æqualitatis: Alio modo, tanquam relatiuum: vtroque enim modo putant intelligi posse vniuersalitatem, nempe, vt formam relatiuam, & etiam vt absolutam, quam tamen consequitur quidam respectus, per quem explicatur: nam vnitas, qua aliquid est commune, & aptitudo prædicandi de multis, formæ absolutæ sunt, sicut vnitas numerica & aptitudo ad ridendum, quas tamẽ explicamus per respectum ad actũ ridendi, & ad obiectum. Idque declarant exemplo vniuersalis Platonici, separati à singularibus: quod verè esset substantia, cùm per se existeret, & ideo vniuersalitas eius forma absoluta, quia substantia res absoluta est, non dicens respectum

62 Besides these three different opinions, I find a fourth, through which certain moderns seem to bring the second and third into agreement, by this distinction. The universal can be taken in two ways. First, after the manner of an absolute, not expressing a respect to another but able to found such a respect, as white or quantity, which are absolute and can found a relation of similarity or equality. In another way, as a relative. For they think that universality can be understood in both ways, namely as a relative form, and also as an absolute one, upon which, however, there follows a certain respect through which it is explained: for the unity by which something is common, and the aptitude of being predicated of many, are absolute forms, just as numerical unity and the aptitude for laughing, which we nevertheless explain through a respect to the act of laughing and to the object. And they illustrate this by the example of the Platonic universal, separated from singulars: which would truly be a substance, since it would exist per se, and therefore its universality would be an absolute form, because substance is an absolute thing, not expressing a respect

p. 53

essentialem ad alterum, & tamen explicaretur à nobis per respectum ad multa, à quibus participaretur: ergo etiam sumi potest vniuersale factum ab intellectu per modum absoluti: Alio modo sumitur tanquam relatiuum, essentialiter respiciens indiuidua. Vniuersale igitur primo modo acceptum, dicunt fieri per primam cognitionem intellectus possibilis, quia habet vnitatem cum aptitudine respiciendi multa, à quibus abstractum est. Si verò accipiatur secundo modo, non fit nisi per comparationem: quia relatiuum non potest cognosci, nisi per comparationem ad suum terminum: & ideo nec vniuersale, vt relatiuum, nisi per comparationem ad multa. Et secundam opinionem, intelligendam esse affirmant de vniuersali, vt absoluto: & ita intellectam esse veram. Tertiam verò, de vniuersali, vt relatiuo.

essential to another, and yet it would be explained by us through a respect to the many by which it would be participated; therefore the universal made by the intellect can also be taken after the manner of an absolute. In another way it is taken as a relative, essentially regarding the individuals. The universal taken in the first way, then, they say is made through the first cognition of the possible intellect, because it has unity with the aptitude of regarding the many from which it has been abstracted. But if it is taken in the second way, it is not made except through comparison: because a relative cannot be cognized except through comparison to its term; and therefore neither can the universal as a relative, except through comparison to the many. And they affirm that the second opinion is to be understood of the universal as absolute, and that so understood it is true; but the third, of the universal as relative.

63 Vt nostram sententiam proponamus, quædam notanda sunt. Primum vniuersale nomen concretum esse, habens materiale significatum, quod est natura, & formale, quod est vniuersalitas, à qua denominatur. Concretum verò duplex est, absolutum, & relatiuum, sicut forma denominans, est etiam absoluta, aut relatiua. Cõcretum absolutum est album: relatiuum verò, simile, vt pater. Hæc est autem differentia inter vnum, & alterum, quòd concretum absolutum, pro materiali significato, solùm habet nudum subiectum, vt album nudum corpus. Concretum verò relatiuum non nudum subiectum, sed aliquid aliud ratione cuius efficitur fundamentum proximum relationis: vt simile præter album, habere debet aliquam vnitatem, aut commensurationem cum alio, ratione cuius sit capax relationis, vnitatem quidem in albedine, & commensurationem in eodem gradu eius. Nam vt aliqua dicantur propriè similia, conuenire debent in albedine, atque etiam in gradu eius, ita vt in vtroque sit, vt tria, vel vt quatuor.

63 In order to propose our view, certain things must be noted. First, that universal is a concrete name, having a material significate, which is the nature, and a formal one, which is universality, from which it is denominated. Now a concrete is twofold, absolute and relative, just as the denominating form is also absolute or relative. An absolute concrete is white; a relative one, similar, or father. And this is the difference between the one and the other, that the absolute concrete has for its material significate only the bare subject, as white the bare body. But the relative concrete has not the bare subject, but something else by reason of which it is made the proximate foundation of the relation: as similar, besides white, must have some unity or commensuration with another, by reason of which it is capable of the relation, namely unity in whiteness and commensuration in the same grade of it. For in order that some things may properly be called similar, they must agree in whiteness, and also in its grade, so that it is in both as three, or as four.

Secundò, notandum est, tria esse fundamenta relationis, Remotissimum, Remotum, & Proximum: vt in similitudine, Fundamentum remotissimum est corpus: remotum est album: proximum verò album habens vnitatem, & commensurationem alio. Vocatur autem fundamentum remotissimum, & remotum, quia ea non sequitur relatio: nam corpus nisi habeat albedinem, aut aliam qualitatem, non dicetur simile: neque etiam, si habeat albedinem, quousque habeat vnitatem, & cõmensurationem cum alio. Tunc autem dicetur fundamentum proximũ, quia eo posito, statim ac necessariò sequitur relatio Ita ergo intelligendum est de vniuersali, si sit relatiuum. Erit enim fundamentum remotum relationis vniuersalitatis, natura à

Second, it should be noted that there are three foundations of a relation: the Most Remote, the Remote, and the Proximate; as in similarity, the most remote foundation is the body; the remote is the white; but the proximate is the white having unity and commensuration with another. And the foundation is called most remote and remote because the relation does not follow upon them: for the body, unless it has whiteness or some other quality, will not be called similar; nor even if it has whiteness, until it has unity and commensuration with another. But then it will be called the proximate foundation, because, once it is posited, the relation follows at once and necessarily. So, then, must it be understood of the universal, if it is a relative. For the most remote foundation of the relation of universality will be the nature on D iij

p. 54

parte rei per vnitatem formalem, qua est vna formaliter in se. Fundamentum verò remotum, dum repræsentatur in specie intelligibili sine conditionibus, aut dum cognoscitur per primam cognitionem intellectus sine illis: si non sequatur statim relatio vniuersalitatis, à qua denominetur. Et tandem erit fundamentum proximum dum comparatur ad inferiora: quia statim sequitur relatio vniuersalitatis ad illa.

the part of the thing, through the formal unity by which it is formally one in itself. The remote foundation, however, is the nature while it is represented in the intelligible species without the conditions, or while it is cognized without them through the first cognition of the intellect, if the relation of universality, from which it is denominated, does not follow at once. And finally it will be the proximate foundation while it is compared to the inferiors, because the relation of universality to them follows at once.

His suppositis, nostra sententia his concl. continetur. Prima: Vniuersale non esse nomen absolutum, sed relatiuum, hæc est aduersus vlt. sententiam: probatur duplici argumento. Primò: Nomen concretum est absolutum, si forma per ipsum significata fuerit absoluta, & relatiuum, si fuerit relatiua: sed forma vniuersalitatis non est absoluta, sed relatiua, ergo nomen vniuersale non erit absolutum, sed relatiuum. Probatur minor ex definitione vniuersalis: Vnum in multis, & aptum prædicari de multis. In qua, per relationem ad multa explicatur vniuersale: nec solùm explicatur, sed vniuersalitas relatio est: non forma absoluta, vt vltima opinio asserit: quod sic probo: Vniuersalitas non est forma conueniens naturæ ex se, aut essentialiter, neque à parte rei, sed per intellectum, vt concedit eadem opinio: ergo non est forma substantialis, sed accidentalis, non est accidens reale, sed rationis: sed omne accidens rationis, quod intellectus attribuit rebus, est relatio rationis: non enim attribuit eis accidens rationis absolutum, per modum qualitatis, aut quantitatis, aut alterius prædicamenti, habens fundamentum in eisdem rebus à se intellectis, vt probabitur: ergo vniuersalitas est relatio rationis, & non forma absoluta. Secundò: Non dicitur natura vniuersalis, ex eo solùm, quòd in se est vna, aut communis, sed quia est vna multorum, multisque communis, aut vna, in qua multa conueniunt: vt Porphyrius docuit, c. de specie, dicens: Participatione speciei plures homines sunt vnus homo. Ergo per vniuersalitatem, essentialiter ordinatur ad inferiora, quorum est vna natura: & ideo vniuersalitas, relatio est, & non forma absoluta: & vniuersale nomen relatiuum, non absolutum Quod intelligens Porphyr. docuit, Nomina prædicabilia (quæ sunt quædam vniuersalia) definienda esse per sua inferiora, vt genus, quod sit prædicabile de pluribus differentibus specie, sicque de reliquis.

These things being supposed, our view is contained in these conclusions. First: The universal is not an absolute name but a relative one. This is against the last opinion, and it is proved by a twofold argument. First: A concrete name is absolute if the form signified by it is absolute, and relative if it is relative; but the form of universality is not absolute but relative; therefore the name universal will not be absolute but relative. The minor is proved from the definition of the universal: One in many, and apt to be predicated of many. In which the universal is explained through a relation to many; and not only is it explained so, but universality is a relation, not an absolute form, as the last opinion asserts: which I prove thus. Universality is not a form belonging to the nature of itself or essentially, nor on the part of the thing, but through the intellect, as the same opinion grants; therefore it is not a substantial form but an accidental one; it is not a real accident, but one of reason; but every accident of reason which the intellect attributes to things is a relation of reason: for it does not attribute to them an absolute accident of reason after the manner of quality, or quantity, or of another category, having its foundation in those same things understood by it, as will be proved; therefore universality is a relation of reason and not an absolute form. Second: The nature is not called universal solely from the fact that it is one or common in itself, but because it is one of many and common to many, or one in which many agree: as Porphyry taught in the chapter on species, saying: By participation in the species many men are one man. Therefore through universality it is essentially ordered to the inferiors, of which it is the one nature; and therefore universality is a relation and not an absolute form, and universal is a relative name, not an absolute one. Understanding which, Porphyry taught that the predicable names (which are certain universals) are to be defined through their inferiors, as genus, that it is predicable of several things differing in species, and so of the rest.

65 Secunda conclusio: Per operationem intellectus agentis solùm datur vniuersale pro fundamento remoto, seu in potentia remota: non pro fundamento proximo, neque actu, & formaliter vniuersale. Hæc sequitur ex præcedenti, atque ex doctrina annotata, & probatur hoc argumento: Vniuersale

65 Second conclusion: Through the operation of the agent intellect the universal is given only as in its remote foundation, or in remote potency; not as in its proximate foundation, nor actually and formally universal. This follows from the preceding and from the doctrine noted, and it is proved by this argument. The universal

p. 55

est relatiuum, ergo non dicitur natura actu, & formaliter vniuersalis, nisi ab vniuersalitate, quæ est relatio, denominetur: sed per operationem intellectus agentis, solùm habet repræsentari in specie intelligibili, non repræsentatis singularibus: ergo nec illa respicit, nec denominari potest ab vniuersalitate, quæ est respectus ad illa: & hoc est non esse actu, & formaliter vniuersalem. Solùm ergo potest esse vniuersalis in potentia, aut in fundamento, non proximo: quia proximum fundamentum statim sequitur relatio, & tamen naturam sic repræsentatam, non sequitur relatio ad indiuidua, quousque intelligatur in ordine ad illa: sed in potentia, & fundamento remoto, quamuis minùs remoto, ac dum est extra causas.

is a relative; therefore the nature is not called actually and formally universal unless it is denominated from universality, which is a relation; but through the operation of the agent intellect it only has being represented in the intelligible species, the singulars not being represented; therefore it neither regards them nor can it be denominated from universality, which is a respect to them: and this is not to be actually and formally universal. Therefore it can only be universal in potency, or in its foundation, not the proximate one, because the relation follows at once upon the proximate foundation, and yet the relation to the individuals does not follow upon the nature so represented until it is understood in order to them; but in potency and in its remote foundation, although less remote than while it is outside its causes.

66 Tertia conclusio: Vniuersale actu, & formaliter, aut in potentia proxima, non fit per primam cognitionem intellectus possibilis, quæ vocatur abstractio. Hæc est aduersus vltimam sententiam. Et probatur primò: Nihil denominatur actu & formaliter tale, nisi à forma propria: sed propria forma vniuersalis est vniuersalitas: quæ est relatio rationis ad indiuidua: ergo non denominatur natura actu, & formaliter vniuersalis, nisi à relatione rationis ad indiuidua: naturam autem cognitam per primam operationem intellectus, non consequitur talis relatio rationis: ergo non est per illam actu, & formaliter vniuersalis. Probatur minor: Per illam cognitionem non cognoscitur in ordine ad indiuidua: immo neque cognoscuntur indiuidua: ergo neque cognoscitur relatio rationis naturæ ad illa: sed relatio rationis non habet aliud esse quàm actu cognosci: ergo si non cognoscitur per illam cognitionem, non est, nec denominat naturam actu, & formaliter vniuersalem.

66 Third conclusion: The universal actually and formally, or in proximate potency, is not made through the first cognition of the possible intellect, which is called abstraction. This is against the last opinion. And it is proved first: Nothing is denominated actually and formally such except from its proper form; but the proper form of the universal is universality, which is a relation of reason to the individuals; therefore the nature is not denominated actually and formally universal except from a relation of reason to the individuals; but no such relation of reason follows upon the nature cognized through the first operation of the intellect; therefore through it it is not actually and formally universal. The minor is proved: Through that cognition it is not cognized in order to the individuals; indeed, the individuals are not even cognized; therefore neither is the relation of reason of the nature to them cognized; but a relation of reason has no other being than to be actually cognized; therefore, if it is not cognized through that cognition, it does not exist, nor does it denominate the nature actually and formally universal.

Secundò, naturam per primam cognitionem non habere aliud, quàm cognosci, vt repræsentatam in specie intelligibili sine conditionibus: ergo solùm consequitur per illam nouam denominationem realem extrinsecam, cognitæ sine conditionibus: quam certum est non esse denominationem vniuersalis: nam hæc, nec realis est, nec solùm denominatio extrinseca, sed rationis, & habens modum, & similitudinem formæ inhærentis, sicut denominatio prædicati, aut subiecti: solùm ergo erit natura per talem cognitionem vniuersalis in potentia, non proxima, sed remota: eodem modo ac per operationem intellectus agentis iam explicato.

Second, the nature through the first cognition has nothing other than to be cognized as represented in the intelligible species without the conditions; therefore only a new real extrinsic denomination follows upon it through that cognition, that of being cognized without the conditions: which it is certain is not the denomination of the universal; for this is neither real nor merely an extrinsic denomination, but one of reason, having the mode and likeness of an inherent form, like the denomination of predicate or subject. Therefore through such a cognition the nature will only be universal in potency, not proximate but remote, in the same way as through the operation of the agent intellect already explained.

67 Vltima cõclusio: Natura fit vniuersalis, nõ solùm in potentia proxima, sed actu, & formaliter, per cognitionem intellectus,

67 Last conclusion: The nature becomes universal, not only in proximate potency but actually and formally, through the cognition of the intellect D iiij

p. 56

quæ dicitur comparatio. Hæc probatur primò, ex tribus præcedentibus: quia si non sit per operationem intellectus agentis, nec per primam cognitionem intellectus possibilis, non restat alia operatio per quam fieri possit, præter comparationem.

which is called comparison. This is proved first from the three preceding: because, if it is not made through the operation of the agent intellect, nor through the first cognition of the possible intellect, there remains no other operation through which it can be made besides comparison.

Sed probatur secundò quòd per eam fiat: quia vniuersalitas est relatio rationis naturæ ad indiuidua: & relatio est comparatio duorum extremorum: ergo relatio rationis naturæ ad indiuidua, est comparatio naturæ ad illa: quare fiet per comparationem vniuersalitas, & vniuersale formaliter.

But it is proved second that it is made through it: because universality is a relation of reason of the nature to the individuals, and a relation is a comparison of two extremes; therefore the relation of reason of the nature to the individuals is a comparison of the nature to them: wherefore universality, and the universal formally, will be made through comparison.

68 Sed, vt cõclusiones istæ meliùs intelligantur, & ex eis cognoscamus aliquo modo fieri vniuersalem, per tres illas operationes intellectus agentis, & possibilis, notanda est illa distinctio vniuersalis, satis manifesta in schola Dialecticorum: Vniuersale duplex est, Logicum & Metaphysicum. Vniuersale Metaphysicum, est natura realis in communi sumpta, hoc est sine conditionibus indiuiduantibus, & non vt denominata à secunda intentione, aut relatione vniuersalitatis. Et vocatur vniuersale Metaphysicum: quia solùm sumitur secundùm essentiam realem, quasi abstractam à materialibus conditionibus, qui est proprius modus, secundùm quem res considerantur in Metaphysica: & vocari etiam potest Vniuersale fundamentaliter, atque etiam Vniuersale in potentia, saltem remota, vt explicatum est. Aliud est Vniuersale Logicum, nempe natura denominata à secunda intentione, aut relatione vniuersalitatis, quæ etiam dicitur Vniuersale in potentia proxima, actu & formaliter: quia dum actu denominatur natura à relatione, proximè dicitur eandem relationem fundare: & vocatur vniuersale Logicum, quia secunda intentio, aut relatio vniuersalitatis, propriè pertinet ad considerationem Logicam. Hac distinctione supposita dicimus, vniuersale Metaphysicum fieri per operationem intellectus agentis, cùm repræsentetur natura in specie intelligibili per eam producta, sine conditionibus: quod est esse vniuersale Metaphysicum. Per primam verò cognitionem intellectus possibilis, fit idem vniuersale Metaphysicum, vel potiùs iam factum per intellectum agentem cognoscitur: sed vniuersale Logicum, fit per solam comparationem.

68 But in order that these conclusions may be better understood, and that from them we may come to know how the universal is in some way made through those three operations of the agent and the possible intellect, that distinction of the universal, sufficiently well known in the school of the Dialecticians, should be noted. The universal is twofold, Logical and Metaphysical. The Metaphysical universal is the real nature taken in common, that is, without the individuating conditions, and not as denominated by second intention or by the relation of universality. And it is called the Metaphysical universal because it is taken only according to its real essence, as it were abstracted from material conditions, which is the proper mode according to which things are considered in Metaphysics; and it can also be called the universal fundamentally, and also the universal in potency, at least remote, as has been explained. The other is the Logical universal, namely the nature denominated by second intention or by the relation of universality, which is also called the universal in proximate potency, actually and formally; because while the nature is actually denominated by the relation, it is said proximately to found that same relation; and it is called the Logical universal because second intention, or the relation of universality, properly pertains to logical consideration. This distinction supposed, we say that the Metaphysical universal is made through the operation of the agent intellect, since the nature is represented without the conditions in the intelligible species produced by it: which is to be the Metaphysical universal. But through the first cognition of the possible intellect the same Metaphysical universal is made, or rather, already made by the agent intellect, it is cognized; but the Logical universal is made through comparison alone.

69 Ad argumenta aliarũ opinionum respondendum est, & ad testimonium Aristo. pro prima opinione duobus modus. Primò, sensum eius esse: quòd lumen facit colores actu visibiles: non quia ipsi actu visibiles non essent in tenebris: sed quia videri non poterant per medium obscurum: illud verò

69 The arguments of the other opinions must be answered, and the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion in two ways. First, that its sense is that light makes colors actually visible not because they were not actually visible in the darkness, but because they could not be seen through an obscure medium; but that light, illuminating

p. 57

illuminans, facit, vt actu videantur. Vel secundò, respondeo: concedendo quòd lumen faciat colores actu visibiles, cùm in tenebris non essent, nisi visibiles in potentia: & ita intellectus agens, quasi lumen quoddam spirituale facit naturam actu intelligibilem: ex quo non sequitur eam facere actu vniuersalem: quia vt sit actu intelligibilis, sufficit esse vniuersalem in potentia quod habet, dum per speciem intelligibilem repræsentatur sine conditionibus, &c.

it, makes them actually seen. Or second, I reply by granting that light makes colors actually visible, since in the darkness they were only potentially visible; and so the agent intellect, as a kind of spiritual light, makes the nature actually intelligible: from which it does not follow that it makes it actually universal, because for it to be actually intelligible it suffices that it be universal in potency, which it has while it is represented through the intelligible species without the conditions, etc.

Ad primum argumentum eiusdem sententiæ, concessa maiori, distinguẽda est minor: nam duobus modis natura est vna. Primò, vnitate negatiua, & hanc habet repræsentata in specie intelligibi: quia sine conditionibus indiuiduantibus repræsentatur: sed per hanc vnitatem solum est vniuersale Metaphysicum, aut in potentia. Alio modo est vna, positiuè, quod non habet, nisi dum comparatur ad indiuidua: & quia hæc requiritur, vt sit actu, & formaliter vniuersalis, non est vniuersalis hoc modo, nisi per comparationem.

To the first argument of the same opinion, granting the major, the minor must be distinguished: for the nature is one in two ways. First, by negative unity, and this it has as represented in the intelligible species, because it is represented without the individuating conditions; but through this unity it is only the Metaphysical universal, or the universal in potency. In another way it is one positively, which it does not have except while it is compared to the individuals; and because this is required for it to be actually and formally universal, it is not universal in this way except through comparison.

Ad secundum respondetur, eadem distinctione, quia natura repræsentata in specie intelligibili, habet vnitatem negatiuam vniuersalis Metaphysici, & in potentia, non vniuersalis Logici, nisi per comparationem.

To the second the reply is by the same distinction: because the nature represented in the intelligible species has the negative unity of the Metaphysical universal, and in potency, not that of the Logical universal, except through comparison.

Ad argumentum secundæ opinionis concedo, quòd natura non est vniuersalis à parte rei, sed fit vniuersalis per cognitionem intellectus: nego tamen, quòd per primam cognitionem intellectus tribuatur ei forma vniuersalitatis: sed solùm ei tribuitur per comparationem.

To the argument of the second opinion, I grant that the nature is not universal on the part of the thing, but becomes universal through the cognition of the intellect; I deny, however, that through the first cognition of the intellect the form of universality is attributed to it: rather, it is attributed to it only through comparison.

Ad tertiam opinionem negandũ est, quod vniuersale possit distingui in absolutũ, & relatiuũ: quia ex propria natura, & essentia relatiuum est, vt probauimus. Falsum igitur est, quòd detur vniuersale absolutum, & non minùs falsum, quòd hoc vniuersale absolutũ, fiat per primam cognitionem intellectus.

To the third opinion it must be denied that the universal can be divided into absolute and relative, because by its proper nature and essence it is relative, as we have proved. It is false, therefore, that an absolute universal is given, and no less false that this absolute universal is made through the first cognition of the intellect.

QUESTION VI

Vtrum Vniuersale Logicum fiat per simplicem comparationem naturæ cum indiuiduis, vel non nisi per compositam quæ vocatur Actualis prædicatio.

Whether the Logical universal is made through a simple comparison of the nature with the individuals, or only through the composite comparison which is called actual predication. 70

70 Vt titulus quæstionis explicetur, notandum est, quòd ab omnibus ferè ponitur intellectus duplex comparatio, vna Simplex, alia Composita.

That the title of the question may be explained, it should be noted that almost all posit a twofold comparison of the intellect, one Simple, the other Composite.

Simplex comparatio est, per quam intellectus vnum in altero, vel in ordine ad alterum cognoscit sine compositione, vt dum simplici cognitione cognoscimus patrem in ordine ad

Simple comparison is that through which the intellect cognizes one thing in another, or in order to another, without composition: as when by a simple cognition we cognize a father in order to

p. 58

filium, non affirmando, quòd habeat filium, vel albedinem in pariete, nõ affirmando, quòd in ea sit Alia est comparatio, per quam cognoscit intellectus duo extrema, & vnum attribuit alteri, affirmando quòd in eo sit: & ideo comparatio hæc vocatur actualis prædicatio. Quærimus ergo, An supposito quod vniuersale fit per comparationem, vt in quæstione præcedenti probauimus, fiat per simplicem, vel per compositam Et sunt duæ opiniones, Prima non admittit comparationem simplicem, sed solùm compositam, & per eam asserit fieri vniuersale: & cùm comparatio hæc sit actualis prædicatio vnius de altero, per actualem prædicationem fieri docet, & ante illam non dari vniuersale actu, & formaliter, sed actualem prædicationem esse vniuersalitatem, à qua natura denominatur vniuersalis: & ita non admittit aptitudinem, nec potentiam prædicandi in natura, sed idem esse, quòd vniuersalis sit & quòd sit actuale prædicatum. Hanc opinionem sequuntur quidam moderni, & eam probant hoc argumento.

the son, without affirming that he has a son; or whiteness in a wall, without affirming that it is in it. The other is the comparison through which the intellect cognizes two extremes and attributes one to the other, affirming that it is in it; and therefore this comparison is called actual predication. We ask, therefore, whether, supposing that the universal is made through comparison, as we proved in the preceding question, it is made through simple or through composite comparison. And there are two opinions. The first does not admit simple comparison, but only composite, and asserts that the universal is made through it; and since this comparison is the actual predication of one thing of another, it teaches that it is made through actual predication, and that before it the universal is not given actually and formally, but that actual predication is the universality from which the nature is denominated universal; and so it does not admit an aptitude or potency of being predicated in the nature, but holds that it is the same for it to be universal and for it to be an actual predicate. This opinion is followed by certain moderns, and they prove it by this argument.

71 Non potest intellectus comparare naturam ad indiuidua, nisi cognoscat in eis esse: sed non potest cognoscere, quòd in eis sit, nisi iudicãdo, quòd eis cõueniat. Iudicare autem quòd in eis sit, & eis cõueniat, est prędicare eam de indiuiduis: ergo non datur simplex comparatio naturæ ad indiuidua, sed solùm composita, quæ est actualis prædicatio: quare si verum est vniuersale fieri per comparationem, necessariò sequitur, quòd fiat per actualem prædicationem, ita vt ante illam non detur.

71 The intellect cannot compare the nature to the individuals unless it cognizes that it is in them; but it cannot cognize that it is in them except by judging that it belongs to them. But to judge that it is in them and belongs to them is to predicate it of the individuals; therefore there is no simple comparison of the nature to the individuals, but only composite, which is actual predication: wherefore, if it is true that the universal is made through comparison, it necessarily follows that it is made through actual predication, so that it is not given before it.

72 Hæc opinio in primis est contra Arist. & D. Th. quod vnico testimonio vtriusque probatur, Arist. enim agens de vniuersali, 1. lib. de interpretatione, cap. 5 definit illud his verbis: Dico autem vniuersale, quod de pluribus aptum est prædicari. Ex quibus euidenter colligitur naturam esse vniuersalem, per aptitudinem prædicandi de indiuiduis, sed aptitudo prædicandi cùm sit potentia, est prior, quàm actualis prædicatio, quæ est actus eiusdem potentiæ: ergo priùs est natura vniuersalis, quã actu prædicetur, ex mente Arist. Quare non fit vniuersalis per comparationem compositam, quæ est actualis prædicatio, sed per aliam comparationem priorem, quæ vocatur simplex.

72 This opinion is, in the first place, against Aristotle and St. Thomas, which is proved by a single testimony of each. For Aristotle, treating of the universal in On Interpretation 1, ch. 5, defines it in these words: And I call universal that which is apt to be predicated of several. From which it is evidently gathered that the nature is universal through the aptitude of being predicated of the individuals; but the aptitude of being predicated, since it is a potency, is prior to actual predication, which is the act of that same potency; therefore the nature is universal before it is actually predicated, according to the mind of Aristotle. Wherefore it does not become universal through composite comparison, which is actual predication, but through another, prior comparison, which is called simple.

Et D. Tho. in eodem loco, declarans eandem definitionem Arist. ait: Bene definisse vniuersale per aptitudinem prædicandi & non per actualem prædicationem: quia aliqua sunt naturæ, vt Sol, & Luna, quæ non prædicantur actu de multis, cum non habeant nisi vnicum indiuiduum, & tamen sunt verè vniuersales per aptitudinem, & potentiam prædicandi de multis. Ponit ergo D. Tho. aptitudinem prædicandi in natura vniuersali, & per illam asserit

And St. Thomas, in the same place, explaining the same definition of Aristotle, says: He defined the universal well through the aptitude of being predicated and not through actual predication, because there are some natures, such as the Sun and the Moon, which are not actually predicated of many, since they have only one individual, and yet they are truly universal through the aptitude and potency of being predicated of many. St. Thomas therefore posits the aptitude of being predicated in the universal nature, and asserts that through it

p. 59

esse vniuersalem cum Arist. Ergo opinio quæ aptitudinem tollit, & non nisi per actualem prædicationem affirmat fieri vniuersale, expressè est contra Arist. & D. Tho.

it is universal, with Aristotle. Therefore the opinion which takes away the aptitude, and affirms that the universal is made only through actual predication, is expressly against Aristotle and St. Thomas.

Deinde est contra rationem, quod sic probo: Si natura est vniuersalis, per actualem prædicationem, sequitur non esse vniuersalem, nisi simul prædicetur de multis: ita vt dicamus Petrum & Ioannem esse homines, nõ hominem, & equum esse animalia, & non, dum de singulis prædicatur: quare neque erit prædicatio vniuersalis: dum species prædicatur de indiuiduo, aut genus de specie: vt in his prædicationibus, Petrus est homo, & homo est animal: consequens autem falsum est, ergo etiam antecedens. Quòd sit vniuersalis natura per actualem prædicationem, probatur consequentia: quia vniuersalitas est actualis prædicatio: sed vniuersalitas est respectus naturæ ad multa, ergo non est natura vniuersalis, nisi actu dum prædicatur de multis, & non de vno tantùm. Quòd verò consequens sit falsum, probo, quia hæc est prædicatio generis, Homo est animal: ergo est prædicatio superioris, quia genus superius est specie: sed prædicatum superius est vniuersale, ergo est prædicatio vniuersalis, & tamen de solo vno: ergo vniuersalis erit natura, dum de vno inferiori prædicatur, quia prædicabilis est de multis: quare non per actualem prædicationem, sed per prædicabilitatem, vt omnes asserunt.

Next, it is against reason, which I prove thus. If the nature is universal through actual predication, it follows that it is not universal unless it is predicated of many at once, so that we say that Peter and John are men, not man, and that man and horse are animals; and not while it is predicated of single ones: wherefore neither will there be a universal predication when the species is predicated of the individual, or the genus of the species, as in these predications: Peter is a man, and Man is an animal; but the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent also. That the nature is universal through actual predication, the consequence is proved: because universality is actual predication; but universality is the respect of the nature to many; therefore the nature is not universal except actually, while it is predicated of many, and not of one only. But that the consequent is false I prove: because this is a predication of the genus, Man is an animal; therefore it is a predication of a superior, because the genus is superior to the species; but a superior predicate is universal; therefore it is a universal predication, and yet of one alone; therefore the nature will be universal while it is predicated of one inferior, because it is predicable of many: wherefore not through actual predication, but through predicability, as all assert.

73 Communis ergo sententia Arist. D.
