Th. & omnium vera est, & tenenda, Quòd natura priùs sit vniuersalis, quàm actu prædicetur, per potentiam prædicandi de multis: & quòd fiat vniuersalis per comparationem simplicem intellectus: per quam cognoscitur in ordine ad indiuidua, & non per compositam, quæ est actualis prædicatio. Quam hoc agumento probo: Intellectus potest cognoscere vnum in altero, aut in ordine ad alterum, sine affirmatione, & negatione, & sine actuali prædicatione: ergo potest cognoscere naturam in ordine ad indiuidua, per simplicem comparationem, sine eo, quòd eam actu prædicet de illis: sed cognita in ordine ad indiuidua, cognoscitur vt vniuersalis: ergo per comparationem simplicem fit vniuersalis, non per compositam. Antecedens probatur duobus modus: primò in intellectu, deinde in sensibus. In intellectu quidem: quia per simplicem cognitionem cognoscimus patrem, ordinatum ad filium, & duos parietes similes in albedine, simul in vtroque cognita: & in tali cognitione nihil componimus nec iudicamus: ergo absque compositione, & iudicio possumus comparare vnum cum altero Deinde in sensibus, de quibus certissimũ est, non iudicare, nec componere, aut diuidere: & non est minùs

73 The common opinion, therefore, of Aristotle, St. Thomas and all, is true and to be held: That the nature is universal before it is actually predicated, through the potency of being predicated of many; and that it becomes universal through the simple comparison of the intellect, through which it is cognized in order to the individuals, and not through the composite comparison, which is actual predication. Which I prove by this argument. The intellect can cognize one thing in another, or in order to another, without affirmation and negation and without actual predication; therefore it can cognize the nature in order to the individuals through simple comparison, without actually predicating it of them; but, cognized in order to the individuals, it is cognized as universal; therefore it becomes universal through simple comparison, not through composite. The antecedent is proved in two ways: first in the intellect, then in the senses. In the intellect indeed: because through a simple cognition we cognize a father ordered to his son, and two walls similar in whiteness, both being cognized at once; and in such a cognition we neither compose nor judge anything; therefore without composition and judgment we can compare one thing with another. Then in the senses, of which it is most certain that they do not judge, nor compose or divide; and it is no less

p. 60

certum, quòd cognoscant vnum in ordine ad alterum, vel comparando ad alterum: ergo idem poterit intellectus facere per simplicem comparationem naturę ad indiuidua. Probatur minor: Sensus communis, cognoscit sensibile vnius sensus externi, vt visus, non esse sensibile alterius sensus, nempe auditus: quod non potest vllo modo fieri sine comparatione vnius cum altero: & ouis cognoscit lupum vt inimicum & ideo fugit ab illo, & agnum vt amicum, à quo non fugit: & inter duos agnos, cognoscit hunc esse filium, & alium: non ergo cognoscit vnum in ordine ad alterum: & per comparationem cum eo, sine formali iudicio, & sine compositione, aut actuali prædicatione; ergo meliùs poterit intellectus cognoscere naturam in ordine ad indiuidua, & eam cum illis comparare, sine compositione, aut actuali prædicatione.

certain that they cognize one thing in order to another, or by comparing it to another; therefore the intellect will be able to do the same through a simple comparison of the nature to the individuals. The minor is proved. The common sense cognizes that the sensible of one external sense, such as sight, is not the sensible of another sense, namely hearing: which cannot in any way be done without comparison of the one with the other. And the sheep cognizes the wolf as an enemy, and therefore flees from it, and the lamb as a friend, from which it does not flee; and between two lambs it cognizes that this one is its offspring, and the other another’s. Does it not, then, cognize one thing in order to another, and through comparison with it, without formal judgment and without composition or actual predication? Therefore the intellect will be all the better able to cognize the nature in order to the individuals and to compare it with them, without composition or actual predication.

Pro solutione argumenti alterius opinionis notandum est, duobus modis posse cognosci vnum in ordine ad alterum, vel comparari ad illud. Primò, cognoscendo vtrumque extremum per se, tãquam conueniens alteri, attribuendo illud álteri: & hoc non potest fieri nisi per formale, & expressum iudicium, & comparationem compositam, quæ consistit in actuali prædicatione vnius de altero. Secundò, non cognoscendo vtrumque extremum per se, neque attribuendo illud alteri, sed vnum tantùm cum ordine ad alterum, vt cõueniens, aut disconueniens: sed non per modum attributionis, aut aliquid affirmando de conuenientia, vel disconuenientia: & hoc fit per simplicem comparationem ab intellectu, atque etiam à sensibus, vt probaui: sic autem comparatur natura ad indiuidua, & fit vniuersalis, & prædicabilis: antequam prædicetur actu de illis. Ad formam igitur argum. distinguenda est minor, quòd non possit intellectus cognoscere naturam esse in indiuiduis, nisi iudicando: nam duplex est iudicium. Vnum formale, & expressum, per quod intellectus iudicat vnum conuenire alteri per modum attributionis: Alterum, quasi virtuale, per quod notitia simplici cognoscit vnum in altero, vel in ordine ad alterum: tanquam ei conueniens aut disconueniẽs, sed non per modum attributionis. Negamus igitur, quòd intellectus non possit cognoscere naturam esse in multis, nisi per expressum, & formale iudicium: & concedimus, quòd non possit sine iudicio virtuali incluso in, comparatione simplici, quam ideo vocamus iudicium virtuale: quia cognoscere vnum, per comparationem ad alterum, fundamentum est formalis, & expressi iudicii, per quod ei attribuitur.

For the solution of the argument of the other opinion it should be noted that one thing can be cognized in order to another, or compared to it, in two ways. First, by cognizing each extreme per se, as agreeing with the other, attributing the one to the other: and this cannot be done except through a formal and express judgment and composite comparison, which consists in the actual predication of one thing of another. Second, by not cognizing each extreme per se, nor attributing the one to the other, but only the one with an order to the other, as agreeing or disagreeing, but not after the manner of attribution, or by affirming anything about the agreement or disagreement: and this is done through simple comparison by the intellect, and also by the senses, as I have proved; and in this way the nature is compared to the individuals and becomes universal and predicable before it is actually predicated of them. To the form of the argument, then, the minor must be distinguished, namely that the intellect cannot cognize that the nature is in the individuals except by judging: for judgment is twofold. One formal and express, through which the intellect judges that one thing belongs to another after the manner of attribution; the other as it were virtual, through which by a simple cognition it cognizes one thing in another, or in order to another, as agreeing or disagreeing with it, but not after the manner of attribution. We deny, therefore, that the intellect cannot cognize that the nature is in many except through express and formal judgment; and we grant that it cannot do so without the virtual judgment included in simple comparison, which we therefore call virtual judgment, because to cognize one thing through comparison to another is the foundation of the formal and express judgment through which it is attributed to it.

p. 61

QUESTION VII

Quæst. 7. An vniuersale sit vniuocum respectu prædicabilium, & verum genus eorum — Whether the universal is univocal with respect to the predicables, and their true genus.

75 Pręsupponit titulus quæstionis, quid sit nomen vniuocum, quid etiam analogum: quod ex Summulis notũ est. Quærit verò quonam modo se habeat vniuersale respectu prædicabilium, vt analogum, vel potiùs, vt vniuocum: ita vt sit genus eorum.

75 The title of the question presupposes what a univocal name is, and also what an analogous one is, which is known from the Summulae. It asks, however, in what manner the universal stands with respect to the predicables: as analogous, or rather as univocal, so that it is their genus.

Prima opinio tenet, analogum esse. Quam diuersis modis defendunt diuersi auctores: sed in eo conueniunt, quòd per prius de vno, aut multis dicatur, per posterius verò de reliquis. Ita docet Albertus Magnus tract. 2. prædicabilium, ca. 9. affirmans primò conuenire generi, deinde speciei, & ratione huius differentiæ. Per posterius verò, & quasi per accidens proprio, & accidenti, tanquam prædicatis accidentalibus. Et eodem ferè modo explicat analogiam Canterus 4. cap. prædicamentorum. Potissimum argumentum huius opinionis est, quia ens reale est analogum ad substantiam, & accidentia: sed tria prædicabilia, vt genus. species, & differentia sunt substantiæ, duo verò alia, vt proprium & accidens, sunt accidentia, ergo vniuersale, quod de omnibus dicitur, cùm omnia prædicabilia sint vniuersalia, non potest esse vniuocum.

The first opinion holds that it is analogous. Different authors defend it in different ways, but they agree in this, that it is said primarily of one, or of several, and secondarily of the rest. So teaches Albert the Great, tract. 2 on the Predicables, ch. 9, affirming that it belongs first to genus, then to species, and by reason of the latter to difference; but secondarily, and as it were per accidens, to property and accident, as to accidental predicates. And Canterus explains the analogy in almost the same way, ch. 4 of the Categories. The chief argument of this opinion is that real being is analogous to substance and accidents; but three predicables, namely genus, species and difference, are substances, while the other two, namely property and accident, are accidents; therefore the universal, which is said of all, since all the predicables are universals, cannot be univocal.

Secundò probari potest hoc modo. Vniuersale, & prædicabile conuertuntur & se habent tanquam essentia, & propria passio: sed prædicabile est analogum, respectu omnium: ergo erit etiam analogum vniuersale. Probatur minor: Prædicatio analogicè, dicitur de prædicatione per se, & per accidens, cùm illa sit simpliciter talis, hæc verò solùm secundùm quid: ergo prædicabile erit etiam analogum, cùm se habeant sicut actus, & potentia, respectu prædicabilis per se; & per accidens: sed tria prędicabilia genus, species, & differentia prædicantur per se, cùm prædicentur essentialiter: & duo alia prędicantur per accidens, cùm prędicentur accidentaliter: ergo prędicabile analogum est respectu omnium.

Secondly, it can be proved in this way. The universal and the predicable are convertible and stand as essence and proper attribute; but the predicable is analogous with respect to all; therefore the universal too will be analogous. The minor is proved: predication is said analogically of predication per se and per accidens, since the former is such simply, the latter only in a qualified sense; therefore the predicable too will be analogous, since they stand as act and potency with respect to the predicable per se and per accidens; but three predicables, genus, species and difference, are predicated per se, since they are predicated essentially; and the two others are predicated per accidens, since they are predicated accidentally; therefore the predicable is analogous with respect to all.

Secunda opinio asserit, Vniuersale vniuocum esse respectu prædicabilium, & verum genus eorum, sicut animal respectu hominis, & equi: & est D Tho. in quæstionibus vniuersalibus, quæst. 2. Scot. quæst. 8, Iauelli tract. 4. de prædicabilibus, ca. 1. 5. & 6 Soti quæst. 4. vniuersalium, & cap. de genere, quæ vnica, & Cardinalis Toleti, quæst. 2. vniuersalium: & iam ferè communis, vera, & tenenda.

The second opinion asserts that the universal is univocal with respect to the predicables, and their true genus, as animal is with respect to man and horse; and it is that of St. Thomas in the questions on universals, q. 2; Scotus, q. 8; Javelli, tract. 4 on the Predicables, ch. 1 and 6; Soto, q. 4 on universals, and the chapter on genus, the only one; and Cardinal Toledo, q. 2 on universals; and it is now almost common, true, and to be held.

76 Sed vt eã efficaciter probemus, notandum est, Vniuersale

76 But in order that we may prove it effectively, it should be noted that the universal

p. 62

cùm sit nomen concretum, & accidentale, duobus modis sumi posse: Materialiter, pro subiecto, seu natura denominata, & Formaliter, pro vniuersalitate eam denominante: sicut album sumitur pro corpore, & pro albedine. Sed adhuc subiectum denominatum consideratur duobus modis, secundùm propriam essentiam, & naturam, aut in quantum denominatur ab vniuersalitate: quemadmodum corpus sumitur, secundùm quod est substantia corporea: aut in quantum denominatur ab albedine: quo pacto visibile est, & ad prædicamentum qualitatis reducitur. Et naturæ, quæ denominantur vniuersales, si secundùm propriam essentiam, aut entitatem sumantur, quædam sunt substantiæ, & quædam accidentia: imò quædam accidentia realia, & quædam accidentia rationis, & cùm nihil possit esse commune vniuocum substantiæ, & accidentibus, nec accidentibus realibus, & rationis: nihil etiam potest esse commune vniuocum diuersis naturis, quæ denominatur vniuersales, hoc modo sumptis. Sed si accipiantur secundo modo, vniuocam rationem habere poterunt: si forma eas denominans vniuoca sit. Exemplum afferre possumus in genere: quod est primum ex quinque vniuersalibus, & considerare vniuersas naturas, quæ à secunda intentione generis denominantur, tanquam à forma, vt substantiam, quantitatem, & qualitatem. Primò quidem secundùm proprias essentias: & hoc modo nihil commune vniuocum habere possunt. Deinde, in quantum denominantur genera, & cùm ratio generis vniuoca sit, per vnam definitionem explicata à Porphyrio: quòd sit prædicabilis de pluribus differentibus specie in quid, vniuocè conueniunt sub ratione generis, substantia, quantitas, & qualitas: quia eodem modo denominantur à tali forma: ita vt non magis, nec priùs substantia sit prædicabilis de pluribus differentibus specie, quàm quantitas, aut qualitas: sed omnino æqualiter.

since it is a concrete and accidental name, can be taken in two ways: Materially, for the subject or nature denominated; and Formally, for the universality that denominates it; just as white is taken for the body and for the whiteness. But further, the subject denominated is considered in two ways: according to its proper essence and nature, or inasmuch as it is denominated by universality; just as body is taken according as it is corporeal substance, or inasmuch as it is denominated by whiteness, in which way it is visible and is reduced to the category of quality. And of the natures that are denominated universal, if they are taken according to their proper essence or entity, some are substances and some accidents; indeed some are real accidents and some accidents of reason; and since nothing univocal can be common to substance and accidents, nor to real accidents and accidents of reason, neither can anything univocal be common to the diverse natures which are denominated universal, taken in this way. But if they are taken in the second way, they will be able to have a univocal ratio, if the form that denominates them is univocal. We can give an example in genus, which is the first of the five universals, and consider the universal natures which are denominated by the second intention of genus as by a form, such as substance, quantity and quality. First, indeed, according to their proper essences; and in this way they can have nothing univocal in common. Then, inasmuch as they are denominated genera; and since the ratio of genus is univocal, explained by Porphyry through one definition, that it is predicable of many differing in species in quid, substance, quantity and quality agree univocally under the ratio of genus, because they are denominated by such a form in the same way, so that substance is not more, nor prior, predicable of many differing in species than quantity or quality, but altogether equally.

77 Ex hac distinctione colligitur argumẽtum, ad probandã nostram sententiam, & cõmunem: Vniuocum est quod multa significat sub eadem ratione: sed vniuersale significat omnia vniuersalia, aut prædicabilia sub eadem ratione: ergo est vniuocum respectu eorum. Probatur minor: illa est vna, & eadem ratio, quæ per vnam definitionem explicatur: sed ratio vniuersalis explicatur ab Aristotele per vnam definitionem, nempe quòd sit vnum in multis, aptum prædicari de multis: ergo est vna, respectu omniũ vniuersaliũ, sub qua vniuocè cõueniunt.

77 From this distinction an argument is gathered to prove our view, which is also the common one: The univocal is that which signifies many things under the same ratio; but universal signifies all universals or predicables under the same ratio; therefore it is univocal with respect to them. The minor is proved: that ratio is one and the same which is explained through one definition; but the ratio of the universal is explained by Aristotle through one definition, namely, that it is one in many, apt to be predicated of many; therefore it is one with respect to all universals, and under it they agree univocally.

Ad primum arg. respondendum est, ex doctrina tradita, distinguendo maiorem hoc modo: Si substantia, & accidentia sumantur secundùm propriam entitatem, & essentiam: nihil

To the first argument one must reply, from the doctrine delivered, by distinguishing the major in this way: if substance and accidents are taken according to their proper entity and essence, nothing

p. 63

commune vniuocum habere possunt: si verò sumantur vt sunt vniuersalia, vniuocè conueniunt: quia eodem modo denominantur ab vniuersalitate: & ideo vniuersale respectu eorum vniuocum est.

univocal can they have in common; but if they are taken as they are universals, they agree univocally, because they are denominated in the same way by universality; and therefore the universal is univocal with respect to them.

Pro solutione secundi notandum est, quòd sicut animal significat solùm naturam sensitiuam, non rationalem, aut irrationalem: quia differentia, vt docet Porph, in prædicabilibus, sunt extra significationem generis: eodem modo vniuersale, solùm dicit vnum in multis, & aptum prædicari de multis: quod verò prædicetur essentialiter aut accidentaliter, per se aut per accidens, extra significationem eius est, & diuersis vniuersalibus conuenit, non sub ratione vniuersalium, vel vt tali nomine significantur: sed secundùm alias rationes particulares, non significatas per nomen vniuersale. vnde licèt rationes illæ ita se habeant, vt vna sit prior altera, vel vna sit talis simpliciter, alia secundùm quid, non ideo commune nomen quo significantur, desinit esse vniuocum.

For the solution of the second, it should be noted that, just as animal signifies only the sentient nature, not the rational or the irrational, because the differences, as Porphyry teaches in the Predicables, are outside the signification of the genus, in the same way universal expresses only one in many, and apt to be predicated of many; but that it is predicated essentially or accidentally, per se or per accidens, is outside its signification, and belongs to the different universals not under the ratio of universals, or as they are signified by such a name, but according to other particular rationes not signified by the name universal. Hence, although those rationes are so related that one is prior to another, or one is such simply and another in a qualified sense, the common name by which they are signified does not on that account cease to be univocal.

Nunc ergo ad formam argumenti neganda est minor: quòd prædicabile, aut prædicatio sit analogum, respectu quinque prædicabilium: nam licèt quædam illorum prædicentur essentialiter, aut per se, alia verò accidentaliter, & per accidens: istæ tamen rationes particulares non pertinent ad significationem prædicabilis: sed solùm potentia prædicandi in communi, quæ cùm sit eadem in omnibus, vniuocè significantur omnia prædicabilia per nomen prædicabile omnibus commune: nec tollitur vniuocatio per particulares rationes, eodem nomine non significatas.

Now, then, to the form of the argument the minor must be denied, namely that the predicable, or predication, is analogous with respect to the five predicables: for although some of them are predicated essentially, or per se, and others accidentally and per accidens, these particular rationes do not pertain to the signification of predicable, but only the potency of predicating in common; and since this is the same in all, all the predicables are signified univocally by the name predicable, common to all; nor is the univocation taken away by particular rationes not signified by the same name.

QUESTION VIII

Quæst. 8. An vniuersale sit adæquatum obiectum libri prædicabilium, vel potiùs prædicabile — Whether the universal is the adequate object of the book of the Predicables, or rather the predicable.

79 Liber prædicabilium pars quædam est totius Logicæ: & ideo aliquod obiectum partiale debet ei correspõdere, quod sit quasi pars totalis, & adæquati obiecti eiusdem scientiæ: de quo inquirimus, An sit vniuersale, vel prædicabile: cùm sit certum nullum aliud, præter hæc, obiectum esse posse: ex quibus illud erit obiectum, cui generales conditiones obiecti quæstione vltima proœmiali à nobis traditæ conueniant, potiùs quàm alteri.

79 The book of the Predicables is a certain part of the whole of Logic, and therefore some partial object ought to correspond to it, which is as it were a part of the total and adequate object of the same science; concerning which we inquire whether it is the universal or the predicable, since it is certain that nothing else besides these can be the object; and of them that one will be the object to which the general conditions of an object, delivered by us in the last proemial question, belong rather than to the other.

Prima opinio defendit, prædicabile esse obiectum, potiùs, quã vniuersale: quę attribui solet Scoto, & defenditur à multis modernis Habétq; duo arg. Primũ, illud est obiectũ alicuius

The first opinion defends that the predicable is the object rather than the universal. It is usually attributed to Scotus, and is defended by many moderns. And it has two arguments. The first: that is the object of any

p. 64

partis, vel scientię, quod continet omnia, de quibus illa agit: sed vniuersale non continet omnia, de quibus agitur in hoc libro: ergo non est eius obiectum: probatur minor. Porphyrius in cap. de specie agit de indiuiduo, atque etiam de specie subiicibili: quæ non sunt vniuersalia: quia indiuiduum nõ est in multis: nec species subiicibilis, in quantum talis, respicit indiuidua.

part or science which contains all the things it treats of; but the universal does not contain all the things treated of in this book; therefore it is not its object. The minor is proved: Porphyry, in the chapter on species, treats of the individual, and also of the subjicible species, which are not universals: because the individual is not in many, nor does the subjicible species, inasmuch as it is such, regard individuals.

Secundũ illud est obiectum formale scientiæ, sub cuius ratione formali cõsiderat omnia, sed omnia quę tractãtur in hoc libro considerantur sub ratione prędicabilis, & non sub ratione vniuersalis: ergo vniuersale non est obiectum, sed prædicabile: Minorem probo ex definitionibus prædicabilium, quas tradit Porphyrius per prædicabile, vt definitionem generis, quòd sit prędicabile de pluribus differẽtibꝰ specie in eo quod quid: & sic de cęteris vnde & librũ prędicabiliũ vocat opꝰ hoc.

The second: that is the formal object of a science under whose formal ratio it considers all things; but all the things treated in this book are considered under the ratio of the predicable, and not under the ratio of the universal; therefore the universal is not the object, but the predicable. I prove the minor from the definitions of the predicables, which Porphyry delivers through the predicable, as the definition of genus, that it is predicable of many differing in species in quid; and so of the others: whence he also calls this work the book of the Predicables.

Secunda opinio asserit vniuersale potiùs esse obiectũ quam tenet D. Tho. q. 9. de obiecto huius libri. Sotus quęst. 4. vniuersalium. Toletus qu. 1. & videtur nobis probabilior, & tenenda. Pro eius declaratione notandũ est ex doctrina D. Th. opusc. 48. cap. 6 quòd intellectus tribuit naturę vniuersalitatẽ, tanquam fundamentum cęterarum denominationũ: quia primum quod in ea intelligit, est esse in multis & ideo vocat eã vniuersalem: & quia ex ratione essẽdi in multis, sequitur posse prædicari de multis statim ei tribuit denominationem prædicabilis: deinde alias denominationes speciales, generis, & speciei. Vnde sequitur, quòd sicut primum, quod est in aliqua re, tanquam fundamentum aliorum, est eius essentia: ita vniuersalitas, quę est prima denominatio naturę, sit quasi essentia eius in ordine Logico: prædicabilitas verò, passio omnibus vniuersalibus communis.

The second opinion asserts that the universal is rather the object. St. Thomas holds it, q. 9, on the object of this book; Soto, q. 4 on universals; Toledo, q. 1; and it seems to us the more probable and to be held. For its explanation it should be noted, from the doctrine of St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 6, that the intellect attributes universality to the nature as the foundation of the other denominations: because the first thing it understands in it is being in many, and therefore it calls it universal; and because from the ratio of being in many there follows being able to be predicated of many, it immediately attributes to it the denomination of predicable; and then other special denominations, of genus and of species. From which it follows that, just as the first thing that is in a thing, as the foundation of the others, is its essence, so universality, which is the first denomination of the nature, is as it were its essence in the logical order, while predicability is an attribute common to all universals.

Ex hac doctrina D. Tho, vera & necessaria, hoc argumentũ colligitur, ad probandam eius sententiam, & nostram. Vniuersale, & prædicabile, considerantur per se in hoc libro, & illud se habet tanquam essentia, hoc verò tanquam propria passio: ergo vniuersale potiùs est obiectum, quàm prędicabile. Probatur consequentia: Quia officium scientiæ est, probare passiones de subiecto: sed in hoc libro probatur de vniuersali, quòd sit prædicabile, tanquam posterius de priori, ergo tanquam propria passio de subiecto, quod non potest conuenire prædicabili; cùm nullam habeat passionem, quę de illo probari possit, ergo nec potest esse obiectum.

From this doctrine of St. Thomas, true and necessary, this argument is gathered to prove his view and ours: The universal and the predicable are considered per se in this book, and the former stands as essence, the latter as proper attribute; therefore the universal is the object rather than the predicable. The consequence is proved: because the office of a science is to prove attributes of the subject; but in this book it is proved of the universal that it is predicable, as the posterior of the prior, therefore as a proper attribute of the subject; which cannot belong to the predicable, since it has no attribute that can be proved of it; therefore neither can it be the object.

81. Ad primum argumentum alterius opinionis, neganda est minor, quia species subiicibilis, & indiuiduum, suo modo

81. To the first argument of the other opinion the minor must be denied, because the subjicible species and the individual, in their own way, are contained

p. 65

continentur sub vniuersali: non quòd vniuersalia sint formaliter, sed quia termini sunt relationis vniuersalitas generis, & speciei: genus enim vniuersale est, quia est in multis speciebus, de quibus aptum est prædicari: & ex hac relatione generis ad species, resultat in eis relatio alia subiicibilitatis, per quam dicuntur illam terminare, vt in cap. de specie explicabitur. Et eadem ratione indiuiduum, est terminus relationis speciei, à qua vniuersalis, & prædicabilis denominatur: quia in multis indiuiduis est, & de illis apta prædicari: & ideo indiuidua, & species subiicibiles, ad genus, speciem, tractatum eorum, reducuntur.

under the universal: not because they are formally universals, but because they are the terms of the relation of universality of the genus and of the species. For the genus is universal because it is in many species, of which it is apt to be predicated; and from this relation of the genus to the species there results in them another relation, of subjicibility, through which they are said to terminate it, as will be explained in the chapter on species. And for the same reason the individual is the term of the relation of the species, by which it is denominated universal and predicable, because it is in many individuals and is apt to be predicated of them; and therefore individuals and subjicible species are reduced to the genus and the species, and to their treatment.

Ad secundum respondeo, distinguendo minorem: quia Vniuersale considerari à Porphyrio in hoc libro, sub ratione prædicabilis, duobus modis intelligi potest. Primo, ita, vt prædicabilitas sit ratio obiectiua, quæ consideratur, & in hoc sensu negandum est, quia cùm vniuersalitas sit essentialis ratio, & fundamentum prædicabilitatis, atque aliarum denominationum, quas intellectus tribuit naturæ, ratio obiectiua est, sub qua considerantur omnia. Secundo modo potest intelligi, sub ratione prædicabilitatis considerari omnia, tanquam sub passione communi, quæ de quinque vniuersalibus in hoc opere demonstratur: & in hoc sensu concedenda est minor: sed ex eo non bene infertur, quòd prædicabile sit obiectum, sed solum, quòd sit passio, quæ de obiecto demonstratur. Demonstratur autem hoc modo: Quidquid est vnum in multis, est prædicabile de multis: sed genus est in multis speciebus: ergo prædicabile de illis est: & sic de cæteris prædicabilibus quæ per prædicabilitatem definiũtur à Porphyrio, tanquam per propriam passionem, magis nobis manifestam: & ideo definitionibus, non quidditatiuis: sed descriptiuis, vt in ca. de genere explicabitur. Et eodem modo intelligendum est, Librum quinque prædicadilium, vocari hoc opus, denominatione sumpta à communi passione, quæ de illis demonstratur magis nota, potiùs quàm ab vniuersali, quòd eius obiectum est.

To the second I reply by distinguishing the minor: for that the universal is considered by Porphyry in this book under the ratio of the predicable can be understood in two ways. First, so that predicability is the objective ratio which is considered; and in this sense it must be denied, because, since universality is the essential ratio and foundation of predicability and of the other denominations which the intellect attributes to the nature, it is the objective ratio under which all things are considered. In the second way it can be understood that all things are considered under the ratio of predicability as under a common attribute which is demonstrated of the five universals in this work; and in this sense the minor must be granted; but from this it is not rightly inferred that the predicable is the object, but only that it is an attribute which is demonstrated of the object. And it is demonstrated in this way: Whatever is one in many is predicable of many; but genus is in many species; therefore it is predicable of them; and so of the other predicables, which are defined by Porphyry through predicability as through a proper attribute more manifest to us; and therefore by definitions that are not quidditative but descriptive, as will be explained in the chapter on genus. And in the same way it must be understood that this work is called the Book of the Five Predicables, the denomination being taken from the common attribute, better known, which is demonstrated of them, rather than from the universal, which is its object.

QUESTION IX

An prædicabilia sint quinque, vel plura, aut pauciora.

Whether the predicables are five, or more, or fewer.

82 Sicut prædicamentorum artem inuenit Arist. vt modos essendi omnium rerum, ad certa quædam capita reduceret, & ita facilè possemus agnoscere earum naturam, cognito prædicamento, in quo collocatur: ita Porphyrius inuenit artem prædicabilium, vt ad certa capita reduceret omnes

82 Just as Aristotle invented the art of the categories in order to reduce the modes of being of all things to certain heads, so that we might easily recognize their nature once the category in which it is placed is known, so Porphyry invented the art of the predicables in order to reduce all predications E

p. 66

prædicationes: & nos facilè possemus cognoscere, qualis sit prædicatio quæcunque, Essentialis, aut Accidentalis: & essentialis, generica, aut specifica: & eodem modo accidentalis, accidentis proprij, aut communis, ex quarum cognitione naturas rerum cognoscere possimus. Vt autem hanc artem prædicabilium meliùs possimus intelligere, necesse est determinatum numerum eorum cognoscere: & ideo quæstio vltima vniuersalis de eorum numero inquirit, An quinque sint. ita vt nec plura, nec pauciora: & licèt non sint diuersæ opiniones, circa numerum: sed omnes Porphyrium sequantur auctorem huius libri, ponentem tantùm quinque.

to certain heads, and so that we might easily know of what kind any predication whatever is, Essential or Accidental; and, if essential, generic or specific; and in the same way, if accidental, of a proper or of a common accident; from the knowledge of which we may know the natures of things. But in order that we may better understand this art of the predicables, it is necessary to know their determinate number; and therefore the last question on universals inquires about their number, whether they are five, so that they are neither more nor fewer. And although there are no differing opinions about the number, but all follow Porphyry, the author of this book, who posits only five,

Quædam tamen argumenta in contrarium proponimus: quæ videntur probare, ex vna parte pauciora esse, ex alia verò esse plura: vt ex eorum solutionibus, veritas manifesta fiat. Probatur ergo, pauciora esse quàm quinque, duobus argumẽtis. Primò, prædicabilia, & prædicata, solùm distinguuntur, tanquam potentiæ, & actus: quia prædicabile est, quod potest prædicari de alio: & prædicatum, quod prædicatur actu: sed Prædicata sunt quatuor, & non plura, vt docet Aristoteles primo lib. Topicorum, c. 2. 3. & 4. nempe Genus, Definitio, Proprium & Accidens: ergo quatuor tantùm erunt prædicabilia.

we nevertheless propose certain arguments to the contrary, which seem to prove, on the one side, that they are fewer, and on the other, that they are more, so that from their solutions the truth may become manifest. That they are fewer than five, then, is proved by two arguments. First, predicables and predicates are distinguished only as potency and act: because the predicable is that which can be predicated of another, and the predicate that which is actually predicated; but the predicates are four, and not more, as Aristotle teaches in Topics 1, ch. 2, 3 and 4, namely Genus, Definition, Property and Accident; therefore there will be only four predicables.

83 Secundò, Porphyrius distinguit duo prædicabilia, generis & differentiæ, quia genus prædicatur in quid, & differentia, in quale quid, sed definitio continet vtrumque: ergo pro duobus prædicabilibus sufficiet. Probatur consequentia: quia de eisdem prędicatur definitio, de quibus prędicantur genus, & differentia: & præterea continet modum prædicandi vtriusque, in quid, & in quale quid, per modum vnius prædicabilis. Nam si definitio sit speciei subalternæ, vt viuens, sensibile, prędicatur de pluribus differentibus specie, nempe de homine, & leone, sicut genus: si verò sit speciei infimæ, vt animal rationale, prædicabitur de pluribus differentibus numero, vt de Petro & Ioanne prædicatur differẽtia, ergo non sunt distinguenda duo prædicabilia generis, & differentiæ, sed sufficiet definitio pro vtroque: & ita erunt quatuor tantùm & non quinque.

83 Second, Porphyry distinguishes two predicables, of genus and of difference, because genus is predicated in quid and difference in quale quid; but definition contains both; therefore it will suffice for two predicables. The consequence is proved: because definition is predicated of the same things of which genus and difference are predicated; and moreover it contains the mode of predicating of both, in quid and in quale quid, by way of one predicable. For if it is the definition of a subalternate species, as living sentient, it is predicated of many differing in species, namely of man and of lion, like a genus; but if it is of a lowest species, as rational animal, it will be predicated of many differing in number, as the difference is predicated of Peter and John; therefore two predicables, of genus and of difference, are not to be distinguished, but definition will suffice for both; and so they will be only four and not five.

Altera verò pars, quòd prædicabilia sint plura, quam quinque, probari potest. Primò, quia Porphyrius in cap de genere, distinguit prædicabilia per ea, de quibus prædicantur, vt genus ab specie: quia prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie: hæc verò de pluribus differentibus numero: & sic de cæteris. sed si ita distinguantur, sequitur septem saltem esse ponenda, ita vt duo sint prædicabilia differentiæ, & duo alia proprij. Probatur consequentia: quia differentia subalterna,

The other part, however, that the predicables are more than five, can be proved. First, because Porphyry, in the chapter on genus, distinguishes the predicables by the things of which they are predicated, as genus from species: because the former is predicated of many differing in species, the latter of many differing in number; and so of the rest. But if they are distinguished in this way, it follows that at least seven must be posited, so that there are two predicables of difference and two others of property. The consequence is proved: because the subalternate difference,

p. 67

vt corporeum, prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie, nempe de corpore viuente, & non viuente: si verò sit infima, vt rationale, solùm de pluribus differentibus numero, nempe de Petro & Ioanne: ergo distincta efficient prædicabilia. Proprium etiam si sit subalternum, vt sensibile, quod sequitur naturam speciei subalternæ animalis, prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie, nempe de equo, & leone: si autem sit infimum, vt risibile, prædicatur solùm de differentibus numero, vt de Petro, & Ioanne: ergo erunt septem prædicabilia.

as corporeal, is predicated of many differing in species, namely of living and non-living body; but if it is a lowest one, as rational, it is predicated only of many differing in number, namely of Peter and John; therefore they will make distinct predicables. Property too, if it is subalternate, as sensible, which follows the nature of the subalternate species animal, is predicated of many differing in species, namely of horse and lion; but if it is a lowest one, as risible, it is predicated only of things differing in number, as of Peter and John; therefore there will be seven predicables.

4 Secundò indiuiduum vagum, vt quidam homo, prædicatur de pluribus differentibus numero, vt de Petro, & Ioanne: & tamen, non est species, quia nõ prædicatur in eo quod quid. Et etiam, actualis existentia idem habet: ergo aliud prædicabile distinctum ab specie, ponendum est pro illis. Probatur minor: quia sicut quidam homo, non dicit essentiam, aut quidditatem indiuiduorum, sed communem rationem indiuidui, quæ vel accidentalis est, vel saltem extra essentiam eorum: ita existentia actualis, non pertinet ad essentiam alicuius creaturæ, facilè eam amittentis per corruptionem, aut potentis eam amittere per annihilationem. Quare non prædicatur in quid, cùm prædicari in quid, idem sit, quod prædicare quidditatem, aut essentiam rei.

4 Second, the vague individual, as a certain man, is predicated of many differing in number, as of Peter and John; and yet it is not a species, because it is not predicated in quid. And actual existence too has the same character; therefore another predicable, distinct from species, must be posited for them. The minor is proved: because, just as a certain man does not express the essence or quiddity of individuals, but the common ratio of individual, which either is accidental or at least is outside their essence, so actual existence does not pertain to the essence of any creature, which easily loses it through corruption, or can lose it through annihilation. Wherefore it is not predicated in quid, since to be predicated in quid is the same as to predicate the quiddity or essence of a thing.

Vera tamen est sententia Porphyrij, & communis in schola. Sed tota difficultas eius consistit in assignanda ratione, per quam sufficienter probetur, prædicabilia non esse plura, aut pauciora, quàm quinque: & diuersæ assignãtur à diuersis. Nam quidam prædicabilia distinguunt per ea, de quibus prædicantur, alij per ea, quæ de re aliqua cognosci possunt, quæ videntur esse quinque. Sed rationes istæ insufficientes mihi videntur: sufficiens verò per quam probatur efficaciter prædicabilia non esse plura, nec pauciora, quàm quinque ex modo formali prædicandi, aut se habendi in ordine ad subiectum, sumenda est: quod sic probatur. Modus prædicandi, qui ex modo se habendi prædicati ad subiectum sumitur, est formalis ratio prædicationis: ergo erit etiam ratio formalis prædicabilium: sed essentialis distinctio rerum, sumitur ex diuersis rationibus formalibus earum: ergo prædicabilia distingui debent per diuersos modos prædicandi.

Yet the opinion of Porphyry, which is also the common one in the schools, is true. But the whole difficulty of it consists in assigning the reason by which it may be sufficiently proved that the predicables are neither more nor fewer than five; and different reasons are assigned by different authors. For some distinguish the predicables by the things of which they are predicated; others by the things that can be known about a thing, which seem to be five. But these reasons seem to me insufficient: the sufficient one, by which it is effectively proved that the predicables are neither more nor fewer than five, must be taken from the formal mode of predicating, or of standing in order to the subject; which is proved thus. The mode of predicating, which is taken from the mode in which the predicate stands to the subject, is the formal ratio of predication; therefore it will also be the formal ratio of the predicables; but the essential distinction of things is taken from their diverse formal rationes; therefore the predicables ought to be distinguished by the diverse modes of predicating.

Hoc igitur discursu probari debet, quòd non sint plura, nec pauciora quàm quinque. Ea quæ constituunt prædicabilia, in primis debent esse vniuersalia, quia prædicabile tamquam propria passio vniuersalis, cum eo conuertitur: sed vniuersale est vnum in multis: ergo nihil erit prædiceabile,

By this discourse, then, it must be proved that they are neither more nor fewer than five. The things that constitute the predicables must, in the first place, be universals, because the predicable, as the proper attribute of the universal, is convertible with it; but the universal is one in many; therefore nothing will be predicable E ij

p. 68

si non sit vnum. Vt autem sit vnum, simplex debet esse, hoc est non complexum: quia complexum non est vnum, sed plura, vt homo albus, aut animal rationale. Præterea, si vnum est, vniuocum erit, non æquiuocum, neque analogum. Per primam igitur conditionem excluduntur prædicata complexa à ratione prædicabilis, vt definitio. Per secundam verò, æquiuoca, & analoga, vt canis, ens, accidens, & similia. Deinde, quod vnum est, hoc est incomplexum, & vniuocum, quinque tantùm modis se habere potest in ordine ad subiectum: ergo quinque tantùm modis potest de illo prædicari: quare quinque tantùm erunt prædicabilia. Probatur antecedens: nam vel prædicatur essentialiter, vel accidentaliter: & si essentialiter, aut per modum totius actualis, quia totam essentiam subiecti actu continet, vt prædicatur homo de Petro & Ioanne: & est prædicabile speciei, aut per modum totius potentialis, quod verè est pars materialis eiusdem speciei, & ideo contrahibile per differentias, tanquam per formas, & est genus: vel per modum partis formalis, actualis, & contrahentis, & est differentia. Si verò prædicetur accidentaliter, aut per modum eius, quod ab essentia procedit, & cum ea conuertitur, & est proprium: & si per modum accidentis extrinseci, aut communis, dicitur prædicabile accidentis: & cùm non sint possibiles alij modi prædicandi, præter istos, & ad eos reduci possint omnes prædicationes, sequitur quinque tantùm esse prædicabilia, ita vt nec plura, nec pauciora. Pro solutione primi argumenti notanda est differentia inter prædicabile, prędicatum, & prędicamentum, quòd prædicamentum est quædam ordinatio essentialis prædicabilium, secundùm debitam subiectionem, & prædicationem, à supremo genere, vsque ad vltimam speciem, & indiuiduum: vt prædicamentum substantiæ, est ordinatio hæc, substantia corpus, viuens, anima, homo, Petrus.

unless it is one. And in order to be one, it must be simple, that is, not complex: because the complex is not one but many, as white man, or rational animal. Moreover, if it is one, it will be univocal, not equivocal or analogous. By the first condition, then, complex predicates, such as definition, are excluded from the ratio of the predicable; by the second, equivocal and analogous ones, as dog, being, accident, and the like. Next, that which is one, that is, incomplex and univocal, can stand in only five ways in order to the subject; therefore it can be predicated of it in only five ways; wherefore there will be only five predicables. The antecedent is proved: for it is predicated either essentially or accidentally; and if essentially, either by way of an actual whole, because it actually contains the whole essence of the subject, as man is predicated of Peter and John, and this is the predicable of species; or by way of a potential whole, which is truly the material part of the same species, and therefore contractible by differences as by forms, and this is genus; or by way of a formal, actual and contracting part, and this is difference. But if it is predicated accidentally, either by way of that which proceeds from the essence and is convertible with it, and this is property; or, if by way of an extrinsic or common accident, it is called the predicable of accident. And since no other modes of predicating besides these are possible, and all predications can be reduced to them, it follows that there are only five predicables, so that they are neither more nor fewer. For the solution of the first argument, the difference between predicable, predicate and category should be noted: namely, that a category is a certain essential ordering of the predicables, according to due subjection and predication, from the supreme genus down to the last species and the individual; as the category of substance is this ordering: substance, body, living, animal, man, Peter.

86 Prædicata verò sumpsit Arist. primo li. Topicorum, c. 2. 3. & 4. per ordinem ad propositionem Dialecticam, seu probabilem, ex qua efficiatur syllogismus Dialecticus, aut probabilis. & quia forma syllogistica petit propositiones de subiecto communi: nam ex propositionibus singularibus non fiunt, nisi syllogismi expositorij, qui non habent modum, nec figuram, nisi per ordinem ad propositiones vniuersales ideo sumit rationem prædicatorum, ex ordine ad subiectum commune.

86 But Aristotle took the predicates, in Topics 1, ch. 2, 3 and 4, in order to the dialectical or probable proposition from which a dialectical or probable syllogism is made; and because the syllogistic form requires propositions about a common subject (for from singular propositions only expository syllogisms are made, which have no mood or figure except in order to universal propositions), he therefore takes the ratio of predicates from their order to a common subject.

Ex quibus sequitur, quatuor tantùm esse prædicata: quod sic probatur. Species non est prædicatum, sed subiectum commune, in ordine ad quem sumitur distinctio prædicatorum: quod adeò verum est, vt non sit aliud subiectum commune

From which it follows that there are only four predicates, which is proved thus. Species is not a predicate but the common subject, in order to which the distinction of the predicates is taken; which is so true that there is no other common subject

p. 69

præter illam. Quo supposito, vel prædicatum conuertitur cum specie, aut vniuersalius est, si conuertitur cum ea: vel est intra essentiam eius, & erit definitio, vt animal rationale: vel ex ea naturaliter sequitur, & erit proprium, vt risibile respectu hominis: si verò vniuersalius est specie, vel ad quidditatem eius pertinet, & est genus: aut extra illam est, & erit commune accidens. differentiam verò, cum genere numerandam esse docet Arist. ca. illo 3. his verbis: Differentia cùm generalis sit, cum genere ordinanda est. Et loquitur de differentia subalterna, quia hæc tantùm generalis est, quia cum genere conuertitur vt corporeum cum corpore: si verò sit infirma, ad definitionem reducitur. In distinguendis verò prædicatis, nihil dicitur de modis prædicandi in quid, aut in quale quid, generis & differentiæ: quia in ordine ad propositionem Dialecticam, & syllogismum, nullam distinctionem efficiunt: cùm idem sit modus disputandi probabiliter in his propositionibus, in quibus prædicatum est vniuersalius subiecto, & intra essentiam eius est, siue sit genus, vel differentia. Nec sunt diuersa prædicata complexa ab incomplexis, si eodem modo se habeant in ordine ad subiectum commune: quia eodem modo disputatur de propositionibus Dialecticis, ex vtroque factis, & ideo definitio inter prędicata numeratur: quæ tamen à prædicabilibus excluditur propter complexionem.

besides it. This supposed, the predicate either is convertible with the species or is more universal. If it is convertible with it, either it is within its essence, and it will be a definition, as rational animal; or it follows naturally from it, and it will be a property, as risible with respect to man. But if it is more universal than the species, either it pertains to its quiddity, and it is a genus; or it is outside it, and it will be a common accident. Difference, however, Aristotle teaches is to be numbered with genus, in that ch. 3, in these words: Difference, since it is generic, is to be ranked with genus. And he is speaking of subalternate difference, because this is generic, since it is convertible with the genus, as corporeal with body; but if it is a lowest one, it is reduced to the definition. In distinguishing the predicates, however, nothing is said of the modes of predicating in quid or in quale quid, of genus and difference: because in order to the dialectical proposition and syllogism they make no distinction, since the mode of disputing probably is the same in those propositions in which the predicate is more universal than the subject and is within its essence, whether it is genus or difference. Nor are complex predicates different from incomplex ones, if they stand in the same way in order to the common subject: because one disputes in the same way about dialectical propositions made from either; and therefore definition is numbered among the predicates, though it is excluded from the predicables on account of its complexity.

87 Prædicabilia tandem in ordine ad prædicamenta sumuntur: & ideo definitio excluditur: quia prædicamentum ex solis simplicibus fit, genus verò, species, & differentia, in eo collocantur. Numerus verò prædicamentorum, ex diuersis modis essendi accipitur: quorum primus est modus essendi per se. Modi verò essendi in alio, qui accidentibus conueniunt, nouem sunt: & ideo sequitur decem esse prædicamenta, quatuor prædicata, & quinque prædicabilia.

87 The predicables, finally, are taken in order to the categories; and therefore definition is excluded, because a category is made of simple things alone, while genus, species and difference are placed in it. The number of the categories, however, is taken from the diverse modes of being, the first of which is the mode of being per se. But the modes of being in another, which belong to accidents, are nine; and therefore it follows that there are ten categories, four predicates, and five predicables.

Et ad formam argumenti, negandum est antecedens, quòd prædicatum, & prædicabile solùm distinguantur tanquam actus, & potentia: nam si prædicatum communissimè accipiatur, non est actus prædicabilis, nec etiam si accipiatur speciali modo, pro prædicato topico, sed solùm se habet ad prædicabile, sicut actus, si accipiatur tali modo, nempe vt petit natura eiusdem prædicabilis. Secundum verò argumentum huius partis, ex doctrina tradita solutum est.

And to the form of the argument, the antecedent must be denied, namely that predicate and predicable are distinguished only as act and potency: for if predicate is taken most commonly, it is not the act of the predicable; nor even if it is taken in a special way, for the topical predicate; but it stands to the predicable as act only if it is taken in such a way, namely as the nature of the same predicable requires. The second argument of this part, however, has been solved from the doctrine delivered.

Ad primum verò alterius partis respondeo, quòd Porphyrius non distinguit genus ab specie per ea, de quibus prędicantur, nisi adiuncto tali modo prædicandi, ex quo essentialis distinctio prædicabilium sumenda est.

To the first argument of the other part I reply that Porphyry does not distinguish genus from species by the things of which they are predicated, except with such a mode of predicating joined to them, from which the essential distinction of the predicables is to be taken. E iij

p. 70

Ad secundum argumentum, respondent quidam, indiuiduum vagum non prædicari vniuocè de Petro & Ioanne, sed æquiuocè: quia cùm indiuidua talia sunt per differentias indiuiduales omnino diuersas, nihil commune habere possunt, præter nomen. Ego verò probabilius esse teneo, quòd à differentiis indiuidualibus, possit abstrahi conceptus communis modalis: quia omnes conueniunt in eo, quòd sint modi particulares, & substantiales, determinantes speciem, vnde ratio modi particularis, in communi considerata, quam significat indiuiduum vagum, vniuoca est respectu indiuiduorum. Ideo alio modo respondeo concedendo, quòd indiuiduum vagum non prædicetur propriè in quid, sicut species, sed prædicatur modo simili, cùm significet modum substantialem: & ratione huius similitudinis reducitur ad prædicabile speciei: quia cùm non sit prædicatum naturę, sed modi eiusdem naturæ, non debet pro eo poni distinctum prædicabile, sed ad prædicabile naturæ reduci. Et eo modo sentiendum est de actuali existentia.

To the second argument some reply that the vague individual is not predicated univocally of Peter and John, but equivocally: because, since such individuals exist through altogether diverse individual differences, they can have nothing in common except the name. I, however, hold it more probable that a common modal concept can be abstracted from the individual differences, because they all agree in this, that they are particular and substantial modes determining the species; whence the ratio of particular mode, considered in common, which the vague individual signifies, is univocal with respect to the individuals. Therefore I reply in another way, granting that the vague individual is not properly predicated in quid, as species is, but is predicated in a similar way, since it signifies a substantial mode; and by reason of this similarity it is reduced to the predicable of species: because, since it is not a predicate of the nature but of a mode of the same nature, a distinct predicable ought not to be posited for it, but it ought to be reduced to the predicable of the nature. And one must think in the same way of actual existence.

Sed duo restant breuissima dubia, quæ aliquo modo pertinent ad numerum prædicabilium: & ideo in fine huius quæstionis soluenda sunt. Primum est, An supposito, quòd quinque prædicabilia sunt species vniuersales, Vniuersale sit genus immediatum eorum, vel remotum: ita vt inter illud, & prædicabilia, detur aliud genus immediatum, sicut viuens dicitur remotum genus hominis, & equi, quia inter ipsum, & species has mediat animal. Cui respondeo, non esse immediatum genus, sed remotum: quod hoc argumento probatur: A quacumque conuenientia essentiali, abstrahi potest conceptus communis eis, quæ essentialiter conueniunt: sed prædicabilia conueniunt essentialiter in aliqua ratione inferiori vniuersali, ergo illius rationis dari poterit conceptus vniuersali inferior, qui prædicabitur de eisdem specie differentibus: & ideo erit genus eorum immediatum, vniuersale verò remotum. Probatur minor, quia tria prædicabilia conueniunt in modo prædicandi intrinseco, aut essentiali, nempe genus, species & differentia: & duo alia in modo prædicandi accidentali, nempe, proprium, & accidens: ergo prædicabile essentialiter erit commune illis, & prædicatum accidentale erit commune his, & magis proximum, quàm vniuersale: & quodlibet prædicatur de pluribus speciebus: illud de tribus, hoc de duobus: ergo erunt genera magis proxima, quàm vniuersale, & consequenter non erit vniuersale genus proximum eorum, sed remotum.

But two very brief doubts remain which pertain in some way to the number of the predicables, and therefore they are to be solved at the end of this question. The first is whether, supposing that the five predicables are universal species, the universal is their immediate genus or a remote one, so that between it and the predicables there is given another immediate genus, as living is called the remote genus of man and horse, because animal mediates between it and these species. To which I reply that it is not the immediate genus but a remote one, which is proved by this argument: from any essential agreement a concept common to the things that agree essentially can be abstracted; but the predicables agree essentially in some ratio inferior to the universal; therefore a concept of that ratio inferior to the universal can be given, which will be predicated of the same things differing in species; and therefore it will be their immediate genus, and the universal a remote one. The minor is proved, because three predicables, namely genus, species and difference, agree in an intrinsic or essential mode of predicating, and two others, namely property and accident, in an accidental mode of predicating; therefore essentially predicable will be common to the former, and accidental predicate will be common to the latter, and nearer than the universal; and each is predicated of several species, the former of three, the latter of two; therefore they will be nearer genera than the universal, and consequently the universal will not be their proximate genus, but a remote one.

Secundum dubium est, An quinque prædicabilia sint

The second doubt is whether the five predicables are species

p. 71

species subalternæ, habentes sub se alias species, sicut animal, aut viuens, vel infimæ non habentes sub se alias species, sed solùm indiuidua, vt homo, vel equus, & reliquæ species infimæ aliorum generum. Si enim dicatur esse species subalternas, sequitur prædicabilia plura esse quàm quinque: quia cum eis debent connumerari species, quas sub se habent: si verò sint infimæ, non erit maior numerus prædicabilium Respondeo esse species infimas, quod ita probo: Prædicabilia distinguuntur specie, per diuersos modos prædicandi, sed isti modi non sunt diuisibiles in alios; ergo prædicabilia non habent alias species. Probatur minor: quia modus prædicandi generis est, quòd prædicetur, vt pars materialis speciei, & per modum totius potentialis, contrahibilis per differentias, sed impossibile est dari genus, quod non prædicetur eodem modo: ergo modus iste non est diuisibilis in alios, & hoc est genus esse speciem infimam vniuersalis, Et idem argumentum fit de cæteris prædicabilibus: quare nullum eorum species subalterna esse potest.

that are subalternate, having other species under them, as animal or living, or lowest ones, not having other species under them but only individuals, as man or horse, and the other lowest species of the other genera. For if they are said to be subalternate species, it follows that the predicables are more than five, because the species they have under them will have to be counted together with them; but if they are lowest, the number of the predicables will not be greater. I reply that they are lowest species, which I prove thus: the predicables are distinguished in species by the diverse modes of predicating; but these modes are not divisible into others; therefore the predicables do not have other species. The minor is proved: because the mode of predicating of genus is that it is predicated as the material part of the species and by way of a potential whole, contractible by differences; but it is impossible that there be a genus which is not predicated in the same way; therefore this mode is not divisible into others; and this is for genus to be a lowest species of the universal. And the same argument is made about the other predicables; wherefore none of them can be a subalternate species.

Tractatus de Natura entis rationis — TREATISE ON THE NATURE OF THE BEING OF REASON, AND OF SECOND INTENTIONS

Septem hoc ordine disputanda sunt de Ente rationis. Primum, An sit. Secundum, Quid sit Tertium, Quotuplex sit. Quartum, An à solo intellectu, vel ratione fiat, aut etiam ab aliis potentiis. Quintum, An à solo intellectu nostro vel etiam ab angelico, & diuino. Sextum, Ad quam scientiam pertineat de eo agere. Postremum, Quonam modo ad ordinem prædicamentalem reducatur.

even things are to be disputed in this order concerning the being of S reason. First, whether it exists. Second, what it is. Third, how manifold it is. Fourth, whether it is made by the intellect or reason alone, or also by other powers. Fifth, whether by our intellect alone, or also by the angelic and divine. Sixth, to which science it pertains to treat of it. Last, in what manner it is reduced to the categorial order.

1 Pauci quidam, & sine fundamento negant Ens rationis esse, vt Vallesius controuersia 9. ad Tyron. & alij: ideo non est opinio vocanda, nec tenenda, sed communi sententia totius scholæ: quod Ens rationis sit. Vt autem eam intelligamus, notandum est: duplex esse ens rationis Primum, quod directè, & per se fit à ratione, vel intellectu, & in eo inhæret,

1 Some few, and without foundation, deny that there is a being of reason, as Vallés, controversy 9, ad Tyron., and others; and therefore it is not to be called an opinion, nor to be held; but it is the common view of the whole school that there is a being of reason. But in order that we may understand it, it should be noted that the being of reason is twofold. The first, that which is made directly and per se by reason or the intellect, and inheres in it, E iiij

p. 72

tanquam in subiecto, & hoc est operatio ipsius intellectus: & ideo est Ens reale, sicut operatio visus: & solùm dicitur Ens rationis, quia fit à ratione: Aliud est Ens rationis: quod non fit directè ab intellectu, nec per se: sed quasi per accidens sequitur operationem eius, vt si intellectus componat hanc propositionem, Homo est animal: compositionem ipsam, quæ est operatio realis intellectus, sequitur denominatio propositionis, & prædicati, atque subiecti, quæ denominationes non sunt aliud, quàm relationes quædam rationis, totius propositionis comparatæ ad prædicatum, & subiectum, tanquam ad partes: & eiusdem prædicati, & subiecti inter se: nam eo ipso, quòd vnum attribuitur alteri, illud dicitur prædicatum, & hoc subiectum. Et primum ens rationis, non propriè dicitur tale, cùm sit Ens reale: & ideo non agimus de eo, sed solùm de secundo: quod non est in aliquo tanquam in subiecto, sed solùm habet esse, dum cognoscitur ab intellectu, & ideò dicitur solùm esse obiectiuè in intellectu De hoc ergo ente rationis est nostra conclusio, quòd sit in rerum natura: quæ colligitur ex Arist. 4. Met. tex 3. lib. 4. 13. & 4. & lib. 6. tex. 8. quibus locis docet, Ens vniuersalissimum, diuidi in illud, quod est in rebus, & aliud, quod non in rebus, sed solùm in mente dicitur esse. Quod est solùm esse obiectiuè in intellectu: & eandem conclusionem sequitur de tota schola.

as in a subject; and this is the operation of the intellect itself, and therefore it is a real being, like the operation of sight; and it is called a being of reason only because it is made by reason. The other is the being of reason which is not made directly by the intellect, nor per se, but follows its operation as it were per accidens: as, if the intellect composes this proposition, Man is an animal, the composition itself, which is a real operation of the intellect, is followed by the denomination of proposition, and of predicate and subject; and these denominations are nothing other than certain relations of reason, of the whole proposition compared to the predicate and the subject as to its parts, and of the same predicate and subject among themselves: for by the very fact that one is attributed to the other, the former is called the predicate and the latter the subject. And the first being of reason is not properly called such, since it is a real being; and therefore we do not treat of it, but only of the second, which is not in anything as in a subject, but only has being while it is known by the intellect; and therefore it is said only to be objectively in the intellect. Of this being of reason, then, is our conclusion, that it exists in the nature of things, which is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 3; bk. 4, 13 and 4; and bk. 6, text 8; in which places he teaches that the most universal being is divided into that which is in things, and that which is said to be not in things but only in the mind, which is only to be objectively in the intellect; and the whole school follows the same conclusion.

Probatur ratione, quia intellectus componit propositionem ex duobus extremis, quæ non distinguuntur à parte rei, vt ex homine & Petro: & ex solo Petro facit propositionem identicam, efficiens ipsum prędicatum, & subiectum: sed distinctio, & attributio vnius ad alterum, est ordinatio ad illud: & ordinatio est relatio inter illa, non realis: quia à parte rei, nec distinguitur Petrus à seipso, nec ad seipsum ordinatur: ergo est, relatio rationis, aut Ens rationis, sequitur ergo, quòd ens rationis detur, & sit.

It is proved by reason, because the intellect composes a proposition out of two extremes which are not distinguished on the part of the thing, as out of man and Peter; and out of Peter alone it makes an identical proposition, making him the predicate and the subject; but the distinction and attribution of one to the other is an ordering to it, and the ordering is a relation between them, not a real one, because on the part of the thing Peter is neither distinguished from himself nor ordered to himself; therefore it is a relation of reason, or a being of reason. It follows, then, that a being of reason is given and exists.

Quid sit Ens rationis.

What the being of reason is. 2

2 Circa essentiam Entis rationis, est prima opinio, asserentium: Omnem denominationem extrinsecam esse Ens rationis, vt denominatio, à qua paries dicitur dexter: quia est à manu dextra hominis, aut lapis dicitur visus, quia videtur à nobis. Quod probant primò, Quia denominatio est opus rationis: ergo non datur ante operationem intellectus: sed denominationes extrinsecæ nihil in rebus denominatis ponunt, præter denominationem ipsam, quam intellectus efficit: ergo sunt entia rationis. Probatur minor, quia lapis nihil acquirit per hoc, quòd sit ad meam dexteram, nisi denominationem

Concerning the essence of the being of reason, the first opinion is that of those who assert that every extrinsic denomination is a being of reason: as the denomination by which a wall is called right, because it is at the right hand of a man, or a stone is called seen, because it is seen by us. Which they prove, first, because denomination is a work of reason; therefore it is not given before the operation of the intellect; but extrinsic denominations posit nothing in the things denominated besides the denomination itself, which the intellect effects; therefore they are beings of reason. The minor is proved, because the stone acquires nothing by being at my right, except the denomination

p. 73

dextri, & sic de reliquis.

of right; and so of the rest.

Secundò, denominationes extrinsecæ sunt relatiuæ, & non fiũt à relationibus realibus: ergo à relationibus rationis, quod est esse Entia rationis. Maiorem sic probo: Quia per denominationes extrinsecas referuntur res denominatæ ad alias, vt paries dexter, ad hominem, ad cuius dexteram est: Minorem verò: quia per tales denominationes nullam relationem realem acquirunt res denominatæ: vt paries ex eo quòd videatur, non acquirit relationem realem ad hominem eum videntem.

Second, extrinsic denominations are relative, and are not made by real relations; therefore by relations of reason, which is to be beings of reason. I prove the major thus: because through extrinsic denominations the things denominated are referred to others, as the wall that is right to the man at whose right it is. And the minor: because through such denominations the things denominated acquire no real relation, as the wall, from the fact that it is seen, does not acquire a real relation to the man seeing it.

Sed hæc sententia falsa est. Probatur duobus argumentis. Primò. Ens rationis non habet aliud esse, quàm cognosci ab intellectu, & ideo non datur ante operationem intellectus: sed denominationes extrinsecæ dantur ante operationem intellectus: ergo non sunt Entia rationis. Probatur minor. Deus dicitur creator, & paries qui videtur ab aliquo animali, dicitur visus, non solùm antequam cognoscantur ab intellectu: sed etiam si nullus sit intellectus in rerum natura: ergo denominationes extrinsecæ dantur ante operationem intellectus, & ideo non possunt esse Entia rationis.

But this opinion is false. It is proved by two arguments. First, the being of reason has no other being than to be known by the intellect, and therefore it is not given before the operation of the intellect; but extrinsic denominations are given before the operation of the intellect; therefore they are not beings of reason. The minor is proved: God is called creator, and a wall that is seen by some animal is called seen, not only before they are known by the intellect, but even if there were no intellect in the nature of things; therefore extrinsic denominations are given before the operation of the intellect, and therefore they cannot be beings of reason.

Secundò: Istæ denominationes (quamuis non fiant ab aliqua forma inhærente in rebus denominatis, & ideo appellentur extrinsecæ) reales sunt: ergo non sunt Entia rationis. Consequentia euidens est: quia Ens rationis nihil habet reale, sed solùm cognosci ab intellectu. Antecedens probatur, quid Deus realiter dicitur creator, & paries realiter visus. Ergo denominationes istæ sunt reales.

Second: these denominations (although they are not made by any form inhering in the things denominated, and are therefore called extrinsic) are real; therefore they are not beings of reason. The consequence is evident, because the being of reason has nothing real, but only to be known by the intellect. The antecedent is proved, because God is really called creator, and the wall really seen. Therefore these denominations are real.

Ad argumentum huius opinionis, distinguendum est antecedens, quòd denominatio sit opus rationis. Nam denominatio duplex est. Vna, quæ fit ab aliqua forma reali, siue inhęreat in re denominata, quales sunt denominationes intrinsecæ: aut in alia ab ea diuersa, vt denominationes extrinsecę: & istę non sunt opus rationis, nec ab intellectu dependent, sicut nec dependet forma realis, à qua fiunt. quia si dependerent: sicut non denominatur paries visus, ante operationem intellectus, ita nec denominaretur homo albus ab albedine, quod patet esse falsum. Alia est denominatio, quæ non fit à forma reali: sed solùm tribuitur ab intellectu rebus intellectis. Vt denominatio subiecti, aut prædicati: & de hac denominatione verum est, quòd sit opus rationis, sicut forma à qua fit. Quæ est relatio rationis, dicitur fieri ab intellectu.

To the argument of this opinion, the antecedent must be distinguished, that denomination is a work of reason. For denomination is twofold. One, which is made by some real form, whether it inheres in the thing denominated, such as intrinsic denominations are, or in another thing diverse from it, as extrinsic denominations; and these are not a work of reason, nor do they depend on the intellect, just as the real form by which they are made does not depend on it; because if they did depend on it, just as the wall is not denominated seen before the operation of the intellect, so neither would a man be denominated white by whiteness, which is plainly false. The other is the denomination which is not made by a real form but is only attributed by the intellect to things understood, as the denomination of subject or of predicate; and of this denomination it is true that it is a work of reason, as is the form by which it is made, which is a relation of reason and is said to be made by the intellect.

Secunda opinio asserit, Non omnes denominationes extrinsecas esse Entia rationis: sed eas tantùm, quas res cognita accipit ab actu intellectu: per quem cognoscitur, & à quo

The second opinion asserts that not all extrinsic denominations are beings of reason, but only those which things known receive from the act of the intellect by which they are known, and from which

p. 74

denominatur intellecta & cognita. Et vt vno verbo sensus huius opinionis declaretur, Ens rationis asserit esse, illud esse cognitum, quod acquirit res, quando cognoscitur ab intellectu: quod patet esse extrinsecam denominationem.

they are denominated understood and known. And so that the sense of this opinion may be declared in one word, it asserts that the being of reason is that being-known which a thing acquires when it is known by the intellect, which is plainly an extrinsic denomination.

Sed hæc opinio eisdem rationibus probatur falsa, quibus falsitas alterius probata est, quia non est minùs realis denominatio cogniti (quamuis sit extrinseca) quàm denominatio visi in pariete, aut denominatio creatoris in Deo: ergo non potest esse Ens rationis, quia Ens rationis nihil reale habet

But this opinion is proved false by the same reasons by which the falsity of the other was proved: because the denomination of known (although it is extrinsic) is no less real than the denomination of seen in the wall, or the denomination of creator in God; therefore it cannot be a being of reason, because the being of reason has nothing real.

Communis sententia duabus conclusionibus explicatur. Prima, Ens rationis non est aliquid inhærens in rebus denominatis, nec denominatio extrinseca ab aliqua forma reali existente in alio, sed sola denominatio, quã eis tribuit intellectus. Probatur hoc argumento: Esse genus, aut esse speciem, non cõuenit homini, aut animali à parte rei, sed has denominationes tribuit eis intellectus per cõparationem ad inferiora: ergo, nec sunt aliquid inhærens, nec fiunt ab aliqua forma reali existente in alio. Probatur cõsequentia, quia id quod inhæret alicui, vel fit à forma inhærente in alio, conuenit illi à parte rei.

The common view is explained in two conclusions. The first: the being of reason is not something inhering in the things denominated, nor an extrinsic denomination from some real form existing in another, but solely a denomination which the intellect attributes to them. This is proved by this argument: to be a genus, or to be a species, does not belong to man or to animal on the part of the thing, but the intellect attributes these denominations to them through comparison to their inferiors; therefore they are neither something inhering, nor are they made by some real form existing in another. The consequence is proved, because that which inheres in something, or is made by a form inhering in another, belongs to it on the part of the thing.

Secunda conclusio: Licèt Ens rationis non sit aliquid inhærens, & ideo possit dici extrinseca denominatio, tamen habet similitudinem cum forma inhærente, & propter hanc similitudinem potest dici denominatio intrinseca. Prima pars huius conclusionis, sequitur euidenter ex conclusione præcedente iam probata: secunda verò pars, quòd possit dici denominatio intrinseca, propter similitudinem, probatur: quia denominatio generis, speciei, prædicati, & subiecti, similes sunt denominationibus realibus, prouenientibus à formis inhærentibus, vt denominationibus albi, & nigri: ergo sicut istæ sunt verè denominationes intrinsecæ, ita illæ possunt dici intrinsecæ per similitudinem.

Second conclusion: although the being of reason is not something inhering, and can therefore be called an extrinsic denomination, it nevertheless has a likeness to an inhering form, and on account of this likeness it can be called an intrinsic denomination. The first part of this conclusion follows evidently from the preceding conclusion, already proved; the second part, that it can be called an intrinsic denomination on account of the likeness, is proved because the denominations of genus, species, predicate and subject are like real denominations proceeding from inhering forms, such as the denominations of white and black; therefore, just as the latter are truly intrinsic denominations, so the former can be called intrinsic by likeness.

Quotuplex sit Ens rationis.

How manifold the being of reason is.

Prima diuisione diuiditur Ens rationis, in illud quod habet fundamentum in re: & aliud, quod non habet fundamentum, sed verè impossibile est. Ens rationis habens fundamentum, est denominatio illa, quæ attribuitur ab intellectu rebus tali modo ab eo cognitis, quam denominationem petit natura earum, vt tali modo cognita. Verbi gratia, dum cognoscit intellectus naturam humanam abstractam ab indiuiduis, & eam comparat cum eis, petit, vt ita cognita, denominationem speciei: & ideo talis denominatio est Ens rationis, habens fundamentum in re.

By the first division the being of reason is divided into that which has a foundation in the thing, and that which has no foundation but is truly impossible. The being of reason having a foundation is that denomination which is attributed by the intellect to things known by it in such a way that their nature, as known in such a way, requires that denomination. For example, when the intellect knows human nature abstracted from individuals and compares it with them, it requires, as so known, the denomination of species; and therefore such a denomination is a being of reason having a foundation in the thing.

p. 75
