Sed fundamentum hoc duobus modis intelligitur à diuersis modernis. Primò, ita vt solùm consistat in modo nostro intelligendi, qui ea quæ verè non sunt distincta, distinguit, & ea quæ verè non sunt separata ab inferioribus, separat, vel abstrahit, non tamen in rebus ipsis. Ab aliis verò non solùm in nostro modo intelligendi, sed in rebus ipsis cognitis fundamentum habere Entia rationis affirmatur.

But this foundation is understood in two ways by different moderns. First, so that it consists only in our mode of understanding, which distinguishes things that are not truly distinct, and separates or abstracts things that are not truly separated from their inferiors, but not in the things themselves. By others, however, it is affirmed that beings of reason have a foundation not only in our mode of understanding but in the known things themselves.

Sed pro huius intelligentia notandum est. Primò: necessarium esse ad efficienda Entia rationis, & attribuenda rebus cognitis, quòd imperfectè cognoscantur: hoc est, per plures conceptus, cùm tamen per vnum cognosci possent ab intellectu perfectè cognoscente. Exempli gratia; vt intellectus attribuat homini denominationem speciei, & prædicati, huius propositionis: Petrus est homo, debet illum cognoscere quasi abstractum, aut separatum, atque distinctum ab eo, cùm tamen à parte rei, non distinguatur, nec separatus sit. Verùm hoc sine mendacio facit, quia sine affirmatione aut negatione, sed per hoc tantùm, quòd vnum cognoscit sine alio: & hoc prouenit ex imperfecto modo cognoscendi, quia non totum simul, sed quasi per partes cognoscit, vel per diuersos gradus. Vt dum distinguit in anima rationali, gradum vegetandi, sentiendi atque intelligendi, cùm tamen anima ipsa sit simplex quædam substantia.

But for the understanding of this it should be noted, first, that for producing beings of reason and attributing them to known things it is necessary that the things be known imperfectly, that is, through several concepts, although they could be known through one by an intellect that knows perfectly. For example, in order that the intellect may attribute to man the denomination of species, and of predicate of this proposition, Peter is a man, it must know it as it were abstracted, or separated and distinct from him, although on the part of the thing it is neither distinguished nor separated. But it does this without falsehood, because it does it without affirmation or negation, but only through knowing one thing without another; and this proceeds from an imperfect mode of knowing, because it knows not the whole at once but as it were by parts, or by diverse grades: as when it distinguishes in the rational soul the grade of vegetating, of sensing and of understanding, although the soul itself is a certain simple substance.

Secundò notandum est, in rebus ipsis cognitis dari etiam fundamentum, vt cognoscantur distinctæ, aut vt eis attribuatur talis denominatio, quæ dicitur Ens rationis: vt in rebus compositis ex materia, & forma, reperitur vnitas formalis, quam tribuit ei forma, & etiam vnitas numerica, quæ ex hac materia, & forma sumitur, aut si ex sola forma diuersa ratione ac sumitur numerica: quia Formalis sumitur à forma, vt est principium, & radix prædicatorum essentialium: Numerica verò ab eadem, vt est principalis pars componens. Ex hoc ergo reperitur fundamentum in natura humana, vt intelligi possit in ea vnitas formalis, non intellecta vnitate numerica: quod est abstrahi ab indiuiduis, atque etiam, vt cum multis eorum comparetur, & denominetur species, aut cum vno tantùm, per modum attributionis, & denominetur prædicatum.

It should be noted, second, that in the known things themselves there is also given a foundation for their being known as distinct, or for such a denomination, which is called a being of reason, being attributed to them: as in things composed of matter and form there is found the formal unity which the form gives it, and also the numerical unity, which is taken from this matter and form, or, if from the form alone, it is taken as numerical under a different ratio: because the Formal unity is taken from the form as it is the principle and root of the essential predicates, but the Numerical unity from the same form as it is the principal component part. From this, then, there is found a foundation in human nature for the formal unity in it to be understood without the numerical unity being understood, which is to be abstracted from the individuals; and also for it to be compared with many of them and denominated species, or with only one, by way of attribution, and denominated predicate.

His suppositis, nostra sententia explicatur duabus conclusionibus. Prima est: Ens rationis aliquando habet fundamentum, nõ solùm in nostro modo intelligendi imperfecto, sed in rebus ipsis quæ ex propria natura habent fundamentum, vt eis tribuatur talis denominatio. Probatur vnico argumento, ex doctrina tradita nõ solùm in nostro modo cognoscẽdi imperfecto,

These things supposed, our view is explained in two conclusions. The first is: the being of reason sometimes has a foundation not only in our imperfect mode of understanding, but in the things themselves, which from their own nature have a foundation for such a denomination being attributed to them. It is proved by a single argument from the doctrine delivered: not only in our imperfect mode of knowing,

p. 76

sed in rebus quas concipimus, datur aliquando fundamentum, vt possit in eis cognosci vnum sine alio, ergo datur fundamentum, vt possint eis tribui denominationes, quæ sunt entia rationis. Probatur antecedens, Primò: In natura humana, in qua datur fundamentum, cognoscendi vnitatem formalem, non cognita vnitate numerica: ergo datur fundamentum abstrahendi eam ab indiuiduis, & comparandi cum multis, comparatione simplici, & attribuendi ei denominationem speciei, aut cum vno tantùm comparatione composita, per modum attributionis, & tribuendi illi denominationem prædicati Secundò: In anima rationali, in qua datur fundamentum distinguendi gradum vegetatiuum, sensitiuum, & rationalem, & hoc fundamentum non est aliud, quàm eminentia seu perfectio eius, ratione cuius sub gradu formæ superioris non dependentis à materia, continet alios gradus, qui in diuersis formis inferioribus reperiuntur.

but in the things we conceive, there is sometimes given a foundation for one thing in them being able to be known without another; therefore there is given a foundation for denominations which are beings of reason being able to be attributed to them. The antecedent is proved. First: in human nature, in which there is given a foundation for knowing the formal unity without the numerical unity being known; therefore there is given a foundation for abstracting it from the individuals, and for comparing it with many by a simple comparison and attributing to it the denomination of species, or with only one by a composite comparison, by way of attribution, and attributing to it the denomination of predicate. Second: in the rational soul, in which there is given a foundation for distinguishing the vegetative, sensitive and rational grade; and this foundation is nothing other than its eminence or perfection, by reason of which, under the grade of a superior form not depending on matter, it contains the other grades which are found in diverse inferior forms.

7 Secunda conclusio. Entia rationis aliquando non habẽt fundamentum in rebus quibus attribuuntur, sed in aliis, aut in solo modo nostro intelligendi imperfecto. In hac conclusione conueniunt omnes, & probatur duplici exemplo. Primò, in Deo, in quo distinguimus iustitiam à misericordia: non propter fundamentum in eis existens, sed in creaturis, in quibus virtutes istæ distinctæ sunt. Secundò in propositionibus, quæ dicuntur Identicæ, quia idem prædicatur de se ipso, vt in hac, Petrus est Petrus: in qua intellectus distinguit Petrum à seipso, cùm faciens quasi duos: & tribuit illi denominationem prædicati, & subiecti, cuius distinctionis nullum est fundamentum in eo, sed solùm in modo cognoscendi imperfecto, qui distinguit quasi in duo extrema illud, quod in se nec distinctum est, nec habet fundamentum, vt à seipso distinguatur.

7 Second conclusion: beings of reason sometimes have no foundation in the things to which they are attributed, but in other things, or in our imperfect mode of understanding alone. In this conclusion all agree, and it is proved by a twofold example. First, in God, in whom we distinguish justice from mercy, not on account of a foundation existing in them, but in creatures, in which these virtues are distinct. Second, in propositions which are called Identical, because the same thing is predicated of itself, as in this one, Peter is Peter, in which the intellect distinguishes Peter from himself, making him as it were two, and attributes to him the denomination of predicate and of subject; of which distinction there is no foundation in him, but only in the imperfect mode of knowing, which distinguishes as it were into two extremes that which in itself is neither distinct nor has a foundation for being distinguished from itself.

Ex his conclusionibus sequitur, distinctionem rationis duplicem esse, vt communis consensus scholæ asserit. Vna est, quę habet fundamentum in rebus ipsis, & hæc dicitur distinctio Rationis ratiocinatæ, quam ponimus inter vniuersale, & singularia, & inter diuersos gradus vegetandi, sentiendi, & intelligendi animæ rationalis: Alia est distinctio, non habens fundamentum in re ipsa cognita, sed in aliis, aut solùm in nostro modo cognoscendi imperfecto, vt ea, quam ponimus inter Petrum, & seipsum, dum prædicatur in propositione identica. Et hæc de Entibus rationis habentibus fundamẽtum in rebus.

From these conclusions it follows that the distinction of reason is twofold, as the common consensus of the school asserts. One is that which has a foundation in the things themselves, and this is called the distinction of Reasoned Reason, which we posit between the universal and the singulars, and between the diverse grades of vegetating, sensing and understanding of the rational soul. The other is the distinction having no foundation in the known thing itself, but in other things, or only in our imperfect mode of knowing, as that which we posit between Peter and himself when he is predicated in an identical proposition. And so much concerning beings of reason having a foundation in things.

8 Alia sunt Entia rationis, quæ nullũ habent fundamentum in rebus: sed ex quibusdam impossibilibus ab intellectu coniunctis finguntur, vt Chimæra, & Sphinx. Ex impossibilibus

8 There are other beings of reason which have no foundation in things, but are feigned by the intellect out of certain impossible things joined together, as the Chimera and the Sphinx. Out of impossible

p. 77

coniunctis fieri dicimus: non quòd impossibilia in se sint, hoc enim est necessarium: sed quia licèt possibilia sint, coniunctio tamen impossibilis iudicatur: & hoc modo dicitur Chimæra impossibilis: quia ex rebus diuersæ speciei, vt ex parte aliqua hominis, & ex alia parte leonis, alteriúsve animalis quasi composita fingitur. Et huiusmodi Entia rationis, in infinitum possunt multiplicari ab intellectu, sicut infinitis modis potest res diuersæ speciei coniungere.

joined together we say they are made: not because they are impossible in themselves, for this is necessary, but because, although they are possible, their conjunction is judged impossible. And in this way the Chimera is called impossible, because it is feigned as it were composed of things of different species, as of some part of a man and of another part of a lion or of some other animal. And beings of reason of this kind can be multiplied to infinity by the intellect, just as it can join things of different species in infinite ways.

9 Secunda diuisio Entis rationis, quasi subdiuisio est primi membri. nam Ens rationis habens fundamentum in rebus, diuiditur in tria membra, nempe, in Negationem, Priuationẽ, & Relationem quam diuisionem insinuauit Arist. 4. li. Met. tex. 2. & li. 5. c. 7. tex. 14. asserens priuationem, & negationem, esse non Entia: vt significarent non esse vera Entia realia, sed ad similitudinem eorũ facta ab intellectu. Et in secundo loco, præter vera Entia quædam alia esse docet, non tam vera secundùm entitatem, quam secũdùm veritatem prędicationis, tam affirmatiuę, quam negatiuæ: quæ non possunt esse, nisi Entia rationis, quæ vocantur priuationes, & negationes. De relatione verò rationis, egit ca 15. eiusdem libri, explicans relationes tertij generis mensurabilis, & mensuræ, docénsque mensuram referri ad mẽsurabile, non per relationem intrinsecam, sed extrinsecam, mensurabilis ad ipsam, cùm tamen certum sit, nihil posse ad aliud ordinari, nisi per relationem in se existentem, quam certum est etiam non habere mensuram in se, quæ potiòr est res absoluta. Intelligit ergo Arist. inferri, per relationem factam ab intellectu, eandem mensuram ordinare ad mensurabile, ac si ex propria natura ordinaretur. Eandem diuisionem videtur colligere ex his locis D. Tho. qu. 21. de veritate art. 1. d. 1. qu. 1. art. 3 & d. 13. q 1. art. 1. & est iam communis in schola.

9 The second division of the being of reason is as it were a subdivision of the first member. For the being of reason having a foundation in things is divided into three members, namely into Negation, Privation and Relation; which division Aristotle intimated in Metaph. bk. 4, text 2, and bk. 5, ch. 7, text 14, asserting that privation and negation are non-beings, so as to signify that they are not true real beings, but made by the intellect after their likeness. And in the second place he teaches that besides true beings there are certain others, true not so much according to entity as according to the truth of predication, affirmative as well as negative; which cannot be anything but beings of reason, which are called privations and negations. Of the relation of reason, however, he treated in ch. 15 of the same book, explaining the relations of the third kind, of the measurable and the measure, and teaching that the measure is referred to the measurable not by an intrinsic relation but by an extrinsic one, of the measurable to it; although it is certain that nothing can be ordered to another except by a relation existing in itself, which it is also certain that the measure does not have in itself, since it is rather an absolute thing. Aristotle therefore means it to be inferred that, through a relation made by the intellect, the same measure is ordered to the measurable as if it were ordered from its own nature. St. Thomas seems to gather the same division from these places: q. 21 On Truth, a. 1; d. 1, q. 2, a. 3; and d. 13, q. 1, a. 1; and it is also common in the school.

Sed circa Negationem: & Priuationem, duo sunt adnotanda, vt eorum natura, & distinctio intelligatur: Primum est, duobus modis posse vtramque considerari: Primò secundùm se, aut secundùm suas essentias, nempè, vt sunt negationes alicuius formę realis, & in hac significatione dicuntur ab Aristotele non Entia realia: quia cùm Ens reale habeat esse ab aliqua forma reali, negatio aut priuatio quæ formam realem negant, consequenter dicuntur negare Ens reale: & ideo non esse entia realia, sed potiùs non entia, vt Arist. 1. & 5. lib. Physicorum docuit. Quod de Ente simpliciter intelligendum est, nam negationes formæ realis, entia realia secundùm quid vocantur, hoc est, non positiua, sed negatiua. In hac etiam significatione docuit Aristoteles 1. lib. Physicorum de priuatione, quòd

But concerning Negation and Privation two things are to be noted, so that their nature and distinction may be understood. The first is that both can be considered in two ways. First, according to themselves, or according to their essences, namely as they are negations of some real form; and in this signification they are called by Aristotle not real beings: because, since real being has being from some real form, negation or privation, which deny the real form, are consequently said to deny real being, and therefore not to be real beings, but rather non-beings, as Aristotle taught in Phys. 1 and 5. Which is to be understood of being simply; for negations of a real form are called real beings in a qualified sense, that is, not positive but negative ones. In this signification too Aristotle taught in Phys. 1, concerning privation, that

p. 78

sit principium rei naturalis. Et de negationibus, docet D. Thõ. in opusculo de Ente, & Essentia, quòd sint de essentia naturæ realis. Vt de essentia hominis est esse non equum, aut non hennibilem. In hac tandem significatione sumptæ, verum est, & necessarium, quòd dentur ante operationem intellectus, & ab eo non dependeant. Probatur euidenter, quia non potest priuatio esse principium generationis naturalis, si dependeat ab intellectu, ante cuius operationem certum est eandem generationem dari. Non potest esse negatio de essentia naturæ realis, si non detur ante operationem intellectus, hoc modo sumpta.

it is a principle of a natural thing. And of negations St. Thomas teaches, in the opusculum On Being and Essence, that they belong to the essence of a real nature: as it is of the essence of man to be not a horse, or not capable of neighing. Taken, finally, in this signification, it is true and necessary that they are given before the operation of the intellect and do not depend on it. This is proved evidently: because privation cannot be a principle of natural generation if it depends on the intellect, before whose operation it is certain that that same generation is given. Negation cannot belong to the essence of a real nature if it is not given before the operation of the intellect, taken in this way.

Alio modo sumi possunt Priuatio, & Negatio, vt attribuuntur rebus in propositione: & hoc modo non accipiuntur secundùm rationem negationis & priuationis, sed ad similitudinem formæ positiuæ, quia quod alteri attribuitur forma positiua esse debet, aut similitudinem eius habere: & quia sumi per modum formæ positiuæ non habent ex se, sed solùm ab intellectu, ideo hoc modo sumptæ, ab eo dependent: ante operationem eius non dantur. neque vllo modo possunt esse Entia realia, sed sunt Entia rationis. Quod hoc exemplo explicare possumus: dum dicimus hominem esse cæcum, non sumimus cæcitatem vt negationem, sed priuationem visus: quia hoc modo sumpta, non propriè dicitur esse in alio, sed potiùs tollere formam ab eo, ergo nec vt priuatio est, alteri attribuitur in propositione, sed in quantum concipitur ad similitudinem formæ positiuæ: & cùm hoc habeat à solo intellectu, ab eo etiam necessariò dependere dicitur, & ante operationem eius non dari: quæ sunt conditiones propriæ Entis rationis.

In another way Privation and Negation can be taken as they are attributed to things in a proposition; and in this way they are not taken according to the ratio of negation and privation, but after the likeness of a positive form, because what is attributed to another must be a positive form or have its likeness; and since they do not have of themselves to be taken by way of a positive form, but only from the intellect, therefore, taken in this way, they depend on it: they are not given before its operation, nor can they in any way be real beings, but they are beings of reason. Which we can explain by this example: when we say that a man is blind, we do not take blindness as a negation but as a privation of sight; because, taken in this way, it is not properly said to be in another, but rather to take away a form from it; therefore neither is it attributed to another in a proposition as it is a privation, but inasmuch as it is conceived after the likeness of a positive form; and since it has this from the intellect alone, it is also said necessarily to depend on it and not to be given before its operation; which are the proper conditions of a being of reason.

Secundò notandum est, pro intelligenda distinctione priuationis à negatione, quòd in vno cõueniunt, & in alio distinguuntur: Conueniunt in eo, quòd vtraqne est negatio formæ realis in subiecto. differunt verò: quia Negatio solùm negat formam subiectio, siue sit aptum eam habere, siue non: Priuatio verò dicit negationem formæ, non in quocunque subiecto, sed apto habere illam: vnde non dicitur lapis cæcus, etiam si non habeat visum, quia non habet aptitudinem habendi illum, sed bene homo, vel animal: in quibus si non sit, est tamen aptitudo habendi visum.

It should be noted, second, for understanding the distinction of privation from negation, that they agree in one thing and are distinguished in another. They agree in this, that each is a negation of a real form in a subject. But they differ, because Negation only denies the form of the subject, whether it is apt to have it or not; whereas Privation expresses the negation of a form not in any subject whatever, but in one apt to have it. Whence a stone is not called blind, even if it does not have sight, because it does not have the aptitude for having it; but a man or an animal is rightly so called, in which, if it is not present, there is nevertheless the aptitude for having sight.

Ex quibus intelligitur, quonam modo distinguantur Priuatio, & Negatio: distinguuntur enim distinctione formali, quæ vocari solet Includentis, & inclusi: quia priuatio includit negationem, & addit supra illam ordinem ad determinatum subiectum, aptum habere formam, qua caret, cùm tamen negatio

From which it is understood in what manner Privation and Negation are distinguished: for they are distinguished by a formal distinction, which is usually called that of the Including and the included; because privation includes negation and adds over it an order to a determinate subject apt to have the form which it lacks, whereas negation

p. 79

non dicat ordinem, nisi ad subiectum non habens, siue aptum sit habere, siue non.

does not express an order except to a subject without it, whether it is apt to have it or not.

Ex his, quæ de diuersitate Entium rationis dicta sunt, sequitur non esse absolutè asserendum, quòd ens rationis, sit Ens confictum ab intellectu, sed solùm esse verã hanc locutionem, de Ente rationis non habente fundamentum in rebus, quibus attribuitur: vt Chimæra aut Sphinge, non verò de iis, quę habent fundamentum. Et huius ratio est manifesta: quia fingere solùm dicitur ille, qui sine aliquo fundamento loquitur: locutio verò aliquo modo fundata in veritate, aut natura rerum, non propriè dicitur ficta: sed propriè loquendum est, de his Entibus rationis, dicendum est, quòd facta sint ab intellectu, præsupposito fundamento in rebus.

From what has been said about the diversity of beings of reason, it follows that it is not to be asserted absolutely that a being of reason is a being feigned by the intellect, but that this way of speaking is true only of the being of reason having no foundation in the things to which it is attributed, as the Chimera or the Sphinx, but not of those which have a foundation. And the reason for this is manifest: because only he is said to feign who speaks without any foundation; but speech in some way founded in the truth or nature of things is not properly called feigned; but, speaking properly of these beings of reason, it must be said that they are made by the intellect, a foundation in things being presupposed.

Per quam potentiam, & operationem fiat Ens rationis.

By what power and operation the being of reason is made.

AD hoc dubium respondent aliqui, nõ solùm intellectum efficere Entia rationis, sed etiam sensus interiores præsertim imaginationem, vel phantasiam, de qua scimus, quòd fingat montem aureum, qui cùm non detur in rerum natura, vocabitur Ens fictum ab imaginatione, quod est Ens rationis.

To this doubt some reply that not only the intellect produces beings of reason, but also the interior senses, especially the imagination or phantasy, of which we know that it feigns a golden mountain, which, since it is not given in the nature of things, will be called a being feigned by the imagination, which is a being of reason.

Nos verò sub distinctione respõdendum esse asserimus: nam Entia rationis ficta, hoc est, non habentia fundamẽtum in re, non solùm ab intellectu, sed etiam à phantasia, fieri possunt: ea verò, quæ habent fundamentum, solùm ab intellectu. Et de primis patet, fieri à phantasia, quasi componente vnum aliquid non existens in rerum natura ex duobus verè existentibus, vt ex speciebus montis, & auri, componit montem aureum, quod non potest fieri ab aliquo alio sensu, nec à voluntate aut appetitu: quia non habent talem virtutem componendi. Entia verò rationis, quę habent fundamentum in rebus, non possunt fieri ab alia potentia, nisi à solo intellectu. Et ratio huius est, quia hæc Entia rationis sunt denominationes quædam vel relationes, quas intellectus tribuit naturis, iam cognitis à se, per aliam cognitionem: vnde quasi per cognitionem reflexam fieri dicuntur: sed nulla alia potentia præter intellectum habet hanc virtutem reflexiuam, per quam possit sumere pro obiecto rem, vt à se cognitam alia cognitione: ergo nec habet virtutem efficiendi Entia rationis. Maior est manifesta ex his, quæ diximus in quæst. 5. Vniuersalium, de modo, quo Vniuersale fit ab intellectu per simplicem comparationem. Diximus enim Comparationem esse cognitionem, per quam intellectus quasi reflectitur supra naturam iam cognitam, per simplicem abstractionem: & naturam ita cognitam comparat ad

We, however, assert that one must reply with a distinction: for beings of reason that are feigned, that is, that have no foundation in the thing, can be made not only by the intellect but also by the phantasy; but those which have a foundation, only by the intellect. And of the first it is plain that they are made by the phantasy, as it were composing some one thing not existing in the nature of things out of two truly existing ones: as out of the species of mountain and of gold it composes a golden mountain; which cannot be done by any other sense, nor by the will or appetite, because they do not have such a power of composing. But beings of reason which have a foundation in things cannot be made by any other power except by the intellect alone. And the reason for this is that these beings of reason are certain denominations or relations which the intellect attributes to natures already known by it, through another cognition; whence they are said to be made as it were by a reflex cognition; but no other power besides the intellect has this reflexive power, by which it can take as object a thing as known by itself through another cognition; therefore neither does it have the power of producing beings of reason. The major is manifest from what we said in q. 5 on Universals, about the mode in which the universal is made by the intellect through simple comparison. For we said that Comparison is a cognition by which the intellect as it were reflects upon the nature already known through simple abstraction, and compares the nature so known to

p. 80

inferiora. Minor verò manifesta est, quia reflexio hæc non potest conuenire voluntati, quæ nihil cognoscit, sed tendit in obiectum cognitum ab intellectu: nec minùs potest tribui sensibus, quorum cognitio imperfectissima est: & ideo non possunt operari circa rem, vt à se iam cognitam: quamuis possit contingere, quòd eandem rem cognitam, iterum cognoscant, non tamen cognitione reflexa, sed pluribus cognitionibus quasi directis.

its inferiors. The minor, however, is manifest, because this reflection cannot belong to the will, which knows nothing but tends to the object known by the intellect; nor can it be attributed to the senses, whose cognition is most imperfect; and therefore they cannot operate about a thing as already known by themselves; although it may happen that they know again the same thing already known, yet not by a reflex cognition, but by several cognitions that are as it were direct.

Sed iam, quòd à solo intellectu fiant entia rationis, poterit quis dubitare, per quam operationem eius fiant: An per primam, quæ est apprehensio simplicium, aut per secundam, quæ est compositio, & diuisio, per discursum: qui est tertia. Respondent quidam, non posse fieri per primam, & probant hac ratione: Entia rationis fiunt per comparationem naturæ cum inferioribus, aut prædicati cum subiecto: sed omnis comparatio est compositio, aut diuisio, & actualis prędicatio: ergo non possunt fieri per simplicem apprehensionem.

But now, granted that beings of reason are made by the intellect alone, someone could doubt by which of its operations they are made: whether by the first, which is the apprehension of simples, or by the second, which is composition and division, or by discursive reasoning, which is the third. Some reply that they cannot be made by the first, and they prove it by this reason: beings of reason are made through the comparison of the nature with its inferiors, or of the predicate with the subject; but every comparison is a composition or division, and an actual predication; therefore they cannot be made through simple apprehension.

Communis tamen sententia à nobis sequenda tenet, (vt vidimus in quæst. 5. vniuersali) quædam entia rationis fieri per primam operationem intellectus, alia per secundum, & quædam alia per tertiam. Quod hoc argumento probatur. Quædam Entia rationis conueniunt simplicibus, priusquam ex eis fiat compositio: alia conueniunt eisdem simplicibus, vt sunt iam in compositione, vel ipsi compositioni: alia denique compositionibus, vt sunt in syllogismo: ergo per singulas has operationes fiunt diuersa Entia rationis. Probatur antecedens, quia per simplicem comparationem naturæ cum inferioribus fit ens rationis, quod est vniuersale. fit etiam genus, & species, quæ omnia conueniunt prædicabilibus, priusquam actu prædicentur: ergo priusquam ex eis fiat propositio. Quare necesse est fieri per simplicem apprehensionem, per quam cognoscimus vnum in ordine ad alterum. Nam hæc simplex cognitio, prior est compositione. De Entibus rationis, quæ conueniunt compositioni, & discursui, manifestum est fieri per secundam, & tertiam operationem intellectus, & talia sunt denominatio prædicati, & subiecti, atque etiam propositionis: & præterea denominationes argumentationis & syllogismi.

The common view, however, to be followed by us, holds (as we saw in q. 5 on universals) that some beings of reason are made through the first operation of the intellect, others through the second, and some others through the third. Which is proved by this argument. Some beings of reason belong to simples before a composition is made out of them; others belong to the same simples as they already are in a composition, or to the composition itself; others, finally, to compositions as they are in a syllogism; therefore different beings of reason are made through each of these operations. The antecedent is proved, because through the simple comparison of the nature with its inferiors there is made the being of reason which is the universal; there are made also genus and species, all of which belong to the predicables before they are actually predicated, therefore before a proposition is made out of them. Wherefore it is necessary that they be made through simple apprehension, through which we know one thing in order to another; for this simple cognition is prior to composition. Of the beings of reason which belong to composition and to discursive reasoning, it is manifest that they are made through the second and third operation of the intellect; and such are the denominations of predicate and subject, and also of proposition; and moreover the denominations of argumentation and syllogism.

Ad argumentum verò alterius opinionis, negandum est, quòd omnis comparatio sit compositio, aut diuisio, cùm probatum sit in quæst. 5. vniuersali, dari comparationem, quæ sit simplicium apprehensio, per quam cognoscimus vnum in ordine ad aliud, vel ad multa.

To the argument of the other opinion, however, it must be denied that every comparison is a composition or division, since it was proved in q. 5 on universals that there is given a comparison which is an apprehension of simples, through which we know one thing in order to another, or to many.

p. 81

An Entia rationis fiant ab intellectu diuino, vel angelico:

Whether beings of reason are made by the divine or the angelic intellect.

PRima opinio affirmat, diuinum & angelicum intellectum efficere entia rationis: quam tenent moderni quidam. Et probatur 1. testimonio D. Tho. 1. part. qu. 15. art. 2. ad 3. vbi habentur hæc verba: Huiusmodi respectus quibus multiplicantur ideæ non causantur à rebus, sed ab intellectu diuino, comparante essentiam suam ad res, &c. Ex quibus hoc argumentum colligitur: Distinctio idearum in Deo non est realis, cùm ideæ cõueniant essentiæ diuinæ, in qua non potest esse distinctio realis: ergo solùm est distinctio rationis: sed distinctio rationis est relatio rationis: ergo Ens rationis fit ab intellectu diuino secundùm mentem D. Tho. Probatur consequentia, quia dicit distinctionem idearum, causari ab intellectu diuino.

The first opinion affirms that the divine and the angelic intellect produce beings of reason; it is held by certain moderns. And it is proved, first, by the testimony of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 15, a. 2, ad 3, where these words are found: Respects of this kind, by which the ideas are multiplied, are not caused by things but by the divine intellect, comparing its essence to things, etc. From which this argument is gathered: The distinction of the ideas in God is not real, since the ideas agree with the divine essence, in which there can be no real distinction; therefore it is only a distinction of reason. But a distinction of reason is a relation of reason; therefore a being of reason is made by the divine intellect, according to the mind of St. Thomas. The consequence is proved, because he says that the distinction of the ideas is caused by the divine intellect.

Probatur etiam duplici ratione. Primò, Intellectus diuinus cognoscit perfectissimè Entia rationis: sed Entia rationis non habent aliud esse, quàm cognosci: ergo habent esse ab intellectu diuino, quod est fieri ab eo.

It is proved also by a twofold argument. First, the divine intellect knows beings of reason most perfectly; but beings of reason have no other being than to be known; therefore they have being from the divine intellect, which is to be made by it.

Secundò, Intellectus diuinus distinguit ea, quæ à parte rei non sunt distincta: sed hoc non potest fieri, nisi efficiendo Ens rationis: ergo diuinus intellectus efficit Entia rationis. Maior est manifesta: quia distinguit suam iustitiam, & misericordiam, atque etiam ideas in se existentes, quæ non distinguuntur à parte rei. Probatur minor, quia distinguere ea, quæ non sunt distincta, fit per relationem rationis, quæ est Ens rationis.

Second, the divine intellect distinguishes things which are not distinct on the part of the thing; but this cannot be done except by producing a being of reason; therefore the divine intellect produces beings of reason. The major is manifest, because it distinguishes its justice and mercy, and also the ideas existing in itself, which are not distinguished on the part of the thing. The minor is proved, because distinguishing things which are not distinct is done through a relation of reason, which is a being of reason.

Secunda opinio asserit, diuinum intellectum non efficere Entia rationis, & hæc est probabilior, & tenenda. Quam explico duabus conclusionibus. Prima intellectus diuinus perfectissimè cognoscit Entia rationis, quæ fiunt ab intellectu nostro. Hanc omnes concedunt: & probatur euidenti ratione. Entia rationis fiunt ab intellectu nostro: ergo cognoscuntur ab eo: sed quidquid ab intellectu cognoscitur, continetur sub obiecto eius: ergo entia rationis, continentur sub obiecto intellectus nostri: sed obiectum diuini intellectus non est minùs vniuersale, quàm nostrum: quin diminuta, & imperfectissima comprehendit: ergo non minùs continet Entia rationis, nec minùs ea cognoscit.

The second opinion asserts that the divine intellect does not produce beings of reason; and this is the more probable and is to be held. I explain it by two conclusions. The first: the divine intellect most perfectly knows the beings of reason which are made by our intellect. All grant this, and it is proved by an evident argument. Beings of reason are made by our intellect; therefore they are known by it. But whatever is known by the intellect is contained under its object; therefore beings of reason are contained under the object of our intellect. But the object of the divine intellect is not less universal than ours, since it comprehends things diminished and most imperfect; therefore it no less contains beings of reason, nor knows them less.

Secunda conclusio: Diuinus intellectus nullum Ens rationis facit: sed nec potest illud facere. Quam vt probemus supponendum est, quòd ad efficiendum Ens rationis, duę sunt imperfectiones necessariò requisitæ, in modo intelligendi. Prima quòd res, quę non sunt à parte rei distinctæ, sed vnum,

The second conclusion: the divine intellect makes no being of reason, nor can it make one. In order to prove this, it must be supposed that two imperfections are necessarily required for producing a being of reason, in the mode of understanding. The first, that things which are not distinct on the part of the thing, but one, be distinguished F

p. 82

distinguantur ab intellectu, & per plures cõceptus concipiantur.

by the intellect and conceived through several concepts.

Secunda, quòd obiectum repræsentetur intellectui, & ab eo intelligatur, non sicut se habet in se, aut à parte rei, sed alio modo. Vtraque conditio manifestatur hoc exemplo: Vt intellectus efficiat naturam vniuersalem genus, aut speciem, necesse est, vt eam distinguat ab inferioribus à quibus non est distincta, & eam ab eis abstrahat: cùm non sit secundùm se abstracta, sed à parte rei sit eis coniuncta: & hoc est alio modo eam intelligere, atque est à parte rei, hoc est pluribus conceptibus, atque distinctis intelligere ea, quæ à parte rei sunt vnum. Sed vtrumque facit intellectus sine mendacio: quia sine affirmatione, & negatione. Et quod de his Entibus rationis dicimus, euidens est in cæteris.

The second, that the object be represented to the intellect and understood by it, not as it is in itself or on the part of the thing, but in another mode. Both conditions are made manifest by this example. In order that the intellect may make the universal nature genus or species, it is necessary that it distinguish it from the inferiors from which it is not distinct, and abstract it from them, since it is not abstracted of itself but is joined to them on the part of the thing; and this is to understand it in another mode than it is on the part of the thing, that is, to understand by several and distinct concepts what on the part of the thing is one. But the intellect does both without falsehood, because without affirmation and negation. And what we say of these beings of reason is evident in the rest.

Ex his colligitur argumentum, ad probandum efficaciter nostram sententiam. Entia rationis non possunt fieri ab intellectu, nisi distinguendo ea, quæ à parte rei, aut secundùm se non sunt distincta, & concipiendo per plures conceptus ea, quæ in se sunt vnum, atque etiam alio modo ea intelligendo, atque se habent à parte rei: sed modus sic intelligendi, est imperfectissimus, & qui non potest conuenire intellectui diuino: ergo nec poterit efficere Entia rationis. Probatur minor: nam diuinus intellectus vnica cognitione & vnico conceptu, & simplissimo intelligit omnia, & secundùm eundem modum, quem habent à parte rei: vt si sint vnum, cognoscit ea per modum vnius: si verò sint distincta, tanquam distincta: ergo non potest ei conuenire talis modus imperfectus intelligendi, per quem necessariò dębet fieri Ens rationis: & ideo nec poterit illud efficere.

From these things an argument is gathered to prove our view effectively. Beings of reason cannot be made by the intellect except by distinguishing things which on the part of the thing, or according to themselves, are not distinct, and by conceiving through several concepts things which in themselves are one, and also by understanding them in another mode than they are on the part of the thing. But such a mode of understanding is most imperfect, and one that cannot belong to the divine intellect; therefore neither will it be able to produce beings of reason. The minor is proved: for the divine intellect understands all things by a single cognition and a single and most simple concept, and according to the same mode which they have on the part of the thing: so that if they are one, it knows them in the mode of one; but if they are distinct, as distinct. Therefore such an imperfect mode of understanding, through which a being of reason must necessarily be made, cannot belong to it; and therefore neither will it be able to produce one.

Ad arg. alterius opinionis respondeo, & ad primum testimonium D. Tho. Sensum eius ex alio loco colligi, nempe ex quæst. 17. de potentia art. 6, vbi docet distinctionem rationis, quæ reperitur inter diuina attributa: vt inter iustitiam, & misericordiam, aut inter ideas, diuerso modo reperiri in intellectu diuino, & nostro: quia in illo reperitur tanquam in radice, & quasi virtualiter: in nostro verò formaliter Quod hoc modo explicandum est: Ideo non est aliud quàm essentia diuina, prout participare potest à creaturis. Et cùm plures creaturæ sint distinctæ secundùm essentiam, distinguimus in ea plures ideas, ita, vt ea ratione, qua potest participari ab homine, sit idea hominis, & non leonis: & vt participari potest à leone, sit idea leonis & non elephantis, & sic de cæteris. Quamuis autem diuinus intellectus intelligat essentiam diuinam, vt imitabilem ab omnibus creaturis, vnico ac simplissimo conceptu,

To the arguments of the other opinion I reply, and to the first, the testimony of St. Thomas, that his sense is gathered from another place, namely from De potentia, q. 17, a. 6, where he teaches that the distinction of reason which is found among the divine attributes, as between justice and mercy, or among the ideas, is found in a different way in the divine intellect and in ours: because in the former it is found as in its root and as it were virtually, but in ours formally. Which is to be explained in this way. An idea is nothing other than the divine essence as it can be participated by creatures. And since there are several creatures distinct according to essence, we distinguish in it several ideas, so that by the ratio by which it can be participated by man, it is the idea of man and not of lion; and as it can be participated by the lion, it is the idea of lion and not of elephant; and so of the rest. But although the divine intellect understands the divine essence as imitable by all creatures by a single and most simple concept,

p. 83

& ideo non distinguat in ea plures ideas, per illum tamen vnicum conceptum intelligit, quòd à nostro intellectu imperfecto modo eam concipiente, hoc est per plures ac distinctos conceptus, distinguatur in plures ideas, hominis, leonis, & aliarum rerum. Nam vnico conceptu intelligimus nos essentiam diuinam, vt participari potest ab homine, & per alium conceptum distinctum, vt participari potest à leone: & hoc est distinguere in essentia diuina plures ideas distinctione rationis, & ideo efficere entia rationis, intelligendo diuinas ideas.

and therefore does not distinguish several ideas in it, yet through that single concept it understands that, by our intellect conceiving it in an imperfect mode, that is, through several and distinct concepts, it is distinguished into several ideas, of man, of lion, and of other things. For by one concept we understand the divine essence as it can be participated by man, and by another, distinct concept as it can be participated by the lion; and this is to distinguish several ideas in the divine essence by a distinction of reason, and therefore to produce beings of reason by understanding the divine ideas.

Ex quibus intelligitur differentia inter diuinum intellectum, & nostrum: quòd ille, non distinguit ideas in essentia diuina distinctione actuali, aut formali, sed fundamentali, aut virtuali, in quantum cognoscit distingui posse à nostro: noster verò intellectus actualem distinctionem rationis inter ideas facit: & quia omnis nostra intellectio causatur, & regulatur per diuinam, docuit D. Tho. intellectum diuinum causare distinctionem idearum, non efficiẽdo eam actualiter, sed solùm virtualiter, in quantum intelligit essentiam diuinam, vt intelligi potest à nostro intellectu per plures conceptus, & ideo distingui possunt à nobis plures ideæ: quam distinctionem à nobis factam, causat intellectus ipse diuinus per suam intellectionem, & iste est sensus illius testimonij.

From which is understood the difference between the divine intellect and ours: that the former does not distinguish the ideas in the divine essence by an actual or formal distinction, but by a fundamental or virtual one, inasmuch as it knows that they can be distinguished by ours; whereas our intellect makes an actual distinction of reason among the ideas. And because all our understanding is caused and regulated by the divine, St. Thomas taught that the divine intellect causes the distinction of the ideas, not by producing it actually, but only virtually, inasmuch as it understands the divine essence as it can be understood by our intellect through several concepts, and that therefore several ideas can be distinguished by us; which distinction, made by us, the divine intellect itself causes through its understanding. And this is the sense of that testimony.

Ad primum argumentum cõcedendum est antecedẽs, quòd diuinus intellectus, perfectissima cognitione cognoscat Entia rationis, sed neganda est consequentia, quòd ea faciat. & ratio est, quia non cognoscit res cum duabus illis imperfectionibus necessariò requisitis ad efficienda Entia rationis. Et vt vno verbo solutionem declaremus, dicendum est: diuinum intellectum non cognoscere Entia rationis, cognitione factiua eorum: sed cognitione, per quam facta à nobis intelligit.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be granted, that the divine intellect knows beings of reason by a most perfect cognition; but the consequence is to be denied, that it makes them. And the reason is that it does not know things with those two imperfections necessarily required for producing beings of reason. And to declare the solution in one word, it must be said that the divine intellect does not know beings of reason by a cognition productive of them, but by a cognition through which it understands them as made by us.

Ad secundum distinguenda est maior: quia distinguere ea quæ non sunt distincta, duobus modis potest intelligi, Primò, efficiendo actualem distinctionem inter ea, & in hoc sensu neganda est: Alio modo, solùm efficiendo distinctionem quasi virtualiter, aut fundamentaliter, & hoc modo concedi potest. Nam cùm intellectus diuinus intelligit ea quæ non sunt didistincta: vt distingui possunt à nobis imperfectè cognoscentibus per plures conceptus, virtualiter dicitur efficere distinctionem, quam noster intellectus facit actualiter: in quantum intellectio nostra causatur, & regulatur per diuinam Et quæ de diuino intellectu dicimus, de angelico etiam, suo modo intelligi debent: qui cùm perfectè intelligat, non dicitur facese Entia rationis: sed ea cognoscere à nobis facta.

To the second, the major is to be distinguished: because “to distinguish things which are not distinct” can be understood in two ways. First, by producing an actual distinction among them; and in this sense it is to be denied. In another way, by producing the distinction only as it were virtually or fundamentally; and in this way it can be granted. For since the divine intellect understands things which are not distinct as able to be distinguished by us, who know imperfectly through several concepts, it is said virtually to produce the distinction which our intellect makes actually, inasmuch as our understanding is caused and regulated by the divine. And what we say of the divine intellect must also be understood, in its own way, of the angelic: which, since it understands perfectly, is not said to make beings of reason, but to know them as made by us. E ij

p. 84

Ad quam scientiam pertineat agere de Ente rationis.

To which science it pertains to treat of being of reason.

DVabus distinctionibus præsuppositis respondendum est huic dubio. Prima est, quam superiùs adduximus de Ente rationis habente fundamentum in rebus, & non habente tale fundamentum. Et de hoc secundo certum est, ad nullam scientiam per se pertinere. Quod duobus argumentis probatur: Primo, Quia ea de quibus scientia per se agit, determinata esse debent: sed Entia rationis, quæ non habent fundamentum, possunt in infinitum multiplicari ab intellectu: ergo nulla scientia potest per se agere de illis. Secundo, Illud de quo agit scientia, debet habere determinata principia, per quæ probentur de illo determinatæ passiones: sed hæc Entia rationis non habent determinata principia, ergo nulla scientia potest agere per se de illis. Minorem probo, quia componuntur ex rebus disparatis, aut specie diuersis: ergo ex eis non potest sumi determinatum principium, nec tale compositum impossibile, potest habere determinatas passiones.

This doubt must be answered with two distinctions presupposed. The first is the one we adduced above, of being of reason having a foundation in things and not having such a foundation. And concerning the second it is certain that it pertains per se to no science. Which is proved by two arguments. First, because the things of which a science treats per se must be determinate; but beings of reason which have no foundation can be multiplied to infinity by the intellect; therefore no science can treat of them per se. Second, that of which a science treats must have determinate principles, through which determinate attributes are proved of it; but these beings of reason do not have determinate principles; therefore no science can treat of them per se. I prove the minor, because they are composed of disparate things, or things diverse in species; therefore no determinate principle can be taken from them, nor can such an impossible composite have determinate attributes.

Alia distinctio est Entis rationis, habentis fundamentum in re. Quòd si sit relatio rationis, duobus modis considerari potest. Primò, secundùm se aut secundùm propriam entitatem: & hoc modo pertinet ad Metaphysicam: non per se, quia obiectum per se huius scientiæ est Ens reale: sed quasi per accidens, in quantum habet quandam similitudinem cum relatione reali, de qua per se agit hæc scientia. Secundò potest considerari, vt est denominatio naturæ, cui attribuitur, vt denominatio generis, speciei, prædicati, & subiecti. Et secundùm hanc considerationem dicitur Ens rationis logicum, de quo agit per se Logica, tanquam de proprio obiecto. Si verò sit priuatio, aut negatio, ad illam scientiam reduci debet, quæ per se agit de forma, aut essentia, quam negat, vel qua priuat: vt priuatio formæ naturalis, pertinet ad Philosophiam, tanquam vnum ex tribus principiis naturalis generationis, vt docet Aristoteles 1. lib. Physicorum, & negatio quæ est de Essentia huius, aut illius naturæ, reducitur ad scientiam, quæ per se agit de tali natura, vt non esse equum, ad scientiam de homine: & sic de cæteris.

The other distinction is of being of reason having a foundation in the thing. If it is a relation of reason, it can be considered in two ways. First, according to itself, or according to its proper entity; and in this way it pertains to Metaphysics, not per se, because the per se object of this science is real being, but as it were per accidens, inasmuch as it has a certain likeness to real relation, of which this science treats per se. Second, it can be considered as it is a denomination of the nature to which it is attributed, as the denomination of genus, species, predicate and subject. And according to this consideration it is called logical being of reason, of which Logic treats per se as of its proper object. But if it is a privation or a negation, it must be reduced to that science which treats per se of the form or essence which it denies or of which it deprives: as the privation of a natural form pertains to Philosophy, as one of the three principles of natural generation, as Aristotle teaches in Phys. 1; and a negation which is of the essence of this or that nature is reduced to the science which treats per se of such a nature, as not to be a horse to the science of man; and so of the rest.

Quonam modo Ens rationis reducatur ad ordinem prædicamentalem.

In what way being of reason is reduced to the categorial order.

DE Ente rationis non habente fundamentum in rebus, certum est non posse reduci ad ordinem prædicamentalem: quia componitur ex rebus diuersis secundùm essentiam

Concerning being of reason not having a foundation in things, it is certain that it cannot be reduced to the categorial order, because it is composed of things diverse according to essence,

p. 85

& ideo non habet vnam aliquam determinatam naturam, secundùm quem possit in prædicamento ordinari. De Ente autem rationis, habet fundamentum, quantum ad priuationem, & negationem: etiam est certum habere quandam similitudinem cum qualitatibus. Quod sic probo. Priuatio, & Negatio, sunt Entia rationis, vt considerantur ab intellectu, tanquam formæ positiuæ, & attribuuntur alicui subiecto in propositione: vt dum dicimus, Hominem esse cæcum: sed ita consideratæ habent similitudinem cum qualitatibus: ergo ad prædicamentum earum reducuntur. Probatur minor. Quia sic prædicatur cæcitas de homine, sicut albedo, aut color, ergo similitudinem habet cum his, & aliis qualitatibus.

and therefore it does not have some one determinate nature according to which it could be ordered in a category. But concerning being of reason having a foundation, as regards privation and negation, it is also certain that it has a certain likeness to qualities. Which I prove thus. Privation and negation are beings of reason as they are considered by the intellect as positive forms and are attributed to some subject in a proposition, as when we say that a man is blind; but so considered they have a likeness to qualities; therefore they are reduced to their category. The minor is proved: because blindness is predicated of a man just as whiteness or color is; therefore it has a likeness to these and to other qualities.

Solum restat Relatio rationis, quæ possit ordinari in speciali prædicamento. Quod tamen non erit proprium: quia prædicamentum, propriè ex solis entibus realibus fieri potest: sed maximam habebit similitudinem cum vero prædicamento ad aliquid, ex relationibus realibus ordinato Prædicamentum igitur relationis rationis sic ordinandum est, vt supremũ genus sit relatio rationis, (nam Ens rationis vniuersalissimum, ab hoc prædicamento excludi debet, propter trãscendentiam: sicut Ens reale excluditur ab omnibus prædicamentis realibus) quod diuidi potest in tria genera, siue species subalternas, secundùm diuersa fundamenta: quæ sunt diuersæ operationes intellectus. Vt apprehensio simplicem, compositio, & diuisio, atque discursus. Quemadmodum Arist. diuisit supremum genus prædicamenti ad aliquid, quod est relatiuum, vt relatio realis: per diuersa fundamenta. Ita vt primum genus sit relationum, quæ fundantur in vnitate, vt relationis identitatis, similitudinis, & æqualitatis. Secundum, relationum quæ fundantur in actione, & passione: vt paternitas, & filiatio. Tertiũ, earum quæ fundantur in mensura, vt sunt relationes scientiæ ad scribile, & potentiæ ad obiectum. Ita diuidenda est relatio rationis: In eam quæ fundatur in cognitione simplicium, & eisdem simplicibus attribuitur; & hoc est primum genus, habens sub se diuersas species, vt relationis vniuersalis, generis, speciei, & aliorum prædicabilium, Deinde in eam, quæ fundatur in compositione, & diuisione, ad quod genus pertinent variæ species propositionum: & tandem in eam, quæ fundatur in tertia operatione, quæ est discursus, sub quo genere continentur diuersæ species argumentationum, & syllogismorum. Itaque hæc tria genera habent sub se alia, vsque ad species infimas, ex quibus omnibus sic ordinatis resultat prædicamentum proprium Entis rationis.

There remains only relation of reason, which could be ordered in a special category. This, however, will not be proper, because a category can properly be made only of real beings; but it will have the greatest likeness to the true category of relation, ordered out of real relations. The category of relation of reason, therefore, is to be ordered thus: that the supreme genus be relation of reason (for being of reason, the most universal, must be excluded from this category on account of its transcendence, just as real being is excluded from all the real categories), which can be divided into three genera, or subalternate species, according to its diverse foundations, which are the diverse operations of the intellect, namely simple apprehension, composition and division, and discursive reasoning. Just as Aristotle divided the supreme genus of the category of relation, which is the relative, or real relation, through its diverse foundations, so that the first genus is of relations which are founded on unity, as the relations of identity, likeness and equality; the second, of relations which are founded on action and passion, as paternity and filiation; the third, of those which are founded on measure, as are the relations of science to the knowable and of a power to its object: so relation of reason is to be divided into that which is founded on the cognition of simples and is attributed to the simples themselves, and this is the first genus, having under it diverse species, as the relation of universal, genus, species and the other predicables; next, into that which is founded on composition and division, to which genus the various species of propositions pertain; and finally into that which is founded on the third operation, which is discursive reasoning, under which genus are contained the diverse species of argumentations and syllogisms. And so these three genera have others under them, down to the lowest species, from all of which, so ordered, the proper category of being of reason results. F iij

p. 86

Tract. De modo, quo fiunt prædicationes in concretis, & abstractis primarum, & secundarum intentionum — TREATISE ON THE WAY I N W H I C H P R E D I C AT I O N S A R E M A D E IN CONCRETES AND ABSTRACTS

OF FIRST AND SECOND INTENTIONS

TRACTATVS DE MODO, QVO PRÆDICATIONES FIVNT IN CONCRETIS ET ABSTRACTIS Primarum & secundarum intentionum.

[…]

AD finem tractatus præcedentis, diximus de Ente rationis agere Dialecticam, vt est relatio quædam, aut denominatio attributa naturis ab intellectu. In qua acceptione vocatur Ens rationis Logicum. Ideo in hoc tractatu secundo, agendum est de modo, & ordine, quem habet ad prędicationes concretorum, & abstractorum, in quibus denominationes exercentur, quas naturę accipiunt ab eo. Et quoniam prędicationes possunt fieri in primis intentionibus, quę sunt naturæ reales: atque etiam in secundis, quę sunt Entia rationis, in duas partes diuidemus præsentem tractatum: ita vt in prima tractetur de prędicationibus concretorum, & abstractorum primę intentionis, & in secunda de eisdem abstractis, & concretis secundarum intentionum.

t the end of the preceding treatise we said that Dialectic treats of A being of reason as it is a certain relation, or a denomination attributed to natures by the intellect; in which acceptation it is called logical being of reason. Therefore in this second treatise we must treat of the mode and order which it has with respect to the predications of concretes and abstracts, in which are exercised the denominations which natures receive from it. And since predications can be made in first intentions, which are real natures, and also in second intentions, which are beings of reason, we shall divide the present treatise into two parts: so that in the first we treat of the predications of concretes and abstracts of first intention, and in the second of the same abstracts and concretes of second intentions.

Et in primis intentionibus quatuor modis exerceri possunt. Primo, ita vt concretum prędicetur de concreto, vt homo est animal. Secundo, abstractum de abstracto: vt humanitas est animalitas. Tertio, abstractum de concreto, vt homo est humanitas. Quarto, concretum de abstracto, vt humanitas est homo. Et vt ea quę sunt certa supponamus, quantum ad veritatem, & falsitatem propositionum, de his tantùm propositionibus loquendum est, in quibus prędicatum & subiectum aliquo modo sunt ordinata, ita vt se habeant tanquam superius, & inferius, aut tanquam ęqualia, quorum vnum pertinet ad alterum, quia in eo includitur: vel propria passio eius est, vel commune accidens.

And in first intentions they can be exercised in four ways. First, so that a concrete is predicated of a concrete, as man is animal. Second, an abstract of an abstract, as humanity is animality. Third, an abstract of a concrete, as man is humanity. Fourth, a concrete of an abstract, as humanity is man. And so that we may suppose what is certain as regards the truth and falsity of propositions, we must speak only of those propositions in which the predicate and subject are in some way ordered, so that they are related as superior and inferior, or as equals, one of which pertains to the other because it is included in it, or is its proper attribute, or a common accident.

Quibus explicatis, certum est primò, Veram esse illam propositionem, in qua concretum prędicatur de concreto inferiori, aut superiori; vel etiam ęquale, siue sit de Essentia eius, aut propria passio, vel commune accidens: tales sunt istę, homo est animal, homo est rationalis, homo est risibilis, homo est albus: verę etiam sunt alię, in quas conuertuntur istæ, sed indirectè, atque impropriè.

These things explained, it is certain, first, that a proposition is true in which a concrete is predicated of a concrete inferior or superior, or also equal, whether it be of its essence, or a proper attribute, or a common accident: such are these, man is animal, man is rational, man is risible, man is white. True also are the others into which these are converted, but indirectly and improperly.

Secandò certum est, propositiones in quibus abstractum prędicatur de concreto, aut cõcretum de abstracto, falsas esse, siue se habeant tanquam superius, & inferius, vel sint ęqualia:

Second, it is certain that propositions in which an abstract is predicated of a concrete, or a concrete of an abstract, are false, whether they be related as superior and inferior, or be equals;

p. 87

vt homo est humanitas, homo est rationalitas, aut risibilitas, vel albedo. Et ratio huius est manifesta: Primò, propter diuersum modum significandi terminorum: quia abstractum significatur per modum partis, concretum verò per modum totius, pars autem non prædicatur de toto, vt pes, vel manus de homine. Secundò, quia subiectum in eisdem propositionibus aliquid includit, quod nullo modo includit prædicatum: vt album includit corpus, quod non includit albedo: vel è contra aliquid includit prædicatum, quod non includit subiectum, vt in propositionibus indirectis, ex eisdem terminis factis, quod sufficit, vt non sit verum, quòd vnum sit aliud, vt significatur per propositionem.

as man is humanity, man is rationality, or risibility, or whiteness. And the reason for this is manifest. First, on account of the diverse mode of signifying of the terms: because the abstract is signified by way of a part, but the concrete by way of a whole; but a part is not predicated of the whole, as foot or hands of a man. Second, because the subject in these propositions includes something which the predicate in no way includes, as white includes body, which whiteness does not include; or, conversely, the predicate includes something which the subject does not include, as in the indirect propositions made from the same terms. Which suffices for it not to be true that the one is the other, as is signified by the proposition.

Ex quo sequitur: Primò, falsam esse sententiam Soti, q. 3. vniuersalium, asserentis, propositionem, in qua prędicatur abstractum de concreto, vt homo est humanitas, solùm esse falsam, propter diuersum modum significandi terminorum, nam falsæ etiam sunt propter inclusionem alicuius in vno, & non in alio: quia vt suo loco videbimus, non potest esse vera propositio aliqua, nisi totum quod includitur in subiecto, aliquo modo includat prædicatum.

From which it follows, first, that the opinion of Soto, q. 3 on Universals, is false, who asserts that a proposition in which an abstract is predicated of a concrete, as man is humanity, is false only on account of the diverse mode of signifying of the terms; for they are false also on account of the inclusion of something in the one and not in the other: because, as we shall see in its place, no proposition can be true unless the whole that is included in the subject in some way includes the predicate.

Secundò sequitur magis falsam esse sententiam Durandi, in 1. d. 24. q. vltima. Vbi regulam vniuersalem assignauit, dicens, in creaturis veras esse omnes propositiones, in quibus prædicatur abstractum substantiale de concreto substantiali, vt homo est humanitas: quamuis sint falsæ in concretis & abstractis accidentalibus, vt homo est albedo, & aliæ similes.

It follows, second, that the opinion of Durandus, in 1, d. 24, last q., is even more false, where he laid down a universal rule, saying that in creatures all propositions are true in which a substantial abstract is predicated of a substantial concrete, as man is humanity; although they are false in accidental concretes and abstracts, as man is whiteness, and others like it.

Tertiò certum est, propositiones in quibus abstractum generis prædicatur de abstracto differentiæ, vel è contra, abstractum differentiæ de abstracto generis, vt rationalitas est animalitas, vel animalitas est rationalitas, falsas esse. Et ratio huius est: quia gradus genericus, & differentialis, formaliter sunt diuersi; & in abstracto significati, non se includunt, quia neque animalitas includit rationalitatem, neque rationalitas animalitatem, ergo neque vna prædicatur formaliter de altera. Probatur consequentia, nam vt propositio vera sit, prædicatum debet includi in subiecto.

It is certain, third, that propositions in which the abstract of a genus is predicated of the abstract of a difference, or conversely the abstract of a difference of the abstract of a genus, as rationality is animality, or animality is rationality, are false. And the reason for this is that the generic and the differential grade are formally diverse, and, signified in the abstract, they do not include each other, because neither does animality include rationality nor rationality animality; therefore neither is predicated formally of the other. The consequence is proved, for in order that a proposition be true, the predicate must be included in the subject.

An abstractum superius prædicetur de abstracto inferiori.

Whether a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract.

14 SOlùm potest esse quæstio de propositionibus, in quibus abstractũ superius prædicatur de abstracto inferiori, aut ęquali: sed istæ duobus modis sumi possunt, nempe in

14 The question can only be about propositions in which a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior, or equal, abstract; but these can be taken in two ways, namely in terms F iiij

p. 88

terminis Accidentalibus aut Essentialibus. Et si in accidentalibus fiant, certum est omnes esse falsas. Vt humanitas est risibilitas, aut humanitas est albedo. Et ratio huius est, quia prædicatum, & subiectum harum propositionum sępe distinguuntur realiter, & nunquam includitur vnum in altero: nam licèt homo includat albedinem, tanquam subiectum eius, tamen humanitas cùm significetur vt forma, non est subiectum accidentium, neque ea includit, vt significata in abstracto. Solùm ergo potest esse quęstio de propositionibus abstractorum, quę fiunt in terminis substantialibus, quales sunt istæ, humanitas est animalitas, humanitas est rationalitas, an veræ sint, vel falsæ.

that are accidental or essential. And if they are made in accidental terms, it is certain that all are false, as humanity is risibility, or humanity is whiteness. And the reason for this is that the predicate and the subject of these propositions are often distinguished really, and the one is never included in the other: for although man includes whiteness as its subject, yet humanity, since it is signified as a form, is not the subject of accidents, nor does it include them, as signified in the abstract. The question can therefore only be about the propositions of abstracts which are made in substantial terms, such as these, humanity is animality, humanity is rationality: whether they are true or false.

Et prima opinio asserit esse veras: quam sequuntur Sotus quęst. 3. Vniuersalium. Canterus cap. de differentia, & ex modernis multi. Et probatur duobus argumentis. Primò: Illa propositio in qua concretum superius prædicatur de inferiori, vt homo est animal, est vera: quia prædicatum includitur in subiecto, vt animal in homine: sed etiam abstractum superius includitur in abstracto inferiori, vt animalitas in humanitate: ergo vera erit hæc, humanitas est animalitas. Probatur minor, quia humanitas componitur ex animalitate, & rationalitate, sicut homo ex animali, & rationali: ergo includit vtramque.

And the first opinion asserts that they are true; it is followed by Soto, q. 3 on Universals, Canterus, chapter on difference, and many of the moderns. And it is proved by two arguments. First, that proposition in which a superior concrete is predicated of an inferior, as man is animal, is true, because the predicate is included in the subject, as animal in man; but the superior abstract is also included in the inferior abstract, as animality in humanity; therefore this will be true, humanity is animality. The minor is proved, because humanity is composed of animality and rationality, just as man of animal and rational; therefore it includes both.

Secundò probatur, in formis substantialibus & accidentalibus. Et primò in substantialibus, quales sunt anima rationalis, & sensitiua, ex quibus hæc est superior, & illa inferior: & vtraque significatur nomine abstracto: & tamen vera est hæc, anima rationalis est sensitiua: ergo vera etiam erit, humanitas est animalitas. Probatur consequentia, quia ideo forma superior prædicatur de inferiori, quia in ea includitur: sed animalitas est forma superior respectu humanitatis: ergo includitur in ea: & consequenter verè prædicabitur. In formis etiam accidentalibus, quales sunt albedo, & color, manifestum est, nam hæc est vera apud omnes, albedo est color: & prædicatur in ea abstractum superius de abstracto, inferiori, sicut in alia, humanitas est animalitas: ergo vera etiam est hæc, & concedenda.

It is proved, second, in substantial and accidental forms. And first in substantial ones, such as are the rational and the sensitive soul, of which the latter is superior and the former inferior; and both are signified by an abstract name; and yet this is true, the rational soul is sensitive; therefore this too will be true, humanity is animality. The consequence is proved, because a superior form is predicated of an inferior precisely because it is included in it; but animality is a superior form with respect to humanity; therefore it is included in it, and consequently it will be truly predicated. In accidental forms too, such as whiteness and color, it is manifest: for this is true among all, whiteness is color; and in it a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract, just as in the other, humanity is animality; therefore this too is true and to be granted.

Secunda opinio tenet, tales propositiones esse falsas. Quam sequitur Scotus in 1. dist. 5. qu. 1. art. 1. Niphus 3. Meta. quæst. 2. concl. 5. ad 3. Canariensis 1. p. qu. 28. ar. 2. dispu. 2. Ferra. 1. lib. contra gentes c 18. 2. 3. §. considerandum, & lib. 4. ca. 81. Caie. in opusc. de ente, & essentia, & cap 3. & 4. Sed Scotus, falsas esse defendit, quia existimat prædicatum, & subiectum distingui ex natura rei, seu formaliter, ante operationem intellectus: alij verò, qui solam distinctionem rationis ponunt inter illa

The second opinion holds that such propositions are false. It is followed by Scotus, in 1, d. 5, q. 1, a. 1; Nifo, Metaph. 3, q. 2, concl. 5, ad 3; Canariensis, 1 p., q. 28, a. 2, disp. 2; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 18, 2, 3, § Considerandum, and bk. 4, ch. 81; Cajetan, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 3 and 4. But Scotus maintains that they are false because he thinks that the predicate and the subject are distinguished from the nature of the thing, or formally, before the operation of the intellect; but the others, who posit only a distinction of reason between them,

p. 89

propter modum significandi abstractorum à quibus significatur animalitas, vt principium, aut pars animalis, & humanitas, vt principium hominis, & principium vnius non prædicatur de principio alterius. Et hæc sententia colligitur euidenter ex D. Tho. duobus locis citatis, & videtur nobis probabilior, & sequenda.

do so on account of the mode of signifying of abstracts, by which animality is signified as a principle or part of animal, and humanity as a principle of man; and the principle of one is not predicated of the principle of another. And this opinion is gathered evidently from St. Thomas in the two places cited, and it seems to us more probable and to be followed.

15 Sed vt efficaciùs eam probemus, duo sunt annotãda. Primum est, Concretum & Abstractum eandem rem significare, diuersa tamẽ ratione: nam Concretum significat eam per modum habentis: Abstractum verò, per modum principii, aut formæ eiusdem habentis. Gratia exempli, homo & humanitas, significant eãdem naturam humanam: sed homo significat eam per modum totius actualis, atq; completi: & ideo per modum habentis: humanitas verò, non nisi per modum principii & formæ, eiusdem totius completi, aut habentis. Quod ex communi modo loquendi, & intelligendi manifestum est: dicimus namque, hominem idem esse, habentem humanitatem: & humanitatem esse quasi principium, & formam hominis.

15 But in order that we may prove it more effectively, two things are to be noted. The first is that the concrete and the abstract signify the same thing, but by a different ratio: for the concrete signifies it by way of the haver, but the abstract by way of the principle or form of that same haver. For example, man and humanity signify the same human nature; but man signifies it by way of an actual and complete whole, and therefore by way of the haver; humanity, on the other hand, only by way of the principle and form of that same complete whole, or haver. Which is manifest from the common way of speaking and understanding: for we say that a man is the same as one having humanity, and that humanity is as it were the principle and form of man.

Ex quo primò colligitur, concretum signare naturam, non omnino pręcisam à conditionibus singularibus. sed vt eas continens: confusè saltem, & in potentia: nam licèt abstrahatur à singularibus, abstractione, per quam fit aliquo modo vniuersalis: & ideo non significet, neque contineat eadem singularia actu, continet tamen in potentia: quia ex proprio modo significandi, determinari potest per conditiones singulares, ad hoc, & illud indiuiduum, aut ad Petrum, aut Ioannem. Abstractum verò significat eandem naturam, vt omnino præcisam à singularibus, nec vt determinabilem per conditiones singulares eorum: quia cùm non significet eam per modum habentis, sed principii, aut formæ, principium verò, aut forma, non habeat modum determinabilis per aliud, sed potiùs determinantis aliud, illud nempe, cuius est principium, vel forma, non potest natura in abstracto significata per modum habentis intelligi: & ideo nec potest ita significata continere actu, nec potentia conditiones singulares, per quas contrahatur ad hoc, vel illud singulare. Et quod de natura specifica dicimus respectu singularium, eodem modo intelligendum est de natura generica, in concreto, aut in abstracto significata, vt de animali, aut animalitate. Ita, vt animal significet naturam sensitiuam, vt contrahibilem, aut perfectibilem per differentias, rationale, & irrationale, quas continet in potentia: animalitas verò nullo modo, seu potiùs, vt forma, vel principium eiusdem animalis, atque specierum eius.

From which it is gathered, first, that the concrete signifies the nature not as altogether prescinded from the singular conditions, but as containing them, at least confusedly and in potency. For although it is abstracted from singulars by an abstraction through which it becomes in some way universal, and therefore does not signify or contain the same singulars in act, yet it contains them in potency: because from its proper mode of signifying it can be determined through singular conditions to this and that individual, or to Peter or John. But the abstract signifies the same nature as altogether prescinded from singulars, and not as determinable through their singular conditions: because, since it does not signify it by way of the haver but of the principle or form, and a principle or form does not have the mode of what is determinable through another, but rather of what determines another, namely that whose principle or form it is, the nature signified in the abstract cannot be understood by way of the haver; and therefore, so signified, it can contain neither in act nor in potency the singular conditions through which it would be contracted to this or that singular. And what we say of the specific nature with respect to the singulars is to be understood in the same way of the generic nature signified in the concrete or in the abstract, as of animal or animality: so that animal signifies the sensitive nature as contractible or perfectible through the differences rational and irrational, which it contains in potency; but animality in no way, or rather as the form or principle of that same animal and of its species.

p. 90

Secũdò colligitur, abstracta significare naturam per modum partis, sicut concreta per modum totius. Quod probatur duplici ratione euidenti. Primò, quia abstracta significant naturam per modum principii, & formæ eiusdem, vt significatur nomine concreto: vt animalitas, significat naturam sensitiuam prout est principium, & quasi forma animalis: sed illud, quod est principium, & forma alterius, habet se vt pars illius: ergo abstractum significat naturam per modum partis. Secundò, animalitas non significat naturam sensitiuam per modum totius, ergo per modum partis. Probatur antecedens: quia sic significaret eam per modum totius, aut totius actualis, aut potentialis: sed neutro modo eam significat: ergo non per modum totius. Minorem probo: quia totum potentiale, vel actuale, significat rem per modum habentis, abstractum verò, non nisi per modum formæ eius, quod habet: ergo non per modum totius, sed partis. Et hinc prouenit, quòd nec animalitas prędicatur de animali, nec humanitas de homine: quia pars non potest prædicari de toto.

It is gathered, second, that abstracts signify the nature by way of a part, just as concretes do by way of a whole. Which is proved by a twofold evident argument.
