First, because abstracts signify the nature by way of the principle and form of that same thing as it is signified by the concrete name: as animality signifies the sensitive nature as it is the principle and as it were the form of animal; but that which is the principle and form of another is related as a part of it; therefore the abstract signifies the nature by way of a part. Second, animality does not signify the sensitive nature by way of a whole; therefore by way of a part. The antecedent is proved: because if it signified it by way of a whole, it would be either of an actual or of a potential whole; but it signifies it in neither way; therefore not by way of a whole. I prove the minor: because a potential or actual whole signifies the thing by way of the haver, but the abstract only by way of the form of that which has it; therefore not by way of a whole but of a part. And hence it comes about that neither is animality predicated of animal, nor humanity of man: because a part cannot be predicated of the whole.

Tertiò sequitur, abstracta non esse genera, nec species, sed principia generum, & specierum: quod asseruit Auicẽna 5. Meta. cap. 7. vt testatur Caie. in opusc. de Ente, & Essentia, ca. 4. & probauit D. Tho ibidem, hoc argumento. Genus ex propria natura habet modum totius potentialis, & species modum totius actualis, sed abstracta non significant naturam per modum totius potentialis, nec actualis, sed per modum partis: ergo non sunt genera, nec species: & propterea non denominantur à secundis intentionibus generis. aut speciei, vel aliorum prædicabilium. Tota hæc doctrina annotata habetur, apud D. Th. opusc. de ente & essentia, cap. 4.

It follows, third, that abstracts are not genera or species, but principles of genera and species; which Avicenna asserted, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, as Cajetan testifies in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4; and St. Thomas proved it in the same place by this argument. A genus by its proper nature has the mode of a potential whole, and a species the mode of an actual whole; but abstracts do not signify the nature by way of a potential or of an actual whole, but by way of a part; therefore they are not genera or species, and for that reason they are not denominated by the second intentions of genus or species, or of the other predicables. All this doctrine that has been noted is found in St. Thomas, opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4.

Ex qua duo argumenta colliguntur, ad probandam nostram sententiam. Quòd hæc prædicatio, humanitas est animalitas, & similes, sint falsæ. Primum est: Vt vera sit aliqua prædicatio, necessariò requiritur, quòd quidquid continet subiectum, contineat prædicatum actu, vel potentia: sed animalitas non continet actu, nec potentia, quidquid cõtinet humanitas: ergo nõ potest verè prędicari de illa. Maior certissima est, quia non potest esse verum, quòd hoc sit illud, vt per propositionem affirmatur, nisi totum quod continet hoc, etiam contineat illud: & hæc est ratio propter quam pars non prędicatur de toto, nec genus posset prædicari de specie, nisi differentiam quam species continet actu, continet in potentia, vt bene D. Tho. vbi supra. Sed probatur minor: quia humanitas continet animalitatem, & rationalitatem, ex quibus componitur: sed euidẽs est

From it two arguments are gathered for proving our view, that this predication, humanity is animality, and similar ones, are false. The first is: for any predication to be true, it is necessarily required that whatever the subject contains, the predicate contain in act or in potency; but animality does not contain, in act or in potency, whatever humanity contains; therefore it cannot be truly predicated of it. The major is most certain, because it cannot be true that this is that, as is affirmed through the proposition, unless the whole that this contains that also contains; and this is the reason why a part is not predicated of the whole, nor could a genus be predicated of a species unless it contained in potency the difference which the species contains in act, as St. Thomas says well in the place above. But the minor is proved: because humanity contains animality and rationality, of which it is composed; but it is evident

p. 91

animalitatem non cõtinere rationalitatem actu, nec potentia, cùm non habeat modum totius actualis, nec potentialis, sed partis vel formę: ergo nõ potest verè prędicari de humanitate.

that animality does not contain rationality in act or in potency, since it does not have the mode of an actual or a potential whole, but of a part or form; therefore it cannot be truly predicated of humanity.

Secundum. Pars actualis non prędicatur de toto, vt concedunt omnes: sed animalitas est pars actualis humanitatis: ergo non verè prædicatur de illa. Probatur minor: quia sicut homo componitur ex animali, & rationali, ita humanitas ex animalitate, & rationalitate. Et si dicas, hoc arg. etiam probari, quòd hæc propositio non sit vera, homo est animal: quia animal est pars actualis hominis: Respondeo, animal esse quidem partẽ; non tamen significari per modum partis, sed per modum totius potentialis: & ideò verè prædicatur de homine: animalitas verò non solùm est pars, sed significatur per modum partis, quæ non potest prædicari de toto: & hæc est ratio propter quam hæc est vera, Homo est animal, & hæc falsa, Humanitas est animalitas.

The second. An actual part is not predicated of the whole, as all grant; but animality is an actual part of humanity; therefore it is not truly predicated of it. The minor is proved: because just as man is composed of animal and rational, so humanity is composed of animality and rationality. And if you say that this argument also proves that this proposition is not true, man is animal, because animal is an actual part of man: I reply that animal is indeed a part, yet it is not signified by way of a part, but by way of a potential whole, and therefore it is truly predicated of man; animality, on the other hand, is not only a part but is signified by way of a part, which cannot be predicated of the whole. And this is the reason why this is true, Man is animal, and this false, Humanity is animality.

Ad primum argumentum respondetur, Non satis esse quòd prædicatum includatur in subiecto, vt propositio sit vera: quia si id sufficeret, sequeretur veram esse propositionem, in qua pars prędicatur de toto: cùm certum sit partem includi in toto. Requiritur ergo, non solùm quòd includatur in eo, sed quòd totum quod continet subiectum, contineat prædicatum actu, vel potentia, vt explicatum est: & cùm animalitas non contineat totum, quod continet humanitas, quia non continet rationalitatem actu, nec potentia, sequitur non verè prædicari de illa.

To the first argument it is replied that it is not enough for the truth of a proposition that the predicate be included in the subject: because if that sufficed, it would follow that a proposition in which a part is predicated of the whole is true, since it is certain that the part is included in the whole. It is required, therefore, not only that it be included in it, but that the whole that the subject contains the predicate contain in act or in potency, as has been explained. And since animality does not contain the whole that humanity contains, because it does not contain rationality in act or in potency, it follows that it is not truly predicated of it.

Secundum argumentum duas habet partes. Prima procedit de formis substantialibus. Secunda de accidentalibus. Ad primam ergo respondeo, negando antecedens: quòd prædicatio illa, anima rationalis est sensitiua, sit abstracti de abstracto: & de prædicato, nempe, sensitiua, euidẽs est, quòd non sit abstractum nomen, sed concretum: quod etiam est verum de anima: nam licèt sit forma, per modum tamen habentis gradum sentiendi significatur: non quidem sicut habet homo, qui ex ea componitur: sed sicut forma, quæ composito eum tribuit, significata tamen quasi per modum totius, & ideo per modum concreti. Quod ex eo fit manifestum: quia nisi per modum concreti significaretur anima: non posset sensitiua, quæ concretum nomen est, de ea veré prædicari: & eo ipso, quòd verè prædicatur idem significans, quod habens gradum sentiendi, negari non potest, quòd per modum concreti etiam significetur anima: vnde non bene infertur, quòd vera etiam sit hæc: Humanitas est animalitas: in qua certum est abstractum

The second argument has two parts. The first proceeds about substantial forms, the second about accidental ones. To the first, therefore, I reply by denying the antecedent: that that predication, the rational soul is sensitive, is of an abstract of an abstract. And concerning the predicate, namely sensitive, it is evident that it is not an abstract name but a concrete one. Which is also true of soul: for although it is a form, yet it is signified by way of what has the grade of sensing; not indeed as man has it, who is composed of it, but as the form, which gives that grade to the composite, yet signified as it were by way of a whole, and therefore by way of a concrete. Which is made manifest from this: because unless soul were signified by way of a concrete, sensitive, which is a concrete name, could not be truly predicated of it; and by the very fact that it is truly predicated, signifying the same as what has the grade of sensing, it cannot be denied that soul too is signified by way of a concrete. Hence it is not well inferred that this too is true, Humanity is animality, in which it is certain that an abstract

p. 92

prædicari de abstracto: & ideo diuersam habere rationem.

is predicated of an abstract; and therefore it has a different ratio.

Pro solutione secundæ partis, annotanda est triplex differentia inter abstracta substantiarum, & accidentium. Prima: quòd illa abstrahuntur abstractione metaphysica à generibus, speciebus, aut differentiis. Vt animalitas ab animali, & humanitas ab homine. Abstracta verò accidentium, abstrahuntur abstractione physica à subiecto, in quo forma accidentalis significata realiter inhæret. Vnde eo ipso quòd significatur vt abstracta ab eo, non significatur vt inhærẽs, aut dependens ab eo: sed ad modum naturæ completæ per se subsistentis. Secunda. Quia abstracta substantiarũ, semper habẽt modum formæ, aut principi eius, à quo abstrahuntur, abstracta verò accidentium, potiùs habent modum completum naturæ totalis, ac per se subsistentis: quod prouenit ex proprio modo abstractionis physicæ. Postrema differentia est, quòd abstracta substantiarum, quia metaphysicè abstrahuntur, sunt abstracta vltima: quia abstractio metaphysica vltima est. Vnde nõ potest ab eis alia abstractio fieri: nihil enim amplius ab humanitate, aut animalitate abstrahi potest. Abstracta verò accidentium, nõ sunt vltima: quia nec abstractio physica vltima est, sed adhuc potest ei succedere abstractio metaphysica: ita, vt ab albedine, quæ abstrahitur abstractione physica, possit aliud abstractum metaphysicum sumi: quod erit ratio albedinis, vel albedineitas (barbaro vocabulo, sed naturã rei explicãte significata) ex quo intelligitur, abstracta accidentiũ solùm vocari abstracta in ordine physico, in ordine verò metaphysico cõcreta potiùs esse.

For the solution of the second part, a threefold difference is to be noted between the abstracts of substances and those of accidents. The first: that the former are abstracted by metaphysical abstraction from genera, species or differences, as animality from animal and humanity from man; but the abstracts of accidents are abstracted by physical abstraction from the subject in which the accidental form signified really inheres. Hence, by the very fact that it is signified as abstracted from it, it is not signified as inhering in it or dependent on it, but after the manner of a complete nature subsisting per se. The second: because the abstracts of substances always have the mode of the form or principle of that from which they are abstracted, whereas the abstracts of accidents rather have the complete mode of a total nature, subsisting per se; which comes from the proper mode of physical abstraction. The last difference is that the abstracts of substances, because they are abstracted metaphysically, are ultimate abstracts, because metaphysical abstraction is ultimate; hence no other abstraction can be made from them: for nothing further can be abstracted from humanity or animality. But the abstracts of accidents are not ultimate, because neither is physical abstraction ultimate, but metaphysical abstraction can still follow upon it: so that from whiteness, which is abstracted by physical abstraction, another, metaphysical abstract can be taken, which will be the ratio of whiteness, or albedineitas [whitenessness] (a barbarous word, but one that signifies by explaining the nature of the thing). From which it is understood that the abstracts of accidents are called abstracts only in the physical order, but in the metaphysical order are rather concretes.

Ex his differentiis ad formam argumenti respondere possumus, concedendo maiorem, quòd vera sit hæc: albedo est color, sed negando minorem, quòd in ea prædicetur abstractum superius de abstracto inferiori: sed potiùs est prædicatio concretorum in ordine metaphysico, sicut hæc, homo est animal. Vnde nec prædicatum significatur per modum partis, sed per modum totius completi, & per se subsistentis atque continentis, quidquid cõtinet subiectum, quod se habet sicut genus ad speciem: vt in hac, homo est animal. Illa verò, humanitas est animalitas, prædicatio abstractorum est in eodem ordine metaphysico: & ideo est falsa. Et eodem modo, erit falsa prædicatio abstractorum in accidentibus, si abstrahantur abstractione metaphysica: vt si ab albedine & colore, metaphysicè abstrahamus albedineitatem, & coloreitatem, vel ratione albedinis, & rationem coloris, falsa erit, albedineitas est coloreitas: quia abstracta metaphysica, per modum principij, & formæ significantur: & ideo non possunt efficere veram prædicationem.

From these differences we can reply to the form of the argument, granting the major, that this is true, whiteness is color, but denying the minor, that in it a superior abstract is predicated of an inferior abstract; rather it is a predication of concretes in the metaphysical order, like this, man is animal. Hence neither is the predicate signified by way of a part, but by way of a complete whole, subsisting per se and containing whatever the subject contains, which is related as genus to species, as in this, man is animal. But that one, humanity is animality, is a predication of abstracts in the same metaphysical order, and therefore it is false. And in the same way a predication of abstracts in accidents will be false if they are abstracted by metaphysical abstraction: as if from whiteness and color we metaphysically abstract albedineitas and coloreitas, or the ratio of whiteness and the ratio of color, this will be false, albedineitas is coloreitas: because metaphysical abstracts are signified by way of principle and form, and therefore cannot make a true predication.

p. 93

SECVNDA PARS HVIVS

S E C O N D PA RT O F T H I S

TRACTATVS, DE PRÆDICATIOnibus secundarum intentionum.

T R E AT I S E , O N T H E P R E D I C A-tions of Second Intentions.

Secundæ intentiones, sunt relationes quædam rationis, quas intellectus attribuit primis intentionibus, nempe naturis realibus, quæ ab eis denominantur: vt secunda intentio speciei, est relatio rationis naturæ specificæ, quam ei attribuit intellectus, dum eam comparat ad indiuidua: & prædicabilia omnia, sunt quædam relationes rationis diuersæ, quia diuersis naturis attribuuntur, & in ordine ad inferiora diuersa, vel de quibus diuerso modo prædicantur. Vt prædicabile generis, est secunda intentio, aut relatio rationis in ordine ad plures species, de quibus prædicatur in quid tanquam totum potentiale. Prædicabile differentiæ, est secunda intentio aut relatio rationis, in ordine ad plures species, aut indiuidua, de puibus prædicatur in quale quid. Prædicabile proprij, est secunda intentio, aut relatio rationis propriæ passionis ad species, aut indiuidua, vt sensibilis ad hominem, & equum: aut risibilis ad hominem, ac Petrum, & Ioannem. Et prædicabile accidentis, est secunda intentio, aut relatio rationis, accidentis ad plura subiecta specie aut numero distincta, vt relatio rationis albi, ad hominem & equum, vel ad Petrum, & Ioannem. Et tandem vniuersale, quod est commune omnibus prædicabilibue: est secunda intentio, aut relatio rationis ad omnia, & singula prædicabilia: quæ de omnibus prædicatur in quid, tanquam genus.

econd intentions are certain relations of reason which the intellect S attributes to first intentions, that is, to real natures, which are denominated by them: as the second intention of species is a relation of reason of the specific nature, which the intellect attributes to it when it compares it to the individuals; and all the predicables are certain relations of reason, diverse because they are attributed to diverse natures, and in order to diverse inferiors, or to inferiors of which they are predicated in diverse ways. Thus the predicable of genus is a second intention, or a relation of reason in order to several species, of which it is predicated in quid as a potential whole. The predicable of difference is a second intention, or a relation of reason in order to several species or individuals, of which it is predicated in quale quid. The predicable of property is a second intention, or a relation of reason of a proper attribute to species or individuals: as of sensible to man and horse, or of risible to man, and to Peter and John. And the predicable of accident is a second intention, or a relation of reason of an accident to several subjects distinct in species or in number: as the relation of reason of white to man and horse, or to Peter and John. And finally the universal, which is common to all the predicables, is a second intention, or a relation of reason to all and each of the predicables, of which it is predicated in quid as a genus.

His suppositis, duobus modis comparari possunt secundæ intentiones. Primò, inter sese, in quantum vna prædicatur de alia: & si ita comparentur, siue in cõcreto, siue in abstracto, eodem modo se habent ac primę intentiones: ita vt si vna aliquo modo pertineat ad aliam, concreta de concretis prædicentur essentialiter, vel accidentaliter, tanquam accidens propriũ, vel commune. Ideo veræ sunt omnes istæ, Genus est vniuersale, species est vniuersalis: & etiam hæc, Vniuersale est genus, sed illæ sunt essentiales: ista verò accidentalis. Hæc verò, Vniuersale est prædicabile, est prædicatio proprij, aut quarti prædicabilis, Concreta verò de abstractis vel abstracta de concretis, semper efficiunt propositiones falsas: vt genus est genereitas, aut specietas est species: vel genus est vniuersalitas. Solùm est

These things supposed, second intentions can be compared in two ways. First, among themselves, inasmuch as one is predicated of another; and if they are compared in this way, whether in the concrete or in the abstract, they behave in the same way as first intentions: so that if one pertains in some way to another, concretes are predicated of concretes essentially or accidentally, as a proper or a common accident. Therefore all of these are true: Genus is universal, Species is universal; and also this: Universal is genus; but the former are essential, the latter accidental. This one, however, The universal is predicable, is a predication of a property, or of the fourth predicable. But concretes of abstracts, or abstracts of concretes, always make false propositions: as Genus is genericity, or Specificity is species, or Genus is universality. Only

p. 94

differentia in prædicationibus abstractorum: quia in secundis intentionibus, vera est prædicatio abstracti superioris, de abstracto inferiori, vt genereitis est vniuersalitas: quam tamen in primis intẽtionibus diximus esse falsam, vt humanitas est animalitas. Et ratio huius differentiæ est: quia secundæ intentiones sunt relationes rationis, & ideo accidentia rationis: quare sicut accidentia realia, in abstracto significata, non habent modum partium, sed totius per se subsistentis, quia nõ abstrahuntur abstractione metaphysica generibus, aut speciebus, sed abstractione physica à subiectis: eodem modo secundæ intentiones, habent similitudinem cum formis accidentalibus, & ideo non significantur per nomina abstracta, tanquam formæ aut principia generum, aut specierũ, sed per modum totius ac per se subsistentis. Et hæc est ratio, propter quam veram constituunt prædicationẽ: quãuis in primis intentionibus sit falsa.

in the predications of abstracts is there a difference: because in second intentions the predication of a superior abstract of an inferior abstract is true, as genericity is universality; which, however, in first intentions we said is false, as humanity is animality. And the reason for this difference is that second intentions are relations of reason, and therefore accidents of reason. Wherefore, just as real accidents signified in the abstract do not have the mode of parts but of a whole subsisting per se, because they are not abstracted by metaphysical abstraction from genera or species, but by physical abstraction from their subjects, in the same way second intentions have a likeness to accidental forms, and therefore are not signified through abstract names as forms or principles of genera or species, but by way of a whole subsisting per se. And this is the reason why they constitute a true predication, although in first intentions it is false.

Secundò, cum primis. Si secundæ intentiones comparentur ad primas, semper comparantur accidentaliter, cùm sint relationes, & accidentia eis attributa: & eodem etiam modo, se habent in omnibus, vt diximus se habere primas inter se. Dum comparantur accidentaliter, in hoc solo differunt: quòd accidentia realia quæ verè prędicantur de inferioribus verè etiam prædicantur de superioribus: & si verè prædicantur de superioribus, verè etiam prædicantur de aliquo inferiori: vt si album prædicatur de Petro, necesse est verè prædicari de homine: & si prædicatur de homine, necesse est verè prædicari de aliquo homine singulari. Quod non reperitur in secundis intentionibus, sed contrarium: quia nec secundæ intentiones, quæ prædicantur de inferioribus, possunt vetè prædicari de superioribus, nec etiam verè prædicantur de inferioribus: quæ prædicantur de superioribus: vt his exemplis fit manifestum. Species prædicatur de homine, & non de animali, nec Petro: & genus prædicatur de animali, & non de homine: & secunda intentio indiuidui, verè prædicatur de Petro, dum dicimus, Petrus est indiuiduum, & tamen non prædicatur de homine: sed falsa est hæc, homo est indiuiduum. Et ratio huius differentiæ est, quia accidentia realia conueniunt subiectis absolutè, & vt sunt à parte rei: sed secundę intentiones, quę sunt relationes & accidentia rationis, non conueniunt naturis absolutè, nec à parte rei, sed vt tali modo concipiuntur ab intellectu, nempe in communi, in ordine ad species, vel indiuidua: aut etiam in singulari, & ideo quę conueniunt inferiori, nempe indiuiduo, non possunt conuenire speciei, nec illa quę conuenit speciei, potest conuenire generi: quia secunda intentio

Second, with first intentions. If second intentions are compared to first ones, they are always compared accidentally, since they are relations and accidents attributed to them; and they also behave in the same way in all things as we said first intentions behave among themselves when they are compared accidentally. In this alone they differ: that real accidents which are truly predicated of inferiors are truly predicated also of superiors; and if they are truly predicated of superiors, they are truly predicated also of some inferior: as if white is predicated of Peter, it must be truly predicated of man; and if it is predicated of man, it must be truly predicated of some singular man. Which is not found in second intentions, but the contrary: because neither can the second intentions which are predicated of inferiors be truly predicated of superiors, nor are those which are predicated of superiors truly predicated of inferiors, as is made manifest by these examples. Species is predicated of man, and not of animal, nor of Peter; and genus is predicated of animal, and not of man; and the second intention of individual is truly predicated of Peter when we say Peter is an individual, and yet it is not predicated of man, but this is false, man is an individual. And the reason for this difference is that real accidents belong to their subjects absolutely and as they are on the part of the thing; but second intentions, which are relations and accidents of reason, do not belong to natures absolutely, nor on the part of the thing, but as they are conceived in such a mode by the intellect, namely in common, in order to species or individuals, or also in the singular; and therefore those which belong to the inferior, namely to the individual, cannot belong to the species, nor can that which belongs to the species belong to the genus: because the second intention

p. 95

indiuidui conuenit Petro, vt concipitur tamquam indiuisibile in alia indiuidua: & hoc modo concipi repugnat speciei: & secunda intentio generis, conuenit naturæ, vt concipitur in ordine ad species, sed in ordine ad indiuidua concipitur.

of individual belongs to Peter as he is conceived as indivisible into other individuals, and to be conceived in this way is repugnant to the species; and the second intention of genus belongs to the nature as it is conceived in order to species, but it is conceived in order to individuals.

CHAPTER II

De Genere

On Genus.

Videtur autem neque genus, neque species simpliciter dici, &c.

But it seems that neither genus nor species is said simply, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

Intentum Porphyrij in pręsenti capite est, explicare naturam generis, quod est primum prædicabile. Diuiditur autem in tres partes. In prima ponit duas acceptiones reales generis, & inter se eas comparat, ex quarum similitudine, in secunda parte, colligit tertiam acceptionem eius Logicam. In tertia verò, tradit definitionem generis, & simul eam exponit.

The intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of genus, which is the first predicable. And it is divided into three parts. In the first he lays down two real acceptations of genus and compares them with each other; from their likeness, in the second part, he gathers its third, logical acceptation. And in the third he hands down the definition of genus and at the same time expounds it.

Prima acceptio realis generis est, qua accipitur pro collectione aliqua hominum, habentium ordinem inter sese, & ad vnum primum, à quo omnes deriuantur: in qua significatione, Romanam gentem solemus vocare genus, Romanorum, quia inter sese per tales leges ordinantur, & à Romulo, tanquam à primo principio, descendunt.

The first real acceptation of genus is that in which it is taken for some collection of men having an order among themselves and to one first, from whom all are derived: in which signification we are accustomed to call the Roman people the genus of the Romans, because they are ordered among themselves by such laws, and descend from Romulus as from their first principle.

Secundò, accipitur genus pro principio ipso generationis, à quo deriuantur alij: siue sit pater aut patria, in qua significatione loquitur poëta, dum dicit: Mantua me genuit, &c. Genus suum, aut principium generationis, patriam vocans. Sed propriè loquendo, non tam pater, vel patria, quàm origo, per quam ab eis deriuantur homines, genus vocatur: quia non ita Romanos ducere genus ab eo. Ex his autem duabus acceptionibus, secundam esse magis propriam, quàm primam, docet Porphyrius. Primò, quia frequentiùs ea vtimur. Secundò, quia collectio hominum, ideo vocatur genus, quia homines illius ab vno primo ducunt originem: ergo origo: per quam ab eo deriuantur, magis propriè vocatur genus quàm collectio ipsa.

Second, genus is taken for the very principle of generation from which others are derived, whether it be the father or the fatherland: in which signification the poet speaks when he says: Mantua begot me, etc., calling his fatherland his genus, or principle of generation. But properly speaking, it is not so much the father or the fatherland as the origin through which men are derived from them that is called genus: for we do not so much call him their genus as say that the Romans draw their genus from him. And of these two acceptations Porphyry teaches that the second is more proper than the first. First, because we use it more frequently. Second, because a collection of men is called a genus precisely because the men of it draw their origin from one first; therefore the origin through which they are derived from him is more properly called genus than the collection itself.

In secunda parte, ex vtraque acceptione reali, colligit Porphyrius Logicam, quam per se intendit, dicens: Logicum genus accipi pro eo, cui supponuntur species, id est, sub quo collocantur, vt animal est genus, quia sub eo ponuntur, homo,

In the second part, from both real acceptations, Porphyry gathers the logical one, which he intends per se, saying: The logical genus is taken for that under which the species are placed, that is, under which they are set, as animal is a genus, because under it are placed man,

p. 96

& leo: quæ species habẽt ordinem, & similitudinem quandam inter se, ratione eiusdem naturæ, quam participant ab ipso genere, à quo etiam dicuntur suo modo ducere originem.

and lion: which species have an order and a certain likeness among themselves by reason of the same nature, which they participate from the genus itself, from which they are also said in their own way to draw their origin.

In tertia parte cap. definit genus Logicum, secundùm vltimam acceptionem sumptum, & definitio talis est: Genus est, quod prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie, in eo quod quid. Quam ita explicat: Ea quæ prædicantur, aut prædicantur de vno, vt indiuiduum: aut de pluribus, vt vniuersalia. Per particulam ergo de pluribus, separatur genus ab indiuiduo, quod de vno solo prædicatur. Per particulam verò, de differentibus specie, separatur ab specie, quæ est secundum prædicabile, & solùm prædicatur de differentibus numero. Per vltimum particulam, in eo quod quid, separatur à tribus aliis prædicabilibus, differentia, proprio, & accidenti: nam illa, in quale quid, proprium, & accidens, in quale genus non nisi in quid prædicatur: quia ad quæstionem factam per quid, non bene per illa, sed per genus respondemus, vt si inquiras, quid est homo, bene respondeo, quòd sit animal: Hæc Porphyrius.

In the third part of the chapter he defines the logical genus, taken according to the last acceptation; and the definition is this: Genus is what is predicated of many differing in species, in quid. Which he explains thus: Things that are predicated are predicated either of one, as the individual, or of many, as universals. By the particle of many, therefore, genus is separated from the individual, which is predicated of one alone. By the particle differing in species, it is separated from species, which is the second predicable and is predicated only of things differing in number. By the last particle, in quid, it is separated from the three other predicables, difference, property and accident: for difference is predicated in quale quid, property and accident in quale, genus only in quid; because to a question put through what we do not answer well through those, but through genus: as if you ask what man is, I answer well that he is an animal. Thus far Porphyry.

QUESTION I

Quæst. 1. Quodnam sit definitum definitionis generis — What the defined of the definition of genus is.

Quòd definitio generis assignata à Porphyrio, nullum habeat definitum, duobus argumentis probo. Primum, si aliquod haberet, maximè genus: sed genus non est definibile, ergo nullum habet. Probatur minor: Bona definitio debet constare genere, & differentia, aut aliquo loco generis, & alio loco differentiæ: sed generis non datur genus: nam si daretur, illius generis daretur aliud genus, & sic procederemus in infinitum: sequitur ergo, genus non esse definibile, & ideo nullum habere definitum prædictam definitionem.

That the definition of genus assigned by Porphyry has no defined, I prove by two arguments. First: if it had any, it would above all be genus; but genus is not definable; therefore it has none. The minor is proved: A good definition must consist of genus and difference, or of something in place of the genus and something else in place of the difference; but there is no genus of genus: for if there were, there would be another genus of that genus, and so we should proceed to infinity. It follows, therefore, that genus is not definable, and therefore that the aforesaid definition has no defined.

Secundò: Definitio debet dari per genus, & differentiam: ergo nihil potest definiri, nisi species, quia hæc sola componitur ex genere, & differentia: imò nec definiri potest aliquid, nisi in quantum est species, quia habere genus & differentiam, conuenit speciei, in quantum est species: ergo genus non potest definiri. Probatur consequentia, quia non est species, sed aliud prædicabile distinctum ab specie: & ideo nullum habebit definitum præsens definitio.

Second: a definition must be given through genus and difference; therefore nothing can be defined except species, because this alone is composed of genus and difference; indeed, nothing can be defined except inasmuch as it is a species, because to have genus and difference belongs to the species inasmuch as it is a species; therefore genus cannot be defined. The consequence is proved, because it is not a species but another predicable distinct from species; and therefore the present definition will have no defined.

Tenendum tamen est, Bonam esse definitionem generis, & certum habere definitum, cuius naturam explicat. Et quòd bona sit definitio probatur primò ex Aristot. 1. lib. Topic. cap. 4. vbi eam posuit Arist. Et à quo illam desumpsit

It must be held, however, that the definition of genus is good and has a definite defined, whose nature it explains. And that the definition is good is proved, first, from Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 4, where Aristotle laid it down; and it was from him that

p. 97

Porphyrius. Secundò, ratione: Quia bona definitio est, quę ita naturam definiti explicat, vt illud distinguat, à quibuscunque aliis rebus, cum quibus conuenire posset: sed per hanc, definitionem explicatur quid sit genus, nempe prædicabile de pluribus differentibus specie, in quid, & distinguitur ab indiuiduo, & reliquis prædicabilibus, vt vidimus in explicatione tex. Est igitur bona.

Porphyry took it. Second, by argument: because a good definition is one that so explains the nature of the defined that it distinguishes it from any other things with which it could agree; but through this definition it is explained what genus is, namely a predicable of many differing in species, in quid, and it is distinguished from the individual and from the remaining predicables, as we saw in the explanation of the text. It is therefore good.

Secundum verò, quòd habeat certum, ac determinatum definitum, sic probo.

And the second point, that it has a definite and determinate defined, I prove thus.

3 Prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie in quid, est communis ratio, eodem modo, atque æqualiter conueniens omnibus generibus: ergo est vna, & per vnam definitionem potest explicari: quare hæc erit determinatum definitum, eiusdem definitionis.

3 To be predicated of many differing in species, in quid, is a common ratio, belonging in the same way and equally to all genera; therefore it is one and can be explained through one definition; wherefore this will be the determinate defined of that definition.

Sed vt hæc veritas meliùs intelligatur, & argumenta soluantur, annotandum est: secundam intentionem generis, quæ est primum prædicabile, relationem quandam rationis esse, & vniuersalissimam rationem denominandi omnes naturas genericas, etiam si sint suprema genera prædicamentorum, vt substantia, quantitas, & qualitas, & simul esse speciem quandam vniuersalis: vnde cùm species quælibet componatur ex genere & differentia, hæc etiam secunda intentio, componitur ex vniuersali, quod est commune genus prædicabilium, & ex differentia, quæ est esse respectiuum ad plures species, de quibus prędicari potest in quid. Itaque genus conuenit cum cæteris prædicabilibus, in ratione communi vniuersalis, quæ est esse vnum in multis: & distinguitur ab eis, quia est in multis speciebus, de quibus prædicari potest in quid: & ideò licèt sit vniuersalissima ratio denominandi, quia naturæ, quas denominat genera, sunt etiam magna ex parte vniuersalissimæ, cùm sint suprema genera prædicamentorum: nihilominus secundùm essentiam est particularis, & determinata species cuiusdam generis, quod est vniuersale. Ex quo intelligitur: quòd per determinatam definitionem possit definiri, & quòd definitio eius tradita à Porphyrio, determinatum habeat definitum.

But in order that this truth may be better understood and the arguments solved, it should be noted that the second intention of genus, which is the first predicable, is a certain relation of reason, and a most universal ratio of denominating all generic natures, even if they are the supreme genera of the categories, as substance, quantity and quality; and at the same time it is a certain species of universal. Hence, since every species is composed of genus and difference, this second intention too is composed of universal, which is the common genus of the predicables, and of a difference, which is to be relative to several species of which it can be predicated in quid. And so genus agrees with the other predicables in the common ratio of universal, which is to be one in many; and it is distinguished from them because it is in many species, of which it can be predicated in quid. And therefore, although it is a most universal ratio of denominating, because the natures which it denominates as genera are also for the most part most universal, since they are the supreme genera of the categories, nevertheless according to its essence it is a particular and determinate species of a certain genus, which is universal. From which it is understood that it can be defined through a determinate definition, and that its definition handed down by Porphyry has a determinate defined.

Ad formam primi argumenti respondendum est, negando minorem primi syllogismi: & dum dicitur in minori secundi syllogismi, quòd generis non datur genus, distinguendo, quia secunda intentio generis, dupliciter sumi potest, in ratione denominandi, aut in ratione essendi. Et primo modo, non habet aliud genus, à quo denominetur: quia non est genus denominatiuè, aut accidentaliter, sed essentialiter: sed in ratione essendi, determinata species est, & habet genus superius, quod

To the form of the first argument it must be replied by denying the minor of the first syllogism; and when it is said in the minor of the second syllogism that there is no genus of genus, by distinguishing: because the second intention of genus can be taken in two ways, in the ratio of denominating or in the ratio of being. And in the first way it has no other genus by which it is denominated, because it is not a genus denominatively or accidentally, but essentially; but in the ratio of being it is a determinate species, and has a superior genus, which G

p. 98

est vniuersale, ex quo simul ac differẽtia componitur.

is universal, of which, together with the difference, it is composed.

Etsi dicatur, etiam vniuersale denominari genus, ab hac secunda intentione generis, quæ est primum prædicabile, sicut reliqua genera: & ideo esse inferius respectu illius: Respondetur, verum esse antecedens, sed distinguendum consequens: nam in ratione denominandi, est superius vniuersali, sed in ratione essendi inferius: & quia denominatio est accidentalis, respectu eius, quod denominatur: vt denominatio albi respectu corporis: & ratio essendi essentialis: ideò secunda intentio generis per hanc definitionem explicata, accidentaliter est superior vniuersali, sed essentialiter inferior, tanquam vera species eius.

And if it is said that universal too is denominated genus by this second intention of genus, which is the first predicable, like the remaining genera, and therefore is inferior with respect to it: it is replied that the antecedent is true, but the consequent must be distinguished. For in the ratio of denominating it is superior to universal, but in the ratio of being inferior; and because denomination is accidental with respect to that which is denominated, as the denomination of white with respect to body, while the ratio of being is essential, therefore the second intention of genus explained by this definition is accidentally superior to universal, but essentially inferior, as its true species.

Ad formam secundi argumenti respondeo: Nihil definiri propria definitione, nisi speciem: sed genus, quod est primum prædicabile, esse speciem alterius generis, nempe vniuersalis, quod accidentaliter denominat: & ideo propriè definiri posse. Ad illud verò, quod in argumento additur, Omne quod definitur, definiri in quantum est species, hac distinctione respõdendum est. Definiri aliquid in quantum est species, duplicem sensum habere potest. Primum, quòd ratio speciei explicetur per definitionem: & hoc est falsum: quia licèt homo sit species, dum definitur, quòd sit animal rationale, non tamen explicatur per talem definitionem, quòd sit species. Secundus sensus est, definiri in quantum est species: ita vt esse speciem sit conditio necessaria, ad propriam definitionem, & hoc est verum: sed non explicatur per definitionem, nisi propria & essentialis ratio definiti, quæ tamen accidentaliter denominatur species, à secundo prædicabili.

To the form of the second argument I reply: nothing is defined by a proper definition except a species; but genus, which is the first predicable, is a species of another genus, namely of universal, which it denominates accidentally; and therefore it can properly be defined. But to what is added in the argument, that everything which is defined is defined inasmuch as it is a species, it must be replied with this distinction. “Something is defined inasmuch as it is a species” can have a twofold sense. The first, that the ratio of species is explained through the definition; and this is false: because although man is a species, when he is defined as rational animal, yet it is not explained through such a definition that he is a species. The second sense is “to be defined inasmuch as it is a species” in such a way that to be a species is a necessary condition for a proper definition; and this is true. But nothing is explained through the definition except the proper and essential ratio of the defined, which nevertheless is accidentally denominated species by the second predicable.

QUESTION II

Quæst. 2. An definitum proprium eiusdem definitionis sit natura realis, quæ denominatur genus, vel secunda intentio, à qua denominatur — Whether the proper defined of the same definition is the real nature which is denominated genus, or the second intention of genus by which it is denominated.

6 Genus in communi consideratum, quatuor modis sumi potest. Primò, pro natura, quæ denominatur genus, secundùm suam essentiam considerata, vt si animal accipiamus, pro natura sensitiua. Secundò, accipiatur pro aggregato ex natura denominata, & secũda intẽtione denominante, quemadmodum album sumi potest pro aggregato ex corpore, & albedine. Tertiò, accipitur pro natura generica, non secũdum suam essentiam, sed in quantum denominatur genus à secunda, intentione generis. Quartò, pro eadem secunda intentione, denominante eandem naturam genus. Ex his autem quatuor,

6 Genus considered in common can be taken in four ways. First, for the nature which is denominated genus, considered according to its essence: as if we take animal for the sensitive nature. Second, it is taken for the aggregate of the nature denominated and the second intention denominating, just as white can be taken for the aggregate of body and whiteness. Third, it is taken for the generic nature, not according to its essence, but inasmuch as it is denominated genus by the second intention of genus. Fourth, for that same second intention denominating the same nature genus. And of these four,

p. 99

certum est aggregatum non esse definitum; quia est ens per accidens, ex duobus entibus in actu compositum: nempe ex natura, & secunda intentione: Ens autem per accidens non habet vnam essentiam, sed duplicem: & ideo non potest per vnam definitionem explicari, vt expressè docet Arist. 7. Meta. tex. 21.

it is certain that the aggregate is not the defined, because it is a being per accidens, composed of two beings in act, namely of the nature and of the second intention. But a being per accidens does not have one essence but a twofold one, and therefore it cannot be explained through one definition, as Aristotle expressly teaches, Metaph. 7, text 21.

Quæstio ergo procedit de tribus aliis. Et sunt circa eam tres opiniones. Prima asserit, definitum huius definitionis esse naturam genericam, secundùm essentialia, ita vt animal sit genus, & prædicabile de pluribus differentibus specie in quid, vt est viuens sensibile: & sic de cæteris generibus. Hæc attribuitur Scoto: qui cùm affirmet naturam esse vniuersalem secundùm se, & ante operationem intellectus, videtur consequenter asserere, quòd sit genus, vel species essentialiter. Et probatur ratione: Quia illud est definitum, cui conuenit definitio: sed prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie, conuenit naturæ secundùm essentiam, & non vt denominatur à secunda intentione: ergo illa est definitum. Minor probatur, quia animal secundùm quod est viuens sensibile, prædicatur de homine, & leone, & non vt denominatur à secunda intẽtione: nam si hoc modo prædicaretur, dum dicimus, homo est animal, ergo sensus esset, homo est genus. Probatur consequentia: Quia animal, vt denominatur à secunda intentione, est genus.

The question therefore proceeds about the three others. And there are three opinions concerning it. The first asserts that the defined of this definition is the generic nature according to its essentials, so that animal is a genus and a predicable of many differing in species, in quid, as it is a sensible living thing; and so of the other genera. This is attributed to Scotus, who, since he affirms that the nature is universal according to itself and before the operation of the intellect, seems consequently to assert that it is a genus or a species essentially. And it is proved by argument: because that is the defined to which the definition belongs; but to be predicated of many differing in species belongs to the nature according to its essence, and not as it is denominated by the second intention; therefore that is the defined. The minor is proved, because animal, according as it is a sensible living thing, is predicated of man and lion, and not as it is denominated by the second intention: for if it were predicated in this way, when we say man is animal, then the sense would be, man is a genus. The consequence is proved: because animal, as it is denominated by the second intention, is a genus.

Hæc sententia nec est Scoti, nec ex vera, sed falsa. Probatur, primùm: quia licèt Scotus asserat, dari vnitatem formalem à parte rei, quæ est fundamentum generis, & speciei: genera tamen, & species denominationes tributas naturis ab intellectu esse docet: quare non tenet naturam realem secundùm essentiam esse definitum. Quòd verò talis opinio sit falsa, hoc argumento probatur. Si natura generica secundùm propriam essentiam est definitum: ergo secundùm propriam essentiam est genus, vel saltem esse genus, erit propria passio eius: sed quæ sunt essentialia naturæ genericæ, aut propriæ passiones eius, conueniunt necessariò speciebus, vt quæcunque sunt essentialia animali, aut tanquam propriæ passiones ei conueniunt, sunt essentialia equo, & leoni, aut propriæ passiones eorum: ergo genus, aut prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie, conueniet speciebus: quod patet esse falsum.

This opinion is neither Scotus’s, nor true, but false. The first is proved: because although Scotus asserts that there is a formal unity on the part of the thing which is the foundation of genus and species, yet he teaches that genera and species are denominations attributed to natures by the intellect; wherefore he does not hold that the real nature according to its essence is the defined. But that this opinion is false is proved by this argument. If the generic nature according to its proper essence is the defined, then according to its proper essence it is a genus, or at least to be a genus will be its proper attribute; but whatever things are essential to the generic nature, or are its proper attributes, necessarily belong to its species, as whatever things are essential to animal, or belong to it as proper attributes, are essential to horse and lion, or are their proper attributes; therefore to be a genus, or to be predicated of many differing in species, will belong to the species; which is plainly false.

Secunda opinio est Caietani in opus. de Ente, & Essentia, ca. 4. vbi tenet nec naturam genericam secundùm Essentialia, nec vt denominatur à secunda intentione, esse definitum, sed secundam intentionem. Quam tamen dupliciter posse considerari ait: Primò, vt Quo: hoc est, vt ratio est denominandi naturam genericam: sicut albedo est ratio denominandi

The second opinion is that of Cajetan in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4, where he holds that neither the generic nature according to its essentials, nor as it is denominated by the second intention, is the defined, but the second intention. Which, however, he says can be considered in two ways. First, as That by which, that is, as the ratio of denominating the generic nature, just as whiteness is the ratio of denominating G ij

p. 100

corpus album: & hoc est considerare illam in abstracto. Secundò, potest considerari, in quantum refertur ad species: nam cùm sit relatio rationis, essentialiter respicit terminum: terminus autem relationis generis, sunt species: & ideo considerari potest in ordine ad illas, & hoc modo sumitur vt Quod, & in concreto: & est proprium definitum huius definitionis, non verò primo modo sumpta.

a white body; and this is to consider it in the abstract. Second, it can be considered inasmuch as it is referred to the species: for since it is a relation of reason, it essentially regards its term; but the term of the relation of genus is the species; and therefore it can be considered in order to them; and in this way it is taken as That which, and in the concrete, and it is the proper defined of this definition, but not when taken in the first way.

Probat Caie. hoc argum. Definitio debet conuenire definito essentialiter, si sit quidditatiua: aut tanquam propria passio, si sit descriptiua: sed prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie, conuenit naturæ genericæ, vt animali, aut colori accidentaliter, etiam consideratæ in communi: & secundæ intentioni in concreto essentialiter, quia secunda intentio generis, essentialiter respicit species, cùm sit relatio ad illas: ergo hæc, & non illa, erit definitum.

Cajetan proves it by this argument. A definition must belong to the defined essentially, if it is quidditative, or as a proper attribute, if it is descriptive; but to be predicated of many differing in species belongs to the generic nature, as to animal or to color, accidentally, even considered in common; and to the second intention in the concrete essentially, because the second intention of genus essentially regards the species, since it is a relation to them; therefore this, and not that, will be the defined.

8 Hæc opinio etiam est falsa: quod probo. Primò, prædicari de pluribus, conuenit generi in concreto: quia quod prædicatur de pluribus, concretum est, sicut disgregare visum, conuenit albo in concreto: sed hæc opinio non ponit genus in concreto definiri: ergo est falsa. Probatur minor. Quia concretum accidentale, quale est genus, significat formam, nempe secundam intentionem: & connotat subiectum, nempe naturam genericam, cui conuenit prędicari de pluribus: si ergo natura generica non est definitum, sed secunda intentio: ergo non definitur genus in concreto, sed in abstracto, quod contradicit verbis definitionis.

8 This opinion too is false, which I prove. First, to be predicated of many belongs to genus in the concrete, because what is predicated of many is a concrete, just as to disperse sight belongs to white in the concrete; but this opinion does not hold that genus in the concrete is defined; therefore it is false. The minor is proved: because an accidental concrete, such as genus is, signifies the form, namely the second intention, and connotes the subject, namely the generic nature, to which it belongs to be predicated of many. If, therefore, the generic nature is not the defined, but the second intention, then genus is not defined in the concrete but in the abstract, which contradicts the words of the definition.

Secundò, etiam si consideretur secunda intentio generis, in quantum relatio ad species: non est concretum, sed abstractum: ergo falsò eam vocat concretum Caie. Probatur antecedens, quia concretum relationis est relatiuum, sicut concretum albedinis est album: sed secunda intentio generis, etiam in ordine ad species, non est relatiuum, quia non est id quod refertur, sed ratio referendi: ergo non est concretum, sed abstractum.

Second, even if the second intention of genus is considered inasmuch as it is a relation to the species, it is not a concrete but an abstract; therefore Cajetan falsely calls it a concrete. The antecedent is proved, because the concrete of relation is the relative, just as the concrete of whiteness is white; but the second intention of genus, even in order to the species, is not the relative, because it is not that which is referred but the ratio of referring; therefore it is not a concrete but an abstract.

9 Tertia opinio, est D. Tho. in opusc. de ente & essentia, ca. 4. vbi asserit, definitum adæquatum ex natura generica, & secunda intentione constare: hoc modo consideratis, nempe, natura generica, non secundùm se, sed vt denominatur à secunda intentione, & secunda intentione denominante: ita vt natura hoc modo considerata, sit definitum materiale, & vt Quod: quia illa est, quæ prædicatur de pluribus differentibus namero. Et secunda intentio, sit definitum formale, & vt Quo: quia non est id quòd prædicatur, sed ratio prædicandi: ex vtraque verò

9 The third opinion is that of St. Thomas in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 4, where he asserts that the adequate defined consists of the generic nature and the second intention, considered in this way: namely the generic nature not according to itself but as it is denominated by the second intention, and the second intention as denominating; so that the nature considered in this way is the material defined, and as That which, because it is that which is predicated of many differing in number; and the second intention is the formal defined, and as That by which, because it is not that which is predicated but the ratio of predicating; and from both

p. 101

resultat vnum definitum adæquatum, & per se: quia non consideratur tanquam aggregatum ex eis: sed tanquam includens vnum in ordine ad alterum: quę verò per se sunt ordinata, non efficiunt vnum per accidens. Exemplum habemus in hac definitione, Disgregatiuum visus. Cuius definitum materiale, & vt Quod, est corpus, vt denominatur ab albedine: quia ei conuenit disgregare visum: formale verò, & vt Quo, albedo: quę potiùs est ratio disgregandi visum: sed ex vtroque vt ordinato ad alterum, resultat vnum definitum adæquatum, & per se. Hanc sententiam sequuntur Iauel. in sua Logica, tit. 4. c. 2. Paulus Venetus c. de genere. Sotus ibidem q. vnica. Toletus qu. 1. Et videtur nobis probabilior, & sequenda.

there results one adequate and per se defined, because it is not considered as an aggregate of them, but as including the one in order to the other; and things that are ordered per se do not make something one per accidens. We have an example in this definition, Dispersive of sight. Its material defined, and as That which, is body as denominated from whiteness, because to disperse sight belongs to it; its formal defined, and as That by which, is whiteness, which is rather the ratio of dispersing sight; but from both, as ordered to each other, there results one adequate and per se defined. This opinion is followed by Javelli in his Logic, tit. 4, ch. 2, Paul of Venice in the chapter on genus, Soto in the same place, the single question, Toledo q. 1. And it seems to us more probable, and to be followed.

Et probatur hoc argumento. Illud est definitum alicuius definitionis, cui per se conuenit definitio: sed prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie in quid, per se conuenit naturæ genericæ, vt denominatur à secunda intentione genatis, & cum ea per se conuertitur: nec alteri potest conuenire: ergo hæc sola potest esse definitum. Probatur minor: quia sicut corpori, vt denominatum, vel informatum albedine, per se conuenit esse disgregatiuum visus, ita natura generica, vt denominatur à secunda intentione, per se prędicabilis est de pluribus differentibus specie: & quidquid est prædicabile, de pluribus differentibus specie in quid, est natura generica: vt denominata, à secunda intentione. Quòd verò ei soli conueniat per se, probatur, quia eidem naturæ non conuenit essentialite, vt cõtra primam opinionem probatum est, sed solùm potest ei conuenire accidentaliter, & secundæ intentioni solùm potest conuenire, vt Quo, cùm non prædicetur de pluribus differentibus specie, sed tantùm sit ratio prædicandi: Solùm ergo conuenire potest per se eidem naturæ, vt denominatæ à secunda intentione.

And it is proved by this argument. That is the defined of a definition to which the definition belongs per se; but to be predicated in quid of many differing in species belongs per se to the generic nature as denominated by the second intention of genus, and is convertible with it per se, and it cannot belong to anything else; therefore this alone can be the defined. The minor is proved: because just as it belongs per se to body, as denominated or informed by whiteness, to be dispersive of sight, so the generic nature, as denominated by the second intention, is per se predicable of many differing in species; and whatever is predicable in quid of many differing in species is the generic nature as denominated by the second intention. That it belongs per se to it alone is proved because it does not belong essentially to the same nature, as was proved against the first opinion, but can only belong to it accidentally; and it can belong to the second intention only as That by which, since this is not predicated of many differing in species, but is only the ratio of predicating. Therefore it can belong per se only to the same nature as denominated by the second intention.

Pro solutione argumenti primæ opinionis, notandum est: Duo esse consideranda in prædicatione cuiuscunque prædicabilis ex parte prædicati.

For the solution of the argument of the first opinion it should be noted that two things are to be considered in the predication of any predicable on the part of the predicate.

Primum, Ratio formalis, quam prædicat de subiecto. Secundum, Conditio sub qua de illo prædicatur: vt dum prædicatur species de indiuiduo in hac prædicatione: Petrus est homo, ratio formalis quam prædicat de illo, est essentia hominis, sed conditio sub qua prædicatur, est esse speciem: quod est denominari à secunda intentione speciei, quæ est relatio speciei ad indiuidua

First, the formal ratio which it predicates of the subject. Second, the condition under which it is predicated of it: as when species is predicated of the individual in this predication, Peter is a man, the formal ratio which it predicates of him is the essence of man, but the condition under which it is predicated is being a species, which is to be denominated by the second intention of species, which is the relation of the species to the individuals.

Ex hac distinctione, respõdeo ad formam arg. distinguendo minorem hoc modo, Si in prędicatione generis de specie, dum dicimus, Homo est animal, consideretur ratio formalis, quam

From this distinction I reply to the form of the argument by distinguishing the minor in this way: if in the predication of genus of species, when we say Man is an animal, the formal ratio is considered which G iij

p. 102

animal prædicat de homine, verum est quòd prædicetur secundùm essentiam, in quantum est viuens sensibile: si verò consideretur conditio sub qua prædicatur, est secunda intentio generis, à qua denominatur: & ideo ratione talis conditionis conuenit ei prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie in Quid, & non secundùm essentiam, aut prædicata essentialia: quamuis hæc prædicet de eisdem speciebus. Et ex hoc intelligitur sensus huius propositionis, Homo est animal: & aliarum, in quibus genus prædicatur de specie: qui non est, hominem esse genus, sed esse viuens sensibile: nam hæc est ratio formalis, quam prædicat de illo, ex qua accipiendus est sensus propositionis, & non ex conditione sub qua prædicatur, quæ est secunda intentio.

animal predicates of man, it is true that it is predicated according to essence, inasmuch as it is sensible living thing; but if the condition under which it is predicated is considered, it is the second intention of genus, by which it is denominated; and therefore by reason of such a condition it belongs to it to be predicated in quid of many differing in species, and not according to essence or essential predicates, although it predicates these of the same species. And from this the sense of this proposition, Man is an animal, is understood, and of the others in which genus is predicated of species: which is not that man is a genus, but that he is a sensible living thing; for this is the formal ratio which it predicates of him, from which the sense of the proposition is to be taken, and not from the condition under which it is predicated, which is the second intention.

Pro solutione argumenti Caie. aliud est notandum, nempe duplex esse materiale significatum generis, in concreto significati, sicut aliorum concretorum accidentalium. Vnum proximum, adæquatum, & per se, Aliud remotum, inadæquatum & per accidens: vt materiale significatum albi, adęquatum, & per se, est corpus: inadæquatum, & per accidens, paries, aut aliud quodcunque corpus particulare: ita significatum materiale, per se adæquatum, & proximum generis est, natura generica in communi, quæ denominatur genus, à secundo prædicabili: Remotum verò, inadæquatum, & per accidens, est animal, vel color. Et ex hoc respondetur ad formam arg. distinguendo minorem: Nam licèt animali, aut colori conueniat accidentaliter definitio generis: quia sunt significata materialia, remota, & per accidens, naturæ tamen genericæ, vt denominatæ à secunda intentione generis, per se conuenit, & non accidentaliter. Sicut corpori, vt habenti albedinem, per se conuenit esse disgregatiuum visus: secundæ autem intentioni, etiam in ordine ad plures species, non conuenit definitio, nisi, vt Quo: sicut probatum à nobis est, contra Caiet.

For the solution of Cajetan’s argument something else should be noted, namely that the material significate of genus, in the concrete signified, is twofold, as of other accidental concretes: one proximate, adequate, and per se; the other remote, inadequate, and per accidens. As the material significate of white, adequate and per se, is body; inadequate and per accidens, a wall or any other particular body: so the material significate of genus, per se, adequate, and proximate, is the generic nature in common, which is denominated genus from the second predicable; the remote, or inadequate and per accidens, is animal or color. And from this one replies to the form of the argument by distinguishing the minor: for although the definition of genus belongs accidentally to animal or to color, because they are remote and per accidens material significates, yet to the generic nature, as denominated by the second intention of genus, it belongs per se and not accidentally. Just as to be dispersive of sight belongs per se to body as having whiteness; but to the second intention, even in order to several species, the definition does not belong except as That by which, as was proved by us against Cajetan.

QUESTION III

Quæst. 3. An definitio generis sit quidditatiua, vel descriptiua — Whether the definition of genus is quidditative or descriptive.

Duo sunt explicanda, vt soluatur quæstio præsens. Primum, qualis nam sit definitio generis, quidditatiua, vel descriptiua. Secundum, quidnam pro genere in ea ponatur, vniuersale, aut prædicabile, vel quid aliud: ideo in duas partes diuidenda est quæstio. Circa primam verò, duæ sunt opiniones, quasi extremæ, & altera media.

Two things are to be explained in order that the present question may be solved. First, of what kind the definition of genus is, quidditative or descriptive. Second, what is placed in it for its genus: universal, or predicable, or something else; and so the question is to be divided into two parts. Concerning the first there are two opinions, as it were extreme, and another in the middle.

Prima opinio extrema asserit. Non solùm non esse quidditatiuam, aut essentialem definitionem generis, sed nullo modo

The first extreme opinion asserts that the definition of genus is not only not quidditative or essential, but that genus can in no way

p. 103

posse definiri genus definitione quidditatiua. Quam sequuntur Albertus Magnus, tract. 1. prædicabiliũ. cap. 3. Villalpandus in præsenti cap. & pro eadem citat Ammonium Toletus qu. 1. huius cap. Probaturque hoc argumento. Genus est concretum accidentale, includens pro materiali naturam genericam: quæ potest esse substantia, aut accidens reale: & pro formali secũdam intentionẽ, quæ est ens rationis: hæ autẽ diuersas habẽt essentias, ergo non possunt vna definitione explicari, quare nõ poterit genus definiri definitione quidditatiua.

be defined by a quidditative definition. It is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 1 of the Predicables, ch. 5; Villalpando on the present chapter, who also cites Ammonius for the same view; Toledo, q. 1 on this chapter. And it is proved by this argument. Genus is an accidental concrete, including as its material the generic nature, which can be a substance or a real accident, and as its formal the second intention, which is a being of reason; but these have diverse essences; therefore they cannot be explained by one definition; wherefore genus cannot be defined by a quidditative definition.

Secunda opinio extrema, Non solùm asserit, posse genus definiri definitione quidditatiua, sed hanc definitionem eius à Porphyrio assignatam, esse quidditatiuam. Ita Scot. qu. 14 & 15. vniuersalium: quem sequitur Caiet. qu. 1. huius ca. in solutione ad primum. Probat Scotus hac ratione. Genus consideratur à Porphyrio in hoc opere sub ratione prædicabilis, sicut & cætera prædicabilia: sed definitur per prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie: ergo definitio est quidditatiua. Probatur consequentia: quia prædicabile dicit potentiam prædicandi, & prædicari est proprius actus talis potentiæ, sed potentia definitur quidditatiuè per propriũ actum, à quo sumit suã essentiam, aut speciem: ergo definitur genus, vt prędicabile quidditatiuè.

The second extreme opinion asserts not only that genus can be defined by a quidditative definition, but that this definition of it assigned by Porphyry is quidditative. So Scotus, q. 14 and 15 on Universals, whom Cajetan follows, q. 1 on this chapter, in the solution to the first. Scotus proves it by this reasoning. Genus is considered by Porphyry in this work under the ratio of predicable, as are the other predicables too; but it is defined by being predicated of many differing in species; therefore the definition is quidditative. The consequence is proved: because predicable means the potency of predicating, and to predicate is the proper act of such a potency; but a potency is defined quidditatively through its proper act, from which it takes its essence or species; therefore genus, as predicable, is defined quidditatively.

Tertia opinio est communis, quæ duo affirmat. Primum, quòd genus potest definiri quidditatiuè Secundum, quòd definitio Porphyrij, non est quidditatiua, sed descriptiua. Et quantum ad hoc secundum, eam tenet D. Th. opusc. 84. tract. 1. Cap 2. & 3 Albertus Magnus tract. 3. prædicabilium, ca. 34, Ammonius & Villalpandeus, vbi suprà. Scotus qu. vnica huius capitis §. vltimo. Toletus quæst. 2. Mercatus cap. de specie, fol. 16. col. 2. Et hæc est probabilior & sequenda.

The third opinion is the common one, which affirms two things. First, that genus can be defined quidditatively. Second, that the definition of Porphyry is not quidditative but descriptive. And as regards this second point it is held by St. Thomas, opusc. 84, tract. 1, ch. 2 and 3; Albert the Great, tract. 3 of the Predicables, ch. 34; Ammonius and Villalpando in the places above; Scotus, the single question on this chapter, the last §; Toledo, q. 2; Mercado, chapter on species, fol. 16, col. 2. And this is more probable and to be followed.

Probatur autem primum, quod affirmat, genus posse definiri quidditatiuè, hoc argumento. Vniuersale est genus ad quinque prædicabilia, vt qu. 8. vniuersalium probauimus, ergo primum prædicabile, quod est genus, est species vniuersalis: sed quælibet species componitur ex genere, & differẽtia, tanquam ex partibus essentialibus, ergo per eas potest definiri: & definitio tradita per genus, & differentiam, est quidditatiua, ergo genus potest definiri definitione quidditatiua.

The first thing it affirms, that genus can be defined quidditatively, is proved by this argument. Universal is a genus to the five predicables, as we proved in q. 8 on Universals; therefore the first predicable, which is genus, is a species of universal; but every species is composed of genus and difference as of essential parts; therefore it can be defined through them; and a definition delivered through genus and difference is quidditative; therefore genus can be defined by a quidditative definition.

Probatur secundò, Quòd definitio Porphyrij non sit quidditatiua: primò ex verbis eiusdem cap. præsenti, quæ sic habent. Quod etiam describentes assignarunt, genus esse dicentes, quod de pluribus, & differentibus specie, in eo, quod quid, prædicatur. Deinde ratione, quia duo habent prædicabilia, vt superiùs probauimus: Primum, quòd sint vniuersalia: hoc est, vnum in

It is proved second that the definition of Porphyry is not quidditative: first, from his words in the present chapter, which run thus: Which those describing it also assigned, saying that genus is that which is predicated of many, and differing in species, in what it is. Next, by reason, because the predicables have two things, as we proved above. First, that they are universals, that is, one in G iiij

p. 104

multis: Deinde, quòd prædicari possint de eisdem: & primum se habet tanquam essentia eorum, secundum vt propria passio. Sed genus definitur per prędicari de multis: ergo definitur per propriam passionem: definitio autem quæ datur per propriam passionem, est descriptiua: vt si definiatur homo per risibilitatem: ergo definitio generis est descriptiua.

many; next, that they can be predicated of the same; and the first stands as their essence, the second as a proper attribute. But genus is defined by being predicated of many; therefore it is defined through a proper attribute; and a definition that is given through a proper attribute is descriptive, as if man were defined through risibility; therefore the definition of genus is descriptive.

Ad argum primæ opinionis, respondetur, diuersa esse, quæ includit genus: sed ordinata inter se: nam includit naturam, vt ordinatam ad secundam intentionem, tanquam ad formam denominantem: & secundam intentionem, vt ordinatam ad naturam, tanquam ad subiectum denominatum: & ex hoc efficiunt vnum ordinem, quod vna definitione possit explicari.

To the argument of the first opinion the reply is that the things which genus includes are diverse, but ordered among themselves: for it includes the nature as ordered to the second intention, as to a denominating form, and the second intention as ordered to the nature, as to a denominated subject; and by this they make one order, so that it can be explained by one definition.

Ad argumentum Scoti respondeo, distinguendo antecedens: nam si intelligatur genus, & reliqua prædicabilia considerari à Porphyrio, vt prædicabilia, in eo sensu, vt prædicabilitas sit ratio essentialis eorum: falsum est: nam essentialis ratio potiùs est vniuersalitas. Si verò intelligatur considerari, vt prædicabilia, ita vt prædicabilitas sit passio communis, quæ de illis probatur, verum est: & ideo per illam definiuntur omnia tanquam per communem passionem, quod est definiri definitionibus descriptiuis: & tales debent omnes reputari.

To Scotus’s argument I reply by distinguishing the antecedent: for if it is understood that genus and the remaining predicables are considered by Porphyry as predicables in the sense that predicability is their essential ratio, it is false, for the essential ratio is rather universality. But if it is understood that they are considered as predicables in such a way that predicability is a common attribute which is proved of them, it is true; and therefore they are all defined through it as through a common attribute, which is to be defined by descriptive definitions; and all are to be reckoned such.

Secunda pars quæstionis.

S E C O N D PA R T O F T H E Q U E S T I O N . 13

13 Sed supposito, quòd sit descriptiua definitio, quæritur in secunda parte quæstionis: Quidnam ponatur in ea pro genere. Et prima opinio asserit, genus huius definitionis esse vniuersale: quia licet non ponatur expresso verbo, refertur tamen per illud relatiuum, quod prædicatur de pluribus: idem enim est dicere, Genus esse quod prædicatur de pluribus, ac dicere, Genus esse vniuersale. Hæc tamen sententia nõ potest in primis defendi, apud Porphyrium: quod sic probo. Porphyrius exponens eandem definitionem, inquit, per illam particulam, prædicari de pluribus, excludi indiuiduum: quod non potest esse verum, si vniuersale sit genus: nam iam esset exclusum per illud: cùm indiuiduum non sit vniuersale. Deinde, nõ potest defendi, quòd definitio sit descriptiua: nam si auferas illas particulas, prædicari de pluribus, & loco earum ponas vniuersale: sensus definitionis erit, Genus est vniuersale in multis, differentibus specie in quid: & ideo auferetur propria passio: qua ablata, non erit definitio descriptiua, contra communem sententiam, ex Porphyrio, & ratione probatam.

But supposing that the definition is descriptive, it is asked in the second part of the question: What is placed in it for its genus? And the first opinion asserts that the genus of this definition is universal, because although it is not placed there in an express word, it is nevertheless referred to by that relative, which is predicated of many: for it is the same to say, Genus is that which is predicated of many, as to say, Genus is universal. This opinion, however, cannot in the first place be defended in Porphyry, which I prove thus. Porphyry, expounding the same definition, says that by the particle predicated of many the individual is excluded; which cannot be true if universal is the genus, for it would already be excluded by that, since the individual is not universal. Next, it cannot be defended that the definition is descriptive: for if you take away the particles predicated of many and put universal in their place, the sense of the definition will be: Genus is universal in many differing in species in quid; and thus the proper attribute will be taken away; and once it is taken away, the definition will not be descriptive, against the common opinion, proved from Porphyry and by reason.

Secunda opinio asserit, genus in hac definitione esse prędicabile

The second opinion asserts that the genus in this definition is predi

p. 105

: quod explicatur per illa verba, quod prædicatur de pluribus: nam verba in definitione, non dicitur actum, sed aptitudinem: idem ergo est dicere genus est, quod prædicatur de pluribus: ac si dicatur, quod aptum est prædicari de pluribus, sed esse aptum prædicari de pluribus, idem est, ac esse prædicabile de pluribus: ergo prædicabile ponitur loco generis in hac definitione.

cable, which is expressed by the words which is predicated of many: for a verb in a definition does not express act but aptitude; it is the same, therefore, to say Genus is that which is predicated of many, as if one said, that which is apt to be predicated of many; but to be apt to be predicated of many is the same as to be predicable of many; therefore predicable is placed for the genus in this definition.

14 Tertia opinio est cõmunis & tenenda: quòd loco generis ponatur natura generica, nõ quidem eodem modo sumpta, ac dum dicitur esse definitum, sed alio: nam dum definitũ est, sumitur simul cum secunda intentione, à qua denominatur, & cũ qua vnum definitum per se facit, vnitate ordinis: sed pro genere ponitur solùm, vt in communi sumitur, non vt ordinata ad secundam intentionem. Quod possumus explicare exemplo albi, quod dum hoc modo definitur, Albũ est disgregatiuum visus, definitum est corpus, vt denominatur ab albedine: ita vt ex vtroque, nempe ex corpore, & albedine, ordinatis, fiat vnũ definitum completum, & per se: sed loco generis ponitur corpus absolutè sumptum: hoc est, non considerato sub denominatione albedinis, nec simul cum illa. Hanc sententiam sic explicatam sequuntur, Ammonius, Albertus Magnus, & Canterus, locis superiùs citatis. Et videtur nobis probabilior.

14 The third opinion is the common one and to be held: that in place of the genus the generic nature is put, not indeed taken in the same way as when it is said to be the defined, but in another: for when it is the defined, it is taken together with the second intention by which it is denominated, and with which it makes one per se defined, by a unity of order; but for the genus it is put only as it is taken in common, not as ordered to the second intention. This we can explain by the example of white: when it is defined in this way, White is dispersive of sight, the defined is body as denominated from whiteness, so that from both, namely from body and whiteness, as ordered, one complete and per se defined is made; but in place of the genus body is put, taken absolutely, that is, not considered under the denomination of whiteness, nor together with it. This opinion, so explained, is followed by Ammonius, Albert the Great, and Canterus, in the places cited above. And it seems to us more probable.

15 Nam in primis colligitur ex doctrina D. Th. 1. lib. de interpretatione, ca. 1. lect. 4. & opus. de ente & essentia ca. 7. vbi tradit modum definiendi accidentia in concreto, per subiectũ loco generis: & in abstracto, per verum genus, & subiectũ loco differentiæ: vt risibile, quòd sit homo aptus ad ridendum: risibilitatem verò, quòd sit aptitudo hominis ad ridendum.
