Et rationem vtriusque esse: quia posse inhærere subiecto, est de essentia accidentis: sed inhærentia in subiecto, propriè explicatur per idem subiectum positum in definitione: ergo propriè definiuntur accidentia, per subiectum loco generis, si definiantur in concreto, & loco differentiæ, si in abstracto.

15 For in the first place it is gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, On Interpretation 1, ch. 1, lect. 4, and the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 7, where he teaches the mode of defining accidents: in the concrete, through the subject in place of the genus; and in the abstract, through a true genus, and the subject in place of the difference: as risible, that it is man apt to laugh; but risibility, that it is the aptitude of man to laugh. And that the reason of both is this: because to be able to inhere in a subject is of the essence of an accident; but inherence in a subject is properly expressed through the same subject placed in the definition; therefore accidents are properly defined through the subject, in place of the genus if they are defined in the concrete, and in place of the difference if in the abstract.

16 Deinde, ex hac doctrina conficitur hoc argumentum ad illam probandam. Genus definitur à Porphyrio in concreto, vt significant verba definitionis. Quod prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie in quid. Nam concretum est, quod prædicatur, non abstractum: sed genus est concretum accidentale, sicut album: ergo definitur per subiectum loco generis: subiectum verò est natura generica, sicut subiectum albedinis est album, ergo per illam loco generis in definitione positam definitur, & sensus definitionis est, Genus est natura, quæ prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie in quid.

16 Next, from this doctrine this argument is constructed to prove that opinion. Genus is defined by Porphyry in the concrete, as the words of the definition signify: That which is predicated of many differing in species in quid. For what is predicated is the concrete, not the abstract; but genus is an accidental concrete, like white; therefore it is defined through the subject in place of the genus; and the subject is the generic nature, just as the subject of whiteness is white; therefore it is defined through this nature placed in the definition in place of the genus, and the sense of the definition is: Genus is a nature which is predicated of many differing in species in quid.

p. 106

Ad argumentum primæ opinionis respondetur, Accidentia meliùs definiri in concreto, per subiectum, quàm per genus: quia meliùs explicatur per illud inhærentia aptitudinalis, quæ est de essentia eorum. Vnde magis propriè refertur subiectum generis, quod est natura, per illud relatiuum, quod prędicatur, quàm vniuersale. Et eodem modo respondetur ad argumentum secundæ opinionis.

To the argument of the first opinion the reply is that accidents are better defined in the concrete through the subject than through the genus, because through it the aptitudinal inherence, which is of their essence, is better expressed. Hence the subject of genus, which is the nature, is more properly referred to by the relative which is predicated than universal is. And in the same way one replies to the argument of the second opinion.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Vtrùm genus includat differentias, & species actu, vel solùm potentia.

Whether genus includes the differences and species in act, or only in potency.

17 Valde vtilis est quæstio hæc, ad intelligendam naturam generis: sed pro breuiori resolutione eius notandum est: Tribus modis intelligi posse, quòd vnum contineat alterum actu: Primò, actu distincto, sicut definitio cõtinet vtramque sui partem, nempe genus, & differentiam. Secundò, actu determinato, sed non expresso: sicut species continet genus, & differentiam, vt homo, animal, & rationale. Tertiò, confusè, & indeterminatè: vt ens continet modos intrinsecos substantiæ, & accidentis: qui sunt per se, & in alio: non solùm confusè, sed neutrum determinando potiùs, quàm alterutrum.

17 This question is very useful for understanding the nature of genus; but for a briefer resolution of it, it should be noted that one thing can be understood to contain another in act in three ways. First, in distinct act, as a definition contains each of its parts, namely genus and difference. Second, in determinate act, but not expressed: as the species contains genus and difference, as man contains animal and rational. Third, confusedly and indeterminately: as being contains the intrinsic modes of substance and of accident, which are per se and in another; not only confusedly, but determining neither one rather than the other.

Ex his tribus modis, Primò certum est, genus non continere differentias actu distincto, sicut definitio continet genus & differentiam. Probatur euidenter: quia si animal contineret actu distincto rationale, per illud solum possemus definire hominem, dicentes hominem esse animal: quia in animali etiam includitur actu, atque distinctè rationale: & ideo talis definitio constaret genere, & differentia: & ideo esset sufficiens, quod patet esse falsum.

Of these three modes, first, it is certain that genus does not contain the differences in distinct act, as a definition contains genus and difference. This is proved evidently: because if animal contained rational in distinct act, we could define man through it alone, saying that man is an animal, because in animal rational too would be included in act and distinctly; and therefore such a definition would consist of genus and difference, and would therefore be sufficient, which is plainly false.

Secundò, certum est genus non continere differentias actu determinato, licèt confuso contineat, vt animal non continet rationale, sicut homo. Quod probatur, quia si animal contineret actu rationale, & irrationale, falsæ essent omnes prædicationes, in quibus prædicatur de suis speciebus, vt homo est animal, leo est animal: quia sensus esset, homo est rationalis, & irrationalis: & similiter leo, quod est absurdum.

Second, it is certain that genus does not contain the differences in determinate act, even if it contains them confusedly, as animal does not contain rational as man does. This is proved because if animal contained rational and irrational in act, all the predications in which it is predicated of its species would be false, as Man is an animal, A lion is an animal: because the sense would be, man is rational and irrational, and likewise the lion, which is absurd.

Solùm ergo potest esse dubium, an genus contineat differentias actu indeterminato, & confuso, ita vt nullam particularem potiùs, quàm alteram exprimat, sed omnes indeterminatè dicatur continere, diuerso modo, ac species quælibet cõtinet suam differentiam: nam homo, licèt non expressè contineat rationale, tamen determinatè, ita vt hanc differentiam

The only doubt, then, can be whether genus contains the differences in indeterminate and confused act, so that it expresses no particular one rather than another, but is said to contain them all indeterminately, in a different way from that in which any species contains its difference: for man, although he does not contain rational expressly, yet contains it determinately, so that this difference

p. 107

, & non aliam contineat: animal verò non sic potest continere rationale, & irrationale: quia non magis vnam quàm alteram dicit, sed sub eadem confusione vtramque. Nihilominus posset intelligi actu confuso, & indeterminato, eas continere, iuxta tertium modum. Et de hoc modo continendi actu differentias, procedit quæstio: cuius sensus est, An genus actu confuso, atque indeterminato contineat differentias, vel solùm in potentia: sicut materia continet formas, solùm in potentia.

and not another is contained in it; but animal cannot contain rational and irrational in that way, because it expresses the one no more than the other, but both under the same confusion. Nevertheless it could be understood to contain them in confused and indeterminate act, according to the third mode. And it is of this mode of containing the differences in act that the question proceeds; its sense is: whether genus contains the differences in confused and indeterminate act, or only in potency, as matter contains forms only in potency.

18 Et prima opinio asserit, Genus hoc tertio modo continere actu differentias. Probatur duobus testimoniis Arist. Primum habetur 1. lib. Physic. textu 4. vbi ita ait: Vniuersale autem totum quoddam est, multa enim comprehendit, vt partes. Secundum verò, 7. lib. Physic. textu 31. vbi de genere sic loquitur: Genus non vnum quid est, sed in hoc latent multa. Ex quibus sic argumentor. Genus continet multa, tanquam partes, ergo continet illa actu: quia omne totum actu continet partes, cùm ex eis componatur: sed ea, quæ ita continet genus, non possunt esse alia præter differentias, & species, vt notum est: ergo eas continet actu, & non in potentia: ex mente Arist.

18 And the first opinion asserts that genus contains the differences in act in this third mode. It is proved by two testimonies of Aristotle. The first is found in Phys. 1, text 4, where he speaks thus: But the universal is a certain whole, for it comprehends many things as parts. The second in Phys. 7, text 31, where he speaks of genus thus: Genus is not some one thing, but in it many things lie hidden. From which I argue thus. Genus contains many things as parts; therefore it contains them in act, because every whole contains its parts in act, since it is composed of them; but the things that genus contains in this way cannot be other than the differences and species, as is known; therefore it contains them in act, and not in potency, according to the mind of Aristotle.

Deinde probatur hac ratione: Vt vera sit prædicatio, necesse est, id totum quod continet subiectum, continere prædicatum, non solùm in potentia, sed etiam actu: at genus prædicatur de specie: ergo debet actu continere, quidquid species continet, nempe differentiam, ex qua simul cum genere componitur Probatur maior, Quia cùm animal prędicatur de homine, sensus prædicationis est, hominem esse animal actu: quod verum non erit, si animal solùm dicat actu naturam sensitiuam: nam cùm hæc sit pars hominis, prædicabitur pars de toto: vt ergo sit vera, debet etiam animal actu continere rationalitatem, & non sufficit in potentia: cùm actu, & non potentia prædicetur.

Next it is proved by this reasoning. For a predication to be true, it is necessary that the whole which contains the subject contain the predicate, not only in potency but also in act; but genus is predicated of species; therefore it must contain in act whatever the species contains, namely the difference, of which together with the genus it is composed. The major is proved: because when animal is predicated of man, the sense of the predication is that man is an animal in act; which will not be true if animal expresses in act only sensitive nature: for since this is a part of man, the part will be predicated of the whole; in order, then, that it be true, animal must also contain rationality in act, and in potency is not enough, since it is predicated in act and not in potency.

Secunda opinio tenet, Genus non actu, sed in potentia tantùm continere species, & differentias, vt animal, rationale, & irrationale, de posteriori resolutione. textu 17. vbi ita ait: Supponatur enim tale esse genus, vt sit secundùm potentiam in plus. Esse autem in plus quàm speciem, est esse vniuersalius, & plus continere quàm singulas species: hoc est, alias species, & earum differentias, si ergo est in plus secundùm potentiam, in potentia tantùm continebit species, & differentias. Hæc est etiam expressa sententia Porphyrij, cap. de differentia, vbi de genere loquens sic ait: Potestate quidem habet omnes, quæ sub se sunt differentias, actu verò nullum. Et D. Tho. super verba Arist. citata, & opusc. 42. cap. 9. quam sequuntur

The second opinion holds that genus contains the species and differences not in act but only in potency, as animal contains rational and irrational. Posterior Analytics, text 17, where he speaks thus: For let genus be supposed to be such that it is in more according to potency. But to be in more than the species is to be more universal and to contain more than the single species, that is, other species and their differences; if, then, it is in more according to potency, it will contain the species and differences only in potency. This is also the express opinion of Porphyry in the chapter on difference, where, speaking of genus, he says thus: In potency indeed it has all the differences that are under it, but in act none. And St. Thomas on the words of Aristotle cited, and opusc. 42, ch. 9, whom follow

p. 108

Albertus Magnus, tractatu 5. prędicabilium c. 4. Iauellus tract. 4. prædicab. c. 4 ante medium. Caiet Sotus, Banterus, Toletus, ca. de differentia, in expositione textus, Mercatus quæst. vnica huius capitis. Et est vera, ac tenenda. Sed vt eam probemus, duo sunt notanda. Primò, Genus significare gradum superiorem naturæ, differentiam verò gradum inferiorem, per quem determinatur ad constituendam speciem, vt animal, significat gradum naturæ sensitiuæ, qui superior est gradu rationalitatis, quem significat differentia rationalis, per hanc contrahitur ad constituendam speciem hominis.

Albert the Great, tract. 5 of the Predicables, ch. 4; Javelli, tract. 4 of the Predicables, ch. 4, before the middle; Cajetan, Soto, Banterus, Toledo, on the chapter on difference, in the exposition of the text; Mercado, the single question on this chapter. And it is true and to be held. But in order to prove it, two things should be noted. First, that genus signifies a superior grade of the nature, and difference an inferior grade, by which it is determined to constitute the species: as animal signifies the grade of sensitive nature, which is superior to the grade of rationality, which the difference rational signifies; by this it is contracted to constitute the species of man.

Secundò notandum est, duobus modis considerari genus. Primò, vt partem actualem componentem speciem simul cum differentia. Secundò, vt totum potentiale, contrahibile per differentias: vt animal, quod est pars actualis speciei humanæ, quam componit simul cum differentia rationali: & vt totum potentiale est, quod determinatur per eandem differentiam, ad constituendum hominem, & per differentiam equi, ad constituendum equum.

Second, it should be noted that genus is considered in two ways. First, as an actual part composing the species together with the difference. Second, as a potential whole, contractible by the differences: as animal is an actual part of the human species, which it composes together with the difference rational; and as a potential whole it is that which is determined by the same difference to constitute man, and by the difference of horse to constitute horse.

19 Ex his duobus notabilibus, duo colliguntur argumenta, ad probandam nostram sententiam. Primum est, genus significat gradum naturæ diuersum, ac superiorem, à gradu, quem significat differentia: & est abstractum ab speciebus, & differentiis, vt animal ab homine, & equo: & consequenter à rationali, & irrationali: sed id quod ab inferioribus abstrahitur, vt sic abstractum, non includit illa: cùm abstrahi ab illis, sit cognosci sine illis: ergo genus non potest includere actu species & differentias, à quibus abstrahitur, sed solùm in potentia.

19 From these two notes two arguments are gathered to prove our opinion. The first is: genus signifies a grade of nature diverse from and superior to the grade which the difference signifies, and it is abstracted from the species and differences, as animal from man and horse, and consequently from rational and irrational; but that which is abstracted from its inferiors, as so abstracted, does not include them, since to be abstracted from them is to be known without them; therefore genus cannot include in act the species and differences from which it is abstracted, but only in potency.

Secundum argumentum. Genus solùm potest considerari, vt pars actualis speciei, vel vt totum potentiale, contrahibile per differentias: sed neutro modo includit eas actu: ergo solùm in potentia. Probatur minor: quia non includit eas actu, vt est pars speciei: nam vna pars actualis, non includit alteram, quia eo ipso, quòd eam actu includeret, non posset cum ea componere totum: cùm componentia distincta esse debeant, & ideo non se includentia: sed nec vt est totum potentiale includere potest eas, nisi solũ in potentia: quia solùm sunt partes potestatiuæ eius, ex quibus vt tale totum potestatiuum componitur. Et confirmari potest, quia si genus cõtineret actu differentias, cùm illæ sint omnino diuersæ, vt rationale, & irrationale, contineret actu plura diuersa, & ideo esset æquiuocum respectu specierum, de quibus prædicatur, vel saltem analogum: sicut ens, respectu substantiæ & accidentis, quæ actu confusio, atque determinato contineat: sicut genus continet differentias,

The second argument. Genus can be considered only as an actual part of the species, or as a potential whole contractible by the differences; but in neither way does it include them in act; therefore only in potency. The minor is proved: because it does not include them in act as it is a part of the species, for one actual part does not include another, since by the very fact that it included it in act it could not compose the whole with it, as the components must be distinct and therefore not including each other; but neither as it is a potential whole can it include them except only in potency, because they are only its potestative parts, of which it is composed as such a potestative whole. And it can be confirmed: because if genus contained the differences in act, since these are altogether diverse, as rational and irrational, it would contain in act many diverse things, and would therefore be equivocal with respect to the species of which it is predicated, or at least analogous, like being with respect to substance and accident, which it contains in confused and indeterminate act, as genus contains the differences,

p. 109

secundùm opinionem oppositam: consequens autem falsum est, cùm genus sit vniuocum: ergo etiam erit falsum, quòd genus contineat actu differentias.

according to the opposite opinion; but the consequent is false, since genus is univocal; therefore it will also be false that genus contains the differences in act.

Ad testimonia Aristotelis, pro alia sententia adducta, respondeo. Genus continere multa in potentia, hoc est, species, & differentias, non tanquam partes actuales, sed potestatiuas: nam sicut totum, aliud est actuale, & aliud potentiale, ita partes, alię sunt actuales, & aliæ potentiales. Actuales sunt, quæ essentiam actualem componunt: potentiales verò aut potestatiuæ, per quas, vel ad quas constituendas contrahitur, aut determinatur totum: idem namque est, esse partes, ad quas actu constituendas determinatur totum, & esse partes suæ potestatis.

To the testimonies of Aristotle adduced for the other opinion I reply: genus contains many things in potency, that is, species and differences, not as actual parts but as potestative ones; for just as among wholes one is actual and another potential, so among parts some are actual and others potential. The actual are those which compose an actual essence; the potential or potestative, those through which, or to constitute which, the whole is contracted or determined: for it is the same to be the parts to constitute which in act the whole is determined, and to be the parts of its potency.

20 Ad argumentũ, neganda est maior: Quia non requiritur ad veritatem propositionis, quòd prædicatum contineat actu, quidquid continet species, sed sufficit quòd aliquid contineat actu, & aliquid in potentia: sic enim prædicabit partem speciei, inclusam in specie: non tamen per modum partis, sed totius: & ideo veram efficiet propositionem, in qua dicitur hominem esse animal: cuius sensus est, hominem includere animal, quod determinatur, per rationale ad constitutionem eius. Hoc est enim includere rationale, ac cæteras differentias in potentia. Quod sic declarandum est. Contrahibile, aut determinabile, dicit potentiam, & contrahens actum: sed genus est contrahibile per differentiam, tanquam per actum, ergo est potentia respectu differentiæ, & speciei, quam cum ea potest constituere: quare non potest continere species, & differentias actu, sed potestate tantùm.

20 To the argument, the major is to be denied: because it is not required for the truth of a proposition that the predicate contain in act whatever the species contains, but it is enough that it contain something in act and something in potency; for thus it will predicate a part of the species, included in the species, yet not by way of a part but of a whole; and therefore it will make true the proposition in which it is said that man is an animal, whose sense is that man includes animal, which is determined by rational to constitute him. For this is to include rational and the other differences in potency. Which is to be explained thus. Contractible or determinable means potency, and the contracting means act; but genus is contractible by the difference as by an act; therefore it is a potency with respect to the difference and to the species which it can constitute with it; wherefore it cannot contain the species and differences in act, but only in potency.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Vtrùm genus prædicetur de specie tanquam totum, vel etiam vt pars illius.

Whether genus is predicated of species as a whole, or also as a part of it.

Genus tribus modis considerari potest Primò, vt dicit naturam genericam abstractam ab speciebus, vt animal in quantum dicit naturam sensitiuam, abstractam ab homine & equo: & hoc modo sumptum non est pars, sed totum: quia significatur per modum habentis naturam: non est tamen totum actuale, sed potentiale quia significatur vt habens naturam perfectibilem, per differentias: Quod verò perfectibile est, significatur tanquam in potentia ad vlteriorem perfectionem, quod est, significari vt potentiale. Alio modo sumitur: genus, tanquam altera pars speciei, componens eam simul cum differentia: & tunc non accipitur, vt abstractum à speciebus,

Genus can be considered in three ways. First, as it expresses the generic nature abstracted from the species, as animal inasmuch as it expresses sensitive nature abstracted from man and horse; and taken in this way it is not a part but a whole, because it is signified by way of something having the nature; yet it is not an actual whole but a potential one, because it is signified as having a nature perfectible by the differences; and what is perfectible is signified as in potency to further perfection, which is to be signified as potential. In another way genus is taken as the other part of the species, composing it together with the difference; and then it is not taken as abstracted from the species,

p. 110

sed solùm vt actu dicit partialem naturam earum. Sed adhuc per modum partis significatũ, potest sumi tanquam pars actualis, in quantum actu coniunctum est cum differentia componendo speciem, aut tanquam pars potentialis: si illud consideremus, non vt actu componens, sed vt potest componere.

but only as it expresses in act their partial nature. But further, signified by way of a part, it can be taken either as an actual part, inasmuch as it is joined in act with the difference in composing the species, or as a potential part, if we consider it not as composing in act but as able to compose.

Et secundùm has tres acceptiones, tres sunt opiniones. Prima tenet, tanquam partem etiam actualem prędicari de specie, quam sequuntur Caiet. cap. præsenti. Venetus cap. sequenti ad finem, & alij. Et probant primò ex Arist. 1. lib. de posteriori resolutione, ca. 4. vbi docet, Integram definitionem, & singulas eius partes, per se prædicari de definito: sed partes definitionis sunt actuales, ex quibus altera est genus: ergo tanquam pars actualis prædicatur de specie.

And according to these three acceptations there are three opinions. The first holds that it is predicated of the species even as an actual part. It is followed by Cajetan on the present chapter, Paul of Venice on the following chapter toward the end, and others. And they prove it first from Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 4, where he teaches that the whole definition and each of its parts are predicated per se of the defined; but the parts of the definition are actual, of which one is the genus; therefore it is predicated of the species as an actual part.

21 Probant deinde ratione: Primò, quia hæc est differentia inter prædicationem generis, & speciei, ab omnibus concessa, quòd prędicatio speciei est completa: prædicatio verò generis incõpleta, prædicatur ergo genus tanquam quid incompletum de specie: sed incompletum est pars: ergo prædicatur vt pars.

21 They prove it next by reason. First, because this is the difference between the predication of genus and of species, granted by all: that the predication of species is complete, but the predication of genus incomplete; genus is therefore predicated of the species as something incomplete; but the incomplete is a part; therefore it is predicated as a part.

Secundò, partes Physicæ, vt materia & forma, magis distinguuntur inter se, & à toto, quàm partes Metaphysicæ, quæ sunt genus, & differentia, cùm illæ sint res distinctæ, istæ verò, non nisi conceptus distincti, eiusdem rei: sed partes Physicæ, in concreto significatæ, verè prædicantur de toto: dum dicimus, Homo est corporeus, aut est animatus: ergo meliùs prædicabuntur partes Metaphysicæ, quæ sunt genus & differentia, in concreto significatæ de specie, quam componunt: & ita vera erit hæc, Homo est animal, etiam si tanquam pars accipiatur genus: sicut etiam est vera hæc, Homo est rationalis, cùm tamen rationale, non sit totum potentiale, sed actualis pars.

Second, physical parts, such as matter and form, are more distinguished among themselves and from the whole than metaphysical parts, which are genus and difference, since the former are distinct things, but the latter only distinct concepts of the same thing; but physical parts, signified in the concrete, are truly predicated of the whole, when we say Man is corporeal, or is animate; therefore the metaphysical parts, which are genus and difference, signified in the concrete, will all the better be predicated of the species which they compose; and so this will be true, Man is an animal, even if the genus is taken as a part; just as this too is true, Man is rational, although rational is not a potential whole but an actual part.

Secunda opinio affirmat, Genus non vt partem actualem prædicari de specie, sed vt partem potentialem: hoc est, non vt actu componens, sed vt potest simul cum differentia componere. Hanc tenet Canterus, cap. præsenti, dub. 3. & probat hoc arg. Vt prædicatio sit vera, prædicatum debet continere totum, quod continet subiectum, sed genus vt pars actualis, non continet aliam partem speciei, quæ est differentia, actu, nec potentia, sed bene vt potentialis: quia vt potest componere speciem non consideratur, vt actu coniunctum cum aliqua differentia, sed vt potest coniungi: quare omnes continebit in potentia: quod satis est, vt dicatur continere totum, quod continet species, nempe vnam partem actu, & alteram in potentia: prædicabitur ergo vt pars potentialis

The second opinion affirms that genus is predicated of the species not as an actual part but as a potential part, that is, not as composing in act but as able to compose together with the difference. Canterus holds this, on the present chapter, doubt 3, and proves it by this argument. For a predication to be true, the predicate must contain the whole that the subject contains; but genus as an actual part does not contain the other part of the species, which is the difference, either in act or in potency, but it does so well as potential: because as able to compose the species it is not considered as joined in act with some difference, but as able to be joined; wherefore it will contain all of them in potency; which is enough for it to be said to contain the whole that the species contains, namely one part in act and the other in potency; it will therefore be predicated as a potential part

p. 111

, non vt pars actualis.

, not as an actual part.

22 Tertia opinio est D. Tho. in 1. dist. 15. & opusc. de ente, & essentia cap. 3. asserentis, genus non prædicari de specie, vt partem, sed vt totum. Verba eius sunt, Si animal non esset totum, quod est homo, non prædicaretur de eo, cùm nulla pars prædicetur de suo toto. Eam sequuntur Boetius lib. de diuisionibus, ferè in principio. Caiet. etiam licèt citetur pro opposita sententia, asserit expressè etiam in eodem cap. 3. opusc. de ente, & essentia, genus non vt partem, sed vt totum potentiale prædicari de specie. Item Sotus quæst. vnica huius capitis, & Pater Franciscus Suarius tom. 1. suæ Metaph. disput. 15. sect. 11. num. 16. Et videtur nobis probabilior.

22 The third opinion is that of St. Thomas, in 1, d. 15, and the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 3, who asserts that genus is predicated of the species not as a part but as a whole. His words are: If animal were not the whole that man is, it would not be predicated of him, since no part is predicated of its whole. It is followed by Boethius, in the book On Division, near the beginning; Cajetan too, although he is cited for the opposite opinion, expressly asserts in the same ch. 3 of the opusc. On Being and Essence that genus is predicated of the species not as a part but as a potential whole. Likewise Soto, the single question on this chapter, and Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 15, sect. 11, no. 16. And it seems to us more probable.

23 Sed vt fundamentum eius explicemus: Notandum est primò, quòd tam genus, quàm differentia, sumuntur à tota natura specifica, aut à tota entitate eius, sub diuersis gradibus considerata, & non à sola parte: vt capite de differentia explicabitur: diuersa tamen ratione: nam genus sumitur à tota natura rei, sub ratione vniuersaliori, atque imperfecta, perfectibili tamen per eandem naturam sub gradu speciali consideratam: differentia verò, à tota etiam natura, vt determinata atque perfecta. Gratia exempli: Animal, vt est genus hominis, sumitur à tota natura eius, secundùm gradum superiorem & imperfectum, hoc est, vt sensitiua, per eandem naturam hominis, vt rationalem, determinabili: & rationale, quod est differentia, sumitur etiam à tota natura hominis: vt perfecta ac determinata: vnde sequitur, tam genus quàm differentiam significare totam naturam speciei: illud quidem sub ratione contrahibilis, hanc verò sub ratione contrahentis.

23 But in order to explain its foundation, it should be noted first that both genus and difference are taken from the whole specific nature, or from its whole entity, considered under diverse grades, and not from a part alone, as will be explained in the chapter on difference; yet by a diverse ratio: for genus is taken from the whole nature of the thing under a more universal and imperfect ratio, which is nevertheless perfectible through the same nature considered under the specific grade; but difference, also from the whole nature, as determined and perfect. For example: animal, as it is the genus of man, is taken from his whole nature according to the superior and imperfect grade, that is, as sensitive, determinable by the same nature of man as rational; and rational, which is the difference, is also taken from the whole nature of man, as perfect and determinate. Whence it follows that both genus and difference signify the whole nature of the species: the former under the ratio of the contractible, the latter under the ratio of the contracting.

Secundò, notandum est, quòd genus sumptum vt totum potentiale, valde diuersum est à seipso, sumpto vt parte actuali, aut potentiali: nam vt totum potentiale: non solùm dicit partem speciei, sed totam naturam eius, sub gradu superiori, & imperfectiori consideratam, & contrahibilem, per gradus inferiores, & speciales indifferentiarum, sed vt pars est speciei, non dicit vllo modo integram naturam speciei, sed partem duntaxat: & ratio huius differentiæ est, quia genus vt totum potentiale, abstrahitur à speciebus abstractione vniuersali, quia abstrahitur commune à particularibus, vt animal abstrahitur ab homine, & leone, tanquam vniuersale à particularibus: & ideo dicit totam naturam eorum: sed sub gradu superiori sensitiuo, idem significans, quod habens naturam sensitiuam determinabilem per rationalem. Si verò idem genus accipiatur vt pars speciei, non abstrahitur abstractione vniuersalis à particularibus, sed potius abstractione

Second, it should be noted that genus taken as a potential whole is very diverse from itself taken as an actual or potential part: for as a potential whole it expresses not only a part of the species but its whole nature, considered under a superior and more imperfect grade, and contractible through the inferior and specific grades of the differences; but as it is a part of the species, it in no way expresses the entire nature of the species, but only a part. And the reason for this difference is that genus as a potential whole is abstracted from the species by universal abstraction, because the common is abstracted from the particulars, as animal is abstracted from man and lion, as a universal from particulars; and therefore it expresses their whole nature, but under the superior sensitive grade, signifying the same as that which has a sensitive nature determinable by rational. But if the same genus is taken as a part of the species, it is not abstracted by the abstraction of the universal from particulars, but rather by the abstraction

p. 112

pręcisiua, quæ pars præscinditur à toto; vt brachiũ ab homine.

of precision, by which a part is prescinded from the whole, as the arm from man.

24 Ex hac doctrina colligitur duplex argumentum ad probandum, quòd genus, vt totum potentiale, & non vt pars, prædicetur de specie. Primùm, genus prædicatur de speciebus, vt vniuersale, ac superius prædicatum abstractum ab eis: sed vniuersale, quod abstrahitur à particularibus, continet totam naturam eorum, sub ratione superiori consideratam: non consideratis rationibus inferioribus, à quibus abstrahitur, vt patet de specie abstracta ab indiuiduis: ergo prædicatur de illis, vt totum potentiale, contrahibile per differentias, & non vt pars. Probatur consequentia, quia pars non potest abstrahi à toto, abstractione vniuersalis à particulari: sed solùm præscindi ab eo, vt brachium ab homine: quod patet non prædicari de toto.

24 From this doctrine a twofold argument is gathered to prove that genus is predicated of the species as a potential whole and not as a part. First: genus is predicated of the species as a universal and superior predicate abstracted from them; but the universal which is abstracted from particulars contains their whole nature, considered under a superior ratio, the inferior rationes from which it is abstracted not being considered, as is plain in the species abstracted from the individuals; therefore it is predicated of them as a potential whole, contractible by the differences, and not as a part. The consequence is proved: because a part cannot be abstracted from the whole by the abstraction of the universal from the particular, but only prescinded from it, as the arm from man; which plainly is not predicated of the whole.

Secundò, vt vera sit prædicatio aliqua, non sufficit quòd prædicatum includatur in subiecto: nam si hoc sufficeret, quælibet pars prædicaretur de toto: ergo requiritur quòd contineat, quidquid continet subiectum. Probatur consequentia, ex sensu ipsius propositionis, per quam significatur hoc esse illud: quod non potest esse verum, nisi totum quod cõtinet subiectum, contineat prædicatum: nam si aliquid subiecti non continet, non erit verum ex parte illius, esse illud. Et hæc est ratio, propter quam, nulla pars prædicari potest de toto: quia ratione alterius partis, quam totum dicit, non potest esse verũ, totum esse partem, vt hominem esse caput. Et argum. hoc eodem modo probat dę partibus Physicis quales sunt materia & forma: quia licèt illæ non distinguantur realiter à toto, satis est distingui ratione formali: propter diuersum modum essendi, & significandi totius & partis, vt ab intellectu conceptis, vt falsam efficiant propositionem.

Second, for any predication to be true, it is not enough that the predicate be included in the subject, for if this were enough any part would be predicated of the whole; therefore it is required that it contain whatever the subject contains. The consequence is proved from the sense of the proposition itself, by which it is signified that this is that; which cannot be true unless the predicate contains the whole that the subject contains: for if it does not contain something of the subject, it will not be true on the part of that something that this is that. And this is the reason why no part can be predicated of the whole: because by reason of the other part, which the whole expresses, it cannot be true that the whole is the part, as that man is a head. And this argument proves in the same way of physical parts, such as matter and form: because although these are not really distinguished from the whole, it is enough that they are distinguished by formal ratio, on account of the diverse mode of being and of signifying of the whole and of the part as conceived by the intellect, for them to make a false proposition.

Ad testimonium Aristot. pro prima opinione respondeo, Partes definitionis prædicari de definito per se, seruato modo prædicandi debito, nempe sumptas per modum totius potentialis, vel actualis: nam sub forma partis impossibile est. Ad intentum verò Aristotelis, in eo loco sufficit, quòd hoc vel illo modo prædicentur.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion I reply that the parts of the definition are predicated per se of the defined, the due mode of predicating being observed, namely taken by way of a potential or an actual whole: for under the form of a part it is impossible. But for Aristotle’s intent in that passage it is enough that they are predicated in this or that way.

Ad primum argumentum eiusdem sententiæ respondetur, distinguendo antecedens. Nam prædicatum, ex duplici parte potest esse incompletum: ex parte eius quod prædicat de subiecto, & ex modo, quo illud prędicat: & in primo sensu incompletè prædicatur genus de specie: quia tantùm prædicat naturam sensitiuam: quæ est pars speciei: sed ex parte modi, completè potiùs prædicatur: quia eandem naturam sensitiuam

To the first argument of the same opinion one replies by distinguishing the antecedent. For a predicate can be incomplete on two counts: on the part of what it predicates of the subject, and from the mode in which it predicates it; and in the first sense genus is predicated incompletely of the species, because it predicates only sensitive nature, which is a part of the species; but on the part of the mode it is rather predicated completely, because it predicates the same sensitive nature

p. 113

prędicata, non per modum partis, sed per modum totius: quia per modum habẽtis illam, non quidem totius actualis, sed potentialis: quia per modum perfectibilis, ac determinabilis, per gradus differentiales.

not by way of a part but by way of a whole, because by way of something having it; not indeed of an actual whole, but of a potential one, because by way of something perfectible and determinable by the differential grades.

25 Ad secundùm respondetur: Concedendo antecedens, quòd pars physica in concreto significata, prædicetur de toto: quia non significatur vt pars, sed sub ratione totius, quia significatur nomine adiectiuo: quod cùm significet per modum adiacentis, rem quoque significat per modum habẽtis, vt dum dicimus, hominem esse materialem, idem est, ac si dicamus, esse habentem materiam: & esse materialem, adiectiuo nomine significatur per modum adiacentis, ac si esset accidens hominis, cùm verè sit pars substantialis. Genus verò etiam in concreto significatum, sumi potest vt pars: quia significatur nomine substantiuo, & ita sumptum non potest prædicari de toto, secundùm verum sensum propositionis, per quam dicitur hoc esse illud. Quod non potest esse verum, ex ea parte, qua totum aliquid aliud importat, diuersum à qualibet parte per se.

25 To the second one replies by granting the antecedent, that a physical part signified in the concrete is predicated of the whole: because it is not signified as a part but under the ratio of a whole, since it is signified by an adjectival name; which, since it signifies by way of something adjacent, also signifies the thing by way of something having: as when we say that man is material, it is the same as if we said that he is having matter; and to be material, signified by an adjectival name, is signified by way of something adjacent, as if it were an accident of man, although it is truly a substantial part. But genus, even signified in the concrete, can be taken as a part, because it is signified by a substantive name; and taken thus it cannot be predicated of the whole according to the true sense of the proposition, by which it is said that this is that. Which cannot be true on the side on which the whole imports something else, diverse from any part per se.

Ad argumentum secundæ opinionis respondetur, Differentiam inter genus, vt partem actualem, & potentialem, non consistere in eo, quòd vt pars actualis, vni tantùm differentię coniunctum sit, vt potentialis verò, omnibus coniungi possit: nam vtroque modo vnam tantùm determinatam differentiam respicit, sed solùm, vt pars actualis distinguitur à se: vt parte potentiali: quia vt actu coniunctum, consideratur cum tali differentia determinata, sed vt pars potentialis, consideratur vt potest coniungi, non omnibus, sed eidem tantùm determinatę differentiæ. Vnde falsum est, quòd vt pars potentialis, contineat differentiam aliquam in potentia, & consequenter est falsum, quòd vt pars potentialis prædicari possit de specie.

To the argument of the second opinion one replies that the difference between genus as an actual part and as a potential part does not consist in this, that as an actual part it is joined to one difference only, while as potential it can be joined to all: for in both ways it regards only one determinate difference; but only in this, that as an actual part it is distinguished from itself as a potential part, because as joined in act it is considered with such a determinate difference, but as a potential part it is considered as able to be joined, not to all, but only to the same determinate difference. Hence it is false that as a potential part it contains some difference in potency, and consequently it is false that as a potential part it can be predicated of the species.

QUESTION VI

An modus prædicandi in quid, separet genus à differentia.

Whether genus is separated from difference by the mode of predicating in quid.

25 PArs negatiua: quòd non distinguatur per modum prædicandi Quid, & in Quale quid, probatur ex Aristotele 1. lib. Posteriorum tex. 12. vbi docet, Vtramque partem definitionis: nempe genus & differentiam, prædicari de specie in quid: & expressius 7. lib. Topicorum cap. 2. loco 31. his verbis. Eorum quæ sunt in assignata oratione, hoc quidem genus, illud autem differentia: & in eo, quod quid est, genus & differentia prædicantur.

25 The negative part, that it is not distinguished by the mode of predicating in Quid and in Quale quid, is proved from Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1, text 12, where he teaches that both parts of the definition, namely genus and difference, are predicated of the species in quid; and more expressly in Topics 7, ch. 2, place 31, in these words: Of those things which are in the assigned expression, this one is genus, that one difference; and genus and difference are predicated in what it is. H

p. 114

Probatur etiam, ratione: Quia modus prædicandi sequitur modum essendi: sed differentia habet modum essendi perfectiorem in compositione speciei, quàm genus, cùm se habeat tanquam forma, & genus, vt materia: ergo habebit modũ perfectiorem prædicandi. Sed modus perfectior prædicandi, est prędicari in Quid, ergo hoc modo potiùs quam in Quale prędicabitur. Minorem probo: quia modus prædicandi in quid, est proprius substantiæ: & modus prædicandi in quale, est modus accidentis: quod non videtur posse negari, cùm sit prædicatum essentiale. Communis tamen sententia Porphyrij, & omnium interpretum eius est, quòd Genus distinguatur à differentia, ex eo, quòd illud prædicatur in quid, hæc verò in quale quid: vera est & tenenda. Quæ probatur expresso testimonio Arist. 4. lib Topicorum, ca. 6. loco 81. vbi sic ait. Quoniam differentia quidem qualitatem generis semper significat, genus autem differentiæ non: nam qui dicit greßibile quiddam, animal dicit: qui verò animal dicit, non dicit quale quiddam greßibile: differentia igitur à genere sic separanda. Et hunc modum distinguendi hęc duo prędicabilia, generis, & differentiæ, per modum prædicandi in quid & in quale quid, sequitur D. Thom. opusc. 58. tract. 1. cap. 4 Probatur deinde ratione: quia genus prædicatur de specie per modum substantię, hoc est per se stantis, cuius euidens signum est, quod nomine substantiuo significatur: sed modus prædicandi in quid, est proprius substantiæ, quæ est quidditas rei: ergo prædicatur in quid. Differentia verò prædicatur per modum formæ, qui non est rei per se stantis: sed inhærentis materiæ, & determinantis, ac modificantis illam, ad similitudinem qualitatis: ergo non prædicatur in quid, sed in quale: non tamen sicut vera qualitas, quia ad essentiam rei pertinet: & ideo non prædicatur in quale simpliciter, sed secundùm quid, & cum addito, hoc est in quale quid: & in hoc distinguitur à genere. pro explicatione testimonij Aristotelis, adducti ad probandam negatiuam partem, notandum est: duo esse consideranda in prædicato alicuius prædicationis. Primum, rem ipsam quæ prædicatur. Secundùm, modum, quo concipitur, & significatur, secundùm quem attribuitur subiecto: & Primum quasi materiale est in prædicatione: ex quo non sumitur modus prædicandi, distinguens prædicabilia, sed ex secundo, in quo consistit ratio formalis prædicationis. Aristoteles ergo in diuersis locis vtrunque considerauit: in eo quidem, cuius verba adduximus, pro negatiua parte, considerauit primum: modum verò concipiendi prædicatum, & attribuendi subiecto, considerauit in secundo loco, quem pro nostra sententia adduximus

It is proved also by reason: because the mode of predicating follows the mode of being; but difference has a more perfect mode of being in the composition of the species than genus, since it stands as form, and genus as matter; therefore it will have a more perfect mode of predicating. But the more perfect mode of predicating is to be predicated in Quid; therefore it will be predicated in this mode rather than in Quale. I prove the minor: because the mode of predicating in quid is proper to substance, and the mode of predicating in quale is the mode of an accident; which it seems cannot be denied, since it is an essential predicate. Nevertheless the common opinion of Porphyry and of all his interpreters, that genus is distinguished from difference in that the former is predicated in quid, the latter in quale quid, is true and to be held. It is proved by an express testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 6, place 81, where he speaks thus: Since difference always signifies a quality of the genus, but genus does not of the difference: for he who says gressible says a certain animal; but he who says animal does not say a certain gressible thing; difference, therefore, is to be separated from genus in this way. And this mode of distinguishing these two predicables, genus and difference, by the mode of predicating in quid and in quale quid, is followed by St. Thomas, opusc. 58, tract. 1, ch. 4. It is proved next by reason: because genus is predicated of the species by way of a substance, that is, of something standing per se, of which an evident sign is that it is signified by a substantive name; but the mode of predicating in quid is proper to substance, which is the quiddity of the thing; therefore it is predicated in quid. But difference is predicated by way of a form, which is not the mode of a thing standing per se, but of one inhering in matter and determining and modifying it, after the likeness of a quality; therefore it is not predicated in quid but in quale; not, however, as a true quality, because it pertains to the essence of the thing; and therefore it is not predicated in quale simply, but in a certain respect and with an addition, that is, in quale quid; and in this it is distinguished from genus. For the explanation of the testimony of Aristotle adduced to prove the negative part, it should be noted that two things are to be considered in the predicate of any predication. First, the thing itself that is predicated. Second, the mode in which it is conceived and signified, according to which it is attributed to the subject; and the first is as it were the material element in the predication, from which the mode of predicating that distinguishes the predicables is not taken, but from the second, in which the formal ratio of predication consists. Aristotle, then, considered both in different places: in the one whose words we adduced for the negative part he considered the first; but the mode of conceiving the predicate and of attributing it to the subject he considered in the second place, which we adduced for our opinion

p. 115

: & ideo distinxit genus à differentia, per modos prædicandi in quid, & in quale: in alio verò eodem modo prædicari docuit: quod verum est ex parte rei, quæ prædicatur, in se consideratæ: nam tam differentia, quàm genus, est pars quidditatis speciei.

; and therefore he distinguished genus from difference by the modes of predicating in quid and in quale; but in the other he taught that they are predicated in the same mode, which is true on the part of the thing that is predicated, considered in itself: for both difference and genus are a part of the quiddity of the species.

Ad argumentum verò respondeo, Distinguendo maiorem. nam modus essendi dupliciter sumi potest, secundùm se, vel vt concipitur à nobis: & ab eo, hoc modo sumpto, accipitur modus prædicandi: quia non prædicantur res, vt sunt à parte rei, sed vt tali modo cognoscuntur: & licèt secundùm primam cõsiderationem, perfectior sit differentia quàm genus, ex modo tamen posteriori, perfectiorem habet modum prędicandi hoc quàm illa, per quem distinctum prædicabile constituit.

To the argument I reply by distinguishing the major: for the mode of being can be taken in two ways, according to itself, or as it is conceived by us; and the mode of predicating is taken from it taken in this latter way, because things are not predicated as they are on the part of the thing, but as they are known in such a way; and although according to the first consideration difference is more perfect than genus, yet in the latter way the latter has a more perfect mode of predicating than the former, by which it constitutes a distinct predicable.

CHAPTER III

De Specie.

On Species.

1 INtentum Porphyrij in hoc capite est, explicare naturam secundi prædicabilis, quod est Species. Diuiditur autem in quatuor partes. In prima, proponit duas acceptiones speciei: primam Physicam & realem, ex cuius similitudine colligit secundam Logicam. In secunda definit speciem duplici definitione. In tertia ponit ordinationem prædicamentalem, prædicamenti substantiæ, vt per eam intelligatur duplex habitudo speciei: Vna quam habet ad genus, sub quo collocatur: Altera ad indiuidua, de quibus prædicatur. In vltima, definit indiuiduum duabus definitionibus. Prima, acceptio realis speciei est, qua accipitur pro forma, ac pulcritudine rei. In qua acceptione dici solet: Præstantissimam speciem dignam esse imperio, Hoc est pulcherrimum hominem dignum esse imperio: quia pulchritudo corporis, signum est virtutis in anima existentis. Et huic acceptioni reali, similis est acceptio Logica, quia accipitur species pro ea quæ sub assignato genere collocatur, inquit Porphyr ) id est sub genere iam definito, & explicato capite præcedenti. Similitudo autem vtriusque acceptionis consistit in hoc: quia quemadmodum forma rei, in qua pulchritudo consistere solet, accidentali modo includit atque ostendit perfectionem essentialem rei: ita species, quæ sub genere collocatur, & ab eo simul cum differentia constituitur, includit modo substantiali, totam perfectionem essentialem rei: vt species humana totam perfectionem essentialem hominis. Et hæc in prima parte capitis.

1 Porphyry’s intent in this chapter is to explain the nature of the second predicable, which is Species. It is divided into four parts. In the first he proposes two acceptations of species: the first physical and real, from whose likeness he gathers the second, the logical. In the second he defines species by a twofold definition. In the third he sets out the categorial ordering of the category of substance, so that through it the twofold relation of species may be understood: one which it has to the genus under which it is placed, the other to the individuals of which it is predicated. In the last he defines the individual by two definitions. The first, real acceptation of species is that in which it is taken for the form and beauty of a thing. In this acceptation it is customarily said: Praestantissimam speciem dignam esse imperio [the most excellent species is worthy of rule]; that is, that the most beautiful man is worthy of rule, because beauty of body is a sign of virtue existing in the soul. And similar to this real acceptation is the logical acceptation, for species is taken for that which is placed under the assigned genus, says Porphyry, that is, under the genus already defined and explained in the preceding chapter. And the likeness of the two acceptations consists in this: that just as the form of a thing, in which beauty usually consists, includes and shows in an accidental way the essential perfection of the thing, so the species, which is placed under the genus and constituted by it together with the difference, includes in a substantial way the whole essential perfection of the thing: as the human species the whole essential perfection of man. And this is in the first part of the chapter. H ij

p. 116

In secunda verò, definit Porphyrius speciem, secundùm hãc acceptionem Logicam, duplici definitione. Prima definitio talis est: Species est, quæ subiicitur generi, & de qua genus in quid prædicatur. Per quam explicatur species secundùm habitudinem, quam habet ad genus, à qua dicitur species subiicibilis.

In the second part Porphyry defines species, according to this logical acceptation, by a twofold definition. The first definition is this: Species is that which is subjected to the genus, and of which the genus is predicated in quid. By it species is explained according to the relation which it has to the genus, from which it is called subjicible species.

Secunda definitio speciei est: Species est quæ prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie in eo, quod quid. Per quam explicatur species, secundùm habitudinem, quam habet ad indiuidua, & vt est secundùm prædicabile: & hæc Porphyrius in 2. part. In tertia, proponit ordinem prædicamentalem in prædicamento substantiæ: quod his quinque prædicatis constat: Substantia, Corpus, Viuens, Animal, Homo. Sed vt intelligatur, tria ait esse in eo consideranda. Primum est, tria in eo reperiri, nempe supremum genus, quod ita est genus, vt non sit species, vt substantia. Infimam speciem, quæ ita est species, vt non sit genus, vt homo, aut leo: & Intermedia genera, quæ simul sunt genera respectu inferiorum specierum, & species respectu superioris generis. Indiuidua verò, non collocantur in prædicamento, tanquam partes eius, sed tanquam fundamentum omnium prædicatorum essentialium: ex quibus tanquam partibus componitur prædicamentum. Gratia exempli: Substantia, est supremum genus: Homo, infima species. Et hæc sunt quasi extrema prædicamenti: Animal, Viuens, & Corpus, dicuntur intermedia: quia ita sunt genera, vt simul sint species: animal enim est genus hominis, & species viuentis: & ideo vocantur hæc genera subalterna: quia ita sunt genera, vt sub alio genere collocentur, respectu cuius species dicuntur: & hoc est simul esse genera, & species respectu diuersorum.

The second definition of species is: Species is that which is predicated of many differing in species in what it is. By it species is explained according to the relation which it has to the individuals, and as it is the second predicable; and this Porphyry does in the 2nd part. In the third he proposes the categorial order in the category of substance, which consists of these five predicates: Substance, Body, Living thing, Animal, Man. But in order that it may be understood, he says three things are to be considered in it. The first is that three things are found in it, namely: the supreme genus, which is a genus in such a way that it is not a species, as substance; the lowest species, which is a species in such a way that it is not a genus, as man or lion; and the intermediate genera, which are at once genera with respect to the inferior species and species with respect to the superior genus. The individuals, however, are not placed in the category as its parts, but as the foundation of all the essential predicates, of which, as of parts, the category is composed. For example: Substance is the supreme genus; Man, the lowest species. And these are as it were the extremes of the category. Animal, Living thing, and Body are called intermediate, because they are genera in such a way that they are at once species: for animal is the genus of man, the species of living thing; and therefore these are called subalternate genera, because they are genera in such a way that they are placed under another genus, with respect to which they are called species; and this is to be at once genera and species with respect to different things.

Secundò, considerandum est, suprema genera esse decem, nempe, Substantiam, Quantitatem Relationem, Qualitatem, Actionem, Passionem, Vbi, Situm, Quando, Habere, & cum hæc sint quasi capita prædicamentorum, decem quoque sunt prædicamenta: species verò infimæ, finitæ sunt: & eodem modo intermedia genera: sed indiuidua in finitum procedunt: quia quibuscunque datis, alia, & alia multiplicantur in infinitum: & ita à scientia prædicamentorum deficiunt.

Second, it is to be considered that the supreme genera are ten, namely Substance, Quantity, Relation, Quality, Action, Passion, Where, Position, When, Having; and since these are as it were the heads of the categories, there are also ten categories; but the lowest species are finite, and in the same way the intermediate genera; but the individuals proceed to infinity, because, whatever ones are given, others and others multiply to infinity; and so they fall outside the science of the categories.

3 Tertiò, considerandum est, hanc esse differentiam, inter ascensum & descensum prædicamentalem: quòd descensus sit per diuisionem vnius in plura, nempe generis, in plures species, per differentias: ascensus verò, per collectionem plurium in vnum: vt dum descendimus, à supremo genere substantiæ, vsque ad infimam speciem hominis, prædicemus diuidendo illud, in Substantiam corpoream, & incorpoream: & hanc in

3 Third, it is to be considered that the difference between categorial ascent and descent is this: that descent takes place by the division of one into many, namely of the genus into several species through the differences; but ascent by the gathering of many into one: as when we descend from the supreme genus of substance down to the lowest species of man, we predicate by dividing it into corporeal and incorporeal substance, and this into

p. 117

viuentem, & non viuentem, vsque ad hominem. Sed dum ascendimus, plures species colligimus in vnum genus, vt hominem, leonem, & cæteras species animalis, in vnum genus animalis: & ita vsq; ad supremum genus substantiæ. Et hęc Porphyrius in 3. parte. In vltima verò, quia speciem vt prædicabilem, definiuit per indiuidua, tanquam per terminum relationis eius, explicat naturã indiuidui, duabus definitionibus: quarũ prima est: Indiuiduum est, quod de vno solo prædicatur. Vt Petrus de seipso, in hac prędicatione idẽtica, Petrus est petrus.

living and non-living, down to man. But when we ascend, we gather several species into one genus, as man, lion, and the other species of animal into one genus of animal; and so on up to the supreme genus of substance. And this Porphyry does in the 3rd part. In the last, since he defined species as predicable through the individuals, as through the term of its relation, he explains the nature of the individual by two definitions, of which the first is: The individual is that which is predicated of one alone: as Peter of himself, in this identical predication, Peter is Peter.

Secunda definitio. Indiuiduum est, cuius collectio proprietatum, quæ in vno est, in alio non potest reperiri. Quæ sic explicatur. Proprietates specificæ, vt risibilitas, & admiratio, cõmunes sunt omnibus indiuiduis humanæ speciei: & plures etiam proprietates indiuiduales cuiuslibet indiuidui, possunt cõuenire aliis: sed collectio omnium, quæ in vno reperiuntur, non potest in alio reperiri. Exempli gratia: quælibet proprietas indiuidualis Petri, potest conuenire Ioanni, sed omnes simul sumptæ non possunt ei conuenire. Porphyr. in toto cap.

The second definition: The individual is that whose collection of properties, which is in one, cannot be found in another. Which is explained thus. The specific properties, such as risibility and wonder, are common to all the individuals of the human species; and even many individual properties of any individual can belong to others; but the collection of all that are found in one cannot be found in another. For example: any individual property of Peter can belong to John, but all of them taken together cannot belong to him. Porphyry, in the whole chapter.

QUESTION I

Vtrum species fuerit definita à Porphyrio duabus vel tribus definitionibus.

Whether species was defined by Porphyry with two definitions or three. 4

4 CIrca numerum definitionum, quibus species definita est à Porphyrio, certum est apud omnes interpretes eius, duabus saltem definitionibus definitam esse, secundùm duas habitudines, vel respectus, quos habet, vnum ad genus, à quo species subiicibilis vocatur, alterum ad indiuidua, à quo dicitur species prædicabilis. Sed an duabus tantùm definita fuerit, vel tribus, diuersæ sunt opiniones.

Concerning the number of definitions by which species was defined by Porphyry, it is certain among all his interpreters that it was defined by at least two definitions, according to the two relations or respects which it has: one to the genus, from which it is called subjicible species, the other to the individuals, from which it is called predicable species. But whether it was defined by two only, or by three, there are different opinions.

Prima est, Soti asserentis, duabus tantùm esse definitam: ita vt prima illa, quæ asserit, Speciem esse, quæ sub assignato genere collocatur, non sit definitio, sed acceptio tantùm logica speciei, aut nuda explicatio vocis. Altera verò, qua dicitur speciem esse, quæ subiicitur generi, & de qua genus in quid prædicatur, definitionem esse: non tamen duplicem, sed vnam tantùm: quia eundem respectum explicat: nam idem est subiici generi, & genus prædicari de illa. Et cùm præter hanc, tantùm sit alia, per quam explicatur species, vt pręcabilis, tantùm erunt duæ. Probat hoc argum. Species solùm habet duos respectus, vnum ad genus, vt est subiicibilis, alterum ad indiuidua. vt est prædicabilis: ergo solùm habet duas rationes formales, explicabiles per definitionem: & ideo duabus solùm definitionibus explicari potest.

The first is that of Soto, who asserts that it was defined by two only, so that the first, which asserts that species is that which is placed under the assigned genus, is not a definition but only the logical acceptation of species, or a bare explanation of the word. But the other, in which it is said that species is that which is subjected to the genus and of which the genus is predicated in quid, is a definition; not, however, a twofold one, but one only, because it explains the same respect: for it is the same to be subjected to the genus and for the genus to be predicated of it. And since besides this there is only another, by which species is explained as predicable, there will be only two. He proves it by this argument. Species has only two respects, one to the genus, as it is subjicible, the other to the individuals, as it is predicable; therefore it has only two formal rationes explicable by definition; and therefore it can be explained by two definitions only. G iij

p. 118

Alij verò omnes, asserunt tribus definitionibus fuisse definitam, sed non eodem modo eas enumerant: nam Toletus primam solùm esse explicationem vocis ait, sed secundam distinguit in duas: ita vt vna sit, Species est quæ subiicitur generi: & altera, Species est de qua genus prædicatur in quid: & ideo cum alia, per quam explicatur species, vt prædicabilis, esse tres. Probat, quia eundem respectum ad genus diuerso modo vtraque explicat: nam aliud est speciem respicere genus, aliud, genus respicere speciem, dum prædicatur de illa.

But all the others assert that it was defined by three definitions, yet they do not enumerate them in the same way. For Toledo says that only the first is an explanation of the word, but he divides the second into two, so that one is: Species is that which is subjected to the genus; and the other: Species is that of which the genus is predicated in quid; and that therefore, with the other, by which species is explained as predicable, there are three. He proves it because each explains the same respect to the genus in a different way: for it is one thing for the species to regard the genus, another for the genus to regard the species when it is predicated of it.

Caietanus verò, & Canterus, ita asserunt tres esse definitiones, vt prima non sit sola acceptio, aut vocis explicatio, sed simul definitio: secundam verò vnam tantùm esse, quia vnam tantùm habitudinem ad genus, omnia illa verba explicant: Et hæc videtur mihi probabilior sententia, & magis ad mentem Porphyrij.

But Cajetan and Canterus assert that there are three definitions in such a way that the first is not only an acceptation or explanation of the word but at the same time a definition, while the second is only one, because all those words explain only one relation to the genus. And this seems to me the more probable opinion, and more in accordance with the mind of Porphyry.

5 Et probatur primum: quòd illa verba, Species est, quæ sub assignato genere collocatur, non sint sola acceptio, sed etiam definitio: quia Porphyr. dum aliam definitionem proposuit, sic asseruit! Assignant ergo & sic speciem: species est, quæ ponitur sub genere, & de qua genus in aliquid prædicatur. Quibus verbis docet, se aliam definitionem, post primam iam traditam, assignare. Præterea, priusquam secundam definitionem proponeret, rationem reddit, propter quam, cùm genus per speciem definierit, cap. præcedenti, nunc speciem per genus explicauerit, quia cùm sint relatiua, vnum per alterum definiendum erat: ergo fatetur iam definisse speciem, antequam secundam definitionem proponeret: quod non esset verum, si prima solùm esset acceptio, & non definitio.

5 And the first point is proved, that the words Species is that which is placed under the assigned genus are not only an acceptation but also a definition: because Porphyry, when he proposed the other definition, asserted thus: They assign species thus too: Species is that which is placed under the genus, and of which the genus is predicated in quid. By which words he teaches that he is assigning another definition after the first one already delivered. Moreover, before proposing the second definition, he gives the reason why, since he defined genus through species in the preceding chapter, he has now explained species through genus: because, since they are relatives, one had to be defined through the other; therefore he admits that he had already defined species before proposing the second definition; which would not be true if the first were only an acceptation and not a definition.

Probatur secundum, quòd sint definitiones distinctæ, prima & secũda, per quas species definiatur vt subiicibilis, hoc argumento, Species vt subiicitur generi, habet duas rationes formales diuersas: ergo non vna, sed duabus definitionibus debuit explicari. Consequentia euidens est, quia vna definitio, vnam tantùm rationem formalem explicare potest. Probatur verò antecedens, quia in genere, diuersæ rationes formales sunt: esse vniuersale, hoc est vnum in multis speciebus & esse prædicabile de illis: & ratio vniuersalis prior est, & essentialis illi: ratio verò prædicabilis posterior, & propria passio eius: & sub vtraque ratione respicit speciem: ergo etiam in specie debent correspondere diuersæ rationes formales: nempe esse subiectum, in quo est genus: & esse subiectum, de quo prædicatur: ita vt illa sit prior, & quasi essentialis speciei, vt subiicibili, hæc verò posterior, & quasi propria

The second point is proved, that the first and second, by which species is defined as subjicible, are distinct definitions, by this argument. Species, as it is subjected to the genus, has two diverse formal rationes; therefore it had to be explained not by one but by two definitions. The consequence is evident, because one definition can explain only one formal ratio. The antecedent is proved: because in genus there are diverse formal rationes, to be universal, that is, one in many species, and to be predicable of them; and the ratio of universal is prior and essential to it, while the ratio of predicable is posterior, and its proper attribute; and under each ratio it regards the species; therefore in the species too diverse formal rationes must correspond, namely to be the subject in which the genus is, and to be the subject of which it is predicated; so that the former is prior and as it were essential to the species as subjicible, the latter posterior and as it were a proper

p. 119

passio eius: sed diuersæ illæ rationes formales in genere, explicantur diuersis definitionibus, nempe vnum in multis speciebus: & prædicabile de illis: ergo etiam diuersæ rationes ex parte speciei, debent explicari per diuersas definitiones. Et ita factum est à Porphyrio, qui per illa verba: Species est, quæ sub assignato genere collocatur, explicuit speciem subiicibilem, vt est subiectum, in quo est genus: per secundam verò, vt est subiectum, de quo prædicatur.

attribute of it; but those diverse formal rationes in genus are explained by diverse definitions, namely one in many species, and predicable of them; therefore the diverse rationes on the part of the species too must be explained by diverse definitions. And so it was done by Porphyry, who by the words Species is that which is placed under the assigned genus explained the subjicible species as it is the subject in which the genus is, but by the second as it is the subject of which it is predicated.

Sed quòd secunda definitio non sit duplex, sed vna, probatur, quia verba, Species est, quæ subiicitur generi, eandem prorsus rationem speciei explicant, quæ per primam definitionem fuerat explicata: nempe esse subiectum in quo est genus: quare solùm videntur repetitio primæ definitionis. Alia verò verba, nempè, De qua genus in quid prædicatur. explicant aliam rationem formalem eiusdem speciei subiicibilis, videlicet esse subiectum, de quo prædicatur genus. Duas igitur tradit Porphyrius speciei subiicibilis definitiones, secundùm duas rationes formales eius, & tertiam eiusdem speciei, vt prædicabilis.

But that the second definition is not twofold but one is proved because the words Species is that which is subjected to the genus explain altogether the same ratio of species that had been explained by the first definition, namely to be the subject in which the genus is; wherefore they seem to be only a repetition of the first definition. But the other words, namely Of which the genus is predicated in quid, explain another formal ratio of the same subjicible species, namely to be the subject of which the genus is predicated. Porphyry therefore delivers two definitions of subjicible species, according to its two formal rationes, and a third of the same species as predicable.

6 Ad argumentum Soti & Toleti, eadem solutione respondetur: nam dum dicitur, Speciem solùm habere respectus ad genus, & indiuidua, concedendum est: dicendum tamen respectum ad genus, duplicem habere formalem rationem diuersam: qua diuerso modo respicit genus, nempe, vt subiectum in Quo, & vt subiectum de Quo: sicut genus diuersa ratione respicit eandẽ speciem, nempe vt subiectum in quo est, & de quo prędicatur: ideo diuersis definitionibꝰ, debuit explicari

6 To the argument of Soto and Toledo one replies with the same solution: for when it is said that species has only respects to the genus and to the individuals, this is to be granted; it must be said, however, that the respect to the genus has a twofold diverse formal ratio, by which it regards the genus in a diverse way, namely as the subject In which and as the subject Of which; just as the genus regards the same species by a diverse ratio, namely as the subject in which it is and of which it is predicated; therefore it had to be explained by diverse definitions.

Sed duo restant breuissima dubia. Primum, qua ratione agat Porphyrius de specie subiicibili: nam cùm opus hoc prædicabilium sit, non pertinet ad ipsum species, nisi vt prædicabililis: sed non est prædicabilis, vt respicit genus, sed indiuidua: ergo non debuit definiri, nisi respectu eorum: & ideo vnica definitione, & non pluribus. Respondetur, agere Porphyrium de specie subiicibili. Primò. Quia est subiectum generis, & subiectum ad eandem considerationem pertinet, ad quam prædicatum, quia terminus relationis eius est: sine quo non potest cognosci. Secundò, Quia subiectum opponitur prædicato: oppositorum verò eadem est scientia: & ideo duabus definitionibus debuit species definiri, vt subiicibilis, quia duobus modis formaliter diuersis est subiectum generis.

But two very brief doubts remain. The first: for what reason Porphyry treats of subjicible species: for since this is a work on the predicables, species does not pertain to it except as predicable; but it is not predicable as it regards the genus, but the individuals; therefore it should not have been defined except with respect to them, and therefore by a single definition, and not by several. The reply is that Porphyry treats of subjicible species, first, because it is the subject of the genus, and the subject pertains to the same consideration as the predicate, because it is the term of its relation, without which it cannot be known. Second, because the subject is opposed to the predicate, and of opposites the science is the same; and therefore species had to be defined by two definitions as subjicible, because it is the subject of the genus in two formally diverse ways.

7 Sed circa vtramq; eius definitionẽ est secundũ dubium: quia videtur conuenire indiuiduis, cùm sub assignato genere collocentur, vt hoc, vel illud animal sub animali, atque etiam

7 But concerning each of its definitions there is the second doubt: because it seems to belong to individuals, since they are placed under the assigned genus, as this or that animal under animal, and also H iij

p. 120

Petrus, & Ioannes, & eidem generi subiiciantur, quod de illis prædicatur in quid, sicut de speciebus. Respondeo, collocari sub genere, aut esse subiectum eius, duobus modis posse intelligi: per se quidem, ratione sui, & immediatè. Per aliud autem, ratione alterius, & remotè. Et primo modo conuenit soli speciei: indiuiduis verò solùm secundo modo. Et ratio huius est: quia genus per se, & immediatè descendit ad species per differentias: ad indiuidua verò, non nisi ratione speciei: ergo species sola est, quæ per se primò collocatur sub genere: indiuidua verò, non nisi per speciem. Definitiones igitur speciei subiicibilis, secundùm primũ modum intelliguntur à Porphyrio: ita vt sensus primæ sit, Species est, quæ sub assignato genere per se primò, atque immediatè collocatur. Sensus verò secundæ, Species est, quæ per se primò, & immediatè subiicitur generi, & de qua genus per se primò, & immediatè prædicatur in quid: & ita excluduntur indiuidua, quæ non sic ponuntur sub genere, nec ei subiiciuntur.

Peter and John, and they are subjected to the same genus, which is predicated of them in quid, as of the species. I reply that to be placed under the genus, or to be its subject, can be understood in two ways: per se, by reason of itself and immediately; and through another, by reason of something else and remotely. And in the first way it belongs to the species alone, but to the individuals only in the second way. And the reason for this is that genus descends per se and immediately to the species through the differences, but to the individuals only by reason of the species; therefore the species alone is what is placed per se and first under the genus, but the individuals only through the species. The definitions of subjicible species, then, are understood by Porphyry according to the first way, so that the sense of the first is: Species is that which is placed per se, first, and immediately under the assigned genus. And the sense of the second: Species is that which is per se, first, and immediately subjected to the genus, and of which the genus is per se, first, and immediately predicated in quid; and so the individuals are excluded, which are not so placed under the genus, nor subjected to it.

QUESTION II

Vtrum species subiicibilis, vt subiicibilis est, sit vniuersalis, vel quonam modo se habeant habitudines istæ speciei inter se, vniuersalitas prædicabilitas, & subiicibilitas.

Whether subjicible species, as subjicible, is universal, or in what way these relations of species are related among themselves: universality, predicability, and subjicibility.

VT intelligatur quæstio, præsupponenda sunt duo, tanquam certa apud omnes. Primum, hos duos respectus speciei, nempe prædicabilitatem, & subiicibilitatem, quasi oppositos esse, cùm conueniant ei respectu diuersorum, & quasi oppositorum terminorum: nam respectus subiicibilitatis conuenit speciei, in ordine ad superius genus: respectus prædicabilitatis, in ordine ad inferiora indiuidua.

To understand the question, two things are to be presupposed as certain among all. First, that these two respects of species, namely predicability and subjicibility, are as it were opposed, since they belong to it with respect to diverse and as it were opposed terms: for the respect of subjicibility belongs to species in order to the superior genus, the respect of predicability in order to the inferior individuals.

Secundò, certum est respectum prædicabilitatis conuenire speciei, vt vniuersali. Probatur, quia vt superiùs probatum est, vniuersalitas se habet tanquam essentia vniuersalis, prædicabilitas verò, tanquam propria passio eius: ergo verum est, speciem, vt vniuersalem, esse prædicabilem, sicut verum est, hominem esse risibilem: vt est rationalis. Quæstio igitur est, An etiam conueniat speciei respectus subiicibilitatis, in quantum est vniuersalis.
