Second, it is certain that the respect of predicability belongs to species as universal. This is proved because, as was proved above, universality stands as the essence of the universal, and predicability as its proper attribute; therefore it is true that species, as universal, is predicable, just as it is true that man is risible as he is rational. The question, then, is whether the respect of subjicibility also belongs to species inasmuch as it is universal.

Circa quam, duæ sunt opiniones. Prima, Caietani cap. præsenti, vbi ait, Ita esse connexas has duas rationes speciei, nempe, vniuersalitatem, & prædicabilitatem cum tertia, quæ est subiicibilitas, vt hæc se habeat tanquam essentia, à qua illæ duæ procedunt, tanquam

On this there are two opinions. The first is Cajetan’s, on the present chapter, where he says that these two rationes of species, namely universality and predicability, are so connected with the third, which is subjicibility, that this stands as the essence from which those two proceed as

p. 121

propriæ passiones. Vnde sequitur, speciem vt subiicibilem, esse vniuersalem: sicut verum est, hominem esse risibilem, in quantum est homo: quia risibilitas procedit à rationalitate, namquam propria passio ab essentia.

proper attributes. Whence it follows that species, as subjicible, is universal, just as it is true that man is risible inasmuch as he is man: because risibility proceeds from rationality, as a proper attribute always does from the essence.

Secunda opinio est Cardinalis Toleti, q. 1. huius capitis. Vbi asserit: Vniuersalitatem esse essentiam speciei, & ab ea procedere duas passiones: Vna est prædicabilitas de multis, respectu indiuiduorum: Altera, subiicibilitas. respectu generis, ex quo sequitur, speciem vt respicit genus, esse vniuersale subiicibile, & vt respicit indiuidua, esse vniuersale prædicabile: & vt vno verbo hanc sententiam explicemus, ita ait speciem, vt subiicibilem, esse vniuersalem: sicut vniuersalis est, in quãtum prædicabilis.

The second opinion is that of Cardinal Toledo, q. 1 of this chapter, where he asserts: Universality is the essence of species, and from it proceed two attributes: one is predicability of many, with respect to the individuals; the other, subjicibility, with respect to the genus. From which it follows that species, as it regards the genus, is a subjicible universal, and as it regards the individuals, a predicable universal; and, to explain this opinion in a word, he says that species, as subjicible, is universal, just as it is universal inasmuch as it is predicable.

Probatur duplici ratione. Prima, Vniuersale (inquit) est genus ad quinque prædicabilia, sicut animal ad hominem, & leonem: ergo quodlibet prædicabile respicit illud, tanquam proprium genus, cuius rationem participat: sed species respectu generis sunt subiicibiles, ergo prædicabilia, vt species subiicibiles, participant rationem genericam vniuersalis, sicut homo & leo rationem animalis: quare, vt subiicibiles, sunt vniuersales.

This is proved by a twofold argument. First: The universal (he says) is a genus to the five predicables, as animal to man and lion; therefore each predicable regards it as its proper genus, whose ratio it participates. But the species are subjicible with respect to the genus; therefore the predicables, as subjicible species, participate the generic ratio of the universal, as man and lion that of animal; wherefore, as subjicible, they are universal.

9 Secunda, Species subiicibilis, vt subiicibilis est, non est singularis: ergo vniuersalis. Consequentia necessaria est, quia inter vniuersale, & singulare, non datur medium. Sed probatur antecedens, quia species subiicibilis, non est natura contracta per conditiones singulares, vt natura Petri, sed abstracta ab illis: natura verò abstracta, communis est multis, ergo est vniuersalis: & ideo in quantum subiicibilis, erit vniuersalis.

9 Second: Subjicible species, as subjicible, is not singular; therefore it is universal. The consequence is necessary, because between universal and singular there is no middle. And the antecedent is proved: because subjicible species is not a nature contracted by singular conditions, as is the nature of Peter, but abstracted from them; but an abstracted nature is common to many; therefore it is universal; and therefore inasmuch as it is subjicible it will be universal.

Et confirmatur: Quia species subiicibilis, in quantum subiicibilis, est communis huic & illi speciei subiicibili, de quibus prædicatur in his prædicationibus, Hæc specie subiicibilis, est species subiicibilis. Et illa species subiicibilis, est species subiicibilis: ergo est vniuersalis. Probatur consequentia: quia prædicabile sequitur ex vniuersali, tanquam propria passio ex essentia.

And this is confirmed: because subjicible species, inasmuch as it is subjicible, is common to this and that subjicible species, of which it is predicated in these predications: This subjicible species is a subjicible species, and That subjicible species is a subjicible species; therefore it is universal. The consequence is proved: because the predicable follows from the universal, as a proper attribute from the essence.

Vtraque hæc sententia falsa est. Probatur hoc argumento. Vniuersalitas, & prædicabilitas, sunt respectus naturæ ad inferiora, Subiicibilitas verò, est respectus eiusdem ad superiora: ergo respectus iste oppositus est illis: sud vnum oppositorum non potest procedere ab alio, tanquam propria passio ab essentia: ergo vniuersalitas, & prædicabilitas, non procedunt à subiicibilitate, tanquam ab essentia, vt affirmat Caie. nec subiicibilitas procedit ab vniuersalitate, tanquam ab essentia, vt affirmat Toletus.

Each of these opinions is false. This is proved by this argument. Universality and predicability are respects of the nature to its inferiors, whereas subjicibility is a respect of the same to its superiors; therefore this respect is opposed to those. But one of two opposites cannot proceed from the other, as a proper attribute from the essence; therefore universality and predicability do not proceed from subjicibility, as from an essence, as Cajetan affirms, nor does subjicibility proceed from universality, as from an essence, as Toledo affirms.

p. 122

Vera igitur sententia, tria affirmat Primum, Vniuersalitatem & prædicabilitatem non esse respectus oppositos, sed se habere tanquam essentiam, & propriam passionem. Probatur hoc: quia vterque respectus habet pro termino inferiora, quãuis diuerso modo considerata, vt quæstione præcedenti explicatum est.

The true opinion, then, affirms three things. First, that universality and predicability are not opposed respects, but are related as essence and proper attribute. This is proved because each respect has the inferiors for its term, although considered in a different way, as was explained in the preceding question.

Secundum. Hos respectus esse quasi oppositos subiicibilitati, & ideo nec ab ea procedere possunt, tanquam propria passio ab essentia, nec subiicibilitas ab illis. Vtrumque probatum est contra Caietanum, & Toletum.

Second, that these respects are as it were opposed to subjicibility, and therefore neither can they proceed from it, as a proper attribute from the essence, nor subjicibility from them. Both have been proved against Cajetan and Toledo.

Tertium, Speciem subiicibilem, vt subiicibilis est, non esse vniuersalem, sed subiectum commune, atque proximum generis. Hoc sequitur euidenter ex duobus primis: & probatur hoc argumento: Respectus oppositi, nõ possunt eidem rei sub eadem ratione formali conuenire: sed vniuersalitas, & subiicibilitas, sunt respectus oppositi, vt probatum est: ergo non possunt speciei sub eadem ratione conuenire: ideo nec vniuersalis, est subiicibilis, neque vt subicibilis, est vniuersalis.

Third, that subjicible species, as it is subjicible, is not universal but the common and proximate subject of the genus. This follows evidently from the first two, and is proved by this argument: Opposed respects cannot belong to the same thing under the same formal ratio; but universality and subjicibility are opposed respects, as has been proved; therefore they cannot belong to species under the same ratio; and therefore neither is it subjicible as universal, nor universal as subjicible.

Ad primum arg. secundę opinionis, concedendum est antecedẽs: Quòd vniuersale sit genus, ad quinque prædicabilia, & etiam prima consequentia, quòd naturam eius participent: sed negandum est, quòd eam participent, vt sunt species subiicibiles: sed eam quidem participant secundùm propriam essentiã: ex participatione verò, resultat in eis accidentaliter respectus subiicibilitatis, secundùm quem non sunt vniuersales, sed subiecta generis. Quod hoc exemplo declaratur. Animal est genus hominis, & leonis, secundùm proprias naturas sensitiuas, & hoc modo naturam eius participant, & animalia sunt formaliter. Ex hoc verò, resultat in eis denominatio specierũ subiicibilium: Accidentalis quidem, cùm sit eis tributa ab intellectu: & ideo vt sunt species subiicibiles: non sunt animalia, sed subiecta. Eadem ratione prædicabilia, secundùm proprias naturas, participant essentiam vniuersalis, quod est genus eorum: propria autem natura prædicabilium est esse, secundas intentiones, denominantes naturas vniuersales, vt primi prædicabilis, denominare naturam vniuersalem in multis speciebus: secundi prædicabilis, in multis differentibus numero in Quid, & sic de reliquis. Vnde hoc modo participant naturam vniuersalis, & essentialiter sunt vniuersalia: sed denominatio speciei subiicibilis, accidentaliter ea consequitur: & ideo secundùm eam, non possunt esse vniuersales, sicut neque homo, & leo, vt sunt species subiicibiles, sunt animalia.

To the first argument of the second opinion, the antecedent must be granted, that the universal is a genus to the five predicables, and also the first consequence, that they participate its nature; but it must be denied that they participate it as they are subjicible species. Rather, they participate it according to their proper essence; and from the participation there results in them accidentally the respect of subjicibility, according to which they are not universal but subjects of the genus. This is made clear by this example. Animal is the genus of man and of lion according to their proper sensitive natures, and in this way they participate its nature and are formally animals. But from this there results in them the denomination of subjicible species: an accidental one, indeed, since it is attributed to them by the intellect; and therefore, as they are subjicible species, they are not animals but subjects. By the same reasoning the predicables, according to their proper natures, participate the essence of the universal, which is their genus. But the proper nature of the predicables is to be second intentions denominating universal natures: that of the first predicable, to denominate a universal nature in many species; that of the second predicable, in many things differing in number, in quid; and so of the rest. Whence in this way they participate the nature of the universal, and are essentially universals; but the denomination of subjicible species follows on them accidentally; and therefore according to it they cannot be universal, just as neither are man and lion animals as they are subjicible species.

Ad secundùm, Concedendum est antecedens, nempe speciem

To the second, the antecedent must be granted, namely that

p. 123

, vt subiicibilem non esse singularem: sed neganda est consequentia, quòd sit vniuersalis: nam inter vniuersale, & singulare datur medium, quod est subiectum commune: id est natura abstracta communis negatiuè: quia nulli singulari appropriata est, neque illa respicit, sed solùm genus, ad quod comparatur, & sub quo collocatur: vt autem vniuersalis sit formaliter, necesse est indiuidua comparetur, & referatur.

species, as subjicible, is not singular; but the consequence must be denied, that it is universal: for between universal and singular there is a middle, which is the common subject, that is, the abstracted nature, common negatively, because it is appropriated to no singular, nor does it regard them, but only the genus to which it is compared and under which it is placed; whereas for it to be formally universal it is necessary that it be compared and referred to the individuals.

Ad cõfirmationem respondeo, Speciem subiicibilem, comparatam ad hanc, & illam speciem subiicibilem, non esse secundùm rem subiicibilem, sed solo nomine: quia non comparatur ad genus, nec illud respicit: verè autem prædicabilem, & vniuersalem, cùm sit vnum in multis, & de multis: quare non probatur, quòd, vt subiicibilis, secundùm rem sit vniuersalis.

To the confirmation I reply that subjicible species, compared to this and that subjicible species, is not subjicible in reality but in name only, because it is not compared to the genus nor does it regard it; but it is truly predicable and universal, since it is one in many and of many. Wherefore it is not proved that, as subjicible, it is in reality universal.

Ex dictis in hac quæstione, tria intelliguntur. Primum, Quòd ex duplici respectu prædicabilitatis, & subiicibilitatis, secundus conuenit primò speciei. Cuius ratio est, quia primum, quod habet species, est esse compositam ex genere & differentia: postquam verò composita ex eis est, participatur ab indiuiduis, ergo primò consequitur naturam eius respectu ad genus quàm ad indiuidua.

From what has been said in this question three things are understood. First, that of the twofold respect of predicability and subjicibility, the second belongs to species first. The reason for this is that the first thing species has is to be composed of genus and difference; and after it has been composed of them, it is participated by the individuals; therefore it follows on its nature with respect to the genus before it does with respect to the individuals.

Secundum, quod intelligitur, est, respectum prædicabilitatis nobiliorem in ea esse, respectu subiicibilitatis: & ideo nobiliorem denominationem speciei, ab eo consequitur. Quod sic probo. Prædicatum nobilius est subiecto, cùm sit forma eius; ergo respectus prędicabilis, nobilior est respectu subiicibilis. Intelligitur tandem tertiò, Speciem respectu subiicibilis, & prædicabilis, æquiuocum nomen esse. Probatur: quia respectus subiicibilitatis, & prædicabilitatis, sunt oppositi, & omnino diuersi, ita vt sub nomine speciei, in nullo conueniant: ergo solùm habent nomen commune, quod proprium est æquiuocorum.

The second thing understood is that the respect of predicability is nobler in it than the respect of subjicibility, and therefore a nobler denomination of species follows from it. I prove this thus. The predicate is nobler than the subject, since it is its form; therefore the respect of the predicable is nobler than the respect of the subjicible. Finally, it is understood third that species, with respect to the subjicible and the predicable, is an equivocal name. This is proved: because the respects of subjicibility and predicability are opposed and altogether diverse, so that under the name of species they agree in nothing; therefore they have only a common name, which is proper to equivocals.

QUESTION III

An species possit conseruari in vnico indiuiduo, & genus in vnica specie.

Whether a species can be preserved in a single individual, and a genus in a single species.

12 VT facilius intelligatur, atq; soluatur quæstio, annotandum est, Genus & speciẽ tribus modis cõsiderari posse. Primò, secundùm entitatem Physicam, & realem. Secundò, Logicè, in quãtũ Genus est prædicabile de multis differẽtibus specie in Quid: Species de pluribus differentibus numero. Tertiò, Metaphysicè, in quãtum genus, est totum potentiale,

12 That the question may be more easily understood and solved, it should be noted that genus and species can be considered in three ways. First, according to their physical and real entity. Second, logically, inasmuch as genus is predicable in quid of many things differing in species, and species of several things differing in number. Third, metaphysically, inasmuch as genus is a potential whole,

p. 124

contrahibile per oppositas differentias, aut pars speciei, eam componens cum differentia: & secundùm considerationem physicam certum est apud omnes genus posse conseruari in vna specie: imò in vno solo indiuiduo, atque etiam speciem: & huius ratio manifesta est: quia tota entitas generis, & speciei, vt animalis, & hominis, reperitur in quolibet indiuiduo, vt in Petro, aut Ioanne.

contractible by opposed differences, or a part of the species, composing it with the difference. And according to the physical consideration it is certain among all that the genus can be preserved in one species, indeed in one single individual, and the species as well; and the reason for this is manifest: because the whole entity of the genus and of the species, as of animal and of man, is found in any individual whatever, as in Peter or John.

Secundum Logicam etiam considerationem, est certum, Genus non conseruari in vna specie, nec speciem in vno indiuiduo. Probatur hoc, ex definitionibus vtriusque: nam genus est prædicabile de multis speciebus: & species de multis indiuiduis: ergo vtrumque postulat plura, ad sui conseruationem, in quo æqualia sunt. Sed an genus postulet plures species, actu existentes, & species plura indiuidua: vel sufficiat eis vnum actu, dummodo plura sint in potentia, ad sui conseruationem: De specie nemo dubitat, quin possit conseruari in vno indiuiduo, si plura sint possibilia. Probatur euidenti experientia, quia Sol, & Luna, sunt species Logicæ, & non habent nisi vnum indiuiduum actu existens, plura tamen possibilia: ergo hoc sufficiet ad conseruationem Logicæ speciei.

According to the logical consideration, too, it is certain that the genus is not preserved in one species, nor the species in one individual. This is proved from the definitions of each: for genus is predicable of many species, and species of many individuals; therefore each requires several for its preservation, in which they are equal. But whether the genus requires several actually existing species, and the species several individuals, or whether one in act suffices them for their preservation, provided there are several in potency: concerning species no one doubts that it can be preserved in one individual if several are possible. This is proved by evident experience: because the Sun and the Moon are logical species, and they have only one actually existing individual, yet several possible ones; therefore this will suffice for the preservation of a logical species.

13 De genere verò Logico, asserit Toletus, quæstione vnica huius capitis, Non posse conseruari in vna specie actu existente, quãuis plures sint possibiles: sed plures actu existentes postulare, ad sui conseruationem. Probat 1. testimonio Arist 4. lib. Topicorum, cap. 3. vbi ita ait, Dum autem omnis generis plures sint species, inspiciendum, si non contingit alteram speciem esse dicti generis: nam si non est, manifestum, quoniam non erit genus omnino. Deinde ratione, quia genus contrahitur ad speciem per differentiam: sed differentia non constituit speciem, nisi distinguendo illam ab aliis: ergo requirit genus plures species, actu existentes. Probatur consequentia: quia differentia non distinguit speciem ab aliis non existentibus, sed ab his tantùm quæ actu sunt.

13 But concerning the logical genus, Toledo asserts, in the single question of this chapter, that it cannot be preserved in one actually existing species, although several are possible, but requires several actually existing ones for its preservation. He proves it first by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 3, where he speaks thus: But since several species are to be placed under every genus, see whether it is not possible for there to be another species of the said genus: for if it is not manifest, then it will not be a genus at all. Then by reason: because the genus is contracted to the species by the difference; but the difference does not constitute the species except by distinguishing it from others; therefore the genus requires several actually existing species. The consequence is proved: because the difference does not distinguish the species from others that do not exist, but only from those that actually are.

Hęc tamẽ sententia falsa est. Quod probatur hoc argumento, Genus Logicum, est prædicabile de pluribus differentibus specie, etiam si actu non prædicetur, vt definitio eius ostendit, sed etiam si in vna tantùm sit specie actu existente: sufficit alias esse possibiles, vt sit prædicabile de pluribus: ergo conseruabitur in vna si plures sint possibiles, & non requirit plures actu existentes: sed quantùm ad considerationem Logicam, æqualis est ratio de genere, & specie: ita vt vtrumque postulet plura ad sui conseruationem, non actu existentia, sed vnum actu, & plura in potentia. Circa tertiam considerationem Metaphysicam, primò certum est apud omnes de genere, vt est totũ

This opinion, however, is false. This is proved by this argument. The logical genus is predicable of several things differing in species, even if it is not actually predicated, as its definition shows; but even if it is in only one actually existing species, it suffices that others be possible for it to be predicable of several; therefore it will be preserved in one if several are possible, and it does not require several actually existing. But as regards the logical consideration, the reasoning is equal concerning genus and species, so that each requires several for its preservation, not actually existing, but one in act and several in potency. Concerning the third, metaphysical, consideration, it is first certain among all concerning the genus, as it is a whole

p. 125

potentiale, quòd non possit conseruari in vnica specie: nisi aliæ sint possibiles. Et ratio est manifesta, quia vt est totum potentiale, essentialiter est contrahibile per oppositas differentias, ad constitutionem diuersarum specierum: ergo plures saltem possibiles postulat, ad sui conseruationem.

potential, that it cannot be preserved in a single species unless others are possible. And the reason is manifest: because as it is a potential whole it is essentially contractible by opposed differences for the constitution of diverse species; therefore it requires several, at least possible ones, for its preservation.

Secundò certum est, de eodem genere, vt est pars actualis speciei, quòd possit conseruari in vna specie, etiam si plures non sint possibiles. Probatur hoc: quia vt est pars actualis speciei, solùm petit vnam differentiam, cui actu cõiungitur: ergo solùm petit ad sui conseruationem vnam speciem, quam cum ea componit.

Second, it is certain concerning the same genus, as it is an actual part of the species, that it can be preserved in one species even if several are not possible. This is proved: because as it is an actual part of the species it requires only one difference, to which it is actually conjoined; therefore for its preservation it requires only one species, which it composes with it.

De specie verò Metaphysica, non est ita certum: An in vno indiuiduo conseruari possit, vel plura postulet saltem possibilia. Sed duæ sunt opiniones contrariæ. Primam tenet Oña, q. 2 huius capitis art. 2. affirmans Æqualia esse genus & speciem Metaphysicam: ita vt sicut genus postulat plures species, vnam actu, & aliam saltem in potentia: ita species non potest conseruari in vno indiuiduo, si non sint plura possibilia.

But concerning the metaphysical species it is not so certain whether it can be preserved in one individual, or requires several, at least possible ones. On this there are two contrary opinions. The first is held by Oña, q. 2 of this chapter, a. 2, who affirms that genus and metaphysical species are equal: so that, just as the genus requires several species, one in act and another at least in potency, so the species cannot be preserved in one individual if several are not possible.

14 Probat hoc argum. Ideo genus non potest conseruari in vna specie, quia est contrahibile per oppositas differentias specificas: hoc est tales, quæ non possunt esse in eadem specie, vt animal per rationale, & irrationale: sed etiam species est contrahibilis, per differentias indiuiduales oppositas: hoc est non potentes conuenire eidem indiuiduo: vt homo, per differentias Petri, & Ioannis: ergo sicut genus non potest conseruari in vna specie, sic species non poterit conseruari in vno indiuiduo. Sed hæc etiam sententia falsa probatur, hoc argumento. Species Metaphysica, secundùm essentiam, solùm dicit quid compositum ex genere, & differentia: & per solum genus, & differentiam definitur: sed in vno solo indiuiduo, etiamsi alia non sint possibilia, saluari potest compositio ex genere, & differentia: ergo etiam saluabitur, aut conseruabitur species Metaphysica. Probatur minor: quia differentiæ indiuiduales, extra genus, & differentiam sunt: ergo compositio speciei ex genere, & differentia, non dependet essentialiter ab illis. & ideo, non minùs in vno indiuiduo, quàm in multis conseruabitur: & ex consequenti species. Et confirmatur: quia probabile est, species Angelorum nec habere, nec posse habere, nisi vnicum indiuiduum: & tamen nullus negat, quòd sint veræ species, compositæ ex genere, & differentia.

14 He proves this by an argument. The genus cannot be preserved in one species for this reason, that it is contractible by opposed specific differences, that is, such as cannot be in the same species, as animal by rational and irrational; but the species too is contractible by opposed individual differences, that is, ones not able to belong to the same individual, as man by the differences of Peter and of John; therefore, just as the genus cannot be preserved in one species, so the species will not be able to be preserved in one individual. But this opinion too is proved false by this argument. The metaphysical species, according to its essence, signifies only something composed of genus and difference, and is defined by genus and difference alone; but in one single individual, even if others are not possible, the composition of genus and difference can be saved; therefore the metaphysical species too will be saved, or preserved. The minor is proved: because the individual differences are outside the genus and the difference; therefore the composition of the species from genus and difference does not depend essentially on them; and therefore it will be preserved no less in one individual than in many, and consequently the species too. And this is confirmed: because it is probable that the species of the angels neither have nor can have more than a single individual; and yet no one denies that they are true species, composed of genus and difference.

Nostra igitur sententia duo asserit. Primum, quòd genus, & species secundùm Logicam considerationem æqualia sunt, ita vt nec genus possit conseruari in vna specie, nisi alia saltem

Our view, then, asserts two things. First, that genus and species according to the logical consideration are equal, so that neither can the genus be preserved in one species unless others at least

p. 126

sit possibilis, nec species in vno indiuiduo, nisi alterum saltem sit possibile: neutrum tamen postulare plura actu existentia ad sui conseruationem.

are possible, nor the species in one individual unless at least another is possible; yet that neither requires several actually existing ones for its preservation.

Secundum quod asserit, est, Genus, & speciem secundùm considerationem Metaphysicam, non esse æqualia, sed genus vt est totum potentiale, non posse conseruari in vna specie, nisi altera saltem sit possibilis: quamuis vt est pars speciei, in vna conseruari possit: speciem verò conseruari posse in vno indiuiduo, etiam si aliud non sit possibile. Vtrumque autem probatum est iam, ex refutatione aliarum opinionum.

The second thing it asserts is that genus and species according to the metaphysical consideration are not equal; but that the genus, as it is a potential whole, cannot be preserved in one species unless at least another is possible, although as it is a part of the species it can be preserved in one; whereas the species can be preserved in one individual even if no other is possible. Both of these have already been proved from the refutation of the other opinions.

15 Sed vt veritas secundi magis fiat manifesta, & argumentum oppositum faciliùs soluatur, annotandum est: hanc esse differentiam inter genus & speciem, Metaphysicè considerata: quòd genus est totum potentiale, & imperfectum essentialiter, perfectibile tamen per differentias specificas, tanquam per alios gradus perfectionis, essentialiter distinctos. Vt animal, dicit naturam sensitiuam, essentialiter imperfectam, perfectibilem verò per rationale, & irrationale, tanquam per diuersos gradus essentialis perfectionis. Vnde sequitur primò, Genus essentialiter esse contrahibile, per oppositas differentias, ad constitutionem diuersarum specierum. Secies verò, totum actuale, & perfectum est, ita vt nõ possit vlteriorem perfectionem essentialem suscipere, (loquimur autem de specie infima, quæ ita est species, vt non sit genus:) quare non est contrahibilis per differentias essentiales, quę sint gradus essentialis perfectionis: sed solùm multiplicatur in indiuiduis, per differentias indiuiduales: quæ non sunt essentiales, sed omnino extra essentiam eius: accidentales enim sunt, vel ad summum modi quidam substantiales. Secundò, sequitur, Speciem non esse essentialiter contrahibilem per differentias indiuiduales, sed sine tali contractione esse perfectam, & completam essentialiter: & ideo siue per plures determinetur ad plura indiuidua: vel per vnam tantùm ad vnum: & siue aliæ sint possibiles, vel non, perfecta erit atque completa species, essentialiter in vno, non minùs quam in multis: & ideo in solo illo conseruabitur: quia determinatio per tales differentias, non est ei essentialis: sed vel accidentalis, vel modalis, & omnino extra essentiam.

15 But that the truth of the second may become more manifest, and the opposing argument be more easily solved, it should be noted that there is this difference between genus and species considered metaphysically: that the genus is a potential whole, and essentially imperfect, yet perfectible by the specific differences as by other grades of perfection, essentially distinct. As animal signifies a sensitive nature, essentially imperfect, but perfectible by rational and irrational as by diverse grades of essential perfection. Whence it follows, first, that the genus is essentially contractible by opposed differences for the constitution of diverse species. But the species is an actual and perfect whole, so that it cannot receive a further essential perfection (we are speaking of the lowest species, which is a species in such a way that it is not a genus); wherefore it is not contractible by essential differences which are grades of essential perfection, but is only multiplied in individuals by individual differences, which are not essential but altogether outside its essence: for they are accidental, or at most certain substantial modes. It follows, second, that the species is not essentially contractible by individual differences, but without such contraction is essentially perfect and complete; and therefore, whether it is determined by several to several individuals or by one only to one, and whether others are possible or not, it will be a species essentially perfect and complete in one no less than in many; and therefore it will be preserved in that one alone, because determination by such differences is not essential to it, but either accidental or modal, and altogether outside the essence.

16 Ad testimonium Arist. quod adduxit Toletus, respondeo, sensum Aristotelis esse, quòd genus Logicum non possit conseruari, nisi cognoscatur ab intellectu, in ordine ad plures species: quia nõ nisi per cõparationem ad plures fit ab intellectu: nec aliud esse habet, quàm ab eo cognosci: non tamen requirit

16 To the testimony of Aristotle which Toledo adduced, I reply that the sense of Aristotle is that the logical genus cannot be preserved unless it is cognized by the intellect in order to several species, because it is made by the intellect only through comparison to several, nor has it any other being than to be cognized by it; yet it does not require

p. 127

plures existentes, à parte rei, sed in vna conseruantur, si aliæ sint possibiles.

several existing on the part of the thing, but it is preserved in one, if others are possible.

1. Ad argum. eiusdem opinionis respondetur. Differentiam constituere speciem, & distinguere eam ab aliis, existentibus quidem, aut possibilibus: nam cùm distinctio specifica per differentias, sit essentialis; necessariò dependet ab actuali existentia specierum. Quod probatur euidenter, quia diuersæ species florum, nõ minùs distinguuntur specie in hyeme, quãdo actu non existunt, quàm dum actu sunt: Bene ergo potest differentia constituere speciem, & distinguere eam ab aliis, etiam actu non existentibus, sed solùm possibilibus.

To the argument of the same opinion the reply is that the difference constitutes the species and distinguishes it from others, whether existing or possible: for since specific distinction through differences is essential, it does not necessarily depend on the actual existence of the species. This is proved evidently: because the diverse species of flowers are no less distinguished in species in winter, when they do not actually exist, than while they actually are. The difference, then, can well constitute the species and distinguish it from others, even ones not actually existing but only possible.

Ad argumentum secundæ opinionis, quod de specie Metaphysica procedebat, ex annotata doctrina responsum est: Quę sic est applicanda ad formam eius; vt dum dicitur genus non posse conseruari in vna specie, quia est contrahibile per differentias oppositas: concedendum sit antecedẽs: sed minor distinguenda: nam species non essentialiter contrahibilis per differentias indiuiduales, sicut genus per specificas: sed determinatio ad indiuidua extra essentiam eius est: & ideo non minùs in vno, quàm in multis potest conseruari essentialiter.

To the argument of the second opinion, which proceeded concerning the metaphysical species, the reply has been given from the doctrine noted above. It is to be applied to its form thus: when it is said that the genus cannot be preserved in one species because it is contractible by opposed differences, the antecedent must be granted; but the minor must be distinguished: for the species is not essentially contractible by individual differences, as the genus is by specific ones; rather, the determination to individuals is outside its essence; and therefore it can be essentially preserved no less in one than in many.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Quæst. 4. Vtrum definitio postrema speciei illis speciebus conueniat, quæ vnum tantum indiuiduum habere possunt — Whether the last definition of species belongs to those species which can have only one individual.

Vtrùm diffinitio postrema speciei, illis speciebus conueniat, quæ vnum tantùm indiuiduum habere possunt.

[…]

17 NVlla reperitur natura specifica, de qua certum sit nõ posse habere plura indiuidua: sed de Angelis, & corporibus cœlestibus, plures opinantur ita se habere, vt quęlibet species, nec habeat, nec habere vllo modo possit plura: sed omnes Angelos specie distinctos esse, & non posse distingui solo numero, sicut Petrum & Ioannem. Quęstio igitur hęc conditionalis est, & non absoluta, & sensus eius est: An supposito quòd aliquę sint species, quibus repugnet habere plura indiuidua, eis conueniat vltima definitio Porphyrii, quòd sint prædicabiles de pluribus differentibus specie in quid.

17 No specific nature is found of which it is certain that it cannot have several individuals; but concerning the angels and the heavenly bodies many are of the opinion that they are so constituted that each species neither has nor can in any way have several, but that all the angels are distinct in species and cannot be distinguished in number alone, as Peter and John. This question, then, is conditional and not absolute, and its sense is: Whether, supposing that there are some species to which it is repugnant to have several individuals, the last definition of Porphyry belongs to them, namely that they are predicable in quid of several things differing in number.

Sed priusquam probabiles opiniones circa eam proponamus, refutandũ est illud, quod sine fundamento rationis quidam asserunt: nempe his speciebus conuenire definitionẽ Porphirii, per non repugnantiam. Quod ita declarant, vt quamuis non conueniat eis, prædicabiles esse de pluribus, in quantùm tales species sunt, non multiplicabiles per plura indiuidua, tamen si considerentur sub communi ratione speciei, non repugnat eis, de multis prædicari: quia species, vt species,

But before we propose the probable opinions concerning it, we must refute what certain people assert without any foundation in reason: namely, that Porphyry’s definition belongs to these species by non-repugnance. They explain this thus: although it does not belong to them to be predicable of several inasmuch as they are such species, not multipliable through several individuals, yet if they are considered under the common ratio of species, it is not repugnant to them to be predicated of many: because species, as species,

p. 128

prædicabilis est de multis. Quod apertè falsum esse probatur. Primò, quia definitiones debent conuenire rebus positiuè, cùm naturam positiuam earum explicent: sed non repugnantia solùm est quædam negatio: ergo non sufficit, vt definitio eis conueniat. Secundò, quia, si talis non repugnantia sufficeret, vt dicatur his speciebus conuenire, sequitur etiam conuenire cuilibet indiuiduo, vt Petro, aut Ioanni. Probatur consequentia: quia licèt ei repugnet prædicari de multis, in quantum est res singularis, tamen si consideretur sub ratione communi hominis, non repugnabit: cùm homo sit prædicabilis de multis: ideo quodlibet indiuiduum erit species prædicabilis, quod absurdum est.

is predicable of many. That this is false is openly proved. First, because definitions ought to belong to things positively, since they explain their positive nature; but non-repugnance is only a certain negation; therefore it does not suffice for the definition to belong to them. Second, because if such non-repugnance sufficed for it to be said to belong to these species, it follows that it also belongs to any individual whatever, as to Peter or John. The consequence is proved: because although it is repugnant to him to be predicated of many inasmuch as he is a singular thing, yet if he is considered under the common ratio of man, it will not be repugnant, since man is predicable of many; therefore any individual whatever will be a predicable species, which is absurd.

18 Hoc igitur refutato: Prima opinio est Caietani, 1. par. q. 13. art. 9. in opusc. de ente, & essentia, cap. 5 & cap. præsenti, dubio 3. circa vltimam definitionem speciei, asserentis his speciebus verè conuenire. Quod vt declaret, distinguit duplicem potentiam in natura ad plura indiuidua, Physicam, & Logicam: Potentiam Physicam vocat realem, quam habet è parte rei, in quantum ex suis principiis potest multiplicari in pluribus indiuiduis, vt natura humana: Logicam verò, quam non habet, nisi vt à nobis intelligitur: & quia nos intelligimus naturas spirituales Angelorum, per similitudinem specierum, materialium, habentium plura indiuidua, & eas abstrahimus ab illo vno indiuiduo, quod habent, sicut naturas materiales à multis, vt hominem à Petro, & Ioanne: hinc est, quòd non minùs illis attribuamus denominationem prędicabilis de pluribus indiuiduis, quàm his, quæ plura habent indiuidua.

18 This, then, being refuted: the first opinion is Cajetan’s, 1 p., q. 13, a. 9, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 5, and on the present chapter, doubt 3, concerning the last definition of species, who asserts that it truly belongs to these species. To explain this, he distinguishes a twofold potency in a nature toward several individuals, physical and logical. He calls physical potency the real one, which it has on the part of the thing, inasmuch as from its own principles it can be multiplied in several individuals, as human nature; but logical the one which it has only as it is understood by us. And because we understand the spiritual natures of the angels through the likeness of material species having several individuals, and we abstract them from that one individual which they have, as we abstract material natures from many, as man from Peter and John, hence it is that we attribute to them the denomination of predicable of several individuals no less than to those which have several individuals.

Probatur hæc sententia sic explicata, authoritate Aristotelis, qui in cap. de substantia duo asserit. Primum, secundas substantias esse genera, & species, vt homo, & animal: primas verò, indiuidua, vt Petrus, & Ioannes. Secundum, easdem secundas substantias esse prædicabiles de primis: sed naturæ Angelorum sunt genera, & species: vt spiritus est genus, Michael, & Gabriel sunt species: ergo sunt secundæ substantiæ, & consequenter erunt prædicabiles de pluribus.

This opinion, so explained, is proved by the authority of Aristotle, who in the chapter on substance asserts two things. First, that second substances are genera and species, as man and animal, but first substances individuals, as Peter and John. Second, that these same second substances are predicable of the first. But the natures of the angels are genera and species: as spirit is a genus, Michael and Gabriel are species; therefore they are second substances, and consequently they will be predicable of several.

Probatur etiam ratione: quia si species Michaelis non potest habere nisi illud vnicum indiuiduum Michaelis, sequitur differentiam specificam eius, & indiuidualem, eandem esse secundùm rem, ratione tamẽ distinctam: vt specifica est à se ipsa, vt est indiuidualis: quia vt specifica, componit speciem simul cum genere, vt indiuidualis verò, determinat speciẽ iam compositam ad tale indiuiduum. Quo supposito, poterit intellectus considerare naturam Michaelis, vt compositam ex genere

It is proved also by reason: because if the species of Michael cannot have more than that single individual of Michael, it follows that its specific and its individual difference are the same in reality, yet distinct in reason: as specific, it is distinct from itself as individual; because as specific it composes the species together with the genus, but as individual it determines the species already composed to such an individual. This supposed, the intellect will be able to consider the nature of Michael as composed of genus and difference

p. 129

& differentia, vt specificam, non considerata eadem differentia, vt indiuiduali: & hoc erit abstrahere naturam ab illo vno indiuiduo. Sic autem abstracta, prædicari poterit de illo, non prędicatione identica: qua ratione formali distinguitur ab indiuiduo: nec prædicatione æquali, quia indiuiduum inferius est respectu speciei: ergo prædicatione superioris de inferiori: sed prædicatio superioris est prædicatio vniuersalis: ergo prædicabitur prædicatione vniuersali de singulari: eritque verò prædicabilis de multis, cui conueniat definitio speciei. Probatur consequentia: quia vniuersale, & prædicabile conuertuntur. Hanc sententiam sequuntur Canterus in 2. parte huius cap. dub 2. & Mercatus q. vnica, arg. 2.

as specific, without considering the same difference as individual; and this will be to abstract the nature from that one individual. And so abstracted it will be able to be predicated of it, not by an identical predication, by which it is distinguished from the individual by a formal ratio, nor by an equal predication, because the individual is inferior with respect to the species; therefore by the predication of a superior of an inferior. But the predication of a superior is a universal predication; therefore it will be predicated by a universal predication of the singular, and it will be truly predicable of many, so that the definition of species belongs to it. The consequence is proved: because the universal and the predicable are convertible. This opinion is followed by Canterus, on part 2 of this chapter, doubt 2, and Mercado, single question, arg. 2.

19 Secunda opinio est multorum modernorum, quòd his speciebus non conueniat vllo modo definitio Porphyrij. Et videtur mihi probabilior, & tenenda.

19 The second opinion is that of many moderns: that Porphyry’s definition in no way belongs to these species. And it seems to me more probable and to be held.

Sed vt eam efficaciter probemus, vnum est notandum, nempe, ita nos intelligere Deum, & Angelos, per species, aut similitudines rerum materialium, vt ex eis non formemus conceptus eis repugnantes, sed proprios: hoc est, qui eis solis conueniant, & cum eis conuertantur. Gratia exempli, per similitudinem rei corporeæ, intelligimus Deum, imperfectionem ab eo auferentes: & ideo concipientes de illo, quòd corpore careat, & purus spiritus sit: & per naturam compositam ex genere, & differentia, auferentes ab eo imperfectionem compositionis, intelligimus esse simplicissimum. Et eodem modo intelligimus angelicam naturam, per species rerum corporearum, proprium conceptum de ea formantes: nempe, quòd incorporea sit, & spiritualis: & per species naturarum materialium, quæ in pluribus indiuiduis multiplicantur, intelligimus Angelos non posse multiplicari, secundùm probabilem sententiam multorum. Et hæc doctrina vera est: Quia si non formaremus proprios, & veros conceptus de rebus spiritualibus, quamuis imperfectos, & per alienas species rerum corporearum, nec verè eas intelligeremus: quin multa eis attribueremus falsa, & naturæ earum repugnantia.

But in order to prove it efficaciously, one thing should be noted: namely, that we understand God and the angels through the species or likenesses of material things in such a way that from them we do not form concepts repugnant to them, but proper ones, that is, ones that belong to them alone and are convertible with them. For example, through the likeness of a bodily thing we understand God by removing imperfection from him, and therefore conceiving of him that he lacks a body and is pure spirit; and through a nature composed of genus and difference, removing from him the imperfection of composition, we understand that he is most simple. And in the same way we understand the angelic nature through the species of bodily things, forming a proper concept of it: namely, that it is incorporeal and spiritual; and through the species of material natures, which are multiplied in several individuals, we understand that the angels cannot be multiplied, according to the probable opinion of many. And this doctrine is true: because if we did not form proper and true concepts of spiritual things, although imperfect and through the alien species of bodily things, we would not truly understand them; indeed we would attribute to them many things false and repugnant to their nature.

20 Ex eadẽ igitur doctrina, probatur primò nostra sententia, contra Caiet. Quia licèt intelligamus naturas spirituales per species corporũ, non tamen iis attribuimus proprietates corporũ eis repugnantes, sed potiùs eas remouentes ab illis, intelligimus incorporeas esse. ergo supposito, quòd intelligamus nõ posse habere plura indiuidua, sicut habẽt corporeę naturæ, per quarũ species eas intelligimus: impossibile est, quòd eis tribuat intellectus denominationes vniuersaliũ, aut prędicabiliũ,

20 From this same doctrine, then, our view is proved first against Cajetan. Because although we understand spiritual natures through the species of bodies, yet we do not attribute to them the properties of bodies that are repugnant to them; rather, removing these from them, we understand that they are incorporeal. Therefore, supposing that we understand that they cannot have several individuals, as the bodily natures through whose species we understand them have, it is impossible that the intellect should attribute to them the denominations of universals or predicables, I

p. 130

Et in hoc decipitur primò Caiet. quia putat ex eò, quòd per species rerum materialium à nobis intelliguntur, denominari ab intellectu vniuersales, & prædicabiles de pluribus: quod nõ est verum, sicut nec verum est, quòd intelligamus esse corporeas. Secundò, decipitur in sua illa diuisione potentiæ Physicæ & Logicæ: nam potentia Logica, fundamentum saltem remotum habere debet in natura, etiam vt à nobis intelligitur, vt vera sit, & non ficta: sed nullum habet fundamentum in natura angelica, etiam vt à nobis intelligitur, multiplicatio indiuiduorum, cùm potius intelligamus ei repugnare: ergo nec habet potentiam Physicam, nec Logicam, secundùm quam possit denominari prædicabilis de multis.

And in this Cajetan is deceived, first, because he thinks that from the fact that they are understood by us through the species of material things, they are denominated by the intellect universal and predicable of several; which is not true, just as it is not true that we understand them to be bodily. Second, he is deceived in that division of his into physical and logical potency: for logical potency, in order to be true and not fictitious, must have at least a remote foundation in the nature, even as it is understood by us; but the multiplication of individuals has no foundation in the angelic nature, even as it is understood by us, since rather we understand it to be repugnant to it; therefore it has neither a physical nor a logical potency according to which it could be denominated predicable of many.

Secundò probatur: Quia Deum intelligimus per species rerum materialium, sicut Angelos: ergo si angelica natura vniuersalis est, vt sic à nobis abstracta, & intellecta, Deus etiam erit vniuersalis, & prædicabilis de multis: quod patet esse falsum. Et si respondeas, adhuc esse diuersam rationem de Deo, & Angelis: quia species angelica componitur ex genere & differentia: & ideo potest ei attribui intentio vniuersalitatis, Deo verò non potest attribui: quia caret tali compositione. Solutio hæc nihil valet: quia speciei non attribuitur denominatio vniuersalis, aut prædicabilis, ex eo, quòd componatur ex genere, & differentia: sed quia comparatur ad plura indiuidua. Probatur hoc in speciebus subalternis, quæ licèt componantur ex genere, & differentia, non sunt species prædicabiles, sed tantùm subiicibiles: ergo licèt species angelica componatur ex genere, & differentia, non ideò capax est denominationis vniuersalis, aut prædicabilis, sed repugnat ei, sicut multiplicitas indiuiduorum.

It is proved second: because we understand God through the species of material things, just as we do the angels; therefore, if the angelic nature is universal as so abstracted and understood by us, God too will be universal and predicable of many, which is plainly false. And if you reply that the reasoning is still different concerning God and the angels, because the angelic species is composed of genus and difference, and therefore the intention of universality can be attributed to it, whereas it cannot be attributed to God, because he lacks such composition: this solution is worth nothing, because the denomination of universal or predicable is not attributed to the species from the fact that it is composed of genus and difference, but because it is compared to several individuals. This is proved in the subalternate species, which, although they are composed of genus and difference, are not predicable species but only subjicible; therefore, although the angelic species is composed of genus and difference, it is not on that account capable of the denomination of universal or predicable; rather, that is repugnant to it, as is the multiplicity of individuals.

21 Ex quibus sequitur: Nõ omnem speciem subiicibilem esse prædicabilem (etiã si infima sit) sed posse esse subiicibilẽ, & nõ prædicabilem Quod euidens est in speciebus subalternis, quæ non sunt prædicabiles, sed subiicibiles tãtùm: in infimis quoq; verũ erit, si repugnet illis pluralitas indiuiduorũ. Et ratio eius est: quia ad speciẽ subiicibilẽ satis est quòd cõponatur ex genere & differentia: ad prædicabilẽ verò de multis, requiritur necessariò multitudo indiuiduorũ, actu existentiũ, aut possibiliũ.

21 From which it follows that not every subjicible species is predicable (even if it is lowest), but that it can be subjicible and not predicable. This is evident in the subalternate species, which are not predicable but only subjicible; and in the lowest too it will be true, if plurality of individuals is repugnant to them. And the reason for it is that for a subjicible species it is enough that it be composed of genus and difference, but for one predicable of many there is necessarily required a multitude of individuals, actually existing or possible.

Ad testimonium Arist. pro sententia Caietani adductum, respondent aliqui, negando, quòd naturæ Angelorum sint secundæ substantiæ: sed hoc cõtrarium est verbis eiusdem Arist. quod ita probo: Quia Aristoteles asserit expressè, Genera & species, esse secundas substantias: sed naturæ Angelorũ sunt species cõpositæ ex genere, & differentia: ergo sunt secundæ substantiæ

To the testimony of Aristotle adduced for Cajetan’s opinion, some reply by denying that the natures of the angels are second substances; but this is contrary to the words of the same Aristotle, which I prove thus: because Aristotle asserts expressly that genera and species are second substances; but the natures of the angels are species composed of genus and difference; therefore they are second substances

p. 131

. Continent etiam prædicata superiora, & spiritualia accidentia sustentant: & ideò dicuntur eis substare, non minùs quàm species materiales: nec solùm prout singulares sunt, aut primæ substantiæ, sed etiam, vt sunt species: ergo negari non potest in doctrina Arist. quòd sint secundæ substantiæ.

They also contain the superior predicates and sustain spiritual accidents, and therefore they are said to stand under them, no less than the material species; and not only as they are singular, or first substances, but also as they are species; therefore it cannot be denied in Aristotle’s doctrine that they are second substances.

Concedendum est ergo, quòd tales species sint secundæ substantię: negandum verò, quòd eis non conueniat vniuersalis proprietas, assignata ab Aristotele, nempè, quòd de primis prædicentur: nam hæc proprietas singulis speciebus applicanda est, iuxta earum naturam, ità vt si plures habuerint primas substantias, de omnibus prædicentur, si vnam tantùm, solùm de illa: quod satis est ad veritatem vniuersalis locutionis, videlicet, proprium est secundis substantiis prædicari de primis.

It must be granted, then, that such species are second substances; but it must be denied that the universal property assigned by Aristotle does not belong to them, namely that they are predicated of the first: for this property is to be applied to the single species according to their nature, so that if they have several first substances they are predicated of all of them, and if only one, then of that one alone; which is enough for the truth of the universal statement, namely: It is proper to second substances to be predicated of the first.

22 Ad 1 arg. concedendum est, quamlibet harum specierum abstrahi posse, à suo indiuiduo, negandum tamen, quòd sic abstractæ, possit ei attribui relatio rationis, per quam sit prædicabilis de multis, nam idemmet intellectus eam abstrahens, præsupponit ei repugnare plura indiuidua. Nec sequitur, Quòd intellectus eam abstrahat per species rerum materialium, quibus abstrahit alias naturas, plura indiuidua habentes, ergo sicut has denominat vniuersalis, sic illas. Nam ex eo, quòd per tales species rerum materialium eas intelligit, non format eundem conceptum earum, ac materialium rerum, sed diuersum, iuxta naturam cuiuscunque: ita vt has intelligat esse multiplicabiles in pluribus indiuiduis, illas verò ad vnicum esse determinatas. De quo concedimus, prædicari posse, non prædicatione identica, nec prædicatione superioris, sed æqualis, ad modum, quo differentia vltima prædicatur de sua specie. Et ratio huius est: quia supposito, quòd natura Michaelis non potest habere plura indiuidua, solùm dicit ordinem ad vnam differentiam indiuidualem, etiam si ab illa abstrahatur: ideo non magis coarctatur per illam: sed quomodocunque accipiatur, cum ea conuertitur. Talis autem prædicatio, eiusdem speciei de suo indiuiduo, licèt similis sit prædicationi vltimæ, differentiæ, de sua specie, ratione æqualitatis, sed prædicatur in Quid, tanquam totum actuale, & completum, ad secundum prædicabile potiùs reducenda est. Species igitur, quibus repugnat pluralitas indiuiduorum subiicibiles tantùm sunt: quibus conueniunt duæ definitiones assignatæ à Porphyrio: nam species Michaelis, subiicitur suo generi proximo, quod est spiritus, & etiam remoto, quod est substantia corporea aut spiritualis: sed non sunt species prædicabiles: ideò non conuenit eis vltima definitio.

22 To the argument, it must be granted that any one of these species can be abstracted from its individual; but it must be denied that, so abstracted, a relation of reason can be attributed to it through which it would be predicable of many: for the very intellect that abstracts it presupposes that several individuals are repugnant to it. Nor does it follow: The intellect abstracts it through the species of material things by which it abstracts other natures having several individuals; therefore, just as it denominates those universal, so too these. For from the fact that it understands them through such species of material things, it does not form the same concept of them as of material things, but a different one, according to the nature of each: so that it understands the former to be multipliable in several individuals, but the latter to be determined to a single one. Of which we grant that it can be predicated, not by an identical predication, nor by the predication of a superior, but by an equal one, in the way in which the last difference is predicated of its species. And the reason for this is that, supposing that the nature of Michael cannot have several individuals, it signifies an order only to one individual difference, even if it is abstracted from it; and therefore it is not further narrowed by it, but in whatever way it is taken it is convertible with it. Such a predication, however, of the same species of its individual, although it is similar to the predication of the last difference of its species by reason of equality, yet, because it is predicated in quid as an actual and complete whole, is rather to be reduced to the second predicable. The species, then, to which plurality of individuals is repugnant are only subjicible; and to them belong the two definitions assigned by Porphyry: for the species of Michael is subjected to its proximate genus, which is spirit, and also to its remote one, which is substance, corporeal or spiritual; but they are not predicable species; therefore the last definition does not belong to them. I ij

p. 132

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

An species distinguatur à genere, per illas particulis suæ definitionis, prædicari de pluribus differentibus numero.

Whether species is distinguished from genus by those particles of its definition, “to be predicated of several things differing in number.” 23

23 Quæstio hæc occasionem sumpsit ex Porphyrio: qui ca. de genere docuit, Speciem distingui à genere: quia genus de pluribus differentibus specie prædicatur, species verò de pluribus differentibus numero. Sed in pręsenti capite, & etiam in vltimo huius libri concedit, Genus etiam de pluribus differentibus numero prædicari: quia cùm sit prædicatum superius respectu speciei, vt animal respectu hominis, necesse est prædicari, de quibuscunque prædicatur species. Quare non videtur excludi posse à definitione vltima speciei, per illas particulas, prædicari de pluribus differentibus numero: nec est alia per quam excludatur. Et ideo non erit bona definitio, quia non distinguit secundum prædicabile à primo.

This question took its occasion from Porphyry, who in the chapter on genus taught that species is distinguished from genus, because genus is predicated of several things differing in species, but species of several things differing in number. But in the present chapter, and also in the last of this book, he grants that genus too is predicated of several things differing in number: because, since it is a superior predicate with respect to the species, as animal with respect to man, it must be predicated of whatever things the species is predicated of. Wherefore it does not seem that it can be excluded from the last definition of species by those particles, to be predicated of several things differing in number; nor is there any other by which it is excluded. And therefore it will not be a good definition, because it does not distinguish the second predicable from the first.

Est igitur prima opinio Alberti Magni tractatu de prædicabilibus cap. 1. asserentis, speciem distingui à genere per illas particulas (prædicari de pluribus differentibus numero) quia in hoc sensu intelliguntur à Porphyrio, vt species per seipsam, & immediatè prędicetur de indiuiduis: genus verò non per seipsum, aut immediatè: sed mediante specie. Et ratio huius sententiæ est, quia species per se componitur ex genere, & differentia: & ideo per seipsam participat naturam generis: indiuidua verò non componuntur per se ex genere & differentia, sed solùm participant naturam generis: quia participant naturam speciei, in qua continentur: ideo enim Petrus est animal, quia est indiuiduum speciei humanæ, compositæ ex natura sensitiua, & rationali.

The first opinion, then, is that of Albert the Great, in the treatise on the Predicables, ch. 1, who asserts that species is distinguished from genus by those particles (to be predicated of several things differing in number), because they are understood by Porphyry in this sense: that species is predicated of the individuals through itself and immediately, but genus not through itself or immediately, but by means of the species. And the reason for this opinion is that species is per se composed of genus and difference, and therefore through itself participates the nature of the genus; but the individuals are not per se composed of genus and difference, but only participate the nature of the genus because they participate the nature of the species in which they are contained: for Peter is an animal for this reason, that he is an individual of the human species, composed of sensitive and rational nature.

Hæc expositio probatur falsa duobus argumẽtis. Primò, Genus prędicatur per seipsum, aut immediatè de indiuiduis: ergo per hoc nõ distinguitur ab eo species. Probatur antecedens: in his prædicationibus, hoc animal est animal, hoc viuens est viuens, quę verè sunt immediatæ, & non solo nomine: nam prædicatum significat naturam sensitiuam in communi, & subiectum eandem naturam singularizatam: sed inter naturam in communi sumptam, & in singulari, nullum potest esse medium, ergo immediatè prædicatur genus de indiuiduis.

This exposition is proved false by two arguments. First: Genus is predicated of the individuals through itself, or immediately; therefore species is not distinguished from it by this. The antecedent is proved: in these predications, This animal is an animal, This living thing is a living thing, which are truly immediate, and not in name only: for the predicate signifies the sensitive nature in common, and the subject the same nature singularized; but between the nature taken in common and in the singular there can be no middle; therefore the genus is predicated immediately of the individuals.

24 Secundò, Quia indiuidua duobus modis cõsiderari possunt. Primò, vt sunt à parte rei: & sic nullum est, quon non contineatur sub aliqua specie: & ea mediante participet naturam genericam: & ideo vocantur indiuidua speciei, vt Petrus

24 Second, because individuals can be considered in two ways. First, as they are on the part of the thing; and thus there is none that is not contained under some species and by means of it participates the generic nature; and therefore they are called individuals of a species, as Peter

p. 133

, & Ioannes, sub his nominibus. Alio modo, in quantùm concipiuntur ab intellectu, sub gradu naturæ superioris, non considerato gradu specifico: quem reuera participant, vt si Petrus consideretur sub gradu naturæ sensitiuæ, non considerato gradu rationali, quem participat ab specie humana, in qua acceptione significatur nomine huius animalis. Et indiuidua hoc modo considerata, vocantur generica: quia formaliter, & immediatè significant, & participant naturam genericam. Vnde sequitur, quòd licèt de indiuiduis specificis prædicetur genus media specie, de genericis tamen per seipsum & immediatè prædicatur: quare dum prædicatur de indiuiduis, hoc modo consideratis, non distinguetur ab specie.

and John, under these names. In another way, inasmuch as they are conceived by the intellect under the grade of the superior nature, without considering the specific grade which they really participate: as if Peter is considered under the grade of sensitive nature, without considering the rational grade which he participates from the human species; in which acceptation he is signified by the name this animal. And individuals considered in this way are called generic, because they formally and immediately signify and participate the generic nature. Whence it follows that, although the genus is predicated of the specific individuals by means of the species, yet of the generic ones it is predicated through itself and immediately; wherefore, when it is predicated of individuals considered in this way, it will not be distinguished from the species.

Ideo secunda opinio Auicenę, concedens genus per seipsam, & immediatè prædicari de indiuiduis asserit, illa verba definitionis, (quod prædicatur de pluribus differentibus numero) cum duplici limitatione intelligenda esse, vt per ea distinguatur species à genere: nempe de his, quæ solo numero distincta sunt: & de his tantùm, & non de aliis, quæ plusquam numero distinguuntur. Vnde cùm genus non de indiuiduis tantùm, sed etiam de speciebus prædicetur, excluditur per illa verba, sic exposita, à definitione speciei.

Therefore the second opinion, that of Avicenna, granting that genus is predicated through itself and immediately of the individuals, asserts that those words of the definition (which is predicated of several things differing in number) are to be understood with a twofold limitation, so that by them species may be distinguished from genus: namely, of those which are distinct in number alone, and of those only, and not of others which are distinguished by more than number. Whence, since genus is predicated not of individuals only but also of species, it is excluded from the definition of species by those words so expounded.

Sed hæc etiam sententia insufficiens est. Probatur primò: quia sicut definitio debet conuenire definito positiuè, & non tantùm per negationem, sic etiam debet illud distinguere ab aliis, per differentiam positiuam: & non per solã negationem: quia sola negatio non potest esse differentia distinguens species: sed prædicari de indiuiduis, & non de aliis magis diuersis, est pura negatio: ergo non potest distinguere secundum prædicabile à primo.

But this opinion too is insufficient. This is proved first: because, just as a definition must belong to the thing defined positively, and not only through negation, so too it must distinguish it from others by a positive difference, and not by negation alone; because negation alone cannot be a difference distinguishing species; but to be predicated of individuals, and not of others more diverse, is a pure negation; therefore it cannot distinguish the second predicable from the first.

25 Secundò, Si semel concedatur genus immediatè prędicari de indiuiduis, sicut speciem, etiam si de speciebus prædicetur: non sequitur non esse speciem: sed non esse solùm speciem, sed etiam genus, cùm definitio vtriusque ei conueniat: ergo non distinguitur ab specie per illas particulas.

25 Second: if it is once granted that genus is predicated immediately of individuals, as species is, even if it is predicated of species, it does not follow that it is not a species, but that it is not only a species but also a genus, since the definition of each belongs to it; therefore it is not distinguished from species by those particles.

Propterea tertia opinio tenet, Non distingui per illas materialiter consideratas, sed formaliter; hoc est, sub tali modo prędicandi speciei proprio: quia species prædicatur de indiuiduis, completè, hoc est, vt totum actuale, & completum, prædicans de illis totam essentiam: genus verò prædicatur incompletè, quia licèt per modum totius potentialis prædicetur, tamen solùm prædicat partem: vt animal non prædicat totam naturam Petri, sed solùm sensitiuam, quæ pars illius est. Et hoc modo intelligi debet Porphyrius, dum distinguit speciem

For this reason a third opinion holds that it is not distinguished by them considered materially, but formally, that is, under such a mode of predicating as is proper to species: because species is predicated of the individuals completely, that is, as an actual and complete whole, predicating of them the whole essence; but genus is predicated incompletely, because, although it is predicated by way of a potential whole, yet it predicates only a part: as animal does not predicate the whole nature of Peter, but only the sensitive nature, which is a part of it. And in this way Porphyry is to be understood when he distinguishes species I iij

p. 134

à genere, per prædicari de pluribus differentibus numero.

from genus by to be predicated of several things differing in number.

Hæc etiam opinio falsa probatur, argumento ad hominem, ex eo, quod concedit, desumpto: nempe genus prædicari per seipsum, & immediatè de indiuiduis generis, vt animal de hoc, & illo animali. Quo supposito, sic argum. Animal prædicatur per se, & immediatè de hoc & illo animali: ergo natura sensitiua sumitur in his prædicationibus, vt immediatè participata ab eis, & non media aliqua specie: sed non sumitur genus vt totum potentiale, & incompletum, atque contrahibile per differentias, nisi in quantum per illas descendit ad species, ergo nec prædicatur incompletè, nisi de speciebus, aut de indiuiduis eius mediantibus: ideo impossibile est, immediatè prædicari de indiuiduis, & prædicari incompletè. Quare, nec potest distingui ab specie, per modum prædicandi incompletum de indiuiduis.

This opinion too is proved false by an argument ad hominem, taken from what it grants: namely, that genus is predicated through itself and immediately of the individuals of the genus, as animal of this and that animal. This supposed, I argue thus: Animal is predicated per se and immediately of this and that animal; therefore the sensitive nature is taken in these predications as immediately participated by them, and not by means of some species. But genus is not taken as a potential and incomplete whole, contractible by differences, except inasmuch as it descends through them to the species; therefore neither is it predicated incompletely except of the species, or of individuals with the species as means. Therefore it is impossible for it to be predicated immediately of the individuals and to be predicated incompletely. Wherefore neither can it be distinguished from species by an incomplete mode of predicating of the individuals.

27 His sententiis refutatis, duabus conclusionibus explicatur nostra. Prima est, Genus non prædicatur de indiuiduis per seipsum, & immediatè tanquam genus, sed per modum speciei: & ideo tales prædicationes, non ad primum, sed ad secundum prædicabile pertinent. Hæc conclusio primò explicanda est, deinde probanda. Explicatur autem hoc modo: Genus non prædicatur per seipsum, aut immediatè: nisi de indiuiduis genericis: vt animal de hoc & illo animali, & in his prædicationibus significatur natura generica, vt immediatè participata ab indiuiduis, & non mediante aliqua specie: quare non consideratur vt contrahibilis per differentias essentiales: & ideo nec vt imperfecta, & incompleta, sed vt completa ex genere, & differentia, immediatè determinata ad indiuidua, per differentias indiuiduales proprias, & non alterius naturæ inferioris: quæ propria sunt infimæ speciei: vnde in eisdem prædicationibus immediatis formaliter sumitur, per modum infimæ speciei, & non tanquam genus, nec prædicatione generis prædicatur, sed tanquam species, & prædicatione speciei.

27 These opinions being refuted, ours is explained in two conclusions. The first is: Genus is not predicated of the individuals through itself and immediately as genus, but by way of species; and therefore such predications pertain not to the first predicable but to the second. This conclusion is first to be explained, then proved. It is explained in this way: Genus is not predicated through itself or immediately except of generic individuals, as animal of this and that animal; and in these predications the generic nature is signified as immediately participated by the individuals, and not by means of some species; wherefore it is not considered as contractible by essential differences, and therefore not as imperfect and incomplete, but as complete from genus and difference, immediately determined to the individuals by individual differences proper to it and not to another inferior nature, which are proper to the lowest species. Whence in these same immediate predications it is formally taken by way of a lowest species, and not as a genus; nor is it predicated with the predication of a genus, but as a species and with the predication of a species.

28 Sic autẽ explicata conclusio probatur duplici argumẽto. Primò: Cùm genus prædicatur immediatè de indiuiduis generis, concipitur natura generica, vt immediatè participata ab eisdem indiuiduis: ergo vt immediatè contracta per differentias indiuiduales sibi proprias: sed immediatè contrahi per differentias indiuiduales, conuenit speciei, & non generi, vt genus est: ergo in his prædicationibus, non habet modum generis, sed speciei. Probatur minor: quia genus vt genus, non contrahitur immediatè per differentias indiuiduales

28 The conclusion so explained is proved by a twofold argument. First: When genus is predicated immediately of the individuals of the genus, the generic nature is conceived as immediately participated by those same individuals; therefore as immediately contracted by individual differences proper to it. But to be immediately contracted by individual differences belongs to species, and not to genus as it is genus; therefore in these predications it does not have the mode of a genus, but of a species. The minor is proved: because genus, as genus, is not contracted immediately by individual

p. 135

, sed specificas: ergo dum formaliter concipitur in eisdem prædicationibus, tanquam contractum immediatè per differentias indiuiduales propriæ naturæ, non concipitur tanquam genus: sed per modum speciei.

differences, but by specific ones; therefore, when in these same predications it is formally conceived as contracted immediately by individual differences of its proper nature, it is not conceived as a genus, but by way of a species.

Secundò: Id quod concipitur tanquam immediatè contractum, per differentias indiuiduales concipitur, vt quid iam cõpletum in sua natura: sed animal in hac prædicatione, Hoc animal est animal, consideratur, vt immediatè contractum, per differentias indiuiduales eiusdem naturæ sensitiuę: ergo significatur vt quid completum in sua natura, composita ex genere, & differentias: nempe ex viuenti, & sensibili: & ideo non vt incompletum, neque vt genus, sed per modum speciei.

Second: That which is conceived as immediately contracted by individual differences is conceived as something already complete in its nature; but animal in this predication, This animal is an animal, is considered as immediately contracted by individual differences of the same sensitive nature; therefore it is signified as something complete in its nature, composed of genus and differences, namely of living and sensible; and therefore not as incomplete, nor as a genus, but by way of a species.

Secunda conclusio: Genus vt genus non prædicatur de indiuiduis per seipsum, sed per speciem. Hæc satis est manifesta, supposita præcedenti: nam si genus non prædicatur immediatè de indiuiduis, tanquam genus, sed per modum speciei: sequitur, quòd dum prædicatur de illis tanquam genus, non per seipsum, & immediatè prædicatur, sed per speciem, & diuerso etiam modo, atque species: quia per modum totius potentialis, & contrahibilis, solùm prędicant partem essentiæ, cùm tamen species prædicetur, vt totum completum, atque perfectum. Et ex his intelligitur, benè fuisse exclusum à Porphyrio genus à definitione speciei, per illas particulas: Quod prædicatur de pluribus differentibus numero, sic ab eo intellectas, vt per se, & non per aliud prædicetur species de indiuiduis, atq; etiam cõpletę, cùm tamen neutrum conuenire possit generi, vt genus est.

The second conclusion: Genus as genus is not predicated of the individuals through itself, but through the species. This is manifest enough, supposing the preceding one: for if genus is not predicated immediately of the individuals as genus, but by way of species, it follows that when it is predicated of them as genus it is not predicated through itself and immediately, but through the species, and also in a different mode from the species: because by way of a potential and contractible whole they predicate only a part of the essence, whereas species is predicated as a complete and perfect whole. And from these things it is understood that genus was well excluded by Porphyry from the definition of species by those particles, which is predicated of several things differing in number, understood by him in such a way that species is predicated of the individuals per se and not through another, and also completely, whereas neither can belong to genus as it is genus.

29 Ad formam arg. primæ opinionis respondeo: Solam speciem componi per se ex genere, & differentia: & ideo solam speciem per se participare naturam generis, vt genus est: indiuidua verò media specie: sed eadem natura generica, vt consideratur immediatè contracta ad propria indiuidua, immediatè etiam participatur ab eis: non tamen sub ratione generis: sed speciei, cui conuenit immediatè contrahi per differentias indiuiduales. Talia autem indiuidua ita consideratata, non existunt à parte rei, sed formaliter accipiuntur ab intellectu, sub gradu naturæ superioris, & genericæ.

29 To the form of the argument of the first opinion I reply that species alone is per se composed of genus and difference, and therefore species alone per se participates the nature of the genus as it is genus, but the individuals by means of the species; but the same generic nature, as it is considered immediately contracted to its proper individuals, is also immediately participated by them, yet not under the ratio of genus but of species, to which it belongs to be immediately contracted by individual differences.
