Such individuals, however, so considered, do not exist on the part of the thing, but are formally taken by the intellect under the grade of the superior and generic nature.

Quæstio 6. An detur vna ratio communis atque realis indiuiduorum, quæ definiatur per secundam definitionem indiuidui — QUESTION VI. Whether there is one common and real ratio of individuals which is defined by the second definition of the individual.

QVÆSTIO VI.

[…]

An detur vna ratio communis, atque realis indiuiduorum, quæ definiatur per secundam definitionem indiuidui.

[…]

De Indiuiduo agit Porphyrius cap. præsenti, quia est terminus relationis speciei, per quem definita est species

Of the individual Porphyry treats in the present chapter because it is the term of the relation of species, through which species I iiij

p. 136

vltima definitione: & ideo ex eius notitia dependet notitia speciei. Sed duplici definitione definiuit indiuiduum. Prima, In quantum est prædicabile de vno, per terminos secundæ intentionis: & propterea secundo intentionaliter intelligitur talis definitio ab expositoribus. Secundam verò tradidit, per proprietates reales, dicens, Indiuiduum esse, cuius collectio proprietatum quæ in vno sunt, in alio reperiri non possunt: quare hæc veluti fundamentum primæ, & ideo prius est à nobis examinanda, quàm illa. Et quia definitio quæcunque explicare debet aliquam rationem communem omnibus, quæ sub definito continentur, vt definitio hominis, rationem hominis communem omnibus hominibus, quærit titulus quæstionis, An per hanc definitionem Indiuidui, definiatur aliqua ratio realis communis omnibus indiuiduis.

is defined in the last definition; and therefore knowledge of species depends on knowledge of it. And he defined the individual by a twofold definition. The first, inasmuch as it is predicable of one, through terms of second intention; and for this reason such a definition is understood by the expositors in the manner of second intention. The second he delivered through real properties, saying that the individual is that whose collection of properties, which are in one, cannot be found in another. Wherefore this is as it were the foundation of the first, and therefore it is to be examined by us before that one. And because any definition whatever ought to explain some ratio common to all things contained under the thing defined, as the definition of man explains the ratio of man common to all men, the title of the question asks whether by this definition of the individual some real ratio common to all individuals is defined.

30 Et est prima opinio Soti, quæstione vnica huius capitis, in solutione ad secundum asserentis, Nihil dari reale, quod omnibus indiuiduis sit commune, & per hanc definitionem explicetur: sed definitum Formale, & vt Quo, esse secundam intentionem indiuidui, Materiale verò, & vt Quod reale Indiuiduum non secundùm esse commune omnibus, sed vt denominatur à secunda intentione, sicut in definitione generis diximus, definiri naturam genericam, prout denominatur à secunda intentione.

30 And the first opinion is Soto’s, in the single question of this chapter, in the solution to the second, who asserts that nothing real is given which is common to all individuals and is explained by this definition; but that the formal thing defined, and as that by which, is the second intention of the individual, while the material, and as that which, is the real individual, not according as it is common to all, but as it is denominated by the second intention; just as we said in the definition of genus that the generic nature is defined as it is denominated by the second intention.

Habet autem hæc opinio duo argumenta, quibus probatur nihil dari reale commune omnibus indiuiduis, quod definiri possit. Primum, Quia indiuidua duo habent: Vnum est participatio naturæ specificæ, sub qua vniuocè conueniunt, vt Petrus, & Ioannes, in eo quòd vterque est homo. sed communis hæc ratio, specifica est, & non indiuidualis: quare non potest esse definitum huius definitionis, sed per definitionem potiùs speciei explicatur. Alterum quod habent, est differentia indiuidualis, propria atque distincta, per quam contrahitur natura specifica & fit singularis: & per hanc differentiam constituuntur in ratione singularium, aut indiuiduorum, & distinguuntur inter se. Gratia exempli, Petrus habet naturam humanam, per quam est homo, & conuenit cum Ioanne, & differentiam indiuidualem, per quam est talis homo singularis, & distinguitur à Ioanne, & sub prima ratione, certum est non definiri, quia sub ea consideratus, non est singularis, sed sub secunda. Sed sub ratione singularium, non possunt conuenire indiuidua: ergo nihil reale datur eis commune, quod definiatur Minorem sic probo: differentiæ indiuiduales sunt primò diuersæ, & per quas vltimò distinguuntur indiuidua: ergo ratione illarum

This opinion has two arguments by which it is proved that nothing real is given common to all individuals that can be defined. First: because individuals have two things. One is the participation of the specific nature, under which they agree univocally, as Peter and John in that each is a man; but this common ratio is specific and not individual; wherefore it cannot be the thing defined by this definition, but is rather explained by the definition of species. The other thing they have is the individual difference, proper and distinct, by which the specific nature is contracted and becomes singular; and through this difference they are constituted in the ratio of singulars, or individuals, and are distinguished among themselves. For example, Peter has the human nature, through which he is a man and agrees with John, and the individual difference, through which he is such a singular man and is distinguished from John; and under the first ratio it is certain that he is not defined, because considered under it he is not singular, but under the second. But under the ratio of singulars individuals cannot agree; therefore nothing real is given common to them which is defined. I prove the minor thus: the individual differences are primarily diverse, and are those by which individuals are ultimately distinguished; therefore by reason of them

p. 137

non possunt conuenire: quare nihil reale commune habere possunt, quod definiatur, sicut in quantum diuersa sunt, non possunt conuenire.

they cannot agree; wherefore they can have nothing real in common which is defined, just as, inasmuch as they are diverse, they cannot agree.

31 Secundum, Singularia vt distincta sunt, propriis, ac diuersis nominibus significantur, vt Petrus, & Ioannes: ergo sub propria, & vltima ratione singularitatis non conueniunt. Probatur consequentia: quia si sub ea conuenirent per alias differentias indiuiduales deberent distingui, quarum ratione conuenire etiam possent, si ratione earum, quas modò habent, conueniunt: & tunc per alias differentias distinguerentur, daretúrque processus in infinitum.

31 Second: Singulars, as they are distinct, are signified by proper and diverse names, as Peter and John; therefore under the proper and ultimate ratio of singularity they do not agree. The consequence is proved: because if they agreed under it, they would have to be distinguished by other individual differences, by reason of which they could also agree, if they agree by reason of those which they now have; and then they would be distinguished by other differences, and there would be a process to infinity.

Et confirmari potest arg. hoc modo: Si indiuidua vt indiuidua sunt realia, habent conuenientiam vniuocam vt abstractam à Petro, & Ioanne, ac cæteris: sequitur species etiam reales atomas, vt distinctas, habere conuenientiam realem vniuocam: ita vt ab homine & equo non solùm vt conueniunt in animali, sed etiam, vt sunt species distinctæ per rationale, & irrationale, possit abstrahi vnus conceptus realis eis communis & vniuocus: quod patet esse falsum.

And the argument can be confirmed in this way: if individuals, as individuals, are real and have a univocal agreement, as abstracted from Peter and John and the rest, it follows that the real atomic species too, as distinct, have a real univocal agreement: so that from man and horse, not only as they agree in animal but also as they are species distinct by rational and irrational, one real concept common to them and univocal could be abstracted; which is plainly false.

32 Secunda opinio affirmat, Dari aliquid reale commune, & vniuocum indiuiduis, quod per hanc definitionem Porphyrij definiatur. Hæc est D. Th. 1. par. qu. 30. art. 4 Caie. ca. præs. & 1. part. q. 29. art. 1. & Canteri in expositione huius definitionis & ca. de substantia, in expositione definitionis primæ substantiæ, quam sequuntur plures moderni. Et mihi videtur probabilior.

32 The second opinion affirms that something real is given, common and univocal to individuals, which is defined by this definition of Porphyry. This is the opinion of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 30, a. 4; of Cajetan, on the present chapter and on 1 p., q. 29, a. 1; and of Canterus, in the exposition of this definition and in the chapter on substance, in the exposition of the definition of first substance; and many moderns follow it. And it seems to me more probable.

Sed duo sunt probanda, aduersus primam opinionem, vt maior probabilitas secundæ constet. Primum est, quòd non definiatur secunda intentio, vel natura indiuidui, vt ab ea denominatur. Secundum. quod definiatur aliquid reale.

But two things are to be proved against the first opinion, so that the greater probability of the second may be established. The first is that what is defined is not the second intention, or the nature of the individual as it is denominated by it. The second, that something real is defined.

Probatur primum, Quia omnia verba in definitione posita, significant proprietates reales indiuidui, per quarum collectionem distinguitur vnum ab altero: nam licèt in multis conuenire possint, tamen quodlibet habet aliquam sibi propriam, diuersam à propriis aliorum: vnde collectio, quæ ex communibus, & propria constat, distincta est in singulis, & per illam distinguuntur: ergo collectio, per quam definitur indiuiduum, constat ex proprietatibus realibus, vt reales sunt, & non vt denominantur à secunda intentione. Probatur consequentia: quia indiuiduum constituitur per proprietates reales, ante operationem intellectus: ergo sine vllo ordine ad secundam intentionem,

The first is proved: because all the words placed in the definition signify real properties of the individual, through whose collection one is distinguished from another: for although they can agree in many, yet each has some property proper to itself, diverse from the proper ones of the others; whence the collection, which consists of common properties and a proper one, is distinct in each, and by it they are distinguished. Therefore the collection by which the individual is defined consists of real properties, as they are real, and not as they are denominated by second intention. The consequence is proved: because the individual is constituted by real properties before the operation of the intellect; therefore without any order to second intention.

Probatur secundum, duplici ratione. Primò: Definitio hęc,

The second is proved by a twofold argument. First: This definition,

p. 138

communis est omnibus indiuiduis substantiæ, quæ per eam definiuntur: ergo aliquid commune definitur per eam, non sola vox: quia æquiuocum esset, quòd definiretur, vt canis, quod constat non posse definiri: ergo definitur aliquid commune, per vocem significatum, vt reale: vt probatum est, nempe, ratio indiuiduationis realis in concreto.

is common to all the individuals of substance, which are defined by it; therefore something common is defined by it, not the word alone: because what was defined would be equivocal, as canis [dog], which, it is agreed, cannot be defined; therefore something common is defined, signified by the word, as real: as has been proved, namely the ratio of real individuation in the concrete.

33 Secundò: A quacunque conuenientia reali vniuoca, abstrahi potest conceptus realis vniuocus: sed indiuidua conueniunt vniuocè in modo particulari essendi: ergo talis modus abstrahi potest ab eis, vt in eo æqualiter conueniunt, poterunt definiri. Probatur minor: quia æquè conuenit Petro, & Ioanni, modus particularis essendi, per quem determinatur natura humana, vt sit singularis in vtroque. Hoc autem commune definitur, & confirmari potest hoc modo: Syllogismus iste constituitur in Darij: Omne indiuiduum est incõmudicabile: Petrus est indiuiduum: ergo est incommunicabilis: sed si nihil commune datur indiuiduis, sequitur esse vitiosum: ergo dicendum est, aliquid reale commune eis dari. Probatur minor: quia medium erit æquiuocum, nempe indiuiduum, nihil commune indiuiduis significans præter vocem.

33 Second: From any real univocal agreement whatever a real univocal concept can be abstracted; but individuals agree univocally in a particular mode of being; therefore such a mode can be abstracted from them, and, as they agree equally in it, they can be defined. The minor is proved: because the particular mode of being, by which human nature is determined so as to be singular in each, belongs equally to Peter and to John. And this common thing is defined. And it can be confirmed in this way: this syllogism is constituted in Darii: Every individual is incommunicable; Peter is an individual; therefore he is incommunicable. But if nothing common is given to individuals, it follows that it is faulty; therefore it must be said that something real common to them is given. The minor is proved: because the middle, namely individual, will be equivocal, signifying nothing common to the individuals besides the word.

34 Pro solutione argumentorum notandum est, Tribus modis considerari posse indiuidua. Primò, in quantum conueniũt in natura specifica: vt Petrus, & Ioannes, in natura humana: ratione cuius conuenientiæ, quilibet vocatur homo, & conceptus iste non est indiuiduorum, vt indiuidua sunt: sed conceptus speciei. Secundo modo considerantur, vt sunt particulares: ac determinati homines, per proprias differẽtias indiuiduales: & iste conceptus, non est naturæ, sed indiuiduationis. Quem adhuc dupliciter cõsideramus. primò, vt talis indiuidui est, nomine particulari, & proprio significati, Petri, aut Ioannis. Secundò, vt est rei singularis, & indiuiduæ, non determinando hanc differentiam indiuidualem, Petri aut Ioannis: sed differentiam indiuidualem, vt sic, abstrahendo à determinatis, Petri & Ioannis: & secundùm primam considerationem, nihil cõmune habere possunt: in secunda verò, cõmunis est eis conceptus indiuidui, vt sic, per quem significatur differentia indiuidualis, & nõ aliqua determinata, & in concreto indiuiduum sub ratione indiuidui, non determinando hoc, vel illud.

34 For the solution of the arguments it should be noted that individuals can be considered in three ways. First, inasmuch as they agree in the specific nature, as Peter and John in human nature; by reason of which agreement each is called a man; and this concept is not of the individuals as they are individuals, but the concept of the species. In the second way they are considered as they are particular and determinate men through their proper individual differences; and this concept is not of the nature but of individuation. This we consider further in two ways. First, as it is of such an individual, signified by a particular and proper name, of Peter or of John. Second, as it is of a singular and individual thing, not determining this individual difference of Peter or of John, but the individual difference as such, abstracting from the determinate ones of Peter and of John. And according to the first consideration they can have nothing in common; but in the second the concept of the individual as such is common to them, by which is signified the individual difference, and not some determinate one, and in the concrete the individual under the ratio of individual, not determining this or that one.

35 Vnde sequitur, Conceptum communem, quem indiuidua habere dicimus, non esse conceptum rei, aut naturæ: sed conceptum modi determinantis naturam: & sub tali conceptu definiri indiuiduum in hac definitione.

35 Whence it follows that the common concept which we say individuals have is not a concept of the thing or of the nature, but a concept of the mode determining the nature; and under such a concept the individual is defined in this definition.

Ad primum arg. Concessa maiori, negatur minor, quòd

To the first argument: the major being granted, the minor is denied, that

p. 139

indiuidua vt indiuidua sunt, nihil commune habere possint, nam licèt differentiæ indiuiduales sint primò diuersæ, & vt tales nihil propriis rationibus commune habere possint: tamen in officio conueniunt, nempe, in determinando naturam specificam, ad particularem modum essendi: quod est constituere eam in indiuiduo; licèt quælibet secundùm propriam rationem, constituat indiuiduum determinatum ac diuersum.

individuals, as they are individuals, can have nothing in common. For although the individual differences are primarily diverse, and as such can have nothing in common by their proper rationes, yet they agree in function, namely in determining the specific nature to a particular mode of being, which is to constitute it in an individual; although each, according to its proper ratio, constitutes a determinate and diverse individual.

Ad secundum respondetur: Distinguendo consequens: nempe, singularia sub vltima ratione singularitatis, non conuenire. Nam propriæ singularitates Petri, & Ioannis, duobus modis considerari possunt. Primo, vt singularitates sunt. Secundo, vt tales singularitates. Et si primo modo considerentur, conueniunt: quia commune est eis officium singularizandi naturam: si verò secundo modo, conuenire non possunt. Nec datur processus in infinitum: quia sub illa ratione communi, considerata indiuidua, non distinguuntur per alias differentias indiuiduales: sed per easdem, consideratas sub vltima ratione particulari, ac determinata: quibus hoc modo sumptis, nihil commune datur: & ideo nec est necessarium, per alias differentias distingui.

To the second the reply is by distinguishing the consequent, namely that singulars do not agree under the ultimate ratio of singularity. For the proper singularities of Peter and of John can be considered in two ways. First, as they are singularities. Second, as they are such singularities. And if they are considered in the first way, they agree, because the function of singularizing the nature is common to them; but if in the second way, they cannot agree. Nor is there a process to infinity: because individuals considered under that common ratio are not distinguished by other individual differences, but by the same ones considered under the ultimate particular and determinate ratio; and to these, taken in this way, nothing common is given; and therefore it is not necessary that they be distinguished by other differences.

36 Et quod de indiuidualibus differentiis dicimus, de specificis intelligendum est: quæ licèt secundùm proprias rationes, non conueniant in aliquo, sed sint primo diuersæ: vt rationale, & hinnibile: tamen in officio diuidendi genus, & constituendi speciem conueniunt. Quam conuenientiam definiunt Porphyrius, cap. de differentia, dicens: Differentia est, qua diuidit genus, & constituit speciem. Et conuenientia hęc specierum, vt per differentias specificas constituuntur, etiam est modalis: quia non est ratione naturæ differentiarum, sed solùm ratione officij constituendi speciem; & ideo non est media inter proximũ genus, & species, sed natura generis proximè descendit ad species, per differentias: licèt differentiæ ipsæ, & species, per eas modaliter conueniant, vt expositum est. Si autem inquiras, Ad quod prædicabile pertineat indiuiduum reale, sub hac ratione communi, sub qua definitur: Respondet Caiet. speciale prædicabile, distinctum à cæteris, pro eo esse ponendum: quia habet modum prędicandi distinctum: non enim prędicatur in Quid, neq; in Quale quid, sed in cuiusmodi: nec est prædicatum Accidentale, sed Substantiale, Dicendum tamen est: Non posse speciale prædicabile constituere: quia non est prædicatum naturæ, aut alicuius gradus essentialis eius, sed modi substãtialis, eiusdem naturę specificæ: & ideo ad prædicabile speciei reduci

36 And what we say of the individual differences is to be understood of the specific ones: which, although according to their proper rationes they do not agree in anything but are primarily diverse, as rational and able to neigh, yet agree in the function of dividing the genus and constituting the species. This agreement Porphyry defines in the chapter on difference, saying: Difference is that which divides the genus and constitutes the species. And this agreement of the species, as they are constituted by specific differences, is also modal: because it is not by reason of the nature of the differences, but only by reason of the function of constituting the species; and therefore it is not a middle between the proximate genus and the species, but the nature of the genus descends proximately to the species through the differences, although the differences themselves, and the species through them, agree modally, as has been expounded. But if you ask to which predicable the real individual belongs under this common ratio under which it is defined, Cajetan replies that a special predicable, distinct from the others, must be posited for it, because it has a distinct mode of predicating: for it is predicated neither in quid nor in quale quid, but in cuiusmodi; nor is it an accidental predicate, but a substantial one. It must be said, however, that it cannot constitute a special predicable, because it is not a predicate of the nature, or of any essential grade of it, but of a substantial mode of the same specific nature; and therefore it ought to be reduced to the predicable of species

p. 140

debet, propter maximam similitudinem cum ea. quia prædicatur de pluribus differentibus numero, substantialiter.

on account of its very great similarity with it: because it is predicated of several things differing in number, substantially.

QUESTION VII

QVÆSTIO VII.

[…]

An secunda intentio, Indiuidui, per primam definitionem Indiuidui definita sit vna.

Whether the second intention of the Individual, defined by the first definition of the Individual, is one. 37

37 Quæstio hæc præsupponit vnum, & quærit alterum. Illud quod, præsupponit est, quòd secunda intentio Indiuidui, in communi considerata, hoc est abstracta, ab hac, & illa secunda intentione Indiuidui, denominante Petrum, & Ioannem, prædicabilis de vno, sit definitum primæ definitionis Indiuidui: nempe, Indiuiduum est, quod de vno prædicatur. Quærit verò, An sit vna, id est, An habeat vnam rationem communem, & vniuocam, respectu secundarum intentionum, denominantium particularia Indiuidua.

This question presupposes one thing and asks another. What it presupposes is that the second intention of the Individual considered in common, that is, abstracted from this and that second intention of the Individual denominating Peter and John, predicable of one, is the thing defined by the first definition of the Individual: namely, The Individual is that which is predicated of one. What it asks is whether it is one, that is, whether it has one common and univocal ratio with respect to the second intentions denominating the particular Individuals.

Sed hoc quod præsupponit, videtur falsum, vt probant hæc arg. Primò, Secunda intentio Indiuidui, in communi considerata, prædicatur de hac & illa secunda intentione Indiuidui, denominante Petrum & Ioannem: ergo est prædicabilis de multis: sed definitio asserit, Indiuiduum esse prædicabile de vno: ergo non potest illi conuenire, sed potiùs conueniet ei definitio speciei, cùm prædicetur de pluribus differentibus numero in Quid.

But what it presupposes seems false, as these arguments prove. First: The second intention of the Individual, considered in common, is predicated of this and that second intention of the Individual denominating Peter and John; therefore it is predicable of many. But the definition asserts that the Individual is predicable of one; therefore it cannot belong to it; rather, the definition of species will belong to it, since it is predicated in quid of several things differing in number.

Secundò, Probatur quòd non sit vna: ex quo etiam colligitur, quòd non sit definitum: quia definitum vnum debet esse, hoc est vniuocum, respectu omnium, quibus definitio conuenit: sed non omne indiuiduum prædicatur de vno: sed quędam de pluribus: ergo secunda intentio Indiuidui, quæ est eis ratio prædicandi: non habebit vnam rationem communem vniuocam, respectu omnium. Consequentia euidens est: quia ab eo, quod prædicatur de vno, & ab alio, quod prædicatur de pluribus, non potest abstrahi ratio communis prædicandi de vno, cui conuenit definitio hæc. Probatur item antecedens: quia Indiuiduum vagum, vt quidam homo, prædicatur de pluribus vniuocè, vt Petro, & Ioanne: & Indiuiduum ex demonstratione, vt hoc album, prædicatur de eisdem, ergo quædam secunda intentio Indiuidui, erit ratio prædicandi de vno, alia verò ratio prædicandi de multis.

Second, it is proved that it is not one, from which it is also gathered that it is not the thing defined: because the thing defined must be one, that is, univocal with respect to all to which the definition belongs; but not every individual is predicated of one, but some of several; therefore the second intention of the Individual, which is their ratio of predicating, will not have one common univocal ratio with respect to all. The consequence is evident: because from that which is predicated of one, and from another which is predicated of several, a common ratio of predicating of one, to which this definition belongs, cannot be abstracted. The antecedent is likewise proved: because the vague Individual, as some man, is predicated univocally of several, as of Peter and John; and the Individual by demonstration, as this white thing, is predicated of the same; therefore one second intention of the Individual will be the ratio of predicating of one, but another the ratio of predicating of many.

38 Pro solutionibus huius quæstionis notandum est, quòd sicut in definitione generis diximus, duplex esse definitum, Quo, & Quod. Definitum Quod, esse naturam genericam, vt denominatã à secunda intentione generis, & definitum, Quo:

38 For the solutions of this question it should be noted that, just as we said in the definition of genus that the defined is twofold, That by which and That which: the defined That which is the generic nature as denominated by the second intention of genus, and the defined That by which,

p. 141

eandem secundam intentionem, vt denominantem naturam: & ex vtroque sic ordinato, fieri vnum totale, atq; completum, Præterea, tam definitum Quod, quã definitũ Quo, duplex esse: Adęquatum, & Proximum: & Inadęquatum, atq; Remotũ: ita vt natura generica, in cõmuni sumpta, sit definitũ adęquatum, & proximũ: remotum verò, & inadæquatum, quæcunque natura generica particularis, vt animal, vel color: & definitum, Quo, adæquatum & proximum, esse secundam intentionẽ generis in communi sumptam: inadæquatum verò, & remotum particularem intentionem denominantem animal, aut colorẽ. Ita dicendum est modò, Definitum, Quod, proximum, & adęquatum, esse naturam Indiuidui in communi acceptam, vt denominatur à secunda intentione, prædicabilis de vno, in adæquatum, & remotum, quodlibet Indiuiduum in particulari. Et definitum Quo, adęquatum, & proximũ, esse secundam intentionem Indiuidui, In communi sumptam, vt est ratio denominans Indiuiduum in communi prædicabile de vno: remotum verò, & inadæquatum, quæcunque intentionem indiuidui, denominantem Petrum, & Ioannem, prædicabilem de vno. Et ex vtroque definito, Quo, & Quod, vt ordinato ad alterum, fit vnum completum, & adæquatum, quod per definitionem explicatur: quæ definito conuenit, vt Quod, naturæ indiuidui, vt denominatæ à secunda intentione, prædicabili de vno; & secundæ intentioni, vt denominati eandem naturam.

the same second intention, as denominating the nature; and that from both, so ordered, there comes to be one total and complete defined. Moreover, that both the defined That which and the defined That by which are twofold: Adequate and Proximate, and Inadequate and Remote; so that the generic nature taken in common is the adequate and proximate defined, while the remote and inadequate defined is any particular generic nature whatever, as animal or color; and that the adequate and proximate defined That by which is the second intention of genus taken in common, while the inadequate and remote is the particular intention denominating animal or color. So now it must be said that the proximate and adequate defined That which is the nature of the Individual taken in common, as it is denominated by the second intention, predicable of one; and the inadequate and remote, any Individual in particular. And that the adequate and proximate defined That by which is the second intention of the Individual taken in common, as it is the ratio denominating the Individual in common, predicable of one; while the remote and inadequate is any intention of the individual whatever denominating Peter and John, predicable of one. And from both defineds, That by which and That which, as ordered to each other, there comes to be one complete and adequate defined, which is explained by the definition: which belongs to the defined as That which, to the nature of the individual as denominated by the second intention, predicable of one; and to the second intention, as denominating that same nature.

39 Ex quibus colligitur vnica conclusio: per quam respondemus quæstioni: & est talis: Secunda intentio Indiuidui in cõmuni accepta, vt est ratio denominans naturam indiuidui, etiam in cõmuni acceptam, est vna, atque vniuoca: & est etiam definitum formale huius definitionis, sicut natura indiuidui denominata, est vna, & est definitũ materiale. Probatur vtrumque hac ratione: Secunda intentio Indiuidui, æqualiter denominat quodlibet Indiuiduum prædicabile de vno: & natura Indiuidui, in communi æqualiter est denominata ab eo: ergo vtraque est vniuoca, & suo modo definitũ huius definitionis.

39 From which a single conclusion is gathered, by which we answer the question, and it is this: The second intention of the Individual taken in common, as it is the ratio denominating the nature of the individual, also taken in common, is one and univocal; and it is also the formal defined of this definition, just as the denominated nature of the individual is one and is the material defined. Both are proved by this argument: The second intention of the Individual equally denominates every Individual predicable of one; and the nature of the Individual in common is equally denominated by it; therefore each is univocal and, in its own way, the defined of this definition.

Pro solutione primi argumenti, notandum est, Secundã intentionem Indiuidui in communi, dupliciter posse considerari, vt Quo, & vt Quod: & prima cõsideratio formalis est: quia consideratur vt forma denominans naturam indiuidui, prædicabilem de vno. Secunda verò, materialis: quia consideratur tanquam id, quod prædicatur de multis, secundis intentionibus Indiuiduorum. Vnde secundùm primam considerationem tantùm, pertinet ad præsentem definitionem, vt formale definitum eius secundùm aliam verò, ad prædicabile speciei

For the solution of the first argument it should be noted that the second intention of the Individual in common can be considered in two ways: as That by which, and as That which. The first consideration is formal, because it is considered as the form denominating the nature of the individual, predicable of one. The second is material, because it is considered as that which is predicated of many, namely of the second intentions of the Individuals. Hence according to the first consideration only does it pertain to the present definition, as its formal defined; but according to the other, to the predicable species

p. 142

pertinet: quia prædicatur de pluribus differentibus numero, in Quid: pertinet quidem, non propriè, sed reductiuè, & impropriè: quia sicut indiuiduum quodcunque, non prædicatur prædicatione propria, pertinente ad artem, & scientiam, sed impropriissima, & quæ vocatur identica, & naturalis: ita secunda intentio indiuidui, tanquam incompletum quid, & impropriè, prædicatur de hac & illa secunda intentione Indiuidui: & ideò solùm per quandam similitudinem denominatur, à secunda intentione speciei, sicut naturæ completæ, denominantur propriè. Arg. verò procedit de secunda intentione Indiuidui materialiter considerata, & ideo nihil probat contra nostram conclusionem.

because it is predicated of many differing in number in quid. It does pertain to it, but not properly; rather reductively and improperly: because, just as any individual whatever is not predicated with a proper predication pertaining to the art and science, but with a most improper one, which is called identical and natural, so the second intention of the individual, as an incomplete quid, is also predicated improperly of this and that second intention of the Individual; and therefore they are denominated by the second intention of species only through a certain likeness, whereas complete natures are denominated by it properly. The argument, however, proceeds of the second intention of the Individual considered materially, and therefore proves nothing against our conclusion.

40 Ad secundũ respondeo, quòd per hanc definitionem nõ definitur quodlibet Indiuiduum, sed proprium, ac determinatum, quod de vno prædicatur, hoc est de seipso, prædicatione identica: & ideo nec definitum formale est, nisi secunda intentio propria Indiuidui, quæ est ratio prædicandi de vno. De Indiuiduo verò vago, asserunt quidam, non definiri hac definitione, quia est complexum, vt quidam homo. Alij verò dicunt, non definiri: quia nihil determinatum significat, sed vagum quid, quod ad singularia omnia eiusdem naturę se extendit, nullum determinando. Sed vtrumque est falsum. Primum quidem, quia Quidam, vel Aliquis, signa quædam sunt, non significantia rem distinctam à nomine, cui adiunguntur, sed particularem modum essendi, qui est indiuidualis differentia, à qua denominatur: res autem determinata per modum, vna, & eadem est: ergo Indiuiduum vagum, aut ex demonstratione, res simplex est, & nomen, quo significatur, incomplexum, quamuis voce videatur complexum, vt quidam homo significat naturam humanam singularizatam, non significando vltimas rationes singularium, per quas distinguitur in diuersis indiuiduis. Hanc verò rem, determinatam esse, aut determinatum conceptum, manifestum est: quamuis non determinet aliquod indiuiduum, de quo verificetur in propositione, sed sufficit in vno, aut altero verificari. Ex quo patet, falsum esse secundum. Quare dicendum est, Indiuiduum vagum, non esse propriè Indiuiduum, cùm de multis prædicetur: & ideo non pertinere ad præsentem definitionem.

40 To the second I reply that by this definition not every Individual whatever is defined, but the proper and determinate one, which is predicated of one, that is, of itself, with an identical predication; and therefore the formal defined is nothing but the proper second intention of the Individual, which is the ratio of predicating of one. Of the vague individual, however, some assert that it is not defined by this definition because it is complex, as some man. Others say that it is not defined because it signifies nothing determinate, but a vague something that extends itself to all the singulars of the same nature, determining none. But both are false. The first, because Some or A certain are certain signs that do not signify a thing distinct from the noun to which they are joined, but a particular mode of being, which is the individual difference by which it is denominated; but the thing determined by the mode is one and the same; therefore the vague Individual, or the demonstrative one, is a simple thing, and the noun by which it is signified is incomplex, although in word it seems complex: as some man signifies human nature singularized, without signifying the ultimate rationes of the singulars by which it is distinguished into diverse individuals. But that this thing is determinate, or a determinate concept, is manifest, although it does not determine some individual of which it is verified in the proposition, but it suffices that it be verified in one or another. From which it is plain that the second is false. Wherefore it must be said that the vague Individual is not properly an Individual, since it is predicated of many, and therefore does not pertain to the present definition.

41 Si autem aliquis obiiciat, aduersus hanc definitionem Indiuidui: illud quod asserit Arist. in prædicamento substantiæ, nempe, A prima substantia, nulla est prædicatio, quod est idem, ac si dicatur, ab Indiuiduo nulla est prædicatio, cùm indiuiduum, & prima substantia, idem sint: vnde ex eo videtur

41 But if someone should object against this definition of the Individual what Aristotle asserts in the category of substance, namely, Of first substance there is no predication, which is the same as if it were said: of the Individual there is no predication, since the individual and first substance are the same; whence from this it seems

p. 143

sequi, Indiuiduum nullo modo prædicari: consequenter nec de vno, vt in definitione dicitur: Respondetur, duplicem esse prædicationem: Vnam propriam, & doctrinalem, cuius prædicatum aliquo modo diuersum est à subiecto: Alteram impropriam, & non aptam & doctrinam, vel scientiam, sed quasi naturalem, in qua idem est prædicatum, & subiectum: dum ergo Arist. asseruit, A prima substantia, vel ab indiuiduo, nullam dari prædicationem, de doctrinali loquitur, & naturalem seu identicam non excludit, de qua intelligitur hæc definitio Porphyrij, Indiuiduum est, quod de vno solo prædicatur.

to follow that the Individual is in no way predicated, and consequently not of one either, as is said in the definition: the reply is that predication is twofold. One proper and doctrinal, whose predicate is in some way diverse from the subject. The other improper and not apt for doctrine or science, but as it were natural, in which predicate and subject are the same. When, therefore, Aristotle asserted that of first substance, or of the individual, there is no predication, he is speaking of doctrinal predication, and does not exclude the natural or identical, of which this definition of Porphyry is understood: The Individual is that which is predicated of one alone.

CAPVT IV.

C H A P T E R I V.

De Differentia.

On Difference.

TEXTVS PORPHYR.

T E X T O F P O R P H Y R Y.

Differẽtia verò, & cõmuniter, & propriè & propriissimè, dicitur, &c.

But difference is said commonly, and properly, and most properly, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T. 1

1 Intentum Porphyrij in præsenti capite, est explicare naturam tertij prędicabilis, quod est Differentia. Diuiditur autem caput in duas partes, in quarum prima diuidit Differentiam quinque diuisionibus. In secunda, eam definit quinque aliis definitionibus.

The intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of the third predicable, which is Difference. And the chapter is divided into two parts, in the first of which he divides Difference by five divisions; in the second he defines it by five other definitions.

Prima diuisio est, Differentia vna est Communis, alia Propria, & alia Propriissima. Communis differentia, est illa, qua aliqua differunt accidente communi, vt albedo Petri, est differentia communis, qua differt Petrus albus, à Ioanne nigro. Differentia propria est, qua differunt aliqua, accidenti inseparabili, vt albedo cygni, per quam differt à coruo. Propriissima tandem differentia vocatur illa, per quam distinguuntur aliqua specie, vt rationale, per quod differt homo à leone.

The first division is: one Difference is Common, another Proper, and another Most proper. Common difference is that by which some things differ by a common accident, as the whiteness of Peter is a common difference, by which Peter, white, differs from John, black. Proper difference is that by which some things differ by an inseparable accident, as the whiteness of the swan, through which it differs from the raven. Most proper difference, finally, is called that by which some things are distinguished in species, as rational, through which man differs from the lion.

Secunda diuisio differentiæ est, secundùm officiũ proprium eius, quod est diuersum facere, & sic se habet: Differentia quædam est, quæ facit diuersum per se, vt essentialis: alia quæ facit diuersum per accidens: vt accidentalis. Hæc diuisio, non est minùs vniuersalis, quàm præcedens: quamuis duo tantùm membra habeat; quia sub membro eius secundo continentur duo membra primæ, nempe differentia communis & propria.

The second division of difference is according to its proper office, which is to make diverse, and it runs thus: some Difference makes diverse per se, as the essential; another makes diverse per accidens, as the accidental. This division is no less universal than the preceding, although it has only two members, because under its second member are contained two members of the first, namely common and proper difference.

Tertia diuisione diuiditur etiam Differentia secundùm totam suam latitudinem, in Separabilem, & in Inseparabilem: ita vt sub secundo membro, comprehendantur differentia communis, & propria. Nam differentia separabilis est, qua differũt aliqua accidẽti separabili, vt albedo parietis: inseparabilis verò

By the third division Difference is likewise divided, according to its whole latitude, into Separable and Inseparable, so that under the second member are comprehended common and proper difference. For separable difference is that by which some things differ by a separable accident, as the whiteness of a wall; inseparable, however,

p. 144

qua differunt inseparabiliter: vt rationalitate, aut risibilitate.

that by which they differ inseparably, as by rationality or risibility.

Quarta diuisio est Differentiæ inseparabilis, in Inseparabilem per se, vt rationale: & Inseparabilem per accidens, vt albedo cygni: & est minùs vniuersalis, quàm præcedentes: quia subdiuisio est vnius membri, tertiæ diuisionis, nempe, differentiæ inseparabilis: & duo tantùm membra continet primæ, videlicet propriam differentiam, & propriissimam.

The fourth division is of inseparable Difference into Inseparable per se, as rational, and Inseparable per accidens, as the whiteness of the swan; and it is less universal than the preceding ones, because it is a subdivision of one member of the third division, namely of inseparable difference; and it contains only two members of the first, namely proper difference and most proper.

Vltima diuisio est: Differentia vna est, quæ diuidit genus, alia, quæ constituit speciem: Exemplum ponit in animali, cuius differentia constitutiua est sensitiuum, diuisiua verò rationale. Et diuisio hæc minùs comprehendit, quàm præcedens, cùm sit subdiuisio quædam vnius membri eius, nempe differentiæ inseparabilis per se: potéstque vtrumque membrum eius conuenire eidem differentiæ, non tamen eadem ratione, nec respectu eiusdem, sed diuersorum: quia vtrumque officium exercere potest, vt rationale, est differentia diuisiua animalis, & constituta hominis.

The last division is: one Difference is that which divides the genus, another that which constitutes the species. He gives the example in animal, whose constitutive difference is sensitive, while its divisive one is rational. And this division comprehends less than the preceding, since it is a certain subdivision of one of its members, namely of inseparable difference per se. And both of its members can belong to the same difference, yet not by the same ratio, nor with respect to the same thing, but to diverse things: for rational can exercise both offices, since it is a difference divisive of animal and constitutive of man.

2 In secunda parte cap. definit differentiam quinque definitionibus, quarum prima talis est: Differentia est, qua species excedit genus, vt homo excedit animal: quia propter naturam sensitiuam eius continet rationalem, non contentam actu in eodem animali. Hanc verò differentiam asserit habere speciem, non à se, nec ex nihilo: sed ab ipso genere, in cuius potestate continetur, & ab intellectu educitur de potentia eius, & tribuitur speciei, vt ex ea simul cum genere componatur.

2 In the second part of the chapter he defines difference by five definitions, of which the first is this: Difference is that by which the species exceeds the genus, as man exceeds animal: because, besides its sensitive nature, it contains the rational, which is not contained in act in the same animal. And he asserts that this difference has its being not from itself nor from nothing, but from the genus itself, in whose potency it is contained, and is educed by the intellect from its potency and attributed to the species, so that the species may be composed of it together with the genus.

Secunda definitio talis est: Differentia est quæ prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie, in Quale quid. Probat Porphyrius. Differentiam prædicari in quale quid: quia ad quæstionem factam de specie, per Quid: propriè respondemus per Genus, ad quæstionem verò factam per Quale, non minùs propriè per Differentiam, Vt si inquiratur, Quid est homo? propriè respondemus esse animal: si verò Quale animal, non minùs propriè dicimus, esse rationale: ergo Genus prædicatur in Quid sed Differentia in Quale, non quidem absolutè: quia non est qualitas accidentalis, sed pars essentialis speciei: & ideo prædicatur in Quale, addito, quid, vt denotetur prædicari in Quale essentiali.

The second definition is this: Difference is that which is predicated of many differing in species in quale quid. Porphyry proves that difference is predicated in quale quid: because to a question put concerning the species through What we properly answer by the Genus, but to a question put through Of what sort, no less properly by the Difference. As, if it is asked, What is man? we properly answer that he is an animal; but if What sort of animal?, we no less properly say that he is rational. Therefore Genus is predicated in quid, but Difference in quale; not, however, absolutely, because it is not an accidental quality but an essential part of the species; and therefore it is predicated in quale with quid added, so as to denote that it is predicated in essential quale.

Tertia definitio est: Differentia separat ea, quæ sub eodem genere conueniunt, vt rationale, separat hominem à leone, cum quo conueniunt in animali.

The third definition is: Difference separates those things that agree under the same genus, as rational separates man from the lion, with which he agrees in animal.

Quarta definitio: Differentia est, quæ differunt à se singula, vt per rationale differt homo à leone. Differentia enim constituit Speciem, & ab aliis separat eam.

The fourth definition: Difference is that by which singular things differ from one another, as by rational man differs from the lion. For Difference constitutes the Species and separates it from the others.

p. 145

Vltima definitio, magis propria videtur, quàm præcedentes, quia explicat potissimum actum eius. Ait enim: Differentia confert ad substantiam rei, & est pars essentiæ ac definitionis eius. Vtrumque habet rationale: confert enim, hoc est, iuuat per se, ad substantiam hominis, & cum eum componat cum animali, est vera pars essentiæ ipsius: & vltima quidem, vt per hoc distinguatur à Genere. Per has quinque definitiones, solùm definit Porph. Differentiam propriissimam quia hæc sola est essentialis, & sola etiam pertinet ad tertium prædicabile.

The last definition seems more proper than the preceding ones, because it explains its chief act. For he says: Difference contributes to the substance of the thing, and is a part of its essence and definition. Rational has both: for it contributes, that is, it helps per se, to the substance of man; and since it composes him together with animal, it is a true part of his essence, and indeed the last, so that by this it is distinguished from the Genus. By these five definitions Porphyry defines only most proper Difference, because this alone is essential, and this alone pertains to the third predicable.

QUESTION I

Quæst. 1. Vtrum prima diuisio differentiæ in communem, propriam, & propriissimam sit sufficiens — Whether the first division of Difference into Common, Proper, and Most proper is sufficient.

QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

Vtrùm prima diuisio Differentiæ in Communem, Propriam & Propriissimam sit sufficiens.

[…]

Duobus modis intelligi potest, Insufficiẽtem esse aliquam Diuisionem: vel quia aliquod membrum ei deficit: aut quia aliud continet superfluum. Vtroque autem modo insufficiens probatur hæc diuisio Differentiæ. Et primò, quòd aliqua membra contineat, quæ non continentur sub diuiso, hoc arg. Diuisum huius diuisionis est tertium prædicabile: sed Differentia communis, & propria non pertinent ad tertium prædicabile, sed ad quintum: ergo non continentur sub diuiso. Probatur minor: quia Differentia communis, & propria, sunt accidens separabile, & inseparabile: sed hæc pertinent ad quintum prædicabile, vt notum est: ergo non possunt pertinere ad hanc diuisionem.

In two ways a Division can be understood to be insufficient: either because some member is lacking to it, or because it contains another that is superfluous. And this division of Difference is proved insufficient in both ways. And first, that it contains some members which are not contained under the divided, by this argument: The divided of this division is the third predicable; but common and proper Difference do not pertain to the third predicable but to the fifth; therefore they are not contained under the divided. The minor is proved: because common and proper Difference are separable and inseparable accident; but these pertain to the fifth predicable, as is known; therefore they cannot pertain to this division.

Quòd verò alia membra ei desint, duobus aliis argumentis probatur. Primò, quia Differentia indiuidualis, per quam differt vnum Indiuiduum, ab altero, nõ est communis, nec propria, cùm non sit accidens, nec est propriissima: ergo nõ continetur sub aliquo membro diuisionis, sed aliud pro illa addendum est. Probatur non esse propriissimam: quia Differentia propriissima est specifica, vt docet expressè Porphyrius in eadem diuisione: sed indiuidualis non est specifica, vt notum est: ergo nec est propriissima Differentia.

But that other members are lacking to it is proved by two other arguments. First, because the individual Difference, by which one Individual differs from another, is neither common nor proper, since it is not an accident; nor is it most proper; therefore it is not contained under any member of the division, but another must be added for it. That it is not most proper is proved: because most proper Difference is specific, as Porphyry expressly teaches in the same division; but the individual is not specific, as is known; therefore neither is it most proper Difference.

Secundò: Propriæ passiones specierum, vt risibilitas, faciunt differre easdem species, accidenti inseparabili: & tamen non sunt differentiæ propriæ, ergo nec pertinent ad hanc diuisionem. Consequentia euidens est: quia non possunt ad duo alia membra pertinere: cùm nec sint accidentia separabilia, nec Differentiæ specificæ. Item probatur minor: quia Differentiæ propriæ, vt Porphyrius asserit, in explicatione quartæ diuisionis, suscipiunt magis, & minus: quod constat conuenire propriis passionibus specierum.

Second: the proper attributes of species, such as risibility, make those same species differ by an inseparable accident; and yet they are not proper differences; therefore they do not pertain to this division. The consequence is evident, because they cannot pertain to the two other members, since they are neither separable accidents nor specific Differences. The minor is likewise proved: because proper Differences, as Porphyry asserts in the explanation of the fourth division, admit of more and less, which is plainly established to belong to the proper attributes of species. K

p. 146

Tenendum tamen est, Diuisionem hanc sufficientem esse. Quod non solùm probatur authoritate Porphyrij, & expositorum omnium, sed hac ratione: Sufficiens diuisio est illa, cui nullum membrum deest, nec aliquid habet, quod non contineatur sub diuiso: sed talis est hæc, ergo sufficiens. Minor probabitur, ex solutione arg. Et ad primum: quo probabatur communem & propriam differentiam, non pertinere ad hanc diuisionem: distinguenda est minor: nam Differentia Communis, & Propria, dupliciter considerari possunt. Primò, vt sunt accidentia quædam: & hoc modo pertinent ad quartum, vel quintum prædicabile. Secundò, vt faciunt differre vnum ab altero accidenti separabili, aut inseparabili: & hoc modo pertinent ad hanc Diuisionem: cuius diuisum non est tertium prædicabile, sed quid vniuersalius, nempe, Differentia secundùm communem rationem, ad essentialem, & accidentalem, sed tertium prædicabile, sola propriissima constituit. Cæteræ verò explicantur, vt ex earum rationibus magis manifesta fiat. Differentia propriissima, vnde non pertinent ad duo prædicabilia, sed ad vnum tantùm: quamuis in hoc tertio adducantur, ad faciliorem eius intelligentiam.

It must nevertheless be held that this Division is sufficient. This is proved not only by the authority of Porphyry and of all the expositors, but by this argument: A sufficient division is that to which no member is lacking, and which has nothing that is not contained under the divided; but this one is such; therefore it is sufficient. The minor will be proved from the solution of the arguments. And to the first, by which it was proved that common and proper difference do not pertain to this division, the minor must be distinguished: for common and proper Difference can be considered in two ways. First, as they are certain accidents; and in this way they pertain to the fourth or fifth predicable. Second, as they make one thing differ from another by a separable or inseparable accident; and in this way they pertain to this Division, whose divided is not the third predicable but something more universal, namely Difference according to its common ratio, as related to the essential and the accidental; but the third predicable is constituted by the most proper alone. The others, however, are explained so that from their rationes most proper Difference may become more manifest; hence they do not pertain to two predicables, but to one only, although in this third one they are brought in for the easier understanding of it.

Circa Differentiam indiuidualem, de qua procedit primum argumentum alterius partis, moderni quidam asserunt, Essentialem esse: quia indiuiduum non potest sine illa esse, nec intelligi: quod si verum est, erit propriissima differentia. Sed probatur falsum, hoc argumento: Essentialia, ea solùm appellantur, quæ prædicata sunt, ex aliquo gradu ipsius essentiæ desumpta, vt rationale, ex gradu rationalitatis, & sensitiuum, ex gradu sentiendi: sed Differentia indiuidualis; non accipitur ex aliquo gradu essentiæ: ergo non est essentialis. Probatur minor: quia vltimus gradus essentiæ, aut naturæ, est Differentia vltima, per quam constituitur vltima species: sed Differentia indiuidualis determinat vltimam speciem iam constitutam, per vltimam Differentiam: ergo non potest esse essentialis, sed extra essentiam indiuidui.

Concerning the individual Difference, from which the first argument of the other side proceeds, certain moderns assert that it is essential, because the individual can neither be nor be understood without it; and if this is true, it will be most proper difference. But it is proved false by this argument: Those predicates alone are called essential which are taken from some grade of the essence itself, as rational from the grade of rationality, and sensitive from the grade of sensing; but the individual Difference is not taken from any grade of the essence; therefore it is not essential. The minor is proved: because the last grade of the essence or nature is the last Difference, by which the last species is constituted; but the individual Difference determines the last species already constituted by the last Difference; therefore it cannot be essential, but is outside the essence of the individual.

6 Et ita tenendum est, Modum potiùs substantialem esse, extra essentiam, aut naturam, quam determinat, atque constituit singularem, aut indiuiduam: & ideo non est Differentia propriissima, sed propter similitudinem, quam habet cum differentia specifica, reducitur ad propriissimam Differentiam. Quòd verò sine illa non possit esse, nec intelligi indiuiduum, non probat esse essentialem: sed solùm esse modum intrinsecum: naturam vel essentiam determinantem: nam in relatiuis, notum est non posse vnum esse, nec intelligi, sine alio, vt patrem

6 And so it must be held that it is rather a substantial mode, outside the essence or nature which it determines and constitutes as singular or individual; and therefore it is not most proper Difference, but on account of the likeness it has with specific difference it is reduced to most proper Difference. But that the individual can neither be nor be understood without it does not prove that it is essential, but only that it is an intrinsic mode determining the nature or essence: for in relatives it is known that one cannot be nor be understood without the other, as a father

p. 147

sine filio, & tamen vnum, non est de essentia alterius.

without a son, and yet the one is not of the essence of the other.

Circa proprietates deniq; specierum, est prima opinio Soti, Mercati, & Canteri, in expositione textus, asserentium non pertinere ad hanc diuisionem. Quod etiam videtur tenere, Toletus in explicatione huius diuisionis. Et ratio eorum est: quia Porphyrius loquens, de Differentia propria, semper ponit exempla in proprietatibus Indiuiduorum, quibus indiuidua differunt, accidenti inseperabili. Et in quarta diuisione, vocat Differentias proprias, Inseparabiles per accidens: quod non conuenit propriis passionibus specierum, quæ potiùs sunt inseparabiles per se.

Concerning, finally, the properties of species, the first opinion is that of Soto, Mercado, and Canterus, in their exposition of the text, who assert that they do not pertain to this division. Toledo too seems to hold this, in his explanation of this division. And their argument is: because Porphyry, speaking of proper difference, always gives examples in the properties of Individuals, by which individuals differ by an inseparable accident. And in the fourth division he calls proper Differences Inseparable per accidens, which does not belong to the proper attributes of species, which are rather inseparable per se.

Alij verò affirmant, proprias passiones specierum, reducendas esse ad Differentiam propriissimam: quia Porphyrius in 4. diuis. posuit exemplum Differentiarum inseparabilium, per se (quas constat esse propriissimas) in propriis passionibus, vt in capacitate disciplinæ: ergo sentit esse differẽtias propriissimas.

Others, however, affirm that the proper attributes of species are to be reduced to most proper Difference, because Porphyry, in the 4th division, gave the example of Differences inseparable per se (which are plainly most proper) in proper attributes, as in the capacity for learning; therefore he holds them to be most proper differences.

Communis tamen sententia, & vera duo asserit. Primum, Passiones specierum, propriè pertinere ad hanc Diuisionem aduersus primam sententiam. Secundum, Non esse differentias propriissimas, sed proprias: & ideo in secundo membro diuisionis collocari, aduersus secundam. Probatur primò hoc arg. Proprietates indiuiduorum, ideo sunt differentiæ propriæ, quia faciunt differre indiuidua, accidenti inseparabili: sed proprietates specierum, faciunt differre easdem species accidenti inseparabili: ergo sunt differentiæ propriæ.

The common opinion, however, which is also true, asserts two things. First, that the attributes of species properly pertain to this Division, against the first opinion. Second, that they are not most proper differences but proper ones, and are therefore placed in the second member of the division, against the second. The first is proved by this argument: the properties of individuals are proper differences for this reason, that they make individuals differ by an inseparable accident; but the properties of species make those same species differ by an inseparable accident; therefore they are proper differences.

7 Probatur secundò, Quòd nõ sint propriissimæ, testimonio Porph. & ratione. Porphyrius enim in secũda Diuisione, ita ait: Vniuersaliter ergo, omnis differentia addita alicui, alteratũ facit: sed hæc quidem quæ communiter, & propriè sunt, alteratũ faciunt: quæ verò propriissimè aliud. Sed propria passio speciei, facit alteratum & nõ aliud: ergo ex mente Porphyrij, non est Differentia propriissima, sed propria. Probatur primum, quia alteratum, est accidentaliter diuersum, cùm alteratio sit motus circa Qualitatem: sed propria passio speciei, est verum accidens, & vera qualitas, vt risibilitas: ergo facit alteratum. Probatur secundum, quia illud est aliud ab altero, quod differt ab eo essentia, aut natura: sed proprij passio, non facit differre vnam speciem ab altera essentia, aut natura, sed quodã accidenti proprio: ergo nõ est differẽtia propriissima. Probatur etiam ratione: quia Differentia propriissima, est omnium maxima, cùm maximam efficiat differentiã, nempe essentialem, atq; specificam: sed propria passio nõ facit Differentiam essentialẽ inter species, ergo non est maxima Differentia, nec erit Differentia propriissima.

7 The second, that they are not most proper, is proved by the testimony of Porphyry and by reason. For Porphyry in the second Division speaks thus: Universally, then, every difference added to something makes it altered; but those which are common and proper make it altered, while those which are most proper make it other. But the proper attribute of a species makes it altered, and not other; therefore, in the mind of Porphyry, it is not most proper Difference, but proper. The first is proved: because the altered is the accidentally diverse, since alteration is a motion concerning Quality; but the proper attribute of a species is a true accident and a true quality, as risibility; therefore it makes altered. The second is proved: because that is other than another which differs from it in essence or nature; but a proper attribute does not make one species differ from another in essence or nature, but by a certain proper accident; therefore it is not most proper difference. It is proved also by reason: because most proper Difference is the greatest of all, since it effects the greatest difference, namely the essential and specific; but a proper attribute does not make an essential Difference between species; therefore it is not the greatest Difference, nor will it be most proper Difference. K ij

p. 148

Ad vltimum igitur argumentum neganda est minor: quòd propriæ passiones specierum, non sint Differentiæ propriæ: & quod Porphyrius asserit, Differentias proprias, suscipere magis, & minus: non de omnibus intelligit, sed de his, quæ conueniunt indiuiduis, in quibus exempla posuit: potiùs quam in propriis passionibus specierum, quia communiter sunt nobis notiores.

To the last argument, therefore, the minor must be denied, namely that the proper attributes of species are not proper Differences; and what Porphyry asserts, that proper Differences admit of more and less, he does not understand of all of them, but of those which belong to individuals, in which he gave his examples, rather than in the proper attributes of species, because they are commonly better known to us.

QUESTION II

Quæst. 2. An diuisio differentiæ in communem, propriam, & propriissimam sit generis in species, vel analogi in analogata — Whether the Division of difference into Common, Proper, and Most proper is of a genus into species, or of an analogous term into analogates.

An Diuisio differentiæ, in Communem, Propriam, & Propriissimam, sit generis in species, aut analogi in analogata.

[…]

8 VT intelligatur difficultas quæstionis, supponendum est, tanquam certum apud omnes: membra huius Diuisionis non conuenire in sola voce, sicut conueniunt significata nominis æquiuoci: sed etiã aliquo modo, in re significata: quæ est, esse Differẽtias, per quas vnum differt ab altero: iste enim conceptus, faciendi differre, communis est eis: vnde certum est apud omnes, Diuisionem non esse ęquiuocam. Sed an sit Vniuoca, aut Analoga, in hoc consistit difficultas quæstionis.

3 That the difficulty of the question may be understood, it must be supposed, as certain among all, that the members of this Division do not agree in the word alone, as the significates of an equivocal name agree, but also in some way in the thing signified, which is to be Differences by which one thing differs from another: for this concept of making to differ is common to them. Whence it is certain among all that the Division is not equivocal. But whether it is Univocal or Analogous, in this consists the difficulty of the question.

Cuius solutio maximè dependet ex alia: nempe, An sumatur Diuisio realiter, hoc est, pro realibus differentiis, facientibus differre vnum ab altero, ante operationem intellectus: aut pro secundis intentionibus, seu differentiis realibus: non vt reales sunt, sed vt denominatur à secundis intentionibus: & ideo hoc in primis determinandum est.

Its solution depends chiefly on another, namely, whether the Division is taken really, that is, for the real differences that make one thing differ from another before the operation of the intellect, or for second intentions, or for the real differences not as they are real but as they are denominated by second intentions; and therefore this must be determined first of all.

Circa quod, duæ sunt opiniones. Prima tenet, Diuisionem non sumi pro differentiis realibus, vt reales sunt: sed pro eisdem vt denominatur à secundis intentionibus, vel pro eisdem secundis intentionibus, vt eas denominant, quemadmodum Genus, & Species, in suis definitionibus. Hæc est Caiet. cap. præsenti, quem sequuntur aliqui, ex recentioribus.

On this there are two opinions. The first holds that the Division is not taken for the real differences as they are real, but for the same as they are denominated by second intentions, or for those second intentions themselves as they denominate them, in the same way as Genus and Species in their definitions. This is Cajetan’s, on the present chapter, whom some of the more recent follow.

Probatur hoc arg. Quia si pro realibus differentiis acciperetur, membra eius coinciderent: ita vt eadem Differentia esset Communis, Propria, atque Propriissima, & ideo nulla esset diuisio. Probatur antecedens: quia differentia albedinis respectu parietis, est communis, respectu cygni, propria, & respectu sui, propriissima.

It is proved by this argument: Because if it were taken for the real differences, its members would coincide, so that the same Difference would be Common, Proper, and Most proper, and therefore there would be no division. The antecedent is proved: because the difference of whiteness is common with respect to a wall, proper with respect to the swan, and most proper with respect to itself.

Probatur secundò, Quia diuisum huius Diuisionis, est Differentia formaliter, & in communi considerata: & membra sunt differentiæ particulares, etiam formaliter acceptæ: sed Differentia formaliter, est ens rationis, sicut Genus & Species:

It is proved, second: Because the divided of this Division is Difference considered formally and in common, and the members are particular differences, also taken formally; but Difference taken formally is a being of reason, as are Genus and Species;

p. 149

ergo accipienda est Diuisio pro secundis intentionibus.

therefore the Division is to be taken for second intentions.

9 Secunda opinio, est communis, quòd non pro secundis intentionibus accipiatur diuisio, nec pro differentiis, vt denominantur à secundis intentionibus: sed pro eisdem, secundùm actus reales faciendi differre. Ita sentiunt, Auicena, Albertus Magnus, Sotus, & plures moderni in præsenti capite. Et mihi videtur probabilior sententia.

9 The second opinion is the common one: that the division is taken neither for second intentions nor for the differences as they are denominated by second intentions, but for the same differences according to their real acts of making to differ. So hold Avicenna, Albert the Great, Soto, and many moderns, on the present chapter. And to me it seems the more probable opinion.

Probatur testimonio Porphyrij, & ratione. Verba Porphyrij sunt: Differentia quæ alicui adiuncta, facit illud diuersum ab alio: Vna est Communis, alia Propria, Propriissima altera. Sed alicui coniungi, & illud facere diuersum ab altero, non conuenit secundis intentionibus, nec differentiis, vt ab eis denominantur, sed actus reales, faciendi differre vnum ab altero realiter: ergo realiter in Diuisione accipiuntur à Porphyrio, & non pro secundis intentionibus.

It is proved by the testimony of Porphyry and by reason. The words of Porphyry are: Difference which, joined to something, makes it diverse from another: one is Common, another Proper, another Most proper. But to be joined to something and to make it diverse from another does not belong to second intentions, nor to the differences as they are denominated by them, but to the real acts of making one thing differ really from another; therefore they are taken really in the Division by Porphyry, and not for second intentions.

10 Ratio verò talis est: Differentiæ istæ possunt sumi, vt prędicabiles sunt, vel vt faciunt differre vnum ab altero: & in prima consideratione, non pertinent ad tertium prædicabile, sed ad quartum, & quintum: cùm prædicentur in Quale accidentale, & non in Quale quid: in secunda verò non possunt sumi, vt denominantur à secundis intentionibus: quia actus faciendi differre vnum ab altero, realis est, & ante operationem intellectus eis conuenit, imò sine vlla dependentia ab intellectu: vt patet in albedine, quæ sine dependentia ab intellectu, facit differre hominem album à nigro: ergo non potest sumi Diuisio hæc, pro secundis intentionibus.

10 The argument from reason is this: these Differences can be taken as they are predicable, or as they make one thing differ from another. And in the first consideration they do not pertain to the third predicable, but to the fourth and fifth, since they are predicated in accidental quale, and not in quale quid; but in the second they cannot be taken as they are denominated by second intentions, because the act of making one thing differ from another is real, and belongs to them before the operation of the intellect, indeed without any dependence on the intellect: as is plain in whiteness, which without dependence on the intellect makes a white man differ from a black one; therefore this Division cannot be taken for second intentions.

Ad primum argum. respondeo, Membra bonæ Diuisionis, concidere posse in eadem re, dummodo distinguantur ratione formali: quod patet in Diuisione, Boni, in Honestum, Vtile, & Delectabile, cuius membra in virtute realiter coincidunt, sed satis est, distingui rationes eorum formales: quia alia est ratio honestatis, alia vtilitatis, & alia delectabilitatis, in eadem virtute. Ita ergo Differentia Communis, Propria, & Propriissima, coincidunt in eadem re, sed semper habent rationes formales distinctas: quia alia est ratio eiusdem differentiæ albedinis, vt Communis est differentia: alia, vt est propria, aut propriissima.

To the first argument I reply that the members of a good Division can coincide in the same thing, provided they are distinguished by a formal ratio: which is plain in the Division of the Good into the Virtuous, the Useful, and the Pleasant, whose members coincide really in virtue; but it is enough that their formal rationes be distinguished, because the ratio of virtuousness is one, that of usefulness another, and that of pleasantness another, in the same virtue. So, then, common, proper, and most proper Difference coincide in the same thing, but always have distinct formal rationes: because the ratio of the same difference of whiteness as it is a Common difference is one, and as it is proper or most proper another.

11 Ad secundum, Distinguenda est maior: quia ratio formalis Differentiæ duplex est, Vna est ratio prædicabilis, alia est ratio faciendi differre: dum ergo dicitur, Differentiam in hac Diuisione, sumi formaliter: si sensus sit de ratione formali prædicandi, falsum est antecedens: si verò de ratione formali faciendi differre, verum: sed tunc neganda est minor, quòd Differentia

11 To the second, the major must be distinguished: because the formal ratio of Difference is twofold. One is the ratio of the predicable, the other the ratio of making to differ. When, therefore, it is said that Difference in this Division is taken formally, if the sense is of the formal ratio of predicating, the antecedent is false; but if of the formal ratio of making to differ, it is true; but then the minor must be denied, namely that Difference K iij

p. 150

hoc modo considerata, formaliter sit ens rationis: est enim, reale potiùs, per realem actum faciendi differre vnum ab altero.

considered in this way is formally a being of reason: for it is rather real, through the real act of making one thing differ from another.

Hoc iam supposito, de alio agendum est, quo principaliter quæritur: An Diuisio sit vniuoca, vel Analoga. Et est prima opinio eorum, qui tenent Diuisionem sumi, pro secundis, intentionibus, & propterea esse Diuisionem Vniuocam generis in species, ita, vt Differentia in communi, prout denominatur à secunda intentione, Genus sit ad Differentiam Communem, Propriam, & Propriissimam, prout denominantur etiam à secundis intentionibus, consideratas.

This being now supposed, we must treat of the other point, which is principally asked: whether the Division is univocal or Analogous. And the first opinion is that of those who hold that the Division is taken for second intentions, and that it is therefore a Univocal Division of a genus into species, so that Difference in common, as it is denominated by the second intention, is a Genus with respect to Common, Proper, and Most proper Difference, considered as they too are denominated by second intentions.

Probant ex Porphyrio, qui in textum, vocat membra huius Diuisionis tres species Differentiæ: sentit ergo diuisam esse tanquam genus in suas species.

They prove it from Porphyry, who in the text calls the members of this Division three species of Difference; he holds, therefore, that it is divided as a genus into its species.

Deinde ratione: quia licèt sumpta Diuisione realiter, non possint membra eius vniuocè conuenire: cùm sola Differentia Propriissima faciat differre simpliciter, cæteræ verò, non nisi secundùm quid: quia solùm faciunt differre accidentaliter: nihilominus, vt denominantur à secunda intentione Differentiæ, æqualiter conuenit illis ratio Differentiæ: sicut ratio Generis, pro secunda intentione, æqualiter conuenit generibus substantiæ, & accidentis.

Next, by reason: because, although, if the Division is taken really, its members cannot agree univocally, since most proper Difference alone makes to differ simply, while the others do so only in a certain respect, because they make to differ only accidentally; nevertheless, as they are denominated by the second intention of Difference, the ratio of Difference belongs to them equally: just as the ratio of Genus, for the second intention, belongs equally to the genera of substance and of accident.

12 Secunda sententia est aliorum omnium, qui tenuerunt Diuisionem hanc sumi realiter à Porphyrio, & consequenter asserunt, esse Analogi in analogata: quod etiam tenet Caiet. quamuis sentiat sumi pro secundis intentionibus. Et hæc est probabilior sententia.

12 The second opinion is that of all the others, who have held that this Division is taken really by Porphyry, and consequently have asserted that it is of an analogous term into analogates: which Cajetan also holds, although he thinks it is taken for second intentions. And this is the more probable opinion.

Itaque duo asserimus. Primum est, Diuisionem sumptam realiter, esse Analogi in analogata, quod concedunt auctores vtriusque opinionis. Et probatur euidenter: quia illa quæ differunt substantialiter, differunt simpliciter: quę verò differunt accidentaliter, differunt secundùm quid: sed sola Differentia Propriissima, facit differre substantialiter, duæ verò aliæ solùm accidentaliter: ergo in ratione faciendi differre realiter: non vniuocè, solùm analogicè conuenire possunt.

We assert, then, two things. The first is that the Division, taken really, is of an analogous term into analogates, which the authors of both opinions grant. And it is evidently proved: because things that differ substantially differ simply, while things that differ accidentally differ in a certain respect; but most proper Difference alone makes to differ substantially, while the two others do so only accidentally; therefore in the ratio of making to differ really they cannot agree univocally, but only analogically.

Secundò asserimus, Quòd, etiamsi accipiatur Diuisio pro secundis intentionibus, aut pro differentiis, vt ab eis denominantur: non est Generis in Species, sed Analogi in analogata, vt asseruit Caieta. Quod probatur hoc argum. Membra huius diuisionis, vel considerantur sub ratione prædicabilis, vel sub ratione faciendi differre, & in prima consideratione, Communis, & Propria, non pertinent ad tertium Prędicabile: quia nõ prædicantur in Quale quid, sed ad quartum, & quintum: cùm

Second, we assert that, even if the Division is taken for second intentions, or for the differences as they are denominated by them, it is not of a Genus into Species but of an analogous term into analogates, as Cajetan asserted. This is proved by this argument: The members of this division are considered either under the ratio of the predicable or under the ratio of making to differ; and in the first consideration Common and Proper do not pertain to the third Predicable, because they are not predicated in quale quid, but to the fourth and fifth, since

p. 151

prædicentur in Quale accidentale, proprio, vel communi. Et certè, si in ratione prædicabilis Differentia in communi esset Genus, & membra essent Species, distinguerentur specie, in ratione prædicabilis: & ideo duo, aut tria prædicabilia Differentiæ essent multiplicanda. In secunda verò, non denominantur à secundis intentionibus: quia facere differre accidenti proprio, aut communi, non dependet ab intellectu: sed est actus realis, ante operationem intellectus eis conueniens: in quo non possunt vniuocè conuenire cum Differentia Propriissima, quia istæ non faciunt differre, nisi secundùm quid, & per attributionem ad Differentiam propriissimam, quæ sola facit differre substantialiter, & simpliciter: ergo repugnat membra huius Diuisionis habere conuenientiam vniuocam. Sed etiam si in ratione faciendi differre, denominarentur à secundis intentionibus, non possent conuenire vniuocè.
