Probatur, Quia facere differre in communi sumptum, Analogum est, cùm primò, & per se conueniat Differentiæ propriissimæ, facienti differre substantialiter; & solùm secundùm quid, cæteris facientibus differre accidentaliter: ergo nec secundæ intentiones denominãtes hęc membra, possunt conuenire vniuocè. Probatur consequentia: Quia vna est ratio faciendi differre simpliciter: alia faciendi differre secundùm quid: ergo sicut facere differre in communi est Analogum: sic etiam ratio faciendi differre in communi, erit Analoga.

they are predicated in accidental quale, proper or common. And certainly, if in the ratio of the predicable Difference in common were a Genus and the members were Species, they would be distinguished in species in the ratio of the predicable; and therefore two or three predicables of Difference would have to be multiplied. In the second consideration, however, they are not denominated by second intentions, because to make to differ by a proper or common accident does not depend on the intellect, but is a real act belonging to them before the operation of the intellect; in which they cannot agree univocally with most proper Difference, because these do not make to differ except in a certain respect, and by attribution to most proper Difference, which alone makes to differ substantially and simply; therefore it is repugnant that the members of this Division should have a univocal agreement. But even if, in the ratio of making to differ, they were denominated by second intentions, they could not agree univocally. It is proved: Because to make to differ, taken in common, is Analogous, since it belongs first and per se to most proper Difference, which makes to differ substantially, and only in a certain respect to the others, which make to differ accidentally; therefore neither can the second intentions denominating these members agree univocally. The consequence is proved: Because one is the ratio of making to differ simply, another that of making to differ in a certain respect; therefore, just as to make to differ in common is Analogous, so too the ratio of making to differ in common will be Analogous.

13 Ad testimonium Porphyrij, pro alia sententia, facilè respondeo, tres species Differentię, appellasse membra huius diuisionis, id est, tres modos differentiæ, non propriè de Specie loquens, sed per similitudinem,

13 To the testimony of Porphyry for the other opinion I easily reply that he called the members of this division three species of Difference, that is, three modes of difference, not speaking properly of Species but by likeness.

Ad Arg. Negandum est antecedens ex ea parte: qua dicit membra, huius Diuisionis, vt denominantur à secundis intentionibus, Vniuocè conuenire: quia nec denominantur ab illis, cùm non pendeant ab intellectu, in ratione faciendi differre: & etiam si denominarentur, non possent Vniuocè denominari: quia conceptus faciendi differre, quantumcumque abstrahatur, non potest ęqualiter participari ab his, quæ non faciunt differre, nisi accidentaliter: & ab eo, quod facit differre substantialiter, sicut conceptus entis non potest abstrahi, quin diuerso modo participalis sit, ab ente simpliciter, quod est substantia, & ab ente secundùm quid, quod est accidens.

To the argument: the antecedent must be denied in the part where it says that the members of this Division, as they are denominated by second intentions, agree Univocally: because they are not even denominated by them, since in the ratio of making to differ they do not depend on the intellect; and even if they were denominated, they could not be denominated Univocally: because the concept of making to differ, however much it is abstracted, cannot be participated equally by those which make to differ only accidentally and by that which makes to differ substantially; just as the concept of being cannot be abstracted without being participated in a diverse mode by being simply, which is substance, and by being in a certain respect, which is accident.

14 Et, si dicatur, verum hoc esse, si membra Diuisionis accipiantur realiter, sed vt denominantur à secundis intentionibus, æqualiter eis conuenire rationem communem faciendi differre, sicut Generibus Substantiæ, & Accidentis, vt animali

14 And if it is said that this is true if the members of the Division are taken really, but that as they are denominated by second intentions the common ratio of making to differ belongs to them equally, just as to the Genera of Substance and Accident, as to animal K iiij

p. 152

& colori, vniuocè conuenit ratio Generis, quia æqualiter denominantur à secunda intentione: quamuis sumpta realiter, nihil commune vniuocum habere possint. Respondeo, diuersam essei rationem de Generibus, & differentiis, sub ratione faciendi dfferre sumptis: quia Genera Substantiæ, & Accidentis, eodem modo sunt in multis speciebus, & de illis prædicantur in Quid: & ideo vniuoca est eis denominatio Vniuersalis, & Generis à secunda intentione: sed differentiis substantialibus, & accidentalibus, non potest esse vniuoca, ratio faciendi differre, sed semper est inæqualis: quia simpliciter à Propriissima, tanquam à substantiali, & secundùm quid participatur ab aliis, tanquam ab accidentalibus: sicut ratio Entis à Substantia, & Accidenti. Vnde quantuncunque abstrahatur, aut consideretur in ordine ad secundas intentiones, semper adducit secum inæqualitatem, & Analogiam.

and color the ratio of Genus belongs univocally, because they are equally denominated by the second intention, although, taken really, they can have nothing univocal in common. I reply that the ratio is diverse for Genera and for differences taken under the ratio of making to differ: because the Genera of Substance and of Accident are in many species in the same mode, and are predicated of them in quid; and therefore the denomination of Universal and of Genus by the second intention is univocal to them. But for substantial and accidental differences the ratio of making to differ cannot be univocal, but is always unequal: because it is participated simply by the Most proper, as by the substantial, and in a certain respect by the others, as by the accidental ones; just as the ratio of Being is participated by Substance and Accident. Whence, however much it is abstracted, or considered in order to second intentions, it always brings inequality and Analogy with it.

QUESTION III

An verum sit, Genus sumi à materia, & Differentiam à forma, & quomodo intelligendum.

Whether it is true that Genus is taken from matter and Difference from form, and how it is to be understood.

15 HIs locutionibus, Genus sumitur à materia, & differentia sumitur à forma, vtitur Arist. 8. Meta. tex. 9 vbi inquit: Aliquid de aliquo significat ratio definitiua, & oportet, hoc quidem, vt materiam, illud verò, vt formam esse. Et eas sumpsit ab eo tota schola, præcipuè D. Tho. in opus. de ente & essentia, c. 7, & 9. & 1. p. quæst. 85. art 5. ad 3.

15 These expressions, Genus is taken from matter and difference is taken from form, are used by Aristotle, Metaph. 8, text 9, where he says: The definitive ratio signifies something of something, and it must be that this one is as matter, and that one as form. And the whole school took them from him, especially St. Thomas in the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 7 and 9, and 1 p., q. 85, a. 5, ad 3.

Sed hoc arg. probantur falsæ. Multa sunt, in quibus dantur vera Genera, & veræ differentiæ, quæ non possunt sumi à materia, nec à forma: ergo locutiones istæ non sunt vniuersaliter veræ. Probatur antecedens: In Angelis, in quibus est, aut esse potest distinctio specifica: ergo verum Genus, & vera Differentia: sed non habent materiam, nec formam, à quibus sumantur, cùm sint substantiæ spirituales, & simplices, hoc est non compositæ ex materia, & forma: ergo non est verum, Genus sumi à materia, & Differentia à forma.

But they are proved false by this argument: There are many things in which true Genera and true differences are found which cannot be taken from matter nor from form; therefore these expressions are not universally true. The antecedent is proved: In Angels there is, or can be, a specific distinction; therefore a true Genus and a true Difference; but they do not have matter or form from which these might be taken, since they are spiritual and simple substances, that is, not composed of matter and form; therefore it is not true that Genus is taken from matter and Difference from form.

Tota difficultas huius quæst. consistit in explicandis his locutionibus: nam ex earum explicatione constabit, in quo sensu veræ sint. Tria autem sunt, in quibus reperiuntur Genus, & Differentia, nempe Substantiæ Corporeæ, Substantiæ Spirituales, & Accidentia: ideo de singulis eodem ordine explicandum est, quomodo, à quo in eis sumatur Genus, & Differentia.

The whole difficulty of this question consists in explaining these expressions: for from their explanation it will be established in what sense they are true. Now there are three things in which Genus and Difference are found, namely Corporeal Substances, Spiritual Substances, and Accidents; therefore it must be explained of each, in the same order, how and from what Genus and Difference are taken in them.

16 Et primò, de Substantiis Corporeis, in quibus, vt veritas harum locutionũ intelligatur, tria sunt notanda. Primum est

16 And first, of Corporeal Substances, in which, in order that the truth of these expressions may be understood, three things are to be noted. The first is

p. 153

Compositionem speciei ex Genere, & Differentia, non esse Physicam, sed Metaphysicam: & ideo, non est ex rebus, sed ex conceptibus, non quidem formalibus quia conceptus formales, sunt Qualitates, & accidentia in intellectu inhærentia, sed obiectiuis, quia repræsentantur per formales: vt compositio hominis, non est ex conceptibus formalibus Animalis, & Rationalis, in intellectu existentibus, sed ex gradibus naturæ Sensitiuæ, & Rationalis, qui per ipsos repræsentantur. Vnde Genus, & Differentia, non sunt diuersę res, etiam partiales, sicut materia & forma: nec ex eis componitur aliqua tertia res, distincta à quolibet, sicut componitur ex materia, & forma, tertia quædam res Physica, distincta realiter ab vtraque, quamuis non ab eisdem simul sumptis, & vnitis: sed Genus & Differentia, sunt diuersi conceptus obiectiui, eiusdem rei: & species ex eis composita, non est res distincta ab vtroque, nec à quolibet eorum: sed conceptus quidam obiectiuus totalis, & completus, ex conceptibus Generis, & Differentiæ compositus.

that the composition of the species from Genus and Difference is not Physical but Metaphysical; and therefore it is not from things but from concepts: not, indeed, from formal ones, because formal concepts are Qualities and accidents inhering in the intellect, but from objective ones, which are represented through the formal ones. As the composition of man is not from the formal concepts of Animal and Rational existing in the intellect, but from the grades of the Sensitive and Rational nature, which are represented through them. Whence Genus and Difference are not diverse things, even partial ones, as matter and form are; nor is some third thing, distinct from each, composed of them, as from matter and form there is composed a certain third Physical thing, distinct really from each, though not from both taken together and united; but Genus and Difference are diverse objective concepts of the same thing, and the species composed of them is not a thing distinct from both, nor from either of them, but a certain total and complete objective concept, composed of the concepts of Genus and Difference.

17 Secundò notandum est, Cõceptum Generis, & Differentiæ, sic se habere, vt ille sit potentialis, atque imperfectus, determinabilis tamen, & perfectibilis, per conceptum Differentiæ, & conceptum Differentiæ habere modum actus, eum determinantis atque contrahentis. Vnde sequitur, Genus ex imperfectiori gradu naturæ desumi, Differentiam verò ex perfectiori: & quia radix totius potentialitatis, in rebus materialibus, est materia: quæ in sua essentia nullum habet actum, sed est pura potentia determinabilis per formam, tanquam per proprium actum: & radix totius actualitatis, est forma, per quam determinatur materia ad talem Speciem: ideo dictum est ab Arist. Genus sumi à materia & differentiam à forma: quod solùm intellexit in rebus materialibus: in quibus compositio Metaphysica ex Genere, & Differentia, præsupponit tanquam fundamentũ, Compositionem Physicam, ex materia, & forma.

17 Second, it should be noted that the concept of Genus and that of Difference are so related that the former is potential and imperfect, yet determinable and perfectible by the concept of the Difference; and the concept of the Difference has the mode of an act, determining and contracting it. Whence it follows that Genus is taken from a more imperfect grade of the nature, and Difference from a more perfect one. And because the root of all potentiality in material things is matter, which in its essence has no act, but is pure potency determinable by form as by its proper act; and the root of all actuality is form, by which matter is determined to such a Species: therefore it was said by Aristotle, Genus is taken from matter and difference from form; which he understood only in material things, in which the Metaphysical composition from Genus and Difference presupposes, as its foundation, the Physical composition from matter and form.

Tertiò, notanda est differentia, quam ponit D. Thom. vbi suprà, inter Materiam, & Formam, ex vna parte, & Genus, ac Differentiam, ex alia: quòd illæ, solum habent modum, & officium partium: & ideo nunquam prædicantur de toto, nunquam enim verum est, Hominem esse animam, aut corpus: sed Genus & Differentia, vtrumq; habent respectu speciei, nempe rationem totius, & partis. Et huius ratio est: quia duo officia exercent respectu illius, Prædicatorum, Vniuersalium, & Partium: vtrumque enim per se sumptum, prædicatur de Specie: & ex eisdem, tanquam ex partibus simul concurrentibus, componitur. Vnde, cùm componere sit officium partis, & ex alia

Third, the difference must be noted which St. Thomas lays down in the place cited above between Matter and Form on the one side, and Genus and Difference on the other: namely, that the former have only the mode and office of parts, and therefore are never predicated of the whole (for it is never true that man is soul or body); but Genus and Difference have both with respect to the species, namely the ratio of whole and of part. And the reason of this is that they exercise two offices with respect to it, those of Predicates or Universals, and of Parts: for each, taken by itself, is predicated of the Species, and of the same, as of parts concurring together, it is composed. Whence, since to compose is the office of a part, and on the other

p. 154

parte, nihil prædicetur de altero, formaliter, per modum partis sed per modum totius: sequitur quòd Genus, & Differentia, vt componunt speciem, habeat modum partis: & vt prædicantur de illa, modum totius: Genus quidem modum totius potentialis: Differentia verò, modum totius actualis: ita vt Genus proprium gradum imperfectæ naturæ actu includat: Differentiam verò solùm in potentia: & Differentia, vtrumque gradum actu, sed genericum quasi præsuppositum, & pro materiali: proprium verò, pro formali: vt Animal, gradum naturæ sensitiuæ, actu, & rationalis in potentia: rationale verò, gradum naturæ sensitiuæ pro materiali, & quasi præsuppositum: gradum verò naturæ rationalis, formaliter.

side nothing is predicated of another formally by way of a part, but by way of a whole, it follows that Genus and Difference, as they compose the species, have the mode of a part; and as they are predicated of it, the mode of a whole: Genus, indeed, the mode of a potential whole, but Difference the mode of an actual whole; so that Genus includes its own grade of the imperfect nature in act, but the Difference only in potency; and the Difference includes both grades in act, but the generic one as it were presupposed and as the material, and its own as the formal: as Animal includes the grade of the sensitive nature in act and that of the rational in potency; but rational includes the grade of the sensitive nature as the material and as it were presupposed, but the grade of the rational nature formally.

18 Vltimò notandum, quod compositio Speciei, potest dupliciter cõsiderari: in Fieri, & in Facto esse: vel clariùs, dum fit, vel dum iam est facta: & si consideretur in Fieri, verum est, Speciem componi ex Genere, vt genus est formaliter: hoc est, vt totum potentiale, & ex Differentia, vt totum actuale: sed in Facto esse, non cõponitur ex Genere, vt genus est: nec ex Differentia, vt differentia est: sed ex Natura generica, & differentiali, tanquam ex partibus. Et ratio huius est, quia licèt Genus in principio compositionis, & si totum potentiale, tamen dum iam est actu coniunctum cum Differentia, coarctatum est, atque determinatum: ita vt ad alias species, vt sic, nõ se extendat. In quo differt à Materia: quæ etiam dum est coniuncta vni formæ, habet potentiam ad alias: sed Genus, vt iam actu coniunctum vni differẽtiæ, non habet potentiam ad alias: & ratio huius differentiæ est: quia potentia Materiæ, ad omnes formas est naturalis, & ideo non amittitur, per coniunctionem cum vna, aut altera forma: sed potentia Generis, prouenit illi ex eo quòd tali modo concipitur ab intellectu, nempe per modum habentis, sed imperfecti, & perfectibilis per aliud, quod est cõcipi vt totum potentiale: quando verò actu coniungitur ab intellectu cum Differentia, alio modo concipitur: non quidem per modum habentis, sed per modum actualis componentis, hanc Speciem determinatam, & pertinentis ad naturam eius, cum qua idem est: quia animal in homine, Homo est: vnde vt sic conceptum, limitato modo, non habet potentiam, vt coniungatur Differentiæ Leonis. Itaque potentia generis solùm proueniebat ei, ex eo, quòd concipiebatur per modũ totius cõtrahibilis: sed dum iam cõsideratur actu coniunctũ cum Differentia nõ permanet idẽ modus cõcipiẽdi, sed alio modo diuerso cõcipitur: ergo nõ permanet eadẽ potẽtia: quę tamẽ permanet in materia; quia eã habet à natura, & natura non variatur.

18 Lastly, it should be noted that the composition of the Species can be considered in two ways: in Becoming and in Having-been-made; or more clearly, while it is being made, or when it has already been made. And if it is considered in Becoming, it is true that the Species is composed of Genus as it is formally genus, that is, as a potential whole, and of Difference as an actual whole; but in Having-been-made it is not composed of Genus as it is genus, nor of Difference as it is difference, but of the generic and differential Nature, as of parts. And the reason of this is that, although Genus at the beginning of the composition is also a potential whole, yet when it is already conjoined in act with the Difference, it is restricted and determined, so that as such it does not extend itself to other species. In this it differs from Matter, which even while it is conjoined to one form has potency to others; but Genus, as already conjoined in act to one difference, does not have potency to others. And the reason of this difference is that the potency of Matter to all forms is natural, and therefore is not lost by conjunction with one form or another; but the potency of Genus comes to it from this, that it is conceived by the intellect in such a way, namely by way of something having, but imperfect and perfectible by another, which is to be conceived as a potential whole; but when it is conjoined in act by the intellect with the Difference, it is conceived in another way: not by way of something having, but by way of something actually composing this determinate Species and pertaining to its nature, with which it is the same, because animal in man is Man. Whence, as so conceived in a limited way, it does not have potency to be conjoined with the Difference of Lion. Thus the potency of genus came to it only from this, that it was conceived by way of a contractible whole; but when it is now considered as conjoined in act with the Difference, the same mode of conceiving does not remain, but it is conceived in another, diverse way; therefore the same potency does not remain. Which, however, remains in matter, because matter has it from nature, and nature does not vary.

p. 155

19 Ex tota hac doctrina, sequuntur duæ cõclusiones, quibus respondemus, ad primam partem quæstionis, Prima conclusio est: In rebus materialibus, prima radix totius potentialitatis est Materia: & prima radix totius actualitatis forma. Secunda conclusio: Et ideo verùm est in eis Genus sumi formaliter, à tota ipsa natura, vt concipitur sub gradu imperfecto, & perfectibili per Differentiam, radicaliter verò à Materia. Et differẽtiam sumi formaliter etiam à tota natura, vt concepta sub gradu perfecto, radicaliter verò à forma. Prima pars, per se nota est in rebus Physicis: quare nõ indiget probatione. Secunda verò probatur: quia propria & formalis ratio Generis Metaphysici, est esse totum potentiale, contrahibile per differentias oppositas, & propria ratio Differentiæ, est esse actum, per quem idem Genus contrahitur ad constituendam speciem: & vtrumque est Prædicatum Vniuersale Speciei: quod necesse est totum continere, quod Speciem, secundùm proprium modum: Genus quidem, actu simul, & potentia: Differentiam verò, actu: licèt diuersa ratione, atque species continet. Vnde necesse est vtrumque sumi à tota natura Speciei, formaliter, radicaliter verò à Materia Genus, & differentiam à Forma. Quia verum est, primam radicem Generis, in rebus, esse Materiam, & primam radicem Differentiæ, Formam: in quo sensu, dictum est ab Arist. & à cæteris omnibus intellectum, quòd Genus sumatur à materia, & Differentia à forma: in rebus quidem materialibus, in quibus solum potest esse verum. Et ex hoc solutum est argum. in principio propositum.

19 From this whole doctrine two conclusions follow, by which we answer the first part of the question. The first conclusion is: In material things the first root of all potentiality is Matter, and the first root of all actuality is form. The second conclusion: And therefore it is true that in them Genus is taken formally from the whole nature itself as it is conceived under an imperfect grade, perfectible through the Difference, but radically from Matter; and that difference is likewise taken formally from the whole nature as conceived under a perfect grade, but radically from form. The first part is known per se in Physical things; wherefore it needs no proof. The second is proved: because the proper and formal ratio of the Metaphysical Genus is to be a potential whole, contractible by opposed differences; and the proper ratio of the Difference is to be the act by which the same Genus is contracted to constitute the species; and each is a Universal Predicate of the Species, which must contain the whole that the Species contains, according to its proper mode: Genus, indeed, in act and in potency together, but the Difference in act, though by a diverse ratio; and the species contains it. Whence each must be taken from the whole nature of the Species formally; but radically Genus from Matter, and difference from Form; because it is true that the first root of Genus in things is Matter, and the first root of Difference is Form. In which sense it was said by Aristotle, and is understood by all the others, that Genus is taken from matter and Difference from form: namely in material things, in which alone it can be true. And from this the argument proposed at the beginning is solved.

Secundò, explicandum est breuiter, à quo sumatur ratio Generis, & Differentiæ, in substantiis spiritualibus. In quibus certum est, non sumi à materia, nec à forma, cùm eas non habeant: dicimus ergo, etiam in his sumi Genus ab aliquo, habẽte similitudinem materiæ, & Differentiam, ab aliquo habente similitudinem formæ. Quod hoc modo intelligendum est.

Second, it must be explained briefly from what the ratio of Genus and of Difference is taken in spiritual substances. In these it is certain that they are not taken from matter nor from form, since they do not have them; we say, therefore, that in these too Genus is taken from something having a likeness to matter, and Difference from something having a likeness to form. Which is to be understood in this way.

20 Actualitas, atque perfectio essentiæ creatæ, per quam est, & fit extra causas, est esse actualis existentiæ, realiter, aut sola ratione ab eadem essẽtia distinctum. Vnde, quo magis gradus essentiæ, aut essentialia prædicata, proxima sunt eidem actui, perfectiora esse intelliguntur: & ideo magis habere de actu, & minùs de potentia: & quo magis ab eo distant, minùs actualia & magis potentialia. Gratia exempli, Inter gradus essentiales hominis, proximè accedit ad actum essendi Rationalis: quia ei conuenit proximè, aut immediatè existentia: nam vltimus gradus essentialis perfectionis est, vltra quem non est alius: sed solùm substantialis modus, actualis existentiæ. Gradus

20 The actuality and perfection of a created essence, by which it is and comes to be outside its causes, is the being of actual existence, distinct from that same essence really or by reason alone. Whence, the closer the grades of the essence, or the essential predicates, are to this act, the more perfect they are understood to be, and therefore to have more of act and less of potency; and the farther they are from it, the less actual and the more potential. For example, among the essential grades of man, Rational comes closest to the act of being, because existence belongs to it proximately or immediately: for it is the last grade of essential perfection, beyond which there is no other, but only the substantial mode of actual existence. The grade

p. 156

verò Animalis, minùs proximè: & remotissimè gradus Substantiæ: quare gradus iste, erit magis potentialis, cùm magis distet ab actu. Cùm ergo Genus sit potentiale quid, atque contrahibile per Differentias: & Differentia actus, per quem Genus contrahitur, primum Genus cuiuslibet Speciei, substantialis, à tota ipsa essentia, secundùm gradum substantiæ: sumitur, tanquam à prima potentia in Genere Metaphysico, materiæ simili: & sic de cæteris generibus intermediis, secundùm maiorem vel minorem approximationem ad Speciem vltimam, quæ proxima est actuali existentiæ. Vt genus Corporis, etiam à tota ipsa natura hominis, sub gradu corporeitatis accepta, & Genus Viuentis, à tota natura sub gradu vitæ concepta, & tandem Genus Animalis, à tota natura sub gradu sentiendi: & hoc est vltimũ genus, cùm vltra illud, nullus sit alius gradus potentialis naturæ, sed infimæ tãtùm Species. Vltimus verò gradus, secundùm quem eadem natura hominis proximè capax est actualis existentiæ, Rationalis est: vnde cùm Differentia sit actus, contrahens genus, à tota natura hominis, sub gradu Rationalis considerata, sumitur tanquam ab actu formæ simili: sicque de cæteris Differentiis specierum.

of Animal less proximately, and most remotely the grade of Substance; wherefore this grade will be more potential, since it is more distant from act. Since, then, Genus is something potential and contractible by Differences, and Difference is the act by which the Genus is contracted, the first Genus of any substantial Species whatever is taken from the whole essence itself according to the grade of substance, as from the first potency in the Metaphysical Genus, similar to matter; and so of the other intermediate genera, according to their greater or lesser approximation to the last Species, which is closest to actual existence. As the genus of Body is taken also from the whole nature of man itself, taken under the grade of corporeity; and the Genus of Living, from the whole nature conceived under the grade of life; and finally the Genus of Animal, from the whole nature under the grade of sensing; and this is the last genus, since beyond it there is no other potential grade of the nature, but only the lowest Species. But the last grade, according to which the same nature of man is proximately capable of actual existence, is Rational; whence, since the Difference is the act contracting the genus, it is taken from the whole nature of man considered under the grade of Rational, as from an act similar to form; and so of the other Differences of species.

Ex his intelligitur, quonam modo accipiantur Genus, & Differentia in Angelis. Conueniunt enim cum corporibus, in gradu substantiæ remotissimo, ab actuali existentia: & ideo primum genus eorum à tota ipsa natura spirituali, sub gradu Substantiæ, maximè potentiali, materiæque simili sumitur. Secundum verò, à tota eadem natura, sub gradu spirituali, aut incorporeo, adhuc omnibus communi, sed minùs remoto ab actuali existentia. Et si quæ sunt alia Intermedia genera, nobis incognita, eodem modo sumuntur à tota natura, sub aliquo gradu concepta, magis aut minùs remoto ab existentia. Differentia verò, à tota etiam natura, sub gradu proximo, eidem actuali existentiæ. Loquor autem de Differentia vltima: nam subalternæ, Intermedia genera contrahentes, tanquam imperfectiores, ab aliis gradibus naturæ imperfectioribus sumuntur: quemadmodum Differentiæ, Substantiæ corporeæ, quod facilè potest intelligi.

From these things it is understood in what way Genus and Difference are taken in Angels. For they agree with bodies in the grade of substance, which is most remote from actual existence; and therefore their first genus is taken from the whole spiritual nature itself under the grade of Substance, which is most potential and similar to matter. The second, from the same whole nature under the grade of the spiritual or incorporeal, still common to all, but less remote from actual existence. And if there are any other Intermediate genera, unknown to us, they are taken in the same way from the whole nature conceived under some grade more or less remote from existence. But the Difference is taken likewise from the whole nature, under the grade closest to that actual existence. I am speaking, however, of the last Difference: for the subalternate ones, which contract the Intermediate genera, are taken, as more imperfect, from other, more imperfect grades of the nature, in the same way as the Differences of corporeal Substance, which can easily be understood.

De Accidentibus tandem dicimus, Esse in duplici differentia: nam quædam sunt Relatiua, de quibus in prędicamẽto. Ad aliquid dicetur, quonam modo, vel à quo Genus & Differentiam sumant. Alia verò absoluta, de quibus illud est certum: Quòd essentialis sit eis attributio ab substantiam, cùm aliquid eius sint: & non tam Entia appellentur, quàm Entis Entia: hoc est substantiæ; cui inhærere nata sunt ex propria natura. Primum

Of Accidents, finally, we say that they are of two different kinds. For some are Relative, of which it will be said in the category of Relation in what way, or from what, they take their Genus and Difference. Others are absolute, of which this is certain: that there is in them an essential attribution to substance, since they are something of it; and they are not so much called Beings as Beings of a Being, that is, of the substance in which they are naturally apt to inhere from their own nature. The first

p. 157

igitur eorum genus, sumitur à gradu Essendi, quem participant ab Ente vniuersalissimo, cum attributione ad substantiam, tanquam remotissimo ab actuali existentia: & ideo magis potentiali, ad similitudinem materiæ. Vt primum Genus Quantitatis, à gradu, seu modo extendendi substantiam, & alia intermedia Genera, ab altis gradibus, secundùm proportionem iam explicatam.

genus of these, therefore, is taken from the grade of Being which they participate from the most universal Being, with attribution to substance, as most remote from actual existence, and therefore more potential, after the likeness of matter. As the first Genus of Quantity is taken from the grade or mode of extending substance; and the other intermediate Genera from other grades, according to the proportion already explained.

Differentia verò, desumitur per ordinem ad proprium principium, aut causam, à quo causatur: quod in propriis passionibus manifestum est: nam Differentia Risibilitatis, per ordinem ad Rationalitatem, ex qua tanquam ex proprio principio, naturaliter procedit, desumenda est: & sic de cæteris. Et eodem ferè modo, in Accidentibus communibus: quia licèt plura habeant subiecta: semper tamen habent aliquam propriam causam in eis, ad quam ordinantur, & per ordinem ad illam sumitur differentia eorum: & hæc est caussa, propter quam semper, & necessariò definiuntur Accidentia per subiectum: siue in Concreto, vel in Abstracto definiantur: quia tam in Genere, quàm in Differentia eorum, essentialiter includitur ordo ad Subiectum: quem vocare solent Inhærentiam aptitudinalem.

The Difference, however, is taken by order to the proper principle or cause by which it is caused: which is manifest in proper attributes; for the Difference of Risibility is to be taken by order to Rationality, from which it proceeds naturally as from its proper principle; and so of the others. And in almost the same way in common Accidents: because, although they have several subjects, yet they always have some proper cause in them to which they are ordered, and by order to it their difference is taken. And this is the cause on account of which Accidents are always and necessarily defined through the subject, whether they are defined in the Concrete or in the Abstract: because in their Genus as well as in their Difference there is essentially included the order to the Subject, which they are accustomed to call aptitudinal Inherence.

QUESTION IIII

Qu. 4. An compositio speciei, ex genere, & differentia sit realis, vel tantum rationis — Whether the composition of the species from Genus and difference is real, or only of reason.

An compositio speciei ex Genere, & differentia sit realis, vel tantùm rationis.

[…]

22 DE Speciebus naturæ realis procedit quæstio, An cõpositio Metaphysica earũ sit realis, vel rationis: vt cõpositio hominis, ex animali, & rationali: nam de Speciebus, quæ reperiuntur in Entibus rationis, certum est non esse reales: quia natura Entis rationis non est realis, sed facta ab intellectu: ergo nulla compositio in ea fieri potest, quæ sit realis.

22 The question proceeds of Species of a real nature: whether their Metaphysical composition is real or of reason, as the composition of man from animal and rational. For of the Species that are found in beings of reason it is certain that they are not real, because the nature of a being of reason is not real, but made by the intellect; therefore no composition can take place in it which is real.

Ad compositionem verò realem, duæ sunt conditiones necessariæ, & quæ sufficiunt, vt talis dicatur. Prima est, quòd partes, aut componentia, sint realia. Probatur: Quia ex compositione reali, aliquid etiam reale debet resultare: sed si componentia non sint realia: nihil reale ex eorum compositione resultabit, vt notum est: ergo realia esse debent.

Now for a real composition two conditions are necessary, and they suffice for it to be called such. The first is that the parts, or components, be real. This is proved: Because from a real composition something real too must result; but if the components are not real, nothing real will result from their composition, as is known; therefore they must be real.

23 Secunda conditio est, Quòd sint distincta realiter, aut ex natura rei: nam si solùm per intellectum, non efficient compositionem realem, sed rationis tantùm, & huius ratio est, quia compositio est, quasi vnio multorum: si verò multa hæc non distinguuntur realiter, non erunt multa realiter: ergo non efficient compositionem realem.

23 The second condition is that they be distinct really, or from the nature of the thing: for if only through the intellect, they will not effect a real composition, but only one of reason. And the reason of this is that composition is as it were a union of many; but if these many are not distinguished really, they will not be many really; therefore they will not effect a real composition.

p. 158

Et de prima conditione certum est, apud omnes, concurrere in compositione Metaphysica Speciei, ex Genere, & Differentia: nam conceptus obiectiui in quibus fit, sunt gradus naturæ genericæ, & differentialis, qui verè sunt reales: vt gradus naturæ sensitiuæ, quem dicit animal, & gradus naturæ rationalis, quem dicit rationale, reales sunt: ergo componentia sunt realia.

And of the first condition it is certain among all that it concurs in the Metaphysical composition of the Species from Genus and Difference: for the objective concepts of which it is made are grades of the generic and of the differential nature, which are truly real: as the grade of the sensitive nature, which animal expresses, and the grade of the rational nature, which rational expresses, are real; therefore the components are real.

24 Ad secundam igitur cõditionem, reducitur tota difficultas quæstionis, An gradus isti, vel conceptus abiectiui, sint realiter distincti: nam si distincti fuerint realiter, realis erit compositio: si verò distinguantur sola ratione, non erit compositio realis, sed rationis. Quandoquidem Distinctio triplex est, Vna realis, alia ex natura rei, & tertia est distinctio rationis, Realis dicitur illa, quæ est inter duas res, vt inter Petrum & Ioannem. Distinctio ex natura rei, ponitur inter rem, & modum eius: vt inter punctum, & lineam, vel etiam ponitur ab aliis, inter rationes formales, eiusdem rei, verùm distinctas ante operationem intellectus: vt inter actionem, & passionem, quæ sunt idem motus realiter. Ponit Scotus distinctionem ex natura rei: quia asserit distingui rationem formalem actionis, & passionis, ante operationem intellectus: Distinctio verò rationis, vocatur ab omnibus illa quæ non est inter aliqua distincta à parte rei, sed fit ab intellectu.

24 To the second condition, then, the whole difficulty of the question is reduced: whether these grades, or objective concepts, are really distinct. For if they are really distinct, the composition will be real; but if they are distinguished by reason alone, the composition will not be real, but of reason. Since, indeed, Distinction is threefold: one real, another from the nature of the thing, and the third is the distinction of reason. That is called Real which is between two things, as between Peter and John. The distinction from the nature of the thing is posited between a thing and its mode, as between the point and the line; or it is also posited by others between formal rationes of the same thing, but distinct before the operation of the intellect, as between action and passion, which are really the same motion. Scotus posits the distinction from the nature of the thing because he asserts that the formal ratio of action and of passion are distinguished before the operation of the intellect. But the distinction of reason is called by all that which is not between things distinct on the part of the thing, but is made by the intellect.

His suppositis, duæ sunt opiniones: Prima Scoti, in 2. d. 3. quæst 1. & 7. Metaph. q. 16. vbi affirmat, gradum Generis, & Differentiæ, distingui ex natura rei, in quantum sunt rationes formales distinctæ, ante operationem intellectus: & cùm ex eis fiat compositio Speciei, consequenter debet concedere, talem compositionem esse realem, si non ex rebus diuersis, saltẽ ex rationibus formalibus eiusdem rei, ante operationem intellectus distinctis. Scotum sequuntur Antonius Andreas, in 2. loco citato, Ferra. 1. lib. contra gentes cap. 24. & 42. Fonseca 2. lib. Metaph. cap. 2. tex. 11. & lib. 4. cap. 2. q. 4. sectio. 3.

These things supposed, there are two opinions. The first is that of Scotus, in 2, d. 3, q. 1, and Metaph. 7, q. 16, where he affirms that the grade of Genus and that of Difference are distinguished from the nature of the thing, inasmuch as they are distinct formal rationes before the operation of the intellect; and since the composition of the Species is made from them, he must consequently grant that such a composition is real, if not from diverse things, at least from formal rationes of the same thing distinct before the operation of the intellect. Scotus is followed by Antonius Andreas, in 2, in the place cited; Ferrara, on Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 24 and 42; Fonseca, Metaph. 2, ch. 2, text 11, and bk. 4, ch. 2, q. 4, sect. 3.

25 Probatur primò, Quia gradus differentialis, realiter perficit gradum genericum, & non tantùm per intellectum: ergo Differentia ex natura rei contrahit genus: sed contrahere Genus, est componere cum eo Speciem: ergo realiter componit speciem: quare erit compositio realis. Vtraque consequentia potest probari, hoc exemplo. Quia gradus rationalitatis, perficit gradum naturæ sensitiuæ, & perficit perfectione reali: quia natura sensitiua, magis perfecta est realiter in homine, quàm in animali: ideo realiter dicitur contrahere genus: quia contrahere, nihil aliud est, quàm determinare, atque perficere.

25 It is proved, first: Because the differential grade perfects the generic grade really, and not only through the intellect; therefore the Difference contracts the genus from the nature of the thing; but to contract the Genus is to compose the Species together with it; therefore it composes the species really; wherefore the composition will be real. Both consequences can be proved by this example: Because the grade of rationality perfects the grade of the sensitive nature, and perfects it with a real perfection, because the sensitive nature is really more perfect in man than in animal, therefore it is said to contract the genus really: because to contract is nothing other than to determine and perfect.

p. 159

Secundò probatur, Quia si rationale non esset distinctum realiter ab animali, non esset distinctum realiter ab equo: consequens est falsum: ergo etiam antecedens. Probatur consequentia: nam quæcunque sunt eadem vni tertio, sunt eadem inter se: si ergo rationale est idem cum animali, ergo etiam hinnibile, quod est Differentia equi, erit idem cum eodem animali. Et ita rationale, hinnibile, erunt idẽ realiter, & consequenter rationale: & equus: quod patet esse falsum. Et confirmari potest: quia ea distinguuntur realiter, quorum vnum potest separari ab altero: sed quælibet Differentia, potest separari à Genere, & separabitur, si species quam constituit, pereat: ergo distinguitur realiter ab eo.

It is proved, second: Because if rational were not really distinct from animal, it would not be really distinct from horse; the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent also. The consequence is proved: for whatever things are the same as one third are the same as each other; if, therefore, rational is the same as animal, then neighing too, which is the Difference of horse, will be the same as that same animal; and so rational and neighing will be really the same, and consequently rational and horse: which is plainly false. And it can be confirmed: because those things are distinguished really of which one can be separated from the other; but any Difference whatever can be separated from the Genus, and will be separated if the species it constitutes perishes; therefore it is distinguished really from it.

Secunda opinio tenet Gradum Generis, & Differentiæ, aut conceptus obiectiui vtriusque, nec distingui realiter, nec ex natura rei, sed tantùm per intellectum: & ideo tantùm Distinctione rationis Et consequenter compositionem speciei, non esse realem, sed factam ab intellectu. Hæc est D. Thom. in opus. de ente, & essentia, c. 4. 7. Meta. lect. 4 & 1. part. q. 50. ar. 4. ad 1. & qu. 76. art. 3. ad 4. quam sequuntur Alexan. Alens. 7. Meta. tit. 11 & lib. 5. tit. 10. Duran. in 2. d. 3. qu. 2. num. 14. Heruæus, quodlib. 1. q. 9. Greg. in 1. d. 38. & ibidem Gab. cum cæteris nominalibus. Capreol. in 1. d. 8. qu. 2. art. 3. Caiet. de ente & essentia, ca. 4. quæst. 6. §. ad 2. dubium. Socinas 7. Meta. qu. 36. Iauel. ibidem, qu. 18. Niphus in Elucidario lib. 7. dispu. 15. cap 3. & 4. Sotus qu. 1. vniuersalium, concl. 3 & quæst. 2. art. 2. Toletus quæst. 3. Vniuersalium, Et est communis iam in schola, & vera.

The second opinion holds that the Grade of Genus and that of Difference, or the objective concepts of each, are distinguished neither really nor from the nature of the thing, but only through the intellect, and therefore only by a Distinction of reason; and consequently that the composition of the species is not real, but made by the intellect. This is St. Thomas’s, in the opusc. On Being and Essence, ch. 4; Metaph. 7, lect. 4; and 1 p., q. 50, a. 4, ad 1, and q. 76, a. 3, ad 4; whom Alexander of Hales follows, Metaph. 7, tit. 11, and bk. 5, tit. 10; Durandus, in 2, d. 3, q. 2, no. 14; Hervaeus, Quodlibet 1, q. 9; Gregory, in 1, d. 38, and Gabriel in the same place, with the other nominalists; Capreolus, in 1, d. 8, q. 2, a. 3; Cajetan, On Being and Essence, ch. 4, q. 6, § ad 2. dubium; Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 36; Javelli in the same place, q. 18; Nifo, in the Elucidarium, bk. 7, disp. 15, ch. 3 and 4; Soto, q. 1 on Universals, concl. 3, and q. 2, a. 2; Toledo, q. 3 on Universals. And it is now common in the school, and true.

26 Sed explicanda priùs est, deinde probanda: & pro eius explicatione notandũ primò, Compositionem Speciei, ex Genere, & Differentia, Metaphysicam esse, & non Physicam: & ideo non fieri eis, tanquam ex diuersis rebus, vt fit compositio Physica, ex materia, & forma, quę sunt res diuersæ. sed tanquam ex diuersis gradibus essentialibus, eiusdem, vt compositio hominis, ex gradu naturæ sensitiuæ, & rationalis: Quare de compositione Physica, nõ est dubium, quin sit realis: sed de compositione Metaphysica, maxima dubitandi ratio esse potest: quia non est certum, An gradus isti, aut conceptus, distincti sint ex natura rei, vel solùm distinguantur per intellectum.

26 But it must first be explained, then proved. And for its explanation it should be noted, first, that the composition of the Species from Genus and Difference is Metaphysical and not Physical; and therefore it is not made from them as from diverse things, as the Physical composition is made from matter and form, which are diverse things, but as from diverse essential grades of the same thing, as the composition of man from the grade of the sensitive nature and of the rational. Wherefore of the Physical composition there is no doubt that it is real; but of the Metaphysical Composition there can be the greatest reason for doubting, because it is not certain whether these grades, or concepts, are distinct from the nature of the thing, or are distinguished only through the intellect.

27 Secundò notandum, Genus, & Differentiam, tribus modis sumi posse. Primò, vt sunt in diuersis Speciebus, & indiuiduis: vt Animal in Leone, aut hoc Leone, & Rationale in Homine, & in hoc, aut illo Homine. Et hoc modo, certum est, non solùm ex natura rei, sed realiter

27 Second, it should be noted that Genus and Difference can be taken in three ways. First, as they are in diverse Species and individuals: as Animal in Lion, or in this Lion, and Rational in Man, and in this or that Man. And in this way it is certain that they are distinguished not only from the nature of the thing, but really

p. 160

distingui: nam Animal, quod est in Homine, aliud est essentialiter, ab Animali, quod est in Equo: quia per coniunctionem cum differentia Equi, fit equus: licèt vt abstractum à Differentiis, sit vnum & idem, vnitate solùm Generica: quæ non tollit distinctionem specificam, quam habet in diuersis Speciebus, per diuersas Differentias: vt Animal, quod est in hoc Homine: & Animal, quod est in hoc Leone, distinctam habent entitatem realem. Secundo modo, sumuntur, prout sunt in eadem Specie, aut in eodem indiuiduo, vt in Homine, Animal & Rationale, & in Petro, hoc animal, & hoc Rationale. Tertiò, prout Genus consideratur abstractum ab Speciebus, & Differentiis, & vt contrahibile per eas: & hoc modo, dicitur esse extra rationem differentiarum: qui eas non includit actu, sed gradum proprium suæ naturæ: vt animal abstractum, solùm actu includit gradum naturæ sensitiuæ, non rationalis, aut irrationalis, nisi in potentia tantùm. Et de gradu Generis, & Differentiæ his duobus modis postremis sumptis, affirmat Scotus, ante operationem intellectus, & ex natura rei distingui, sed negat. D. Tho. & qui eum sequuntur: & asserunt, solùm distingui per intellectum, & ideo solùm ratione.

: for the Animal that is in Man is essentially other than the Animal that is in Horse, because through conjunction with the difference of Horse it becomes horse; although, as abstracted from the Differences, it is one and the same by a Generic unity only, which does not take away the specific distinction that it has in diverse Species through diverse Differences: as the Animal that is in this Man and the Animal that is in this Lion have a distinct real entity. In the second way they are taken as they are in the same Species or in the same individual: as in Man, Animal and Rational, and in Peter, this animal and this Rational. Third, as Genus is considered abstracted from the Species and Differences, and as contractible by them; and in this way it is said to be outside the ratio of the differences, because it does not include them in act, but the proper grade of its nature: as animal abstracted includes in act only the grade of the sensitive nature, not of the rational or the irrational, except only in potency. And of the grade of Genus and of Difference, taken in these last two ways, Scotus affirms that they are distinguished before the operation of the intellect and from the nature of the thing; but St. Thomas and those who follow him deny it, and assert that they are distinguished only through the intellect, and therefore only by reason.

Tertiò notandum, Quòd licèt Scotus & alij sentiant, gradus omnes genericos, & differentiales, eiusdem Speciei, à diuersis formis substantialibus procedere, tamen D. Tho. cuius sententia communis est iam in schola, tenet ab eadem forma substantiali promanare, vt omnes gradus essentiales hominis, nempe gradum Substantiæ, gradum Corporis, gradum Viuentis, gradum naturæ Sensitiuæ & Rationalis, ab eadem anima rationali procedere, nec esse aliam formam substantialem in homine. Cùm tamen Scotus, pro gradu Substantiæ & gradu Corporis, ponat vnam formam substantialem, quam vocat formam Corporeitatis, & pro reliquis gradibus inferioribus, aliam distinctam realiter, nempe animam rationalem. Et hæc diuersitas Formarum, videtur arguere Distinctionem aliquam ex natura rei, inter gradus essentiales, ab eis proueniente Sicut Identitas formæ substantialis, apud D. Tho. arguit Identitatem eorum.

Third, it should be noted that, although Scotus and others hold that all the generic and differential grades of the same Species proceed from diverse substantial forms, St. Thomas, whose opinion is now common in the school, holds that they emanate from the same substantial form: so that all the essential grades of man, namely the grade of Substance, the grade of Body, the grade of Living, the grade of the Sensitive and of the Rational nature, proceed from the same rational soul, and there is no other substantial form in man. Whereas Scotus, for the grade of Substance and the grade of Body, posits one substantial form, which he calls the form of Corporeity, and for the remaining lower grades another, really distinct, namely the rational soul. And this diversity of Forms seems to argue some Distinction from the nature of the thing between the essential grades proceeding from them, just as the Identity of the substantial form, according to St. Thomas, argues their identity.

28 His prænotatis, probatur cõmunis sententia duplici arg. Primò: Quia si Genus distinguitur ex natura rei, à Differẽtiis, aut distinguitur vt abstractum ab eis, hoc est tanquam gradus Vniuersalis, à particularibus, vt animal in communi, ab Equo, & Leone, vel vt contractum in Speciebus, & indiuiduis, vt in Petro hoc Animal, & hoc Rationale, sed neutro modo distingui potest: ergo non distinguuntur isti gradus ex natura

28 These things noted beforehand, the common opinion is proved by a twofold argument. First: Because if Genus is distinguished from the Differences from the nature of the thing, either it is distinguished as abstracted from them, that is, as a Universal grade from the particulars, as animal in common from Horse and Lion; or as contracted in the Species and individuals, as in Peter this Animal and this Rational; but it cannot be distinguished in either way; therefore these grades are not distinguished from the nature of the thing.

p. 161

rei. Maior est necessaria: quia his tantùm duobus modis considerari possunt in ordine Metaphysico, vt notauimus. Minor verò probatur: Nam si distinguuntur tanquam Vniuersale à particularibus, ergo datur Vniuersale ante operationem intellectus: quod superiùs probauimus falsum. Quòd verò non possint distingui, tanquam diuersi gradus, singularizati in Petro, probo. Quia in vno indiuiduo, tantùm datur vna Differentia indiuidualis realiter, per quam omnes gradus generici, & differentiales, fiunt singulares, licèt vnicuique gradui correspondeat sua Differentia indiuidualis, sola ratione distincta, vt gradui Gorporis, hoc Corpus, & gradui Animalis, hoc Animal, &c. sed gradus omnes, & singuli, sunt idem ex natura rei, cum Differentia indiuiduali Petri, eos contrahente: ergo sunt idem inter sese. Probatur minor: nam si ex natura rei distingueretur, eodem modo sequeretur dari Vniuersale ex natura rei, & ante operationem intellectus, distinctum à singulari.

The major is necessary, because only in these two ways can they be considered in the metaphysical order, as we noted. The minor is proved: for if they are distinguished as the universal from the particulars, then the universal is given before the operation of the intellect, which we proved above to be false. That they cannot be distinguished as diverse grades singularized in Peter, I prove. Because in one individual there is really given only one individual difference, through which all the generic and differential grades become singular, although to each grade there corresponds its own individual difference, distinct by reason alone: as to the grade of body, this body, and to the grade of animal, this animal, etc.; but all the grades, and each of them, are the same from the nature of the thing with the individual difference of Peter which contracts them; therefore they are the same among themselves. The minor is proved: for if they were distinguished from the nature of the thing, it would follow in the same way that a universal is given from the nature of the thing, and before the operation of the intellect, distinct from the singular.

Secundò, Omnes isti gradus generici, & differentiales, tribuuntur ab eadem forma substantiali: omnes sumuntur ab eadem natura reali: imò omnes reperiuntur, in eadem forma Physica, quæ est eadem Entitas simplex: ergo non possunt distingui, nisi à solo intellectu. Consequentia euidens est: Quia in eadem Entitate simplici, in eadem essentia, & natura, nihil potest esse distinctum ex natura rei. Quocirca probatur Antecedens: quia ab eadem natura humana reali, sumuntur omnes gradus generici, & differentiales, à Substantia vsque ad naturam Sensitiuam, & Rationalem: omnes etiam in eadem natura reali Petri reperiuntur, cum qua eadem res sunt: omnes denique, in eadem Entitate simplicissima animæ rationalis, in qua fundantur, existunt: nam eadem est forma substantialis Corporea, Vitalis, Sensitiua, & Rationalis: ergo sicut gradus isti Physicè loquendo, non possunt distingui, nisi ab intellectu, ita multò minùs distingui poterunt, Metaphysicè eos accipiendo.

Second: all these generic and differential grades are bestowed by the same substantial form; all are taken from the same real nature; indeed all are found in the same physical form, which is the same simple entity; therefore they cannot be distinguished except by the intellect alone. The consequence is evident, because in the same simple entity, in the same essence and nature, nothing can be distinct from the nature of the thing. Accordingly the antecedent is proved: because from the same real human nature are taken all the generic and differential grades, from substance down to sensitive and rational nature; all of them are also found in the same real nature of Peter, with which they are the same thing; finally, all of them exist in the same most simple entity of the rational soul, in which they are founded: for the corporeal, vital, sensitive, and rational substantial form is the same; therefore, just as these grades, speaking physically, cannot be distinguished except by the intellect, so much less will they be able to be distinguished taking them metaphysically.

29 Sed si non distinguuntur, nisi sola ratione, explicandum est, qua distinctione rationis: quia duplex dari solet, Vna habens fundamentum in re ipsa concepta, quæ appellatur Distinctio rationis Ratiocinatæ: Alia in solo intellectu, imperfectè concipiente, hoc est, per plures conceptus, ea quæ per vnũ concipi possunt, quam vocant Distinctionem rationis Ratiocinantis, vt ea qua distinguitur Petrus à seipso, in hac prædicatione identica, Petrus est Petrus. Respondeo, distingui Genus à Differentia, Distinctione rationis Ratiocinatæ. Et ratio est manifesta: quia in eadem essentia specifica, reperitur vterque

29 But if they are not distinguished except by reason alone, it must be explained by which distinction of reason: because a twofold one is customarily given. One having a foundation in the thing itself that is conceived, which is called the distinction of reason reasoned about; the other in the intellect alone, conceiving imperfectly, that is, through several concepts, things that can be conceived through one, which they call the distinction of reason of the reasoning intellect: such as that by which Peter is distinguished from himself in this identical predication, Peter is Peter. I reply that genus is distinguished from difference by a distinction of reason reasoned about. And the reason is manifest: because in the same specific essence is found each L

p. 162

gradus, & secundùm eos habet operationes realiter distinctas: Vt Homo, secundùm gradum Genericum animalis, habet operationes sensitiuas, vt videre, & audire: & secũdum gradum Differentiæ, habet operationes rationalis intellectus, & voluntatis: ergo habet fundamentum ex parte sua, vt intellectus distinguat in ea gradum genericum à differentiali. Verum quidem est, quòd intellectus noster, non distingueret hos gradus nisi imperfecto modo cognosceret: sed nec sufficeret imperfectus modus cognoscendi, nisi in re ipsa daretur fundamentum, & cùm non detur in Petro fundamẽtum distinguendi eum à seipso, non potest intellectus tali distinctione eum distinguere: sed solùm alia minori, quæ vocatur rationis Ratiocinantis.

grade, and according to them it has really distinct operations: as man, according to the generic grade of animal, has sensitive operations, such as seeing and hearing; and according to the grade of difference, he has the operations of the rational intellect and will; therefore it has a foundation on its own part for the intellect to distinguish in it the generic grade from the differential. It is indeed true that our intellect would not distinguish these grades unless it cognized in an imperfect manner; but neither would the imperfect mode of cognizing suffice unless a foundation were given in the thing itself; and since there is not given in Peter a foundation for distinguishing him from himself, the intellect cannot distinguish him by such a distinction, but only by another, lesser one, which is called the distinction of reason of the reasoning intellect.

30 Ex his omnibus, colligitur hæc conclusio, quia respondetur quæstioni: Licèt compositio Speciei ex Genere, & differẽtia realis sit, ex parte componentium realium, tamen ex parte distinctionis eorum, non est realis, sed rationis: & cùm vtraque conditio necessaria sit ad realem compositionem, nempe componentia esse realia, & realiter, aut ex natura rei distincta simpliciter loquendo, non est cõpositio realis vocanda, sed rationis facta ab intellectu: eodẽ modo, quo fieret ex natura rei, si gradus genericus, & differẽtialis essẽt distincti ex natura rei.

30 From all these is gathered this conclusion, by which the question is answered: Although the composition of the species from genus and difference is real on the part of the real components, nevertheless on the part of their distinction it is not real but of reason; and since both conditions are necessary for a real composition, namely that the components be real and really, or from the nature of the thing, distinct, then, speaking simply, it is not to be called a real composition but one of reason, made by the intellect in the same way as it would be made from the nature of the thing if the generic and the differential grade were distinct from the nature of the thing.

Ad primum argu. negandum est Antecedens, quòd gradus differentialis perficiat genericum, ex natura rei: nam cùm non sint distincti ex natura rei, sed idem, nec ex natura rei coniungi possunt: & ideo nec vnus perficere alterum: nam si nõ sunt distincti, non erunt vnus & alter: solùm ergo perficit illum, supposita distinctione facta ab intellectu, inter eos: & ideo, solùm per intellectum vnus perficit alterum: sicut solùm per intellectum distinguentem eos, coniungitur illi. Itaque realis est perfectio, quàm habet gradus genericus, in Specie, per gradum differentialem, & non Ens rationis: sed sicut ex natura rei, nõ sunt distincti, ita ex natura rei, eadem est perfectio in eo semper: sed quia intellectus distinguens ea, quæ ex natura rei non sunt distincta, considerat vnum, non considerato alio, & ideo sub esse quodam imperfecto, & perfectibili per alium, dicitur vnus perficere alium: quod non est verum ex natura rei, cùm nec sint distincti, sed solùm per intellectũ distinguentem, Realis ergo est perfectio ipsa, quam vnus accipit ab illo, supposita distinctione, quam facit intellectus: & ideo propter defectum distinctionis, falsum est, quòd vnus perficiat alterum, ex natura rei: nam vtrumque requiritur, vt verum sit, nempe, quòd sint distincti ex natura rei, & etiam quòd ex natura rei, vnus

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be denied, that the differential grade perfects the generic from the nature of the thing: for since they are not distinct from the nature of the thing, but the same, neither can they be conjoined from the nature of the thing; and therefore neither can one perfect the other: for if they are not distinct, they will not be one and another. It perfects it, then, only on the supposition of a distinction made by the intellect between them; and therefore one perfects the other only through the intellect, just as it is conjoined to it only through the intellect distinguishing them. Thus the perfection which the generic grade has in the species through the differential grade is real, and not a being of reason; but just as they are not distinct from the nature of the thing, so from the nature of the thing the perfection in it is always the same; but because the intellect, distinguishing those things which are not distinct from the nature of the thing, considers the one without considering the other, and therefore under a certain imperfect being, perfectible by the other, the one is said to perfect the other: which is not true from the nature of the thing, since they are not distinct, but only through the intellect distinguishing them. Real, therefore, is the perfection itself which the one receives from the other, on the supposition of the distinction which the intellect makes; and therefore, for lack of a distinction, it is false that one perfects the other from the nature of the thing: for both are required for it to be true, namely that they be distinct from the nature of the thing, and also that from the nature of the thing one

p. 163

contrahat, aut determinet alterum: quare deficiente altero, deficit etiam veritas Antecedentis,

contract or determine the other: wherefore, if one of the two is lacking, the truth of the antecedent also fails.

31 Ad secundum, neganda est consequentia: & dum sic probatur: si Rationale est idem cum Animali: ergo etiam cum Equo, iterum neganda est Consequentia: nam Animal, non est quid tertium respectu Rationalis, & hinnibilis, nisi solùm per intellectum: quia à parte rei, distinctum Animal est in Homine, & Equo: & ideo non sequitur, quòd si Rationale est idem cum Animali, & etiam hinnibile, sint idem inter se: quia non sunt idem cum eo, tanquam cum aliquo tertio, ex natura rei, sed tanquam aliquo tertio, secundùm rationem. Bene autem potest intelligi, quòd duo aliqua sint idem, cum aliquo tertio, sola ratione ab eis distincto: & non sint eadem inter sese: vt Petrus, & Ioannes, sunt idem cum Homine abstracto ab eis, & inter se distinguuntur realiter, Itaque vt principium illud verùm sit, Quæcunque sunt eadem vni tertio, sint eadem inter se, requiritur, quòd sit tertium, ex natura rei distinctum ab vtroque: ex defectu igitur Distinctionis fit, vt cùm Genus non sit tertium, ante operationem intellectus, respectu Differentiarum & Specierum, non possint cum eo comparari ex natura rei, sed solum per intellectum illud abstrahentem, & distinguentem: & ideo vt non possit inferri identitas realis differentiarum oppositarum inter se, ex eo quòd sint idem cum genere ab eis abstracto per intellectum.

31 To the second, the consequence is to be denied; and when it is proved thus: if rational is the same as animal, therefore also as horse, again the consequence is to be denied: for animal is not some third thing with respect to rational and neighing except through the intellect alone, because on the part of the thing animal is distinct in man and in horse; and therefore it does not follow that, if rational is the same as animal, and neighing also, they are the same among themselves: because they are not the same as it as with some third thing from the nature of the thing, but as with some third thing according to reason. But it can well be understood that two things are the same as some third thing distinct from them by reason alone, and yet are not the same among themselves: as Peter and John are the same as man abstracted from them, and are really distinguished among themselves. Thus, in order that that principle be true, Whatever things are the same as one third thing are the same among themselves, it is required that the third thing be distinct from the nature of the thing from each of them. From the lack of distinction, then, it comes about that, since genus is not a third thing with respect to the differences and species before the operation of the intellect, they cannot be compared with it from the nature of the thing, but only through the intellect abstracting and distinguishing it; and therefore that a real identity of the opposed differences among themselves cannot be inferred from the fact that they are the same as the genus abstracted from them by the intellect.

Ad confirmationem, eodem ferè modo respondetur, quòd cùm Genus non sit distinctum à Differentiis, nisi per intellectum illud abstrahentem ab eis: non dicuntur ei aduenire, aut ab eo separari realiter, sed solùm per intellectum, & secundùm rationem: & hoc tantùm modo, potest quælibet ab eo separari, salua eius essentia: ex quo non sequitur distingui realiter, aut ex natura rei, sed sola ratione.

To the confirmation the reply is made in almost the same way: that since genus is not distinct from the differences except through the intellect abstracting it from them, they are not said to come to it, or to be separated from it, really, but only through the intellect and according to reason; and only in this way can any of them be separated from it with its essence preserved: from which it does not follow that they are distinguished really, or from the nature of the thing, but by reason alone.

32 Vnum restat argu. non facilè, aduersus nostram sententiam: quia si compositio ex Genere, & Differentia, non est realis, sed rationis: ergo nihil reale ponit in natura, in qua reperitur: & si nihil reale, nihil etiam perfectionis, aut imperfectionis. Probatur vtraque consequentia, quia ex eo, quòd intellectus aliquid intelligit vno, aut alio modo, solùm prouenit ei denominatio extrinseca, intellecti eo modo: extrinseca verò denominatio, nihil imperfectionis in ea ponere potest. Quæ si ita se habent, sequitur, in Deo posse reperiri compositionem ex Genere, & Differentia: quia non videtur vllo modo concedendum, cùm summæ simplicitati eius repugnet quælibet compositio. Respondetur, Talem compositionem,

32 One argument, not an easy one, remains against our view: because if the composition from genus and difference is not real but of reason, then it posits nothing real in the nature in which it is found; and if nothing real, then nothing of perfection or imperfection either. Each consequence is proved: because from the fact that the intellect understands something in one way or another, there accrues to it only the extrinsic denomination of being understood in that way; but an extrinsic denomination can posit nothing of imperfection in it. If this is so, it follows that composition from genus and difference can be found in God: which does not seem in any way to be granted, since every composition is repugnant to his supreme simplicity. The reply is: Such a composition L ij

p. 164

non esse admittendam in Deo, secundùm communem sententiam scholæ.

is not to be admitted in God, according to the common opinion of the school.

Cuius duplex est ratio immissis aliis. Prima: quia conceptos Generis tria dicit sibi intrinseca, nempe Esse limitatum, & extra rationem differentiarum, esse imperfectum: & per alium perfectibilem essentialiter: & hæc quidem cum fundamento in re ipsa, quæ omnia intrinsecam imperfectionem significant: & ideo aliena sunt à Deo, summè perfecto, in quo nihil limitatum, aut finitum concipimus, neque aliquid, quod essentialiter sit extra alia, aut essentialiter imperfectum, & per aliud perfectibile: sed immensitas diuina, & infinita perfectio eius, atque esse purissimum actum, ea excludunt, etiam vt à nobis imperfecto modo intelligitur.

Of this there is a twofold reason, setting aside others. The first: because the concept of genus implies three things intrinsic to itself, namely to be limited, and to be imperfect outside the ratio of the differences, and to be essentially perfectible through another; and this indeed with a foundation in the thing itself; all of which signify imperfection intrinsically; and therefore they are alien to God, who is supremely perfect, in whom we conceive nothing limited or finite, nor anything which is essentially outside others, or essentially imperfect and perfectible through another; but the divine immensity and his infinite perfection, and his being most pure act, exclude these things, even as he is understood by us in an imperfect manner.

33 Secunda ratio: Quia conceptus genericus duo alia habet intrinseca. Primum, quòd communis esse possit atque vniuocus multis Speciebus: sed talem conceptum in Deo reperiri repugnat: ergo repugnat dari in eo Genus, & Differentiam. Probatur minor: quia conceptus de Deo formatus à nobis, non potest esse communis multis Diis specie differentibus, quos euidenter cognoscimus esse impossibiles: ergo solùm potest esse communis Deo, & creaturis, plusquam specie differentibus: sed Deo, & creaturis, minùs potest dari aliquid commune vniuocum, quàm Substantiæ, & Accidenti: ergo sicut Ens non potest esse Genus ad illa, ita neque in Deo dari potest conceptus vniuocus, à nobis formatus, qui sit vniuocus, & consequenter, neque qui sit Genus.

33 The second reason: because the generic concept has two other things intrinsic to it. The first, that it can be common and univocal to many species; but it is repugnant that such a concept be found in God; therefore it is repugnant that genus and difference be given in him. The minor is proved: because a concept formed by us of God cannot be common to many gods differing in species, whom we evidently know to be impossible; therefore it can only be common to God and creatures, which differ more than in species; but less can something common and univocal be given to God and creatures than to substance and accident; therefore, just as being cannot be a genus to these, so neither can there be given in God a univocal concept, formed by us, which is univocal, and consequently neither one which is a genus.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Quæst. 5. Vtrum differentia superior includatur in inferiori, & de illa prædicetur — Whether a superior difference is included in an inferior one, and is predicated of it.

Vtrùm Differentia superior includatur in inferiori & de illa prædicetur.

[…]

34 DVplex distinctio Differentiæ necessaria est ad explicãdum titulũ quæstionis. Prima est, Differentiæ superioris, & inferioris: & Differentia superior vocatur illa, quæ constituit speciem magis vniuersalem: Inferior verò, quæ constituit speciem inferiorem: vt Differentia superior est Corporeũ respectu Differentiæ Viuentis: & hæc respectu Sensibilis: & Sensibile respectu Rationalis. Petit igitur titulus quæstionis, An Corporeum includatur in Viuente: & Sensibile in Rationali: &, An vera sit prædicatio, Rationale est Sensibile.

34 A twofold distinction of difference is necessary for explaining the title of the question. The first is of superior and inferior difference: and that difference is called superior which constitutes a more universal species; inferior, that which constitutes an inferior species: as corporeal is a superior difference with respect to the difference living, and this with respect to sensible, and sensible with respect to rational. The title of the question therefore asks whether corporeal is included in living, and sensible in rational; and whether the predication Rational is sensible is true.

Secunda distinctio est, Differentiæ cuiuslibet, quæ duobus modis sumi potest Materialiter, & Formaliter: sumitur autem materialiter in quantum totum dicit, quod species ipsa, nempe gradum generis, quasi pro materiali, & gradum proprium, quasi pro formali: vt rationale, dicit pro materiali naturam

The second distinction is of any difference whatever, which can be taken in two ways, materially and formally. It is taken materially inasmuch as it implies the whole that the species itself implies, namely the grade of the genus, as for the material, and its proper grade, as for the formal: as rational implies for the material the nature

p. 165

sensitiuam, pro formali verò gradum rationalitatis: sed formaliter sumitur, pro solo gradu rationalitatis: quemadmodum Album, materialiter sumptum, dicit Corpus affectum albedine, sed dum sumitur formaliter, solam Albedinem denominantem corpus. Et vtramque acceptionem habet differentia, significata in concreto, sicut vtramque habet Album. Nam Rationale, & pro tota natura hominis sumitur, & etiam pro solo vltimo gradu eius significato tamen in concreto. Vnde falsò putant aliqui, Differentiam formaliter sumi, dum significatur in abstracto, vt nomine Rationalitatis, aut Sensibilitatis: hoc enim modo significata, non est Differentia, sed principium differentię, vt natura Generis nomine abstracto significata, solum vt principium Generis, & non vt Genus significatur. In concreto ergo significatur, etiam dum formaliter sumitur, sed tantùm pro gradu vltimo, atque proprio.

sensitive, but for the formal the grade of rationality; but formally it is taken for the grade of rationality alone: just as white, taken materially, implies a body affected with whiteness, but when it is taken formally, only the whiteness denominating the body. And difference, signified in the concrete, has both acceptations, just as white has both. For rational is taken both for the whole nature of man and also for its last grade alone, though signified in the concrete. Hence some falsely think that difference is taken formally when it is signified in the abstract, as by the name rationality or sensibility: for signified in this way it is not difference but the principle of difference, just as the nature of the genus signified by an abstract name is signified only as the principle of the genus, and not as genus. It is signified, then, in the concrete even when it is taken formally, but only for the last and proper grade.

35 Et quidem, si Differentiam inferiorem materialiter accipiamus, certum est, quòd superiorem includat, & hæc de illa prædicetur: vnde vera est hæc, Rationale est Sensibile: quamuis non sit formalis. Nam Rationale, saltem pro materiali, dicit naturam animalis: in qua includitur Differentia eius, nempe Sensibile, ergo includit etiam Sensibile, quæ est differentia superior.

35 And indeed, if we take the inferior difference materially, it is certain that it includes the superior and that the latter is predicated of it; hence this is true, Rational is sensible, although it is not formal. For rational, at least for the material, implies the nature of animal, in which its difference, namely sensible, is included; therefore it also includes sensible, which is the superior difference.

Difficultas igitur quæstionis est, de Differentia inferiori, formaliter sumpta, An includat superiorem, & hæc de illa prædicetur, vt, An Rationale sumptum, prout de formali, dicit vltimum gradum naturæ rationalis, per quem constituitur homo, includat sensibile, & cæteras differentias superiores.

The difficulty of the question, then, concerns the inferior difference taken formally: whether it includes the superior, and the latter is predicated of it; as, whether rational, taken as it implies formally the last grade of rational nature, through which man is constituted, includes sensible and the other superior differences.

Et prima opinio affirmat, formaliter includi, & prædicari: quam Soncinas 7. Meta. qu. 37. asserit, se defendere exercitij gratia, licèt opposita ei magis placeat. In eam etiam inclinat Sotus, cap. de genere: qu. 1. ad 3. sed expressè eam tenet Cant. in expositione huius capitis.

And the first opinion affirms that it is included and predicated formally: which Soncinas, Metaph. 7, q. 37, asserts he defends for the sake of exercise, although the opposite pleases him more. Soto too inclines to it, ch. on genus, q. 1, ad 3; but Cant. expressly holds it in his exposition of this chapter.

Probatur primò ex doctrina Aristot. 7. Meta. tex. 45. vbi tria docet de differentiis. Primum, nihil referre siue sola vltima Differentia ponatur in definitione, vel etiam omnes superiores: quia vltima includit omnes. Vnde eodem modo definimus hominem, si solùm dicamus esse animal rationale, ac si omnes superiores differentias ponamus, dicentes: Homo est Substantia corporea animata, sensitiua, rationalis. Secundò asserit, vltimam differentiam, esse totam Substantiam speciei: & ideo si ea ponatur in definitione non licere superiorem aliam addere: quia committeretur vitium nugationis, idem bis repetendo; vt si dicamus, Homo est animal rationale,

It is proved first from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 7, text 45, where he teaches three things about differences. First, that it makes no difference whether the last difference alone is placed in the definition, or also all the superior ones, because the last includes all. Hence we define man in the same way if we only say that he is a rational animal as if we placed all the superior differences, saying: Man is a corporeal, animate, sensitive, rational substance.
