Second, he asserts that the last difference is the whole substance of the species, and therefore, if it is placed in the definition, it is not permitted to add another superior one, because the fault of nugation would be committed, by repeating the same thing twice: as if we should say, Man is a rational L iij

p. 166

sensibile, nugatoriam definitionem assignamus. Asserit tertiò, ad inueniendam Differentiam vltimam alicuius speciei, diuidendam esse superiorem, per duas inferiores oppositas, vt bipedem, quę est differentia animalis, (accidentalis quidem, sed qua vtitur Arist. loco essentialis) per fissos, & non fissos pedes habentem, hoc est, scissos, vel non scissos: nam fissos habere pedes (inquit) differentia inferior est, respectu bipedis, cùm fissio pedis, sit quædam pedalitas: id est cùm fissio pedis, includat pedalitatem, idem significantem, quod habere pedes.

sensible animal, we assign a nugatory definition. He asserts third that, in order to find the last difference of some species, the superior must be divided by two opposed inferior ones: as biped, which is a difference of animal (an accidental one, indeed, but one which Aristotle uses in place of an essential one), by having cloven and not cloven feet, that is, split or not split. For to have cloven feet (he says) is an inferior difference with respect to biped, since the cleaving of the foot is a certain footedness: that is, since the cleaving of the foot includes footedness, which signifies the same as to have feet.

Ex quolibet autem horum trium, videtur euidenter sequi, quòd Differentia inferior, includat superiorem. Ex primo quidem quia formaliter sumitur Differentia, dum in definitione ponitur: sed vltima Differentia quæ inferior est, posita in definitione, tantum valet, ac si omnes superiores ponantur: ergo eas includit: nam si non includeret, non tantum valeret. Ex secundò verò: quia non posset esse tota substantia rei, nisi superiores includeret, quas certum est ad substantiam infimæ speciei pertinere. Sed ex postremo efficacius sequitur: quia si ad inueniendum vltimam differentiam, diuidenda est superior per duas inferiores oppositas: ergo in vtraque includitur formaliter, & de vtraque formaliter prędicatur. Probatur euidenter consequentia: quia in bona diuisione, Diuisum formaliter sumptum, includitur in singulis membris diuidentibus, & de illis prædicatur, etiam formaliter: vt animal, de animali rationali, & irrationali. Et tandem, Arist. ipse, prædicat Differentiam superiorem de inferiori, formaliter sumpta, dum ait, Verum esse, quòd fissio pedis, sit pedalitas: hæc enim superior Differentia est: & illa inferior dicitur.

But from each of these three it seems evidently to follow that the inferior difference includes the superior. From the first, indeed, because difference is taken formally when it is placed in the definition; but the last difference, which is the inferior, placed in the definition, is worth as much as if all the superior ones were placed; therefore it includes them: for if it did not include them, it would not be worth as much. From the second: because it could not be the whole substance of the thing unless it included the superior ones, which it is certain pertain to the substance of the lowest species. But from the last it follows more efficaciously: because if, in order to find the last difference, the superior is to be divided by two opposed inferior ones, then it is included formally in each and is predicated formally of each. The consequence is proved evidently: because in a good division the divided, taken formally, is included in each of the dividing members and is predicated of them, also formally: as animal of rational and irrational animal. And finally Aristotle himself predicates the superior difference of the inferior, taken formally, when he says, It is true that the cleaving of the foot is footedness: for this is the superior difference, and that is called the inferior.

37 Probatur deinde ratione. Primò, quia Rationale formaliter sumptum, est Substantia: Corporea igitur, aut Incorporea: & cùm Corporea sit, includet formaliter differentiam superiorem, vt etiam probat hic syllogismus in Datisi: Omnis homo formaliter est sensibilis: homo formaliter est rationalis, ergo rationale formaliter est sensibile.

37 It is proved next by reason. First, because rational, taken formally, is a substance: therefore corporeal or incorporeal; and since it is corporeal, it will include formally the superior difference, as this syllogism in Datisi also proves: Every man is formally sensible; man is formally rational; therefore the rational is formally sensible.

Secundò: Si Differentia inferior non includeret superiorem, maximè id fieret, quia est conceptus simplex, & ideò non potest componi, nec resolui in plures alios conceptus: quia iam daretur processus in infinitum: sed conceptus genericus, est etiam simplex: & nihilominus includit genera superiora: vt Animal, includit Viuens, Corpus, & Substantiam: ergo etiam si Differentia simplex conceptus, includere poterit differentias superiores.

Second: if the inferior difference did not include the superior, this would happen chiefly because it is a simple concept, and therefore cannot be composed of or resolved into several other concepts, since then there would be a process to infinity; but the generic concept is also simple, and nevertheless it includes the superior genera, as animal includes living, body, and substance; therefore even if difference is a simple concept, it will be able to include the superior differences.

p. 167

Secunda opinio negat, Differentiam inferiorem formaliter sumptam, includere superiorem: & consequenter negat, quòd hæc prædicetur de illa formaliter. Quam sequuntur Scotus in 4. dist. 11. q. 3. § ad rationes Capreol. in 1. dist. 8. q. 2. in solut. ad 5. arg. Sot. Card. Toletus cap. de substantia, dub. 2. Mercatus 1. post cap. 4. q 3 ad 3 Fonseca 5. Metaphys. cap. 28. q. 18. sect. 1. Et videtur mihi non solùm probabilior, sed vera, & quæ euidenter colligitur ex doctrina Aristotelis, & Diui Thomæ.

The second opinion denies that the inferior difference, taken formally, includes the superior, and consequently denies that the latter is predicated of it formally. It is followed by Scotus, 4, d. 11, q. 3, § ad rationes; Capreolus, 1, d. 8, q. 2, in the solution to the 5th argument; Soto; Cardinal Toledo, ch. on substance, doubt 2; Mercado, 1 post ch. 4, q. 3, ad 3; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 28, q. 18, sect. 1. And it seems to me not only more probable but true, and evidently gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle and St. Thomas.

38 Vt autem hæc ita esse probemus, duo sunt præsupponenda, tanquam fundamenta certa ac necessaria. Primum est, Differentiam quamcunque, siue inferiorem, siue superiorem, includi formaliter in sua specie, quam constituit, vt rationale formaliter in homine, & Sensibile formaliter est in animali. Quod probatur euidenter: quia Differentia formaliter, constituit Speciem: ergo formalis pars illius est: sed pars includitur formaliter in toto: ergo Differentia includitur formaliter in Specie.

38 But in order that we may prove these things to be so, two things are to be presupposed as certain and necessary foundations. The first is that any difference whatever, whether inferior or superior, is included formally in its species, which it constitutes: as rational is formally in man, and sensible is formally in animal. This is proved evidently: because difference formally constitutes the species; therefore it is a formal part of it; but a part is included formally in the whole; therefore difference is included formally in the species.

Secundum fundamentum est, Omnes Species subalternas, esse Genera, respectu inferiorum, vt Animal, respectu equi, & leonis: & Viuens, respectu animalis, & plantæ. Ex quibus sequitur: quòd in quocunque includitur formaliter differentia subalterna, formaliter etiam includitur genus subalternum, quod est subalterna species, per eandem Differentiam constituta. Gratia exempli: Animal est species subalterna, constituta formaliter per Differentiam sensibilem, quam necesse est includere formaliter: ergo in quocunque includitur formaliter sensibile, includitur etiam formaliter animal: sicut in quocunque includitur formaliter rationale, includitur formaliter homo. Eadem igitur est quæstio: An Differentia inferior formaliter sumpta, includat superiorem, &, An includat Genus, quod est Species subalterna, per eam constituta: vt eadem quæstio est, An rationale, formaliter sumptum, includat Sensibile, &, An includat Animal. Vnde si probatum fuerit, non includere Genus superius, probatum erit, quòd non includat Differentiam superiorem: & conclusum, veram esse nostram sententiam.

The second foundation is that all subalternate species are genera with respect to their inferiors: as animal with respect to horse and lion, and living with respect to animal and plant. From which it follows that in whatever a subalternate difference is formally included, the subalternate genus, which is the subalternate species constituted through the same difference, is also formally included. For example: animal is a subalternate species, constituted formally through the difference sensible, which it necessarily includes formally; therefore in whatever sensible is formally included, animal is also formally included, just as in whatever rational is formally included, man is formally included. The question, then, is the same: whether the inferior difference, taken formally, includes the superior, and whether it includes the genus which is the subalternate species constituted through it; just as it is the same question whether rational, taken formally, includes sensible, and whether it includes animal. Hence, if it has been proved that it does not include the superior genus, it will have been proved that it does not include the superior difference, and concluded that our view is true.

Probatur autem expressis testimoniis Aristot. & D. Thom. deinde ratione. Aristot. enim 4. lib. Topic. cap. 2. loco 18. sic ait: Manifestum igitur, quoniam non participat Genus Differentia: quare neque impar Species erit, sed Differentia: quoniam non participat Genus. & loco 22. De pluribus (inquit) Genus quàm Differentiam oportet dici, & non participare differentiam. Et

Now it is proved by express testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas, and then by reason. For Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 2, place 18, speaks thus: It is manifest, therefore, that difference does not participate in genus: wherefore neither will odd be a species, but a difference, since it does not participate in genus. And in place 22: Genus (he says) must be said of more things than difference, and must not participate in difference. And L iiij

p. 168

D. Th. 3. lib. Met. lect. 8. ait: Genus per se sumptum non potest prædicari de differentia, quia differentia non participat genus, vt dicitur in 4. Topicorum, &c.

St. Thomas, Metaph. 3, lect. 8, says: Genus taken per se cannot be predicated of difference, because difference does not participate in genus, as is said in Topics 4, etc.

Probatur etiam ratione. Primò: Quia Genus & Differentia, formaliter sumpta, duo habent. Primum, quòd formaliter important diuersos gradus perfectionis essentialis: vt animal gradum naturæ sensitiuæ, & rationalis. Secundò, Quod se habet, tanquam contrahens, & contrahibile: & ideo tanquam actus & potentia: sed ex vtroque sequitur, quòd non se includant formaliter: ergo nec Differentia inferior, includet superiorem. Minorem sic probo: Gradus diuersi essentialis perfectionis, habent rationes diuersas: Actus quoque & potentia, formaliter differunt: ergo nec illi, nec isti, possunt formaliter se includere, & consequenter nec Genus, & Differentia, per quam contrahitur. Consequentia verò, quòd nec Differentia inferior includat superiorem, probatur hoc syllogismo: Illud quod non est formaliter animal: non est formaliter sensibile: sed rationale formaliter sumptum, non est animal: ergo nec erit formaliter sensibile: quare non includet formaliter differentia superiorem.

It is proved also by reason. First: because genus and difference, taken formally, have two things. The first, that they formally import diverse grades of essential perfection: as animal the grade of sensitive nature, and rational the grade of rational nature. Second, that the one is related as contracting and the other as contractible, and therefore as act and potency; but from each it follows that they do not include each other formally; therefore neither will the inferior difference include the superior. I prove the minor thus: grades of diverse essential perfection have diverse rationes; act and potency also differ formally; therefore neither the former nor the latter can include each other formally, and consequently neither can genus and the difference by which it is contracted. But the consequence, that neither does the inferior difference include the superior, is proved by this syllogism: That which is not formally animal is not formally sensible; but rational, taken formally, is not animal; therefore neither will it be formally sensible: wherefore it will not formally include the superior difference.

39. Secundò: Si Differentiæ inferiores, includerent formaliter superiores: ergo rationale, & irrationale includerent formaliter sensibile: & consequenter conuenirent in eo formaliter: sicut homo, & equus: sed quæcunque conueniunt essentialiter, in aliquo gradu perfectionis essentialis: debent à tali conuenientia separari per differentias: vt homo, & equus, separantur à conuenientia essentiali in eodem sensibili, per differentias, rationale, & hinnibile: ergo Differentiæ ipsæ, per alias deberent separari à tali conuenientia essentiali in gradu sensibilis, & ita daretur processus in infinitum: quia illæ etiam Differentiæ, per quas separentur, haberent similem conuenientiam in differentia superiori, quam includeretur, à qua deberent per alias differentias separari: nec possent separari per seipsas: quia per seipsas formaliter conueniunt: sed per alios gradus perfectionis deberent separari: & consequenter per alias differentias.

39 Second: if the inferior differences included the superior formally, then rational and irrational would include sensible formally, and consequently would agree in it formally, as man and horse do; but whatever things agree essentially in some grade of essential perfection must be separated from such agreement through differences, as man and horse are separated from the essential agreement in the same sensible through the differences rational and neighing; therefore the differences themselves would have to be separated through other differences from such essential agreement in the grade of sensible, and so there would be a process to infinity: because those differences also through which they were separated would have a similar agreement in the superior difference which they would include, from which they would have to be separated through other differences; nor could they be separated through themselves, because through themselves they agree formally; but they would have to be separated through other grades of perfection, and consequently through other differences.

40 Ad testimonium Arist. respondetur, secundùm expositionem D. Thomæ in Comment. ipsius, & Scoti in 4. d. 11. q. 3. §. ad rationes: vbi proprium eius sensum hunc esse asserunt, Vt duobus modis rem definiendam esse docuerit, videlicet, per supremum Genus, & omnes Differentias superiores, & inferiores, vsque ad vltimam vel per solum Genus proximum & vltimam Differentiam, neque vnum modum esse alteri

40 To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is made according to the exposition of St. Thomas in his commentary on him, and of Scotus, 4, d. 11, q. 3, § ad rationes: where they assert that its proper sense is this, that he taught that a thing to be defined is to be defined in two ways, namely through the supreme genus and all the differences, superior and inferior, down to the last, or through the proximate genus alone and the last difference, and that neither way is to

p. 169

contrarium, sed rationem primi esse: quia differentiæ intermediæ constituunt species subalternas, quæ sunt intermedia genera: ideo eisdem differentiis in definitione positis, sufficienter explicantur rationes formales eorum. Quod patet, si sic definiamus hominem, Homo est substantia corporea, animata, sensitiua, rationalis. Rationem verò secundi: quia Genus proximum, formaliter continet rationes omnium superiorum: ergo sola vltima differentia ei addita, sufficienter explicatur tota ratio definiti: & ideo si post eam addatur aliqua ex superioribus, vitium nugationis, aut inutilis repetitionis committitur: quia sufficienter explicatur talis Differentia. posito genere proximo, in quo includitur formaliter. Gratia exempli, Animal, formaliter continet, Viuens, Corpus, & Substantiam, & omnes differentias eorum: quare addito ei solo Rationali, sufficienter explicat totam rationem essentialem hominis: & si post Rationale, addideris Sensibile, vel Corporeum, inutilem repetitionem committis: quia sufficienter explicatæ sunt tales differentiæ, posito animali, in quo formaliter includuntur.

be contrary to the other; but that the reason of the first is that the intermediate differences constitute the subalternate species, which are the intermediate genera; therefore, when the same differences are placed in the definition, their formal rationes are sufficiently explained. Which is plain if we define man thus: Man is a corporeal, animate, sensitive, rational substance. And the reason of the second, that the proximate genus formally contains the rationes of all the superior ones; therefore, when the last difference alone is added to it, the whole ratio of the defined is sufficiently explained; and therefore, if after it some one of the superior ones is added, the fault of nugation or of useless repetition is committed, because such a difference is sufficiently explained once the proximate genus is placed, in which it is formally included. For example, animal formally contains living, body, and substance, and all their differences; wherefore, when rational alone is added to it, it sufficiently explains the whole essential ratio of man; and if after rational you add sensible or corporeal, you commit a useless repetition, because such differences are sufficiently explained once animal is placed, in which they are formally included.

41 Et ex hac explicatione, Respondetur ad primum: Eundem modum definiendi esse, per supremum Genus & omnes Differentias intermedias, vsque ad vltimam, & per solam vltimam cum proximo genere: non quia vltima includit superiores: sed quia in proximo genere includuntur formaliter: & ideo eo solo posito sufficienter explicantur.

41 And from this explanation the reply is made to the first: that the way of defining through the supreme genus and all the intermediate differences down to the last, and through the last alone with the proximate genus, is the same: not because the last includes the superior ones, but because they are formally included in the proximate genus, and therefore, once it alone is placed, they are sufficiently explained.

Dum verò asserit Aristoteles, Vltimam differentiam esse totam substantiam speciei: non totaliter, sed completiuè intelligendum esse docent, ita vt præsupposito genere proximo, quod contrahit, & supra quod cadit in definitione, totam substantiam rei compleat. Tertium verò quod asserit Aristoteles, de diuisione superioris differentiæ, in inferiores oppositas, ita exponunt, vt Differentia non ratione sui, sed ratione Generis, quod constituit, vt speciem subalternam, & quod formaliter includit, diuidatur: non quidem in differentias, sed in species per differentias: vnde nec genus superius, includitur in differentiis inferioribus, sed in speciebus, & multò minùs differentiæ superiores in inferioribus. Illa autem verba Aristo. Fissio pedis, est pedalitas. non sic intelliguntur, vt vnam velit prædicare, de altera formaliter: sed sensus eius est, quòd fissio sit differentia per se diuisiua pedalitatis, & non per accidens.

But when Aristotle asserts that the last difference is the whole substance of the species, they teach that this is to be understood not totally but completively, so that, presupposing the proximate genus, which it contracts and upon which it falls in the definition, it completes the whole substance of the thing. And the third thing which Aristotle asserts, on the division of the superior difference into opposed inferior ones, they expound thus: that the difference is divided not by reason of itself but by reason of the genus which it constitutes as a subalternate species, and which it formally includes; and not, indeed, into differences, but into species through differences: hence neither is the superior genus included in the inferior differences, but in the species, and much less the superior differences in the inferior. And those words of Aristotle, The cleaving of the foot is footedness, are not to be understood as if he meant to predicate the one of the other formally; but his sense is that cleaving is a per se difference dividing footedness, and not a per accidens one.

Ad primum argu. Distinguendum est Antecedens, nempe, Rationale est Substantia: nam si pro Substantia completa quę est supremum Genus prædicamenti, accipiatur, falsum est;

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished, namely, Rational is a substance: for if it is taken for complete substance, which is the supreme genus of the category, it is false;

p. 170

cùm rationale, & quæcunque Differentia, formaliter sit pars speciei, & ideo substantia incompleta: si verò accipiatur Substantia vniuersaliùs, prout abstrahit à completa, & incompleta, verum est, Rationale esse Substantiam, non prædicamentalem, sed analogam, ad completas, & incompleta substantias. Vnde ad formam argumenti negandum est, quòd sit Substantia, quæ diuiditur in corpoream & incorpoream: & consequenter, quòd includat Differentiam superiorem.

since rational, and any difference whatever, is formally a part of the species, and therefore an incomplete substance; but if substance is taken more universally, as it abstracts from complete and incomplete, it is true that rational is a substance, not the categorial one, but one analogous to complete and incomplete substances. Hence, to the form of the argument, it is to be denied that it is a substance which is divided into corporeal and incorporeal, and consequently that it includes the superior difference.

42 Syllogismum verò, qui adducitur, concedimus esse in modo, & figura: & ideo euidenter concludere, quòd Differentia inferior includat superiorem: non tamen in sensu formali: nec id necessarium est ad formam syllogisticam, cuius virtute, infertur quidem, Conclusionem stare in veritate cum præmissis, sed non semper in eodem sensu: vt hoc exemplo, omnino simili, potest probari: Omnis homo est animal, omnis homo est risibilis, ergo risibile est animal: cuius præmissæ, veræ sunt in sensu formali: conclusio verò, non potest esse vera formaliter, sed solùm in sensu materiali.

42 The syllogism which is adduced we grant to be in mood and figure, and therefore to conclude evidently that the inferior difference includes the superior; not, however, in the formal sense: nor is this necessary to the syllogistic form, by virtue of which it is indeed inferred that the conclusion stands in truth with the premises, but not always in the same sense: as can be proved by this altogether similar example: Every man is an animal; every man is risible; therefore the risible is an animal; whose premises are true in the formal sense, but the conclusion cannot be true formally, but only in the material sense.

Ad secundum, Concessa maiori, distinguenda est minor: quia Genus non est tam simplex, sicut Differentia: quod cùm sit species subalterna, componitur ex genere, & differentia, sed Differentia non potest habere talem compositionem, quia cùm ex propria ratione, sit vltimus actus speciei, non potest esse vllo modo composita: nec tamen est purus actus: quia cùm sit pars, potentiam includit ad componendum totum, & intrinsecam imperfectionem, ex ratione partis ei prouenientem.

To the second, the major being granted, the minor is to be distinguished: because genus is not as simple as difference; for since it is a subalternate species, it is composed of genus and difference; but difference cannot have such a composition, because, since by its proper ratio it is the last act of the species, it cannot be composite in any way; nor yet is it pure act, because, since it is a part, it includes potency for composing the whole, and an intrinsic imperfection coming to it from the ratio of a part.

QUESTION VI

Quæst. 6. An differentia semper & necessario sit perfectior genere, quod contrahit — Whether difference is always and necessarily more perfect than the genus which it contracts.

QVÆSTIO VI.

[…]

An Differentia semper, & necessariò sit perfectior Genere, quod contrahit.

[…]

43 QVodlibet Genus contrahitur per plures Differentias oppositas, diuersæ perfectionis, ita vt aliæ sint nobiliores aliis, & ex eis quædam eleuent genus ipsum, ad gradũ altioris naturæ, aliæ verò intra proprium gradum illud contrahant, Gratia exempli, Animal contrahitur per rationale. & irrationale: & rationale eleuat illud ad altiorem gradum naturæ rationalis: irrationale verò non eleuat, sed intra proprium gradum naturæ sensitiuæ reliquit. Et de differentia eleuante, certum est, nobiliorem esse genere ipso: vt de rationali, quòd sit nobilius animali: sed de differentiis non eleuantibus, procedit

ny genus whatever is contracted by several opposed differences of 43 A diverse perfection, so that some are nobler than others; and of them some elevate the genus itself to the grade of a higher nature, while others contract it within its proper grade. For example, animal is contracted by rational and irrational: and rational elevates it to the higher grade of rational nature, whereas irrational does not elevate it, but leaves it within its proper grade of sensitive nature. And of the elevating difference it is certain that it is nobler than the genus itself: as of rational, that it is nobler than animal; but concerning the non-elevating differences the

p. 171

quæstio: An sint nobiliores genere, vel minùs nobiles, aut nobilitate æquales.

question is whether they are nobler than the genus, or less noble, or equal in nobility.

Et prima opinio tenet, Non omnes differentias esse nobiliores genere, quod contrahunt, sed solùm eas, per quas eleuatur ad gradum perfectioris naturæ: cæteras verò minùs nobiles eo esse, vel ad summum eiusdem nobilitatis: vt omnes differentias animales, excepta rationali, & omnes differentias Angelorum, per quas genus eorum, quod est substantia spiritualis, aut incorporea, non eleuatur ad altiorem gradum essentialis perfectionis, Hanc sequuntur moderni quidam.

And the first opinion holds that not all differences are nobler than the genus which they contract, but only those through which it is elevated to the grade of a more perfect nature; but that the others are less noble than it, or at most of the same nobility: as all the differences of animals, except rational, and all the differences of angels, through which their genus, which is spiritual or incorporeal substance, is not elevated to a higher grade of essential perfection. Certain moderns follow this.

Eámque probant duplici arg. Primum est, Quia perfectior gradus naturæ, radix est perfectionis operationis: ergo illa differentia, quæ ad perfectiorem operationem, vel perfectiorem saltem modum operandi, non eleuat naturam generis, non potest esse eo perfectior, sed plures sunt differentiæ, genus neutro modo eleuantes, ergo nulla earum erit nobilior genere. Probatur minor, in differentiis animalis: ex quibus nulla constituit speciem, perfectiorem aliam operationem habentem, sensitiua, quæ gradui generis propria est: & etiam in speciebus Angelorum, non aliam operationem perfectiorem habentibus, præter intellectionem, nec alium modum perfectiorem operandi, præter intelligere sine discursu.

And they prove it by a twofold argument. The first is: because a more perfect grade of nature is the root of perfection of operation; therefore that difference which does not elevate the nature of the genus to a more perfect operation, or at least to a more perfect mode of operating, cannot be more perfect than it; but there are many differences which elevate the genus in neither way; therefore none of them will be nobler than the genus. The minor is proved in the differences of animal, of which none constitutes a species having another operation more perfect than the sensitive, which is proper to the grade of the genus; and also in the species of angels, which have no other more perfect operation besides intellection, nor another more perfect mode of operating besides understanding without discursive reasoning.

44 Secundum: Inter species animalis, plures reperiuntur, adeò imperfectæ, vt pluribus sensibus careant. Vt de talpis, ostreis, & sanguisugis manifestum est, de aliisque, petris semper affixis, quæ præter tactum, nullum alium sensum habere videntur:, ergo in his minùs perfectus reperitur gradus sentiendi, quàm in genere animalis, significante naturam sensitiuam, abstractam ab his defectibus.

44 The second: among the species of animal several are found so imperfect that they lack several senses, as is manifest of moles, oysters, and leeches, and of others always fixed to rocks, which seem to have no other sense besides touch; therefore in these a less perfect grade of sensing is found than in the genus animal, which signifies sensitive nature abstracted from these defects.

Secunda opinio opposita est, affirmans, quamcunque differentiam esse perfectiorem genere, quod contrahit. Hæc est expressa D. Thom. & non solùm probabilior, sed vera. Probatur primùm, duobus testimoniis eiusdem: nam in 2. d 13. quæst. 1. artic. 6. ad 1. ita ait: Differentia, non est nobilior genere, sicut natura vna, est nobilior altera, vel sicut forma vna, nobilior est alia: quia differentia, nullam formam dicit: quia implicitè in natura generis non contineatur: sed dicitur genere nobilior, sicut determinatum indeterminato, & per hunc modum habere intellectum sic, est nobilius, quàm habere intellectum simpliciter: & habere sensum sic, quàm habere sensum simpliciter, &c. Et 1. p. quæst. 75. art 7 ad 2. inquit: Differentia specifica vltima, est nobilissima, in quantum est maximè determinata, per modum, quo actus nobilior est potentia: sic autem intellectuale, non est

The second opinion is the opposite, affirming that any difference whatever is more perfect than the genus which it contracts. This is the express view of St. Thomas, and not only more probable but true. It is proved first by two testimonies of the same: for in 2, d. 13, q. 1, a. 6, ad 1, he speaks thus: Difference is not nobler than genus as one nature is nobler than another, or as one form is nobler than another: because difference implies no form which is not implicitly contained in the nature of the genus; but it is said to be nobler than genus as the determinate than the indeterminate; and in this way to have intellect thus is nobler than to have intellect simply, and to have sense thus than to have sense simply, etc. And 1 p., q. 75, a. 7, ad 2, he says: The last specific difference is most noble inasmuch as it is most determinate, in the way in which act is nobler than potency: but in this way the intellectual is not nobler

p. 172

nobilissimum: quia est indeterminatum, & commune ad multos intellectualitatis gradus: sicut sensibile, ad multos gradus in esse sensibili, &c.

than the sensitive, because it is indeterminate and common to many grades of intellectuality, as sensible is to many grades in sensible being, etc.

45 Ex quibus duo arg. colliguntur, ad probandam eandem sententiam. Primum est, Omnis differentia eleuat genus, ad altiorem gradum essendi, vel ad altiorem modum essendi, intra eundem gradum suę naturę: ergo omnis differentia, est nobilior suo generę. Euidens est consequentia: quia non solùm res est perfectior, quia perfectiorem dicit gradum essendi, sed quia eundem gradum perfectiori modo participat. Sed probatur antecedens: quia differentia duo habet, in quibus excedit genus: Nempe esse actum determinantem, atque perficientem ipsum: cùm tamen genus se habeat, sicut potentia determinabilis: Esse etiam determinatum, atque distinctum gradum naturæ, & modo determinato, atque distincto, eum dicere: cùm tamen genus, licèt determinatum, indeterminatè tamen, & quasi confusè eum includat: sed gradum naturæ determinatum, atque determinatè includere, perfectius est, quàm confusè tantùm: ergo differentia ex proprio modo essendi semper est perfectior.

45 From these two arguments are gathered for proving the same opinion. The first is: every difference elevates the genus to a higher grade of being, or to a higher mode of being within the same grade of its nature; therefore every difference is nobler than its genus. The consequence is evident: because a thing is more perfect not only because it implies a more perfect grade of being, but because it participates the same grade in a more perfect mode. But the antecedent is proved: because difference has two things in which it exceeds the genus: namely, to be the act determining and perfecting it, whereas the genus is related as a determinable potency; and also to be a determinate and distinct grade of nature, and to imply it in a determinate and distinct mode, whereas the genus, although it includes a determinate grade, includes it indeterminately and as it were confusedly; but to include a determinate grade of nature, and determinately, is more perfect than to include it only confusedly; therefore difference, by its proper mode of being, is always more perfect.

Secundò, Genus se habet, tanquam materia in compositione speciei: & differentia tanquam forma: sed forma semper eleuat materiam, ad perfectius esse: ergo differentia semper eleuat genus ad perfectius esse: & forma semper est nobilior materia: ergo semper erit nobilior Differentia Genere. Probatur minor prioris syllogismi: quia forma eleuat materiam, in ordine physico, ad esse specificum determinatum, & actuale, quod ei tribuit, & eodem modo differentia eleuat genus in ordine metaphysico: Esse autem specificum, determinatum, & actuale, perfectius est, confuso, & potentiali, quod habet genus, ergo differentia semper est nobilior genere.

Second: genus is related as matter in the composition of the species, and difference as form; but form always elevates matter to a more perfect being; therefore difference always elevates genus to a more perfect being. And form is always nobler than matter; therefore difference will always be nobler than genus. The minor of the first syllogism is proved: because form elevates matter in the physical order to the determinate and actual specific being which it bestows on it; and in the same way difference elevates the genus in the metaphysical order; but specific, determinate, and actual being is more perfect than the confused and potential being which the genus has; therefore difference is always nobler than genus.

46 Ad primum arg. alterius opinionis respondetur, negando consequentiam primi Enthymematis: quia pręter eleuationem ad perfectiorem operationem, vel perfectiorem modum operandi, reperitur perfectior modus essendi, actualis, ac determinatus, ad quem omnis differentia eleuat genus: & ideo semper est perfectior illo.

46 To the first argument of the other opinion the reply is made by denying the consequence of the first enthymeme: because, besides elevation to a more perfect operation or a more perfect mode of operating, there is found a more perfect mode of being, actual and determinate, to which every difference elevates the genus; and therefore it is always more perfect than it.

Ad secundum, Concesso Antecedenti, neganda est consequentia: nam licèt imperfectè reperiatur gradus sentiendi, in illis speciebus, adhuc reperitur perfectiùs, quàm in genere: quia determinatus, & specificus est; in genere verò, nec determinatus, nec perfectior, sed confusus, abstrahens à perfecto, & imperfecto. quod autem determinatum, atque distinctum est, perfectius est indeterminato, atque confuso. Et ideo adhuc

To the second, the antecedent being granted, the consequence is to be denied: for although the grade of sensing is found imperfectly in those species, it is still found more perfectly than in the genus, because it is determinate and specific; but in the genus it is neither determinate nor more perfect, but confused, abstracting from the perfect and the imperfect. But what is determinate and distinct is more perfect than the indeterminate and confused. And therefore still

p. 173

differentiæ harum specierum, perfectiores genere sunt.

the differences of these species are more perfect than the genus.

QUESTION VII

QVÆSTIO VII.

[…]

An secunda definitio differentiæ, possit conuenire vltimis differentiis.

Whether the second definition of difference can belong to the last differences.

DVo præsupponit titulus quæstionis, tanquam certa. Primò, Duplicem esse differentiam, Subalternam, & Vltimam. Subalterna est, quæ constituit Speciem subalternam, vt Corporeum, & Sensibile. Vltima, quæ constituit Speciem vltimam, vt Rationale. Præsupponit secundò, Secundam definitionem, conuenire differentiis subalternis, cùm notum sit, de pluribus differentibus specie, eam prædicari: vt Sensibile, de homine, & leone. Sed in dubium reuocat, An possit etiam conuenire vltimis, Et ratio dubitandi est manifesta: quia non prędicantur de pluribus speciebus, sed de vna tantùm, & indiuiduis eius: vt rationale, de solo homine, & singularibus hominibus: ergo non cõuenit eis definitio, quæ asserit, Differentiam esse, quæ prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie in Quale quid.

he title of the question presupposes two things as certain. First, T that difference is twofold, subalternate and last. The subalternate is that which constitutes a subalternate species, as corporeal and sensible; the last, that which constitutes a last species, as rational. It presupposes second that the second definition belongs to subalternate differences, since it is known that they are predicated of many things differing in species: as sensible of man and lion. But it calls into doubt whether it can also belong to the last ones. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because they are not predicated of many species, but of one only and its individuals: as rational of man alone and of singular men; therefore the definition does not belong to them which asserts that difference is that which is predicated of many things differing in species in quale quid.

47 Et est prima opinio, quæ tenet, etiam conuenire vltimis differentiis: vt autem modum quo eis conueniat, explicet, sic esse exponendam definitionem docet, vt dum dicitur, Differentia est, quę prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie: sensus sit, de pluribus, quæ inter sese, aut ab aliis distinguuntur Specie. In quo sensu manifestum est, Differentiis subalternis, atque etiam vltimis conuenire: nam illæ prædicantur de pluribus differentibus specie, inter sese, vt Sensibile, de equo, & leone. Differentia verò vltima, vt Rationale prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie, non inter se, sed ab aliis: vt de homine: qui specie differt ab equo: & de Petro, & Ioanne, qui ab indiuiduis aliarum specierum, specie distinguuntur, per idem rationale. Hanc sententiam tenuerunt nonnulli, quos attulit Auicenna cap. præsenti.

47 And there is a first opinion, which holds that it belongs also to the last differences; and in order to explain the way in which it belongs to them, it teaches that the definition is to be expounded thus: that when it is said, Difference is that which is predicated of many things differing in species, the sense is: of many things which are distinguished in species either among themselves or from others. In which sense it is manifest that it belongs to the subalternate differences and also to the last: for the former are predicated of many things differing in species among themselves, as sensible of horse and lion; but the last difference, as rational, is predicated of many things differing in species, not among themselves but from others: as of man, who differs in species from the horse, and of Peter and John, who are distinguished in species from the individuals of other species through the same rational. Some held this opinion, whom Avicenna brought forward in the present chapter.

Sed probatur falsa duplici arg. Primò, Hæc definitio differentiæ eodem modo, & in eodem sensu assignatur à Porphyrio: in quo assignatæ sunt definitiones aliorum prędicabilium: sed aliæ definitiones, vt Speciei & Generis, sic intelliguntur, vt hæc de pluribus differentibus numero inter se, illud de pluribus, inter se differentibus specie, prædicari debeat, vt probant exempla in eis adducta à Porphyrio: ergo eodem modo intelligenda est hæc definitio differentiæ: sed sic intellectas patet non conuenire vltimis differentiis: ergo non fuerunt definitæ à Porphyrio.

But it is proved false by a twofold argument. First: this definition of difference is assigned by Porphyry in the same way and in the same sense in which the definitions of the other predicables were assigned; but the other definitions, as those of species and genus, are understood thus: that the former is to be predicated of many things differing in number among themselves, the latter of many things differing in species among themselves, as the examples adduced in them by Porphyry prove; therefore this definition of difference is to be understood in the same way; but, so understood, it is plain that it does not belong to the last differences; therefore they were not defined by Porphyry.

p. 174

Secundò, Si sensus ille admittendus esset, vt conueniret vltimis differentiis, sequitur euidenter definitionem Generis, etiam conuenire Speciei. Probatur consequentia: quia prædicatur de pluribus differentibus specie, licèt non inter sese, bene tamen ab indiuiduis aliarum specierum distinctis.

Second: if that sense were to be admitted, so that it belonged to the last differences, it follows evidently that the definition of genus also belongs to species. The consequence is proved: because it is predicated of many things differing in species, not indeed among themselves, but certainly distinct from the individuals of other species.

48 Secunda opinio est Caietani, in expositione huius definitionis, dubio vnico, vbi duo præsupponit, ad explicandum sensum definitionis, in quo vltimis differentiis conueniat. Primum est, Per hanc definitionem, definitam esse differentiam, sub ratione communi Differentiæ, abstrahente à Subalterna, & Vltima. Quia sub ratione communi denominatur à secunda intentione, tertij prædicabilis. Secundò, Verba alicuius definitionis, duobus modis posse applicari his, quæ continentur sub definito, positiuè, hoc est affirmatiuè: aut etiam negatiuè, hoc est, per non repugnantiam: & vtroque modo applicatur definitio hæc, diuersis differentiis. Positiuè quidem, Subalternis, quæ verè prædicantur, de pluribus differentibus specie: Vltimis verò, per non repugnantiam: quia verum est, eis in quantum differentiæ sunt, non repugnare, quòd prædicentur de pluribus differentibus specie. Itaque, Vltimæ duobus modis considerantur, nempe sub Communi, ratione differentiæ, & sub Particulari, ratione Vltimarum: & hoc modo, omnino eis repugnat definitio, sed non primo. Nam si eis, vt differentiæ sunt, repugnaret, nullis differentiis etiam subalternis posset conuenire: & cùm non definiantur, vt Vltimæ, sed vt Differentiæ: absolutè dicendum est, eis conuenire definitionem negatiuè, aut per non repugnantiam, Hanc sententiam Caietani sequitur Sotus cap. præsenti, quæstione vnica ad 6. pro qua etiam referuntur, Auicenna cap. vltimo prædicabilium, & Iamblicus, cap. de differentia. Et Toletus quæstione vnica huius capitis, probabilem esse docet, quamuis non ad mentem Porphyrij, Probat Caietanus hoc argu. Definitio Quanti, est, quòd sit definibile in partes, & non conuenit corpori cœlesti positiuè: quia cùm sit incorruptibile, non potest diuidi: alioquin per diuisionem corrumperetur: sed conuenit ei negatiuè, hoc est, per non regnantiam, vt est Quantum, non vt est corpus incorruptibile: quia vt Quantum est, non repugnat ei diuidi: quamuis repugnet ei diuisio, vt tali quanto incorruptibili. Et tamen sufficit, ita ei conuenire, vt dicatur definitio conuenire ei absolutè: ergo sufficiet, quòd vltimis differentiis, conueniat per non repugnantiam, vt differentiæ sunt, quamuis repugnet eis, vt vltimis.

48 The second opinion is that of Cajetan, in his exposition of this definition, in the single doubt, where he presupposes two things for explaining the sense of the definition in which it belongs to the last differences. The first is that by this definition difference is defined under the common ratio of difference, abstracting from subalternate and last, because under the common ratio it is denominated by the second intention of the third predicable. Second, that the words of any definition can be applied in two ways to those things which are contained under the defined: positively, that is, affirmatively, or else negatively, that is, by non-repugnance; and this definition is applied in each way to diverse differences: positively, indeed, to the subalternate ones, which are truly predicated of many things differing in species; but to the last ones by non-repugnance, because it is true that it is not repugnant to them, inasmuch as they are differences, to be predicated of many things differing in species. Thus the last differences are considered in two ways, namely under the common ratio of difference, and under the particular ratio of last ones; and in this latter way the definition is altogether repugnant to them, but not in the first. For if it were repugnant to them as they are differences, it could not belong to any differences, not even the subalternate ones; and since they are not defined as last, but as differences, it is to be said absolutely that the definition belongs to them negatively, or by non-repugnance. This opinion of Cajetan is followed by Soto in the present chapter, in the single question, ad 6; for it are also cited Avicenna, in the last chapter of the Predicables, and Iamblichus, in the chapter on difference. And Toledo, in the single question of this chapter, teaches that it is probable, although not according to the mind of Porphyry. Cajetan proves it by this argument: the definition of quantity is that it is divisible into parts, and it does not belong positively to a celestial body, because, since it is incorruptible, it cannot be divided; otherwise it would be corrupted by division; but it belongs to it negatively, that is, by non-repugnance, as it is quantity, not as it is an incorruptible body: because as it is quantity it is not repugnant to it to be divided, although division is repugnant to it as such an incorruptible quantity. And yet it suffices for it to belong to it in this way for the definition to be said to belong to it absolutely; therefore it will suffice that it belong to the last differences by non-repugnance, as they are differences, although it is repugnant to them as last.

p. 175

49 Mihi verò nullam ferè probabilitatem habere videtur. Vnde neque vllus ferè iam eam defendit. Probatur primò: Definitio rei, si essentialis sit, continet essentiam omnium, quę definiuntur: & si descriptiua, aliam propriã passionem eorum: sed essentia, & propria passio, non possunt rebus conuenire negatiuè, aut per non repugnantiam, sed necesse est eis positiuè conueniant: ergo repugnat definitioni conuenire alicui per non repugnantiam.

49 But to me it seems to have almost no probability. Hence hardly anyone now defends it. It is proved first: the definition of a thing, if it is essential, contains the essence of all the things that are defined; and if it is descriptive, some proper attribute of them; but essence and proper attribute cannot belong to things negatively, or by non-repugnance, but it is necessary that they belong to them positively; therefore it is repugnant to a definition to belong to anything by non-repugnance.

Secundò, Quia si ex eo solùm conuenit definitio vltimis differentiis, quia non repugnat eis, sub communi ratione differentiæ consideratis, prædicari de pluribus differentibus specie: quamuis repugnet, vt sunt differentiæ vltimæ: sequitur definitionem hominis conuenire leoni: imò & definitionem cuiuslibet speciei, conuenire cæteris speciebus eiusdem generis. Consequens est absurdum: ergo & Antecedens erit falsum. Probatur Consequentia, quia licèt definitio hominis, repugnet leoni, sub ratione specifica leonis, non repugnat tamen ei, sub ratione communi animalis considerato.

Second: because, if the definition belongs to the last differences only from the fact that it is not repugnant to them, considered under the common ratio of difference, to be predicated of many things differing in species, although it is repugnant to them as they are last differences, it follows that the definition of man belongs to the lion; indeed, that the definition of any species whatever belongs to the other species of the same genus. The consequent is absurd; therefore the antecedent will also be false. The consequence is proved: because, although the definition of man is repugnant to the lion under the specific ratio of lion, it is nevertheless not repugnant to it considered under the common ratio of animal.

Tertia opinio communis & vera, tenet, Per hanc definitionem solùm definisse Porphyrium differentias Subalternas, non verò Vltimas. Ita Commentator, Auicena, & Alpharabius, quos citat, & sequitur Albertus Magnus, tract. 5. de differentia, cap. 6. Iauellus, Louanienses, Sotus, Canterus, Mercatus, Villalpandeus, Toletus, & Fonseca, cap. præsenti, in explicatione eiusdem definitionis. Et probatur, ex impugnatione aliarum opinionum: quia nullo modo potest conuenire vltimis differentiis.

The third opinion, common and true, holds that by this definition Porphyry defined only the subalternate differences, and not the last. So the Commentator, Avicenna, and Alfarabi, whom Albert the Great cites and follows, tract. 5 on difference, ch. 6; Javelli, the Louvain commentators, Soto, Canterus, Mercado, Villalpando, Toledo, and Fonseca, in the present chapter, in the explanation of the same definition. And it is proved from the refutation of the other opinions: because in no way can it belong to the last differences.

Sed quare has non definiuit Porphyrius? Respondent quidã, quia eas nõ cognouit. Sed falsum hoc est, quia certum est, Species vltimas cognouisse, quarum mentionem fecit cap de specie, in ordinatione prædicamentali: ergo cognouit etiam vltimas differentias, saltem in ratione communi vltimarum: quãuis particulares ignorauerit: & in hoc cap. & vltimo huius libri, differentiam vltimam hominis, dixit esse Rationale Mortale: vnde sequitur etiam in particulari aliquam cognouisse.

But why did Porphyry not define these? Some reply: because he did not know them. But this is false, because it is certain that he knew the last species, of which he made mention in the chapter on species, in the categorial ordering; therefore he also knew the last differences, at least in the common ratio of last ones, although he was ignorant of the particular ones; and in this chapter, and in the last of this book, he said that the last difference of man is rational mortal: whence it follows that he also knew some in particular.

Ideo alij, eas non definisse asserunt, quia existimauit non esse simplices, sed cõpositas, aut complexas: vt rationale mortale, esse differentiam hominis: complexa verò non pertinent ad prædicabilia, quæ simplicia esse debent, aut incomplexa: vt in vltima quæst. vniuersali diximus. Hæc tamen ratio contra mentem Porphyrij est, cap. vlt. huius libri, vbi comparans differentiam cum specie, ita ait: Differentia quidem sæpe in pluribus speciebus consideratur: species verò, in solis his quæ sub speci sunt

Therefore others assert that he did not define them because he thought they were not simple but composite or complex, as rational mortal is the difference of man; but complex ones do not pertain to the predicables, which must be simple, or incomplex, as we said in the last question on universals. This reason, however, is against the mind of Porphyry, in the last chapter of this book, where, comparing difference with species, he speaks thus: Difference indeed is often considered in many species; but species only in those things which are under the species

p. 176

indiuiduis est, &c. Si ergo sæpe in pluribus speciebus differentia est: non semper ex mente Porphyrij, apud quem dabitur vltima differentia prædicabilis, quæ cum specie comparetur.

of the individual, etc. If, then, difference is often in many species, not always according to the mind of Porphyry, there will be given with him a predicable last difference, which is compared with the species.

Dicendum igitur est. ideo solas subalternas definisse Porphyrium: quia cùm nobis notiores sint, frequentiùs eis vtimur in definitionibus. Quod à simili probari potest: nam cùm duplex sit proprium, Subalternum & Infimum, hoc solùm definiuit cap. sequenti: quia frequentiùs eo vtimur in demonstrationibus. Sufficit autem definisse differentias Subalternas: quia cum eodem modo prædicentur omnes, nempe in Quale quid, ex harum notitia, facilè est differentias infimas cognoscere, in quantum pertinent ad tertium prædicabile: facilè est etiam definitionem communem subalternis, & infimis assignare: quæ talis erit: Differentia est, quæ prædicatur de pluribus in Quale quid.

It is to be said, therefore, that Porphyry defined only the subalternate ones because, since they are better known to us, we use them more frequently in definitions. Which can be proved from a like case: for since property is twofold, subalternate and lowest, he defined only the latter in the following chapter, because we use it more frequently in demonstrations. And it suffices to have defined the subalternate differences: because, since all are predicated in the same way, namely in quale quid, from the knowledge of these it is easy to know the lowest differences, inasmuch as they pertain to the third predicable; it is also easy to assign a definition common to the subalternate and the lowest, which will be this: Difference is that which is predicated of many in quale quid.

Ad argum. Caiet. respondetur, falsum esse, quòd definitio Quanti, ab Arist. designata, non conueniat corpori cœlesti positiuè. quia cùm veram habeat quantitatem, verè per se, & positiuè, est diuisibile in partes: quamuis actualis diuisio, per accidens impediatur, propter incorruptibilitatem substantialem, eiusdem corporis.

To the argument of Cajetan the reply is that it is false that the definition of quantity designated by Aristotle does not belong positively to a celestial body: because, since it has true quantity, it is truly, per se, and positively divisible into parts, although actual division is impeded per accidens on account of the substantial incorruptibility of the same body.

CAPVT V.

C H A P T E R V.

De Proprio.

On Property.

TEXTVS PORPHYR.

T E X T O F P O R P H Y R Y.

Proprium verò quadrifariam diuidunt, &c.

But property is divided in four ways, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T. 1

1 INtentum Porphyrij cap. præsenti est, explicare naturam Proprij, quod est quartum Prædicabile. Diuiditur autem in duas partes. In prima, Tradit Porphyrius quatuor acceptiones, seu modos proprij. In secunda, Solam quartam acceptionem eius, docet esse propriam: cæteras verò communes aliis accidentibus.

The intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of property, which is the fourth predicable. And it is divided into two parts. In the first, Porphyry hands down four acceptations, or modes, of property. In the second, he teaches that only its fourth acceptation is proper, but that the others are common to other accidents.

Proprium, primo modo, accipitur pro eo, quod conuenit alicui speciei soli, non tamen omnibus indiuiduis eius: vt esse medicum aut philosophum, proprium hominis dicitur: quia soli homini conuenit: licèt non omni homini conueniat. Secundo modo, accipitur ex opposito, pro eo quod conuenit omni indiuiduo alicuius speciei, non tamen soli, sed etiam indiuiduis aliarum: vt esse bipedem, vel duos habere pedes, omnibus hominibus ex propria natura conuenit, non tamen

Property in the first mode is taken for that which belongs to some one species alone, yet not to all its individuals: as to be a physician or a philosopher is said to be a property of man, because it belongs to man alone, although it does not belong to every man. In the second mode it is taken, in the opposite way, for that which belongs to every individual of some species, yet not to it alone, but also to the individuals of others: as to be a biped, or to have two feet, belongs to all men from their own nature, yet not

p. 177

solis, sed quibusdam etiam aliis animalibus aliarum specierum. Tertio modo accipitur pro eo, quod conuenit alicui speciei, & omnibus indiuiduis eius, non tamen omni tempore, sed quodam determinato: vt canescere conuenit omnibus, & solis hominibus, verùm non semper, sed solùm tempore senectutis. Quarto modo, accipitur Proprium pro eo, quod conuenit alicui speciei, & omnibus indiuiduis eius, non pro determinato tempore, sed semper: vt Risibile conuenit homini, & omni homini, atque etiam semper: quia licèt non semper homo rideat, semper tamen habet aptitudinem ad ridendum: & ideo semper est risibilis.

to them alone, but also to certain other animals of other species. In the third mode it is taken for that which belongs to some species, and to all its individuals, yet not at every time, but at a certain determinate one: as to grow gray belongs to all men and to men alone, but not always, only at the time of old age. In the fourth mode property is taken for that which belongs to some species, and to all its individuals, not for a determinate time but always: as risible belongs to man, and to every man, and also always: because, although a man does not always laugh, he nevertheless always has the aptitude for laughing, and therefore he is always risible.

Ex his quatuor acceptionibus sola quarta propria est, (inquit Porphyrius) quia proprium propriè sumptum, solùm est illud, quod conuertitur cum eo, cuius est proprium, sed solùm proprium quatuor modo acceptum, conuertitur: ergo solùm in quarta acceptione propriè accipitur.

Of these four acceptations, only the fourth is proper (says Porphyry): because property properly taken is only that which is convertible with that of which it is the property; but only property taken in the fourth mode is convertible; therefore only in the fourth acceptation is it taken properly.

QUESTION I

Qu. 1. An proprium solum quarto modo acceptum constituat quartum prædicabile, vel etiam secundum alios modos — Whether property taken only in the fourth mode constitutes the fourth predicable, or also according to the other three modes.

QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

An proprium solùm quarto modo acceptum, constituat quartum prædicabile, vel etiam secundùm alios tres modos.

[…]

2 PRæsupponit tanquam certum, titulus quæstionis, quòd Proprium secundùm quartũ modum, pertineat ad quartum prædicabile: sed dubitat, An hoc solùm constituat quartum prædicabile, & tres alij modi potiùs pertineant ad quintum: vel ex omnibus quatuor modis, efficiatur quartum.

2 The title of the question presupposes as certain that property according to the fourth mode pertains to the fourth predicable; but it doubts whether this alone constitutes the fourth predicable, and the other three modes rather pertain to the fifth, or whether the fourth is made up of all four modes.

Et prima opinio tenet, Proprium non solùm secundùm quartum modum, sed etiam secundùm alios, constituere quartum prædicabile: hoc est, vel secundùm omnes, vel saltem secundùm modum tertium. Sic videtur sentire Albertus Magnus, tract. 6. de proprio, c. 1. & tract. 7. de accidenti, c. etiam 1. Louanienses ca. præs. & ibid. Canter. quos saltem, quantum ad proprium tertio modo sequuntur nonnulli ex modernis.

And the first opinion holds that property not only according to the fourth mode but also according to the others constitutes the fourth predicable: that is, either according to all, or at least according to the third mode. So Albert the Great seems to think, tract. 6 on property, ch. 1, and tract. 7 on accident, also ch. 1; the Louvain commentators, in the present chapter; and in the same place Canter., whom some of the moderns follow, at least as regards property in the third mode.

Probatur primò: Quia licèt Propria aliorum modorum, sumpta pro actu, sint communia accidentia, si tamen sumantur pro aptitudine, vel potentia, propriæ passiones sunt, emanantes ab essentia: ergo non pertinent ad quintum prædicabile, sed ad quartum. Probatur Antecedens, in proprio primi modi: nam esse medicum vel philosophum, hoc est, habere aliquam scientiam ex his, commune accidens est: aptitudo verò ad eas habendas, sicut ad cæteras, propria passio hominis: quam appellare solent capacitatem disciplinæ.

It is proved first: because, although the properties of the other modes, taken for the act, are common accidents, yet if they are taken for the aptitude or potency, they are proper attributes emanating from the essence; therefore they do not pertain to the fifth predicable, but to the fourth. The antecedent is proved in property of the first mode: for to be a physician or a philosopher, that is, to have some science among these, is a common accident; but the aptitude for having them, as for having the others, is a proper attribute of man, which they are accustomed to call the capacity for learning. M

p. 178

Secundò: Quia proprium tertio modo conuenit omni, & soli, ergo est propria passio. Probatur consequentia: Quia esse propriam passionem, in eo solùm consistit, quòd ab essentia emanet: emanatio verò, non tollitur ex eo, quod non semper conueniat, sed tempore à natura statuto: quia eo tempore, & non alio, reperitur dispositio in subiecto, ad talem emanationem: ergo nec tollitur ratio propriæ passionis in emanatione consistentis.

Second: because property in the third mode belongs to every and to only; therefore it is a proper attribute. The consequence is proved: because to be a proper attribute consists only in this, that it emanate from the essence; but emanation is not removed by the fact that it does not always belong, but at a time fixed by nature: because at that time, and not at another, a disposition for such emanation is found in the subject; therefore neither is the ratio of proper attribute, which consists in emanation, removed.

3 Secunda opinio communis & vera. Negat vllam acceptionem proprii, præter quartam, constituere quartum prædicabile, sed tres priores ad quintum prædicabile pertinere affirmat: & solùm proprium quarto modo, constituere quartum prædicabile. Quam tenet D. Tho. opusc. 48 c. 7. Iauel. tract 4. præd. c. 5. Caiet. Sot. & Tol. c. præs. & est expressa, in doctrina Arist. in qua definitio proprii continetur, solùm conueniens Proprio, quarto modo. Et præterea, Proprium secundùm alias acceptiones, ad prędicabile accidẽtis pertinere dicitur. Vtrumque habetur 1. lib. Topicorum, ca. 4 Definitio quidem Proprii his verbis: Proprium est, quod non indicat, quid est esse rei: soli autem inest, & conuersim prædicatur. De aliis etiam acceptionibus Proprii sic ait: Nemo enim proprium dicet, quod contingit alij inesse, neque forsitan per aliquod tempus inest soli, &c. Et in fine capitis inquit: Manifestum est autem ex his, quoniam accidens nihil prohibet, & quando, & ad aliquid proprium fieri: simpliciter autem proprium non erit, &c. Proprium autem ad aliquid: vocat primo & secundo modo acceptum: quia in ordine ad alia tale dicitur, hoc est: quia conuenit soli, & non omni, vel omni, & non soli. Proprium verò, Quando, idem est, atque proprium tertio modo: nam quando significat tempus, & cùm proprium tertio modo, solùm conueniat pro determinato tempore, appellatur ab Aristot. proprium, Quando.

3 The second opinion is common and true. It denies that any acceptation of property besides the fourth constitutes the fourth predicable, but affirms that the three prior ones pertain to the fifth predicable, and that only property in the fourth mode constitutes the fourth predicable. It is held by St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 7; Javelli, tract. 4 on the predicables, ch. 5; Cajetan, Soto, and Toledo, in the present chapter; and it is expressed in the doctrine of Aristotle, in which the definition of property is contained as belonging only to property in the fourth mode. And moreover property according to the other acceptations is said to pertain to the predicable of accident. Both are found in Topics 1, ch. 4: the definition of property in these words: Property is that which does not indicate what the being of the thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly. Of the other acceptations of property, too, he speaks thus: For no one will call property that which can belong to another, nor perhaps that which belongs to it alone for some time, etc. And at the end of the chapter he says: But it is manifest from these things that nothing prevents an accident from becoming a property both when and relative to something; but simply it will not be a property, etc. Property relative to something he calls property taken in the first and second mode, because it is called such in order to other things, that is: because it belongs to only and not to every, or to every and not to only. But property when is the same as property in the third mode: for when signifies time; and since property in the third mode belongs only for a determinate time, it is called by Aristotle property when.

4 Nec minus est expressa sententia Porphyrii, c. vltimo huius libri: vbi in tribus distingui docet, quartum & quintum prædicabile. In primo quidem, quia proprium solùm conuenit vni speciei: cuius essentiam sequitur, eiusque indiuiduis: accidens verò pluribus aliis conuenit. In secundo, differunt, quia proprium conuertibiliter prædicatur de subiecto, non tamen commune accidens. In vltimo verò: quia proprium non suscipit magis & minus, sed communia accidentia suscipiunt. Hæc autem triplex differentia, respectu accidentis, solùm conuenit proprio quarto modo.

4 No less express is the opinion of Porphyry, in the last chapter of this book, where he teaches that the fourth and the fifth predicable are distinguished in three things. In the first, indeed, because property belongs only to one species, whose essence it follows, and to its individuals; but an accident belongs to many others. In the second they differ because property is predicated convertibly of the subject, but not so a common accident. In the last, because property does not admit of more and less, but common accidents do admit of them. But this threefold difference with respect to accident belongs only to property in the fourth mode.

Ratione quoque probatur, ex testimoniis Arist. deducta, Non in communi modo concipiendi, & loquendi, inquit Arist. illud

It is also proved by a reason drawn from the testimonies of Aristotle: Not in the common mode of conceiving and speaking, says Aristotle, is that

p. 179

solùm appellatur Proprium, quod omnibus ita conuenit, vt non sit aliis commune: & præterea, quod semper eis conuenit, quibus est proprium: sed has duas conditiones, solùm habet proprium quarto modo, ergo hoc tantùm erit proprium: reliqua verò accidentia communia: & ideo hoc tantùm constituet quartum prædicabile: reliqua verò potiùs ad quintum pertinebunt. Probatur minor: nam Proprium primo, & secundo modo, vel non conuenit omnibus, vel aliis, etiam commune est: proprium verò tertio modo, multis indiuiduis nunquam conuenit: aliis verò omnibus, multo saltem tempore non conuenit: ergo nullum verè proprium appellari debet, neque ad quartum prædicabile pertinere, intelligendum est.

alone called property which so belongs to all that it is not common to others; and moreover, which always belongs to those of which it is the property; but only property in the fourth mode has these two conditions; therefore this alone will be property, but the others common accidents; and therefore this alone will constitute the fourth predicable, while the others will rather pertain to the fifth. The minor is proved: for property in the first and second mode either does not belong to all, or is common to others as well; but property in the third mode never belongs to many individuals, and to all the others it does not belong at least for a long time; therefore it is to be understood that none of them ought to be called truly property, nor pertain to the fourth predicable.

5 Et si dixeris: Quare ergo propria aliorum modorum adducuntur à Porphyrio in hoc cap. Respondeo, Solùm adduci, quia aliquam habent similitudinem, & analogiam, cum vero proprio quarto modo, ex qua similitudine meliùs cognoscitur natura, & essentia veri proprij, atque etiam ex dissimilitudine, & improprietate eorum. Quare si proprium in communi accipiatur, non vniuocè, sed analogicè, dicitur de omnibus: & solùm de proprio quarto modo simpliciter: de aliis verò non nisi secundùm quid, & per attributionem ad ipsum.

5 And if you say: Why, then, are the properties of the other modes adduced by Porphyry in this chapter? I reply: they are adduced only because they have some likeness and analogy with true property in the fourth mode, from which likeness the nature and essence of true property is better known, and also from their unlikeness and impropriety. Wherefore, if property is taken in common, it is said of all not univocally but analogically: and of property in the fourth mode simply, but of the others only in a certain respect and by attribution to it.

Ad primum arg. Distinguendum est Antecedens: nam aptitudo ad scientias, duplex est, Vniuersalis, & Particularis. Vniuersalis vocatur capacitas, quam habet homo per intellectum: Particularis verò, respectu particularium scientiarum. Nam vnus homo particularem inclinationem, & aptitudinem habet ad vnam scientiam, vel artem, quam non habent alij: licèt vniuersali aptitudine intellectus non careant. Ad formam igitur arg. respondetur, verum esse, quòd proprium primo, & secundo modo, pro aptitudine vniuersali acceptum, sit propria passio, sed hoc modo, non est Proprium primo, aut secundo modo, sed quarto, quia est proprium, dimanans ab essentia hominis specifica: si verò accipiatur pro aptitudine particulari, solùm est proprietas indiuiduorum: neque omnibus conueniens: licèt conueniat solis: & ideo non est proprium simpliciter, sed commune accidens pertinens ad quintum prædicabile.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished: for aptitude for the sciences is twofold, universal and particular. The universal is called the capacity which man has through the intellect; the particular, that with respect to particular sciences. For one man has a particular inclination and aptitude for one science or art which others do not have, although they do not lack the universal aptitude of the intellect. To the form of the argument, then, the reply is that it is true that property in the first and second mode, taken for the universal aptitude, is a proper attribute; but in this way it is not property in the first or second mode but in the fourth, because it is a property flowing from the specific essence of man; but if it is taken for the particular aptitude, it is only a property of individuals, not belonging to all, although it belongs to them alone; and therefore it is not property simply, but a common accident pertaining to the fifth predicable.

6 Pro solutione secundi arg. Duplex proprietas distinguenda est, Specifica, & Indiuidualis. Illa dimanat ex principiis essentialibus speciei, quæ sunt Genus, & Differentia, vt risibilitas ex propriis hominis. Indiuidualis verò, ex complexione indiuiduali, ad quam concurrunt humores, & aliæ qualitates, & dispositiones materiæ. Vnde sequitur, quòd illa

6 For the solution of the second argument, a twofold property is to be distinguished, specific and individual. The former flows from the essential principles of the species, which are genus and difference, as risibility from the proper principles of man. The individual, on the other hand, from the individual complexion, to which the humors and other qualities and dispositions of matter concur. Hence it follows that the former always M ij

p. 180

semper conueniat: quia essentia specifica eodem modo se habet semper: Indiuidualem verò, non necesse est semper conuenire: quia non sunt humores in eadem dispositione: vnde nec vocatur propria passio simpliciter, sed commune accidens. Talis est canities, etiam si pro aptitudine accipiatur: quæ licèt soli homini propriè conueniat, aliis verò animalibus per similitudinem tantùm ad hominem, vt ex causis eius colligitur, quas tradit Arist. lib 4. de generatione animalium, cap. 5. nõ tamen dimanat ab essentia specifica eius, sed ex complexione hominum particulari, & ex aliis etiam causis extrinsecis, in eisdem, & solis hominibus concurrentibus tempore senectutis: ideo non ad quartum prædicabile, sed ad quintum pertinet,

belongs, because the specific essence is always disposed in the same way; but the individual property need not always belong, because the humors are not in the same disposition: hence it is not called a proper attribute simply, but a common accident. Such is grayness of hair, even if it is taken for the aptitude: which, although it belongs properly to man alone, and to other animals only by likeness to man, as is gathered from its causes which Aristotle hands down in On the Generation of Animals 4, ch. 5, nevertheless does not flow from his specific essence, but from the particular complexion of men, and also from other extrinsic causes concurring in the same men, and in men alone, at the time of old age; therefore it pertains not to the fourth predicable but to the fifth.

7 Ad formam igitur arg. Neganda est Consequentia, quòd proprium tertio modo, sit propria passio simpliciter, sed solùm habet similitudinem cum propria passione. Et dum dicitur, Non esse necessarium semper conuenire, vt sit propria passio, negandum est etiam: quia propria passio simpliciter, ex nuda essentia sequitur: vnde non variatur, sed eodem modo se habet, sicut ipsa essentia: proprietates verò indiuiduorum ex aliis causis accidentibus, & extrinsecis dependent, quæ diuerso tempore, diuerso modo se habent: ideo tales proprietates, non sunt propriæ passiones simpliciter, nec sub nomine proprij, constituente quartum prædicabile, comprehenduntur.

7 To the form of the argument, then, the consequence is to be denied, that property in the third mode is a proper attribute simply; it only has a likeness with a proper attribute. And when it is said that it is not necessary for it always to belong in order to be a proper attribute, this too is to be denied: because a proper attribute simply follows from the bare essence; hence it does not vary, but is disposed in the same way as the essence itself; but the properties of individuals depend on other accidental and extrinsic causes, which are disposed in a different way at a different time; therefore such properties are not proper attributes simply, nor are they comprehended under the name of property constituting the fourth predicable.

Quæst. 2. An proprium sit vniuersale, aut quartum prædicabile respectu speciei, vel indiuiduorum — QUESTION II. Whether property is a universal, or the fourth predicable, with respect to the species or to the

QVÆSTIO II.

[…]

An proprium sit vniuersale, aut quartum prædicabile, respectu speciei, vel indiuiduorum.

individuals.

PRo faciliori intelligentia quæst. annotandum est. Primò Duplex esse Proprium: Vnum, quod consequitur naturam generis, aut speciei subalternæ: & ideo vocatur Proprium Subalternum, prædicatúrque de genere ipso conuertibiliter, sed cum qualibet specie, non conuertitur, & ideo respectu generis, est Proprium Adæquatum: & respectu cuiuslibet speciei, Inadæquatum: vt Sensibile, proprium subalternum est, quod sequitur naturam animalis: cum quo conuertitur, sed cum nulla eius specie: ideo proprium adæquatum est, respectu animalis: sed respectu specierum inadæquatum: de omnibus tamen prædicatur eodem modo: ac de genere, quamuis non proximè, sed remotè: hoc est, in Quale proprium: secundùm regulam Anteprædicamentalem ab Arist. traditam, cap. 3. Anteprædicamentorum: Quòd quando aliquid prædicatur de alio,

For an easier understanding of the question it should be noted, first, that property is twofold. One, which follows the nature of a genus or of a subalternate species, and therefore is called subalternate property, and is predicated convertibly of the genus itself, but is not convertible with any species whatever; and therefore with respect to the genus it is adequate property, and with respect to any species inadequate: as sensible is a subalternate property, which follows the nature of animal, with which it is convertible, but with none of its species; therefore it is an adequate property with respect to animal, but inadequate with respect to the species; yet it is predicated of all of them in the same way as of the genus, although not proximately but remotely: that is, in quale as a property, according to the antepredicamental rule handed down by Aristotle in ch. 3 of the Antepredicaments: That when something is predicated of something,

p. 181

quæcunque prædicantur de tali prædicato, prædicantur de eius subiecto, & de omnibus contentis sub illo, & eodem genere prædicationis, secundùm omnes interpretes: vt animal prædicatur de homine, & leone, & sensibile de animali, prædicatione proprij: & ideo necesse est, quòd idem sensibile prædicetur de homine, & leone, sub eodem animali contentis, prædicatione etiam proprij. Aliud est proprium, quod sequitur speciem infimam, & de illa prædicatur proximè, adæquatè, & conuertibiliter: de indiuiduis verò eiusdem, inadæquatè, quia cum nullo conuertitur: & remotè, quia media specie: sed prædicatione proprij, quia in quale proprium.

whatever things are predicated of such a predicate are predicated of its subject and of all things contained under it, and in the same kind of predication, according to all interpreters: as animal is predicated of man and of lion, and sensible of animal, with the predication of a property; and therefore it is necessary that the same sensible be predicated of man and of lion, contained under the same animal, also with the predication of a property. The other property is the one that follows the lowest species, and is predicated of it proximately, adequately, and convertibly; but of the individuals of that species inadequately, because it is convertible with none of them, and remotely, because by means of the species: yet with the predication of a property, because in quale proper.

8 Secundò notandum est, Vtrumque proprium definitum esse ab Arist. 1. li. Topico. cap. 4. illa definitione: Proprium est, quod non indicat, quid est esse rei, soli autem inest & conuersim prædicatur. Quia non minùs conuertitur proprium Subalternum, cum specie Subalterna, quam sequitur: vt sensibile cum animali, ac proprium Infimum, cum Infima specie, vt risibile cum homine: quamuis nec illud conuertatur cum speciebus inferioribus, neque hoc cum indiuiduis: quia respectu inferiorum, neutrum est adæquatum proprium.
