Quod verò dicitur, non indicare quid est esse rei: hoc tantùm significat, quòd est, non pertinere ad essentiam, sed esse accidens eius, quamuis à posteriori, per illud cognoscamus essentiam: & in hoc sensu videatur indicare, quid est esse rei: sed sensus definitionis prior est. Vtrumque est etiam definitum à Porphyrio, dum ait, Proprium quarto modo (quod solùm est proprium simpliciter) esse quod conuenit, omni soli, & semper.

8 It should be noted second that each property was defined by Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 4, with this definition: A property is that which does not indicate what the being of a thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly. For a subaltern property is no less convertible with the subaltern species which it follows (as sensible with animal) than a lowest property with the lowest species (as risible with man); although the former is not convertible with the inferior species, nor the latter with the individuals, because with respect to inferiors neither is an adequate property. And when it is said that it does not indicate what the being of a thing is, this signifies only that it does not pertain to the essence but is an accident of it; although a posteriori we know the essence through it, and in this sense it might seem to indicate what the being of a thing is; but the sense of the definition is the former. Each is also defined by Porphyry, when he says that a property in the fourth mode (which alone is a property simply) is that which belongs to all, to it alone, and always.

De vtroque etiam proprio, tam Subalterno, quàm Infimo, quæritur, An sit vniuersale, & quartum prædicabile, respectu speciei subalternæ, vel infimæ, quam sequitur, vel solùm respectu inferiorum specierum, aut indiuiduorum. Et ratio dubitandi est manifesta: quia nihil est Vniuersale, nisi respectu plurium: sed species, quam sequitur vtrumque proprium vna tantùm est: nam cum ea conuertitur: ergo respectu illius, non erit vniuersale, aut prædicabile, sed solùm respectu specierum inferiorum, aut indiuiduorum, quæ plura sunt.

Concerning each property too, the subaltern as well as the lowest, it is asked whether it is a universal and the fourth predicable with respect to the subaltern or lowest species which it follows, or only with respect to the inferior species or the individuals. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because nothing is universal except with respect to many; but the species which each property follows is only one, for it is convertible with it; therefore with respect to it the property will not be universal or predicable, but only with respect to the inferior species or the individuals, which are many.

9 Prima opinio asserit, Proprium non esse vniuersale, nec quartum prædicabile, respectu generis, aut speciei, quam proximè sequitur, sed respectu inferiorum. Sic Louanienses, cap. præsenti, Fonseca. 5. Metaph. cap. 28, quæst. 19. sectio. 2. Et plures moderni probant, Primò, Quia vniuersale ad plura se extendit, quàm subiectum, de quo prædicatur: ergo si cum eo conuertatur, non erit respectu illius vniuersale. Probatur

9 The first opinion asserts that property is not a universal, nor the fourth predicable, with respect to the genus or species which it proximately follows, but with respect to the inferiors. So the Louvain commentators, on the present chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 28, q. 19, sect. 2; and several moderns. They prove it, first, because the universal extends to more things than the subject of which it is predicated; therefore if it is convertible with it, it will not be universal with respect to it. This is proved M iij

p. 182

Antecedens: nam Vniuersale ex vi nominis, significat id, quod non est particulare, sed ad multa particularia extenditur: ergo repugnat esse Vniuersale, respectu vnius particularis subiecti: vnde cùm species sit vnum particulare subiectum, non erit proprium vniuersale, respectu illius.

the antecedent: for the universal, by the force of the name, signifies that which is not particular but extends to many particulars; therefore it is repugnant for it to be universal with respect to one particular subject; whence, since the species is one particular subject, the property will not be universal with respect to it.

Secundò: Quia ratio Vniuersalis, & ratio Proprij, oppositæ sunt: ergo non possunt eidem respectu eiusdem conuenire: sed proprium dicitur aliquid, respectu speciei, quam sequitur, ergo repugnat dici Vniuersale, respectu eiusdem. Probatur antecedens: nam Vniuersale dicitur, respectu multorum, vt probat definitio eius, quod sit vnum in multis: proprium verò, respectu vnius tantùm, vt ex eius etiam definitione patet, qua dicitur: soli autem inest: ergo sunt rationes oppositæ.

Second, because the ratio of universal and the ratio of property are opposed; therefore they cannot belong to the same thing with respect to the same thing; but something is called a property with respect to the species which it follows; therefore it is repugnant for it to be called universal with respect to the same. The antecedent is proved: for the universal is so called with respect to many, as its definition proves, that which is one in many; but a property with respect to one only, as is also plain from its definition, in which it is said: but belongs to it alone; therefore they are opposed rationes.

Secunda opinio affirmat, Proprium esse vniuersale, & prædicabile, respectu speciei, quam sequitur, & non solùm respectu indiuiduorum. Hanc sequitur Alber. Mag. tract. 5. de proprio, cap. 1. Caiet. & Sot. quæst 1. huius cap. Tolet. in fine eiusdem, & etiam plures moderni.

The second opinion affirms that property is a universal and predicable with respect to the species which it follows, and not only with respect to the individuals. This is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 5, on property, ch. 1; Cajetan; and Soto, q. 1 on this chapter; Toledo, at the end of the same; and also several moderns.

10 Probatur ex Arist. & Porph. Ex Arist. quidem, quia definitio quam tradit de proprio, non conuenit ei respectu inferiorum, sed solùm respectu speciei, ait enim: Soli autem inest, & conuersim prædicatur. hoc est, soli speciei, de qua solùm prædicatur conuertibiliter, & non de inferioribus speciebus, aut indiuiduis, ergo sentit Arist. Proprium, respectu solius speciei, esse proprium, atque adeò vniuersale, & quartum prædicabile. Porphyrius etiam, proprium quarto modo, dicit esse illud, quod conuenit, omni soli, & semper: quas conditiones non videtur habere, nisi respectu speciei: & cap. vlt. huius libri, enumerans ea, quæ conueniunt quarto prædicabili, ait, esse prædicabile de specie, quam sequitur.

10 It is proved from Aristotle and Porphyry. From Aristotle indeed, because the definition which he gives of property does not belong to it with respect to the inferiors, but only with respect to the species; for he says: but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly, that is, to the species alone, of which alone it is predicated convertibly, and not of the inferior species or individuals; therefore Aristotle holds that property, with respect to the species alone, is a property, and therefore a universal and the fourth predicable. Porphyry too says that property in the fourth mode is that which belongs to all, to it alone, and always: which conditions it does not seem to have except with respect to the species; and in the last chapter of this book, enumerating the things that belong to the fourth predicable, he says that it is predicable of the species which it follows.

Item ratione probatur. Primò: Quia modus prædicandi, sequitur modum essendi, quem res habet, ex propria natura, aut ex modo, quo concipitur ab intellectu: sed proprium, ex modo naturali essendi, atque etiam vt concipitur ab intellectu, respicit speciem, tanquam principium proximum, à quo dimanat: species verò inferiores, aut indiuidua, remotè tantùm, & per participationem speciei: ergo rationem vniuersalis, & prædicabilis in Quale, proprium primò habet, respectu speciei, & quasi secundariò, respectu indiuiduorum.

Again, it is proved by reason. First, because the mode of predicating follows the mode of being which a thing has from its own nature, or from the mode in which it is conceived by the intellect; but property, from its natural mode of being, and also as it is conceived by the intellect, regards the species as the proximate principle from which it flows, but the inferior species or the individuals only remotely and through participation in the species; therefore property has the ratio of universal and of predicable in quale primarily with respect to the species, and as it were secondarily with respect to the individuals.

Secundò, Prædicabilia ordinantur ad demonstrationem, sicut prædicamẽta, ergo propositiones necessariæ, & per se: ex quibus demonstratio conficitur, pertinent ad prædicabilia: sed tales sunt illæ, in quibus proprium prædicatur de specie, vt

Second, the predicables are ordered to demonstration, as the categories are; therefore the necessary and per se propositions of which demonstration is composed pertain to the predicables; but such are those in which a property is predicated of the species, as

p. 183

homo est risibilis: pertinebunt igitur ad quartum prædicabile, cùm non sit aliud, ad quod pertinere possint: & ideo proprium erit vniuersale, & prædicabile, respectu speciei.

“man is risible”: they will therefore pertain to the fourth predicable, since there is no other to which they could pertain; and therefore property will be universal and predicable with respect to the species.

11 Nostra sententia duabus conclusionibus explicatur. Prima, Proprium non est vniuersale, respectu solius speciei, sed respectu inferiorum specierum, vel indiuiduorum. Probatur hæc ex definitione vniuersalis: nẽpe, Vnum in multis, & de multis: sed Species, non est multa simpliciter, sed vnum: quamuis sit multa secundùm rationem virtualem, qua participatur à multis: ergo respectu illius, non potest proprium esse vniuersale. Probatur consequentia: quia multa simpliciter non sunt, nec dicuntur, nisi illa quæ actu sunt multa, ac distincta: in specie verò, nec indiuidua multa sunt, nec distincta, sed vnum: nec species ipsa, est in eis multa, sed etiam vnum: ergo proprium respectu solius speciei, non est vniuersale.

11 Our view is explained in two conclusions. The first: Property is not universal with respect to the species alone, but with respect to the inferior species or individuals. This is proved from the definition of the universal, namely one in many and of many; but the species is not many simply, but one, although it is many according to a virtual ratio, by which it is participated by many; therefore with respect to it the property cannot be universal. The consequence is proved: because only those things are, and are called, many simply which are in act many and distinct; but in the species neither are the individuals many or distinct, but one, nor is the species itself many in them, but likewise one; therefore property with respect to the species alone is not universal.

Secunda conclusio. Esse tale vniuersale, hoc est propriũ, aut quartum prædicabile, nec habet proprium in ordine ad solam speciẽ, nec in ordine ad sola indiuidua: sed in ordine ad indiuidua, vt participant rationem speciei. Vt autem conclusio hæc, & præcedens, meliùs intelligatur notandũ est, in proprio, sicut in quocunque alio prædicabili, duo esse consideranda: & rationem communem vniuersalis: quam omnes participant, & in qua conueniunt: & rationẽ specialem, ex tali modo prædicandi desumptam, per quam distinguuntur. Ratio ergo vniuersalis, vt sic, petit plura pro termino: & ideo eam non habet proprium respectu speciei, vt in prima conclusione probatum est: quia species, non est multa simpliciter, sed vnum: rationem verò specialem, talis vniuersalis, & prædicabilis, non habet solùm respectu indiuiduorum: quia non dimanat ab eis, nec primò, & per se, est proprium illorum: sed speciei, à qua primò, & per se emanet, & de qua per se primò prædicatur, in Quale propriũ, vnde in ordine ad illam, habet per se primò, specialem modum prædicandi, per quem distinguitur à cæteris prædicabilibus. Sed quia ad rationem talis vniuersalis, requiruntur talia multa, sicut ad rationem vniuersalis in communi multa simpliciter, adhuc proprium non est tale vniuersale respectu solius speciei nisi cum ordine ad indiuidua, à quibus ratio essentialis eius, & consequenter proprium ipsum ab ea dimanans participatur.

Second conclusion. Property does not have its being such a universal, that is, a property or the fourth predicable, in relation to the species alone, nor in relation to the individuals alone, but in relation to the individuals as they participate the ratio of the species. In order that this conclusion and the preceding one may be better understood, it should be noted that in property, as in any other predicable, two things are to be considered: both the common ratio of universal, which all participate and in which they agree, and the special ratio, taken from such a mode of predicating, by which they are distinguished. The ratio of universal as such, then, requires several things for its term; and therefore property does not have it with respect to the species, as was proved in the first conclusion, because the species is not many simply, but one. But the special ratio of such a universal and predicable it does not have with respect to the individuals alone: because it does not flow from them, nor is it primarily and per se their property, but the species’, from which it flows primarily and per se, and of which it is predicated per se and primarily in quale proper; whence in relation to it, it has per se and primarily the special mode of predicating by which it is distinguished from the other predicables. But because for the ratio of such a universal such many are required, just as for the ratio of the universal in common many simply, property is still not such a universal with respect to the species alone except with an order to the individuals, by which its essential ratio, and consequently the property itself flowing from it, is participated.

12 Ex hac doctrina nõ solùm declaratur vtraque cõclusio, sed colligitur hoc argu. quo probatur secunda. Proprium, vt est quartum prædicabile, sic definiendum est: Proprium est, quod prædicatur de pluribus in Quale proprium sed primum non habet respectu solius speciei: nempe esse prædicabile de multis, nec

12 From this doctrine not only is each conclusion explained, but this argument is gathered by which the second is proved. Property, as it is the fourth predicable, is to be defined thus: A property is that which is predicated of many in quale proper; but it does not have the first with respect to the species alone, namely to be predicable of many, nor M iiij

p. 184

secundum, nempe, in Quale proprium, habet respectu indiuiduorum. nisi cum ordine ad speciem, ratione cuius prædicatur de illis, in Quale proprium, ergo completam definitionem quarti prædicabilis, nec habet à sola specie, nisi cum ordine ad indiuidua, nec à solis indiuiduis, nisi cum ordine ad speciem.

the second, namely in quale proper, with respect to the individuals, except with an order to the species, by reason of which it is predicated of them in quale proper; therefore it has the complete definition of the fourth predicable neither from the species alone, except with an order to the individuals, nor from the individuals alone, except with an order to the species.

Arg. verò primæ opinionis solùm probant, quòd proprium non habet rationem vniuersalis, vt sic, respectu speciei, sed indiuiduorum: non tamen, quòd specialem rationem talis vniuersalis, ex modo prædicandi desumptam, non habeat ab specie, cum ordine ad indiuidua.

The arguments of the first opinion prove only that property does not have the ratio of universal as such with respect to the species, but with respect to the individuals; not, however, that it does not have from the species, with an order to the individuals, the special ratio of such a universal, taken from the mode of predicating.

Arg. secundæ opinionis solùm probat, eandem rationem specialem, talis vniuersalis, aut quarti prædicabilis, habere ab specie, non tamen, sine ordine ad indiuidua: & quia vtrumque continet nostra sententia, non est necessarium, argumenta aliarum in particulari soluere, sed ex annotata doctrina facilè, à quocunque soluentur.

The argument of the second opinion proves only that it has the same special ratio of such a universal, or of the fourth predicable, from the species, yet not without an order to the individuals; and since our view contains both, it is not necessary to solve the arguments of the other opinions in particular, but from the doctrine noted they will easily be solved by anyone.

Solùm restat, vno verbo explicandum id, quod à quibusdam dubitari solet. An proprium, vt est quartum prædicabile, vna, & eadem relatione, secundùm speciem, referatur ad speciem, & indiuidua, aut ad genus, & inferiores species, vel diuersis: ita vt vna ad speciem, & alia ad indiuidua. Cui respondeo, Vna, & eadem referri. Quod ita probo: Relatio, sumit suam vnitatem specificam, à termino formali: sed species, & indiuidua habent eandem rationem terminandi relationem proprij: ergo vna erit respectu omnium. Probatur minor: Proprium refertur ad speciem, & indiuidua: tanquam ad principium, à quo emanat, & tanquam ad subiectum, cum quo conuertitur: sed species, & indiuidua, habent eandem rationem principij, atque subiecti: cùm indiuidua ratione speciei, vtrumque habeant: ergo habent eandem rationem formalem terminandi, & pro vnico termino formali accipienda sunt, à qua vnitatem specificam habet relatio proprij.

It remains only to explain in one word what some are accustomed to doubt: whether property, as it is the fourth predicable, is referred by one and the same relation, according to species, to the species and the individuals, or to the genus and the inferior species, or by different ones, so that one is to the species and another to the individuals. To which I reply that it is referred by one and the same. Which I prove thus: A relation takes its specific unity from the formal term; but the species and the individuals have the same ratio of terminating the relation of property; therefore it will be one with respect to all. The minor is proved: Property is referred to the species and the individuals as to the principle from which it flows and as to the subject with which it is convertible; but the species and the individuals have the same ratio of principle and of subject, since the individuals have both by reason of the species; therefore they have the same formal ratio of terminating, and are to be taken for a single formal term, from which the relation of property has its specific unity.

CHAPTER VI

De Accidenti.

On Accident.

TEX. PORPHYR.

T E X T O F P O R P H Y R Y.

Accidens autem est, quod adest & abest, præter subiecti corruptionem, &c.

But an accident is that which comes and goes without the corruption of the subject, etc.

Breuis explicatio textus.

B R I E F E X P L A N AT I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 INtentum Porphyrii, cap. præsenti est, explicare naturam Accidentis, quod est quintum prædicabile. Agit autem

1 The intent of Porphyry in the present chapter is to explain the nature of Accident, which is the fifth predicable. And he treats

p. 185

tria in toto capite. Primò, Tribus definitionibus definit accidens. Secundò, Quadam diuisione illud diuidit. Tertio, Cuidam tacitæ obiectioni respondet.

three things in the whole chapter. First, he defines accident by three definitions. Second, he divides it by a certain division. Third, he replies to a certain tacit objection.

Prima definitio accidentis est: Accidens est, quod & adest, & abest, præter subiecti corruptionem. Vt albedo inhæret in pariete, & potest separari ab illo sine corruptione eius. Secunda definitio eadem ferè est: Accidens est, quod contingit eidem inesse, & non inesse. Postrema definitio: Accidens est, quod neque est genus, nec differentia, neque species, neque proprium, inest autem subiecto. Datur hæc definitio, per negationem aliorum prædicabilium à Porphyrio, vt explicetur proprius modus prædicandi accidentis.

The first definition of accident is: An accident is that which comes and goes without the corruption of the subject. As whiteness inheres in a wall and can be separated from it without its corruption. The second definition is almost the same: An accident is that which can both belong and not belong to the same thing. The last definition: An accident is that which is neither genus, nor difference, nor species, nor property, but inheres in a subject. This definition is given by Porphyry through the negation of the other predicables, so that the proper mode of predicating of accident may be explained.

2 Diuisio accidentis est: Accidens aliud est Separabile, vt dormire, aliud Inseparabile, vt albedo cygni. Sed poterat obiicere aliquis aduersus Porphyrium, quòd prima definitio accidentis non sit bona, vel quòd hæc diuisio sit mala: quia secundùm primam definitionem, omne accidens potest separari à subiecto: ergo nullum erit inseparabile: sed diuisio asserit, accidens aliud esse Separabile, aliud Inseparabile, ergo sibi contrariantur. Ideo respondet Porphyrius, in 3. par. hac distinctione: Duobus modis contingit separari à subiecto: Secundùm rem, aut secundùm considerationem intellectus: & primo modo, non omne accidens potest separari à subiecto, bene tamen secundo modo; & definito intelligitur primo, aut secundo modo, diuisio verò, solùm secundo modo, ideo non sunt contrariæ.

2 The division of accident is: One accident is separable, as to sleep; another inseparable, as whiteness in a swan. But someone could object against Porphyry that the first definition of accident is not good, or that this division is bad: because according to the first definition every accident can be separated from the subject; therefore none will be inseparable; but the division asserts that one accident is separable and another inseparable; therefore they contradict each other. Therefore Porphyry replies in the 3rd part with this distinction: It happens in two ways that something is separated from the subject: according to the thing, or according to the consideration of the intellect; and in the first way not every accident can be separated from the subject, but it can in the second way; and the definition is understood in the first or in the second way, but the division only in the second way; therefore they are not contrary.

QUESTION I

An accidens sit vniuersale, & respectu quorum id habeat.

Whether accident is a universal, and with respect to which things it has this.

3 PRobatur, Accidens non esse vniuersale, duobus arg. Primò: Quia vniuersale, non habet à parte rei aptitudinem essendi in multis, aut prædicandi de illis: nec respicit inferiora relatione reali, sed solùm habet talem aptitudinem, per intellectum abstrahentem illud, vel comparantem ad inferiora, ad quæ solum dicit respectum rationis: sed Accidens à parte rei, habet aptitudinem essendi in subiecto: ergo etiam habebit aptitudinem prædicandi de illo: & cùm distinguatur ab eo realiter, per relationem realem illud respiciet, vt albedo hominem; ergo accidens non est vniuersale respectu subiecti: imò nec potest prædicari de illo: quia quod ab alio distinguitur realiter, non potest de eo prædicari, cum distinctio realis falsam efficiat prædicationem.

3 It is proved that accident is not a universal by two arguments. First, because the universal does not have on the part of the thing an aptitude for being in many or for being predicated of them, nor does it regard its inferiors by a real relation, but it has such an aptitude only through the intellect abstracting it or comparing it to the inferiors, to which alone it bears a relation of reason; but accident on the part of the thing has an aptitude for being in a subject; therefore it will also have an aptitude for being predicated of it; and since it is really distinguished from it, it will regard it by a real relation, as whiteness regards man; therefore accident is not a universal with respect to the subject; indeed, it cannot even be predicated of it, because what is really distinguished from another cannot be predicated of it, since a real distinction makes the predication false.

p. 186

Secundò Vniuersale dicitur esse in multis, & posse prædicare de multis, etiam si illa multa non sint actu, in rerum natura, sed solùm in potentia: vt patet de Sole & Luna; sed Accidens non potest prædicari de subiectis, nisi actu existentibus: ergo non est vniuersale, nec prædicabile. Probatur minor: quia nullo homine existente, in rerum natura, falsum erit dicere: Homo est albus, aut Petrus est albus.

Second: the universal is said to be in many and to be able to be predicated of many, even if those many do not exist in act in the nature of things but only in potency, as is plain of the Sun and the Moon; but accident cannot be predicated of subjects except of those actually existing; therefore it is not universal or predicable. The minor is proved: because if no man existed in the nature of things, it would be false to say: Man is white, or Peter is white.

Pro solutione huius quæstionis, notandum est primò, Accidens duobus modis considerari. Primò, in ordine ad sua inferiora quidditatiua: vt color respectu albedinis, & nigredinis: aut albedo, respectu huius, & illius albedinis: & hoc modo non constituit quintum prædicabile, sed primum, secundum, vel tertium: nam vel genus est, vel species, aut differentia. Secundò consideratur in ordine ad subiecta, quibus inhæret: vt album in ordine ad hominem, vel parietem. Et hoc modo constituit quintum prædicabile, quia prædicatur in Quale accidentale.

For the solution of this question it should be noted first that accident is considered in two ways. First, in relation to its quidditative inferiors, as color with respect to whiteness and blackness, or whiteness with respect to this and that whiteness; and in this way it does not constitute the fifth predicable, but the first, second, or third, for it is either a genus, or a species, or a difference. Second, it is considered in relation to the subjects in which it inheres, as white in relation to man or a wall. And in this way it constitutes the fifth predicable, because it is predicated in quale accidental.

Secundò notandum: Accidens dupliciter considerari: In abstracto, & in concreto: & primo modo consideratum, non dicit subiectum sed solã formam: vt albedo, & color, & cum hæc distinguatur realiter, à subiecto, non prædicatur de illo, falsum est enim dicere: Homo est albedo: consideratum verò in concreto, dicit subiectum, vt album: & à diuersis subiectis abstractum per intellectum, vt ab homine, & pariete, est vniuersale, & prædicabile respectu aliorum, à quibus solùm distinguitur ratione: nec habet aptitudinem prædicandi de illis à parte rei, sed solùm per intellectum: nec denique ad illa refertur relatione reali, sed rationis: sicut cætera prædicabilia, ad sua inferiora: sed quia accidens, respicit subiectum secundùm modum inhærentiæ actualis in eo, & hoc modo prædicatur de illo, requirit actualem existentiam subiectorum, de quibus prædicatur: aliqui non erunt veræ prædicationes: & in hoc distinguitur à cæteris prædicabilibus, quę cùm essentialia sint, vt genus, species, & differentia, vel propriæ passiones, consequentes essentiam, vt quartum prædicabile, abstrahunt ab existentia, & prædicantur de inferioribus, secundùm naturalem connexionem extremorum: ideoque non requirunt actualem eorum existentiam.

It should be noted second that accident is considered in two ways: in the abstract and in the concrete. Considered in the first way, it does not express the subject but the form alone, as whiteness and color; and since this is really distinguished from the subject, it is not predicated of it, for it is false to say: Man is whiteness. But considered in the concrete, it expresses the subject, as white; and abstracted by the intellect from diverse subjects, as from man and a wall, it is universal and predicable with respect to those from which it is distinguished only by reason; nor does it have an aptitude for being predicated of them on the part of the thing, but only through the intellect; nor, finally, is it referred to them by a real relation, but by one of reason, just as the other predicables are to their inferiors. But because accident regards the subject according to the mode of actual inherence in it, and in this way is predicated of it, it requires the actual existence of the subjects of which it is predicated; otherwise the predications would not be true. And in this it is distinguished from the other predicables, which, since they are essential, as genus, species, and difference, or proper attributes following upon the essence, as the fourth predicable, abstract from existence and are predicated of their inferiors according to the natural connection of the extremes; and therefore they do not require their actual existence.

5 His suppositis, Conclusio respondens quæstioni est: Accidens in concreto sumptum, est quintum prædicabile: non respectu inferiorum quidditatiuè, sed respectu subiectorum, à quibus abstrahitur & de quibus prædicatur, in Quale accidentale; & hoc modo sumptum definitur à Porphyrio, duplici

5 These things supposed, the conclusion answering the question is: Accident taken in the concrete is the fifth predicable, not with respect to its quidditative inferiors but with respect to the subjects from which it is abstracted and of which it is predicated in quale accidental; and taken in this way it is defined by Porphyry by a twofold

p. 187

definitione, inferiùs explicanda. Probatur hæc conclusio: Quia accidens hoc modo sumptum, est vnum in multis accidentaliter, & ideo prædicabile de multis in Quale accidentale distinctúmque à cæteris quatuor prædicabilibus.

definition, to be explained below. This conclusion is proved: because accident taken in this way is one in many accidentally, and therefore predicable of many in quale accidental, and distinct from the other four predicables.

Ad primum arg. Neganda est minor, quòd accidens habeat aptitudinem realem inhærendi, aut essendi in multis, à parte rei: nam si sumatur in abstracto, verum est, sed sic non est vniuersale, nec prædicabile: sed dicit formam accidentalem, realiter distinctam à subiectis, & realiter eis inhærentem: quæ non potest realiter prædicari de illis, propter realem distinctionem: si verò sumatur in concreto, respectu subiectorum, à quibus abstrahitur, vniuersale est, & prædicabile, vt expositum est.

To the first argument, the minor is to be denied, namely that accident has a real aptitude for inhering or being in many on the part of the thing: for if it is taken in the abstract, this is true; but so taken it is not universal or predicable, but expresses an accidental form really distinct from the subjects and really inhering in them, which cannot really be predicated of them, on account of the real distinction; but if it is taken in the concrete, with respect to the subjects from which it is abstracted, it is universal and predicable, as has been explained.

Ad secundum; Distinguenda est minor: nam vt accidens sit vniuersale & prædicabile, satis est, quòd plura subiecta, secundùm potentiam existentia respiciat: sed ad exercitium prædicationum, requirit actualem existentiam subiectorum: & in primo, conuenit cum cæteris prædicabilibus: à quibus distinguitur, in hoc secundo, propter modum distinctum prædicandi, accidentalem, quem habet: nam accidens respicit subiectũ secundùm actualem inhærentiam in eo: actualis verò inhærentia, petit actualem existentiam subiecti: quia nihil potest inhærere, nisi actu existenti: de aliis verò prædicabilibus, diuersa est ratio, quantum ad exercitium prædicandi, iam explicata.

To the second, the minor is to be distinguished: for in order that accident be universal and predicable, it is enough that it regard several subjects existing according to potency; but for the exercise of predications it requires the actual existence of the subjects; and in the first it agrees with the other predicables, from which it is distinguished in this second, on account of the distinct, accidental mode of predicating which it has; for accident regards the subject according to actual inherence in it, and actual inherence requires the actual existence of the subject, because nothing can inhere except in what actually exists; but of the other predicables the ratio is different as regards the exercise of predicating, as has already been explained.

CHAPTER II

An diuisio accidentis, in accidens separabile, & inseparabile, sit bona.

Whether the division of accident into separable and inseparable accident is good.

DVobus argumentis, videtur probari, quòd non sit bona. Primò: Quia accidens secundùm Porphyrium, duobus modis potest separari à subiecto, secundùm rem, & per intellectum: ergo nullum accidens inseparabile. Probatur consequentia: quia accidens inseparabile secundùm rem, est separabile per intellectum: vnde non bene diuiditur accidens, in duo membra.

t seems to be proved by two arguments that it is not good. First, be‐ I cause accident according to Porphyry can be separated from the subject in two ways, according to the thing and through the intellect; therefore no accident is inseparable. The consequence is proved: because an accident inseparable according to the thing is separable through the intellect; whence accident is not well divided into two members.

Secundò: Quia si omne accidens est separabile, per intellectum: ergo hæc diuisio, comprehendit propriam passionem, quæ licèt non possit separari secundùm rem, potest tamen per intellectum: vt risibile, potest separari ab homine: quia cùm nõ sit de essentia eius: potest homo intelligi sine illo. Et ex hoc sequitur, quartum prædicabile, & quintum, non distingui. Probatur consequentia: quia propria passio, quæ constituit

Second: because if every accident is separable through the intellect, then this division comprehends the proper attribute, which although it cannot be separated according to the thing, can nevertheless be through the intellect, as risible can be separated from man: because, since it is not of his essence, man can be understood without it. And from this it follows that the fourth predicable and the fifth are not distinguished. The consequence is proved: because the proper attribute, which constitutes

p. 188

quartum prædicabile, pertinet ad quintum, cùm sit accidens inseparabile.

the fourth predicable, pertains to the fifth, since it is an inseparable accident.

Pro solutione quæstionis, annotanda est distinctio, quam tradit D. Tho. quæst. Vnica, de spiritualibus creaturis, art. vltimo ad 7. vbi ait, Duplicem esse operationem intellectus, per quam vnum separat ab alio Vna est simplex abstractio, per quam illud vnum sine alio cognoscit, sine affirmatione, & negatione: vt dum intelligimus albedinem, existentem in pariete, non intellecto pariete: non tamen negando, quòd in eo sit. Altera est, abstractio composita, per quam vnum sine alio intelligimus, illud de eo negando: vt si dum intelligimus, albedinem sine pariete: negemus eam de pariete, dicẽtes, paries non est albus.

For the solution of the question, the distinction is to be noted which St. Thomas gives in the single question On Spiritual Creatures, last article, ad 7, where he says that the operation of the intellect by which it separates one thing from another is twofold. One is simple abstraction, by which it knows that one thing without the other, without affirmation or negation: as when we understand the whiteness existing in a wall without understanding the wall, yet without denying that it is in it. The other is composite abstraction, by which we understand one thing without the other while denying it of it: as if, when we understand whiteness without the wall, we deny it of the wall, saying: The wall is not white.

8 Secundò notandum est: Quòd hæc est differentia, inter accidens separabile, & propriam passionem, quantum ad secundum modum abstractionis à subiecto: quòd subiectum accidentis inseparabilis, non solùm potest intelligi sine illo, sed etiam cum opposito, salua eius essentia: vt cygnus, non solùm potest intelligi sine albedine, sed cum nigredine, quæ non repugnat essentiæ eius. Sed subiectum propriæ passionis, quãuis possit intelligi sine illa, non tamen cum opposita: cuius ratio est, quia cùm propria passio dimanet ab essentia, & qua impossibile est dimanare oppositam: impossibile est etiam, quod cũ opposita intelligatur, sed accidens inseparabile, nõ dimanat ab essentia subiecti: ideo non repugnat, quòd idem subiectum, cum opposito accidente intelligat. Exempli gratia, Sine risibilitate, potest intelligi homo, nõ tamen cum hinnibilitate, quia repugnat hinnibilitatẽ dimanare ab essentia eius: sed cygnus, non solùm potest intelligi sine albedine, sed etiam cum nigredine: quia cùm albedo non dimanet ab essentia eius, non repugnat, quòd cum nigredine opposita intelligatur.

8 It should be noted second that this is the difference between the inseparable accident and the proper attribute as regards the second mode of abstraction from the subject: that the subject of an inseparable accident can be understood not only without it but also with its opposite, its essence remaining intact; as a swan can be understood not only without whiteness but with blackness, which is not repugnant to its essence. But the subject of a proper attribute, although it can be understood without it, yet cannot be understood with the opposite one; the reason for which is that, since the proper attribute flows from the essence, and it is impossible that the opposite should flow from it, it is also impossible that it be understood with the opposite; but the inseparable accident does not flow from the essence of the subject, and therefore it is not repugnant that the same subject be understood with the opposite accident. For example, man can be understood without risibility, yet not with the capacity to neigh, because it is repugnant that the capacity to neigh should flow from his essence; but a swan can be understood not only without whiteness but also with blackness, because, since whiteness does not flow from its essence, it is not repugnant that it be understood with the opposite blackness.

Conclusio nostra est, Diuisionem esse bonam. Probatur: Quia vtrumque membrum, verè datur in rebus, verum accidens est, & tantum continet, quantum diuisum: ergo adæquata est, & bona diuisio: sed intelligenda est realiter, & non per intellectum: ita vt sensus sit: Accidens, vnum est separabile, à subiecto realiter: & aliud realiter inseparabile, ab eodem: & ex hoc soluitur primum argumentum.

Our conclusion is that the division is good. It is proved: because each member is truly found in things, is truly an accident, and together they contain as much as the thing divided; therefore it is an adequate and good division. But it is to be understood really, and not through the intellect, so that the sense is: one accident is really separable from the subject, and another really inseparable from the same; and by this the first argument is solved.

9 Ad secundum: Neganda est consequentia, quia accidens commune, separari potest per intellectum, vtraque abstractione, simplici, & composita: ita vt non solùm negari possit de subiecto, sed etiam oppositam ei attribui: quod non habet passio, quia cùm dimanet ab essentia: repugnat oppositam passionem conuenire subiecto. Itaque commune accidens, omnibus

9 To the second, the consequence is to be denied: because a common accident can be separated through the intellect by both abstractions, simple and composite, so that not only can it be denied of the subject, but its opposite can also be attributed to it; which the attribute does not have, because, since it flows from the essence, it is repugnant that the opposite attribute should belong to the subject. And so every common accident

p. 189

modis, potest separari per intellectum à subiecto: proprium verò non omnibus modis: & hoc sufficit, vt ad quintum prædicabile non pertineat.

can be separated from the subject through the intellect in all ways, but a property not in all ways; and this suffices for it not to pertain to the fifth predicable.

10 Sed vt meliùs natura huius prædicabilis intelligatur: Triplex alia differentia notanda est, quam habet respectu proprij. Prima est: Quòd proprium dimanat, ex principiis essentialibus subiecti: accidens commune, non dimanat ab eis: sed ex aliis causis prouenit. Secunda: Quòd passio, primò conuenit speciei, secundariò verò indiuiduis accidens commune. ex opposito, primò conuenit indiuiduis, & ratione eorum speciei. Et ratio huius differentiæ est: quia proprium maximè dimanat à natura specifica, sed commune accidens, ex particularibus causis indiuidualibus sequitur. Tertia differentia est: Quòd proprium prædicatur per se, de subiecto, accidens verò quod est quintum prædicabile per accidens.

10 But in order that the nature of this predicable may be better understood, a further threefold difference is to be noted which it has with respect to property. The first is that a property flows from the essential principles of the subject; a common accident does not flow from them, but comes from other causes. The second: that an attribute belongs primarily to the species and secondarily to the individuals; a common accident, on the contrary, belongs primarily to the individuals, and by reason of them to the species. And the reason for this difference is that a property flows chiefly from the specific nature, but a common accident follows from particular individual causes. The third difference is that a property is predicated per se of the subject, but an accident, which is the fifth predicable, per accidens.

QUESTION III

Qu. 3. An definitiones accidentis intelligantur à Porphyrio de inhærentia reali accidentis in subiecto, vel secundæ intentionaliter de affirmatione, & negatione — Whether the definitions of accident are understood by Porphyry of the real inherence of the accident in the subject, or in terms of second intention, of affirmation and negation.

An definitiones accidentis, intelligantur à Porphyrio, de inherentia reali accidentis in subiecto, vel secundo intentionaliter, de affirmatione, & negatione.

[…]

11 VIdetur hoc secundo modo intelligi, & non primo, quod probatur ex eodem Porphyrio: qui Vltimam definitionem, assignauit per negationem aliorum prædicabilium, ergo definit accidens, vt prædicabile: & consequenter, non per realem inhærentiam, sed per prædicationem. Et præterea, quia vt explicaret diuisionem, non esse contrariam primæ definitioni, docuit, Accidens non solùm secundùm rem, sed per intellectum posse separari à subiecto: ergo dum illud asserit posse adesse, & abesse subiecto, in prima definitione, non de reali inhærentia, sed de prædicatione loquitur.

11 It seems that they are understood in this second way and not in the first, which is proved from the same Porphyry, who assigned the last definition through the negation of the other predicables; therefore he defines accident as a predicable, and consequently not through real inherence but through predication. And moreover, because, in order to explain that the division is not contrary to the first definition, he taught that accident can be separated from the subject not only according to the thing but through the intellect; therefore when he asserts in the first definition that it can come to and go from the subject, he speaks not of real inherence but of predication.

Et ratione deinde probatur. Primò: Quia accidens secundùm realem inhærentiam, non pertinet ad Dialecticum, sed ad Philosophum: ergo in Dialectica, non per illam debet definiri, sed per prædicationem Dialecticæ propriam.

And it is then proved by reason. First, because accident according to real inherence does not pertain to the Dialectician but to the Philosopher; therefore in Dialectic it ought not to be defined through it, but through predication, which is proper to Dialectic.

Secundò: Accidentia rationis, qualia sunt secundæ intentiones, dum prædicantur de primis, pertinet ad hoc prædicabile, & non habent realem inhærentiam in subiecto, sed solùm sunt obiectiuè intellectu: & tamen eis conueniunt definitiones accidentis: ergo non intelliguntur de reali inhærẽtia, sed de prædicatione. Hanc sententiam tenent Caiet. cap. præsenti, dubio 1. Iauel. tra. 4. de quinque prædicabilibus, cap. 6. Sotus in expositione textus, & eandem dicit esse probabilem, Tole. dub. 3.

Second, accidents of reason, such as second intentions are when they are predicated of first ones, pertain to this predicable, and do not have real inherence in the subject, but are only objectively in the intellect; and yet the definitions of accident belong to them; therefore they are not understood of real inherence, but of predication. This opinion is held by Cajetan on the present chapter, doubt 1; Javelli, tract. 4, on the five predicables, ch. 6; Soto in the exposition of the text; and Toledo, doubt 3, says that it is probable.

p. 190

12 Secunda opinio affirmat, Easdem definitiones, intelligi à Porphyrio de reali inhærentia accidentis: Et hæc est probabilior. Probatur efficaciter ex Porphyrio, qui vt explicaret primam definitionem, non esse contrariam diuisioni, tradit diuersos modos separationis, accidentis à subiecto, nempe reale, & per intellectum: quod non esset necessarium, si definitio intelligeretur de prædicatione, & non de reali inhæsione: nam prædicatio, separationem dicit per intellectum, si sit negatiua.

12 The second opinion affirms that the same definitions are understood by Porphyry of the real inherence of the accident; and this is more probable. It is proved effectively from Porphyry, who, in order to explain that the first definition is not contrary to the division, gives different modes of separation of the accident from the subject, namely real and through the intellect; which would not be necessary if the definition were understood of predication and not of real inherence: for predication, if it is negative, expresses separation through the intellect.

Probatur secundò: Quia eodem modo sumitur accidens in definitionibus, sicut in diuisione, sed diuisio non potest intelligi de prædicatione, sed de reali separatione: nam in primo sensu, nullum accidens esset inseparabile, ergo definitiones de reali inhærentia intelliguntur.

It is proved second: because accident is taken in the definitions in the same way as in the division; but the division cannot be understood of predication, but of real separation, for in the first sense no accident would be inseparable; therefore the definitions are understood of real inherence.

Ad primum testimonium respondetur: Non per solam negationem aliorum prædicabilium, definiisse Porphyrium accidens, sed per realem inhærentiam, quam in vltimo verbo definitionis posuit. Secundum testimonium, potiùs probat nostram sententiam.

To the first testimony it is replied that Porphyry defined accident not through the negation of the other predicables alone, but through real inherence, which he placed in the last word of the definition. The second testimony rather proves our view.

Ad primum arg. respondetur: Quòd realis inhærentia, fundamentum est secundæ intentionis: quam necesse fuit explicare per definitiones, vt natura huius prædicabilis, meliùs intelligeretur.

To the first argument it is replied that real inherence is the foundation of the second intention, which it was necessary to explain through the definitions, so that the nature of this predicable might be better understood.

Ad secundum dicimus, Entia rationis, non habere realem inhærentiam in subiecto, sed intelligi à nobis per similitudinem, ad accidentia realia, quæ illam habent: & ideo de illis etiam loquimur, ac si realiter inhærent: quare per similitudinem, applicantur eis definitiones accidentis.

To the second we say that beings of reason do not have real inherence in a subject, but are understood by us through likeness to real accidents, which have it; and therefore we also speak of them as if they really inhered; wherefore the definitions of accident are applied to them through likeness.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Quæst. 4. An prima definitio accidentis sit bona — Whether the first definition of accident is good.

An prima definitio accidentis sit bona.

[…]

13 RAtio dubitandi est, quia multa sunt accidentia, quæ subiectum corrumpunt, vt morbus lethalis, combustio & mors: ergo eis non conuenit definitio: quia non possunt adesse, & abesse, præter subiecti corruptionem.

13 The reason for doubting is that there are many accidents which corrupt the subject, as a lethal disease, burning, and death; therefore the definition does not belong to them, because they cannot come and go without the corruption of the subject.

Difficultas huius quæstionis, in eo consistit: An ea quæ enumerantur in argumento, sint accidentia, vel non. Et prima opinio, negat esse accidentia, sed potiùs, dicit esse destructiones substantiæ, vel prædicatata substantialia priuatiua. Probat: quia corruptio vel mors, est dissolutio principiorum vitæ: sed principia vitæ sunt substantialia: ergo corruptio, & mors, erunt potiùs quid substantiale, quàm accidentale.

The difficulty of this question consists in this: whether the things enumerated in the argument are accidents or not. And the first opinion denies that they are accidents, but says rather that they are destructions of substance, or substantial predicates taken privatively. It proves this: because corruption or death is the dissolution of the principles of life; but the principles of life are substantial; therefore corruption and death will be something substantial rather than accidental.

p. 191

Pro solutione quæstionis, notandum est, Mortem dupliciter sumi posse: primò pro corruptione rei, vt in fieri, hoc est, dum fit: aut pro corruptione in facto esse, vel iam facta: & certum est, vtroque modo sumptam, modum saltem accidentis habere, & consequenter subiectum: & cùm sit quasi mutatio priuatiua, non solùm habet subiectum, sed etiam terminum, quasi per eam factum: & subiectum eius est materia, quæ à forma, quæ corrumpitur, ad formam de nouo aduenientem mutatur: vt à forma hominis, quæ desinit esse in materia, ad formam cadaueris, quæ de nouo aduenit. Terminus autem corruptionis, est non esse rei, vt non esse hominis: denominat autem corruptio materiam, tanquam subiectum in quantum est mutatio eius: & etiam terminum, nempe rem corruptam, ad cuius non esse terminatur: & ita materia denominatur priuatiuè, mutata per corruptionem, tanquam subiectum huius accidentis priuatiui: & id quod desinit esse per eam, dicitur non esse, vel esse mortuum, aut corruptum: & sicut est accidens materiæ, tanquam subiecti, in quo intelligitur inhærere, ita respectu illius conuenit ei definitio accidentis: quia adest, & abest materiæ præter eius corruptionem: terminum verò non denominat, vt subiectum, sed tanquam terminum, quem destruit, & ideo non est accidens, respectu eius, nec conuenit ei definitio accidentis,

For the solution of the question it should be noted that death can be taken in two ways: first, for the corruption of a thing in its becoming, that is, while it is coming to be; or for the corruption in its having been made, or already made. And it is certain that, taken in either way, it has at least the mode of an accident, and consequently a subject; and since it is as it were a privative change, it has not only a subject but also a term, as it were the thing made through it. And its subject is the matter, which is changed from the form that is corrupted to the form newly supervening: as from the form of man, which ceases to be in the matter, to the form of the corpse, which newly supervenes. But the term of corruption is the not-being of the thing, as the not-being of the man. And corruption denominates the matter as its subject, inasmuch as it is its change, and also the term, namely the thing corrupted, at whose not-being it terminates; and so the matter is denominated privatively, changed through corruption, as the subject of this privative accident; and that which ceases to be through it is said not to be, or to be dead or corrupted. And just as it is an accident of the matter as of the subject in which it is understood to inhere, so with respect to it the definition of accident belongs to it, because it comes to and goes from the matter without the matter’s corruption; but it does not denominate the term as a subject, but as the term which it destroys, and therefore it is not an accident with respect to it, nor does the definition of accident belong to it.

14 Nostra igitur sententia est: Illa omnia, quæ in arg. enumerantur, esse accidentia, vel saltem modum accidentium habere: quibus suo modo conuenit definitio. Quod probatur euidenter de morbo etiam lethali, hac ratione: Morbus adest, & abest, sine subiecti corruptione: ergo conuenit ei definitio accidentis. Probatur antecedens: quia quamdiu durat morbus, subiectum manet, & eo absente, etiam manet: ergo adesse, & abesse potest, præter corruptionem eius.

14 Our view, then, is that all the things enumerated in the argument are accidents, or at least have the mode of accidents, to which the definition belongs in its own way. This is proved evidently of disease, even lethal disease, by this argument: Disease comes and goes without the corruption of the subject; therefore the definition of accident belongs to it. The antecedent is proved: because as long as the disease lasts the subject remains, and when it is absent it also remains; therefore it can come and go without its corruption.

Secundò, probatur de combustione, & morte: nam ista habent modum mutationis priuatiuę: sed subiectũ, Vnum in multis, vt docet Arist. 1. & 5. li. Phys. ergo est accidens: quare modum accidentium habere debent, quibus definitio conueniat.

Second, it is proved of burning and death: for these have the mode of a privative change; but the subject is one in many, as Aristotle teaches in Phys. 1 and 5; therefore it is an accident: wherefore they must have the mode of accidents, to which the definition may belong.

Ex his responderetur ad arg. Morbum esse accidens, & posse adesse, & abesse subiecto, præter corruptionem eius: quia quamdiu durat, non est corruptum, sed manet. De combustione verò, & morte, dicimus esse accidentia priuatiua, materiæ, cui adsunt, & absunt præter corruptionem eius: non tamen sunt accidentia hominis, vel domus, sed illum, & hanc denominat, tanquam terminos. Quod verò ad veritatem propositionum attinet, nempe: Homo est mortuus, vel Domus

From these things the reply would be given to the argument: disease is an accident and can come to and go from the subject without its corruption, because as long as it lasts the subject is not corrupted but remains. But of burning and death we say that they are privative accidents of the matter, to which they come and from which they go without its corruption; yet they are not accidents of the man or of the house, but they denominate the one and the other as terms. As for the truth of the propositions, namely The man is dead, or The house

p. 192

est combusta: veras esse dicimus, vt communis modus concipiendi, & loquendi tenet: quia sensus est: Homo desiit esse, aut Domus: & verus quidem, quia non denominantur, vt subiecta, sed vt termini corruptionis: quasi dicatur hominem, & domum, per mortem, aut combustionem periisse: mors namque appellatur, corruptio hominis: quia est priuatio vitæ: non verò combustio domus, sed talis combustio.

is burned, we say that they are true, as the common mode of conceiving and speaking holds, because the sense is: The man has ceased to be, or the house; and it is true indeed, because they are denominated not as subjects but as terms of the corruption, as if it were said that the man and the house have perished through death or burning; for death is called the corruption of the man, because it is the privation of life; but burning is not the corruption of the house, but such a burning.

15 Circa rationem tandem Accidentis duo sunt notanda. Primum: Duobus modis sumi accidens, nempe pro accidente Prædicamentorum, & pro accidente Prædicabili: & hæc acceptio est vniuersalior, quia non solùm compræhendit vera accidentia, sed illa etiam, quæ licèt sint substantiæ, modo tamen quodam accidentali se habent ad alia, & ideo ex parte modi se habendi, videntur ea respicere tanquam subiecta, vt differentia, respectu generis, accidens prædicabile vocatur, licèt sæpè sit substantia: quia adesse, & abesse porest generi, salua eius essentia. Accidens verò prædicamentale, solùm comprehendit vera accidentia: sed ex alia parte, idem accidens, vt prędicabile, minùs vniuersale est: quia accidens prædicamentale, absolutè comprehendit omnia accidentia vera: accidens verò prædicabile, non comprehendit ea, nisi sub limitata consideratione: hoc est, quatenus subiecto adesse & abesse possunt, vel prædicari, & non prædicari de illo. Albedo enim, aut nigredo, sicque de cæteris accidentibus, duobus modis considerantur. Primo: Secundùm proprias essentias, vt in eis sunt Genera, Species, & Indiuidua: & sic pertinent ad specialia prædicamenta, & non ad quintum prædicabile, sed ad primum, secundum, vel tertium. Alio modo, In ordine ad subiectum, cui adesse, & abesse possunt: & sic pertinent ad quintum prædicabile.

15 Finally, concerning the ratio of accident, two things are to be noted. The first: accident is taken in two ways, namely for the accident of the categories and for the predicable accident; and this acceptation is more universal, because it comprehends not only true accidents but also those which, although they are substances, yet relate to others in a certain accidental mode, and therefore, on the part of the mode of relating, seem to regard them as subjects: as difference, with respect to the genus, is called a predicable accident, although it is often a substance, because it can come to and go from the genus, its essence remaining intact. But categorial accident comprehends only true accidents; yet on the other side the same accident, as predicable, is less universal: because categorial accident comprehends all true accidents absolutely, but predicable accident does not comprehend them except under a limited consideration, that is, insofar as they can come to and go from the subject, or be predicated and not be predicated of it. For whiteness or blackness, and so of the other accidents, are considered in two ways. First, according to their own essences, as there are in them genera, species, and individuals; and so they pertain to the special categories, and not to the fifth predicable, but to the first, second, or third. In another way, in relation to the subject to which they can come and from which they can go; and so they pertain to the fifth predicable.

Ex quibus intelligitur distinctio quædam, satis necessaria, prædicationis accidentalis: nam vna est Accidentalis, ab accidente prædicamentali, quando prædicatum, verum est accidens, inhærens subiecto, de quo prædicatur. Alia est accidentalis, ab accidente prædicabili, & non prædicamentali, cuius prędicatum, non est verum accidens subiecti, sed modo accidentali se habet ad illud, in quantum adesse & abesse potest ei, præter eius corruptionem: vt hæc prædicatio. Homo est albus, accidentalis est, ab accidente prædicamentali, & etiam prædicabili: hæc verò, Animal est rationale: non ab accidente prædicamentali, sed solùm ab accidente prædicabili.

From these things a certain quite necessary distinction of accidental predication is understood: for one is accidental from a categorial accident, when what is predicated is a true accident inhering in the subject of which it is predicated. The other is accidental from a predicable and not categorial accident, whose predicate is not a true accident of the subject, but relates to it in an accidental mode, inasmuch as it can come to and go from it without its corruption: as this predication, Man is white, is accidental from a categorial accident and also from a predicable one; but this one, Animal is rational, not from a categorial accident, but only from a predicable accident.

16 Secundò notandum est: Quòd Accidens, vt est quintum prædicabile, non est definiendum per plures species, vel plura

16 It should be noted second that accident, as it is the fifth predicable, is not to be defined through several species or several individuals

p. 193

indiuidua, tanquam per subiecta, quia licèt vera sint subiecta accidentis, tam hęc, quàm illa: quodlibet tamen est inadæquatum: itaque definiendum est per illud vniuersalius, quod sit quasi adæquatum subiectum eius & in plurali sumptum, adæquatus terminus relationis eiusdem accidentis, vt prædicabilis. Vnde, talis erit eius adæquata definitio: Accidens est, quod predicatur de pluribus, in Quale accidentale. Per quam definitionem, ratione vltimæ particulæ, patet distingui à cæteris prędicabilibus. Et hæc de prædicabilibus annotasse sufficiat.

as through its subjects: because, although both the former and the latter are true subjects of the accident, yet each is inadequate; and so it is to be defined through that more universal thing which is as it were its adequate subject and, taken in the plural, the adequate term of the relation of the same accident as predicable. Whence its adequate definition will be this: An accident is that which is predicated of many in quale accidental. By this definition, by reason of the last particle, it is plain that it is distinguished from the other predicables. And let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the predicables.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

An inhærentia aptitudinalis, sit de essentia accidentis.

Whether aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident.

17 INhærentia duplex est, Actualis, & Aptitudinalis. Actualis est modus quidam, per quem accidens vnitur subiecto, vt ab eo sustentetur: & proportionatur, modo per se substantiæ, per quem in se, & per se subsistit independenter ab alio: vnde sicut modus Subsistentiæ, est vltimus terminus naturæ substantialis, per se existentis, à quo completur, & constituitur in supposito: ita inhærentia actualis, est vltimus terminus naturę accidentalis, actu existentis, complens eam, & constituens actu, in subiecto: & tandem, sicut subsistentia, præsupponens actualem existentiam, non distinctam realiter à natura substantiali, sed per quam est extra causas, distinguitur ex natura rei, ab eadem natura substantiali, per se existente: eadem ratione, inhærentia actualis accidentis, præsupponens nostro modo intelligendi, naturam accidentalem actu existentem, distinguitur ab ea, ex natura rei.

17 Inherence is twofold, actual and aptitudinal. Actual inherence is a certain mode through which the accident is united to the subject, so as to be sustained by it; and it is proportioned to the per se mode of substance, through which it subsists in itself and per se independently of another. Whence, just as the mode of subsistence is the ultimate term of a substantial nature existing per se, by which it is completed and constituted in a supposit, so actual inherence is the ultimate term of an accidental nature actually existing, completing it and constituting it in act in the subject. And finally, just as subsistence, presupposing actual existence (not really distinct from the substantial nature, but through which it is outside its causes), is distinguished from the nature of the thing from the same substantial nature existing per se, by the same reason the actual inherence of an accident, presupposing, in our mode of understanding, the accidental nature actually existing, is distinguished from it from the nature of the thing.

Alia est inhærentia Aptitudinalis: quæ non est aliud, quàm aptitudo eiusdem naturæ accidentalis, ad actu inhærendum subiecto: vt si Deus separet accidens à subiecto, peribit modus actualis, inhærentiæ eius: per quem actu inhærebat subiecto: sed adhuc erit aptum ei inhærentiæ eius: per quem actu inhærebat subiecto: sed adhuc erit aptum ei inhærere: & hæc aptitudo inhærendi vocatur inhærentia aptitudinalis.

The other is aptitudinal inherence, which is nothing other than the aptitude of the same accidental nature for actually inhering in the subject: as, if God should separate an accident from the subject, the mode of its actual inherence, through which it actually inhered in the subject, will perish; but it will still be apt to inhere in it; and this aptitude for inhering is called aptitudinal inherence.

Et de inhærentia actuali, certum est apud omnes, quòd non sit de essentia accidentis, quia sine illa potest esse accidens, si non naturaliter, saltem diuina virtute: & verè manet quantitas Eucharistiæ, sine inhærentia actuali, quam habebat in substantia panis. Ex quo euidens argumentum deducitur probans non pertinere ad eius essentiam, & cùm eadem ratio sit de cæteris accidentibus, sequitur, actualem inhærentiam, nulli accidenti esse essentialem: in quo etiam assimilatur subsistentiæ substantiali: de qua euidens est, eam nõ pertinere ad essentiam

And concerning actual inherence it is certain among all that it is not of the essence of accident, because without it there can be an accident, if not naturally, at least by divine power; and indeed the quantity of the Eucharist remains without the actual inherence which it had in the substance of the bread. From which an evident argument is deduced proving that it does not pertain to its essence; and since the same reason holds of the other accidents, it follows that actual inherence is essential to no accident; in which it is also likened to substantial subsistence, of which it is evident that it does not pertain to the essence N

p. 194

naturę substantialis, cùm sit in fide certum, Naturam humanam Christi, non habere propriam subsistentiam: sed terminatam esse, subsistentia verbi Diuini. Ideo solùm quærit titulus quæstionis, de inhærentia aptitudinali, An sit de essentia accidentis.

of the substantial nature, since it is certain in faith that the human nature of Christ does not have its own subsistence, but is terminated by the subsistence of the divine Word. Therefore the title of the question asks only about aptitudinal inherence, whether it is of the essence of accident.

18 Et est prima opinio Scoti in 4. d. 12. q. vnica, & Antonij Andreę 7. Meta. q. 1. cum cęteris Scoti discipulis, asserentium, non pertinere ad essentiam eius, sed extra illam esse. Probant id primò: Quia inhærentia, est relatio accidentis ab subiectum, vel relationem saltem includit, ergo non potest esse de essentia alicuius accidentis absoluti: imò aliquam rationem accidentalem debet prę supponere in eo, cui conuenit, per quam fundetur talis relatio: & ex consequenti, essentiam accidentis, eam fundantem: quare extra illam omnino erit.

18 And the first opinion is that of Scotus, In 4, d. 12, single q., and of Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 7, q. 1, with the other disciples of Scotus, who assert that it does not pertain to its essence, but is outside it. They prove this, first, because inherence is a relation of the accident to the subject, or at least includes a relation; therefore it cannot be of the essence of any absolute accident; indeed, it must presuppose some accidental ratio in that to which it belongs, through which such a relation is founded, and consequently the essence of the accident founding it; wherefore it will be altogether outside it.

Secundò: Si inhęrentia aptitudinalis est de essentia accidentis, omnibus ęquè conuenire debet: quia quę essentialia sunt, omnibus illius ordinis debent ęquè conuenire: sed neque conuenit omnibus, neque ęquè potest conuenire: ergo non est essentialis. Probatur minor, quia modus, quem habet quantitas Eucharistiæ, separata à substantia, est accidens; cùm terminet naturam accidentalem: & repugnat ei aptitudo inhęrendi, cùm sit modus essendi per se, & independenter à subiecto, ergo non conuenit omnibus accidentibus: sed neq; ęqualiter: quia iam conueniret eis vniuocè, quod videbimus esse falsum.

Second: if aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident, it must belong to all equally, because the things that are essential must belong equally to all of that order; but it neither belongs to all nor can belong equally; therefore it is not essential. The minor is proved: because the mode which the quantity of the Eucharist has, separated from the substance, is an accident, since it terminates an accidental nature; and the aptitude for inhering is repugnant to it, since it is a mode of being per se and independently of the subject; therefore it does not belong to all accidents; nor yet equally, because then it would belong to them univocally, which we shall see is false.

Secunda opinio est communis, & vera quôd inhęrentia aptitudinalis sit de essentia accidentis. Ita D. Th. in 4. d 18. q. & art. 1. q. etiam 1. Capr. in 4. d. 2. q. 1. ad 1. contra 5. & 6. conc. Herue. quodlib. 4. q. 9. Iauel. 7. Meta. q. 1. Caiet. 7. c. de ente, & essentia, q. 15. Et colligitur euidenter ex doctrina Arist. 7. Meta. text. 2. vbi asserit, Accidentia non esse entia, sed entis entia: hoc est substantię, ad quam in sua entitate, dicunt attributionem: sed esse entia substantię, est posse eam afficere, secundum proprios modos intrinsecos: ergo aptitudo ei inhęrendi, est eis essentialis. ex mente Aristotelis.

The second opinion is the common and true one: that aptitudinal inherence is of the essence of accident. So St. Thomas, In 4, d. 18, q. and a. 1, q. also 1; Capreolus, In 4, d. 2, q. 1, ad 1 against the 5th and 6th conclusions; Hervaeus, Quodlibet 4, q. 9; Javelli, Metaph. 7, q. 1; Cajetan, On Being and Essence, ch. 7, q. 15. And it is gathered evidently from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 7, text 2, where he asserts that accidents are not beings, but beings of a being, that is, of substance, to which in their entity they bear an attribution; but to be beings of substance is to be able to affect it according to their own intrinsic modes; therefore the aptitude for inhering in it is essential to them, according to the mind of Aristotle.

19 Probatur etiam ratione: Quia esse per se, & esse in alio, sunt modi intrinseci substantiæ, & accidentis, diuidentes per se ens, sed esse per se, secundum aptitudinem, hoc est, aptum esse ad subsistendum per se, est de essentia substantiæ: ergo aptum esse ad inhęrendum eidem substantiæ, erit de essentia accidentis. Probatur minor: Quia, substantiam esse talem entitatem, cui debetur subsistentia per se, essentiale est ei: & hoc, est, esse radicem, vnde oritur subsistentia, esse ei essentialem: ergo etiã est essentiale accidentia, esse talem naturam, cui debetur

19 It is proved also by reason: because to be per se and to be in another are the intrinsic modes of substance and accident, dividing being per se; but to be per se according to aptitude, that is, to be apt to subsist per se, is of the essence of substance; therefore to be apt to inhere in the same substance will be of the essence of accident. The minor is proved: because for substance to be such an entity that subsistence per se is due to it is essential to it; and this is for it to be essential to it to be the root from which subsistence arises; therefore it is also essential to accidents to be such a nature that there is due to it

p. 195

actualis inhærentia in subiecto: quod est, esse radicem actualis inhærentiæ: & radix hæc, est inhærentia aptitudinalis, quæ etiam erit ei essentialis

actual inherence in a subject: that is, to be the root of actual inherence; and this root is aptitudinal inherence, which will therefore also be essential to it.

Ad primum argum. Neganda est maior: quòd inhærentia actualis, sit relatio: sed est modus absolutus, includens respectum quendam transcendentalem, de quo neganda est minor: quòd non possit esse, de essentia absoluti, sicut cætera prædicata transcendentalia, vt videbimus in prædicamento Ad aliquid. Vbi probabimus: quòd licèt relatio prædicamentalis, quæ vocatur secundum esse, non possit pertinere ad essentiam absoluti, respectus tamen transcendentales, & secundùm dici, ad essentiam plurium absolutorum necessariò pertinent.

To the first argument, the major is to be denied, namely that actual inherence is a relation; rather it is an absolute mode including a certain transcendental respect, of which the minor is to be denied, namely that it cannot be of the essence of an absolute thing, just as the other transcendental predicates, as we shall see in the category of Relation; where we shall prove that, although categorial relation, which is called relation secundum esse, cannot pertain to the essence of an absolute thing, yet transcendental respects, or respects secundum dici, necessarily pertain to the essence of many absolute things.

Ad secundum: Neganda est prima consequentia, quòd inhærentia aptitudinalis, conueniat æqualiter omnibus accidentibus, aut vniuocè: nam cùm conueniat eis per attributionem ad substantiam vel sit ipsamet attributio ad substantiam, non potest eis conuenire vniuocè: quia repugnat attributio vniuocationi. Et præterea, vnicuique conuenit secundùm proprium modum attributionis ad substantiam, quod sufficit analogiam constituere, vt in anteprædicamentis, c. 2. ostendemus. De modo autem per se, quantitatis Eucharistiæ, non est certum, quòd illum habeat, sed probabile, quòd immediatè sustentetur à Deo, & etiam si illum habere dicatur, non est natura accidentalis, cui debetur actualis inhærentia, sed modus, cui per se non debetur: sicut inhærentiæ actuali, non debetur alia inhærentia: alioqui esset processus in infinitum: sed cùm sit ratio, vel modus inhærendi, non dicitur propriè inhærere: nec modo illi, per se essendi quantitatis, debetur inhærentia: quia non est natura accidentalis: sed entitas quædam modalis, supernaturaliter concessa accidenti: vt sit per se, hoc est, sine dependentia actuali à substantia: quæ entitas, accidentalis est, quia modum essendi tribuit accidenti. Itaque naturæ accidentali, tantùm conuenit aptitudinalis inhærentia, per se, sicut ei solùm debita est actualis: modis verò, non conuenit per se; sed ratione naturæ, cuius sunt modi: sicut nec per se inhærent, sed ratione naturæ: & cùm modus ille, nec sit natura accidentalis, nec modus per se, ex propria natura conueniens accidenti, non est ei vllo modo debita actualis inhærentia, nec erit essentialis ei inhærentia aptitudinalis.

To the second, the first consequence is to be denied, namely that aptitudinal inherence belongs equally to all accidents, or univocally: for since it belongs to them through attribution to substance, or is itself the attribution to substance, it cannot belong to them univocally, because attribution is repugnant to univocation. And moreover, it belongs to each according to its own mode of attribution to substance, which suffices to constitute analogy, as we shall show in the Antepredicaments, ch. 2. But as for the per se mode of the quantity of the Eucharist, it is not certain that it has it, but it is probable that it is sustained immediately by God; and even if it be said to have it, it is not an accidental nature to which actual inherence is due, but a mode to which it is not due per se; just as to actual inherence another inherence is not due, otherwise there would be a process to infinity; but since it is the ratio or mode of inhering, it is not properly said to inhere. Nor is inherence due to that mode of per se being of quantity, because it is not an accidental nature, but a certain modal entity supernaturally granted to the accident, so that it may be per se, that is, without actual dependence on substance; which entity is accidental, because it gives the accident a mode of being. And so aptitudinal inherence belongs per se only to the accidental nature, just as actual inherence is due to it alone; but it does not belong to the modes per se, but by reason of the nature whose modes they are; just as neither do they inhere per se, but by reason of the nature; and since that mode is neither an accidental nature nor a mode belonging per se to the accident from its own nature, actual inherence is in no way due to it, nor will aptitudinal inherence be essential to it. N ij

p. 196

COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK

COMMENTARII IN LIBRVM CATEGORIARVM, ARISTOTELIS Stagiritæ, quæ Prædicamenta appellari consueuerunt, Vnà cum dubiis, & quæstionibus, hac tempestate agitari solitis.

O F T H E C AT E G O R I E S O F A R I S T O T L E the Stagirite, which they have been accustomed to call the Predicaments, together with the Doubts and Questions customarily debated in our time.

BREVE PROEMIVM.

B R I E F P RO E M .

De inscriptione huius libri — On the title of this book.

De inscriptione huius libri.

[…]

1 QVamuis vocabulum Gręcum Categoria, ex prima eius impositione, à prædicatione, seu prædicato dictum sit: communi tamen Dialecticorum, & Philosophorum consensu, iam accipitur, pro integra ordinatione prædicatorum essentialium: eadémque est significatio prędicamenti: quod sic possumus describere: Prædicamentum, est dispositio prædicamentorum essentialium, superiorum atque inferiorum, sub vno quodam supremo genere, quo nihil est superius, vsque ad indiuiduum, quo nihil est inferius. Vnde liber categoriarum, aut prædicamentorum, scribitur opus hoc: id est, Liber ordinationum, quibus prædicata disponuntur secundùm diuersos gradus essendi, à supremo genere, quod quasi caput totius ordinationis est, vsque ad infimas species & indiuidua.

lthough the Greek word Categoria, from its first imposition, is 1 A so called from predication or from the predicate, yet by the common consent of Dialecticians and Philosophers it is now taken for the entire ordering of essential predicates; and the same is the signification of predicament, which we can describe thus: A predicament is the arrangement of essential predicates, superior and inferior, under some one supreme genus, than which nothing is higher, down to the individual, than which nothing is lower. Whence this work is entitled the book of the Categories or Predicaments: that is, the book of the orderings by which predicates are arranged according to the different grades of being, from the supreme genus, which is as it were the head of the whole ordering, down to the lowest species and individuals.

De inuentore artis prædicamentalis — On the inventor of the categorial art.

De inuentore artis prædicamentalis.

[…]

COmmunis consensus scholæ, iam tenet, primum inuentorem huius artis, fuisse Aristotelem. Ille enim primus fuit, qui omnes gradus essendi, sic disponere docuit, vt ad certas quasdam classes reducerentur, omnes res mundi: & facilè possemus naturam, & essentiam cuiuscumq; inuenire, ad propriam eius categoriam, aut prædicamentum recurrendo.

The common consent of the school now holds that the first inventor of this art was Aristotle. For he was the first who taught how to arrange all the grades of being in such a way that all the things of the world might be reduced to certain definite classes, and that we might easily find the nature and essence of anything by recurring to its proper category or predicament.

De fine huius operis — On the end of this work.

De fine huius operis.

[…]

CVm ex simplicibus, aut incomplexis rebus, efficiantur prædicamenta patet ad primam operationem intellectus, quæ est simplicium apprehensio, pertinere: & ad specifiendam secundam, quæ versatus circa compositionem, & diuisionem,
