Since the categories are made from simple or incomplex things, it is plain that they pertain to the first operation of the intellect, which is the apprehension of simples, and that they are ordered, for specifying the second, which is concerned with composition and division,

p. 197

proximè ordinari. Sed tanquam ad finem vltimum, ad Demonstrationem ad quam omnia, quæ in Dialectica tractatur, ordinari constat.

proximately; but as to their ultimate end, to Demonstration, to which it is established that all the things treated in Dialectic are ordered.

An de vocibus, vel de rebus agatur in prædicamentis — Whether the categories treat of words or of things.

An de vocibus, vel de rebus agatur in prædicamentis.

[…]

AB omnibus refutatur sententia nominalium: qui dixerunt. de vocibus principaliter agere opus hoc, sicut & tota scientia Dialecticæ. Quod ex eo probatur falsum: quia voces tantùm sunt instrumenta, quibus loco rerum vtimur, non valentes res, de quibus disputatur, ad scholas afferre: vt Arist. docet 1. lib. Elenchorum. Res igitur sunt. ex quibus ordinatio prædicamentalis constituitur, mediis vocibus significatæ: & ideo de rebus principaliter, minùs principaliter de vocibus, tanquam de conditionibus necessariis agit ars prædicamentalis.

By all is refuted the opinion of the Nominalists, who said that this work, like the whole science of Dialectic, treats principally of words. Which is proved false from this: because words are only instruments which we use in place of things, since we are unable to bring the things that are disputed about into the schools, as Aristotle teaches in Sophistical Refutations 1. It is things, therefore, from which the categorial ordering is constituted, signified by means of words; and therefore the categorial art treats principally of things, and less principally of words, as of necessary conditions.

De obiecto huius operis — On the object of this work.

De obiecto vnius operis.

[…]

OBiectum verò huius partis Dialecticæ est categoria, seu prædicamentum, in communi consideratum, prout omnes ordinationes prædicamẽtales, sub se comprehendit. Quod probatur inde: quia sub eo proximè continentur, omnia, quæ in arte hac tractatur, & rationem eius proximè participant: quæ duo propriæ conditiones obiecti sunt.

The object of this part of Dialectic is the category or predicament considered in common, as it comprehends under itself all the categorial orderings. Which is proved from this: because under it are proximately contained all the things treated in this art, and they proximately participate its ratio; which two are the proper conditions of an object.

De modo procedendi, & ordinatione huius operis, cum cæteris partibus Dialecticæ — On the mode of proceeding, and on the ordering of this work with the other parts of

De modo procedendi, & ordinatione huius operis, cum cæteris partibus Dialecticæ.

Dialectic.

2 MOdus procedendi, quem Aristot. seruat, in hoc opere, simplex est. Quia per definitionem, & diuisionem, procedit: per quas docet, quonam modo simplicia sunt ordinanda in prædicamentis.

2 The mode of proceeding which Aristotle observes in this work is simple, because he proceeds by definition and division, through which he teaches in what way simples are to be ordered in the categories.

Quod verò ad ordinem huius operis inter cæteras partes Dialecticæ attinet, sic explicari debet: vt primum locum teneat, inter omnes: quia ordinatio simplicium, & ordinata cognitio eorum, quasi ianua est, per quam ad reliquas partes Dialecticæ, & ad totam ipsam scientiam ingredimur.

As for the order of this work among the other parts of Dialectic, it must be explained thus: that it holds the first place among them all, because the ordering of simples, and the ordered cognition of them, is as it were the door through which we enter the remaining parts of Dialectic and the whole science itself.

Ad quam scientiam pertineat de prædicamentis agere — To which science it pertains to treat of the categories.

Ad quam scientiam pertineat, de prædicamentis agere,

[…]

LIcèt nonnulli asserant, ad nullam scientiam determinatam pertinere, artem prædicamentalem, sed intellectum

Although some assert that the categorial art pertains to no determinate science, but that the intellect N iij

p. 198

per lumen naturale, nulla scientia media, notitiam huius artis habere posse, & adeo, nec ad Dialecticam, nec ad Metaphysicam pertinere: Nihilominus, cùm prædicatorum ordinationes, non possint fieri sine arte, vel scientia, necessariò dicendum est, ad scientiam pertinere, & in primis ad Metaphysicam: cuius ratio satis est per se manifesta, & nota: quia de ente reali vniuersalissimo agit: ergo ad eam pertinet, omnes modos entis realis considerare, secundùm rationem propriam, abstrahendi à materia: sed prædicamenta non sunt aliud, quam rerum ordinationes, ex quibus proprios modos entis cognoscimus: ergo hæc ars ordinandi res secundùm diuersos modos essendi, ad Metaph. propriè pertinebit: & etiam ad Dialecticam, sed diuersa ratione: nam ad illam, secundùm proprias entitates, ad Dialecticam verò, in ordine ad prędicationes, enunciationes, & syllogismos.

through the natural light, without any intermediate science, can have cognition of this art, and that it therefore pertains neither to Dialectic nor to Metaphysics; nevertheless, since the orderings of predicates cannot be made without an art or science, it must necessarily be said that it pertains to a science, and first of all to Metaphysics. The reason for this is sufficiently manifest and known per se: because Metaphysics treats of the most universal real being; therefore it pertains to it to consider all the modes of real being according to its proper ratio of abstracting from matter; but the categories are nothing other than orderings of things, from which we know the proper modes of being; therefore this art of ordering things according to the different modes of being will pertain properly to Metaphysics; and also to Dialectic, but under a different ratio: for to the former according to their proper entities, but to Dialectic in relation to predications, enunciations, and syllogisms.

CHAPTER I

CAP. I. De æquiuocis, & vniuocis, & denominatiuis, cum exposit. text. — On Equivocals, Univocals, and Denominatives.

De æquiuocis, vniuocis, & denominatiuis.

[…]

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Æquiuoca dicuntur, quorum nomen solum commune est, secundum verò nomen, substantiæ ratio diuersa.

Those things are called equivocal whose name alone is common, but the ratio of substance according to the name is different.

Textus expositio.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

3 INtentum Arist. in hoc primo capite est, explicare naturam nominum Æquiuocorum, Vniuocorum, & Denominatiuorum: nam cùm ex rebus fiant prædicamenta, vt significantur per voces, ex modo significandi vocum, maximè dependet distinctio rerum, quæ in prædicamento collocandæ sunt: & ita, ex applicatione harum trium vocum, tria alia constabunt Primum, quænam sint à prædicamentis excludenda. Secundum, ex quibus prædicamenta constituenda sint. Tertium, quonam modo res vnius prædicamenti, prædicari possint de rebus alterius.

3 The intent of Aristotle in this first chapter is to explain the nature of Equivocal, Univocal, and Denominative names: for since the categories are made from things as they are signified by words, the distinction of the things that are to be placed in a category depends chiefly on the mode of signifying of words; and so, from the application of these three words, three other things will be established. First, which things are to be excluded from the categories. Second, from which things the categories are to be constituted. Third, in what way the things of one category can be predicated of the things of another.

Diuiditur autem caput, in tres partes, in quarum Prima, proponit Arist. definitionem Æquiuocorum: in Secunda, definitionem Vniuocorum: & in Tertia, definitionem Denominatiuorum.

And the chapter is divided into three parts, in the first of which Aristotle proposes the definition of Equivocals; in the second, the definition of Univocals; and in the third, the definition of Denominatives.

Definitio Æquiuocorum talis est, Æquiuoca dicuntur, quorum nomen commune est, ratio verò substantiæ nomini accommodata, diuersa. Quæ duas continet partes. In prima dicitur, quòd Æquiuoca debent habere nomen commune, vt significetur

The definition of Equivocals is this: Those things are called equivocal whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is different. Which contains two parts. In the first it is said that equivocals must have a common name, so that it may be signified

p. 199

distincta esse ab eodem nomine: & esse res significatas per ipsum: vt canis latrabilis, sydus cæleste, & piscis marinus, quæ sunt res significatæ, per hoc nomen canis: distincta quidem hæc sunt ab eo, sed non dicuntur Æquiuoca, nisi vt per nomen significantur: quia res non pertinent ad Dialecticam, nisi vt significantur per voces.

that they are distinct from that same name and are the things signified by it: as the barking dog, the heavenly constellation, and the sea fish, which are the things signified by this name canis [dog]; these are indeed distinct from it, but they are not called equivocals except as they are signified by the name, because things do not pertain to Dialectic except as they are signified by words.

Et ex hoc desumpta est communis illa distinctio, qua distinguuntur Æquiuoca, in æquiuoca æquiuocata, & Æquiuoca æquiuocantia: ita vt Æquiuoca æquiuocata, sint res, quæ, vt significãtur tali nomine, dicũtur fieri æquiuoca in eo: AEquiuoca verò æquiuocãtia, sint voces ipsæ, quæ, ex tali modo significandi, res efficiunt æquiuocas.

And from this is taken that common distinction by which equivocals are distinguished into equivocated equivocals and equivocating equivocals: so that equivocated equivocals are the things which, as they are signified by such a name, are said to become equivocal in it; but equivocating equivocals are the words themselves, which, from such a mode of signifying, make the things equivocal.

4 Secunda pars definitionis est, in qua dicitur, Quòd ratio substãtia, accommodata nomini æquiuoco, sit diuersa Per rationẽ verò, intelligitur definitio: vel conceptus quidditatiuus, in his quæ non habent definitionem. Definitio igitur, vel cõceptus AEquiuocorũ, vt significantur nomine æquiuoco, omnino diuersus esse debet: ita vt in eo nullo modo conueniant: sed solùm habeant nomen commune.

4 The second part of the definition is the one in which it is said that the ratio of substance accommodated to the equivocal name is different. By ratio is understood the definition, or the quidditative concept in those things which do not have a definition. The definition, therefore, or the concept of equivocals, as they are signified by the equivocal name, must be altogether different, so that they in no way agree in it, but have only the name in common.

Definitio Vniuocorum hæc est. Vniuoca dicuntur, Quorum & nomen commune est, & secundum nomen eadem substantiæ ratio. In qua, per rationem substantiæ, definitio, vel conceptus Vniuocorum intelligitur: qui idem esse debet. & non diuersus, sicut diuersam esse diximus in AEquiuocis.

The definition of Univocals is this: Those things are called univocal whose name is common, and the ratio of substance according to the name is the same. In which by the ratio of substance is understood the definition or concept of univocals, which must be the same and not different, as we said it is different in equivocals.

Definitio Denominatiuorum sic habet: Denominatiua dicũtur, quæcunque ab aliquo, solo differentia casu, secundum nomen habent appellationem: vt à fortitudine, fortis. In qua tria continẽtur, quia in denominatione tria sunt: Forma denominans: Res denominata: & Denominatiuum nomen: tali ordine intelligenda, vt Res denominata dicatur talis, à Denominatiuo nomine: & hoc dicatur Denominatiuum, à forma: & ita forma, sit quasi origo, totius denominationis. Gratia exempli: Fortis, nomen denominatiuum est, in quo res denominata est Petrus ipse. Forma verò, à qua denominatur, est fortitudo. A qua nomen ipsum denominatiuum, casu debet differre: vt significetur deriuatio denominationis eiusdem, quam à forma res denominata accipit.

The definition of Denominatives runs thus: Those things are called denominative which, differing only in case, have their appellation according to the name from something: as from fortitudo [courage], fortis [courageous]. In which three things are contained, because in denomination there are three: the denominating form, the thing denominated, and the denominative name; to be understood in such an order that the thing denominated is called such from the denominative name, and this is called denominative from the form; and so the form is as it were the origin of the whole denomination. For example: courageous is a denominative name, in which the thing denominated is Peter himself; but the form from which he is denominated is courage. From which the denominative name itself must differ in case, so that the derivation of that denomination which the thing denominated receives from the form may be signified.

SINGLE QUESTION

Vtrùm definitio Vniuocorum, conueniat, Denominatiuis.

Whether the definition of univocals belongs to denominatives.

5 PRima opinio tenet, Denominatiua simul esse Vniuoca, sed diuersa ratione: nam in quãtum appellationem habẽt

5 The first opinion holds that denominatives are at the same time univocals, but under a different ratio: for insofar as they have their appellation N4

p. 200

bent ab alio, dicuntur Denominatiua: in ordine tamen ad res denominatas: de quibus prædicantur, verè sunt vniuoca: vt album, respectu albedinis, à qua denominatur, Denominatiuum dicitur: sed respectu huius, & illius corporis, nempe parietis, & hominis, de quibus prædicatur, Vniuocum est, quare omnibus Denominatiuis conuenit definitio Vniuocorum. Ita Sotus q. vniuoca huius ca. ad secundum. Quam sententiam probabilem dicit esse Caiet. in expositione definitionis Denominatiuorum. Et videtur probari ex definitione Vniuocorum: quia nomen Denominatiuum commune est omnibus subiectis, de quibus dicitur: vt album, homini, & parieti: & ratio significatã, quæ est forma accidentalis, eadem est etiam in eis, vt albedo in eisdem, ergo conuenit eis integra definitio.

from another, they are called denominatives; but in relation to the things denominated, of which they are predicated, they are truly univocal: as white, with respect to whiteness, from which it is denominated, is called denominative; but with respect to this and that body, namely a wall and a man, of which it is predicated, it is univocal; wherefore the definition of univocals belongs to all denominatives. So Soto, in the single question on this chapter, ad 2. Which opinion Cajetan says is probable, in the exposition of the definition of denominatives. And it seems to be proved from the definition of univocals: because the denominative name is common to all the subjects of which it is said, as white to man and to a wall; and the ratio signified, which is the accidental form, is also the same in them, as whiteness in the same; therefore the whole definition belongs to them.

Et potest probari secundò: quia omne vniuersale debet esse vniuocum: vt in quæst. vltima Vniuersalium diximus, sed inter Vniuersalia, quartum, & quintum prædicabile, sunt denominatiua, vt risibile, & album probant: ergo Denominatiua sunt Vniuoca, & eis verè & propriè conuenit definitio Vniuocorum.

And it can be proved second: because every universal must be univocal, as we said in the last question on universals; but among the universals, the fourth and fifth predicables are denominatives, as risible and white prove; therefore denominatives are univocal, and the definition of univocals truly and properly belongs to them.

Secunda opinio, est Toleti: qui quamuis negare omnino videatur, Denominatiua esse Vniuoca: vnum tamen asserit, ex quo videtur contrarium colligi: nempe illam particulam definitionis vniuocorum (ratio substantiæ) intelligi, de definitione quidditatiua, vel descriptiua: ita, vt sufficiat ad rationem Vniuoci, quòd definitio descriptiua, eadem sit in omnibus vniuocatis. Ex quo colligitur nomina propriæ passionis, vt sensibile, aut risibile, esse Vniuoca, respectu subiectorum, de quibus prædicantur: vt sensibile, respectu hominis & equi.

The second opinion is that of Toledo, who, although he seems altogether to deny that denominatives are univocal, nevertheless asserts one thing from which the contrary seems to be gathered: namely, that that particle of the definition of univocals (ratio of substance) is understood of the quidditative or of the descriptive definition, so that it suffices for the ratio of a univocal that the descriptive definition be the same in all the univocates. From which it is gathered that the names of proper attributes, as sensible or risible, are univocal with respect to the subjects of which they are predicated, as sensible with respect to man and horse.

6 Nostra tamen sententia est, Denominatiuis nullo modo conuenire definitionem vniuocorum, ita tenet Caiet. cap. præsenti, & est expressa sententia Arist. cap. de substantia. Vbi Denominatiua asserit, non prædicari de subiectis, nomine, & ratione: quia forma significata per nomen, non est quidditatiuè in eis, sed accidentaliter.

6 Our view, however, is that the definition of univocals in no way belongs to denominatives. So holds Cajetan on the present chapter, and it is the express opinion of Aristotle in the chapter on substance, where he asserts that denominatives are not predicated of their subjects in name and in ratio: because the form signified by the name is not in them quidditatively, but accidentally.

Et ratione probatur: Quia in definitione Vniuocorum dicitur (quorum nomen est cõmune, ratio verò substãtiæ eadẽ.) Per rationem autem substantiæ, intelligunt omnes, aut definitionem quidditatiuam, aut quidditatiuum conceptũ: quæ propriè ad substantiam rei pertinent: sed hoc non reperitur in Denominatiuis: quia res significata per illa, neque est definitio quidditatiua respectu inferiorum, nec quidditatiuus conceptus eorum, sed forma accidentalis: ergo non sunt Vniuoca.

And it is proved by reason: because in the definition of univocals it is said (whose name is common, and the ratio of substance the same); but by the ratio of substance all understand either the quidditative definition or the quidditative concept, which properly pertain to the substance of the thing; but this is not found in denominatives: because the thing signified by them is neither the quidditative definition with respect to the inferiors nor their quidditative concept, but an accidental form; therefore they are not univocal.

Ad primum arg. Distinguenda est minor: Nam ratio significata

To the first argument, the minor is to be distinguished: for the ratio signified

p. 201

per nomen, duobus modis potest esse cõmunis, vel eadem in inferioribus essentialiter, aut accidentaliter: & primo modo, communis esse debet, vt nomen sit Vniuocum, hoc enim intelligit Arist. per illa verba (ratio substantiæ nomini accõmodata) in definitione Vniuocorum: quia ratio substantiæ: idem est ac ratio essentialis, significatum verò Denominatiuorum, solùm est commune, & vnum in inferioribus, accidentaliter: & ideo non potest eis conuenire definitio Vniuocorum.

by the name can be common in two ways: either as the same in the inferiors essentially, or accidentally. And in the first way it must be common for the name to be univocal; for this is what Aristotle means by those words (the ratio of substance accommodated to the name) in the definition of univocals, because the ratio of substance is the same as the essential ratio. But the significate of denominatives is common and one in the inferiors only accidentally; and therefore the definition of univocals cannot belong to them.

7 Secundum arg. soluitur alia distinctione. Vniuocum duobus modis accipitur, propriè pro eo, cuius non solùm nomen commune est vniuocatis, sed definitio, vel conceptus quidditatiuus: & hoc tantum definiuit Aristot. cap. præsenti. Aliud est Vniuocum, improprium: cuius significatum, commune est inferioribus, solùm accidentaliter: & hoc modo impropria, Denominatiua possunt dici Vniuoca: qui licèt non sufficiat, vt eis conueniat definitio Vniuocorum, sufficit tamen vt sint Vniuersalia, & prædicabilia: nam ad rationem Vniuersalis, sufficit aliquid esse Vniuocum, solùm, vt distinguitur contra æquiuocum & analogum: quod habent Denominatiua, per impropriam vniuocationem.

7 The second argument is solved by another distinction. Univocal is taken in two ways: properly, for that of which not only the name is common to the univocates, but also the definition or quidditative concept; and only this did Aristotle define in the present chapter. The other is improper univocal, whose significate is common to the inferiors only accidentally; and in this way, improperly, denominatives can be called univocal. And although this does not suffice for the definition of univocals to belong to them, it does suffice for them to be universals and predicables: for to the ratio of universal it suffices that something be univocal only as it is distinguished against the equivocal and the analogous, which denominatives have through an improper univocation.

TRACTATVS DE NOMINVM ANALOGIA.

T R E AT I S E O N T H E A N A L O G Y

OF NAMES

8 TRactatio de natura, & ratione Analogiæ, maxima ex parte pertinet ad Metaphysicam: cùm præcipuè reperiri possit in ente vniuersalissimo, quod proprium obiectum eius est: atq; etiam in passionibus eius, & in accidenti, quod nomen prædicamentis est commune: sed propriè pertinet ad Logicam, vt ex ea cognoscatur. Analoga excludenda esse à prędicamentis, atque etiam à syllogismis, & aliis argumentationibus: quæ in solis terminis vniuocis commodè fieri possunt. Aristoteles verò non definiuit analoga cap. præsenti, sed solùm æquiuoca & vniuoca: quia cùm sint quasi media, inter hęc extrema, cognitis vniuocis, & æquiuocis facile est analoga cognoscere. De quibus quinque tantum disputanda sunt. Primum, quid sit analogia. Secundum, quotuplex sit. Tertium, vtrum Analogum possit abstrahi, aut præscindi ab analogatis. 4. An ens sit analogum, ad Deum & creaturas; & ad entia creata, substantialia, & accidentalia: & qua analogia, hæc omnia significet. 5. An accidens, respectu nouem prædicamentorum accidentium, analogum sit, vel vniuocum.

he treatment of the nature and ratio of analogy pertains for the 8 T most part to Metaphysics, since it is found chiefly in being taken most universally, which is its proper object, and also in its attributes, and in accident, a name common to the categories. But it pertains properly to Logic in order that from it we may know that analogous terms are to be excluded from the categories, and also from syllogisms and other argumentations, which can conveniently be made only in univocal terms. Aristotle, however, did not define analogous terms in the present chapter, but only equivocal and univocal ones: because, since analogous terms are as it were midway between these extremes, once univocals and equivocals are known it is easy to know analogous ones. Concerning these only five things are to be disputed. First, what analogy is. Second, how manifold it is. Third, whether the analogous term can be abstracted or prescinded from the analogates. 4. Whether being is analogous with respect to God and creatures, and to created beings, substantial and accidental; and by what analogy it signifies all these. 5. Whether accident, with respect to the nine categories of accidents, is analogous or univocal.

p. 202

Explicatur, quid sit Analogia.

It is explained what analogy is.

9 SI Analogiam ex ipsiusmet nominis significatione definire velimus; dicendum erit, non esse aliud; quàm proportionem, aut conuenientiam, seu comparationem inter multa, eodem nomine significata: nam Græcum nomen est; quod in Latinum transferens Quintilianus, proportionem vocauit: Tullius verò, in vno loco, conuenientiam, in alio verò, comparationem, aut proportionem. Et omnes istæ significationes, diuersis analogis conuenire possunt, vel eisdem sub diuersa consideratione: vt dũ diuersas analogiæ species enumerabimus, cõstare poterit.

9 If we wish to define analogy from the very signification of the name, we shall have to say that it is nothing other than a proportion, or agreement, or comparison among many things signified by the same name. For it is a Greek name, which Quintilian, rendering it in Latin, calls proportion; while Cicero in one place calls it agreement, and in another comparison, or proportion. And all these significations can belong to different analogous terms, or to the same ones under different consideration, as will be able to appear when we enumerate the different species of analogy.

Si verò rem potius significatam nomine analogiæ, consideremus, quàm etymologiam eiusdem nominis: definitionem analagorum, ex definitionibus æquiuocorum, & vniuocorum assignatis ab Arist. cap. præsenti facilè possumus colligere. Nam Analoga, ex communi sententia scholæ, medium quoddam sunt, inter Æquiuoca & Vniuoca. Æquiuoca veró sic definit Arist. Quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ nomini acommodata, omnino diuersa: vt canis, respectu latrabilis, piscis, & syderis cœlestis. Vniuoca quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ, nomini accommodata, omnino eadem. Analoga igitur erunt, Quorum nomen est commune: ratio verò substantiæ nomini accommodata, neque omnino diuersa, neque omnino eadem. Secundùm quam analoga vtrumque extremum participant: conueniunt enim cum æquiuocis, & vniuocis in nomine, quod commune debet esse in omnibus: in re verò, aut conceptu per nomen significato: partim conueniunt, & partim differunt: conueniunt quidem cum æquiuocis, in eo; quòd diuersus debet esse simpliciter: & in hoc differunt ab vniuocis, in quibus idem simpliciter debet esse: sed differunt ob eisdem æquiuocis, in eo, quod non omnino diuersus est, sed aliquo modo vnus vel idem: & in hoc assimilantur vniuocis. Vnde sequitur maiorem similitudinem habere cum æquiuocis. Et hæc est ratio, propter quam cum æquiuocis enumerari solent, & etiam æquiuoca appellari: quia parum ab eis distinguuntur.

But if we consider rather the thing signified by the name of analogy than the etymology of the same name, we can easily gather the definition of analogous terms from the definitions of equivocals and univocals assigned by Aristotle in the present chapter. For analogous terms, according to the common opinion of the school, are something midway between equivocals and univocals. Now Aristotle defines equivocals thus: Those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether different: as dog, with respect to the barking animal, the fish, and the heavenly star. Univocals: those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether the same. Analogous terms, therefore, will be those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is neither altogether different nor altogether the same. According to this, analogous terms participate in both extremes: for they agree with equivocals and univocals in the name, which must be common in all of them; but in the thing or concept signified by the name they partly agree and partly differ. They agree with equivocals in this, that it must be different simply; and in this they differ from univocals, in which it must be the same simply. But they differ from the same equivocals in this, that it is not altogether different, but in some way one or the same; and in this they resemble univocals. From which it follows that they have greater similarity with equivocals. And this is the reason why they are customarily enumerated with equivocals, and are even called equivocal: because they are distinguished from them only a little.

10 Itaque conceptus analogi, quantum ad res significatas, non est vnus, sed plures: quia analogata diuersa sunt: ratione tamen proportionis, vel attributionis, seu proportionalitatis, quãdam habent similitudinem: & eius ratione, aliqualem vnitatem: & hoc est, rationem substantiæ nomini accommodatam, non esse omnino diuersam, nec omnino eandem, sed proportionalem, vel similem.

10 Thus the concept of the analogous term, as regards the things signified, is not one but several, because the analogates are different; yet by reason of proportion, or attribution, or proportionality, they have a certain similarity, and by reason of it some unity; and this is for the ratio of substance accommodated to the name to be neither altogether different nor altogether the same, but proportional or similar.

p. 203

Quotuplex sit analogia — How manifold analogy is.

11 CAietanus in opusc. de Analogia nominum, ca. 1. 2 & 3. triplicem Analogiam distinguit. Primam Inæqualitatis, quæ reperitur in generibus, respectu suarum specierum, à quibus ratione differentiarum, secundùm inæqualitatem perfectionis participatur: vt in animali, respectu hominis, & leonis, perfectiùs enim participatur ab homine, ratione perfectioris differentiæ, & ideo inæqualiter ab vtroque: sed hanc analogiam dicit, non esse talem simpliciter, nec facere nomen analogum: quia in generibus verè vniuocis, reperitur, & solum potest vocari Analogia physica, quia procedit ex diuersis formis physicis, maioris & minoris perfectionis.

11 Cajetan, in the opuscule On the Analogy of Names, ch. 1, 2 and 3, distinguishes a threefold analogy. The first, of Inequality, which is found in genera with respect to their species, by which, by reason of the differences, they are participated according to an inequality of perfection: as in animal with respect to man and lion; for it is participated more perfectly by man, by reason of the more perfect difference, and therefore unequally by the two. But he says that this analogy is not such simply, nor does it make a name analogous, because it is found in truly univocal genera; and it can only be called physical analogy, because it proceeds from different physical forms of greater and lesser perfection.

Secunda species Analogiæ est, Proportionis, vnius ad alterum, vel plurium ad vnum: & hoc etiam vocatur Attributionis: quia proportio quam habet vnum ad alterum, vel multa ad vnum, habitudo quædam ad illud est, quę attributio etiam vocatur: vt sanum, dicitur analogum proportionis, & attributionis: quia de vrina, & medicina dicitur, secundùm proportionem, quam habent cum sanitate animalis: in quantum vrina, est signum sanitatis, medicina verò causa: & hoc est dici per attributionem ad illa: quare sanum respectu animalis, vrinæ, & medicinæ, dicitur analogum proportionis, seu attributionis.

The second species of analogy is that of Proportion of one to another, or of several to one; and this is also called analogy of Attribution, because the proportion that one has to another, or many to one, is a certain relation to it, which is also called attribution. Thus healthy is called an analogous term of proportion and attribution, because it is said of urine and medicine according to the proportion they have with the health of the animal, inasmuch as urine is a sign of health and medicine a cause; and this is to be said by attribution to it. Wherefore healthy, with respect to animal, urine, and medicine, is called an analogous term of proportion or attribution.

12 Tertia species Analogiæ est, Proportionalitatis: Proportionalitas verò, non est aliud, quam similitudo, vel proportio duarum proportionum. Gratia exempli: Inter tria & sex, reperitur proportio dupla: & eadem reperitur inter quatuor, & octo: deinde inter has duas proportiones duplas, reperitur alia proportio, aut similitudo, in eo consistens, quod sicut se habent tria ad sex, ita quatuor ad octo. Hæc igitur proportio, & similitudo duarum proportionum, vocatur proportionalitas. Et ideo nomen illud, quod significat plura, inter quæ reperitur, vocatur analogum proportionalitatis. Vt risus, significat risum hominis verum, & quasi metaphoricum risum prati; quod dum floret, quandam hilaritatem ostendit, similem ei, quam ostendit homo, dum ridet. Dicitur autem de vtroque nomen risus: nempe de homine ridente, & de prato florido secundùm proportionalitatem: quia sicut se habet risus hominis, ad hominem: sic floriditas prati, ad pratum. Quare analogum proportionalitatis vocatur.

12 The third species of analogy is that of Proportionality. Proportionality is nothing other than the similarity or proportion of two proportions. For example: between three and six there is found a double proportion, and the same is found between four and eight; then between these two double proportions there is found another proportion or similarity, consisting in this, that as three is to six, so four is to eight. This proportion and similarity of two proportions, therefore, is called proportionality. And therefore the name that signifies several things among which it is found is called an analogous term of proportionality.

Ex his tribus speciebus analogiæ, prima à nullo reputatur vera, nec sufficiens ad constituendum nomen analogum: sed omnes dicunt, non esse analogiam simpliciter, sed solùm

Thus laughter signifies the true laughter of man and the as it were metaphorical laughter of a meadow, which, when it flowers, shows a certain cheerfulness similar to that which a man shows when he laughs. Now the name laughter is said of both, namely of the laughing man and of the flowering meadow, according to proportionality: because as the laughter of a man is to the man, so the floweriness of the meadow is to the meadow. Wherefore it is called an analogous term of proportionality. Of these three species of analogy, the first is reputed by no one to be true, nor sufficient to constitute an analogous name; but all say that it is not analogy simply, but only

p. 204

secundùm quid. Et ratio omnium est, quia in generibus, & pluribus aliis vniuocis, reperitur, sine præiudicio vniuocationis.

in a certain respect. And the reason of all is that it is found in genera and in many other univocals without prejudice to univocation.

13 Analogiam verò proportionis, seu attributionis, recipiunt omnes, tanquam veram, & sufficientem, ad constituendum nomen analogum. Et ratio est manifesta: Quia sola attributio vnius ad alterum, vel multorum ad vnum, efficit, vt non omnia eodem modo, nec æqualiter significentur: sed illud vnum, simpliciter tale appelletur, cætera verò non, nisi secundùm quid: ergo sola attributio facit nomen analogum. Probatur consequentia ex definitione analogorum: Analoga sunt quorum nomen est commune: ratio verò substantiæ, nec omnino eadem, nec omnino diuersa: sed eo ipso, quòd significata ita se habent, vt omnia dicantur per attributionem ad vnum: ratio, sub qua, significata primo, per se, & principaliter ei conuenit: cæteris verò per attributionem ad illud: ergo non est omnino eadem in omnibus: quia si eadem esset æquè primo, & sine dependentia ab aliis, conueniret singulis, vt patet in vniuocis: quare necesse est dicere, quòd sola attributio efficiat analogiam.

13 But the analogy of proportion, or of attribution, all receive as true and sufficient to constitute an analogous name. And the reason is manifest: because attribution alone, of one to another or of many to one, brings it about that not all are signified in the same way or equally, but that the one is called such simply, while the others are not, except in a certain respect; therefore attribution alone makes a name analogous. The consequence is proved from the definition of analogous terms: Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance is neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but by the very fact that the significates are so related that all are said by attribution to one, the ratio under which they are signified belongs to that one first, per se, and principally, and to the others by attribution to it; therefore it is not altogether the same in all: because if it were the same, it would belong to each one equally first and without dependence on the others, as is plain in univocals. Wherefore it is necessary to say that attribution alone produces analogy.

Secundò, Sola attributio tollit vniuocationem: ergo sola facit nomen analogum. Euidens est consequentia: quia vbi est attributio significatorum, non est æquiuocatio nominis, cùm aliquid sit eis commune, præter nomen, nempe similitudo illa, & correspondentia, quam facit attributio: si ergo attributio tollit vniuocationem, necesse est eandem efficere nomen analogum: quia nullum datur medium, inter vniuocum & æquiuocum, præter analogum. Cæterum probatur primum antecedẽs, ex definitione vniuocorum. Vniuoca sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ, nomini accommodata, omnino eadem: sed attributio efficit vt ratio non sit omnino eadem, nec ęqualiter participetur ab omnibus, sed primo ab vno, à reliquis verò cum dependentia ab eo: ergo tollit vniuocationem.

Second, attribution alone takes away univocation; therefore it alone makes a name analogous. The consequence is evident: because where there is attribution of the significates there is no equivocation of the name, since something is common to them besides the name, namely that similarity and correspondence which attribution produces. If, therefore, attribution takes away univocation, it must make the name analogous, because no middle is given between univocal and equivocal besides the analogous. Moreover, the first antecedent is proved from the definition of univocals: Univocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether the same; but attribution brings it about that the ratio is not altogether the same, nor equally participated by all, but first by one, and by the rest with dependence on it; therefore it takes away univocation.

14 De analogia verò proportionalitatis non est certum, quòd sit talis simpliciter, ita vt sola sufficiat efficere nomen analogum: sed prima opinio tenet, quòd sufficiens sit, non minùs quàm analogia attributionis. Ita Caietanus vbi suprà: ita etiam videtur sentire D. Thom. de veritate, qu. 2. art. 11. ita denique plures moderni.

14 But concerning the analogy of proportionality it is not certain that it is such simply, so that it alone suffices to make a name analogous. The first opinion holds that it is sufficient, no less than the analogy of attribution. So Cajetan in the place cited above; so also St. Thomas seems to think, On Truth, q. 2, a. 11; so, finally, many moderns.

Secunda opinio, est aliorum modernorum, qui hac distinctione vtuntur. Proportionalitas, duobus modis potest reperiri, inter significata nominis: Primò, ita vt non significetur ipsa per illud nomen, sed alia ratio communis eorum: & hoc modo sumpta, non sufficit ad efficiendum nomen analogum

The second opinion is that of other moderns, who use this distinction. Proportionality can be found among the significates of a name in two ways. First, such that it is not itself signified by that name, but another ratio common to them; and taken in this way it does not suffice to make a name analogous

p. 205

. Quòd verò non significetur per nomen, videtur manifestum: quia animal, solùm significat naturam sensitiuam, communem speciebus: non proportionalitatem inter eas repertam.

That it is not signified by the name seems manifest: because animal signifies only the sensitive nature common to the species, not the proportionality found among them.

15 Secundò, ita, vt per nomen ipsa analogia significetur, & hæc sufficiens erit ad constituendum illud analogum: & quia nullum est nomen impositum, quo significetur, nulla datur talis analogia: daretur tamen, si imponeretur nomen ad eam significandam. Cuius rationem, vel exemplum non afferunt. Sed vtrumque afferre possumus exemplum quidem, in hoc nomine Principium: quòd analogicè dicitur, de fundamento domus, de puncto: quod est principium lineæ, & de præmissis demonstrationis, per se notis: & inter hæc, nulla est attributio, sed omnia æqualiter, & per se significantur: sola proportionalitas reperitur: quia sicut se habet fundamentum domus, ad domum ab eo incipientem, sic se habet punctum ad lineam, & principia demonstrationis ad demonstrationem: & quia per nomen significatur (cùm ratione proportionalitatis, videantur significare tria illa & non ratione alterius conceptus eis communis) sufficit constituere analogiam.

15 Second, such that the analogy itself is signified by the name; and this will be sufficient to constitute that name analogous. And because no name has been imposed by which it is signified, no such analogy is given; it would be given, however, if a name were imposed to signify it. Of which they do not bring a reason or an example. But we can bring both: an example, indeed, in this name principle, which is said analogically of the foundation of a house, of the point, which is the principle of a line, and of the premises of a demonstration known per se; and among these there is no attribution, but all are signified equally and per se; only proportionality is found: because as the foundation of a house is to the house that begins from it, so the point is to the line, and the principles of a demonstration to the demonstration. And because it is signified by the name (since they seem to signify those three by reason of proportionality, and not by reason of another concept common to them), it suffices to constitute analogy.

Ratione verò probari potest: quia proportionalitas præsupponit necessariò, diuersa esse illa, inter quæ reperitur, sed ab ea recipere aliquam similitudinem, & vnitatem: ergo efficit, vt ratio significata per nomen, non sit omnino diuersa, sed nec omnino eadem: quia aliqualis est similitudo, & vnitas in ea: quare sola efficiet nomen analogum.

It can also be proved by reason: because proportionality necessarily presupposes that the things among which it is found are different, but that they receive from it some similarity and unity; therefore it brings it about that the ratio signified by the name is not altogether different, but not altogether the same either, because there is some similarity and unity in it. Wherefore it alone will make a name analogous.

16 Tertia opinio tenet, Proportionalitatem quomodocunque repertam, inter significata eiusdem nominis, non sufficere ad constituendum nomen analogum: sed necesse est, vt sic reperiatur: quòd vnum eorum sit absolutè tale, per suam formam, aut per suum esse: aliud non verò nò sit absolutè tale per suum esse, sed vt substat tali proportioni, vel comparationi ad aliud. Exemplum esse potest in risu: qui ita significat risum hominis & floriditatem prati, vt ille quidem per proprium esse sit absolutè talis: hæc verò non, nisi in quantum talem habet proportionem, aut proportionalitatem cum eo. Manifestum est enim floriditatem prati, non esse nec vocari risum, nisi per ordinem ad risum hominis. Ita sentit pater Franciscus Suarius, to. 2. suæ Meta. disp. 28. sect. 3. n. 11.

16 The third opinion holds that proportionality, found in whatever way among the significates of the same name, does not suffice to constitute an analogous name; but it is necessary that it be found in such a way that one of them is absolutely such through its form or through its being, while the other is not absolutely such through its being, but as it underlies such a proportion or comparison to another. An example can be in laughter, which signifies the laughter of man and the floweriness of the meadow in such a way that the former is absolutely such through its own being, but the latter not, except inasmuch as it has such a proportion or proportionality with it. For it is manifest that the floweriness of the meadow neither is nor is called laughter except through its order to the laughter of man. So thinks Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaph., disp. 28, sect. 3, no. 11.

Nostra sententia tribus conclusionibus explicatur. Prima est: Proportionalitas non est vera analogia, nec sufficit analogum nomen facere, nisi per illud significetur. Hæc videtur mihi euidens, vt probat hoc arg. Res non habent analogiam, aut

Our view is explained in three conclusions. The first is: Proportionality is not true analogy, nor does it suffice to make a name analogous, unless it is signified by it. This seems to me evident, as this argument proves. Things do not have analogy, or

p. 206

vniuocationem, nisi in quantum per voces significantur: ergò nec sunt analoga proportionis vel attributionis, nisi in quantum, vt eam habentes, significantur. Cuius euidens signum est quòd quia diuerso modo significantur, per diuersas voces, fieri potest, vt æquiuocè per vnam, vniuocè verò per aliam significentur: vt Canis, nomine bestiæ latrabilis, Piscis, & Sydus, æquiuocè significantur, & vniuocè eadem designantur per nomen substantia: ex eo, quòd substantia significat conuenientiam essentialem eorum: canis verò nullam. Vt igitur nomen sit vniuocum: necesse est, significet conuenientiam multorum: & eodem modo, vt sit analogum, necesse est, vt significet diuersitatem simul, & conuenientiam multorum, sed analogata, habent conuenientiam, aut similitudinem, ratione proportionalitatis: aut attributionis: cùm diuersa simpliciter: ergo non possunt, vt analogata significari: nisi proportionalitas ipsa, vel attributio significetur.

univocation except inasmuch as they are signified by words; therefore neither are they analogous terms of proportion or attribution except inasmuch as they are signified as having it. Of which there is an evident sign: that, because they are signified in different ways by different words, it can happen that they are signified equivocally by one and univocally by another. Thus dog, the barking beast, the fish, and the star are signified equivocally by the name dog, and the same are designated univocally by the name substance, because substance signifies their essential agreement, but dog none. Therefore, for a name to be univocal it is necessary that it signify the agreement of many; and in the same way, for it to be analogous it is necessary that it signify at once the diversity and the agreement of many. But analogates have agreement or similarity by reason of proportionality or attribution, since they are different simply; therefore they cannot be signified as analogates unless the proportionality itself, or the attribution, is signified.

17 Secundò probatur: Quia licèt significata alicuius nominis, vniuocam habeant conuenientiam, si tamen non significentur, vt eam habent, non erunt vniuocata, nec nomen quo significantur, vniuocum, sed conuenientia se habebit materialiter tantùm, aut concomitanter, & erit, quasi non esset, ad effectum efficiendi nomen analogum: ergo licèt aliqua habeant inter se conuenientiam analogicam, si hæc non significetur, materialiter, & quasi concomitanter se habebit, & erit quasi non esset, ad effectum constituendi nomen analogum. Quare necesse est per nomen significari.

17 Second, it is proved: because, although the significates of some name have a univocal agreement, yet if they are not signified as having it, they will not be univocates, nor will the name by which they are signified be univocal; but the agreement will stand only materially or concomitantly, and will be as if it were not, as regards the effect of making the name univocal. Therefore, although some things have an analogical agreement among themselves, if this is not signified it will stand materially and as it were concomitantly, and will be as if it were not, as regards the effect of constituting an analogous name. Wherefore it is necessary that it be signified by the name.

Secunda conclusio: Proportionalitas, aliquando significatur per nomen analogum: & ideo si significata sufficit constituere speciem distinctam, ab analogia attributionis, efficiet eam distinctam: & ita fatendum erit, esse actu, in rerum natura, diuersas species analogiæ. Hæc est contra secundam opinionem quæ negat, diuersas esse species analogiæ, & analogorum, nempe proportionalitatis, & attributionis: quamuis fateatur, esse possibiles, si nomen imponatur, ad significandam proportionalitatem multorum.

Second conclusion: Proportionality is sometimes signified by an analogous name; and therefore, if when signified it suffices to constitute a species distinct from the analogy of attribution, it will make it distinct; and so it will have to be admitted that there are in act, in the nature of things, different species of analogy. This is against the second opinion, which denies that there are different species of analogy and of analogous terms, namely of proportionality and of attribution, although it admits that they are possible, if a name is imposed to signify the proportionality of many.

Probatur efficaciter, exemplo risus, quo significatur, floriditas prati, simul cum risu vero hominis, ex eo solùm, quia sic se habet pratum, dum floret, præ se ferens quandam hilaritatem, sicut se habet homo, dum ridet: sed hæc est proportionalitas: ergo significatur floriditas prati, in quantum habet proportionalitatem cum risu hominis: quare falsum erit, quòd proportionalitas nunquam significetur, per nomen analogũ, & consequenter erit necessarium, secũdùm eandem sententiam,

It is proved effectively by the example of laughter, by which the floweriness of the meadow is signified together with the true laughter of man, solely because the meadow, when it flowers, displaying a certain cheerfulness, is related as a man is related when he laughs; but this is proportionality; therefore the floweriness of the meadow is signified inasmuch as it has proportionality with the laughter of man. Wherefore it will be false that proportionality is never signified by an analogous name; and consequently it will be necessary, according to the same opinion,

p. 207

quòd ita significata, efficiat distinctam speciem analogiæ, & analogum, specie distinctum, ab analogia, & analogis attributionis. Et si dicatur per nomen risus, non significari floriditatem prati, nisi vt habet similitudinem cum risu hominis, non proportionalitatem: & ideo, nec significari ipsam proportionalitatem, sed attributionem: Contra hoc est, quòd floriditas prati, non significatur, vt habet similitudinem in communi, sed in particulari: hoc est talem, vt sicut risus est actus vitalis, quo ostenditur hilaritas cordis, in hoc si similis ei floriditas prati: quia ostendit quandam hilaritatem, hoc est, ita se habet atque homo, declarans hilaritatem: & hæc est proportionalitas quæ verè significatur per nomen risus. Et certè, non potest aliud nomen imponi, quo meliùs significetur proportionalitas hæc, quàm nomen risus.

that, signified in this way, it makes a distinct species of analogy, and an analogous term distinct in species from the analogy and analogous terms of attribution. And if it is said that by the name laughter the floweriness of the meadow is signified only as it has similarity with the laughter of man, not proportionality, and that therefore it is not the proportionality itself that is signified, but attribution: against this is the fact that the floweriness of the meadow is not signified as having a similarity in common, but in particular, that is, such that, as laughter is a vital act by which the cheerfulness of the heart is shown, in this the floweriness of the meadow is similar to it, because it shows a certain cheerfulness; that is, it is related just as a man declaring his cheerfulness; and this is the proportionality which is truly signified by the name laughter. And certainly no other name could be imposed by which this proportionality would be better signified than the name laughter.

18 Tertia Conclusio: Proportionalitas, etiam significata per nomen analogum, & adhuc in his analogatis reperta, quorum vnum est tale, per suum esse, aliud verò non, nisi ratione proportionalitatis, non facit ex se, aut per se sola, veram speciem, & distinctam analogiæ, nec nomen analogum, sed ratione attributionis, cui coniungitur: & ideò eandem cum analogia attributionis, & ita nec secundùm actum, nec secundùm possibilitatem, distinguendæ sunt diuersæ species analogiæ, sed sola analogia attributionis ponenda est.

18 Third conclusion: Proportionality, even when signified by an analogous name, and moreover found in those analogates of which one is such through its own being while the other is not, except by reason of proportionality, does not of itself or by itself alone make a true and distinct species of analogy, nor an analogous name, but by reason of the attribution with which it is joined; and therefore it is the same as the analogy of attribution. And so neither according to act nor according to possibility are different species of analogy to be distinguished, but the analogy of attribution alone is to be posited.

Conclusio hęc, est contra secundam & tertiam opinionem: & priùs declaranda est, deinde probanda. Declaratur autem sic: Proportionalitas ex se differens est, vt reperiri possit, inter significata: quorum vtrique conueniat formaliter, & intrinsecè appellatio, & significatio nominis, & inter ea, quorum solum vni conueniat formaliter, alijs verò, per extrinsecam denominationem; imò & inter ea etiam, quæ sub tali nomine, nullam habent conuenientiam, vt æquiuocata. Probatur euidenter: quia inter species eiusdem generis, reperitur: vt inter hominem, & leonem: & etiam, inter canem latrabilem, piscem, & sydus: & tandem, inter risum hominis, & floriditatem prati: quia verum est, de his omnibus, quòd sicut se habet vnum eorum, ad suũ esse, sic aliud ad suum: & quamuis per nomẽ idem significetur, potest eodẽ modo, seu diuerso, reperiri in eisdem.

This conclusion is against the second and third opinions, and it must first be explained, then proved. It is explained thus: Proportionality of itself is indifferent, so that it can be found among significates to both of which the appellation and signification of the name belongs formally and intrinsically, and among those to only one of which it belongs formally, and to the others by extrinsic denomination; indeed, even among those which under such a name have no agreement, as equivocates. This is proved evidently: because it is found among species of the same genus, as between man and lion; and also among the barking dog, the fish, and the star; and finally between the laughter of man and the floweriness of the meadow: because it is true of all these that as one of them is related to its own being, so is the other to its own; and although they are signified by the same name, it can be found in the same things in the same way or in a different way.

Quod non minus efficaciter sic probatur: Quia ita se habere quodlibet, ad suum esse, sicut aliud ad suum, non efficit ea, magis vel minùs diuersa, in apprehensione intellectus, quàm si id non haberent: ergo nec efficiet ea magis, aut minùs diuersa, nec magis, & minus eadem, etiam si per nomen idem seu aliud significetur. Euidens est consequentia, quia res significantur,

Which is proved no less effectively thus: because the fact that any one thing is related to its own being as another to its own does not make them more or less different in the apprehension of the intellect than if they did not have this; therefore neither will it make them more or less different, nor more or less the same, even if they are signified by the same name or by another. The consequence is evident, because things are signified

p. 208

per voces, vt apprehenduntur ab intellectu. Probatur porrò antecedens: quia æqualiter reperitur in apprehensione intellectus, inter res omnino diuersas, ac inter res eiusdem rationis: non enim, vt minùs diuersa apprehenduntur significata canis, ex eo, quòd intelligantur, sic se habere quodlibet ad suum esse, sicut aliud ad suum: nec minùs dissimilia sunt, album, & nigrum, ex eo, quòd apprehendantur, sub eadem proportionalitate, quàm ea non apprehensa. Probatur iam conclusio, sic explicata, aduersus secundam opinionem, hac ratione.

by words as they are apprehended by the intellect. Further, the antecedent is proved: because it is found equally, in the apprehension of the intellect, among things altogether different and among things of the same ratio. For the significates of dog are not apprehended as less different from the fact that they are understood each to be related to its own being as another to its own; nor are white and black less dissimilar from the fact that they are apprehended under the same proportionality than if that were not apprehended. The conclusion, thus explained, is now proved against the second opinion by this argument.

20 Analoga sunt media inter æquiuoca, & vniuoca, ergo nõ possunt requiri simul, cum aliquo extremorum, ita vt idem nomen, respectu eorundem significatorum, sit analogum simul, & æquiuocum, vel analogum & vniuocum: sed proportionales sola, etiam per nomen significata, potest reperiri simul cum vno, & altero extremo: ergo non facit medium, quod est, non efficere nomen analogum. Probatur minor: Quia etiam si species animalis, apprehendantur ab intellectu, sub proportionalitate, hoc est, vt ita se habet leo, ad suum esse animalis, quod participat ab animali, sicut homo, ad suum, quod ab eodem participat, eadem intelligitur natura animalis in eis: ergo non desinunt esse vniuoca: & ex consequi non apprehenditur, vt analoga: nec essent analoga, si sub eadem proportionalitate significarentur, per nomen: quia vt probatum est, eodem modo significantur per nomen: quo apprehenduntur per intellectum.

20 Analogous terms are midway between equivocals and univocals; therefore they cannot be found together with either of the extremes, so that the same name, with respect to the same significates, is at once analogous and equivocal, or analogous and univocal. But proportionality alone, even signified by the name, can be found together with the one extreme and with the other; therefore it does not make a middle, which is not to make a name analogous. The minor is proved: because even if the species of animal are apprehended by the intellect under proportionality, that is, as the lion is related to its being of animal, which it participates from animal, just as man to his own, which he participates from the same, the same nature of animal is understood in them; therefore they do not cease to be univocal, and consequently they are not apprehended as analogous. Nor would they be analogous if they were signified by the name under the same proportionality: because, as has been proved, they are signified by the name in the same way in which they are apprehended by the intellect.

21 Probatur deinde aduersus tertiam: Quia proportionalitas ratione sui, non facit floriditatem prati esse, aut vocari risum sub ratione attributionis, quam causat in ea, ad risum hominis, ergo nec ratione sui, facit eam analogatum risus, aut risum esse analogum, sed ratione attributionis. Probatur minor: Quia si ratione sui, faceret eam analogatum, omnia alia, in quibus reperitur, faceret analogata: sed probauimus, eam non facere: ergo nec facit floriditatem prati analogatum risus, nisi ratione attributionis, quam causat in ea: quia attributio, vera est analogia, & per se efficit nomen analogum.

21 It is proved next against the third: because proportionality, by reason of itself, does not make the floweriness of the meadow be or be called laughter, but under the ratio of the attribution which it causes in it to the laughter of man; therefore neither by reason of itself does it make it an analogate of laughter, or laughter to be analogous, but by reason of attribution. The minor is proved: because if by reason of itself it made it an analogate, it would make all the other things in which it is found analogates; but we have proved that it does not make them so; therefore neither does it make the floweriness of the meadow an analogate of laughter except by reason of the attribution which it causes in it: because attribution is true analogy and per se makes a name analogous.

Ex his conclusionibus sequitur, proportionalitatem, non esse veram analogiam, nisi vt per se coniunctam attributioni: & ratione huius, non ratione sui: & ideo non facere distinctam speciem analogorum, vllo modo, sed omnia analoga, esse attributionis, vt docuit expressè D. Tho. 1. p. q. 13. art. 6. vbi ita ait: In omnibus nominibus, quæ de pluribus analogicè dicuntur, necesse est, quòd omnia dicantur per respectum ad vnum: & ideo illud vnum, oportet, quòd ponatur definitione omnium.

From these conclusions it follows that proportionality is not true analogy except as joined per se to attribution, and by reason of this, not by reason of itself; and therefore that it does not in any way make a distinct species of analogous terms, but that all analogous terms are of attribution, as St. Thomas expressly taught, 1 p., q. 13, a. 6, where he says thus: In all names which are said analogically of many, it is necessary that all be said with respect to one; and therefore that one must be posited in the definition of all. And

p. 209

22 Et probatur, hac ratione: Inæqualitas sola non sufficit analogum facere, nec sola proportionalitas, etiam per nomen significata: sed præter has, sola attributio restat, de qua probatum est, per se facere nomen analogum: ergo solùm datur analogia attributionis, & sola analoga attributionis. Nomine autem Attributionis, intelligimus, quamcunque habitudinem, vnius ad alterum, vel multorum ad vnum, per ordinem, ad quod dicantur talia. Et hoc modo intellecta, tertia opinio vera esse potest, asserens, proportionalitatem non facere analogiam: nisi vnum eorum, inter quæ reperitur, dicatur absolutè tale per suum esse, aliud verò, non nisi per habitudinem ad illud: eiusmodi enim habitudo, sub nomine attributionis comprehenditur, & proportionalitas, à qua causatur ratione illius, & non ratione sui facit nomen analogum.

22 And it is proved by this argument: inequality alone does not suffice to make an analogous term, nor proportionality alone, even signified by the name; but besides these there remains only attribution, of which it has been proved that it per se makes a name analogous; therefore only the analogy of attribution is given, and only analogous terms of attribution. By the name of attribution, however, we understand any relation of one to another, or of many to one, by order to which such things are said. And understood in this way the third opinion can be true, which asserts that proportionality does not make analogy unless one of the things among which it is found is said to be absolutely such through its own being, and the other not, except through a relation to it: for a relation of this kind is comprehended under the name of attribution; and the proportionality by which it is caused makes the name analogous by reason of that, and not by reason of itself.

Ad exemplum primæ opinionis, Respondent aliqui: Principium esse ęquiuocum, à consilio: quia à consilio impositum est ad diuersa significanda. Alij verò dicunt: Esse analogum proportionalitatis. Sed vtrumque videtur falsum, primum quia Arist. 5. lib. Meta. c. 1. enumerans principia omnia, diuersæ rationis, asserit, conuenire in ratione principij his verbis: Omnibus igitur principiis commune est esse primum, vnde aut est, aut fit, aut cognoscitur. Ergo principium, non est æquiuocum. Probatur consequentia: quia æquiuoca non possunt conuenire nisi in solo nomine. Quod verò non sit analogum proportionalitatis, ex dictis consequitur, quia proportionalitas non sufficit ad efficiendum nomen analogum. Dici ergo posset, Principium esse analogum attributionis: quia primò, & per se significat: principium, à quo per veram originem procedit aliud secundùm esse: & per attributionem ad hoc principium, dicitur de reliquis. Vel, cui non placuerit, analogum hoc modo esse dicat potiùs, esse vniuocum, quàm æquiuocum: quia hoc vltimum expressè, est contra Arist.

To the example of the first opinion, some reply that principle is equivocal by design, because it was imposed by design to signify different things. Others say that it is an analogous term of proportionality. But both seem false. The first, because Aristotle, Metaph. bk. 5, ch. 1, enumerating all principles, of different ratio, asserts that they agree in the ratio of principle, in these words: It is common, then, to every principle to be the first thing from which something either is, or comes to be, or is known. Therefore principle is not equivocal. The consequence is proved: because equivocals cannot agree except in the name alone. That it is not an analogous term of proportionality follows from what has been said, because proportionality does not suffice to make a name analogous. It could be said, then, that principle is an analogous term of attribution: because first and per se it signifies the principle from which something else proceeds according to being by a true origin, and by attribution to this principle it is said of the rest. Or, whoever is not pleased that it is analogous in this way, let him rather say that it is univocal than equivocal, because this last is expressly against Aristotle.

Ad rationem verò: Negandum est antecedens, quòd proproportionalitas præsupponat diuersa esse illa, inter quæ reperitur: nam licèt supponat esse distincta, tamen indifferenter potest reperiri inter ea, quæ vniuocè conueniunt: & inter ea, quæ conueniunt solo nomine: & ideo, non facit per se nomen analogum.

To the argument, the antecedent is to be denied, namely that proportionality presupposes that the things among which it is found are different: for although it supposes that they are distinct, yet it can be found indifferently among those which agree univocally and among those which agree in name alone; and therefore it does not per se make a name analogous.

Ad testimonium D. Thom. respondeo, Eam sententiam, absque dubio, rectè tractasse in eodem loco primæ partis, à nobis citato, vbi tam expressè tenet oppositam.

To the testimony of St. Thomas I reply that without doubt he retracted that view in the same place of the First Part cited by us, where he so expressly holds the opposite. O

p. 210

An necesse sit rem, vel conceptum, significatum nomine analogi, intrinsecè solùm reperiri in principali analogato, in cæteris verò, solùm per extrinsecam denominationem — Whether it is necessary that the thing or concept signified by the name of the analogous term be found intrinsically only in the principal analogate, and in the others only by extrinsic denomination.

25 SVpposito, quòd solùm dentur analoga proportionis, seu attributionis, dubitatur: An necesse sit, quòd significatum eorum, solùm reperiatur formaliter in principali analogato, in cæteris verò, non formaliter: sed solùm per extrinsecam denominationem: vt videmus, in hoc nomine, sanum, quod significat sanitatem: & hæc, solùm reperitur formaliter in animali, quod est principale analogatum: in vrina verò, & medicina, solùm per extrisecam denominationem: in illa quidem, tanquam in signo, & in hac, tanquam in causa.

25 Supposing that only analogous terms of proportion, or attribution, are given, it is doubted whether it is necessary that their significate be found formally only in the principal analogate, and in the others not formally, but only by extrinsic denomination: as we see in this name healthy, which signifies health; and this is found formally only in the animal, which is the principal analogate, but in urine and medicine only by extrinsic denomination: in the former as in a sign, in the latter as in a cause.

Et prima opinio aliquorum asserit, necessarium esse, quòd in solo principali reperiantur formaliter, & intrinsecè. Quod probari potest, quia in eo solo hoc modo reperitur, per se primò, cætera verò, solùm videntur esse, quasi attributiones ad illud: ideo Arist. de accidentibus dixit, Non esse entia, sed entis entia, hoc est, aliquid substantiæ: sed attributio, non videtur esse, nisi quædam extrinseca denominatio: ergo solùm in eis reperietur, per extrinsecam denominationem.

And the first opinion, of some, asserts that it is necessary that it be found formally and intrinsically in the principal one alone. Which can be proved, because it is found in this way in it alone, per se and first, while the others seem to be only as it were attributions to it. Hence Aristotle said of accidents that they are not beings, but of a being, that is, something of substance. But attribution does not seem to be anything but a certain extrinsic denomination; therefore it will be found in them only by extrinsic denomination.

Secunda opinio est communis, omnium modernorum, negans hoc esse necessarium: sed indifferenter esse posse, in omnibus formaliter, vel solùm in principali, secundùm diuersam naturam, & conditionem eorum. Et hæc est expressa sententia D. Th. in 1. d. 19. q. 5. & ex vera, & à nobis amplectenda. Probatur: Ratione, & Exemplis: Ratione quidem, quia attributio est, quæ facit analogiam: sed hæc potest reperiri inter ea, quæ formaliter participant rationem vel conceptum analogi, sicut reperitur inter ea, quorum vnum tantùm formaliter eam participat: ergo vtroque modo se habere possunt analoga, & non vno tantùm, vt asserit prima opinio. Probatur minor: quia bene potest intelligi, quòd vnum, vel plura participent rationem formalem significatam, quam non habeant, nisi cum dependẽtia, & attributione ad vnum, in quo per se primò reperiatur.

The second opinion is the common one of all the moderns, denying that this is necessary, but holding that it can indifferently be in all formally, or only in the principal one, according to their different nature and condition. And this is the express opinion of St. Thomas, In 1, d. 19, q. 5; and it is true, and to be embraced by us. It is proved by reason and by examples. By reason, indeed: because it is attribution that makes analogy; but this can be found among things which formally participate the ratio or concept of the analogous term, just as it is found among things of which only one formally participates it; therefore analogous terms can stand in both ways, and not in one only, as the first opinion asserts. The minor is proved: because it can well be understood that one or several things participate the formal ratio signified, which they do not have except with dependence on and attribution to one, in which it is found per se and first.

24 Probatur secundò Exemplis. Nam ens dicitur analogicè, de substantia & accidente, atque etiam, de Deo, & creaturis, vt inferiùs probatur: sed entitas, quam significat, non solùm reperitur formaliter, in substantia, sed etiam in accidentibus: nec solùm in Deo, sed etiam in creaturis: ergo, non est necessarium, quòd solùm in principali analogato reperiatur formaliter

24 It is proved second by examples. For being is said analogically of substance and accident, and also of God and creatures, as is proved below; but the entity which it signifies is found formally not only in substance but also in accidents, and not only in God but also in creatures; therefore it is not necessary that it be found formally only in the principal analogate

p. 211

. Probatur minor: Quia creatura, entitatem habet intrinsecam, & formalem, productam in rerum natura, per creationem, aut per aliam actionem: ergo non reperitur in solo Deo: quamuis, per se, in eo tantùm, & per participationem, & attributionem, ad ipsum in creatura. Et in accidentibus, reperitur etiam entitas propria, formalis, & intrinseca: quamuis non sine intrinseca dependentia à substantia, vt quantitate, & qualitate, manifestum est.

The minor is proved: because a creature has an intrinsic and formal entity, produced in the nature of things by creation or by another action; therefore it is not found in God alone, although it is found per se in him alone, and by participation and attribution to him in the creature. And in accidents too there is found a proper, formal, and intrinsic entity, though not without an intrinsic dependence on substance, as is manifest in quantity and quality.

Sed respondent aliqui, pro prima opinione, Accidens non esse ens, sed entis ens: hoc est, esse aliquid substantiæ: vt sæpe asserit Arist. & hoc est non habere aliam entitatem, nisi attributionem ad substantiam, in quadam denominatione extrinseca consistentem, sibi autem intrinsecam, & essentialem. Sed hoc non potest esse verum, vt ex eadem solutione, in primis colligitur. Nam si accidens, est entis ens: ergo est ens substantiæ: habet igitur veram entitatem, per quam afficit substantiam. Quod videtur probari euidẽter, his experientiis: Quantitas in Eucharistia, non inhæret substantiæ, sed ab ea est separata: & tamen est vera entitas, quam videmus, & tangimus. Albedinem etiam sentimus, per visum, & calorem, per tactum: ergo euidenter probatur, quòd hæc accidentia, & similia, non sint extrinsecæ attributiones, aut denominationes: sed veræ entitates reales: quia sola denominatio extrinseca, non sentitur, nec potest esse per se, obiectum sensus.

But some reply, for the first opinion, that accident is not a being but of a being, that is, that it is something of substance, as Aristotle often asserts; and this is to have no other entity than attribution to substance, consisting in a certain denomination extrinsic to substance but intrinsic and essential to itself. But this cannot be true, as is gathered first of all from the same solution. For if accident is of a being, then it is of the being of substance; it has, therefore, a true entity, through which it affects substance. Which seems to be evidently proved by these experiences. Quantity in the Eucharist does not inhere in substance, but is separated from it; and yet it is a true entity, which we see and touch. Whiteness too we perceive by sight, and heat by touch. Therefore it is evidently proved that these accidents and the like are not extrinsic attributions or denominations, but true real entities: because an extrinsic denomination alone is not perceived, nor can it be a per se object of sense.

25 Et confirmari potest: Quia accidentia hæc, habent suos effectus formales, in subiectis, in quibus sunt: nec solùm formales, sed reales, & physicos: vt albedo, facit parietem, realiter, & formaliter album: & calor, facit aquam realiter, & formaliter calidam: sed effectus isti, non possunt procedere à causis in sola denominatione extrinseca consistentibus, sed ab his, quæ veram, & intrinsecam habent entitatem realem: per cuius realem virtutem eos producunt: ergo accidentia, veram & intrinsecam habent entitatem: alioqui, intellectus, & voluntas, quæ sunt accidentia, superaddita substantiæ animæ rationalis, ad operandum, non erunt nisi denominationes extrinsecæ, ei superadditæ. Quod patet esse falsum: cùm sint potentiæ reales, per quas tanquam per virtutes reales, elicit anima veras & reales operationes.

25 And it can be confirmed: because these accidents have their formal effects in the subjects in which they are; and not only formal but real and physical ones: as whiteness makes the wall really and formally white, and heat makes water really and formally hot. But these effects cannot proceed from causes consisting in extrinsic denomination alone, but from those which have a true and intrinsic real entity, by whose real power they produce them; therefore accidents have a true and intrinsic entity. Otherwise the intellect and will, which are accidents superadded to the substance of the rational soul for operating, will be nothing but extrinsic denominations superadded to it. Which is plainly false, since they are real powers, through which, as through real powers, the soul elicits true and real operations.

Ad argumentum verò, Neganda est consequentia: quia licèt solùm in principali analogato, reperiatur prima & per se ratio significata per analogum, in cæteris verò, solùm per attributionem ad illud, intrinsecè tamen, & formaliter reperiri potest: quia attributio, hoc non tollit, vt probatum est.

To the argument, the consequence is to be denied: because, although the ratio signified by the analogous term is found first and per se only in the principal analogate, and in the others only by attribution to it, yet it can be found in them intrinsically and formally, because attribution does not take this away, as has been proved. O ij

p. 212

An conceptus formalis analogorum sit vnus, & abstractus ab analogatis, vel multiplex, & ab eis an abstrahi possit — Whether the formal concept of analogous terms is one and abstracted from the analogates, or manifold; and whether it can be abstracted from them.

26 COnceptus, quem format intellectus de aliquo: duplex est, vt cap. de differentia notauimus: formalis, & obiectiuus. Conceptus formalis, est qualitas mentis, quam intellectus producit, vbi sibi faciat obiectum actu præsens, & illud intelligat: nam per hanc qualitatem, sibi perfectè repræsentatur. Conceptus verò obiectiuus, est obiectum, quod intelligitur, in quantum per formalem repræsentatur. Et de vtroque procedit quæstio: & ideo habebit duplicem partem. In prima disputabimus, de vnitate conceptus formalis. In secunda, de vnitate conceptus obiectiui.

26 The concept that the intellect forms of something is twofold, as we noted in the chapter on difference: formal and objective. The formal concept is a quality of the mind which the intellect produces when it makes the object actually present to itself and understands it: for through this quality it is perfectly represented to it. The objective concept is the object that is understood, inasmuch as it is represented through the formal one. And the question proceeds concerning both, and therefore it will have two parts. In the first we shall dispute about the unity of the formal concept; in the second, about the unity of the objective concept.

Sed conceptus formalis, etiam est duplex: Vnus est, conceptus vocis significantis, Alter, conceptus rei significatæ. Et de primò certum est, quòd sit vnus: quia nomen analogum, est vna vox simplex: ergo per vnum simplicem conceptum, à nobis intelligitur. De conceptu verò formali rei significatæ, per nomen analogum, procedit quæstio, An sit vnus.

But the formal concept is also twofold: one is the concept of the signifying word, the other the concept of the thing signified. And concerning the first it is certain that it is one, because the analogous name is one simple word; therefore it is understood by us through one simple concept. But concerning the formal concept of the thing signified by the analogous name, the question proceeds whether it is one.

Prima opinio tenet, Dari vnum conceptum formalem rei significatæ, per analogum, ita Scotus, loco inferiùs citando. Herueus quodlib. 2. q. 7. Sotus cap. præsenti. Fonseca 4. Meta. cap 2. q. 12. sect. 5. P. Franciscus Suarius, tomo. 1. suæ Met. dist. 2. sect. 1. sed diuerso modo procedunt: nam Scotus vnum conceptum formalem ponit: quia tenet, ens esse vniuocum: Vniuoca verò, vnico conceptu formali medio, sua vniuocata significant. P. Suarius, ideo ponit vnum conceptum formalem: quia vnum etiam ponit obiectiuum, abstractum ab analogatis. Herueus & Sotus, licèt non ponant eundem conceptum obiectiuum, asserunt tamen formalem esse vnum. Et tandem Fonseca ponit vnum formalem, non distinctum, sed confusum: quia non repræsentat distinctè analogata, sed confusè.

The first opinion holds that there is given one formal concept of the thing signified by the analogous term. So Scotus, in the place to be cited below; Hervaeus, Quodlibet 2, q. 7; Soto, on the present chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, q. 12, sect. 5; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 2, sect. 1. But they proceed in different ways. For Scotus posits one formal concept because he holds that being is univocal, and univocals signify their univocates by means of a single formal concept.
