53 And for the analogous term to be able to be the object of the intellect and of science, the same unity suffices: because a science or a power does not take its specific unity from the material object, but from the formal objective ratio under which the power tends to it, or under which it is considered by the science; from which the analogous term receives a greater unity when it is the object of a power or of a science.

An ens sit vniuocum respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, aut analogum, & qua analogia — Whether being is univocal with respect to substance and accident, or analogous, and by what analogy.

Hoc est quartum, quod proposuimus tractandum. Sed pro eius notitia notari debet, Ens duobus modis sumi posse: pro ente creato, quod diuiditur in decem prædicamenta, aut vniuersaliùs pro Ente communi respectu creati, & increati, aut Dei, & creaturarum: & de ente vtroque modo sumpto, potest esse quæstio, quam ideo in duas partes diuidimus. In prima agemus de ente creato, an sit vniuocum respectu prædicamentorum, vel analogum, & qua analogia. In secunda eadem inquiremus de eodem ente, respectu Dei, & creaturarum.

This is the fourth thing which we proposed to treat. But for knowledge of it, it should be noted that being can be taken in two ways: for created being, which is divided into the ten categories; or more universally, for being common with respect to the created and the uncreated, or to God and creatures. And concerning being taken in either way there can be a question, which we therefore divide into two parts. In the first we shall treat of created being, whether it is univocal with respect to the categories, or analogous, and by what analogy. In the second we shall inquire into the same things concerning the same being with respect to God and creatures.

Prima pars quæstionis.

First Part of the Question. 54

54 Circa primã partem duæ sunt opiniones extremæ, & altera media. Prima opinio extrema, est Aureoli apud Capreolum in d. 1. d. 2. q. 1. asserentis, Ens esse æquiuocũ respectu substantię, & accidentis. Probatur testimoniis Arist. & Porphyrij: nam Arist. 8. Meta. cap. 6. tex. 16. ait: Quodlibet prædicamentum statim quippiam esse, hoc est seipso esse tale, atque diuersum ab alio, quod aliis verbis dici solet, prædicamenta seipsis esse diuersa,

Concerning the first part there are two extreme opinions and one intermediate. The first extreme opinion is that of Auriol, in Capreolus on 1, d. 2, q. 1, who asserts that being is equivocal with respect to substance and accident. It is proved by testimonies of Aristotle and Porphyry: for Aristotle, Metaph. 8, ch. 6, text 16, says: that each category is straightway something, that is, is such by itself and diverse from another; which is customarily said in other words, that the categories are diverse by themselves, P ij

p. 228

& non per differentias, sed esse seipsis diuersa, & si se totis esse diuersa, & se totis esse diuersa idem est, ac esse omnino diuersa, quod & proprium est æquiuocatorum. Erit igitur æquiuocum ens.

and not through differences, but are diverse by themselves; and if they are diverse with their whole selves, to be diverse with their whole selves is the same as to be altogether diverse, which is proper to equivocates. Being, therefore, is equivocal.

Porphy. verò cap. de specie ex mente eiusdem Arist. dixit Ens æquiuocum esse,

And Porphyry, in the chapter on Species, according to the mind of the same Aristotle, said that being is equivocal.

Hæc tamen sententia (si de propria æquiuocatione loquitur, & non de communi, prout comprehendit analogiam) contraria est doctrinæ eiusdem Arist. & rationi. Probatur primum ex 4. Meta. cap. 2. & tex. 2. vbi ait Arist. Ens autem multipliciter dicitur, non æquiuocè, sed ad vnam naturam, sicut sanum, hoc est, per attributionem multorum ad vnum.

This opinion, however (if it speaks of proper equivocation, and not of common equivocation, as it comprehends analogy), is contrary to the doctrine of the same Aristotle and to reason. The first is proved from Metaph. 4, ch. 2, and text 2, where Aristotle says: But being is said in many ways, not equivocally, but with respect to one nature, as healthy; that is, by attribution of many to one.

Probatur secundum, quòd sit contra rationem, ex definitione æquiuocorũ. Æquiuoca sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ nomini accommodata omnino diuersa: sed substantia, & accidens conueniunt aliquo modo in ratione entis cùm vtrumque sit ens, licèt vnum diuersum ab alio, & ei attributum, ergo non sunt omnino diuersa: quare nec ens potest esse æquiuocum.

The second, that it is against reason, is proved from the definition of equivocals. Equivocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is altogether different; but substance and accident agree in some way in the ratio of being, since each is a being, although one is diverse from the other and attributed to it: therefore they are not altogether diverse; wherefore neither can being be equivocal.

55 Secunda opinio extrema tenet, Ens esse vniuocum, ita Scotus, in 1. d. 3. q. 3. & in 3. d. 8. qu. 2. & omnes eius discipuli, Antonius, Andreas 4. Meta. ca. 2. atque etiam Nominales omnes, vt testatur Gab. in 1. d. 2. qu. 4 Et probatur duplici ratione. Prima, ex definitione vniuocorum desumpta: Vniuoca sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ nomini accommodata eadem: hoc est, conceptus per nomen significatus: sed nomen ens constat esse commune substantiæ, & accidenti, & conceptus tam formalis quàm obiectiuus est vnus, & idem in inferioribus, ergo nomen erit vniuocum. Probatur minor, quia substantia & accidens conueniunt in ratione entis, & distinguuntur per modos intrinsecos per se, & in alio: sed modi distinguuntur ratione ab entitate, cùm eam determinent, atque contrahant ad substantiam & accidens, ergo potest intellectus concipere entitatem, nullo modo conceptis modis. Probatur hæc vltima consequentia: nam ea quæ distinguuntur ratione, bene potest intellectus separare, & vt sic separata, non se includent, quare poterit concipere rationem entis communem substantiæ, & accidenti, in qua non includantur modi. Et talis conceptus formalis, & obiectiuus, erit vnus simpliciter, nullam includens diuersitatem.

55 The second extreme opinion holds that being is univocal. So Scotus, on 1, d. 3, q. 3, and on 3, d. 8, q. 2, and all his disciples; Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 4, ch. 2; and also all the Nominalists, as Gabriel attests on 1, d. 2, q. 4. And it is proved by a twofold argument. The first, taken from the definition of univocals: Univocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is the same, that is, the concept signified by the name; but it is established that the name being is common to substance and accident, and the concept, both formal and objective, is one and the same in the inferiors: therefore the name will be univocal. The minor is proved: because substance and accident agree in the ratio of being, and are distinguished by the intrinsic modes per se and in another; but the modes are distinguished by reason from entity, since they determine and contract it to substance and accident: therefore the intellect can conceive entity without conceiving the modes in any way. This last consequence is proved: for things which are distinguished by reason the intellect can well separate, and, as thus separated, they will not include each other; wherefore it will be able to conceive the ratio of being common to substance and accident, in which the modes are not included. And such a concept, formal and objective, will be one simply, including no diversity.

Secundò: Quia si aliquid obstaret, quominus conceptus entis non esset vnus simpliciter & communis substantiæ, & accidenri, esset maximè diuersitas in modo essendi vtriusque, quia substantia habet modum essendi per se, accidens verò modum

Second: because, if anything stood in the way of the concept of being’s being one simply and common to substance and accident, it would above all be the diversity in the mode of being of each, because substance has the mode of being per se, but accident the mode

p. 229

essendi in alio: sed hæc non obstant: ergo erit vnus simpliciter. Probatur minor, quia hęc ratio diuersitatis non est in in entitate, nisi ratione modorum, ergo non tollit vnam rationem entitatis, atque adeò vniuocam, quemadmodum non tollit vnitatem conceptus animalis diuersitas per rationale, & irrationale, quia non est ratione naturæ sensitiuæ, sed differentiarum.

of being in another; but these things do not stand in the way: therefore it will be one simply. The minor is proved: because this ratio of diversity is not in the entity except by reason of the modes; therefore it does not take away the one ratio of entity, and so not the univocal one either; just as the diversity through rational and irrational does not take away the unity of the concept of animal, because it is not by reason of the sensitive nature, but of the differences.

Tertiò: Intellectus potest esse certus de aliquo, quòd sit ens, & dubius an sit substantia, vel accidens: vt si quis dubitet, an aliqua Hostia sit consecrata, vel non, certò cognoscit esse ens, dubitat verò, an ibi sit substantia, vel solùm accidens. Hoc autem non posset contingere, nisi intellectus conceptus rationem entis, non conceptis rationibus particularibus substantiæ, & accidentis: qui conceptus communis erit eis, & vnus simpliciter, cùm non includat aliquid, ratione cuius possit vllam diuersitatem habere. Et ex consequenti, nomen ens significans talem conceptum, erit vniuocum.

Third: the intellect can be certain of something that it is a being, and doubtful whether it is substance or accident: as, if someone doubts whether some Host is consecrated or not, he knows with certainty that it is a being, but doubts whether there is substance there, or only accident. But this could not happen unless the intellect conceived the ratio of being without conceiving the particular rationes of substance and accident; and this concept will be common to them, and one simply, since it does not include anything by reason of which it could have any diversity. And consequently the name being, signifying such a concept, will be univocal.

56 Tertia sententia media inter hæc extrema asserit, Ens non esse æquiuocum, neque vniuocum, sed analogum. Et est communis in schola, & vera, quam sequuntur Auerroes, Alexander, & D. Tho. in commentariis locorum Arist. inferiùs citandis, Porphyrius, Albertus, & Ammonius, cap. de specie in prædicabilibus, & cæteri omnes, præter citatos pro sententia Scoti,

56 The third, intermediate opinion between these extremes asserts that being is neither equivocal nor univocal, but analogous. And it is common in the school, and true; it is followed by Averroes, Alexander, and St. Thomas in their commentaries on the places of Aristotle to be cited below; Porphyry, Albert, and Ammonius, in the chapter on Species in the Predicables; and all the others, except those cited for the opinion of Scotus.

Colligitur efficaciter ex doctrina Arist. 4. Meta. ca. 2. lib. 7. cap. 1. & 4, & 1. l. Ethic. c. 6. vbi expressè docet, Ens multipliciter dici, & non æquiuocè, sed sicut sanum de vrina, Medicina, & animali ad vnam naturam, hoc est, per attributionem multorum ad vnum. Quibus verbis excludit vtramque extremam sententiam: nam dum dicit, Ens multipliciter dici sicut sanum, tollit vniuocationem, contra Scotum: dum verò addit non æquiuocè, tollit æquiuocationem, contra Aureolum.

It is gathered effectively from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 4, ch. 2; bk. 7, ch. 1 and 4; and Ethics 1, ch. 6, where he expressly teaches that being is said in many ways, and not equivocally, but as healthy is said of urine, medicine, and animal, with respect to one nature, that is, by attribution of many to one. By these words he excludes both extreme opinions: for when he says being is said in many ways, as healthy, he takes away univocation, against Scotus; but when he adds not equivocally, he takes away equivocation, against Auriol.

Probatur deinde ratione. Primò, ex definitione analogorum. Analoga sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ nomini accommodata, nec omnino eadem, neque omnino diuersa: sed ita se habet ens respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, ergo est analogum, & non vniuocum. Minorem ita probo: Substantia est primum ens, habens entitatem per se independentem ab alio: accidens verò est entitas alterius, nempe substantię, & ideo Arist. 4. Met. c. 2. dixit, Accidens non est ens, sed entis ens, ergo non habet per se entitatem, sed per attributionem ad substantiam: quare in ipsamet ratione entitatis, reperitur imprimis maxima diuersitas, & ob id etiam in conceptu significato per nomen ens. Deinde reperitur aliqualis conuenientia ratione eiusdem attributionis; ergo ratio entis per

It is next proved by reason. First, from the definition of analogous terms. Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but being stands thus with respect to substance and accident: therefore it is analogous and not univocal. I prove the minor thus: substance is the first being, having entity per se, independent of another; but accident is the entity of another, namely of substance, and therefore Aristotle said in Metaph. 4, ch. 2, Accident is not a being, but a being of a being; therefore it does not have entity per se, but by attribution to substance; wherefore in the very ratio of entity there is found, first of all, the greatest diversity, and on that account also in the concept signified by the name being. Then there is found some agreement by reason of the same attribution: therefore the ratio of being by P iij

p. 230

nomen significata, nec est omnino diuersa, neque omnino eadem. Et hoc est ens esse analogum, & ideo non vniuocum.

the name signified is neither altogether different nor altogether the same. And this is for being to be analogous, and therefore not univocal.

Si autem dixerit Scotus, diuersitatem inter substãtiam, & accidens non prouenire ex parte entitatis, sed ex parte modorum per se, & in alio, à quibus abstrahi potest ratio entitatis: & sic abstracta erit vna, quia sic à diuersitate abstrahitur, ergo vt sic abstracta nõ includit eam, quare erit vna, simpliciter, & nomen ens, eam immediatè significans, erit vniuocum. Non ergo probatur, analogum esse, aut non esse vniuocum? Hoc non tollit vim arg. quia modi intrinseci substantiæ, & accidentis, nõ sunt gradus perfectionis distincti ab entitate, sed ipsamet entitas expressiùs concepta, & significata, quæ significatur nomine entis: vnde nec ens est extra rationem eorum, nec ipsi extra rationem entis: vnde sequitur primò, quòd nec possit entitas concipi, sine illis actu saltem confuso inclusis, nec ipsi sine entitate. Secundò sequitur idem esse, quòd diuersitas substantiæ, & accidentis, vt significantur nomine entis, proueniat ex modis intrinsecis per se, & in alio, & quòd proueniat ex ipsamet entitate; idem etiam esse, quòd per eosdem modos sint diuersa, & quòd seipsis sine diuersa: & tandem, quòd sicut entitas nõ potest à seipsa abstrahi, sic nec possit abstrahi, ab eisdem modis & ideo, neque conceptus entis eos necessariò includens, possit esse vnus simpliciter, nec vniuocus. An verò ens non in tota sua vniuersalitate sumptũ, sed pro ente tantũ completo, abstrahi possit à substantia, & accidẽti, & respectu eorũ sit vniuocum, statim dicemus.

But if Scotus says that the diversity between substance and accident does not come from the side of the entity, but from the side of the modes per se and in another, from which the ratio of entity can be abstracted; and that thus, abstracted, it will be one, because thus it is abstracted from the diversity, and therefore, as abstracted, does not include it; wherefore it will be one simply, and the name being, signifying it immediately, will be univocal: is it not then proved that it is analogous, or that it is not univocal? This does not take away the force of the argument: because the intrinsic modes of substance and accident are not grades of perfection distinct from the entity, but the very entity, more expressly conceived and signified, which is signified by the name being; whence neither is being outside their ratio, nor are they outside the ratio of being. Whence it follows first that neither can the entity be conceived without them, included at least in confused act, nor they without the entity. Second, it follows that it is the same that the diversity of substance and accident, as they are signified by the name being, comes from the intrinsic modes per se and in another, and that it comes from the entity itself; it is likewise the same that they are diverse through these same modes and that they are diverse by themselves; and finally, that just as the entity cannot be abstracted from itself, so neither can it be abstracted from the same modes; and therefore neither can the concept of being, which necessarily includes them, be one simply, nor univocal. But whether being, taken not in its whole universality but only for complete being, can be abstracted from substance and accident, and is univocal with respect to them, we shall say presently.

58 Ad testimoniũ. Arist. pro prima sententia respondeo, Prędicamenta esse primò diuersa, hunc sensum efficere, quòd non differant, sicut species per differentias, continentes diuersum gradũ perfectionis, à genere in quo cõueniunt, sed per modos, qui sunt ipsamet prædicamentorum entitas speciali modo concepta: vnde verum est, per proprias entitates ita conceptas, esse diuersa Et hoc est etiam seipsis differre. Et cùm infertur se totis differre, distinguendum est: nam si sensus sit, Per totam entitatem suã vnum esse diuersum ab alio, verum est, si verò, Per totã entitatem omnibus modis conceptam, falsum, quia entitates eorum concipi possunt tanquã diuersæ simpliciter, atque etiam tanquam similes, & eædem secundùm quid, ratione attributionis, & ideo non concipiuntur, vt omnibus modis diuersæ. Neque in hoc sensu verum est, se totis differre, esse tamen necessarium vt ens esset ęquiuocũ: quia ęquiuocata, vt sub eo nomine cõcipiuntur, & significãtur, nullo modo cõueniunt. Et ideo non probatur ex illo testimonio quòd ens sit æquiuocum, Porphyrius verò de æquiuoco loquitur secũdùm cõmunem acceptionẽ

58 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion I reply that the categories’ being primarily diverse has this sense: that they do not differ as species do, through differences containing a different grade of perfection, from the genus in which they agree, but through the modes, which are the very entity of the categories conceived in a special way: whence it is true that they are diverse through their proper entities so conceived. And this is also to differ by themselves. And when it is inferred that they differ with their whole selves, a distinction is to be made: for if the sense is, One is diverse from the other through its whole entity, it is true; but if, Through its whole entity conceived in all ways, it is false: because their entities can be conceived as diverse simply, and also as similar and the same in a certain respect, by reason of attribution; and therefore they are not conceived as diverse in all ways. Nor, though in this sense it is true that they differ with their whole selves, is it necessary that being be equivocal: because equivocates, as they are conceived and signified under that name, agree in no way. And therefore it is not proved from that testimony that being is equivocal. Porphyry, however, speaks of the equivocal according to the common acceptation,

p. 231

, sub qua analogũ cõprehendit: nã ad intentũ eius, quod erat, ens non esse genus rerũ omniũ, sufficiebat esse analogũ.

under which he comprehends the analogous term: for for his purpose, which was that being is not the genus of all things, it sufficed that it be analogous.

59 Ad primum arg. secundæ opinionis: Neganda est minor, quòd conceptus entis sit vnus simpliciter. Et cùm dicitur modos distingui ratione ab entitate, distinguendum: nam duobus modis contingit aliqua distingui ratione. Primò, distinctione totali, ita vt conceptus vnius sic distinguatur ab alio, vt illum non includat, & hoc modo distinguitur ratione differentia à genere. Secundò, non distinctione totali, sed includentis, & inclusi, & ita verum est, quòd conceptus entis distinguatur à modis, quos includit, & à quibus includitur, in quantum addunt supra conceptum eius rationem expressionis. Et si distingueretur conceptus entis ratione à modis in primo sensu, posset abstrahi ab eis: sed cùm non distinguatur, nisi in secundo: negandum est, quòd possit abstrahi, aut sine illis concipi.

59 To the first argument of the second opinion: the minor is to be denied, that the concept of being is one simply. And when it is said that the modes are distinguished by reason from the entity, a distinction is to be made: for things happen to be distinguished by reason in two ways. First, by a total distinction, so that the concept of one is so distinguished from the other that it does not include it; and in this way the difference is distinguished by reason from the genus. Second, not by a total distinction, but by that of the including and the included; and so it is true that the concept of being is distinguished from the modes, which it includes and by which it is included, inasmuch as they add above its concept the ratio of expression. And if the concept of being were distinguished by reason from the modes in the first sense, it could be abstracted from them; but since it is not distinguished except in the second, it is to be denied that it can be abstracted, or conceived without them.

Ad secundum: Neganda est minor, quòd ratio diuersitatis substantiæ, & accidentis, non sit in entitate, sed ratione modorum: impossibile est enim, quòd ratione modorum sit, & non ratione entitatis, cùm modi entitates sint, & ideo in conceptu entitatis includantur. Est igitur ratione vtriusque: & ideo repugnat concipiens sine diuersitate, aut ab ea abstrahi, ita vt conceptus eius sit vnus simpliciter.

To the second: the minor is to be denied, that the ratio of the diversity of substance and accident is not in the entity, but by reason of the modes. For it is impossible that it be by reason of the modes and not by reason of the entity, since the modes are entities, and are therefore included in the concept of the entity. It is therefore by reason of both; and therefore it is repugnant that it be conceived without diversity, or be abstracted from it, so that its concept is one simply.

Ad vltimum, Concessa maiori, distinguenda est minor: nam concipere rationem entis, non conceptis rationibus particularibus substantiæ, & accidentis duobus modis cõtingit, Primò, non conceptis distinctè, & expressè. Secũdò non cõceptis actu implicito, & confuso. Et in casu argumenti concedendum est, quòd concipiatur sine modis in primo sensu, non tamen in secundo: ex eo autem quod concipitur, non conceptis modis in primo sensu, fit, vt possit dubitare intellectus, An ens quod concipit, sit substantia, vel accidẽs. Quare talis dubitatio non probat, quòd detur conceptus entis vnus simpliciter abstractus à substantia, & accidenti, ratione cuius vniuocum esse possit.

To the last: granting the major, the minor is to be distinguished. For to conceive the ratio of being without conceiving the particular rationes of substance and accident happens in two ways. First, without conceiving them distinctly and expressly. Second, without conceiving them in implicit and confused act. And in the case of the argument it is to be granted that it is conceived without the modes in the first sense, but not in the second; and from its being conceived without the modes being conceived in the first sense, it comes about that the intellect can doubt whether the being which it conceives is substance or accident. Wherefore such a doubt does not prove that there is given a concept of being one simply, abstracted from substance and accident, by reason of which it could be univocal.

An saltem ens completum sit vniuocum respectu substantiæ, & accidentis completi — Whether at least complete being is univocal with respect to complete substance and accident.

60 Ratio dubitandi pro affirmatiua parte specialis est de ente completo, quia non videtur includi posse, in differentiis, nec in modis intrinsecis, per quos diuersa sunt, accidens, & substantia: quia de modis atque differentiis manifestum est, esse entia incompleta: ergo abstrahi poterit ab eis conceptus entis nullam diuersitatem includens. Probatur consequentia, quia totam diuersitatem efficiunt modi.

60 The special reason for doubting in favor of the affirmative side concerns complete being: because it does not seem that it can be included in the differences, nor in the intrinsic modes, through which accident and substance are diverse: because concerning the modes and differences it is manifest that they are incomplete beings; therefore a concept of being including no diversity could be abstracted from them. The consequence is proved: because the modes cause the whole diversity. P iiij

p. 232

Communis tamen sententia tenenda est tanquam vera, Quòd ens completum non possit esse vniuocum ad substantiã cõpletam & accidens completum; sed non minus hoc modo esse analogum, quàm si in tota sua vniuersalitate accipiatur. Cuius ratio non eadem assignatur ab omnibus, qui ita sentiunt. Sed mihi videtur eodem ferè modo probandum esse, quòd ens completum non sit vniuocum, sed analogum, quo probatum est, vniuersaliter sumptum analogum esse. Probatur ergo duplici ratione. Prima: Sicut ens vniuersaliter sumptum includit actu quamlibet entitatem, quãtumcunque minimam, siue sit entitas rei, siue modus, & etiam includitur in ea formaliter, & esseatialiter: ita ens completum includit actu quamcunque entitatem completam, tam accidentalem, quàm substantialem, quia esse entitatem substantialem, aut accidentalem, non sunt gradus perfectionis ab eadem entitate distincti, sed sunt eademmet entitas expressori quodam modo cõcepta, & significata: ergo tota diuersitas, tota attributio, quam habent inter sese, includitur in conspectu entis completi, & ex consequenti tota analogia, Quare repugnat conceptum entis completi, esse vnum simpliciter, & vniuocum.

The common opinion, however, is to be held as true: that complete being cannot be univocal to complete substance and complete accident, but is analogous in this way no less than if it is taken in its whole universality. The reason for this is not assigned in the same way by all who think so. But it seems to me that it must be proved in almost the same way that complete being is not univocal but analogous as it was proved that being taken universally is analogous. It is proved, therefore, by a twofold argument. The first: just as being taken universally includes in act any entity whatever, however minimal, whether it be the entity of a thing or a mode, and is also included in it formally and essentially, so complete being includes in act any complete entity whatever, accidental as well as substantial: because to be a substantial or an accidental entity are not grades of perfection distinct from the same entity, but are the very same entity conceived and signified in a certain more express way; therefore the whole diversity and the whole attribution which they have among themselves is included in the concept of complete being, and consequently the whole analogy. Wherefore it is repugnant that the concept of complete being be one simply, and univocal.

61 Secunda ratio sumitur ex definitione vniuocatorum. Vniuoca sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ omnino eadem; ergo vniuocata debent participare ex æquo, & simpliciter cõceptum vniuoci: sed substantia, & accidens completum, non participant ex æquo, nec simpliciter rationem entis completi: ergo ens non potest esse vniuocum respectu eorum. Probatur minor, quia illa participant ex æquo rationem communem, quorum quodlibet participat eam per se, hoc est, sine dependentia essentiali in eadem ab altero: & illa participant eam simpliciter, quorum quodlibet dicitur simpliciter tale, vt eam participat: sed accidens completum non participat rationem entis completi, nisi cum essentiali dependentia à substantia, nec dicitur simpliciter ens completum, sed tantùm secundùm quid, imò non dicitur ens completum, sed entis ens, vt ex Aristot. attulimus: ergo non potest participare vniuocè rationem entis completi, neque ens completum potest esse vniuocum respectu vtriusque. Et quod diximus de ente completo, dicendum est de ente perfecto in ordine ad substantiam perfectam, & accidens perfectum, quia quantùm ad præsentem diuisionem entis attinet, eadem est ratio de vtroque: & ideo eædem rationes eodem modo probant de vtroque.

61 The second argument is taken from the definition of univocates. Univocals are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance altogether the same; therefore univocates must participate the concept of the univocal term equally and simply; but complete substance and accident do not participate the ratio of complete being equally, nor simply: therefore being cannot be univocal with respect to them. The minor is proved: because those things participate a common ratio equally each of which participates it per se, that is, without essential dependence on another; and those participate it simply each of which is called such simply, as it participates it; but complete accident does not participate the ratio of complete being except with essential dependence on substance, nor is it called complete being simply, but only in a certain respect; indeed it is not called complete being, but a being of a being, as we adduced from Aristotle: therefore it cannot participate univocally the ratio of complete being, nor can complete being be univocal with respect to both. And what we have said of complete being must be said of perfect being in relation to perfect substance and perfect accident, because, as far as the present division of being is concerned, the ratio is the same for both; and therefore the same arguments prove the same thing in the same way of both.

Ad argumentum pro ratione dubitandi positum respondetur; Quòd licèt ens completum non includat modos intrinsecos

To the argument put forward for the reason for doubting it is replied that, although complete being does not include the intrinsic modes

p. 233

per se, & in alio, vt separatim conceptus à substantia, & accidenti, & eodem modo, nec differentias, nec etiam in eis sic conceptus includatur: nihilominus tamen eos includit, & in eis includitur, vt concipiuntur in constitutione substantiæ, & accidentis, aut specierum. Et ratio huius est manifesta, quia ens completum, vt probauimus, includit substantiam, & accidens completum, & ab eis includitur formaliter, & essentialiter: sed non est substantia completa & incompleta sine modis, vt eam constituentibus: ergo, vt sic concepta includuntur in ente completo, & illud includunt. Quæ inclusio sufficit: vt conceptus entis diuersitatem includat sufficientem ad tollendam vniuocationem, & efficiendam analogiam.

per se and in another as concepts separate from substance and accident, and in the same way neither the differences, nor again is it included in them as thus conceived, it nevertheless includes them and is included in them as they are conceived in the constitution of substance and accident, or of the species. And the reason for this is manifest: because complete being, as we have proved, includes complete substance and accident, and is included by them formally and essentially; but there is no complete and incomplete substance without the modes that constitute it: therefore, as thus conceived, they are included in complete being and include it. Which inclusion suffices for the concept of being to include a diversity sufficient to take away univocation and to produce analogy.

An ens sit vniuocum respectu aliquarum rerum eiusdem prædicamenti, vel diuersorum prædicamentorum — Whether being is univocal with respect to some things of the same category, or of different categories.

62 Explicata iam, analogia entis vniuersalissimi respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, & entis competi, respectu substantiæ cõpletæ, & accidentis completi, restant duæ aliæ comparationes entis magis particulares. Prima est, An respectu duarum specierum eiusdem prædicamenti, vt hominis & equi, Petri & Ioannis, aut albedinis, & nigredinis. Secunda; An respectu duarum rerum diuersorum prædicamentorum accidentium, vt albedinis & quantitatis, ens sit vniuocum, vel analogum: & non loquimur de ente vt completo, sed secundùm se sumpto.

62 Having now explained the analogy of being taken most universally with respect to substance and accident, and of complete being with respect to complete substance and complete accident, there remain two other, more particular comparisons of being. The first is whether, with respect to two species of the same category, as man and horse, Peter and John, or whiteness and blackness; the second, whether, with respect to two things of different categories of accidents, as whiteness and quantity, being is univocal or analogous. And we are not speaking of being as complete, but taken according to itself.

63 Prima opinio tenet. Ens vniuocum esse, respectu duarum rerum eiusdem prædicamenti, tam substantiæ, quàm accidentis, atque etiam diuersorum prædicamentorum accidentium. Eam tenet quantum ad primum Fons. 4. Met. cap. 1. q. 1. sect. 3. non negans secundum, & quantum ad vtrumque P. F. Suarius in Met, dis. 32. sect. 2. n. 21. Probat vtrumque hoc arg. Duæ substantiæ, & duo accidentia eiusdem prædicamenti, aut diuersorum, participant rationem entis sine vlla attributione vnius ad alterum, imò sine vllo ordine, sed æquè primo: ergo non conuenit illis analogicè, sed vniuocè.

63 The first opinion holds that being is univocal with respect to two things of the same category, of substance as well as of accident, and also of different categories of accidents. Fonseca holds it as to the first, Metaph. 4, ch. 1, q. 1, sect. 3, not denying the second; and as to both, Father F. Suárez, in Metaph., disp. 32, sect. 2, no. 21. He proves both by this argument: two substances, and two accidents of the same category or of different ones, participate the ratio of being without any attribution of one to the other, indeed without any order, but equally primarily: therefore it does not belong to them analogically, but univocally.

Secunda opinio est aliorum, qui tenent vtroque modo comparatum ens esse analogum proportionalitatis. Probant: Quia ens est analogum attributionis simul, & proportionis: sed in his comparationibus non significat membra illa, secundùm attributionem vnius ad alterum: ergo nõ potest habere aliam analogiam, nisi proportionalitatis. Quod verò hanc habeat, manifestum est: quia verum est, ita se habere quamlibet speciem

The second opinion is that of others, who hold that being, compared in either way, is analogous by analogy of proportionality. They prove it: because being is analogous by analogy of attribution and of proportion at once; but in these comparisons it does not signify those members according to the attribution of one to the other: therefore it cannot have any other analogy except that of proportionality. That it has this, however, is manifest: because it is true that any species

p. 234

eiusdem, vel diuersorum prędicamentorum accidentium ad suam entitatem, quam participat ab ente: sicut alteram ad suam, & hæc est proportionalitas: ergo erit ens, respectu illarum, analogum attributionis.

of the same category, or of different categories of accidents, stands to its entity, which it participates from being, as the other does to its own; and this is proportionality: therefore being, with respect to them, will be analogous by analogy of proportionality.

64 Pro solutione huius dubij notandum est, quòd in his cõparationibus duobus modis potest sumi ens. Primò secundùm limitatum conceptum eiusdẽ prędicamenti: & hoc modo cõparatum ad duas substantias, idem est cum supremo genere substantiæ. Secundò modo potest sumi in tota sua vniuersalitate, prout significat substantiam & accidens. Omitto tertiam considerationem eius, quam ponunt alij quasi mediam inter vtramque, ita vt accipiatur pro conceptu minùs vniuersali, eo quem habet in secunda acceptatione: sed magis vniuersali, quàm supremum genus prædicamenti: & ita si eo superius, quia conceptus iste coincidit cum secundo, quantum pertinet ad analogiam, aut vniuocationem: nam repugnat accipi vniuersaliùs, quàm pro rebus vnius prædicamenti, & non accipi, pro communi aliquo modo multis prædicamentis. Idem est autem accipi pro duobus ac prout est commune omnibus, quantum pertinet ad analogiam, aut vniuocationem, iuxta communem, & probabiliorem sententiam: ergo de hac acceptione non est curandum.

64 For the solution of this doubt it should be noted that in these comparisons being can be taken in two ways. First, according to the limited concept of the same category; and compared in this way to two substances, it is the same as the supreme genus of substance. In the second way it can be taken in its whole universality, as it signifies substance and accident. I omit a third consideration of it, which others posit as it were midway between the two, so that it is taken for a concept less universal than the one it has in the second acceptation, but more universal than the supreme genus of the category, and so superior to it: because this concept coincides with the second as far as analogy or univocation is concerned. For it is repugnant for it to be taken more universally than for the things of one category, and not to be taken for something in some way common to many categories. But to be taken for two and as it is common to all is the same, as far as analogy or univocation is concerned, according to the common and more probable opinion: therefore this acceptation need not concern us.

Hoc supposito, duo asserit nostra sententia. Primum: Ens primo modo sumptũ, vniuocum esse respectu rerum eiusdem prædicamenti. Probatur: Quia idem est ens ita sumptum, cum supremo genere eiusdem prædicamenti, sed hoc est vniuocum respectu rerum eiusdem prædicamẽti: ergo etiam ens.

This supposed, our view asserts two things. The first: being taken in the first way is univocal with respect to things of the same category. It is proved: because being so taken is the same as the supreme genus of the same category; but this is univocal with respect to things of the same category: therefore being is too.

Secundum est: Si ens secundo modo accipiatur in omnibus his comparationibus, est analogum, & non vniuocum. Quod sic probo: Analogum in sua propria, & integra significatione prædicatur analogicè de singulis analogatis per se sumptis, vt sanum de animali per se, aut de vrina, & medicina per se: sed ens in sua propria, & integra significatione est analogum: ergo, vt analogum, prædicatur de substantia per se, & de quolibet accidenti per se, & ex consequenti de rebus eiusdem prædicamenti, vel diuersorum prædicamentorum accidentium; sed sic sumitur in secunda acceptione: ergo prædicatur analogicè de singulis analogatis.

The second is: if being is taken in the second way, in all these comparisons it is analogous and not univocal. I prove it thus: the analogous term, in its proper and integral signification, is predicated analogically of the individual analogates taken by themselves, as healthy of animal by itself, or of urine and medicine by themselves; but being in its proper and integral signification is analogous: therefore, as analogous, it is predicated of substance by itself and of any accident by itself, and consequently of things of the same category or of different categories of accidents; but it is so taken in the second acceptation: therefore it is predicated analogically of the individual analogates.

65 Ad arg. primæ sententiæ, Distinguendum est antecedens, secundùm diuersas confiedrationes entis explicatis: nam si secundùm primam accipiatur, verum est sine attributione, aut respectu participari à duabus speciebus eiusdem prædicamenti: sicut participatur supremum genus eiusdem prædicamenti

65 To the argument of the first opinion: the antecedent is to be distinguished according to the different considerations of being that have been explained. For if it is taken according to the first, it is true that it is participated without attribution or respect by two species of the same category, just as the supreme genus of the same category is participated

p. 235

cum quo conuertitur: si verò accipiatur iuxta secundam, negandum est, quia licèt duæ illæ species non participent rationem entis, cum attributione inter sese, eam tamen participant cum attributione accidentium ad ipsas, quemadmodum verum est, ac necessarium, supremum genus earum, participare rationem entis cum attributione accidentium ad illud in hac prædicatione, Substantia est ens: alioqui nõ esset prædicatio analogi formaliter. Quod patet esse falsum.

with which it is convertible; but if it is taken according to the second, it is to be denied: because, although those two species do not participate the ratio of being with attribution between themselves, they nevertheless participate it with the attribution of accidents to them; just as it is true, and necessary, that their supreme genus participates the ratio of being with the attribution of accidents to it in this predication, Substance is a being; otherwise it would not formally be a predication of the analogous term, which is plainly false.

Ad rationem alterius opinionis, Respondetur ex doctrina superiùs tradita, quòd proportionalitas nullo modo efficit per se nomen analogum: vnde eo ipso, quòd ens non prædicatur secundùm attributionem, non potest prædicari vt analogum. Sed de hoc statim dicemus.

To the argument of the other opinion it is replied, from the doctrine handed down above, that proportionality in no way makes a name analogous per se: whence, by the very fact that being is not predicated according to attribution, it cannot be predicated as analogous. But of this we shall speak presently.

Secunda pars quæstionis.

Second Part of the Question.

An ens sit analogum comparatum ad ens creatum & increatum, vel ad Deum, & creaturas — Whether being is analogous when compared to created and uncreated being, or to God and creatures.

66 Diuersa est hæc entis comparatio à præcedentibus, quia nõ sumitur ens in sua vniuersalitate, respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, sed respectu Dei, & creaturarum. Per creaturas verò non intelligimus accidentia: nam cùm Deus sit substantia, manifestum est ex dictis in prima parte quęstionis, non posse conuenire vniuocè sub nomine entis cum accidentibus, solùm ergo intelligitur nomine creaturarum substantia creata: vnde sensus quæstionis est, An substantia creata, & increata, vniuocè conueniant sub nomine entis.

66 This comparison of being is different from the preceding ones, because being is not taken in its universality with respect to substance and accident, but with respect to God and creatures. And by creatures we do not understand accidents: for, since God is a substance, it is manifest from what was said in the first part of the question that he cannot agree univocally with accidents under the name of being; therefore by the name of creatures only created substance is understood. Whence the sense of the question is whether created and uncreated substance agree univocally under the name of being.

Et prima opinio asserit, Ens ad Deum & creaturas, non esse vniuocum sed æquiuocum Huius sententiæ mentionem fecit D. Th. 1. p. q. 13. art. 5. & qu 7. de potentia, art. 7. & eam videtur tenere Aureolus in 1, p. 2. qu. 1, (nisi fortè de æquiuoco loquitur sub communi acceptione, vt comprehendit analogum) Et potest probati: Quia entitas creata, alterius longè rationis est ab increata, & in infinitum ab ea diuersa: ergo nihil potest habere commune cum increata, præter solam vocem. Et hoc est, nomen vtramque significans esse æquiuocum.

And the first opinion asserts that being is not univocal to God and creatures, but equivocal. St. Thomas made mention of this opinion, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5, and On Power, q. 7, a. 7; and Auriol seems to hold it, on 1, d. 2, q. 1 (unless perhaps he speaks of the equivocal in the common acceptation, as it comprehends the analogous). And it can be proved: because created entity is of a far different ratio from the uncreated, and infinitely diverse from it: therefore it can have nothing in common with the uncreated except the word alone. And this is for the name signifying both to be equivocal.

Secunda opinio, est Scoti in 1. d. 3. quæst, 1. & 3 asserentis, Ens respectu substantiæ creatæ, & increatæ, habere vnum conceptum communem, & distinctum ex natura rei ab vtraque, sicut superiùs dixerat de conceptu entis, & ideo esse vniuocum. Eum sequuntur eius discipuli.

The second opinion is that of Scotus, on 1, d. 3, q. 1 and 3, who asserts that being, with respect to created and uncreated substance, has one common concept, distinct from the nature of the thing from both, as he had said above of the concept of being, and that it is therefore univocal. His disciples follow him.

67 Probatur sufficienti diuisione, Ens ita comparatum non est æquiuocũ, non est analogũ; ergo erit vniuocum. Probatur

67 It is proved by a sufficient division: being so compared is not equivocal, nor is it analogous: therefore it will be univocal. It is proved

p. 236

prima pars antecedentis, Nam substantia creata non est omnino diuersa ab increata, sed ei similis: ergo non conuenit cum ea in sola voce, sed aliquo modo in entitate ipsa: quare non potest ens respectu vtriusque esse æquiuocum. Probatur secunda pars hoc modo: Ens non est analogum proportionalitatis, neque attributionis: ergo nullo modo. Antecedens probo: quia nomen ens respectu Dei & creaturarum, non significat proportionalitatem, quod necessarium est, vt sic analogum: ergo non est analogum proportionalitatis, sed nec significat attributionem: nam creatura simpliciter est ens, ergo non per attributionem ad Deum.

the first part of the antecedent: for created substance is not altogether diverse from the uncreated, but similar to it: therefore it does not agree with it in the word alone, but in some way in the entity itself; wherefore being cannot be equivocal with respect to both. The second part is proved in this way: being is not analogous by analogy of proportionality, nor of attribution: therefore in no way. I prove the antecedent: because the name being, with respect to God and creatures, does not signify proportionality, which is necessary for it to be thus analogous: therefore it is not analogous by analogy of proportionality. But neither does it signify attribution: for the creature is a being simply, therefore not by attribution to God.

Tertia opinio est D Tho. 1. p. q. 13. art. 5. Quòd Ens respectu Dei, & creaturarum, non sit æquiuocum, nec vniuocum, sed analogum. Quam sequuntur iam ferè omnes, præsertim Ferta. 1. contra gent. cap. 32. Sot. q. 4. anteprædicam. P. F. Suarius in Met. disp. 28. sect. 3. P. Vazquez 1. par. d. 22. c. 5. in fine & est vera & tenenda. Et quòd non sit æquiuocum contra primam opinionem, efficaciter probatum est arg. secundæ opinionis. Sed probatur, quòd non sit vniuocum aduersus secundam, hac ratione: Analogum est, quod non participatur æqualiter, nec simpliciter ab analogatis, sed ab vno per se primò, atque simpliciter, ab alio, vel aliis non per se primò nec simpliciter, sed cum essentiali attributione, ad dependentia ab illo: sed ita se habet ens respectu Dei, & creaturæ: ergo analogum est, & non vniuocum. Probatur minor, quia entitas conuenit Deo per se, & à se, & conuenit ei simpliciter: creaturæ verò, vt creatura est, non per se primò, nec à se, sed per participationem, & ideo non simpliciter, sed secũdùm quid.

The third opinion is that of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5: that being, with respect to God and creatures, is neither equivocal nor univocal, but analogous. Almost all now follow it, especially Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 32; Soto, q. 4 on the Antepredicaments; Father F. Suárez, in Metaph., disp. 28, sect. 3; Father Vázquez, 1 p., d. 22, ch. 5, at the end; and it is true and to be held. And that it is not equivocal, against the first opinion, has been effectively proved by the argument of the second opinion. But that it is not univocal, against the second, is proved by this argument: the analogous is that which is not participated equally nor simply by the analogates, but by one per se primarily and simply, and by another or others not per se primarily nor simply, but with essential attribution and dependence on that one; but being stands thus with respect to God and creature: therefore it is analogous and not univocal. The minor is proved: because entity belongs to God per se and from himself, and belongs to him simply; but to the creature, as it is a creature, not per se primarily nor from itself, but by participation, and therefore not simply, but in a certain respect.

68 Ad arg. primę opinionis, Concesso antecedenti, neganda est consequentia. Nam licèt infinita sit distantia inter entitatem creatam, & increatam, aliqua tamen est similitudo, per attributionem significata, quia entitas creata est quędam participatio entitatis diuinæ. Et hoc sufficit, vt non sint omnino diuersæ, & vt respectu illarum, ens non sit nomen æquiuocum.

68 To the argument of the first opinion: granting the antecedent, the consequence is to be denied. For although the distance between created and uncreated entity is infinite, there is nevertheless some similarity, signified through attribution, because created entity is a certain participation of the divine entity. And this suffices for them not to be altogether diverse, and for being not to be an equivocal name with respect to them.

Ad arg. secundæ opinionis, Negandum est antecedens. Et rursus dum probatur, quòd ens non significat Deum, & creaturam secundùm attributionem, quia creatura est ens simpliciter, distinguendum est: Nam duobus modis potest significari creatura. Primo, nomine entis, Secundo, nomine entis creati, vt significatur comparatione Dei per nomen ens, vt commune ad ens creatum, & increatum. Et si primo modo accipiatur, non significatur cum attributione ad Deum, sed absolutè: & ideo dicitur simpliciter ens; significata verò secundo modo

To the argument of the second opinion: the antecedent is to be denied. And again, when it is proved that being does not signify God and creature according to attribution, because the creature is a being simply, a distinction is to be made. For the creature can be signified in two ways: first, by the name being; second, by the name created being, as it is signified in comparison with God through the name being, as common to created and uncreated being. And if it is taken in the first way, it is not signified with attribution to God, but absolutely, and therefore it is called a being simply; but signified in the second way,

p. 237

attributionem dicit, & ratione illius non vocatur ens simpliciter, sed secundùm quid, hoc est, ens per participationem. Et ex hoc habetur, quòd nomen ens, vt significat ens creatum, & increatum, analogum sit, & non vniuocum.

it says attribution, and by reason of it it is not called a being simply, but in a certain respect, that is, a being by participation. And from this it is had that the name being, as it signifies created and uncreated being, is analogous and not univocal.

Qua analogia dicatur ens respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, atque etiam respectu Dei, & creaturarum — By what analogy being is said with respect to substance and accident, and also with respect to God and creatures.

Prima opinio est aliquorum modernorum, qui vtramque analogiam proportionalitatis, & attributionis tribuunt enti, respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, atque etiam respectu Dei, & creaturarum. Probant hoc arg. Illud est analogum proportionalitatis, & attributionis, inter cuius analogata reperitur proportionalitas, & attributio: sed inter substantiam, & accidens, & inter ens creatum, & increatum, reperitur vtraque, ergo dicetur analogum proportionalitatis, & attributionis. Probatur minor, nam verum imprimis est, quòd sicut se habet substantia ad suum esse, quòd participat ab ente, ita accidens ad suum, quod participat ab eodem: ergo habent inter se proportionalitatem. De attributione verò videtur manifestum, quia accidens dicitur ens per attributionem ad substantiam, & ens creatum per participationem, & attributionem, ad increatum.

The first opinion is that of some moderns, who attribute both analogies, of proportionality and of attribution, to being with respect to substance and accident, and also with respect to God and creatures. They prove this by this argument: that is analogous by analogy of proportionality and of attribution among whose analogates proportionality and attribution are found; but between substance and accident, and between created and uncreated being, both are found: therefore it will be called analogous by analogy of proportionality and of attribution. The minor is proved: for it is true, first of all, that as substance stands to its being, which it participates from being, so accident stands to its own, which it participates from the same: therefore they have proportionality among themselves. But concerning attribution it seems manifest: because accident is called a being by attribution to substance, and created being by participation and attribution to the uncreated.

69 Secunda opinio est, Non esse analogum attributionis, sed proportionalitatis tantùm, quia accidens vocatur absolutè ens in communi modo loquendi, & multò meliùs substantia creata: ergo non sunt entia per attributionem. Probatur consequentia, quia quod tale est per solam attributionem ad aliud, non dicitur tale simpliciter sed secundùm, quid, vt de vrina, & medicina patet.

69 The second opinion is that it is not analogous by analogy of attribution, but only of proportionality: because accident is called a being absolutely in the common way of speaking, and much more so created substance: therefore they are not beings by attribution. The consequence is proved: because what is such only by attribution to another is not called such simply, but in a certain respect, as is plain of urine and medicine.

Tertia sententia est, Non esse analogum proportionalitatis sed solius attributionis. Hæc est conformis doctrinæ D. Tho. & probabilior, ideo eam sequitur iam maior modernorum pars, sed non omnes in eodem sensu, aut propter eandem rationem eam tenent: nam quidam fatentur, non solam attributionem reperiri inter analogata, sed etiam proportionalitatem, sed hanc ideo non facere ens analogum, quia non significatur per illud, non enim significantur substantia, & accidens nomine entis in quantum quodlibet sic se habet ad suum esse, sicut alterum ad suum, licèt hanc proportionalitatem habeant, & secundùm eam possint concipi ab intellectu: ergo talis proportionalitas non efficit ens analogum proportionalitatis. Probatur consequentia, quia non dicuntur aliqua analogata alicuius nominis analogi, nec nomen ipsum dicitur analogum

The third opinion is that it is not analogous by analogy of proportionality, but only of attribution. This is in conformity with the doctrine of St. Thomas, and more probable; therefore the greater part of the moderns now follow it, but not all hold it in the same sense or for the same reason. For some grant that not only attribution is found among the analogates, but also proportionality, but that the latter does not make being analogous because it is not signified by it: for substance and accident are not signified by the name being inasmuch as each stands to its being as the other to its own, although they have this proportionality and can be conceived according to it by the intellect: therefore such proportionality does not make being analogous by analogy of proportionality. The consequence is proved: because things are not called analogates of some analogous name, nor is the name itself called analogous

p. 238

respectu illorum, nisi ea significet, vt talem habent analogiam, sed non potest ea ita significare, nisi analogiam significando: ergo si eam non significet, vt probatum est non significare ens, non dicetur ab illa analogum, quamuis inter res significatas reperiatur.

with respect to them unless it signifies them as they have such an analogy; but it cannot so signify them except by signifying the analogy: therefore, if it does not signify it, as it has been proved that being does not, it will not be called analogous by that analogy, although it is found among the things signified.

70 Nos verò alia via hanc sententiam defendimus. (vt superiùs diximus.) Fatemur enim, proportionalitatem reperiri inter vtraque analogata entis, & diximus proportionalitatem, siue significetur per nomen analogum, siue non sufficientem non esse ad efficiendum illud analogum, quòd superiùs agentes de speciebus analogiæ probauimus. Ideo non datur analogum proportionalitatis, nec eius tale vocari debet, sed analogum attributionis, quia sola attributio vera analogia reputanda est, & sola illa analogum facit nomen, & semper significatur per nomen analogum. Necessarium est enim analogiam significari per nomen, vt illud analogum constituat. Quod efficaciter probatum est argumento illo pro nostra sententia ab his qui eam alia via defendunt.

70 We, however, defend this opinion by another way (as we said above). For we grant that proportionality is found between both analogates of being; and we said that proportionality, whether it is signified by the analogous name or not, is not sufficient to make it analogous, as we proved above when treating of the species of analogy. Therefore there is not given an analogous term of proportionality, nor ought it to be called such, but an analogous term of attribution: because attribution alone is to be reputed true analogy, and it alone makes a name analogous, and it is always signified by the analogous name. For it is necessary that the analogy be signified by the name in order that it constitute it analogous. This was effectively proved by that argument for our view put forward by those who defend it by the other way.

Sed ad argumentum alterius opinionis distinguendum est antecedens, dum dicitur, Accidens vocari simpliciter ens, & etiam ens creatum. Nam aliquid esse, aut dici simpliciter ens, duplicem sensum habere potest. Primus est, vt sit ens intrinsecè, formaliter, & non per solam denominationem extrinsecam. Et in hoc sensu verum est, accidens esse ens simpliciter, & etiam ens creatum. Alter sensus est, quòd aliquid sit ens sine addito. Et hoc modo de nullo analogato minùs principali prędicatur simpliciter analogum, sed de omnibus cum illo addito (secundùm quid) Et ratio huius est, quia licèt formaliter participet rationem analogi, hoc tamen non nisi per essentialem dependentiam, & attributionem ad principale analogatum, & ideo non nisi secundùm quid. Quod vt significaret Arist. asseruit, Accidens non esse ens, sed entis ens. Et ita loquendum est de quocunque alio analogato minùs principali cuius libet analogi, cùm probatum sit, omne analogum esse attributionis. Et hoc significat etiam illud commune proloquium (analogum per se sumptum stat pro famosiori significato.) Cuius sensus est, quod licèt omnia significet, principale tamen tantùm simpliciter, & sine addito. Quare dum absolutè profertur analogum, pro eò tantùm supponit.

But to the argument of the other opinion the antecedent is to be distinguished, when it is said that accident is called a being simply, and also created being. For that something is, or is called, a being simply can have a twofold sense. The first is that it is a being intrinsically and formally, and not by extrinsic denomination alone; and in this sense it is true that accident is a being simply, and also created being. The other sense is that something is a being without an addition; and in this way the analogous term is predicated simply of no less principal analogate, but of all of them with that addition (in a certain respect). And the reason for this is that, although it formally participates the ratio of the analogous term, it does so only through essential dependence and attribution to the principal analogate, and therefore only in a certain respect. To signify which, Aristotle asserted that accident is not a being, but a being of a being. And so one must speak of any other less principal analogate of any analogous term whatever, since it has been proved that every analogous term is of attribution. And this is also what that common saying signifies (The analogous term taken by itself stands for its more famous significate), whose sense is that, although it signifies all, it signifies only the principal one simply and without an addition. Wherefore, when an analogous term is uttered absolutely, it supposits for that one alone.

Et si dixeris, ex hoc sequi, hanc propositionem esse veram: Omne ens est substantia, imò esse identicam, quod sic probatur: Ens absolutè sumptum solum supponit pro substantia, ergo subiectum, & prædicatum idem sunt. Respondeo neutrum

And if you say that from this it follows that this proposition is true, Every being is substance, and indeed that it is identical, which is proved thus: being taken absolutely supposits only for substance; therefore subject and predicate are the same: I reply that neither

p. 239

sequi. Non primum quòd propositio sit vera, quia analogum absolutè sumptum semper significat omnia sua analogata, sed pro solo primo stare dicitur, si per se accipiatur: quia reliqua non sunt talia sine addito: in subiecto autem illius propositionis, Omne ens est substantia, non sumitur absolutè, aut per se ens sed cum addito distributionis, quę in nomen analogum fertur, secundùm significationem analogi, & ideo in omnia analogata. Quare sicut non pro solo principali distribuitur, sic non pro solo illo supponit, & ideo non est vera perfectio, quia prædicatum solum continet vnum analogarum, subiectum verò distributiuè omnia: & hæc est ratio, propter quam non potest verificari de subiecto. Quòd verò non sit identica, ex eodem est manifestum, cùm plus significet subiectum, quàm prædicatum: atque etiam ex alio, quia licèt subiectum solum pro substantia supponeret, non significat eam expressè ac distinctè, sed confusè tantùm, & in prędicato significatur distinctè, & expressè: diuersus autem modus significandi prædicati, & subiecti sufficit, vt propositio non sit identica.

follows. Not the first, that the proposition is true: because the analogous term taken absolutely always signifies all its analogates, but is said to stand for the first alone if it is taken by itself, because the rest are not such without an addition; but in the subject of that proposition, Every being is substance, being is not taken absolutely or by itself, but with the addition of distribution, which is carried onto the analogous name according to the signification of the analogous term, and therefore onto all the analogates. Wherefore, just as it is not distributed for the principal one alone, so it does not supposit for that one alone; and therefore it is not a true proposition, because the predicate contains only one of the analogates, but the subject all of them distributively; and this is the reason why it cannot be verified of the subject. And that it is not identical is manifest from the same thing, since the subject signifies more than the predicate; and also from another: because, although the subject supposited only for substance, it does not signify it expressly and distinctly, but only confusedly, while in the predicate it is signified distinctly and expressly; and the different mode of signifying of predicate and subject suffices for the proposition not to be identical.

72 Ad arg. primæ opinionis dupliciter responpetur. Primò, distinguendo antecedens. Nam duobus modis potest reperiri proportionalitas inter analogata: Primò, ita vt per nomen analogum significetur: & si ita reperiretur, sufficeret facere illud analogum: alio modo reperitur non significata, sed quam potest intellectus in eis concipere, & sic non facit nomen analogum. Et hoc modo non solùm in analogis, sed in æquiuocis, & vniuocis reperitur: primò verò modo in nullis, sed si imponeretur nomen aliquod, à quo significarentur analogata, vt habent proportionalitatem, ex ea sola esset analogum. Sed per nomen ens non significatur, & ideo non probatur, quòd sit analogum attributionis.

72 To the argument of the first opinion a twofold reply is given. First, by distinguishing the antecedent. For proportionality can be found among analogates in two ways. First, so that it is signified by the analogous name; and if it were found in this way, it would suffice to make it analogous. In another way it is found not signified, but such that the intellect can conceive it in them; and so it does not make a name analogous. And in this way it is found not only in analogous terms but in equivocals and univocals; but in the first way in none: but if some name were imposed by which the analogates were signified as they have proportionality, it would be analogous from that alone. But by the name being it is not signified; and therefore it is not proved that it is analogous by analogy of proportionality.

Secundò, respondetur negando absolutè antecedens, quòd proportionalitas ex se, siue significata, siue non significata, efficiat, nomen analogum: vnde licèt reperiatur inter significata entis, non sequitur esse analogum proportionalitatis.

Second, it is replied by denying absolutely the antecedent, that proportionality of itself, whether signified or not signified, makes a name analogous: whence, although it is found among the significates of being, it does not follow that it is analogous by analogy of proportionality.

Ad argumentum secundæ, distinguendum est antecedens. Nam si ens simpliciter idem sit, quòd ens intrinsecè, & formaliter, verum est, si verò simpliciter sumatur prout distinguitur contra secundùm quid, falsum est, vt probauimus: & cùm ex attributione proueniat, quòd minùs principalia analogata non dicantur talia, nisi secundùm quid: non probatur, quòd ens non sit analogum attributionis.

To the argument of the second: the antecedent is to be distinguished. For if being simply is the same as being intrinsically and formally, it is true; but if simply is taken as it is distinguished against in a certain respect, it is false, as we have proved; and since it comes from attribution that the less principal analogates are not called such except in a certain respect, it is not proved that being is not analogous by analogy of attribution.

p. 240

Vtrum accidens sit vniuocum ad nouem prædicamenta accidentium, vel analogum — Whether accident is univocal to the nine categories of accidents, or analogous.

Maior difficultas est de accidenti respectu omnium accidentium, An sit vniuocum, vel analogum. in qua præsupponendum est primò, quæstionem non procedere de accidenti vniuersalissimè sumpto prout est commune ad accidentia realia, & rationis: nam sic certum est, esse analogum, cùm accidentia rationis non sint accidentia, nisi per similitudinem, & attributionem ad accidentia realia: quare non potest abstrahi ab vtrisque conceptus communis vniuocus. Secundò, certum est, nec etiam procedere de accidenti reali, prout significat tam accidentia intrinseca, hoc est, verè inhærentia in subiecto, quàm extrinsecas denominationes reales, vt dexteritatem & similes, quæ passim reperiuntur in sex vltimis prædicamentis, quamuis ergo non intelligam, ex sola denominatione extrinseca posse fieri prædicamentum reale, vt suo loco probabo.) Nam denominationes istæ non sunt vera accidentia, sed solùm per attributionem, & similitudinem ad ea, quæ inhærent subiecto, dicuntur: vnde respectu omnium, non potest accidens esse vniuocum Sed solùm loquimur de accidenti reali, prout significat ea solùm, quæ inhærent subiectis, de quo inquirimus, An sit vniuocum, vel analogum.

The greater difficulty concerns accident with respect to all accidents: whether it is univocal or analogous. In which it must be presupposed, first, that the question does not proceed concerning accident taken most universally, as it is common to real accidents and accidents of reason: for so it is certain that it is analogous, since accidents of reason are not accidents except by similarity and attribution to real accidents; wherefore a common univocal concept cannot be abstracted from both. Second, it is certain that neither does it proceed concerning real accident as it signifies both intrinsic accidents, that is, those truly inhering in a subject, and real extrinsic denominations, such as rightness and the like, which are found here and there in the last six categories (although I, for my part, do not understand that a real category can be made from extrinsic denomination alone, as I shall prove in its place). For these denominations are not true accidents, but are so called only by attribution and similarity to those which inhere in a subject: whence, with respect to all of them, accident cannot be univocal. But we speak only of real accident, as it signifies only those things which inhere in subjects, concerning which we inquire whether it is univocal or analogous.

73 Et prima opinio asserit esse vniuocum. Ita Sotus quæst. 2. anteprædicamentorum, & plures moderni: sed differunt à Soro in eo, quòd ita asserunt esse vniuocum, vt etiam sit genus, constituens vnum prædicamentum omnium accidentium, sicut substantia constituit vnum prædicamentum omnium substantiarum: Sotus verò negat esse genus.

73 And the first opinion asserts that it is univocal. So Soto, q. 2 on the Antepredicaments, and many moderns; but they differ from Soto in this, that they assert it to be univocal in such a way that it is also a genus, constituting one category of all accidents, as substance constitutes one category of all substances; whereas Soto denies that it is a genus.

Duo possunt probari pro hac sententia. Primum, quòd accidens non sit analogum. Secundum, quòd sit vniuocum. Et hoc secundum eisdem prorsus argumentis probari solet, quibus probatum est superius ens esse vniuocum, & ideo non sunt hoc loco repetenda, sed solùm probabitur primum ex definitione analogorum. Analoga sunt quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ, nec omnino eadem, nec omnino diuersa: sed ratio accidentis omnino est eadem: ergo non est analogum, sed vniuocum. Probatur minor: Ratio accidentis est, Esse in subiecto, sed Esse in subiecto, non solùm formaliter & intrinsecè conuenit omnibus accidentibus, sed etiam æqualiter & simpliciter, ergo non est diuersa in eis, sed eadem.

Two things can be proved for this opinion. The first, that accident is not analogous; the second, that it is univocal. And this second is customarily proved by exactly the same arguments by which it was proved above that being is univocal, and therefore they need not be repeated in this place; but only the first will be proved, from the definition of analogous terms. Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but the ratio of accident is altogether the same: therefore it is not analogous, but univocal. The minor is proved: the ratio of accident is to be in a subject; but to be in a subject belongs to all accidents not only formally and intrinsically, but also equally and simply: therefore it is not diverse in them, but the same.

74 Huic argumento solet responderi: Quòd licèt accidentia non dicantur per attributionem ad vnum accidens, tamen

74 To this argument it is customarily replied that, although accidents are not called such by attribution to one accident, yet

p. 241

omnia dicunt attributionem ad substantiam, & intrinsecam dependentiam ab ea. Et hæc sufficit vt inter sese dicantur analogicè sub nomine accidentis. Sed probatur hoc non sufficere, duplici ratione. Primò, quia vt attributio constituat analogiam, inter significata analogata versari debet, sicut analogia ipsa: sed substantia non est analogatũ accidentis, cùm nõ significetur eo nomine, ergo attributio accidentium ad illam, non constituit accidens analogum, sed solùm ens, à quo significantur omnia.

all of them express attribution to substance and intrinsic dependence on it. And this suffices for them to be called analogically among themselves under the name of accident. But it is proved that this does not suffice, by a twofold argument. First, because in order that attribution constitute analogy, it must obtain among the analogated significates, just as analogy itself does; but substance is not an analogate of accident, since it is not signified by that name; therefore the attribution of accidents to it does not constitute accident as analogous, but only being, by which all of them are signified.

Secundò, attributio ad substantiam æquè primò conuenit omnibus accidentibus, atque etiam intrinsecè, & formaliter, ergo vniuocè conueniunt in ea: sed secundùm talem attributionem significantur nomine accidentis, ergo vniuocè, & non analogicè significantur.

Second, attribution to substance belongs equally and primarily to all accidents, and also intrinsically and formally; therefore they agree univocally in it; but according to such attribution they are signified by the name of accident; therefore they are signified univocally, and not analogically.

Secunda opinio tenet, Accidens non esse vniuocum, sed analogum, Ita Sonc. 4. Meta. q. 4. ad 1. Caie. de ente, & essentia, c. 7. q. 15. ad 4. P. F. Suarius in Met. disp. 39. q. 3. Pater Vazquez, 1. p. d. 14. c. 2. Fonseca 5. Met. c. 7. q. 1. sect. 4. & hæc est probabilior & tenenda.

The second opinion holds that accident is not univocal, but analogous. So Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 4, ad 1; Cajetan, On Being and Essence, ch. 7, q. 15, ad 4; Fr. Francisco Suárez in Metaph., disp. 59, q. 3; Father Vázquez, 1 p., d. 14, ch. 2; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 1, sect. 4. And this is more probable and to be held.

Sed diuersis modis probatur à diuersis. Ratio aliquorum est, proportionalitas, quæ reperitur inter accidẽtia. Quia sicut vnũ se habet ad suum esse, quod ab accidenti participat, sic se habet aliud. Et sufficit, vt accidens sit analogum respectu omniũ. Sed hęc ratio insufficiens est, nam vt superiùs probauimus, proportionalitas non significatur per nomen, & ideo non sufficit illud facere analogum, & etiam si significaretur, non sufficeret.

But it is proved in different ways by different authors. The argument of some is the proportionality which is found among accidents: because just as one is related to its own being, which it participates from accident, so is the other related. And this suffices for accident to be analogous with respect to all. But this argument is insufficient: for, as we proved above, proportionality is not signified by the name, and therefore it does not suffice to make it analogous; and even if it were signified, it would not suffice.

75 Ideo alij, qui solam attributionem veram constituere analogiam, nobiscum sentiunt, dicunt reperiri attributionem inter accidentia, quia omnia dicuntur talia in ordine ad quantitatem, ratione cuius inhęrent subiecto. Sed hoc probatur falsum. Quia nullum accidẽs spirituale inhæret subiecto media quantitate, neque enim omnia accidentia sunt corporea: nam generatio substantialis inhæret materiæ primæ ante quantitatem, & relatio totius substantialis ad materiam, & formam, & relatio materiæ, & formæ inter sese, ergo falsum est, quòd dicantur per attributionem ad quantitatem.

75 Therefore others, who agree with us that attribution alone constitutes true analogy, say that attribution is found among accidents, because all are called such in order to quantity, by reason of which they inhere in the subject. But this is proved false: because no spiritual accident inheres by the mediation of quantity, for not all accidents are corporeal; for substantial generation inheres in prime matter before quantity, and so do the relation of the substantial whole to matter and form, and the relation of matter and form to each other; therefore it is false that they are so called through attribution to quantity.

Alij denique probant accidens non esse vniuocum. Quia saltem respectu accidentis absoluti, & relatiui, non potest habere rationem vniuocam: nam vel conceptus abstractus ab vtroque est absolutus, vel relatiuus. Non absolutus, quia non conueniret inferiori accidenti relatiuo. Nec potest esse relatiuus, quia non conueniret inferiori absoluto: ergo nec potest esse vniuocus. Et si dicas, non esse relatiuum, nec absolutum,

Others, finally, prove that accident is not univocal because, at least with respect to absolute and relative accident, it cannot have a univocal ratio: for the concept abstracted from both is either absolute or relative. Not absolute, because it would not belong to the inferior relative accident. Nor can it be relative, because it would not belong to the inferior absolute accident; therefore neither can it be univocal. And if you say that it is neither relative nor absolute, Q

p. 242

sed abstrahere ab vtraque ratione, vt abstrahunt cætera vniuoca à particularibus rationibus vniuocatorum. Probatur hoc esse falsum, quia si talis conceptus abstrahit à relatiuo, & absoluto, eo ipso debet esse absolutus. Nam si abstrahit à relatiuo, ergo iam non respicit terminum: sed quod non respicit terminum, est absolutum, ergo talis conceptus absolutus erit, & non abstrahet ab absoluto, & relatiuo.

but that it abstracts from both rationes, as the other univocal terms abstract from the particular rationes of the univocates, this is proved to be false: because if such a concept abstracts from the relative and the absolute, by that very fact it must be absolute. For if it abstracts from the relative, then it no longer regards a term; but what does not regard a term is absolute; therefore such a concept will be absolute, and will not abstract from the absolute and the relative.

76 Hæc tamen ratio insufficiens mihi videtur, quia non probat talem conceptum non posse abstrahere ab absoluto, & relatiuo; & ideo non probat quòd vniuocus esse non possit. Nam dicam ergo relationem duplicem conceptum habere. Primum, quo respicit subiectum, & hic est ei communis cum accidentibus absolutis. Secundum quo respicit terminum, & iste est conceptus specialis, quo distinguitur à cæteris prædicamentis, & per primum conceptum non respicit relatio terminum, sed per secundum. Dum autem sic arguitur, Ille conceptus non respicit terminum: ergo est absolutus, neganda est consequentia, quia medium dari potest inter conceptum absolutum, & respicientem terminum, & tale medium est conceptus abstrahens ab absoluto, & relatiuo, qui nec respicit terminum, nec excludit respectum ad terminum, sed solùm dicit rationem communem, contrahibilem per respectum ad terminum, & per rationem absolutam, quæ non solùm non dicit respectum ad terminum, sed eum excludit, quem non excludit conceptus communis, abstrahens à relatiuo, & absoluto. Non ergo probatur illa ratione, quòd accidens non possit esse vniuocum.

76 This argument, however, seems to me insufficient, because it does not prove that such a concept cannot abstract from the absolute and the relative, and therefore it does not prove that it cannot be univocal. For I shall say, then, that relation has a twofold concept. The first, by which it regards the subject, and this it has in common with absolute accidents.
