The second, by which it regards the term, and this is the special concept by which it is distinguished from the other categories; and through the first concept relation does not regard the term, but through the second it does. When, then, one argues thus: That concept does not regard a term; therefore it is absolute, the consequence must be denied, because a middle can be given between an absolute concept and one regarding a term; and such a middle is the concept abstracting from the absolute and the relative, which neither regards a term nor excludes respect to a term, but only expresses a common ratio, contractible through respect to a term and through an absolute ratio, which not only does not express respect to a term but excludes it, which the common concept abstracting from the relative and the absolute does not exclude. It is not proved, therefore, by that argument that accident cannot be univocal.

77 Vt igitur hoc efficaciter probetur, Annotãda est doctrina D. Th. 1. p. q. 13 art. 5. vbi de analogis loquens ait: Nomen analogum duobus modis significare attributionem vnius ad alterum, vel multorum ad vnum. Et ponit exemplum vtriusque in sano, quod analogum est attributionis, respectu medicinæ, & animalis per attributionem vnius ad alterum. Nam medicina dicitur sana, quia est causa sanitatis animalis: sed idem sanum dicitur analogicè respectu vrinę, & medicinę, nõ quia vnũ horum habeat attributionem ad alterum, sed quia vtrumque dicitur tale per attributionem ad tertium, nempe ad animal, vrina quidem tanquam signum sanitatis eius, medicina verò tanquam causa.

77 In order, then, that this may be proved efficaciously, the doctrine of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5, must be noted, where, speaking of analogous terms, he says: An analogous name signifies in two ways: the attribution of one to another, or of many to one. And he gives an example of each in healthy, which is analogous by attribution with respect to medicine and animal through the attribution of one to the other: for medicine is called healthy because it is the cause of the animal’s health. But the same healthy is said analogically with respect to urine and medicine, not because one of these has attribution to the other, but because each is called such through attribution to a third, namely to the animal: urine as the sign of its health, medicine as the cause.

Ex hac doctrina applicata ad propositum colligi potest argumentum efficax, ad probandum accidens esse analogum. Nam vterque modus attributionis, nempe vnius ad alterum, vel multorum ad vnum, efficit nomen analogum: sed in accidentibus reperitur secundus modus attributionis: ergo accidens erit

From this doctrine, applied to our purpose, an efficacious argument can be gathered for proving that accident is analogous. For each mode of attribution, namely of one to another or of many to one, makes a name analogous; but in accidents the second mode of attribution is found; therefore accident will be

p. 243

analogũ attributionis, respectu eorũ, sicut sanũ respectu vrinę & medicinæ. Probatur consequentia, quia omnia accidentia significantur cũ intrinseca attributione ad substantiã. Sed contra hoc sic arg. Nam in primis videtur nõ bene colligi argum. ex doctrina D. Th. neq; habere vllã vim ad probandũ analogiã accidentis, quia D. Th. vtrũque illum modum attributionis assignat: inter significata eiusdẽ nominis, sani, nẽpe animal vrinam, & medicinã. Et ita significari necessarium est, vt probat hoc arg. Analogia solùm reperitur inter significata eiusdẽ nominis analogi, & nõ inter significata diuersorum nominũ, vt ex definitione cõstat: Analogia sunt, quorũ nomen est cõmune, &c. Sed nomine accidentis non significatur substãtia, sed solo accidentia: ergo attributio inter hæc versari debet, vt efficiat nomen accidentis analogum, ita vt attributio sit vnius ad alterũ, vel multorũ ad vnũ per tale nomen significatũ, & nõ sufficit esse inter illa, & substantiam, nõ significatam eodem nomine.

analogous by attribution with respect to them, just as healthy is with respect to urine and medicine. The consequence is proved: because all accidents are signified with an intrinsic attribution to substance. But against this one argues thus. For in the first place it seems that the argument is not well gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, nor to have any force for proving the analogy of accident: because St. Thomas assigns each of those modes of attribution among the significates of the same name, healthy, namely animal, urine, and medicine. And it is necessary that they be so signified, as this argument proves: analogy is found only among the significates of the same analogous name, and not among the significates of different names, as is clear from the definition: Analogous are those whose name is common, etc. But by the name of accident substance is not signified, but only accidents; therefore the attribution must obtain among these, in order that it make the name of accident analogous, so that the attribution be of one to another, or of many to one, signified by such a name; and it does not suffice that it be between them and substance, which is not signified by the same name.

78 Quod confirmari potest, & declarari simul: nam attributio accidentium ad substantiam, facit quidem, analogiam attributionis multorum ad vnum in ente, à quo significantur omnia, sed non potest facere analogiam in accidente, à quo nõ significantur omnia, sicut non facit analogiam in nomine, substantia, licèt sit vnũ analogatũ entis cum accidentibus: & ob id solùm attribuatur ei accidẽtia, quòd nomine substantiæ nõ significantur: Nam ergo videtur hac via, efficaciter probari, quòd accidẽs sit analogum. Probatur minor: quia ex eo quòd accidentia attribuantur substantiæ, solùm sequitur, quòd non sint entia simpliciter, non verò, quòd non sint accidentia simpliciter: ergo talis attributio ad substantiam facit analogiam in ente, à quo significantur omnia, non in accidenti. Probatur consequentia, quia necessarium est in omnibus analogis, vnum esse tale simpliciter, aliud, vel alia secundùm quid.

78 This can be confirmed and declared at the same time: for the attribution of accidents to substance does indeed make an analogy of attribution of many to one in being, by which all are signified; but it cannot make an analogy in accident, by which not all are signified; just as it does not make an analogy in the name of substance, although substance is one analogate of being together with accidents; and for this reason accidents are attributed to it only because they are not signified by the name of substance. It does not seem, then, that it is efficaciously proved in this way that accident is analogous. The minor is proved: because from the fact that accidents are attributed to substance it follows only that they are not beings simply, but not that they are not accidents simply; therefore such attribution to substance makes an analogy in being, by which all are signified, not in accident. The consequence is proved: because it is necessary in all analogous terms that one be such simply, and the other or others in a certain respect.

His tamen non obstantibus, expressa mens D. Thom. est, sufficere talem attributionem ad analogiam, quia non possunt distingui duo illi modi attributionis vnius ad alterum, & multorum ad vnum, vt eos distinguit D. Thom. nisi duobus etiam modis accipiatur, sanum, in quo vtrumque contineri affirmat. Primò quidem respectu solius medicinæ, & vrinæ, deinde respectu solius medicinæ, & animalis: nam si respectu omnium sumatur, necesse est plura attribui eidem: ergo nõ habebit locum attributio secunda, quæ est vnius ad alterum. Probatur consequentia: quia impossibile est, sumere ens in ordine ad decem prædicamenta: & cõstituere in eo attributionem vnius ad alterum, sed solùm est multorum ad vnum: quia

These things notwithstanding, the express mind of St. Thomas is that such attribution suffices for analogy: because those two modes of attribution, of one to another and of many to one, cannot be distinguished as St. Thomas distinguishes them unless healthy, in which he affirms that both are contained, is also taken in two ways: first with respect to medicine and urine alone, then with respect to medicine and animal alone. For if it is taken with respect to all, it is necessary that several be attributed to the same thing; therefore the second attribution, which is of one to another, will have no place. The consequence is proved: because it is impossible to take being in order to the ten categories and to constitute in it the attribution of one to another; rather it is only of many to one: because Q ij

p. 244

attributio vnius ad alterum, inter duo tantum potest reperiri, non inter multa, nisi omnia sumantur pro vno: ergo impossibile est constituere in sano, attributionem vnius ad alterum, hoc est, medicinæ ad animal, nisi sumendo illud, prout solùm significat hæc duo, & ex consequenti constituitur alius modus attributionis distinctus, qui est multorum ad vnum, accipiẽdo idem nomẽ prout ea tantũ significat, quæ attribuuntur tertio.

the attribution of one to another can be found only between two, not among many, unless all are taken for one; therefore it is impossible to constitute in healthy the attribution of one to another, that is, of medicine to animal, except by taking it as it signifies only these two; and consequently another, distinct mode of attribution is constituted, which is of many to one, by taking the same name as it signifies only those things which are attributed to a third.

79 Sed ratione probatur, sufficere talem attributionem multorum ad vnum, etiam si illud vnum non significetur per idem nomen, quia quando attributio multorum ad vnum intrinseca est eis, vt per tale nomen significantur, vera est attributio & per nomen significata, licèt non significetur per nomen illud vnum, ad quod est attributio, non minùs, quàm si per nomen significaretur: ergo non minùs sufficit nomen analogum. Probatur consequentia ex definitione analogorum: quia tale nomen significat plura in quantum habent attributionem: ergo est analogum: deinde quia attributio significata per nomen, vera est analogia: & ea quæ cum tali attributione significantur, vera analogata, impertinens igitur est, per nomen significari illud, respectu cuius est attributio.

79 But it is proved by argument that such attribution of many to one suffices, even if that one is not signified by the same name: because when the attribution of many to one is intrinsic to them, so that they are signified by such a name, the attribution is true and signified by the name, although that one to which the attribution is made is not signified by the name, no less than if it were signified by the name; therefore it no less suffices for an analogous name. The consequence is proved from the definition of analogous terms: because such a name signifies several things inasmuch as they have attribution; therefore it is analogous. Then because the attribution signified by the name is true analogy, and the things which are signified with such attribution are true analogates; it is irrelevant, therefore, that that with respect to which the attribution is made be signified by the name.

80 Ad obiectionem principalem propositam respondetur, negando imprimis, quòd hæc analogia non sit ex mente D. Th. deinde negando etiam, quòd vtrumque modum attributionis vnius ad alterum, & multorum ad vnum, ponat D. Th. inter ea tantùm, quæ significantur eodem nomine. Nam expressè asserit, sanum respectu vrinæ, & medicinæ, esse analogum attributionis multorum ad vnum: sed respectu medicinę, & animalis, attributionis vnius ad alterum, ergo non sumit sanum vt significat omnia. Nec id reputat necessarium, sed vt significat minùs principalia cum attributione ad principale, etiam non significatum. Probatur consequentia: quia si illud accipiat secundùm integram significationem omniũ, non potest vtrumque modum attributionis distinguere; quia attributio vnius ad alterum, non est nisi inter duo. Præterea D. Tho. expresè docet, quemlibet modum attributionis, per se facere analogiam, sed modus attributionis multorum ad vnum, reperitur in analogatis, etiamsi illud vnum non significetur per nomen, vt iam probaui: ergo sufficit nomen analogum facere.

80 To the principal objection proposed, it is replied by denying, first, that this analogy is not according to the mind of St. Thomas; and then by denying also that St. Thomas places each mode of attribution, of one to another and of many to one, only among those things which are signified by the same name. For he expressly asserts that healthy, with respect to urine and medicine, is analogous by attribution of many to one; but with respect to medicine and animal, by attribution of one to another; therefore he does not take healthy as it signifies all. Nor does he consider this necessary, but takes it as it signifies the less principal things with attribution to the principal, even when the latter is not signified. The consequence is proved: because if he took it according to the entire signification of all, he could not distinguish each mode of attribution, since the attribution of one to another is only between two. Moreover, St. Thomas expressly teaches that any mode of attribution makes analogy per se; but the mode of attribution of many to one is found in the analogates even if that one is not signified by the name, as I have already proved; therefore it suffices to make an analogous name.

Ad arg. verò distinguendum est antecedens: quia modus attributionis, efficiens nomen analogum, duplex est, vt asserit D. Th. vel vnius ad alterum, & secundùm hunc modum attributionis non potest esse analogia, nisi vtrumque significetur eodem nomine: vel multorum ad vnum, & modus iste, reperitur

But to the argument, the antecedent must be distinguished: because the mode of attribution that makes a name analogous is twofold, as St. Thomas asserts: either of one to another, and according to this mode of attribution there cannot be analogy unless both are signified by the same name; or of many to one, and this mode is indeed found

p. 245

quidem inter significata eiusdem nominis, sed quia est ordine ad tertium, vtroque modo contingit, nempe ad tertium significatum eodem nomine, vel diuerso. Et ratio huius est: quia cùm ea quæ attribuuntur alteri, sint multa, potest talis attributio adæquatè, atque completè significari per nomen commune omnium, vel quasi inadæquatè, & partialiter, quod est, quasi diuidi in totalem, & partialem. Et ita est in sano, atque etiam in ente, & accidente: nam sanum potest accipi in sua integra significatione, & tunc efficit completam analogiam: vel potest coarctari ad sola analogata minùs principalia: & efficit quasi incompletam, aut partialem, sed sufficientem: quia cùm attributio ad principale, sit eis intrinseca, non possunt sine illa significari, significata autem cum attributione non possunt, nisi analogicè significari. Probatur efficaciter: quia vniuocis repugnat significari cum attributione ad principale analogatum, cum quo apta sunt, analogiam facere: ergo analogata sunt, siue eodẽ nomine significetur principale, siue diuerso, analogia quidẽ quasi inadæquata, & partiali: cùm tamẽ ex modo, quo significantur, apta sint efficere analogiã completam, sub nomine vniuersaliori, quo significãtur omnia, & hoc modo intelligenda est analogia accidẽtis. Secundò possemus etiam respõdere, aliquo modo significari substantiã nomine accidẽtis, nõ in recto, sed in obliquo, quia accidens idem est ac entis ens, vt dixit Arist. id est, ens substantiæ: sufficit autem ita significari, vt attributio accidentiũ ad substantiam aliquo modo dicatur esse inter significata eiusdẽ nominis analogi: atque etiã vt aliquo modo nomẽ accidẽtis sit cõmune accidentibus, & substantiæ.

among the significates of the same name; but because it is in order to a third, it happens in either way, namely to a third signified by the same name or by a different one. And the reason for this is: because, since the things that are attributed to another are many, such attribution can be signified adequately and completely by the name common to all, or as it were inadequately and partially, which is as it were to be divided into total and partial. And so it is in healthy, and also in being and accident: for healthy can be taken in its entire signification, and then it makes a complete analogy; or it can be restricted to the less principal analogates alone, and it makes an analogy as it were incomplete or partial, but sufficient: because, since the attribution to the principal is intrinsic to them, they cannot be signified without it; and being signified with attribution, they cannot be signified except analogically. This is proved efficaciously: because it is repugnant to univocal terms to be signified with attribution to a principal analogate, with which they are apt to make an analogy; therefore they are analogates, whether the principal is signified by the same name or by a different one: an analogy indeed as it were inadequate and partial, but since, from the mode in which they are signified, they are apt to make a complete analogy under a more universal name by which all are signified. And in this way the analogy of accident is to be understood. Second, we could also reply that substance is in some way signified by the name of accident, not in recto but in obliquo, because accident is the same as being of a being, as Aristotle said, that is, being of substance; and it suffices that it be so signified in order that the attribution of accidents to substance may in some way be said to be among the significates of the same analogous name, and also in order that the name of accident may in some way be common to accidents and substance.

81 Nec contrarium est hoc definitioni analogiæ, quæ dicitur nomen analogum commune esse analogatis: nam commune est nomen his, quibus conuenit attributio, licèt non sit commune ei, ad quod habent attributionem: quia hoc non est analogatum talis nominis, sed illa tantùm.

81 Nor is this contrary to the definition of analogy, which says that the analogous name is common to the analogates: for the name is common to those to which the attribution belongs, although it is not common to that to which they have attribution, because this is not an analogate of such a name, but those only.

Ad confirmationem negandum est antecedens, quòd attributio accidentium ad substantiam, solùm efficiat analogiam in ente, & non in accidente, sed dicendum in vtroque eam efficere, quia per vtrumque nomen significatur: sed in ente efficit quasi completam, & totalem, in accidente verò incompletam, & partialem. quia intrinsecè præsupponit illam & intrinsecè ab ea dependet. In nomine autem substantiæ, non fit analogia: quia nec substantia habet attributionem ad accidentia, nec etiam si haberet eam, significaretur eo nomine, vt superius probatum est.

To the confirmation, the antecedent must be denied, that the attribution of accidents to substance makes an analogy only in being and not in accident; rather it must be said that it makes it in both, because it is signified by both names; but in being it makes one as it were complete and total, in accident one incomplete and partial, because it intrinsically presupposes substance and intrinsically depends on it. But in the name of substance there is no analogy, because substance neither has attribution to accidents, nor, even if it had it, would it be signified by that name, as was proved above.

82 Aliud tandem quod in eadem confirmatione dicitur,

82 The other thing, finally, which is said in the same confirmation, that the attribution Q iij

p. 246

attributionem accidentium ad substantiam solùm efficere, quòd sint entia secundùm quid, non verò quòd sint accidentia secũdùm quid, concedendum est, neganda tamen consequentia, quòd non efficiat analogiam sub nomine accidentis. Nam ad analogiam attributionis non requiritur necessariò, quòd analogata, vel aliquod eorum sit tale secundùm quid, sub particulari nomine, quo ea tantùm significantur, sed sufficit, quòd sint talia secundùm quid respectu eius, ad quod attribuantur: nam ex hoc habetur esse analogata cum eo, sub nomine vniuersaliori, completa & totali analogia, & consequenter analogia incompleta, ac dependenti sub particulari nomine, quo significantur, sub quo non est necessarium, dici talia secundùm quid. Sed illud esse secundùm quid, quod habent ex propria natura, dicitur de eis simpliciter, vt significantur particulari nomine, & ideo sub eo dicuntur talia secundùm quid simpliciter (vt sic loquamur) Et hoc patet in accidentibus: nam dici accidentia simpliciter secundùm quid, non est aliud, quàm dici simpliciter entia secundùm quid, quod etiam de sano dicetur respectu solius medicinæ, & vrinæ. Imò ex hoc satis clarè intelligitur, vtroque nomine analogicè significari, cùm vtroque nomine significentur cum attributione, & propter eandem attributionem, cum qua significantur, fit vt sub vtroque nomine significata, dicantur talia secundùm quid formaliter, vel præsuppositiuè, præsuppositione eis intrinseca, quæ omnia vniuocis repugnant. Et si tandem obiiciatur, Omnes potentias ordinari ad obiectum: & hoc non sufficere vt potentia in communi, sit analogum ad illas; Respondeo, non dicere ordinem attributionis, sicut accidentia ad substantiam, sed specificationis tantùm, & ideo non esse analogata.

of accidents to substance brings about only that they are beings in a certain respect, but not that they are accidents in a certain respect, must be granted; but the consequence must be denied, that it does not make an analogy under the name of accident. For analogy of attribution does not necessarily require that the analogates, or some one of them, be such in a certain respect under the particular name by which they alone are signified; but it suffices that they be such in a certain respect with respect to that to which they are attributed: for from this it follows that they are analogates together with it under a more universal name, with a complete and total analogy, and consequently with an incomplete and dependent analogy under the particular name by which they are signified, under which it is not necessary that they be called such in a certain respect. But that being in a certain respect which they have from their own nature is said of them simply, as they are signified by the particular name, and therefore under it they are called such in a certain respect simply (if we may speak so). And this is plain in accidents: for to be called accidents simply in a certain respect is nothing other than to be called simply beings in a certain respect, which will also be said of healthy with respect to medicine and urine alone. Indeed, from this it is quite clearly understood that they are signified analogically by both names, since they are signified by both names with attribution, and on account of that same attribution with which they are signified it comes about that, signified under both names, they are called such in a certain respect, formally or presuppositively, by a presupposition intrinsic to them; all of which are repugnant to univocal terms. And if it is finally objected that all powers are ordered to their object, and that this does not suffice for power in common to be analogous to them, I reply that this does not express an order of attribution, as accidents have to substance, but only of specification, and therefore they are not analogates.

An necesse sit accidens esse genus, si sit vniuocum — Whether accident must be a genus, if it is univocal.

84 Multi ex his, qui tenent accidens esse vniuocum, negant esse genus, vt Iauellus, & Sotus vbi supra, sed nõ assignant eandem rationem. Nam Iauell. ait, ideo non esse genus, quia non est extra rationem differentiarum & modorum: sed cùm transcendens sit, in eis necessariò includitur, at hoc est cõtra rationem generis, quod, vt supra probauimus, debet esse extra rationem differentiarum, alioqui non poterit per eas cõtrahi.

84 Many of those who hold that accident is univocal deny that it is a genus, as Javelli and Soto in the places cited above; but they do not assign the same reason. For Javelli says that it is not a genus because it is not outside the ratio of the differences and modes; but since it is transcendental, it is necessarily included in them; and this is against the ratio of genus, which, as we proved above, must be outside the ratio of the differences; otherwise it could not be contracted by them.

85 Hæc tamen ratio insufficiens est, quia, vt superiùs probauimus, non potest accidens includi in modis intrinsecis, & vltimis differentiis, quin eas etiam in se includat actu, licèt cõfuso, cùm sint entitates quædam accidentales: sed eas includẽs non potest habere conspectum ab eis abstractum, vt constat:

85 This argument, however, is insufficient, because, as we proved above, accident cannot be included in the intrinsic modes and ultimate differences without also including them in itself in act, although confusedly, since they are certain accidental entities; but including them it cannot have a concept abstracted from them, as is clear:

p. 247

ergo neque vniuocum. Probatur consequentia, quia talis conceptus non abstrahit à diuersitate, sed eam includit, ergo non est vniuocus, si non sit genus.

therefore neither is it univocal. The consequence is proved: because such a concept does not abstract from diversity but includes it; therefore it is not univocal, if it is not a genus.

Secunda opinio est Soti asserentis, Ideo accidens non est genus, licèt sit vniuocum, quia genus pertinet ad quidditatem specierum: sed accidens non significat quidditatem accidentium, sed esse eorum in substantia, ergo non est genus. Hoc autem probatur falsum duplici ratione. Prima, quia non minùs pertinet ad rationem vniuoci, esse de quidditate inferiorum quàm ad rationem generis, si ergo accidens ideò non est genus, quia non dicit quidditatem accidentium, sequitur eadem ratione non esse vniuocum. Probatur maior ex definitione vniuocorum. Vniuoca enim sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ eadem. Per rationem autem substantiæ intelligit Aristoteles & omnes, & definitionem, vel conceptum quidditatiuum, in his quæ definitione carent, ergo repugnat aliquid esse vniuocum, & non esse de quidditate inferiorum.

The second opinion is that of Soto, who asserts that accident is not a genus, although it is univocal, because genus pertains to the quiddity of the species; but accident does not signify the quiddity of accidents, but their being in substance; therefore it is not a genus. But this is proved false by a twofold argument. The first, because it pertains no less to the ratio of the univocal than to the ratio of genus to be of the quiddity of the inferiors; if, then, accident is not a genus because it does not express the quiddity of accidents, it follows by the same argument that it is not univocal. The major is proved from the definition of univocal terms: For univocal are those whose name is common, and the ratio of substance the same. But by the ratio of substance Aristotle and everyone understand the definition, or the quidditative concept in those things that lack a definition; therefore it is repugnant that something be univocal and not be of the quiddity of the inferiors.

Secunda, quia falsum est, quòd accidens non dicat quidditatem accidentium, quod sic probo: Ens pertinet ad quidditatem entium particularium, & diuiditur, vt tale, in substantiam, & accidens, tanquam in membra opposita, & adæquata rationi eius: sed substantia dicit quidditatem substantiarum inferiorum, ergo accidens quidditatem inferiorum accidentium.

The second, because it is false that accident does not express the quiddity of accidents, which I prove thus: being pertains to the quiddity of particular beings, and is divided, as such, into substance and accident, as into opposed members adequate to its ratio; but substance expresses the quiddity of the inferior substances; therefore accident expresses the quiddity of the inferior accidents.

Nostra igitur sententia est, Non posse accidens esse vniuocum, quin eo ipso sit genus omnium accidentium, vnde qui asserit vniuocum esse, consequenter dicere debet esse genus. Probatur, quia nulla potest assignari ratio sufficiens excludendi vniuocum à ratione generis, vt probatum est ex refutatione aliarum opinionum.

Our view, then, is that accident cannot be univocal without by that very fact being the genus of all accidents; whence whoever asserts that it is univocal must consequently say that it is a genus. This is proved: because no sufficient reason can be assigned for excluding the univocal from the ratio of genus, as has been proved from the refutation of the other opinions.

An saltem respectu aliquorum accidentium, aut prædicamentorum, possit esse accidens vniuocum — Whether at least with respect to some accidents, or categories, accident can be univocal.

56 Prima opinio tenet, Accidens respectu aliquorum accidentium, vt quantitatis, & qualitatis, an etiam cæterorum intrinsecorum, esse vniuocum. Ita Pater Franciscus Suarius in Met. disp. 39. sect. 3 num. 15. & probat hoc arg. Accidens respectu horum non est analogum proportionalitatis, nec attributionis: ergo nullam habet analogiam, sed est vniuocum. Euidens est consequentia, quia nullus ponit plures modos analogiæ. Sed probatur antecedens, quia analoga proportionalitatis nullam habent conuenientiam intrinsecam, vt patet de risu hominis, & prati: sed accidentia hæc, habent conuenientiam

56 The first opinion holds that accident with respect to some accidents, such as quantity and quality, and perhaps also the other intrinsic ones, is univocal. So Father Francisco Suárez in Metaph., disp. 39, sect. 3, no. 15; and he proves it by this argument: accident with respect to these is not analogous by proportionality nor by attribution; therefore it has no analogy, but is univocal. The consequence is evident, because no one posits more modes of analogy. But the antecedent is proved: because analogous terms of proportionality have no intrinsic agreement, as is plain in the laughter of a man and of a meadow; but these accidents have an agreement Q iiij

p. 248

intrinsecam cùm omnia inhæreant realiter subiecto: ergo non potest esse analogum proportionalitatis accidens respectu eorum. De analogia verò attributionis probat, quia nullum accidens horum dicitur tale, per attributionem ad alterum, vt satis est manifestum: ergo accidens respectu eorum non est analogum attributionis.

that is intrinsic, since all of them really inhere in the subject; therefore accident cannot be analogous by proportionality with respect to them. And concerning analogy of attribution he proves it because none of these accidents is called such through attribution to another, as is quite manifest; therefore accident with respect to them is not analogous by attribution.

87 Nostra tamen sententia opposita est, quòd nec respectu horum accidentium possit accidens esse vniuocum, sed analogum. Probatur duplici ratione. Prima, quia sicut accidens respectu omnium accidentium, non potest abstrahi à modis intrinsecis eorum: ita nec respectu accidentium intrinsecorum, potest abstrahi à modis eorum, ergo sicut non est vniuocum, sed analogum respectu omnium, ita nec respectu horum. Probatur antecedens, quia ideo respectu omnium non potest abstrahi à modis, quia modi non sunt aliud quàm entitates quædam accidentales, expressiùs significatæ, & propterea necesse est, vt sub significatione vniuersali accidentis, actu, licèt confuso, comprehendantur. Quo supposito, conceptus accidentis nec abstractus, neque vnus esse potest, sed eodem modo se habet ad intrinseca, si cum illis solis comparetur, vt ex se patet: ergo nec respectu eorum potest esse vniuocum.

87 Our view, however, is the opposite: that not even with respect to these accidents can accident be univocal, but it is analogous. This is proved by a twofold argument. The first, because just as accident with respect to all accidents cannot be abstracted from their intrinsic modes, so neither with respect to the intrinsic accidents can it be abstracted from their modes; therefore, just as it is not univocal but analogous with respect to all, so too with respect to these. The antecedent is proved: because the reason why with respect to all it cannot be abstracted from the modes is that the modes are nothing other than certain accidental entities, signified more expressly, and therefore it is necessary that they be comprehended in act, although confusedly, under the universal signification of accident. This supposed, the concept of accident can be neither abstracted nor one, but is related in the same way to the intrinsic accidents, if it is compared with them alone, as is plain of itself; therefore neither with respect to them can it be univocal.

88 Quòd verò sit analogum, eadem ratione probatur, qua probauimus esse analogum respectu omnium, quia intrinseca accidentia, significant cum attributione ad substantiam, sicut sanum, si respectu sanorum extrinsecorum, quæ sunt vrina, & medicina, solùm accipiatur, ergo continet modum attributionis multorum ad vnum, sufficientem ad efficiendum nomen analogum, vt probandum est.

88 That it is analogous is proved by the same argument by which we proved that it is analogous with respect to all: because the intrinsic accidents are signified with attribution to substance, just as healthy is, if it is taken only with respect to the extrinsic healthy things, which are urine and medicine; therefore it contains the mode of attribution of many to one, sufficient to make a name analogous, as has been proved.

Ad argumentum alterius sententiæ, negandum est antecedens, quòd accidens respectu intrinsecorum non sit analogum attributionis quia licèt nõ significet ea cũ modo attributionis vnius ad alterum, benè tamen cum attributione multorum ad vnum, nempe ad substantiam, cuius aliquid sunt, & vt aliquid eius significantur vt de accidenti respectu omnium diximus.

To the argument of the other opinion, the antecedent must be denied, that accident with respect to the intrinsic ones is not analogous by attribution. Because although it does not signify them with the mode of attribution of one to another, it does signify them with the attribution of many to one, namely to substance, of which they are something, and they are signified as something of it, as we said of accident with respect to all.

Ex quibus sequitur, qua analogia accidens sit analogum, tam respectu omnium accidentium, quàm solùm respectu intrinsecorum, nempe analogia attributionis multorum ad vnum.

From which it follows by what analogy accident is analogous, both with respect to all accidents and with respect to the intrinsic ones alone: namely, by the analogy of attribution of many to one.

An verò respectu accidentium completorum vniuocum esse possit, vel etiam sit analogum, eodem modo respondendum est, & eisdem rationibus probandum, quòd non sit vniuocum, sed analogum, quibus probatum est de ente in ordine ad sola entia incompleta. Et hæc sint satis de analogia nominum.

But whether with respect to complete accidents it can be univocal, or rather is analogous, must be answered in the same way, and it must be proved that it is not univocal but analogous by the same arguments by which it was proved of being in order to incomplete beings alone. And let these things suffice concerning the analogy of names. Are.

p. 249

CHAPTER II

CAP. II. De diuisione eorum quæ dicuntur, & sunt, cum exposit. tex. — On the division of the things that are said and that are.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Eorum quæ sunt, alia de subiecto aliquo dicuntur, in subiecto verò nullo sunt, &c.

Of the things that are, some are said of some subject, but are in no subject, etc.

Textus expositio.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 Intentum Aristotelis est tradere duas diuisiones, vnam eorum quæ dicuntur, aliam, eorum quæ sunt, in hoc tantùm agit in toto capite, quod ideo non eget diuisione.

he intent of Aristotle is to hand down two divisions, one of the 1 T things that are said, the other of the things that are; in this alone he is occupied in the whole chapter, which therefore does not need division.

Prima diuisio non est rerum, sed vocum, vt significant res, quia complexio non conuenit rebus, sed vocibus, vt eas significant. Asserit ergo Arist. Ea quæ dicuntur: quædam cum complexione, alia sine complexione dicuntur. quasi dicat, voces quæ significant res alias esse complexas, vt homo albus, alias, incomplexas, vt color, aut animal. Quod idem est, ac si dicatur: quasdam esse simplices, alias compositas.

The first division is not of things but of words, as they signify things, because combination does not belong to things but to words, as they signify them. Aristotle therefore asserts: Of the things that are said, some are said with combination, others without combination; as if to say that of the words which signify things, some are complex, as white man, others incomplex, as color or animal. Which is the same as if it were said that some are simple, others composite.

Secunda diuisio rerum est. Sed vt intelligatur, notari debet, quòd Esse in subiecto, & dici de subiecto, particulari quodam modo sumuntur ab Arist. in hoc capite. Nam esse in subiecto, sumit pro vera, & reali inhærentia in eo, & dici de subiecto, tanquam de quidditatiuè inferiori, vt animal de homine, & homo de Petro.

The second division is of things. But in order that it may be understood, it should be noted that to be in a subject and to be said of a subject are taken by Aristotle in this chapter in a particular way. For to be in a subject is taken for true and real inherence in it; and to be said of a subject, as of a quidditatively inferior thing, as animal of man and man of Peter.

Hoc supposito, diuisio talis est: Eorum quæ sunt, quædam de subiecto dicuntur, & in subiecto non sunt, vt homo, qui dicitur de Petro, non est tamen in eo per realem inhærentiam, sed substantialiter, ideò non vt in subiecto. Alia in subiecto sunt, sed de nullo subiecto dicuntur, vt accidentia singularia: nam hæc albedo in pariete inhæret, sed de nullo subiecto dicitur, quia non habet inferiora quidditatiuè, de quibus prædicari possit, licèt accidentaliter dicatur de pariete, & aliis corporibus. Alia de subiecto dicuntur, & in subiecto sunt, vt accidentia abstracta à suis inferioribus, nempe genus à speciebus, & species ab indiuiduis, color enim de albedine, & nigredine dicitur, & in pariete, & homine inhæret. Alia denique sunt, quæ nec sunt in subiecto, nec dicuntur de subiecto, vt singulares substantiæ, Petrus, & Ioannes.

This supposed, the division is as follows: Of the things that are, some are said of a subject and are not in a subject, as man, which is said of Peter, yet is not in him by real inherence but substantially, and therefore not as in a subject. Others are in a subject, but are said of no subject, as singular accidents: for this whiteness inheres in the wall, but is said of no subject, because it does not have quidditatively inferior things of which it could be predicated, although it is said accidentally of the wall and of other bodies. Others are said of a subject and are in a subject, as accidents abstracted from their inferiors, namely the genus from the species and the species from the individuals: for color is said of whiteness and blackness, and inheres in the wall and in man. Others, finally, are neither in a subject nor said of a subject, as singular substances, Peter and John.

p. 250

CHAPTER III

CAP. III. De regulis prædicamentorum essentialium, cum exposit. tex. — On the rules of essential predicates.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Quando alterum de altero prædicatur vt de subiecto, quæcunque de eo, quod prædicatur, dicuntur, omnes etiam de subiecto dicuntur.

When one thing is predicated of another as of a subject, whatever things are said of that which is predicated will all be said of the subject too.

Textus expositio.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 Intentum Arist. est tradere duas regulas prædicatorũ essentialium, & hoc tantùm agit in toto ca Prima regula est, Quando aliquid prædicatur de aliquo tanquam de subiecto, hoc est, tanquam de quidditatiuè inferiori quæcunque dicuntur de prædicato, necesse est prædicari de subiecto. Ita se habent quæcunque prædicata, posita in recta linea prædicamentali, vt animal prædicatur de homine, & leone, ideo quæcunque prædicantur de animali, necesse est prædicari de homine.

he intent of Aristotle is to hand down two rules of essential predicates, 1 T and in this alone he is occupied in that whole chapter. The first rule is: When something is predicated of something as of a subject, that is, as of a quidditatively inferior thing, whatever things are said of the predicate must be predicated of the subject. So it is with whatever predicates are placed in the categorial straight line: as animal is predicated of man and lion, and therefore whatever things are predicated of animal must be predicated of man.

Secunda regula obscurior est, & sic habetur in translatione Boëtij: Diuersorum generum, & non subalternatim positorum, diuersæ sunt specie differentiæ, vt animalis, & scientiæ, Si verò subalternatim ponantur, easdem differentias habere possunt. Vt animal, & viuens, eandem habent differentiam, quia differentiæ viuentis includuntur in animali.

The second rule is more obscure, and runs thus in the translation of Boethius: Of diverse genera, and not placed subalternately, the differences are diverse in species, as of animal and of science. But if they are placed subalternately, they can have the same differences: as animal and living have the same difference, because the differences of living are included in animal.

SINGLE QUESTION

An genera non subalternatim posita, possint habere aliquam differentiam communem.

Whether genera not placed subalternately can have some common difference.

2 Duas habet partes quæstio hæc. Prima quærit, quid intelligat Arist. per genera subalternatim posita, & non subalternatim posita. Secunda, an possint habere aliquam differentiam communem.

2 This question has two parts. The first asks what Aristotle understands by genera placed subalternately, and not placed subalternately. The second, whether they can have some common difference.

Prima pars quæstionis.

First Part of the Question.

Circa primam partem duæ sunt opiniones. Prima asserit genera subalternatim posita ea solùm esse, quorum vnum collocatur sub altero, vt animal, & viuens: & non subalternatim posita ea, quorum vnum non est sub altero, sed ambo sunt sub tertio, vt animal, & planta: vel etiam, quę nec vnum sub altero, nec ambo sub tertio, vt sunt ea, quæ in diuersis prædicamentis collocantur, qualia sunt animal, & scientia. Ita Sotus in expositione huius regulæ.

On the first part there are two opinions. The first asserts that genera placed subalternately are only those of which one is placed under the other, as animal and living; and not placed subalternately those of which one is not under the other, but both are under a third, as animal and plant; or also those of which neither is one under the other nor both under a third, as are those that are placed in different categories, such as animal and science. So Soto in his exposition of this rule.

Probat duobus testimonium Arist. Primum est in hoc cap. vbi secundùm translationem Argyropyli vocantur genera sub

He proves it by two testimonies of Aristotle. The first is in this chapter, where, according to the translation of Argyropoulos, those are called genera subalternately

p. 251

alternatim posita ea, quorum vnum est sub altero: & non subalternatim posita, quorum vnum non est sub altero. Alterum testimonium, habetur 1 lib. Topic. cap. 13. vbi genera subalternata vocat Aristotel. subalternatim posita: sed genera subalternata sunt, quorum vnum est sub altero: ergo non subalternatim posita erunt illa, quorum vnum non est sub altero, licèt vtrumque sit sub tertio.

placed of which one is under the other, and not placed subalternately those of which one is not under the other. The other testimony is found in Topics 1, ch. 15, where Aristotle calls subalternate genera genera placed subalternately; but subalternate genera are those of which one is under the other; therefore not placed subalternately were those of which one is not under the other, although both are under a third.

Probat deinde ratione, quia si per genera subalternatim posita non solùm intelliguntur ea, quorum vnum non est sub altero, sed etiam illa, quæ sunt sub tertio, sequitur, genera non subalternatim posita, ea solùm esse, quæ in diuersis prædicamentis sunt, de quibus euidens est, non posse habere differentiam communem, cùm sint in diuerso gradu essendi: quare nihil difficultatis habere regula hæc. Quam tamen difficilem efficiunt omnes interpretes.

He proves it next by reason: because if by genera placed subalternately are understood not only those of which one is under the other, but also those which are under a third, it follows that genera not placed subalternately are only those which are in different categories, of which it is evident that they cannot have a common difference, since they are in a different grade of being; so that this rule would have no difficulty. Which nevertheless all the interpreters make difficult.

3 Nostra sententia est, Per genera non subalternatim posita, intelligi non solùm ea, quorum vnum non est sub altero: sed etiã quæ sunt sub tertio. Et ideò non subabternatim posita, ea solùm esse, quæ in diuersis prædicamentis sunt.

3 Our view is that by genera placed subalternately are understood not only those of which one is under the other, but also those which are under a third; and therefore that those not placed subalternately are only those which are in different categories.

Probatur expresso testimonio Arist. 6. lib. Topic. cap. 2. loco 41. vbi duo asserit. Primum; Genera subalterna non solùm appellari ea, quorum vnum est sub altero: sed etiam quæ sunt sub tertio. Secundum: Genera illa quæ sunt sub tertio, habere differentiam communem: vt animal gressibile, & animal volatile, habent bipedem pro differentia communi. Ex quo sequitur, quòd vel non dicantur non subalternatim posita, vel falsa sit regula Aristotelis, quòd genera non subalternatim posita, non possint habere differentiam communem.

This is proved by an express testimony of Aristotle, Topics 6, ch. 2, locus 41, where he asserts two things. The first: That not only are those called subalternate genera of which one is under the other, but also those which are under a third. The second: That those genera which are under a third have a common difference: as walking animal and flying animal have biped as a common difference. From which it follows that either they are not called not placed subalternately, or Aristotle’s rule is false, that genera not placed subalternately cannot have a common difference.

Deinde probatur ratione. Primò, quia genera non subalternatim posita, ex Arist. non possunt habere differentiam communem: sed ea quorum vnum non est sub altero: sed ambo sub tertio, habent differentiam communem: ergo non dicuntur non subalternatim posita ab Aristotele. Probatur minor: quia quantitas diuiditur in successiuam, & permanentem, tanquam in duo genera, quorum vnum non est sub altero, & habent differentiam communem: nam differentia continui, communis cum vtrique atque etiam differentia discreti, si quidem tam quantitas permanens, quàm successiua diuiditur in continuam & discretam.

It is proved next by reason. First, because genera not placed subalternately, according to Aristotle, cannot have a common difference; but those of which one is not under the other, but both under a third, have a common difference; therefore they are not called not placed subalternately by Aristotle. The minor is proved: because quantity is divided into successive and permanent, as into two genera of which one is not under the other, and they have a common difference: for the difference of the continuous is common to both, and also the difference of the discrete, since both permanent and successive quantity are divided into continuous and discrete.

Secundò, quia eadem sunt genera subalterna, & subalternatim posita: sed ea quorũ vtrũq; est sub tertio, sunt subalterna respectu illius: cũ vtrumq; sit sub eo: ergo erunt subalternatim posita.

Second, because subalternate genera and genera placed subalternately are the same; but those of which each is under a third are subalternate with respect to it, since each is under it; therefore they will be placed subalternately.

Ad primum testimonium respondetur, Quòd cùm diuerso

To the first testimony it is replied that, since a different

p. 252

modo habeatur in diuersis translationibus, per illud expressum à nobis citatum, explicari, & intelligi debet. in quo non potest esse dubium, nostram sententiam contineri.

way it is found in different translations, it must be explained and understood through that express passage cited by us, in which there can be no doubt that our view is contained.

Ad aliud testimonium dicimus, genera subalterna, aut subalternatim posita, vtraque comprehendere: nempe ea, quorum vnum est sub altero, & quorum ambo sunt sub tertio.

To the other testimony we say that subalternate genera, or genera placed subalternately, comprehend both: namely, those of which one is under the other, and those of which both are under a third.

Ad arg. Concedendum est antecedens cum consequentia, & dicendum: Quòd regula Aristotelis, quantum ad hanc partem, clarissima est, si per alia testimonia expressa eiusdem intelligatur, eam verò difficilem fecerunt, qui prædicta testimonia non viderunt.

To the argument: the antecedent must be granted together with the consequence, and it must be said that Aristotle’s rule, as far as this part is concerned, is very clear if it is understood through other express testimonies of the same author; but those who did not see the aforesaid testimonies have made it difficult.

Secunda pars quæstionis.

Second Part of the Question. 4

4 Secunda pars quæstionis quærit, An genera non subalternatim posita, possint habere differentiam communem. Quod vt meliùs intelligatur notandum est, duplicem esse differentiam: Constitutiuam, & Diuisiuam, Superiorem etiam, atque Inferiorem: Vt sensibile est constitutiua animalis, & diuisiua viuentis, & corporeum est differentia superior respectu viuentis, sensibile verò inferior respectu eiusdẽ. Intelligitur ergo quæstio de inferiori diuisiua: nam de superioribus non est dubiũ, quin possint esse communes. Circa quam est prima opinio Scoti asserentis, Genera non subalternatim posita, quorum vnum non est sub altero in eodem prædicamento, sed vtrumque sub tertio, non posse habere differentiam communem, & multo minus genera diuersorum prædicamentorum. Quem etiam sequuntur alij, etiam si nobiscum dicant, hæc esse subalternatim posita.

The second part of the question asks whether genera not placed subalternately can have a common difference. In order that this may be better understood, it should be noted that difference is twofold: Constitutive and Divisive; and also Superior and Inferior. As sensible is constitutive of animal and divisive of living; and corporeal is a superior difference with respect to living, but sensible an inferior one with respect to the same. The question, then, is understood of the inferior divisive difference: for concerning the superior ones there is no doubt that they can be common. On this the first opinion is that of Scotus, who asserts that genera not placed subalternately, of which one is not under the other in the same category, but each is under a third, cannot have a common difference, and much less the genera of different categories. Others also follow him, even if they say with us that these are placed subalternately.

Probant duplici testimonio Arist. 1. lib. Topic. c 2. loco 22. vbi affirmat, De pluribus prædicari genus, quàm differentiam. Secundum habetur 1. lib. de partibus animalium, cap. 3. vbi dicit Tot esse differentias, quot sunt species: sed si eadem differentia duobus generibus, quæ sunt sub tertio, communis sit, vtrumque erit falsum: ergo non est admittendum. Probatur minor: nam si eadem differentia diuisiua viuentis, communis est duabus speciebus subalternis, sub eo contentis: cùm de illis prædicetur genus, prædicabitur etiam hæc differentia communis, & ideo non prædicabitur differentia de paciuoribus, quàm genus. Et præterea, in minori numero erunt differentiæ, quàm species: cùm vna differentia sit communis duabus speciebus.

They prove it by a twofold testimony of Aristotle: Topics 1, ch. 2, locus 22, where he affirms that the genus is predicated of more things than the difference. The second is found in On the Parts of Animals 1, ch. 3, where he says that there are as many differences as there are species. But if the same difference is common to two genera which are under a third, each will be false; therefore it is not to be admitted. The minor is proved: for if the same divisive difference of living is common to two subalternate species contained under it, since the genus is predicated of them, this common difference will also be predicated of them, and therefore the difference will not be predicated of fewer things than the genus. And moreover, the differences will be fewer in number than the species, since one difference is common to two species.

Probant deinde ratione: Quia sicut repugnat idem indiuiduum esse sub duplici specie, ita repugnat eandem speciem esse sub duplici genere: sed si eadẽ differentia Diuisiua sit communis duobus generibus, sequitur eandem speciem contineri sub

They prove it next by reason: because just as it is repugnant that the same individual be under two species, so it is repugnant that the same species be under two genera; but if the same Divisive difference is common to two genera, it follows that the same species is contained under

p. 253

duplici genere: ergo impossibile erit. Probatur minor: Quia differentia Diuisiua generis constituit speciem sub eo, vt rationale diuidens animal constituit hominem sub eo: ergo si animal, & planta habent differentiam communem, talis differentia constituet speciem sub vtroque genere, & eadem erit species animalis, & plantæ, quod absurdum est.

two genera; therefore it will be impossible. The minor is proved: because the Divisive difference of a genus constitutes a species under it, as rational, dividing animal, constitutes man under it; therefore if animal and plant have a common difference, such a difference will constitute a species under each genus, and the same species will be of animal and of plant, which is absurd.

Secunda opinio tenet, Genera nõ subalternatim posita, non semper, aut necessariò habere differẽtiam cõmunem: sed aliqua posse eam habere. Et hæc est probabilior & tenenda. Et explicatur duabus conclusionibus. Prima, Genera subalternatim posita, quorum vnum est sub altero, habent omnes differentias Constitutiuas superiorum generum communes, & Diuisiuas, aliquas, non tamen omnes. Exempli gratia: Animal & viuens, habent differentiam Diuisiuam substantiæ communem, vt corporeum, & etiam Constitutiuam corporis: sed neutrum habet differentiam Constitutiuam alterius, quæ Diuisiua est proximi generis. Ita Arist. in vltimis verbis huius capitis. Et colligitur euidenter ex prima regula huius capitis: quia si genus superius, prædicatur de generibus inferioribus, quæ sunt species subalternæ: sequitur de eisdem prædicari differentiam Constitutiuam eiusdem generis superioris, quæ illud constituit, & de illo prædicatur.

The second opinion holds that genera not placed subalternately do not always or necessarily have a common difference, but that some can have one. And this is more probable and to be held. And it is explained by two conclusions. The first: Genera placed subalternately, of which one is under the other, have all the Constitutive differences of the superior genera in common, and some Divisive ones, though not all. For example: Animal and living have in common the Divisive difference of substance, such as corporeal, and also the Constitutive difference of body; but neither has the Constitutive difference of the other, which is the Divisive difference of the proximate genus. So Aristotle in the last words of this chapter. And it is evidently gathered from the first rule of this chapter: because if the superior genus is predicated of the inferior genera, which are subalternate species, it follows that the Constitutive difference of the same superior genus, which constitutes it and is predicated of it, is predicated of them.

Secunda conclusio: Genera non subalternatim posita secundùm primam opinionem: quorum vnum nõ est sub altero, sed vtrumque sub tertio, easdem differentias Constitutiuas superiorum generum habent communes: & aliquam Diuisiuam superioris generis, possunt habere communem, licèt non necessariò, nec semper habeant: sed genera diuersorum prædicamentorum, quæ sola dicuntur non subalternatim posita, nullã. Prima pars huius conclusionis euidens est in animali, & planta quæ habent differentiam Diuisiuam, & Constitutiuam corporis communem. Secunda verò, expressa est apud Arist. 6. Topic. ca. 2 loco 41. vbi eam probat hac ratione: Animal diuiditur in gressibile, & volatile, tanquã in diuersas species subalternas, & ideo in diuersa genera, quæ sub se habent alias species, & tamen vtrique generi, communis est, differentia bipedis: ergo duo genera, non subalternatim posita, communem habent differentiam Diuisiuam superioris generis. Vtitur autem Aristoteles his differentiis loco essentialium, quas ignoramus. Et confirmatur: Quia quantitas diuiditur in successiuam, & permanentem, tanquam in diuersas species subalternas: quarum vna non est sub altera, sed vtraque sub tertia, & habent communes differentias continui, & discreti. Si autem dicatur, quæ sit ratio propter quam non semper, nec necessariò habeant talia genera differentiam

The second conclusion: Genera not placed subalternately according to the first opinion, of which one is not under the other but each is under a third, have the same Constitutive differences of the superior genera in common; and they can have some Divisive difference of the superior genus in common, although they do not necessarily or always have it; but the genera of different categories, which alone are called not placed subalternately, have none. The first part of this conclusion is evident in animal and plant, which have the Divisive and Constitutive difference of body in common. The second is expressly found in Aristotle, Topics 6, ch. 2, locus 41, where he proves it by this argument: Animal is divided into walking and flying, as into diverse subalternate species, and therefore into diverse genera which have other species under them; and yet the difference biped is common to each genus; therefore two genera not placed subalternately have a common Divisive difference of the superior genus. Aristotle, however, uses these differences in place of the essential ones, which we do not know. And this is confirmed: because quantity is divided into successive and permanent as into diverse subalternate species, of which one is not under the other but each is under a third, and they have the common differences of continuous and discrete. But if it is asked what the reason is why such genera do not always or necessarily have a difference

p. 254

communem, sed aliqua habeant illam, & alia non: Respondeo, rationem esse, quia aliqua sunt magis similia aliis, & ideo possunt habere maiorem conuenientiam.

in common, but some have it and others do not: I reply that the reason is that some are more similar to others, and therefore can have a greater agreement.

Pro solutione argumenti, notãdum primò, Quòd differentia communis, quam habent aliquando illa genera, quorum vnum non est sub altero, sed vtrũque sub tertio: eo ipso, quòd communis est, non est vltimatè Constitutiua eorum, quia differentia vltimatè Constitutiua, distinguit speciem, quam constituit, à quacunque alia: sed differentia communis non distinguit inter se illas species, quibus est communis: ergo non est vltimatè constitutiua earum. Gratia exempli: Differentiæ cõtinui, & discreti, communes permananenti & successiuæ quãtitati, non distingunt eas inter se: sed solùm quantitatem continuam à discreta: & ideo harum sunt vltimatè constitutiuæ non illarum.

For the solution of the argument, it should be noted first that the common difference which those genera sometimes have, of which one is not under the other but each is under a third, by the very fact that it is common, is not ultimately Constitutive of them: because the ultimately Constitutive difference distinguishes the species which it constitutes from any other whatever; but the common difference does not distinguish among themselves those species to which it is common; therefore it is not ultimately constitutive of them. For example: the differences of continuous and discrete, common to permanent and successive quantity, do not distinguish these among themselves, but only continuous quantity from discrete; and therefore they are ultimately constitutive of these, not of those.

Secundò notandum, Differentias quasdam esse vniuersales, quæ totam lineam prædicamenti diuidunt: vt corporeum, & incorporeum: Alias verò particulares solùm diuidentes, vnum vel alterum genus particulare alicuius partialis lineæ, vt differentiæ diuidentes animal. Et ideo genera etiam sunt duplicia: Quædam vniuersalia, quorum quodlibet continet integram lineã, vt corpus, & spiritus: Alia particularia partiales lineæ, vt animal, vel planta. Et differentiæ vniuersales, non possunt esse communes, vt vniuersalia genera, possunt habet aliquam differentiam communem. Et huius ratio est manifesta: quia vniuersales differentiæ habent vniuersalem oppositionem: Particulares verò oppositæ non sunt, formaliter oppositæ, sed diuersæ, ideo repugnat illas esse communes, non istas. Tertiò notandum, Quòd cùm dicimus, Genera vniuersalia quæ continentur sub tertio non posse habere differentiam communem, & particularia posse habere, non loquimur de differentia Constitutiua superiori, quam certum est, & necessarium habere communem: nam corpus, & spiritus, sunt vniuersalia genera, & habent communem modum intrinsecum substantiæ, qui licèt non sit differentia, quia substantia non est genus, est tamen similis superiori differentiæ: & non minùs eum includeret, si esset vera differentia. Et ratio huius est euidens, quia, quidquid includitur in prædicato superiori, debet includi in inferiori, sed differentia Constitutiua superioris generis includitur in eo, ergo necesse est includi in quolibet genere inferiori. Loquimur ergo de differentia Diuisiua superioris generis. De qua dicimus, Communem esse posse inferioribus, licèt hoc nõ sit necessarium, nec semper contingat, sed aliquando, vt

It should be noted second that some differences are universal, which divide the whole line of the category, as corporeal and incorporeal; others particular, dividing only one or another particular genus of some partial line, as the differences dividing animal. And therefore genera too are twofold: some universal, each of which contains an entire line, as body and spirit; others particular, of partial lines, as animal or plant. And universal differences cannot be common, nor can universal genera have any common difference. And the reason for this is manifest: because universal differences have a universal opposition; but particular ones are not opposed, formally opposed, but diverse; therefore it is repugnant that the former be common, not the latter. It should be noted third that when we say that universal genera which are contained under a third cannot have a common difference, and that particular ones can, we are not speaking of the Constitutive difference of the superior genus, which it is certain and necessary that they have in common: for body and spirit are universal genera, and they have the common intrinsic mode of substance, which, although it is not a difference, because substance is not a genus, is nevertheless similar to a superior difference, and would include it no less if it were a true difference. And the reason for this is evident: because whatever is included in the superior predicate must be included in the inferior; but the Constitutive difference of the superior genus is included in it; therefore it must necessarily be included in any inferior genus whatever. We are speaking, then, of the Divisive difference of the superior genus, of which we say that it can be common to the inferiors, although this is not necessary nor does it always happen, but sometimes, as the difference

p. 255

differentiæ continui & discreti, quæ sunt diuisiuæ quantitatis, communes sunt quantitati permanenti, atque successiuæ.

of continuous and discrete, which are divisive of quantity, are common to permanent and successive quantity.

6 Notandum quartò: Quòd hæc differẽtia Diuisiua superioris generis, quam dicimus posse esse communem duobus generibus sub eo contentis, non est adęquata alicui eorum, sed inadæquata, ita vt per alias differentias distinctas ab ea, adæquatè constituantur. Gratia exempli: Bipes communis est differentia, gressibilis, & volatilis animalis. sed inadæquata vtrique, quia per proprias differentias gressibilem & volatilem, adæquatè constituuntur.

6 It should be noted fourth that this Divisive difference of the superior genus, which we say can be common to two genera contained under it, is not adequate to either of them but inadequate, so that they are adequately constituted through other differences distinct from it. For example: biped is a common difference of walking and flying animal, but inadequate to each, because they are adequately constituted through the proper differences walking and flying.

Ex his responderetur ad vtrumque testimonium Arist. Negando minorem, nempe quòd ex nostra sententia sequatur, Genus non prædicari de pluribus, quàm differentia, aut, Non esse tot differentias, quot sunt species. Neutrum enim sequitur Nam cùm differentia, quæ potest esse communis duobus generibus, quæ continentur sub tertio superiori, non sit Constitutiua eiusdem superioris generis, sed Diuisiua, ideo inferiorem necesse est de paucioribus prædicari, quàm genus ipsum, vt bipes de paucioribus, quàm animal. Et de hac loquitur Aristo. in primo testimonio, non de constitutiua, de qua manifestum est, Quòd de eisdem omninò prædicetur, de quibus prædicatur genus, quod constituit. De tot enim prædicatur sensibile, de quot prædicatur animal. Quod verò dixit Aristoteles in secundo testimonio, Tot esse differentias, quot sunt species, verissimum est, nam licèt vna possit esse communis duabus speciebus subalternis, positis sub tertio genere superiori, non tamen est vltimatè constitutiua earum, sed habent alias, per quas constituuntur, & distinguuntur. Illa verò quæ communis est, licèt non constituat eas adęquatè, tamen suam habet speciem propriam, quam adęquatè constituit. Vt bipes non constituit adæquatè animal volatile, aut gressibile, sed adæquatè constituit animal habens duos pedes. Vnde intelligitur, quòd etiam si vna differentia inadæquata, communis sit duabus speciebus, nihilominus tot sunt differentiæ, quot species, cùm nulla sit species, quæ non habeat propriam differentiam adæquatè constitutiuam: neque vlla differentia, quæ non constituat adæquatè suam speciem.

From these things one would reply to each testimony of Aristotle by denying the minor, namely that from our view it follows that the genus is not predicated of more things than the difference, or that there are not as many differences as there are species. For neither follows. For since the difference which can be common to two genera that are contained under a third, superior genus is not Constitutive of that superior genus but Divisive, it is therefore necessary that the inferior be predicated of fewer things than the genus itself, as biped of fewer than animal. And it is of this that Aristotle speaks in the first testimony, not of the constitutive difference, of which it is manifest that it is predicated of altogether the same things of which the genus that it constitutes is predicated: for sensible is predicated of as many things as animal is predicated of. And what Aristotle said in the second testimony, that there are as many differences as there are species, is most true: for although one may be common to two subalternate species placed under a third, superior genus, it is nevertheless not ultimately constitutive of them, but they have others through which they are constituted and distinguished. But that which is common, although it does not constitute them adequately, nevertheless has its own proper species, which it constitutes adequately: as biped does not adequately constitute flying or walking animal, but adequately constitutes animal having two feet. Whence it is understood that, even if one inadequate difference is common to two species, there are nonetheless as many differences as species, since there is no species which does not have its proper adequately constitutive difference, nor any difference which does not adequately constitute its own species.

Ad argumentum: Negandum est antecedẽs, Quòd sicut non potest idem indiuiduum esse sub duplici specie, sic non possit vna species, esse sub duplici genere, est enim diuersa ratio de indiuiduo, ac de specie. Nam differẽtia indiuidualis adæquatè & vltimatè determinat speciem, & ideo repugnat, eandem differẽtiam indiuidualem, determinare duplicem speciem diuersam: sed differentia specifica, cùm sit prædicatum commune, &

To the argument: the antecedent must be denied, that just as the same individual cannot be under two species, so one species cannot be under two genera; for the ratio of the individual and of the species is different. For the individual difference adequately and ultimately determines the species, and therefore it is repugnant that the same individual difference determine two different species; but the specific difference, since it is a common predicate, and

p. 256

possit inadæquatè conuenire duobus, & neutrum adæquatè, aut vltimatè constituere, potest ex consequenti esse communis illis.

can belong inadequately to two, and constitute neither adequately or ultimately, it can consequently be common to them.

CAPVT IV.

C H A P T E R I V.

CAP. IIII. Continens diuisionem incomplexorum in decem prædicamenta, cum expositione text. — Containing the division of incomplexes into ten categories.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Eorum, quæ secundùm nullam complexionem dicuntur, vnum quodque aut substantiam significat, aut quantum, &c.

Of the things that are said without any combination, each one signifies either substance, or quantity, etc.

Textus expositio.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 Intentum Aristot. in præsenti ca. est, explicare, simplicia esse debere illa, ex quibus prędicamenta constituenda sunt. Diuiditur autem in duas partes, in quarum prima ponit Arist. Vniuersalem diuisionem incomplexorum in decem prædicamenta. In secunda asserit, & probat, Eadem incomplexa, ex quibus prædicamentum fit, non esse affirmationes, aut negationes, sed ex eis posse affirmationes & negationes fieri.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain that those 1 T things of which the categories are to be constituted must be simple. And it is divided into two parts, in the first of which Aristotle sets down the universal division of incomplexes into ten categories. In the second he asserts and proves that the same incomplexes of which a category is made are not affirmations or negations, but that affirmations and negations can be made from them.

Diuisio talis est: Ens incomplexum, aut simplex, aliud est substantia, vt homo, vel equus, aliud quantum, vt corpus, aut linea, aliud quale, vt album, aliud ad aliquid, vt duplum, dimidium, aliud, vbi, vt esse in foro, aliud, quando, vt heri, aut hodie, aliud, situs, vt iacere, sedere, aliud habere, vt armatum esse, aliud agere, vt secare, aliud pati, vt secari.

The division is as follows: Of incomplex or simple being, one is substance, as man or horse; another quantity, as body or line; another quality, as white; another relation, as double, half; another where, as to be in the forum; another when, as yesterday or today; another position, as to lie, to sit; another having, as to be armed; another acting, as to cut; another being acted upon, as to be cut.

Sed simplicia hæc (inquit Arist. in secunda parte) secundùm se considerata non sunt affirmationes, nec negationes, quamuis ex eis si aliquo verbo, aut copula vniantur, possint fieri affirmationes, & negationes. Quod ita probat: Omnis affirmatio & negatio, est vera aut falsa: sed simplicia, vt homo, aut albedo per se sumpta, non dicunt veritatem aut falsitatem, vt notum est, ergo non sunt affirmationes, aut negationes. Sed si ea coniungas verbo aliquo, affirmationem, aut negationem statim efficies, vt si homini & albo adiungas verbum, est, resultabit hæc affirmatio, homo est albus, in qua iam reperitur veritas aut falsitas.

But these simple things (says Aristotle in the second part), considered in themselves, are not affirmations nor negations, although, if they are united by some verb or copula, affirmations and negations can be made from them. Which he proves thus: Every affirmation and negation is true or false; but simple things, as man, or whiteness, taken by themselves, do not express truth or falsity, as is known; therefore they are not affirmations or negations. But if you join them by some verb, you will at once make an affirmation or negation: as, if you add the verb is to man and white, there will result this affirmation, Man is white, in which truth or falsity is now found.

QUESTION I

Ex quibúsnam rebus per se componatur prædicamentum.

Of which things the category is composed per se.

1 Quinque sunt, de quibus dubitari potest, An & quomodo pertineant ad prædicamentum, vt exclusis his, quæ ad

1 There are five things concerning which it can be doubted whether and how they pertain to the category, so that, once those things are excluded which

p. 257

ipsum non possunt pertinere, intelligi possit, ex quibúsnam per se componatur. Primum, est ens rationis, quod ex eo videtur primò ad prædicamentum pertinere, quia prædicamentum, sicut propositio, aut syllogismus, quoddam ens rationis est, ergo non quomodocunque, sed formaliter, pertinebit ens rationis ad prædicamentum.

cannot pertain to it, it may be understood of which things it is composed per se. The first is the being of reason, which seems to pertain primarily to the category from this: that a category, like a proposition or a syllogism, is a certain being of reason; therefore the being of reason will pertain to the category not in just any way, but formally.

Secundò, Prædicamentum fit ex generibus & speciebus: sed genera, & species sunt entia rationis: ergo ex entibus rationis fiet prædicamentum.

Second, a category is made of genera and species; but genera and species are beings of reason; therefore a category will be made of beings of reason.

Vera tamen sententia est, ex solis entibus realibus fieri, & ideo entia rationis, non pertinere ad prædicamentum, nisi per quandem similitudinem, ratione entis, quoddam prædicamẽtum, vel potiùs similitudinem prædicamenti excogitare possumus, vt in tractatu nostro, de natura entis rationis, diximus. Ita sentiunt D. Th. 5. lib. Meta. lect. 9. & q. 7. de potentia, art. 9. Capreol. in 1. d. 8 q. 2. & d 29 qu. 1. ad 5. Sotus cap. 4. anteprædicam. quæst. 2. ad 4. Fonseca 5. Meta. cap. 7. q. 6. sect. 1. & cæteri omnes.

The true view, however, is that it is made of real beings alone, and therefore that beings of reason do not pertain to the category, except that, through a certain likeness in the ratio of being, we can devise a certain category, or rather a likeness of a category, as we said in our treatise on the nature of the being of reason. So hold St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 9, and On Power, q. 7, a. 9; Capreolus on 1, d. 8, q. 2, and d. 29, q. 1, ad 5; Soto, ch. 4 of the Antepredicaments, q. 2, ad 4; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 6, sect. 1; and all the others.

Probatur testimonio Arist. 5 lib. Met. c. 7. tex. 14. vbi docet, Entia per se diuidi in decem prædicamenta: ens autem per se, apud ipsum (vbicunque de eo loquitur) & ens reale idem sunt.

This is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, text 14, where he teaches that beings per se are divided into ten categories; but being per se, in his usage (wherever he speaks of it), and real being are the same.

Probatur deinde ratione: Quia entia rationis, nec veram habent entitatem, nec veram essentiam, sed ab intellectu excogitatam ad similitudinem entitatis, & essentiæ realis: sed verũ prædicamentum ex vero ente, vtramque essentiam habente debet fieri: ergo non fit ex entibus rationis, sed solùm ex realibus. Quod constabit, si per singula prædicamenta discurramus: videbimus enim prædicamentum substantiæ, qualitatis, & quantitatis, ex veris naturis realibus fieri.

It is proved next by reason: because beings of reason have neither true entity nor true essence, but one devised by the intellect after the likeness of real entity and essence; but a true category must be made of true being, having both entity and essence; therefore it is not made of beings of reason, but only of real beings. Which will be clear if we run through the categories one by one: for we shall see that the category of substance, of quality, and of quantity is made of true real natures.

3 Sed pro solutione arg. notandum est, Prædicamentum fieri ex prædicatis realibus: non tamen realiter, aut ex natura rei distinctis: quia, vt probauimus cap. de differentia, Genus, & differentia, eiusdem rei conceptus reales obiectiui sunt, diuersos gradus essentiales significantes, & solùm ab intellectu distincti. Species verò ex eis componitur, nõ tanquam tertia res ab eis distincta, sed tanquam tertius conceptus obiectiuus, totalis atque completus: & ideo non est compositio realis, sed rationis, quia licèt reales sint conceptus componẽtes, & compositi, non tamen distincti, nisi ratione: quare non possum realem compositionem facere. Ita ergo de prædicamento intelligendum est, ab intellectu distinguente prædicata essentialia fieri: ita vt sicut ante operationem eius, non sunt distincta prędicata, nec ideo plurali, sic non potest prædicamentum dari,

3 But for the solution of the argument it should be noted that a category is made of real predicates, yet not of predicates distinct really or from the nature of the thing: because, as we proved in the chapter on difference, genus and difference are real objective concepts of the same thing, signifying different essential grades, and distinguished only by the intellect. But the species is composed of them, not as a third thing distinct from them, but as a third objective concept, total and complete; and therefore the composition is not real but of reason, because, although the composing and the composite concepts are real, they are nevertheless not distinct except by reason; wherefore they cannot make a real composition. So, then, it must be understood of the category that it is made by the intellect distinguishing the essential predicates, so that, just as before its operation there are no distinct predicates, and therefore no plurality, so a category cannot be given, R

p. 258

sed est opus eiusdem intellectus, qui distinguens prædicata, ea ordinat, ac disponit, prædicamentumque ex eis efficit.

but it is the work of the same intellect, which, distinguishing the predicates, orders and disposes them, and makes a category out of them.

4 Secundò notandum, Prædicamentum duobus modis considerari.
