Primò, quasi pro materiali, nempe pro naturis rerum, ac prædicatis earum, quæ in linea prædicamentali ordinantur, & sic acceptum reale est, quia tam prædicata essentialia, quàm naturæ, in quibus fundantur, realia sunt, licèt non realiter distincta. Secundo modo consideratur quasi pro formali, hoc est, pro ordinatione ipsa, ac dispositione prædicatorum, quæ necessariò supponit distinctionem eorum: & hoc modo sumptum non est quid reale, sed rationis: vnde sequitur prædicamentum formaliter sumptum, ens rationis esse, & pro fundamento esse ens reale, & hoc secundo modo consideratur à Meta. sed primo modo à Dialectica.

4 It should be noted second that a category is considered in two ways. First, as it were for its matter, namely for the natures of things and their predicates, which are ordered in the categorial line; and so taken it is real, because both the essential predicates and the natures in which they are founded are real, although not really distinct. In the second way it is considered as it were for its formal element, that is, for the very ordering and disposition of the predicates, which necessarily supposes their distinction; and taken in this way it is not something real but of reason. Whence it follows that the category taken formally is a being of reason, and for its foundation is a real being; and in this second way it is considered by Metaphysics, but in the first way by Dialectic.

His explicatis, ad vtrumque arg. simul respondemus. Concedendo, quòd genera, species, & prædicamentum formaliter sumpta, entia rationis sint; negamus tamen, quòd aliquo modo pertineant ad prædicamentum: quia illa solùm, dicuntur pertinere ad prædicamentum, ex quibus prædicamentum fit: sed prædicamentum solùm fit ex prædicatis, quæ in eo ordinatur, & non ex ordinatione ipsa, sicut cætera entia artificialia solùm dicuntur fieri ex materia, vt statua ex ligno, domus ex lignis, & lapidibus: ergo entia rationis non pertinent ad prædicamentum, nec genera, & species formaliter sumpta, sed solùm pro fundamentis realibus.

These things explained, we reply to both arguments at once by granting that genera, species, and the category, taken formally, are beings of reason; but we deny that they pertain in any way to the category: because only those things are said to pertain to the category of which the category is made; but the category is made only of the predicates which are ordered in it, and not of the ordering itself, just as other artificial beings are said to be made only of their matter, as a statue of wood, a house of timbers and stones; therefore beings of reason do not pertain to the category, nor do genera and species taken formally, but only taken for their real foundations.

De Complexis.

On Complexes. 5

5 Secundum, de quo dubitari potest, sunt complexa, quæ sic distinguuntur à quibusdam: Quædam sunt complexa, quæ vnam tantum rem significant, & æquiualent voci simplici eam significanti. Et talia sunt definitiones substantiarum, vt animal rationale, aut viuens sensibile. Alia sunt complexa, quæ non vnam rem, sed plures significant. Et talia sunt definitiones accidentium, in quibus præter illa, quæ pertinent ad essentiam accidentis, includitur subiectum, vt per illud, explicetur intrinsecus ordo accidentis ad ipsum, & complexa illa pertinent per se ad prædicamentum, hæc verò ab eo excludenda sunt.

The second thing about which it can be doubted is complexes, which are distinguished by some thus: some are complexes which signify only one thing, and are equivalent to a simple word signifying it. And such are the definitions of substances, as rational animal or sensible living thing. Others are complexes which signify not one thing but several. And such are the definitions of accidents, in which, besides those things which pertain to the essence of the accident, the subject is included, so that through it the intrinsic order of the accident to it may be explained. And the former complexes pertain per se to the category, but the latter must be excluded from it.

Probatur ex Porphyrio, cap. de specie, vbi prædicamentum substantiæ constituens, pro genere viuentis posuit, corpus animatum, & etiam animal rationale, pro quodam genere, in quo existimauit homines, cum dæmonibus conuenire, sed hęc sunt complexa substantialia; ergo ex mente Porphyrij ponenda sunt in prædicamentis.

This is proved from Porphyry, in the chapter on species, where, constituting the category of substance, he placed ensouled body as the genus of living thing, and also rational animal as a certain genus in which he thought men agree with demons; but these are substantial complexes; therefore according to the mind of Porphyry they are to be placed in the categories.

p. 259

Deinde ratione, quia loco definiti, licet ponere definitionem eius, nihil extrinsecum includentem, vt loco hominis, animal rationale, quia talis definitio simplici definito æquiualet: ergo in recta linea prædicamentali licebit ponere loco generis, & speciei, cuiuscunque propriam definitionem, quæ cùm sit cõplexum quid, sequitur ex complexis substantialibus fieri per se prædicamentum.

Next by reason: because in place of the thing defined it is permitted to put its definition, including nothing extrinsic, as rational animal in place of man, because such a definition is equivalent to the simple thing defined; therefore in the categorial straight line it will be permitted to put in place of any genus and species its proper definition, which, since it is something complex, it follows that a category is made per se of substantial complexes.

6 Nostra sententia est opposita: Quòd nullum complexum pertineat ad prædicamentum, & est expressa apud Arist. c. præsenti, vbi ita ait: Eorum, quæ secundùm nullam complexionem dicuntur, vnumquodque aut substantiam significat, aut quantum, aut quale, aut ad aliquid, &c. Quibus verbis complexa omnia, siue substantialia, siue accidentalia sint, excludit à prædicamento, & solùm ens incomplexum diuidit in decem prædicamenta.

6 Our view is the opposite: that no complex pertains to the category. And it is expressly found in Aristotle, in the present chapter, where he speaks thus: Of the things that are said without any combination, each one signifies either substance, or quantity, or quality, or relation, etc. By which words he excludes all complexes from the category, whether they are substantial or accidental, and divides only incomplex being into ten categories.

Sed ratione probatur, quia recta linea prædicamentalis ex solis generibus, & speciebus fit, vt in prædicamento substantiæ, ex substantia, corpore, viuenti, animali, & homine: sed cõplexa siue sint definitiones substantiarum, siue accidẽtium non sunt genera, neque species: ergo ex eis non fit prędicamẽtum. Quod probatur etiam ex definitione eius: nam prædicamentum est prædicabilium ordinatio: sed prædicabilia sunt quædam vniuersalia, de quorum ratione est esse simplicia, vt quæstione vltima vniuersali vidimus: ergo ex solis simplicibus fit prædicamentum, non ex complexis.

But it is proved by reason: because the categorial straight line is made of genera and species alone, as in the category of substance, of substance, body, living thing, animal, and man; but complexes, whether they are definitions of substances or of accidents, are not genera or species; therefore a category is not made of them. Which is proved also from its definition: for a category is an ordering of predicables; but predicables are certain universals, of whose ratio it is to be simple, as we saw in the last question on universals; therefore a category is made of simple things alone, not of complexes.

7 Ad Porphyrium respondetur: Complexa posuisse loco simplicium, non quia intelligeret ad prædicamentorum pertinere, sed vel maioris explicationis gratia, vel quia simplicia genera non cognouit. Propter primam rationem, posuit corpus animatum pro viuenti, & propter secundam, animal rationale pro genere hominum, ac demonum.

7 To Porphyry it is replied that he placed complexes in place of simple things not because he understood that they pertain to the categories, but either for the sake of greater explanation, or because he did not know the simple genera. For the first reason he placed ensouled body for living thing; and for the second, rational animal as the genus of men and demons.

Ad rationem verò negamus, quòd semper loco definiti, liceat ponere definitionem, etiam nihil includentem extrinsecum, sed solùm licet quantum ad ęquiualentiam veritatis, quia de quibus prædicatur definitum, necesse est prædicari definitionem: sed vbi modus significandi determinatus esse debet, atque distinctus in definitione, & definito, non licet eam loco definiti ponere. Et ita est in proposito, quia res non ponitur in prædicamento, quomodocunque significata, aut concepta, sed per modum generis, aut speciei, & ideo per modum incomplexi, cùm ergo definitio non habeat modum generis, aut speciei ratione complexionis, sequitur nec habere modum prædicamentalem, quare non potest loco definiti in prędicamento poni. Ad formam ergo argum. dum dicitur, Definitio licèt sit

To the argument, however, we deny that it is always permitted to put the definition, even one including nothing extrinsic, in place of the thing defined; rather it is permitted only as regards the equivalence of truth, because of whatever things the thing defined is predicated, the definition must be predicated; but where the mode of signifying must be determinate, and is distinct in the definition and in the thing defined, it is not permitted to put it in place of the thing defined. And so it is in the case at hand, because a thing is not placed in a category as signified or conceived in just any way, but by way of a genus or species, and therefore by way of an incomplex. Since, then, the definition, by reason of its being complex, does not have the mode of a genus or species, it follows that it does not have the categorial mode either; wherefore it cannot be placed in the category in place of the thing defined. To the form of the argument, then: when it is said, Although the definition is R ij

p. 260

complexa, æquiualet simplici definito. distinguendum est antecedens, quasi æquiualet definito, quantum ad veritatem rei, non tamen quantum ad modum significandi simplicem, & omnino necessarium ad lineam prædicamentalem, & ideo non potest loco eius in prædicamento poni, quamuis in propositione, vel in aliis casibus ponatur.

complex, it is equivalent to the simple thing defined, the antecedent must be distinguished: it is as it were equivalent to the thing defined as regards the truth of the thing, but not as regards the simple mode of signifying, which is altogether necessary for the categorial line; and therefore it cannot be placed in its stead in the category, although it may be so placed in a proposition or in other cases.

De partibus Physicis, & Metaphysicis.

On Physical and Metaphysical Parts.

Partes rei duplices sunt, Physicæ, & Metaphysicæ, & partes Physicæ adhuc duplices, quædam sunt, Essentiales, vt materia, & forma, & aliæ Integrantes, quæ adhuc sunt in duplici differentia: nam quædam sunt eiusdem rationis, vt partes æquę aut ligni, & ideo vocari solent homogeneæ, aliæ diuersæ rationis vt caput, & manus, & vocantur eterogeneæ & integrantes quæ non sunt essentiales, sed substantiales, aut entitatiuæ appellari possunt. Partes Meta. sunt genus, & differentia: sed de genere certum est, quòd per se pertineat ad prædicamentum, quia habet modum substantiæ completæ. De solis ergo differentia, tanquam de partibus Meta. & de materia, & forma, ac partibus integrantibus, tanquam Physicis procedit quæstio, An per se sint in prædicamento. Et primo de his dicendum est, deinde, de partibus Metaphysicis.

The parts of a thing are twofold, Physical and Metaphysical. And the Physical parts are again twofold: some are Essential, as matter and form, and others Integral, which again are of two kinds: for some are of the same ratio, as the parts of water or of wood, and therefore they are usually called homogeneous; others of a different ratio, as the head and the hands, and they are called heterogeneous; and the integral parts, which are not essential, can be called substantial or entitative. The Metaphysical parts are genus and difference: but concerning the genus it is certain that it pertains per se to the category, because it has the mode of a complete substance. The question therefore proceeds concerning the difference alone, as concerning the Metaphysical parts, and concerning matter and form and the integral parts, as the Physical ones: whether they are per se in the category. And first we must speak of these, then of the Metaphysical parts.

Sed priùs explicandum est, Quid sit per se pertinere ad prædicamentum. Duo sunt in prædicamento. Primum est, series ipsa seu ordinatio prædicamentalis superiorum, & inferiorum, ex quibus fit, quasi quædam linea recta, per quam ascendere, atque descendere possumus, ab indiuiduo, quod totius lineæ fundamentum est, vsque ad genus supremum, quod est quasi caput. Sic linea prædicamenti substantię, procedit à genere supremo, quod est substantia, per diuisionem eius in species, quæ sunt corpus, & spiritus: & rursus per diuisionem corporis in viuens, & non viuens: deinde per diuisionem viuentis in animal, & plantam: & tandem per diuisionem animalis in hominem, equum & leonem, & ex his diuisionibus generum in species per differentias, resultat linea hæc, quæ appellatur series, aut ordinatio, nempe substantia, corpus viuens, animal, homo, Petrus. Et pro hac linea recta supponit prædicamentum, quotiescunque de eo loquimur. Præter hanc verò habet prædicamentum quasi duo latera, quibus quasi circundatur, & lata hæc fiunt ex differentiis oppositis, per quas genus diuiditur in species. Vt latus eiusdem prædicamenti substantiæ nobis fit notissimum ex his quatuor differentiis, corporeum, animatum, sensitiuum, rationale,

But first it must be explained what it is to pertain per se to the category. There are two things in a category. The first is the very series or categorial ordering of superiors and inferiors, from which is made as it were a certain straight line, through which we can ascend and descend from the individual, which is the foundation of the whole line, up to the supreme genus, which is as it were its head. So the line of the category of substance proceeds from the supreme genus, which is substance, through its division into species, which are body and spirit; and again through the division of body into living and non-living; then through the division of living into animal and plant; and finally through the division of animal into man, horse, and lion. And from these divisions of genera into species through differences there results this line, which is called the series or ordering: namely substance, body, living thing, animal, man, Peter. And it is for this straight line that the category stands whenever we speak of it. But besides this the category has as it were two sides, by which it is as it were surrounded, and these sides are made of the opposed differences through which the genus is divided into species. As one side of the same category of substance is best known to us from these four differences: corporeal, animate, sensitive, rational,

p. 261

Ex his intelligitur iam. Quid sit esse per se in prædicamento, vel ex quibus fiat per se prædicamentum, idem est enim, ac poni in recta linea prædicamentali, vel ex aliquo fieri eandem rectam lineam, nam latera prædicamenti extra ipsum sunt, & quasi ornatus eius. Dum ergo quærimus de partibus tam Physicis, quàm Metaphysicis, An per se sint in prædicamento, vel ex eis fiat prædicamentum, sensus est: An per se sint in recta linea prædicamentali.

From this it is now understood what it is to be per se in a category, or what things a category is made of per se: for it is the same as to be placed in the straight categorial line, or for the same straight line to be made out of something; for the sides of a category are outside it, and as it were its ornament. When, therefore, we ask concerning parts, both Physical and Metaphysical, whether they are per se in a category, or whether a category is made of them, the sense is: whether they are per se in the straight categorial line.

Et de partibus Physicis tenet prima opinio, quòd per se collocentur in prædicamento, ita Villalpandus, & Louanienses, cap. de substantia, quos sequuntur alij. Probant primò: Quia completa substantia componitur essentialiter ex materia, & forma: & integratur substantialiter ex partibus integrantibus: ergo repugnat completam substantiam poni per se in prædicamento, quin partes etiam ponantur, & per se quidem, cùm per se eam componant.

And concerning Physical parts the first opinion holds that they are placed per se in the category; so Villalpando and the Louvain commentators, ch. on substance, whom others follow. They prove it first: because a complete substance is composed essentially of matter and form, and is integrated substantially out of integral parts; therefore it is repugnant that a complete substance be placed per se in the category without the parts also being placed there, and indeed per se, since they compose it per se.

Secundò, quia in partibus substantiæ intelligimus genera, & species, ergo ex his potest ordinari prędicamentum, sicut ordinatur ex generibus, & speciebus substantiæ totalis. Probatur antecedens: quia sicut diuidimus completam substantiam in corpoream, & incorpoream, & sic de cæteris generibus, sic possumus diuidere partialem.

Second, because in the parts of substance we understand genera and species; therefore a category can be ordered out of these, just as it is ordered out of the genera and species of total substance. The antecedent is proved: because just as we divide complete substance into corporeal and incorporeal, and so on with the other genera, so we can divide partial substance.

10 Et confirmari potest de partibus homogeneis, quia eiusdem rationis sunt cum tota substantia, & possunt per diuisionem fieri completæ substantię: vt si diuidamus aquam, tot substantias completas efficiemus, quot partes separamus: nam postquam separatæ sunt, nec dependent à tota substantia, nec partes eius sunt, sed quælibet incipit esse completa substantia: ergo per se etiam pertinens ad prædicamentum.

10 And it can be confirmed concerning homogeneous parts: because they are of the same ratio as the whole substance, and by division they can become complete substances: as, if we divide water, we shall make as many complete substances as we separate parts; for after they have been separated they neither depend on the whole substance nor are parts of it, but each begins to be a complete substance; therefore it also pertains per se to the category.

Secunda opinio excludit partes substantiæ Physicas à prædicamento, & D. Tho. 1. p. q. 29. art. 4. ad 5. & de veritate q. 27. art. 1. ad 8. Scoti quæst. 15. prædicamentorum, Ægidij Romani in d. 2. qu. 3. Caiet. & Soti, cap. de substantia, Toleti, qu. 5. eiusdem prædicamenti, Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 7. q. 7. sect. 2. & c. 8. q. 3. Et hæc est vera & tenenda.

The second opinion excludes the Physical parts of substance from the category; and it is that of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 29, a. 4, ad 5, and On Truth, q. 27, a. 1, ad 8; of Scotus, q. 15 on the Categories; of Giles of Rome, on d. 2, q. 3; of Cajetan and Soto, ch. on substance; of Toledo, q. 5 on the same category; of Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 7, sect. 2, and ch. 8, q. 3. And this is true and to be held.

Probatur primò, quia prædicamentum solum fit per se ex generibus, & speciebus, vt iam ostendimus, sed genera, & species sunt substantiæ completæ: ergo partes, quæ incompletæ sunt substantiæ, non possunt prædicamentum per se constituere, aut in eo per se collocari.

It is proved first: because a category is made per se only out of genera and species, as we have already shown; but the genera and species are complete substances; therefore the parts, which are incomplete substances, cannot constitute the category per se, or be placed in it per se.

11 Secundò, Substantiæ completę, & incompletæ nihil datur commune vniuocum: ergo nec dabitur genus commune vtrisque, sub quo collocari possint incompletæ: quare non pertinebunt

11 Second, nothing univocal common to complete and incomplete substance is given; therefore neither will a genus common to both be given, under which the incomplete could be placed; wherefore they do not pertain R iij

p. 262

per se ad prædicamentum.

per se to the category.

Ad primum, Concedendum est antecedens, sed neganda consequentia, quia res non pertinent ad prædicamentum secundùm entitatem, quam à parte rei habent, sed secundùm modum, quo talis entitas concipitur ab intellectu, & modus iste ad constitutionem prædicamenti necessarius, completæ entitatis esse debet, vnde cùm partes, solùm sint incompleta entia, non possunt, vt talia, per se efficere prædicamentum, quamuis componant per se substantiam completam, ex qua per se fit. Solùm autem concedi potest partibus, quòd reductiuè, aut quasi indirectè collocentur in recta linea prædicamentali, vbi collocatur species, aut genus, cuius partes sunt.

To the first: the antecedent is to be granted, but the consequence denied; because things do not pertain to the category according to the entity they have on the side of the thing, but according to the mode in which such an entity is conceived by the intellect; and this mode, necessary for the constitution of the category, must be that of a complete entity. Hence, since the parts are only incomplete beings, they cannot, as such, make up a category per se, although they compose per se the complete substance out of which it is made per se. The only thing that can be granted to the parts is that they are placed reductively, or as it were indirectly, in the straight categorial line, where the species or genus whose parts they are is placed.

Ad secundum, negandum est, quòd in partibus possint intelligi vera genera, & veræ species, sed solùm possunt ex eis formari conceptus, quodammodo similes generibus, & speciebus, Et ratio est, quia non possunt concipi partes, nisi tanquam incompletæ, quamuis in communi concipiantur abstractæ à partibus singularibus, in quo consistit aliqua similitudo: & cùm genera, & species ex proprio modo, quo concipiuntur, sint completa, repugnat, in partibus vera genera, & veras species concipere, aut esse veram ordinationem prædicamentalem.

To the second: it is to be denied that true genera and true species can be understood in the parts; only concepts in some way similar to genera and species can be formed out of them. And the reason is that the parts cannot be conceived except as incomplete, although in common they are conceived abstracted from the singular parts, in which some similarity consists; and since genera and species, by the proper mode in which they are conceived, are complete, it is repugnant to conceive true genera and true species in the parts, or that there be a true categorial ordering among them.

12 Ad confirmationẽ de partibus integrãtibus homogeneis, concedimus, quòd sint eiusdem rationis cum tota, quantum ad entitatem, atque etiam quòd possint fieri substantię completę; negamus tamen, quòd per se pertineant ad prædicamẽtum. Et ratio est, quia quamdiu sunt in toto, ab eo depẽdent, & incompletum modum essendi habent. Quod verò separari possint ab eo, solùm probat, quòd dum separatæ fuerint, pertinebunt per se ad prædicamentum, quia non erunt iam partes, hoc verò solùm est, posse pertinere, non verò pertinere actu.

12 To the confirmation concerning homogeneous integral parts, we grant that they are of the same ratio as the whole as regards entity, and also that they can become complete substances; we deny, however, that they pertain per se to the category. And the reason is that as long as they are in the whole they depend on it and have an incomplete mode of being. That they can be separated from it proves only that, once they have been separated, they will pertain per se to the category, because they will then no longer be parts; but this is only to be able to pertain, not to pertain in act.

De partibus verò Met. quales sunt differentiæ, dixerunt quidam, quos citat Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 8. q. 2. pertinere ad prædicamentum qualitatis, cùm prędicẽtur de speciebus in quale quid. Sed hoc apertè falsum est, quia licèt aliquam similitudinem habeant cum qualitatibus in modo prædicandi, verè sunt conceptus essentiales, & vt tales concipiuntur ab intellectu componente speciem ex eis simul, ac generibus, ergo non sunt verè qualitates, nec vt verè qualitas concipiuntur, sed per quandam similitudinem earum, & ideo non possunt pertinere ad prædicamentum qualitatis. Solum potest esse dubium, An singulæ differentiæ per se pertineant ad illud prædicamentum, in quo collocantur genera quæ diuidunt, & species quas cõstituunt.

But concerning Metaphysical parts, such as the differences are, some, whom Fonseca cites, Metaph. 5, ch. 8, q. 2, have said that they pertain to the category of quality, since they are predicated of the species in quale quid. But this is plainly false: because although they have some similarity with qualities in their mode of predicating, they are truly essential concepts, and as such they are conceived by the intellect, which composes the species out of them together with the genera; therefore they are not truly qualities, nor are they conceived as truly quality, but through a certain likeness to them; and therefore they cannot pertain to the category of quality. The only thing that can be doubtful is whether each of the differences pertains per se to that category in which the genera they divide and the species they constitute are placed.

13 Et est prima sententia Ammonij, c. de substantia, asserentis

13 And the first opinion is that of Ammonius, ch. on substance, who asserts

p. 263

per se pertinere quaslibet differentias ad proprium prædicamentũ, quod probat hoc. arg. Nam aut differentiæ excluduntur à prędicamento, quia simplices conceptus sunt, vel quia incompleti: sed vtraque ratio concurrit in generibus: ergo vel genera excludi debent, vel collocari differentiæ: sed genera excludi non possunt. vt notum est: ergo nec differentiæ excludi debent. Probatur minor, quia conceptus generis, vt talis non est compositus, quamuis, si sit species subalterna, in quantum est species, componatur: ergo est simplex: & est vera pars speciei, non minùs, quàm differentia, ergo incompletum quid.

that any differences whatever pertain per se to their own category; which he proves by this argument. For either the differences are excluded from the category because they are simple concepts, or because they are incomplete; but both reasons concur in the genera; therefore either the genera must be excluded or the differences placed there; but the genera cannot be excluded, as is known; therefore neither must the differences be excluded. The minor is proved: because the concept of the genus as such is not composite, although, if it is a subalternate species, it is composed inasmuch as it is a species; therefore it is simple; and it is a true part of the species no less than the difference; therefore something incomplete.

Nec soluitur argu. si dicatur genus esse totum potentiale: quia etiam differentia est totum actuale, vt prædicatur de specie, continens totum, quod species: nam vt pars non posset de ea prædicari: ergo pertinebit ad prædicamentum sicut genus.

Nor is the argument solved if it is said that the genus is a potential whole: because the difference too is an actual whole, as it is predicated of the species, containing the whole that the species contains; for as a part it could not be predicated of it; therefore it will pertain to the category just as the genus does.

Communis sententia omnium expositorum, cap. præsenti, & sequenti, differentias excludit à recta linea prædicamentali, & solùm eis concedit, vt latera prædicamenti constituant: quod est extra prædicamentum simpliciter esse.

The common opinion of all the expositors, in the present chapter and the following, excludes the differences from the straight categorial line, and only grants them that they constitute the sides of the category; which is to be simply outside the category.

14 Et probatur duplici ratione. Prima, Differentia formaliter sumpta, solùm dicit partem speciei: ergo formaliter est quid incompletum: sed recta linea prædicamenti solùm constituitur ex prædicatis completis, quæ sunt genera, & species: ergo differentiæ non pertinent per se ad illam.

14 And it is proved by a twofold argument. First: the difference, taken formally, signifies only a part of the species; therefore formally it is something incomplete; but the straight line of the category is constituted only out of complete predicates, which are the genera and species; therefore the differences do not pertain per se to it.

Et si dicas totum includere, quod species, cùm includat genus saltem materialiter: ergo habet modum totius completi, sicut genus, ex eo solùm, quòd includit differentias in potentia, dicitur habere modum totius completi, & pertinere per se ad prædicamentum. Contra hos est, quòd differẽtia eodem modo includit genus, ac accidens in concreto, nempe per modũ subiecti, & ideo significatur nomine adiectiuo, vt rationale, quare non includit per se totum, quod species, sed quasi per accidens: vnde nec habet modum vnius per se. Sed genus per se, & formaliter est totum potentiale, per se, & formaliter includens totum, quod species, quamuis vnum actu, nempe gradum propriæ naturæ, & aliud in potentia, nempe gradum differentialem, & ideo modum habet totius, atque completi per se, & per se efficitur ex eo prædicamentum.

And if you say that it includes the whole that the species includes, since it includes the genus at least materially, and therefore has the mode of a complete whole, just as the genus, from this alone, that it includes the differences in potency, is said to have the mode of a complete whole and to pertain per se to the category: against these it is that the difference includes the genus in the same way as an accident in the concrete does, namely by way of a subject, and therefore it is signified by an adjectival name, as rational; wherefore it does not include per se the whole that the species includes, but as it were per accidens; hence neither does it have the mode of something one per se. But the genus is per se and formally a potential whole, per se and formally including the whole that the species includes, though one part in act, namely the grade of its proper nature, and the other in potency, namely the differential grade; and therefore it has the mode of a whole, and of something complete per se, and a category is made out of it per se.

15 Secundò probatur: Recta linea prædicamenti constituitur ex prædicatis per se, formaliter & essentialiter ordinatis: sed differentia nõ ordinatur per se & formaliter cum genere: ergo non pertinet per se ad rectam lineam prædicamenti. Probatur minor: quia differẽtia non includit per se, & formaliter genus, vt rationale non includit per se & formaliter animal, sed extra

15 It is proved second: the straight line of the category is constituted out of predicates ordered per se, formally and essentially; but the difference is not ordered per se and formally with the genus; therefore it does not pertain per se to the straight line of the category. The minor is proved: because the difference does not include the genus per se and formally, as rational does not include animal per se and formally, but outside R iiij

p. 264

rationem eius animal est, ergo non potest cum eo constituere lineã prædicamẽtalem, nec per se pertinere ad prędicamẽtum.

its ratio is animal; therefore it cannot constitute a categorial line with it, nor pertain per se to the category.

Ad arg. alterius opinionis iam responsum est, quia differentia formaliter, & per se non est totum, sed pars, genus verò formaliter, & essentialiter habet rationem totius potentialis, & completi, & ideo per se, & formaliter collocatur in prædicamento, à quo excluditur differentia, propter rationem incompletam.

To the argument of the other opinion a reply has already been given: because the difference is formally and per se not a whole but a part, whereas the genus formally and essentially has the ratio of a potential and complete whole, and therefore it is placed per se and formally in the category, from which the difference is excluded on account of its incomplete ratio.

An, & quomodo indiuidua ponantur in prædicamento — Whether and how individuals are placed in the category.

16 Prima opinio est Iauelli in sua Logic. tit. 5. c. 1. asserentis, Indiuiduum per se non pertinere ad prædicamentum, sed reductiuè ratione speciei, quam participat. Quod probari potest ex Porphyrio ca. de specie, vbi Terminos, quibus clauditur prædicamentum, asserit esse supremũ genus, & infimam speciem, vltra quam non licet ascendere ad indiuidua, quia sunt infinita: ergo sentit non pertinere per se ad prædicamentum, & pręterea si infinita sunt, quemadmodũ de illis non datur scientia, ita ad prædicamẽtum non per se pertinebũt: quia pars ista, sciẽtię Dialecticæ pars est.

16 The first opinion is that of Javelli in his Logic, tit. 5, ch. 1, who asserts that the individual does not pertain per se to the category, but reductively, by reason of the species in which it participates. This can be proved from Porphyry, ch. on species, where he asserts that the Terms by which the category is closed are the supreme genus and the lowest species, beyond which it is not permitted to ascend to the individuals, because they are infinite; therefore he holds that they do not pertain per se to the category. And besides, if they are infinite, just as there is no science of them, so they will not pertain per se to the category: because this part is a part of the science of Dialectic.

Sed opposita opinio, quod indiuiduum per se sit in prædicamento tanquam basis, & fundamentum eius) vera est & tenenda, Eam sequitur Fonseca 5. Met. c. 7. q. 7 sect. 2. & q. 8 sect. 3.

But the opposite opinion, that the individual is per se in the category as its base and foundation, is true and to be held. Fonseca follows it, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 7, sect. 2, and q. 8, sect. 3.

Et ratione probatur, quia Indiuiduum est ens per se completum, & in se continens omnia prædicata rectæ lineæ prædicamentalis, quibus per se subiicitur, & de quo per se, & formaliter prędicantur, Substantia, Corpus, Viuẽs, Animal & Homo, ergo nihil ei deficit, vt in prędicamento sit tanquam fundamentum eius.

And it is proved by reason: because the individual is a being complete per se, and containing in itself all the predicates of the straight categorial line, to which it is subjected per se, and of which Substance, Body, Living, Animal, and Man are predicated per se and formally; therefore nothing is lacking to it for it to be in the category as its foundation.

17 Ad arg. respondetur, Porphyrium posuisse pro extremis prædicatis essentialibus prædicamenti genus supremum, & infimam speciem: præsupponendo indiuiduum esse extremum, tanquam fundamentum omnium prædicamentorum. Quòd verò sint infinita indiuidua, non tollit indiuiduum pertinere per se ad prædicamentum, etiam si actu essent infinita: quia nõ pertinent ad prædicamentum vt distincta, vel vt efficiunt numerum: sed vt participant de prædicatis essentialibus, & ea sustentant. & hæc ratio eadem est in omnibus, siue sint infinita, aut solùm finita. Ex quo etiam intelligitur, indiuiduum ad scientiam prædicamentalem pertinere posse, non quidem vt obiectum eius, sed tanquam id, ex quo, vt fundamento, integratur obiectum, nempe prædicamentum, quod est pars totius obiecti Dialecticæ scientiæ.

17 To the argument it is replied that Porphyry posited the supreme genus and the lowest species as the extreme essential predicates of the category, presupposing that the individual is an extreme, as the foundation of all the categories. That the individuals are infinite, however, does not take away that the individual pertains per se to the category, even if they were infinite in act; because they do not pertain to the category as distinct, or as making up a number, but as participating in the essential predicates and sustaining them; and this ratio is the same in all, whether they are infinite or only finite. From which it is also understood that the individual can pertain to the science of the categories, not indeed as its object, but as that out of which, as from a foundation, the object is integrated, namely the category, which is part of the total object of the science of Dialectic.

p. 265

Quonam modo res infinitæ ponantur, aut excludantur à prædicamento — In what way infinite things are placed in, or excluded from, the category.

18 In communi tantùm dicendum est hoc loco de rebus infinitis: nam in particulari suis locis de illis agemus, nempe in prædicamento substantiæ & quantitatis. Nunc verò hac distinctione explicandum est dubium hoc: Duobus modis potest esse aliquid infinitum, aut secũdùm essentiam, vt Deus, aut secundùm aliquam rationem accidentalem extensionis, aut intentionis, vt linea, si daretur infinita, aut albedo habens infinitos gradus intentionis. Et infinitum secundùm essentiam non pertinet ad prædicamentum, vt probabitur cap. sequenti, de reliquis verò probabitur cap. de quantitate, quod ad prædicamenta propria per se pertineant. non minùs quàm finitæ quantitates, aut qualitates.

18 Only in general need we speak in this place about infinite things; for we shall deal with them in particular in their own places, namely in the category of substance and of quantity. But now the following doubt is to be explained by this distinction: a thing can be infinite in two ways, either according to essence, as God, or according to some accidental ratio of extension or of intension, as a line, if an infinite one were given, or a whiteness having infinite degrees of intension. And what is infinite according to essence does not pertain to the category, as will be proved in the following chapter; but of the rest it will be proved in the chapter on quantity that they pertain per se to their proper categories no less than finite quantities or qualities.

QUESTION II

Quæst. 2. An res sint ponendæ in prædicamentis sub nominibus abstractis, vel concretis — Whether things are to be placed in the categories under abstract names or concrete ones.

19 De his, quæ pertinent ad prædicamentum substantiæ, certum est, sub nominibus concretis collocanda esse in prædicamento, & non sub nominibus abstractis, vt species humana, & genus animalis, sub nominibus hominis, & animalis, & non sub nominibus animalitatis, & humanitatis, & sic de reliquis. Et huius ratio est, quia prædicamentum fit, ex rebus completis, sed per nomina abstracta nõ significantur substantiæ, tanquam entia completa, sed solùm per concreta: ergo sub concretis, & non abstractis ad prædicamentum pertinebunt. Probatur minor, quia per nomina abstracta significantur, non vt species, vel genera, sed vt principia generis, & speciei, vt nomine animalitatis significatur natura sensitiua, vt principium animalis, & nomine humanitatis natura rationalis, vt principium hominis: ergo significantur modo incompleto, & non prædicamentali.

19 Concerning the things that pertain to the category of substance, it is certain that they are to be placed in the category under concrete names, and not under abstract names: as the human species and the genus of animal under the names man and animal, and not under the names animality and humanity; and so of the rest. And the reason for this is that a category is made out of complete things; but by abstract names substances are not signified as complete beings, but only by concrete ones; therefore they will pertain to the category under concrete names, and not under abstract ones. The minor is proved: because by abstract names they are signified not as species or genera, but as principles of the genus and of the species: as by the name animality the sensitive nature is signified as the principle of animal, and by the name humanity the rational nature as the principle of man; therefore they are signified in an incomplete and non-categorial mode.

De solis ergo accidentibus procedit quæstio, An abstracta, vel albedo, & color: vel concreta potiùs, vt album & coloratum, ponantur in prædicamento qualitatis: & sic de cæteris prædicamentis.

The question therefore proceeds concerning accidents alone: whether the abstract ones, as whiteness and color, or rather the concrete ones, as white and colored, are placed in the category of quality; and so of the other categories.

20 Et antequam alias sententias proponamus, reiicienda est ea, quam Caiet. tenet, opusc. de ente, & essentia, c. 7. vbi distinguit duas considerationes prędicamentorum, Logicam, & Metaphysicam, & in prędicamentis Logicè consideratis. abstracta

20 And before we propose the other opinions, that one is to be rejected which Cajetan holds, in the opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 7, where he distinguishes two considerations of the categories, the Logical and the Metaphysical; and in the categories logically considered, the abstract

p. 266

esse collocanda, non concreta: quia ordinantur ad prædicationes, quæ meliùs in abstractis, quàm in concretis exercentur: sed sub cõsideratione Metaphysica, concreta, & non abstracta. Hoc tamen ab omnibus refutatur, quia prædicamenta eadem sunt in Logica, & Metaphysica: ergo ex eisdem rebus, & eodem modo conceptis significantur. Quòd verò in ordine ad prædicationes potiùs abstracta, quàm concreta ponenda sint, etiam est falsum, quia cùm concreta, quibus significantur formæ accidentales, vt sunt in subiecto, notiora nobis sint, meliùs in concretis exercentur prædicationes. Sed hæc ratio non est sufficiens ad variandum modum significandi rerum prædicamentalium, & ideo sub vtraque consideratione Logica, & Metaphysica disponendæ sunt in prædicamentis.

are to be placed, not the concrete: because they are ordered to predications, which are better exercised in abstract terms than in concrete ones; but under the Metaphysical consideration, the concrete and not the abstract. This, however, is refuted by all: because the categories are the same in Logic and in Metaphysics; therefore they are signified out of the same things, conceived in the same way. And that in relation to predications the abstract rather than the concrete are to be placed is also false: because, since the concrete terms, by which accidental forms are signified as they are in a subject, are better known to us, predications are better exercised in concrete terms. But this reason is not sufficient to vary the mode of signifying of the things of the categories; and therefore under both considerations, Logical and Metaphysical, they are to be arranged in the categories.

Tenet ergo prima opinio: Abstracta accidentium non collocari in prædicamento, sed sola concreta. Ita Niphus 5 Meta qu 3. & 7. Toletus q. 2. postprædicamentorum, & alij ex modernis. Et probant ex Aristotele ipso, cap. præsenti, vbi prædicamenta in concreto enumerauit, iuxta translationem Boetij, quamuis Argyropylus in abstracto ea posuerit, & lib. Topic. c. 7. & li 4. c 1. loco 4. etiam in concreto secundùm vtrãque trãslationem.

The first opinion therefore holds: that the abstract terms of accidents are not placed in the categories, but only the concrete. So Nifo, Metaph. 5, q. 3 and 7; Toledo, q. 2 on the Postpredicaments; and others among the moderns. And they prove it from Aristotle himself, in the present chapter, where he enumerated the categories in the concrete, according to the translation of Boethius (although Argyropoulos put them in the abstract), and in Topics bk. 1, ch. 7, and bk. 4, ch. 1, locus 4, also in the concrete according to both translations.

21 Probant deinde ratione. Primò, quòd abstracta non ponantur, Secundò, quòd ponantur concreta. Ratio primi est, quia perfectior est substantia accidentibus: sed substantiæ non ponuntur in abstracto, quia significantur tanquam partes, & ideo modo incompleto: ergo multò minùs collocanda erunt accidentia in abstracto.

21 They prove it next by reason: first, that the abstract are not placed; second, that the concrete are placed. The reason for the first is that substance is more perfect than the accidents; but substances are not placed in the abstract, because they are signified as parts, and therefore in an incomplete mode; therefore much less will accidents be placed in the abstract.

Ratio secundi est, quia sic non ponerentur concreta: maximè quia sunt entia per accidens, cùm significent formam, & connotent subiectum, vt album, & ex forma, & subiecto tanquam ex duobus entibus in actu non fiat vnum per se, sed per accidens: sed hoc est falsum: ergo non sunt à prædicamento excludenda. Probatur minor, quia ex actu & potentia, secundùm Arist. 2. lib. de anima, tex. 2. fit vnum per se: sed subiectum se habet vt potentia, & forma vt actus: ergo ex tali compositione resultabit vnum per se, quod est concretum.

The reason for the second is that if the concrete were not placed in this way, it would be chiefly because they are beings per accidens, since they signify a form and connote a subject, as white, and out of a form and a subject, as out of two beings in act, there is made not something one per se but something one per accidens; but this is false; therefore they are not to be excluded from the category. The minor is proved: because out of act and potency, according to Aristotle, On the Soul 2, text 2, something one per se is made; but the subject behaves as potency, and the form as act; therefore out of such a composition there will result something one per se, which is the concrete.

Secunda opinio opposita est, quia sola abstracta, accidentium dicit collocanda esse in prædicamento, ita D. Th. opusc. de Ente, & essentia, cap. 7. ad finem. Scotus quæst. 5. vniuersalium, & quæst. 11. prædicamentorum, Auicenna lib. 3. suæ Met. c. 3 Iauellus 5. Meta. quæst. 16 Sotus ca. de quantitate, quæst. 1. Venetus cap. præsenti. Villalpandus cap. de genere, q. 4.

The second opinion is the opposite one, which says that only the abstract terms of accidents are to be placed in the category; so St. Thomas, opusculum On Being and Essence, ch. 7, toward the end; Scotus, q. 5 on Universals and q. 11 on the Categories; Avicenna, bk. 3 of his Metaph., ch. 3; Javelli, Metaph. 5, q. 16; Soto, ch. on quantity, q. 1; Paul of Venice, on the present chapter; Villalpando, ch. on genus, q. 4.

22 Probatur testimonio Arist. 3. li. Topic. c. 1. loco 3. & 4. vbi asserit, Iustitiam esse in genere, hoc est, in prędicamẽto, non iustũ.

22 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics bk. 4, ch. 1, loci 3 and 4, where he asserts that justice is in a genus, that is, in a category, not the just

p. 267

Et etiam ratione, quia concretum significat res diuersorum prædicamentorum, nempe subiectum, quod est substantia, & formam, quæ est accidens: ergo non potest pertinere ad vnum prædicamentum determinatum. Imo ad nullum potest pertinere, quia prædicamenta fiunt ex entibus per se: sed ex rebus diuersorum prædicamentorum, cùm sint primò diuersa, & in actu, non potest fieri vnum per se: ergo concretum non potest collocari in prædicamento. Probatur minor, quantum ad hoc vltimum ex Arist. 7. Meta tex. 25. vbi docet expressè, Album, & musicum non habere vnam essentiam determinatam, & per se, & ideo non posse per vnam definitionem essentialem explicari, sed esse entia per accidens.

And also by reason: because the concrete signifies things of different categories, namely the subject, which is substance, and the form, which is accident; therefore it cannot pertain to one determinate category. Indeed it can pertain to none, because categories are made out of beings per se; but out of things of different categories, since they are primarily diverse and in act, something one per se cannot be made; therefore the concrete cannot be placed in the category. The minor is proved, as to this last point, from Aristotle, Metaph. 7, text 15, where he teaches expressly that the white and the musical do not have one determinate essence per se, and therefore cannot be explained by one essential definition, but are beings per accidens.

23 Pro solutione huius quæstionis duo notanda sunt circa concreta, & abstracta accidentium. Primum est circa naturam concreti, quę explicanda est per similitudinem increti substantialis. Natura autem substantialis habet actualem existentiam, per quam est in rerum natura sola ratione ab ea distinctam, & vltra hanc habet subsistentiam, quę est modus quidam substantialis, per quam vltimò terminatur, atque completur, & constituitur in supposito si non sit rationalis, & si rationalis sit constituitur in supposito simul, & persona, vt natura humana Petri habet actualem existentiam, per quam est in rerum natura, & subsistentiam quæ est vltimus actus eius, & per quam constituitur persona: vnde persona Petri, est composita ex humanitate actu existente, & subsistentia, aut personalitate. Et cùm humanitas se habeat per modum potentiæ, hoc est, terminabilis per subsistentiam: & subsistentia sit tanquam actus substantialis eam terminans, atque complens, sequitur personam esse vnum per se substantiale. Et etiam concretum singulare quælibet persona, & à multis personis abstrahitur. Natura communis sic terminata & completa. Et sic abstracta significatur nomine concreto communi: vt nomen homo, significat naturam humanam subsistentem, & completam in communi, quæ est idem, ac homo in communi.

23 For the solution of this question two things are to be noted concerning the concrete and abstract terms of accidents. The first concerns the nature of the concrete, which is to be explained by likeness to the substantial concrete. Now a substantial nature has actual existence, through which it is in the nature of things, distinct from it by reason alone; and beyond this it has subsistence, which is a certain substantial mode through which it is ultimately terminated and completed, and constituted in a supposit if it is not rational, and, if it is rational, constituted at once in a supposit and a person: as the human nature of Peter has actual existence, through which it is in the nature of things, and subsistence, which is its ultimate act and through which it is constituted a person. Hence the person of Peter is composed of humanity actually existing and of subsistence, or personality. And since humanity behaves by way of potency, that is, as terminable by subsistence, and subsistence is as a substantial act terminating and completing it, it follows that the person is something one per se and substantial. And each person is also a singular concrete, and from many persons there is abstracted a common nature thus terminated and complete. And thus abstracted it is signified by a common concrete name: as the name man signifies the human nature subsisting and complete in common, which is the same as man in common.

24 Simili modo natura accidentalis vt albedo, habet actualẽ existentiam, per quam est in rerum natura sola ratione à se distinctam, & etiam alium modum per quem vltimò terminatur, & completur, qui modus non est subsistentia, sed actualis inhærentia in subiecto. Ex hac igitur natura accidentali actu existenti in rerum natura, & ex modo actualis inhærentiæ in subiectó, componitur hoc concretum, quod est hoc album, vel illud. Et ab his concretis singularibus abstrahitur concretum commune, vt album, significans naturam albedinis actu inhærentem

24 In a like manner an accidental nature, such as whiteness, has actual existence, through which it is in the nature of things, distinct from itself by reason alone, and also another mode through which it is ultimately terminated and completed; which mode is not subsistence but actual inherence in a subject. Out of this accidental nature, then, actually existing in the nature of things, and out of the mode of actual inherence in a subject, there is composed this concrete, which is this white thing or that. And from these singular concretes there is abstracted the common concrete, as white, signifying the nature of whiteness actually inhering

p. 268

in subiecto. Et compositio hæc est per se, quia fit ex natura accidentali, se habente tanquam potentia quasi substantiali, hoc est, ex natura, vt determinabili, & ex modo actualis inhærentiæ, tanquam ex actu quasi substantiali eam terminante. Ex potentia autem substantiali, & actu substantiali, fit vnum per se, & ideo concretum accidentale resultans ex tali compositione, est vnum per se, sed quia modus iste, quo terminatur natura accidentalis, est actualis inhærentia in subiecto, concretum hoc per se, vt album, connotat subiectum, in quo inhæret natura accidentalis, ita completa, & terminata. Connotare autem subiectum non est aliud, quàm simul denotare illud, tanquam quid extrinsecum, cui quasi affixa est natura accidentalis. Et ratio huius connotationis est, quia modus per quem terminatur hæc natura, imperfectus est sicut ipsa, & ideo non potest per se illam sustentare, sed indiget adminiculo subiecti extrinseci, qui quasi affixa sit. Et propterea talis modus non dicitur substantia, aut existentia per se, sed actualis inhærentia, vel actualis inexistentia.

in a subject. And this composition is per se, because it is made out of the accidental nature, behaving as a quasi-substantial potency, that is, out of the nature as determinable, and out of the mode of actual inherence as out of a quasi-substantial act terminating it. Now out of a substantial potency and a substantial act something one per se is made; and therefore the accidental concrete resulting from such a composition is something one per se. But because this mode by which the accidental nature is terminated is actual inherence in a subject, this concrete per se, as white, connotes the subject in which the accidental nature, thus complete and terminated, inheres. Now to connote the subject is nothing other than to denote it at the same time, as something extrinsic to which the accidental nature is as it were affixed. And the reason for this connotation is that the mode by which this nature is terminated is imperfect, as the nature itself is, and therefore cannot sustain it by itself, but needs the support of an extrinsic subject to which it may be as it were affixed. And for this reason such a mode is not called subsistence, or existence per se, but actual inherence, or actual in-existence.

Ex quibus intelligitur, Concretum accidentale duobus modis sumi posse. Primò, vt solùm significat compositum quid ex natura accidentali, & proprio modo actualis inhærentiæ: connotat verò ex consequenti subiectum, in quo inhæret, & concretum hoc, est vnum per se, quia non componitur ex natura accidentali, & subiecto: sed ex sola illa, & termino, seu actu proprio substantiali, qui est actualis inhærentia, eo modo, quo componitur concretum substantiale ex natura substantiali, & proprio modo substantiæ: subiectum verò non pertinet ad hanc compositionem, sed extra illam connotatur, tanquam quid extrinsecum, cui affixa est naturę per actualem inhærentiam, connotatur tamen per se. Alio modo sumitur concretum accidentale per modum aggregati ex vtroque, nempe ex natura accidentali, & subiecto, ita vt tanquam compositum ex vtroque significetur. Et hoc modo non est vnum per se sed per accidens: quia licèt componatur ex subiecto, vt ex potentia, & ex forma accidentali, vt ex actu potentia tamen illa subiecti, quam habet ad recipiendam formam accidentalem, accidentalis est, quia omnibus modis est extra essentiam eius, iam omnino completam per principia, & partes substantiales. Ex potentia autem accidentali, & actu etiam accidentali, non potest fieri vnum per se, sed per accidens, quia fit ex duobus entibus iam completis in proprio esse substantiali & ad diuersa prædicamenta pertinentibus, nempe ex subiecto, & natura accidentali, iam completa per proprium modum actualis inhærentiæ.

From which it is understood that the accidental concrete can be taken in two ways. First, as signifying only something composed of the accidental nature and its proper mode of actual inherence, while it connotes consequently the subject in which it inheres; and this concrete is something one per se, because it is not composed of the accidental nature and the subject, but of the nature alone and its term, or proper substantial act, which is actual inherence, in the way in which the substantial concrete is composed of the substantial nature and the proper mode of substance; but the subject does not pertain to this composition, but is connoted outside it, as something extrinsic to which the nature is affixed through actual inherence; yet it is connoted per se. In another way the accidental concrete is taken by way of an aggregate of both, namely of the accidental nature and the subject, so that it is signified as composed of both. And in this way it is not something one per se but per accidens: because although it is composed of the subject as of potency and of the accidental form as of act, yet that potency of the subject which it has for receiving the accidental form is accidental, because it is in every way outside its essence, already wholly complete through its substantial principles and parts. But out of an accidental potency and an act that is also accidental, something one per se cannot be made, but only per accidens, because it is made out of two beings already complete in their own substantial being and pertaining to different categories, namely out of the subject and the accidental nature, already complete through its proper mode of actual inherence.

p. 269

Et hoc est fieri ex duobus entibus in actu, ex quo infertur esse vnum per accidens. Et si dicatur, quòd sicut ex potentia substantiali, & actu substantiali fit vnum per se substantia, ita ex potentia accidentali subiecti, & actu accidentalis formæ, potest fieri vnum per se accidentale: Respondeo impossibile esse, quòd sit vnum accidentale, & per se, quia potentia accidentalis subiecti non potest esse per se respectu illius, quia est alterius generis à substantia: ergo respectu subiecti est potentia per accidens: sed subiectum concurrit per talem potentiam ad componendum concretum, simul cum forma accidentali, ergo concurrit per potentiam, non per se, sed per accidens: quare non potest per illam efficere vnum per se componendo simul cum alio, sed eo ipso, quòd efficit vnum accidentale, cùm ipsummet sit substantia, efficit vnum per accidens.

And this is to be made out of two beings in act, from which it is inferred that it is something one per accidens. And if it is said that just as out of a substantial potency and a substantial act there is made something one per se, a substance, so out of the accidental potency of the subject and the act of the accidental form there can be made something one per se and accidental: I reply that it is impossible that it be something one, accidental and per se, because the accidental potency of the subject cannot be per se with respect to it, since it is of another genus than substance; therefore with respect to the subject it is a potency per accidens; but the subject concurs through such a potency to compose the concrete, together with the accidental form; therefore it concurs through a potency not per se but per accidens; wherefore it cannot through it make something one per se in composing together with another, but by the very fact that it makes something accidental one, since it is itself a substance, it makes something one per accidens.

27 Secundò notandum est, circa naturam abstractionem accidentium, quòd vt in communi modo concipiendi, & loquendi accipiuntur, significant naturam accidentalem, vt abstractam à subiecto, abstractione Physica, & non Metaphysica, qua abstrahuntur vniuersalia à particularibus: vnde significant eam, non per modum inhærentis, in subiecto, sed per modum quasi per se subsistens, ad similitudinem substantiarum: vt albedo quæ verè inhæret subiecto, nomine albi significatur per modum inhærentis: sed nomine abstracto albedinis significatur, vt abstracta Physicè à subiecto, & propterea non per modum inhærentis, sed per modum per se subsistentis completi, & ideo tanquam vnum per se.

27 It is to be noted second, concerning the nature of the abstract terms of accidents, that as they are taken in the common way of conceiving and speaking, they signify the accidental nature as abstracted from the subject by Physical abstraction, and not by the Metaphysical abstraction by which universals are abstracted from particulars. Hence they signify it not by way of something inhering in a subject, but by way of something as it were subsisting per se, after the likeness of substances: as whiteness, which truly inheres in a subject, is signified by the name white by way of something inhering; but by the abstract name whiteness it is signified as abstracted Physically from the subject, and therefore not by way of something inhering, but by way of something complete subsisting per se, and therefore as something one per se.

Ex tota hac doctrina colligo tres conclusiones, quibus nostra sententia explicatur. Prima est: Concretum accidentale ex sola natura accidentali, & proprio modo actualis inhærentiæ compositum, per se collocatur in prædicamento. Probatur hac ratione: Prædicamentum fit ex entibus per se, & completis, sed concretum hoc est vnum per se, & completum: ergo per se pertinet ad prædicamentum. Probatur minor: Ex potentia substantiali, & actu substantiali componitur vnum per se, vt docet Arist. 2. lib. de anima, tex. 2. sed concretum accidentale compositum ex natura accidentali, vt terminabili, & ex proprio modo actualis inhærentiæ terminante, componitur ex eadem natura, vt in potentia substantiali ad suum terminum, tanquam ad actum substantialem, & ex termino ipso, tanquam actus eius substantialis, ergo est vnum per se, atque completum, cùm contineat natura accidentalem completam per proprium modum.

From this whole doctrine I gather three conclusions by which our view is explained. The first is: the accidental concrete composed solely of the accidental nature and its proper mode of actual inherence is placed per se in the category. It is proved by this argument: a category is made out of beings that are per se and complete; but this concrete is something one per se and complete; therefore it pertains per se to the category. The minor is proved: out of a substantial potency and a substantial act something one per se is composed, as Aristotle teaches, On the Soul 2, text 2; but the accidental concrete composed of the accidental nature as terminable and of its proper mode of actual inherence terminating it is composed of that same nature, as in substantial potency to its term as to a substantial act, and of the term itself, as its substantial act; therefore it is something one per se and complete, since it contains the accidental nature complete through its proper mode.

p. 270

Secunda conclusio: Concretum secundo modo sumptum, vt significat compositum Physicũ ex subiecto, & forma accidentali, non ponitur in prędicamẽto. Probatur, quia prædicamentum fit ex entibus per se: sed concretum accidentale hoc modo sumptum est ens per accidens, ergo non pertinet ad prædicamentum. Minorem probo, quia ens per accidens est, quod componitur ex pluribus entibus in actu, hoc est, iam completis in suo esse substantiali: sed concretum sic sumptum, componitur ex subiecto iam completo in toto suo esse substantiali, & ex natura accidentali, etiam complexa per proprium modum actualis inhærentiæ, ergo ex multis entibus in actu.

The second conclusion: the concrete taken in the second way, as it signifies a Physical composite of the subject and the accidental form, is not placed in the category. It is proved: because a category is made out of beings per se; but the accidental concrete taken in this way is a being per accidens; therefore it does not pertain to the category. I prove the minor: because a being per accidens is that which is composed of several beings in act, that is, already complete in their substantial being; but the concrete so taken is composed of the subject, already complete in its whole substantial being, and of the accidental nature, also complete through its proper mode of actual inherence; therefore of many beings in act.

Tertia conclusio: Abstracta Physica accidentium, vt in communi modo concipiendi, & loquendi significantur, per se pertinent ad prædicamentum, vt albedo, color, &c. Probatur quia significant naturam accidentalem per modum per se existentis, ac subsistentis, ergo tanquam vnum quid per se, & prædicamentale. Si verò ab his abstractis abstractione Physica (quæ potiùs habent modum concretorum substantialium) accipiantur alia abstracta Metaphysica, vt ab albedine albedineitas, & à colore coloreitas, abstracta hæc non pertinent per se ad prædicamentum, sicut nec abstracta substantiarum, quia significant naturam modo incompleto, hoc est non tanquam genus, aut speciem, sed tanquam principia generis, & speciei.

The third conclusion: the Physical abstract terms of accidents, as they are signified in the common way of conceiving and speaking, pertain per se to the category, as whiteness, color, etc. It is proved: because they signify the accidental nature by way of something existing and subsisting per se; therefore as something one per se and categorial. But if from these abstract terms, abstracted by Physical abstraction (which rather have the mode of substantial concretes), other Metaphysical abstract terms are taken, as from whiteness whiteness-ness, and from color color-ness, these abstract terms do not pertain per se to the category, just as neither do the abstract terms of substances, because they signify the nature in an incomplete mode, that is, not as a genus or species, but as principles of the genus and of the species.

29 Ad testimonium Arist. pro prima sententia, Concedendum est, vtroque modo enumerasse prædicamenta, in concreto, & in abstracto, quia tam concretum per se, quàm abstractum per se, pertinent ad prædicamenta, & solùm concretum per accidens excluditur.

29 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion: it is to be granted that he enumerated the categories in both ways, in the concrete and in the abstract, because both the concrete per se and the abstract per se pertain to the categories, and only the concrete per accidens is excluded.

Ad primum arg. distinguenda est maior, quia duobus modis possumus loqui de rebus aut secundùm se, & hoc modo perfectiora sunt abstracta substantiarum, quàm accidentium, vel, vt tali modo abstrahuntur ab intellectu, & sic accepta perfectiora sunt abstracta accidentium, in communi modo concipiendi, & loquendi, quia significant naturam, licèt accidentalem, vt abstractam abstractione Physica, & ideo per modum naturarum per se subsistentium, atque completarum, abstracta verò substantiarum significant naturam, licèt substantialem, abstractam tamen abstractione Metaphysica, & ideo modo quodam incõpleto, tanquã principiũ generis, & speciei. Quare illa pertinent per se ad prędicamentũ, hoc non, sed abstracta accidentiũ, quæ accipiuntur Metaphysicè, etiam excluduntur à prędicamento.

To the first argument the major is to be distinguished: because we can speak of things in two ways. Either according to themselves, and in this way the abstract terms of substances are more perfect than those of accidents; or as they are abstracted in such a way by the intellect, and so taken the abstract terms of accidents are more perfect, in the common way of conceiving and speaking, because they signify the nature, although accidental, as abstracted by Physical abstraction, and therefore by way of natures subsisting per se and complete; whereas the abstract terms of substances signify the nature, although substantial, yet abstracted by Metaphysical abstraction, and therefore in a certain incomplete mode, as the principle of the genus and of the species. Wherefore the former pertain per se to the category, the latter do not; but the abstract terms of accidents that are taken Metaphysically are also excluded from the category.

30 Ad aliud, quod de cõcretis dicitur in eodẽ arg. Respõdeo. Concretum, vt compositũ ex subiecto, & accidenti, esse vnum

30 To the other point, which is said about concretes in the same argument, I reply: the concrete, as composed of the subject and the accident, is something one

p. 271

per accidens, licèt componatur ex potentia, & actu, quia potentia, & actus, non sunt substantiales, ex quibus Arist. affirmat fieri vnum per se, sed potentia accidentalis substantiæ, & actus accidentalis formæ, ex quibus fit vnum per accidens.

per accidens, although it is composed of potency and act: because the potency and act are not the substantial ones out of which Aristotle affirms that something one per se is made, but the accidental potency of the substance and the accidental act of the form, out of which something one per accidens is made.

Ad testimonium Aristo. pro secunda opinione respondetur, quòd si loquatur de genere pro prædicamento, iustum, sumit pro concreto accidentali, & hoc modo sumptum, verum est, non esse in genere, hoc est, in prædicamento, vt expositum est.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the second opinion it is replied that, if he is speaking of genus for category, he takes just for the accidental concrete; and taken in this way it is true that it is not in a genus, that is, in a category, as has been explained.

Et eodem modo respondetur ad arg. quòd concretum, vt significat compositum ex rebus diuersorum prædicamentorum, non potest pertinere ad vnum prædicamentum determinatum, imò nec ad vllum prædicamentum, bene tamen, vt significat compositum ex sola natura, & proprio eius modo actualis inhærentiæ, quod est vnum per se.

And in the same way it is replied to the argument that the concrete, as it signifies something composed of things of different categories, cannot pertain to one determinate category, indeed not to any category; but it can, as it signifies something composed solely of the nature and its proper mode of actual inherence, which is something one per se.

Si autem aduersus nostram sententiam aliquis ita arguat, Accidentia in concreto definiuntur vnica definitione, vt album quòd sit disgregatiuum visus, & definiuntur, vt dicũt subiectum, & formam accidentalem, ita, vt subiectum sit definitũ materiale, tanquam denominatum à forma, & hæc sit definitum formale, vt denominans subiectum. ergo sunt vnum per se, etiam vt includunt subiectum, & ideo pertinebunt ad prædicamentum, contra secundam conclusionem nostram. Respondeo, quòd concretum duobus modis includit subiectum, vt ex nostra doctrina est manifestum. Primo, tanquam per se connotatum, & non significatum, & tunc concretum est vnum per se: quia solùm significat naturam per proprium modum actualis inhærentiæ completam: subiectum verò per se connotat. Secundo modo includit subiectum, vt per se significatum, & hoc modo est vnum per accidens. Dum ergo definitur in concreto, primo modo sumitur, & est vnum per se, includens naturam, & subiectum, vt per se connotatum, non vt componentia vnum, sed vt ordinata; quia cum subiectum per se connotetur, per se ordinatur cum natura completa illud connotante: ideo efficit vnum per se, non entitate, sed ordine, quod per vnam definitionem explicari potest.

But if someone should argue thus against our view: accidents in the concrete are defined by a single definition, as white, that it is what disperses sight; and they are defined as they signify the subject and the accidental form, in such a way that the subject is the material definitum, as denominated by the form, and the form is the formal definitum, as denominating the subject; therefore they are something one per se even as they include the subject, and therefore they will pertain to the category, against our second conclusion: I reply that the concrete includes the subject in two ways, as is manifest from our doctrine. First, as connoted per se and not signified; and then the concrete is something one per se, because it signifies only the nature complete through its proper mode of actual inherence, while it connotes the subject per se. In the second way it includes the subject as signified per se, and in this way it is something one per accidens. When, therefore, it is defined in the concrete, it is taken in the first way and is something one per se, including the nature, and the subject as connoted per se, not as components of something one but as ordered; because, since the subject is connoted per se, it is ordered per se with the complete nature that connotes it; therefore it makes something one per se, not in entity but in order, which can be explained by one definition.

QUESTION III

An necesse sit prædicamenta distingui realiter, aut ex natura rei, vel sufficiat distingui ratione.

Whether it is necessary that the categories be distinguished really, or from the nature of the thing, or whether it suffices that they be distinguished by reason. 31

31 Prima opinio affirmat, Necessariò esse ponendã distinctionẽ realẽ inter prædimenta. Ita Ven. 3. l. suæ Met. c. 31. Niph 4. Met. q. 4 & l. 5. 12. quos videtur sequi Caiet. 1. par. q. 28. art. 1.

The first opinion affirms that a real distinction must necessarily be posited between the categories. So Paul of Venice, bk. 3 of his Metaph., ch. 31; Nifo, Metaph. 4, q. 4, and bk. 5, 12; whom Cajetan seems to follow, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1.

Probant primò, quia diuisio entis in decem prædicamenta

They prove it first: because the division of being into ten categories

p. 272

est realis: ergo diuiditur ens in diuersas entitates reales: sed diuersæ entitates reales sunt realiter distinctæ, quia quæ sola ratione distinguuntur, sunt eadem entitas realis: ergo necesse est prædicamenta distingui realiter. Probatur prima consequentia: Quia sicut animal diuiditur in diuersa animalia: & color in diuersos colores, ita ens in diuersas entitates.

is real; therefore being is divided into diverse real entities; but diverse real entities are really distinct, because things that are distinguished by reason alone are the same real entity; therefore it is necessary that the categories be distinguished really. The first consequence is proved: because just as animal is divided into diverse animals, and color into diverse colors, so being into diverse entities.

Secundò: Prædicamenta sunt primò diuersa: ergo in entitate non conueniunt vniuocè: sed si non distinguerẽtur realiter, conuenirent in vna aliqua entitate multis communi: ergo sicut repugnat eis talis conuenientia, sic repugnat identitas realis, at non distinctio, necesse est ergo distingui realiter.

Second: the categories are primarily diverse; therefore they do not agree univocally in entity; but if they were not distinguished really, they would agree in some one entity common to many; therefore just as such agreement is repugnant to them, so real identity is repugnant to them, but not distinction; it is necessary, therefore, that they be distinguished really.

32 Secunda opinio, non ponit distinctionem realem inter omnia prædicamenta, sed realem, vel formalem, saltem ante operationem intellectus, ita vt necessarium sit illa habere rationes formales ex se, & sine dependentia ab intellectu distinctas. Et quia hanc distinctionem formalem solent vocare ex natura rei, dicunt necessarium esse quòd prædicamenta distinguantur realiter, aut ex natura rei: ita vt non sit possibile solùm per intellectum distingui. Ita Ioannes Gandauen. quem citat Fonseca 5. Met. c. 7. q. 6. sect. 1. & licèt eum refutare videatur, sect. 2. concl. 2. sect. tamen 3. in fine sententiam eius sequi videtur: affirmans, Prædicamentorum distinctionem, non pendere ab intellectu, sed ante operationem eius omnia distingui.

32 The second opinion does not posit a real distinction between all the categories, but a real or formal one, at least prior to the operation of the intellect, so that it is necessary that they have formal rationes distinct of themselves and without dependence on the intellect. And because they are accustomed to call this formal distinction “from the nature of the thing,” they say it is necessary that the categories be distinguished really or from the nature of the thing, so that it is not possible that they be distinguished only by the intellect. So John of Jandun, whom Fonseca cites, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 6, sect. 1; and although he seems to refute him in sect. 2, concl. 2, yet in sect. 3, at the end, he seems to follow his opinion, affirming that the distinction of the categories does not depend on the intellect, but that they are all distinguished before its operation.

33 Et probatur hoc arg. Prædicamenta continens diuersos modos essendi, ergo diuersas rationes formales, ante operationem intellectus distinctas, quòd est non distingui sola ratione, sed quasi ex natura rei. Probatur consequentia, quia modus essendi rerum non pendet ab intellectu: ergo nec dependebit ab eius operatione, quòd diuersi sint, vel non, sed ex propria natura erunt distincti.

33 And it is proved by this argument: the categories contain diverse modes of being; therefore diverse formal rationes, distinct before the operation of the intellect, which is not to be distinguished by reason alone, but as it were from the nature of the thing. The consequence is proved: because the mode of being of things does not depend on the intellect; therefore neither will it depend on its operation whether they are diverse or not, but they will be distinct from their own nature.

Tertia opinio ferè communis est iam in schola, Quòd nec prædicamenta necessariò distinguantur realiter, nec ex natura rei: sed satis sit, aliqua distingui ratione, cum fundamento in re. Ita D. Tho. 11. lib. Met. lect. 7. q. 2. ad 18. Sotus cap. de quantitate, q. 1. Toletus q. 5. ex communibus prædicamentis omnibus, & ex modernis multi.

The third opinion is now almost common in the school: that the categories are not necessarily distinguished really, nor from the nature of the thing, but that it is enough that they be distinguished by some distinction of reason, with a foundation in the thing. So St. Thomas, Metaph. bk. 11, lect. 7; q. 2, ad 18; Soto, ch. on quantity, q. 1; Toledo, q. 5 on the categories in common; and many among the moderns.

34 Et quòd non sit necessaria distinctio realis inter prędicamenta, euidenter colligitur ex duobus locis Arist. Nam in hoc lib. prędicamentorum distinguit duo prędicamenta, actionis, & passionis. Et 3. lib. Phys. tex. 19. asserit, & probat, Actionem & passionem non distingui realiter, sed eundem motum realem esse actionem, prout procedit ab agente, & passionem prout recipitur in passo, vt eandem calefactionem, per quam ignis calefacit lignum,

34 And that a real distinction between the categories is not necessary is evidently gathered from two passages of Aristotle. For in this book of the Categories he distinguishes two categories, of action and of passion. And in Phys. 3, text 19, he asserts and proves that action and passion are not distinguished really, but that the same real motion is action as it proceeds from the agent, and passion as it is received in the patient: as that the same heating, by which fire heats wood,

p. 273

esse actionem, prout ab eodem igne procedit, & passionem, prout recipitur in ligno, ergo euidenter sequitur ex vtroque testimonio non esse necessariò ponendam distinctionem realem inter prædicamenta.

is action as it proceeds from the same fire, and passion as it is received in the wood; therefore it follows evidently from both testimonies that a real distinction is not necessarily to be posited between the categories.
