35 Probatur secundum, quòd non sit necessariò ponenda distinctio ex natura rei, sed rationis sufficiat. Primò, quia inter diuersos gradus essentiales eiusdem rei, non est necessariò ponenda distinctio ex natura rei, sed sufficit per intellectum distingui, vt cap. de differentia probauimus, sed prædicamenta possunt in eadem entitate conuenire, in qua reperiatur ratio vtriusque, & non distinguantur rationes eorum per diuersos gradus essentiales, sed solùm per diuersos modos essendi, vt substantia ab accidentibus per modum per se, & accidentia inter sese per diuersos modos inhærendi in substantia, ergo non est necessarium distingui ex natura rei, sed sufficit per intellectum. Probatur consequentia, quia minùs differunt modi, quàm gradus essentiales.

35 The second point is proved, that a distinction from the nature of the thing is not necessarily to be posited, but that one of reason suffices. First, because between the diverse essential grades of the same thing a distinction from the nature of the thing is not necessarily to be posited, but it suffices that they be distinguished by the intellect, as we proved in the chapter on difference; but the categories can agree in the same entity, in which the ratio of both is found, and their rationes are not distinguished by diverse essential grades, but only by diverse modes of being, as substance from the accidents by the mode of being per se, and the accidents among themselves by diverse modes of inhering in substance; therefore it is not necessary that they be distinguished from the nature of the thing, but it suffices that they be distinguished by the intellect. The consequence is proved: because modes differ less than essential grades.

Secundò probatur, quia non est ponenda distinctio ex natura rei, vbi sufficit distinctio per intellectum, sed sufficit distinctio rationis ab intellectu facta inter prædicamenta, ergo non est ponenda formalis, aut ex natura rei. Minorem probo, quia quotiescunque aliqua sunt distincta ex natura rei, non possunt in eodem reperiri, nisi per realem compositionem, cùm sint multa, ex quibus resultat vnum: quod non potest fieri, nisi per compositionem: sed actio, & passio, quæ sic distinguuntur, sunt in eodem motu sine compositione, & in multis aliis plures reperiuntur rationes formales sine compositione reali, vt in attributis diuinis, iustitiæ, & misericordiæ, ergo non debent poni distinctæ ex natura rei, vel ante intellectum, sed satis est ab intellectu distingui.

It is proved second: because a distinction from the nature of the thing is not to be posited where a distinction by the intellect suffices; but a distinction of reason made by the intellect between the categories suffices; therefore a formal distinction, or one from the nature of the thing, is not to be posited. I prove the minor: because whenever some things are distinct from the nature of the thing, they cannot be found in the same thing except through real composition, since they are many, out of which something one results, which cannot come about except through composition; but action and passion, which are distinguished in this way, are in the same motion without composition, and in many other things several formal rationes are found without real composition, as in the divine attributes of justice and mercy; therefore they ought not to be posited as distinct from the nature of the thing, or before the intellect, but it is enough that they be distinguished by the intellect.

36 Sed talis distinctio facta ab intellectu inter aliqua prædicamenta, quæ non sunt dictincta realiter, necessariò esse debet cum fundamento in re, & ideo distinctio rationis ratiocinatæ, Nam cùm sint rationes formales primò diuersæ, non possunt separari ab intellectu in eadem re, nisi virtualiter in ea contineantur. Et hæc virtualis continentia fundamentum est, vt possit intellectus vtramque separare, ac distinguere, concipiendo vnam sine alia. Gratia exempli, in Petro nullum est fundamentum distinguendi illum à seipso, quia repugnat, quòd differat à se formaliter, & ideo non potest distingui distinctione rationis ratiocinatæ, sed solùm rationis ratiocinantis, hoc est, solo officio intellectus. Sed actio, & passio, quæ reperiuntur in eodem motu, quasi virtualiter distinctæ sunt ante intellectum,

36 But such a distinction, made by the intellect between some categories which are not really distinct, must necessarily be with a foundation in the thing, and therefore a distinction of reasoned reason. For since they are primarily diverse formal rationes, they cannot be separated by the intellect in the same thing unless they are virtually contained in it. And this virtual containment is the foundation by which the intellect can separate and distinguish both, conceiving one without the other. For example, in Peter there is no foundation for distinguishing him from himself, because it is repugnant that he differ formally from himself; and therefore he cannot be distinguished by a distinction of reasoned reason, but only of reasoning reason, that is, by the sole work of the intellect. But action and passion, which are found in the same motion, are as it were virtually distinct before the intellect, S

p. 274

quia verè ante operationem eius reperitur in motu, quod procedat ab agente, & recipiatur in passo, & ideo fundamentum tribuunt eidem intellectui, vt concipiat motum, vt procedentem ab agente, non concipiendo illum, vt receptum in passo eodem conceptu, sed alio, & diuerso quidem: quia verum est, procedere ab agente ita conceptum, non essẽ recipi in passo. Et hoc est distincta esse ab intellectu actu, & formaliter illa, quæ à parte rei solùm erant distincta virtualiter: esse autem distincta virtualiter non est aliud, quàm posse formaliter distingui. Et hanc distinctionem rationis ratiocinatæ, dicimus sufficere inter aliqua prædicamenta, licèt alia distinguantur realiter, sed nulla esse distincta formaliter ante operationem intellectus, quia talem distinctionem formalem non admittimus.

because truly, before its operation, it is found in the motion that it proceeds from the agent and is received in the patient; and therefore they give a foundation to the same intellect to conceive the motion as proceeding from the agent, not conceiving it as received in the patient by the same concept, but by another, and indeed a different one: because it is true that to proceed from the agent, so conceived, is not to be received in the patient. And this is for those things which on the side of the thing were only virtually distinct to be distinct by the intellect actually and formally; but to be virtually distinct is nothing other than to be able to be formally distinguished. And this distinction of reasoned reason we say suffices between some categories, although others are distinguished really; but that none are formally distinct before the operation of the intellect, because we do not admit such a formal distinction.

37 Ad primum arg. Distinguendum est antecedens, quia duobus modis potest intelligi diuisionem esse realem. Primo ita vt tam diuisum, quàm membra sint realia, & non entia rationis. In quo sensu admittimus diuisionem entis in decem prædicamenta, esse realem. Secundo, potest intelligi esse realem, ita vt membra sint realiter distincta. & in hoc sensu negamus, quòd sit realis. Et possumus exemplum ponere in diuisione boni in honestum, vtile, & delectabile, quam omnes concedunt esse realem in primo sensu, & negant in secundo, quia sæpe contingit membra non esse distincta realiter, aut ex natura rei, sed sola ratione. Et hac distinctione supposita, neganda est etiam consequentia, quòd sit diuisio entis in diuersas entitales reales, si per diuersas, entitates reales intelligantur realiter distinctæ.

37 To the first argument: the antecedent is to be distinguished, because a division can be understood to be real in two ways. First, in such a way that both the thing divided and the members are real and not beings of reason; in which sense we admit that the division of being into ten categories is real. Second, it can be understood to be real in such a way that the members are really distinct; and in this sense we deny that it is real. And we can give an example in the division of good into the honest, the useful, and the pleasant, which all grant to be real in the first sense and deny in the second, because it often happens that the members are not distinct really or from the nature of the thing, but by reason alone. And, this distinction being supposed, the consequence must also be denied, that the division of being is into diverse real entities, if by diverse real entities are understood ones really distinct.

Ad secundum, Respondeo distinguendo antecedens, quòd prædicamenta sint primò diuersa, hoc enim dupliciter potest intelligi. Primò, secundùm rationes formales, & in hoc sensu verum est, sed sic intelligẽdum, vt non conueniant vniuocè in aliquo gradu superioris naturæ, nec distinguantur per alios gradus inferiores essentialis perfectionis, sicut distinguuntur species per gradus essentialis perfectionis diuersos à genere, sed vt distincta sint prædicamenta, per diuersos modos essendi intrinsecos, atque inclusos in eadem ratione entitatis, in qua analogicè conueniunt, & ita verum est per easdem suas entitates, & non per alios gradus perfectionis esse diuersa, & ideo seipsis esse diuersa, quod verè, & propriè est esse primò diuersa, nec speciebus conuenit, sed per differentias dicuntur differre. Secundò modo potest intelligi esse primò diuersa secũdùm entitates reales, ita vt non possint in eadem entitate reali plura

To the second, I reply by distinguishing the antecedent, that the categories are primarily diverse; for this can be understood in two ways. First, according to their formal rationes; and in this sense it is true, but it is to be understood thus: that they do not agree univocally in any grade of a superior nature, nor are they distinguished by other, inferior grades of essential perfection, as species are distinguished by grades of essential perfection diverse from the genus; but that the categories are distinct through diverse intrinsic modes of being, included in the same ratio of entity in which they agree analogically. And so it is true that they are diverse through their very entities, and not through other grades of perfection, and therefore diverse by themselves, which truly and properly is to be primarily diverse, and does not belong to species, which are said to differ through differences. In the second way it can be understood that they are primarily diverse according to real entities, so that several cannot be in the same real entity

p. 275

conuenire, & hoc modo apertè falsum est, vt de actione, & passione ostendimus, quarum rationes formales in eodem motu reali reperiuntur, sed nihilominus sic reperta, & ab intellectu distincta, primò diuersa sunt modo iam explicato.

agree; and in this way it is plainly false, as we have shown of action and passion, whose formal rationes are found in the same real motion; but nonetheless, so found and distinguished by the intellect, they are primarily diverse in the way already explained.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Vtrum prædicamenta sint decem, ita vt nec plura esse possint, nec pauciora.

Whether the categories are ten, so that there can be neither more nor fewer.

38 Quidam quos citat Plot. li. 1. Ænead. 6. vsque adeò prędicamenta multiplicarunt, vt infinita posuerint. Sed eorum sentẽtia hac ratione falsa probatur: Quia si verum est, de omnibus rebus à Deo factis, quòd in numero, pondere, & mensura sint ab eo factæ, vt sacræ literæ docent: quantò magis de generibus atquę speciebus, quibus essentię rerum continentur: sed ex his efficiuntur prędicamenta: ergo finita erunt.

38 Some, whom Plotinus cites, Ennead 6, bk. 1, multiplied the categories so far that they posited infinitely many. But their opinion is proved false by this argument: because if it is true of all things made by God that they were made by him in number, weight, and measure, as Sacred Scripture teaches, how much more of the genera and species in which the essences of things are contained; but the categories are made out of these; therefore they will be finite.

Sed inter eos, qui pro certo tenent finita esse, tres sunt opiniones diuersę. Prima eorum, qui plura quàm decem posuerunt: quos citat Simplicius in commento prędicamentorum; & potest probari hoc argumento: Pro causa efficiente ponitur prædicamentum actionis: & pro causa materiali receptiua eiusdem actionis, ponitur prædicamentum passionis: ergo pro aliis duabus causis, formali, & finali, debent poni duo alia prædicamenta, quia non est maior ratio, ob quam pro illis, quàm pro his, multiplicentur.

But among those who hold for certain that they are finite, there are three different opinions. The first is that of those who posited more than ten, whom Simplicius cites in his commentary on the Categories; and it can be proved by this argument: for the efficient cause the category of action is posited, and for the material cause receptive of the same action the category of passion is posited; therefore for the other two causes, formal and final, two other categories ought to be posited, because there is no greater reason why they should be multiplied for the former than for the latter.

Secunda opinio fuit eorum, qui pauciora, quàm decem posuerunt, sed diuisi sunt. Nam Plato in dialogis de ente, & vno, qui aliis nominibus vocantur, Sophista, seu Parmenides etiam tantùm prędicamentum videtur ponere vniuersalissimum entis, quod supremum genus rerum omnium vocat, sub quo particularia genera, & species collocantur.

The second opinion was that of those who posited fewer than ten; but they were divided. For Plato, in the dialogues on being and the one, which are called by other names the Sophist or Parmenides, seems to posit only one category, the most universal one of being, which he calls the supreme genus of all things, under which the particular genera and species are placed.

39 Probatur hoc arg. Ens est genus vniuersalissimum entis: ergo sub eo ordinari possunt genera omnia, & species: sed vna ordinatio sub vno primo genere, est vnum prædicamentum, ergo vnum tantum prædicamentum ponendum est, & non plura. Probatur maior, quia si ens nõ esset genus, ideo maximè quia est transcendens, & propter transcendentiam includitur in omnibus differentiis, contra propriam conditionem generis, quod debet esse extra rationem differentiarum: sed hæc ratio non est sufficiens: nam licèt ens vniuersaliter sumptum, prout cõmune est, tam entibus incompletis, quàm completis, hoc habeat, si tamen pro solis completis accipiatur, non includetur

39 This is proved by the argument: being is the most universal genus of being; therefore all genera and species can be ordered under it; but one ordering under one first genus is one category; therefore only one category is to be posited, and not more. The major is proved: because if being were not a genus, it would be chiefly because it is transcendent, and on account of its transcendence is included in all the differences, against the proper condition of a genus, which must be outside the ratio of the differences; but this reason is not sufficient: for although being taken universally, as it is common both to incomplete and to complete beings, has this, yet if it is taken for complete beings alone, it is not included S ij

p. 276

in differentiis, quia differentiæ non sunt entia completa, & eadem ratione, neque in modis intrinsecis, & ideo poterit esse vniuersalissimum genus omnium rerum completarum, ex quibus fit prædicamentum. Sed etiam si ens non posset esse genus omnium rerum, accidens saltem videretur esse genus omnium accidentium, & ideo vnum tantùm prædicamentum omnium accidentium esse ponendum, & aliud substantiæ, & ita duo tantùm, & hæc fuit sententia Zenocratis, & Andronici quos citat Simplicius vbi suprà.

in the differences, because the differences are not complete beings, and for the same reason neither in the intrinsic modes; and therefore it could be the most universal genus of all complete things, out of which the category is made. But even if being could not be the genus of all things, accident at least would seem to be the genus of all accidents, and therefore one category alone of all accidents would have to be posited, and another of substance, and so only two. And this was the opinion of Xenocrates and Andronicus, whom Simplicius cites in the place above.

40 Alij verò antiquiores Philosophi, quos citat Plotinus, lib. 1. Ænead. cap. 29. posuerunt quatuor, nempe substantiam, qualitatem, relationem, & modum rei. Et potest probari ex doctrina Arist. qui 1. lib. Topicorum, cap. 7. quatuor posuit prædicata: sed prædicamentum non est aliud, quàm prædicatorum ordinatio: ergo ex quatuor prædicatis non possunt plura, quàm quatuor fieri prædicamenta. Plotin. verò lib. 2. Æneade 6. cap. 18. quinque posuit, nempe, motum, quietem, identitatem, diuersitatem, & ens.

40 But other, more ancient Philosophers, whom Plotinus cites, Ennead bk. 1, ch. 29, posited four, namely substance, quality, relation, and the mode of the thing. And it can be proved from the doctrine of Aristotle, who in Topics bk. 1, ch. 7, posited four predicates; but a category is nothing other than an ordering of predicates; therefore out of four predicates no more than four categories can be made. Plotinus, however, in bk. 2 of Ennead 6, ch. 18, posited five, namely motion, rest, identity, diversity, and being.

Scaliger verò exercitatione 65. posuit nouem, quia prædicamentum vbi, vel prædicamentum quando, ad quantitatem reducit.

Scaliger, however, in exercitation 65, posited nine, because he reduces the category of where, or the category of when, to quantity.

Tertia opinio est eorum qui decem tantùm prædicamenta ponunt, ita vt nec plura sint, nec pauciora. Quam primus videtur insinuasse Archytas Tarentinus, Pythagoræ discipulus, & postea Arist. eam in scholas introduxit. Et hæc iam est communis & tenenda. quam secutus est D. Aug. lib. 10. Categoriarum, c. 8. & D. Th. non solùm eam sequitur, sed probat 3. lib. Phys. lect. 9. & 5. Meta. lect. 5.

The third opinion is that of those who posit only ten categories, so that there are neither more nor fewer. Archytas of Tarentum, the disciple of Pythagoras, seems to have been the first to suggest it, and afterwards Aristotle introduced it into the schools. And this is now common and to be held; St. Augustine followed it, bk. 10 of the Categories, ch. 8; and St. Thomas not only follows it but proves it, Phys. 3, lect. 9, and Metaph. 5, lect. 5.

41 Ratio autem D. Th. hęc est. Prima substantia, quę est indiuiduum substantiæ, vt Petrus, aut Ioannes, est fundamentum omnium prædicatorum essentialium: ergo secundùm diuersos modos essendi, & prædicandi de illa, numerus prædicamentorum sumi debet, sed vno ex tribus modis potest se habere prædicatum respectu illius. Nam vel pertinet ad quidditatem eius, vel extra illam est: & si ad quidditatem pertinet, est prædicamentum substantiæ: si verò est extra illam, vel sumitur ab aliquo ei formaliter inhęrente, & ex hoc distinguuntur tria prędicamenta: Quia prędicatum ab aliquo inhęrente sumptum, vel conuenit primę substantiæ modo absoluto, aut cum respectu ad aliud: Si modo absoluto, tunc vel ratione materiæ, & est prædicamentum quantitatis, vel ratione formæ, & est prædicamentum qualitatis: si verò conuenit cum respectu ad aliud est prædicamentum ad aliquid. Vel sumitur ab aliquo

41 Now the argument of St. Thomas is this. First substance, which is the individual of substance, as Peter or John, is the foundation of all essential predicates; therefore the number of the categories must be taken according to the diverse modes of being and of being predicated of it; but a predicate can stand in one of three ways with respect to it. For either it pertains to its quiddity, or it is outside it; and if it pertains to its quiddity, it is the category of substance; but if it is outside it, either it is taken from something formally inhering in it, and from this three categories are distinguished: because a predicate taken from something inhering belongs to the first substance either in an absolute mode or with a respect to another; if in an absolute mode, then either by reason of matter, and it is the category of quantity, or by reason of form, and it is the category of quality; but if it belongs with a respect to another, it is the category of relation. Or it is taken from something

p. 277

extrinseco, hoc est, non inhęrente primæ substantiæ, & ex hoc distinguuntur sex alia prædicamenta. Quia vel sumitur ab eo, quod est mensura extrinseca, quasi per modum continentis, quæ dicitur locus, & erit prædicamentum vbi. nam vbi, naturaliter saltem, dicitur esse in loco, aut circunscribi loco: aut ex tali dispositione, quam corpus habet in loco, quia stat, vel sedet, & est prædicamentum situs: Vel ab eo, quod est mensura extrinseca successiua, quale est tempus, & est prædicamentum quando, quod non videtur esse aliud quàm tempori accomodari, & ab eo mensurari. Si verò prædicatum accipiatur ab extrinseco, quod non est mensura, sed propriè dicitur habere: vt habere vestem aut arma, quod est vestimentum, aut armatum esse, efficitur prędicamentum habitus. Et, si accipiatur ab extrinseco, à quo procedit efficienter, est prędicamentum actionis. Et, si ab extrinseco, cui actio, aut effectus imprimitur, est prędicamentum passionis. Sequitur ergo decem tantùm esse prędicamenta, nec plura esse multiplicanda, quia ad hęc decem capita facilè reduci possunt omnia entia creata.

extrinsic, that is, not inhering in the first substance; and from this six other categories are distinguished. Because either it is taken from that which is an extrinsic measure, as it were by way of a container, which is called place, and it will be the category of where; for where, at least naturally, is said to be in place, or to be circumscribed by place; or from such a disposition as a body has in place, because it stands or sits, and it is the category of position. Or from that which is a successive extrinsic measure, such as time is, and it is the category of when, which seems to be nothing other than to be fitted to time and measured by it. But if the predicate is taken from something extrinsic which is not a measure, but is properly said to be had, as to have a garment or arms, which is to be clothed or armed, the category of habit is produced. And if it is taken from something extrinsic from which it proceeds efficiently, it is the category of action. And from something extrinsic on which the action or effect is impressed, it is the category of passion. It follows, therefore, that there are only ten categories, and that more are not to be multiplied, because all created beings can easily be reduced to these ten heads.

42 Ad arg. primæ opinionis respondet D. Tho. 3. lib. Phys. lect. 5. post medium, negando consequentiam, quòd pro causa formali, & finali, ponenda sint duo alia prædicamenta: quia causa formalis simul cum materiali, intrinsecæ partes substantiæ sunt, ex quibus componitur, & ideo ad prædicamentum eiusdem substantiæ reducuntur: causa autem finalis non habet specialem modum prædicamentalem, sicut efficiens, sed solùm mouet voluntatem, attrahendo eam ad sui amorem, & motio hæc extrinseca quædam ratio est, minimè prædicamentalis: quare pro ea non est multiplicandum prædicamentum, sicut pro efficiente, à quo egreditur actio, secundùm specialem modum prędicamentum constituentem.

42 To the argument of the first opinion St. Thomas replies, Phys. 3, lect. 5, after the middle, by denying the consequence that for the formal and final causes two other categories are to be posited: because the formal cause, together with the material, are intrinsic parts of the substance, of which it is composed, and therefore they are reduced to the category of the same substance; but the final cause does not have a special categorial mode, as the efficient cause does, but only moves the will, attracting it to love of itself; and this motion is a certain extrinsic ratio, not at all categorial; wherefore a category is not to be multiplied for it, as for the efficient cause, from which action issues according to a special mode constituting a category.

Ad argumenta de ente, & accidente, in fauorem Platonis, & aliorum Philosophorum, vnum vel duo tantùm prędicamenta ponentium, proposita: Respondetur, Ideo ens non esse genus omnium entium, nec accidens omnium accidentium, qua genus debet esse vniuocum: ens verò, & accidens non sunt vniuoca, sed analoga, vt superiùs probauimus: ergo non sunt genera.

To the arguments proposed concerning being and accident, in favor of Plato and the other Philosophers who posit only one or two categories, it is replied that being is not the genus of all beings, nor accident of all accidents, for this reason: because a genus must be univocal; but being and accident are not univocal but analogous, as we proved above; therefore they are not genera.

Ad arg. illorum, qui quatuor ponebant prædicamenta, propter quatuor prędicata Dialectica, quę posuit Arist. Respondeo, prędicata Dialectica diuerso modo sumi, ac prędicamenta, nempe ex ordine ad commune subiectum, cum quo possunt constituere propositionem Dialecticam: prędicamenta verò ex diuersis modis essendi vniuersalissimis, & ideo

To the argument of those who posited four categories on account of the four Dialectical predicates which Aristotle posited, I reply that the Dialectical predicates are taken in a different way from the categories: namely, by their order to a common subject with which they can constitute a Dialectical proposition; but the categories by the diverse most universal modes of being; and therefore a greater S iij

p. 278

maiorem extensionem habent, & maiorem numerum efficiunt, quàm prædicata, vt q. 5. vniuersalium probauimus.

extension they have, and they make up a greater number, than the predicates, as we proved in q. 5 on Universals.

Ad arg. tandem pro sententia Scaligeri de reductione prædicamenti, vbi ad locum, vel predicamenti, quando ad quantitatem: Respondemus diuersam rationem formalem habere, vbi, à loco. & quando, etiam à quantitate (vt suis locis probabitur) & ideo non posse ad prædicamentum quãtitatis reduci, sed distincta prædicamenta ab ea constituere. Quare nec pauciora sunt ponenda prædicamenta, quàm decem, nec plura.

To the argument, finally, for the opinion of Scaliger, about the reduction of the category of where to place, or of the category of when to quantity: we reply that where and when have a formal ratio different from place, and also from quantity (as will be proved in their own places), and therefore they cannot be reduced to the category of quantity, but constitute categories distinct from it. Wherefore neither fewer categories than ten are to be posited, nor more.

CAPVT V.

C H A P T E R V.

CAP. V. Continens prædicamentum substantiæ, cum expositione tex. — Containing the category of substance.

Continens prædicamentum substantiæ.

[…]

TEXTVS ARISTOT. Substantia autem est quæ propriè & principaliter, & maximè dicitur, quæ neque in subiecto aliquo est, neque de subiecto aliquo dicitur, &c.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. Substance, moreover, which is said properly, principally, and most of all, is that which neither is in any subject nor is said of any subject, etc.

Textus expositio.

E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

INtentum Arist. est explicare naturam substantiæ, quæ est primum prædicamentum. Diuiditur autem caput in tres partes. In prima, præsupposita diuisione substantiæ in primam, & secundam substantiam, explicat, quid sit prima, & quid sit secunda substantia. In secunda parte comparat primã & secundam substantiam inter se, atque etiam inter se secundas, & docet, quænã sit perfectior altera. In tertia enumerat sex proprietates substantiæ. Definitio primæ substantiæ his verbis continetur: Substantia, quæ propriè, principaliter & maximè dicitur, est quæ neque de subiecto aliquo dicitur, neque in subiecto aliquo est. Et tria illa verba, quæ propriè, principaliter, & maximè dicitur, ad definitum pertinẽt, non ad definitionem. Et sensus eorum est: Substantia non sub ratione communi, & impropriè accepta pro essentia rei, siue substantialis, aut accidẽtalis, sed propriè pro ente per se: & quæ ratione sui, hoc est, propria virtute substat, siue sustentat tam accidentia, quàm secundas substantias, & ideo maximè vocatur substantia: est illa, quæ neque de subiecto aliquo dicitur, id est, de quidditatiuè inferiori, nec in subiecto aliquo est per realem inhęrentiam. Vt Petrus propriè est substãtia, cùm sit ens per se, & propria virtute substet, siue sustentet, nõ solùm albedinem, & cætera accidẽtia, sed etiã secũdas substantias, quæ sunt prędicata vniuersalia superiora, vt hominẽ, animal, viuens & substantiã.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the nature of substance, which is T the first category. And the chapter is divided into three parts. In the first, presupposing the division of substance into first and second substance, he explains what first substance is and what second substance is. In the second part he compares first and second substance with each other, and also the second substances among themselves, and teaches which is more perfect than the other. In the third he enumerates six properties of substance. The definition of first substance is contained in these words: Substance which is said properly, principally, and most of all is that which neither is said of any subject nor is in any subject. And those three phrases, which is said properly, principally, and most of all, pertain to the definitum, not to the definition. And their sense is: substance, not under the common ratio and taken improperly for the essence of a thing, whether substantial or accidental, but properly for being per se; and which by reason of itself, that is, by its own power, stands under, or sustains, both the accidents and the second substances, and is therefore most of all called substance, is that which neither is said of any subject, that is, of a quidditatively inferior one, nor is in any subject through real inherence. As Peter is properly substance, since he is a being per se, and by his own power stands under, or sustains, not only whiteness and the other accidents, but also the second substances, which are the superior universal predicates, as man, animal, living, and substance.

p. 279

Et nõ dicitur de subiecto, quia nullũ habet inferius se quidditatiuè, de quo dicatur, nec est in subiecto, quia nõ inhęret alicui.

And he is not said of a subject, because he has nothing quidditatively inferior to himself of which he might be said; nor is he in a subject, because he does not inhere in anything.

2 Definit deinde secundum substantiam. Et in plurali dicẽs, Secundæ substantiæ sunt species, & genera, in quibus primæ substãtiæ insunt: Vt homo, & animal, sunt secundæ substantiæ, in quibus primæ substantiæ, vt Petrus & Ioannes insunt, id est, sub quibus, tanquam subiecta sub prædicatis continentur. Nam secũdæ substantiæ sunt in primis, tanquam superiora prædicata in subiectis quidditatiuè inferioribus, & ideo actu & formaliter. Primæ verò in secundis, tanquàm subiecta, de quibus prædicãtur, & propterea, non actu, & formaliter, sed quasi sub potentia earum, eo ferè modo, quo species dicuntur esse in genere.

2 He next defines second substance, and says in the plural: Second substances are the species and genera in which the first substances are: as man and animal are second substances, in which the first substances, as Peter and John, are, that is, under which they are contained as subjects under predicates. For the second substances are in the first as superior predicates in quidditatively inferior subjects, and therefore actually and formally; but the first are in the second as subjects of which they are predicated, and therefore not actually and formally, but as it were under their potency, in almost the same way in which the species are said to be in the genus.

Comparat in tertia parte primas substantias cum secundis, deinde secundas inter se. Et inter primam & secundas substãtias asserit, Primam esse perfectionem, probatque, quia substantia est quæ substat alijs, aut quæ sustentat alia: sed prima substantia propria virtute sustentat, & omnibus substat, id est non solùm accidentibus, sed ipsimet secundis substantiis, secunda verò substantia non substat ratione sui, sed ratione primæ, in qua, & à qua sustentatur, nec substat primis substantiis: ergo prima substantia est magis substantia, quàm secunda. Vt Petrus est magis substantia, quàm homo, quia ratione sui substat albedini, & reliquis accidentibus, atque etiam eidem homini, homo verò non ratione sui, sed ratione Petri in quo sustentatur, dicitur sustentare accidentia, nec Petrum ipsum sustentat, sed ab eo sustentatur.

In the second part he compares the first substances with the second, and then the second among themselves. And between first and second substance he asserts that the first is more perfect, and proves it: because substance is that which stands under others, or which sustains others; but first substance by its own power sustains and stands under all things, that is, not only the accidents but the second substances themselves, whereas second substance does not stand under by reason of itself, but by reason of the first, in which and by which it is sustained, nor does it stand under the first substances; therefore first substance is more substance than second. As Peter is more substance than man, because by reason of himself he stands under whiteness and the other accidents, and also under man itself; whereas man is said to sustain the accidents not by reason of itself but by reason of Peter, in whom it is sustained, nor does it sustain Peter himself, but is sustained by him.

Comparat deinde secundas substantias, & ait, Quòd si species comparetur cum genere, magis substantia est quàm genus: si verò cum alia specie, æqualis est ratio substantię in vtraque. Probat primum duplici argumento. Primò, quia illud est perfectius in quocunque ordine rerũ, quod magis accedit ad perfectissimum eiusdem ordinis. Et inter species animalis illa erit perfectior, quæ magis accedit ad humanam, quæ est perfectissima species talis generis. Sed species magis quàm genus accedit ad primam substãtiam, quæ est perfectissima, vt homo, magis accedit ad Petrum quàm animal: ergo erit perfectior substantia genere. Secundò inter substantias illa est perfectissima, quæ omnibus substat, ergo ex aliis illa erit perfectior altera quæ pluribus substat, sed species pluribus substat quàm genus, ergo erit perfectior illo. Probatur minor, quia substat omnibus quibus substat genus, hoc est, eisdẽ accidentibus, & eisdẽ prędicatis superioribus: & præterea substat eidẽ generi: genus verò nõ substat speciei. Gratia exẽpli, homo substat omnib.

He then compares the second substances, and says that if the species is compared with the genus, it is more substance than the genus; but if with another species, the ratio of substance is equal in both. He proves the first by a twofold argument. First, because that is more perfect in any order of things which approaches more closely to the most perfect of the same order: as among the species of animal that one will be more perfect which approaches more closely to the human, which is the most perfect species of such a genus. But the species approaches more closely than the genus to first substance, which is the most perfect, as man approaches Peter more closely than animal does; therefore it will be more perfect substance than the genus. Second, among substances that one is the most perfect which stands under all things; therefore of the others that one will be more perfect than another which stands under more; but the species stands under more than the genus; therefore it will be more perfect than it. The minor is proved: because it stands under all the things under which the genus stands, that is, the same accidents and the same superior predicates, and besides it stands under the genus itself; but the genus does not stand under the species. For example, man stands under all the accidents S iiij

p. 280

accidẽtibus, & omnibus prædicatis superioribus, quibus substat animal, & etiam ipsi animali, at verò animal non substat homini, sed in eo sustentatur.

and all the superior predicates under which animal stands, and also under animal itself; but animal does not stand under man, but is sustained in it.

3 Si verò species comparentur inter se, vt homo cum leone, neutra dicitur magis substantia quàm alia. Probat, quia vna non substat pluribus, sed eisdem prorsus accidentibus, & prædicatis superioribus substat: & vna non substat alteri, quia neutra in alia.

3 But if the species are compared among themselves, as man with lion, neither is said to be more substance than the other. He proves it: because one does not stand under more things than the other, but stands under exactly the same accidents and superior predicates; and one does not stand under the other, because neither is in the other.

In vltima parte capitis enumerat sex proprietates substantię, quarum prima est, Non esse in subiecto. Et de prima substantia euidentis esse ait, quia Petrus in nullo subiecto est, sed in se, & per se subsistit. Sed quòd conueniat secundis substantiis, probat duplici ratione. Prima, quia si in aliquo essent tanquam in subiecto, maximè in prima substantia, in qua inhærent omnia accidentia: sed in ea non possunt esse tanquam in subiecto, ergo in nullo. Probat minorem, quia secundæ substantiæ prædicantur de primis, tanquam de quidditatiuè inferioribus, ergo non sunt in illis, tanquam in subiectis. Probatur consequentia, quia esse in aliquo tanquam subiecto, est esse in eo per realem inhærentiam, sicut est accidens: sed secundæ substantiæ sunt de quidditate primarum, vt homo, & animal de quidditate Petri, ergo non sunt tanquam in subiecto.

In the last part of the chapter he enumerates six properties of substance, of which the first is not to be in a subject. And of first substance he says that it is evident, because Peter is in no subject, but subsists in himself and per se. But that it belongs to the second substances he proves by a twofold argument. First, because if they were in anything as in a subject, it would be chiefly in first substance, in which all the accidents inhere; but they cannot be in it as in a subject; therefore in nothing. He proves the minor: because second substances are predicated of the first as of quidditatively inferior things; therefore they are not in them as in subjects. The consequence is proved: because to be in something as in a subject is to be in it through real inherence, as an accident is; but the second substances are of the quiddity of the first, as man and animal are of the quiddity of Peter; therefore they are not as in a subject.

4 Secunda ratio est, Quæ sunt in aliquo tanquam in subiecto, vt accidentia, prædicantur quidem nomine de subiectis, sed ratione non possunt prædicari, quia ratio, est definitio, seu conceptus quidditatiuus: sed definitio albi non est definitio hominis, ergo non prædicatur de illo nomine & ratione, sicut prædicantur vniuoca, sed solo nomine: at verò secundæ substantiæ prædicantur de primis nomine, & ratione, vt homo de Petro, quia definitio hominis, est definitio Petri, ergo non possunt esse in eis tanquam in subiecto. Et ideò non solùm primis substantiis conuenit hæc proprietas, videlicet, Non esse in subiecto, sed etiam secundis.

4 The second argument is: things that are in something as in a subject, as accidents, are indeed predicated of their subjects in name, but they cannot be predicated in ratio, because the ratio is the definition, or quidditative concept; but the definition of white is not the definition of man; therefore it is not predicated of it in name and ratio, as univocals are predicated, but in name alone. But second substances are predicated of the first in name and ratio, as man of Peter, because the definition of man is the definition of Peter; therefore they cannot be in them as in a subject. And therefore this property, namely not to be in a subject, belongs not only to the first substances but also to the second.

5 Secunda proprietas Substantiæ est, vniuocè prædicari: quod non intelligitur de prima substantia. Et ideo certum est hanc proprietatem solùm conuenire secundis. Sed non solùm conuenire ait generibus & speciebus, quæ verè & propriè sunt secundæ substantiæ, sed etiam differentiis earum: quia de quibus prædicatur species vniuocè, necesse est etiam prædicetur eius differentia. Quòd verò secundis substantiis, & differentiis conueniat, probat Arist. hac ratione, Vniuoca sunt, quorum nomen est commune, ratio verò substantiæ eadem: sed nomen secundæ substantiæ commune est primis, de quibus prædicatur, &

5 The second property of Substance is to be predicated univocally, which is not understood of first substance. And therefore it is certain that this property belongs only to the second. But he says that it belongs not only to the genera and species, which are truly and properly second substances, but also to their differences: because of whatever the species is predicated univocally, its difference too must necessarily be predicated. And that it belongs to the second substances and to the differences Aristotle proves by this argument: Univocals are those whose name is common, and the ratio of substance the same; but the name of second substance is common to the first, of which it is predicated, and

p. 281

definitio eadem, vt nomen homo commune ex Petro, & Ioanni, & definitio eius etiam est eadem, atque illis communis, vt notum est: ergo prædicatur de eis vniuocè.

definition is the same: as the name man is common to Peter and John, and its definition is also the same and common to them, as is well known; therefore it is predicated of them univocally.

Tertia proprietas est: Hoc aliquid significare. Quid autem intelligat, per, Hoc aliquid: certum est intelligere substantiam singularem, & per se subsistentem, & ideo asserit, quòd licèt videatur hæc proprietas conuenire secundis substantiis, quia homo, & animal videntur significare aliquid per se subsistens, solùm tamen conuenit primis. Secundæ verò non significant hoc aliquid, sed potiùs Quale quid. Quale quidem significant, quia sunt quasi formæ vniuersales primarum substantiarum: & formæ videntur habere similitudinem qualitatis, cuius vna species est forma, & figura: sed quia sunt prædicata substantialia, dicuntur significare Quale quid.

The third property is: To signify a this something. As for what he understands by this something: it is certain that he understands a singular substance, subsisting per se; and therefore he asserts that, although this property seems to belong to second substances, because man and animal seem to signify something subsisting per se, it nevertheless belongs only to first substances. Second substances, however, do not signify a this something, but rather a what-like [quale quid]. They signify a what-like, because they are as it were universal forms of first substances, and forms seem to bear a likeness to quality, one species of which is form and figure; but because they are substantial predicates, they are said to signify a what-like.

6 Quarta proprietas substantiæ est, Nullum habere contrarium. vt Petro & Ioanni nihil contrarium esse potest. Et hæc proprietas tam primis, quàm secundis substantiis conuenit, sed nõ quarto modo (inquit Aristoteles) quia aliis etiam, vt quantitati est communis.

6 The fourth property of substance is: To have no contrary, as nothing can be contrary to Peter and John. And this property belongs both to first and to second substances, but not in the fourth mode (says Aristotle), because it is common to others also, as to quantity.

Quinta proprietas est, Non suscipere magis, & minus, quemadmodum suscipiunt qualitates: nam vnum calidum magis est calidum quàm alterum, quia plus habet gradus intensionis: hoc autem gradus non habet substantia, & ideo dicitur non suscipere magis & minus,

The fifth property is: Not to admit of more and less, in the way that qualities admit of them: for one hot thing is more hot than another, because it has more degrees of intension; but substance does not have these degrees, and therefore it is said not to admit of more and less.

Vltima proprietas substantiæ est, Vt vna numero permanens contraria suscipere possit: vt Petrus idem numero permanens, modò potest esse calidus, & postea frigidus. Hæc autem proprietas non videtur conuenire secundis substantiis, sed solùm primis, quia solùm prima substantia est vna numero, secunda verò vna specie, vel genere, ergo quòd vna numero perseuerans, suscipiat in se contraria, soli primæ conuenire potest.

The last property of substance is: That, remaining one in number, it can receive contraries: as Peter, remaining the same in number, can now be hot and afterwards cold. But this property does not seem to belong to second substances, but only to first ones, because only first substance is one in number, while second substance is one in species or in genus; therefore that, persevering one in number, it should receive contraries in itself can belong only to first substance.

7 Sed aduersus hanc proprietatem proponit arg. Aristot. Quia videtur conuenire alteri, nempe propositioni, quæ vna numero permanens, de vera fit falsa, & de falsa fit vera. Vt hæc propositio. Petrus sedet, vera est eo sedente, stante verò falsa, & permanet eadem, ergo conuenit illi, quòd vna numero permanens suscipiat contraria. Et respondet duobus modis. Primò, quòd licèt suscipiat contraria, non tamen eodem modo, ac substantia, sed diuerso: Nam substantia suscipit contraria per sui mutationem, quia suscipit ea in se formaliter, & ideo mutatur ea suscipiens. Sed propositio sine sui mutatione, sed solùm per mutationem alterius extrinseci, nempe rei, de qua aliquid enuntiatur. Dum ergo dicitur, proprium esse

7 But against this property Aristotle proposes an argument: because it seems to belong to something else, namely to a proposition, which, remaining one in number, from true becomes false and from false becomes true. As this proposition, Peter is sitting, is true while he sits, but false while he stands, and it remains the same; therefore it belongs to it that, remaining one in number, it receives contraries. And he replies in two ways. First, that although it receives contraries, it does not do so in the same way as substance, but in a different way: for substance receives contraries through a change of itself, because it receives them in itself formally, and therefore the thing receiving them is changed. But a proposition does so without a change of itself, and only through a change of something else extrinsic, namely of the thing about which something is enunciated. When, therefore, it is said that it is proper to substance

p. 282

substantiæ suscipere contraria, intelligitur per sui mutationem, & hoc modo. nec propositioni, neque aliis conuenit. Secunda solutio eadem ferè est, negat enim propositionem suscipere contraria, quia suscipere contraria est subiectum moueri ab vno in alterum, amittendo vnum, & acquirendo alterum. Propositio verò, dum ex vera fit falsa, non mouetur à veritate in falsitatem, nec amittit vnam, & adquirit alteram, sed mutatio solùm se tenet ex parte rei significatæ, & ideo propositio non dicitur suscipere contraria.

to receive contraries, this is understood as through a change of itself, and in this way it belongs neither to a proposition nor to anything else. The second solution is almost the same: for he denies that a proposition receives contraries, because to receive contraries is for a subject to be moved from one to the other, losing the one and acquiring the other. But a proposition, while from true it becomes false, is not moved from truth to falsity, nor does it lose the one and acquire the other; rather, the change holds only on the side of the thing signified, and therefore the proposition is not said to receive contraries.

QUESTION I

Quodnam sit supremum genus prædicamenti substantiæ.

Which is the supreme genus of the category of substance.

VIdetur nullum habere genus supremum, quod sic probatur: Si haberet aliquod, maximè esset substantia, sed hæc non potest esse genus, ergo nullum habebit. Minorem probo, quia si substantia in communi, vt ab omnibus substantiis abstracta, esset supremum genus huius prædicamenti, sub quo comprehenderentur omnes substantiæ, & ideò vnum tantùm esset prædicamentum pro eis constituendum, sequeretur, etiam accidens in communi, esse supremum genus omnium accidentium, & ita vnum prædicamentum constituere, sub quo ponãtur accidentia omnia: quare duo tantùm prædicamenta erunt. Probatur consequentia, quia sicut substantia vniuersaliter sumpta, prout communis est completis, & partialibus, transcendens est, & in vltimis differentiis includitur, nec est vniuoca respectu omnium, sed analoga, quia prius de completis substantiis: posterius verò de partibus, & cum intrinseca dependentia ab illis dicitur, & ideo non potest esse genus, quia genus debet esse vniuocum, & non transcendens, ne includatur in vltimis differentiis, sed extra rationem earum sit. Si tamen pro substantia in communi accipiatur nec erit transcendens, quia non includetur in differentiis, nec analoga, sed vniuoca, quia æqualiter de omnibus dicetur, & ideo poterit esse genus. Eodem modo accidens quamuis vniuersaliter sumptum, sit transcendens, & analogum, & ideo non possit esse genus, si tamen pro completo tantùm sumatur, non erit transcendens, neque analogum, sed vniuocum, quia æqualiter dicetur de omnibus accidentibus completis, & ideo poterit esse genus.

t seems that it has no supreme genus, which is proved thus: If it had Ione, it would above all be substance; but this cannot be a genus; therefore it will have none. I prove the minor: because if substance in common, as abstracted from all substances, were the supreme genus of this category, under which all substances would be comprehended, and therefore only one category were to be constituted for them, it would follow that accident in common also is the supreme genus of all accidents, and so constitutes one category, under which all accidents would be placed: wherefore there will be only two categories. The consequence is proved: because, just as substance taken universally, as it is common to complete and partial substances, is transcendent, and is included in the ultimate differences, and is not univocal with respect to all, but analogous, because it is said first of complete substances and afterwards of parts, and with an intrinsic dependence on the former, and therefore cannot be a genus, because a genus must be univocal and not transcendent, lest it be included in the ultimate differences, but must be outside their ratio; if, however, it is taken for substance in common, it will neither be transcendent, because it will not be included in the differences, nor analogous, but univocal, because it will be said equally of all, and therefore it will be able to be a genus. In the same way accident, although taken universally it is transcendent and analogous, and therefore cannot be a genus, yet if it is taken only for complete accident, it will not be transcendent, nor analogous, but univocal, because it will be said equally of all complete accidents, and therefore it will be able to be a genus.

Pro solutione huius quæstionis notandum est, Quinque esse acceptiones substantiæ, vt colligitur ex doctrina Arist. c. præsenti,

For the solution of this question it should be noted that there are five acceptations of substance, as is gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle in the present chapter,

p. 283

& 5. Meta. c. 8. tex. 15. atque etiam ex D. Th. in Commentariis eiusdem loci, & potentia, q. 9. art. 1. ad 4. & 5.

and Metaph. 5, ch. 8, text 15, and also from St. Thomas in his Commentaries on the same place, and On Power, q. 9, a. 1, ad 4 and 5.

Primò accipitur pro Essentia rei. Et hęc acceptio communis est accidẽtibus, in quibus etiam reperitur essentia, & ideo non est propria, neque vniuoca: sed analoga: quia nihil reale potest dari commune, & vniuocum substantiæ, & accidentibus.

First, it is taken for the Essence of a thing. And this acceptation is common to accidents, in which an essence is also found, and therefore it is not proper, nor univocal, but analogous: because nothing real can be given that is common and univocal to substance and accidents.

Secundò accipitur substantia, pro Ente per se: in quo duo includuntur: vnum negatiuum, quod est non esse in alio: Aliud positiuũ, quod est esse entitatem, adeò perfectam, cui debetur existentia, & subsistentia per se, ita vt sine adminiculo alterius sustentetur. Vnde acceptio hæc duas includit. Primam, & quæ in ordine erit secunda, qua accipitur sustantia pro ente, quod non inhæret alteri, vel vt dici solet, prout distinguitur contra accidens, quod constat inhærere. Et hæc etiam acceptio communis est, & analoga, & ideo impropria, quia sub ea cõprehendit substantias, non solùm completas substantias, sed etiam incompletas, seu partiales, de quibus verum est, quod non inhæreant. Nam licèt sint in toto: non tamen per realem inhærentiam, sed componendo illud substantialiter. Substantia verò de completis, & incompletis non vniuocè, sed analogicè dicitur.

Second, substance is taken for Being per se, in which two things are included: one negative, which is not to be in another; the other positive, which is to be an entity so perfect that existence and subsistence per se are due to it, so that it is sustained without the support of another. Hence this acceptation includes two. The first, which in order will be the second, in which substance is taken for a being that does not inhere in another, or, as is commonly said, as it is distinguished against accident, which is established to inhere. And this acceptation too is common and analogous, and therefore improper, because under it it comprehends not only complete substances but also incomplete or partial ones, of which it is true that they do not inhere. For although they are in the whole, yet they are not so by real inherence, but by composing it substantially. And substance is said of complete and incomplete substances not univocally but analogically.

Tertia acceptio in ordine est, pro illo positiuo, quod includit eadem particula per se, nempe pro entitate completa, cui debetur existentia, & subsistentia per se. Sed adhuc acceptio hæc communis est, & analoga, & ideo non ita propria, quia comprehendit substantiam finitam, & infinitam, creatam, & increatam, quibus nihil potest esse commune vniuocum: nam substantia creata intrinsecam dependentiam & attributionem dicit ad increatam, quæ est Deus. Quare substantia completa, cui debetur existentia, & subsistentia per se, analoga erit respectu vtriusque.

The third acceptation in order is for that positive element which the particle per se includes, namely for a complete entity to which existence and subsistence per se are due. But this acceptation is still common and analogous, and therefore not so proper, because it comprehends finite and infinite, created and uncreated substance, to which nothing univocal can be common: for created substance implies an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to uncreated substance, which is God. Wherefore complete substance, to which existence and subsistence per se are due, will be analogous with respect to both.

10 Quarto modo accipitur pro substantia completa, & finita, in cõmuni, hoc est, abstracta à particularibus substantiis completis, & finitis Et hoc modo sumpta, est supremum genus prædicamenti substantiæ, quod diuiditur in corpoream, & in incorpoream prima diuisione, ex qua resultat secundum genus corporis, quod diuiditur in viuens, & non viuens, & rursus, viuens, in sensibile, & in insensibile, & tandem, sensibile, quod est animal, in hominem, equum, & leonem Ex his diuisionibus, resultat, prædicamentum substantiæ, his prædicatis constans: substantia, corpus, viuens, animal, homo, vsque ad Petrum.

10 In a fourth way it is taken for complete and finite substance in common, that is, abstracted from particular complete and finite substances. And taken in this way it is the supreme genus of the category of substance, which is divided into corporeal and incorporeal by the first division, from which there results the second genus, body, which is divided into living and non-living; and again living into sensible and insensible; and finally sensible, which is animal, into man, horse, and lion. From these divisions there results the category of substance, consisting of these predicates: substance, body, living thing, animal, man, down to Peter.

Vltima acceptio est, pro completa substantia secundùm quandam proprietatem eius, quæ est substare accidentibus, aut etiam prædicatis superioribus quidditatiuis. Substare verò idem significat

The last acceptation is for complete substance according to a certain property of it, which is to stand under accidents, or also under superior quidditative predicates. But to stand under [substare] signifies the same

p. 284

quod sustentare illa. Et substantiam hoc modo sumptam diuisit Arist. in principio huius capitis in primam & secundam. Sed in hac acceptione non potest prædicamentum constituere, quia non sumitur essentialiter.

as to sustain them. And substance taken in this way Aristotle divided, at the beginning of this chapter, into first and second. But in this acceptation it cannot constitute a category, because it is not taken essentially.

Ex his colligitur conclusio hęc, per quam respondetur quęstioni: Prædicamentum substantiæ habet supremum genus determinatum, & hoc est substantia completa, & finita, in communi considerata. Probatur hoc arg. Supremum genus prædicamenti est illud, à quo deriuantur genera, & species eiusdem prædicamenti, & ipsum non deriuatur ab alio: sed has conditiones habet substantia completa, & finita: ergo est supremum genus prædicamenti substantiæ. Probatur minor, quia hęc non deriuatur ab alio prædicato superiori vniuoco, sed immediatè continet sub ente analogo, & ab ea deriuantur genera, & species, ex quibus efficitur recta linea prædicamenti, vt exemplis probatum est.

From these things this conclusion is gathered, by which the question is answered: The category of substance has a determinate supreme genus, and this is complete and finite substance considered in common. This is proved by an argument: The supreme genus of a category is that from which the genera and species of the same category are derived, and which itself is not derived from another; but complete and finite substance has these conditions; therefore it is the supreme genus of the category of substance. The minor is proved: because this is not derived from another superior univocal predicate, but is immediately contained under analogous being, and from it are derived the genera and species out of which the straight line of the category is made, as has been proved by examples.

11 Ad arg. respondetur, negando consequentiam, quia diuersa ratio de substantia, & accidenti, in duobus: In primo quidem, Nam substantia dicit particularem, & determinatum modum essendi, accidens verò plures modos essendi dicit, nullum determinans, sed confusa ratione. Secundò, accidens quantumcunque abstrahatur, aut sumatur pro solo accidẽti incompleto, analogum est, propter intrinsecam attributionẽ ad substantiam, cum qua significat accidentia omnia, & ideò non potest esse genus, nec determinatum genus vnius prædicamenti. Substantia verò sumpta pro completa, & finita, vniuocam rationem, atque communem dicit respectu omnium substantiarum completarum, ex quibus fit prædicamentum, & propterea potest esse supremum genus determinati prædicamenti.

11 To the argument the reply is by denying the consequence, because the ratio of substance and of accident is different in two respects: In the first, indeed, because substance implies a particular and determinate mode of being, whereas accident implies several modes of being, determining none, but with a confused ratio. Second, accident, however much it is abstracted, or taken for incomplete accident alone, is analogous, on account of its intrinsic attribution to substance, together with which it signifies all accidents, and therefore it cannot be a genus, nor the determinate genus of one category. But substance, taken for complete and finite substance, implies a univocal and common ratio with respect to all complete substances, out of which the category is made, and therefore it can be the supreme genus of a determinate category.

QUESTION II

Vtrùm Deus ponatur in prædicamento substantiæ.

Whether God is placed in the category of substance.

12 QVamuis ex his, quæ in quæstione præcedenti diximus, nempe substantiam completam, & finitam, esse supremum genus prædicamenti substantiæ, colligi posset, Deum qui substantia infinita est, non pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum, plures tamen eum in prædicamento esse affirmãt, & ideo specialem disputationem postulat.

12 Although from what we said in the preceding question, namely that complete and finite substance is the supreme genus of the category of substance, it could be gathered that God, who is infinite substance, does not pertain to this category, yet many affirm that he is in the category, and therefore it calls for a special disputation.

Tenet igitur prima opinio, Deum esse in prædicamento substantiæ. Ita Greg. & Gab. in 1. d. 8. quæst. 3. Holcoth quæst. 6. & Ioannes Baconius d. 9. qu. 1. & probatur testimonio Arist. 4. Topicorum ca. 2. loco 17. vbi ait, Deum esse in genere

The first opinion, then, holds that God is in the category of substance. So Gregory of Rimini and Gabriel on 1, d. 8, q. 3; Holcot, q. 6; and John Baconthorpe, d. 9, q. 1; and it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics 4, ch. 2, place 17, where he says that God is in the genus of animal

p. 285

animalis & separari ab homine per propriam differentiam immortale, his verbis, Si differentiam, vt genus assignauit, vt si immortale, genus Dei: nam differentia est animalis immortale. Et loco secundo eiusdem capitis: Si differentiam in specie posuit, vt immortale id ipsum quod est, Deum esse, &c.

and is separated from man by the proper difference immortal, in these words: If he has assigned the difference as the genus, as if immortal were the genus of God: for immortal is a difference of animal. And in the second place of the same chapter: If he has placed the difference in the species, as that immortal is that very thing which God is, etc.

Deinde probatur ratione. Primò, quia si aliquid obstaret quo minus Deus esset in prædicamento, maximè, esse substantiam infinitam: sed hoc non obstat, ergo nihil. Probo minorem, quia esse aliquid infinitum non obstat quo minus sit in aliis prædicamentis: vt si daretur linea infinita, esset in prædicamento substantiæ & si daretur calor infinitè perfectus, secundùm intentionem, esset in prædicamento qualitatis: ergo etiam si Deus sit substantia infinita, poterit esse in prædicamento substantiæ.

Next it is proved by reason. First, because if anything stood in the way of God’s being in the category, it would above all be that he is infinite substance; but this does not stand in the way; therefore nothing does. I prove the minor: because to be something infinite does not prevent a thing from being in the other categories: as, if an infinite line were given, it would be in the category of quantity; and if a heat infinitely perfect according to intension were given, it would be in the category of quality; therefore even if God is infinite substance, he will be able to be in the category of substance.

13 Secundò, per mysterium incarnationis Deus factus est homo vniuocè nobiscum; ergo verè & propriè est in specie humana tanquam indiuiduum huius naturæ: & etiam sub genere animalis; sed quod est sub genere, & specie, est etiam in prædicamento, quod ex generibus atque speciebus fit, ergo Deus verè & propriè est in prædicamento substantiæ per humanam naturam, quam assumpsit.

13 Second, through the mystery of the incarnation God was made man univocally with us; therefore he is truly and properly in the human species as an individual of this nature, and also under the genus of animal; but what is under a genus and a species is also in the category, which is made of genera and species; therefore God is truly and properly in the category of substance through the human nature which he assumed.

Secunda opinio negat Deum, vt Deus est, in prædicamento collocari. Et hæc est communis, & vera, quam ex Philosophis tenuerunt Mercurius Trismegistus in Epimandro c. 1. Auerroes, disputatione 7. & con. Algazelem c. vltimo. Auicenna 8. Meta. cap. 4. & cum his omnes interpretes Ari. Ex sanctis patribus August. lib. de Cognitione veræ vitæ, c. 3. Anselmus in Monologio c. 26. & cum eis Boëtius 1. lib. de Trinitate, cap. 6. Ex scholasticis verò omnes, pręter Nominales illos pro opposita sententia citatos. Ita mag. in 1. d. 8. & ibidem Albertus Magnus, Scotus d. bona. Richar. Duran. Ægidius, D. Tho. 1. lib. contra gentes cap. 24. & 25. & ibidem Ferra. & 1. par. q. 3. art. 5. & ibid. Caiet. Alexand. Alẽsis 1. par. q. 48. memb. 5. art. 2. & 3.

The second opinion denies that God, as God, is placed in the category. And this is the common and true opinion, which among the Philosophers was held by Hermes Trismegistus in the Pimander, ch. 1; Averroes, disputation 7, and against Algazel, the last chapter; Avicenna, Metaph. 8, ch. 4; and with these all the interpreters of Aristotle. Among the holy Fathers, Augustine in the book On the Knowledge of the True Life, ch. 3; Anselm in the Monologion, ch. 26; and with them Boethius, On the Trinity bk. 1, ch. 6. And among the scholastics, all except those Nominalists cited for the opposite opinion. So the Master on 1, d. 8, and in the same place Albert the Great, Scotus, Bonaventure, Richard, Durandus, Giles of Rome; St. Thomas, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 24 and 25, and there the Ferrariensis; and 1 p., q. 3, a. 5, and there Cajetan; Alexander of Hales, 1 p., q. 48, memb. 5, a. 2 and 3.

Et probatur duplici ratione. Prima, quia Deus ita est purus actus, vt tam essentiale sit ei suum esse actuale, quàm sua essentia: ergo nihil est potentiale in Deo, quod per modum contrahibilis concipi possit. Quare repugnat in Deo esse genus. Probatur vltima consequentia, quia genus essentialiter est contrahibile: sed quod non est in genere, non est in prædicamento, ergo repugnat Deum esse in prædicamento.

And it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because God is pure act in such a way that his actual being is as essential to him as his essence; therefore there is nothing potential in God that could be conceived after the manner of something contractible. Wherefore it is repugnant that there be a genus in God. The last consequence is proved: because a genus is essentially contractible; but what is not in a genus is not in a category; therefore it is repugnant that God be in a category.

Secundò, quia si Deus esset in prędicamento, aliquod genus daretur commune Deo & creaturis: sed nullum genus potest dari eis commune: ergo non erit Deus in prędicamento.

Second, because if God were in a category, some genus would be given common to God and creatures; but no genus can be given common to them; therefore God will not be in a category. The

p. 286

Minorem probo, quia genus debet esse vniuocum: sed nihil potest dari commune vniuocum Deo, & creaturis, propter intrinsecam dependentiam, & attributionem creaturarum ad Deum, qua non possunt intelligi: ergo nec potest dari genus cõmune.

minor I prove: because a genus must be univocal; but nothing univocal can be given common to God and creatures, on account of the intrinsic dependence and attribution of creatures to God, without which they cannot be understood; therefore neither can a common genus be given.

Ad testimonium Arist. Respondetur, Deorum nomine non veros Deos intelligere: cùm certum fuerit apud ipsum, vnum tantùm esse, sed substantias quasdam superiores, subtilissima corpora habentes, quas plures philosophi rationales esse dixerunt, homine quidem perfectiores, quia immortales: cum eo tamen conuenientes sub genere animalis rationalis, distingui verò per differentias, mortale & immortale, de quibus asserit, quòd in pradicamẽto sint collocãda, si verum est, quòd dẽtur.

To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is that by the name of gods he does not mean true gods, since it was certain for him that there is only one, but certain superior substances having most subtle bodies, which many philosophers said were rational, more perfect indeed than man, because immortal, yet agreeing with him under the genus of rational animal, and distinguished by the differences mortal and immortal; and of these he asserts that they are to be placed in the category, if it is true that they are given.

14 Ad primum arg. Cõcessa maiori, distinguenda est minor: quia esse aliquid infinitum, dupliciter intelligi potest, aut secundùm essentiam: aut secundùm aliquam rationẽ accidentalem extensionis, aut intentionis. Et infinitum primo modo, non potest esse in aliquo prędicamento, ideóque Deus excluditur à prædicamento, quia est ens infinitum secundùm essentiam. Infinitum secundo modo ad prædicamentum pertinere potest: quia licèt sit infinitum secundùm rationem accidentalem, finitum tamen est secundùm essentiam, per quam in prædicamento collocari debet, & non ratione accidentis. Et talis esset linea infinita, si daretur, aut calor infinitus secundùm intentionem: nam linea finitã haberet essentiam quantitatis continuę, & calor etiam finitam essentiam qualitatis: licèt illa haberet infinitam extensionem longitudinis accidentalem, & calor infinitam intensionem gradualem: quæ accidentia infinita non obstarent, quo minus in suis prædicamentis collocarentur. Et huius ratio est, quia prędicamenta constituuntur ex rerum essentiis, non ex earum accidentibus.

14 To the first argument: granting the major, the minor is to be distinguished: because to be something infinite can be understood in two ways: either according to essence, or according to some accidental ratio of extension or of intension. And what is infinite in the first way cannot be in any category; and therefore God is excluded from the category, because he is a being infinite according to essence. What is infinite in the second way can pertain to a category: because although it is infinite according to an accidental ratio, yet it is finite according to essence, by reason of which it must be placed in the category, and not by reason of the accident. And such would be an infinite line, if it were given, or a heat infinite according to intension: for the line would have the finite essence of continuous quantity, and the heat too the finite essence of quality, although the former would have an infinite accidental extension of length, and the heat an infinite gradual intension; and these infinite accidents would not prevent them from being placed in their categories. And the reason of this is that the categories are constituted from the essences of things, not from their accidents.

15 Ad secundum arg. Respondeo, Christum verè, & propriè esse in genere, & specie, atque etiam in prędicamento, ratione humanæ naturæ, & consequenter verbum Diuinum, cui natura humana vnita est in persona, per illam ponitur in prædicamento substantiæ. Sed ex hoc non sequitur, quòd verbum Diuinum ratione diuinæ naturę, aut diuinę personę ponatur in prędicamento. Sic igitur loquendum est in hac materia, vt absolutè dicamus. Primò, Christum esse in prædicamento substantiæ, quia simpliciter, & absolutè est homo, & hic homo. Secundò, Deum etiam absolutè esse in prædicamento substantię. quia absolutè verum est, Deum esse hominem, sed quia hoc habet ratione humanę naturę, & non ratione naturę diuinę aut diuinę personę, negandum est, Deum vt Deus

15 To the second argument I reply that Christ is truly and properly in a genus and a species, and also in the category, by reason of his human nature; and consequently the divine Word, to which the human nature is united in person, is placed through it in the category of substance. But from this it does not follow that the divine Word is placed in the category by reason of the divine nature or of the divine person. Thus, then, one must speak in this matter, so that we say absolutely: First, that Christ is in the category of substance, because simply and absolutely he is a man, and this man. Second, that God too is absolutely in the category of substance, because it is absolutely true that God is a man; but because he has this by reason of the human nature, and not by reason of the divine nature or the divine person, it must be denied that God as God

p. 287

est, vel, vt persona est diuina, esse in prædicamento: Et hoc modo intelligitur communis, & vera opinio, quam sequimur, quæ non minùs vera est modò, quàm fuit priusquam Deus fieret homo, quia ea, quæ conueniunt Deo post incarnationem, pertinentia ad humanam naturam, non conueniunt ratione sui sed ratione eiusdem humanæ naturæ, & ideo nihil ponunt in Deo, vt Deus est, quod non habuerit semper. Sed quæret aliquis, An licèt Deus non sit per se prædicamento. reductiuè saltem in aliquo possit collocari. Cui respondet Fonseca, posse quidem in illis prædicamentis, quæ extrinsecam denominationem continent, vt prædicamento, vbi, in prædicamento actionis, & habitus. Ego verò nec reductiuè in prædicamento esse admitto, quia ita tenet D. Tho. 1. p. qu. 3. art. 5. & cum eo Richardus in 1. dist. 8. artic. 4. qu. 1. Probatque hac ratione: Res illa dicitur pertinere ad aliquod prædicamentum reductiuè, quæ deficit à ratione perfecta, & completa talis prædicamenti, vt partes, & modi, sic enim punctum pertinet ad prædicamentum quantitatis, & brachium ad prædicamentum substantiæ: sed Deus excedit potiùs in infinitum omnes rationes prædicamentales, ergo non est reductiuè in aliquo prædicamento. Quod D. Augustinus his verbis docuit. 5. lib. de Trinitate cap. 1. Sic intelligamus Deum (si possumus) sine qualitate bonum, sine quantitate magnum, sine intelligentia creatorem, sine situ præsentem, sine habitu omnia continentem, sine loco vbique totum, sine tempore sempiternum, sine vlla sui mutatione mirabilia facientem, nihilque patientem.

is, or as he is a divine person, in the category. And in this way is understood the common and true opinion which we follow, which is no less true now than it was before God became man: because the things that belong to God after the incarnation, pertaining to the human nature, do not belong to him by reason of himself but by reason of that same human nature, and therefore they posit nothing in God, as he is God, which he did not always have. But someone will ask whether, although God is not per se in a category, he can at least be placed reductively in some category. To which Fonseca replies that he can indeed be in those categories which contain an extrinsic denomination, as in the category of where, in the category of action, and of having. But I do not admit that he is in a category even reductively, because so holds St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 3, a. 5, and with him Richard on 1, d. 8, a. 4, q. 1. And he proves it by this argument: That thing is said to pertain to some category reductively which falls short of the perfect and complete ratio of such a category, as parts and modes; for so the point pertains to the category of quantity, and the arm to the category of substance; but God rather exceeds all the categorial rationes infinitely; therefore he is not reductively in any category. Which St. Augustine taught in these words, On the Trinity bk. 5, ch. 1: Thus let us understand God (if we can) as good without quality, great without quantity, a creator without need, present without position, containing all things without having, whole everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making changeable things without any change of himself, and undergoing nothing.

Hæc August. ex quibus intelligitur, etiam denominationes extrinsecas aliquorum prædicamentorum, non propriè, sed abusiuè Deo conuenire, ideo non eadem ratione, aut vniuocè in eisdem conuenire cum creaturis, & consequenter propter illas, nec reductiuè pertinere ad aliquod prædicamentum,

Thus Augustine; from which it is understood that even the extrinsic denominations of some categories belong to God not properly but improperly, and therefore not for the same reason, nor univocally, do they belong to him and to creatures in common; and consequently that on account of them he does not pertain even reductively to any category.

QUESTION III

Vtrùm Angeli & corpora cœlestia sint in prædicamento substantiæ.

Whether angels and the heavenly bodies are in the category of substance.

16 CIrca corpora cœlestia, & Angelos in ordine ad cõstitutionem prædicamentalem, Prima opinio fuit Commẽtatoris 10. Meta. ca. vltimo, commento 16. excludentem vtrasque substantias à prædicamento. Quam sententiam secuti sunt Ioannes Gandauensis 18 Metap. quæst. 22. Niphus ibidem quæst. 9 & quantùm ad solos Angelos. Plotinus lib. 1. Æneade 6. Ægidius Romanus in commentariis huius prædicamenti, &

16 Concerning the heavenly bodies and the angels, in relation to the categorial constitution, the first opinion was that of the Commentator, Metaph. 10, last chapter, comment 16, which excludes both kinds of substance from the category. This opinion was followed by John of Jandun, Metaph. 18, q. 22; Niphus in the same place, q. 9, and that as regards the angels alone; Plotinus, Enneads 6, bk. 1; Giles of Rome in his commentaries on this category, and

p. 288

quodlib. 1. quæst. 8. Albertus Magnus in prædicamentis, tract. de substantia, cap. 12.

Quodlibet 1, q. 8; Albert the Great on the Categories, treatise on substance, ch. 12.

Et de corporibus cœlestibus probant hoc arg. Corruptibile & incorruptibile differunt genere, ergo differunt prędicamento: sed corpora cœlestia sunt substantiæ incorruptibiles, ergo differunt prædicamento à substantiis corruptibilibus. Probatur antecedens ex Arist. Meta. cap. vltimo, vbi id expressè docet. Deinde substantiæ corruptibiles ponuntur in hoc prædicamento, ergo corpora cœlestia non sunt in eodem, nec etiam in alio, cùm non sint in aliquo prædicamento accidentium, quare non erunt omnino in prædicamento.

And concerning the heavenly bodies they prove it by this argument: The corruptible and the incorruptible differ in genus; therefore they differ in category; but the heavenly bodies are incorruptible substances; therefore they differ in category from corruptible substances. The antecedent is proved from Aristotle, Metaph., last chapter, where he teaches it expressly. Next, corruptible substances are placed in this category; therefore the heavenly bodies are not in the same one, nor in another either, since they are not in any category of accidents; wherefore they will not be in a category at all.

De Angelis verò probatur testimonio Arist. 10. Meta. tex. 30. vbi præter primum principium, quod est Deus, ponit quasdam alias substantias, quas vocat intelligentias, ad mouendum corpora cælestia. Et has dicit non habere materiam, sed esse puros actus, ac sempiternos: sed substantia, quæ est purus actus, nihil habet potentię, ergo non habet genus. Probatur consequẽtia, quia genus est totum potentiale. Deinde ea, quæ non habent genus non possunt habere speciem, nec prædicamentum, quia species componitur ex genere, & differentia, & prædicamentũ fit ex generibus, & speciebus, ergo ex sententia Arist. intelligentiæ, quas nos vocamus Angelos, non sunt in prædicamento, qui simplices etiam substantias eas appellauit, 9. lib.
