Meta, tex 22. quasi nullam habentes compositionem: ex quo etiam sequitur nec habere prædicamentum, quia ea quæ sunt in prædicamento, composita esse debent, saltem ex genere, & differentia.

Concerning the angels, it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 10, text 30, where, besides the first principle, which is God, he posits certain other substances, which he calls intelligences, for moving the heavenly bodies. And these he says have no matter, but are pure and everlasting acts; but a substance that is pure act has nothing of potency; therefore it has no genus. The consequence is proved: because a genus is a potential whole. Next, those things that have no genus cannot have a species, nor a category, because a species is composed of genus and difference, and a category is made of genera and species; therefore, in the opinion of Aristotle, the intelligences, which we call angels, are not in a category, who also called them simple substances, Metaph. bk. 9, text 22, as having no composition; from which it also follows that they do not have a category, because the things that are in a category must be composite, at least of genus and difference.

Vnde sequitur euidenter falsam esse sententiam Duran. & contradictionem implicare in 2. d. 3. quæst. 1. num. 12. & Marsilii in 1 q. 2. qui cùm Angelo ponant in hoc prędicamento, negant nihilominus vllam prorsus habere compositionem, etiam ex genere, & differentia.

Hence it follows evidently that the opinion of Durandus on 2, d. 3, q. 1, no. 12, and of Marsilius on 1, q. 2, is false and implies a contradiction; for though they place the angel in this category, they nevertheless deny that it has any composition whatever, even of genus and difference.

Probatur deinde ratione, quia Angeli sunt substantiæ, simplices, in quibus non est compositio ex materia, & forma, ergo nec est compositio realis ex potentia, & actu: sed compositio ex genere & differentia, quæ est ex potentia & actu Metaphysicis, fundatur in compositione reali ex potentia, & actu, ergo nec est in illis compositio ex genere, & differentia, & consequenter non sunt in prædicamento,

It is proved next by reason: because angels are simple substances, in which there is no composition of matter and form; therefore neither is there a real composition of potency and act; but the composition of genus and difference, which is of metaphysical potency and act, is founded on a real composition of potency and act; therefore neither is there in them a composition of genus and difference, and consequently they are not in a category.

Secunda opinio tenet, Non solùm corpora cælestia sed etiam Angelos collocari in hoc prædicamento. Et hæc est communis & vera, quam sequuntur quantùm ad corpora cælestia, omnes interpretes Aristotelis in præsenti capite. Et quantum ad Angelos non solùm illi, sed scholastici omnes præter citatos pro

The second opinion holds that not only the heavenly bodies but also the angels are placed in this category. And this is the common and true opinion, which as regards the heavenly bodies all the interpreters of Aristotle follow in the present chapter; and as regards the angels not only they, but all the scholastics except those cited for the opposite opinion

p. 289

opposita) cum magistro in 1 d. 8. & D. Th. 1. p. q. 50. art. 2. ad 1. & 3. & q. 88. art. 2. ad 4. Et probatur imprimis de corporibus cœlestibus testimonio Arist. 5. Meta. tex. 15. 7. Meta. tex. 5. & lib. 8. tex. 1. quibus locis expressè docet esse composita, non solùm ex materia & forma, sed etiam ex partibus integrantibus, eo modo, quo corpus nostrum cõponitur ex capite, brachio, & cæteris membris. Ergo etiam ex mente eius erunt cõposita ex genere & differentia. Probatur consequentia, quia compositio hæc minor est aliis, & in cõpositione ex materia, & forma fundatur.

together with the Master on 1, d. 8, and St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 50, a. 2, ad 1 and 3, and q. 88, a. 2, ad 4. And it is proved first of all concerning the heavenly bodies by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, text 15; Metaph. 7, text 5; and bk. 8, text 1, in which places he teaches expressly that they are composite, not only of matter and form, but also of integral parts, in the way in which our body is composed of head, arm, and the other members. Therefore, in his mind too, they will be composed of genus and difference. The consequence is proved: because this composition is less than the others, and is founded on the composition of matter and form.

18 Probatur etiam ratione, quia corpora cœlestia, præter compositiones physicas ex materia, & forma, atque ex partibus integrantibus, habent aliam etiam physicam, ex subiecto, & accidenti materialibus, nam & quantitatem habent, & lucem recipiunt à sole: ergo habent omnes compositiones physicas possibiles, quia præter prædictas res, non possunt aliæ excogitari: ergo necesse est esse composita ex genere, & differentia. Probatur consequentia, quia vbi potentia realis est, & actus realis, poterit intellectus conceptum potentialem sub ratione contrahibilis formare, quia est conceptus genericus, & etiam conceptum actualem, & contrahentem, qui est conceptus differentialis, & ex vtroque componere speciem. Quod verò genus, & speciem habet, in prædicamento ponitur: ergo euidens est corpora cœlestia in prædicamento substantiæ collocari.

18 It is proved also by reason: because the heavenly bodies, besides the physical compositions of matter and form and of integral parts, have another, also physical, of material subject and accident: for they both have quantity and receive light from the sun; therefore they have all possible physical compositions, because besides the aforesaid no others can be thought of; therefore they must be composed of genus and difference. The consequence is proved: because where there is real potency and real act, the intellect will be able to form a potential concept under the ratio of something contractible, which is the generic concept, and also an actual and contracting concept, which is the differential concept, and to compose the species from both. But what has a genus and a species is placed in a category; therefore it is evident that the heavenly bodies are placed in the category of substance.

De Angelis verò, tria asserunt doctores omnes citati, præcipuè D. Th. Primum, Quòd in eis sit vera & realis compositio ex actu, & potentia, aut ex esse & essentia. Secundum, Quòd verè componantur ex genere, & differentia. Tertium. Quòd per se ponantur in prædicamento substantiæ. Et omnia sunt vera, ac necessaria.

Concerning the angels, all the doctors cited, and especially St. Thomas, assert three things. First, that there is in them a true and real composition of act and potency, or of being and essence. Second, that they are truly composed of genus and difference. Third, that they are placed per se in the category of substance. And all are true and necessary.

19 Sed probanda sunt singula. & vt probet primũ D. Th. vbi suprà, nempe, quòd in Angelis sit compositio realis ex actu, & potentia, præsupponit, quòd in rebus materialibus duplex cõpositio realis reperitur. Prima ex materia, & forma, ex quibus natura earum cõponitur, vt natura humana ex corpore, & anima. Natura verò ita composita adhuc non est completa, sed respicit actum realem, per quem cõpletur, & actus iste vocatur esse eius, per quod constituitur suppositum, aut persona: ergo natura est potentia realis respectu proprij esse, per quod cõpletur, & esse est actus realis eius, & ex vtroq; fit vnum, nẽpe suppositum, aut persona, quod non potest fieri, nisi per realẽ compositionem, quia compositio realis est, per quam ex duobus ex natura rei distinctis fit vnũ: ergo pęter cõposionem ex

19 But each must be proved. And in order that St. Thomas, in the place above, may prove the first, namely that there is in the angels a real composition of act and potency, he presupposes that in material things a twofold real composition is found. The first, of matter and form, of which their nature is composed, as human nature of body and soul. But a nature so composed is still not complete, but looks to a real act by which it is completed, and this act is called its being, by which the supposit or person is constituted: therefore the nature is a real potency with respect to its own being, by which it is completed, and being is its real act, and from both is made one thing, namely the supposit or person, which cannot be done except through a real composition; because a real composition is that through which one thing is made from two things distinct from the nature of the thing; therefore, besides the composition of matter T

p. 290

materia, & forma reperitur in his rebus compositio realis ex essentia, & esse, siue ex natura, & proprio actu, per quod completur.

and form, there is found in these things a real composition of essence and being, or of the nature and its proper act, by which it is completed.

20 Hoc supposito probat, Quòd licèt prima compositio non reperiatur in Angelis, quia carent materia, secunda tamen necessariò sit in eis ponenda. Quia hæc est differentia inter esse diuinum, & creatum, quòd diuinum non est receptum ab alio, sed essentialiter habetur. quia prædicatum est essentiale Dei, sicut esse bonum, aut sapientem: esse autem creatum, extra essentiam rei creatæ est, & ideo non habet illud essentia, nisi à Deo communicetur, & hoc est esse receptum à Deo: ergo essentia creata, verè, & realiter est in potentia ad recipiendum esse à Deo, & esse receptum à Deo, actus realis eius est. Vnde sequitur, intra substantiam Angeli reperiri potentiam realem, & realem actum, ex quibus cùm fiat vnum, nempe completa substantia eius, non potest fieri nisi per realem compositionem. Et ita probatum est primum.

20 This supposed, he proves that, although the first composition is not found in the angels, because they lack matter, the second must nevertheless necessarily be posited in them. Because this is the difference between divine and created being: that divine being is not received from another, but is had essentially, because it is an essential predicate of God, as to be good or wise; but created being is outside the essence of the created thing, and therefore the essence does not have it unless it is communicated by God, and this is to be being received from God; therefore the created essence is truly and really in potency to receive being from God, and the being received from God is its real act. Hence it follows that within the substance of the angel there is found a real potency and a real act, and since from these one thing is made, namely its complete substance, this cannot be done except through a real composition. And so the first has been proved.

Ex quo probari potest secundum, quòd sit eis compositio ex genere, & differẽtia, hoc arg. Intellectus cognoscit naturam Angeli tanquam potentiam realem determinabilem per actũ essendi: ergo potest formare in eadem natura conceptum perfectibilem, ac determinabilem, & conceptum perficientem, ac determinantem: sed isti sunt conceptus genericus, & differentialis, ex quibus componitur species: ergo in Angelo est compositio speciei, ex genere & differentia.

From which the second can be proved, namely that there is in them a composition of genus and difference, by this argument: The intellect knows the nature of the angel as a real potency determinable by the act of being; therefore it can form in the same nature a perfectible and determinable concept, and a perfecting and determining concept; but these are the generic and the differential concepts, of which the species is composed; therefore in the angel there is a composition of the species from genus and difference.

Ex quo euidenter probatur tertium, quòd Angelus sit in prædicamento. Quia prædicamentum fit ex generibus, & speciebus essentialiter ordinatis: sed Angelus habet genus, & speciem: ergo ordinabilis erit in prædicamento.

From which the third is evidently proved, that the angel is in a category. Because a category is made of genera and species essentially ordered; but the angel has a genus and a species; therefore it will be orderable in a category.

21 Ad arg. primæ opinionis de corporibus cœlestibus, respondet D. Th. 1. p. quæst. 66. art. 2. ad 2. & quæst. 88. art. 2. ad 4. distinguendo maiorem: quia genus duplex est, Physicum, & Logicum, seu Metaphysicum. Genus Physicum est materia, quia primò reperitur in ea potentia realis, quæ prima radix est, & fundamentum Metaphysici generis in rebus materialibus. Genus autem Logicum, aut Metaphysicum, est natura abstracta à speciebus, & differentiis, vt substantia à corporea, & incorporea. Ad formam igitur argumenti, dum in maiori dicitur, corruptibile, & incorruptibile differre genere: distinguendum est, de genere physico, & logico, & de illo concedendum, quia corpora incorruptibilia constant materia diuersæ speciei, à materia corporum corruptibilium, & ideo dicuntur differre genere physico, quod est materia.

21 To the argument of the first opinion concerning the heavenly bodies, St. Thomas replies, 1 p., q. 66, a. 2, ad 2, and q. 88, a. 2, ad 4, by distinguishing the major: because genus is twofold, Physical and Logical, or Metaphysical. The physical genus is matter, because real potency is found first in it, which is the first root and foundation of the metaphysical genus in material things. But the logical or metaphysical genus is a nature abstracted from species and differences, as substance from corporeal and incorporeal. To the form of the argument, then: where it is said in the major that the corruptible and the incorruptible differ in genus, one must distinguish between the physical and the logical genus, and grant it of the former, because incorruptible bodies consist of matter of a different species from the matter of corruptible bodies, and therefore they are said to differ in physical genus, which is matter.

22 Et ita intelligendum est testimonium Aristotelis, in quo

22 And in this way is to be understood the testimony of Aristotle, in which

p. 291

propositio illa continetur. Sed de genere logico non est verum, nec de eo loquitur Aristoteles, quia corpus corruptibile, & incorruptibile, commune genus habent, nempe corpus abstractum ab vtroque, & sub illo collocantur in prædicamento substantiæ. Non ergo sequitur, differunt genere physico, ergo differunt prædicamento, quia genus physicum, quod est materia, non est genus prædicamentale, sequeretur autem bene, si differrent genere logico.

that proposition is contained. But of the logical genus it is not true, nor does Aristotle speak of it: because corruptible and incorruptible body have a common genus, namely body abstracted from both, and under it they are placed in the category of substance. It does not follow, therefore: they differ in physical genus, therefore they differ in category; because the physical genus, which is matter, is not a categorial genus; but it would follow well if they differed in logical genus.

Quamuis etiam posset secundò responderi, loqui Aristotelem de genere logico, aut metaphysico. Sed alio modo esset eadem maior distinguenda, dum dicitur, corruptibile, & incorruptibile, differunt genere. Nam genus prædicamentale duplex est, supremum & intermedium, & concedendum est differre genere intermedio, non supremo, quia corpus diuiditur in corpus corruptibile, & incorruptibile, tanquam in duo genera intermedia. Et sub vno continentur corpora cælestia, sub alio corruptibilia: & ita differunt genere intermedio, sed non supremo, quia sub eodem genere corporis & substantiæ continentur, & in eo conueniunt. Vnde nec differunt prædicamento, quia ea solùm dicuntur differre prodicamento, quæ sub diuersis generibus supremis continentur, vt animal, & scientia, illud enim sub supremo genere substantiæ, scientia verò sub supremo genere qualitatis continetur.

Although one could also reply, second, that Aristotle speaks of the logical or metaphysical genus. But in another way the same major would have to be distinguished, where it is said that the corruptible and the incorruptible differ in genus. For the categorial genus is twofold, supreme and intermediate; and it must be granted that they differ in intermediate genus, not in supreme genus: because body is divided into corruptible and incorruptible body as into two intermediate genera, and under one are contained the heavenly bodies, under the other the corruptible ones; and so they differ in intermediate genus, but not in supreme genus, because they are contained under the same genus of body and of substance, and agree in it. Hence neither do they differ in category, because only those things are said to differ in category which are contained under different supreme genera, as animal and science: for the former is contained under the supreme genus of substance, but science under the supreme genus of quality.

23 Ad testimonia Arist. in quibus loquitur de intelligentiis: Respondeo, sempiternas esse, & materia carere, & ideo non habere potentiam ad non essendum, quia non habent principium corruptionis, sicut substantiæ corruptibilium, quæ ratione materię habeant in se principium non essendi. Et ideo vocantur ab Aristotele intelligentiæ actus, non tamen puri, quia cùm triplicem compositionem habeant necessariò, nempe ex esse, & essentia, ex subiecto, & accidenti, habent enim intellectum. & voluntatem, quæ sunt vera accidentia superaddita substantiæ eorum, & præterea ex genere, & differentia, necesse est triplicem quoque potentiam habere, quia quælibet compositio suo modo fit ex actu, & potentia. Quare sicut ab his potentiis, eas non excludit, sic nec potuit excludere à prædicamento.

23 To the testimonies of Aristotle in which he speaks of the intelligences, I reply that they are everlasting and lack matter, and therefore do not have a potency to not being, because they do not have a principle of corruption as the substances of corruptible things do, which by reason of matter have in themselves a principle of not being. And therefore they are called by Aristotle acts, yet not pure acts: because, since they necessarily have a threefold composition, namely of being and essence; of subject and accident (for they have intellect and will, which are true accidents superadded to their substance); and besides, of genus and difference, they must also have a threefold potency, because every composition in its own way is of act and potency. Wherefore, just as he does not exclude them from these potencies, so neither could he exclude them from the category.

24 Ad Arg. negandum est antecedens, quòd Angeli, ita sint substantiæ simplices, vt in eis non sit compositio realis ex potentia, & actu, atq; etiam ex genere, & differentia: non enim sequitur, nõ habent compositione ex materia, & forma, ergo nec ex actu, & potentia: quia cõpositio ex actu, & potẽtia,

24 To the argument: the antecedent must be denied, that angels are simple substances in such a way that there is in them no real composition of potency and act, and so too of genus and difference. For it does not follow: they do not have a composition of matter and form, therefore not of act and potency either; because the composition of act and potency is more universal T ij

p. 292

vniuersalior est compositione ex materia & forma, & communis substantiis materialibus, & immaterialibus, quia non fundatur necessariò in materia, sed in natura ipsa reperitur, ex eo quòd creata est, & esse receptum ab alio habet. Et cùm talis sit natura Angelorum (licèt spiritualis) necessariò includit hanc compositionem intra propriam substantiam, & consequenter compositionem ex genere, & differentia, quæ proximè in ea fundatur, quamuis radicaliter, & remotè fundetur in materia, in rebus materialibus.

than the composition of matter and form, and common to material and immaterial substances, because it is not necessarily founded on matter, but is found in the nature itself from the fact that it is created and has its being received from another. And since such is the nature of the angels (although spiritual), it necessarily includes this composition within its own substance, and consequently the composition of genus and difference, which is proximately founded on it, although in material things it is radically and remotely founded on matter.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Quæst. 4. Qualisnam sit diuisio substantiæ in primam, & secundam: vniuoca, vel analoga — Of what kind the division of substance into first and second is: univocal or analogous.

Qualisnam sit diuisio substantiæ in primam, & secundam: vniuoca, vel analoga.

[…]

25 VT meliùs intelligatur quæstio, notandum est, quatuor modis accipi posse tam diuisum quàm membra huius diuisionis. Primo sic accipiuntur, vt diuisum sit reale, & membra sint secundæ intentiones. Sed tunc diuisum secundùm esse reale duobus modis accipi potest: Aut pro substantia reali secundùm essentiam, aut secundùm proprietatem substandi: & si primo modo accipiatur, sensus diuisionis erit: Substantia realis, vna est vniuersalis, alia particularis, aut vna est subiectum, alia prædicatum. Et erit diuisio subiecti realis in diuersa accidentia rationis. Si verò secundo modo, diuersus erit sensus, nempe, Substantia realis, vt substans, vna est primum subiectum in propositione, alia secundum. Et erit diuisio quasi accidentis realis, in diuersa accidentia rationis.

25 In order that the question may be better understood, it should be noted that both the thing divided and the members of this division can be taken in four ways. In the first way they are taken so that the thing divided is real and the members are second intentions. But then the thing divided, according to its real being, can be taken in two ways: either for real substance according to its essence, or according to the property of standing under. And if it is taken in the first way, the sense of the division will be: Of real substance, one is universal, another particular; or one is subject, another predicate. And it will be a division of a real subject into different accidents of reason. But if in the second way, the sense will be different, namely: Of real substance, as standing under, one is the first subject in a proposition, another the second. And it will be a division as it were of a real accident into different accidents of reason.

26 Secundo modo potest accipi, ex opposito, ita vt diuisum sit ens rationis & membra realia, videlicet prima, & secunda substantia secundùm esse reale: eritque sensus: Subiectum in propositione, vnum est prima substantia realis, aliud, secunda substantia realis. Et erit diuisio accidentis rationis, in diuersa subiecta realia.

26 In the second way it can be taken conversely, so that the thing divided is a being of reason and the members are real, namely first and second substance according to their real being; and the sense will be: Of the subject in a proposition, one is first real substance, another second real substance. And it will be a division of an accident of reason into different real subjects.

Tertiò modo accipitur, ita vt tam diuisum quàm membra sint entia rationis, & sensus sit: Subiectum propositionis aliud est primum, aliud secundum, vel aliud particulare, aliud commune, & cùm hæc diuersa subiecta, sint quasi species subiecti abstracti à communi, & particulari, erit diuisio sic sumpta generis in species. Vltimò accipi possunt, tã diuisum, quàm membra pro substantia reali, secundùm proprietatem realem substandi, eritque sensus: Substantia realiter substãs accidentibus, & prædicatis superioribus, vna est prima, quæ propria virtute substat, alia secunda, quæ substat virtute primæ. Et erit diuisio

In the third way it is taken so that both the thing divided and the members are beings of reason, and the sense is: Of the subject of a proposition, one is first, another second, or one is particular, another common; and since these different subjects are as it were species of subject abstracted from the common and the particular, the division so taken will be of a genus into species. Lastly, both the thing divided and the members can be taken for real substance according to the real property of standing under, and the sense will be: Of substance really standing under accidents and superior predicates, one is first, which stands under by its own power; another second, which stands under by the power of the first. And the division will be

p. 293

analogi in analogata, quia secunda substantia non dicitur substare, nisi per attributionẽ ad primam, cùm eius virtute substet.

of an analogous term into its analogates, because second substance is not said to stand under except through attribution to first substance, since it stands under by its power.

27 Ex his quatuor modis sumendi hanc diuisionem, secundus excludi debet, quia nullus est, qui sic accipiat diuisionem, & verè est præter mentem Arist. atque impertinens ad propositum eius, quia cùm diuisum ordinetur ad cognitionem membrorum, si pro ente rationis accipiatur, non poterit deseruire ad ea cognoscenda. Hoc ergo modo prætermisso, secundùm alios tres, sunt quatuor opiniones diuersæ.

27 Of these four ways of taking this division, the second must be excluded, because there is no one who takes the division so, and it is truly beside the mind of Aristotle and irrelevant to his purpose: because, since the thing divided is ordered to the cognition of the members, if it is taken for a being of reason it will not be able to serve for knowing them. This way, then, being passed over, according to the other three there are four different opinions.

Prima asserit, esse diuisionem subiecti in accidentia, quia primo modo eam considerat. Ita Can. in principio huius capitis. Probat à sufficienti diuisione, quia hæc diuisio non est æquiuoci in æquiuocata, cùm aliquid præter nomen diuidatur. Nec est diuisio totius in partes, quia diuisum prædicatur de membris, imò vnum membrum de alio: nam verum est, quòd prima substantia sit substantia: & cùm secunda substantia sit vniuersalis, verum est etiam prædicari de prima, quæ est singularis, & tamen neque totum prędicatur de partibus, neque vna pars de alia: ergo non diuiditur per hanc diuisionem substantia, tanquam totum in suas partes. Nec est diuisio generis in species, quia vna species non prędicatur de alia, secunda verò substantia prædicatur de prima. Et præterea si diuisio esset generica, daretur genus superius generalissimo huius prædicamenti, quòd cùm sit secunda substantia, erit alterum membrum huius diuisionis, & ideo inferius diuiso, tanquam species sub genere. Nec tandem est analoga, primò quia si substantia realis in ratione substandi diuiditur, cùm substare non sit essentia substantiæ, sed proprietas eius, non diuideretur substantia, sed quædam propria passio eius. Deinde diuisum non conueniret secundæ substantiæ, quia diuisum est substantia sub ratione substandi, cum substare sit subiectum, & secunda substantia cùm non possit esse subiectum, sed prædicatum, non posse ei conuenire.

The first asserts that it is a division of a subject into accidents, because it considers it in the first way. So Canterus at the beginning of this chapter. He proves it from a sufficient division: because this division is not of an equivocal term into its equivocates, since something besides the name is divided. Nor is it a division of a whole into parts, because the thing divided is predicated of the members, indeed one member of the other: for it is true that first substance is substance; and since second substance is universal, it is true also that it is predicated of first substance, which is singular; and yet neither is the whole predicated of the parts, nor one part of another; therefore substance is not divided by this division as a whole into its parts. Nor is it a division of a genus into species, because one species is not predicated of another, but second substance is predicated of first. And besides, if the division were generic, a genus would be given superior to the most general genus of this category, which, since it is second substance, will be the other member of this division, and therefore inferior to the thing divided, as a species under a genus. Nor, finally, is it analogous: first, because if real substance is divided in the ratio of standing under, since to stand under is not the essence of substance but its property, it would not be substance that is divided, but a certain proper attribute of it. Next, the thing divided would not belong to second substance: because the thing divided is substance under the ratio of standing under, since to stand under is to be a subject; and second substance, since it cannot be a subject but a predicate, could not have it belong to it.

28 Secunda opinio eodẽ modo accipit diuisum, pro substantia reali, & membra pro secundis intentionibus, non tamẽ pro substantia reali secundùm essentiam, sed secundùm proprietatem realem substandi. Et affirmat esse diuisionem accidentalis realis, in accidentia rationis, quia propria passio substandi, accidens reale est, membra verò, accidẽtia rationis nempe substantia vniuersalis, & particularis. Pro hac sententia referuntur Louanienses, & To. sed nihil tale apud eos inuenire potui.

28 The second opinion takes the thing divided in the same way for real substance, and the members for second intentions, yet not for real substance according to its essence, but according to the real property of standing under. And it affirms that it is a division of a real accidental into accidents of reason: because the proper attribute of standing under is a real accident, while the members are accidents of reason, namely universal and particular substance. For this opinion the Louvain commentators and Toledo are cited, but I have been unable to find anything of the kind in them.

29 Tertia opinio, integram diuisionem sumens pro secundis intentionibus, asserit esse generis in species: quam sequuntur

29 The third opinion, taking the whole division for second intentions, asserts that it is of a genus into species: which is followed T iij

p. 294

plures moderni. Et probant hac ratione: Diuisum, quod est subiectum in communi, æqualiter participatur à prima & secunda substantia, & ab vna sine dependentia ab altera, ergo est diuisio vniuoca, atque generica. Probatur antecedens, quia quando in propositione copula absoluitur à tempore, non pendet veritas eius à singularibus, vt in hac, homo est risibilis: ergo non substat homo, qui est secunda substantia, prædicata risibili, cum dependentia à prima substantia. Et in propositionibus contingentibus singularibus, non dependet veritas à secundis substantiis, sed solùm à primis, quibus conueniunt accidentia sine dependentia à secundis.

by many moderns. And they prove it by this argument: The thing divided, which is subject in common, is participated equally by first and second substance, and by the one without dependence on the other; therefore it is a univocal and generic division. The antecedent is proved: because when in a proposition the copula is absolved from time, its truth does not depend on singulars, as in this one, Man is risible; therefore man, which is second substance, does not stand under the predicate risible with dependence on first substance. And in contingent singular propositions the truth does not depend on second substances, but only on first ones, to which accidents belong without dependence on second substances.

Vltima sententia tenet, Diuisionem esse anologi in analogata. Sed qui eam sequuntur, non eodem modo eam accipiunt, sed quidam diuisum pro reali substantia, & membra pro secundis intentionibus secundum primum modum, & ita substantia realis diuiditur in diuersas secundas intentiones, Vniuersalem, & Singularem, aut Subiecti, & Prædicati. Ita Sotus, quęst. 1. ad primum, & Caiet. ca. etiam præsenti. Sed plures alij analogam esse affirmant, tam diuisum, quàm membra accipientes realiter. Ita Albertus Magnus in prædicamentis tract. 2. de substantia, c. 3. Iauel. 5 Meta. q. 7. Toletus, q. 1. & expressè D. Tho. q. 9. de potentia, art. 1. ad 6 Et hæc videtur mihi probabilior.

The last opinion holds that the division is of an analogous term into its analogates. But those who follow it do not take it in the same way: some take the thing divided for real substance and the members for second intentions, according to the first way, and so real substance is divided into different second intentions, Universal and Singular, or of Subject and Predicate. So Soto, q. 1, ad 1, and Cajetan on the present chapter also. But many others affirm that it is analogous, taking both the thing divided and the members really. So Albert the Great on the Categories, tract. 2, on substance, ch. 3; Javelli, Metaph. 5, q. 7; Toledo, q. 1; and expressly St. Thomas, On Power, q. 9, a. 1, ad 6. And this seems to me more probable.

30 Sed duo sunt probãda, vt maior probabilitas eius fiat manifesta. Primum, quòd tam diuisum, quàm membra sumantur realiter, & non pro secundis intentionibus. Secundum, quòd sic accepta sit diuisio analogi in analogata. Probatur primum ex Arist. qui non posuit hanc diuisionem expressè, sed eam posuisse intelligimus ex eo, quòd vtrumque membrum definiuit, Ergo sic sunt mẽbra diuisionis, sicut definiuntur. Sed definiuntur secundùm esse reale, ergo efficiunt diuisionem realem. Probatur minor, quia prima sic definitur, Substantia quę propriè, principaliter, & maximè dicitur, &c. Sed excellentiæ istæ nõ conueniunt ei ratione secundæ intentionis, sed propter naturam realem perfectissimam, ergo realiter, & non per secundam intentionem definitur. Secundæ etiam substantiæ definiuntur, quòd sint genera, & species, quibus insunt, primę id est, sub quibus ponuntur in prædicamento, ergo definiuntur, vt ponuntur in prędicamento: sed non ponuntur in prędicamento, vt denominantur à secundis intentionibus, sed vt sunt genera & species Metaphysicæ, atque reales, ergo realiter definiuntur.

30 But two things must be proved, in order that its greater probability may become manifest. First, that both the thing divided and the members are taken really, and not for second intentions. Second, that so taken it is a division of an analogous term into its analogates. The first is proved from Aristotle, who did not posit this division expressly, but we understand that he posited it from the fact that he defined each member. Therefore the members of the division are such as they are defined. But they are defined according to their real being; therefore they make a real division. The minor is proved: because the first is defined thus: Substance which is said properly, principally, and most of all, etc. But these excellences do not belong to it by reason of a second intention, but on account of its most perfect real nature; therefore it is defined really, and not by a second intention. Second substances too are defined as being the genera and species in which the first are, that is, under which they are placed in the category; therefore they are defined as they are placed in the category; but they are not placed in the category as they are denominated by second intentions, but as they are metaphysical and real genera and species; therefore they are defined really.

31 Præterea, comparans Arist. vtrumque membrũ deuisionis, ait, Primam substantiam esse magis substantiam, quàm secundam, quia propria virtute substat accidentibus: sed substare est

31 Besides, comparing the two members of the division, Aristotle says that first substance is more substance than second, because it stands under accidents by its own power; but to stand under is

p. 295

actus realis, cùm sit realiter sustentare accidentia: ergo comparantur secundùm esse reale, & non intentionale, & ideo realem diuisionem efficiunt.

a real act, since it is really to sustain accidents; therefore they are compared according to real being and not intentional being, and therefore they make a real division.

Probatur tandem: quia eandem substantiam diuidit Arist. in primam, & secundam, cuius proprietates postea enumerat, sed proprietates sunt reales, vt manifestum est: ergo substantia realiter diuiditur in primam, & secundam.

It is proved finally: because Aristotle divided into first and second the same substance whose properties he afterwards enumerates; but the properties are real, as is manifest; therefore substance is really divided into first and second.

Probatur deinde ratione. Primò, quia repugnat, diuisum, & membra, sumi pro secundis intentionibus, vt ponunt aliæ sententiæ: ergo omnes sunt falsæ. Probatur antecedens de diuiso: nam membra diuisionis sunt secundæ intentiones subiecti, & prædicati, vt ex definitionibus vtriusque colligitur, secundò intentionaliter intellectis; sed nulla datur secunda intentio communis subiecto, & prædicato, præter rationem vniuersalem entis rationis: ergo hæc erit diuisum. Et sensus diuisionis erit: Ens rationis aliud est subiectum, aliud prædicatum: quod patet esse absurdum, cùm ens rationis in communi consideratum nihil denominet, & si denominaret, non magis substantiam, quàm accidentia. Ex quo intelligitur, nec diuisum huius diuisionis posse esse subiectum in communi: quia non magis denominat substantiam, quàm accidens, siquidem vtrumque potest indifferenter esse subiectum propositionis. Probatur etiam de membris, quòd non accipiantur pro secundis intentionibus: nam membra sunt subiectum, & prædicatum, vt asserit prima opinio: sed prædicatum est nobilius subiecto, cùm sit forma propositionis: ergo secunda substantia, vt est membrum diuisionis, erit nobilior prima, quod expressè est contra Arist. sæpè docentem in textu, Primam substantiam esse nobiliorem secunda.

It is proved next by reason. First, because it is repugnant that the thing divided and the members be taken for second intentions, as the other opinions posit; therefore all of them are false. The antecedent is proved concerning the thing divided: for the members of the division are the second intentions of subject and predicate, as is gathered from the definitions of each, understood in the second, intentional, way; but no second intention is given common to subject and predicate except the universal ratio of being of reason; therefore this will be the thing divided. And the sense of the division will be: Of being of reason, one is subject, another predicate; which is plainly absurd, since being of reason considered in common denominates nothing, and if it did denominate, it would not denominate substance more than accidents. From which it is understood that neither can the thing divided in this division be subject in common: because it does not denominate substance more than accident, since either can indifferently be the subject of a proposition. It is proved also concerning the members, that they are not taken for second intentions: for the members are subject and predicate, as the first opinion asserts; but the predicate is nobler than the subject, since it is the form of the proposition; therefore second substance, as it is a member of the division, will be nobler than first, which is expressly against Aristotle, who often teaches in the text that first substance is nobler than second.

32 Hoc supposito probandum est secundum, quòd diuisio sit analogi in analogata. Sed vt probetur, notandum est, Substantiam tribus modis posse considerari, secundùm essentiam: secundùm vltimum actum substantialem eius, qui est subsistentia: vel secundùm proprietatem susteutandi accidentia. Essentia substantiæ est, esse gradum quendam entitatis realis perfectæ, hoc est, independentis ab alio, & cui debetur subsisteniia per se: & licèt non possit esse in rerum natura, nisi actu existens: neque completa, nisi per subsistentiam: neutra tamen pertinet ad essentiam eius, sed extra illam est. Nec tamen sunt accidentia: sed actus quidam substantiales eius, ita vt per existentiam sit in rerum natura: & per subsistentiam vltimò compleatur, & in persona, aut supposito constituatur. Proprietas verò substandi, sequitur substantiam iam completam, aut iam

32 This supposed, the second must be proved, that the division is of an analogous term into its analogates. But in order that it may be proved, it should be noted that substance can be considered in three ways: according to its essence; according to its ultimate substantial act, which is subsistence; or according to the property of sustaining accidents. The essence of substance is to be a certain grade of perfect real entity, that is, independent of another, and to which subsistence per se is due; and although it cannot be in the nature of things except as actually existing, nor complete except through subsistence, yet neither pertains to its essence, but is outside it. Nor, however, are they accidents, but certain substantial acts of it, such that through existence it is in the nature of things, and through subsistence it is ultimately completed and constituted in a person or supposit. But the property of standing under follows substance already completed, or already T iiij

p. 296

subsistentem. Itaque hæc tria ita se habent: vt esse entitatem perfectam, & ex se independentem, sit essentia substantiæ, ex quo duo alia procedunt hoc ordine, vt subsistentia sit prius, deinde verò illa mediante, procedit substare: illa quidem tanquam modus substantialis, substare verò tanquam proprietas, sed vtramque extra essentiam, eiusdem naturæ, quæ quidem ponitur in prædicamento secundùm essentiam. Sed quia hæc non facilè cognoscitur à nobis, voluit eam Arist. manifestare per intimam proprietatem, sustentandi accidentia: & ideo substantiam diuisit, secundùm proprietatem substandi, vt defininitio primæ substantiæ euidenter ostendit: vnde sensus diuisionis est: Substantia, quę est ens completum atque perfectum, cui debetur subsistentia per se, ratione cuius est quasi sustentatatiua aliorum, vna est prima, alia secunda, hoc est, primò, & per se habet esse in singulari, & quasi secundariò in vniuersali.

subsisting. These three, then, are related thus: to be a perfect entity, independent of itself, is the essence of substance, from which the two others proceed in this order: that subsistence is first, and then, by means of it, standing under proceeds; the former as a substantial mode, standing under as a property, but both outside the essence of the same nature, which is placed in the category according to its essence. But because this is not easily known by us, Aristotle wished to make it manifest through the intimate property of sustaining accidents; and therefore he divided substance according to the property of standing under, as the definition of first substance evidently shows. Hence the sense of the division is: Of substance, which is a complete and perfect being, to which subsistence per se is due, by reason of which it is as it were sustentative of other things, one is first, another second; that is, it has being first and per se in the singular, and as it were secondarily in the universal.

33 Ex hac doctrina colligitur hoc arg. quo probatur diuisionem realiter sumptam esse analogi in analogata. Analogum est nomen, quod ita conuenit suis significatis, vt vni per se primò, atque simpliciter: aliis verò non nisi cum intrinseca dependentia, & attributione ad illud: sicut ens conuenit substantiæ, & accidenti. Sed substantia sumpta realiter in ratione substandi (vt probatum est sumi in hac diuisione) conuenit primę substantiæ primò, & per se: secundæ verò non nisi cum intrinseca dependentia, & attributione ad illam: ergo habet se vt analogum respectu vtriusque, & vt tale diuiditur in ea tanquã in analogata. Probatur minor, quia substare, aut sustentare, alia propria virtute, conuenit primæ substantiæ, & per participationem eius conuenit secundis.

33 From this doctrine is gathered this argument, by which it is proved that the division taken really is of an analogous term into its analogates. An analogous term is a name that belongs to its significates in such a way that it belongs to one per se, first, and simply, but to the others only with an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to it: as being belongs to substance and accident. But substance taken really in the ratio of standing under (as it has been proved to be taken in this division) belongs to first substance first and per se, but to second substance only with an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to the first; therefore it stands as analogous with respect to both, and as such it is divided into them as into its analogates. The minor is proved: because to stand under, or to sustain other things by its own power, belongs to first substance, and by participation of it belongs to second substances.

Ad arg. primæ sententiæ, quæ contendebat probare. Diuisionem non esse analogam propter duo. Primum, quia diuisum est substantia in ratione substãdi: ergo non diuiditur substantia, sed quædam propria passio eius. Et respondemus, concedendo, quòd non diuiditur substantia secundùm essentiam: sed in quantum conuenit illi propria passio substandi, per quam manifestatur eius essentia, sicut posset diuidi animal, in quantum est sensibile. Secundum erat, quòd si substantia diuiditur in ratione substandi, non poterit conuenire secundæ substantiæ: quia substare est esse subiectum, & secunda substantia est prædicatum. Respondetur, secundas substantias vtramque rationem habere subiecti, & prædicati: & ad hanc diuisionem potiùs pertinent, tanquam subiecta, quæ realiter substant accidentibus, quàm vt prædicata. Fuit autem conuenientius diuidere substantiam, per illam proprietatem realem

To the argument of the first opinion, which contended to prove that the division is not analogous on account of two things. First, because the thing divided is substance in the ratio of standing under; therefore it is not substance that is divided, but a certain proper attribute of it. And we reply by granting that substance is not divided according to its essence, but inasmuch as there belongs to it the proper attribute of standing under, through which its essence is made manifest, just as animal could be divided inasmuch as it is sensible. The second was that if substance is divided in the ratio of standing under, it will not be able to belong to second substance, because to stand under is to be a subject, and second substance is a predicate. The reply is that second substances have both rationes, of subject and of predicate; and they pertain to this division rather as subjects, which really stand under accidents, than as predicates. But it was more fitting to divide substance through that real property

p. 297

substandi, quàm per secundas intentiones: vt ratio prædicamentalis eius manifesta fieret, & etiam constaret, quomodo potest esse fundamentum secundæ intentionis.

of standing under than through second intentions, so that its categorial ratio might become manifest, and it might also be established how it can be the foundation of a second intention.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Quod sit formale definitum definionis primę substantię.

What the formal definitum of the definition of first substance is.

35 PRima opinio est Soti, quam sequuntur plures moderni. Definitum formale huius definitionis, Esse secundam intentionem primę substantię in communi, quæ abstrahitur à particularibus, secundis intentionibus, denominantibus Petrum, & Ioannem, cæterasque secundas substantias. Materiale verò, Rationem primę substantię realem, in qua conueniunt omnes primę substantię, non vt realis est, sed vt denominatur à secunda intentione: & ex vtraque fieri vnum definitum totale, atque completum. Sicut in definitione generis diximus, formale definitum, esse secundam intentionem generis: materiale verò naturam genericam in communi, ab eo denominatam.

35 The first opinion is that of Soto, which many moderns follow: that the formal definitum of this definition is the second intention of first substance in common, which is abstracted from the particular second intentions denominating Peter and John and the other first substances. And the material definitum is the real ratio of first substance, in which all first substances agree, not as it is real, but as it is denominated by the second intention; and from both is made one total and complete definitum. Just as in the definition of genus we said that the formal definitum is the second intention of genus, and the material definitum the generic nature in common, denominated by it.

Probatur ex definitione primæ substantiæ tradita ab Arist. quæ sic habet: Prima substantia est, quę nec de subiecto aliquo dicitur, nec in subiecto aliquo est, & continet negationem prædicationis, & negationem fundamenti. Nam ex eo non prædicatur de subiecto prima substantia, quia non est in subiecto: ergo definitum erit prima substantia realis pro fundamento, & quasi pro materiali, & secunda intentio, aut negatio eius, pro formali.

It is proved from the definition of first substance given by Aristotle, which runs thus: First substance is that which is neither said of any subject nor is in any subject; and it contains a negation of predication and a negation of the foundation. For first substance is not predicated of a subject because it is not in a subject; therefore the definitum will be real first substance as the foundation and as it were as the material element, and the second intention, or its negation, as the formal element.

Deinde probatur ratione, quia primæ substantiæ, vt Petrus, & Ioannes, duobus modis possunt considerari: aut secundùm esse reale substantiæ singularis: vel vt denominantur à secunda intentione: & si primo modo considerentur, nihil reale commune, & vniuocum habere possunt: ergo neque aliquid reale eis commune potest esse definitum. Probatur antecedens: quia singularia, vt singularia, sunt primò diuersa, sicut sunt vltimò distincta: ergo non possunt habere vniuocam conuenientiam: nam si eam haberent, per alias differentias essent ab ea separanda, & sic procederetur in infinitum. Ex quo sequitur, solum posse definiri primam substantiam, vt denominatam à secunda intentione.

Next it is proved by reason: because first substances, as Peter and John, can be considered in two ways: either according to the real being of singular substance, or as they are denominated by the second intention; and if they are considered in the first way, they can have nothing real common and univocal; therefore neither can anything real common to them be the definitum. The antecedent is proved: because singulars, as singulars, are primarily diverse, just as they are ultimately distinct; therefore they cannot have a univocal agreement: for if they had it, they would have to be separated from it by other differences, and so one would proceed to infinity. From which it follows that first substance can be defined only as denominated by the second intention.

36 Tertiò, si aliquid reale commune esset definitum, duo absurda sequerentur: primum, quòd Definitio non conueniret definito. Quod sic probo: Definitum est aliquid reale, commune omnibus primis substantiis: ergo prædicatur de illis atque in illis est: sed definitio asserit primam substantiam non

36 Third, if something real and common were the definitum, two absurdities would follow. First, that the definition would not belong to the definitum. Which I prove thus: The definitum is something real, common to all first substances; therefore it is predicated of them and is in them; but the definition asserts that first substance is not

p. 298

dici de subiecto, nec esse in subiecto: ergo non potest ei conuenire. Secundum, quod sequitur, est: Definitum non esse primam substantiam, sed secundam. Probatur consequentia: quia prima substantia non est prędicatum commune, sed subiectum singulare: Secunda verò substantia est prædicatum commune, quod prædicatur de primis: sed illud est reale prędicatum commune, quod prædicatur de primis substantiis: ergo est secunda substantia. Quare non potest esse definitum in definitione primæ.

said of a subject nor is in a subject; therefore it cannot belong to it. The second absurdity that follows is that the definitum is not first substance but second. The consequence is proved: because first substance is not a common predicate but a singular subject, whereas second substance is a common predicate, which is predicated of first substances; but that is a real common predicate which is predicated of first substances; therefore it is second substance. Wherefore it cannot be the definitum in the definition of first substance.

37 Secunda opinio est Caiet. cap. præsenti, vbi asserit, Indiuidua, seu primas substantias, vt Petrus, & Ioannes, duobus modis considerari posse, vel vt participant naturam humanam, vel vt habent modum particularem subsistendi. Et vtroque modo habent conuenientiam vniuocam, sed prima est conuenientia naturæ: secunda verò modi: & ideo illa vocatur specifica, hæc modalis: nam subsistentia in qua conueniunt, modus est naturæ. Et prima cõuenientia significatur per hoc nomen (homo,) secunda per hoc nomen (prima substantia:) quia prima substantia significat substantiam per se subsistentem, abstractam ab hac, & illa prima substantia, vt à Petro, & Ioanne. Definitum ergo huius definitionis, quasi materiale, Sunt omnes primę substantię: Formale verò est communis illa ratio particulariter subsistendi, & adæquatum, primę istę substantię, vt conueniunt in eadem ratione modali Hæc est expressa sententia D. Tho. 1 part. q. 29. art. 1. ad 1. vbi ita ait: Licet hoc singulare, vel illud definiri non possit, tamen id, quod pertinet ad communem rationem singularitatis, definiri potest. Et sic Philosophus definit substantiam primam: & hoc modo definit Boëtius personam, & quæst. 30. art. 4. ad 2. licet persona sit incommunicabilis, tamen ipse modus existendi incommunicabiliter, potest esse pluribus communis. Et hæc videtur mihi probabilior & tenenda.

37 The second opinion is that of Cajetan on the present chapter, where he asserts that individuals, or first substances, as Peter and John, can be considered in two ways: either as they participate the human nature, or as they have a particular mode of subsisting. And in both ways they have a univocal agreement, but the first is an agreement of nature, the second of mode; and therefore the former is called specific, the latter modal: for the subsistence in which they agree is a mode of the nature. And the first agreement is signified by this name (man), the second by this name (first substance): because first substance signifies substance subsisting per se, abstracted from this and that first substance, as from Peter and John. The definitum of this definition, then, as it were the material one, is all first substances; but the formal one is that common ratio of subsisting particularly, and adequate to these first substances, as they agree in the same modal ratio. This is the express opinion of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 29, a. 1, ad 1, where he says thus: Although this or that singular cannot be defined, yet that which pertains to the common ratio of singularity can be defined. And thus the Philosopher defines first substance; and in this way Boethius defines person. And q. 30, a. 4, ad 2: although a person is incommunicable, yet the very mode of existing incommunicably can be common to many. And this seems to me more probable and to be held.

38 Quæ probatur testimonio Arist. & ratione. Aristot. enim volens definire primam substantiam, his verbis eam explicauit: Substantia, quę propriè, principaliter, & maximè dicitur, &c. Quibus, euidens est significari, proprias excellentias primæ substantiæ, quæ non possunt ei conuenire, in ordine ad secundam intentionem: sed secundùm propriam naturam realem per se subsistentem: ergo secundùm eam definitur, & non vt denominata à secunda intentione. Et sic potiùs definiri debuit, quàm per secundam intentionem, quia nisi cognoscatur natura realis eius, non potest intelligi modus, qua fundamentum est secundæ intentionis.

38 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle and by reason. For Aristotle, wishing to define first substance, explained it in these words: Substance which is said properly, principally, and most of all, etc. By which it is evident that the proper excellences of first substance are signified, which cannot belong to it in relation to the second intention, but according to its own real nature, subsisting per se; therefore it is defined according to that nature, and not as denominated by the second intention. And so it had to be defined rather than through the second intention, because unless its real nature is known, the mode by which it is the foundation of the second intention cannot be understood.

Sed ratione probatur eadem sententia, Primò quia prima

But the same opinion is proved by reason. First, because first

p. 299

substantia, ad quamlibet naturam substantialem se extendit, persona verò solùm ad naturam rationalem, atque intellectualem: sed personam definiuit Boëtius, secũdùm modum realem subsistendi, li. de duabus naturis, in principio (inquiens) Persona est rationalis naturæ indiuidua substantia, Ita enim intellexit hanc definitionem schola Theologorum, ergo prima substantia eodem modo potuit definiri ab Arist. Quòd verò sic fuerit definita, probat testimonium citatum.

substance extends to any substantial nature whatever, whereas person extends only to rational and intellectual nature; but Boethius defined person according to the real mode of subsisting, in the book On the Two Natures, at the beginning, saying: A person is an individual substance of a rational nature. For so the school of the Theologians understood this definition; therefore first substance could be defined by Aristotle in the same way. And that it was so defined, the testimony cited proves.

39 Secundo, quia prima substantia definitur secundùm rationem per quam punitur in prædicamẽto, tanquam fundamentũ reale totius prædicamenti: sed euidens est, in prædicamento non collocari, vt denominatur à secunda intentione, quia sic nõ est fundamentum reale, sed secundùm realem naturam per se subsistentem, & sustentantem omnia, ergo secundùm eam definitur, & nõ vt denominatur à secunda intentione subiecti.

39 Second, because first substance is defined according to the ratio by which it is placed in the category, as the real foundation of the whole category; but it is evident that it is not placed in the category as it is denominated by the second intention, because so it is not a real foundation, but according to its real nature, subsisting per se and sustaining all things; therefore it is defined according to that nature, and not as it is denominated by the second intention of subject.

Ad testimonium Arist. pro prima sententia, Respondetur, quòd prima substãtia per proprium modum realem subsistendi habet etiam reales negationes inhærendi in subiecto, & prędicandi de illo, & ideo definitio, secundùm has negationes reales, intelligenda est, & non secundùm negationes intẽtionales.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, the reply is that first substance, through its proper real mode of subsisting, also has the real negations of inhering in a subject and of being predicated of it; and therefore the definition is to be understood according to these real negations, and not according to intentional negations.

Ad primum arg. Respondetur, negando minorem, quòd Petrus, & Ioannes, vt sunt singulares homines, non conueniant, quia à modo singularitatis vtriusque abstrahi potest conceptus communis modi singularitatis. Et eodem modo, primæ substantiæ, conueniunt in modo subsistendi per se, à quá conuenientia non est necesse, vt separentur per alias differentias, sed per easdem subsistẽtias, vt determinatas, atque distinctas, sufficienter separantur, & ideo non dabitur processus in infinitum.

To the first argument the reply is by denying the minor, that Peter and John, as they are singular men, do not agree: because from the mode of singularity of each a common concept of the mode of singularity can be abstracted. And in the same way first substances agree in the mode of subsisting per se; from which agreement it is not necessary that they be separated by other differences, but they are sufficiently separated by the same subsistences as determinate and distinct, and therefore there will be no process to infinity.

40 Ad secundum negamus, quòd duo illa absurda sequantur, si definiantur aliquid commune primis substantiis, nam illud commune non est, cui non conuenit definitio: sed ratio sub qua conuenit primis substantiis: quare nec est in subiecto, nec de subiecto dicitur, sed est communis ratio eorum, quæ nec sunt in subiecto, nec dicuntur de subiecto.

40 To the second, we deny that those two absurdities follow if something common to first substances is defined: for that common thing is not something to which the definition does not belong, but the ratio under which it belongs to first substances; wherefore it neither is in a subject nor is said of a subject, but is the common ratio of those things which neither are in a subject nor are said of a subject.

Nec etiam sequitur secundum, quòd conueniat definitio secundis substantiis, quia secunda substantia non est, quodcunque prædicatur de prima: sed quod prædicatur de illa, tanquam natura generica, aut specifica: quod probatur ex definitione secundarum substantiarum, quæ sic habet Secundæ substantiæ sunt genera, & species, quibus primæ substantię insunt, communis autem illa ratio, sub qua definiuntur primæ substantiæ, non est naturæ, & ideo non est generica nec differentialis, sed solùm modalis.

Nor does the second follow either, that the definition belongs to second substances: because second substance is not whatever is predicated of first substance, but what is predicated of it as a generic or specific nature; which is proved from the definition of second substances, which runs thus: Second substances are the genera and species in which first substances are. But that common ratio under which first substances are defined is not of the nature, and therefore it is neither generic nor differential, but only modal.

p. 300

PRIMVM DVBIVM CIRCA COMparationes primarum, & secundarum substantiarum.

F I R S T D O U B T, C O N C E R N I N G T H E

COMPARISONS OF FIRST AND SECOND SUBSTANCES

41 DVo restant explicanda circa textum Arist. Primum pertinet ad comparationes, quas fecit inter primas, & secundas substantias. Secundum ad proprietates eiusdem substantiæ. Hæc autem breuitatis gratia, quibusdam dubiis explicabuntur. Et primum est circa comparationes, an sint veræ. Sunt autem quatuor. Nam primò comparat primas substantias cum secundis, & asserit, Primam esse magis substantiam, quàm secundam. Secundò, comparat secundas substantias inter se dupliciter, nempe genus cum specie, & species inter se, & affirmat Speciem esse magis substantiam, quàm genus: sed inter species, vnam non esse magis substantiam, quàm alteram. Vltimò comparat primas inter se, affirmans, etiam Vnum non esse magis substantiam, quàm aliam.

41 Two things remain to be explained concerning the text of Aristotle. The first pertains to the comparisons which he made between first and second substances; the second to the properties of the same substance. These, for brevity’s sake, will be explained in certain doubts. And the first is about the comparisons, whether they are true. Now they are four. For first he compares first substances with second ones, and asserts that first substance is more substance than second. Second, he compares second substances among themselves in two ways, namely genus with species, and species among themselves; and he affirms that the species is more substance than the genus, but that among species one is not more substance than another. Lastly he compares first substances among themselves, affirming also that one is not more substance than another.

Sed aduersus has comparationes, tria argumenta proponuntur. Primum aduersus omnes, quia videntur contradicere cuidam proprietati eiusdem substantiæ, qua dicitur, Substantiam non suscipere magis, & minùs: quod si ita est, falsum erit, quòd vna substantia sit magis substantia quàm alia, siue prima sit vel secunda.

But against these comparisons three arguments are proposed. The first against all of them: because they seem to contradict a certain property of the same substance, by which it is said that substance does not admit of more and less; and if this is so, it will be false that one substance is more substance than another, whether it be first or second.

Secundum argumentum est contra primam comparationem, in qua dicitur, quòd prima substantia est magis substantia, quàm secunda, nam secunda substantia est species, vt homo, & prima substantia est indiuiduum, vt Petrus: sed species perfectior est indiuiduo, ergo secunda substãtia erit perfectior prima, & ideo erit magis substantia, quàm illa. Probatur minor, quia perfectior essentialis rei, sumitur ex prædicatis essentialibus: sed prædicata essentialia primò conueniunt speciei, & per participationẽ eius indiuiduo, ergo perfectior erit species.

The second argument is against the first comparison, in which it is said that first substance is more substance than second: for second substance is the species, as man, and first substance is the individual, as Peter; but the species is more perfect than the individual; therefore second substance will be more perfect than first, and therefore it will be more substance than it. The minor is proved: because the perfection of an essential thing is taken from the essential predicates; but the essential predicates belong first to the species, and by participation of it to the individual; therefore the species will be more perfect.

42 Tertium est contra comparationem secundarum substantiarum atque primarum inter se, in qua dicit Arist. Vnam speciem, non esse magis substantiam, quàm alteram. Quod probo esse falsum: nam illa est magis substantia, quàm altera, quæ pluribus substat, sed vna species pluribus substat quàm alia, ergo erit magis substantia. Probatur minor, quia coruus substat pluribus prædicatis, quàm homo: quia substat omnibus, quibus substat homo, & duobus aliis, nempe bruto, & aui, quæ sunt genera inferiora animali: & inter primas substantias, vna etiam

42 The third is against the comparison of second substances, and of first ones, among themselves, in which Aristotle says that one species is not more substance than another. Which I prove to be false: for that one is more substance than another which stands under more things; but one species stands under more things than another; therefore it will be more substance. The minor is proved: because crow stands under more predicates than man: because it stands under all those under which man stands, and under two others, namely brute and bird, which are genera inferior to animal; and among first substances too, one

p. 301

substat pluribus, quàm alia: nam coruus iste singularis, substat eisdem generibus, quibus sicut non substat homo, ita nec Petrus: ergo erit magis substantia quàm Petrus.

stands under more things than another: for this singular crow stands under the same genera under which, just as man does not stand, so neither does Peter; therefore it will be more a substance than Peter.

Pro solutione primi argumenti, notandum est, Magis & Minus, duobus modis sumi posse, Propriè, & Impropriè. Sumitur autem Propriè, pro intensione graduali qualitatis: secundùm quam, Calidum, vt quatuor, magis calidum dicitur propriè, quàm Calidum, vt duo: quia plures habet gradus intensionis eiusdem caloris. Impropriè verò sumuntur magis, & minus, pro magis, & minùs perfecto, sub quacunque consideratione, siue essentiali, siue accidentali, siue intensiua, aut extensiua: in qua acceptione homo dicitur magis substantia, quàm equus, hoc est, perfectior essentialiter. Dum ergo Aristoteles in principio capitis dicit, Primam substantiam esse magis substantiam, quàm secundam, & inter secundas, speciem magis substantiam, quàm genus: in secunda significatione accipit verba illa, Magis, & Minus: sed dum asserit in fine capitis, substantiam non suscipere magis, & minus, accipit ea primo modo: & ideo non est sibi contrarius.

For the solution of the first argument, it should be noted that More and Less can be taken in two ways, Properly and Improperly. They are taken Properly for the gradual intension of a quality: according to which Hot as four is properly called more hot than Hot as two, because it has more degrees of intension of the same heat. But improperly more and less are taken for more and less perfect, under any consideration whatever, whether essential or accidental, whether intensive or extensive: in which acceptation man is said to be more a substance than a horse, that is, more perfect essentially. When, therefore, Aristotle says at the beginning of the chapter that the first substance is more a substance than the second, and among the second substances the species is more a substance than the genus, he takes those words More and Less in the second signification; but when he asserts at the end of the chapter that substance does not admit of more and less, he takes them in the first way; and therefore he does not contradict himself.

Pro solutione secundi argumenti, notandum est, Substantiam duobus modis sumi posse. Primo, quantum ad essentiam abstrahentem ab actuali existentia, & subsistentia: & ideo, quæ solùm respicit essentialia prædicata. Secundo, sumitur pro essentia, in ordine ad actualem entitatem, quam habet extra causas, per actualem existentiam, & completam quidem, per subsistentiam: & substantiam hoc modo sumptam, sequitur proprietas substandi accidentibus, & prędicatis superioribus: nam ex eo, quòd substantia per se subsistit, potest sustentare omnia: nunc ergo, si substantia primo modo accipiatur, perfectiùs conuenit secundæ substantiæ, quàm primæ: & hoc probat argumentum: sed non sic accipitur ab Aristotele: verùm in secunda acceptione, & in quantum illi conuenit proprietas substandi: & hoc modo verum est, quòd prima substantia, sit perfectior, quàm secunda: quia propria virtute substat, secunda verò, non nisi virtute eius.

For the solution of the second argument, it should be noted that Substance can be taken in two ways. First, as to the essence abstracting from actual existence and subsistence; and therefore as it regards only the essential predicates. Second, it is taken for the essence in order to the actual entity which it has outside its causes through actual existence, and complete entity through subsistence; and upon substance taken in this way there follows the property of standing under accidents and superior predicates: for from the fact that substance subsists per se, it can sustain all things. Now, then, if substance is taken in the first way, it belongs more perfectly to the second substance than to the first; and this is what the argument proves. But it is not so taken by Aristotle, but in the second acceptation, and insofar as the property of standing under belongs to it; and in this way it is true that the first substance is more perfect than the second, because it stands under by its own power, but the second only by the power of the first.

43 Tertium argumentũ, alia distinctione soluendũ est: nam substare, duobus modis sumitur, Intensiuè, & Extensiuè: Intensiuè, accipitur in ordine ad virtutem substandi, & hoc modo, illud dicitur magis substare, quod propria virtute substat, & illud minus, quod virtute alterius: Extensiuè autem, in ordine ad plura, vel pauciora, quibus aliquid substat. Et ex hoc respondetur ad argumentum, quòd dum Aristoteles ait, Primam substantiam esse magis substantiam quàm secundam, vtroque modo

43 The third argument is to be solved by another distinction: for to stand under is taken in two ways, Intensively and Extensively. Intensively it is taken in order to the power of standing under, and in this way that is said to stand under more which stands under by its own power, and that less which does so by the power of another. But Extensively, in order to the more or fewer things under which something stands. And from this it is replied to the argument that when Aristotle says that the first substance is more a substance than the second, in both

p. 302

intelligit hanc comparationem: tam intensiuè, quàm extensiuè. Et vtroque modo verum est: quia prima substantia pluribus substat, quàm secunda: & etiam propria virtute substat, secunda verò non nisi virtute primæ: aliæ verò comparationes intensiuè intelliguntur, non extensiuè: & ideo verum est inter species, nullam esse, quæ substet virtute alterius. Argumentum verò solùm probat, magis substare extensiuè, quod est, pluribus substare: & eodem modo, verum est, inter primas substantias, vnam, non magis substare, quàm alteram intensiuè: quia vna non substat virtute alterius, sed quælibet virtute propria. Species verò magis substantia dicitur, quàm genus, vtroque modo: extensiuè quidem: nam & pluribus substat, cùm substet ipsi generi, & cæteris. Et etiam intensiuè, quia licèt non substet propria virtute, sicut nec genus, tamen propinquiùs accedit ad id, quod substat propria virtute, nempe ad primam substantiam: & hoc sufficit, vt dicatur, magis substare intensiuè.

he understands this comparison both intensively and extensively. And in both ways it is true: because the first substance stands under more things than the second, and also stands under by its own power, while the second does so only by the power of the first. But the other comparisons are understood intensively, not extensively: and therefore it is true that among species there is none that stands under by the power of another. The argument, however, proves only that one stands under more extensively, that is, that it stands under more things. And in the same way it is true that among first substances one does not stand under more than another intensively: because one does not stand under by the power of another, but each by its own power. But the species is said to be more a substance than the genus in both ways: extensively indeed, for it stands under more things, since it stands under the genus itself and the rest. And also intensively, because, although it does not stand under by its own power, any more than the genus does, yet it comes nearer to that which stands under by its own power, namely to the first substance; and this suffices for it to be said to stand under more intensively.

SECOND DOUBT CONCERNING THE THIRD

DVBIVM SECVNDVM CIRCA tertiam proprietatem substantiæ.

P RO P E RT Y O F S U B S TA N C E .

An verum sit, & in quo sensu, Secundas substantias significare Quale quid.

Whether it is true, and in what sense, that Second substances signify Quale quid.

QVòd secundæ substantiæ, non significent Quale quid, vt Aristoteles docet, duobus argumentis probo. Primo, quia duo tantùm possunt considerari in nomine aliquo, ex quibus intelligatur significare, Quid, vel Quale quid: nempe, res significata, an sit Substantia, vel qualitas, & modus eam significandi. Nomina secundarum substantiarum ex parte vtriusque significant Quid, hoc est, Substantiam, & non Quale quid: ergo falsum est, Quale quid significare. Probatur minor: quia ex parte rei significatæ, substantiam, significant, & etiam ex parte modi, cùm sint nomina substantiua, significantia rem per modum subsistentis.

That second substances do not signify Quale quid, as Aristotle teaches, I prove by two arguments. First, because only two things can be considered in any name from which it may be understood to signify Quid or Quale quid: namely, the thing signified, whether it is Substance or quality; and the mode of signifying it. The names of second substances, on the part of both, signify Quid, that is, Substance, and not Quale quid; therefore it is false that they signify Quale quid. The minor is proved: because on the part of the thing signified they signify substance, and also on the part of the mode, since they are substantive names, signifying the thing by way of something subsisting.

Secundò: Ex modo significandi, sumitur modus prædicandi, ergo si secundæ substantiæ, quæ sunt genera, & species, significant Quale quid, sequitur, quòd prędicẽtur de primis in Quale quid. Consequens est falsum, ergo & antecedens, probo minorem auctoritate, & ratione: nam Porphyrius cap. de genere, & specie docuit expressè, Genus & speciem prædicari in Quid. Et ratio ipsa coniunxit: quia ad interrogationem factam de specie, per Quid, respondemus, per genus: & ad interrogationem factam de indiuiduo, per speciem, vt si inquiras, quid est

Second: the mode of predicating is taken from the mode of signifying; therefore if second substances, which are genera and species, signify Quale quid, it follows that they are predicated of the first in Quale quid. The consequent is false; therefore so is the antecedent. I prove the minor by authority and by reason: for Porphyry, in the chapter on genus and species, expressly taught that Genus and species are predicated in Quid. And reason itself joins with this: because to a question asked about the species by Quid, we reply by the genus; and to a question asked about the individual, by the species: as if you ask what is Peter

p. 303

homo? respondemus esse animal: & si inquiras, quid sit Petrus? Esse hominem: ergo vtraque secunda substantia prædicatur in Quid, & non in Quale quid.

man, we reply that it is an animal; and if you ask what Peter is, that he is a man: therefore each second substance is predicated in Quid, and not in Quale quid.

Circa sensum huius proprietatis, diuerso modo loquuntur auctores: & primus modus dicendi, est Alberti Magni, tract. 7. prædicamentorum, cap. 8. vbi inquit: Genera, & species, quę sunt secundę substantię, ratione naturę genericę, significare Quid: sed propter differentiam, quam species continet actu, & genus potentia: significant Quale, & ideo ratione vtriusque, Quale quid: & hunc fuisse sensum Arist.

Concerning the sense of this property, authors speak in different ways. And the first way of speaking is that of Albert the Great, Categories, tract. 7, ch. 8, where he says: Genera and species, which are second substances, by reason of the generic nature signify Quid; but on account of the difference, which the species contains in act and the genus in potency, they signify Quale, and therefore by reason of both, Quale quid; and that this was the sense of Aristotle.

Hic tamen modus dicendi, hoc arg. probatur falsus: Si genus, & Species, ratione vtriusque partis essentialis, significant Quale quid, ergo prędicantur in Quale quid, contra sententiã Porph. qui sciens speciem continere genus & differentiam, & genus differentiã, docuit expressè, vtrumque prædicari in Quid, & non in Quale quid, & est contra rationem: quia si prędicarẽtur in Quale quid, non distinguerentur à prędicabili differentiæ. Ideo hanc sententiã meritò refutauit Caiet. cap. præsenti.

This way of speaking, however, is proved false by this argument: If genus and Species, by reason of each essential part, signify Quale quid, then they are predicated in Quale quid, against the opinion of Porphyry, who, knowing that the species contains genus and difference, and the genus difference, expressly taught that each is predicated in Quid, and not in Quale quid; and it is against reason: because if they were predicated in Quale quid, they would not be distinguished from the predicable difference. Therefore Cajetan rightly refuted this opinion, in the present chapter.

Ipse verò Caiet. secundum modum dicendi proponit, duo distinguens in genere, & specie nempe naturam genericam, aut specificam, quæ denominatur genus: & secundam intentionem, à qua denominantur: & propter naturam genericam, atque specificam, quę sunt substantiæ, significant aliquid: sed propter secundam intentionem: quæ est accidens, & modum habet qualitatis, sicut albedo, & color, significant Quale, & ideo propter vtramque significant Quale quid.
