But we regard both of these as the same, and judge that they differ in name alone. For since the extension of parts is the root of impenetrability, as of the other attributes, it is the same to say that the essence of quantity consists in the extension of parts, and in the fact that quantity is the root of impenetrability. But we say that the extension is more clearly explained by that which is to have one part outside another according to bulk, or magnitude occupative of a different part of place, as already declared by us.

15 Conclusio igitur nostræ sententiæ, & communis est, quòd essentia quantitatis non consistat in diuisibilitate, ac mensura, sed in extensione partium. Probatur hoc arg. ex doctrina tradita desumpto. Essentia rei, in eo debet consistere, quod primò de illa concipimus, non in aliis, quæ ex eo consequi intelligimus: sed

15 The conclusion, then, of our view, and the common one, is that the essence of quantity does not consist in divisibility and measure, but in the extension of parts. This is proved by an argument taken from the doctrine delivered. The essence of a thing ought to consist in that which we first conceive of it, not in the other things which we understand to follow from it; but

p. 319

primum, quod concipimus de quantitate, est extensio partium, ex qua intelligimus sequi diuisibilitatem, & mensuram: ergo extensio erit essentia quantitatis, potiùs quàm diuisibilitas, aut mensura. Minorẽ probo: quia primũ est habere partes, quã esse diuisibile in eas, aut per eas mensurabile: ergo priùs est habere partes extensas, quã esse diuisibile in partes extẽsas, aut per eas mensurabile, & ex illo sequuntur hæc: & ideo illud erit essentia quãtitatis, diuisibilitas verò, & mẽsura, propriæ passiones eius.

the first thing that we conceive of quantity is the extension of parts, from which we understand divisibility and measure to follow; therefore extension will be the essence of quantity rather than divisibility or measure. I prove the minor: because it is prior to have parts than to be divisible into them or measurable by them; therefore it is prior to have extended parts than to be divisible into extended parts or measurable by them, and these follow from that; and therefore that will be the essence of quantity, but divisibility and measure its proper attributes.

16 Ad testimonium Aristotelis pro prima opinione, Respondeo: quò dum dixit, Tempus esse numerum motus, per numerum, non intellexit mensuram, sed discretionem, aut distinctionem partium motus, secundùm prius & posterius: hanc enim propriè significat numerus: vt in nostris Commentariis super 4. librum Physicorum, expositum reperitur.

16 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, I reply that when he said that Time is the number of motion, by number he did not understand measure, but the discreteness or distinction of the parts of motion according to before and after; for this is what number properly signifies, as is found explained in our Commentaries on the fourth book of the Physics.

Ad arg. eiusdem opinionis, Concedenda est maior, sed minor neganda: Quia si locus species est distincta à superficie, non potest distingui, per solam rationem mensuræ, sed prius debet distingui, per extensionem, ratione cuius conuenit ei mensura.

To the argument of the same opinion, the major is to be granted, but the minor denied: Because if place is a species distinct from surface, it cannot be distinguished by the ratio of measure alone, but must first be distinguished by extension, by reason of which measure belongs to it.

17 Ad testimonium Arist. pro sententia Scoti, Concedimus, Aristotelem definisse quantitatem per diuisibilitatem: sed neganda est minor, quòd definitio sit essentialis, sed descriptiua potiùs censenda est: quia datur per propriam passionem diuisibilitatis. Aristoteles autem, per passionem, voluit describere quantitatem: quia notior nobis est diuisibilitas, quàm extensio partium: & ita per illam fit nobis extensio manifesta. Vel secundò, respondemus, Diuisibilitatem duobus modis sumi posse. Primò, pro formali aptitudine ad diuisionem. Secundò pro radice eius, quam possumus appellare diuisibilitatem radicalem: & est idem prorsus, cum extensione partium à qua diximus, procedere diuisibilitatem formalem tanquam ab essentia. Hoc supposito, concedere possumus, eandem minorem arg. quòd definitio sit essentialis: sed per diuisibilitatem in ea positam, non intelligitur formalis, sed radicalis: quæ idem est cum extensione. Quare idem est etiam per diuisibilitatem sic sumptam, definitam esse quantitatem, ac per extensionem: in qua potiùs consistit essentia quantitatis, quàm in diuisibilitate formali.

17 To the testimony of Aristotle for the opinion of Scotus: We grant that Aristotle defined quantity by divisibility; but the minor is to be denied, that the definition is essential; rather it is to be judged descriptive, because it is given through the proper attribute of divisibility. And Aristotle wished to describe quantity through an attribute because divisibility is better known to us than the extension of parts, and so through it extension becomes manifest to us. Or, second, we reply that Divisibility can be taken in two ways. First, for the formal aptitude to division. Second, for its root, which we can call radical divisibility; and this is altogether the same as the extension of parts, from which we said formal divisibility proceeds as from its essence. This supposed, we can grant the same minor of the argument, that the definition is essential; but by the divisibility placed in it is understood not formal but radical divisibility, which is the same as extension. Wherefore it is also the same for quantity to be defined by divisibility so taken as by extension, in which the essence of quantity consists rather than in formal divisibility.

Ad secundum, Concedimus, per diuisibilitatem distingui, à multis, species quantitatis, tanquam per propriam passionem nobis notiorem, ex qua cognoscimus distinctionem essentialem, quam habet per extensionem. Vel secundò, dicimus, distinguere eas per diuisibilitatem, radicaliter sumptã, quæ idem est, cum extensione: & tunc distinctione est essentialis.

To the second, we grant that the species of quantity are distinguished by many through divisibility, as through a proper attribute better known to us, from which we come to know the essential distinction which it has through extension. Or, second, we say that they distinguish them through divisibility taken radically, which is the same as extension; and then the distinction is essential.

p. 320

QUESTION II

Quæst. 2. Vtrùm Linea, Superficies & Corpus, sint tres species distinctæ quantitatis continuæ — Whether Line, Surface and body are three distinct species of continuous quantity.

Vtrùm Linea, Superficies, & corpus, sint tres species distinctæ quantitatis continuæ.

[…]

18 Vt ratio harum specierum intelligatur, notandum est, ex D. Tho. opus. 48. tract. 5. ca. 3. Quòd licèt punctum, à linea non separetur realiter, nec linea à superficie, nec superficies à corpore: per intellectum tamen apprehẽdere possumus, punctum, quod omnino est indiuisibile, realiter separatum à linea, & fingere, quod per planum ducatur: & tunc ex ductu eius, remanebit vestigium longum, sed nec latum, nec profundum, quod vestigium, si versus latera extendatur, relinquetur aliud, non solùm longum, sed etiam latum, & tandem, si hoc eleuetur, aut deprimatur, relinquetur tertium aliud vestigium, longum, latum atque profundum: hoc est habens grossitiem.

18 In order that the ratio of these species may be understood, it should be noted, from St. Thomas, opusc. 48, tract. 5, ch. 3, That although the point is not really separated from the line, nor the line from the surface, nor the surface from the body, yet by the intellect we can apprehend the point, which is altogether indivisible, as really separated from the line, and imagine that it is drawn across a plane; and then from its drawing there will remain a trace that is long, but neither broad nor deep. Which trace, if it is extended sideways, will leave another, not only long but also broad; and finally, if this is raised or lowered, it will leave a third trace, long, broad and deep, that is, having thickness.

19 Primum ergo vestigium, est continuum, & diuisibile secũdùm longitudinem, & appellatur linea: & cùm sit vestigium relictum ex ductu puncti, continuatur punctis: continuari verò est quaslibet duas partes eius copulari puncto indiuisibili, & ita efficit vnum continuum. Vestigium secundum, est longum, & latum, sed caret profunditate: quia non habet grossitiem (vt sic loquamur) & ideo est diuisibile, secundùm longitudinem & latitudinem, sed caret profunditate: & ideo est indiuisibile secundum profunditatem, & cùm sit vestigium, relictum ex extensione lineæ, continuatur lineis, & appellatur superficies. Tertium vestigium, est longum, latum & profundùm, & cùm sit relictum ex eleuatione, aut depressione superficiei, partes eius continuantur superficiebus: & est diuisibile, secundùm longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem, quæ appellantur dimensiones quantitatis: quia quantitatem continuam, his tribus modis, quasi dimetiri possumus, hoc est, secundùm longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem: & quia non sunt plures dimensiones, corpus dicitur diuisibile secundùm omnem dimensionem.

19 The first trace, then, is continuous and divisible according to length, and is called a line; and since it is a trace left from the drawing of a point, it is continued by points. Now to be continued is for any two of its parts to be joined by an indivisible point, and thus it makes one continuum. The second trace is long and broad, but lacks depth, because it does not have thickness (so to speak); and therefore it is divisible according to length and breadth, but lacks depth, and therefore is indivisible according to depth; and since it is a trace left from the extension of the line, it is continued by lines, and is called a surface. The third trace is long, broad and deep; and since it is left from the raising or lowering of the surface, its parts are continued by surfaces, and it is divisible according to length, breadth and depth, which are called the dimensions of quantity, because we can as it were measure continuous quantity in these three ways, that is, according to length, breadth and depth; and because there are no more dimensions, body is said to be divisible according to every dimension.

20 De his ergo tribus, linea, superficie, & corpore, duo possent disputari. Primum: An distinguantur realiter, aut ex natura rei, possintque separari realiter: sed quæstio hæc Philosophica est, & ideo non pertinet ad propositum nostrum. Nunc verò supponenda est, tanquam communis opinio, quòd distinguuntur realiter aut ex natura rei, sine dependentia ab intellectu: & quòd naturaliter saltem nullum eorum potest separari realiter ab aliis. Secundum quod potest disputari, est, An

20 Of these three, then, line, surface and body, two things could be disputed. The first: Whether they are distinguished really or from the nature of the thing, and whether they can be separated really. But this question is a Philosophical one, and therefore does not pertain to our purpose. For now it is to be supposed, as the common opinion, that they are distinguished really or from the nature of the thing, without dependence on the intellect; and that, naturally at least, none of them can be separated really from the others. The second thing that can be disputed is Whether they

p. 321

distinguantur specie, & ideo sint species distinctæ quantitatis continuæ: & hoc quærit titulus quæstionis.

are distinguished in species, and are therefore distinct species of continuous quantity: and this is what the title of the question asks.

Circa quam, est prima opinio Duran. in 2. d. 2. q. 4. asserentis, lineam, & superficiem, non esse veras species quantitatis, sed solùm negationes quasdam dimensionum: vt lineam, negationem latitudinis, superficiem, negationem profunditatis. Probat hoc argumento: Quia differentia constituens, atque distinguens speciem, debet esse positiua, cùm se habeat tanquam forma: sed linea, & superficies, non habent differentiam positiuam, per quam constituantur, & distinguantur: ergo non sunt veræ species quantitatis. Probatur minor, quia solùm distinguitur linea à superficie, quod careat latitudine, & superficies à corpore, quòd careat profunditate, ergo solùm sunt negationes quædam latitudinis, & profunditatis, & non veræ species.

On this the first opinion is that of Durandus, in 2, d. 2, q. 4, who asserts that line and surface are not true species of quantity, but only certain negations of dimensions: line, the negation of breadth; surface, the negation of depth. He proves it by this argument: The difference that constitutes and distinguishes a species must be positive, since it stands as a form; but line and surface do not have a positive difference by which they are constituted and distinguished; therefore they are not true species of quantity. The minor is proved: because a line is distinguished from a surface only in that it lacks breadth, and a surface from a body in that it lacks depth; therefore they are only certain negations of breadth and of depth, and not true species.

21 Secunda opinio tenet, lineam, & superficiem, esse entitates positiuas, & non solas negationes, sed non distingui specie. Probat hac ratione. Si linea, & superficies, distinguerentur specie inter sese, & à corpore, maximè per longitudinem: distinguerentur, & latitudine: sed per has non: ergo nullo modo. Probatur minor: quia superficies includit longitudinem, & latitudinem, ergo non distinguitur ab ea linea, per longitudinem. Deinde corpus, includit longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem, ergo non distinguuntur ab eo, linea, & superficies, per longitudinem & latitudinem.

21 The second opinion holds that line and surface are positive entities, and not mere negations, but that they are not distinguished in species. It proves this by the following reasoning. If line and surface were distinguished in species from each other and from body, they would be distinguished above all by length and breadth; but they are not distinguished by these; therefore in no way. The minor is proved: because a surface includes length and breadth; therefore a line is not distinguished from it by length. Next, a body includes length, breadth, and depth; therefore line and surface are not distinguished from it by length and breadth.

Tertia sententia est communis, & vera: Quòd linea, superficies, & corpus sint veræ species quantitatis continuæ, atque distinctæ. Hæc est expressa apud Aristot. non solùm cap. præsenti, sed 5. Meta. c. 13. vbi singulas has species, suis descriptionibus explicat: & omnes eius interpretes in Commentariis vtriusque loci eam sequuntur.

The third opinion is the common and true one: that line, surface, and body are true species of continuous quantity, and distinct ones. It is expressly found in Aristotle, not only in the present chapter but in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, where he explains each of these species by its own description; and all his interpreters follow it in their Commentaries on both passages.

Præterea ratione probatur primò: quòd sint veræ species quantitatis: quia extensio partium, intrinseca ratio quantitatis est, & diuisibilitas in partes, propria passio eius: sed vtraque ratio conuenit formaliter lineæ, & superficiei: illi quidem secundùm longitudinem, huic verò secundùm latitudinem, & corpori secundùm profunditatẽ, secundùm quas dimensiones extenduntur partes eorum: ergo sunt veræ species quantitatis.

Moreover, it is proved by reason, first, that they are true species of quantity: because extension of parts is the intrinsic ratio of quantity, and divisibility into parts its proper attribute; but each ratio belongs formally to line and to surface: to the former according to length, to the latter according to breadth, and to body according to depth, the dimensions according to which their parts are extended; therefore they are true species of quantity.

22 Probatur deinde, quòd sint species distinctæ. Primò, quia multa demonstrantur in Mathematicis de his speciebus, tanquam de distinctis: Geometra enim agit de sola linea, tanquam de proprio obiecto, nihil considerans de latitudine aut superficie: & perspectiuus de linea visuali: ergo distincta species est à superficie, & corpore. Secundò, Quia rationes

22 It is proved next that they are distinct species. First, because many things are demonstrated in Mathematics about these species as about distinct ones: for the geometer treats of the line alone as of his proper object, considering nothing of breadth or surface; and the student of perspective of the visual line: therefore it is a species distinct from surface and body. Second, because the formal X

p. 322

formales diuersæ, distinguunt diuersas species: sed longitudo, quam dicit linea, est diuersa ratio formalis à latitudine, quam dicit superficies, & à profunditate, quam dicit corpus, vt ex se patet: ergo distinguitur species ab eis: & idem potest probari de superficie, & corpore.

ratios, when diverse, distinguish diverse species; but length, which line expresses, is a formal ratio diverse from breadth, which surface expresses, and from depth, which body expresses, as is plain of itself; therefore it is distinguished in species from them; and the same can be proved of surface and body.

23 Sed tota difficultas distinguendi has species, in eo consistit: quòd videntur posteriores includere priores: vt corpus superficiem: & lineam, & superficies lineam. Vt ergo fiat manifestum: hanc inclusionem non tollere differentiam specificam, notandum est primò, lineam, & superficiem duobus modis sumi posse. Primò, vt sunt indiuisibiles, linea quidem secundùm latitudinem, & superficies secundùm profunditatem: & hoc modo, non sunt species quantitatis: sicut punctum, non est species quantitatis, sed terminatiuum, & continuatiuum partium lineæ. Probatur vtrumque: quia quantitas essentialiter est diuisibilis: ergo linea, & superficies, vt sunt indiuisibiles, non possunt esse species quantitatis, sed sunt terminatiuæ, & continuatiuæ alterius speciei: linea continuatiua partium superficiei, & superficies continuatiua partium corporis. Secundo modo accipiuntur, vt diuisibiles sunt, secundùm proprias dimensiones: linea secundùm longitudinem, & superficies secundùm latitudinem, & habent sua indiuisibilia, quibus partes eorum continuantur, & terminantur: linea terminatur, & continuatur punctis: superficies verò continuatur lineis, vt indiuisibilibus secundùm latitudinem. Et hoc modo sunt species quantitatis distinctæ, & pertinent per se, & directè, ad prædicamentum: sed secundùm primam considerationem, solùm pertinent reductiuè ad speciem illam, cuius partes copulant, vt linea ad speciem superficiei, & hæc ad speciem corporis. Sed dum dicimus, lineam esse indiuisibilem, secundùm latitudinem, & superficiem secundùm profunditatem, per indiuisibilitatem, non debemus intelligere puram negationem dimensionis: sed modum positiuum, qui per negationem indiuisibilitatis explicatur: sicut per punctum omnino indiuisibile, non intelligimus puram negationem, sed modum positiuum, quo copulantur partes lineæ. Ratio huius est: quia officium copulandi partes, reale est, & positiuum: ergo non potest à pura negatione fieri, sed ab entitate positiua. Secundò notandũ est, ex doctrina D. Th. vbi suprà, sic se habere has duas species, superficiem, & corpus, vt quęlibet dicat vnam tantùm dimensionem, de formali, nempe vltimam: aliã verò, vel alias, de materiali, & quasi præsuppositiuè, vt superficies, de formali solùm dicit latitudinem, de

23 But the whole difficulty of distinguishing these species consists in this: that the later ones seem to include the earlier, as body includes surface and line, and surface includes line. In order, then, that it may become manifest that this inclusion does not remove the specific difference, it should be noted, first, that line and surface can be taken in two ways. First, as they are indivisible: line according to breadth, and surface according to depth; and in this way they are not species of quantity, just as the point is not a species of quantity but what terminates and continues the parts of the line. Both are proved: because quantity is essentially divisible; therefore line and surface, as they are indivisible, cannot be species of quantity, but are what terminates and continues another species: the line what continues the parts of the surface, and the surface what continues the parts of the body. In the second way they are taken as they are divisible according to their proper dimensions: the line according to length, and the surface according to breadth; and they have their own indivisibles, by which their parts are continued and terminated: the line is terminated and continued by points, while the surface is continued by lines, as by indivisibles according to breadth. And in this way they are distinct species of quantity, and belong per se and directly to the category; but according to the first consideration they belong only reductively to that species whose parts they join, as the line to the species of surface, and this to the species of body. But when we say that the line is indivisible according to breadth, and the surface according to depth, by indivisibility we must not understand a pure negation of dimension, but a positive mode which is explained through the negation of divisibility; just as by the altogether indivisible point we do not understand a pure negation, but the positive mode by which the parts of the line are joined. The reason for this is that the office of joining parts is real and positive; therefore it cannot be performed by a pure negation, but by a positive entity. It should be noted, second, from the doctrine of St. Thomas in the place cited above, that these two species, surface and body, are so related that each of them expresses only one dimension formally, namely the last, but the other or others materially and as it were presuppositively: as surface formally expresses only breadth,

p. 323

materiali verò, longitudinem: & corpus profunditatem de formali, longitudinem verò, & latitudinem, quasi de materiali: & ratio huius est: quia cùm profunditas sit dimensio continua: copulari debent partes eius, indiuisibilibus secundùm profunditatem: & tales sunt superficies, quæ cùm habeant dimensionem latitudinis: necesse est eam habere corpus: & quia superficies copulari debet indiuisibilibus, secundùm latitudinem, quæ sunt lineæ, habentes longitudinem: ideo necesse est superficiem habere longitudinem: sed ex hoc fit manifestum, quòd eas non habeat formaliter, sed solùm materialiter, & quasi per accidens: quia propria indiuisibilia, quæ per se includunt, simul sunt diuisibilia, secundùm easdem dimensiones. Vnde quia indiuisibilia lineæ, quæ sunt puncta, non sunt diuisibilia secundùm aliam dimensionem: nec linea, de materiali, aut per accidens, vllam aliam dimensionem, præter longitudinem importat.

but length materially; and body formally depth, but length and breadth as it were materially. And the reason for this is that, since depth is a continuous dimension, its parts must be joined by indivisibles according to depth; and such are surfaces, which, since they have the dimension of breadth, body must necessarily have it; and because a surface must be joined by indivisibles according to breadth, which are lines having length, therefore the surface must necessarily have length. But from this it becomes manifest that it does not have them formally, but only materially and as it were per accidens: because the proper indivisibles which they include per se are at the same time divisible according to those same dimensions. Whence, because the indivisibles of the line, which are points, are not divisible according to another dimension, neither does the line, materially or per accidens, import any other dimension besides length.

24 Vltimò notandum est, Genus, & differentiam, ita esse accipienda in his speciebus, vt definitiones earum possimus designare, quòd commune & proximum genus earum sit, quantitas continua, sub qua collocantur: differentia verò accipienda est, in ordine ad proprias dimensiones singularum: & ita definitio lineæ talis erit: Linea, est quantitas continua, extensa secundùm dimensionem formalem longitudinis. Superficies, est quantitas continua, extensa secundùm dimensionem formalem latitudinis. Corpus verò, quantitas continua, extensa secundùm dimensionem formalem profunditatis. Nec enim ponitur longitudo in definitione superficiei, nec latitudo, in definitione corporis: quia, licèt has etiam dimensiones necessariò includant, non tamen formaliter, sed solùm materialiter: imò nec per se, sed per accidens: quod hac ratione probatur: Vna species, nec componitur ex altera formaliter, nec in ea excludi potest: sed linea, superficies, & corpus, sunt species diuersæ quantitatis, ergo nulla potest aliam, aut alias includere formaliter.

24 It should be noted, lastly, that genus and difference are to be taken in these species in such a way that we can assign their definitions: so that their common and proximate genus is continuous quantity, under which they are placed; but the difference is to be taken in relation to the proper dimensions of each; and so the definition of line will be this: A line is a continuous quantity extended according to the formal dimension of length. A surface is a continuous quantity extended according to the formal dimension of breadth. A body is a continuous quantity extended according to the formal dimension of depth. For length is not placed in the definition of surface, nor breadth in the definition of body, because, although they necessarily include these dimensions too, yet they do not do so formally but only materially; nay, not even per se but per accidens. This is proved by the following reasoning: One species is neither composed formally of another, nor can it be included in it; but line, surface, and body are diverse species of quantity; therefore none can include another or others formally.

25 Ex tota hac doctrina intelligitur, quonam modo distinguantur linea, superficies, & corpus: non quidem, vt nonnulli opinantur, per negationem alicuius dimensionis: vt linea à superficie, per negationẽ latitudinis: & superficies à corpore, per negationem profunditatis: sed distinguuntur, per positiuam extensionem, secundùm dimensionem propriam: ita vt linea distinguatur à superficie, per positiuam extensionem partium, secũdùm longitudinem: & superficies à corpore, per positiuam extensionem latitudinis: & corpus ab vtraque, per positiuam extensionem, secundùm dimensionem profunditatis.

25 From this whole doctrine it is understood in what way line, surface, and body are distinguished: not indeed, as some think, by the negation of some dimension, as line from surface by the negation of breadth, and surface from body by the negation of depth; but they are distinguished by positive extension according to their proper dimension: so that the line is distinguished from the surface by the positive extension of its parts according to length; and the surface from the body by the positive extension of breadth; and the body from both by positive extension according to the dimension of depth. X ij

p. 324

Si autem dicatur, Aristotelem 5. Meta. cap. 13. alio modo has species definisse, nempe, Lineam esse magnitudinem continuam ad vnum: hoc est, secundùm vnam dimensionem longitudinis. Superficiem, ad duo, id est, secundùm duas dimensiones, longitudinis, & latitudinis. Et corpus, ad tria, id est, secundùm tres dimensiones, longitudinis, latitudinis, & profunditatis. Respondeo, ita, definisse, sed definitiones istæ, non sunt distinctæ à nostris, verùm eædem cum eis: & differre videntur, quia Aristoteles, non solùm formales dimensiones posuit, per quas constituuntur, ac distinguuntur: sed etiam materiales, in quibus superficies, & corpus conueniunt. Nos verò, solùm per formales definimus eas, non curantes de materialibus, quas præsupponimus necessariò includere.

But if it is said that Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, defined these species in another way, namely: A line is a magnitude continuous in one, that is, according to the one dimension of length; a surface, in two, that is, according to two dimensions, of length and breadth; and a body, in three, that is, according to three dimensions, of length, breadth, and depth: I reply that he did so define them; but these definitions are not distinct from ours, rather they are the same as them; and they seem to differ because Aristotle placed not only the formal dimensions by which they are constituted and distinguished, but also the material ones, in which surface and body agree. We, however, define them only by the formal ones, not caring about the material ones, which we presuppose that they necessarily include.

26 Ad arg. primæ opinionis, neganda est minor, quòd solùm per negationem alicuius dimensionis, distinguantur linea & superficies. Non enim distinguuntur, nisi per positiuam extensionem, secundùm propriam extensionis rationem: quamuis vna dicat negationem dimensionis, quam includit altera: quod commune est omnibus speciebus cuiuscunque generis: nam homo eo ipso, quòd est rationalis, dicit negationem cuiuscunque speciei irrationalis.

26 To the argument of the first opinion, the minor must be denied, namely that line and surface are distinguished only by the negation of some dimension. For they are not distinguished except by positive extension according to the proper ratio of extension; although the one expresses the negation of a dimension which the other includes; which is common to all the species of any genus whatever: for man, by the very fact that he is rational, expresses the negation of every irrational species.

Ad arg. secundæ opinionis, Concessa maiori, neganda est minor, quòd non distinguantur linea, & superficies, per longitudinem, & latitudinem: quia licèt superficies includat longitudinem, nõ tamen formaliter, sicut linea, sed materialiter tantùm: & licèt corpus includat latitudinem, non formaliter, sed materialiter: & cùm distinctio debeat esse per aliquid formale, distinguuntur istæ species, per singulas dimensiones, quas includunt formaliter, & quæ non includunt formaliter ab aliis, vt expositum est. Et si aliquis dicere vellet, superficiem dicere longitudinem aliam, distinctam à longitudine lineæ, & corpus aliam longitudinem, distinctam à longitudine lineæ, & superficiei, & aliam latitudinem, distinctam à latitudine superficiei, & ita distingui à superficie, & linea, non solùm per vnam dimensionem formalem, sed per tres etiam formales, & sibi proprias, & superficiem à linea, & corpore, per duas formales, & sibi proprias, longitudinis, & latitudinis: quod manifestum fieret, si istæ species, saltem per potentiam Dei absolutam, separarentur realiter: tunc enim corpus haberet trinam dimensionem, essẽtque longum, latum, & profundum, & superficies, longa, & lata, linea verò, solùm longa. Respondetur, hunc modum distinguendi has species, per solam imaginationem excogitari posse: sed secundùm rationem implicare contradictionem.

To the argument of the second opinion, granting the major, the minor must be denied, namely that line and surface are not distinguished by length and breadth: because, although surface includes length, yet not formally, as the line does, but only materially; and although body includes breadth, it does so not formally but materially; and since distinction must be through something formal, these species are distinguished by the several dimensions which they include formally, and which the others do not include formally, as has been explained. And if someone wished to say that the surface expresses another length, distinct from the length of the line, and the body another length, distinct from the length of the line and of the surface, and another breadth, distinct from the breadth of the surface; and so that it is distinguished from surface and line not only by one formal dimension but by three, all formal and proper to itself; and the surface from line and body by two formal ones proper to itself, of length and breadth (which would become manifest if these species were separated really, at least by the absolute power of God: for then the body would have a threefold dimension and be long, broad, and deep, and the surface long and broad, but the line only long): the reply is that this way of distinguishing these species can be devised by the imagination alone, but that according to reason it implies a contradiction.

p. 325

Probatur, quia ex eo sequeretur, Corpus habere tres longitudines distinctas, & distinctas solo numero, & eas includere formaliter: & eodem modo, duas latitudines: imò, & triplicata puncta, quibus continuantur diuersæ longitudines: & vtrumque est impossibile.

This is proved: because from it it would follow that the body has three distinct lengths, distinct by number alone, and includes them formally; and in the same way two breadths; nay, even a threefold set of points, by which the diverse lengths are continued: and both are impossible.

27 Primum quidem: quia longitudines omnes, sunt eiusdem speciei, cùm habeant eundem modum extensionis partium, eundem modum continuationis per puncta, & eundem effectum formalem in subiecto: repugnat autem, quòd aliquid includat formaliter, & essentialiter, tria prædicata eiusdem speciei. Probatur secundum esse, impossibile: quia repugnat multa accidentia, purè absoluta, & eiusdem speciei, qualia sunt dimensiones, simul esse in eodem subiecto, à quo aliquo modo accipiunt indiuiduationem, Hoc autem sequeretur, si superficies, & corpus, tot haberent longitudines, & latitudines, quas omnes tribuerunt subiecto, in quo inhærerent.

27 The first indeed, because all lengths are of the same species, since they have the same mode of extension of parts, the same mode of continuation through points, and the same formal effect in the subject; but it is repugnant that something should include formally and essentially three predicates of the same species. The second is proved to be impossible: because it is repugnant that many accidents that are purely absolute and of the same species, such as dimensions are, should be at the same time in the same subject, from which they in some way receive their individuation. But this would follow if surface and body had so many lengths and breadths, all of which they would impart to the subject in which they inhered.

Quòd verò dicitur, has species posse realiter separari, per potentiam Dei absolutam: falsum est, quia manifestam contradictionem implicat. Quod sic probo: Si corpus esset separatum à superficie, esset quantitas continua diuisibilis, secundùm longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem: ergo longitudo eius, continuaretur punctis, & ideo esset linea: Linea nihil aliud est, nisi longitudo continuata punctis: latitudo etiam eius continuaretur lineis: & ideo esset superficies, quare non esset separatum à linea, & superficie, vt supponitur: implicat ergo contradictionem separari: quod potest eodem modo probari, de superficie, vt intelligenti patet.

But what is said, that these species can be separated really by the absolute power of God, is false, because it implies a manifest contradiction. I prove it thus: If a body were separated from the surface, it would be a continuous quantity divisible according to length, breadth, and depth; therefore its length would be continued by points, and so it would be a line (a line is nothing else but length continued by points); its breadth also would be continued by lines, and so it would be a surface; wherefore it would not be separated from line and surface, as is supposed: therefore it implies a contradiction that it be separated. And this can be proved in the same way of the surface, as is plain to one who understands.

28 Ratio autem fundamentalis, propter quam repugnat separari vllo modo has species, est: Quia non est dabilis, imò nec intelligibilis substantia, cui quantitas inhærere possit, nisi corporea: quę ex sua natura, & essentia, non potest suscipere quantitatem, nisi trinę dimensionis, nempe longitudinis, latitudinis, & profunditatis: quare non potest dari quantitas, quæ illas omnes non habeat.

28 But the fundamental reason why it is repugnant that these species be separated in any way is this: because no substance can be given, nay none can even be understood, in which quantity can inhere, except a corporeal one; and this, by its nature and essence, cannot receive any quantity except of threefold dimension, namely of length, breadth, and depth: wherefore no quantity can be given which does not have all of them.

QUESTION III

Vtrùm tempus, sit vera species quantitatis continuæ.

Whether time is a true species of continuous quantity.

Occasionem dedit Aristo. ipse huic quæstioni: nam capite præsenti, tempus enumerauit inter species quantitatis continuæ. Sed Metaph. ca. 13. idem tempus cum motu, docuit esse quantum per accidens, ita vt à mobili, & spatio: seu alia forma,

Aristotle himself gave occasion to this question: for in the present chapter he enumerated time among the species of continuous quantity. But in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, he taught that time, together with motion, is quantified per accidens, so that from the mobile and the space, or another form,

p. 326

circa quam versatur, motus continuationem, & extensionem accipiat: sicut albedo eam accipit à corpore, cui inhæret. Ideo diuersæ sunt opiniones.

with which it is concerned, motion receives its continuation and extension, just as whiteness receives it from the body in which it inheres. Hence the opinions are diverse.

Prima tenet, Tempus non esse speciem quantitatis, nec habere extensionem per se, sed per accidens, sicut motum: ita Pater Franciscus Suarius, tomo 2. suæ Met. disp. 40. lect. 9. nu. 8. & cum eo multi recentiores, Habetque hæc sententia, præter testimonium Arist. plura argum. sed tria hæc sunt potissima, & difficilia. Primum, Species quantitatis, debent esse entia realia: quia quantitas est prædicamentum reale. Sed tempus, non est ens reale: ergo non est species quantitatis. Probatur minor: nam ens reale, quod est totum, debet habere partes reales: sed tempus, cùm sit totum comprehendens sub se præteritum tempus, præsens, & futurum, non habet partes reales: ergo non est reale. Probo iterum minorem: quia reale est illud, quod est in rerum natura: sed nulla pars temporis est in rerum natura, nam tempus præteritum iam non est, futurum nondum est, præsens verò solùm potest esse instans, seu momentum indiuisibile, quia cùm tempus sit successiuum, nullam partem potest habere præsentem, præter indiuisibile: ergo nullam habebit præsentem, & ideo nec realiter existentem.

The first holds that time is not a species of quantity, nor has extension per se, but per accidens, like motion. So Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, disp. 40, lect. 9, no. 8, and with him many of the more recent authors. And this opinion has, besides the testimony of Aristotle, several arguments, but these three are the strongest and difficult. The first: The species of quantity must be real beings, because quantity is a real category. But time is not a real being; therefore it is not a species of quantity. The minor is proved: for a real being that is a whole must have real parts; but time, since it is a whole comprehending under itself past, present, and future time, does not have real parts; therefore it is not real. I prove the minor again: because that is real which is in the nature of things; but no part of time is in the nature of things, for past time no longer is, future time is not yet, while the present can only be an instant, or indivisible moment, because, since time is successive, it can have no part present except the indivisible: therefore it will have none present, and so none really existing.

29 Secundò probatur, quia Tempus, vt definit Arist. lib. 4. Phys. ca. 11. tex 100. est numerus motus secundùm prius, & posterius: sed non est numerus discretus, qui sit species quantitatis discretæ, cùm verè sit continuum, nec habet aliam extensionem distinctam, ab extensione motus, cum quo identificatur realiter: ergo sicut motus, non est quantus per se, sed per accidens, sic etiam tempus. Probatur minor: quia tempus nõ est aliud, quàm duratio motus: ergo non potest habere aliam extensionem partium, distinctam ab extensione partium motus; de quo Aristo. affirmat, & omnes ferè expositores eius, quòd sit quantus per accidens.

29 Second, it is proved because time, as Aristotle defines it, Phys. 4, ch. 11, text 100, is the number of motion according to before and after; but it is not a discrete number, which would be a species of discrete quantity, since it is truly continuous; nor does it have another extension distinct from the extension of motion, with which it is really identified; therefore, just as motion is not quantified per se but per accidens, so neither is time. The minor is proved: because time is nothing other than the duration of motion; therefore it cannot have another extension of parts distinct from the extension of the parts of motion, of which Aristotle affirms, and almost all his expositors, that it is quantified per accidens.

Tertiò, Impossibile est, quòd species alicuius generis pertineat ad aliquod prædicamentum, quin genus eius ac cæteræ species, ad idem prædicamentum pertineant: vt si homo pertinet ad prædicamentum substantię, necesse est animal in eodem prædicamento substantiæ collocari: sed duratio est genus, ad durationem Angelorum, quæ vocatur æuum ad durationem substantiæ corporeæ, & ad durationem motus, quæ vocatur tempus: ergo omnes collocantur in eodem prædicamento: sed durationes substantiarum, non collocantur in hoc prædicamento, cùm sint indiuisibiles, nullam habentes extensionem, ergo nec poterit in eo collocari tempus.

Third: It is impossible that the species of some genus should belong to some category without its genus and the other species belonging to the same category: as, if man belongs to the category of substance, animal must necessarily be placed in the same category of substance. But duration is a genus to the duration of angels, which is called aeviternity, to the duration of corporeal substance, and to the duration of motion, which is called time; therefore all are placed in the same category. But the durations of substances are not placed in this category, since they are indivisible, having no extension; therefore neither can time be placed in it.

p. 327

30 Secunda opinio distinguit duplicem considerationem temporis, & ait: Si tempus consideretur sub ratione extensionis partium, & diuisibilitatis in eas, non est quantum per se, sed per accidens: vnde nec est species quantitatis Si verò consideretur sub ratione mensuræ, hoc est, in quantum est mensura motus, sic est quantum per se, & species quantitatis continuæ. Aristoteles verò loquitur de eo 5. Meta. sub prima consideratione: & propter ipsum connumerat inter quanta per accidens: sed cap. præsenti, sub secunda, & ideo dicit esse speciem per se quantitatis continuæ. Hanc sententiam, videntur sub hac distinctione temporis excogitasse antiqui interpretes Aristot. vt commentator, D. Th. & alij ad concilianda diuersa loca Aristot. citata: & eos sequitur Soncinas 5. Meta. q 8.

30 The second opinion distinguishes a twofold consideration of time, and says: If time is considered under the ratio of extension of parts and of divisibility into them, it is not quantified per se but per accidens; whence neither is it a species of quantity. But if it is considered under the ratio of measure, that is, insofar as it is the measure of motion, then it is quantified per se and is a species of continuous quantity. And Aristotle speaks of it in Metaph. 5 under the first consideration, and on that account numbers it among things quantified per accidens; but in the present chapter under the second, and therefore he says it is a species of continuous quantity per se. The ancient interpreters of Aristotle, such as the Commentator, St. Thomas, and others, seem to have devised this opinion under this distinction of time in order to reconcile the diverse passages of Aristotle cited; and Soncinas follows them, Metaph. 5, q. 8.

Tertia opinio, affirmat tempus esse speciem quantitatis, per se distinctam à cæteris: non solùm in ratione mensuræ, sed extensionis. Sic Fonsec. 5. Meta. c. 13 q. 10. Tolet. q. 1. huius capitis, & alij interpretes Arist. & Aristoteles ipse c. præsenti. Et hæc videtur nobis probabilior, & tenenda. Probatur hac potissimùm ratione, insinuata à D. Th. opus. 42. c. 2. Essentialis ratio quantitatis, est extensio partium: sed tempus habet distinctam extensionem partium à motu: ergo non accipit extensionem ab eo, sed habet per se. Probatur minor, nam fieri potest, vt motus habeat paruam extensionem, & tempus magnam: & ex opposito, tempus paruam, & motus magnam: ergo sunt distinctæ extensiones, & vna non accipitur ab alia. Antecedens probo, quia motus factus per idemmet spatium eiusdem longitudinis, non habet maiorem extensionem, siue sit tardus, siue velox, & tamen extensior est duratio eius. Nam si velox sit, durabit per dimidiam horam: si verò tardus, per integram: ergo habet maiorem extensionem, atque distinctam à motu.

The third opinion affirms that time is a species of quantity per se, distinct from the others not only in the ratio of measure but of extension. So Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, q. 10; Toledo, q. 1 of this chapter; and other interpreters of Aristotle; and Aristotle himself in the present chapter. And this seems to us the more probable and is to be held. It is proved chiefly by this argument, hinted at by St. Thomas, opusc. 42, ch. 2: The essential ratio of quantity is extension of parts; but time has an extension of parts distinct from motion; therefore it does not receive extension from it, but has it per se. The minor is proved: for it can happen that a motion has a small extension and the time a great one, and conversely the time a small one and the motion a great one; therefore they are distinct extensions, and the one is not received from the other. I prove the antecedent: because a motion made through the very same space of the same length has no greater extension whether it be slow or swift, and yet its duration is more extended. For if it is swift, it will last half an hour; but if slow, a whole hour: therefore it has a greater extension, and one distinct from the motion.

31 Respondent huic arg. moderni, quòd si duratio tardioris motus, cõparetur ad tempus extrinsecum, quod est duratio motus primi mobilis, vel ad tempus imaginarium, maior dicetur: si verò ad durationem intrinsecam, eiusdem motus: non erit maior, vel extensior, quàm motus ipse: sed potiùs in motu velociori, quasi comprimuntur partes eius: sicut comprimuntur partes motus, ratione velocitatis: vnde non sequitur, durationem intrinsecam habere distinctam extensionem à suo motu, quem sequitur: licèt distinctam habeat extensionem ab eo duratio extrinseca primi mobilis: quæ etiam non erit distincta à suo illo motu primi mobilis, quem sequitur: vt ita verum semper sit, nullam durationem, habere extensionem distinctam à suo motu: sed eam quam habet, ab eo accipere.

31 The moderns reply to this argument that if the duration of the slower motion is compared to extrinsic time, which is the duration of the motion of the first mobile, or to imaginary time, it will be called greater; but if to the intrinsic duration of the same motion, it will not be greater or more extended than the motion itself; rather, in the swifter motion its parts are as it were compressed, just as the parts of the motion are compressed by reason of the swiftness; whence it does not follow that the intrinsic duration has an extension distinct from its motion, which it follows, although the extrinsic duration of the first mobile has an extension distinct from it; and this too will not be distinct from that motion of its own, of the first mobile, which it follows; so that it is always true that no duration has an extension distinct from its motion, but receives what it has from it. X iiij

p. 328

Contra hanc tamen solutionem sic arguo: Non solùm duratio extrinseca cœlestis motus, maiorem habet extensionem, quàm motus ille velox, sed etiam duratio propria eius: ergo solutio est falsa. Probatur antecedens: quia duratio propria, æquiualet horæ, & ei coexistit coexistentia formali: quia vtraque duratio, est formaliter successiua: sed hora, est duratio extrinseca, temporis cœlestis: ergo sunt formaliter æquales: duratio autem extrinseca, extensior est motus tardioris: ergo erit etiam extensior duratio intrinseca, & propria: quare non erit accepta ab eo.

Against this solution, however, I argue thus: Not only the extrinsic duration of the celestial motion has a greater extension than that swift motion, but also its proper duration; therefore the solution is false. The antecedent is proved: because the proper duration is equivalent to an hour and coexists with it by a formal coexistence, since each duration is formally successive; but the hour is the extrinsic duration of celestial time; therefore they are formally equal; but the extrinsic duration of the slower motion is more extended; therefore the intrinsic and proper duration too will be more extended: wherefore it will not be received from it.

32 Vnde sequitur, non minùs falsum esse, quod in eadem solutione dicitur, partes intrinsecas durationis comprimi, sicut partes motus: quia partes motus comprimuntur, ratione velocitatis, quæ est quidam modus earum: sicut condensatio, est modus, quo partes aquæ, aut alterius corporis comprimuntur: sed tempus, non est capax velocitatis, aut tarditatis, vt docet, & probat Aristot. 4. lib. Phys. tex. 96. his verbis: Mutatio quidem omnis, velocior aut tardior est: tempus autem non est: tardum enim, & velox, tempore definiuntur: velox enim est, quod in pauco tempore multum mouetur. Tardum autem quod in multo parum: tempus autem non definitur tempore. &c. Ergo repugnat, partes durationis comprimi: & ideò falsum est, quòd duratio ipsa non sit maior, vel extensior tardioris motus.

32 Whence it follows that what is said in the same solution is no less false, namely that the intrinsic parts of duration are compressed like the parts of motion: because the parts of motion are compressed by reason of swiftness, which is a certain mode of them, just as condensation is the mode by which the parts of water or of another body are compressed; but time is not capable of swiftness or slowness, as Aristotle teaches and proves, Phys. 4, text 96, in these words: Change indeed is in every case swifter or slower, but time is not: for slow and swift are defined by time; for that is swift which is moved much in a little time, and that slow which is moved little in much; but time is not defined by time, etc. Therefore it is repugnant that the parts of duration be compressed; and so it is false that the duration itself of the slower motion is not greater or more extended.

Secundò probatur, In tempore, quod est duratio motus primi mobilis. Nam si vna circulatio cœli, per quam sol mouetur ab Oriente in Occidentem, quæ modò fit spatio 12. horarum, fieret spatio 24. horarum: euidens esset, durationem in tali motu consumptam, duplo maiorem esse ea, quæ modò consumitur: & ideo habere extensionem duplo maiorem ea quàm modò habet: sed circulatio ipsa, non haberet maiorem extensionem, quàm habet modò: ergo extensio durationis, distincta est ab extensione motus. Probatur minor, quia extensio motus, sumitur ab extensione spatij, aut localis præsentiæ, quæ per motum acquiritur: sed spatium est idem, & ex consequenti, præsentia localis in eo est eiusdem extensionis: ergo motus per illud factus, siue tardus, aut velox, eiusdem erit extensionis, & non maioris: cùm euidens sit durationem eius, duplo maiorem extensionem habere.

Second, it is proved in the time which is the duration of the motion of the first mobile. For if one revolution of the heavens, by which the sun is moved from East to West, which is now made in the space of 12 hours, were made in the space of 24 hours, it would be evident that the duration consumed in such a motion would be twice as great as that which is now consumed, and so would have an extension twice as great as that which it now has; but the revolution itself would not have a greater extension than it has now; therefore the extension of the duration is distinct from the extension of the motion. The minor is proved: because the extension of motion is taken from the extension of the space, or of the local presence which is acquired through the motion; but the space is the same, and consequently the local presence in it is of the same extension; therefore the motion made through it, whether slow or swift, will be of the same extension and not greater, while it is evident that its duration has an extension twice as great.

33 Vt autem nostra sententia, & communis, meliùs intelligatur, notandum est, Tempus sic esse definitum ab Arist. 4 lib. Physic. Tempus est, numerus motus, secundùm prius, & posterius. In qua definitione, duo dicuntur de motu. Primum, quòd sit duratio prioris, & posterioris motus: ex quo sequitur aliud, nempe,

33 But in order that our opinion, which is the common one, may be better understood, it should be noted that time was defined thus by Aristotle, Phys. 4: Time is the number of motion according to before and after. In which definition two things are said concerning motion. The first, that it is the duration of the prior and posterior of motion; from which another follows, namely

p. 329

quòd sit numerus partium eius: sed numerus, dicit discretionem, seu separationem, quæ duobus modis sumitur. Primò, secundùm quantitatem: & sic est species quantitatis discretæ: vt tria corpora, quæ realiter sunt discreta, aut separata: sed cum certo ordine numerabilitatis inter sese, secundùm prius, & posterius: quia secunda vnitas, est posterior prima, & prior tertia: alio modo sumitur discretio, seu separatio: non secundùm quantitatem, sed secundùm qualitatem: ita vt licèt partes sint continuæ secundùm quantitatem, tamen diuersas habeant qualitates, quarum ratione discretæ, aut separatæ dicantur. Dum ergo dicitur: Tempus esse numerum motus, non de numero quantitatiuo, sed secundùm qualitatem intelligitur: quia pars prior distinctam habet qualitatem, à posteriori: & qualitas hæc, modus ipse prioritatis, & posterioritatis esse intelligitur. Ideo tempus non est species quantitatis, in quantum numerus dicitur: sed in quantum est duratio continua motus, habens partes priores, & posteriores, copulatas termino communi, quod est instans.

that it is the number of its parts. But number expresses discreteness, or separation, which is taken in two ways. First, according to quantity: and thus it is a species of discrete quantity, as three bodies, which are really discrete or separate, but with a certain order of numerability among themselves according to before and after, because the second unit is posterior to the first and prior to the third. In another way discreteness, or separation, is taken not according to quantity but according to quality: so that, although the parts are continuous according to quantity, yet they have diverse qualities, by reason of which they are called discrete or separate. When, therefore, it is said that time is the number of motion, this is understood not of quantitative number but according to quality: because the prior part has a quality distinct from the posterior; and this quality is understood to be the very mode of priority and posteriority. Hence time is not a species of quantity insofar as it is called number, but insofar as it is the continuous duration of motion, having prior and posterior parts joined by a common term, which is the instant.

34 Secundò notandum est, non esse certum, quo modo distinguatur tempus à motu: sed quidam dicunt distingui ex natura rei. & ante intellectum, quod ego probabilius esse existimo, vt in nostris Commentariis, super quartum librum Physicorum ostenditur: Alij verò, non nisi ratione distingui tenent, rationata tamen, hoc est habente fundamentum in re ipsa: sicut distinguuntur actio, & passio, in eodem motu. Siue autem hoc, vel illud dicatur, satis est, vt possimus intelligere, Tempus habere distinctam extensionem realem, vel formalem, à motu, quæ est extensio durationis.

34 It should be noted, second, that it is not certain in what way time is distinguished from motion. Some say that it is distinguished from the nature of the thing and prior to the intellect, which I judge to be the more probable, as is shown in our Commentaries on the fourth book of the Physics; but others hold that it is distinguished only by reason, yet by reasoned reason, that is, reason having a foundation in the thing itself, as action and passion are distinguished in the same motion. But whether this or that be said, it is enough for us to be able to understand that time has a real or formal extension distinct from motion, which is the extension of duration.

Tertiò notandum est, Motum, duplicem habere extensionem: Vnam, in quantum est via inter duos terminos A quo, & Ad quem, Aliam, in quantum durat, & dicitur extensio durationis: & neutram habet à se, sed primam à mobili, & spatio, seu termino Ad quem: secundam verò à tempore, quæ propriè loquendo est extensio durationis. Ex quo intelligitur, vtroque modo, & omni ratione esse quantum per accidens. Tempus verò neutro modo habet extensionem à motu, aut mobili, vel spatio: sed eam habet propriã, & à se: & vocatur extensio prioris, & posterioris, secundùm durationem, distincta ex natura rei, à motu, à mobili, & spatio: & ideo dicitur intrinseca. Sed eam habet dependentem à causa efficiente motum, à qua producitur idem tempus, secundùm suum esse, medio motu: non tanquam causa, sed tanquam causatione: quod patet non tollere, quin eam habeat per se, & ab intrinseco; nam cæteræ

It should be noted, third, that motion has a twofold extension: one insofar as it is a way between two terms, the From-which and the To-which; the other insofar as it lasts, and this is called the extension of duration. And it has neither from itself, but the first from the mobile and the space, or the To-which term; the second from time, which, properly speaking, is the extension of duration. From which it is understood that in both ways and in every respect it is quantified per accidens. Time, however, has its extension in neither way from motion, or from the mobile or the space, but has it as its own and from itself; and it is called the extension of prior and posterior according to duration, distinct from the nature of the thing from motion, from the mobile, and from the space; and therefore it is called intrinsic. But it has it as dependent on the cause efficient of motion, by which the same time is produced according to its being by means of the motion, not as by a cause, but as by a causation; which plainly does not prevent it from having it per se and from within; for all the other

p. 330

omnes species quantitatis, habent suas extensiones; sicut & suas entitates à causa efficiente, à qua producuntur.

species of quantity have their extensions, as they also have their entities, from the efficient cause by which they are produced.

35 Quartò notandum: Quòd cùm tempus sit duratio motus: & motus sit duplex, duplex est etiam duratio. Vna est duratio primi motus, hoc est cœlestis: qui cùm sit primum corpus, motus eius dicitur primus: & cùm motus iste primus sit regularissimus, hoc est, eodem modo se habens semper quantum ad velocitatem, & ab eo dependeant cæteri motus inferiorum corporum, omnes etiam per eum mensurantur: & ideo dicitur mensura omnium, quia mensura debet esse certissima: & propterea eodem modo semper se habens. Et hæc est ratio, propter quam in communi modo loquendi, hæc sola duratio vocatur tempus: quia tempus videtur communis mensura omnium motuum, est tamen mensura extrinseca, cùm sit distincta à cæteris motibus, per eam mensuratis. Aliæ sunt durationes particularium, & inferiorum motuum: quia cuilibet motui correspondet sua duratio particularis, & intrinseca, sicut quilibet habet suas partes priores, & posteriores: quæ necessariò inferunt particulares, & proprias durationes. Sed quia istæ non sequuntur ex motibus regularibus, sed modò velocioribus, modò tardioribus; ideo nec vocantur propriè tempora: sed tempus absolutè dicitur vnum, pro illa prima duratione primi motus.

35 It should be noted, fourth, that since time is the duration of motion, and motion is twofold, duration too is twofold. One is the duration of the first motion, that is, the celestial one; since that is the first body, its motion is called the first; and since this first motion is most regular, that is, always behaving in the same way as regards swiftness, and the other motions of the lower bodies depend on it, all are also measured by it; and therefore it is called the measure of all, because a measure must be most certain, and for that reason always behaving in the same way. And this is the reason why, in the common way of speaking, this duration alone is called time: because time seems to be the common measure of all motions; yet it is an extrinsic measure, since it is distinct from the other motions measured by it. The others are the durations of particular and lower motions: because to each motion there corresponds its own particular and intrinsic duration, just as each has its own prior and posterior parts, which necessarily imply particular and proper durations. But because these do not follow from regular motions, but now from swifter, now from slower ones, therefore they are not properly called times; but time, absolutely, is said to be one, for that first duration of the first motion.

36 Ex his credo intelligetur aliquo modo natura temporis: & ex ea: quem sensum tenuerit Aristoteles, dum tempus enumerauit inter quanta per accidens, in 5. Metaphysicorum, videlicet non habere extensionem omnino absolutam, sicut cæteras species quantitatis, sed cum ordine ad aliud, nempe ad motum, & ideo esse quasi quantum per aliud, non tamen per accidens, sicut motus: qui non habet propriam extensionem, sed quam accipit à spatio & subiecto. Tempus verò habet quidem propriam, non omnino absolutam, sed cum ordine ad aliud: ideo non est tam per se quantum, ac cætera species. Sed primum argumentum petit distinctionem illam rerum permanentium, & successiuarum, quæ etiam habent partes diuersæ rationis: nam res permanentes habent partes, quæ simul existunt, vt lignum, vel lapis: res verò successiuæ, non habent partes simul existentes, sed in successione, & transitu, vt motus: cuius partes non simul existunt, sed quædam sunt futuræ, aliæ præteritæ: & futuræ fiunt primò præsentes: deinde præteritæ; sed nec præsentes sunt per modum permanentis, aut simul existentis; sed per modum successiuè transeuntis Denique tam partes futuræ, quàm præsentes, & præteritæ, copulantur

36 From these things, I believe, the nature of time will be understood in some way, and from it what sense Aristotle held when he enumerated time among things quantified per accidens, in Metaph. 5: namely, that it does not have an altogether absolute extension, like the other species of quantity, but one with an order to something else, namely to motion; and therefore that it is as it were quantified through another, yet not per accidens, like motion, which does not have its own extension but one which it receives from the space and the subject. Time, however, does indeed have its own, not altogether absolute, but with an order to something else; therefore it is not so much quantified per se as the other species. But the first argument calls for that distinction of permanent and successive things, which also have parts of a diverse ratio: for permanent things have parts which exist at the same time, as wood or stone; but successive things do not have parts existing at the same time, but in succession and passage, as motion, whose parts do not exist at the same time, but some are future, others past; and the future ones first become present, then past; yet not even the present ones are present after the manner of something permanent or existing at the same time, but after the manner of something passing successively. Finally, the future parts as well as the present and the past are joined

p. 331

per instantia indiuisibilia, etiam fluentia, & fiunt vnum tempus, & vna quantitas continua, & successiua. Quare licèt nulla pars temporis sit præsens, vel existens permanenter, aut tota simul, habet tamen vtrumque per modum successionis, & fluxus.

by indivisible instants, themselves also flowing, and they become one time and one continuous and successive quantity. Wherefore, although no part of time is present, or existing permanently, or whole at once, yet it has both after the manner of succession and flux.

Ad formam autem primi argum. neganda est minor, Quòd tempus non sit ens reale, aut non habeat partes reales actu existentes; quia licèt non existant per modum permanentis, existunt tamen per modum successiui, hoc est, continuè fluẽtis: & ita tempus futurum, fit præsens, & præteritum. Et licèt tempus futurum nondum sit, & præteritum iam non sit: est tamen tempus præsens, non solùm ratione instantis, sed etiam vt tempus est: non tamen habet præsentiam permanentem, sed fluentem: fit autem vnum tempus continuum, cum præterito, & futuro, ratione instantis, per quod cum eis copulatur.

But to the form of the first argument, the minor must be denied, namely that time is not a real being, or does not have real parts actually existing: because, although they do not exist after the manner of something permanent, yet they exist after the manner of something successive, that is, continually flowing; and so future time becomes present and past. And although future time is not yet, and past time is no longer, yet there is present time, not only by reason of the instant but also as it is time; yet it does not have a permanent presence, but a flowing one; and it becomes one continuous time with the past and the future by reason of the instant through which it is joined with them.

37 Vnde sequitur falsam esse, & non necessariã ad entitatem realem temporis dependentiam ab intellectu, quam aliqui ponunt in tẽpore: dicentes, Tempus complementum suæ essentiæ ab ea accipere: ita vt ante operationem intellectus, nõ sit completa. Quia cùm sit numerus motus, & numerus compleatur ab intellectu: ergo ita complebitur & tempus. Dico falsum hoc esse: quia ex eo sequitur, Tempus formaliter esse ens rationis, & non dari ante operationem intellectus. Probatur consequentia: quia nihil reale potest accipere ab intellectu: si ergo accipit essentiale complementum: ergo complementum hoc, est ens rationis, & ita essentia temporis, erit ens rationis, cùm per ipsum compleatur. Quare non dabitur ante operationem intellectus, quod constat esse falsum, cùm ante operationem intellectus, detur duratio primi motus, quæ est verum tempus. Quòd verò tale complementum non sit necessarium, probatur, quia sine illo habet tempus veras, ac reales partes, in fluxu reali consistentes, iuxta naturam entis successiui, non minùs quàm motus: de quo euidens est, non dependere ab intellectu: sicut videbimus non dependere numerum.

37 Whence it follows that the dependence on the intellect which some place in time is false and not necessary for the real entity of time: they say that time receives the complement of its essence from the intellect, so that before the operation of the intellect it is not complete; because, since it is the number of motion, and number is completed by the intellect, therefore time too will be so completed. I say that this is false: because from it it follows that time is formally a being of reason, and is not given before the operation of the intellect. The consequence is proved: because nothing real can be received from the intellect; if, therefore, it receives its essential complement, then this complement is a being of reason, and so the essence of time will be a being of reason, since it is completed by it. Wherefore it will not be given before the operation of the intellect, which is certainly false, since before the operation of the intellect there is given the duration of the first motion, which is true time. That such a complement is not necessary is proved: because without it time has true and real parts, consisting in a real flux according to the nature of successive being, no less than motion, of which it is evident that it does not depend on the intellect; just as we shall see that number does not depend on it.

Ad secundum, Concedenda est minor, quòd tempus non sit numerus, realiter discretus, discretione quantitatiua, neque species quantitatis, ex eo quòd sit numerus, sed ex eo, quòd est continua duratio motus: à quo negãdum est, non distingui realiter: & licèt solùm distinguatur ratione formali, sufficit, vt sit ens completum, & per se extensum: quamuis motus sit incompletus, atque extensus per accidens: nam actio, & passio, identificãtur realiter cum motu, tamen sufficit distinctio rationis, vt actio, & passio, sint entia completa, & prædicamentalia:

To the second, the minor must be granted, namely that time is not a number really discrete by quantitative discreteness, nor a species of quantity from the fact that it is a number, but from the fact that it is the continuous duration of motion; from which it must be denied that it is not really distinguished; and although it is distinguished only by a formal ratio, this suffices for it to be a complete being and extended per se, although motion is incomplete and extended per accidens: for action and passion are really identified with motion, yet a distinction of reason suffices for action and passion to be complete and categorial beings:

p. 332

quamuis motus neutrum habeat.

although motion has neither.

38 Ad vltimum, Concessa maiori, neganda est minor: quòd duratio in communi, sit genus, ad durationes substantiarum, & ad tempus: sed est analogum: quod præsertim verum est, ac necessarium, apud eosdem modernos, qui asserunt, durationem sola ratione distingui, ab existentia rei durantis. Quo supposito, duratio substantiarum erit idem, ac existentia earum: & duratio accidentium, idem ac actualis inhærentia eorum: sed substantiæ, & accidenti, nihil datur commune vniuocum: ergo nec durationibus eorum. Et etiam si ex natura rei distinguatur duratio, ab existentia rei durantis, cùm eam consequatur naturaliter: non potest tamen duratio in communi, esse vniuoca, respectu vtriusque: quia sicut accidens habet esse secundùm quid, ita duratio consequens naturam eius, erit talis secundùm quid, per attributionem ad durationem substantiæ: nec habere poterunt rationem vniuocam durationis: quare nec sequitur durationem motus, non esse speciem quantitatis: quia durationes substantiarum, non sunt in hoc prædicamento.

38 To the last, granting the major, the minor must be denied, namely that duration in general is a genus to the durations of substances and to time; rather it is analogous. This is especially true, and necessary, according to those same moderns who assert that duration is distinguished only by reason from the existence of the enduring thing. On this supposition, the duration of substances will be the same as their existence, and the duration of accidents the same as their actual inherence; but nothing univocal is given common to substance and accident; therefore neither to their durations. And even if duration is distinguished from the nature of the thing from the existence of the enduring thing, since it follows upon it naturally, yet duration in general cannot be univocal with respect to both: because, just as an accident has being in a qualified sense, so the duration following upon its nature will be such in a qualified sense, by attribution to the duration of substance; nor will they be able to have a univocal ratio of duration. Wherefore neither does it follow that the duration of motion is not a species of quantity because the durations of substances are not in this category.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

An locus sit species quantitatis continuæ, distincta à superficie.

Whether place is a species of continuous quantity distinct from surface.

39 OCcasionem dedit Aristoteles huic quęstioni: quia licèt capite præsenti, enumerauit locum inter species quantitatis, tamen 5. Metaph. c. 13. vbi de eodem prædicamento ex professo agit, & alias species quantitatis enumerauit, nullam fecit mentionem loci. Ideo prima opinio asserit, Locum esse speciem quantitatis, distinctam à superficie: non quidem in ratione extensionis essentiali quantitatis, sed solùm in ratione mensuræ. Probat vtrumque, quia illa distinguuntur specie, in ratione extensionis, quæ habent distinctam extensionem: sed locus & superficies, non habent extensionem distinctam, sed eandem: ergo in ratione extensionis distinguuntur. Minor probatur; quia locus est superficies quædam: ergo est extensa secundùm longitudinem, & latitudinem: addit verò continentiam locati, ratione cuius non habent nouam aliquam dimensionem, sed solùm nouam correspondentiam ad locatum: ergo non habet nouam aut distinctam extensionem, bene tamen habet nouam rationem mensuræ: quia ex eo, quod continet locatum, est mensura extrinseca eius: superficies verò, non est mensura extrinseca locati, sed intrinseca locantis in quo inhæret. Ideo Aristoteles

39 Aristotle gave occasion to this question: because, although in the present chapter he enumerated place among the species of quantity, yet in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, where he treats of the same category expressly and enumerated the other species of quantity, he made no mention of place. Hence the first opinion asserts that place is a species of quantity distinct from surface: not indeed in the ratio of the essential extension of quantity, but only in the ratio of measure. It proves both: because those things are distinguished in species in the ratio of extension which have a distinct extension; but place and surface do not have a distinct extension, but the same; therefore they are not distinguished in the ratio of extension. The minor is proved: because place is a certain surface; therefore it is extended according to length and breadth; but it adds the containing of the located thing, by reason of which it does not have any new dimension, but only a new correspondence to the located thing; therefore it does not have a new or distinct extension; but it does indeed have a new ratio of measure: because, from the fact that it contains the located thing, it is its extrinsic measure; whereas the surface is not the extrinsic measure of the located thing, but the intrinsic measure of the locating body in which it inheres. Hence Aristotle

p. 333

capite præsenti, vbi rationem mensuræ præcipuè considerabat, in quantitate locum numerauit, tanquam speciem distinctam à superficie: sed 5. Metaphysicorum, vbi de quantitate agebat, præcipuè secundum rationem essentialem extensionis, non fecit mentionem loci: quia sub hac consideratione, non distinguitur à superficie. Vnde connumerans superficiem, sufficienter connumerauit locum. Ita sentit Sotus, in hoc cap. & Masius disp. de quantitate, sect. 3. quæst. 4.

in the present chapter, where he chiefly considered the ratio of measure, numbered place within quantity as a species distinct from surface; but in Metaph. 5, where he treated of quantity chiefly according to the essential ratio of extension, he made no mention of place, because under this consideration it is not distinguished from surface. Whence, in enumerating surface, he sufficiently enumerated place. So thinks Soto, on this chapter, and Masius, disp. on quantity, sect. 3, q. 4.

40 Secunda opinio tenet, Locum esse distinctam speciem à superficie, etiam sub ratione essentiali extensionis: non quidem realiter, sed solùm formaliter. Hanc sequuntur Albertus Magnus, tract. 8. prædicamentorum, cap. 5. Iauellus, tractat. 5. Canter. in extensione textus, & Toletus, quæst. 2. huius capitis. Probatur testimonio Aristo. in hoc cap. vbi non solùm docuit, sed probauit, Locum esse speciem quantitatis continuæ, distinctam ab aliis.

40 The second opinion holds that place is a species distinct from surface even under the essential ratio of extension: not indeed really, but only formally. This is followed by Albert the Great, tract. 8 on the categories, ch. 5; Javelli, tract. 5; Canter., in the extension of the text; and Toledo, q. 2 of this chapter. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in this chapter, where he not only taught but proved that place is a species of continuous quantity distinct from the others.

Deinde ratione. Primò: Quia distinctus modus formalis extensionis, sufficit distinguere rationem formalem, & specificam duarum quantitatum: sed locus habet distinctum modum formalem extensionis: ergo distinguitur formaliter, atque specie à superficie. Probatur minor, quia superficies, vt superficies, solùm habet extensionem secundùm longitudinem, & latitudinem: sed vt locus, addit nouum modum extensionis, correspondentem locato, quod circumscribit, in quantum partes eius, correspondent partibus locati, & puncta punctis, & ex tali correspondentia, habet nouum modum diuisibilitatis: quia diuisibilis est, ad diuisionem locati: ergo habet distinctam rationem quantitatiuam, quæ sufficit, vt sit distincta specie à superficie, licèt non distinguatur ab ea realiter.

Next, by reason. First: because a distinct formal mode of extension suffices to distinguish the formal and specific ratio of two quantities; but place has a distinct formal mode of extension; therefore it is distinguished formally, and in species, from surface. The minor is proved: because surface, as surface, has extension only according to length and breadth; but as place, it adds a new mode of extension corresponding to the located thing which it circumscribes, insofar as its parts correspond to the parts of the located thing, and points to points; and from such correspondence it has a new mode of divisibility, because it is divisible upon the division of the located thing; therefore it has a distinct quantitative ratio, which suffices for it to be a species distinct from surface, although it is not distinguished from it really.

Secundò, quia proprietas maxima quantitatis est, æquale, & inæquale: sed locus, vt locus, est æqualis locato, vt docet Arist. 4. lib. Phy. tex. 13. ergo vt talis, conuenit ei essentia quantitatis, per quam erit distincta species à superficie: cui, sicut non conuenit æqualitas cum locato, ita nec conueniet formalis ratio, & propria extensionis loci.

Second, because the chief property of quantity is the equal and the unequal; but place, as place, is equal to the located thing, as Aristotle teaches, Phys. 4, text 15; therefore, as such, the essence of quantity belongs to it, through which it will be a species distinct from surface; to which, just as equality with the located thing does not belong, so neither will the formal and proper ratio of the extension of place belong.

41 Tertia opinio duo asserit. Primum, Quòd locus sit vera species quantitatis. Secundum, Quòd non sit species distincta, à superficie, nec in ratione extensionis, nec in ratione mensuræ, sed solùm distinguatur ab ea, per quandam rationem accidẽtalem, & extrinsecam: quæ est continentia, aut circumscriptio locati. Hæc est expressa D. Th. 5. Meta. lect. 15. & in 2. d. 12. qu. vnica, ar. 5. ad 2. & eam sequuntur Soncinas 5. Meta. quæ. 40. Albertus Saxoniæ 4. lib. Phys. q. 1. Venetus cap. præsenti. Vallesius,

41 The third opinion asserts two things. The first, that place is a true species of quantity.
