The second, that it is not a species distinct from surface, neither in the ratio of extension nor in the ratio of measure, but is distinguished from it only by a certain accidental and extrinsic ratio, which is the containing or circumscription of the located thing. This is expressly the view of St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 15, and in 2, d. 12, single q., a. 5, ad 2; and it is followed by Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 40; Albert of Saxony, Phys. 4, q. 1; Paul of Venice on the present chapter; Vallés,

p. 334

controuersia 23. ad tyrones, Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 13. q. 5. P. F. Suarius 2. tomo suæ Meta. disp. 51. sect. 2. nu. 9. & multi ex modernis. Et hæc videtur mihi probabilior.

controversy 13, for beginners; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, q. 5; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, disp. 51, sect. 2, no. 9; and many of the moderns. And this seems to me the more probable.

Vt autem illam probemus, notandum est, Locum duobus modis considerari. Primò, Mathematicè solùm pro superficie continente aliud corpus. Secundò, Physicè, prout addit quandam immobilitatem, ratione cuius respicit motum localem, aut etiam virtutem conseruatiuam locati. Et vtramque rationem eius explicuit Arist. 4. li. Phys. textu 36. sic eum definiens, Locus est, vltima superficies corporis, continentis immobilis. Capite autem præsenti, solùm considerat locum, secundùm primam rationem, vt est vltima superficies continens corpus: immobilitatem verò, ad libros Physic. remittit, & secundùm illam, asserit esse speciem quantitatis. Et hoc est primum, quod nostra sententia affirmat.

But in order that we may prove it, it should be noted that place is considered in two ways. First, mathematically, only for the surface containing another body. Second, physically, as it adds a certain immobility, by reason of which it regards local motion, or also the conserving power of the located thing. And Aristotle explained both its ratios, Phys. 4, text 36, defining it thus: Place is the ultimate immobile surface of the containing body. But in the present chapter he considers place only according to the first ratio, as it is the ultimate surface containing a body; but he refers immobility to the books of the Physics; and according to that first ratio he asserted that it is a species of quantity. And this is the first thing which our opinion affirms.

42 Probatur verò secundum, Quòd non sit species distincta à superficie. Primò quia species distinguuntur per differentias cõtentas sub eodem genere: ergo si species quantitatis continuæ, per differentias eiusdem generis, quæ aliquem gradum perfectionis supra illud addant. Vt igitur superficies, quatenus locus, distincta species sit à superficie, vt superficie, nouam rationem formalem extensionis, aut mensuræ, supra eam addere debet: sed nullam addit: ergo non est distincta species.

42 The second is proved, namely that it is not a species distinct from surface. First, because species are distinguished by differences contained under the same genus: therefore, if species of continuous quantity are distinguished, it is by differences of the same genus which add some grade of perfection above it. In order, then, that surface insofar as it is place may be a species distinct from surface as surface, it must add a new formal ratio of extension or of measure above it; but it adds none; therefore it is not a distinct species.

Probatur minor: quia vel consideramus superficiem, vt actu continentem locatum, vel solùm, vt aptam continere: quod habebit, si locus, qui modò repletur corpore, vacuus remaneat, non est enim alia ratio considerandi eam, vt locum: sed neutro modo considerata addit nouam rationem extensionis, aut mensuræ: ergo non est vllo modo distincta species, à se ipsa, vt superficie. Probo iterum minorem: quia vt actu continere, nihil addit intrinsecum, sed continere, vel circunscribere aliud, sola denominatio extrinseca est, in circunscribẽte, vt patet: aptitudo verò continendi, talis debet esse, qualis est actualis continentia: cùm potentia ab actu sumat speciem: ergo solùm erit potentia denominandi aliud, extrinsecè contentum, vel circundatum: sicut aptitudo in veste, denominandi corpus vestitum: sed sola denominatio extrinseca, vel sola aptitudo ad illam, non potest esse nouus gradus perfectionis, sub genere extensionis quantitatiuæ: quod ex se dicit aliquid intrinsecum, & formale: cùm sit accidens purè absolutum: ergo non potest distingui specie locus à superficie.

The minor is proved: because either we consider the surface as actually containing the located thing, or only as apt to contain it, which it will have if the place which is now filled by a body should remain empty; for there is no other ratio of considering it as place. But considered in neither way does it add a new ratio of extension or of measure; therefore it is in no way a species distinct from itself as surface. I prove the minor again: because as actually containing it adds nothing intrinsic, but to contain or circumscribe another is merely an extrinsic denomination in the circumscribing thing, as is plain; and the aptitude for containing must be such as the actual containing is, since potency takes its species from act; therefore it will only be a potency of denominating another as extrinsically contained or surrounded, just as is the aptitude in a garment of denominating the body as clothed. But a merely extrinsic denomination, or a mere aptitude for it, cannot be a new grade of perfection under the genus of quantitative extension, which of itself expresses something intrinsic and formal, since it is a purely absolute accident; therefore place cannot be distinguished in species from surface.

43 Et confirmari potest: quia si continere actiuè locatum, quamuis extrinsecè addit nouum modum extensionis, distinctum

43 And it can be confirmed: because if containing the located thing actively, although extrinsically, added a new mode of extension, a distinct

p. 335

à superficie vt tali, ideo facit distinctam speciem quantitatis, sequitur corpus passiuè contineri à loco, addere nouum modum supra dimensiones eiusdem corporis contenti: & ideo pro continentia passiua, aliam speciem esse distinguendam, quod nemo concedit.

one from surface as such, and therefore made a distinct species of quantity, it follows that the body’s being passively contained by the place adds a new mode above the dimensions of that same contained body; and so for passive containing another species would have to be distinguished, which nobody grants.

Secundò probatur, quia continere locatum extrinsecè, vel aptam esse superficiem, ad illud continendum, aut etiam respondentia illa partium, aut punctorum, cum partibus, & punctis locati, non potest intelligi aliud esse, præter relationem, sed sola relatio, non potest distinguere species quantitatis: quia differentia quantitatis, debet esse absoluta, sicut genus: ergo non distinguitur locus specie, à superficie, sub genere quantitatis, per continentiam locati: nec aliud addere intelligitur, per quod sub eodem genere distinguatur.

Second, it is proved: because extrinsically containing the located thing, or the surface’s being apt to contain it, or also that correspondence of parts or points with the parts and points of the located thing, cannot be understood to be anything other than a relation; but a relation alone cannot distinguish species of quantity, because the difference of quantity must be absolute, as the genus is; therefore place is not distinguished in species from surface under the genus of quantity by the containing of the located thing; nor is it understood to add anything else by which it might be distinguished under the same genus.

Ad argumentum primæ opinionis Distinguenda est minor, ex ea parte, qua dicit locum addere nouam rationem mensuræ: nam mensura duplex est, vt inferiùs explicabitur, Actiua, & Passiua: & illa solùm est extrinseca ratio quantitatis: passiua verò, quæ appellatur mensurabilitas est extrinseca, & propria passio eius: ab illa igitur, non possunt distingui species quantitatis, quia extrinseca: sed neque ab hac, quia communis omnibus, licèt omnibus intrinseca, tamquam communis passio.

To the argument of the first opinion, the minor must be distinguished, in the part which says that place adds a new ratio of measure: for measure is twofold, as will be explained below, Active and Passive; and the former is only an extrinsic ratio of quantity, while the passive, which is called measurability, is an intrinsic and proper attribute of it. By the former, therefore, the species of quantity cannot be distinguished, because it is extrinsic; but neither by the latter, because it is common to all, although intrinsic to all, as a common attribute.

Ad primum arg. secundæ opinionis, Concessa maiori, neganda est minor: quia continentia actiua locati, aut correspondentia secundùm partes, & puncta, non est nouus modus extensionis: sed sola denominatio extrinseca, in superficie, & fortè noua relatio, ad corpus contentum: quæ non possunt locum distinguere à superficie, sub genere quantitatis continuæ.

To the first argument of the second opinion, granting the major, the minor must be denied: because the active containing of the located thing, or the correspondence according to parts and points, is not a new mode of extension, but only an extrinsic denomination in the surface, and perhaps a new relation to the contained body; and these cannot distinguish place from surface under the genus of continuous quantity.

44 Ad secũdum, negandum est antecedens, Quòd proprium sit quantitati esse æqualem, vel inæqualem alteri: sed est accidens commune: proprietas verò eius est, quòd secundùm eam, omnia dicãtur æqualia, vel inæqualia: & hæc proprietas, communis est omnibus speciebus: & ideo nõ potest eas distinguere: vnde, quòd superficies continens sit æqualis locato, accidens eius est: sicut est accidens, vnum corpus, aut vnam lineam, esse æqualem alteri: quare non potest ex hoc distingui à superficie, sicut nec superficies locati potest distingui specie, à superficie loci, ex eo, quòd sit ei æqualis.

44 To the second, the antecedent must be denied, namely that it is proper to quantity to be equal or unequal to another; rather this is a common accident. But its property is that according to it all things are called equal or unequal; and this property is common to all the species, and therefore cannot distinguish them. Whence that the containing surface is equal to the located thing is an accident of it, just as it is an accident that one body or one line is equal to another; wherefore it cannot on this account be distinguished from surface, just as neither can the surface of the located thing be distinguished in species from the surface of the place on the ground that it is equal to it.

Ad Aristotelem verò Respondetur, numerasse locum capite præsenti, tanquam speciem distinctam à superficie: quia nondum determinauerat quid nam locus esset, vsque ad quartum

To Aristotle, the reply is that he numbered place in the present chapter as a species distinct from surface because he had not yet determined what place was, until the fourth

p. 336

lib. Physic. Et iuxta varias sententias, posse distingui, vel non distingui, à superficie: interim tamen, propter extrinsecam continentiam, distingui, non essentialiter, sed accidentaliter. Vt ex hac distinctione, intelligeretur, modo quodam diuerso se habere ad prædicationes. In Metaph. verò, vbi iam constabat esse vltimam superficiem continentem, non fecit mentionem eius: sed connumerata superficie, à qua non distinguitur specie, sufficienter connumerari intellexit.

book of the Physics; and that according to various opinions it can be distinguished or not distinguished from surface; meanwhile, however, on account of the extrinsic containing, it is distinguished, not essentially but accidentally, so that from this distinction it might be understood to be related in a somewhat diverse manner to predications. But in the Metaphysics, where it was already established that it is the ultimate containing surface, he made no mention of it; but he understood that, surface having been enumerated, from which it is not distinguished in species, it was sufficiently enumerated.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Quæst. 5. An motus sit species quantitatis continuæ — Whether motion is a species of continuous quantity.

An motus sit species quantitatis continuæ.

[…]

45 PRima opinio, affirmat, Esse speciem distinctam à cæteris, quam tenet Fonsec. 5. lib. Met. cap. 33. q. 8. sect. 1. 2. & 3. & cum eo Conimbricenses 3. lib. Physic. c. 2. q. 2. art. 3. in fine. Vbi asserunt, Motum sex modis considerari posse, Primò, vt procedit ab agente: & sic pertinent ad prædicamentum actionis. Secundò, vt recipitur in passo, & pertinet ad prædicamentum passionis. Tertiò, vt quasi forma imperfecta, tendens ad perfectionem. Quartò, vt est acquisitio perfectæ formæ. Quintò, vt est successiuus: & his tribus modis, ad nullum prædicamentum per se pertinet: quia est quid incompletum essentialiter. Sed potest sexto modo considerari: vt est continuus, & hoc modo pertinet ad hoc prædicamentum, sicut tempus: sed est distincta species ab eo: quia partes temporis copulantur instantibus diuisibilibus, partes verò motus, copulantur mutatis esse, etiam indiuisibilibus: quæ valde diuersa sunt ab sese inuicem: & ideo arguunt distinctas esse species quantitatis.

45 The first opinion affirms that it is a species distinct from the others. It is held by Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 33, q. 8, sect. 1, 2 and 3, and with him by the Coimbra commentators, Phys. 3, ch. 2, q. 2, a. 3, at the end, where they assert that motion can be considered in six ways. First, as it proceeds from the agent; and thus it belongs to the category of action. Second, as it is received in the patient; and it belongs to the category of passion. Third, as a quasi-imperfect form tending to perfection. Fourth, as it is the acquisition of a perfect form. Fifth, as it is successive; and in these three ways it belongs per se to no category, because it is something essentially incomplete. But it can be considered in a sixth way, as it is continuous; and in this way it belongs to this category, like time; but it is a species distinct from time, because the parts of time are joined by indivisible instants, while the parts of motion are joined by mutata esse, also indivisible, which are very diverse from each other; and therefore they argue that they are distinct species of quantity.

46 Probatur testimonio Arist. 3. lib. Phys. in principio, vbi ait Motum esse de genere continuorum: sed genus continuorum non reperitur, nisi in hoc prædicamento: ergo sentit collocari sub genere continuæ quantitatis, quod est esse speciem eius.

46 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Phys. 3, at the beginning, where he says that motion is of the genus of continuous things; but the genus of continuous things is not found except in this category; therefore he thinks that it is placed under the genus of continuous quantity, which is to be a species of it.

Probatur deinde ratione, quia continuum est genus quantitatis: ergo species eius erit, quidquid habet continuitatem per se: & distincta species, si habeat distinctam continuitatem: sed motus, habet vtrumque: ergo est species quantitatis continuæ, distinctæ à cæteris. Probatur minor: quia continuitas motus, est distincta à continuitate spatij, aut termini, qui fit per eum: & etiam à continuitate subiecti, mobilis, cui inhæret, & tandem, à continuitate temporis: ergo non accipit eam, ab aliquo horum, sed à se illam habet: & ideo erit per se quantum atque continuum. Minor probatur: quia continuitas mobilis, spatij, aut termini, qui fit per motum, siue sit qualitas siue

It is proved next by reason: because the continuous is a genus of quantity; therefore whatever has continuity per se will be a species of it, and a distinct species if it has a distinct continuity; but motion has both; therefore it is a species of continuous quantity distinct from the others. The minor is proved: because the continuity of motion is distinct from the continuity of the space or of the term which is made through it, and also from the continuity of the subject, the mobile, in which it inheres, and finally from the continuity of time; therefore it does not receive it from any of these, but has it from itself; and therefore it will be per se quantified and continuous. The minor is proved: because the continuity of the mobile, of the space, or of the term which is made through motion, whether it be quality or quantity,

p. 337

quantitas, vel quid aliud, est permanens: sed continuitas motus est successiua, sicut ipse motus, ergo est distincta à continuitate eorum, atque etiam à continuitate temporis successiua; quia cùm motus tardus est, continuitas cuius est breuis, si breue sit spatium, quod mobile pertransit, continuitas temporis lingua, ergo diuersa est vna ab altera. Quod etiam colligitur ex continuatiuis, quę in tempore sunt instantia, in motu verò mutata esse valde diuersa.

or anything else, is permanent; but the continuity of motion is successive, like motion itself; therefore it is distinct from their continuity, and also from the successive continuity of time: because, when the motion is slow, its continuity is short, if the space which the mobile traverses is short, while the continuity of the time is long; therefore the one is diverse from the other. This is also gathered from the continuatives, which in time are instants, but in motion mutata esse, which are very diverse.

Secunda opinio, negat motum esse quantum per se: & ex consequenti speciem quantitatis, & est communis, & vera, quam tenet expressè Arist. non solùm cap. præsenti, sed etiam 5. lib. Meta. cap. 13. quibus locis expressis verbis docet, Motum esse quantum per accidens, sicut album. Et cum eo omnes ferè expositores. D. Tho. 5. Meta. lect. 15. Albertus Magnus tractat. 8. de quantitate, c. 4. Soncinas 5. Meta. q. 24. Louanienses, Caie. Iauellus, Sotus, Toletus, Mercatus in Commentariis huius ca. P. Pereira lib. 13. c. Pater Franciscus Suarius 2. tomo suæ Meta. d. 40. sect. 8. & probatur duplici argu. Primò, quia motus est continuus, quia est successiuus: si enim in instanti fieret, nullam posset habere successionem: At non habet per se successionem, sed ratione termini, qui fit per ipsum, ergo nec habet per se continuitatem, sed ab eo.

The second opinion denies that motion is quantified per se, and consequently that it is a species of quantity; and it is the common and true one. Aristotle expressly holds it, not only in the present chapter but also in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, in which places he teaches in express words that motion is quantified per accidens, like the white. And with him almost all the expositors: St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 15; Albert the Great, tract. 8 on quantity, ch. 4; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 24; the Louvain commentators, Cajetan, Javelli, Soto, Toledo, Mercado, in their Commentaries on this chapter; Father Pereira, bk. 13, ch.; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, d. 40, sect. 8. And it is proved by a twofold argument. First, because motion is continuous because it is successive: for if it were made in an instant, it could have no succession. But it does not have succession per se, but by reason of the term which is made through it; therefore neither does it have continuity per se, but from the term.

47 Minorem probo: Quia motus calefactionis, ideo successiuus est, quia calor per eum factus habet quandam latitudinem gradualem, contrariam frigiditati existenti in eodem subiecto: quam frigiditatem, quia non potest agens naturale, finitum, simul & in momento vincere, sed paulatim, vincitur successiuè: & ideo successiuè producitur calor: vnde si detur agens infinitæ virtutis, quale est Deus, potens in momento vincere totam resistentiam frigiditatis, in momento etiam, & sine successione producetur calor, & non habebit calefactio vllam successionem, neque continuationem. Signum igitur euidens est, quòd vtramque habet à termino, & non per se: quare nec erit continuum per se, sed per accidens.

47 I prove the minor: because the motion of heating is successive for this reason, that the heat made through it has a certain gradual latitude, contrary to the coldness existing in the same subject; and because a natural, finite agent cannot overcome this coldness all at once and in a moment, but little by little, it is overcome successively; and therefore heat is produced successively. Whence, if an agent of infinite power be given, such as God is, able to overcome in a moment the whole resistance of the coldness, heat will also be produced in a moment and without succession, and the heating will have no succession, nor continuation. It is therefore an evident sign that it has both from the term, and not per se; wherefore neither will it be continuous per se, but per accidens.

Secundò, quia motus essentialiter est via, fluxus, & tendentia inter duos terminos, A quo, & ad quem: & est ipsum fieri termini; ergo secundùm propriam entitatem, & essentiam est quid incompletum. A quo non constituitur mobile in esse simpliciter, sed in via ad illud: & ideo excluditur ab Aristotele, & eius interpretibus, ad omnibus prædicamentis, & inter post prædicamenta collocatur qui sunt modi quidam incompleti rerum: siue ergo continuitas pertineat ad essentiam eius, siue sit propria passio, erit etiam quid incompletum formaliter: quare

Second, because motion is essentially a way, a flux, and a tending between two terms, the From-which and the To-which, and is the very becoming of the term; therefore according to its proper entity and essence it is something incomplete, by which the mobile is not constituted in being simply, but on the way to it; and therefore it is excluded by Aristotle and his interpreters from all the categories, and is placed among the postpredicaments, which are certain incomplete modes of things. Whether, then, continuity pertains to its essence or is a proper attribute, it too will be something formally incomplete; wherefore Y

p. 338

non pertinebit ad prædicamentum per se, nec motus ipse ratione illius. Falsum est ergo, quòd ratione continuitatis, motus sit species per se quantitatis continuæ.

it will not belong to the category per se, nor will motion itself by reason of it. It is false, therefore, that by reason of continuity motion is a species of continuous quantity per se.

48 Ad testimonium Aristotelis, Respondetur, verba illius generalia esse, quæ hunc sensum faciunt: Motus inter res continuas numerari debet: ex quo non sequitur, esse per se continuum, sed habere continuitatem essentialem, vel accidentalem: quemadmodum, si quis diceret, lignum esse de genere grauium corporum, eo ipso, non cogeretur admittere, grauitatem esse ei essentialem, sed satis esset, ad veritatem generalis locutionis, modo accidentali ei conuenire.

48 To the testimony of Aristotle, the reply is that his words are general, and make this sense: Motion must be numbered among continuous things; from which it does not follow that it is continuous per se, but that it has continuity, essential or accidental: just as, if someone said that wood is of the genus of heavy bodies, he would not by that very fact be forced to admit that heaviness is essential to it, but it would be enough, for the truth of the general statement, that it belong to it in an accidental manner.

Et eodem ferè modo respondetur ad argumentum, Concessa minori, quòd motus habet continuitatem, distinctam à spatio, & termino: sed negata consequentia, quòd eam habeat per se: nam aliud est habere distinctam, aliud habere per se, quia habere per se, dicit ex intrinseca sua ratione habere: habere verò distinctam, commune est respectu eius, quod est, habere per se, & ab alio, aut per accidens: cùm sit euidens, posse habere distinctam, & communicatam ab alio: vt hoc exemplo sit manifestum. Albedo, habet extensionem, quam participat à superficie corporis, in quo extenditur, & eo ipso, distinctam ab extensione eiusdem superficiei: quia repugnat, eandem extensionem alicui inesse, à se, & ab alio: & nihilominus extensio superficiei, non est per se, sed per accidens: quocirca licèt motus habeat extentionem, distinctam à mobili, spatio, & termino: non sequitur eam habere per se: sed habet communicatam ab eis: & ideo habet per accidens: quamuis eam quoque habeat distinctam, ab extensione temporis.

And in almost the same way the reply is made to the argument: granting the minor, that motion has a continuity distinct from the space and the term, but denying the consequence, that it has it per se. For it is one thing to have a distinct one, another to have it per se: because to have it per se means to have it from its own intrinsic ratio, whereas to have a distinct one is common with respect to having it per se and having it from another, or per accidens; since it is evident that it can have one that is distinct and communicated by another, as may be made manifest by this example. Whiteness has an extension which it participates from the surface of the body in which it is extended, and by that very fact one distinct from the extension of that same surface, because it is repugnant that the same extension should be in something from itself and from another; and nevertheless the extension of whiteness is not per se but per accidens. Wherefore, although motion has an extension distinct from the mobile, the space, and the term, it does not follow that it has it per se; but it has it communicated by them, and therefore has it per accidens, although it also has it distinct from the extension of time.

QUESTION VI

QVÆSTIO VI.

[…]

An numerus sit species quantitatis discretæ.

Whether number is a species of discrete quantity. 49

49 EXaminatis iam speciebus quantitatis cõtinuæ, ad quantitatem discretam veniendum est: quæ duas habet species, Numerum, & Orationem, Et priùs, de numero quærimus, An sit vera species quantitatis discretæ. Et difficultas consistit in hoc, an numerus sit vnum per se: nam si ita sit, non erit difficile intelligere, sitne species quantitatis discretæ, vel non sit: si verò non sit, nisi vnum per accidens, certum est, non pertinere id ad prædicamentum.

Having examined the species of continuous quantity, we must come to discrete quantity, which has two species, Number and Speech. And first we ask about number, whether it is a true species of discrete quantity. And the difficulty consists in this: whether number is one per se; for if it is so, it will not be difficult to understand whether or not it is a species of discrete quantity; but if it is only one per accidens, it is certain that it does not belong to the category.

Prima opinio tenet, numerum esse vnum per accidens: & ideo nõ pertinere ad prædicamentum, nec esse speciem quantitatis, sed esse vnum tantum per aggregationem, sicut cumulũ lapidum, aut aliorum corporum: Aristotelem verò eũ enumerasse inter

The first opinion holds that number is one per accidens, and therefore does not belong to the category, nor is a species of quantity, but is one only by aggregation, like a heap of stones or of other bodies; and that Aristotle enumerated it among

p. 339

species quantitatis: quia habet quandam extensionem discretam, similem extensioni quantitatiuæ, & modum quendam vnitatis, in vulgari modo loquendi fundatum, quo dicimus, ternarium esse vnum quendam numerum, & quaternarium, esse alium distinctum. Ita Fonseca 5. lib. Met. cap. 13. q. 4. sect. 4. Pater Franciscus Suarius 2. tom. suæ Meta. & ex modernis multi.

the species of quantity because it has a certain discrete extension, similar to quantitative extension, and a certain mode of unity founded on the common way of speaking, by which we say that the ternary is one particular number and the quaternary another, distinct one. So Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, q. 4, sect. 4; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics; and many of the moderns.

50 Probatur testimonio Arist. 3. li. Phys. c. 7. tex. 68. vbi de numero ait: Numerus est vna plura, quantáve quædam. Et 10. Met. c. 9. tex. 20. Numerus est multa vna & lib. 8. c. 3. tex. 10. Numerum, inquit, oportet aliquid esse, quo vnus, si vnus est: aut enim non est, sed quasi congeries, aut dicendum est, quodnam illud sit quod vnum ex multis facit. Ex quibus sequitur, numerum ex mente Arist. non esse vnum per se, sed per accidens: & ideo non esse speciem quantitatis.

50 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Phys. 3, ch. 7, text 68, where he says of number: Number is one-many, and certain how-manys. And Metaph. 10, ch. 9, text 20: Number is many ones. And bk. 8, ch. 3, text 10: Of number, he says, there must be something by which it is one, if it is one: for either it is not, but is as it were a heap, or one must say what it is that makes one out of many. From which it follows that number, in Aristotle’s mind, is not one per se but per accidens, and therefore is not a species of quantity.

Quod probatur duplici arg. Primò: Ens per accidens, dicitur illud, quod constat ex pluribus entibus in actu: sed talis est numerus, ergo est ens per accidens. Probatur minor: Nam siue accipiamus tres homines, vel tres quantitates separatas, quales sunt tres Hostiæ cõsecratæ, quælibet est ens actu: ergo numerus ternarius ex eis constans, erit vnum per accidens. Et si respondeas, Vnitas secundùm entitates consideratas, non efficere vnum per se, sed vt ordinatas, secundùm ordinem prioris, & posterioris, in quantũ secunda præsupponit primam, & tertia primam, & secundam: & sicut per se ordinantur, ita efficere vnum per se ordine, non vnum per se entitate. Contra hoc est primò, quia ordo iste, non est realis, sed rationis, ergo non potest facere vnum per se reale, etiam vnitate ordinis. Probatur antecedens, nam vnitates ipsæ, non sunt ex se ordinatæ, cùm ex se non sit vna prior altera, ergo solùm ab intellectu ordinari possunt: sed ordo, quem ab intellectu suscipiunt, non potest esse realis, sed rationis, ergo per talem ordinem non efficiunt vnum reale, quod in prædicamento collocari possit, sed vnum rationis. Secundò, quia etiam si ordo esset realis, & numerus esset vnus ordine, licèt non entitate, non sufficit, vt ponatur per se in prædicamento: non prædicamenta sunt entia realia, ergo debent esse vnum per se, non solùm ordine, sed entitate reali: & certè, si vnitas ordinis sufficeret, non esset numerus alio modo vnus per se, quàm ciuitas, aut exercitus, de quibus constat, non esse entia prædicamentalia.

This is proved by a twofold argument. First: A being per accidens is said to be that which consists of several beings in act; but such is number; therefore it is a being per accidens. The minor is proved: for whether we take three men or three separate quantities, such as are three consecrated Hosts, each is a being in act; therefore the ternary number consisting of them will be one per accidens. And if you reply that the units, considered according to their entities, do not make one per se, but as ordered according to the order of prior and posterior, inasmuch as the second presupposes the first, and the third the first and second; and that, as they are ordered per se, so they make one per se by order, not one per se by entity: against this is, first, that this order is not real but of reason; therefore it cannot make a real one per se, even by unity of order. The antecedent is proved: for the units themselves are not of themselves ordered, since of itself one is not prior to another; therefore they can be ordered only by the intellect; but the order which they receive from the intellect cannot be real, but of reason; therefore by such an order they do not make a real one, which could be placed in the category, but a one of reason. Second, because even if the order were real, and the number were one by order, though not by entity, this does not suffice for it to be placed per se in the category: for the categories are real beings; therefore they must be one per se, not only by order but by real entity. And certainly, if unity of order sufficed, number would not be one per se in any other way than a city or an army, of which it is certain that they are not categorial beings.

Secundò: Vnitates non concurrunt ad compositionem numeri, per aliquam vnionem, aut vnitatem realem, ergo non possunt efficere vnum per se, quod sit in prædicamento.

Second: Units do not concur in the composition of number through any real union or unity; therefore they cannot make one per se which would be in the category. Y ij

p. 340

Euidens est consequentia, quia repugnat plura efficere vnum per se, nisi per se vniantur. Probatur autem antecedens: quia de ratione quantitatis, discretæ est, quòd partes eius non copulentur termino communi, ergo repugnat eis quælibet vnio, & ex consequenti, quòd efficiat vnum per se.

The consequence is evident, because it is repugnant that several things make one per se unless they are united per se. The antecedent is proved: because it is of the ratio of discrete quantity that its parts are not joined by a common term; therefore any union is repugnant to them, and consequently that they make one per se.

Et confirmari potest, ac declarari simul: quia ideo fatentur omnes cumulum non esse vnum per se, sed per accidens: quia solùm dicit aggregationem plurium vnitatum, absque aliqua vnione superaddita, per quam fiant vnum: sed numerus nihil dicit, præter vnitates: ergo non erit per se vnum, magis quàm cumulus, nec pertinebit ad prædicamentum. Minorem ita probo: quia quælibet vnitas, ex qua fit numerus, solùm habet quantitatem quandam continuam, cum negatione diuisionis, ergo tres vnitates, nihil aliud continebunt, præter tres quantitates, cum suis negationibus diuisionis: quantitates autem per se, non vniuntur: sed separatæ sunt, per negationes verò, vniri non possunt, cùm vnio debeat esse modus positiuus, per quem, vnum positiuum per se fiat, ex multis diuersis, ergo neque potest ex eis resultare aliquid per se vnum, & prædicamentale.

And it can be confirmed and at the same time explained: because all admit that a heap is not one per se but per accidens for this reason, that it expresses only the aggregation of several units, without any superadded union by which they become one; but number expresses nothing besides units; therefore it will not be one per se any more than a heap, nor will it belong to the category. I prove the minor thus: because each unit of which number is made has only a certain continuous quantity with the negation of division; therefore three units will contain nothing else besides three quantities with their negations of division; but quantities are not united per se, but are separate, while by negations they cannot be united, since union must be a positive mode by which one positive thing per se is made out of many diverse ones; therefore neither can anything one per se and categorial result from them.

52 Probatur tandem, quia non potest fieri vnum per se, nisi ex potentia per se, & actu per se, vt docet Arist. 1. lib. de anima, cap. 1. sed vnitates non se habent tanquam potentia per se, & actus per se, ergo non efficiunt vnum per se prædicamentale. Minorem probo: quia omnes vnitates sunt entia in actu, ergo nulla se habet tanquam potentia: imò nec potest se habere sic: quia non est maior ratio, quare vna se habeat, vt potentia, quàm aliæ: vnde nulla earum talem rationem habere poterit.

52 It is proved finally: because one thing per se cannot be made except out of potency per se and act per se, as Aristotle teaches, On the Soul 1, ch. 1; but units are not related as potency per se and act per se; therefore they do not make a categorial one per se. I prove the minor: because all units are beings in act; therefore none is related as potency; nay, none can be so related, because there is no greater reason why one should be related as potency than the others; whence none of them can have such a ratio.

Secunda opinio, tenet, Numerum esse vnum per se, & ideo speciem quantitatis discretæ: hæc est expressa apud Aristot. cap. præsenti, & 5. Met. cap. 13. de prædicamento quantitatis: quibus locis eum enumerat inter species quantitatis discretæ. Nec potest textus vtriusque capitis, vllam admittere expositionem, tum quia verba expressa sunt, tum etiam, quia ita sentiunt omnes expositores: Auicenna 3. lib. suæ Meta. cap. 4. D. Tho. 7. Met. lect. vlt. Scot. 5. Meta. quæst. 9. Henri. 1. p. summæ, ar. 29. q. 7. & quodlib. 6. Capr. in 1. d. 24. concl. Soncin. 10. Metaph. quæst. 7. Argent. in 1. dist. 24. quæst. 1. Iauel. 8. Met. q. 9. Caiet. Sot. Toletus, Canter. cum cæteris, cap. præsenti, atque etiam ex modernis multi. Et quod plus est, sancti Patres ita sentiunt, præsertim Gregor. Nyssenus, in libr. de historia sex dierum, & Ioannes Damascen. cap. 49. suæ Dialecticæ in principio. Et videtur nobis, non quidem facilior, sed probabilior, & tenenda.

The second opinion holds that number is one per se, and therefore a species of discrete quantity. This is expressly found in Aristotle, in the present chapter, and in Metaph. 5, ch. 13, on the category of quantity, in which places he enumerates it among the species of discrete quantity. Nor can the text of either chapter admit any other exposition, both because the words are express, and also because all the expositors think so: Avicenna, bk. 3 of his Metaphysics, ch. 4; St. Thomas, Metaph. 7, last lect.; Scotus, Metaph. 5, q. 9; Henry of Ghent, 1 p. of the Summa, a. 29, q. 7, and Quodlibet 6; Capreolus, in 1, d. 24, concl.; Soncinas, Metaph. 10, q. 7; Thomas of Strasbourg, in 1, d. 24, q. 1; Javelli, Metaph. 8, q. 9; Cajetan, Soto, Toledo, Canter., with the rest, on the present chapter; and also many of the moderns. And what is more, the holy Fathers think so, especially Gregory of Nyssa, in the book on the history of the six days, and John Damascene, ch. 49 of his Dialectic, at the beginning. And it seems to us, not indeed easier, but more probable, and is to be held.

p. 341

Probatur hac potissimùm ratione: Vna scientia, versatur circa obiectum per se vnum, à quo sumit suam vnitatem specificam: sed de numero, tanquam de proprio, & vnico obiecto, agit Arithmeticus, & de numero sonoro, agit Musicus: & sunt veræ scientiæ: ergo habet vnius per se, & poterit collocari in hoc prædicamento, tanquam vera species eius.

It is proved above all by this argument: One science is concerned with an object that is one per se, from which it takes its specific unity; but the Arithmetician deals with number as with his proper and only object, and the Musician with sonorous number; and these are true sciences: therefore it has a per se unity, and can be placed in this category as a true species of it.

53 Et potest confirmari, & declarari simul hoc modo: Officium scientiæ, est demonstrare passiones de subiecto: ergo quod est subiectum scientiæ, debet habere proprias passiones, de se demonstrabiles: sed determinatæ passiones, procedunt à determinata essentia; ergo debet habere determinatam essentiam: & cùm numerus, sit subiectum prædictarum scientiarum, habebit determinatas passiones, & determinatam, essentiam: erit igitur vnum per se prædicamentale. Probatur hæc vltima consequentia, quia de ente per accidens, non potest dari scientia, vt docet expressè Arist. 6. lib. Met. tex. 4.

53 And this can be confirmed and explained at the same time in this way: The office of science is to demonstrate attributes of a subject; therefore what is the subject of a science must have proper attributes, demonstrable of it; but determinate attributes proceed from a determinate essence; therefore it must have a determinate essence; and since number is the subject of the aforesaid sciences, it will have determinate attributes and a determinate essence; it will therefore be one per se and categorial. This last consequence is proved because of a being per accidens there cannot be science, as Aristotle expressly teaches, Metaph. 6, text 4.

Sed duobus modis, intendunt aduersarij hoc arg. soluere. Primò, distinguentes ens per accidens, quod duplex esse inquiunt, primum, secundùm entitatem, quod ex multis entibus in actu constat, vt album, aut musicum: aliud casuale, aut fortuitum, quale est inuentio thesauri: & de primo ente per accidens, scientia esse potest, de quo non loquitur Arist. sed non de secundo: quod ideo non potest esse obiectum scientiæ: quia non habet esse certum, vel fixum, sed casuale, & contingens. Verùm hæc solutio, contraria est verbis Arist. & rationi. Probatur primum, ex his verbis eiusdem loci: Signum autem, quòd nulli scientia cura est illud, neque actiua, neque factiua, neque speculatiua, neque enim qui facit domum, facit simul quæ accidunt, &c.

But the adversaries try to answer this argument in two ways. First, by distinguishing being per accidens, which they say is twofold: the first according to entity, which is made up of many beings in act, as a white thing or a musical thing; the other casual or fortuitous, such as the finding of a treasure. And of the first being per accidens there can be science, and Aristotle is not speaking of it; but not of the second, which therefore cannot be the object of science, because it does not have a certain or fixed being, but a casual and contingent one. But this solution is contrary to the words of Aristotle and to reason. The first is proved from these words of the same place: And a sign of this is that no science takes care of it, neither active, nor factive, nor speculative; for he who makes a house does not at the same time make the things that befall it, etc.

54 Probatur etiam secundum: Quia ens per accidens secundùm entitatem, non habet vnam essentiam determinatam, aut per se, sed multiplicem: ergo vt tale est, nec potest habere determinatas passiones, neque vnam definitionem, per quam possint de eo demonstrari in scientia, ergo falsum est, quòd possit esse scientia de illo.

54 The second is also proved: because a being per accidens according to entity does not have one determinate essence, or one per se, but a manifold one; therefore, as such, it cannot have determinate attributes, nor one definition through which they could be demonstrated of it in a science; therefore it is false that there can be a science of it.

55 Alij verò, vt Fonseca, vbi suprà, alio modo intendunt soluere idem arg. dicentes numerum dupliciter considerari. Primò, vt est à parte rei, & sic solùm dicit vnitates reales: & ideo ens reale est, non per se vnum, sed per accidens: de quo non potest esse scientia. Alio modo consideratur, in quantum vnitates eius ordinantur ab intellectu, secundùm prius, & posterius: & hoc modo, per se vnum est, non entitate, sed ordinatione: nec vnum reale, sed rationis: hoc tamen sufficit, vt sit obiectum Arithmeticæ. Nec est inconueniens, quòd scientia realis

55 Others, however, such as Fonseca in the place cited, try to answer the same argument in another way, saying that number is considered in two ways. First, as it is on the part of the thing; and thus it signifies only real unities, and therefore it is a real being, one not per se but per accidens, of which there cannot be science. In another way it is considered inasmuch as its unities are ordered by the intellect according to prior and posterior; and in this way it is one per se, not by entity but by ordination; nor is it one real thing, but one of reason: yet this suffices for it to be the object of Arithmetic. Nor is it unfitting that a real science Y iij

p. 342

, versetur circa ens rationis: nam multæ sunt scientiæ reales, quæ versantur circa entia rationis; vt scientia de republica (quam politicam vocant) Musica, & Dialectica.

should be concerned with a being of reason: for there are many real sciences which are concerned with beings of reason, such as the science of the commonwealth (which they call politics), Music, and Dialectic.

Sed hæc etiam solutio insufficiens est, & falsum supponit: nam licèt scientiæ diuidantur in reales, & rationales; & rationales sint, quæ versantur in dirigendis operibus rationis, quibus non repugnat versari, circa ens rationis, vt de Dialectica constat: nullus tamen vocauit Mathematicas disciplinas rationales scientias, nempe Geometriam, agentem de linea, aut Arithmeticam, de numero, sed verè reales sunt, ex communi omnium consensu: quia non versantur circa operationes dirigendas, vt Dialectica, sed circa determinatas res. Sed nec politica potest inter rationales scientias numerari: quia non in dirigendis operibus rationis, sed in ordinandis actionibus ciuium, ac reipublicæ versatur: alioqui Ethica, & omnes, scientiæ morales, vocarẽtur rationales: quod satis falsum est. Ità ergo de politica, sicut de his, verum est, apud omnes, non esse rationales scientias: sed reales, & quæ circa entia realia versari debent, non circa ens rationis. Vnde sequitur, quòd si numerus formaliter est ens rationis, vt hæc solutio asserit, non possit esse obiectum Arithmeticæ.

But this solution too is insufficient, and supposes something false. For although sciences are divided into real and rational, and the rational are those which are concerned with directing the works of reason, to which it is not repugnant to be concerned with a being of reason, as is evident of Dialectic, yet no one has called the mathematical disciplines rational sciences, namely Geometry, which deals with line, or Arithmetic, which deals with number; rather they are truly real, by the common consent of all: because they are not concerned with directing operations, as Dialectic is, but with determinate things. But neither can politics be numbered among the rational sciences: because it is concerned not with directing the works of reason, but with ordering the actions of the citizens and of the commonwealth; otherwise Ethics and all the moral sciences would be called rational, which is quite false. Thus, therefore, of politics, as of these, it is true, in the judgment of all, that they are not rational sciences, but real ones, and ones which must be concerned with real beings, not with a being of reason. From which it follows that if number is formally a being of reason, as this solution asserts, it could not be the object of Arithmetic.

56 Probatur secundò nostra sententia, Quia numerus est sensibile per se, vt docet Arist. 2. lib. de anima, cap. 6. ergo est ens reale, & per se vnum. Probatur consequentia, quia operationes sensuum, non dependent ab intellectu, sed priores sunt actibus eius: ergo nec obiecta sensuum, dependere possunt ab intellectu, sed ante operationem eius dantur in rerum natura: & ideo vera entia realia sunt. Quòd verò habeant vnitatem per se, probo, quia potentia sensitiua, suam vnitatem accipit ab obiecto per se, sub quo comprehenditur numerus: ergo debet esse vnum per se, non, vt ab intellectu concipitur, sed à parte rei: quia sensus non versantur circa sensibilia, vt apprehenduntur per intellectum, sed vt in rebus sunt.

56 Our view is proved, second, because number is sensible per se, as Aristotle teaches, On the Soul 2, ch. 6; therefore it is a real being, and one per se. The consequence is proved: because the operations of the senses do not depend on the intellect, but are prior to its acts; therefore neither can the objects of the senses depend on the intellect, but they are given in the nature of things before its operation; and therefore they are true real beings. That they have per se unity I prove, because the sensitive power receives its unity from its per se object, under which number is comprehended; therefore it must be one per se, not as it is conceived by the intellect, but on the part of the thing: because the senses are not concerned with sensibles as they are apprehended through the intellect, but as they are in things.

Vt autem probabilitas communis sententiæ, quam defendimus, magis pateat, & argu. quæ verè sunt difficilia, soluantur, explicãdum est: quonam modo numerus sit ens reale, & à quo habeat, quòd sit vnum per se: in hoc enim consistit tota difficultas eiusdem sententiæ. Et de numero quantum ad vnitates, nemo potest dubitare, quin sit ens reale; quia tres quantitates hominum, vel lapidum, reales sunt: sed quæ sit illa ratio realis, à qua constituantur in ratione vnius numeri realis, ita vt separetur à cumulo lapidum, difficilè explicatur, & non eodem modo ab omnibus, qui eandem sententiam sequuntur.

But in order that the probability of the common opinion which we are defending may be more evident, and that the arguments, which are truly difficult, may be solved, it must be explained in what way number is a real being, and from what it has its being one per se: for in this consists the whole difficulty of this opinion. And as for number with respect to its unities, no one can doubt that it is a real being, because three quantities of men or of stones are real; but what that real ratio is by which they are constituted in the ratio of one real number, so that it is separated from a heap of stones, is explained with difficulty, and not in the same way by all who follow this opinion.

p. 343

Itaque prima opinio est Toleti q. 2. huius c. concl. 2. asserentis, Numerum esse ens reale, ex parte vnitatum, sed accipere complementum essentiale ab intellectu: hoc autem complementum, ait esse, ordinem prioris, & posterioris, quem intellectus tribuit vnitatibus, numerans vnam post aliam, tertiam post duas, & quartam post tres: & ita constituens numerum ternarium, & quaternarium. Numerus itaque secundùm hanc sententiam, constat ex ente reali, nempe ex vnitatibus, & ex ente rationis quod est ordo prioris, & posterioris: & per talem ordinem vniuntur vnitates, & efficiunt vnum per se.

Thus the first opinion is that of Toledo, q. 2 of this chapter, concl. 2, who asserts that number is a real being on the part of its unities, but receives its essential complement from the intellect; and this complement, he says, is the order of prior and posterior which the intellect attributes to the unities, numbering one after another, the third after two, and the fourth after three, and thus constituting the number three and the number four. According to this opinion, therefore, number is composed of a real being, namely of the unities, and of a being of reason, which is the order of prior and posterior; and through such an order the unities are united and make something one per se.

57 Hic tamen modus dicendi sustineri nõ potest: quia iuxta eum, nec numerus potest esse ens reale, nec species quantitatis. Probo primũ, quia vel tres vnitates efficiunt numerũ ternariũ, ante operationem intellectus, vel expectanda est operatio intellectus, vt efficiat numerum, si primum dicatur, falsum erit, quod dependeat ab intellectu, vel ab eo accipiat complementum essentiale: si verò dicatur secundum, sequitur non esse ens reale formaliter, sed ens rationis: nec esse vnum per se, quia ex ente reali, & rationis, non potest fieri vnum per se, quod sit species realis prædicamenti: ergo si numerus pro materiali, est realis, & pro formali ens rationis, nõ poterit esse ens prædicamentale, nec prædicamẽtalis species. Vtrumque ergo debet habere numerus, ante operationem intellectus: & quòd ens reale sit, & aliquid per se vnum. Vt autem quomodo ea habeat, ostendamus, notandum est, Vnitates, ex quibus fit numerus, duo habere. Primum, quòd quælibet sit quantitas continua, distincta ab altera. Aliud, quòd sint numerabiles ab intellectu, secundùm prius, & posterius: & hoc est etiam in eis reale, & intrinsecum, sicut realis est aptitudo cuiuscunque rei, vt ab intellectu intelligatur: & sicut hæc aptitudo, vocatur intelligibilitas, ita aptitudo vnitatum, vt secundùm ordinem prioris & posterioris ordinentur, vocatur numerabilitas: sed sicut rem actu intelligi ab intellectu non est aliquid reale intrinsecum in ea: nec est ens rationis, sed denominatio realis extrinseca, ab actu reali intellectus, per quem intelligitur: ita numeratio actualis vnitatum, non est aliquid reale intrinsecum in eis nec est ens rationis, sed denominatio realis extrinseca, ab actu intellectus reali, quo numerantur. Vnitates igitur numeri, licèt sint plura entia in actu, secundùm quantitatem continuam consideratæ, tamen aptitudo realis, vt numerentur realiter secundùm prius, & posterius, tribuit eis vnitatẽ: quia ex ea habent, vt constituant vnũ numerum realem per se. Gratia exẽpli: tres homines aut tres lapides, reales vnitates sunt, secundùm quãtitatis reales, quas habent

57 This way of speaking, however, cannot be sustained: because according to it number can be neither a real being nor a species of quantity. I prove the first: because either three unities make the number three before the operation of the intellect, or the operation of the intellect must be awaited for them to make the number. If the first is said, it will be false that it depends on the intellect, or receives its essential complement from it; but if the second is said, it follows that it is not formally a real being, but a being of reason; nor is it one per se, because from a real being and a being of reason there cannot come to be something one per se which is a real species of a category. Therefore, if number on its material side is real, and on its formal side a being of reason, it cannot be a categorial being, nor a categorial species. Number, therefore, must have both before the operation of the intellect: both that it is a real being and that it is something one per se. And in order that we may show how it has them, it should be noted that the unities of which number is made have two things. The first, that each is a continuous quantity, distinct from the other. The other, that they are numerable by the intellect according to prior and posterior; and this too is real and intrinsic in them, just as the aptitude of any thing whatever to be understood by the intellect is real; and just as this aptitude is called intelligibility, so the aptitude of the unities to be ordered according to the order of prior and posterior is called numerability. But just as a thing’s being actually understood by the intellect is not something real intrinsic in it, nor is it a being of reason, but a real extrinsic denomination from the real act of the intellect by which it is understood, so the actual numbering of the unities is not something real intrinsic in them, nor is it a being of reason, but a real extrinsic denomination from the real act of the intellect by which they are numbered. Therefore, although the unities of a number are several beings in act, considered according to continuous quantity, yet the real aptitude to be really numbered according to prior and posterior gives them unity: because from it they have their constituting one real number per se. For example, three men or three stones are real unities according to the real quantities which they have, Y iiij

p. 344

& secundùm aptitudinem realẽ, quam habet quælibet, vt numeretur realiter ab intellectu, post aliam, vel ante alia, efficiunt numerum ternarium per se vnum: ex potentia per se, & actu per se, suo modo compositum: nam quælibet vnitas est in potentia, vt numeretur ante aliam, vel post aliam: & quæ ante aliam numeratur, se habet vt potẽtia, determinabilis per aliam posteriùs numerabilem. Et cùm vtrumque habeant vnitates, ante operationem intellectus, nempe esse reales quantitates, & realiter numerabiles, secundùm prius, & posterius, per actum realem intellectus, efficiunt vnum per se reale, & prædicamentale, nullum complementum accipiens ab intellectu.

and according to the real aptitude which each has to be really numbered by the intellect after another or before another, they make the number three, one per se: composed in its own way of potency per se and act per se. For each unity is in potency to be numbered before another or after another; and the one that is numbered before another stands as potency, determinable by another that is numerable after it. And since the unities have both before the operation of the intellect, namely, being real quantities and being really numerable according to prior and posterior through a real act of the intellect, they make something one per se, real and categorial, receiving no complement from the intellect.

58 Ex hac doctrina duo colliguntur. Primũ, quòd sicut Arist. sæpe asserit, Non esse quærendam eandem certitudinem in omni materia, vel obiecto, de quo potest esse scientia: neque in omni scientia: sed quasdam scientias esse certiores aliis: quia certior est materia, circa quam versantur, secundùm maiorem, vel minorem abstractionem à materia. Ita nec est quærenda in quibuscunque rebus prædicamentalibus, eadẽ vnitas, aut idem modus vnius per se, sed quasdam habere, maiorem vnitatem, & magis esse vnum per se, alias verò longè minorem, secundùm minorem perfectionem suæ naturæ. Verùm dummodo habeant aliquam vnitatem, sufficiet, vt in prædicamento per se collocentur, tanquam genera, vel species eius. Gratia exempli, in substantia maior reperitur vnitas, & perfectior modus vnius per se quàm in accidentibus: & inter accidentia, maior in vno, quàm alio: sed aliqualis sufficit, vt per se sint species prædicamentales, saltem imperfectè. Et huius conditionis est numerus, & omnis quantitas discreta, quæ cùm ex propria natura debeat habere partes actu separatas, minorem possunt habere vnitatem, sufficientem tamen ad constituendas species quasdam prædicamentalis imperfectas.

58 From this doctrine two things are gathered. The first, that just as Aristotle often asserts that the same certitude is not to be sought in every matter, or object of which there can be science, nor in every science, but that some sciences are more certain than others, because the matter with which they are concerned is more certain according to a greater or lesser abstraction from matter, so neither is the same unity, or the same mode of being one per se, to be sought in all categorial things whatsoever; but some have a greater unity and are more one per se, while others have a far lesser one, according to the lesser perfection of their nature. But provided they have some unity, it will suffice for them to be placed per se in a category, as its genera or species. For example, in substance a greater unity and a more perfect mode of being one per se is found than in accidents; and among accidents, a greater one in one than in another; but some degree suffices for them to be per se categorial species, at least imperfectly. And of this condition is number, and all discrete quantity, which, since by its own nature it must have parts separated in act, can have a lesser unity, yet one sufficient to constitute certain imperfect categorial species.

59 Colligitur secundum, nempe, quòd ea, quę in vno genere sunt entia per accidens, in alio sunt entia per se: vt domus, in genere naturæ, ens per accidens, est cùm contineat plura entia naturalia in actu, vt ligna, & lapides: sed in genere artificiali, est vnum per se, ita ergo de numero dicendum est, quòd vnitates eius, in genere quantitatis continuæ, sunt multa in actu, quæ in eodem genere non efficiunt vnum per se, etiam si in cumulo congregentur: sed in genere quantitatis discretæ, efficiunt per se vnum numerum propter numerabilitatem realem, per quam suo modo vniuntur per se, vt explicatum est.

59 It is gathered, second, that things which are beings per accidens in one genus are beings per se in another: as a house, in the genus of nature, is a being per accidens, since it contains several natural beings in act, such as timbers and stones; but in the artificial genus it is one per se. So, then, it must be said of number that its unities, in the genus of continuous quantity, are many in act, which in that same genus do not make something one per se, even if they are gathered into a heap; but in the genus of discrete quantity they make per se one number, on account of the real numerability through which they are united per se in their own way, as has been explained.

Ex hac doctrina, Respondetur ad argum. & primò ad testimonium Arist. dicimus, loqui de numero pro materiali significato

From this doctrine the reply is made to the arguments. And first, to the testimony of Aristotle, we say that he is speaking of number with respect to its material significate,

p. 345

, nempe pro vnitatibus: & hoc modo quanta quædam dicuntur, & vna quædam, sed ratione formalis numerabilitatis, fiunt vnum per se, quam numerabilitatem, non excludit ibi Arist. sed potiùs quærit: ideo nihil contra nostram sententiam continent illa testimonia.

namely, for the unities; and in this way they are called certain quantities and certain ones; but by reason of the formal numerability they become one per se, which numerability Aristotle does not exclude there, but rather seeks it: hence those testimonies contain nothing against our view.

60 Ad primum arg. Distinguenda est minor: nam vnitates numeri, duobus modis considerantur. Primò, secundùm rationem materialem, qua sunt plures quantitates, actu separatæ: & hoc modo, non efficiunt vnum per se. Secundò, considerantur vt sunt numerabiles ab intellectu, secundùm prius & posterius: & ex hoc habent vnitatem per quam constituunt vnum numerum. Et cùm dicitur, Ordinem prioris, & posterioris inter vnitates, non esse realem: etiam est distinguendum: nam prius, & posterius potest sumi, vt connotatur per aptitudinem numerabilitatis: & sic est aliquid reale, in eisdem vnitatibus, quia quælibet, ex propria natura potest numerari, secundùm prius, & posterius: si verò consideretur in actuali numeratione, solùm est intrinseca denominatio, in eisdem vnitatibus, sicut intelligibilitas, in quacunque re, est aliquid reale, sed actu intelligi, solùm est denominatio extrinseca. Et ad aliud, quod tandem dicitur: Non satis esse, quòd numerus sit vnus ordine, sed requiritur, quòd sit vnus entitate: Respondetur numerabilitatẽ, nõ dicere solùm respectum, sed aliquid etiã absolutũ, in quo conueniunt omnes vnitates, nempe aptitudinem numerabilitatis: & ideo licèt numerus sit vnus ordine, aliqua tamen ex parte est etiam vnus entitate: & hoc sufficit, vt sit species prædicamentalis.

60 To the first argument. The minor must be distinguished: for the unities of a number are considered in two ways. First, according to their material ratio, by which they are several quantities, separated in act; and in this way they do not make something one per se. Second, they are considered as they are numerable by the intellect according to prior and posterior; and from this they have a unity through which they constitute one number. And when it is said that the order of prior and posterior among the unities is not real, this too must be distinguished: for prior and posterior can be taken as connoted through the aptitude of numerability, and thus it is something real in those same unities, because each, by its own nature, can be numbered according to prior and posterior; but if it is considered in the actual numbering, it is only an extrinsic denomination in those same unities: just as intelligibility in any thing whatever is something real, but being actually understood is only an extrinsic denomination. And to the other point, which is said at the end, that it is not enough that number be one by order, but it is required that it be one by entity: the reply is that numerability does not signify only a respect, but also something absolute in which all the unities agree, namely the aptitude of numerability; and therefore, although number is one by order, yet in some respect it is also one by entity; and this suffices for it to be a categorial species.

61 Ad secundum, Negandum est antecedens, quòd vnitates non concurrant ad componendum numerum per aliquam vnionem: nam licèt separatæ sint, in quantum sunt quantitates continuæ inter se distinctæ, tamen per aptitudinem numerabilitatis, quam habent in ordine ad intellectum, vniuntur inter sese, ad efficiendum vnam quantitatem discretam: de cuius ratione est, vt partes eius non copulentur termino communi materiali; hoc est, puncto indiuisibili, aut quouis alio, non tamen quòd non vniantur formaliter, ad constituendum vnum discretum: vnde licèt separatæ sint vnitates, separatione continui, sunt tamen vnitæ, vnione discreti; & ideo, licèt non efficiant vnum continuum, efficiunt tamen vnum discretum, vt expositum est.

61 To the second. The antecedent must be denied, namely that the unities do not concur to compose number through some union: for although they are separated inasmuch as they are continuous quantities distinct from one another, yet through the aptitude of numerability which they have in order to the intellect they are united with one another to make one discrete quantity, of whose ratio it is that its parts are not joined by a common material term, that is, by an indivisible point or any other, but not that they are not united formally to constitute one discrete thing. Hence, although the unities are separated with the separation of the continuous, they are nevertheless united with the union of the discrete; and therefore, although they do not make one continuous thing, they nevertheless make one discrete thing, as has been set forth.

Et eodem modo respondetur ad confirmationem, Negando minorem, quòd numerus nihil aliud dicat, præter vnitates; dicit enim aptitudinem numerabilitatis, secundùm prius, & posterius earundem vnitatum, in ordine ad intellectum, à quo

And in the same way the reply is made to the confirmation, by denying the minor, that number signifies nothing other than the unities: for it signifies the aptitude of numerability of those same unities according to prior and posterior, in order to the intellect, by which

p. 346

habent vnitatem sufficientem, ad efficiendum vnum per se discretum: quod non habent eædem vnitates, vt sunt in cumulo: in quo talem ordinem numerabilitatis non dicunt, & ideo cumulus est vnum per accidens: sed numerus vnum per se.

they have a unity sufficient to make one discrete thing per se, which the same unities do not have as they are in a heap, in which they do not signify such an order of numerability; and therefore a heap is one per accidens, but number one per se.

62 Ad tertiũ, Concessa maiori, distinguenda est minor, quòd vnitates numeri, non se habeant, tanquam potenti per se, & actus per se: nam duplex est potentia, Vna receptiua actus per modum informationis: qualis est materia Physica, ex qua fit ens naturale: Alia, non receptiua, sed determinabilis per actum: & est similis potentiæ generis, quod non recipit in se actum differentiæ, sed determinatur per eum, ad constitutionem speciei: & talis est potentia, in qualibet vnitate, vt determinetur per aliam, ad constituendum numerum: & ita determinans se habet tanquam actus per se, & determinata tanquam potentia per se: & hoc sufficit, vt ex eis fiat vnum per se, imperfecta quadam vnitate, per quam constituunt vnam speciem quantitatis discretæ. Hæc doctrina colligitur ex Arist. 8. Met. c. 8. tex. 15.

62 To the third. Granting the major, the minor must be distinguished, namely that the unities of a number do not stand as potency per se and act per se: for potency is twofold. One receptive of act by way of information, such as is physical matter, from which a natural being comes to be. The other not receptive, but determinable by the act; and it is like the potency of a genus, which does not receive in itself the act of the difference, but is determined by it to the constitution of the species. And such is the potency in each unity, to be determined by another to constitute number; and thus the determining one stands as act per se, and the determined one as potency per se; and this suffices for something one per se to come to be from them, by a certain imperfect unity, through which they constitute one species of discrete quantity. This doctrine is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 8, ch. 8, text 15.

QUESTION VII

QVÆSTIO VII.

[…]

An forma numeri sumenda sit ab vltima vnitate, vel ab omnibus.

Whether the form of number is to be taken from the last unity, or from all.

63 QVæstio hæc procedit, supposita communi opinione, quam secuti sumus, quæstione præcedenti, quòd numerus sit vera species quantitatis discretæ: nam si esset ens per accidens, & non pertineret ad prædicamentum, nullam haberet formam, aut differentiam: & ideo non esset inquirendum, an ab vltima vnitate desumenda sit, vel ab omnibus.

his question proceeds on the supposition of the common opinion, 63 T which we followed in the preceding question, that number is a true species of discrete quantity: for if it were a being per accidens and did not pertain to the category, it would have no form or difference; and therefore it would not need to be inquired whether it is to be taken from the last unity or from all.

Est igitur prima opinio Capreoli in 1. d. 24. quæst. 1. concl. 5. distinguentis duplicem formam numeri, Partialem, & Totalem, sicut debet distingui, in quibuscunque speciebus substantiæ. Vt in homine, forma partialis est illa, quæ cum materia componit naturam hominis: & natura ipsa composita ex materia, & forma, dicitur forma totalis: vt humanitas, dicitur forma totalis hominis: quia simul cum suo modo substantiali, qui est subsistentia, componit hominem: significantem naturam completam in supposito. Formam igitur partialem numeri, ait esse vltimam vnitatem, quæ determinat præcedentes: & ita se habet, per modum actus, & formæ: & præcedentes per modum materiæ: vt forma binarij, est secunda vnitas, determinans primam, ad constitutionem talis speciei: forma ternarij, est tertia, præsupponens duas tanquam materiam, & eas determinans per modum formæ. Formam verò totalem (inquit) non esse

The first opinion, then, is that of Capreolus, on 1, d. 24, q. 1, concl. 5, who distinguishes a twofold form of number, Partial and Total, as must be distinguished in any species of substance whatever. As in man, the partial form is that which with matter composes the nature of man; and the nature itself, composed of matter and form, is called the total form: as humanity is called the total form of man, because together with its substantial mode, which is subsistence, it composes man, signifying the complete nature in the supposit. The partial form of number, then, he says is the last unity, which determines the preceding ones; and thus it stands by way of act and form, and the preceding ones by way of matter: as the form of the number two is the second unity, determining the first to the constitution of such a species; the form of the number three is the third, presupposing two as matter and determining them by way of form. But the total form (he says) is not

p. 347

vltimam vnitatem, neque omnes, sed naturam ipsam numeri, resultantem ex compositione: ex qua natura simul, cum modo actualis inhærentiæ, fit completus numerus in concreto. Probat hoc vltimum hac ratione, quia in quibuscunque rebus, forma totalis, quæ est natura, resultat ex vnione partium: sed nec vltima vnitas, nec omnes simul, resultant ex vnione partium: sed potiùs sunt partes, ex quibus resultat natura ipsa numeri: ergo non possunt esse forma totalis eius. Primum verò non probat, quia per se est manifestum. Hanc sententiam sequutus est priùs Albert. Mag. in prædicamentis, tit. 8. quantitate, & in Comment. sup. 5. c. D. Dionys. de diuinis nominibus, Imò & D. Th. 8. Met. lect. 3. & postea Iauel. 8. Meta. q. 10.

the last unity, nor all of them, but the very nature of number resulting from the composition; from which nature, together with the mode of actual inherence, the complete number in the concrete comes to be. He proves this last point by this argument: because in any things whatever the total form, which is the nature, results from the union of the parts; but neither the last unity nor all of them together result from the union of the parts, but rather they are the parts from which the very nature of number results; therefore they cannot be its total form. The first point, however, he does not prove, because it is manifest of itself. This opinion was followed earlier by Albert the Great, in the Categories, the treatise on quantity, and in his Commentary on ch. 5 of St. Dionysius, On the Divine Names; indeed also by St. Thomas, Metaph. 8, lect. 3; and afterward by Javelli, Metaph. 8, q. 10.

64 Secundam opinionem tenet Sonci. 10. Meta. q. 9. vbi alio modo distinguit numerum, In eum qui abstrahitur à particularibus vnitatibus: & solùm dicit duo, tria, vel quatuor: & in eum, qui contrahitur ad particulares vnitates, & in eis consideratur: vt dum dicimus tria corpora, tres lapides, vel tres homines. Formam igitur numeri abstracti, dicit esse vltimam vnitatem, non tamen numeri contracti: sed numerum contractum seipso cõstitui, in specie, hoc est, per suas vnitates simul acceptas, absque ordine primę, vel vltimæ: vt ternarium hominum, aut quaternarium lapidum. Et hæc sententia, videtur opposita præcedenti: quia quæstio hæc de numero reali pro quantitatibus ipsis accepto, procedit: cuius formam, dicit, prima opinio, sumendam esse ab vltima vnitate, quod negat hæc secunda.

64 The second opinion is held by Soncinas, Metaph. 10, q. 9, where he distinguishes number in another way: into that which is abstracted from particular unities, and signifies only two, three, or four; and into that which is contracted to particular unities and is considered in them, as when we say three bodies, three stones, or three men. The form of abstract number, then, he says is the last unity, but not that of contracted number; rather contracted number is constituted in its species by itself, that is, by its unities taken together, without an order of first or last: as the number three of men, or the number four of stones. And this opinion seems opposed to the preceding one, because this question proceeds concerning real number, taken for the quantities themselves, whose form the first opinion says is to be taken from the last unity, which this second one denies.

65 Probat porrò Sonc. 1. par. suæ opinionis, Quòd forma numeri abstracti, sit vltima vnitas, hac ratione: Quia numerus abstractus, solùm reperitur obiectiuè in intellectu, constituente ordinem prioris, & posterioris, inter vnum, duo, & tria: ita vt sicut ad binarium, non perueniat, nisi per vnitatem, & ad ternarium, per binarium; sicque ad cæteros semper: ergo vltima vnitas, in apprehensione intellectus, præsupponit cæteras: & ideo habet se ad illas, per modum formæ determinantis.

65 Soncinas, further, proves the first part of his opinion, that the form of abstract number is the last unity, by this argument: because abstract number is found only objectively in the intellect, which constitutes the order of prior and posterior among one, two, and three, so that just as it does not arrive at two except through one, so it does not arrive at three except through two, and so always to the others; therefore the last unity, in the apprehension of the intellect, presupposes the others, and therefore stands to them by way of a determining form.

Secundam verò partem, quòd forma numeri contracti, non sit vltima vnitas, probat duplici argument. Primò, quia vbi est primum, & vltimum realiter, aliquis est ordo realis inter ea: sed inter vnitates numeri, nullus est ordo realis: ergo nec datur prima vnitas realiter, neque vltima, quæ possit esse forma numeri. Probatur minor, quia si ordo realis daretur inter vnitates: aut ille ordo esset naturæ aut dignitatis, loci, vbi, vel situs, sed nullus talis datur: ergo nec habebunt realem ordinem. Probo iterum minorem, quia simul tempore, possunt fieri duo, vel tria corpora, ex quibus efficitur ternarius: & ita vt

But the second part, that the form of contracted number is not the last unity, he proves by a twofold argument. First, because where there is a first and a last really, there is some real order between them; but among the unities of number there is no real order; therefore neither is there really a first unity, nor a last, which could be the form of number. The minor is proved: because, if a real order were given among the unities, that order would be either of nature, or of dignity, of place, of where, or of position; but none such is given; therefore they will not have a real order. I prove the minor again: because two or three bodies, from which the number three is made, can come to be at the same time; and thus

p. 348

vnum non sit causa alterius, nec sit eo dignius: sed nec necesse est habere ordinem loci, vel situs, cùm possint in vacuo constitui: quare nullum habebunt ordinem realem.

one is not the cause of another, nor is it more worthy than it; nor is it necessary that they have an order of place or of position, since they can be constituted in a vacuum: wherefore they will have no real order.

Secundò: Vel vltima vnitas, est forma numeri realis, in quantum est vnitas, vel in quantum est vltima; non vt vnitas, quia hæc ratio communis est omnibus: sed nec, vt vltima, propter duo. Primum quia esse vltimam, habet ab intellectu numerante: ergo non potest esse forma realis. Secundò, quia forma rei, debet esse fixa, & inuariabilis: sed esse vltimam, sæpe variatur, pro voluntate numerantis: ita vt vnitas, quæ modò numeratur post alias, possit rursus numerari prima; vnde esse vltimam, per omnes variatur: quare non potest esse forma numeri.

Second: Either the last unity is the form of real number inasmuch as it is a unity, or inasmuch as it is last. Not as a unity, because this ratio is common to all; but neither as last, for two reasons. First, because it has its being last from the intellect that numbers; therefore it cannot be a real form. Second, because the form of a thing must be fixed and invariable; but being last often varies according to the will of the one numbering, so that a unity which is now numbered after the others can in turn be numbered first; hence being last varies through all of them; wherefore it cannot be the form of number.

66 Pro solutione huius quæst. notandum est, ex D. Th. 12. q. 54. art. 4. in corpore: In accidentibus, non esse compositionem essentialem Physicam, ex materia, & forma, sed esse naturas quasdam adeò imperfectas, vt potiùs sint formæ subiectorum, per actualẽ inhęrentiam in eo: & huius ratio est manifesta, quia materia, & forma, sunt partes essentiales entis naturalis, quod est substantia: accidentia verò, non sunt entia naturalia: sed aliquid entis naturalis: ergo non possunt habere compositionem ex materia, & forma. Vnde ex tribus compositionibus, quæ reperiuntur in substantia, nempe Physica essentialis ex materia, & forma: & quasi Entitatiua, aut substantialis, ex partibus integrantibus: & Metaphysica, essentialis ex genere, & differentia: solùm in accidentibus reperiuntur duæ postremæ: in quibus explicandum est: an vltima vnitas habeat rationem differentiæ: vel ab ea sumatur differentia essentialis.

66 For the solution of this question it should be noted, from St. Thomas, 1- 2, q. 54, a. 4, in the body, that in accidents there is no essential physical composition of matter and form, but that they are certain natures so imperfect that they are rather forms of the subject, through actual inherence in it. And the reason for this is manifest: because matter and form are essential parts of a natural being, which is substance; but accidents are not natural beings, but something of a natural being; therefore they cannot have composition of matter and form. Hence, of the three compositions which are found in substance, namely the physical essential one, of matter and form; the quasi-entitative or substantial one, of integral parts; and the metaphysical essential one, of genus and difference, only the last two are found in accidents; in which it must be explained whether the last unity has the ratio of difference, or whether the essential difference is taken from it.

Et à compositione ex genere & differentia tanquam ab essentiali incipiamus: idem est in ea forma, & differentia: quia cùm fiat ex genere, & differentia, genus se habet, vt materia, & differentia tanquam forma.
