This is proved by this reason: The son proceeds from the father as from the actual principle of his being; but he is not an actual principle through potency alone, except by means of generation, as is known; therefore neither is potency a sufficient foundation unless it is reduced to act by means of generation.

114 Tertiò dicimus, Actionem non esse fundamentum harum relationum. Quod probatur primò, quia non est certum, sed in opinione positum, quòd relatio distinguatur ex natura rei, à fundamento: sed euidens erit, distingui has relationes, si fundamentum earum sit actio, & non potentia: ergo non est asserendum. Probatur minor: quia generatio actiua, non permanet in patre, sed transit ad filium: aut saltem in materia prima, ex qua generatur, est tanquam in subiecto: sed relatio paternitatis, est in patre: ergo euidens erit distingui realiter ab actione, quia euidens est, accidentia inhærentia in subiectis adæquatis, & realiter distinctis, ex natura rei esse distincta.

114 Third, we say: Action is not the foundation of these relations. This is proved first, because it is not certain, but placed in opinion, that a relation is distinguished from its foundation from the nature of the thing; but it will be evident that these relations are distinguished if their foundation is action and not potency; therefore it is not to be asserted. The minor is proved: because active generation does not remain in the father but passes into the son, or at least is in the prime matter from which he is generated as in a subject; but the relation of paternity is in the father; therefore it will be evident that it is distinguished really from the action, because it is evident that accidents inhering in adequate and really distinct subjects are distinct from the nature of the thing.

Secundò: Quia relatio filiationis consequitur hominem genitum: ergo idem est principium vtriusque: sed generatio non est principium, neque causa, sed causatio, aut medium, quo procedit genitum à principio, & consequenter relatio filiationis: ergo nec potest esse fundamentum relationis, Probatur hæc vltima cõsequenti, quia in his relationibus, processionis vnius ab alio, idem est esse principium, à quo procedit aliud, & fundamentum relationis eiusdem principij ad ipsum.

Second: Because the relation of filiation follows upon the man begotten; therefore the principle of both is the same; but generation is not the principle, nor the cause, but the causation or medium by which the begotten proceeds from the principle, and consequently the relation of filiation; therefore it cannot be the foundation of the relation either. This last consequence is proved: because in these relations of the procession of one from another, it is the same to be the principle from which another proceeds and to be the foundation of the relation of the same principle to it. Dd iiij

p. 424

115 Vltimò dicimus: Fundamentum proximum harum relationum esse potentiam, vt reductam ad actum per actionem: ita vt actio solùm sit conditio, potentia verò, vt ab ea procedit actio, fundamentum. Hæc est expressa sententia Arist. 5. Meta. cap. 15. vbi fundamentum earum assignans, ait: Actiua verò, & passiua secundum actiuam, & passiuam potentiam, & potentiarum actiones. Quibus verbis vtramque pertinere ad fundamentum docet, nempe potentiam, & actionem: illam quidem tanquam principium, & ideo tanquam fundamentum: hanc verò, vt conditionem necessariam, sine qua non potest illa esse fundamentum.

115 Lastly, we say: The proximate foundation of these relations is potency, as reduced to act through action: so that the action is only a condition, but the potency, as the action proceeds from it, is the foundation. This is the express opinion of Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, where, assigning their foundation, he says: But the active and the passive, according to the active and passive potency, and the actions of the potencies. In which words he teaches that both pertain to the foundation, namely potency and action: the former as principle, and therefore as foundation; the latter as a necessary condition, without which the former cannot be the foundation.

Et probatur rationibus primæ, & secundæ opinionis: quibus hæc addenda est: Filius procedit à patre, tanquam à principio efficienti actuali suæ generationis: & ad ipsum, vt tale refertur: sed non constituitur in ratione actualis principij, nisi per potentiam simul cum actione generandi per quam reducitur potentia ad actũ, & denominat hominem generantem, vel actuale principium generationis: ergo potentia, vt ab ea procedit actio, est fundamentum relationis. Argumenta primæ, & secundæ opinionis, ex parte probant nostram sententiam; ideo non est eis respondendum.

And it is proved by the reasons of the first and second opinions, to which this is to be added: The son proceeds from the father as from the actual efficient principle of his generation, and is referred to him as such; but he is not constituted in the ratio of actual principle except through potency together with the action of generating, through which the potency is reduced to act and denominates the man generating, or the actual principle of generation; therefore potency, as the action proceeds from it, is the foundation of the relation. The arguments of the first and second opinions in part prove our view; therefore they need no reply.

116 Pro solutione arg. tertiæ opinionis, de separabilitate fundamenti à relatione, explicandum est [quom]odo se habeat fundamentum ad relationem: & quo etia[m mo]do hæc dependeat ab illo. Et fundamentum quidem relationis, non est adeo materialiter accipiendum, sicut fundamentum domus, aut parietis: super quod materialiter consurgunt: sed in hoc sensu dicitur res aliqua fundamentum relationis: quia illa media fit, aut producitur relatio in subiecto: dependentia verò relationis à fundamento, non est eadem in omnibus relationibus, sed maior, vel minor, secundùm naturam cuiuslibet relationis. Est autem differentia inter relationes secundi generis, ex vna parte, & alias omnes ex altera: quòd in relationibus primi, & tertij generis, fundamentum habet modum formæ, per quam constituuntur extrema, in ratione extremorum: vt albedo, quæ est fundamentum similitudinis, extremorum forma est, quia media relatio inhæret extremis: vnde si ab eis tolleretur, non haberent capacitatem recipiendi relationem, vt si albedinem tollas ab extremis similitudinis, implicat contradictionem, talem relationem eis in esse: vnde sequitur, relationes has non solùm in esse, & fieri, sed etiam, in conseruari dependere à fundamentis: ita vt non possint vllo modo sine illis consistere.

116 For the solution of the argument of the third opinion, concerning the separability of the foundation from the relation, it must be explained how the foundation is related to the relation, and also in what way the latter depends on the former. And the foundation of a relation is not to be taken so materially as the foundation of a house or a wall, upon which they materially rise; but a thing is called the foundation of a relation in this sense: because by means of it the relation comes to be or is produced in the subject. But the dependence of a relation on its foundation is not the same in all relations, but greater or lesser according to the nature of each relation. And there is a difference between the relations of the second kind on the one side and all the others on the other: that in relations of the first and third kind the foundation has the mode of a form, through which the extremes are constituted in the ratio of extremes: as whiteness, which is the foundation of likeness, is the form of the extremes, because by means of it the relation inheres in the extremes; whence, if it were removed from them, they would not have the capacity of receiving the relation: as, if you remove whiteness from the extremes of likeness, it implies a contradiction that such a relation be in them; whence it follows that these relations depend on their foundations not only in being and in becoming, but also in being conserved, so that they can in no way subsist without them.

p. 425

Fundamenta verò relationum secundi generis, alio modo se habent: non enim sunt formæ extremorum, sed virtutes, aut media tantùm: & quibus effectiuè procedit relatio, vt à principio efficiente non quidem per se, sed quasi per accidens: quia nullum est agens, quod per se intendat relationem.

But the foundations of relations of the second kind are related in another way: for they are not forms of the extremes, but powers or media only, by which the relation proceeds effectively, as from an efficient principle, not indeed per se but as it were per accidens, because there is no agent that intends a relation per se.

117 Gratia exempli: potentia generandi est virtus efficientis, per quem producit effectum, & ex cõsequenti relationem, eum consequentem: vnde relatio proximè inhęret substantię, quamuis media potentia, & actione fiat: vnde sequitur, has relationes solùm dependere à suis fundamentis, in esse & fieri: quia eis mediis fiunt ab effici[ente]: non tamen dependere in conseruari: quia non depende[nt] ab eis tanquam à formis extremorum, sicut de cæteris relationibus dictum est.

117 For example: the potency of generating is the power of the efficient cause, through which it produces the effect, and consequently the relation consequent upon it; whence the relation inheres proximately in the substance, although it comes to be by means of the potency and the action; whence it follows that these relations depend on their foundations only in being and in becoming, because by means of them they are made by the efficient cause; yet they do not depend on them in being conserved, because they do not depend on them as on forms of the extremes, as was said of the other relations.

Et ex his respondetur ad formam argument. Negandum est enim antecedens, quòd relationes huius secundi generis, non possint permanere in subiectis sine fundamentis: vnde nec repugnat, quòd separata potentia generatiua ab homine, qui genuit, & permanente, filio genito, permaneat relatio paternitatis, & filiationis: imò, extremis permanentibus, necesse est eam permanere. Et ratio huius est: quia non dependent à fundamentis, in conseruari: sed tantùm esse, & fieri: vt explicatum est.

And from these things the reply is made to the form of the argument. For the antecedent must be denied, that relations of this second kind cannot remain in their subjects without their foundations: whence it is not repugnant that, when the generative potency is separated from the man who begot, and the begotten son remains, the relation of paternity and of filiation should remain; indeed, if the extremes remain, it must necessarily remain. And the reason of this is: because they do not depend on their foundations in being conserved, but only in being and becoming, as has been explained.

QUESTION XIII

Quæst. 13. An relationes tertij generis sint reales, & prædicamentales — Whether relations of the third kind are real and categorial.

QVÆSTIO XIII.

[…]

An relationes tertij generis sint reales, & prædicamentales.

[…]

118 Tertium genus relationum est, mensurabilis, & mensuræ, de quibus non est apud omnes certum, An sint veræ relationes, neque an sint prædicamentales.

118 The third kind of relations is that of the measurable and of the measure, concerning which it is not certain among all whether they are true relations, nor whether they are categorial.

sed prima opinio, tenet, Non esse veras relationes, sed solo nomine ita vocari: & hanc esse causam, ob quam dicuntur ab Arist relationes secundum dici; quasi titulum solum eis concedat, in re verò nihil sint: quare nec pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum, neque ad aliud.

And the first opinion holds: They are not true relations, but are so called in name only; and that this is the reason why they are called by Aristotle relations according to being said, as if he grants them only the title, but in reality they are nothing; wherefore they belong neither to this category nor to any other.

Ita Henricus, quodlib. 2. quæst. 4. quem sequuntur moderni quidam: & probant testimonio Aristot. 5. lib Metaph. cap. 15. vbi Mensurabile, scibile, & intelligibile, ait non esse ad aliquid, quia ipsa referantur, sed quia alia referuntur ad ipsa: ergo ex parte mensurabilis nulla datur relatio, sed longè minùs ex parte mensuræ: nam mensura absolutum quid est, quare solo nomine dicuntur relatiua, & re ipsa nullam relationem habent:

So Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 2, q. 4, whom certain moderns follow; and they prove it by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. bk. 5, ch. 15, where he says that the measurable, the knowable, and the intelligible are not relatives because they themselves are referred, but because other things are referred to them; therefore on the side of the measurable no relation is given, and much less on the side of the measure; for the measure is something absolute, wherefore they are called relative in name only, and in reality have no relation;

p. 426

& hoc est esse relatiua secundùm dici, & ad nullum prædicamentum pertinere.

and this is to be relative according to being said, and to belong to no category.

Alij verò, Eiusmodi relatiua vera, & realia esse, concedunt, sed transcendentalia vocant, non prædicamentalia: quia ad multa prædicamenta pertinere possunt, vt ad qualitatem, & quantitatem: & ideo non collocantur in hoc prædicamento. Quare secundùm has duas sententias, duo tantùm sunt genera relationis prædicamentalis. Primum, Quod fundatur in vnitate. Secundum: In potentia, & actione. Tertium verò, Res est de solo tituli, vel, titulus sine re.

Others, however, grant that such relatives are true and real, but they call them transcendental, not categorial, because they can belong to many categories, as to quality and quantity; and therefore they are not placed in this category. Wherefore, according to these two opinions, there are only two kinds of categorial relation. The first, that which is founded in unity. The second, in potency and action. But the third is a thing of title only, or a title without a thing.

119 Tertia opinio est Caiet. quàm superiùs citauimus, asserentis, has relationes non solum esse reales, & prædicamentales, tertium genus huius prædicamenti constituentes, sed mutuas, hoc est, reales ex parte vtriusque extremi: quorum vnum refertur ad aliud, per veram relationem in se existentem, nempe mensurabile ad mensuram: hæc verò refertur ad mensurabile, non per relationem in se existentem, sed per relationem eiusdem mensurabilis ad ipsam. Idque probat eodem testimonio Arist. citato pro prima sententia.

119 The third opinion is that of Cajetan, whom we cited above, asserting that these relations are not only real and categorial, constituting the third kind of this category, but mutual, that is, real on the side of both extremes: of which one is referred to the other through a true relation existing in itself, namely the measurable to the measure; but the latter is referred to the measurable not through a relation existing in itself, but through the relation of the same measurable to it. And he proves this by the same testimony of Aristotle cited for the first opinion.

Communis tamen sententia, totius ferè scholæ est, Relationes mensurabilis, & mensuræ veras, & reales esse, & tertium genus huius prædicamenti constituere, sed non mutuas: quia reales sunt tantùm ex parte mensurabilis, non ex parte mensuræ. Ita D. Tho. expressè 5. Metaph. lect. 17. & 1. partic. quæst. 13. art. 7. & omnes interpretes Aristot. non solùm capite præsenti, sed 5. Metaph. cap 15. Imò ipsemet Aristot. etiam expressè ibidem, postquam primum, & secundum genus relationum posuit, tertium addit: in quo posuit mensurabile, scibile, & intelligibile.

The common opinion, however, of almost the whole school is: The relations of the measurable and of the measure are true and real, and constitute the third kind of this category, but are not mutual, because they are real only on the side of the measurable, not on the side of the measure. So St. Thomas expressly, Metaph. 5, lect. 17, and 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, and all the interpreters of Aristotle, not only in the present chapter but on Metaph. 5, ch. 15. Indeed, Aristotle himself also expressly in the same place, after he has laid down the first and second kind of relations, adds a third, in which he placed the measurable, the knowable, and the intelligible.

120 Sed notandum est primò: Quòd hoc tertium genus relationum explicat, & distinguit à primo, & secundo, D. Tho. eisdem locis hanc differentiam inter ipsum, & alia assignans, quòd relationes primi, & secundi generis sunt mutuæ, hoc est, reales ex parte vtriusque extremi: ita vt in duobus extremis, duæ sint relationes reales, quarum vtraque suum extremum denominat formaliter: vt in patre, & filio, simili, & æquali, est manifestum: in relatiuis verò tertij generis, solùm vna relatio realis reperitur, à qua vtrumque extremum denominatur: vnum quidem denominatione formali & extrinseca, alterum verò solùm denominatione extrinseca: vt in scientia, & scibili, solùm reperitur vna relatio realis: per quam scientia dicitur formaliter mensurabilis, & per eandem denominatur obiectum mensura eiusdem scientiæ: sed denominatione

120 But it should be noted first: St. Thomas explains this third kind of relations and distinguishes it from the first and second in the same places, assigning this difference between it and the others: that relations of the first and second kind are mutual, that is, real on the side of both extremes, so that in the two extremes there are two real relations, each of which denominates its own extreme formally, as is manifest in father and son, in the like and the equal; but in relatives of the third kind only one real relation is found, by which both extremes are denominated: the one by a formal and intrinsic denomination, the other only by an extrinsic denomination; as in science and the knowable only one real relation is found, through which science is formally called measurable, and through the same the object is denominated the measure of the same science; but by a denomination

p. 427

solùm extrinseca: & ideo relationes huius generis dicuntur non mutuæ.

only extrinsic; and therefore relations of this kind are called not mutual.

121 Secundò notat D. Tho. rationem, propter quam in his relatiuis, tantùm sit vna relatio realis, à qua vtrumque extremum denominetur: cùm tamen in aliis duobus generibus, singulæ relationes denominent singula extrema, & ideo dicantur relatiua huius tertij generis non mutua.

121 Second, St. Thomas notes the reason why in these relatives there is only one real relation, by which both extremes are denominated, whereas in the other two kinds the single relations denominate the single extremes, and therefore relatives of this third kind are called not mutual.

Rationem autem huius esse ait, quia extrema harum relationum non sunt eiusdem ordinis, sed diuersi: & ideo licèt vnum ad aliud ordinetur realiter, per intrinsecam relationem, non ordinatur tamen aliud ad illud, sed solùm dicitur tale à relatione reali alterius. Gratia exempli: Scientia, & potentia ordinantur ad propria obiecta, quæ secundùm se absoluta sunt, nec pertinent ad ordinem scientiarum, & potentiarum: quare nec ordinantur ex se ad easdem scientias, & potentias: & ideo non habent relationem realem intrinsecam, & qua denominentur mensuræ, sed solùm denominantur à relationibus earum: ita vt eo ipso, quòd scientia, & potentia denominantur formaliter mẽsurabiles, per obiecta propriis relationibus realibus, obiecta ipsa ex se absoluta, consequantur denominationem extrinsecam relatiuam mensuræ, ab eisdem relationibus.

And he says the reason of this is that the extremes of these relations are not of the same order, but of different ones; and therefore, although one is ordered to the other really, through an intrinsic relation, yet the other is not ordered to it, but is only called such by the real relation of the other. For example: science and a potency are ordered to their proper objects, which are absolute in themselves and do not belong to the order of the sciences and potencies; wherefore neither are they of themselves ordered to the same sciences and potencies; and therefore they do not have a real intrinsic relation by which they are denominated measures, but are denominated only by the relations of the former: so that by the very fact that science and potency are formally denominated measurable by their objects, through their own real relations, the objects themselves, absolute of themselves, acquire the extrinsic relative denomination of measure from the same relations.

122 Et hunc esse sensum Arist. (ait D. Tho. dum asseruit 5. Met. c. 15. relatiua primi, & secundi generis esse talia, quia referuntur ad aliud: sed relatiua tertii generis, non quia referuntur ad alia, sed quia alia referuntur ad ipsa: quod asseruisse docet, non propter vtrumque extremum: nam scientia, & potentia etiam dicitur talis: quia refertur ad obiectum: sed propter alterum tantùm, nempe propter ipsum obiectum: quod non dicitur scibile, nisi quia scientia versatur circa ipsum: vnde hoc non fuit aliud, quàm dicere, has relationes non esse mutuas, sed vnam pro vtroque extremo deseruire, & vtrumque denominare, formaliter quidem vnum, & extrinsecè aliud.

122 And this is the sense of Aristotle (says St. Thomas) when he asserted, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, that relatives of the first and second kind are such because they are referred to another, but relatives of the third kind not because they are referred to others, but because others are referred to them: which he teaches that Aristotle asserted not on account of both extremes, for science and potency are also called such because they are referred to the object, but on account of the other alone, namely on account of the object itself, which is not called knowable except because science is concerned with it: whence this was nothing else than to say that these relations are not mutual, but that one serves for both extremes and denominates both, the one formally and the other extrinsically.

Tertiò notat D. Thom. quòd illud extremum harum relationum, in quo non est relatio realis, duobus modis dicitur tale.

Third, St. Thomas notes that that extreme of these relations in which there is no real relation is called such in two ways.

Primo quidem, denominatione reali extrinseca, à relatione reali existente in alio extremo.

First, by a real extrinsic denomination, from the real relation existing in the other extreme.

Secundo, denominatione quasi formali, & intrinseca, non reali, sed rationis.

Second, by a quasi-formal and intrinsic denomination, not real but of reason.

Nam ex eo, quòd intellectus videt denominari obiectum à relatione scientiæ, & eandem relationem terminare, concipit illud, ac si verò ordinaretur ad scientiã: & tribuit illi relationem

For from the fact that the intellect sees the object denominated by the relation of science, and terminating the same relation, it conceives it as if it were truly ordered to science, and attributes to it a relation

p. 428

rationis, per quam ipsum ordinat ad eandem scientiam. Inter vtramque verò denominationem, hæc est differentia: quòd prima, & realis est denominatio relatiua, quia à relatione suscepta: per eam tamen non refertur scibile ad scientiam: sed ad aliquid dicitur: hoc est, relatiuè denominatur, quia aliud refertur ad ipsum: denominatio verò, quam ei tribuit intellectus, cùm sit relatio ex parte ipsius, aut in ipso concepta, eique attributa, non solùm illud denominat relatiuè, sed etiam refert ad aliud.

of reason, through which it orders it to the same science. And between the two denominations there is this difference: that the first and real one is a relative denomination, because it is received from a relation; yet through it the knowable is not referred to science, but is said to be relative, that is, is denominated relatively, because another is referred to it; whereas the denomination which the intellect attributes to it, since it is a relation on its side, or conceived in it and attributed to it, not only denominates it relatively but also refers it to another.

123 Vltimò notandũ est, Potentiam, habitum, & scientiam, duos habere respectus: Vnum, qui includitur in ratione absoluta earum, & eandẽ complet essentialiter: Alterum, qui extra essentiam absolutã est: & ideo ei cõuenit solùm accidentaliter: & primum respectum, includunt sub nominibus potentiarum, habituum, & scientiarum: & ideo secundùm illum non sunt relatiua secundùm esse, sed secundùm dici: quare nec ipsæ, nec talis eorum respectus pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum, sed ad prædicamentum qualitatis. Per secundum autem respectum denominantur mensurabiles ab obiectis, neque aliquid absolutum includunt sub his nominibus, sed solam relationem: & ideo sunt relatiua secundùm esse, & constituunt hoc tertium genus relationum: quę omnia tradit D. Th. eisdem locis: & nos ex mente eius copiosius explicuimus q. 6. huius prædicamenti.

123 Lastly, it should be noted that potency, habit, and science have two respects: one, which is included in their absolute ratio and completes it essentially; the other, which is outside the absolute essence, and therefore belongs to it only accidentally. And they include the first respect under the names of potencies, habits, and sciences; and therefore according to it they are not relatives according to being, but according to being said: wherefore neither they themselves nor such a respect of theirs belong to this category, but to the category of quality. But through the second respect they are denominated measurable by their objects, and they include nothing absolute under these names, but only a relation; and therefore they are relatives according to being and constitute this third kind of relations: all of which St. Thomas teaches in the same places, and we have explained it more fully according to his mind in q. 6 of this category.

124 Testimonium Arist. quod pro se adducit prima opinio Henrici, & modernorum, explicatum est iam, à D. Tho. secundùm germanum sensum, in fauorem cõmunis sententiæ, quam sequimur: quia eam, absque dubio, continent, sed à modernis in oppositum sensum trahitur. Intelligunt enim Arist. de iis relatiuis dixisse, quòd neutrum extremum eorum sit verè relatiuum, sed solo nomine talia dicantur: hoc verò falsum est, & verbis Arist. contrarium: qui de solo vno extremo eorum dixit, non denominari tale per relationem, qua ipsum refertur ad aliud, sed per eam, qua aliud refertur ad ipsum: quod non potest esse verum, nisi ex parte alterius extremi daretur vera relatio realis: nam si non datur, nec erit, à quo denominetur. Sensus igitur Arist. est, Vnum extremum esse ad aliquid, quia per propriam relationem refertur ad aliud: alterum verò dici ad aliquid, non quia referatur, sed quia denominationem relatiuam à relatione alterius suscipit. Ex quo etiam patet, non bene intellexisse Caiet. idem testimonium Arist. ex eo colligentem vtrumque extremum harum relationum referri ad aliud, vnum quidem per relationem propriam, aliud verò per relationem alterius: cùm tamen repugnet aliquid referri ad aliud, nisi per

124 The testimony of Aristotle which the first opinion, that of Henry of Ghent and the moderns, adduces for itself has already been explained by St. Thomas according to its genuine sense, in favor of the common opinion which we follow: for it contains that opinion beyond doubt, but is drawn by the moderns into the opposite sense. For they understand Aristotle to have said of these relatives that neither of their extremes is truly relative, but that they are called such in name only: but this is false and contrary to the words of Aristotle, who said of one extreme of them alone that it is not denominated such through the relation by which it is itself referred to another, but through that by which another is referred to it: which cannot be true unless on the side of the other extreme a true real relation were given: for if it is not given, there will be nothing by which it is denominated. The sense of Aristotle, therefore, is: one extreme is relative because it is referred to another through its own relation; but the other is said to be relative not because it is referred, but because it receives a relative denomination from the relation of the other. From which it is also plain that Cajetan did not understand the same testimony of Aristotle well, gathering from it that both extremes of these relations are referred to another, the one through its own relation, the other through the relation of the other: whereas it is repugnant that anything be referred to another except through

p. 429

relationem in se existentem. Arist. ergo relatiuum denominari docuit à relatione alterius: quia relatio non potest tribuere, nisi denominationem relatiui, quod verò referatur per alienam relationem, nec vnquam somniauit.

a relation existing in itself. Aristotle, therefore, taught that a relative is denominated by the relation of the other, because a relation cannot attribute anything but the denomination of a relative; but that it is referred through another’s relation he never dreamed.

QVÆSTIO XIV.

Q U E S T I O N X I V.

An relatio distinguatur realiter à fundamento, vel solùm ratione.

Whether a relation is distinguished from its foundation really, or only by reason.

125 Fundamentum relationis primi generis, diximus iam, Esse substantiam, qualitatem, & quantitatem, sub ratione Vnitatis, aut diuersitatis genericæ, vel specificæ. Fundamentum relationis secundi generis: Potentiam, actiuam, & passiuam, reductam ad actum per actionem, & passionem. Adæquationem verò, aut commensurationem vnius rei cum alia, vt scientiæ, cum suo obiecto, fundamentum relationis tertij generis. Quærimus igitur modo: An relationes mediis his fundamentis in extremis insurgentes, distinguantur ab eisdem fundamentis realiter, & ante operationem intellectus, vel solùm ratione per intellectum? vt paternitas à potentia generatiua, similitudo ab albedine, & æqualitas à quantitate.

125 The foundation of a relation of the first kind, we have already said, is substance, quality, and quantity, under the ratio of unity or of diversity, generic or specific. The foundation of a relation of the second kind: potency, active and passive, reduced to act through action and passion. And the adequation or commensuration of one thing with another, as of science with its object, is the foundation of a relation of the third kind. We ask, therefore, now: Whether relations arising in the extremes by means of these foundations are distinguished from the same foundations really, and before the operation of the intellect, or only by reason, through the intellect? As paternity from the generative potency, likeness from whiteness, and equality from quantity.

126 Et prima opinio, Nullam relationem distinguitur realiter à suo fundamento, sed ratione tantùm ratiocinata, habente fundamentum in re. Ita sentiunt Nominales, Ocham, & Maior, in 1. d. 3. quæst. 1. Greg. d. 28. qu. 2. art. 1. Marsilius in 1. q. 32. art. 1. Herueus d. 3. q. 1. Iauellus 5. Meta. q. 22. Soncinas ibidem, q. 28. Duran. in 1. d. 5. q. 2 num. 17. Probatur testimonio Aristotelis, 5. lib. Physic. tex. 11. & lib. 11. Meta. cap. penultimo. Quibus locis asserit, Relationem non terminare motum per se: quia sæpe acquiritur sine mutatione subiecti: Compluti fit vnum corpus album, & fiat aliud album Romæ, illud acquirit nouam relationem similitudinis, sine aliqua sui mutatione: imò sine mutatione albedinis in eo existentis: ergo non acquirit nouam entitatem realem, distinctam ab albedine. Probatur consequentia: quia si relatio esset noua entitas realis, distincta ab albedine, acquireret nouam formam realem, quæ sine mutatione subiecti non potest acquiri: imò nec produceretur ab aliquo talis entitas relationis, quia non est, à quo produci possit, nisi ab eodem agente à quo Romæ producitur nouum album: sed ab eo produci repugnat cum non possit agere ad tantam distantiam.

126 And the first opinion: No relation is distinguished really from its foundation, but only by reasoned reason having a foundation in the thing. So hold the Nominalists, Ockham, and Major on 1, d. 3, q. 1; Gregory of Rimini, d. 28, q. 2, a. 1; Marsilius on 1, q. 32, a. 1; Hervaeus, d. 3, q. 1; Javelli, Metaph. 5, q. 22; Soncinas in the same place, q. 28; Durandus on 1, d. 5, q. 2, no. 17. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Phys. bk. 5, text 11, and Metaph. bk. 11, the penultimate chapter. In which places he asserts that relation does not terminate motion per se, because it is often acquired without change of the subject: one white body is made at Alcalá, and another white is made at Rome; the former acquires a new relation of likeness without any change of itself; indeed, without change of the whiteness existing in it; therefore it does not acquire a new real entity distinct from the whiteness. The consequence is proved: because if the relation were a new real entity distinct from the whiteness, it would acquire a new real form, which cannot be acquired without change of the subject; indeed, such an entity of relation would not even be produced by anything, because there is nothing by which it could be produced except the same agent by which the new white is produced at Rome; but it is repugnant that it be produced by that agent, since it cannot act at so great a distance.

Probatur etiam ratione. Primò, quia illa quæ distinguuntur

It is proved also by reason. First, because those things which are distinguished

p. 430

realiter, separari possunt inter sese, saltem per potentiam Dei absolutam: vel impediri potest consecutio vnius, ex altero, sed posito fundamento in vtroque extremo, repugnat non sequi relationem: & permanente etiam vtroque, repugnat non permanere relationem: sicut in duobus albis eiusdem gradus est manifestum, à quibus repugnat separari similitudinem: ergo relatio non est entitas realis, distincta à fundamento.

really can be separated from one another, at least by the absolute power of God, or the consequence of one upon the other can be impeded; but once the foundation is posited in both extremes, it is repugnant that the relation not follow; and while both also remain, it is repugnant that the relation not remain: as is manifest in two whites of the same degree, from which it is repugnant that likeness be separated; therefore relation is not a real entity distinct from its foundation.

Secundò probatur: Quia non sunt multiplicandæ entitates sine vrgenti necessitate: sed posita distinctione reali relationis à fundamento, multiplicantur penè infinitæ entitates, in singulis relatiuis, præsertim si ad distinctos terminos referuntur, per distinctas relationes, (vt probabile est) ergò non est ponenda talis distinctio realis. Probatur consequentia: quia nulla vrget ratio efficax, per quàm probetur esse ponendam: sed cùm relatio non sit aliud, quam modus se habendi ad aliud, absque noua entitate possumus intelligere, alio modo se habere, quod est, referri ad aliud.

Second, it is proved: Because entities are not to be multiplied without urgent necessity; but once a real distinction of relation from its foundation is posited, almost infinite entities are multiplied in single relatives, especially if they are referred to distinct terms through distinct relations (as is probable); therefore such a real distinction is not to be posited. The consequence is proved: because no efficacious reason urges by which it could be proved that it must be posited; but since relation is nothing else than a mode of being disposed toward another, we can understand without a new entity that a thing is disposed in another way, that is, is referred to another.

128 Secunda opinio: distinctione vtitur. Nam relationes, quæ possunt separari ab extremis, ita vt extrema permanentia cum fundamentis, possint esse sine relatione, asserit distingui realiter à fundamentis: illas verò quæ ab eisdem fundamentis, in extremis positis, non possunt separari, non distingui ab eis, nisi ratione: quæ autem sint, quæ separari possint ab extremis: & quæ non possint, non explicat: imò neque rationem vllam affert, ad id confirmandum: quare confusè satis loquitur: id solùm declarans, quòd relationes secundi generis, quas putat in potentia nuda fundari, & non in potentia reducta ad actum, non distinguuntur à fundamento. Addit autem, quòd relationes, quæ identificantur cum substantia, quæcunque illæ sint, non pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum: quia repugnat accidens identificari cum substantia. Alij verò moderni relationes omnes fundatas in substantia, realiter distinguunt à fundamento, propter eandem rationem.

128 The second opinion makes use of a distinction. For it asserts that the relations which can be separated from the extremes, so that the extremes, remaining with their foundations, can be without the relation, are distinguished really from their foundations; but that those which cannot be separated from the same foundations once posited in the extremes are not distinguished from them except by reason. But which they are that can be separated from the extremes, and which cannot, it does not explain; indeed, it does not even bring forward any reason to confirm this: wherefore it speaks quite confusedly, declaring only this, that relations of the second kind, which it thinks are founded in bare potency and not in potency reduced to act, are not distinguished from their foundation. And it adds that relations which are identified with substance, whatever they may be, do not belong to this category, because it is repugnant for an accident to be identified with substance. But other moderns distinguish all relations founded in substance really from their foundation, on account of the same reason.

Tertia opinio, Distingui omnes relationes reales, à suis fundamentis realiter: quam sequuntur ferè omnes Thomistæ. Caiet. 1. par. quæst. 28. art. 2. & ibid. Bannes, Capr. in 1. dist. 3. quæst. 1. Ferrar. 4 lib. contra gentes, cap. 14. Sotus qu. 2 huius prædicamenti. Fonseca 5. lib. Meta. cap. 15. quæst. 2. sect. 1. Et eandem videtur sequi Scotus, in 2. d 1. q. 5. & in 3. d. 8. q. 1. Et videtur mihi probabilior, & tenenda. Hoc solùm addendum est, quòd talis distinctio, non est ita realis, qualis reperitur inter duas res, sed qualis reperitur inter rem, & modum eius: nam cùm relatio non possit esse in rerum natura, sine relatiuo (vt

The third opinion: All real relations are distinguished from their foundations really: which almost all the Thomists follow: Cajetan, 1 p., q. 28, a. 2, and Báñez in the same place; Capreolus on 1, d. 3, q. 1; Ferrara on bk. 4 Against the Gentiles, ch. 14; Soto, q. 2 of this category; Fonseca, Metaph. bk. 5, ch. 15, q. 2, sect. 1. And Scotus seems to follow the same, on 2, d. 1, q. 5, and on 3, d. 8, q. 1. And it seems to me more probable and to be held. Only this is to be added: that such a distinction is not so real as is found between two things, but such as is found between a thing and its mode: for since a relation cannot be in the nature of things without a relative (as

p. 431

postea probabitur) non se habet, tanquam alia res distincta ab eo: sed tanquam modus eius; ideo non distinguitur tanquam vna res ab alia: sed per distinctam quidem entitatem realem, & sine dependentia ab intellectu: solùm tamen modalem, & distinctione non rei, sed modi: & eam sic explicatam, sequuntur iam omnes ferè moderni.

will be proved afterwards) it is not related to it as another thing distinct from it, but as its mode; therefore it is not distinguished as one thing from another, but through a distinct entity, indeed real and without dependence on the intellect, yet only modal, and by a distinction not of thing but of mode; and, explained in this way, almost all the moderns now follow it.

129 Probatur autem ex doctrina D. Th. qui tria docet de relationibus creaturarum. Primum, quòd aliud esse habeant distinctum, ab esse substantiæ: & secundùm hoc esse ei inhæreant. Secundum, quòd in relatiuis creatis, præter id, quod significatur nomine relatiuo, inueniatur aliquid aliud, quod est res alia diuersa ab ea: quæ significatur per nomen relatiuum. Tertium quòd relatio creata, sic inhæret subiecto, vt faciat cum eo compositionem realem: relatio verò diuina, non faciat compositionem. Primum & tertium asserit 4. li. contra gentes, cap. 14. Secundum verò 1. p. q. 28. ar. 2. ad 2. Ex quibus euidenter sequitur, relationem distingui ex natura rei, saltem à substantia, cui inhæret, & quam ordinat ad aliud: quia realis compositio, & realis inhærentia, supponit distinctionem realem componentium, atque etiam subiecti, & formæ inhærentis: sed superiùs probatum est, ex communi sententia, relationes primi generis, fundari proximè in substantia; ergo de his saltem relationibus euidens est in doctrina D. Th. distingui à substantia ex natura rei: & cùm sit eadem ratio de cæteris, sequitur eum sentire, quòd omnes distinguantur ex natura rei, à suis fundamentis.

129 And it is proved from the doctrine of St. Thomas, who teaches three things about the relations of creatures. First, that they have a being distinct from the being of substance, and inhere in it according to this being. Second, that in created relatives, besides what is signified by the relative name, something else is found which is another thing, different from what is signified by the relative name. Third, that a created relation so inheres in its subject as to make a real composition with it, whereas a divine relation does not make a composition. The first and third he asserts in Against the Gentiles bk. 4, ch. 14; the second in 1 p., q. 28, a. 2, ad 2. From which it evidently follows that relation is distinguished from the nature of the thing, at least from the substance in which it inheres and which it orders to another: because real composition and real inherence presuppose a real distinction of the components, and also of the subject and the inhering form; but it was proved above, from the common opinion, that relations of the first kind are founded proximately in substance; therefore, at least of these relations, it is evident in the doctrine of St. Thomas that they are distinguished from substance from the nature of the thing; and since the ratio is the same for the others, it follows that he holds that all are distinguished from their foundations from the nature of the thing.

Idem ratione probatur. Primò, Ex noua, atque reali acquisitione relationis, & ex reali eius deperditione. Nam dum corpus erat album, & nõ erat simile, fit de nouo simile, per productionem noui albi: & dum hoc album corrũpitur, desinit esse simile: ex quo sic arguo: Primum albũ non erat realiter simile, antequam produceretur secũdum, ergo cũ producitur, fit realiter, & formaliter simile, per realem relationem similitudinis: quam priùs nõ habebat, licèt haberet albedinem, quæ est eius fundamentum: sed relatio realis, est realis forma relatiua: ergo acquirit formam realem relatiuam, quam non habebat: & realis forma, est realis entitas: ergo acquirit realem entitatem, quam non habebat, licèt haberet fundamentum: relatio igitur res est à fundamento distincta. Et idem sequitur ex reali separatione eiusdem relationis à subiecto: nam corrupto alio albo, corrũpitur in hoc realis similitudo, ergo realis forma relatiua: & ideo realis entitas permanente entitate reali fundamenti: quod non potest esse verum, nisi sint entitates reales distinctæ.

The same is proved by reason. First, from the new and real acquisition of a relation, and from its real loss. For while a body was white and was not like, it becomes like anew through the production of a new white; and while this white is corrupted, it ceases to be like. From which I argue thus: The first white was not really like before the second was produced; therefore when it is produced it becomes really and formally like, through a real relation of likeness, which it did not have before, although it had whiteness, which is its foundation; but a real relation is a real relative form; therefore it acquires a real relative form which it did not have; and a real form is a real entity; therefore it acquires a real entity which it did not have, although it had the foundation: the relation, therefore, is a thing distinct from the foundation. And the same follows from the real separation of the same relation from the subject: for when the other white is corrupted, the real likeness in this one is corrupted, therefore a real relative form, and therefore a real entity, while the real entity of the foundation remains; which cannot be true unless they are distinct real entities.

p. 432

131 Hoc argumentum duobus modis conantur soluere moderni. Primo asserentes, quòd dum nouum album producitur, nihil nouum acquirit antiquum album, sed solùm id habere nouum ex eo, quod de nouo factum est simile: vt nouum extremum connotet, quod priùs non connotabit: vnde relatio similitudinis, non est aliud (inquiunt) quàm albedo, vt connotans terminum, ad quem refertur. Hæc tamen solutio non satisfacit argumento: quia album illud denominatur de nouo simile realiter, & formaliter, atque etiam accidentaliter, cùm priùs nullo modo denominaretur: sed denominatio realis, & accidentalis, non potest fieri, nisi à forma reali inhærente: ergo noua denominatio non potest fieri, nisi à noua forma reali, & inhærente: Falsum igitur est, quòd esse de nouo simile, solùm sit noua connotatio termini. Probatur consequentia: quia talis connotatio, quæ supponit nouam denominationem realem, formalem, & accidentalem, nec potest esse, nec intelligi, sine noua acquisitione realis formę.

131 The moderns try to solve this argument in two ways. First, asserting that while the new white is produced, the old white acquires nothing new, but only has this new thing from the fact that it has been made like anew: namely, that it connotes a new extreme, which it did not connote before; whence the relation of likeness is nothing else (they say) than whiteness as connoting the term to which it is referred. Yet this solution does not satisfy the argument: because that white is denominated like anew, really and formally, and also accidentally, whereas before it was in no way so denominated; but a real and accidental denomination cannot come about except from a real inhering form; therefore a new denomination cannot come about except from a new real and inhering form. It is false, therefore, that to be like anew is only a new connotation of the term. The consequence is proved: because such a connotation, which presupposes a new real, formal, and accidental denomination, can neither be nor be understood without a new acquisition of a real form.

Quare alij respondent secundo: Negari non posse, quin antiquum album acquirat aliquid nouum, non tamen distinctum à fundamento realiter: sed sola ratione: &, vt vno verbo dicatur, non comparare nouam entitatem realem, sed nouam rationem formalem relatiuam: à qua nouam denominationem realem suscipit. Hæc tamen solutio verba solùm continet, & nihil aliud: quare nec potest argumento satisfacere: quod sic probo: Ante operationem intellectus, antiquum album fit realiter, formaliter, & accidentaliter simile, cùm priùs non esset simile, licèt haberet albedinem: sed talis denominatio, non potest prouenire, nisi a forma inhærente de nouo acquisita: cùm denominatio sit noua, & acquirat talem denominationem nouam, sine dependentia ab intellectu, imò licèt nunquam ab eo cognoscatur: ergo acquirit nouam formam, absque dependentia, vel distinctione intellectus: & ideo ex natura distinctam a fundamento quod habebat prius.

Wherefore others reply, second: It cannot be denied that the old white acquires something new, yet not distinct from the foundation really, but by reason alone; and, to say it in one word, that it does not acquire a new real entity, but a new formal relative ratio, from which it receives a new real denomination. Yet this solution contains only words and nothing else: wherefore it cannot satisfy the argument either; which I prove thus: Before the operation of the intellect, the old white becomes really, formally, and accidentally like, whereas before it was not like, although it had whiteness; but such a denomination cannot come except from an inhering form newly acquired, since the denomination is new, and it acquires such a new denomination without dependence on the intellect, indeed even though it is never known by it; therefore it acquires a new form, without dependence on or distinction by the intellect, and therefore distinct from the nature of the thing from the foundation which it had before.

132 Secundo: De relationibus fundatis in substantia, specialiter probatus, quia substantia est ens per se, nulli inhęrens: & accidens reale, ea propria natura inhęret substantiæ: sed relatio est accidens reale: ergo inhæret realiter substantiæ. Sed repugnat; quòd eadem entitas realis, sit per se, & inhæreat alteri: quia esset simul per se, & non per se ergo repugnat, quòd relatio sit eadem entitas realis, cum substantia: quare necesse est relationem fundatam in substantia, distingui realiter à suo fundamento. Neque aliquid valet, quòd solet responderi; relationem non inhærere substantiæ, nisi vt distinctam

132 Second: Concerning relations founded in substance, it is proved specially, because substance is a being per se, inhering in nothing, and a real accident by its proper nature inheres in substance; but relation is a real accident; therefore it inheres really in substance. But it is repugnant that the same real entity be per se and inhere in another, because it would be at once per se and not per se; therefore it is repugnant that relation be the same real entity with substance; wherefore it is necessary that a relation founded in substance be distinguished really from its foundation. Nor is there any force in what is customarily replied, that relation does not inhere in substance except as distinct

p. 433

ratione ab ea. Hoc enim apertè falsum est, quia ante operationem intellectus, vna substantia refertur ab alteram, per relationem realem, & accidentalem: ergo ante operationem intellectus, relatio est in substantia. Tunc ergo: vel est ens per se, ante operationem intellectus, vel ens in alio non per se, quia erit substantia, & non relatio accidentalis: ergo est ens in alio, quod non potest intelligi, nisi per realem inhærentiam: & cùm idem non possit sibi realiter inhærere, sequitur relationem realiter inhærentem, distinctam entitatem esse à substantia, cui inhæret, & in qua fundatur.

by reason from it. For this is openly false, because before the operation of the intellect one substance is referred to another through a real and accidental relation; therefore before the operation of the intellect the relation is in the substance. Then, therefore, it is either a being per se, before the operation of the intellect, or a being in another, not per se: if the former, it will be substance and not an accidental relation; therefore it is a being in another, which cannot be understood except through real inherence; and since the same thing cannot really inhere in itself, it follows that the relation really inhering is an entity distinct from the substance in which it inheres and in which it is founded.

133 Ad testimonium Arist Respõdetur hac distinctione: mutari aliquid, duobus modis contingit, Per se, & per accidens, Per se mutatur illud cuius mutatio intenta est à natura, vel ab aliquo agente naturali: vt dum lapis mutatur, à loco superiori ad inferiorem. Per accidens verò mutatur, si mutatio eius casu contingat, vel ex mutatione alterius extrinseci. Dum ergo Arist. ait, Ad relationem non terminari motum per se: quia relatio solet acquiri sine mutatione subiecti, in quo consurgit: de mutatione per se loquitur: sed non excludit, quin mutetur saltem per accidens illud quod solam relationem de nouo recepit: nec ad intentum eius hoc requirebatur, sed satis est, quòd per se non mutetur, vt verum sit, quòd ad relationem non sit per se motus.

133 To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is made with this distinction: for something to be changed happens in two ways, per se and per accidens. That is changed per se whose change is intended by nature or by some natural agent: as when a stone is changed from a higher place to a lower. But it is changed per accidens if its change happens by chance, or from the change of something else extrinsic. When, therefore, Aristotle says that motion does not terminate at relation per se, because a relation is customarily acquired without change of the subject in which it arises, he is speaking of per se change; but he does not exclude that what has newly received only a relation is changed at least per accidens: nor was this required for his intent, but it is enough that it is not changed per se, for it to be true that there is no motion per se to relation.

134 Ad secundum arg priùs est respondendum, quam ad primum. Respondemus igitur, Concessa maiore, & minore, sed negando consequentiam, quòd sine vrgenti necessitate distinguamus entitatem relationis ab entitate fundamenti: nam rationes adductæ, satis vrgentes sunt.

134 The second argument must be answered before the first. We reply, therefore, granting the major and the minor, but denying the consequence, that we distinguish the entity of the relation from the entity of the foundation without urgent necessity: for the reasons adduced are urgent enough.

Dubium de separatione relationis à fundamento — Doubt on the separation of a relation from its foundation.

Dubium de separatione relationis à fundamento.

[…]

Circa solutionem secundi arg. dubitatur: An posito fundamento relationis in vtroque extremo, sic necessariò consurgat relatio, vt nec per potentiam Dei absolutam, impediri possit talis consecutio: & an postquam iam est in vtroque extremo posita, possit ab eis separari ita vt permaneant duo alba eiusdem gradus intensionis, sine relatione similitudinis.

Concerning the solution of the second argument, it is doubted: Whether, once the foundation of the relation is posited in both extremes, the relation so necessarily arises that such a consequence cannot be impeded even by the absolute power of God; and whether, after it has already been posited in both extremes, it can be separated from them, so that two whites of the same degree of intensity remain without the relation of likeness.

Et prima opinio tenet: Nec posse impediri, quin sequatur, nec postquam iam est in extremis, separari ab eis: ita nonnulli ex modernis. Et quòd impediri non possit, consecutio eius, posito fundamento in vtroque extremo, probant: quia intelligi non potest, quòd vnus homo genuerit alterum, quin ille sit pater, & iste filius (si vterque permaneant) nec possunt intelligi duo alba in eodem gradu, quin intelligantur similia. Ergo fieri

And the first opinion holds: It cannot be impeded from following, nor, after it is already in the extremes, be separated from them: so some of the moderns. And that its consequence cannot be impeded once the foundation is posited in both extremes they prove: because it cannot be understood that one man has begotten another without the former being father and the latter son (if both remain); nor can two whites in the same degree be understood without being understood to be like. Therefore it cannot happen Ee

p. 434

non potest, quin relatio sequatur posito fundamento, in vtroque extremo. Quòd verò postquam relatio iam est in vtroque extremo, non possit ab eis separari vllo modo, probant hoc argumen. Relatio, non est aliud, quàm ita se habere vnum extremum ad alterum, præsupposito fundamento, ergo est modus relatiuorum: sed modus non potest esse separatus à re, cuius est: alioqui iam non esset modus, sed res: ergo nec relatio poterit separari à fundamentis in vtroque extremo existentibus.

that the relation does not follow once the foundation is posited in both extremes. And that, after the relation is already in both extremes, it cannot in any way be separated from them, they prove by this argument: Relation is nothing else than that one extreme is so disposed toward the other, the foundation being presupposed; therefore it is a mode of the relatives; but a mode cannot be separated from the thing whose mode it is, otherwise it would no longer be a mode but a thing; therefore neither can the relation be separated from the foundations existing in both extremes.

136 Nostra tamen sententia est: quòd supposita distinctione ex natura rei, inter relationem, & fundamentum: quam defendimus, separari potest relatio ab eo, etiam posito in vtroque extremo: ita vt impediri possit à Deo, ne sequatur in extremis, atque etiam postquam in eis reperitur, in eisdem esse desinat: non quidem sine eis existens in rerum natura, sed extrema sine illa.

136 Our view, however, is that, supposing the distinction from the nature of the thing between the relation and the foundation, which we defend, the relation can be separated from it even when it is posited in both extremes: so that God can impede it from following in the extremes, and also, after it is found in them, make it cease to be in them: not indeed so that it exists without them in the nature of things, but so that the extremes exist without it.

Probantur duo priora hoc arg. Relatio est entitas ex natura rei distincta à fundamento, & non pertinet ad essentiam eius, aut extremorum, in quibus est: ergo etiam si naturaliter sequatur ex eo, iam posito in vtroque extremo, non implicat contradictionem: quòd talis consecutio impediatur. Antecedens ex nostra sententia est manifestum, quia relatio non solùm est entitas distincta à fundamento, sed rationem etiam formalem, & prædicamentalem habet ab eo diuersam: ergo nulla est repugnantia, quin impediatur à Deo consecutio eius, ex fundamento in vtroque extremo posito: sicut non repugnat, propriam passionem distinctam realiter ab essentia, à qua procedit, ab ea non procedere: vt risibilitas ab essentia hominis. Et eadem ratione probatur, quòd postquam in eis reperitur, possint sine illa permanere.

The two former points are proved by this argument: Relation is an entity distinct from the nature of the thing from its foundation, and does not belong to its essence, or to that of the extremes in which it is; therefore, even if it naturally follows from it once it is posited in both extremes, it does not imply a contradiction that such a consequence be impeded. The antecedent is manifest from our view, because relation is not only an entity distinct from the foundation, but also has a formal and categorial ratio different from it; therefore there is no repugnance in its consequence from the foundation posited in both extremes being impeded by God: just as it is not repugnant that a proper attribute really distinct from the essence from which it proceeds should not proceed from it, as risibility from the essence of man. And by the same reason it is proved that, after it is found in them, they can remain without it.

137 Sed quia duobus modis intelligi potest: Quod ab eis separetur: Primò, ita, vt sine illis permaneat in rerum natura, atque etiam extrema sine illa: vel secundò non sic, sed ita, vt relatio destruatur, aut desinat esse: & extrema sine illa permaneant. Dicimus ergo hoc secundo modo posse ab eis separari, non primo. Probatur primum: quia non est de essentia extremorum, & habet distinctam entitatem relatio ab eis: ergo non repugnat, quòd à Deo destruatur, permanentibus sine illa extremis Probatur secundum: quia relatio est modus extremorum, per quem taliter se habet vnum, in ordine ad alterum: ergo intrinsecum est illi actu referre vnum ad alterum: & ideo repugnat permanere in rerum natura, quin actu referat: quia si separata ab eis daretur, nihil referret ad aliud.

137 But since its being separated from them can be understood in two ways: first, so that it remains in the nature of things without them, and the extremes also without it; or second, not so, but so that the relation is destroyed or ceases to be, and the extremes remain without it: we say, therefore, that it can be separated from them in this second way, not in the first. The first is proved: because it is not of the essence of the extremes, and the relation has an entity distinct from them; therefore it is not repugnant that it be destroyed by God while the extremes remain without it. The second is proved: because relation is a mode of the extremes, through which one is so disposed in order to the other; therefore it is intrinsic to it actually to refer one to the other; and therefore it is repugnant that it remain in the nature of things without actually referring: because if it were given separated from them, it would refer nothing to another.

p. 435

Ad primum arg. oppositæ opinionis: Distinguendum est antecedens: quia duo alba esse similia, duobus modis intelligi potest, formaliter, aut fundamentaliter: & si separetur ab eis relatio, intelligerentur similia fundamentaliter, non formaliter: in quo nulla est repugnantia: & eodem modo generans, & genitus, quasi in fundamento proximò intelligerentur, pater, & filius, non formaliter.

To the first argument of the opposite opinion: The antecedent must be distinguished: because that two whites are like can be understood in two ways, formally or fundamentally; and if the relation were separated from them, they would be understood to be like fundamentally, not formally: in which there is no repugnance; and in the same way the one generating and the one generated would be understood to be father and son as it were in the proximate foundation, not formally.

Ad secundum, Concedendum est antecedens, quòd relatio sit modus extremorum: ex quo solùm sequitur, quòd ipsa non possit esse in rerum natura sine extremis: non tamen, quòd extrema non possint esse, sine illa.

To the second: The antecedent must be granted, that relation is a mode of the extremes; from which it follows only that it cannot be in the nature of things without the extremes, but not that the extremes cannot be without it.

Primum dubium.

F I R S T D O U B T.

An relationi conueniat habere contrarium.

Whether it belongs to relation to have a contrary.

Dvo restant dubia, circa duas proprietates relatiuorum: quarum prima est: Quòd in eis reperiatur contrarietas. Videtur enim Arist. sibi contrarius in hac proprietate. Nam capite de quantitate, negat expressè, Quod relatiua habeant contrarium: capite verò præsenti, tanquam proprietatem tribuit illis, Quod contrarium habeant. Et videntur eam habere: quia simile, & dissimile, contraria sunt: & etiam æquale, & inæquale, & sunt relatiua primi generis.

Two doubts remain concerning two properties of relatives, of which the first is: That contrariety is found in them. For Aristotle seems to be contrary to himself in this property. For in the chapter on quantity he expressly denies that relatives have a contrary; but in the present chapter he attributes it to them as a property, that they have a contrary. And they seem to have one: because like and unlike are contraries, and also equal and unequal, and they are relatives of the first kind.

138 Prima opinio, est Toleti in expositione textus, qui hac distinctione vtitur: Relatiua dupliciter considerari possunt. Primò, formaliter, prout relatiua sunt. Secundò, materialiter, pro fundamentis relationum, vt duo alba considerantur in quantum similia, & in quantum alba: & sub prima consideratione, inquit, non habent contrarium, bene tamen ratione fundamenti, habere possunt, & dum Arist. negauit habere contrarium, formaliter locutus est: sed dum eis tribuit contrarietatem, loquitur fundamentaliter: nam hoc modo contraria sunt dissimilia, vt album, & nigrum

138 The first opinion is that of Toledo in his exposition of the text, who uses this distinction: Relatives can be considered in two ways. First, formally, as they are relatives. Second, materially, for the foundations of the relations, as two whites are considered inasmuch as they are like, and inasmuch as they are white. And under the first consideration, he says, they do not have a contrary, but by reason of the foundation they can well have one; and when Aristotle denied that they have a contrary, he spoke formally; but when he attributes contrariety to them, he speaks fundamentally: for in this way unlike things are contraries, as white and black.

Nostra tamen sententia est: Propriam contrarietatem, non conuenire relatiuis, nec formaliter, nec ratione fundamenti, sed impropria, pro quocunque genere oppositionis, etiam formaliter eis conuenit. Probatur, quòd non conueniat eis formaliter propria contrarietate, hac ratione, Contraria sunt, quæ sub eodem genere maximè distant, & ab eodem subiecto mutuò se expellunt: Ergo contraria, vt talia sunt, formaliter, & expressè respiciunt subiectum, circa quod se expellunt: sed relatiua, vt relatiua, non respiciunt formaliter, & expressè subiectum, sed terminum: ergo, vt relatiua non sunt propriè

Our view, however, is: Proper contrariety does not belong to relatives, neither formally nor by reason of the foundation; but improper contrariety, for any kind of opposition whatever, belongs to them even formally. That proper contrariety does not belong to them formally is proved by this reason: Contraries are those which, under the same genus, are most distant, and mutually expel one another from the same subject; therefore contraries, as such, formally and expressly regard the subject around which they expel one another; but relatives, as relatives, do not formally and expressly regard the subject, but the term; therefore, as relatives, they are not properly Ee ij

p. 436

contraria. Quod verò, nec ratione fundamenti, probatur: quia licèt fundamenta aliquorum relatiuorum contraria sint, vt albedo, & nigredo: quę sunt fundamenta dissimilitudinis, tamen per accidens se habet contrarietas ad rationem dissimilitudinis. Probatur euidenter: quia sola diuersitas specifica, sine vlla contrarietate, fundat relationem dissimilitudinis: vt albedo, & nigredo, vel alia quæcunque contraria, quæ sunt fundamenta dissimilitudinis: at eodem modo eam fundarent; quamuis contraria non essent, per solam differentiam specificam: ergo contrarietas per accidens etiam se habet ad fundandam relationem, & ideo, nec ratione fundamenti per se considerari, vel vt fundamentum est, conuenit relationi.

contraries. And that they are not so by reason of the foundation either is proved: because, although the foundations of some relatives are contraries, as whiteness and blackness, which are foundations of unlikeness, yet contrariety is related per accidens to the ratio of unlikeness. This is proved evidently: because specific diversity alone, without any contrariety, founds the relation of unlikeness: as whiteness and blackness, or any other contraries which are foundations of unlikeness, would found it in the same way even if they were not contraries, through the specific difference alone; therefore contrariety is also related per accidens to founding the relation, and therefore it does not belong to relation by reason of the foundation considered per se, or as it is a foundation.

Ad Aristotelem verò, Respondeo, non esse sibi contrarium: quia capite de quantitate, secundùm propriam sententiam loquitur, negans, Quòd relatiuis aliquid sit contrarium: præsenti verò cap. tribuit eis contrarietatem, non quòd sentiat veram esse proprietatem eorũ, sed vt ostendat definitionem antiquorum, minùs bonam esse: cùm ex ea sequatur, accidentia absoluta, in quibus reperitur contrarietas, esse relatiua: & relatiuis aliquid esse contrarium; quæ cùm sint falsa, sequitur non esse bonam definitionem illam: nec est verum, quòd veris relatiuis aliquid sit contrarium: nec ex propria sententia id aliquando docuit Arist. Quòd denique impropria contrarietas, pro quocunque genere oppositionis eis cõueniat, vt relatiuis, euidens est: cùm relatio formaliter sumpta, includat oppositionem relatiuam, quæ est vnum genus ex quatuor oppositionibus.

To Aristotle, however, I reply that he is not contrary to himself: because in the chapter on quantity he speaks according to his own view, denying that anything is contrary to relatives; but in the present chapter he attributes contrariety to them, not because he thinks it is a true property of theirs, but to show that the definition of the ancients is not good: since from it follows that absolute accidents in which contrariety is found are relatives, and that something is contrary to relatives; and since these things are false, it follows that that definition is not good; nor is it true that something is contrary to true relatives, nor did Aristotle ever teach this from his own view. Finally, that improper contrariety, for any kind of opposition whatever, belongs to them as relatives is evident, since relation, taken formally, includes relative opposition, which is one kind out of the four oppositions.

Dubium Secundum.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

An relatiua suscipiant magis, & minus.

Whether relatives admit of more and less.

140 Dvbium hoc de solis relatiuis secundùm esse, & prædicamentalibus, procedit. Et ratio dubitandi sumitur ex Aristotele, qui asserit: Proprium esse relatiuorum, suscipere magis, & minus. Et ne videretur alicui, eum non loqui de veris relatiuis, atque ex propria sententia, sed ex sententia antiquorum, & secundùm definitionem eorum, ponit exemplum huius proprietatis, in simili, & dissimili: quæ sunt vera relatiua, & prædicamentalia.

140 This doubt proceeds concerning relatives according to being and categorial relatives alone. And the reason for doubting is taken from Aristotle, who asserts: It is proper to relatives to admit of more and less. And lest he should seem to anyone not to be speaking of true relatives and from his own view, but from the view of the ancients and according to their definition, he gives an example of this property in the like and the unlike, which are true and categorial relatives.

Prima opinio, distinguit relatiua: Nam alia sunt secundum esse quæ propriè pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum: alia secundùm dici, quæ verè sunt absoluta, tamen includunt quosdam respectus, secundùm dici, tanquam complementum essentiale:

The first opinion distinguishes relatives: for some are according to being, which properly belong to this category; others according to being said, which are truly absolute, yet include certain respects according to being said, as an essential complement:

p. 437

& illa priora non suscipiunt magis & minus: hæc verò suscipere possunt. Ita Albertus Mag. tract. de prædicamento ad aliquid, cap 3. Et huius sententiæ videtur esse D. Th. c. 12. q. 82. art. 4 Quam etiam sequuntur alij, qui aiunt secundùm veritatem, non suscipere magis, & minus vnum relatiuum, vel secundùm opinionem vulgi aliqua suscipere: vt æqualia, vel similia appellari solent, quæ licèt verè æqualia, aut similia non sint, parum tamen à verá æqualitate, aut similitudine distant: & quo minus distant, eo dicuntur magis æqualia, aut similia. Ita Canterus in expositione huius proprietatis.

and the former do not admit of more and less, while the latter can admit of them. So Albert the Great, in the treatise on the category of relation, ch. 3. And St. Thomas seems to be of this opinion, c. 12, q. 82, a. 4. Others also follow it, who say that according to the truth no relative admits of more and less, but that according to the opinion of the common people some do admit them: as things are customarily called equal or like which, although they are not truly equal or like, yet are little distant from true equality or likeness; and the less they are distant, the more they are called equal or like. So Canterus in the exposition of this property.

Probatur primùm, quia suscipere magis & minus, prouenit ex maiori, vel minori admixtione contrarij, vt illud dicitur magis calidum, quod minùs habet de frigiditate admixta: illud verò minùs calidum, quod plus habet frigiditatis admixtæ: sed vera relatiua prædicamentalia, non habent contrarium, vt probatum est dubio præcedenti: ergo non suscipiunt magis & minus.

The first is proved: because to admit of more and less comes from a greater or lesser admixture of a contrary, as that is called more hot which has less cold admixed, and that less hot which has more cold admixed; but true categorial relatives do not have a contrary, as was proved in the preceding doubt; therefore they do not admit of more and less.

Secunda opinio, Distinguit relationem, ex parte sui: aut, ex parte fundamenti: & ex parte sui, negat veram relationem huius prædicamenti suscipere magis, & minus: sed ratione fundamenti suscipere concedit. Ita Caietanus, Sotus, & Toletus, cap. præsenti.

The second opinion distinguishes relation on its own side or on the side of the foundation; and on its own side it denies that a true relation of this category admits of more and less, but grants that it admits of them by reason of the foundation. So Cajetan, Soto, and Toledo, in the present chapter.

141 Quod probatur experientia. Nam dum albedo intenditur in extremo, in quo erat remissa, consequenter fit magis simile alteri, in quo est intensa: ergo albedo, quæ est fundamentum similitudinis, per se suscipit magis, & minùs, & eius ratione similitudo; & eodem modo, dum aliquid est alteri inæquale, quò magis aufertur de quantitate eius, magis inæquale efficitur, & hoc est, relationem inæqualitatis, minorem fieri, ratione fundamenti. Sed addit hæc sententia, non esse necessarium, vt relatio suscipiat magis & minùs ratione fundamenti, quod fundamentum suscipiat magis & minùs: nam quantitas, ratione cuius inæqualitas, maior est, vel minor, non suscipit magis & minùs: sed ratione fundamenti dicitur relatio suscipere in hoc sensu: quod non potest suscipere, nisi aliqua variatio fiat in fundamento, quæcunque illa sit: vnde magis & minus, distinguenda putat Caietanus: quia vel sumuntur Physicè: & hoc modo non fiunt, nisi per admixtionem contrarij; aut Logicè, & sic sumpta, in eo tantùm consistunt, quod est aliquid prædicari de alio, cum his aduerbiis magis & minus, vndecunque id proueniat. Et Physicè quidem sumpta, non conueniunt verè relationi: Logicè verò conuenire illi possunt.

141 This is proved by experience. For while whiteness is intensified in an extreme in which it was remiss, consequently it becomes more like the other, in which it is intense; therefore whiteness, which is the foundation of likeness, per se admits of more and less, and by reason of it likeness does; and in the same way, while something is unequal to another, the more is taken away from its quantity, the more unequal it is made; and this is for the relation of inequality to become less by reason of the foundation. But this opinion adds that it is not necessary, for the relation to admit of more and less by reason of the foundation, that the foundation admit of more and less: for quantity, by reason of which inequality is greater or less, does not admit of more and less; but the relation is said to admit of them by reason of the foundation in this sense: that it cannot admit of them unless some variation take place in the foundation, whatever it may be. Whence Cajetan thinks that more and less must be distinguished: because either they are taken Physically, and in this way they come about only through admixture of a contrary; or Logically, and taken so they consist only in this, that something is predicated of another with these adverbs more and less, from wherever that may come. And taken Physically they do not truly belong to relation; but Logically they can belong to it.

Hæc tamen distinctio, confundit potiùs rem, quàm eam

This distinction, however, confuses the matter rather than Ee iij

p. 438

explicat: quia prædicationes Logicæ, in re ipsa debent fundari: ergo nunquam poterunt, magis & minùs, Logicè sumpta, conuenire relationi, nisi ratione fundamenti realis, & Physici: quare si Physicè sumpta, nullo modo ei conueniunt, nec Logicè poterunt ei conuenire.

explains it: because Logical predications must be founded in the thing itself; therefore more and less, taken Logically, can never belong to relation except by reason of a real foundation, and Physically; wherefore, if taken Physically they in no way belong to it, neither will they be able to belong to it Logically.

Nostra igitur sententia, hac distinctione præsupposita explicanda est: Magis, & minus, duobus modis accipiuntur, Communiter: & Propriè: Communiter quidem: pro magis aut minùs perfectum, magis aut minùs proximum, vel distans: vnde cùm perfectio maior, vel minor, proueniat ex fundamento, ab eo proueniet magis & minus, in relatione impropriè sumptum. Propriè verò accipitur magis & minùs, prout ex maiori, vel minori intentione procedit.

Our view, therefore, is to be explained presupposing this distinction: More and less are taken in two ways, Commonly and Properly. Commonly, for more or less perfect, more or less near or distant: whence, since greater or lesser perfection comes from the foundation, from it will come more and less in relation, taken improperly. But more and less are taken properly as they proceed from greater or lesser intensity.

Nunc verò duabus conclusionibus explicatur. Prima est, Relationibus prædicamentalibus (de quibus solùm loquimur) non conuenit ratione sui magis, aut minus suscipere, propriè, nec impropriè. Probatur hæc conclusio: Quia experientia constat, relationem ratione sui, non mutari ab eo statu in quo emergit, nisi aliquo modo varietur fundamentum; & si hoc inuariabile permaneat: nunquam ipsa nec magis & minùs suscipit: ergo non conuenit illi ratione sui.

And now it is explained by two conclusions. The first is: To categorial relations (of which alone we are speaking) it does not belong by reason of themselves to admit of more or less, either properly or improperly. This conclusion is proved: Because it is established by experience that a relation, by reason of itself, does not change from the state in which it emerges unless the foundation is varied in some way; and if this remains invariable, it never admits of more and less; therefore this does not belong to it by reason of itself.

143 Secunda conclusio: Magis & minus propriè & impropriè sumpta, conueniunt quibusdam relationibus ratione fundamenti: non tamen omnibus. Probatur vtrumque, in relationibus primi generis: nam quædam dicuntur magis & minùs inæqualia, magis, & minùs similia: sed hoc non conuenit illis ratione sui: ergò ratione fundamenti: & similitudini quidem, ac dissimilitudi propriè: quia qualitates, in quibus fundantur, propriè suscipiunt magis & minùs: vt calor, albedo, & nigredo. Quando autem dicimus: his relationibus conuenire magis & minùs, ratione fundamenti: sensus est, quòd aliqua mutatione facta in fundamento, semper eis conueniat: & hæc mutatio, potest esse in fundamento remissio, & in relatione intentio, quia fundamentum absolutè intenditur, cùm sit qualitas: relatio verò, non nisi comparatione alterius. Quòd verò non conueniat hoc, nisi quibusdam relationibus, primi generis, manifestum est, quòd solùm illis quarum fundamenta mutari possunt.

143 The second conclusion: More and less, taken properly and improperly, belong to certain relations by reason of the foundation, yet not to all. Both are proved in relations of the first kind: for some things are called more and less unequal, more and less like; but this does not belong to them by reason of themselves; therefore by reason of the foundation; and to likeness and unlikeness properly, because the qualities in which they are founded properly admit of more and less, as heat, whiteness, and blackness.
