And when we say that more and less belong to these relations by reason of the foundation, the sense is that, when some change is made in the foundation, they always belong to them; and this change can be remission in the foundation and intensification in the relation, since the foundation is intensified absolutely, as it is a quality, but the relation only by comparison with another. And that this does not belong except to certain relations of the first kind is manifest, because it belongs only to those whose foundations can be changed.

144 Ad Arist. verò respondetur: quòd dum relationibus tribuit proprietatem suscipiendi magis & minus, etiam de prædicamentalibus loquitur, non tamen intelligit eis conuenire ratione sui, sed ratione fundamenti, vt explicatum est, nec etiam intelligit eis adhuc in hoc sensu conuenire, quarto modo,

144 To Aristotle the reply is that, when he attributes to relations the property of admitting of more and less, he is indeed speaking of categorial ones, yet he does not understand that it belongs to them by reason of themselves, but by reason of the foundation, as has been explained; nor does he understand that it belongs to them even in this sense in the fourth mode,

p. 439

cùm constet, non omnibus conuenire, neque etiam solis: quia præcipuè conuenit qualitatibus. Proprietas verò, conueniens relatiuis prædicamentalibus, quarto modo, est, Esse simul natura, & cognitione: ita vt qui definitiuè cognoscit vnum, necessariò debeat cognoscere alterum.

since it is established that it belongs neither to all nor to them alone, because it belongs chiefly to qualities. But the property belonging to categorial relatives in the fourth mode is to be simultaneous by nature and in cognition: so that whoever knows one definitively must necessarily know the other.

Sed dicet aliquis: Suscipere magis & minùs procedit ex maiori vel minori admixtione contrarij: sed dictum est, relatiua, nec ratione sui, nec ratione fundamenti habere contrarium: ergo nec ratione sui, nec ratione fundamenti conueniet illis suscipere magis, & minùs. Respondetur, Quòd ratione sui neutrum illis conuenit, sed ratione fundamenti non repugnat eis conuenire secundum, licèt non conueniat primum, etiam ratione fundamenti: quia contrarietas fundamenti, per accidens se habet ad illas relationes, in quibus posset esse contrarietas, vt ad similitudinem, & dissimilitudinem (vt probatum est in primo dubio) Magis autem, & minùs ex parte fundamenti, non se habet omnino per accidens, ad magis, & minus relationum, sed quasi naturaliter ex eo sequitur. Ex eo verò, quòd relatiua carent contrarietate omnibus modis, solùm sequitur, quòd non possent ratione sui suscipere magis, & minùs.

But someone will say: To admit of more and less proceeds from a greater or lesser admixture of a contrary; but it has been said that relatives have a contrary neither by reason of themselves nor by reason of the foundation; therefore to admit of more and less will belong to them neither by reason of themselves nor by reason of the foundation. The reply is that by reason of themselves neither belongs to them; but by reason of the foundation it is not repugnant that the second belong to them, although the first does not belong even by reason of the foundation: because the contrariety of the foundation is related per accidens to those relations in which there could be contrariety, as to likeness and unlikeness (as was proved in the first doubt); but more and less on the side of the foundation are not related altogether per accidens to the more and less of relations, but follow from it as it were naturally. And from the fact that relatives lack contrariety in all ways, it follows only that they could not admit of more and less by reason of themselves.

CHAPTER VIII

CAP. VIII. Continens prædicamentum qualitatis, cum exposit. text. — Containing the category of Quality.

CAPVT VIII.

[…]

Continens prædicamentum Qualitatis.

[…]

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

TEXTVS ARIST.

[…]

Qualitatem verò dico, secundùm quam, quales quidam esse dicuntur, &c.

But I call quality that according to which certain things are said to be qualified, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 Intentum Aristo. capite præsenti est, explicare naturam, & essentiam qualitatis: quam numerat quarto loco ante sex alia prædicamenta: quia accidens intrinsecum est, formaliter inhærens substantiæ: & ideo perfectius reliquis, quæ magna ex parte, in quibusdam extrinsecis denominationibus consistunt. Diuiditur caput in tres partes. In prima, definit qualitatem in abstracto, & connumerat quatuor eius species subalternas, quas ideo genera vocat, In secunda parte, definit qualitatem in concreto, hoc est, per ordinem ad subiectum, quod denominat: vt per illud magis fiat manifesta. Et in tertia, tres proprietates eius assignat. Definitio qualitatis est hæc: Qualitas est qua quales esse dicimur

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the nature 1 T and essence of quality, which he numbers in the fourth place before the six other categories, because it is an intrinsic accident, formally inhering in substance, and therefore more perfect than the rest, which for the most part consist in certain extrinsic denominations. The chapter is divided into three parts. In the first, he defines quality in the abstract and enumerates its four subaltern species, which he therefore calls genera. In the second part, he defines quality in the concrete, that is, through its order to the subject which it denominates, so that through this it may become more manifest. And in the third, he assigns three properties of it. The definition of quality is this: Quality is that by which we are said to be qualified Ee iiij

p. 440

vt albedo, à qua albus denominatur homo, & ideo qualis, quia si interroges, qualis sit homo? bene respondebitur, si dicatur, esse album.

as whiteness, by which a man is denominated white, and therefore qualified, because if you ask, What kind is the man? it will be well answered if it is said that he is white.

Prima species qualitatis est, Habitus, & dispositio. Habitus sic definitur: Est qualitas difficile mobilis à subiecto, vt habitus virtutum & scientiarum. Dispositio verò: Qualitas facilè mobilis à subiecto, vt calor, quem ignis producit in aqua, facilè ab ea remouetur.

The first species of quality is Habit and disposition. Habit is defined thus: It is a quality difficult to move from the subject, as the habits of the virtues and sciences. But disposition: A quality easily movable from the subject, as heat, which fire produces in water, is easily removed from it.

2 Secundum genus qualitatis est, Naturalis potentia, & impotentia; secundùm quam naturalem habent inclinationem, vel aptitudinem aliqui, ad aliquem actum, aliquódue exercitium, vt ad pugnam, vel ad luctam, & dicuntur pugillatores. Alij verò inepti sunt, aut impotentes ad eundem actum. Dicitur autem naturalis: quia ab ipsa natura habetur, & non est acquisita per actus: nam si talis esset, potiùs erit habitus, aut dispositio.

2 The second genus of quality is Natural potency and impotency, according to which some have a natural inclination or aptitude to some act or some exercise, as to boxing or to wrestling, and are called boxers. Others are inept or impotent for the same act. And it is called natural because it is had from nature itself and is not acquired through acts: for if it were such, it would rather be a habit or disposition.

Tertium genus est, Passio, aut Passibilis qualitas: & hæc est qualitas, nata causare passionem in sensu, vel quæ est effectus passionis permanentis: vt qualitates tangibiles, quæ causant sensationem in tactu, vt calor, & frigiditas, & sic de aliis: & albedo, quæ causatur in cera, ex nimio calore solis dicitur etiam passibilis qualitas: quia est effectus illius impressionis, quam Sol causat in cera: & permanens quidem, quia albedo producta in cera, non statim transit, sed permanet in ea. Passio verò dicitur qualitas, si sit effectus passionis citò transeuntis: vt rubor causatus in facie ex verecundia, & quia passio non est qualitas permanens non denominat subiectum tale simpliciter, sed passum secundùm eam: vnde à rubore causato ex verecundia non dicitur homo rubeus, sed ruborem passus, & sic de cæteris passionibus.

The third genus is Passion or passible quality; and this is a quality apt to cause passion in the sense, or which is the effect of a permanent passion; as the tangible qualities, which cause sensation in touch, as heat and cold, and so of the others; and whiteness, which is caused in wax by the excessive heat of the sun, is also called a passible quality, because it is the effect of that impression which the Sun causes in the wax; and permanent, because the whiteness produced in the wax does not pass at once, but remains in it. But a quality is called a passion if it is the effect of a quickly passing passion; as the redness caused in the face by shame; and because a passion is not a permanent quality, it does not denominate the subject such simply, but as having suffered according to it: whence from redness caused by shame a man is not called red, but one who has suffered redness, and so of the other passions.

3 Quartum genus qualitatis est, Forma & Figura, vt rectitudo, curuitas, statua, aut cathedra, formæ, ac figuræ dicuntur & species huius generis.

3 The fourth genus of quality is Form and Figure, as straightness, curvature; a statue or a chair are called forms and figures and species of this genus.

In secunda parte cap. definit Arist. qualitatem in concreto, hoc modo: Quale est, quod secundùm qualitatem denominatur, vt album, & dulce.

In the second part of the chapter Aristotle defines quality in the concrete in this way: Qualified is that which is denominated according to quality, as white and sweet.

In tertia parte, enumerat tres proprietates qualitatis: quarum prima est, Qualitatem habere contrarium: vt calori contrariatur frigiditas: nec tamen conuenit omnibus qualitatibus proprietas hæc, quia plures sunt non habentes contrarium, vt rubrum, pallidum, & alij colores medij.

In the third part he enumerates three properties of quality, of which the first is That quality has a contrary: as cold is contrary to heat; yet this property does not belong to all qualities, because there are several that have no contrary, as red, pale, and the other intermediate colors.

Secunda proprietas est, Suscipere magis & minus: quòd cùm procedat ex maiori aut minori admixtione contrarij, necesse est, habentibus propriè contrarium conuenire: sed nec omnibus

The second property is To admit of more and less; which, since it proceeds from a greater or lesser admixture of a contrary, must necessarily belong to those that properly have a contrary; but neither does it belong to

p. 441

qualitatibus conuenit hoc: quia plures sunt non suscipientes magis & minùs, vt figuræ & similes.

all qualities: because there are many that do not admit of more and less, such as figures and the like.

Tertia proprietas qualitatis est, Quòd secundùm eam res dicantur similes, aut dissimiles: vt secundùm albedinem, dicuntur corpora similia. Hæc autem proprietas, quarto modo conuenit qualitati, quia omnibus qualitatibus solis, & semper conuenit.

The third property of quality is that according to it things are called like or unlike: as according to whiteness bodies are called like. And this property belongs to quality in the fourth mode, because it belongs to all qualities, to them alone, and always.

QUESTION I

Quæst. 1. An qualitas sit supremum genus huius prædicamenti: & diuersæ qualitates, enumeratæ ab Arist., diuersæ species eius — Whether quality is the supreme genus of this category, and the diverse qualities enumerated by Aristotle are diverse species of it.

QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

An qualitas sit supremum genus huius prædicamenti: & diuersæ qualitates, enumeratæ ab Arist. diuersæ species eius.

[…]

4 Vt meliùs intelligatur quæstio, explicandæ sunt diuersæ acceptiones qualitatis: quæ (omissis aliis) tres sunt, vt colligitur ex Aristo. cap. præsenti, & 5. Metaph cap 14. Qualitas in generali, significat determinationem, seu modificationem substantiæ: & ideo prima acceptio eius, est pro quocunque determinante, aut modificante aliud: quòd non solùm conuenit omnibus accidentibus, sed etiam substantiis, aut differentiis earum. Secundo modo, accipitur pro forma quacunque accidentali, quæ secundùm proprium modum essendi modificat, aut determinat substantiam: vt quantitas, relatio, ac cætera accidenti pro hæc etiam acceptio communis est. Tertia verò propria, a: & forma, non solùm secundùm communem rationem accidentalem determam sibi inhærentem. tali modo se habeat substantia, vt forminante subiectum, sed propriè: ita vt per eam, tanquam per formaliter denominetur, non extensa, non relata ad aliud, sed qualis: quia ad quæstionem de ea factam per quale, propriè respondeamus per talem formam, vt si quæratur, Qualis sit substantia: propriè respondemus, esse albam, aut calidam, & ideo formæ istæ accidentales propriè dicuntur qualitates. Et secundùm hanc solam acceptionem, non secundùm duas alias, sumitur qualitas ab Aristotele, capite præsenti, & distinguitur à cæteris prædicamentis: de qua quærit titulus quæstionis: An sit supremum genus huius prædicamenti, & qualitates particulares enumeratæ ab Arist. veræ species eius.

hat the question may be better understood, the different accepta4 T tions of quality must be explained; of which (omitting others) there are three, as is gathered from Aristotle in the present chapter and Metaph. 5, ch. 14. Quality in general signifies a determination or modification of substance; and therefore its first acceptation is for anything whatever that determines or modifies another: which belongs not only to all accidents but also to substances, or to their differences. In the second way it is taken for any accidental form whatever which, according to its own proper mode of being, modifies or determines substance: as quantity, relation, and the other accidents; and this acceptation too is common. But the third is the proper one, for a form which determines the subject not only according to the common accidental ratio, but properly: so that it makes the substance inhering in it be disposed in such a way that through it, as through a form, it is formally denominated not extended, not related to another, but qualified; because to the question put about it through what kind, we properly reply through such a form: as, if it is asked, What kind is the substance? we properly reply that it is white, or hot. And therefore these accidental forms are properly called qualities. And it is according to this acceptation alone, not according to the other two, that quality is taken by Aristotle in the present chapter and is distinguished from the other categories; and concerning it the title of the question asks: Whether it is the supreme genus of this category, and the particular qualities enumerated by Aristotle are true species of it.

5 Prima opinio tenet, Qualitatem sic acceptam, non esse verum genus, quod diuidatur in illas qualitates enumeratas ab Arist. tanquam in veras species: sed tanquam analogum in sua analogata, vel tanquam res in diuersos modos. Primum affirmat Simplicius cap. præsenti, & probat ex eodem Aristotele, qui priusquam illas qualitates enumeraret, sic loquitur: Est autem

5 The first opinion holds that quality so taken is not a true genus which is divided into those qualities enumerated by Aristotle as into true species, but as an analogous term into its analogates, or as a thing into its different modes. The first is affirmed by Simplicius on the present chapter, and he proves it from the same Aristotle, who, before enumerating those qualities, speaks thus: But

p. 442

qualitas eorum, quæ multipliciter dicuntur. Secundum verò tenet Scotus capite præsenti, quæst 36. & in 4. dist 6. quæst. 10. §. Sed tunc est dubium, & etiam probat testimonio Aristotelis, qui postquam enumerauit omnes has qualitates, dicit, Fortasse quidem alius quispiam modus apparuerit qualitatis: sed ferè qui maximè dicuntur, hi sunt.

quality is among the things that are said in many ways. The second is held by Scotus on the present chapter, q. 36, and in 4, d. 6, q. 10, § But then there is a doubt; and he too proves it by the testimony of Aristotle, who, after enumerating all these qualities, says: Perhaps indeed some other mode of quality might appear; but those which are most of all spoken of are these.

7 Probat etiam ratione: Quia esse naturalem potentiam, vel aptitudinem acquisitam, esse causam, vel effectum passionis, diuersas habitudines qualitatis ad subiectum significant, accidentales tamen, & quasi extrinsecè denominantes: quia extrinsecum est qualitati, parum aut multum durare in subiecto, causam esse, aut effectum passionis. Vnde eiusdem speciei sunt, rubor causatus ex verecundia, aut ex alia causa permanenti; & quod amplius est, eidem qualitati omnino inuariatæ, conueniunt isti modi: ergo non sunt differentiæ essentiales, sed accidentales. Probatur hoc vltimum antecedens, Quia idem calor si citò transeat, erit dispositio, si multùm duret in subiecto, erit habitus, & vt virtus naturalis ignis ad calefaciendum, erit naturalis potentia: & tandem, in quantum causat passionem in sensum tactus, aut productus est per motum calefactionis, erit passibilis qualitas; ex quibus considerationibus, constat non variari,

7 It is proved also by reason: Because to be a natural potency, or an acquired aptitude, to be a cause or an effect of passion, signify different relations of quality to the subject, but accidental ones, and denominating as it were extrinsically: since it is extrinsic to quality to last a short or a long time in the subject, to be a cause or an effect of passion. Hence redness caused by shame and redness caused by some other permanent cause are of the same species; and, what is more, these modes belong to the same quality wholly unchanged: therefore they are not essential differences but accidental ones. This last antecedent is proved: Because the same heat, if it passes quickly, will be a disposition; if it lasts long in the subject, it will be a habit; and as the natural power of fire to heat, it will be a natural potency; and finally, insofar as it causes a passion in the sense of touch, or is produced by the motion of heating, it will be a passible quality: from which considerations it is plain that it does not vary.

Huic opinioni, addunt Boëtius & Simplicius, cap. præsenti, diuisionem qualitatis in hos modos, aut in hæc analogata: non esse sufficientem: quia alia dantur membra huius diuisionis, ab Arist. prætermissa: quod sic probatur: Pulchritudo, & sanitas, sunt qualitates, & non pertinent ad aliquod membrum ex his quatuor: cùm nec sint habitus, aut dispositiones: quia non sunt acquisitæ, sed naturales: nec potentiæ, aut impotentiæ: quia non ordinantur ad actus aliquos exercendos: nec passiones, aut passibiles qualitates: quia nec per se sunt effectus passionis, nec eam in sensu causant: nec tandem sunt forma, & figura: quod de sanitate patet: & de pulchritudine probatur, quæ magis, & minus suscipit, cùm dentur quidam pulchriores aliis: figura autem, & forma, id non habeant,

To this opinion Boethius and Simplicius, on the present chapter, add that the division of quality into these modes, or into these analogates, is not sufficient: because there are other members of this division passed over by Aristotle. This is proved thus: Beauty and health are qualities, and they do not pertain to any member of these four: since they are neither habits nor dispositions, because they are not acquired but natural; nor potencies or impotencies, because they are not ordered to exercising any acts; nor passions or passible qualities, because they neither are per se effects of passion nor cause it in the sense; nor finally are they form and figure, which is plain of health, and is proved of beauty, which admits of more and less, since some are more beautiful than others; but figure and form do not have this.

Communis sententia à nobis tenenda, duo asserit. Primum, Qualitatem verum genus esse, & supremum huius prædicamenti, diuisum in particulares qualitates, enumeratas ab Aristotele, tanquam in veras species: contra Simplicium, & Scotum. Secundum, Diuisionem eius in quatuor illa membra sufficientem esse: ita vt nulla detur vera qualitas quæ sub eis non comprehendatur, contra eundem Simplicium, & Boëtium.

The common opinion, to be held by us, asserts two things. First, that quality is a true genus, and the supreme genus of this category, divided into the particular qualities enumerated by Aristotle as into true species: against Simplicius and Scotus. Second, that its division into those four members is sufficient, so that no true quality is given which is not comprehended under them: against the same Simplicius and Boethius.

Hæc est expressa sententia Arist, non solùm in hoc c. sect. 5,

This is the express opinion of Aristotle, not only in this chapter, sect. 5,

p. 443

Meta. cap. 14. & recepta ab vniuersa schola: quæ prædicamentum qualitatis distinctum ab aliis, cum eo ponit: sed impossibile est constituere prædicamentum qualitatis, ex alio genere, & in aliis speciebus; ergo qualitas in communi, pro genere supremo recipienda est, & inferiores illæ qualitates, pro veris speciebus. Minorem probo, quia nec ab his autoribus, contrarium opinantibus: nec ab alio excogitatum est aliud genus: nec aliæ species.

Metaph. ch. 14, and received by the whole school: which posits a category of quality distinct from the others, with it; but it is impossible to constitute the category of quality out of another genus and in other species; therefore quality in common is to be received as the supreme genus, and those inferior qualities as true species. I prove the minor: because neither by these authors who hold the contrary, nor by anyone else, has any other genus or other species been thought up.

Nihilominus probatur ratione: Quia communis conceptus qualitatis, abstractus ab illis, prædicatur de singulis quidditatiuè, & vniuocè: ergo est genus, vel species respectu illarum: Species esse non potest, quia non habet genus aliud supra se: ergo erit genus. Probatur antecedens: quia negari non potest, quidditatiuas esse has prædicationes: Habitus est qualitas, Naturalis potentia, est qualitas, cùm eis conueniat definitio qualitatis, tradita ab Arist. & æqualiter eis conuenit, sine attributione vnius ad aliam: ergo est prædicatum vniuocum, & quidditatiuum. Quod autem qualitates illæ distinguantur specie, non est minùs manifestum: quia ratio formalis habitus, valde diuersa est à naturali potentia: & hæc à forma, & figura, sed diuersæ rationes formales, constituunt, & distinguunt, diuersas species: ergo specie distinguuntur illæ quatuor qualitates, sub communi genere qualitatis.

It is proved nonetheless by reason: Because the common concept of quality, abstracted from them, is predicated of each of them quidditatively and univocally; therefore it is a genus or a species with respect to them. A species it cannot be, because it has no other genus above itself; therefore it will be a genus. The antecedent is proved: because it cannot be denied that these predications are quidditative: A habit is a quality, A natural potency is a quality, since the definition of quality given by Aristotle belongs to them, and belongs to them equally, without attribution of one to another; therefore it is a univocal and quidditative predicate. And that those qualities are distinguished in species is no less manifest: because the formal ratio of habit is very different from natural potency, and this from form and figure; but different formal rationes constitute and distinguish different species: therefore those four qualities are distinguished in species under the common genus of quality.

8 Probatur tandem, quòd sufficiens sit diuisio qualitatis, in has quatuor species, ita vt nec plures sint, nec pauciores, ratione D. Th. quam adduxit 12. q. 49. art. 2. Ratio intrinseca, & propria qualitatis, est esse determinatum substantiæ, secundùm modum accidentalem qualificatiuum eius: sed modus iste qualificatiuus substantiæ, quatuor modis tantùm potest se habere, in ordine ad substantiam: ergo quatuor tantùm possunt sub species distingui. Probatur minor: quia vel qualitas inhæret substantiæ ea disponens, vt bene vel malè se habeat, vt est primò in se: & cùm hæc sit prima consideratio substantiæ hæc erit prima species qualitatis, quæ est habitus & dispositio, ita disponens substantiam. Secunda consideratio substantiæ est, in quantum est principium operationis: cùm vnumquodque sit propter suam operationem. Et ideo secundus modus qualitatis, est afficere substantiam tanquam principium operationis, & hæc est secunda species naturalis potentia.

8 It is proved, finally, that the division of quality into these four species is sufficient, so that there are neither more nor fewer, by the argument of St. Thomas which he adduced in 1-2, q. 49, a. 2: The intrinsic and proper ratio of quality is to be a determination of substance according to its accidental qualifying mode; but this qualifying mode of substance can stand in only four ways in relation to substance; therefore only four species can be distinguished under it. The minor is proved: because either quality inheres in substance disposing it so that it is well or ill disposed, as it is first in itself; and since this is the first consideration of substance, this will be the first species of quality, which is habit and disposition, so disposing substance. The second consideration of substance is insofar as it is a principle of operation, since each thing exists for the sake of its operation. And therefore the second mode of quality is to affect substance as a principle of operation, and this is the second species, natural potency.

9 A substantia autem habente iam potentiam operandi, statim procedit tertio motus, continens actionem, & passionem: quia motus, vt procedit ab agente, est actio: & vt recipitur in passo, est passio; ideo qualitas, vt acquisita per motum, est tertia

9 But from substance already having the potency of operating there proceeds at once, third, motion, containing action and passion: because motion, as it proceeds from the agent, is action, and as it is received in the patient, is passion; therefore quality, as acquired through motion, is the third

p. 444

species, quæ vocatur passio, & passibilis quantitas. Nam si habeat modum permanentis, & passibilis qualitas: si verò citò transeat, est passio. Vltima consideratio substantiæ est, vt iam extensa per quantitatem: & ita qualitas inhærens ei, ratione quantitatis, constituit quartam speciem: quæ est forma, & figura: nam figura vel est terminatio quantitatis, vel ex terminis eius resultat. Et ad hos quatuor modos, constituentes quatuor species, facilè reduci possunt omnes qualitates: vt constabat ex solutione argumentorum. Hoc solum est notandum, quòd argumentum hoc sumit sufficientiam harum specierum, aut ex præcipuo, cui conuenit specialis illa ratio qualificandi substantiam, aut ex primo: vnde est necessarium, quòd in omnibus, quæ sub tali ratione comprehenduntur, reperiatur illa ratio. Exempli gratia: Prima species sumitur ex modo afficiendi substantiam, vt bene, vel malè se habeat, secundùm propriam naturam: quòd solùm habent habitus, aut dispositiones naturales, quæ primò conueniunt substantiæ corporeæ, vt sanitas: ægritudo, & similes: non tamen habitus, aut dispositiones liberè acquisitæ: sed cùm omnes conueniant in ratione habitus & dispositionis, in quantum sunt facilè mobiles à subiecto: omnes constituunt idem genus qualitatis, distinctum à cæteris, sed quasi radicaliter sumptum à naturalibus, tanquam à primis.

species, which is called passion and passible quality. For if it has a permanent mode, it is a passible quality as well; but if it passes quickly, it is a passion. The last consideration of substance is as already extended through quantity; and so the quality inhering in it by reason of quantity constitutes the fourth species, which is form and figure: for figure either is the termination of quantity or results from its terms. And to these four modes, constituting four species, all qualities can easily be reduced, as was plain from the solution of the arguments. Only this is to be noted: that this argument takes the sufficiency of these species either from the principal member, to which that special ratio of qualifying substance belongs, or from the first; whence it is not necessary that that ratio be found in all the things which are comprehended under such a ratio. For example: the first species is taken from the mode of affecting substance so that it is well or ill disposed according to its proper nature; which only natural habits or dispositions have, which belong first to corporeal substance, such as health, sickness, and the like; not, however, habits or dispositions freely acquired. But since all agree in the ratio of habit and disposition, insofar as they are easily or not easily removable from the subject, all constitute the same genus of quality, distinct from the others, but taken as it were radically from the natural ones, as from the first.

10 Ad primum testimonium Arist. pro prima opinione adductum: Respondetur, multis modis dici qualitatem: non sicut analogum, vel æquiuocum, sed propter differentias, inæquales perfectionis, per quas contrahitur ad diuersas species: quarum diuersitas, non tollit vniuocationem generis, quod ab eis abstrahi potest. Vel secundò respondeo, Aristotelem asseruisse, quòd qualitas dicitur multis modis, vt ostendere qualitatem esse modum substantiæ, & species eius sumi ex diuersis modis afficiendi substantiam, vt explicatum est.

10 To the first testimony of Aristotle adduced for the first opinion: it is replied that quality is said in many ways, not as an analogous or equivocal term, but on account of differences of unequal perfection by which it is contracted to different species; whose diversity does not take away the univocation of the genus, which can be abstracted from them. Or, second, I reply that Aristotle asserted that quality is said in many ways in order to show that quality is a mode of substance, and that its species are taken from the different modes of affecting substance, as has been explained.

Ad secundum testimonium, pro opinione Scoti, Respondetur, Aristotelem ita locutum fuisse, vt significaret facilè ad has quatuor species reduci posse, cæteras omnes qualitates quamuis aliquæ diuersæ appareant ab eis.

To the second testimony, for the opinion of Scotus, it is replied that Aristotle spoke thus to signify that all other qualities can easily be reduced to these four species, although some appear different from them.

11 Ad arg. Scoti: Negandum est antecedens, quòd rationes formales diuersæ harum qualitatum, sint accidentales, aut extrinsecæ: nam specialis ratio, quam habet quælibet qualificandi substantia, intrinseca sibi est, & per quam distinguitur à cæteris, tanquam per differentiam essentialem: vt esse ex propria natura, facilè aut difficilè mobilem à subiecto, essentialis ratio, habitus, & dispositionis, est valde diuersa à naturali potentia.

11 To the argument of Scotus: the antecedent must be denied, that the different formal rationes of these qualities are accidental or extrinsic: for the special ratio of qualifying substance which each has is intrinsic to it, and is that through which it is distinguished from the others, as through an essential difference: as to be, by its own nature, easily or not easily removable from the subject, the essential ratio of habit and disposition, is very different from natural potency,

p. 445

Quòd verò eidẽ qualitati cõuenire possint omnes rationis formales specierũ: concedimus: negamus tamen, quod ex hoc infertur, non esse veras species: quia distinctio specifica, non necessariò est realis: sed eadem res, potest pertinere ad diuersas species, sub diuersis rationibus formalibus, quas habet: imò ad diuersa prædicamenta, vt de actione, & passione constat: quæ cùm sint eadem entitas realis modus, efficiunt tamen diuersa prædicamenta, propter rationes formales diuersas.

And that all the formal rationes of the species can belong to the same quality, we grant; but we deny what is inferred from this, that they are not true species: because specific distinction is not necessarily real; but the same thing can pertain to different species under the different formal rationes which it has; indeed, to different categories, as is plain of action and passion: which, although they are the same real entity or mode, nevertheless make different categories on account of their different formal rationes.

Ad arg. Boëtij, negandum est antecedens, quòd dentur alia membra prætermissa ab Aristotele, præter illa quatuor: nam sanitatem posuit ipse in prima specie: & ad eandem pertinet pulchritudo: & vtraque est habitus naturalis: quia habitus, vt est primum genus qualitatis, vniuersaliter sumitur pro quacunque qualitate difficilè mobili à subiecto, siue sit naturalis, siue acquisita: quamuis specialis, & propriissima ratio habitus, solùm reperiatur in potentiis aliquo modo liberis: & ideo solùm sint acquisiti, vel infusi habitus. Species verò intentionales sensibiles, aut intelligibiles, si sint impressæ, pertinent ad speciẽ habitus: quia ex propria natura sunt permanentes si verò sint expressæ, pertinent ad dispositionem: & eodem modo intelligendum est de cæteris qualitatibus, ad has quatuor species reducendis.

To the argument of Boethius: the antecedent must be denied, that there are other members passed over by Aristotle besides those four: for he himself placed health in the first species, and beauty pertains to the same; and both are natural habits: because habit, as it is the first genus of quality, is taken universally for any quality not easily removable from the subject, whether it be natural or acquired; although the special and most proper ratio of habit is found only in powers that are in some way free, and therefore only acquired or infused habits are habits in that sense. But intentional species, sensible or intelligible, if they are impressed, pertain to the species of habit, because by their own nature they are permanent; but if they are expressed, they pertain to disposition. And the same is to be understood of the other qualities that are to be reduced to these four species.

QUESTION II

Quæ. 2. An habitus, & dispositio distinguantur specie — Whether habit and disposition are distinguished in species.

QVÆSTIO II.

[…]

An habitus, & dispositio distinguantur specie.

[…]

12 PRima opinio tenet, Habitum, & dispositionem non esse distinctas species, sed eandem: & solum differre accidentaliter: ita Sotus q. 9. huius cap. §. ad secundam quæstionem. Boëtius, Ammonius, Titelmanus, Villalpand. Louanienses, cap. etiam præsenti: & probatur testimonio Arist. quia tria dicit in textu de his qualitatibus. Primum, Quòd sunt vna species. Secundum, Quòd omnes habitus sunt dispositiones, licet non omnes dispositiones sint habitus Tertium, Dispositionem fieri habituum, procedente tempore, si nimis radicetur in subiecto. Ex quibus sequitur ex mente eius, non esse species distinctas, sed solùm distingui accidentaliter. Probatur consequentia: quia si distinctæ species essent, neque essent vna, nec prædicaretur vna de alia, nec vna posset conuerti in aliam.

he first opinion holds that habit and disposition are not distinct species, 12 T but the same, and differ only accidentally: so Soto, q. 9 on this chapter, § To the second question; Boethius, Ammonius, Titelmans, Villalpando, the Louvain commentators, also on the present chapter; and it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, because he says three things in the text about these qualities. First, that they are one species. Second, that all habits are dispositions, although not all dispositions are habits. Third, that a disposition becomes a habit, as time goes on, if it takes very deep root in the subject. From which it follows, in his mind, that they are not distinct species, but are distinguished only accidentally. The consequence is proved: because if they were distinct species, they would neither be one, nor would one be predicated of the other, nor could one be converted into the other.

13 Et ratione probatur. Primò quia habitus, & dispositio, distinguuntur ex eo, quòd ille difficilè separatur à subiecto, hæc verò facilè remouetur ab eo: sed istæ sunt differentiæ accidentales

13 And it is proved by reason. First, because habit and disposition are distinguished by this, that the former is separated from the subject with difficulty, while the latter is easily removed from it; but these are accidental

p. 446

: ergo solùm differunt accidentaliter. Probatur minor: nam qualitas fit difficilè mobilis à subiecto, quia magis radicatur in eo: sed maior radicatio, procedit ex multiplicatione actuum, aut ex diuturnitate temporis, aut ex vtroque, vt patet in febri, quæ ex eo solùm, quòd multum durat in subiecto, radicatur in eo, & fit difficilè mobilis: sed magis aut minùs perseuerare in subiecto, vel actus multiplicari, sunt accidentia eiusdem qualitatis: ergo hæc differentia habitus, & dispositionis, accidentalis est.

differences; therefore they differ only accidentally. The minor is proved: for a quality becomes not easily removable from the subject because it is more deeply rooted in it; but greater rooting proceeds from the multiplication of acts, or from length of time, or from both, as is plain in a fever, which, from the mere fact that it lasts long in the subject, is rooted in it and becomes not easily removable; but to persevere more or less in the subject, or for acts to be multiplied, are accidents of the same quality: therefore this difference of habit and disposition is accidental.

Secundò, Scientia, & virtus quælibet, eiusdem speciei est, per primum, aut secundum actum acquisita; & successu temporis magis radicata in subiecto, per frequentationem actuũ: sed in principio habet rationem dispositionis, quia facilè potest remoueri à subiecto, & postea fit habitus, quia iam est difficilè mobilis: ergo accidentales sunt istæ differentiæ: facilè, & difficilè mobilem esse à subiecto: Probatur maior: quia distinctio specifica scientiæ, & virtutis, sumitur ex obiecto: sed idem obiectum, habet scientia, aut virtus in principio suæ acquisitionis, & dum iam est radicata in subiecto, per plures actus: ergo est eiusdem speciei.

Second: any science and virtue is of the same species, whether acquired through the first or the second act, and, with the passage of time, more deeply rooted in the subject through the frequent repetition of acts; but in the beginning it has the ratio of disposition, because it can easily be removed from the subject, and afterwards it becomes a habit, because it is now not easily removable: therefore these differences, to be easily and not easily removable from the subject, are accidental. The major is proved: because the specific distinction of science and of virtue is taken from the object; but science or virtue has the same object at the beginning of its acquisition and when it is already rooted in the subject through many acts: therefore it is of the same species.

14 Secunda opinio distinguit habitum, & dispositionem, tanquam duas species subalternas: ita vt sub habitu, distinguantur plures aliæ diuersorum habituum, atque etiam sub dispositione. Hæc est sententia D. Th. 1. 2. qu. 49. art. 2. ad 3 Iauelli, Caiet. Soti, Toleti, atque Canteri cap. præsenti: quam sequuntur etiam Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 14. q. 2 sect 1. & 2. Pater Franciscus Suarius tom. 2. suæ Meta. disp. 42. sect. 6. num. 6. Et videtur nobis probabilior, & tenenda.

14 The second opinion distinguishes habit and disposition as two subalternate species, so that under habit several others, of different habits, are distinguished, and likewise under disposition. This is the opinion of St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 49, a. 2, ad 3; of Javelli, Cajetan, Soto, Toledo, and Canterus on the present chapter; which is followed also by Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 14, q. 2, sect. 1 and 2, and by Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics, disp. 42, sect. 6, no. 6. And it seems to us more probable, and to be held.

Sed vt eam explicemus, & probemus, duo sunt notanda. Primum est: Qualitatem esse facilè aut difficilè mobilem à subiecto, dupliciter contingere: nempe ex natura suæ causæ, per quam producitur in subiecto, & in ordine, ad quam sumit suam speciem: aut ex aliis causis, aut rationibus extrinsecis. Et si primò modo consideretur, essentialis est differentia, vnius qualitatis ab alia: ita, vt quæ sic est difficilè mobilis à subiecto, sit distincta specie ab alia, quæ eodem modo considerata, facilè mobilis est. Si verò considerentur secundo modo, solùm sunt differentiæ accidentales. Exemplum primæ considerationis, habemus in scientia, & opinione: nam illa habet pro causa demonstrationem, à qua producitur, & in ordine ad quam specificatur, demonstratio verò, causa efficax est, cùm sit argumentum euidens, & necessarium: & ideo scientia per eam acquisita, etiam per primum actum, difficilè mobilis est à

But in order that we may explain and prove it, two things are to be noted. The first is: that a quality’s being easily or not easily removable from the subject comes about in two ways: namely, from the nature of its cause, through which it is produced in the subject and in relation to which it obtains its species; or from other causes or extrinsic reasons. And if it is considered in the first way, it is an essential difference of one quality from another, so that one which is in this way not easily removable from the subject is distinct in species from another which, considered in the same way, is easily removable. But if they are considered in the second way, they are only accidental differences. An example of the first consideration we have in science and opinion: for the former has as its cause demonstration, by which it is produced and in relation to which it is specified; and demonstration is an efficacious cause, since it is an evident and necessary argument; and therefore science acquired through it, even through the first act, is not easily removable from

p. 447

subiecto. Sed opinio habet pro causa argumentum probabile, quod non est efficax, sed facilè destrui potest per demonstrationem oppositam, aut per oppositum argumentum probabilius: ideo opinio, facilè mobilis est, ex natura suæ causæ.

the subject. But opinion has as its cause a probable argument, which is not efficacious, but can easily be destroyed by an opposite demonstration, or by an opposite and more probable argument: therefore opinion is easily removable, from the nature of its cause.

15 Vnde sequitur: quòd licèt versentur circa idem obiectum, tamen specie distinguãtur sub hoc genere qualitatis, per differentias essentiales, facilè & difficilè mobilis, ex natura suarum causarum. Exemplum verò considerationis secundæ, est in calore febrili: qui propter debilitatem subiecti, aut particularem complexionem eius, aliásve accidentales causas extrinsecas, ita solet radicari in subiecto, vt non solùm sit difficilè mobilis ab eo, sed naturaliter sit impossibile ab eo separari: & tamen eiusdem speciei est in principio, & fine, & solùm distinguitur à seipso accidentaliter.

15 Whence it follows that, although they are concerned with the same object, they are nevertheless distinguished in species under this genus of quality, by the essential differences of easily and not easily removable, from the nature of their causes. An example of the second consideration is in feverish heat: which, on account of the weakness of the subject, or its particular complexion, or other accidental extrinsic causes, is wont to be so rooted in the subject that not only is it not easily removable from it, but it is naturally impossible for it to be separated from it; and yet it is of the same species at the beginning and at the end, and is distinguished from itself only accidentally.

Secundò notandum est, Quòd licèt facilè, & difficilè moueri ex causis accidentalibus, nempe ex frequentatione actuũ, vel ex diuturnitate tẽporis, sint differẽtiæ accidentales habitus, & dispositionis, sunt tamen quasi accidentia congruentia naturæ harum qualitatum: ita vt cùm habitus sit difficilè mobilis à subiecto, essentialiter, propter naturam suæ causæ, etiam accidens sit consonũ naturæ eius, esse difficilè mobilem per radicationẽ in subiecto.

The second thing to be noted is: that although to be easily and not easily removed from accidental causes, namely from the frequent repetition of acts or from length of time, are accidental differences of habit and disposition, they are nevertheless as it were accidents congruent with the nature of these qualities: so that, since habit is essentially not easily removable on account of the nature of its cause, it is also an accident conformable to its nature to be not easily removable through rooting in the subject.

16 Et cùm dispositio sit facilè mobilis, propter naturam suæ causæ, accidens etiam consonum sit naturæ eius, non esse radicatam in subiecto, sed facilè etiam posse ab eo separari, ex parte causarum accidentalium. Et istæ differentiæ accidentales, tribuunt eis statum habitus, & dispositionis: ita vt tunc habeat habitus statum suæ naturæ congruentem, quando sit radicatus in subiecto: dispositio verò, quando non sit radicata. Vnde fieri potest: vt qualitas aliqua, habeat essentiam habitus, statum verò dispositionis: & è contra, essentiam dispositionis, & statum habitus, & tunc distinguuntur essentialiter, quamuis vni conueniant accidens alterius: & ideo verum sit, habitum esse accidentaliter dispositionem: & dispositionem, accidentaliter habitum. Vtrumque habet scientia, aut virtus, per primum actum acquisita: quia essentialiter est habitus, & accidentaliter dispositio: essentiam quoque habitus habet, & statum dispositionis: opinio verò, radicata in subiecto, per frequentationem actuum, ex opposito, essentialiter est dispositio, & accidentaliter habitus habet etiam essentiam dispositionis, & statum habitus.

16 And since disposition is easily removable on account of the nature of its cause, it is also an accident consonant with its nature not to be rooted in the subject, but to be able to be separated from it easily also on the part of accidental causes. And these accidental differences give them the state of habit and of disposition: so that habit then has the state congruent with its nature when it is rooted in the subject, and disposition when it is not rooted. Whence it can come about that some quality has the essence of habit but the state of disposition; and conversely, the essence of disposition and the state of habit; and then they are distinguished essentially, although the accident of the other belongs to one; and therefore it is true that habit is accidentally disposition, and disposition accidentally habit. Science or virtue acquired through the first act has both: because it is essentially habit and accidentally disposition: it has, that is, the essence of habit and the state of disposition. But opinion, rooted in the subject through the frequent repetition of acts, conversely, is essentially disposition and accidentally habit: it has the essence of disposition and the state of habit.

17 Ex hac doctrina, intelligitur differẽtia, inter primam & secundam opinionem: nam prima, facilè, & difficilè mobilem esse solùm ex parte subiecti, aut causarum accidentalium, prouenire

17 From this doctrine the difference between the first and the second opinion is understood: for the first holds that to be easily and not easily removable comes only from the side of the subject, or of accidental causes,

p. 448

posse credit: & ideo solùm esse differentias accidentales. Sed D. Tho. alium modum magis intrinsecum earundem differentiarum inuenit, & ideo docuit essentiales esse: quem modum ex mente Arist. esse, probant hæc verba huius ca. Differre autem habitum à dispositione, quòd permanentior, ac diuturnior est: tales verò sunt scientiæ, & virtutes: scientia enim videtur esse permanentium & diuturnorum, vt si quis vel mediocriter sumat scientiam, nisi grandis permutatio facta sit, vel ab ægritudine, vel ab aliquo eiusmodi. Quibus scientiam, antequam radicetur in subiecto, per frequentationem actuum, sed solùm sit mediocriter acquisita dicit esse difficilè mobilem à subiecto: & hoc habere ex natura sua, hoc est ex efficacitate suæ causæ naturalis, quæ est demonstratio: & ideo differre à dispositione. Quasi dicat differre essentialiter, per facilè & difficilè mobilem esse, desumptum ex parte causæ. Vnde sequitur, opinionem D. Thom. quam sequimur, esse ex mente Aristotelis.

it believes can come about, and therefore that they are only accidental differences. But St. Thomas found another, more intrinsic mode of these same differences, and therefore taught that they are essential: and that this mode is in the mind of Aristotle is proved by these words of this chapter: But habit differs from disposition in that it is more permanent and more lasting: such are the sciences and the virtues; for science seems to be among the permanent and lasting things, if one has acquired science even moderately, unless a great change has been made, either by sickness or by something of that kind. By which words he says that science, before it is rooted in the subject through the frequent repetition of acts, but is only moderately acquired, is not easily removable from the subject; and that it has this from its own nature, that is, from the efficacy of its natural cause, which is demonstration; and that therefore it differs from disposition. As if to say that it differs essentially, through being easily or not easily removable, taken from the side of the cause. Whence it follows that the opinion of St. Thomas, which we follow, is in the mind of Aristotle.

18 Tamen probatur hac ratione, quæ colligitur ex eadem doctrina. Ea distinguuntur specie, quæ differunt per differentiam essentialem: sed habitus, & dispositio, distinguuntur per differentias essentiales facilè, & difficilè moueri: ergo distinguuntur specie sub genere qualitatis. Probatur minor: Quia esse difficilè mobilem, conuenit habitibus ex natura suæ causę, à qua sumunt speciem: nempe ex ordine ad demonstrationem, si sit habitus scientiæ: aut ex ordine ad bonum honestum, si sit habitus virtutis: quia bonum honestum, efficax causa virtutis est ex se, cùm sit consonum rationi: ergo est differentia essentialis eius, per quam distinguitur specie à dispositione facilè mobili, ex eadem causa.

18 It is proved, however, by this argument, which is gathered from the same doctrine. Those things are distinguished in species which differ by an essential difference; but habit and disposition are distinguished by the essential differences of being easily and not easily moved: therefore they are distinguished in species under the genus of quality. The minor is proved: Because to be not easily removable belongs to habits from the nature of their cause, from which they take their species: namely, from their relation to demonstration, if it is a habit of science; or from their relation to the honorable good, if it is a habit of virtue, because the honorable good is of itself an efficacious cause of virtue, since it is consonant with reason: therefore it is its essential difference, through which it is distinguished in species from disposition, which is easily removable from the same cause.

Pro explicatione verborum Aristo. notandum est, Dispositionem duobus modis sumi posse: In genere, aut in specie. In genere sumpta, dicit qualitatem disponentem subiectum, vt bene se habeat, in ordine ad propriam naturam, vel operationem: quæ, si sit difficilè mobilis, ex natura suæ causæ, à qua sumit speciem, erit habitus: si verò solùm ex parte subiecti, aliorum accidentium, erit dispositio. Itaque dispositio primo modo sumpta, genus est ad habitum, & seipsam, sumptam secundo modo.

For the explanation of Aristotle’s words, it is to be noted that disposition can be taken in two ways: in genus, or in species. Taken in genus, it means a quality disposing the subject so that it is well disposed in relation to its proper nature or operation: which, if it is not easily removable from the nature of its cause, from which it takes its species, will be a habit; but if only from the side of the subject or of other accidents, it will be a disposition. And so disposition taken in the first way is a genus with respect to habit and to itself taken in the second way.

19 Et ex hoc patet, quem sensum habeat primum dictum Arist. Nempe habitum, & dispositionem, esse vnam speciem qualitatis: id est, conuenire in vna ratione superiori dispositionis, quæ vna species subalterna est, vtrique communis. Dictum verò secundùm: quòd omnis habitus sit dispositio: non tamen omnis dispositio, sit habitus, verum est etiam,

19 And from this it is plain what sense the first dictum of Aristotle has: namely, that habit and disposition are one species of quality: that is, that they agree in one superior ratio of disposition, which is one subalternate species, common to both. And the second dictum, that every habit is a disposition, but not every disposition is a habit, is true also, disposition

p. 449

sumpta dispositione in genere. Tertium verò, quòd dispositio per nimiam radicationem fiat habitus, non de habitu essentialiter considerato intelligit, sed accidentaliter, aut secundùm statum, vt expositum est.

taking disposition in genus. And the third, that disposition through excessive rooting becomes habit, he understands not of habit considered essentially, but accidentally, or according to its state, as has been explained.

Ad primum arg. Distinguenda est minor: Nam si facilè & difficilè mobile sumuntur ex parte subiecti, temporis, aut ex frequentatione actuum, accidentales sunt differentiæ: si verò ex natura causæ intrinsecæ, per quam producuntur, & specificantur, essentiales sunt. Arg. verò, solùm procedit ex eis primo modo consideratis: quo pacto concedimus: solùm esse differentias accidentales: & per eas ita acceptas, solùm differre accidentaliter habitum, & dispositionem, sed differunt essentialiter per easdem, consideratas secundo modo.

To the first argument: the minor must be distinguished. For if easily and not easily removable are taken from the side of the subject, of time, or of the frequent repetition of acts, they are accidental differences; but if from the nature of the intrinsic cause through which they are produced and specified, they are essential. But the argument proceeds only from them considered in the first way: in which manner we grant that they are only accidental differences, and that through them so taken habit and disposition differ only accidentally; but they differ essentially through the same differences considered in the second way.

20 Ad secundum: Concedenda est maior, quòd eiusdem speciei sit scientia acquisita, per primum actum, & iam radicata in subiecto per frequentationem demonstrationum: minor tamen distinguenda: nam si intelligatur, quòd in principio habeat rationem dispositionis essentialem, falsa est, & neganda: si verò de dispositione quantùm ad statum, & rationem accidentalem, vera, & concedenda. Vnde nec fit habitus essentialiter, per frequentationem actuum: quia per primum actum acquisita, habebit essentialem rationem habitus, tamen solùm acquirit statum habitus in quadam ratione accidentali consistentem: quare nunquam mutat speciem, sed solùm statum, & rationem accidentalem.

20 To the second: the major must be granted, that science acquired through the first act and science already rooted in the subject through the frequent repetition of demonstrations are of the same species; but the minor must be distinguished: for if it is understood that in the beginning it has the essential ratio of disposition, it is false and must be denied; but if of disposition as to its state and accidental ratio, it is true and must be granted. Whence it does not become a habit essentially through the frequent repetition of acts: because, acquired through the first act, it will have the essential ratio of habit; yet it acquires only the state of habit, consisting in a certain accidental ratio: wherefore it never changes its species, but only its state and accidental ratio.

QUESTION III

QVÆSTIO III.

[…]

Vtrùm naturalis potentia, & impotentia sit species qualitatis distincta.

Whether natural potency and impotency are a distinct species of quality.

DVo sunt explicanda circa hanc speciem qualitatis. Primum: quo modo differant naturalis potentia, & impotentia, ab habitu, & dispositione. Secundum, quo modo differant inter sese, nempe, essentialitérne, tanquam duæ species eiusdem generis, vel solùm accidentaliter: & ideo in duas partes diuidimus quæstionem hanc claritatis gratia.

wo things are to be explained concerning this species of quality. T First: in what way natural potency and impotency differ from habit and disposition. Second: in what way they differ from each other, namely, whether essentially, as two species of the same genus, or only accidentally; and therefore, for the sake of clarity, we divide this question into two parts.

Prima pars quæstionis.

F I R S T PA R T O F T H E Q U E S T I O N . 21

21 CIrca primum notandum est, quòd naturalis potentia, & impotentia, in vno conueniunt cum habitu, & dispositione, & in duobus differunt. Conueniunt enim in eo, quòd aliquo modo ordinantur ad operationem: quia substantia creata sicut

Concerning the first, it is to be noted that natural potency and impotency agree with habit and disposition in one thing, and differ in two. For they agree in this, that they are in some way ordered to operation: because created substance, just as Ff

p. 450

est limitata quantum ad esse, sic etiam quantum ad modum operãdi: non enim potest per seipsam operari, sed indiget quibusdam accidentibus superadditis: quibus mediis exerceat operationes sibi conuenientes: & per hæc accidentia, formaliter fit potens, ad eliciendas tales operationes: cùm ex se solùm sit quasi radicaliter, aut virtualiter potens: & ideo hæc accidentia superaddita, vocantur potentiæ eius ad operandum: quæ partim sunt naturales, partim acquisitæ: inter quas numerantur, habitus, & dispositiones. Ex quibus licèt quædam disponant eam, vt bene se habeat in suo esse, aut in sua natura, vt sanitas: aliæ verò, vt bene se habeat in ordine ad operationes, vt scientiæ, & virtutes: omnes tamen ordinantur ad operationes, vt docet D. Th. 1. 2. q 49. art. 2. ad 3. sed non omnes eodem modo: nam istæ immediatè, illæ verò priores remotè: quia proximè disponunt substantiam, vt bene se habeat, secundùm propriam naturam. Et cùm natura sit principium operationum, consequenter, & quasi remotè ordinantur ad operationes: vt docet Arist. 10. lib. de historia animalium, cap. 1. dicens: Sanum vocari hominem, aut membrum aliquod, sui corporis, quando potest facere operationem sani. Itaque tam habitus, & dispositio, quàm naturalis potentia, & impotentia, ordinantur aliquo modo ad operationes.

it is limited as to being, so also as to the mode of operating: for it cannot operate through itself, but needs certain superadded accidents, by means of which it exercises the operations befitting it; and through these accidents it becomes formally capable of eliciting such operations, since of itself it is capable only as it were radically or virtually. And therefore these superadded accidents are called its potencies for operating: which are partly natural, partly acquired; among which habits and dispositions are numbered. Of which, although some dispose it so that it is well disposed in its being or in its nature, as health, and others so that it is well disposed in relation to operations, as the sciences and the virtues, all nevertheless are ordered to operations, as St. Thomas teaches, 1- 2, q. 49, a. 2, ad 3; but not all in the same way: for the latter immediately, but the former remotely; because they proximately dispose substance so that it is well disposed according to its proper nature. And since nature is the principle of operations, consequently, and as it were remotely, they are ordered to operations: as Aristotle teaches in History of Animals 10, ch. 1, saying: A man, or some member of his body, is called healthy when it can perform the operation of a healthy one. And so both habit and disposition, and natural potency and impotency, are ordered in some way to operations.

22 Sed differunt in duobus: quia naturalis potentia, & impotentia, tribuuntur ipsi substantiæ à natura, & ex vi suæ generationis: & ferè semper, sunt quasi propriè passiones eius: vt intellectus, & voluntas, respectu animæ, aut potentia motiua, respectu hominis: & propterea, semper ordinantur ad simpliciter operandum, tanquam proxima principia operationum: quia sine illis non potest operari substantia. Habitus verò, & dispositio, ferè semper sunt acquisitæ per nostros actus, vt de scientiis, & virtutibus est manifestum. Præterea, vel non ordinantur proximè ad operandum: vel si proximè, non ad operãdum simpliciter, sed ad facilè operandum. Exempli gratia: Sanitas, licèt sit à natura tributa, non ordinatur tamen proximè ad operandum: virtutes autem, & scientiæ, licèt ordinentur proximè ad operandum: non tamen ad operandum simpliciter: quia per naturalem potentiam, potest substantia operari, sed ad facilè operandum: vnde per eas consequitur substantia facilitatem in suis operationibus. Et istæ duæ differentiæ, manifestè ostendunt, naturalem potentiam, & impotentiam distingui essentialiter, ab habitu, & dispositione, & ideo meritò Aristotelem eas posuisse, pro distinctis generibus, aut speciebus subalternis qualitatis.

22 But they differ in two things: because natural potency and impotency are bestowed on substance itself by nature and by virtue of its generation; and almost always they are as it were proper attributes of it: as intellect and will with respect to the soul, or the motive power with respect to man; and on that account they are always ordered to operating simply, as proximate principles of operations, because without them substance cannot operate. But habit and disposition are almost always acquired through our acts, as is manifest of the sciences and the virtues. Moreover, either they are not ordered proximately to operating, or, if proximately, not to operating simply, but to operating easily. For example: health, although it is bestowed by nature, is nevertheless not ordered proximately to operating; and the virtues and the sciences, although they are ordered proximately to operating, are nevertheless not ordered to operating simply, because substance can operate through natural potency, but to operating easily: whence through them substance obtains facility in its operations. And these two differences manifestly show that natural potency and impotency are distinguished essentially from habit and disposition; and therefore Aristotle rightly posited them as distinct genera, or subalternate species, of quality.

p. 451

Secunda pars quæstionis.

S E C O N D PA R T O F T H E Q U E S T I O N .

SEd circa distinctionem naturalis potentiæ, & impotentiæ, versatur secunda pars eiusdem quæstionis, quæritque: An sint species distinctæ: vel eadem, & ideo non essentialiter, sed solùm accidentaliter distinguantur.

But the second part of the same question turns on the distinction of natural potency and impotency, and asks: Whether they are distinct species, or the same, and therefore are distinguished not essentially but only accidentally.

23 Prima opinio est, Soti, quæstione vnica huius capitis, in solutione ad confirmationem tertij argumenti, vbi ait, Esse duas species subalternas, sicut habitum, & dispositionem. Probatur hoc argum. Naturalis potentia, & impotentia, dicunt oppositas rationes, nempe posse, & non posse: ergo non sunt eiusdem speciei; sed diuersæ: probatur consequentia: quia distinctio per rationes formales est essentialis, & specifica.

23 The first opinion is that of Soto, in the single question on this chapter, in the solution to the confirmation of the third argument, where he says: that they are two subalternate species, like habit and disposition. This argument proves it: Natural potency and impotency imply opposite rationes, namely to be able and not to be able; therefore they are not of the same species, but of different ones. The consequence is proved: because distinction through formal rationes is essential and specific.

Secundam opinionem tenet Fonseca 5. Met. c. 14. q. 2. sect. 3. Quòd non distinguantur essentialiter, sed solùm accidentaliter, & ideo non sint diuersæ species, sed vna: Et hæc est magis ad mentem Arist. & tanquam probabilior tenenda.

The second opinion is held by Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 14, q. 2, sect. 5: that they are not distinguished essentially but only accidentally, and therefore are not different species, but one. And this is more in the mind of Aristotle, and to be held as more probable.

Sed vt fiat vtrumque manifestum, tria sunt præsupponenda, tanquam certa, & ab omnibus recepta. Primum, Impotentiam non accipi ab Arist. pro pura negatione, aut priuatione potentiæ. Probatur euidenter: quia dicit esse qualitatem: qualitas verò positiua entitas est: negatio autem, & priuatio, non sunt entitates positiuæ, vt per se patet: ergo non sunt qualitates, nec intelliguntur ab Aristotole, per impotentiam naturalem, sed per impotentiam intelligit qualitatem positiuam, tributam substantiæ à naturá, ad aliquid agendum, vel ad resistendum contrariis: sed cum difficultate vtrumque. Itaque substantia per hanc qualitatem naturalem potest aliquid facere, aut potest resistere contrariis, ægrè tamen, & difficulter: vnde principium est alicuius operationis, aut resistentiæ, debile tamen, & quasi infirmum: & ideo non tam potentia vocatur, quàm impotentia, vt defectus, & imperfectio eius manifestetur.

But that each may become manifest, three things are to be presupposed as certain and received by all. First, that impotency is not taken by Aristotle for a pure negation or privation of potency. This is proved evidently: because he says it is a quality; but quality is a positive entity, while negation and privation are not positive entities, as is self-evident: therefore they are not qualities, nor are they understood by Aristotle by natural impotency; but by impotency he understands a positive quality, bestowed on substance by nature, for doing something or for resisting contraries, but each with difficulty. And so substance through this natural quality can do something, or can resist contraries, yet hardly and with difficulty: whence it is a principle of some operation or resistance, but a weak and as it were infirm one; and therefore it is called not so much a potency as an impotency, so that its defect and imperfection may be made manifest.

24 Secundò: Certum est, Impotentiam naturalem, non solùm sumi ab Aristot. in ordine ad resistendum cum difficultate: sed etiam ad agendum cum difficultate: vtrumque enim expressis verbis explicuit in textu. Tertiò, Certum est, Naturalem potentiam, & impotentiam, dum ordinantur ad operationes specie diuersas, vel vna ad agendum, & alia ad resistendum, specie distingui. Vt hebetudo ingenij, quæ ordinatur ad intelligendum cum difficultate, specie distinguitur, à potentia visiua, ordinata ad videndum. Probatur efficaciter: quia potentiæ distinguuntur specie per actus, ad quos ordinantur: sed videre, & intelligere sunt actus specie

24 Second: it is certain that natural impotency is taken by Aristotle not only in relation to resisting with difficulty, but also to acting with difficulty: for he explained both in express words in the text. Third, it is certain that natural potency and impotency, when they are ordered to different operations, or one to acting and the other to resisting, are distinguished in species. As dullness of wit, which is ordered to understanding with difficulty, is distinguished in species from the visual power, ordered to seeing. This is proved efficaciously: because potencies are distinguished in species through the acts to which they are ordered; but seeing and understanding are acts Ff ij

p. 452

distincti: ergo potentiæ ad eos ordinatæ, distinguuntur specie. Nec minùs euidenter probatur, de potentia ad agendum, & impotentia ad resistendum: quia agere, & resistere contrariis, diuersa sunt: vt potentia nutritiua, distincta est, à mollitudine ceræ, quæ est impotentia, ad ægrè resistendum diuisioni.

distinct in species: therefore the potencies ordered to them are distinguished in species. Nor is it less evidently proved of a potency for acting and an impotency for resisting: because to act and to resist contraries are different things: as the nutritive power is distinct from the softness of wax, which is an impotency for resisting division with difficulty.

25 Difficultas igitur quæstionis, in hoc posita est: An naturalis potentia ad aliquid agendum, & naturalis impotentia, ad illud idem ægre, aut difficulter agendum, distinguentur specie: & eodem modo, naturalis potentia ad resistendum fortiter diuisioni, & naturalis impotentia ad ægre resistendum, an distinguantur specie: vt durities ferri per quam fortiter resistit diuisioni, distinguatúrne à mollitudine ceræ, per quam modo quodam debili resistit eidem diuisioni hæc enim quasi durities quædam imperfecta videtur, & prima opinio distingui specie docet: Nostra verò, talem distinctionem negat.

25 The difficulty of the question, then, lies in this: Whether a natural potency for doing something, and a natural impotency for doing the same thing hardly or with difficulty, are distinguished in species; and in the same way, whether a natural potency for resisting division strongly and a natural impotency for resisting it hardly are distinguished in species: as, whether the hardness of iron, by which it strongly resists division, is distinguished from the softness of wax, by which it resists the same division in a certain weak manner; for this seems to be as it were a certain imperfect hardness. And the first opinion teaches that they are distinguished in species; ours denies such a distinction.

Probatur autem testimonio Arist. capite præsenti, vbi potentiam naturalem vocat qualitatem, per quam substantia simpliciter potest aliquid agere, vel contrario resistere: impotentiam verò, qualitatem quandam debilem, & quasi infirmam, ad eadem præstanda: sed debili quodam modo, & cum difficultate, quod est imperfectè illa præstare: sed perfectè, & imperfectè idem agere, aut eidem contrario resistere, non distinguuntur essentialiter: ergo nec naturalis potentia, & impotentia, ad idem agendum, vel eidem resistendum, distinguuntur essentialiter, ex mente Arist. Probatur consequentia, quia perfectè aut imperfectè efficere eandem operationem, solùm potest esse differentia accidentalis.

And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he calls natural potency a quality through which substance can simply do something or resist a contrary; and impotency a certain weak and as it were infirm quality for accomplishing the same things, but in a certain weak manner and with difficulty, which is to accomplish them imperfectly. But to do the same thing, or to resist the same contrary, perfectly and imperfectly, are not distinguished essentially: therefore neither are natural potency and impotency, for doing the same thing or resisting the same thing, distinguished essentially, in the mind of Aristotle. The consequence is proved: because to effect the same operation perfectly or imperfectly can be only an accidental difference.

26 Probatur deinde ratione: Quia potentiæ distinguuntur specie, per actus, & obiecta: sed potentia, & impotentia, sunt facultates quædam naturales, aut potentiæ: ergo si ordinentur ad eundem actum, erunt eiusdem speciei. Probatur consequentia: quia solùm differunt, tanquam principium eiusdem actus, aut eiusdem resistentiæ, perfectum & imperfectum, quod patet solùm esse differentiam accidentalem.

26 It is proved next by reason: Because potencies are distinguished in species through their acts and objects; but potency and impotency are certain natural faculties or potencies: therefore, if they are ordered to the same act, they will be of the same species. The consequence is proved: because they differ only as perfect and imperfect principle of the same act or of the same resistance, which plainly is only an accidental difference.

Ad argu. primæ opinionis negandum est antecedens: Quòd naturalis potentia, & impotentia, dicant rationes formales verè oppositas: nam licèt nomina ipsa potentiæ, & impotentiæ, videantur opposita, ratione negationis, quam videtur significare impotentia, tamen verè, nec rationes significatæ opponuntur: nec nomina: quia impotentia non dicit puram negationem, sed qualitatem positiuam, debilem tamen atque imperfectam: & imperfectio hæc, quasi negatio est perfectionis, quam dicit potentia: & propter ea negationem videtur significare nomen

To the argument of the first opinion, the antecedent must be denied, that natural potency and impotency imply truly opposite formal rationes: for although the names themselves, of potency and impotency, seem opposed by reason of the negation which impotency seems to signify, yet in truth neither are the rationes signified opposed, nor the names: because impotency does not imply a pure negation, but a positive quality, yet a weak and imperfect one; and this imperfection is as it were a negation of the perfection which potency implies; and on account of this negation the name seems to signify

p. 453

impotentia: sed quia perfecta, & imperfecta facultas, aut potentia: respectu eiusdem actus, non possunt distingui Specie, nec esse verè oppositæ: ideo nec rationes formales earum oppositæ sunt, nec nomina significant rationes verè oppositas: sed se habent, sicut hæc duo nomina, perfectum, & imperfectum: quæ etiam videntur significare oppositas rationes, & specie diuersas, cùm tamen semper sint eiusdem speciei, si solùm secundùm rationem perfectæ, & imperfectæ distinguantur. Et eodem modo intelligendum est, de mollitudine, & duritie, vt ordinatis, ad fortiter, & debiliter resistendum: quæ licèt videantur specie differre, non tamen differunt: quia mollitudo hoc modo considerata, quasi durities quædam imperfecta est.

impotency. But because a perfect and an imperfect faculty or potency, with respect to the same act, cannot be distinguished in species nor be truly opposed, therefore neither are their formal rationes opposed, nor do the names signify truly opposed rationes; but they stand as these two names, perfect and imperfect: which also seem to signify opposed rationes, different in species, although they are always of the same species, if they are distinguished only according to the ratio of perfect and imperfect. And the same is to be understood of softness and hardness, as ordered to resisting strongly and weakly: which, although they seem to differ in species, nevertheless do not differ; because softness, considered in this way, is as it were a certain imperfect hardness.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

De his quæ pertinent ad passionem, & passibilem qualitatem.

On the things that pertain to passion and passible quality.

27 QVatuor sunt disputanda, circa passionem, & passibilem qualitatem. Primum, An sint veræ species qualitatis. Secundum, An sint species distinctæ: vel vna tantùm, & ita solùm distinguantur accidentaliter. Tertium, An passiones animæ, vt ira, gaudium, & similes, pertineant ad hanc speciem. Quartum, An etiam in eadem ponantur obiecta omnium sensuum externorum. Ideo, quatuor dubiis propositis, & solutis, maioris distinctionis, & claritatis gratia, soluta erit quæstio.

our things are to be disputed concerning passion and passible 27 F quality. First, whether they are true species of quality. Second, whether they are distinct species, or only one, and so are distinguished only accidentally. Third, whether the passions of the soul, such as anger, joy, and the like, pertain to this species. Fourth, whether the objects of all the external senses are also placed in it. Therefore, four doubts having been proposed and solved, for the sake of greater distinction and clarity, the question will be solved.

Primum dubium.

F I R S T D O U B T.

An passio, & passibilis qualitas, sint veræ species qualitatis.

Whether passion and passible quality are true species of quality.

PAssio, vt à significatione nominis incipiamus: quatuor modis accipitur. Primò, pro quacunque, siue sit rei disconuenientis, aut nociuæ affectio, siue conuenientis, ac perficientis: in qua acceptione, non minùs vocatur passio, receptio speciei visibilis, aut visionis in oculo, quàm receptio caloris in aqua: vnde hæc acceptio passionis communissima est, & impropria.

Passion, to begin from the signification of the name, is taken in four ways. First, for any affection whatever, whether of a thing disagreeing or harmful, or of one agreeing and perfecting: in which acceptation the reception of a visible species, or of vision, in the eye is no less called passion than the reception of heat in water; whence this acceptation of passion is the most common and improper.

Ideo accipitur secundò modo, pro sola receptione contrariæ qualitatis, aut disconuenientis, per quam subiectum recipiens, disponitur ad corruptionem: & hæc receptio propriè vocatur passio.

It is taken, therefore, in a second way, for the sole reception of a contrary or disagreeing quality, through which the receiving subject is disposed toward corruption; and this reception is properly called passion.

Sed accipitur tertiò, pro operatione animæ sensitiuæ, facta cum

But it is taken, third, for an operation of the sensitive soul, accompanied Ff iij

p. 454

aliqua passione corporali secundæ acceptionis. in qua acceptione, ira, gaudium, dolor, & tristitia dicuntur passiones: quia ex propria natura, fiunt cum aliqua alteratione corporali: hoc est, cum calefactione, aut frigefactione, aut alia simili: vnde passiones istæ, duo includunt, nempe operationem sensibilem appetitus sensitiui: & alterationem naturalem corporis: nempe calefactionem, aut infrigidationem: illam formaliter, hanc verò quasi materialiter, & antecedenter, vel concomitanter. Ex quo factum est, vt duobus modis definiantur, definitione materiali, & formali, seu finali. Materialiter definiuntur pro alteratione reali. Formaliter verò, pro operatione sensitiua.

by some bodily passion in the second acceptation: in which acceptation anger, joy, pain, and sadness are called passions, because by their own nature they come about with some bodily alteration, that is, with heating or cooling or something similar. Whence these passions include two things, namely the sensible operation of the sensitive appetite, and the natural alteration of the body, namely heating or chilling: the former formally, the latter as it were materially, and antecedently or concomitantly. From which it has come about that they are defined in two ways, by a material definition and by a formal or final one. Materially they are defined by the real alteration; formally, by the sensitive operation.

28 Vt ira definitur, materialiter, quòd sit accensio sanguinis circa cor: formaliter verò, quòd sit appetitus vindictæ. Et hæc acceptio tertia, includit primam, & secũdam.
