ARistoteles non definiuit, Quando, nec docuit, in quonam formalis ratio eius consistat: sed definiuit Gilber. quamuis obscura admodum definitione, dicens: Quando est id quod ex adiacentia temporis relinquitur: per adiacentiam verò videtur significare, esse aliquam denominationem, prouenientem rebus ex tempore, aut ex eo, quod in tempore sint.

Aristotle did not define When, nor did he teach in what its formal ratio consists; but Gilbert defined it, although with a quite obscure definition, saying: When is that which is left over from the adjacency of time. By adjacency he seems to signify that it is a certain denomination coming to things from time, or from the fact that they are in time.

Hæc autem definitio Gilberti, diuersis modis explicatur, & D. Tho. duas posuit explicationes eius, opusc. 48. tract. de sex vltimis prædicamentis, cap. 1. & 2. ex diuersis auctoribus collectas. Prima asserit, tempus duobus modis considerari. Primo, vt

This definition of Gilbert, however, is explained in diverse ways, and St. Thomas posited two explanations of it, collected from diverse authors, in Opusculum 48, treatise on the six last categories, ch. 1 and 2. The first asserts that time is considered in two ways. First, as Gg iij

p. 470

est mensura successiua, & continua. Secundo, vt explicatur ad mensurandam substantiam, & motum, vel operationem eius: ex qua applicatione procedit vt denominentur mensurata à tempore, denominatione quadam extrinseca: & dicantur esse, fuisse, aut futura esse: & actio dicatur hesterna, vel hodierna. Hæc igitur denominatio extrinseca, est illud, quod ex adiacentia temporis relinquitur: hoc est, ex eo, quòd tempus circumstat substantiam, & eius operationes: circumstare verò non est aliud, quàm intrinseca ratione ad eas pertinere, & non per inhæsionem.

it is a successive and continuous measure. Second, as it is applied to measure substance and motion, or its operation; from which application it comes about that the thing measured is denominated by time with a certain extrinsic denomination, and things are said to be, to have been, or to be going to be, and an action is said to be yesterday’s or today’s. This extrinsic denomination, then, is that which is left over from the adjacency of time: that is, from the fact that time stands around substance and its operations; and to stand around is nothing other than to pertain to them by an intrinsic ratio, and not by inherence.

2 Secunda, non est multum diuersa: asserit enim, id quod ex tempore relinquitur esse, quòd substantia, & operationes eius tempori subditæ dicantur: in quantùm, non totum suum esse habẽt simul, sed quasi augmentum, vel extensionem, aut intentionem à tempore accipiunt: & in eo dicuntur crescere, consenescere, ac tandem ab eo consumi: & hoc est prædicamentum, Quando, nempe tempori subdi.

2 The second is not very different: for it asserts that that which is left over from time is that substance and its operations are said to be subject to time, inasmuch as they do not have their whole being at once, but receive as it were augmentation, or extension, or intension from time; and in this they are said to grow, to grow old, and finally to be consumed by it: and this is the category When, namely to be subject to time.

Duæ istæ explicationes, in eo conueniunt: quòd vtraque ponit prædicamentum Quando, in sola denominatione extrinseca à tempore consistere: & ideo falsa est: quod sic probo: Prædicamentalis ordinatio (si vera est) ex veris generibus, & speciebus, licèt imperfectis, ac diminutis fieri debet, sed ex sola denominatione extrinseca, nec genus, nec species sumi possunt: ergo ex ea sola non potest constare prædicamentum. Probatur minor, quia genus & species dicunt aliquam naturam, & entitatem realem: sed denominatio extrinseca, nec est aliqua natura nec aliqua entitas realis in rebus, quibus prædicamentum hoc conuenire potest, vt patet: ergo non potest ex ea sola prædicamentum constitui.

These two explanations agree in this: that each posits that the category When consists in an extrinsic denomination alone from time; and therefore it is false, which I prove thus: the categorial ordering (if it is true) must be made from true genera and species, albeit imperfect and diminished ones; but from an extrinsic denomination alone neither a genus nor a species can be taken: therefore a category cannot consist of it alone. The minor is proved: because genus and species express some nature and real entity; but an extrinsic denomination is neither any nature nor any real entity in the things to which this category can belong, as is plain: therefore a category cannot be constituted from it alone.

3 Secundò: Si aliquid intrinsecum ponunt, non potest esse absolutum: quia nulla entitas absoluta resultat in rebus, aut in tempore ipso, ex adiacentia eius, sed ad summum relatio aliqua: quæ si realis sit, pertinebit ad prędicamentum Ad aliquid: si rationis ad nullum: ergo non potest ex tali adiacentia temporis, constitui reale prædicamentum: aut certè, non distinctum à prædicamento Ad aliquid.

3 Second: if they posit something intrinsic, it cannot be absolute, because no absolute entity results in things, or in time itself, from its adjacency, but at most some relation, which, if it is real, will belong to the category Relative, and if it is of reason, to none: therefore from such an adjacency of time a real category cannot be constituted, or at least not one distinct from the category Relative.

Propterea moderni quidam asserunt, tria esse consideranda in hoc prædicamento, sicut in cæteris: nempe, Formam denominantem subiectum: & hanc dicunt esse Durationem: & subiectum denominatum ab ea: & hoc esse Motum, aut rem aliam durãtem, & effectum formalem. Effectum verò formalem, non esse alium, quàm durare in esse: ideo cõcretum esse, Durans, vt sic. Sed qui hanc opinionem tenẽt, diuisi sunt: nam quidam ab hoc prædicamento

Therefore certain moderns assert that three things are to be considered in this category, as in the others: namely, the Form denominating the subject, and this they say is Duration; and the subject denominated by it, and this is Motion, or another enduring thing; and the formal effect. But the formal effect, they say, is nothing other than to endure in being; therefore the concrete is Enduring, as such. But those who hold this opinion are divided: for some, from this category

p. 471

excludunt, non solùm æternitatem, quæ duratio infinita est, sed iam tempus: quia cùm pertineat ad prædicamentum quantitatis, non potest in isto collocari, vnde abstractum huius prædicamenti, asserunt esse, durationem creatam indiuisibilem: sub qua collocatur æuum Angelorum, & duratio substantiæ corporeæ, tanquam genera subalterna: quarum quælibet durationum, aiunt, diuiditur in diuersas durationes eiusdem generis, sed diuersæ speciei, secundùm diuersitatem specificam Angelorum, & substantiarum corporearum.

exclude not only eternity, which is infinite duration, but also time, because, since it belongs to the category of quantity, it cannot be placed in this one. Whence they assert that the abstract of this category is created indivisible duration, under which are placed the aevum of the Angels and the duration of corporeal substance, as subalternate genera; each of which durations, they say, is divided into diverse durations of the same genus but of diverse species, according to the specific diversity of the Angels and of corporeal substances.

4 Hæc tamen sententia primo est contra Arist. in hoc lib. prædicamentorum, ca. 4. vbi cùm enumerasset prædicamenta, & peruenisset ad hoc, ita ait, Quando autem, vt heri, superiori anno, &c. Quæ verba tempus expressè significant, vt patet.

4 This opinion, however, is first against Aristotle in this book of the Categories, ch. 4, where, having enumerated the categories and come to this one, he says thus: But When, as yesterday, last year, etc. Which words expressly signify time, as is plain.

Deinde est contra rationem: Quia vel æuum, & duratio alia substantiæ corporeæ, pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum: quia durationes creatæ sunt: vel, quia indiuisibiles: non propter secundum, quia ratio diuisibilis, vel indiuisibilis impertinens est ad hoc prædicamentum, cùm id non sit quantitas, sed quando: ergo pertinent: quia sunt durationes creatæ, sed tempus est vera duratio creata: ergo non potest excludi ab hoc prædicamento.

Next, it is against reason: because either the aevum and the other duration of corporeal substance belong to this category because they are created durations, or because they are indivisible; not on account of the second, because the ratio of divisible or indivisible is impertinent to this category, since it is not quantity but When: therefore they belong because they are created durations; but time is a true created duration: therefore it cannot be excluded from this category.

Nostra igitur sententia est: quòd Quando in abstracto significat durationem creatam in communi, vt comprehendit æuum, durationem indiuisibilem substantiæ corporeæ, & durationem successiuam motus, quæ est tempus, in concreto verò rem durantem, duratione creata: ita tenent plures moderni.

Our view therefore is that When in the abstract signifies created duration in common, as it comprehends the aevum, the indivisible duration of corporeal substance, and the successive duration of motion, which is time; but in the concrete, the thing enduring by created duration. So hold many moderns.

5 Et probatur, à sufficienti diuisione: quia Quando, dicit aliquo modo durationem, vt manifestum est, non tamen durationem comprehendit infinitam Dei: quia hæc non pertinet ad prædicamentum: ergo dicit durationem creatam comprehendentem successiuam, & momentaneam, siue sit Angelica, vel alia quæcunque creata. Probatur consequentia: quia successiua non potest excludi, vt probatum est: nec etiam momentanea, vel indiuisibilis: quia talis duratio, cùm sit accidens creatum, & completum, per se debet pertinere ad aliquod prædicamentum: sed ad nullum, præter hoc, pertinere potest: ergo in eo erit per se collocanda: & ita supremum genus erit duratio creata, prout vtramque comprehendit: vel res durans, vt comprehendit ea, quæ durant, vtraque duratione. Probatur minor, quia certum est, durationem indiuisibilem non pertinere ad prædicamentum quantitatis: cuius propria ratio est extensio, & diuisibilitas propria passio: quòd verò non

5 And it is proved from a sufficient division: because When expresses in some way duration, as is manifest; yet it does not comprehend the infinite duration of God, because this does not belong to a category: therefore it expresses created duration, comprehending successive and momentary duration, whether it be Angelic or any other created duration. The consequence is proved: because successive duration cannot be excluded, as has been proved; nor momentary or indivisible duration either, because such a duration, since it is a created and complete accident, must per se belong to some category; but it can belong to none besides this one: therefore it will be placed per se in it. And so the supreme genus will be created duration, as it comprehends both; or the enduring thing, as it comprehends the things which endure by either duration. The minor is proved: because it is certain that indivisible duration does not belong to the category of quantity, whose proper ratio is extension, and divisibility its proper attribute; but that it does not Gg iiij

p. 472

pertineat ad alia prædicamenta, ostendunt rationes eorum diuersissimæ à duratione.

belong to the other categories is shown by their rationes, which are most diverse from duration.

6 Arg. verò alterius opinionis, quo probatur, tempus esse excludendum ab hoc prædicamento, quia pertinet se ad prædicamentum quantitatis: nihil probat aduersus eos, qui asserunt tempus esse quantum per accidens: & ideo non pertinere ad prædicamentum quantitatis: apud quos pertinere poterit ad hoc prædicamentum. Sed habet apud nos difficultatem maximam, qui tenemus, Esse quantum per se, & speciem quantitatis. Hac tamen distinctione soluitur. Duo possunt considerari in tempore: nempe, quòd successiua duratio sit: & quòd continua: quo pacto abstrahit ab extensione & diuisibilitate per se, & per accidens. Probatur, nam euidens est apud omnes, tempus esse durationem successiuam: & tamen non est euidens, quòd sit per se extensa: sed satis probabile, quòd sit extensa per accidens, ergo ratio successiuæ durationis, abstrahit ab extensione per se, & per accidens. Nos igitur, qui tenemus, tempus esse extensum per se possumus ipsum hac ratione collocare in prædicamento Quantitatis: sed in ratione successiuæ durationis in prædicamento Quando: & hac distinctione solutum est argumentum.

6 But the argument of the other opinion, by which it is proved that time is to be excluded from this category because it belongs to the category of quantity, proves nothing against those who assert that time is a quantity per accidens and therefore does not belong to the category of quantity; according to whom it will be able to belong to this category. But it has the greatest difficulty for us, who hold that it is a quantity per se, and a species of quantity. It is solved, however, by this distinction. Two things can be considered in time, namely that it is a successive duration, and that it is continuous; in the former respect it abstracts from extension and divisibility per se and per accidens. This is proved: for it is evident to all that time is a successive duration, and yet it is not evident that it is extended per se, but fairly probable that it is extended per accidens: therefore the ratio of successive duration abstracts from extension per se and per accidens. We, therefore, who hold that time is extended per se, can place it by this ratio in the category of Quantity, but by the ratio of successive duration in the category When; and by this distinction the argument is solved.

Quot, & quæ habeat genera, & species hoc prædicamentum — How many and which genera and species this category has.

7 SVpremum genus huius prædicamenti, quod est Duratio creata, vel Durans creatum, diuiditur, in durationem Permanentem, & Successiuam: tanquam in duas species subalternas: & rursus, Duratio permanens, in Æuum, quod est duratio Angelorum, & in Durationem substantiæ corporeæ, Duratio verò successiua: in durationem primam motus cælestis, quæ per antonomasiam vocatur tempus, & in durationem, motus inferioris: & adhuc quęlibet species subalterna durationis permanentis, habet alias species infimas, secundùm distinctionem specificam, Angelorum, & substantiarum corporearum: & ex his generibus, & speciebus, fit ordinatio prædicamenti Quando.

7 The supreme genus of this category, which is created Duration, or the created Enduring thing, is divided into Permanent and Successive duration, as into two subalternate species; and again, permanent Duration into the Aevum, which is the duration of the Angels, and into the Duration of corporeal substance; but successive Duration into the duration of the first heavenly motion, which by antonomasia is called time, and into the duration of the lower motion. And further, each subalternate species of permanent duration has other lowest species, according to the specific distinction of the Angels and of corporeal substances; and from these genera and species the ordering of the category When is made.

Quot, & quas proprietates habeat hoc prædicamentum — How many and which properties this category has.

8 TRes proprietates tribuit Gilbert. huic prædicamento: sed omnes videntur aliis etiam esse communes. Prima est, Non habere contrarium: Secunda, Non suscipere magis: & minus: de quibus manifestum est aliis conuenire. Tertiam dicit

8 Gilbert attributes three properties to this category, but all of them seem to be common to the others as well. The first is Not to have a contrary; the second, Not to admit of more and less: of which it is manifest that they belong to the others. The third

p. 473

esse, quòd duratio creata solùm conuenit his, quæ incipiunt esse, vel apta nata sunt incipere esse: de qua etiam probatur: quòd conueniat aliis: quia alia etiam sunt accidentia, quæ solùm conueniunt his, quæ incipere apta nata sunt: vt mutatio, & motus, aliaque huiusmodi Nullam igitur habet proprietatem prædicamentum hoc, nobis notam: sed aliquam absque dubio habebit, quam ignoramus: nam cùm debilissimæ sit naturæ, mirum non est, si intimas eius proprietates non cognoscamus.

he says is that created duration belongs only to those things which begin to be, or are apt by nature to begin to be; of which too it is proved that it belongs to others: because there are other accidents too which belong only to those things that are apt by nature to begin, such as change and motion and others of this kind. This category, therefore, has no property known to us; but without doubt it will have some, which we do not know: for since it is of a most feeble nature, it is no wonder if we do not know its inmost properties.

Prædicamentum Vbi — T H E C AT E G O RY W H E R E .

1 CIrca prædicamentum Vbi, quatuor etiam explicanda sunt. Primum, Quid per nomen, Vbi significetur. Secũdum, In quo consistat ratio formalis eius. Tertium, Quot, & quæ genera, & species habeat, ex quibus ordinatio eius prædicamentalis fiat. Quartum, Quot, & quæ sint proprietates eius.

1 Concerning the category Where, four things are likewise to be explained. The first, What is signified by the name Where. The second, In what its formal ratio consists. The third, How many and which genera and species it has, from which its categorial ordering is made. The fourth, How many and which are its properties.

Circa primum, Nomen Vbi, vno tantùm modo accipitur, pro reali præsentia: per quam aliquid dicitur præsens esse loco, aut spatio loci: nam & si corpus sit in vacuo habebit pręsentiam realem: cùm sit certum, & ab omnibus concessum, posse moueri in vacuo: in quo, sicut verum, & realem motum haberet, ita verum terminum motus acquireret: est autem Vbi, terminus proprius motus localis: quare verum haberet Vbi, verámque ac realem præsentiam.

Concerning the first, the name Where is taken in one way only, for real presence, through which something is said to be present to a place, or to the space of a place: for even if a body were in a vacuum it would have real presence, since it is certain, and conceded by all, that it can be moved in a vacuum; in which, just as it would have a true and real motion, so it would acquire a true term of motion; and Where is the proper term of local motion: wherefore it would have a true Where, and a true and real presence.

Quid sit Vbi, aut in quo consistit ratio formalis eius — What Where is, or in what its formal ratio consists.

VBi, sic definitur à Gilberto: Vbi, est circumscriptio corporis, à circumscriptione loci proueniens: quibus verbis duplicem circumscriptionem insinuat. Prima est, Circumscriptio loci à locato. & hæc potest vocari actiua. Secunda verò passiua est, Quia locatum dicitur à loco circumscribi: & hanc dicit esse de ratione, Vbi: nam alia ad locum potiùs pertinet, & ad prędicamentum quantitatis reduci potest, in quo ponitur locus: sed in circumscriptione passiua, præsentiam localem virtualiter includit Gilbertus: quia non potest corpus circumscribi loco, nisi sit ei pręsens. Nihilominus definitio hæc limitata est, & non omnino completa: quia solùm compræhendit, Vbi, pro locali præsentia, cùm tamen corpus habere verum, Vbi sine illa.

Where is defined thus by Gilbert: Where is the circumscription of a body, proceeding from the circumscription of place: by which words he intimates a twofold circumscription. The first is the Circumscription of the located by the place, and this can be called active. The second is passive: that the located is said to be circumscribed by the place; and this he says is of the ratio of Where: for the other rather pertains to place, and can be reduced to the category of quantity, in which place is posited; but in the passive circumscription Gilbert virtually includes local presence, because a body cannot be circumscribed by a place unless it is present to it. Nevertheless this definition is limited and not altogether complete, because it comprehends Where only for local presence, although a body could have a true Where without it.

Sic ergo definiendum est, Vbi, definitione adæquata, & comprehendente, Vbi, quodcunque: Vbi est realis præsentia, quam habet corpus in loco, aut in spatio loci.

Thus, then, Where is to be defined, by an adequate definition comprehending every Where: Where is the real presence which a body has in a place, or in the space of a place.

p. 474

Ex qua definitione intelligimus, quatuor habere conditiones Vbi. Primum est: Esse aliquid reale: quia non potest esse aliquid præsens alteri, nisi per aliquid reale: & cùm Vbi sit terminus realis motus, necesse est aliquid etiam reale esse: alioqui per realem motum, nihil reale acquireretur, à quo tanquam à termino haberet speciem realem.

From this definition we understand that Where has four conditions. The first is: To be something real; because something cannot be present to another except through something real; and since Where is the term of a real motion, it must also be something real: otherwise nothing real would be acquired through a real motion, from which, as from its term, it would have a real species.

Habet secundò, Quòd sit aliquid inhærens subiecto realiter: quia cùm per motum tendat mobile ad acquirendum sibi aliquem terminum: & motus sit realis: non solùm realem terminum debet acquirere, sed in se manentem. Probatur consequentia: quia motus & terminus in eodem subiecto recipi debent, vt manifesta inductione probari potest, in omnibus motibus, Habet tertiò Vbi, quòd sit entitas realis, distincta ex natura rei à subiecto, in quo est.

It has, second, that it is something really inhering in the subject: because, since through motion the mobile tends to acquire some term for itself, and the motion is real, it must acquire not only a real term but one remaining in itself. The consequence is proved: because the motion and the term must be received in the same subject, as can be proved by a manifest induction in all motions. Where has, third, that it is a real entity, distinct from the nature of the thing from the subject in which it is.

5 Probatur hoc, ex noua acquisitione, & separatione à subiecto: nam illud, quod separatur ab alio realiter, necesse est distingui ab eo, absque operatione intellectus: cùm ante illam separetur: sed hoc Vbi, desinit esse in corpore, & acquiritur aliud nouum: ergo vtrumque separatur à corpore, ante operationem intellectus: & ideo ante illam distinguitur, & ex natura rei.

5 This is proved from the new acquisition and from the separation from the subject: for that which is really separated from another must be distinguished from it without the operation of the intellect, since it is separated before that operation; but this Where ceases to be in the body, and another new one is acquired: therefore each is separated from the body before the operation of the intellect; and therefore it is distinguished before it, and from the nature of the thing.

Quartum quod habet, Vbi, est, non esse puram relationem, sed aliquid absolutum includens, & etiam respectum secundùm dici ad locum, quo circumscribitur corpus, vel ad spacium loci. Probatur hac ratione: quia sola relatio non potest per se terminare motum, vt docet expressè Arist. 5 lib. Phys. sed, Vbi, terminat per se motum localem, vt ibidem asserit: ergo non dicit solam relationem, sed modum quendam realem absolutum, quem per respectum ad extrinsecum explicamus. Hic autem modus absolutus, non est aliud, quàm accommodatio rei pręsentis ad locum, vel ad spacium loci: ita vt si corpus sit, sic se accommodet illi, vt totum corpus respondeat toti loco, aut spatio, & singulæ partes singulis etiam partibus loci: si verò sit res indiuisibilis, tota correspondeat toti loco, aut spatio: & tota etiam singulis partibus: quòd verò simul cum hoc modo absoluto, includat respectum realem ad extrinsecum locum, vel spatium, certum esse debet: quia talis accommodatio, intrinsecam dicit correspondentiam: ergo intrinsecum etiam respectum.

The fourth which Where has is not to be a pure relation, but including something absolute, and also a respect, as it is said, to the place by which the body is circumscribed, or to the space of the place. This is proved by the following argument: because a relation alone cannot per se terminate motion, as Aristotle expressly teaches in Phys. 5; but Where terminates local motion per se, as he asserts in the same place: therefore it does not express a relation alone, but a certain real absolute mode, which we explain through a respect to something extrinsic. And this absolute mode is nothing other than the accommodation of the present thing to the place, or to the space of the place; so that if it is a body, it so accommodates itself to it that the whole body corresponds to the whole place or space, and the single parts also to the single parts of the place; but if it is an indivisible thing, the whole corresponds to the whole place or space, and the whole also to the single parts. But that, together with this absolute mode, it includes a real respect to the extrinsic place or space ought to be certain: because such an accommodation expresses an intrinsic correspondence: therefore also an intrinsic respect.

Quot, & quæ habeat genera, & species, Vbi — How many and which genera and species Where has.

4 VBi potest diuidi, in Circumscriptiuum, & Definitiuum. Circumscriptiuum est, quod habet corpus quantum, quod ita

4 Where can be divided into Circumscriptive and Definitive. Circumscriptive is that which a quantified body has, which so

p. 475

est præsens spatio, vt toti spatio correspondeat totum corpus, & partibus correspondeant partes: & id suo modo potest habere res spiritualis, sic se accommodans loco, vt singulis partibus loci correspondeat tota, & tota etiam toti loco. Vbi Definitiuum, potest vocari simplex præsentia, per quam res potest dici præsens alicui, sine commensuratione, vel accommodatione ad illud: & hoc modo erunt fortasse præsentes Angeli in Cœlo empyreo, in quo non sunt tanquam in loco, secundùm sententiam D. Th. magis communem in schola: licèt adhuc sit hoc positũ in opinione, An Angeli moueantur per motum realem, eis inhærentem: & ex consequenti, An verum Vbi acquirant: aut solùm per extrinsecam denominationem à corpore: quod mouent.

is present to the space in such a way that the whole body corresponds to the whole space, and the parts correspond to the parts; and a spiritual thing can have this in its own way, so accommodating itself to the place that the whole of it corresponds to the single parts of the place, and the whole also to the whole place. Definitive Where can be called simple presence, through which a thing can be said to be present to something without commensuration or accommodation to it; and in this way perhaps the Angels will be present in the empyrean Heaven, in which they are not as in a place, according to the opinion of St. Thomas more common in the school; although it is still placed in opinion Whether the Angels are moved by a real motion inhering in them, and consequently Whether they acquire a true Where, or only by an extrinsic denomination from the body which they move.

Secunda diuisione diuiditur Vbi, ab Arist. 7. & 8. lib. Phys. in Vbi, Sursum, & Deorsum, tanquam in diuersas species, per quas, tanquam per proprios terminos distinguuntur specie motus localis, sursum, & deorsum: quamuis moderni plures, hanc distinctionem specificam, Vbi, & motuum localium non admittant: sed nos Aristot. sequentes, probamus admittendam esse, 5. lib. Phys. in nostris Commentariis.

By the second division, Where is divided by Aristotle, Phys. 7 and 8, into the Where Up and Down, as into diverse species, through which, as through their proper terms, the species of local motion, up and down, are distinguished; although many moderns do not admit this specific distinction of Where and of local motions; but we, following Aristotle, prove that it is to be admitted, Phys. 5, in our Commentaries.

Quot, & quas proprietates habeat Vbi — How many and which properties it has.

5 DVas proprietates ei concedit Gilbertus, videlicet, Non habere contrarium: & Non suscipere magis, & minus: quas patet non ei soli conuenire, sed multis aliis. Et prima proprietas, (si vera est de propriissima contrarietate, quæ in solis qualitatibus, se expellentibus ab eodem subiecto, intelligi debet: nam aliam ei concedit Arist. non ita propriam, locis creatis. Alij etiam tribuunt, Vbi, duas alias proprietates: nempe, Esse immobile, cùm constet moueri non posse cum corpore, in quo est, sed moto corpore, statim desinere esse in eo: & ideo aliam eius proprietatem dicunt esse, Quod corrumpi possit: vtraque tamen proprietas, communis est ei cum aliis: nam immobilitatem, loco etiam concedit Arist. 4. lib. Phys. & multæ sunt aliæ res corruptibiles. Ego verò quintam proprietatem ei concederem, quia nulli potest conuenire, sed quarto modo ei conuenit: quia cum eo conuertitur: & hæc est, Acquisibile, aut producibile esse per se, per motum localem.

5 Gilbert concedes two properties to it, namely, Not to have a contrary, and Not to admit of more and less: which plainly belong not to it alone but to many others. And the first property, if it is true, must be understood of the most proper contrariety, which is in qualities alone that expel each other from the same subject: for Aristotle concedes another, not so proper, to created places. Others also attribute two other properties to Where: namely, To be immobile, since it is plain that it cannot be moved with the body in which it is, but that when the body is moved it at once ceases to be in it; and therefore they say that another property of it is That it can be corrupted. Each property, however, is common to it with others: for Aristotle also concedes immobility to place, Phys. 4, and many other things are corruptible. I, however, would concede to it a fifth property, because it can belong to no other, but belongs to it in the fourth mode, because it is convertible with it: and this is, To be acquirable, or producible, per se through local motion.

Prædicamentum Situs — T H E C AT E G O RY P O S I T I O N .

6 QVatuor alia de Situ declaranda sunt. Primum. Quid per Situm constituentem hoc prædicamentum intelligatur,

6 Four other things are to be declared concerning Position. The first, What is understood by the Position that constitutes this category.

p. 476

Secundum in quo consistat ratio formalis eius. Tertium, In quot, & quæ genera, & species diuidatur. Quartum, Quot, & quæ proprietates ei attribuantur.

The second, in what its formal ratio consists. The third, Into how many and which genera and species it is divided. The fourth, How many and which properties are attributed to it.

Circa primum, variis modis accipitur Situs. Primò, pro loco, aut vbi, in quo res sita est: sed hæc nimis est impropria: ideo accipitur secundò pro quadam relatione ordinis, quam res habet in loco: per quam dicitur esse sursum, aut deorsum, priorem aut posteriorem habere locum: sed hoc non ad Situm, sed ad Vbi pertinet: & ideo nimis est impropria respectu situs. Quare se secundùm has duas acceptiones, non potest constituere speciale, aut distinctum prædicamentum ab aliis.

Concerning the first, Position is taken in various ways. First, for the place, or the where, in which a thing is situated; but this is too improper. Therefore it is taken, second, for a certain relation of order which a thing has in place, through which it is said to be up or down, to have a prior or posterior place; but this pertains not to Position but to Where, and therefore it is too improper with respect to position. Wherefore according to these two acceptations it cannot constitute a special category, or one distinct from the others.

Tertia igitur acceptio, & propria, colligitur ex Arist. 5. lib. Meta. c. 19. vbi ait, Dispositio dicitur ordo partes habentis, secundùm locum Quæ verba intelligunt omnes Interpretes, de prædicamento Situs, quod sub nomine dispositionis explicare voluit.

The third and proper acceptation, therefore, is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 19, where he says: Disposition is called the order of that which has parts, according to place. Which words all the Interpreters understand of the category of Position, which he wished to explain under the name of disposition.

In quo consistat formalis ratio huius præd. — In what the formal ratio of this category consists.

2 DEfinitio Situs, secundùm hanc vltimam conceptionem, ex Arist. colligenda est: erit autem talis: Situs est, dispositio partium in loco, secundùm quam aliquis sedere, stare, aut iacere dicitur.

2 The definition of Position, according to this last conception, is to be gathered from Aristotle; and it will be this: Position is the disposition of the parts in place, according to which someone is said to sit, to stand, or to lie.

Sed distinguere situm à prædicamento vbi, difficilè est: quia esse aliquid extensum, & esse tali modo extensum, ad idem prædicamentum pertinet: ergo esse aliquid in loco, & esse tali modo in loco, pertinebit ad idem prædicamentum: sed situs non est aliud, quàm tali modo esse in loco, hoc est cum tali dispositione, partium: ergo non efficiet distinctum prædicamentum, à prædicamento Vbi, quod est esse in loco. Probatur minor, nam stare, aut sedere, non est aliud, quàm tali modo esse in loco: ideo tenuit Fonseca 5. Meta. cap. 7. qu. 2. sect. 4. quòd licèt vulgò dicatur situm, & vbi, diuersa efficere prædicamenta, tamen secundùm vnitatem Philosophicam, non distinguitur situs, à prædicamento vbi.

But it is difficult to distinguish position from the category Where: because to be something extended, and to be extended in such a way, belong to the same category: therefore to be something in place, and to be in place in such a way, will belong to the same category; but position is nothing other than to be in place in such a way, that is, with such a disposition of the parts: therefore it will not make a category distinct from the category Where, which is to be in place. The minor is proved: for to stand or to sit is nothing other than to be in place in such a way. Therefore Fonseca held, Metaph. 5, ch. 7, q. 2, sect. 4, that although position and where are commonly said to make diverse categories, yet according to Philosophical unity position is not distinguished from the category where.

3 Hæc tamen sententia expressè in primis contraria est Arist. & toti Peripatecicæ scholæ, decem prædicamenta recipienti: & inter ea, situm. si enim non distinguatur à prædicamento vbi, non erunt nisi nouem: est etiam contra rationem: quia situs, distinctam saltem rationem formalem habet à prædicamento vbi: vt statim ostendemus.

3 This opinion, however, is first of all expressly contrary to Aristotle and to the whole Peripatetic school, which receives ten categories, and among them position: for if it is not distinguished from the category where, there will be only nine. It is also against reason: because position has at least a formal ratio distinct from the category where, as we shall show at once.

Sed in quo consistat hæc ratio, non est certum apud omnes. Itaque secunda opinio, tenet in sola denominatione extrinseca à loco, consistere. Quæ etiam falsa probatur, Primò: Quia sola denominatio

But in what this ratio consists is not certain among all. And so the second opinion holds that it consists in an extrinsic denomination alone from place. Which is also proved false. First: because an extrinsic

p. 477

extrinseca, non sufficit prædicamentum constituere, vt probauimus. Secundò: Quia qui sedet, vel stat in loco, eodem modo stabit, & sedebit, si locus in quo est, corrumpatur, & in vacuo remaneat: ergo eodem modo habebit situm, sicut est certum habere vbi: sed tunc non denominaretur extrinsecè à loco, cùm non sit in loco: ergo nihil erit prædicamentum situs.

denomination does not suffice to constitute a category, as we have proved. Second: because he who sits or stands in a place will stand and sit in the same way if the place in which he is is corrupted and he remains in a vacuum: therefore he will have position in the same way, just as it is certain that he has a where; but then he would not be denominated extrinsically by the place, since he is not in a place: therefore the category of position will be nothing.

Propterea tertia opinio asserit, non esse solam denominationem extrinsecam, sed relationem corporis, & partium eius ad locum, vel spatium loci. Sed nec potest hæc opinio defendi. Quia si solam relationem dicit: vel est relatio secundùm esse, & ita non distingueretur situs à prædicamento ad aliquid: vel est relatio secundùm dici, & hoc non: quia relatio secundùm dici, est de essentia absoluti, vt probauimus in prædicamento ad aliquid, ergo non potest per solam relationem secundùm dici, constitui prædicamentum situs: sed aliquid absolutum habere debet in quo respectus secundùm dici includatur,

Therefore the third opinion asserts that it is not an extrinsic denomination alone, but the relation of the body and of its parts to the place, or to the space of the place. But neither can this opinion be defended. Because if it expresses a relation alone, either it is a relation according to being, and so position would not be distinguished from the category relative; or it is a relation according to being said, and this not: because a relation according to being said is of the essence of the absolute, as we proved in the category relative: therefore the category of position cannot be constituted by a relation according to being said alone; but it must have something absolute in which the respect according to being said is included.

4 Ideo vltima opinio, quam sequuntur omnes ferè Iterpretes Arist cap. præsenti, & 5. Meta. cap. 19. asserit, Situm dicere quid absolutum: nempe specialem modum se habendi totius corporis, & partium eius in loco, aut spatio loci, in quo modo absoluto, includitur respectus secundùm dici, ad locum, & partes eius: vnde ex absoluto, & respectiuo, constat ratio adæquata huius prædicamenti, sicut & prædicamentum vbi. Quam rationem explicuit Arist. vbi suprà, nomine dispositionis partium in loco: sed situs à prædicamento vbi, non distinguitur realiter, sed solùm ratione ratiocinata, sicut actio à passione. Præsupponit enim vbi, tanquam aliquid prius secundùm rationem, & addit supra illud, specialem illum modum dispositionis partium in loco: nam prius intelligimus corpus esse præsens loco, aut spatio loci, quàm intelligamus talem habere dispositionem partium in eo: sed hæc dispositio partium, non est alia entitas realis. ab entitate, vbi, sed alia ratio formalis: quam certum est, non dicere, vbi, sed solùm præsentiam in loco, aut spatio loci, & nihil aliud: præsentia autẽ in loco, sine tali dispositione, & ideo, sine ratione situs intelligitur: & hoc est, in eadẽ entitate reali, distinguere intellectu, duplicem rationem prædicamentalem: sicut distinguimus in eadem entitate realis motus, prædicamentum actionis, & passionis.

4 Therefore the last opinion, which almost all the Interpreters of Aristotle follow on the present chapter and on Metaph. 5, ch. 19, asserts that position expresses something absolute: namely, a special mode of being disposed of the whole body and of its parts in place, or in the space of place; in which absolute mode is included a respect according to being said to the place and its parts: whence the adequate ratio of this category consists of the absolute and the respective, as does the category where as well. Which ratio Aristotle explained in the place cited above by the name of the disposition of the parts in place. But position is not distinguished from the category where really, but only by reasoned reason, as action from passion. For it presupposes where, as something prior according to reason, and adds over it that special mode of disposition of the parts in place: for we understand a body to be present to a place, or to the space of a place, before we understand it to have such a disposition of the parts in it; but this disposition of the parts is not another real entity from the entity of where, but another formal ratio: since it is certain that where expresses only presence in place, or in the space of place, and nothing else; and presence in place is understood without such a disposition, and therefore without the ratio of position. And this is to distinguish, by the intellect, a twofold categorial ratio in the same real entity: just as in the same entity of real motion we distinguish the category of action and of passion.

5 Ad arg. primæ opinionis, distinguenda est maior: quia esse & esse tali modo, dupliciter contingit. Primò, ita, vt talis modo essendi, comprehendatur sub eodem esse: & tunc verum est, ad idem prædicamentum pertinere. Alio modo, ita, vt extra rationem

5 To the argument of the first opinion, the major is to be distinguished: because to be, and to be in such a way, happens in two ways. First, so that such a mode of being is comprehended under the same being; and then it is true that it belongs to the same category. In another way, so that it is outside the

p. 478

eius sit: & tunc non ad idem, sed ad aliud pertinebit: quod patet in eodem exemplo quantitatis: nam esse extensum, constituit prædicamentum quantitatis: sed corpus tali modo esse extensum, vt sit alteri æqualiter extensum, non comprehenditur sub extensione: & ideo non iam ad prædicamentum quantitatis, sed ad prædicamentum ad aliquid pertinet: & ita se habet situs, in ordine ad vbi: quod simpliciter dicit esse in loco, non comprehendens per se, nec per suas species, speciales modos, aut dispositiones, se habendi in loco: & ideo situs specialem modum se habendi in loco dicit, non comprehensum, in ratione formali vbi: quare aliud prædicamentum constituere potest.

ratio of it; and then it will belong not to the same but to another category. Which is plain in the same example of quantity: for to be extended constitutes the category of quantity; but for a body to be extended in such a way that it is equally extended with another is not comprehended under extension; and therefore it belongs no longer to the category of quantity but to the category relative. And so position stands in order to where, which expresses simply being in place, not comprehending per se, nor through its species, the special modes or dispositions of being disposed in place; and therefore position expresses a special mode of being disposed in place which is not comprehended in the formal ratio of where: wherefore it can constitute another category.

Quot, & quæ sint genera, & species Situs — How many and which are the genera and species of Position.

6 GEnera, & species huius prædicamenti, ita colligunt Albertus Mag. lib. de sex principiis, tractatu de positione, cap. 1. & D. Th. opusc. 48. cap. 2. vt supremum genus, quod est dispositio partium in loco, aut in spatio loci, diuidatur in id, quod est, Rectè esse positum, aut Reflexe: tanquam in duo genera subalterna deposita: sub quibus continentur, Sedere, Stare, Iacere, Cubare, & huiusmodi alia, tanquam species, in quas diuiduntur eadem genere: & ex omnibus fit ordinatio prædicamentalis.

6 The genera and species of this category are gathered thus by Albert the Great, book on the Six Principles, treatise on position, ch. 1, and by St. Thomas, Opusculum 48, ch. 2: that the supreme genus, which is the disposition of the parts in place, or in the space of place, is divided into that which is To be placed upright, or bent, as into two subalternate genera laid down; under which are contained To sit, To stand, To lie, To recline, and other things of this kind, as species into which the same genera are divided; and from all of them the categorial ordering is made.

Quot, & quæ sint proprietates huius præd. — How many and which are the properties of this category.

7 DVas proprietates ei attribuunt Alb Mag. & D. Th. vbi supra: videlicet, Contrario carere, & Suscipere magis & minus: quæ etiam conueniunt pluribus aliis: quibus tertiam addit Gilbertus, nempe, Assistere proximè substantiæ: quæ etiam conuenit prædicamento, vbi, & immediatius, cùm sit prius secundùm rationem, vt probauimus: sed cùm sint idem realiter, vtrique conuenit immediatè, realiter aliquando: sed non est sic intelligendum quòd situs assistat substantiæ vt extrinsecè prorsus se habeat ad illam: nam verè ei inhæret, tanquam modus eius: sed assistere dicitur, quia ab extrinseco dependet.

7 Albert the Great and St. Thomas, in the places cited above, attribute two properties to it: namely, To lack a contrary, and To admit of more and less, which also belong to many others; to which Gilbert adds a third, namely, To stand by substance most closely; which also belongs to the category where, and more immediately, since it is prior according to reason, as we have proved; but since they are the same really, it belongs to both immediately, really at some time. But it is not to be understood thus, that position stands by substance in such a way that it is disposed toward it altogether extrinsically: for it truly inheres in it, as its mode; but it is said to stand by because it depends on something extrinsic.

Prædicamentum Habere — T H E C AT E G O RY H AV I N G .

1 EAdem quæ de cæteris prædicamentis explicata sunt, de habere, vel habitu, qui est vltimum prędicamentum, sunt

1 The same things that have been explained concerning the other categories are, concerning having, or habit, which is the last category,

p. 479

declaranda. Primum, Quid per habere sit intelligendum? Secundum, Quid sit habere, aut in quo consistat ratio formalis eius. Tertium, Quot genera, & species habeat. Quartum, Quot etiam, & quæ sint proprietates eius.

to be declared. The first, What is to be understood by having? The second, What having is, or in what its formal ratio consists. The third, How many genera and species it has. The fourth, How many and which are its properties.

2 Circa primum, multis modis accipitur habere, vt docet Aristot. 5. lib. Meta. cap. 10. text. 25. sed tres sunt præcipuæ acceptiones eius. Prima vniuersalis: ita vt inter habentem, & rem habitam, solùm sit distinctio rationis: vt homo dicitur habere substantiam & cætera prædicata essentialia. Secunda acceptio est minùs vniuersalis: ita vt respectus realis, & ex consequenti realis distinctio sit, inter habentem, & rem habitam. In qua significatione, idem est habere aliquid, quod illud respicere: vt pater dicitur habere filium. Sed vtraque hæc acceptio inpropria est, & secundùm quam habere non constuit speciale prædicamentum: quare Tertiò accipitur, pro eo, quod est habere aliquid, non quomodocunque, sed ita: vt habens, sit speciali ratione accommodatum, vel commensuratum rei habitæ, cum respectu reali ad illam: non tanquam ad terminum: sed tanquam ad aliquid cui habens speciali modo adaptatur. Et secundùm diuersum modum huius adaptionis, vel accommodationis ad illam, diuerso modo dicetur eam habere, & diuersum prædicamentum constituere. Habere locum, vel spatium, est prædicamentum vbi: habere durationem, prædicamentum, quando: habere positionem partium in loco, prædicamentum, situs: habere vestes, aut arma, prædicamentum, Habere: quia specialis est accommodatio corporis ad vestes, & arma: vnde generale nomen habere, specialiter ei attribuitur.

2 Concerning the first, having is taken in many ways, as Aristotle teaches in Metaph. 5, ch. 10, text 25; but there are three principal acceptations of it. The first is universal, such that between the one having and the thing had there is only a distinction of reason: as man is said to have substance and the other essential predicates. The second acceptation is less universal: such that there is a real respect, and consequently a real distinction, between the one having and the thing had. In which signification to have something is the same as to regard it: as a father is said to have a son. But each of these acceptations is improper, and according to it having does not constitute a special category. Wherefore, third, it is taken for that which is to have something, not in any way whatever, but so that the one having is accommodated, by a special ratio, or commensurated to the thing had, with a real respect to it: not as to a term, but as to something to which the one having is adapted in a special mode. And according to the diverse mode of this adaptation or accommodation to it, it will be said to have it in a diverse way, and will constitute a diverse category. To have a place or a space is the category where; to have duration, the category when; to have a position of the parts in place, the category position; to have clothes or arms, the category Having: because there is a special accommodation of the body to clothes and arms; whence the general name having is attributed to it specially.

Et secundùm hanc acceptionem, definitur à Gilberto hac definitione: Habitus est corporum, & eorum, quæ circa corpus versantur, adiacentia. Quasi dicatur, vestes circundare, aut operire corpus, per specialem accommodationem eiusdem corporis ad eas, tanquam ad aliquid extrinsecum ei non inhærens: itaque ratio formalis huius prædicamenti, consistit in modo speciali, quo corpus sese accommodat vestibus, aut armis: qui modus diuersus est ab aliis: quibus se accommodat loco, aut durationi: & ideo speciale constituit prædicamentum: quod in Concreto, dicitur Habere, aut Habitus: Abstractum verò, nomen non habet, sed abstractum eius vocatur, ratio habitus, vel ratio habendi.

And according to this acceptation it is defined by Gilbert with this definition: Habit is the adjacency of bodies and of the things which are about the body. As if it were said that clothes surround or cover the body through a special accommodation of the same body to them, as to something extrinsic not inhering in it. And so the formal ratio of this category consists in the special mode by which the body accommodates itself to clothes or arms; which mode is diverse from the others by which it accommodates itself to place or to duration; and therefore it constitutes a special category, which in the Concrete is called Having, or Habit; but the Abstract has no name, but its abstract is called the ratio of habit, or the ratio of having.

Quot, & quæ sunt genera, & species habere — How many and which are the genera and species of Having.

3 HAbere diuiditur, tanquã supremũ genus, in diuersos modos habendi, distinctos per diuersas res habitas, quibus

3 Having is divided, as a supreme genus, into diverse modes of having, distinguished by the diverse things had, to which

p. 480

diuersis modis se accomodat corpus: vt, Habere vestes: aliud genus est ac, Habere arma: & quodlibet horum, diuiditur in alias species, quales sunt, Tunicatum esse, Loricatum esse, & aliæ similes: & ex his generibus, & speciebus, vsque ad indiuidua, quæ sunt, Petrum aut Ioannem, esse calceatum, tunicatum, aut loricatum, constituitur ordinatio prædicamentalis.

the body accommodates itself in diverse modes: as To have clothes is one genus, and another To have arms; and each of these is divided into other species, such as are To be tunicked, To be cuirassed, and others like them; and from these genera and species, down to the individuals, which are Peter or John being shod, tunicked, or cuirassed, the categorial ordering is constituted.

Quot, & quæ sint proprietates huius præd. — How many and which are the properties of this category.

PRima proprietas, Habere, est: Quod magis & minus suscipiat, nam eques, armatior est pedite: & magis calceatus dicitur qui caligis simul, & calceamentis ornatus est, quàm qui solis calceamentis. Secunda proprietas est: Non habere contrarium. Nam esse calceatum, & loricatum, non sunt opposita. Sed vtraque hæc proprietas, communis est aliis rebus: circa quas notat bene D Tho. opusc. 48. tractat. de sex vltimis prædicamentis, cap. 3. non esse inter se repugnantes: quia licèt suscipere magis & minus, propriè sumptum, procedat ex maiori vel minori admixtione contrarij: & ideo nihil possit ea suscipere, nisi contrarium habeat: tamen magis & minus, non attribuuntur huic prædicamento propriè sumpta, sed impropriè: hoc est, secundùm quandam extensionem: quia pluribus vestibus, aut armis, paucioribusve ornatur corpus: ideo bene hoc modo sumpta, magis, & minus, conuenire possunt huic prædicamento: licèt non habeat contrarium.

The first property of Having is: That it admits of more and less; for the horseman is more armed than the foot soldier, and he is said to be more shod who is furnished with greaves and shoes together than he who is furnished with shoes alone. The second property is: Not to have a contrary. For to be shod and to be cuirassed are not opposites. But each of these properties is common to other things; concerning which St. Thomas well notes, Opusculum 48, treatise on the six last categories, ch. 3, that they are not repugnant to each other: because, although to admit of more and less, taken properly, proceeds from a greater or lesser admixture of the contrary, and therefore nothing can admit them unless it has a contrary, yet more and less are not attributed to this category taken properly, but improperly: that is, according to a certain extension, because the body is adorned with more or fewer clothes or arms; therefore, taken well in this way, more and less can belong to this category, although it does not have a contrary.

Vltima proprietas eius est, Quòd adiacentiam inter plura necessariò dicat, ita, vt vnum sit actu in alio: nisi enim vestes, aut arma sint in homine, non dicetur vestitus, vel armatus, nec habere illa, secundùm specialem significationem huius prædicamenti: (quamuis alio titulo possessionis possit ea habere) quod in aliis non est necessarium: nam corpus potest habere vbi, & situm, etiam si actu non circumscribatur loco: ideo hæc proprietas, videtur conuenire quarto modo, huic prædicamento.

Its last property is That it necessarily expresses adjacency between several things, so that one is actually in the other: for unless the clothes or arms are on the man, he will not be called clothed or armed, nor be said to have them according to the special signification of this category (although by another title, of possession, he can have them); which in the others is not necessary: for a body can have a where and a position even if it is not actually circumscribed by a place. Therefore this property seems to belong to this category in the fourth mode.

QVÆSTIO VNICA.

SINGLE QUESTION.

An habere sit aliquid intrinsecum, & inhærens, vel in sola denominatione extrinseca consistat.

Whether having is something intrinsic and inhering, or consists in an extrinsic denomination alone.

CIrca hanc qu. reiicienda in primis est opinio quorundam modernorum, qui nihil intrinsecum inuenientes in eo quod est habere, dixerunt non esse speciale prædicamentum. Sed hoc est contra communem consensum totius scholæ, quæ

Concerning this question, there must first of all be rejected the opinion of certain moderns who, finding nothing intrinsic in that which is having, said that it is not a special category. But this is against the common consensus of the whole school, which

p. 481

cum Arist. tenet decem esse prædicamenta: & Habere, esse vnum ex iis: quod si excludatur, nouem erunt tantùm. Et etiam contra rationem, qua probabitur specialem rationem & prædicamentalem habere, licèt imperfectam, ac diminutam.

with Aristotle holds that there are ten categories, and that Having is one of them: if it is excluded, there will be only nine. And it is also against reason, by which it will be proved that it has a special and categorial ratio, although an imperfect and diminished one.

5 Hac ergo refutata sententia: est alia modernorum, qui in sola denominatione extrinseca, à vestibus, aut armis, consistere aiunt hoc prædicamentum, præter quam, nihil intrinsecum, vel inhęrens dicit. Probant primò: Quia habere non est aliud, quàm esse vestitum, vel armatum: ergo forma, à qua denominatur corpus, sunt vestes, vel arma: sed hæc non inhærent ei, sed extrinsecè adiacent, illud circundantes: ergo non dicit aliquid intrinsecum, vel inhærens, sed extrinsecam solùm denominationem ab eis.

5 This opinion, then, being refuted, there is another of certain moderns, who say that this category consists in an extrinsic denomination alone, from clothes or arms, beyond which it signifies nothing intrinsic or inhering. They prove it first: Because to have is nothing other than to be clothed or armed: therefore the form by which the body is denominated is the clothes or the arms; but these do not inhere in it, but lie extrinsically beside it, surrounding it: therefore it does not signify something intrinsic or inhering, but only an extrinsic denomination from them.

Secundò: Ex eo, quòd homo habeat vestes, vel arma, nullus modus realis, & intrinsecus potest ei aduenire, præter relationem propinquitatis, vel contactus ab illa: sed constat hunc respectum generalem esse, & ideo non pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum: ergo nihil speciale intrinsecum dicit, sed solam denominationẽ extrinsecam à vestibus, vel armis: cuius signum est, quod etiam si vestitus, vel armatus homo, vestibus, aut armis spolietur, nihil reale intrinsecum, aut sibi inhærens amittit: ergo neque aliquid sibi inhærens acquirit, dum induitur vestibus, aut armis, sed solùm acquirit, & admittit extrinsecam denominationem ab eis: quare in hac sola consistit ratio formalis huius prædicamenti. Hæc tamen opinio falsa probabitur quæst. sequenti, vbi ostendam, solam denominationem extrinsecam non posse efficere prędicamentum speciale.

Second: From the fact that a man has clothes or arms, no real and intrinsic mode can come to him, besides the relation of proximity or of contact with them; but it is certain that this respect is general, and therefore does not pertain to this category: therefore it signifies nothing special and intrinsic, but only an extrinsic denomination from the clothes or arms. A sign of which is that even if a clothed or armed man is stripped of his clothes or arms, he loses nothing real and intrinsic, or inhering in him: therefore neither does he acquire anything inhering in him while he is dressed in clothes or arms, but he acquires and admits only an extrinsic denomination from them; wherefore the formal ratio of this category consists in this alone. This opinion, however, will be proved false in the following question, where I shall show that an extrinsic denomination alone cannot make a special category.

6 Nostra igitur sententia opposita est, nempe, habere, præter denominationem extrinsecam à vestibus, aut armis, modum aliquem formaliter inhęrentem corpori continere: & hunc modum esse entitatem realem absolutam, includere tamen respectum secundùm dici ad vestes, vel arma: ita vt ratio formalis huius prædicamenti, absoluto simul cum respectu constet.

6 Our view, then, is the opposite, namely that having, besides the extrinsic denomination from clothes or arms, contains some mode formally inhering in the body; and that this mode is an absolute real entity, which nevertheless includes a respect secundum dici to the clothes or arms: so that the formal ratio of this category consists of the absolute together with the respect.

Sed quinam sit modus iste inhærens corpori, ex doctrina Arist. colligi debet: qui lib. 5. Meta. cap. 10. sic loquitur de hoc prædicamento: Habitus autem dicitur, tanquam quidam habentis, & habiti actus, sicut actio quædam aut motus: nam cùm hoc quidem efficit, illud verò fit, media est effectio: ita, & habentis vestem, & vestis habitæ, est medius habitus: hunc itaque habitum, quod non contingit habere manifestum est: ad infinita enim progrederetur, si habiti esset habitum habere. Quibus verbis duo expressè docet. Primum, quòd inter vestem, & hominem vestitum, aliquid est medium, sicut inter agens, & effectum, media est actio: & hoc

But what this mode inhering in the body is must be gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle, who in Metaph. 5, ch. 10, speaks thus of this category: Having is said as a certain act of the one having and of the thing had, as a certain action or motion: for when the one makes and the other is made, the making is in between; thus too between the one having clothing and the clothing had there is a habit in between: this habit, then, it is manifest, cannot be had; for it would proceed to infinity, if there were a having of the habit had. In which words he expressly teaches two things. First, that between the clothing and the clothed man there is something in between, just as between the agent and the effect the action is in between: and this Hh

p. 482

medium, inter vestem, & hominem, vocat actum habendi, seu habitationem, (vt sic loqui liceat ad hæc explicanda) Docet secundò, quòd hic actus medius, non habetur medio alio habitu, ne in infinitum procedatur: quia non est quod habetur: sed ratio habendi: vnde seipsa, & non per aliud medium conuenit homini vestito, aut armato.

in between, between the clothing and the man, he calls the act of having, or “habitation” (if one may speak so to explain these matters). He teaches second that this middle act is not had through another middle habit, lest there be a process to infinity: because it is not that which is had, but the ratio of having; whence it belongs to the clothed or armed man by itself, and not through another medium.

Et ex vtroque colligo hoc arg. ad probandam nostram sententiam. Si inter corpus & vestem est aliquid medium, haberi dicuntur vestes, medium hoc ex parte corporis se tenet: ergo aliquid reale in eo est: & accidentale quidem, cùm adesse, & abesse possit, dum homo induitur, & spoliatur vestibus: quare necesse est formaliter inhærere eidem nomini. Præterea, Si medium hoc non habetur per aliud medium, sed seipso, quia est ratio habendi: sequitur non esse extrinsecum homini, sicut vestes: nam si extrinsecum esset, per aliud medium haberetur, sicut habentur vestes: ergo est aliquid intrinsecum ei inhærens.

And from both I gather this argument to prove our view. If between the body and the clothing by which the clothes are said to be had there is something in between, this medium holds itself on the side of the body: therefore it is something real in it; and indeed accidental, since it can be present and absent while the man is dressed in and stripped of his clothes: wherefore it must formally inhere in that same man. Moreover, if this medium is not had through another medium but by itself, because it is the ratio of having, it follows that it is not extrinsic to the man, as the clothes are: for if it were extrinsic, it would be had through another medium, as the clothes are had: therefore it is something intrinsic, inhering in him.

7 Sed quid sit hoc medium intrinsecum, in quo consistit formalis ratio huius prædicamenti, ex doctrina eiusdem Arist. 3. lib. de partibus animalium, cap. 1 colligendum est: vbi asserit, naturam dedisse animalibus vestes, quibus operiantur, vt cutem, pilos, lanam, aut quid simile, & arma, quibus possint se defendere ab aliis, & etiam ea offendere, si opus fuerit, hominem verò nudum edidisse: intellectum tamen ei tribuisse, quo propria industria posset sibi vestes, & arma quærere, & ex rebus aliis ea conficere.

7 But what this intrinsic medium is, in which the formal ratio of this category consists, must be gathered from the doctrine of the same Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals 3, ch. 1, where he asserts that nature gave the animals clothing with which to be covered, such as skin, hair, wool, or something similar, and arms with which they might defend themselves from others, and also attack them if need be; but that it brought forth man naked, while giving him intellect, by which through his own industry he might seek clothes and arms for himself, and make them from other things.

Ex quibus, duo colliguntur valde notanda, in quibus differt homo à cæteris animalibus. Primum est, quòd vestes, & arma eorum, sunt partes integrantes suorum corporum: vnde non dicuntur ea habere propriè, sed communissima, atque impropriissima ratione, non pertinente ad hoc prędicamentum: sicut dicuntur habere pedes, aut caput: vestes verò, & arma solius hominis sunt, quædam alia corpora sibi extrinseca, quæ propriè dicuntur ei adiacere: & ideo propriè dicitur ea habere, & speciali, ac propriissima ratione dicitur vestitus, & armatus: quare ei soli propriè conuenit prædicamentum, habere. Vestimus quidem simias, & armamus equos, tamen non dicuntur vestiti, vel armati propriè, sed per quandam analogiam, & similitudinem ad hominem: quare nec dicuntur propriè habere vestes, & arma secundùm rationem formalem huius prædicamenti.

From this two things are gathered that are very much to be noted, in which man differs from the other animals. The first is that their clothing and arms are integral parts of their bodies: whence they are not said to have them properly, but by a most common and most improper ratio, not pertaining to this category, just as they are said to have feet or a head; but the clothes and arms of man alone are certain other bodies extrinsic to him, which are properly said to lie beside him: and therefore he is properly said to have them, and by a special and most proper ratio is said to be clothed and armed: wherefore the category Having belongs properly to him alone. We do indeed clothe monkeys and arm horses, yet they are not said to be clothed or armed properly, but by a certain analogy and likeness to man: wherefore neither are they said properly to have clothes and arms according to the formal ratio of this category.

8 Secundum, quod colligitur, est, Naturam loco vestium, & armorum, dedisse homini naturalem aptitudinem, & accommodationem

8 The second thing that is gathered is that in place of clothes and arms nature gave man a natural aptitude, and an accommodation

p. 483

ad illa induenda, per quam aptitudinem speciali modo eisdem sese aptaret, & accommodaret, dum eis indueretur: & ratione huius accommodationis, specialem ornatum & quasi naturalem ei tribuunt vestes, & arma: cæteris verò animalibus suas vestes, & arma, tanquam partes integrantes corporum habentibus, nec dedit natura, nec necesse fuit dare talem aptitudinem, & accommodationem ad extrinsecas vestes, & arma: vnde nec eis tribuunt quasi naturalem ornatum, sicut homini, sed quasi artificiatum, & nimis improprium.

for putting them on, by which aptitude he might in a special manner fit and accommodate himself to them while he was dressed in them: and by reason of this accommodation, clothes and arms give him a special and as it were natural adornment; but to the other animals, which have their clothing and arms as integral parts of their bodies, nature neither gave, nor was it necessary to give, such an aptitude and accommodation to extrinsic clothes and arms: whence these do not give them an adornment as it were natural, as they do to man, but as it were artificial, and excessively improper.

Ex quibus infero, quòd dum homo nudus est, solùm habet aptitudinem naturalem, & quasi aptitudinalem accõmodationem, & coaptationem ad vestes, & arma: sed dum eis induitur, exit in actum talis aptitudo: non quidem in actum, qui sit actio, sed qui sit modus formalis actualis accõmodationis, & coaptationis in eo productus: aliquo modo similis actioni, & passioni, in quantũ vestes, & arma dicuntur vestire, & armare hominẽ, & homo ipse dicitur vestiri, & armari, vestitusque & armatus esse.

From which I infer that while a man is naked he has only a natural aptitude, and an as it were aptitudinal accommodation and coaptation, to clothes and arms; but while he is dressed in them, such an aptitude goes out into act: not indeed into the act which is an action, but into the act which is the formal mode of actual accommodation and coaptation produced in him, in some way similar to action and passion, inasmuch as clothes and arms are said to clothe and arm a man, and the man himself is said to get clothed and armed, and to be clothed and armed.

9 Et modus iste actualis accommodationis, & coaptationis, vocatur habitus, seu habitio, quem Aristot. docuit esse medium, inter vestes, & hominem: & non habere per alium modum, sed seipso inesse homini, tanquam medio habendi vestes & arma. In hoc igitur modo absoluto, includente tamen respectum secundùm dici ad vestes, & arma, & extrinsecas etiam denominationes ab eis, consistit ratio formalis huius prædicamenti: quam extrinsecam vocant aliquando D. Tho. & alij antiquiores Interpretes, propter easdem denominationes extrinsecas quas includit: non certè modum intrinsecum, & inhærentem excludere volentes.

9 And this mode of actual accommodation and coaptation is called habit, or “habition,” which Aristotle taught is the medium between the clothes and the man, and is not had through another mode, but inheres in the man by itself, as the medium of having clothes and arms. In this absolute mode, then, which nevertheless includes a respect secundum dici to the clothes and arms, and also extrinsic denominations from them, the formal ratio of this category consists: which St. Thomas and other older Interpreters sometimes call extrinsic, on account of the same extrinsic denominations which it includes; not, certainly, wishing to exclude an intrinsic and inhering mode.

Ad primum arg. alterius opinionis, Neganda est prima consequentia quòd à solis vestibus, & armis denominaretur homo vestitus, & armatus: sed primò atque formaliter denominatur, ab actuali modo accommodationis, & coaptationis ei inhærente, deinde à vestibus, & armis denominatione extrinseca: in qua non consistit principaliter ratio huius prædicamenti, sed in alia denominatione formali.

To the first argument of the other opinion: The first consequence must be denied, that the man would be denominated clothed and armed by the clothes and arms alone: rather he is denominated first and formally by the actual mode of accommodation and coaptation inhering in him, and then by the clothes and arms with an extrinsic denomination; in which the ratio of this category does not principally consist, but in the other, formal denomination.

Ad secundum: Negandum est primum antecedens, quòd nullus modus realis oriatur in homine, ex eo, quòd vestibus induatur: oritur enim modus actualis accommodationis inhærens, vt explicatum est: quem modum amittit, dum vestibus, & armis spoliatur: & alium de nouo acquirit, si iterum induatur. Ratione igitur huius modi formalis, & intrinseci, intrinsecum quoque, atque formalem concretum habet hoc prædicamentum.

To the second: The first antecedent must be denied, that no real mode arises in the man from the fact that he is dressed in clothes: for there arises an actual inhering mode of accommodation, as has been explained; which mode he loses while he is stripped of his clothes and arms, and acquires another anew if he is dressed again. By reason, then, of this formal and intrinsic mode, this category also has an intrinsic and formal concrete. Hh ij

p. 484

Quæstio generalis pro omnibus sex vltimis prædicamentis — GENERAL QUESTION FOR ALL THE LAST

QVÆSTIO GENERALS PRO omnibus sex vltimis prædicamentis.

S I X C AT E G O R I E S .

An ratio formalis eorum consistat in aliquo intrinseco, & formaliter inhærenti, vel in sola denominatione extrinseca — Whether their formal ratio consists in something intrinsic and formally inhering, or in an extrinsic denomination alone.

An ratio formalis eorum consistat in aliquo intrinseco, & formaliter inhærente, vel in sola denominatione extrinseca.

[…]

10 PRiusquam probabiles sententias adducamus, excludenda est illa, tanquam improbabilis, eorum qui tenuerunt: Ex decem prædicamentis, sola quatuor prima, nempe substantiam, quantitatem, relationem, & qualitatem, esse propriè prædicamenta: reliqua verò sex: solùm esse quasdam complicationes, seu aggregationes quorundam prædicatorum, minùs imperfectorum: ex quibus, nec genera, neque species, sed nec prędicamentales ordinationes constitui possunt: nisi per quandam similitudinem, & analogiam, ad illa quatuor: & ideo inquiunt, Aristotelem paucissimis verbis, & perfunctoriè admodum genera & species eorum distinxisse. Hoc verò probabilitate prorsus caret: cùm Aristo ca. de incomplexis absque distinctione enumerauit decem prædicamenta: & postea quatuor illis propositis, enumerauit actionem, & passionem cum reliquis: & suis locis, de singulis probatum sit, proprias rationes prædicamentales habere genera etiam atque species, quamuis imperfectissima, & quorum non est adeò frequens vsus in scientiis: & ideo paucis verbis explicata sunt ab Aristotele.

10 Before we bring forward the probable opinions, that of those who held the following is to be excluded as improbable: Of the ten categories, only the first four, namely substance, quantity, relation, and quality, are proper categories; while the remaining six are only certain complications or aggregations of certain less imperfect predicates, from which neither genera nor species, nor even categorial orderings, can be constituted, except through a certain likeness and analogy to those four: and therefore, they say, Aristotle distinguished their genera and species in very few words and quite perfunctorily. But this altogether lacks probability; since Aristotle, in the chapter on incomplexes, enumerated ten categories without distinction, and afterwards, having set out those four, enumerated action and passion with the rest; and since it has been proved of each in its own place that they have proper categorial rationes, and also genera and species, although most imperfect ones, and of which the use in the sciences is not so frequent: and therefore they were explained by Aristotle in few words.

11 Hac igitur exclusa sententia falsa. Prima opinio est Scoti, in 3. d. 1. qu. 1. in 4. d. 13. quæst. 1. & quodlib. 11. qu. 4. quibus locis hanc distinctionem relationum excogitauit: Quædam sunt relationes, (inquit) Intrinsecus aduenientes: quæ posito fundamento, & extremis, necessariò insurgunt in eis, vt paternitas, & filiatio. Aliæ sunt, Extrinsecus aduenientes, quæ adhuc posito fundamento, & extremis non necessariò insurguut: & ideo non ex natura extremorum proueniunt, sed ab extrinseco: tales sunt relatio vnionis, inter materiam, & formam, & relatio inter locatum & locum: de quibus constat: quòd existentibus extremis, nempe materia, & forma, vt dum separatur anima à corpore, atque etiam locatum à loco, eum deferens, non sequitur relatio vnionis, aut locationis inter illa: nisi rursus ab aliqua causa efficienti, & proinde extrinseca vniantur. Et in his relationibus extrinsecus aduenientibus, ait consistere rationes horum sex prædicamentorum. Erit itaque secundùm Scotum prædicamentum Actionis: relatio ad principium, seu causam efficientem, à qua procedit effectus, & Passio, relatio

11 This false opinion, then, being excluded, the first opinion is that of Scotus, in 3, d. 1, q. 1; in 4, d. 13, q. 1; and Quodlibet 11, q. 4; in which places he devised this distinction of relations: Some relations (he says) come intrinsically, which, once the foundation and the extremes are posited, necessarily arise in them, such as paternity and filiation. Others are extrinsically coming, which even when the foundation and the extremes are posited do not necessarily arise: and therefore they do not come from the nature of the extremes, but from something extrinsic. Such are the relation of union between matter and form, and the relation between the located thing and the place: of which it is certain that while the extremes exist, namely matter and form (as when the soul is separated from the body), and also the located thing and the place that carries it away, the relation of union or of location between them does not follow, unless they are united again by some efficient, and consequently extrinsic, cause. And in these extrinsically coming relations, he says, the rationes of these six categories consist. According to Scotus, then, the category of Action will be the relation to the principle, or efficient cause, from which the effect proceeds; and Passion, the relation

p. 485

ad eandem, vt imprimentem effectum in passo. Vbi, relatio corporis ad locum, aut spatium, loci Quando, relatio rei ad propriam durationem. Situs, relatio corporis, secundùm suas partes ad locum. Et, Habere, relatio eiusdem corporis ad vestes, vel arma. Distingui autem sufficienter hæc sex prædicamenta ait.

to the same, as impressing the effect on the patient; Where, the relation of the body to the place or space; When, the relation of the thing to its proper duration; Position, the relation of the body, according to its parts, to the place; and Having, the relation of the same body to the clothes or arms. And he says these six categories are sufficiently distinguished.

12 Probat Scotus hoc argu. Petrum esse in loco, vel habere vbi, non est Petrus ipse: nec locus eum circundans: ergo cùm sit aliquid, erit relatio eius ad locum dumtaxat. Probatur consequentia, quia cùm superficies continens Petrum, ei non inhæreat: nihil aliud acquirit dum incipit esse in loco, præter relationem ad locum: nec aliquid aliud amittit, dum recedit à loco, præter eandem relationem: ergo, Vbi, nihil aliud præter relationem erit. Sicque de cæteris quinque prædicamentis: quibus idem arg. applicari potest. Eandem ferè sententiam Scoti sequuntur, Capreol. in 2. d. 2. q. 1. & Soncinas 5. Meta. q. 6. ad 4. nam licèt illam distinctionem relationum non admittant, asserunt tamen sex vltima prædicamenta, non consistere in aliquo absoluto, nec in absoluto simul cum respectu: sed puros quosdam & solos respectus includere.

12 Scotus proves it with this argument: Peter’s being in a place, or having where, is not Peter himself, nor the place surrounding him: therefore, since it is something, it will be only his relation to the place. The consequence is proved: because, since the surface containing Peter does not inhere in him, he acquires nothing else when he begins to be in a place besides the relation to the place; nor does he lose anything else when he withdraws from the place besides the same relation: therefore Where will be nothing besides a relation. And so of the other five categories, to which the same argument can be applied. Almost the same opinion as Scotus is followed by Capreolus, in 2, d. 2, q. 1, and Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 6, ad 4: for although they do not admit that distinction of relations, they nevertheless assert that the last six categories do not consist in something absolute, nor in the absolute together with a respect, but include certain pure respects alone.

Hæc tamen opinio duo continet falsa. Nam primò falsum est: quòd dentur tales relationes: quas vocat Scotus extrinsecus aduenientes. Secundò, falsum est etiam: quòd si darentur, in eis solis posita esset ratio formalis horum prædicamentorum.

This opinion, however, contains two falsehoods. For first, it is false that there are such relations as Scotus calls extrinsically coming. Second, it is also false that, if there were, the formal ratio of these categories would be placed in them alone.

13 Probatur autem primò: quòd non dentur. Relationem extrinsecus aduenientem, vocat Scotus eam quæ posito fundamento, & extremis, non sequitur, aut non consurgit: sed impossibile est: quòd positis extremis cum fundamento, non consurgat in eis relatio: ergo impossibiles sunt tales relationes. Probatur minor: quia extrema omnia relationis, sunt talia per fundamentum: siue ab extrinseco eis proueniat relatio, siue ab intrinseco: ergo repugnat poni fundamentum in eis, quin sequatur relatio.
