Gratia exempli: duo alba, sunt extrema similitudinis, per albedinem in vtroque positam: duo homines, extrema sunt paternitatis, & filiationis, per generationem actiuam, & passiuam: & ideo repugnat naturaliter, quòd posito fundamento, & extremis, non sequatur in eis relatio. Quòd in exemplis etiam Scoti, non est minus euidens: nam relatio vnionis, inter materiam, & formam, fundatur in actione, per quam ab agente vniuntur, (quam vocant vnitionem:) & relatio loci ad locatum, & locati ad locum: (si ex parte vtriusque realis est) fundatur in approximatione, seu commensuratione locati ad locum, aut circumscriptione loci ad locatum; sed naturaliter est impossibile, quòd locatum sit approximatum

13 Now the first is proved, that there are none. Scotus calls an extrinsically coming relation that which, once the foundation and the extremes are posited, does not follow or does not arise; but it is impossible that, once the extremes are posited with the foundation, the relation should not arise in them: therefore such relations are impossible. The minor is proved: because all the extremes of a relation are such through the foundation, whether the relation comes to them from something extrinsic or from something intrinsic: therefore it is repugnant that the foundation be posited in them without the relation following. For example: two white things are the extremes of likeness through the whiteness posited in each; two men are the extremes of paternity and filiation through active and passive generation: and therefore it is naturally repugnant that, once the foundation and the extremes are posited, the relation should not follow in them. Which is no less evident in Scotus’s own examples: for the relation of union between matter and form is founded on the action by which they are united by the agent (which they call “unition”); and the relation of the place to the located thing, and of the located thing to the place (if it is real on the part of both), is founded on the approximation or commensuration of the located thing to the place, or the circumscription of the place to the located thing; but it is naturally impossible that the located thing be approximated Hh iij

p. 486

, aut commensuratum loco, aut quòd locus circumscribat locatum, & non sequatur talis relatio: ergo impossibiles sunt tales relationes.

or commensurated to the place, or that the place circumscribe the located thing, and such a relation not follow: therefore such relations are impossible.

14 Deceptio verò Scoti fit manifesta: quia in suis exẽplis, solùm ponit extrema, & non fundamentum eorum: nempe materiam, & formam, nulla facta mentione vnitionis, quæ fundamentum est: locatum quoque, & locum sine circumscriptione, aut approximatione: quod est, ponere extrema nuda, aut materialiter accepta, non formaliter, vt sunt extrema relationis, quod habent per fundamentum: quare non est mirum, si eis sic positis, non sequatur relatio, positis verò cum fundamento, impossibile est non sequi. Quod etiam reperitur in cæteris relationibus: nam licèt ponas duos homines, nisi ponas vnum procedere ab alio per generationem, quæ est fundamentum relationis, non sequitur in eis relatio paternitatis, & filiationis: hac verò posita, necessariò sequitur. Et ecce patet, quo pacto friuola est, & sine fundamento, distinctio Scotica relationum.

14 And Scotus’s deception becomes manifest: because in his examples he posits only the extremes and not their foundation, namely matter and form, making no mention of the unition, which is the foundation; and also the located thing and the place, without the circumscription or approximation: which is to posit the extremes bare, or taken materially, not formally, as they are extremes of the relation, which they are through the foundation: wherefore it is no wonder if, when they are posited in this way, the relation does not follow, whereas when they are posited with the foundation it is impossible that it not follow. Which is found also in the other relations: for although you posit two men, unless you posit that one proceeds from the other by generation, which is the foundation of the relation, the relation of paternity and filiation does not follow in them; but once this is posited, it necessarily follows. And so it is plain how frivolous and without foundation the Scotist distinction of relations is.

15 Item probatur secundùm, quòd etiam si darentur tales relationes non posset in eis solis consistere ratio formalis horum prædicamentorum. Et sumo ad id probandum, prædicamenta actionis, & passionis: argumentórque hoc modo, Actio, & passio, sunt idem motus: ita vt actio non sit aliud, quàm motus, vt procedit ab agente, & passio, motus, vt receptus in passo: sed motus, vt procedit ab agente, dicit entitatem absolutam viæ, præter respectum ad agens: & passio, eandem entitatem receptam, præter respectum ad passum: ergo de his duobus prædicamẽtis euidenter probatur, non posse consistere in solo respectu. Et eodem modo potest probari de aliis: quamuis in his duobus magis sit manifestum.

15 Likewise the second is proved, that even if there were such relations, the formal ratio of these categories could not consist in them alone. And to prove it I take the categories of action and passion, and argue in this way: Action and passion are the same as motion, so that action is nothing other than motion as it proceeds from the agent, and passion motion as received in the patient; but motion as it proceeds from the agent signifies the absolute entity of the way, besides the respect to the agent; and passion signifies the same entity as received, besides the respect to the patient: therefore it is evidently proved of these two categories that they cannot consist in a respect alone. And in the same way it can be proved of the others, although in these two it is more manifest.

16 Probatur secundò: Quia si prædicamenta hæc, in solis, & puris relationibus consistunt, impossibile est distingui à prædicamento ad aliquid: ergo cùm certum sit, & à Scoto concedatur, ab eo distingui, non possunt consistere in sola relatione. Probatur antecedens, ex definitione prædicamenti ad aliquid. Relatiua prædicamenti ad aliquid sunt, quorum totum suum esse, est ad aliud referri: sed totum esse horum prædicamentorum, est referri ad aliud: ergo sunt relatiua illius prædicamenti. Probatur minor: quia si in sola & pura relatione consistunt, cùm relatio nihil absolutum dicat, sed solùm esse rationem referendi ad aliud: totum esse horum erit relatio, & ex consequenti totum erit referri ad aliud.

16 It is proved second: Because if these categories consist in relations alone and pure, it is impossible that they be distinguished from the category of relation: therefore, since it is certain, and is granted by Scotus, that they are distinguished from it, they cannot consist in relation alone. The antecedent is proved from the definition of the category of relation. Relatives of the category of relation are those whose whole being is to be referred to another; but the whole being of these categories is to be referred to another: therefore they are relatives of that category. The minor is proved: because if they consist in relation alone and pure, since relation signifies nothing absolute, but only the ratio of referring to another, the whole being of these will be relation, and consequently the whole will be to be referred to another.

Secunda opinio opposita est, asserens hæc vltima prædicamenta

The second opinion is the opposite, asserting that these last categories

p. 487

, in ratione purè absoluta consistere: non quidem intrinseca, aut inhærente, sed purè extrinseca: quam consequitur, respectus ad extrinsecum, non tamen pertinens ad rationem formalem, aut essentialem eorum, sed quasi accidentalis: vt prędicamentum, vbi, non est aliud, quàm locus: vt denominans extrinsecè locatum: sicque de reliquis. Ita Herueus, quodlib. 1. q. 9. Iauellus 5. Meta. q. vltima, Sotus qu. vnica de sex vltimis prædicamentis, Fonseca 5. Met. c. 15. q. 7. sect. 3.

consist in a purely absolute ratio: not indeed an intrinsic or inhering one, but a purely extrinsic one, which a respect to something extrinsic follows, not pertaining, however, to their formal or essential ratio, but as it were accidental: as the category of where is nothing other than the place, as extrinsically denominating the located thing; and so of the rest. So Hervaeus, Quodlibet 1, q. 9; Javelli, Metaph. 5, last q.; Soto, sole q. on the last six categories; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 7, sect. 3.

17 Probatur à sufficienti partium enumeratione: nam hæc prædicamenta, non dicunt nudam relationem, vt probatum est contra Scotum: nec absolutum simul cum respectu: quia hoc est aggregatum per accidens, ex rebus diuersorum prædicamentorum. Nec etiam dicunt rationem purè absolutam, intrinsecam, seu inhærentem: quia Aristoteles, & cum ea tota schola, vocat ea prædicamenta adiacentia, atque extrinseca: & meritò, cùm vbi, non sit aliud, quàm extrinsecè circunscribi loco: & vestitum esse, extrinsecè circunscribi vestibus: sicque de cæteris: ergo necesse est, rationem formalem eorum, absolutam, & omnino extrinsecam ponere.

17 It is proved by a sufficient enumeration of the parts: for these categories do not signify a bare relation, as has been proved against Scotus; nor the absolute together with a respect, because this is an aggregate per accidens out of things of diverse categories. Nor again do they signify a purely absolute ratio, intrinsic or inhering; because Aristotle, and with him the whole school, calls these categories adjacent and extrinsic; and rightly, since where is nothing other than to be extrinsically circumscribed by a place, and to be clothed, to be extrinsically circumscribed by clothes; and so of the others: therefore it is necessary to posit their formal ratio as absolute and altogether extrinsic.

Hæc etiam sententia falsa probatur duplici argumento. Primo: Quia prædicamentum dicit ordinationem ex generibus, & speciebus constitutam: sed genera, & species non possunt constare, aut fieri ex sola denominatione extrinseca, cùm dicant naturam realem, & intrinsecam: ergo nec prædicamentum ex sola denominatione extrinseca constare potest. Præterea, Denominatio extrinseca, nihil ponit in re denominata: & ideo nouam denominationem extrinsecam, admittunt omnes in Deo, vt quòd sit creator in tempore: quam denominationem non habuit ab æterno: ergo, si sola denominatio extrinseca sufficit constituere hæc sex prædicamenta, Deus poterit in eis collocari, absque vlla sui imperfectione, aut limitatione: quod superiùs probauimus falsum.

This opinion too is proved false by a twofold argument. First: Because a category signifies an ordering constituted of genera and species; but genera and species cannot consist of, or be made from, an extrinsic denomination alone, since they signify a real and intrinsic nature: therefore neither can a category consist of an extrinsic denomination alone. Moreover, an extrinsic denomination posits nothing in the thing denominated: and therefore all admit a new extrinsic denomination in God, as that He is creator in time, a denomination which He did not have from eternity: therefore, if an extrinsic denomination alone suffices to constitute these six categories, God could be placed in them without any imperfection or limitation of Himself: which we proved above to be false.

Secundò: Quia de duobus saltem prædicamentis euidenter probatur, non consistere in sola denominatione extrinseca: nempe, de prædicamento passionis, &, vbi: propria enim. & formalis ratio passionis, consistit in receptione motus, vel actionis in passo: ergo formaliter dicit rationem inhærentem, & non solùm extrinsecam. Vbi etiam, est proprius terminus motus localis: ergo in eodem mobili debet recipi, in quo recipitur motus: sed motus formaliter inhæret mobili, cùm sit actus mobilis, prout mobile est; vt definit Aristoteles 3. Physicorum in principio: ergo, Vbi etiam inhærebit mobili, & non erit sola denominatio extrinseca.

Second: Because of two categories at least it is evidently proved that they do not consist in an extrinsic denomination alone, namely of the category of passion and of where. For the proper and formal ratio of passion consists in the reception of motion or action in the patient: therefore it formally signifies an inhering ratio, and not only an extrinsic one. Where, too, is the proper term of local motion: therefore it must be received in the same mobile in which the motion is received; but motion formally inheres in the mobile, since it is the act of the mobile insofar as it is mobile, as Aristotle defines it at the beginning of Phys. 3: therefore Where too will inhere in the mobile, and will not be an extrinsic denomination alone. Hh iiij

p. 488

Vltima opinio, quam tenent cæteri omnes interpretes Aristotelis, non solùm cap. præsenti, sed etiam 5. Metaph. cap. 15. asserit, rationem formalem horum prædicamentorum, in modo aliquo absoluto, & inhærente in subiecto, consistere, simul includente respectum secundùm dici ad aliquid extrinsecum, atque etiam extrinsecam denominationem ab eo: vt prædicamentum Vbi, includere realem pręsentiam in loco, aut spatio loci: & hanc pręsentiam modum esse absolutum, in corpore inhærentem, cum respectu secundùm dici ad locum, aut spatium, & præter hanc includere etiam denominationem à loco ipso, si localis sit præsentia. Hæc est probabilior sententia, & tenenda.

The last opinion, which all the other interpreters of Aristotle hold, not only in the present chapter but also in Metaph. 5, ch. 15, asserts that the formal ratio of these categories consists in some absolute mode, inhering in the subject, which at the same time includes a respect secundum dici to something extrinsic, and also an extrinsic denomination from it: as that the category Where includes real presence in the place, or in the space of the place; and that this presence is an absolute mode inhering in the body, with a respect secundum dici to the place or space; and that besides this it includes also the denomination from the place itself, if the presence is local. This is the more probable opinion, and to be held.

Probaturque ex refutatione aliarum opinionum, hoc modo: Hæc prædicamenta, non dicunt solùm respectum, vt probauimus contra Scotum: nec solam denominationem extrinsecam: ergo dicunt aliquam rationem absolutam, & intrinsecam, quia respectus, in aliquo absoluto debet includi, vt non pertineat ad prædicamentum ad aliquid.

And it is proved from the refutation of the other opinions, in this way: These categories do not signify a respect alone, as we proved against Scotus; nor an extrinsic denomination alone: therefore they signify some absolute and intrinsic ratio, because the respect must be included in something absolute, so as not to pertain to the category of relation.

19 Quòd verò absolutum cum respectu, non sit vnum per accidens, probatum est in prędicamento ad aliquid: nam cùm includatur respectus essentialiter in ratione absoluta, non concurrunt ad constituendum vnum per modum compositionis: & ideo non efficiunt vnum per accidens: sed absolutum, includens essentialiter respectum, vnum per se est: ad cuius prædicamentum pertinet respectus ipse, & non ad prædicamentum ad aliquid: quod in potentiis, habitibus, & scientiis, necessariò concedendum esse probauimus: nec respectus isti sunt transcendentales: quia nec omnibus prædicamentis, nec pluribus sunt communes; sed ad solum prędicamentum absoluti, in quo includuntur, & cuius essentiam complent, reducuntur.

19 And that the absolute with the respect is not one per accidens was proved in the category of relation: for since the respect is included essentially in the absolute ratio, they do not concur to constitute one thing by way of composition; and therefore they do not make one thing per accidens: but the absolute, essentially including the respect, is one per se, to whose category the respect itself pertains, and not to the category of relation: which we proved must necessarily be granted in powers, habits, and sciences. Nor are these respects transcendental: because they are not common to all the categories, nor to several, but are reduced to the sole category of the absolute in which they are included and whose essence they complete.

Ad arg. Scoti, Neganda est consequentia, quòd, Vbi, sit sola relatio ad locum: sed est realis pręsentia in modo absoluto, & inhęrente locato consistens, atque includens respectum ad locum, vel denominationem extrinsecam ab eo.

To the argument of Scotus: The consequence must be denied, that Where is a relation to the place alone; rather it is a real presence, consisting in an absolute mode inhering in the located thing, and including a respect to the place, or an extrinsic denomination from it.

20 Ad argu. secundæ opinionis, Neganda est secunda pars antecedentis: quòd prædicamenta hæc non dicant absolutum cum respectu: negandum est etiam: quòd tale absolutum cum respectu, sit ens per accidens: quia cùm respectus ipse, non pertineat ad prędicamentum ad aliquid, nec concurrat simul cum absoluto, ad constituendum vnum tertium per modum compositionis, sed tanquam cõplementum essentiale eiusdem absoluti, in eo includatur, & ad idemmet prędicamentum reducatur, vnum per se est absolutum cum respectu: & vnam rationem prędicamentalem, licèt imperfectam, constituere potest.

20 To the argument of the second opinion: The second part of the antecedent must be denied, that these categories do not signify the absolute with a respect; it must also be denied that such an absolute with a respect is a being per accidens: because, since the respect itself does not pertain to the category of relation, nor concur together with the absolute to constitute one third thing by way of composition, but is included in it as an essential complement of that same absolute, and is reduced to the very same category, the absolute with the respect is one per se, and can constitute one categorial ratio, although an imperfect one.

p. 489

VLTIMA PARS LIBRI PRÆDICAMENTORVM, QVAM POSTprædicamenta vocant.

CHAPTER XI, ON OPPOSITES

CAPVT XI, DE OPPOSITIS,

[…]

TEXTVS ARISTOT.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE.

De Oppositis autem, quot modis solent opponi, dicendum est

Now concerning opposites, in how many ways things are wont to be opposed, we must speak.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

POST explicationem prædicamentorum, quædam proponit Arist. declaranda: quæ sunt quasi modi quidam, aut rationes incompletæ, multis prædicamentis communes: quas à prædicamentis, propter vtramque rationem excludit, nempe propter Transcendentem, & Incompletam. Sunt autem quinque Oppositio, Prius & Posterius, Simul, Motus, & diuersi modi Habere: ideo per quinque capita sequentia, vsque ad decimum quintum, explicationem eorum, & totum librum absoluit.

fter the explanation of the categories, Aristotle proposes certain A things to be declared, which are as it were certain modes, or incomplete rationes, common to many categories: which he excludes from the categories for both reasons, namely on account of the transcendent ratio and the incomplete one. And there are five: Opposition, Prior and Posterior, Simultaneous, Motion, and the diverse modes of Having: therefore through the five following chapters, up to the fifteenth, he completes their explanation and the whole book.

Intentum Aristotelis in hoc vndecimo capite est, explicare naturam Oppositionis & species eius: & in duas partes diuiditur. In prima diuidit oppositionem in quatuor genera: & explicat singula membra. In secunda, Speciales, conditiones contrariæ oppositionis enumerat. Oppositio, inquit Aristoteles, quadruplex est, Relatiua, Contraria, Contradictoria, & Priuatiua.

The intent of Aristotle in this eleventh chapter is to explain the nature of Opposition and its species; and it is divided into two parts. In the first he divides opposition into four genera, and explains the single members. In the second he enumerates the special conditions of contrary opposition. Opposition, says Aristotle, is fourfold: Relative, Contrary, Contradictory, and Privative.

Relatiuè opposita dicuntur illa, quorum totum suum esse, est ordinari ad aliud, vt pater, & filius, simile, & aliud sibi simile opponuntur relatiuè. Contrariè opposita, ait esse illa, quæ cùm ad inuicem non ordinantur, sunt tamen sibi repugnantia: vt calor, & frigus. Sibi autem repugnare idem est, ac esse formas sibi repugnãtes circa idem subiectum: & per hoc distinguuntur ab oppositis contradictoriè, & priuatiuè, per primam verò particulam à relatiuè oppositis.

Relatively opposed are said to be those whose whole being is to be ordered to another: as father and son, a like thing and another like it, are opposed relatively. Contrarily opposed, he says, are those which, though they are not ordered to each other, are nevertheless repugnant to each other: as heat and cold. And to be repugnant to each other is the same as to be forms repugnant to each other with respect to the same subject: and by this they are distinguished from things opposed contradictorily and privatively, and by the first particle from things opposed relatively.

Oppositio priuatiua, est eorum, quæ nata sunt fieri circa idem subiectum, vt cæcitas, & visus, aut cæcum, & videns; hoc est circa subiectum aptum habere vtrumque vt cæcitas, & visus circa lapidem, in quo nulla est aptitudo ad visum: ideo homo dicitur propriè cæcus: lapis verò solùm dicitur, non videns.

Privative opposition is that of things which are apt by nature to come to be with respect to the same subject, as blindness and sight, or blind and seeing; that is, with respect to a subject apt to have both: as blindness and sight with respect to a stone, in which there is no aptitude for sight; therefore a man is properly called blind, while a stone is only called not seeing.

p. 490

Vltima oppositio, & maior, aut perfectior omnibus est Contradictoria, quæ nullum habet medium, cùm tamen reliqui medium habeant. Nec conuenit rebus, nisi vt à nobis concipiuntur, & vocibus significantur: & ideo eam definit Aristoteles: per affirmationem & negationem, dicens: Ea opponuntur contradictoriè, quæ tanquam affirmatio, & negatio repugnant: id est, quæ per affirmationem, & negationem repugnare censetur, vt Petrus sedet, & non sedet.

The last opposition, and the greater or more perfect than all, is the Contradictory, which has no middle, although the others have a middle. Nor does it belong to things except as they are conceived by us and signified by words: and therefore Aristotle defines it through affirmation and negation, saying: Those things are opposed contradictorily which are repugnant as affirmation and negation; that is, which are judged to be repugnant through affirmation and negation, as Peter sits and does not sit.

In secunda parte capitis, explicat conditiones contrariorum: quarum prima est, quòd bono necessariò, contrariatur malum, malo verò non solùm bonum: sed etiam aliud malum. Secunda conditio est, Posse vnum existere in rerum natura, sine altero: vt album sine nigro: in quo distinguuntur à relatiuis, quorum vnum esse sine altero repugnat. Tertia conditio, Contraria possunt simul esse in eodem subiecto, vt idem corpus, non potest simul esse album, & nigrum: Quarta conditio, Contraria non possunt fieri circa idem subiectum genere, vel specie, vt, album, & nigrum circa Petrum, & Ioannem, qui sunt eiusdem speciei, atque etiam, circa hominem, & equum, qui sunt eiusdem generis. Vltima conditio est, Quod contraria sint sub eodem genere proximo, aut sub diuersis, vt album, & nigrum, sub eodem genere proximo coloris: virtus, & vitium, sub diuersis, quod tamen sic intelligi debet: vt semper, & necessariò, sint sub eodem genere proximo, aut remoto, intermedio vel supremo: vt virtus, & vitium, sunt sub eodem genere remoto Habitus: & sub eodem genere supremo Qualitatis.

In the second part of the chapter he explains the conditions of contraries, of which the first is that to good evil is necessarily contrary, but to evil not only good but also another evil. The second condition is that one can exist in the nature of things without the other, as white without black: in which they are distinguished from relatives, of which it is repugnant that one exist without the other. The third condition: Contraries cannot be at the same time in the same subject, as the same body cannot be at the same time white and black. The fourth condition: Contraries cannot come to be with respect to a subject the same in genus or in species, as white and black with respect to Peter and John, who are of the same species, and also with respect to man and horse, who are of the same genus. The last condition is that contraries are under the same proximate genus, or under diverse ones, as white and black under the same proximate genus of color, virtue and vice under diverse ones; which, however, must be understood thus: that they are always and necessarily under the same genus, proximate or remote, intermediate or supreme; as virtue and vice are under the same remote genus of Habit, and under the same supreme genus of Quality.

CAP. XII. De modis prioris, cum expositione textus — On the Modes of Prior.

De modis prioris.

[…]

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

TEX. ARISTOTELIS.

[…]

Prius autem alterum altero, dicitur quadrupliciter, primò quidem, & maximè propriè.

One thing is said to be prior to another in four ways: first, indeed, and most properly.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 INtentum huius capitis, est explicare modos Prioritatis, nec diuisione indiget: quia solùm in eo explicat Aristoteles, quatuor modos prioritatis: quia suo tempore circumferebantur in schola, quibus ipse addit quintum à se inuentum. Primus modus prioritatis est secundùm quem vnum dicitur prius tempore altero; vt qui hodie nascitur, dicitur prius tempore eo, qui nascitur cras. Secundò

he intent of this chapter is to explain the modes of Priority; and it 1 T needs no division, because in it Aristotle only explains the four modes of priority which were current in the school in his time, to which he himself adds a fifth found by himself. The first mode of priority is that according to which one thing is said to be prior in time to another: as he who is born today is said to be prior in time to him who is born tomorrow. Second,

p. 491

modo illud dicitur prius altero, à quo non valet subsistendi consequentia: quia ratione vnum dicitur prius duobus: & quodlibet prædicatum superius, prius inferiori: quia valet consequentia. Sunt duo, ergo est vnum: non valet tamen, Est vnum, ergo sunt duo. Est homo, ergo est animal: non tamen sequitur, Est animal: ergo est homo. Tertius modus, prioritatis, nõ est in ratione essendi, sed ordinis, & reperitur inter illa, quæ sic sunt ordinata, vel ordinabilia: vt in tali ordinatione, vnum sit prius, aliud posterius: vt in oratione, priora sunt elementa, seu litteræ, syllabis, & syllabæ priores dictionibus: & in numero ternario, prima, & secunda vnitas, priores sunt tertia. Quarto modo, digniora, aut honorabiliora dicuntur priora minus dignis. In qua significatione, priores apud se vocare solent aliqui eos, quos plus diligunt, vel alia de causa pluris faciunt. Sed hunc modum prioritatis, improprium dicit esse Arist. quia non fundatur in esse rerum, vel in naturali ordinabilitate earum, sed solùm in apprehensione hominum His quatuor modis quintum addit Arist. quo prius dicitur vnum respectu alterius: quia causa illius est: quamuis sit simul tempore cum eo: vt homo, dicitur prius, quàm risibile, quia est causa eius: & vniuersaliter omnis causa prior est suo effectu hoc genere prioritatis. Ex his autem quinque modis, secundus, tertius, & quintus, dicuntur prioritates naturæ: omnes verò sunt prioritates reales, quibus addere possumus, prioritatem secundùm rationem, qua illud dicitur prius altero, quod licèt non sit reipsa eo prius, bene tamen nostro modo intelligendi: vt in secundis intentionibus, & relationibus rationis, est manifestum. Omnia, quæ dicta sunt de modo prioris, intelliguntur de modo posterioris, secundùm eandem proportionem.

in the mode in which that is said to be prior to another from which the consequence of subsisting does not hold: for which reason one is said to be prior to two, and any superior predicate prior to the inferior: because the consequence holds, There are two, therefore there is one; but this does not hold, There is one, therefore there are two. It is a man, therefore it is an animal; but it does not follow, It is an animal, therefore it is a man. The third mode of priority is not in the ratio of essence, but of order, and is found among those things which are so ordered, or orderable, that in such an ordering one is prior, the other posterior: as in speech the elements, or letters, are prior to syllables, and syllables prior to words; and in the number three the first and second unit are prior to the third. In the fourth mode the worthier or more honorable are said to be prior to the less worthy. In which signification some are wont to call prior in their esteem those whom they love more, or for some other reason value more. But Aristotle says this mode of priority is improper, because it is not founded on the being of things or on their natural orderability, but only on the apprehension of men. To these four modes Aristotle adds a fifth, by which one thing is said to be prior with respect to another because it is its cause, although it is simultaneous in time with it: as man is said to be prior to risible, because it is its cause; and universally every cause is prior to its effect in this genus of priority. Of these five modes, the second, the third, and the fifth are called priorities of nature; but all are real priorities, to which we can add priority according to reason, by which that is said to be prior to another which, although it is not in reality prior to it, is so nevertheless according to our mode of understanding: as is manifest in second intentions and relations of reason. Everything that has been said of the mode of prior is understood of the mode of posterior, according to the same proportion.

CAP. XIII. De modis simul, cum expositione textus — On the Modes of Simultaneous.

De modis simul.

[…]

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

TEXT. ARIST.

[…]

Simul autem dicuntur simpliciter quidem, & propriissimè, quorum generatio in eodem est tempore.

Those things are called simultaneous simply, and most properly, whose generation is at the same time.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 INtentum Arist. est explicare modos quibus vnum dicitur simul cum altero: nec diuisione indiget ca. quia solùm in eo tradit Arist. tres modos simultatis, quorum primus est: quo aliqua dicuntur simul tempore, quæ simul generantur vel fiunt in rerum natura.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the modes in which one thing is said 1 T to be simultaneous with another; nor does it need division, because in it Aristotle only hands down three modes of simultaneity, of which the first is that in which some things are said to be simultaneous in time, which are generated or come to be in the nature of things at the same time.

p. 492

Secundus modus est: quo aliqua dicuntur simul natura: & sunt ea, quæ dicuntur ad conuertentiam: & neutrum est causa alterius: vt pater, & filius: simile, & aliud sibi simile: & in vniuersum omnia relatiua, prædicamenti ad aliquid: quorum proprietatem esse diximus, ex mente Arist. quòd sint simul natura, & cognitione. Licèt enim materialiter sumpti, pater & filius, hoc est, vt generans & genitus, ille sit prior natura: quia est causa, & iste posterior, quia effectus: tamen sub formali ratione relatiua patris, & filij, simul natura sunt.

The second mode is that in which some things are said to be simultaneous by nature: and these are the things which are said to reciprocate, and neither is the cause of the other: as father and son, a like thing and another like it, and universally all the relatives of the category of relation: whose property, we said, according to the mind of Aristotle, is that they are simultaneous by nature and in cognition. For although, taken materially, father and son, that is, as generator and generated, the former is prior by nature because he is the cause, and the latter posterior because he is the effect, nevertheless under the formal relative ratio of father and son they are simultaneous by nature.

Tertius modus simultatis, versatur inter differentias ex æquo diuidentes genus, & species per eas constituas: ex æquo autem diuidere genus, est, æquè proximè illud diuidere: vt rationale, & irrationale, dicuntur simul natura: non tamen rationale, & reptibile, aut aquatile: quia rationale, & reptibile, non diuidunt æquè proximè animal: sed reptibile, solùm diuidit animal iam contractum, per irrationale: rationale verò, immediatè. Ideo non sunt simul natura. Et quæ de differentiis dicimus, de speciebus quoque per eas constitutis, secundùm eandem proportionem intelligendum est.

The third mode of simultaneity concerns the differences dividing a genus equally, and the species constituted by them; and to divide a genus equally is to divide it equally proximately: as rational and irrational are said to be simultaneous by nature; but not rational and creeping, or aquatic: because rational and creeping do not divide animal equally proximately, but creeping divides only animal already contracted by irrational, whereas rational divides it immediately. Therefore they are not simultaneous by nature. And what we say of the differences must be understood also of the species constituted by them, according to the same proportion.

CAP. XIV. De speciebus motus, cum expositione text. — On the Species of Motion.

De speciebus motus.

[…]

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

TEXTVS ARIST.

[…]

Motus autem species sunt sex.

The species of motion, moreover, are six.

Generatio, Corruptio, Augmentum, Diminutio, Alteratio, & secundùm locum Mutatio, &c

Generation, Corruption, Augmentation, Diminution, Alteration, and Change according to place, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 INtentum Arist. est, explicare naturam specierum motus, & diuiditur caput hoc in duas partes. In prima enumerat sex species motus. In secunda, quot, & quæ sint contraria motui, & speciebus eius. Sumit autem motum Arist. vniuersaliter, pro omni mutatione physica: quo pacto eum definiuit 3. lib. Physico. Quòd sit actus entis in potentia: secundùm quod in potentia: nec vocat

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the nature of the species of mo1 T tion; and this chapter is divided into two parts. In the first he enumerates six species of motion. In the second, how many and which things are contrary to motion and to its species. Now Aristotle takes motion universally, for every physical change: in which way he defined it in Phys. 3: That it is the act of a being in potency, according as it is in potency; nor does he call

p. 493

species motus eas, quas enumerat: quòd intelligat veras esse species aut motum verum esse genus. Quia cùm motus, & species eius, sint entia incompleta, & ideo non prædicamentalia: nec verum genus ipse motus est, nec illæ sunt veræ species, sed dicuntur quodammodo species, id est, modi essentialiter diuersi eiusdem motus. In hoc igitur sensu asserit, Species motus esse sex. Prima est Generatio, per quam producitur substantia, vt homo. Secunda. Corruptio, per quam desinit esse substantia, vt mors, vel desitio hominis. Tertia est Augmentatio, per quam res maiorem quantitatem acquirit quam habeat: & ideo augeri dicitur. Quarta, Deminutio, per quam deperdit aliquam quantitatem ex ea, quam habebat prius: & propterea fit minor Quinta est, Alteratio, per quam res acquirit qualitatem, quam prius non habebat, vel contrariam ei, quam habeat prius: aut denique intensionem, aut extensionem in eadem, quam iam habebat: vt dum aqua calida magis calefit, quia plures gradus acquirit in eisdem partibus calidis, vel ad nouas nondum calefactas extenditur calor. Motus autem localis est sextus, per quem corpus acquirit, vbi, aut realem præsentiam.

those which he enumerates species of motion because he understands them to be true species, or motion to be a true genus. For since motion and its species are incomplete beings, and therefore not categorial, neither is motion itself a true genus, nor are those true species; but they are called species in a certain manner, that is, essentially diverse modes of the same motion. In this sense, then, he asserts that the species of motion are six. The first is Generation, by which a substance is produced, as a man. The second, Corruption, by which a substance ceases to be, as the death or ceasing of a man. The third is Augmentation, by which a thing acquires a greater quantity than it has, and therefore is said to be augmented. The fourth, Diminution, by which it loses some quantity out of that which it had before, and on that account becomes smaller. The fifth is Alteration, by which a thing acquires a quality which it did not have before, or one contrary to that which it had before; or finally an intension or extension in the same quality which it already had: as when hot water becomes hotter because it acquires more degrees in the same hot parts, or the heat is extended to new parts not yet heated. Local motion, finally, is the sixth, by which a body acquires where, or real presence.

2 Itaque non dicitur localis, quia proprius terminus eius sit locus, sed vbi quod acquirit, semper est præsentia localis: hoc est commensurata loco, à quo circumscribitur, licèt supernaturaliter possit acquirere vbi sine loco.

2 And so it is not called local because its proper term is place, but because the where which it acquires is always a local presence: that is, commensurated to the place by which it is circumscribed; although supernaturally it can acquire a where without a place.

In secunda parte capitis, docet Aristoteles motum in communi consideratum, habere vnum contrarium, nempe quietem: quemlibet verò motum specialem, duo asserit habere opposita, vnum sub ratione communi motus, aliud sub ratione speciali, vt est talis motus. Exempli gratia, Generatio, vt est motus, habet quietem in communi, pro contrario: sed vt est motus ad substantiam, habet pro contrario quietem in substantia: & eodem modo intelligendum est de cæteris speciebus motus: sed dum asserit Aristoteles, motum in communi habere pro contrario quietem in communi, & motum in speciali quietem in communi & in speciali: non de propria contrarietate loquitur, sed de communi, & impropria pro quocunque genere oppositionis: quia motus, & quies, aut talis motus, & talis quies, non opponuntur contrariè, sed priuatiuè.

In the second part of the chapter Aristotle teaches that motion considered in common has one contrary, namely rest; but he asserts that any special motion has two opposites, one under the common ratio of motion, the other under the special ratio, as it is such a motion. For example, Generation, as it is a motion, has rest in common as its contrary; but as it is a motion to substance, it has as its contrary rest in substance; and the same is to be understood of the other species of motion. But when Aristotle asserts that motion in common has as its contrary rest in common, and motion in particular rest in common and in particular, he is not speaking of proper contrariety, but of a common and improper contrariety, for any genus of opposition whatever: because motion and rest, or such a motion and such a rest, are not opposed contrarily but privatively.

p. 494

CAPVT XV.

C H A P T E R X V.

CAP. XV. De modis habere, cum expositione text. — On the Modes of Having.

De modis habere.

[…]

TEXTVS ARIST.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE.

Habere secundùm plures modos dicitur, aut enim vt habitum, & dispositionem, aut aliam aliquam qualitatem.

To have is said according to several modes: for either as a habit and disposition, or some other quality.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

INtentum Aristotelis est, tradere omnes modos, vel acceptiones, quibus aliquid habere dicimur. Caput diuisione non indiget, quia solùm in eo enumerat Aristot. septem modos, habere: quorum Primus est, secundùm quem dicimur habere qualitatem: vt intellectum, virtutes, & scientias. Secundus modus est, habere quantitatem, vt corpus, dicitur habere magnitudinem bicubitam, aut tricubitam. Tertius est, habere non ea quæ inhærent corpori, sed quæ illud circumstant, vel extrinseca sunt ei, vt habere vestem, vel arma. Quarto modo dicitur aliquid habere aliud, non in toto corpore, sed in aliqua eius parte, ratione cuius totum corpus dicitur illud habere: vt habere nasi curuitatem, vel annulum manu, aut pileum in capite. Quintus modus, est habere partem ipsam: vt caput, vel manum. Sexto modo, dicitur vnum habere aliud, quia continet illud: vt amphora dicitur habere vinum. Vltimus modus habendi, est per possessionem: vt vir dicitur habere vxorem, vxor virum, atque etiam homo habere pecunias. Plures alios modos habendi enumerat Aristoteles 5. Metaphy. cap. 23. tex. 18. sed hos ait magis esse in vsu: & ideo pro Dialecticorum vsu & captu sufficere. Et nos etiam sufficere dicimus hæc adnotasse, circa librum prædicamentorum, ad maiorem Dei gloriam, & studiosorum vtilitatem.

he intent of Aristotle is to hand down all the modes or accepta‐ T tions in which we are said to have something. The chapter needs no division, because in it Aristotle only enumerates seven modes of having, of which the First is that according to which we are said to have a quality: as intellect, virtues, and sciences. The second mode is to have quantity, as a body is said to have a magnitude of two cubits or three cubits. The third is to have not things that inhere in the body, but things that surround it, or are extrinsic to it, as to have clothing or arms. In the fourth mode something is said to have another thing, not in the whole body, but in some part of it, by reason of which the whole body is said to have it: as to have a hooked nose, or a ring on the hand, or a hat on the head. The fifth mode is to have the part itself: as a head or a hand. In the sixth mode one thing is said to have another because it contains it: as a jar is said to have wine. The last mode of having is by possession: as a husband is said to have a wife, a wife a husband, and also a man to have money. Aristotle enumerates many other modes of having in Metaph. 5, ch. 23, text 18; but he says these are more in use, and therefore suffice for the use and capacity of Dialecticians. And we too say that it suffices to have noted these things on the book of the Categories, to the greater glory of God and the benefit of students.

FINIS.

The End.

p. 495

COMMENTARIES ON THE WHOLE DIALECTIC OF ARISTOTLE, TOGETHER WITH THE DOUBTS and Questions customarily debated

COMMENTARIORVM IN VNIVERSAM ARIST. DIALECTICAM, VNA CVM DVBIIS & quæstionibus hac tempestate agitari solitis.

in this age.

SECVNDA PARS,

S E C O N D PA R T,

CONTINENS LIBROS DE INTERpretatione, de priori, & posteriori resolutione, libr. Topicorum, & Elenchorum.

C O N TA I N I N G T H E B O O K S O N I N T E R P R E TAT I O N , ON PRIOR AND POSTERIOR RESOLUTION, T H E B O O K S O F T H E T O P I C S , A N D O F T H E S O P H I S T I C A L R E F U TAT I O N S .

Lib. 1. Arist. περὶ Ἑρμηνείας; seu de Interpretatione.

Book 1 of Aristotle, περὶ ἑρμηνείας, or On Interpretation.

Proœmium totius operis — P RO E M O F T H E W H O L E WO R K .

PROEMIVM TOTIVS OPERIS

[…]

OPVS hoc, iam ad secundam operationem intellectus pertinet, quæ vocatur Compositio, & diuisio: & ideo inscribitur ab Arist. περὶ Ἑρμηνείας, seu de interpretatione: quia ille solus dicitur aliquid interpretari, qui veritatem, aut falsitatem in aliquo contentam exponit: & ideo interpretatio, solùm de oratione continente veritatem, aut falsitatem (quę est enuntiatio) propriè dicitur: vt asserit bene D. Thom. lectione prima horum commentariorum: simplicia verò vt nomen, & verbum, partes potiùs interpretationis vocantur: sic & quædam alia, quibus naturales effectus exprimuntur, vt suspiria, & gemitus, nimis impropriè dicuntur interpretationes. Vnde sequitur, idem esse, quòd opus hoc de interpretatione appelletur, ac de enuntiatione.

his work now pertains to the second operation of the intellect, which T is called Composition and division: and therefore it is entitled by Aristotle περὶ ἑρμηνείας, or On Interpretation: because he alone is said to interpret something who sets forth the truth or falsity contained in something; and therefore interpretation is properly said only of a speech containing truth or falsity (which is the enunciation), as St. Thomas rightly asserts in the first lecture of these commentaries: but simple things, such as the noun and the verb, are rather called parts of interpretation; so too certain other things by which natural affections are expressed, such as sighs and groans, are quite improperly called interpretations. Whence it follows that it is the same for this work to be called On Interpretation as On Enunciation.

Quodnam sit obiectum huius operis — What the object of this work is.

Quodnam sit obiectum huius operis.

[…]

EX inscriptione iam explicata, intelligitur, Enuntiationem esse obiectum adæquatum huius operis, in quo conueniunt omnes interpretes Arist. quia hæc est de qua principaliter agitur in eo: & cuius partes explicantur, quæ sunt, nomen, & verbum: hæc est etiam, cuius passiones probantur, & in quam cætera de quibus disputatur, tanquam in finem ordinantur: quæ sunt propriæ conditiones obiecti.

From the title now explained it is understood that the enunciation is the adequate object of this work, in which all the interpreters of Aristotle agree: because this is what is principally treated in it, and whose parts are explained, which are the noun and the verb; this is also the one whose attributes are proved, and to which the other things that are disputed are ordered as to their end: which are the proper conditions of an object.

p. 496

Verùm enuntiatio duplex est: Vna Simplex, quam vocant Categoricam, & alia Composita, quæ appellatur Hypothetica: & ideo vel pro sola simplici, tanquam pro pręcipua parte accipi potest, dum dicimus esse obiectum, aut in communi, prout abstrahit ab vtraque, & eas comprehendit: & prima opinio tenet, solam enuntiationem simplicem esse obiectum, ita Boëtius Amonius, & Louanienses in proœmio huius operis, & quidam alij ex modernis: videturque idem sentire D. Th. cùm dicat de sola simplici determinatè agere Arist.

But the enunciation is twofold: one Simple, which they call Categorical, and the other Composite, which is called Hypothetical: and therefore it can be taken either for the simple alone, as for the principal part, when we say that it is the object, or in common, as it abstracts from both and comprehends them. And the first opinion holds that the simple enunciation alone is the object: so Boethius, Ammonius, and the Louvain commentators in the proem of this work, and certain others among the moderns; and St. Thomas seems to think the same, since he says that Aristotle determinately treats of the simple alone.

Et probatur ratione prima: Quia Arist. solùm agit in hoc opere de partibus enuntiationis simplicis, aut categoricæ, non de partibus hypotheticæ: ergo illa sola obiectum est.

And it is proved, first, by reason: Because in this work Aristotle treats only of the parts of the simple or categorical enunciation, not of the parts of the hypothetical: therefore that alone is the object.

Secunda: Quia hoc opus ordinatur proximè ad tractatum de syllogismo: sed syllogismus solùm componitur ex propositionibus categoricis: ergo de hac sola, tanquam de proprio obiecto, agit.

Second: Because this work is ordered proximately to the treatise on the syllogism; but the syllogism is composed only of categorical propositions: therefore it treats of this alone, as of its proper object.

Secunda opinio asserit: Enuntiationem in communi, prout comprehendit simplicem, & compositam, esse obiectum. ita Villalpandeus, & Toletus, in eodem proœmio. Et hæc videtur nobis probabilior. Probatur testimonio Arist. quia cap. 4. huius 1. li. vbi ex professo ait de enuntiatione, eam diuidit in simplicem, & compositam, tanquam in proprias species: & vtramque explicat propria definitione: ergo de vtraque per se disputat, & vtraque per se comprehenditur sub adæquato obiecto.

The second opinion asserts: The enunciation in common, as it comprehends the simple and the composite, is the object. So Villalpando and Toledo, in the same proem. And this seems to us more probable. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle: because in ch. 4 of this first book, where he speaks expressly of the enunciation, he divides it into simple and composite as into proper species, and explains each by its proper definition: therefore he disputes of both per se, and both are comprehended per se under the adequate object.

Probatur etiam ratione: Quia enuntiatio composita, per se pertinet ad Dialecticam: & non ad aliam partem, quàm ad istam: ergo per se consideratur in ea, & ideo sub obiecto eius per se comprehenditur. Probo minorem: quia non pertinet ad partes præcedentes, in quibus solùm de simplicibus agitur, nec ad sequentes, in quibus agitur per se de syllogismo, & speciebus eius: ergo solùm consideratur per se in hoc opere.

It is proved also by reason: Because the composite enunciation pertains per se to Dialectic, and to no other part than to this one: therefore it is considered per se in it, and therefore is comprehended per se under its object. I prove the minor: because it does not pertain to the preceding parts, in which only simple things are treated, nor to the following ones, in which the syllogism and its species are treated per se: therefore it is considered per se only in this work.

Ad primum arg oppositæ sententiæ, Negandum est, solùm agere Arist. de partibus enuntiationis simplicis. Licèt enim de enuntiatione simplici, & partibus eius præcipuè disputet, tanquam de præcipua specie enuntiationis in communi consideratæ: non est tamen negandum, etiam eum de hypotheca agere: cùm eam definiat: ac etiam de partibus eius, quæ sunt simplices enuntiationes. Sed pauca admodum de ea tradit: quia non est tam frequens vsus eius in Dialectica: & hoc voluit D. Th. dum dixit Arist. solùm de simplici determinatè agere, non tamen eam excludere ab obiecto huius operis.

To the first argument of the opposite opinion: It must be denied that Aristotle treats only of the parts of the simple enunciation. For although he disputes principally of the simple enunciation and its parts, as of the principal species of the enunciation considered in common, it must nevertheless not be denied that he also treats of the hypothetical, since he defines it, and also of its parts, which are simple enunciations. But he hands down very few things about it, because its use in Dialectic is not so frequent: and this is what St. Thomas meant when he said that Aristotle determinately treats only of the simple, not, however, that he excludes it from the object of this work.

2 Ad secundum: Neganda est minor, quòd syllogismus solùm componatur ex enuntiationibus categoricis: nam duplex

2 To the second: The minor must be denied, that the syllogism is composed only of categorical enunciations; for the syllogism is twofold

p. 497

est syllogysmus: Categoricus, & Hypotheticus: vt expressè docet Aristo. 1. lib. de priori resolutione, vbi de vtroque per se agit: licèt præcipuè de categorico, tanquam de perfectiori eius specie: & ita etiam in hoc opere, de vtraque enunciatione agit, tanquam de præcipua specie: vtraque ergo pertinent per se ad obiectum: sicut vterque syllogismus ad obiectum priorum.

the categorical and the hypothetical, as Aristotle expressly teaches in Prior Analytics 1, where he treats of each per se, although principally of the categorical, as of its more perfect species: and so also in this work he treats of both enunciations, of the one as of the principal species: both therefore pertain per se to the object, just as each syllogism pertains to the object of the Prior Analytics.

De loco quem hoc opus obtineat inter cæteras partes dialecticæ, & diuisione eius — On the place which this work holds among the other parts of Dialectic, and on its division.

De loco quem hoc opus obtineat inter cæteras partes Dialecticæ, & de diuisione eius.

[…]

OPus hoc secundum locum obtinet inter partes Dialecticæ: quia de secunda operatione intellectus agit: ideo immediatè collocatur post librum prædicamentorum, agentem de prima, & ante libros de priori resolutione, ac cæteros, in quibus agitur de tertia.

This work holds the second place among the parts of Dialectic, because it treats of the second operation of the intellect: therefore it is placed immediately after the book of the Categories, which treats of the first, and before the books of the Prior Analytics and the others, in which the third is treated.

Diuisio verò, non est eadem apud omnes interpretes: nam Græci, sub vno eodemque libro totum opus includunt: Latini verò quos sequimur, in duos libros illud diuidunt: in quorum Primo, de enunciatione, & eius partibus: nomine videlicet, verbo, affirmatione, & negatione agitur. In secundo verò, de variis modis enunciationum: quod idem est, ac de enunciationibus modalibus.

The division, however, is not the same among all the interpreters: for the Greeks include the whole work under one and the same book, while the Latins, whom we follow, divide it into two books: in the first of which the enunciation and its parts are treated, namely the noun, the verb, affirmation, and negation; and in the second, the various modes of enunciations: which is the same as of modal enunciations.

Liber primus sex habet capita. Primum, quasi proœmium est totius operis: in quo Arist. proponit materiã, de qua acturus est. In secũdo, agit de nomine. In tertio de verbo. In quarto de enunciatione. In quinto de oppositione enunciationum. In vltimo, de particularibus enunciationibus, (quas vocat de futuro contingenti) explicans modum quo in eis reperiantur veritas, & falsitas.

The first book has six chapters. The first, as it were the proem of the whole work, in which Aristotle proposes the matter he is going to treat. In the second he treats of the noun. In the third of the verb. In the fourth of the enunciation. In the fifth of the opposition of enunciations. In the last, of particular enunciations (which he calls about future contingents), explaining the mode in which truth and falsity are found in them.

CHAPTER I

CAPVT I.

[…]

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

TEXTVS ARIST.

[…]

Primum oportet ponere quid sit nomen, & quid verbum, &c.

First it is necessary to establish what a noun is, and what a verb, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

1 INtentum Arist. in præsenti ca. est, explicare modum significandi cõceptum, vocum, & scripturarum. Diuiditur autem caput hoc in duas partes. Prima, quasi proœmium est totius operis, in quo proponit ea de quibus acturus est. In secunda agit, de conceptibus, vocibus, atque scripturis. Explicans modum significandi omnium.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the mode 1 T of signifying of concepts, words, and writings. And the chapter is divided into two parts. The first, as it were the proem of the whole work, in which he proposes the things he is going to treat. In the second he treats of concepts, words, and writings, explaining the mode of signifying of all of them. Ii

p. 498

Ea de quibus agendum est in hoc opere, sex esse ait, nempe, Nomen, Verbum, Affirmatio, Negatio, Enunciatio, & Oratio: & singula propriis definitionibus explicanda esse.

The things to be treated in this work, he says, are six, namely the Noun, the Verb, Affirmation, Negation, the Enunciation, and Speech; and each is to be explained by its proper definitions.

In secunda parte, de conceptuum vocum atque scripturarum significatione agendum esse ait. Inter quæ, talis est ordo: vt à rebus ipsis, tanquam ab obiectis intellectui, imprimantur species intelligibiles, quibus informatus operatur: & per propriam operationem producit aliam speciem, quæ vocatur expressa, atque etiam conceptus, seu verbum mentis, repręsentans rem, vt actu, aut expressè intellectam: sed quia res per conceptum repræsentata, debet significari aliis: ideo adinuentæ sunt voces, & scripturæ, vt per voces significentur præsentibus, per scripturas, absentibus. Ex quo colligit Arist. conceptus significare immediatè res: voces verò easdem res, mediis conceptibus: scripturas tandem voces, quæ omnia his verbis docet: Sunt ergo ea, quæ sunt in voce, earum quæ sunt in anima passionum notæ: & ea quæ scribuntur, eorum quæ sunt in voce. Per passiones animæ, conceptus intelligens, secundùm omnes expositiones: quia cùm in eodẽ intellectu, à quo producuntur, recipiantur, & receptio sit quasi quædam passio, meritò dicuntur passiones: quarum voces notas esse ait, id est signa.

In the second part he says that the signification of concepts, words, and writings is to be treated. Among which the order is this: that from the things themselves, as from objects, intelligible species are impressed on the intellect, informed by which it operates; and through its proper operation it produces another species, which is called expressed, and also the concept, or word of the mind, representing the thing as actually or expressly understood: but since the thing represented through the concept must be signified to others, therefore words and writings were invented, so that it might be signified through words to those present, through writings to those absent. From which Aristotle gathers that concepts signify things immediately; words signify the same things by means of the concepts; writings, finally, signify words: all of which he teaches in these words: Those things, therefore, which are in the voice are signs of the passions which are in the soul; and those which are written, of those which are in the voice. By passions of the soul he means concepts, according to all the expositions: because, since they are received in the same intellect by which they are produced, and the reception is as it were a certain passion, they are rightly called passions; of which he says words are the marks, that is, signs.

Itaque Conceptus, significant res Voces, res, & conceptus. Scriptura verò, voces immediatè, & remotè conceptus, & res. Diuersa tamen ratione: nam conceptus, inquit, significant naturaliter: voces verò, atque scripturæ, non nisi ad placitum. Probat vtrumque hoc argumento: Natura semper se habet eodem modo, apud omnes nationes: ergo quę se habent eodem modo apud omnes, naturalia sunt, & quæ non sunt eadem apud omnes non sunt naturalia, sed ex diuerso hominum placito variantur: at conceptus cuiuscunque rei, est idem apud omnes: voces verò, atque scripturæ, sunt diuersæ apud diuersas nationes: ergo conceptus significant naturaliter: voces verò, & scripturæ ad placitum. Probatur minor: quia tam Græci, quàm Latini, eundem conceptum formant de homine, sed diuersis vocibus illum significant, pro diuersitate linguæ.

And so Concepts signify things; Words, things and concepts; and Writings, words immediately, and concepts and things remotely. Yet by a diverse ratio: for concepts, he says, signify naturally; but words and writings only by convention. He proves both by this argument: Nature always behaves in the same way among all nations: therefore things which behave in the same way among all are natural, and things which are not the same among all are not natural, but vary according to the diverse convention of men: but the concept of any thing whatever is the same among all, whereas words and writings are diverse among diverse nations: therefore concepts signify naturally, but words and writings by convention. The minor is proved: because the Greeks as well as the Latins form the same concept of man, but signify it with diverse words, according to the diversity of the language.

Porro in ordine ad veritatem, & falsitatem, diuerso modo se habere docet, conceptas voces, atque scripturas simplices, & cõpositas: nam simplices, nihil verum, aut falsum continent, nisi eis addatur, est, vel non est, compositę verò, cum eodẽ verbo, iam significant verum, & falsum. Probat primum hac ratione: quia si simplicia, aut incomplexa significarent per se verum, vel falsum, maximè id haberent nomina composita, vt centimanus: sed qui hoc nomen proferret, non diceret verũ aliquid vel falsum

Further, he teaches that simple and composite concepts, words, and writings stand in a diverse way in order to truth and falsity: for the simple contain nothing true or false unless is or is not is added to them; but the composite, with that same verb, already signify the true and the false. He proves the first by this reason: because if simple or incomplex things signified the true or the false per se, composite nouns would have this most of all, as centimanus [hundred-handed]; but he who uttered this noun would not say something true or false,

p. 499

, quia non mentiretur, nec veritatem diceret, nisi addas esse, vel non esse: ergo in vocibus, aut conceptibus simplicibus, nulla est veritas: quod verò compositæ cum verbo, est, aut non est, veritatem, aut falsitatem contineant: tanquam per se notum relinquit.

because he would not lie, nor would he speak the truth, unless is or is not were added: therefore in simple words or concepts there is no truth. That composite ones, with the verb is or is not, contain truth or falsity, he leaves as known per se.

SOLE QUESTION

QVÆSTIO VNICA.

[…]

Quæst. 1. An voces significent conceptus & res, atque scripturæ voces ad placitum, conceptus verò naturaliter res — Whether words signify concepts and things; and whether writings signify words by convention, but concepts signify things naturally.

An voces significent conceptus, & res: atque scripturæ voces ad placitum, conceptus verò naturaliter res

[…]

4 CIrca hanc quæst. quædam sunt apud omnes certa. Primum, quòd conceptus significent res naturaliter: propter rationem Arist. quia eiusdem rei eundem etiam conceptum omnes formant, si eandem rationem eius concipiant, & diuersum, si diuersam: ergo conceptus semper sunt idem apud omnes: & ex consequenti naturaliter significant res. Probatur antecedens, quia de ente eundem conceptum omnes formant: si entitatem solùm in eo considerent: & similiter si vniuocationem eius respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, vel etiam analogiam: nam licèt, qui putant esse vniuocum, diuersum conceptum eius forment, ab his qui putãt esse analogum, hoc tamen ideo est, quia diuersam rationem in eo considerant, nempe vniuocationem, & analogiam, omnes nihilominus qui vniuocationem considerant, eundem conceptum eius formant: & etiam qui considerant analogiam: & qui illam considerant, semper diuersum ab his qui considerant hanc: & ita intelligitur Arist. dum ait, conceptus significare naturaliter res, quia sunt iidem apud omnes, si eiusdem rei sint, vel eiusdem rationis formalis eius: si verò rei diuersæ, aut diuersæ rationis eiusdem rei, diuersi sunt conceptus. Ex quo etiam ostenditur conceptus naturaliter significare: quia non est minùs naturale diuersum esse apud omnes, quod ex propria natura diuersum est, quàm esse idem, quod ex propria natura est idem.

4 Concerning this question certain things are certain among all. First, that concepts signify things naturally: on account of Aristotle’s reason, because all form the same concept of the same thing if they conceive the same ratio of it, and a diverse one if a diverse one: therefore concepts are always the same among all, and consequently signify things naturally. The antecedent is proved: because all form the same concept of being if they consider only entity in it; and likewise if they consider its univocation with respect to substance and accident, or also its analogy: for although those who think it is univocal form a diverse concept of it from those who think it is analogous, this nevertheless is because they consider a diverse ratio in it, namely univocation and analogy; nonetheless all who consider univocation form the same concept of it, and so too those who consider analogy; and those who consider the latter always form a diverse one from those who consider the former. So Aristotle is understood when he says that concepts signify things naturally, because they are the same among all if they are of the same thing, or of the same formal ratio of it; but if of a diverse thing, or of a diverse ratio of the same thing, the concepts are diverse. From which it is shown also that concepts signify naturally: because it is no less natural that what is diverse by its own nature be diverse among all, than that what is the same by its own nature be the same.

Certum est secundò: Scripturam significare vocem ad placitum: quod probatur euidenter, quia ab hominibus inuentæ sunt: & diuersæ, ad significandas voces diuersas, ab eisdem pro libitu applicantur: ergo significant voces, ex libera hominum impositione.

It is certain, second, that writing signifies the word by convention: which is proved evidently, because writings were invented by men, and diverse ones are applied by the same men at will to signify diverse words: therefore they signify words by the free imposition of men.

Difficultas igitur quæst. consistit, in significatione vocum, & in modo significandi earum. In significatione quidem: An voces significent non solum res, sed etiam conceptus, quos de eisdem rebus formamus. In modo etiam significandi. An significent res naturaliter, vel ad placitum.

The difficulty of the question therefore consists in the signification of words and in their mode of signifying. In the signification, indeed: Whether words signify not only things, but also the concepts which we form of the same things. In the mode of signifying, also: Whether they signify things naturally or by convention. Ii ij

p. 500

Et est prima opinio quorundam modernorum, quæ asserit voces solùm significare res: conceptus verò non significare, sed exprimere. Quod sic probant: Illud significat, vox, pro quo supponitur in propositione: sed voces non supponuntur pro conceptibus, sed pro rebus: ergo non significant conceptus, sed res. Probatur minor, primò ex Arist. 1. lib. Elench. c. 1. vbi asserit: Quia non possumus res, de quibus disputamus, ad scholas adducere, vtimur, vocibus loco rerum: sicut ludentes, vtuntur calculis pro pecuniis: ergo intelligit Aristot. pro solis rebus voces supponi. Prob. secundò: quia in hac propositione, Homo disputat, non supponitur vox homo, pro conceptu hominis, sed pro homine ipso: de quo verificatur disputatio, & non de conceptu.

And the first opinion is that of certain moderns, which asserts that words signify only things; concepts, however, they do not signify, but express. Which they prove thus: A word signifies that for which it supposits in a proposition; but words do not supposit for concepts, but for things: therefore they do not signify concepts, but things. The minor is proved, first, from Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations 1, ch. 1, where he asserts: Since we cannot bring the things about which we dispute into the schools, we use words in place of things; just as those who play use counters in place of money: therefore Aristotle understands that words supposit for things alone. It is proved, second: because in this proposition, Man disputes, the word man does not supposit for the concept of man, but for man himself, of whom disputing is verified, and not of the concept.

Iam quòd voces exprimant conceptus, sic explicant: voces non solùm inuentæ sunt, vt pro rebus ponantur in propositione: sed etiam vt per eas conceptus nostros internos manifestemus aliis, quibus non possunt per se innotescere: ergo voces sunt quasi manifestatiuæ & declaratiuæ conceptuum: declarare autem, atque exprimere, idem sunt: & ideo licèt voces non significent reconceptus, eos tamen propriè dicuntur exprimere.

Now, that words express concepts they explain thus: words were invented not only so that they might be put in a proposition in place of things, but also so that through them we might manifest to others our internal concepts, which cannot become known to them by themselves: therefore words are as it were manifestative and declarative of concepts; but to declare and to express are the same: and therefore, although words do not signify concepts, they are nevertheless properly said to express them.

5 Secunda opinio tenet, voces non solas res, sed etiam conceptus significare: ita D. Th. expressè quæst. 8. de Potentia, art. 1. & 1. part. q. 27. art. 1. quem sequuntur omnes ferè interpretes Arist. cap. præsenti, & Arist. ipse expressè id docet, his verbis: Sunt ergo ea quæ sunt in voce, earum quæ sunt in anima passionum notæ, &c. Per passionem animæ, conceptus ipsos intelligens: & non res conceptas, vt volunt moderni: quia passiones animæ, actus eius significant in ea manentes: qui sunt conceptus, non res intellectæ: res enim nihil sunt ipsius animæ, nec in ea manent, sed solùm sunt obiecta actus eius, extra eam existentia: asserit autem esse notas eorum, id est signa: ergo sentit eos significare. Et ita tenendum est.

5 The second opinion holds that words signify not only things, but also concepts: so St. Thomas expressly, On Power, q. 8, a. 1, and 1 p., q. 27, a. 1, whom almost all the interpreters of Aristotle follow on the present chapter; and Aristotle himself expressly teaches it in these words: Those things, therefore, which are in the voice are signs of the passions which are in the soul, etc.; by passion of the soul meaning the concepts themselves, and not the things conceived, as the moderns would have it: because passions of the soul signify its acts remaining in it, which are the concepts, not the things understood: for the things are nothing of the soul itself, nor do they remain in it, but are only objects of its act, existing outside it: and he asserts that words are marks of them, that is, signs: therefore he holds that they signify them. And so it is to be held.

Sed vt eam explicemus, & probemus simul, notandum est, Signum quatuor diuisionibus diuidi.

But in order that we may explain and prove it at the same time, it should be noted that the sign is divided by four divisions.

Prima diuisio est: Signum aliud est Proprium, aliud improprium. Signum proprium, duas habet conditiones. Primam, vt faciat nos venire in cognitionem alicuius rei, à se distinctæ, quam dicitur significare. Secundam, vt à natura ipsa, vel hominum voluntate, ad talem rem significandam sit institutum: vtramque conditionem habent suspiria, & gemitus: & ideo propria signa naturalia sunt alicuius affectus interni. Cæterùm defectu primæ conditionis, voces nullam rem extra se significantes, non sunt propria signa, sed nimis impropria: vt blictri,

The first division is: One sign is Proper, another improper. The proper sign has two conditions. The first, that it make us come into the cognition of some thing distinct from itself, which it is said to signify. The second, that it be instituted, by nature itself or by the will of men, to signify such a thing. Sighs and groans have both conditions, and therefore they are proper natural signs of some internal affection. But for lack of the first condition, words that signify no thing outside themselves are not proper signs, but quite improper ones: as blictri,

p. 501

& similes. Defectu verò secundæ, risus non est signum rationalitatis, licèt per eum cognoscatur à nobis: quia non est à natura institutus ad significandam rationalitatem, licèt per eum possit à nobis demonstratiuè cognosci.

and the like. But for want of the second condition, laughter is not a sign of rationality, although rationality is known by us through it: because it is not instituted by nature to signify rationality, although rationality can be known demonstratively by us through it.

Secunda diuisione diuiditur signum proprium. relicto improprio, in signum Naturale, Ad placitum, & Ex consuetudine. Naturale est, quòd à natura institutum est, ad rem aliquam significandam, vt gemitis. Ad placitum: quod ex voluntate hominum, vt homo ad significandum hominem. Ex consuetudine verò, quod consuetudo facit, vt per vnam rem intelligamus aliam, ad quam significandam communiter ordinatur, vt mappæ appositæ, signa sunt prandij.

By the second division the proper sign, the improper being left aside, is divided into the sign Natural, By Convention, and From Custom. Natural is that which is instituted by nature to signify some thing, as groaning. By convention: that which is instituted by the will of men, as the word man to signify man. From custom, that which custom brings about, so that through one thing we understand another which it is commonly ordered to signify: as napkins laid out are signs of a meal.

Tertia diuisio signi est, In Internum: & Externum. Internum est, quod intra animam nostram permanet, vt conceptus: externum verò, quod per externos sensus, vt visum, & auditum percipitur: & talia sunt signa, voces, & scripturæ: hoc tantùm signum descripsit D. Aug. lib. de Doctrina Christ. cap. 1. his verbis: Signum est res, quæ præter speciem quam ingerit sensibus, alterius rei à se facit in cognitionem venire.

The third division of the sign is into Internal and External. Internal is that which remains within our soul, as a concept; external, that which is perceived through the external senses, such as sight and hearing: and such signs are words and writings. This sign alone St. Augustine described in the book On Christian Doctrine, ch. 1, in these words: A sign is a thing which, besides the species that it impresses on the senses, makes something other than itself come into cognition.

Quarta diuisio signi est: Signum aliud est Manifestatiuum tantum: aliud Manifestatiuum simul, & Suppositiuum. Manifestatiuum tantum, est illud quod rem aliquam à se distinctam significat, aut repræsentat, pro qua non sustituitur, vel supponitur in propositione: vt sonus campanæ signum lectionis futuræ est, sed non ponitur pro ea in propositione. Manifestatiuum verò, & suppositiuum simul est, quod non solùm rem significat, sed pro ea ponitur: vt hęc vox homo, ponitur in propositione pro homine, quem significat.

The fourth division of the sign is: one sign is Manifestative only, another Manifestative and Suppositive at once. Manifestative only is that which signifies or represents some thing distinct from itself, for which it is not substituted, or does not supposit, in a proposition: as the sound of the bell is a sign of the lecture to come, but is not put for it in a proposition. Manifestative and suppositive at once is that which not only signifies a thing but is put for it: as this word man is put in a proposition for the man whom it signifies.

6 Secundò notandum: Significatum duplex esse posse, Quo, & Quod. Significatum, Quo, dicitur res illa ad quam significandam ordinatur signum. Significatum, Quod, dicitur medium, quo eam significat. Præterea, Significatum, aliud est Proximum, aliud Remotum, & quasi vltimatum: Et iuxta hanc doctrinam, intelligendum est, quo pacto voces significent res, & conceptus. Nam conceptus significant immediatè quidem, non vt quod, sed solùm vt quo: quia mediis conceptibus, quos de rebus formamus, significamus eas per voces: res verò significant etiam immediatè vt quod, sed quasi remotè, & vltimatè, comparatas ad significatum, quo, nempe conceptus. Præterea, Voces sunt signa conceptuum significatiua tantùm, non suppositiua, rerum verò significatiua simul, & suppositiua: quia pro eis, & non pro conceptibus supponuntur in propositione.

6 Second, it should be noted that the significate can be twofold, Quo and Quod. The significate Quod is the name given to that thing which the sign is ordered to signify. The significate Quo is the name given to the medium by which it signifies it. Moreover, one significate is Proximate, another Remote and as it were ultimate. And according to this doctrine it is to be understood in what way words signify things and concepts. For they signify concepts immediately indeed, not as quod, but only as quo: because by means of the concepts which we form of things we signify those things through words; but things they signify also immediately as quod, yet as it were remotely and ultimately, compared with the significate quo, namely the concept. Moreover, words are signs of concepts that are significative only, not suppositive; but of things they are significative and suppositive at once: because in a proposition they supposit for things, and not for concepts.

His suppositis, Opinio Arist. D. Tho. & nostra duabus conclusionibus

These things supposed, the opinion of Aristotle, of St. Thomas, and our own is set out in two conclusions. I i iij

p. 502

explicatur. Prima est: Voces significant conceptus immediatè, & vt quo: ideo minùs principaliter: res verò immediatè quidem, vt Quod, & ideo principaliter: sed respectu conceptuum, quasi remotè, & vltimatè & tam conceptus, quàm res ad placitum. Probatur prima pars hoc argumento: Plures voces impositæ sunt ad significandas naturas vniuersales, vt homo, & animal: sed res non sunt vniuersales: vt sunt ad extra, sed vt per conceptus communes à nobis abstractæ, atque cognitæ: ergo non significantur per voces, nisi mediis conceptibus communibus, quos de eis formamus. Et ex consequenti, conceptus significant immediatè, vt quo: & ideo minùs principaliter: & ipsis mediis res vltimatè, principaliter. Probatur hæc vltima consequentia: quia conceptus non sunt nisi media quædam, quibus significantur res, ad quas significandas ordinantur.

The first is: Words signify concepts immediately, and as quo, and therefore less principally; but things immediately indeed, as Quod, and therefore principally, but with respect to the concepts as it were remotely and ultimately; and both concepts and things by convention. The first part is proved by this argument: Many words have been imposed to signify universal natures, as man and animal; but things are not universal as they exist outside, but as abstracted and known by us through common concepts: therefore they are not signified by words except by means of the common concepts which we form of them. And consequently, words signify concepts immediately, as quo, and therefore less principally; and by means of these, things ultimately and principally. This last consequence is proved: because concepts are nothing but certain media by which the things are signified which they are ordered to signify.

Secunda verò pars: quòd voces significant res, & conceptus ad placitum, euidens est.: quia non habent significationem à natura, sed soni quidam sunt, nihil præter se, & prolatotem impropriè significantes: ab hominibus verò ordinatæ sunt ad significandum res alias, mediis conceptibus: ergo significant ad placitum, quod colligitur ex verbis Scripturæ sacræ, Gen. 2. Formatis igitur Dominus Deus de humo cunctis animantibus terræ, & vniuersis volatilibus cœli, adduxit ad Adam, vt videret, quid vocaret ea: omne enim quod vocauit Adam animæ viuentis, ipsum est nomen eius.

The second part, that words signify things and concepts by convention, is evident: because they do not have their signification from nature, but are certain sounds, improperly signifying nothing besides themselves and the speaker; but they have been ordered by men to signify other things by means of concepts: therefore they signify by convention.
