This is gathered from the words of sacred Scripture, Gen. 2: Therefore the Lord God, having formed out of the ground all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of the air, brought them to Adam to see what he would call them: for whatever Adam called a living creature, that is its name.

Quod autem de vocibus dicimus, solùm est intelligendum de his, quæ Dearticulatæ sunt, hoc est, lingua, dentibus, & palato formatæ: his enim tantùm vtuntur homines ad significandum conceptus, & res: & ideo dicuntur significare ad placitum. Inarticulata verò, quales sunt voces brutorum, gemitus etiam, & suspiria nostra: naturaliter significant aliquem affectum internum, nisi fortè eum explicemus dearticulata voce: nam tunc iam per eam significaretur ad placitum: quia diuersæ nationes, diuersis aliquando dearticulatis vocibus, in hunc finem significandi affectum internum vtuntur.

But what we say of words is to be understood only of those which are articulate, that is, formed by the tongue, teeth, and palate: for only these do men use to signify concepts and things, and therefore they are said to signify by convention. But inarticulate ones, such as the sounds of brute animals, and also our groans and sighs, signify some internal affection naturally, unless perhaps we express it by an articulate word: for then it would at once be signified by that word by convention, because different nations sometimes use different articulate words for this purpose of signifying an internal affection.

Ad arg. alterius opinionis, Distinguenda est maior, nam signum significatiuum tantùm, & non suppositiuum, non significat id, pro quo supponitur, sed id pro quo non supponitur, signum verò significatiuum, & suppositiuum simul id tantùm significat, pro quo supponitur. Et ideo non est vniuersaliter verum quòd voces illud tantùm significent, pro quo supponuntur: quia licèt respectu rerum, sint signa significatiua, & suppositiua simul, tamen respectu conceptuum, solùm sunt significatiua: vnde possunt eos significare quamuis non supponantur

To the argument of the other opinion: The major is to be distinguished. For a sign that is significative only, and not suppositive, does not signify that for which it supposits, but that for which it does not supposit; whereas a sign that is significative and suppositive at once signifies only that for which it supposits. And therefore it is not universally true that words signify only that for which they supposit: because, although with respect to things they are signs significative and suppositive at once, yet with respect to concepts they are only significative: whence they can signify concepts although they do not supposit

p. 503

pro eis in propositione. Et in hoc sensu intelligitur testimonium Aristotelis, qui de vocibus, vt sunt signa significatiua simul, & suppositiua rerum, loquitur; hoc tamen non tollit, quin etiam possint significare conceptus, vt media, licèt pro eis non supponantur.

for them in a proposition. And in this sense is to be understood the testimony of Aristotle, who speaks of words as they are signs of things significative and suppositive at once: this, however, does not exclude that they can also signify concepts, as media, although they do not supposit for them.

CHAPTER II

De Nomine.

On the Noun.

TEXTVS ARIST.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE.

Nomen igitur est vox significatiua secundùm placitum, sine tempore, cuius nulla pars significatiua est separata.

A noun, then, is a word significative by convention, without time, no part of which is significative when separated.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

INtentum huius capitis, est explicare naturam nominis: de quo agit Aristo. tanquam de parte actuali enunciationis, & priusquam de verbo, tanquam de simpliciori: nam verbum non solùm rem aliquam significat, sed etiam actionem cum tempore, nomen verò solam rem, vel quia nomen est quasi materia propositionis, & ideo primum eius fundamentum: verbum verò quasi forma. Caput autem hoc non eget diuisione; quia nihil aliud in eo facit Arist. quàm definitionem nominis assignare, & singulas eius particulas explicare.

he intent of this chapter is to explain the nature of the noun, T which Aristotle treats as an actual part of the enunciation, and before the verb, as being simpler: for the verb signifies not only some thing but also action with time, whereas the noun signifies only a thing; or because the noun is as it were the matter of the proposition, and therefore its first foundation, while the verb is as it were its form. This chapter, moreover, needs no division, because Aristotle does nothing else in it than assign the definition of the noun and explain each of its particles.

Definitio nominis ita habet: Nomen est vox significatiua secundùm placitum, sine tempore, cuius nulla pars significatiua est separata. Vox ponitur in hac definitione loco generis, & accipitur pro sola dearticulata humanis instrumentis prolata, nempe, lingua, dentibus, palato, ac cæteris: Quam sic definiuit idem Aristo. 2. lib. de anima, textu 90. Vox est sonus, ab animalis ore prolatus, cum imaginatione quadam. Vnde per vocem, excluduntur soni inarticulati brutorum, atque etiam soni instrumentorum, qui alio modo satis imperfecto dicuntur voces. Significatiua etiam vocatur, vt excludantur voces humanæ dearticulatæ, nihil tamen significantes, vt blictri. Secundùm placitum, vt excludantur signa omnia naturalia. Sine tempore, vt excludatur verbum, quod cum tempore significat. Quid sit autem significare sine tempore, constabit capitulo sequenti, in quo explicatur, quid sit cum tempore significare. Cuius nulla pars significatiua est separata: ad differentiam orationis: cuius partes per se separatæ significant: vt partes

The definition of the noun runs thus: A noun is a word significative by convention, without time, no part of which is significative when separated. Word is put in this definition in place of the genus, and is taken only for the articulate word uttered by the human instruments, namely the tongue, teeth, palate, and the rest; which the same Aristotle defined thus in On the Soul 2, text 90: A word is a sound uttered from the mouth of an animal with a certain imagination. Hence by word are excluded the inarticulate sounds of brute animals, and also the sounds of instruments, which are called voices in another, rather imperfect way. It is also called significative, so that human words which are articulate but nevertheless signify nothing, such as blictri, may be excluded. By convention, so that all natural signs may be excluded. Without time, so that the verb, which signifies with time, may be excluded. What it is to signify without time, however, will be clear from the following chapter, in which it is explained what it is to signify with time. No part of which is significative when separated: in distinction from speech, whose parts signify per se when separated: as the parts I i iiij

p. 504

huius orationis, homo albus. Probat tandem hanc particulam hoc argum. Si partes alicuius nominis separatæ significarent, maximè partes nominis compositi, vt partes huius nominis, Equiferus: sed partes eius separatæ, nihil significant: ergo nec partes separatæ alicuius nominis significabunt. Maior euidens est, quia cùm nomen compositum sæpe contineat plura nomina simplicia, tanquam partes, maior ratio erat in eo, vt partes eius separatæ significarent, quàm in nomine simplici, cuius partes non nisi syllabæ, & literæ sunt. Minorem verò probat: quia partes huius nominis, equiferus, ab eo separatæ, si tanquam partes eius accipiantur, nullam significationem retinent: cùm equiferus, non significet equum ferocem, sed aliud animal ab eo diuersum. A ratione tandem nominis, excludit nomina infinita vt non homo, non leo: quia non habent determinatam significationem, sed de omnibus dicuntur, præterquam de re significata per nomen, supra quod cadit negatio, vt Non homo, de omnibus dicitur, præter hominem. Verum autem nomen, aliquid determinatum significare debet. Excludit etiam casus obliquos, vt hominis, & hominem: quia non tam nomina: quàm deriuationes quædam à nomine ipso recto, censentur.

of this speech, white man. He proves this particle, finally, by this argument: If the parts of any noun signified when separated, most of all would the parts of a composite noun, as the parts of this noun equiferus [wild horse]: but its parts, when separated, signify nothing: therefore neither will the separated parts of any noun signify. The major is evident, because, since a composite noun often contains several simple nouns as parts, there was greater reason in it for its parts to signify when separated than in a simple noun, whose parts are nothing but syllables and letters. The minor he proves: because the parts of this noun equiferus, separated from it, if they are taken as its parts, retain no signification: since equiferus does not signify a fierce horse, but another animal different from it. Finally, by the ratio of noun he excludes infinite nouns, as non-man, non-lion: because they do not have a determinate signification, but are said of all things except the thing signified by the noun on which the negation falls, as Non-man is said of all things except man. But a true noun must signify something determinate. He also excludes the oblique cases, as hominis [of a man] and hominem [man, accusative]: because they are judged not so much nouns as certain derivations from the direct noun itself.

QUESTION I

Quæst. 1. An bene definiatur nomen per vocem — Whether the noun is rightly defined through word.

An bene definiatur nomen per vocem.

[…]

RAtio dubitandi est: quia nomen, & verbum, sunt partes propositionis, sed in mente & scriptura sunt propositiones non minùs quàm in vocibus: ergo erunt etiam nomina, & verba: si igitur per vocem definiatur nomen, diminuta erit definitio, non comprehendens omnia nomina.

The reason for doubting is: because the noun and the verb are parts of the proposition; but in the mind and in writing there are propositions no less than in words: therefore there will also be nouns and verbs there: if, then, the noun is defined through word, the definition will be deficient, not comprehending all nouns.

Circa modum intelligendi hanc definitionem, est prima opinio Louaniensium cap. præsenti: qui asserunt accommodari posse nominibus mentalibus, & scriptis, paucis mutatis. Mentalibus quidem, mutatis duabus particulis, nempe, vox, & secundùm placitum. Scriptis verò, mutata sola voce: & ideo non esse diminutam: quia licèt non comprehendat omnia nomina vt iacet, potest tamen omnia comprehendere, per accommodationem.

On the manner of understanding this definition, the first opinion is that of the Louvain commentators on the present chapter, who assert that it can be accommodated to mental and written nouns, a few things being changed: to mental ones, indeed, by changing two particles, namely word and by convention; to written ones, by changing word alone; and that it is therefore not deficient, because, although it does not comprehend all nouns as it stands, it can nevertheless comprehend them all by accommodation.

Hæc tamen opinio sustineri non potest: quia cùm definitio sit quasi indiuisibilis terminus definiti, sub qua tota eius essẽtia contineri debet, mutata qualibet particula, vel addita mutatur tota definitio; ergo si hæc definitio non potest conuenire omnibus nominibus, nisi detractis aliquibus particulis; sequitur

This opinion, however, cannot be sustained: because, since the definition is as it were an indivisible term of the definitum, under which its whole essence must be contained, if any particle whatever is changed or added the whole definition is changed: therefore, if this definition cannot fit all nouns unless some particles are taken away, it follows

p. 505

non posse eis conuenire, sed diminutam esse. Probatur consequentia: quia detractis illis particulis, non est eadem definitio, sed alia: ergo repugnat, hanc definitionem conuenire omnibus nominibus: vnde diminuta censebitur, si solùm potest conuenire cum detractione illarum particularum.

that it cannot fit them, but is deficient. The consequence is proved: because, when those particles are taken away, it is not the same definition, but another: therefore it is impossible that this definition should fit all nouns; whence it will be judged deficient if it can fit them only with the removal of those particles.

Nostra igitur sententia est, vera nomina solùm in vocibus reperiri simpliciter, in mente verò solùm conceptus rerum significatarum per nomina, qui potiùs dicuntur termini mentales, ex quibus propositio mentalis componitur. In scripturis verò solùm reperiuntur nomina per deriuationem à vocibus, quarum quasi supplementa sunt, vt cum absentibus agere possimus. Vnde sequitur bene definitum esse nomen ab Aristo. per vocem.

Our view, therefore, is that true nouns are found, simply speaking, only in words; but in the mind there are only the concepts of the things signified by the nouns, which are rather called mental terms, and of which the mental proposition is composed. In writings, on the other hand, nouns are found only by derivation from words, of which they are as it were supplements, so that we may deal with those who are absent. Whence it follows that the noun was rightly defined by Aristotle through word.

Probatur testimonio Arist. c. 2. Anteprædicamentorum, vbi definiens æquiuoca, ait: Ea esse, quorum nomen commune est, ratio verò substantiæ nomini accommodata, diuersa. Per rationem verò substantiæ, secundùm communem expositionem omnium, conceptus intelligitur: ergo sentit Arist. nomen à conceptu distingui, & ideo conceptum non esse nomen, sed in solis vocibus nomina reperiri. Probatur consequentia: quia vbi nomen est commune, conceptum asserit esse diuersum.

This is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, ch. 2 of the Antepredicaments, where, defining equivocals, he says: They are those whose name is common, but the ratio of the substance accommodated to the name is different. But by the ratio of the substance, according to the common exposition of all, the concept is understood: therefore Aristotle holds that the name is distinguished from the concept, and that therefore the concept is not a name, but that names are found in words alone. The consequence is proved: because where the name is common, he asserts that the concept is different.

Probatur etiam ratione: Quia antequam nomina imponeret rebus Adam, innominatæ censebantur, etiam si haberet proprios conceptus earum: & cùm primùm nomina eis imposuit, dixit Deus. Omne quod vocauit Adam animæ viuentis, ipsum est nomen eius. Quasi diceret, tunc primò cœpisse nomina. Et nos etiam dum non habemus vocem propriam, ad aliquam rem significãdum impositam, dicimus talem rem innominatam esse; quamuis proprium eius conceptum in mente habeamus. Ex quibus sequitur, in mente non esse nomina, sed conceptus, qui dicuntur termini mentales, ex quibus componitur compositio mentrlis: & rationem termini vniuersaliorem esse, nomine & verbo, ex quibus sola propositio vocalis propriè ac simpliciter componitur: in scriptura verò, solùm per quandam analogiam ad vocem per eam significatam, reperiuntur nomina, & verba: sunt enim scripturæ quasi nomina, & verba depicta. Non est igitur necessarium particulas detrahere à definitione Arist. vt conceptibus, & scripturis accommodetur: quia nec eis potest propriè conuenire: & ideo bene definiuit nomen per vocem.

It is proved also by reason: Because before Adam imposed names on things, they were held to be nameless, even if he had proper concepts of them; and as soon as he imposed names on them, God said: Whatever Adam called a living creature, that is its name. As if to say that names then first began. And we too, as long as we do not have a proper word imposed to signify some thing, say that such a thing is nameless, although we have its proper concept in the mind. From which it follows that in the mind there are not nouns but concepts, which are called mental terms, of which the mental composition is composed; and that the ratio of term is more universal than noun and verb, of which alone the vocal proposition is properly and simply composed; but in writing nouns and verbs are found only through a certain analogy to the word signified by it: for writings are as it were nouns and verbs depicted. It is not necessary, therefore, to take particles away from Aristotle’s definition in order that it be accommodated to concepts and writings, because it cannot properly fit them either; and therefore he rightly defined the noun through word.

Ad arg. pro ratione dubitandi propositum, Concessa maiori, & minori, neganda est consequentia; quia propositio in communi, non componitur ex nomine, & verbo, sed ex terminis:

To the argument proposed for the reason for doubting: Granting the major and the minor, the consequence is to be denied: because the proposition in common is not composed of noun and verb, but of terms

p. 506

quorum ratio vniuersalior est: sola autem propositio vocalis, ex nomine, & verbo componitur. Vnde non sequitur, vera nomina, & verba reperiri, vbicunque reperitur propositio, sed solùm quòd reperiantur termini, ex quibus componatur: qui in mentali, sunt conceptus extremorum, & copulæ, in scripta verò nomina, & verba depicta: & ideo non talia simpliciter, sed secundùm quid.

whose ratio is more universal; but only the vocal proposition is composed of noun and verb. Whence it does not follow that true nouns and verbs are found wherever a proposition is found, but only that terms are found of which it is composed: which in the mental proposition are the concepts of the extremes and of the copula, and in the written one nouns and verbs depicted; and therefore not such simply, but in a certain respect.

QUESTION II

An nomen definiatur per vocem, tanquam per verum genus.

Whether the noun is defined through word as through a true genus.

DVobus modis potest considerari vox. Primò Materialite, prout solùm dicit sonum dearticulatum humanis instrumentis. Secundo, Formaliter, prout significatiua: ex quo habet, quòd sit nomen, aut verbum: & primo modo considerata, habet se, tanquam subiectum eiusdem significationis, commune ad nomen, & verbum: sicut lignum, commune subiectum est, respectu cathedræ, & portæ, potens suscipere formam artificialem vtriusque: si verò, consideretur, vt significatiua, verum genus est ad nomen, & verbum. Quæstio igitur est, An nomen definiatur per eam materialiter sumptam, tanquam per subiectum, sicut statua definitur per lignum: vel potiùs, sumptam formaliter, prout significatiuam, tanquam per verum genus: ita vt vox significatiua, genus sit huius definitionis, & reliquæ particulæ, sint differentiæ.

Word can be considered in two ways. First, Materially, as it denotes only an articulate sound made by the human instruments. Second, Formally, as significative, from which it has it that it is a noun or a verb. And considered in the first way, it stands as the subject of that same signification, common to the noun and the verb: just as wood is a common subject with respect to a chair and a door, able to receive the artificial form of both. But if it is considered as significative, it is a true genus with respect to the noun and the verb. The question, then, is whether the noun is defined through word taken materially, as through a subject, as a statue is defined through wood; or rather through word taken formally, as significative, as through a true genus: so that significative word is the genus of this definition, and the remaining particles are differences.

Et prima opinio tenet, Nomen non definiri per vocem, tanquam per subiectum, sed per vocem significatiuam, tanquam per verum genus nomini & verbo commune: ita Niphus, Lemosius, & Psallus, c. præsenti: & probatur. Quia res quælibet, per definitionem quidditatiuam definienda est, si fieri potest, cùm iste sit optimus definiendi modus: sed posita significatiua, pro vero genere, erit quidditatiua definitio nominis: posita verò sola voce pro subiecto, non erit quidditatiua: cùm subiectum non sit genus accidentis, sed extra quidditatem eius: ergo primo modo intelligi debet definitum nomen ab Arist. potiùs quàm secundo.

And the first opinion holds that the noun is not defined through word as through a subject, but through significative word, as through a true genus common to the noun and the verb. So Nifo, Lemosius, and Psellus, on the present chapter; and it is proved: Because any thing whatever is to be defined by a quidditative definition, if that can be done, since this is the best mode of defining; but if significative is posited as a true genus, the definition of the noun will be quidditative, whereas if word alone is posited as a subject it will not be quidditative, since the subject is not the genus of an accident but outside its quiddity: therefore the noun as defined by Aristotle ought to be understood in the first way rather than in the second.

Secunda opinio est D. Tho. & Ammonij, ca. præsenti: Quòd non definiatur nomen ab Arist. per vocem significatiuam, tanquam per verum genus, sed per solam vocem, tanquam per subiectum, loco generis positum & hæc probabilior: cuius potissimum fundamentum colligitur ex Arist. 8. lib. Metaph. textu 6. vbi

The second opinion is that of St. Thomas and Ammonius, on the present chapter: that the noun is not defined by Aristotle through significative word as through a true genus, but through word alone, as through a subject, put in the place of the genus. And this is the more probable; its chief foundation is gathered from Aristotle, Metaph. 8, text 6, where

p. 507

proprium modum definiendi artificialia, ait, esse per subiectum loco generis, & per formam artificialem, loco differentiæ, vt si domum definire velis, dices, esse lapides, & ligna, ita composita, Et D. Th. opusc. de ente, & essentia, c. 7 non solùm artificialia, sed etiam accidentia omnia, meliùs definita ait per subiectum loco generis, quàm per verum genus. Et ratio huius est manifesta: quia essentia accidentis, & modus essendi eius, sumuntur per ordinem ad subiectum: ergo vtrumque fit magis notum per subiectum: & cùm definitio eo fine tradatur: vt per eam cognoscamus naturam definiti, melior modus definiendi accidentia erit per subiectum, pro genere positum, quàm per verum genus, quod per idem subiectum innotescit. Sea nomen, & verbum, sunt accidentia quædam artificialia, ab intellectu facta, & in concreto significata: ergo melius per vocem, tanquam per subiectum definienda sunt, quàm per vocem significatiuam, tanquam per verum genus: & sic censendum est ab Arist. esse definita.

he says that the proper mode of defining artificial things is through the subject in place of the genus, and through the artificial form in place of the difference: as, if you wish to define a house, you will say that it is stones and timbers so put together. And St. Thomas, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 7, says that not only artificial things but also all accidents are better defined through the subject in place of the genus than through a true genus. And the reason for this is manifest: because the essence of an accident and its mode of being are taken from its order to the subject: therefore both become better known through the subject; and since the definition is handed down for this end, that through it we may know the nature of the definitum, the better mode of defining accidents will be through the subject, put in place of the genus, rather than through the true genus, which becomes known through that same subject. But the noun and the verb are certain artificial accidents, made by the intellect and signified in the concrete: therefore they are better defined through word, as through a subject, than through significative word, as through a true genus; and so they are to be judged to have been defined by Aristotle.

Ad arg. alterius opinionis: Distinguenda est maior: nam si res, quæ definitur, sit substantia, quidditatiuè definienda est per genus, & differentiam, si fieri possit: si verò sit accidens, præsertim artificiale, & in concreto significatum, modus magis naturalis, & per quem essentia eius clariùs explicabitur, erit, illud definire per subiectum loco generis: quia verum genus, & vera eius differentia, per subiectum respectu cuius accipiuntur, potiùs quàm per se cognoscenda sunt: & ex consequenti quidditas, & essentia eius, ad quam cognoscendam ordinatur per se definitio.

To the argument of the other opinion: The major is to be distinguished. For if the thing that is defined is a substance, it is to be defined quidditatively through genus and difference, if that can be done; but if it is an accident, especially an artificial one and signified in the concrete, the more natural mode, and that through which its essence will be more clearly explained, will be to define it through the subject in place of the genus: because its true genus and its true difference are to be known through the subject with respect to which they are taken, rather than through themselves; and consequently so are its quiddity and essence, for the knowing of which a definition is per se ordered.

QUESTION III

An verum sit nomen significare ad placitum, vt in definitione dicitur.

Whether the noun truly signifies by convention, as is said in the definition.

10 CIrca modum significandi Vocum, Tres opinines refert D. Th. in Comment. huius capitis. Prima fuit eorum qui tenuerunt esse naturalia signa rerum: sicut nos dicimus de conceptibus: quam Pythagoræ, & eius discipulis, tribuit Dexippus, lib. 1. q. in categorias, c. 6. & videtur etiam fuisse Heracliti, & Cratilli. Probaturq; hoc arg. Quia quibus natura tribuit facultatẽ, seu potentiã ad aliquẽ actũ exercendum, consequenter tribuit instrumẽta naturalia, quibus illũ possint exercere: vt homini tribuit facultatem ad ambulandũ: & ideo tribuit eis pedes tali modo fabricatos, quib, ambulare possit: sed facultas loquẽdi naturalis est: ergo natura tribuit homini cum

10 Concerning the mode of signifying of Words, St. Thomas reports three opinions in the commentary on this chapter. The first was that of those who held that they are natural signs of things, as we say of concepts: which Dexippus, bk. 1 of the Questions on the Categories, ch. 6, attributes to Pythagoras and his disciples; and it seems also to have been that of Heraclitus and Cratylus. And it is proved by this argument: Because to those to whom nature has given a faculty, or power, for exercising some act, it consequently gives natural instruments by which they can exercise it: as it gave man the faculty of walking, and therefore gave him feet so fashioned that he can walk with them; but the faculty of speaking is natural: therefore nature gave man, together with

p. 508

ea, naturalia instrumenta, per quæ loqueretur: hæc autem instrumenta sunt voces, non nudæ: alioqui bruta etiam loqui possent, sed dearticulatæ, ac significatiuæ, sicut brutis, dedit voces naturaliter significantes, quibus possent suos effectus internos manifestare: ergo voces significatiuę sunt à natura datę hominibus, quibus possint aliis manifestare conceptus mentis internos. Ex quo euidenter sequitur, significationem earum esse naturalem, & non ex impositione hominum: quia naturale est quidquid à natura conceditur.

it, natural instruments through which he might speak; but these instruments are words, not bare ones (otherwise brute animals too could speak), but articulate and significative ones, just as to brute animals nature gave sounds signifying naturally, by which they might manifest their internal affections: therefore significative words were given by nature to men, by which they might manifest to others the internal concepts of the mind. From which it evidently follows that their signification is natural, and not from the imposition of men: because whatever is granted by nature is natural.

Secunda opinio ex diametro opposita est, asserens, significationem vocum non solùm non esse à natura: sed sic ex beneplacito hominum procedere, vt possit quisque pro libito, his nominibus iam impositis vti, vel alia noua excogitare, & ad significandum imponere, eisque vti, prout sibi placuerit ad loquendum: & postmodum eisdem relictis, noua alia imponere: quam videtur tenuisse Hermogenes quidam Philosophus Platone, & Aristotel. antiquior, vt Plato ipse testatur in Dialogo Cratyllo.

The second opinion is diametrically opposed, asserting that the signification of words not only is not from nature, but proceeds from the good pleasure of men in such a way that anyone may at his discretion use these names already imposed, or devise other new ones and impose them for signifying, and use them in speaking as he pleases, and afterward, leaving these, impose other new ones. This seems to have been held by a certain Hermogenes, a Philosopher older than Plato and Aristotle, as Plato himself testifies in the dialogue Cratylus.

Ratio huius sententiæ est: quia si vocum significatio ex libera voluntate hominum dependet, mutari poterit pro libitu: ita vt voces hodie impositæ ad significandum, crastino die nihil iam significent aut à prima significatione mutentur, ac de nouo imponantur ad alias res diuersas significandas: & ideo cadere dicantur à significatione, ex quo nullum sequetur inconueniens.

The reason for this view is: because, if the signification of words depends on the free will of men, it can be changed at discretion; so that words imposed today for signifying may tomorrow signify nothing any longer, or be changed from their first signification and be imposed anew to signify other different things, and therefore be said to fall away from their signification; from which no inconvenience follows.

Tertia opinio media est inter hæc extrema, Concedens voces non significare naturaliter; sed ex impositione hominum: non tamen ita esse liberam, vt quisque pro libitu possit, his aut illis vocibus vti, easque de nouo ad significandum imponere, sed congruentem naturis rerum, ad quas significandas imponuntur: ita vt singulis rebus, iuxta propriam naturam talia sunt nomina accommodata. Itaque libera hominum impositio, quandam considerationem discretam habuit concomitantem vel præcedentem: per quam impositor, cognoscens rerum naturas, eis accommodauit propria nomina, quibus congruenter significarentur: & talis impositio perpetuò durat, & ab omnibus sic inuiolabiliter recepta est, vt nemini liceat pro libitu eam mutare, aut nouas impositiones vocum introducere. Hanc sententiam secuti sunt grauissimi Philosophi, Plato vbi suprà, Aristot. in his capitibus, Tullius lib. 1. Academicarum quæstionum, Quintilianus lib. 8. institutionum, cap. 6. D. Th. Albertus Magnus, cum cæteris expositoribus huius capitis. Et hæc est vera & tenenda.

The third opinion is midway between these extremes, granting that words do not signify naturally, but from the imposition of men; yet that this imposition is not so free that anyone may at his discretion use these or those words and impose them anew for signifying, but is congruent with the natures of the things they are imposed to signify: so that to each thing, according to its proper nature, such names are accommodated. And so the free imposition of men had a certain discerning consideration accompanying or preceding it, through which the imposer, knowing the natures of things, accommodated to them proper names by which they might be congruently signified; and such an imposition lasts perpetually, and has been so inviolably received by all that no one may change it at his discretion or introduce new impositions of words. This view has been followed by the weightiest Philosophers: Plato in the place cited above; Aristotle in these chapters; Cicero, bk. 1 of the Academic Questions; Quintilian, bk. 8 of the Institutes, ch. 6; St. Thomas; Albert the Great, with the other expositors of this chapter. And this is true and to be held.

p. 509

11 Quam vt explicemus simul, & probemus, notandum est, Res esse in duplici differentia: nam quædam sunt Naturales, quibus certum est, à primo nostro parente, diuina sapientia prædito, per quam perfectè cognouit naturam singularum rerum nomina fuisse accommodata ex directione Dei, vt verba hæc Genes. 2. ostendunt: Formatis igitur Dominus Deus de humo, cunctis animantibus terræ, & vniuersis volatilibus cœli, adduxit ea ad Adam, vt videret, quid vocaret ea: omne enim quod vocauit Adam animæ viuentis, ipsum est nomen eius. Quasi dicat Deus vniuersalem hanc impositionem, ex eius commissione factam sic esse perpetuam: vt nunquam omnino, aut vbicunque ab aliquo mutanda sit: licèt diuersa sint nomina, iuxta diuersitatem nationum, & linguarum: in quibus etiam est euidens, nulli vnquam licuisse pro libitu mutare impositionem. Aliæ sunt res Artificiales, quibus etiam ab hominibus arte præditis & per eam perfectè cognoscentibus earum conditionem, iuxta eam conuenientia, accommodata sunt nomina: hoc est talia, vt significatio eorum, aut ex modo quo fiunt, aut ex aliqua earum proprietate, vel vsu in quem ordinantur per artem, desumatur. Quod maiori ex parte, verum esse intelligendum est: nam aliquando contingit, vt nulla talis similitudo, nobis saltem cognita, in nominis impositione seruetur: & hæc doctrina simul explicat, & probat veritatem communis sententiæ, quam sequimur.

11 In order to explain and prove it at the same time, it should be noted that things are of two different kinds. For some are Natural, to which it is certain that names were accommodated, at God’s direction, by our first parent, endowed with divine wisdom, through which he perfectly knew the nature of each thing, as these words of Gen. 2 show: Therefore the Lord God, having formed out of the ground all the living creatures of the earth and all the birds of the air, brought them to Adam to see what he would call them: for whatever Adam called a living creature, that is its name. As if God were saying that this universal imposition, made by his commission, is perpetual in such a way that it is never altogether, or anywhere, to be changed by anyone, although names are different according to the diversity of nations and languages; in which also it is evident that no one has ever been permitted to change the imposition at his discretion. Others are Artificial things, to which also names have been accommodated by men endowed with art, who through it perfectly know their condition, names agreeing with that condition: that is, such that their signification is taken either from the way in which they are made, or from some property of theirs, or from the use to which they are ordered by art. This is to be understood as true for the most part: for it sometimes happens that no such likeness, at least none known to us, is preserved in the imposition of a name. And this doctrine at once explains and proves the truth of the common view, which we follow.

Ad arg. verò primæ sententiæ: Concessa maiori, neganda est minor: quòd voces sint instrumenta facultatis naturalis ad loquendum, sed potiùs instrumenta huius facultatis sunt, lingua, dentes, & palatum, quibus formantur eædem voces: & iam formatæ imponuntur ad significandum, vt media esse possint, quibus homo proprios conceptus aliis explicet: quare licèt ex parte soni voces sint naturales, ex parte tamen significationis per artem, vel scientiam fiunt: sicut cathedra, ex parte ligni naturalis est: sed artificialis ex parte formæ, per artem factam: & ideo simpliciter vocatur artificialis, sic etiam nomina, & verba artificialia sunt vocanda.

But to the argument of the first opinion: Granting the major, the minor is to be denied, namely that words are the instruments of the natural faculty of speaking; rather, the instruments of this faculty are the tongue, teeth, and palate, by which those same words are formed; and once formed they are imposed for signifying, so that they may be media by which a man may express his own concepts to others. Wherefore, although on the part of the sound words are natural, yet on the part of the signification they come about through art or science: just as a chair is natural on the part of the wood, but artificial on the part of the form, made through art, and therefore is called simply artificial; so too nouns and verbs are to be called artificial.

Argumentum verò secundæ opinionis, ex doctrina tradita solutum est: quia licèt libera sit impositio vocum ad significandum, conformis tamen naturis rerum: & ideo non à quocunque facta: sed à sapientibus qui perfectè cognoscentes earum naturas, talia nomina, eis congruentia accommodarunt: vnde nec variari potest pro libitu significatio nominum: nec ab ea nomina cadere possunt.

But the argument of the second opinion is solved by the doctrine handed down: because, although the imposition of words for signifying is free, it is nevertheless conformed to the natures of things, and therefore not made by just anyone, but by wise men who, perfectly knowing their natures, accommodated to them such names as were congruent with them; whence neither can the signification of names be varied at discretion, nor can names fall away from it.

p. 510

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

An verum sit, partes nominis separatas, non esse significatiuas.

Whether it is true that the parts of a noun, when separated, are not significative.

HAnc particulam definitionis probauit Arist. ex nomine composito, cuius partes separatæ, ait, non sunt significatiuæ, vt partes eius sunt: etiam si sint integra nomina: ergo multò minùs partes nominis simplicis separatæ, erunt significatiuæ: cùm non sint integra nomina, sed syllabæ, & literæ: sed hæc ratio nihil valet: ergo non probatur per eam, quòd partes nominis separatæ, non sint significatiuæ, nec verum hoc erit. Probatur antecedens: Quia partes nominis compositu, sunt integra nomina, vel nomen integrum, & verbum, vt patet in hoc nomine agricola: & separatæ retinent eandem significationem, per quam componebant nomen: ergo partes nominis compositi separatæ, etiam vt partes eius, vel iuxta significationem totius, sunt significatiuæ Probatur minor, nam hoc nomen ager, & hoc verbum, colo, componebant nomen, agricola, per proprias significationes, nempe, & ager significas agrum, & colo actionem colendi: vnde agricola, significant colentem agrum & hanc eandem significationem retinent separata à compositione: vt notum est: ergo verè significant iuxta significationem totius, vel vt sunt partes eius: quare nec ratio Arist. probat, partes nominis separatas non significare; nec verum esse potest, saltem in nomine composito,

Aristotle proved this particle of the definition from a composite noun, whose parts when separated, he says, are not significative as they are its parts, even though they are whole nouns: therefore much less will the parts of a simple noun be significative when separated, since they are not whole nouns but syllables and letters. But this reasoning is worth nothing: therefore it is not proved by it that the parts of a noun when separated are not significative; nor will this be true. The antecedent is proved: Because the parts of a composite noun are whole nouns, or a whole noun and a verb, as is plain in this noun agricola [farmer]; and when separated they retain the same signification through which they composed the noun: therefore the parts of a composite noun when separated are significative even as its parts, or according to the signification of the whole. The minor is proved: for this noun ager [field] and this verb colo [I till] composed the noun agricola through their proper significations, namely, ager signifying a field and colo the action of tilling: whence agricola signifies one tilling a field; and they retain this same signification when separated from the composition, as is well known: therefore they truly signify according to the earlier signification, or as they are its parts. Wherefore neither does Aristotle’s reasoning prove that the parts of a noun do not signify when separated, nor can it be true, at least in a composite noun.

Probatur secundò: Quia si nomina simplicia caderẽt à propria significatione, & imponerentur ad significãdas res diuersas, etiam caderet à sua significatione nomen cõpositum: ergo pendet significatio eius, ex propriis significationibus partium: sed partes separatæ, retinent proprias significationes: ergo separatę significabunt iuxta significationem totius Pro solutione huius quæst. notandum est, Nomen compositum, sic ex nominibus integris, aut ex nomine & verbo componi, vt ex pluribus, ac diuersis significationibus eorum, resultet tertia quædam significatio indiuisibilis eiusdem nominis compositi: quæ significatio, non potest in eisdem iam separatis conseruari: in quo simile est nomen compositum, naturali composito viuẽti ex anima, & corpore facto, non quocunque, sed eterogeneo: hoc est partes habenti diuersæ rationis, vt brachium, caput, & pedes: non enim componitur nomen aliquod, ex multis nominibus, eandem rem significantibus, vt ex gladio,

It is proved second: Because if simple nouns fell away from their proper signification and were imposed to signify different things, the composite noun too would fall away from its signification: therefore its signification depends on the proper significations of the parts; but the parts when separated retain their proper significations: therefore when separated they will signify according to the signification of the whole. For the solution of this question it should be noted that a composite noun is composed of whole nouns, or of a noun and a verb, in such a way that from their several and different significations there results a certain third, indivisible signification of that composite noun; which signification cannot be preserved in those same parts once separated. In which respect the composite noun is like a natural living composite made of soul and body, not any body whatever but a heterogeneous one, that is, one having parts of different ratio, as the arm, the head, and the feet: for no noun is composed of many nouns signifying the same thing, as from gladius [sword],

p. 511

& ense: sed ex significantibus res diuersas: quare ex his diuersis significationibus, resultat tertia significatio totius, diuersa à partibus. Vt patet in nomine, respublica, & in nomine equiferus: quia nec respublica, significat rem quamlibet, vel negotium publicum: sed congregationem ciuium sub his legibus, & tali ordine dispositam: quæ diuersum quid est, à significatione vtriusque partis separatæ: & equiferus, significat non equum ferocem, quem significant partes separatæ, sed aliud animal valde diuersum. Vnde, sicut anima non informat partes separatas corporis, sed dum separantur à toto, aliam formam diuersam consequuntur: ita forma nominis compositi, quæ est significatio eius, non informat partes separatas, sed alias habent significationes sibi proprias partes atque diuersas significatione totius, quam participabant, dum illud componebant.

and ensis [sword], but of nouns signifying different things: wherefore from these different significations there results a third signification of the whole, different from the parts. As is plain in the noun respublica [commonwealth], and in the noun equiferus: because neither does respublica signify any thing whatever, or public business, but the gathering of citizens disposed under such laws and in such an order, which is something different from the signification of either part when separated; and equiferus signifies not a fierce horse, which the parts signify when separated, but another, very different animal. Whence, just as the soul does not inform the separated parts of the body, but while they are separated from the whole they acquire another, different form: so the form of the composite noun, which is its signification, does not inform the separated parts, but the parts have other significations proper to themselves and different from the signification of the whole, in which they participated while they composed it.

13 Itaque sicut quælibet pars nominis compositi, per se sumpta, habet propriam significationem vnam, & indiuisibilem, quæ non conuenit syllabis, nec in eis separatis permanet, sed desinit esse, & quasi corrumpitur separatis syllabis: sic etiam nomen compositum ex aliis nominibus, aut ex nomine, & verbo, propriam habet significationem, distinctam à significatione partium, & indiuisibilem quidem, & ideo talem, quę non prædicatur de partibus, nec in eis separatis permanere potest. Et ratio huius est: quia nomen compositum, distincta impositione imponitur, ad significandum totum, atque ad significandas partes: & ad significandum rem diuersam ab ea quam partes significant: similem tamen aliquo modo, & quæ non resultaret, nisi ex his partibus. Vnde sequitur, diuersa nomina, ita per proprias significationes concurrere ad ponendum aliud, vt cùm media alia impositione, & ad aliam rem significandam concurrant, proprias significationes amittant in tali compositione, & aliam diuersam participent: licèt similem propriis: sed dum à compositione separantur, illam rursus significationem quam in toto habebant, amittunt, & proprias retinent. Et hoc est, quod dici solet, separatas non significare, iuxta significationem totius. Licèt videantur significare, propter similitudinem, quæ reperitur inter significationem totius, & proprias earum: Dependet enim significatio totius, ex eis, verùm distincta est, & in eis permanere non potest.

13 And so, just as each part of a composite noun, taken by itself, has its own one and indivisible signification, which does not belong to the syllables nor remain in them when separated, but ceases to be and is as it were corrupted when the syllables are separated: so also a noun composed of other nouns, or of a noun and a verb, has its own signification, distinct from the signification of the parts, and indivisible indeed, and therefore such that it is not predicated of the parts nor can remain in them when separated. And the reason for this is: because the composite noun is imposed by a distinct imposition to signify the whole, and not to signify the parts, and to signify a thing different from the one which the parts signify, yet in some way similar, and which would not result except from these parts. Whence it follows that different nouns so concur through their proper significations to compose another that, since they concur by means of another imposition and to signify another thing, they lose their proper significations in such a composition and participate in another, different one, although similar to their own; but when they are separated from the composition, they lose again that signification which they had in the whole, and retain their own. And this is what is commonly said: that when separated they do not signify according to the signification of the whole, although they seem to signify on account of the likeness found between the signification of the whole and their own; for the signification of the whole depends on them, but it is distinct, and cannot remain in them.

Ex hac doctrina respondetur quæstioni: verum esse, quòd asserit Arist. in definitione nominis, quòd partes eius, si vt partes accipiantur, non sunt significatiuæ, dum ab eo separantur:

From this doctrine the question is answered: that what Aristotle asserts in the definition of the noun is true, that its parts, if they are taken as parts, are not significative when they are separated from it;

p. 512

quamuis proprias significationes separatæ retineant: quia cùm significatio totius, distincta sit à propriis partium significationibus, & sit quasi forma rei heterogeneæ, partes diuersæ rationis informans, corrumpitur separatis partibus. Et ideo potest in eis permanere.

although when separated they retain their proper significations: because, since the signification of the whole is distinct from the proper significations of the parts, and is as it were the form of a heterogeneous thing, informing parts of different ratio, it is corrupted when the parts are separated; and therefore it cannot remain in them.

Ad primum arg. Distinguenda est minor, quòd partes nominis compositi componant illud per proprias significationes: nam si ita intelligatur, quòd significatio totius, non sit alia à significatione partium, falsum est: cùm distincta impositione, & ad rem distinctam significandam, vel saltem modum distinctum habentem, imponatur. Si verò per proprias significationes concurrere intelligatur, ita, vt tertia significatio, à propriis distincta, atque indiuisibilis, cui simplex etiam & distinctus conceptus correspondet in mente, à conceptibus partium per se sumptarum, verum est: sed ex eo non sequitur: quòd partes separatæ retineant eandem significationem totius, vel quam ab eo participabant: quia hæc statim corrumpitur, quam primum partes separantur: sicut corrumpitur nomine ipsum compositum: ideo non potest in eis permanere. Quocirca bene Arist. dixit, nihil iam significare, iuxta significationem totius, vel vt partes eius.

To the first argument: The minor is to be distinguished, namely that the parts of a composite noun compose it through their proper significations. For if it is understood in this way, that the signification of the whole is not other than the signification of the parts, it is false, since it is imposed by a distinct imposition and to signify a distinct thing, or at least one having a distinct mode. But if they are understood to concur through their proper significations in such a way that a third signification results, distinct from their own and indivisible, to which there also corresponds in the mind a simple concept, distinct from the concepts of the parts taken by themselves, it is true; but from this it does not follow that the parts when separated retain that same signification of the whole, or the one they participated from it: because this is corrupted at once, as soon as the parts are separated, just as the composite noun itself is corrupted; therefore it cannot remain in them. Wherefore Aristotle rightly said that they no longer signify anything according to the signification of the whole, or as its parts.

Ad secundum: Concedendum est primum enthymema, sed neganda vltima consequentia quòd partes separatæ significent iuxta significationem totius: nam licèt significatio totius pendeat ex significatione partium, & desinat esse partibus cadentibus à propria significatione: nihilominus cùm distincta sit significatio totius, à propriis partium significationibus, atque indiuisibilis, corrumpitur eis separatis: vnde permanere non potest in eis: sed licèt proprias significationes retineant, verum est, nihil significare separatas, iuxta significationem totius: quia nihil retinent de significatione eius: licèt eam aliquando retinere videantur, propter similitudinem, quam habent propriæ, cum significatione totius, iam corruptæ.

To the second: The first enthymeme is to be granted, but the last consequence is to be denied, namely that the parts when separated signify according to the signification of the whole. For although the signification of the whole depends on the signification of the parts, and ceases to be when the parts fall away from their proper signification, nevertheless, since the signification of the whole is distinct from the proper significations of the parts, and indivisible, it is corrupted when they are separated; whence it cannot remain in them. But although they retain their proper significations, it is true that when separated they signify nothing according to the signification of the whole, because they retain nothing of its signification, although they sometimes seem to retain it, on account of the likeness which their own significations have with the signification of the whole, now corrupted.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

An nomen infinitum, omninò sit excludendum à definitione.

Whether the infinite noun is to be altogether excluded from the definition.

14 SEx sunt explicanda de nomine infinito. Primum, Quid sit, Secundum, Quid, & quomodo significet. Tertium, De quibus dicatur. Quartum, An nomina transcendentia possint fieri infinita.

14 Six things are to be explained concerning the infinite noun. First, What it is. Second, What and how it signifies. Third, Of what things it is said. Fourth, Whether transcendental nouns can be made infinite.

p. 513

Quintum, An nomen infinitum sit inter absoluta, vel inter connotatiua numerandum. Vltimum, An dicatur vniuocè de entibus, & non entibus, vel analogicè.

Fifth, Whether the infinite noun is to be counted among absolute or among connotative terms. Last, Whether it is said univocally of beings and non-beings, or analogically.

Circa primum notandum est: Negationem duobus modis sumi posse: Primò neganter, quod est sumi in tota vi negationis: quo pacto, etiamsi in principio propositionis ponatur, copulã eiusdem propositionis, & totam ipsam propositionem negat: & propterea de ea dictũ est, esse malignantis naturæ, ita, vt quidquid post se inueniat, destruat, & oppositum efficiat. Secundo modo, accipitur, non secundùm totam vim negationis, sed secundum limitatam: ita vt solùm neget significatum illius vocis, cui proxissiè adiungitur, nec vis eius vlteriùs transeat. Vnde, si adiungatur subiecto propositionis, non transit vis eius ad copulam, nec negatiuam reddit propositionem: & hoc est accipi Infinitanter: quia effectus eius, solùm est negare significatum nominis, cui adiungitur, & ex hoc, quasi infinitum illud efficere: quia cætera omnia significat, præter rem illam, supra quam cadit: vt non homo, significat cætera omnia præter hominem, nihil eorum determinans: & ideo dicitur habere significationem infinitam, Nomen igitur infinitum negationem includit, non neganter sumptam, hoc est, non in tota vi negationis, sed sumptam infinitanter: hoc est, secundùm vim negandi, determinatam ad proprium eius significatum.

Concerning the first it should be noted that negation can be taken in two ways. First, negatingly, which is to be taken in the whole force of the negation: in which way, even if it is placed at the beginning of the proposition, it negates the copula of that proposition and the whole proposition itself; and for this reason it has been said of it that it is of a malignant nature, so that whatever it finds after itself it destroys and makes into its opposite. In the second way it is taken not according to the whole force of the negation, but according to a limited force: so that it negates only the significate of the word to which it is most immediately joined, and its force does not pass further. Whence, if it is joined to the subject of the proposition, its force does not pass to the copula, nor does it render the proposition negative; and this is to be taken Infinitizingly: because its effect is only to negate the significate of the noun to which it is joined, and thereby, as it were, to make it infinite: because it signifies all other things except the thing on which it falls: as non-man signifies all other things except man, determining none of them; and therefore it is said to have an infinite signification. The infinite noun, then, includes a negation taken not negatingly, that is, not in the whole force of the negation, but taken infinitizingly, that is, according to a force of negating determined to its proper significate.

Ex quibus intelligitur, nomen infinitum hoc modo esse definiendum: Nomen infinitum, est nomen compositum ex nomine simplici, & negatione, infinitanter accepta: vt non homo, non leo: & hæc de quidditate eius.

From which it is understood that the infinite noun is to be defined in this way: The infinite noun is a noun composed of a simple noun and a negation taken infinitizingly: as non-man, non-lion. And so much for its quiddity.

De modo significandi nominis infiniti — On the mode of signifying of the infinite noun.

De modo significandi nominu infiniti.

[…]

QVantum verò ad modum significandi eius pertinet, aliqui dicunt, de materiali, significare rem illam, quæ negatur, de formali verò, cæteras omnes vt non homo, de materiali hominem, de formali verò, leonem, & bouem, ac cætera omnia præter hominem. Melius tamen dicendum est, non significare rem illam, quam negat, sed de mateirali, cæteris præter illam: de formali verò puram negationem eius: vt non homo, de materiali, leonem, & bouem cum cæteris, & de formali, solam negationem hominis. Quid sic probatur: quia non homo, nõ significat leonem, aut bouem, secundùm naturas positiuas eorum: sed in quantum sub negatione hominis cadunt, vel continentur: ergo secundùm naturas positiuas, materialiter pertinent ad significationem nominis infiniti. Formaliter verò secundùm negationem talis naturæ, in propria inclusam.

As for what pertains to its mode of signifying, some say that materially it signifies the thing which is negated, but formally all the others: as non-man materially signifies man, but formally the lion and the ox and all other things except man. It is better to say, however, that it does not signify the thing which it negates, but materially the others besides it, and formally the pure negation of it: as non-man materially signifies the lion and the ox with the rest, and formally only the negation of man. This is proved thus: because non-man does not signify the lion or the ox according to their positive natures, but inasmuch as they fall or are contained under the negation of man: therefore according to their positive natures they pertain materially to the signification of the infinite noun; but formally according to the negation of such a nature, included in its own signification. Kk

p. 514

Circa significatum verò eius omnes conueniunt: adeò extensum esse, vt cætera omnia, præter rem illam quam negat, significet non solùm existentia actu, sed etiam possibilia: imò etiam impossibilia, vt Chimæram, & Centimanum, & ratio huius est manifesta ex dictis. Nam si formale significatum eius, est negatio illius rei, cui adiungitur: ergo materiale erit omne illud, cui potest conuenire talis negatio: sed hæc conuenit cæteris omnibus existentibus, aut possibilibus, imò etiam impossibilibus: ergo hæc omnia comprehenduntur sub materiali significatu eius: sed omninò indeterminatè, atque confusè: & ideo modo quasi infinito: quia non magis aliquod Ens vnum, quàm aliud determinat, vt ex se est manifestum.

Concerning its significate, however, all agree that it is so extended that it signifies all other things except the thing which it negates, not only those actually existing but also possible ones, and indeed even impossible ones, such as the Chimera and the Hundred-handed. And the reason for this is manifest from what has been said. For if its formal significate is the negation of that thing to which it is joined, then its material significate will be everything to which such a negation can belong; but this belongs to all other things, existing or possible, and indeed even impossible: therefore all these are comprehended under its material significate, but altogether indeterminately and confusedly, and therefore in an as it were infinite mode: because it does not determine one Being more than another, as is manifest of itself.

Ex quibus sequitur: Duo habere nomen infinitum, in quibus deficit à vera ratione nominis. Primum, ex parte formalis significati, quòd nullam rem, aut naturam, vel rationem positiuam significat formaliter, sed puram, & solam negationem illius rei, supra quam cadit: vt non homo: solam negationem hominis. Secundum, ex parte significati materialis: quia nihil determinatum significat, sed tam illud quod est, quàm quod non est, imò quod impossibile est. Et propter hæc duo, excludit Aristot. nomen infinitum à definitione nominis: quia verum nomen, determinatam significationem habere debet, & naturam aliquam positiuam, vel saltem positiuam rationem eius debet significare.

From which it follows that the infinite noun has two things in which it falls short of the true ratio of a noun. The first, on the part of the formal significate: that it formally signifies no positive thing, or nature, or ratio, but the pure and sole negation of that thing on which it falls: as non-man signifies only the negation of man. The second, on the part of the material significate: because it signifies nothing determinate, but as much that which is as that which is not, and indeed that which is impossible. And on account of these two things Aristotle excludes the infinite noun from the definition of the noun: because a true noun must have a determinate signification, and must signify some positive nature, or at least a positive ratio of it.

De quibusnam dicatur nomen infinitum in propositione — Of what things the infinite noun is said in a proposition.

De quibusnam dicatur nomen infinitum in propositione.

[…]

15 PRima opinio asserit: quòd licèt nomen infinitum significet, tam ea quæ sunt, quàm quæ non sunt, & tam possibilia, quã impossibilia: tamen in propositione non potest verificari, nisi de solis existentibus, non de possibilibus, vel impossibilibus. Ita Sotus 2. lib. Summularum, c. 1. notabili quinto: quod probat hoc arg. Nomen infinitum, non potest dici de non existentibus, atque impossibilibus, nisi in propositione affirmatiua, de subiecto non supponente: sed talis propositio, est falsa secundùm regulas Summularum: ergo nunquam de his verificabitur, sed de solis existentibus. Maiorem probat: quia vt subiectum propositionis supponi pro aliquo dicatur, requiritur quòd res significata existit in rerum natura, tempore significata per copulam: ergo solùm potest supponi pro existentibus, non pro possibilibus, vel impossibilibus: quare propositio in qua de his dicitur, erit de subiecto non supponente. Minorem verò, quòd affirmatiua de subiecto nõ supponẽte sit falsa, manifestam esse ait in his propositionibus: Adam est albus, Antichristus

15 The first opinion asserts that, although the infinite noun signifies as much the things that are as those that are not, and as much possible as impossible things, yet in a proposition it cannot be verified except of existing things alone, not of possible or impossible ones. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 1, fifth notable; which he proves by this argument: The infinite noun cannot be said of non-existing and impossible things except in an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject; but such a proposition is false according to the rules of the Summulae: therefore it will never be verified of these, but of existing things alone. He proves the major: because, for the subject of a proposition to be said to supposit for something, it is required that the thing signified exist in the nature of things at the time signified by the copula: therefore it can supposit only for existing things, not for possible or impossible ones; wherefore a proposition in which it is said of these will be about a non-suppositing subject. And the minor, that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false, he says is manifest in these propositions: Adam is white, Antichrist

p. 515

est niger: euidens namque est consequentia, à propositione, de tertio adiacente, ad propositionem de secundo, vt Petrus est albus: ergo Petrus est: ergo euidens erit consequentia, Adam est non homo: ergo Adam est: sed consequens est falsum: ergo & antecedens, quod est propositio affirmatiua de subiecto non supponente.

is black: for the consequence is evident from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second, as Peter is white: therefore Peter is; therefore this consequence will be evident: Adam is non-man: therefore Adam is; but the consequent is false: therefore the antecedent is too, which is an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject.

Secunda opinio: affirmat, Nomen infinitum, non solùm significare existentia, & possibilia, atque impossibilia, sed etiam verificari posse de omnibus in propositione. Ita D. Tho. c. præsenti, cum Boëtio, & Ammonio, quos sequuntur moderni omnes interpretes: & est expressa sententia Aristo. cap. præsenti, vbi ita ait: Non homo verò, non est nomen: quoniam similiter in quolibet est, & quod est, & quod non est. Et ita tenendum est. Probatur duplici argum. Primò, ex intrinseca conditione nominis infiniti, quæ talis est, vt nullam formam ponat in subiecto, imò neque vllam rationem positiuam, sed puram negationem illius rei, cui adiungitur: vt non homo, solam negationem hominis: sed sola negatio non postulat existentiam subiecti: imò nec possibilitatem eius: quia etiam de re impossibili verificatur, vt de chimæra, negatio hominis: ergo de his omnibus verificari potest nomen infinitum. Probatur consequentia: quia euidens argu. ducitur à propositione negatiua ad affirmatiuam, de prædicato infinito, in eisdem terminis, vt leo non est homo: ergo leo est non homo: sed nomen infinitum, negatur de impossibilibus: quia vera est hæc, Chimera non est homo: ergo affirmabitur de eisdem, in propositione de prædicato infinito: & ita vera etiam erit hæc, chimæra est non homo. Probatur iterum consequentia: nam ideo vera est propositio negatiua, de subiecto impossibili: quia negatio nihil positiuum ponit in subiecto: sed nomen infinitum nihil positiuum ponit in subiecto; sed solam negationem: ergo secundùm hanc, potest de eadem re possibili verificari in propositione affirmatiuę.

The second opinion affirms that the infinite noun not only signifies existing and possible and impossible things, but can also be verified of all of them in a proposition. So St. Thomas, on the present chapter, with Boethius and Ammonius, whom all the modern interpreters follow; and it is the express view of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he says thus: But non-man is not a noun: since it is in anything whatever alike, both what is and what is not. And so it is to be held. It is proved by a twofold argument. First, from the intrinsic condition of the infinite noun, which is such that it posits no form in the subject, indeed not even any positive ratio, but the pure negation of the thing to which it is joined: as non-man posits only the negation of man; but negation alone does not require the existence of the subject, indeed not even its possibility, because the negation of man is verified even of an impossible thing, such as the chimera: therefore the infinite noun can be verified of all these. The consequence is proved: because there is an evident argument from a negative proposition to an affirmative one with an infinite predicate in the same terms, as A lion is not a man: therefore a lion is non-man; but the infinite noun is denied of impossible things, because this is true: A chimera is not a man: therefore it will be affirmed of the same in a proposition with an infinite predicate; and so this too will be true: A chimera is non-man. The consequence is proved again: for the reason a negative proposition about an impossible subject is true is that the negation posits nothing positive in the subject; but the infinite noun posits nothing positive in the subject, but only a negation: therefore according to this it can be verified of the same possible thing in an affirmative proposition.

Secundò, Prædicata contradictoria, habent immediatam oppositionem: ergo de quolibet ente, aut non ente, necesse est alterum eorum verificari: sed homo, & non homo sunt prædicata contradictoria: ergo necesse est alterum eorum verificari de quacunque re possibili, vel impossibili: sed de re impossibili vt de chimæra, non verificatur homo: ergo verificabitur non homo: sicque de cæteris nominibus infinitis, quæ de rebus etiam impossibilibus verificari debent.

Second, contradictory predicates have an immediate opposition: therefore of any being or non-being whatever one of them must be verified; but man and non-man are contradictory predicates: therefore one of them must be verified of any thing whatever, possible or impossible; but of an impossible thing, such as the chimera, man is not verified: therefore non-man will be verified; and so of the other infinite nouns, which must be verified even of impossible things.

16 Pro solutione arg. alterius opinionis: Notandum est, Prædicatum propositionis affirmatiuæ duobus modis se habere ad subiectum, nam vel accidens eius est, modùmve accidentis habet,

16 For the solution of the argument of the other opinion it should be noted that the predicate of an affirmative proposition stands toward the subject in two ways: for either it is its accident, or it has the mode of an accident, Kk ij

p. 516

vel ad essentiam eius pertinet, aut tanquam propria passio se habet. Et si primo modo se habeat, certum est subiecto actu existenti attribui: quia accidentia non conueniunt subiectis, nisi secundùm actualem inhærentiam in eis: quam constat necessariò supponere actualem existentiam: Si verò secundo modo se habeat, certum est non conuenire ei secundùm actualem existentiam, sed secundùm naturalem connexionem cum eo: quæ cùm nullum tempus determinet, sed perpetua sit, eodem modo semper se habens, propositio etiam perpetuæ veritatis est: & copula (vt aiunt) absoluitur à tempore: quod est, extrema non coniungere, pro vlla differentia temporis: cùm tamen in propositione accidentali, pro determinata differentia temporis, in qua existunt extrema, ea coniungat.

or it pertains to its essence, or stands toward it as a proper attribute. And if it stands in the first way, it is certain that it is attributed to an actually existing subject: because accidents do not belong to subjects except according to actual inherence in them, which, it is agreed, necessarily presupposes actual existence. But if it stands in the second way, it is certain that it does not belong to it according to actual existence, but according to a natural connection with it; and since this determines no time, but is perpetual, always standing in the same way, the proposition too is of perpetual truth, and the copula (as they say) is absolved from time: that is, it does not join the extremes for any difference of time; whereas in an accidental proposition it joins them for a determinate difference of time, in which the extremes exist.

Ex quibus sequitur, solùm in propositionibus accidentalibus, extrema supponi: & ideo solùm in his requiri actualem existentiam extremorum, ad veritatem propositionis affirmatiuæ. Et etiam in his solùm intelligi illam regulam summulistarum, quòd propositio affirmatiua de subiecto non supponente est falsa: ac tandem solùm in his esse bonam consequentiam, à propositione de tertio adiacente, ad propositionem de secundo. In propositionibus autem necessariis, nec supponuntur subiecta, nec vniuntur secundùm actualem existentiam, nec secundùm aliquam differentiam temporis, sed solùm secundùm naturalem connexionem, abstrahentem ab existentia, & tempore: vnde in eis hæc sola regula vera semper est, & obseruanda: quòd omnes propositiones affirmatiuæ, sunt semper veræ: & omnes negatiuæ semper falsæ. Quare nec in his valet consequentia, à propositione de tertio adiacente, ad propositionem de secundo: quia in propositione de tertio, prædicatum coniungitur subiecto, secundùm naturalem connexionem cum eo: in propositione verò de secundo, dicit actualem existentiam, vt si dicas: Homo est rationalis, ergo homo est: antecedens erit verum, nullo homine existente, & consequens falsum. Quam doctrinam, si ad nomen infinitum applicemus, inueniemus significare omnia possibilia, & impossibilia, quasi modo essentiali, cùm per se omnia significet. Et ex hoc sequitur, de illis verificari in propositione, quasi per modum naturalis connexionis, & non secundùm actualem existentiam: quare omnes propositiones affirmatiuæ sunt veræ: & omnes negatiuæ falsæ: quia extrema non supponuntur nec valet in eis consequentia, à propositione de tertio adiacente, ad propositionem de secundo.

From which it follows that only in accidental propositions do the extremes supposit, and therefore only in these is the actual existence of the extremes required for the truth of an affirmative proposition. And also that only in these is that rule of the summulists to be understood, that an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject is false; and finally that only in these is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second good. But in necessary propositions the subjects neither supposit, nor are united according to actual existence, nor according to any difference of time, but only according to a natural connection, abstracting from existence and from time: whence in them this rule alone is always true and to be observed, that all affirmative propositions are always true, and all negative ones always false. Wherefore neither is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second valid in these: because in the proposition of the third adjacent the predicate is joined to the subject according to a natural connection with it, but in the proposition of the second it denotes actual existence: as if you say, Man is rational: therefore man is, the antecedent will be true when no man exists, and the consequent false. If we apply this doctrine to the infinite noun, we shall find that it signifies all possible and impossible things in an as it were essential mode, since it signifies them all per se. And from this it follows that it is verified of them in a proposition as it were by way of a natural connection, and not according to actual existence: wherefore all affirmative propositions are true, and all negative ones false, because the extremes do not supposit; nor is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second valid in them.

Ad formam igitur arg. Concedenda est maior, quòd nomen

To the form of the argument, then: The major is to be granted, that the infinite

p. 517

infinitum non possit verificari de impossibilibus, aut non existentibus, nisi in propositione affirmatiua de subiecto non supponente: sed minor distinguẽda, quòd affirmatiua de subiecto non supponente sit falsa: nam si accidentalis sit, concedendum est, quia vniuntur extrema secundùm actualem existentiam, quam habere debet tempore significato per copulam: & si eam non habuerint, falsa erit propositio. In propositionibus verò necessariis, nõ requiritur actualis existentia extremorum: quia solùm vniuntur secundùm naturalem connexionem: & ideo affirmatiua, licèt sit de subiecto non supponente, vera est. Et cùm propositiones affirmatiuæ de prædicato infinito, modum habeant necessarium, negandum est etiam in eis quòd affirmatiua de subiecto, non supponente sit falsa.

noun cannot be verified of impossible or non-existing things except in an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject; but the minor is to be distinguished, that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false. For if it is accidental, it is to be granted, because the extremes are united according to actual existence, which they must have at the time signified by the copula; and if they do not have it, the proposition will be false. But in necessary propositions the actual existence of the extremes is not required, because they are united only according to a natural connection; and therefore the affirmative, although it is about a non-suppositing subject, is true. And since affirmative propositions with an infinite predicate have the mode of necessary ones, it is to be denied in them too that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false.

An transcendentia nomina possint infinitari — Whether transcendental nouns can be made infinite.

An transcendentia nomina possint infinitari.

[…]

17 PRima opinio, tenet, infinitari non posse transcendentia, si in tota sua vniuersalitate accipiantur: vt ens absolutè sumptum: Si verò cum limitatione, vt pro ente reali tantùm, aut pro ente rationis, infinitari posse. Ita Alber. Magnus in Comment. huius lib. tract. 2. c. 5. cum Auicenna, quos sequuntur Toletus, & alij c. præsenti. Probatur ex natura nominis infiniti, quod tam de entibus, quàm de non entibus dicitur: sed si infinitetur ens absolutè sumptum, solùm de entibus dici poterit: ergo non potest infinitari.

17 The first opinion holds that transcendentals cannot be made infinite if they are taken in their whole universality, as being taken absolutely; but if they are taken with a limitation, as for real being only, or for being of reason, that they can be made infinite. So Albert the Great in the commentary on this book, tract. 2, ch. 5, with Avicenna, whom Toledo and others follow on the present chapter. It is proved from the nature of the infinite noun, which is said as much of beings as of non-beings; but if being taken absolutely were made infinite, it could be said only of beings: therefore it cannot be made infinite.

Secunda opinio, adhuc hoc modo sumpta, transcendentia infinitari posse, concedit: ita Sotus 2. li. Summularum, c. 1. notab. 6. Suesanus, & Louanienses c. præsenti. Probãt: Quia prædicationes istæ, Chimæra est non ens; Nihil est, non ens, sunt de prædicato infinito: & prędicatum est ens in sua vniuersalitate: ergo transcendentia in sua vniuersalitate sumpta, infinitari possunt.

The second opinion grants that transcendentals can be made infinite even when taken in this way. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 1, notable 6, Suesanus, and the Louvain commentators on the present chapter. They prove it: Because these predications, A chimera is non-being, Nothing is non-being, have an infinite predicate; and the predicate is being in its universality: therefore transcendentals taken in their universality can be made infinite.

Pro solutione dubij: Distinguenda sunt transcendentia, hoc modo: Quædam sunt Vniuersalissima, vt Ens, alia minùs vniuersalia: vt passiones eius, Verum, Bonum, & Vnum, quæ minùs vniuersalia dicuntur: quia secundùm rationes formales non se includunt, nec enim bonum, est verum formaliter; nec verum, est formaliter vnum. Et rursus, vniuersalissimum transcendens, vt ens, potest sumi absolutè, vel cum alia limitatione. Videlicet pro solo ente reali, vel pro sola substantia. Et de transcendentibus minùs vniuersalibus, euidens est infinitari posse: quia non verum, aut non bonum, adhuc verificari possunt de entibus, & non entibus: nam verum est non bonum: & vnum est non verum formaliter. Certum est etiam, ens cum limitatione acceptum, infinitari posse, propter eandem rationem: sed an possit

For the solution of the doubt, transcendentals are to be distinguished in this way: some are Most universal, as Being; others less universal, as its attributes, True, Good, and One, which are called less universal because according to their formal ratios they do not include one another: for neither is good formally true, nor is true formally one. And again, the most universal transcendental, such as being, can be taken absolutely, or with some limitation: namely for real being alone, or for substance alone. And of the less universal transcendentals it is evident that they can be made infinite, because non-true or non-good can still be verified of beings and non-beings: for the true is non-good, and the one is formally non-true. It is certain also that being taken with a limitation can be made infinite, for the same reason; but whether it can Kk iij

p. 518

possit sine limitatione acceptum; de hoc solùm potest esse dubium.

be made infinite when taken without limitation: about this alone can there be doubt.

Et nostra sententia est infinitari posse. Probatur, ex propria definitione nominis infiniti, à nobis assignata in principio, secundùm quam solum dicit esse compositum ex nomine simplici, & negatione ei adiuncta: sed non ens, componitur ex vtroque: ergo simpliciter est nomen infinitum: & hoc etiam probat arg. secundæ opinionis.

And our view is that it can be made infinite.
