Et ita in definitione orationis ponuntur ea, quæ conueniunt ei in genere, nempe, vt oratio est abstrahens à simplici, & composita: ex quibus vnum est, quòd partes eius non sint significatiuæ, vt affirmationes, sed solùm, vt dictiones. Quòd verò oratio aliqua, nempe composita, habeat partes significatiuas, vt affirmationes, non conuenit ei, vt est oratio, aut ex ratione generica orationis, quæ definitur, sed ex ratione specifica orationis compositæ: vnde, hoc non contradicit definitioni, nec tollit, quin sub ea comprehendatur;

To the second argument, St. Thomas and Alexander reply that in the definition only those things are placed which belong to the defined as such, not those which can belong to it under another particular ratio: as in the definition of animal only those things are placed which pertain to sentient nature, not others which can belong to animal considered in this or that species by reason of some difference. And so in the definition of speech those things are placed which belong to it in general, namely as speech abstracts from simple and composite; among which one is that its parts are not significant as affirmations, but only as words. But that some speech, namely composite speech, has parts significant as affirmations does not belong to it as it is speech, or from the generic ratio of speech which is defined, but from the specific ratio of composite speech: hence this does not contradict the definition, nor prevent its being included under it. Ll iij

p. 534

QUESTION II

QVÆSTIO II.

[…]

An enuntiatio sit ens reale, vel rationis.

Whether the enunciation is a real being or a being of reason.

31 TRia sunt consideranda in enunciatione, seu propositione. Primum, Voces ipsæ, scripturæ, aut conceptus. Secundum, Ordinatio eorum in propositione, secundùm rationem prædicati, subiecti, & copulæ. Tertium, Actus intellectus per quem ordinantur, & ex eis sic ordinatis efficitur propositio. Et de primo, & tertio, certum est, esse realia, & de quo nemo dubitauit: sed quia in his non consistit formalis ratio Enunciationis, sed solùm materialis, tertium vero pertinet ad formalem rationem eius: certum etiam erit, quòd enunciatio materialiter accepta, & quasi pro fundamẽto, sit ens reale. Dubiũ verò, An enunciatio formaliter sit realis, vel ens rationis.

31 Three things are to be considered in the enunciation, or proposition. First, the vocal sounds themselves, the writings, or the concepts. Second, their ordering in the proposition according to the ratio of predicate, subject, and copula. Third, the act of the intellect by which they are ordered, and from which, once they are so ordered, the proposition is effected. Concerning the first and the third it is certain that they are real, and no one has doubted it; but because the formal ratio of the Enunciation does not consist in these, but only the material, while the second pertains to its formal ratio, it will also be certain that the enunciation taken materially, and as it were for its foundation, is a real being. The doubt, then, is whether the enunciation formally is real, or a being of reason.

Prima opinio, Distinguit de enunciatione vocali, scripta, atque mentali & de duabus primis, asserit formaliter esse ens rationis: sed de mentali docet formaliter esse ens reale. Ita tenent moderni quidam: & vtrumque probant hoc arg. Enunciatio vocis, & scripta, solùm sunt reales ex parte vocum, & scripturarum. sed ex parte significationis, & veritatis, sunt entia rationis, cùm significatio earum, ex libera impositione hominum dependeat, quæ nihil reale in eis ponit. Veritas etiam cùm non sit in eis formaliter, sed solùm tanquam in signo: ideo nihil habent etiam reale, sed rationis: ad rationem autem formalem propositionis, non pertinent scripturæ, & voces, nisi vt significatiuæ rerum, & veritatis in mente existentis: ergo propositio vocalis, & scripta, materialiter tantùm est ens reale, formaliter verò ens rationis: Quòd verò mentalis sit ens reale formaliter probant: quia conceptus ex quibus fit, non solùm sunt reales: sed significatio (quæ inest à natura) & veritas quoque reperitur in eis formaliter: ergo tam ex formali significatione, & veritate, in quibus consistit formalis ratio propositionis, quàm ex materiali conceptuum, erit ens reale.

The first opinion distinguishes between the vocal, the written, and the mental enunciation; and of the first two it asserts that they are formally beings of reason, but of the mental it teaches that it is formally a real being. So certain moderns hold; and they prove both points by this argument: The vocal and the written enunciation are real only on the side of the vocal sounds and the writings, but on the side of signification and of truth they are beings of reason, since their signification depends on the free imposition of men, which posits nothing real in them. Truth too, since it is not in them formally but only as in a sign, therefore has nothing real in them either, but only of reason; but to the formal ratio of the proposition the writings and vocal sounds do not pertain except as significant of things and of the truth existing in the mind: therefore the vocal and the written proposition is a real being only materially, but formally a being of reason. That the mental one is formally a real being they prove: because the concepts of which it is made are not only real, but signification (which is in them by nature) and truth are also found in them formally: therefore, both from the formal signification and truth, in which the formal ratio of the proposition consists, and from the material ratio of the concepts, it will be a real being.

Hæc sententia quantùm ad enunciationem vocalem, & scriptam, vera est: non tamen quantũ ad mentalem, quod ita probo: nam licèt duo illa realia sint in conceptibus nempe significatio, & veritas, ordinatio tamen in modum cõpositionis, prædicati, subiecti, & copulæ, non potest esse ens reale: quia nihil reale ponit in eis, sed sicut in vocibus, & scripturis, esse subiectum, & prædicatum, & propositionem, solùm est relatio rationis, quæ consequitur actum realem intellectus ea ordinantis: ita in conceptibus, quantumuis naturaliter significantibus, &

This opinion is true as regards the vocal and the written enunciation, but not as regards the mental, which I prove thus: for although those two real things, namely signification and truth, are in the concepts, yet the ordering after the manner of a composition of predicate, subject, and copula cannot be a real being, because it posits nothing real in them; but just as in vocal sounds and writings to be subject, and predicate, and proposition is only a relation of reason, which follows the real act of the intellect ordering them, so in concepts, however naturally they signify, and

p. 535

formalem rationem veritatis continentibus, solùm est relatio rationis, esse ordinatos in ratione subiecti & prædicati, ac mentalis propositionis: quare non minùs in his quàm in scripturis, & vocibus ens rationis est, formalis ratio enunciationis. Quod verò de veritate reali conceptuum dicitur (licèt in optione sit positum) tamen amittendum est: sed non sequitur ex eo, enunciationem mentalem formaliter esse ens reale: quia licèt conceptus, eo ipso quòd formantur ab intellectu, habeant veritatem realem simplicem: complexam tamen seu compositam nõ habent, nisi supposita ordinatione intellectus, & constitutione eorum in ratione prædicati, & subiecti, ac propositionis, quæ cùm relationes tantùm rationis sint, efficitur propositionem mentalem formaliter esse ens rationis.

which contain the formal ratio of truth, it is only a relation of reason that they are ordered in the ratio of subject and predicate, and of a mental proposition: wherefore, no less in these than in writings and vocal sounds, the formal ratio of the enunciation is a being of reason. As for what is said about the real truth of concepts, although it is left to choice, it must nevertheless be admitted; but it does not follow from it that the mental enunciation is formally a real being: because, although concepts, by the very fact that they are formed by the intellect, have simple real truth, yet they do not have complex or composite truth except on the supposition of the ordering of the intellect and of their constitution in the ratio of predicate and subject, and of proposition; and since these are only relations of reason, the result is that the mental proposition is formally a being of reason.

Non igitur sententia est, non solùm enunciationem vocalem & scriptam formaliter esse entia rationis, sed etiam mentalem absolutè loquendo. Quia licèt aliquid reale habeat, pertinens ad rationem formalem propositionis, nempe significationem, & veritatem: nihilominus vltimum, per quod constituitur enunciatio, in ratione formali enunciationis, est ens rationis nempe ordinatio conceptuum in ratione prædicati, & subiecti, atque compositionis ex his: & ideo absolutè pronunciandum est, enunciationem mentalem formaliter, esse ens rationis: & ex consequenti: omnes, & singulas enunciationes, esse entia rationis formaliter: & ex his solutum est arg. oppositæ opinionis.

Our opinion, therefore, is that not only the vocal and the written enunciation are formally beings of reason, but also the mental one, speaking absolutely. Because, although it has something real pertaining to the formal ratio of the proposition, namely signification and truth, nevertheless the ultimate thing through which the enunciation is constituted in the formal ratio of an enunciation is a being of reason, namely the ordering of the concepts in the ratio of predicate and subject, and of the composition from these; and therefore it must be pronounced absolutely that the mental enunciation is formally a being of reason, and consequently that each and every enunciation is formally a being of reason. And by these things the argument of the opposite opinion is solved.

QUESTION III

QVÆSTIO III.

[…]

An enunciatio quidditatiuè sit definita ab Aristo. per veritatem & falsitatem.

Whether the enunciation was defined quidditatively by Aristotle through truth and falsity.

2 ARist. ca. præsenti definit enunciationem, per veritatem, & falsitatem: & ideo dubitamus, An veritas, & falsitas, pertineant ad essentiam enunciationis, & ideo talis definitio sit, essentialis: vel potiùs sit accidens, aut propria passio eius, & ita accidentalis, aut descriptiua sit.

32 Aristotle, in the present chapter, defines the enunciation through truth and falsity: and therefore we ask whether truth and falsity pertain to the essence of the enunciation, and so whether such a definition is essential; or rather whether truth is an accident or proper attribute of it, and so the definition is accidental or descriptive.

Et est prima opinio, quorundam modernorum, asserentium, Veritatem, & falsitatem pertinere ad essentiam enunciationis: & ideo essentialiter esse per eas definitam. Probatur hoc argum. Quia illa est differentia essentialis alicuius speciei per quam à cæteris eiusdem generis distinguitur: sed enunciationem distinguit Arist. à cæteris orationibus non enunciatiuis, per significationem veri, & falsi: ergo veritas, & falsitas, sunt differentia essentialis eius, per quam separatur à cæteris speciebus orationis.

And the first opinion is that of certain moderns, who assert that truth and falsity pertain to the essence of the enunciation, and that it is therefore essentially defined through them. This is proved by this argument: That is the essential difference of a species by which it is distinguished from the others of the same genus; but Aristotle distinguishes the enunciation from the other, non-enunciative speeches through the signification of the true and the false: therefore truth and falsity are its essential difference, by which it is separated from the other species of speech. Ll iiij

p. 536

Secunda opinio tenet, Essentiam enunciationis non consistere in significatione veri, aut falsi, sed in eo quod est vnum de altero enunciare: veritatem verò, aut falsitatem, extra essentiam enunciationis esse, tanquam accidens, vel ad summum vt propriam passionem, per quam descripsit eam Aristot. Ita Alexander, Ammonius, & Niphus cap. pręsenti, & omnes ferè moderni; & nos etiam verum id existimamus esse, & doctrinæ Arist. valde consonum.

The second opinion holds that the essence of the enunciation does not consist in the signification of the true or the false, but in this, that it enunciates one thing of another; and that truth or falsity is outside the essence of the enunciation, as an accident, or at most as a proper attribute, through which Aristotle described it. So Alexander, Ammonius, and Nifo on the present chapter, and almost all the moderns; and we too judge this to be true, and very consonant with the doctrine of Aristotle.

Probatur testimonio Arist. capit. de substantia in prædicamentis. Vbi docet, eandem enunciationem, secundùm speciem suscipere veritatem, & falsitatem, & mutari de vera in falsam ab extrinseco, nempe ex mutatione rei ad extra. Vt hæc propositio, Petrus sedet, eadem numero permanens; vera nunc est, sedẽte Petro, stante verò fit falsa; & hanc mutationem ab extrinseco ei prouenire; & ideo suscipere contraria, sine sui mutatione: ex quo tale argum colligo. Eadem propositio immutata permanet, sub veritate, & falsitate: ergo veritas, & falsitas, non est de essentia propositionis; aut enunciationis. Probatur consequentia: quia, si de essentia eius esset, non permaneret eadem, sed alia esset secundùm speciem, & numerum vera, & falsa: quare ex mente Aristot. non pertinet ad essentiam enunciationis verum, aut falsum significare.

It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in the chapter on substance in the Categories, where he teaches that the same enunciation, according to species, receives truth and falsity, and is changed from true to false extrinsically, namely by a change of the thing outside. As this proposition, Peter is sitting, remaining the same in number, is true now while Peter is sitting, but becomes false when he is standing; and this change comes to it from without; and therefore it receives contraries without change of itself. From which I gather this argument: The same proposition remains unchanged under truth and falsity: therefore truth and falsity are not of the essence of the proposition, or of the enunciation. The consequence is proved: because if they were of its essence, it would not remain the same, but the true and the false would be different according to species and number: wherefore, according to the mind of Aristotle, to signify the true or the false does not pertain to the essence of the enunciation.

Pręterea Propositionem definiens Aristot. lib. 1. Priorum, cap. 1. ait, esse orationem, quæ aliquid de aliquo affirmat, aut negat, & 1. lib. Poste. cap. 2. asserit, propositionem esse alterã partem enunciationis, in qua vnum de vno enunciatur, nulla facta mentione veri, aut falsi: ergo sentit non in his, sed in eo, quod est enunciare vnum de altero, consistere essentiam eius. Probatur etiam ratione: Primò: Quia si veritas, & falsitas pertinent ad essentiam enuntiationis: ergo enunciatio vera, & falsa, distinguuntur specie: sicut veritas ipsa, & falsitas, specie diuersæ sunt: sed differentiæ specierum essentiales, non pertinent ad essentiam generis, sed extra eam sunt, vt ex Arist. & Porphyrio adduximus, in tertio prædicabili: vt differentia rationalis, & irrationalis, non pertinent ad essentiam animalis; ergo verum, & falsum significare, extra essentiam enunciationis in genere sumptæ esse debent: quare aliquid aliud de essentia eius erit, quod per verum & falsum contrahatur ad diuersas species: & hoc erit enunciare vnum de altero: quod aliud erit verum, aliud falsum.

Moreover, Aristotle, defining the proposition in Prior Analytics bk. 1, ch. 1, says that it is a speech which affirms or denies something of something; and in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 2, he asserts that a proposition is one part of an enunciation, in which one thing is enunciated of one, no mention being made of the true or the false: therefore he thinks that its essence consists not in these but in this, that it enunciates one thing of another. It is proved also by reason. First: Because if truth and falsity pertain to the essence of the enunciation, then the true and the false enunciation are distinguished in species, just as truth itself and falsity are diverse in species; but the essential differences of species do not pertain to the essence of the genus, but are outside it, as we adduced from Aristotle and Porphyry on the third predicable, as the differences rational and irrational do not pertain to the essence of animal: therefore to signify the true and the false must be outside the essence of the enunciation taken in general: wherefore there will be something else of its essence which is contracted through the true and the false to diverse species; and this will be to enunciate one thing of another, which is in one case true, in another false.

33 Et si dixeris: Totum disiunctum, nempe verum, aut falsum, pertinere ad essentiam enunciationis in genere: & alterutrum eorum per se, esse differentiam specificam: probatur hoc esse

33 And if you say: The disjunctive whole, namely true or false, pertains to the essence of the enunciation in general, and either of them per se is the specific difference: this is proved to be

p. 537

falsum: quia totum disiunctum, componitur ex partibus oppositis: ergo non potest esse de essentia vnius, & eiusdem rei.

false: because the disjunctive whole is composed of opposite parts: therefore it cannot be of the essence of one and the same thing.

Secundò probatur eadem sententia: Quia enunciatio genus est, ad mentalem, vocalem, & scriptam: ergo conueniet eis vniuocè: sed veritas, & falsitas, non possunt eis vniuocè conuenire: ergo nec pertinere ad essentiam eius. Probatur minor: quia in sola enunciatione mentali, reperiuntur formaliter, in vocali verò, & scripta, solùm tanquam in signo: & ideo per attributionem ad mentalem; ergo conuenit eis analogicè.

Second, the same opinion is proved: Because the enunciation is a genus with respect to the mental, the vocal, and the written: therefore it will belong to them univocally; but truth and falsity cannot belong to them univocally: therefore neither can they pertain to its essence. The minor is proved: because they are found formally only in the mental enunciation, but in the vocal and the written only as in a sign, and therefore by attribution to the mental: therefore they belong to them analogically.

Tertiò: Quia hæc causalis est vera: quia enunciatio enunciat vnum de altero est vera, aut falsa, Et hæc causalis est falsa: quia enunciatio est vera aut falsa: enunciat vnũ de altero: ergo prius natura est, enunciationem enunciare vnum de altero: quàm esse veram aut falsam: in illo: ergo consistit essentia eius, quam sequuntur verum, & falsum, vt proprium accidens. Et certè ita est: quod eo ipso quòd intelligimus vnum enunciari de altero, intelligimus orationem enunciatiuam: quamuis nihil de vero aut falso intelligimus: ergo in eo solùm consistit essentia enunciationis, hæc verò extra eam sunt.

Third: Because this causal proposition is true: Because the enunciation enunciates one thing of another, it is true or false. And this causal proposition is false: Because the enunciation is true or false, it enunciates one thing of another: therefore it is prior by nature that the enunciation enunciates one thing of another than that it is true or false: therefore its essence consists in the former, upon which the true and the false follow as a proper accident. And certainly it is so: for by the very fact that we understand one thing to be enunciated of another, we understand an enunciative speech, although we understand nothing of the true or the false: therefore the essence of the enunciation consists only in that, while these are outside it.

Ad arg. alterius sententiæ, Distinguenda est maior, nam distingui ab aliis speciebus eiusdem generis, dupliciter contingit. Primò distinctione specifica; & hoc modo non potest vnum distingui ab alio, nisi per differentiam essentialem. Secundò non distinctione specifica: sed accidentali: & sic distinguuntur enunciatio vera, & falsa, nõ essentialiter. Voluit autem Arist. enunciationem definire cap. præsenti, per verum, & falsum, tanquam per accidentia eius nobis notiora: ex quibus innotesceret nobis essentia eiusdem enunciationis, in eo solùm consistens, quòd vno de altero enuncietur.

To the argument of the other opinion: The major must be distinguished: for to be distinguished from the other species of the same genus happens in two ways. First, by a specific distinction; and in this way one thing cannot be distinguished from another except through an essential difference. Second, not by a specific distinction but by an accidental one; and so the true and the false enunciation are distinguished, not essentially. And Aristotle chose in the present chapter to define the enunciation through the true and the false, as through its accidents more known to us, from which the essence of the same enunciation might become known to us, which consists only in this, that one thing is enunciated of another.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Quæst. 4. An enunciatio mentalis sit vna simplex qualitas — Whether the mental enunciation is one simple quality.

An enunciatio mentalis sit vna simplex qualitas.

[…]

DE sola enunciatione mentali quærimus, An sit vna qualitas simplex, vel composita potiùs ex multis simplicibus, non de vocali, & scripta. de quibus certum est, compositas esse ex multis vocibus simplicibus, aut scripturis. Circa mentalem verò, notandum est primò, quòd si accipiatur pro actu intellectus, quo apprehendimus res, aut de rebus apprehensis iudicamus, non est quid compositum, sed simplex. Nam iudicium intellectus, quo iudicamus veram esse hanc enunciationem, homo est albus, vnicus est, atque simplex actus intellectus: nec

We ask about the mental enunciation alone, whether it is one simple quality, or rather composed of many simple ones; not about the vocal and the written, about which it is certain that they are composed of many simple vocal sounds or writings. Concerning the mental, then, it should be noted first that if it is taken for the act of the intellect by which we apprehend things, or judge about things apprehended, it is not something composite but simple. For the judgment of the intellect by which we judge this enunciation to be true, man is white, is a single and simple act of the intellect; nor

p. 538

propriè sumitur pro eo enunciatio mentalis, ideo de hoc non procedit quæstio, sed de conceptibus, quos format intellectus de rebus ipsis: quibus formatis, iudicat vnum conuenire alteri, & iudicando, componit vnum cum altero, & hæc compositio, & propositio mentalis, de qua inquirimus, An sit vna qualitas simplex, vel non nisi ex multis composita.

is the mental enunciation properly taken for it; therefore the question does not proceed about this, but about the concepts which the intellect forms of the things themselves; when these are formed, it judges that one agrees with another, and in judging it composes one with the other; and it is about this composition and mental proposition that we inquire: Whether it is one simple quality, or only composed of many.

Secundò notandum est: Sic se habere intellectum in formanda enunciatione mentali, vt primò apprehendat simplicia, per plures, ac simplices conceptus: deinde, ex his efficiat compositionem, priusquam iudicet de conuenientia vnius respectus alterius: vel aliquando integram apprehensionem totius enunciationis habeat, ante iudicium: quia prius apprehendit compositionem integram, quàm iudicet, de conuenientia prædicati cum subiecto: vt patet, dum audimus hanc propositionem; astra sunt paria: quam integram apprehendimus, antequam iudicemus de veritate, aut falsitate eius: imò cùm apprehensionem eius habeamus: nunquam habemus iudicium: quia nulla apparet ratio iudicandi veram esse potiùs quàm falsam. De propositione igitur mentali apprehensa, euidens est, non esse simplicem qualitatem: quare difficultas quæstionis reducitur, ad propositionem mentalem iudicatam, an sit simplex qualitas, vel composita. Nam duobus modis possumus intelligere, quòd intellectus iudicet veram esse hanc propositionem apprehensam, homo est albus, ex tribus conceptibus compositam. Primò ita, vt iudicet conceptum simplicem albedinis conuenire conceptui simplici hominis: & tunc euidens est, propositionem mentalem iudicatam, quæ est quasi terminus iudicij, non esse qualitatem simplicem, sed compositam, sicut propositionem mentalem apprehensam. Alio modo potest se habere intellectus in iudicio, non iudicando vnum conceptum simplicem conuenire alteri, sed ex tota apprehensione composita, vel ex tribus conceptibus simplicibus, prædicati, subiecti, copulæ, formando quemdam alium distinctum, per quem repræsententur significata totius compositionis, nempe prædicati, subiecti, & copulæ: ita vt simul per vnum illum conceptum iudicet de veritate, aut falsitate totius compositionis, eo modo, quo phantasia ex duplici specie montis, & auri, format tertiam quandam simplicem, repræsentantem montem aureum. Eo etiam modo, quo Angelus per vnum simplicem conceptum, intelligit integram compositionem à nobis factam. Si enim ita fiat, enunciatio mentalis erit vnicus simplex conceptus, & vna simplex qualitas, per quam repræsententur prædicatum, subiectum, & copula.

Second, it should be noted that the intellect behaves thus in forming the mental enunciation: it first apprehends the simple things through several simple concepts; then from these it effects a composition, before it judges of the agreement of the one with respect to the other; or sometimes it has an entire apprehension of the whole enunciation before the judgment: because it apprehends the entire composition before it judges of the agreement of the predicate with the subject: as is plain when we hear this proposition, the stars are even, which we apprehend entire before we judge of its truth or falsity; indeed, though we have its apprehension, we never have a judgment, because no reason appears for judging it true rather than false. Of the mental proposition as apprehended, therefore, it is evident that it is not a simple quality: wherefore the difficulty of the question is reduced to the mental proposition as judged, whether it is a simple quality or composite. For we can understand in two ways that the intellect judges true this apprehended proposition, man is white, composed of three concepts. First, in such a way that it judges that the simple concept of whiteness agrees with the simple concept of man: and then it is evident that the judged mental proposition, which is as it were the term of the judgment, is not a simple quality but composite, like the apprehended mental proposition. In another way the intellect can behave in judgment, not by judging that one simple concept agrees with another, but by forming, from the whole composite apprehension, or from the three simple concepts of predicate, subject, and copula, some other distinct concept through which the significates of the whole composition, namely of predicate, subject, and copula, are represented; so that through that one concept it judges at once of the truth or falsity of the whole composition, in the way in which the imagination, from the twofold species of a mountain and of gold, forms a certain third, simple species representing a golden mountain; and in the same way also as an angel, through one simple concept, understands the entire composition made by us. For if it is done so, the mental enunciation will be a single simple concept, and one simple quality, through which predicate, subject, and copula are represented.

p. 539

Et prima opinio tenet, Ita fieri: & ideò enunciationem mentalem iudicatam, esse vnam simplicem qualitatem. Ita Sotus 2. lib. Summularum, ca. 5. Toletus 3. de anima, quæst. 19. Probaturque hoc argum. Intellectus, cùm sit potentia superior phantasia, habet eandem, aut maiorem virtutem componendi, quàm illa: sed phantasia est duplici specie simplici diuersarum rerum, elicit vnam etiam simplicem repræsentantem, quidquid per suas illas repræsentabatur: ergo eandem habebit intellectus: & ita poterit sic iudicare de apprehensione composita, vel de conuenientia vnius conceptus simplicis cum alterò, vt vnum conceptum eliciat repræsentantem, quidquid per vtrumque conceptum repræsentabatur, vel per totam compositionem apprehensam; & ita enunciatio iudicata, & repræsentata per vnum illum conceptum, erit vna simplex qualitas.

And the first opinion holds that it happens so, and that therefore the judged mental enunciation is one simple quality. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 5; Toledo, On the Soul 3, q. 19. And it is proved by this argument: The intellect, since it is a power superior to the imagination, has the same or a greater power of composing than it; but the imagination, from a twofold simple species of diverse things, elicits also one simple species representing whatever was represented by those species of its own: therefore the intellect will have the same power; and so it will be able to judge of the composite apprehension, or of the agreement of one simple concept with another, in such a way that it elicits one concept representing whatever was represented by each concept, or by the whole apprehended composition; and so the enunciation judged and represented through that one concept will be one simple quality.

Secunda opinio tenet: Hoc est impossibile; & omnino necessarium, vt sicut intellectus apprehendit subiectum, predicatum, & copulam propositionis, non per vnum, sed per plures conceptus: ita vnum attribuat alteri per iudicium: & per hanc attributionem, componat enunciationem iudicatam, ex eisdem simplicibus conceptibus, per apprehensionem formatis. Et sic propositio mentalis iudicata, non sit vnus conceptus simplex neque vna simplex qualitas, sed composita ex multis conceptibus, & qualitatibus simplicibus. Ita pater Gabriel Vazques tomo 2. 1. part. distinct. 13. cap. 13 Et videtur mihi vera sententia, & expressa apud D. Thom. 1. part. quæst. 58. art. 4. ad 1, vbi de enunciatione mentali, sic loquitur: Non qualiscunque multitudo intellectuum compositionem causat, sed multitudo illorum intellectuum quorum vnum attribuitur alteri. Per multitudinem namque intellectuum, multitudinem conceptuum intelligit: ex quibus intellectum, componere ait, enunciationem mentalem iudicatam, per attributionem vnius ad alterum.

The second opinion holds: This is impossible; and it is altogether necessary that, just as the intellect apprehends the subject, the predicate, and the copula of the proposition not through one but through several concepts, so it attributes one to the other through judgment; and through this attribution composes the judged enunciation from the same simple concepts formed through apprehension. And thus the judged mental proposition is not one simple concept, nor one simple quality, but composed of many concepts and simple qualities. So Father Gabriel Vázquez, vol. 2 on 1 p., d. 13, ch. 13. And it seems to me the true opinion, and expressed in St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 58, a. 4, ad 1, where he speaks thus of the mental enunciation: Not any multitude whatever of understandings causes composition, but a multitude of those understandings of which one is attributed to another. For by the multitude of understandings he means the multitude of concepts, from which, he says, the intellect composes the judged mental enunciation through the attribution of one to another.

35 Probatur etiam ratione. Primò: Quia intellectus efficit enunciationem mentalem iudicatam, per attributionem vnius ad alterum, hoc est affirmando vnum de altero, vel negando illud de eo. Sed attribuere vnum alteri, ab eò diuerso, dicit multiplicitatem: ergo cùm id quod attribuitur alteri in propositione mentali, sit conceptus attributus alteri conceptui, sicut in propositione vocali, est vna vox attributa alteri: sic propositio mentalis, non est minus composita qualitas, quàm vocalis.

35 It is proved also by reason. First: Because the intellect effects the judged mental enunciation through the attribution of one to another, that is, by affirming one of another, or by denying it of it. But to attribute one thing to another, diverse from it, expresses multiplicity: therefore, since that which is attributed to another in the mental proposition is a concept attributed to another concept, just as in the vocal proposition it is one vocal sound attributed to another, the mental proposition is no less a composite quality than the vocal one.

Secundò: Voces significant res mediis conceptibus: ergo

Second: Vocal sounds signify things by means of concepts: therefore

p. 540

propositio vocalis est signum propositionis mentalis: sed illa non est vna vox simplex, sed composita ex multis: ergo neque propositio mentalis erit vnus simplex conceptus, vel qualitas, sed ex multis conceptibus prædicati, subiecti, & copulæ composita. Quod præsertim verum est, ac necessarium vbi prædicatum, & subiectum, sola ratione distinguuntur, vt in propositione identica: quam repugnat intellectum efficere, nisi ea distinguendo, quæ à parte rei non sunt distincta; hæc autem distinguere non potest, nisi per plures conceptus ea intelligat, & vnum eorum alteri attribuat: ergo repugnat talem enunciationem mentalem, esse vnum simplicem conceptum, vel vnam simplicem qualitatem.

the vocal proposition is a sign of the mental proposition; but the former is not one simple vocal sound, but composed of many: therefore neither will the mental proposition be one simple concept or quality, but composed of many concepts, of predicate, subject, and copula. Which is especially true and necessary where the predicate and the subject are distinguished by reason alone, as in an identical proposition: which it is impossible for the intellect to effect except by distinguishing those things which are not distinct on the side of the thing; but it cannot distinguish these unless it understands them through several concepts and attributes one of them to the other: therefore it is impossible for such a mental enunciation to be one simple concept, or one simple quality.

Ad arg. alterius sententiæ, Concessa maiore, distinguenda est minor. quia ex duplici conceptu simplici diuerso, elicere tertium etiam simplicem, repræsentantem plura, quæ repræsentabantur per illa, duobus modis intelligi potest. Primò, per modum simplicis expressionis: ita, vt vno illo conceptu exprimatur, quidquid per plures repræsentabatur. Secundò, per attributionem, & compositionem vnius cum altero. Et primo modo, fieri potest à phantasia, & intellectu nostro: sed secundo modo fieri repugnat: quia componere vnum cum altero, dicit multiplicitatem conceptuum: & cùm sic fieri debeat per iudicium, quo constituitur enunciatio mentalis: non potest per vnum conceptum fieri, sed necessariò per plures, ex quibus enunciatio mentalis componatur: & propterea non potest esse enunciatio mentalis conceptus simplex, aut simplex qualitas, sed composita ex pluribus conceptibus, & qualitatibus. In Angelis verò, simplex conceptus, & simplex qualitas est: quia non iudicant componendo vnum cum altero: vel vnum alteri attribuendo: sed vno simplici conceptu exprimendo vtrumque. Modus autem iste pugnat cum imperfectione nostri intellectus, non intelligentis, nisi componendo & diuidendo.

To the argument of the other opinion: Granting the major, the minor must be distinguished: because to elicit, from a twofold diverse simple concept, a third, also simple, representing the several things that were represented by those, can be understood in two ways. First, by way of simple expression, so that by that one concept is expressed whatever was represented by several. Second, by attribution and composition of one with another. And in the first way it can be done by the imagination and by our intellect; but in the second way it is impossible: because to compose one with another expresses a multiplicity of concepts; and since it must be done so through the judgment by which the mental enunciation is constituted, it cannot be done through one concept, but necessarily through several, of which the mental enunciation is composed; and therefore the mental enunciation cannot be a simple concept or a simple quality, but is composed of several concepts and qualities. In the angels, however, it is a simple concept and a simple quality, because they do not judge by composing one with another, or by attributing one to another, but by expressing both by one simple concept. But this mode is incompatible with the imperfection of our intellect, which does not understand except by composing and dividing.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

An diuisio enunciationis, in affirmatiuam, & negatiuam, sit generis in species, vel analogi in analogata.

Whether the division of the enunciation into affirmative and negative is that of a genus into species, or of an analogous term into analogates.

Prima opinio est Alexandri: quem citat D. Tho. cap. præsenti, asserentis esse diuisionem analogi, in analogata, quam sequuntur etiam Philoponus, 1. lib. Poster. cap. 21. Aspasius, & Burana, 1. lib. Priorum, cap. 1. Probatur hac ratione: Analogum est, quod de vno membro dicitur per prius, & de

he first opinion is that of Alexander, whom St. Thomas cites on the T present chapter, who asserts that it is the division of an analogous term into analogates; which Philoponus also follows, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 21, and Aspasius and Burana, Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1. It is proved by this reason: An analogous term is that which is said of one member by priority, and of

p. 541

alio per posterius: sed enunciatio dicitur per prius de affirmatiua, & per posterius de negatiua: ergo analogum est respectu earum: & ita diuisio erit analogi in analogata. Probatur minor. Primò ex Arist. cap. præsenti, vbi sic ait: Est autem vna prima oratio enuntiatiua, affirmatio: deinde negatio. Probatur etiam ratione: Quia affirmatio dicit compositionem, negatio diuisionem: compositio autem prior est diuisione. Præterea, affirmatio dicit formam positiuam, qua priuat negatio: forma verò prior est priuatione. Et tandem negatio cadit supra affirmationem: cùm propositio negatiua non sit aliud, quam affirmatiua, addita negatione: illa igitur prior est posterior hæc.

of the other posteriorly; but enunciation is said priorly of the affirmative and posteriorly of the negative; therefore it is analogous with respect to them, and so the division will be of an analogous term into its analogates. The minor is proved: first, from Aristotle in the present chapter, where he says: But the first one enunciative speech is affirmation; then negation. It is proved also by reason: because affirmation signifies composition, negation division; but composition is prior to division. Moreover, affirmation signifies a positive form, of which negation deprives; but form is prior to privation. And finally, negation falls upon affirmation, since a negative proposition is nothing other than an affirmative one with a negation added: the former, therefore, is prior, the latter posterior.

Secunda opinio est Soti, 2. lib. Summularum, asserentis, affirmationem & negationem esse diuersas qualitates enuntiationis: & cùm qualitas sit accidens, diuidetur enunciatio in affirmatiuam, & negatiuam, tanquam subiectum in diuersa accidentia Probatur hoc arg. Accidens est, quod potest adesse, & abesse subiecto, præter corruptionem eius: sed affirmatio, & negatio, ita se habent respectu enunciationis: ergo sunt accidentia eius. Probatur minor: quia enunciatio eadem permanens secundùm essentiam, transit de affirmatiua in negatiuam, vt hæc eadem: Petrus currit, fit negatiua addita negatione Petrus non currit.

The second opinion is that of Soto, Summulae bk. 2, who asserts that affirmation and negation are different qualities of the enunciation; and since quality is an accident, enunciation will be divided into affirmative and negative as a subject into different accidents. This is proved by this argument: An accident is that which can be present to and absent from a subject without its corruption; but affirmation and negation are so related to the enunciation; therefore they are its accidents. The minor is proved: because the enunciation, remaining the same according to its essence, passes from affirmative to negative, as this same one, Peter runs, becomes negative when a negation is added: Peter does not run.

Tertia opinio est communis: quòd diuisio enunciationis sit generis in species, ita Porphyrius, Ammonius, Boëtius, Simplicius, D. Th. Louanien. Suesan. Lemosius, & Toler. cap. præsenti. Et hæc est probabilior, & tenenda.

The third opinion is the common one: that the division of the enunciation is of a genus into species. So hold Porphyry, Ammonius, Boethius, Simplicius, St. Thomas, the Louvain commentators, Suessanus, Lemos, and Toledo on the present chapter. And this is more probable and is to be held.

Probatur Primò: Quia essentia enunciationis, vt superiùs probauimus, consistit in eo, quod attribuere vnum alteri, aut enũciare de illo: sed hoc fit per affirmationem, & negationem: ergo istæ sunt differentiæ essentiales, diuidentes enunciationem. Erit ergo diuisio generis in species.

It is proved, first: because the essence of the enunciation, as we proved above, consists in attributing one thing to another, or enunciating something of it; but this comes about through affirmation and negation; therefore these are essential differences dividing the enunciation. The division, therefore, will be of a genus into species.

Secundò: Enunciatio affirmatiua, & negatiua, conueniunt in ratione communi enunciationis, quæ de vtraque prædicatur: nam vera est hæc, Enunciatio affirmatiua, est enunciatio: est enunciatio negatiua, est enuntiatio, est æquè vera quæ distinguuntur specie: ergo enunciatio est genus ad vtranque. Probatur minor: quia affirmatiua dicit vnionem, & compositionem prædicati cum subiecto, negatiua verò diuisionem & separationem ab illo: at isti sunt modi enunciandi, formaliter, & essentialiter diuersi, vt patet: ergo constituunt enunciationes formaliter, & essentialiter diuersas.

Second: the affirmative and the negative enunciation agree in the common ratio of enunciation, which is predicated of both; for this is true, An affirmative enunciation is an enunciation, A negative enunciation is an enunciation; and they are distinguished in species; therefore enunciation is a genus with respect to both. The minor is proved: because the affirmative signifies the union and composition of the predicate with the subject, but the negative its division and separation from it; and these are modes of enunciating formally and essentially different, as is plain; therefore they constitute enunciations formally and essentially different.

Ad arg. primæ opinionis, Distinguenda est maior: nam dici

To the argument of the first opinion: the major must be distinguished; for to be said

p. 542

per prius de vno, & per posterius de altero, duobus modis contingit: vel ratione prædicati superioris, in quo conueniunt, vel ratione differentiarum per quas distinguuntur, & primus modus tollit vniuocationem, & efficit analogiam: secundus verò nullo modo: cùm in omnibus generibus reperiatur: in quibus semper datur vna species, prior aliis, propter minorem perfectionem suæ differentiæ: quod non impedit, quin natura generica ex sua parte, æqualiter, & vniuocè participetur ab omnibus speciebus. Et ita contingit in enunciatione, cuius ratio ex parte sua æquè participatur ab affirmatiua, & negatiua, & non secundùm prius & posterius: sed enunciatio affirmatiua, propter maiorem perfectionem suæ differentiæ, prior est negatiua, vt asserit Arist. & probat argumentum: hoc tamen non tollit vniuocationem nec rationem genericam.

priorly of one and posteriorly of another happens in two ways: either by reason of the superior predicate in which they agree, or by reason of the differences by which they are distinguished; and the first way takes away univocation and produces analogy, but the second in no way, since it is found in all genera, in which there is always one species prior to the others on account of the lesser perfection of their difference; which does not prevent the generic nature, on its own side, from being participated equally and univocally by all the species. And so it happens in the enunciation, whose ratio, on its own side, is participated equally by the affirmative and the negative, and not according to prior and posterior; but the affirmative enunciation, on account of the greater perfection of its difference, is prior to the negative, as Aristotle asserts and the argument proves; this, however, does not take away univocation nor the generic ratio.

Ad arg. secundæ opinionis, Distinguenda est minor. quia propositio eadem permanens, solùm materialiter: hoc est, secundùm materiales terminos, transit de affirmatiua in negatiuam: non tamen eadem permanens formaliter, & essentialiter: sed diuersæ speciei fit, addita negatione, propter diuersum modum enunciandi, vt probauimus: quare affirmatio, & negatio, differentiæ essentiales sunt enunciationis, & non qualitates: nisi eo modo, quo differentiæ essentiales, dicuntur qualitates generis essentiales: quare nec sunt vllo modo accidentia eius.

To the argument of the second opinion: the minor must be distinguished; for the proposition, remaining the same only materially, that is, according to its material terms, passes from affirmative to negative; but not remaining the same formally and essentially: rather, when the negation is added, it becomes of a different species, on account of the different mode of enunciating, as we proved. Wherefore affirmation and negation are essential differences of the enunciation, and not qualities, except in the way in which essential differences are called essential qualities of the genus; wherefore neither are they in any way its accidents.

Quæstio 5. An diuisio enunciationis in affirmatiuam, & negatiuam, sit generis in species, vel analogi in analogata — QUESTION VI. Whether the division of the enunciation into simple and composite is of a genus into species, or of an analogous term into its analogates.

QVÆSTIO VI.

[…]

An diuisio enunciationis in simplicem & compositam, sit generis in species? vel analogi in analogata.

[…]

Prima opinio tenet, Vniuocam esse hanc diuisionem: & ideo generis in suas species. Ita Sotus 2. lib. Summularum, cap. 6. & alij. Probant primò: Quia enunciatio simplex, & composita, conueniunt vniuocè in genere orationis: ergo etiam in genere enunciationis, quod est oratione inferius. Probatur consequentia: quia quæ conueniunt vniuocè sub genere superiori, necesse est etiam vniuocè conuenire, sub genere inferiori: vt si duo animalia conueniunt sub genere viuentis superiori, necesse est sub genere animalis viuente inferiori, etiam vniuocè conuenire.

The first opinion holds that this division is univocal, and therefore of a genus into its species. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 6, and others. They prove it, first: because the simple and the composite enunciation agree univocally in the genus of speech; therefore also in the genus of enunciation, which is inferior to speech. The consequence is proved: because things that agree univocally under a superior genus must also agree univocally under an inferior genus; as, if two animals agree under the superior genus of living thing, they must also agree univocally under the genus of animal, inferior to living thing.

Secundò: Significare verum, aut falsum, vel est de essentia enunciationis, vel propria passio eius: sed enunciatio simplex, & composita, conueniunt vniuocè in eo, quod est significare, verum, aut falsum: nam enunciatio composita, simpliciter

Second: to signify the true or the false is either of the essence of the enunciation or its proper attribute; but the simple and the composite enunciation agree univocally in signifying the true or the false; for the composite enunciation, simply

p. 543

est vera, aut falsa, sicut simplex: ergo cõueniunt etiam vniuocè in ratione cõmuni enunciationis, tanquam species sub genere.

is true or false, just like the simple one; therefore they also agree univocally in the common ratio of enunciation, as species under a genus.

Secunda opinio quorundam modernorum, asserit diuisionem hanc esse, Subiecti in accidentia. Probatur hoc ar. Quòd magis, & minùs compositum, solùm differunt ex hoc accidentaliter: vt paries à tota domo: & enunciatio omnino simplex, ab ea, quæ componitur ex parte subiecti, ex alia simplici enunciatione, vt hæc: homo est albus, est propositio: solùm differt accidentaliter ab illa, homo est albus: quia magis composita est: sed enunciatione composita, solùm differt à simplici, penes magis, & minus, compositum: quia simplex, solùm componitur ex subiecto prædicato, & copula: composita verò, ex his quidem remotè, proximè verò ex multis enuntiationibus simplicibus: ergo solùm distinguuntur accidentaliter.

The second opinion, of certain moderns, asserts that this division is of a subject into accidents. This is proved by this argument: the more and the less composite differ by this only accidentally, as the wall from the whole house; and the wholly simple enunciation differs from one which is composed, on the side of the subject, of another simple enunciation, such as this, “Man is white” is a proposition, only accidentally from the former, Man is white, because it is more composite. But the composite enunciation differs from the simple only according to more and less composite: because the simple is composed only of subject, predicate, and copula, whereas the composite is composed of these remotely, but proximately of many simple enunciations; therefore they are distinguished only accidentally.

Tertia opinio est communis: Quòd hæc diuisio sit analogi in analogata. Ita Boëtius, Ammonius, Suesanus, Toletus c. præsenti. D. Tho. opusc. 48. cap. 6. & moderni plures. Videtúrque nobis probabilior, & magis conformis doctrinæ Aristot. qui enuntiationem simplicem vocauit vnam, propter vnum significatum: & ideo vnam simpliciter: compositam verò vnam coniunctione, quod est, esse vnam secundùm quid: & ideo secundùm quid enuntiationem.

The third opinion is the common one: that this division is of an analogous term into its analogates. So Boethius, Ammonius, Suessanus, Toledo on the present chapter, St. Thomas, opusc. 48, ch. 6, and many moderns. And it seems to us more probable and more in conformity with the doctrine of Aristotle, who called the simple enunciation one, on account of its one significate, and therefore one simply; but the composite one by conjunction, which is to be one in a qualified sense, and therefore an enunciation in a qualified sense.

Probatur id ratione. Primò: quia ratio formalis enunciationis, vt superiùs probauimus, consistit in enunciando, vnum de altero: sed enunciatio composita, non enunciat vnum de altero: quia non componitur proximè ex subiecto, & prædicato, sed solùm dicitur enunciatio ratione simplicium, ex quibus constat, coniunctione vnitis: & solùm ratione earum significat veritatem, aut falsitatem: ergo ratio formalis enunciationis, conuenit per se primò simplici, compositæ verò solùm per participationem, & attributionem ad illam: quod est analogicè conuenire.

This is proved by reason. First: because the formal ratio of the enunciation, as we proved above, consists in enunciating one thing of another; but the composite enunciation does not enunciate one thing of another, because it is not composed proximately of subject and predicate, but is called an enunciation only by reason of the simple ones of which it consists, united by a conjunction, and only by reason of them does it signify truth or falsity; therefore the formal ratio of enunciation belongs per se and primarily to the simple, but to the composite only by participation and attribution to it, which is to belong analogically.

Secundò: Vna species non componitur formaliter ex altera licèt materialiter componi non repugnet: sed composita enunciatio, componitur ex simplicibus formaliter: hoc est, inquantum enunciant vnum de altero, & inquantum veritatem etiam simplicem habent: cum quolibet horum ab eis sublato non consistat enunciatio composita: ergo non possunt esse species enunciationis: sed erunt analogata eius, contra primam opinionem. Item probatur contra secundam, quòd non differant solùm accidentaliter: quia differunt per modum formalem, & essentialem: quia in simplici est enunciatiuus, in composita verò non: sed forma eius potius consistit in vnione

Second: one species is not composed formally of another, although it is not repugnant for it to be composed of it materially; but the composite enunciation is composed of simple ones formally, that is, inasmuch as they enunciate one thing of another and inasmuch as they also have simple truth, since if any one of these is taken from them the composite enunciation does not stand; therefore they cannot be species of the enunciation, but will be its analogates, against the first opinion. It is likewise proved against the second that they do not differ only accidentally: because they differ by a formal and essential mode, since in the simple the mode is enunciative, but in the composite it is not; rather, its form consists in the union

p. 544

simplicium, aut enunciatiuarum: ergo differunt essentialiter: quare diuisio non potest esse subiecti in accidentia, sed erit analogi in analogata, vt probauimus aduersus secundam opinionem.

of simple ones, or of enunciative ones; therefore they differ essentially. Wherefore the division cannot be of a subject into accidents, but will be of an analogous term into its analogates, as we proved against the second opinion.

Ad cuius arg. Respondendum est, & ad primum, Concesso antecedente, neganda est consequentia, & ratio est: quia ratio enunciationis, est longè perfectior oratione: quam non potest per se attingere composita enunciatio, sed solùm per participationem simplicis: quamuis per se, & simpliciter, possit attingere rationem orationis. Et licèt simile exemplum, non facilè inueniatur in entibus naturalibus, quia eorum natura, non est ita variabilis: inuenitur tamen in eisdem rebus artificialibus, ab intellectu factis: nam species, & indiuiduum vniuocè conueniunt sub genere relationis rationis, tanquam species eius: sub genere tamen inferiori, relationis prædicabilitatis, non conueniunt nisi analogicè: quia indiuiduum, non attingit perfectionem eius, cùm non prædicetur, nisi impropriè, de seipso. Itaque ratio inferior, adeò perfecta esse potest, & ratio superior, adeo imperfecta, vt non per se, aut non vniuocè eam possit participare: sed solùm per attributionem, ad aliud membrum perfectius, cum quo in genere superiori, valde imperfectiori, vniuocè conueniebat: & hoc satis est, vt non sit bona consequentia ita arguentis: hæc duo conueniunt vniuocè in prædicato superiori, ergo etiam in prædicato inferiori.

To whose arguments one must reply, and to the first: granting the antecedent, the consequence must be denied; and the reason is that the ratio of enunciation is far more perfect than speech, and the composite enunciation cannot attain it per se, but only by participation in the simple, although per se and simply it can attain the ratio of speech. And although a similar example is not easily found among natural beings, because their nature is not so variable, it is nevertheless found in those artificial things that are made by the intellect: for species and individual agree univocally under the genus of relation of reason, as its species; yet under the inferior genus, of the relation of predicability, they agree only analogically, because the individual does not attain its perfection, since it is not predicated except improperly, of itself. So the inferior ratio can be so perfect, and the superior ratio so imperfect, that one member cannot participate the former per se, or not univocally, but only by attribution to the other, more perfect member, with which it agreed univocally in the superior, much more imperfect genus; and this suffices for the consequence of one who argues thus not to be good: These two agree univocally in a superior predicate; therefore also in an inferior predicate.

Ad secundum: neganda est minor: quòd enunciatio simplex, & composita conueniant vniuocè in eo, quod est verum, vel falsum significare; nam hoc solùm conuenit compositæ per participationem simplicis: quare negandum est etiam, quòd sit vera, vel falsa simpliciter.

To the second: the minor must be denied, that the simple and the composite enunciation agree univocally in signifying the true or the false; for this belongs to the composite only by participation in the simple; wherefore it must also be denied that it is true or false simply.

Ad arg. secundæ opinionis, neganda est etiam minor: quòd enunciatio simplex, & composita, solùm differant penes magis & minùs compositum, nam differunt per diuersos modos formales enunciationis: quia simplex habet modum formalem enunciandi, composita verò non habet per se modum enunciandi: vnde nec per se enunciat, sed solùm per participationem simplicis: per se verò solùm habet modum coniunctionis enunciatiuarum: & ideo essentialiter sunt diuersæ.

To the argument of the second opinion, the minor must also be denied, that the simple and the composite enunciation differ only according to more and less composite; for they differ by different formal modes of enunciation: because the simple has the formal mode of enunciating, whereas the composite does not have the mode of enunciating per se, whence neither does it enunciate per se, but only by participation in the simple; per se, however, it has only the mode of a conjunction of enunciatives; and therefore they are essentially different.

CAP. V. De modis oppositionum — C H A P T E R V. O N T H E M O D E S of Oppositions.

CAPVT V. DE MODIS oppositionum.

[…]

Capite quinto, agit Aristotel. de modis oppositionum, inter enunciationes repertis. Quod caput non à nobis

In the fifth chapter Aristotle treats of the modes of opposition found among enunciations. This chapter is not to be expounded by us

p. 545

exponendum: quia de oppositione propositionum, & modis omnibus eius, satis disputant Summulistæ, regulas eorum ex hoc capite, atque ex lib. 2. huius operis deducentes: quare non putamus necessarium hac in parte eas repetere.

because concerning the opposition of propositions and all its modes the Summulists have disputed sufficiently, deducing their rules from this chapter and from bk. 2 of this work; wherefore we do not think it necessary to repeat them in this part.

CHAPTER VI

CAPVT VI.

[…]

CAP. VI. De oppositione, & veritate enunciationum de futuro contingenti, cum expositione textus — On the Opposition and Truth of Enunciations about the Contingent Future.

De oppositione, & veritate enunciationum de futuro contingenti.

[…]

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

TEX. ARISTOTELIS.

[…]

In his ergo quæ sunt, & quæ facta sunt, necesse est affirmationem & negationem veram esse, vel falsam, &c.

In those things, then, which are and which have been, it is necessary that the affirmation and the negation be true or false, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

33 Intentum Arist. ca. præsenti est, ostendere regulam propositionum contradictoriarum: quæ est talis: Si vna est vera, altera necessariò debet esse falsa: non esse veram eodem modo in propositionibus singularibus, de futuro contingenti: quemadmodum vera est in propositionibus materiæ necessariæ, & remotæ, atque etiam in propositionibus contingentibus de subiecto vniuersali. Diuiditur autem hoc in duas partes, nam in prima proposita quæstione & soluta, duplici ratione probat propriam sententiam. In 2. verò, duplicem distinctionem necessarij: circa res & propositiones tradit.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to show that the 33 T rule of contradictory propositions, which is this: If one is true, the other must necessarily be false, is not true in the same way in singular propositions about the contingent future as it is true in propositions of necessary and remote matter, and also in contingent propositions with a universal subject. And it is divided into two parts: for in the first, having proposed and solved the question, he proves his own view by a twofold argument; in the second, he delivers a twofold distinction of the necessary, concerning things and propositions.

Egerat Arist. cap. præcedenti, sub finem, de natura contradictionis, aut oppositionis in propositionibus repertæ: dixerâtque necessariam esse conditionem contradictoriarum enunciationum, vt si vna sit determinatè vera, altera determinatè sit falsa. Cap. verò præsenti, proponit hanc quæst. videlicet: An hæc conditio contradictoriarum vera sit, non solùm in propositionibus materiæ necessariæ, & remotæ sed etiam materiæ contingentis. Loquitur autem non de contingenti raro, quale est fodientem inuenire thesaurum: nec de contingente frequenter, quale est hominem noctu cubare: sed de contingente ad vtrumlibet: hoc est, ad vtramque partem, quod æquè potest esse, & non esse: vt Petrum peccare, vel honestè viuere.

Aristotle had treated in the preceding chapter, toward the end, of the nature of contradiction, or opposition, found in propositions; and he had said that it is a necessary condition of contradictory enunciations that, if one is determinately true, the other is determinately false. But in the present chapter he proposes this question, namely: Whether this condition of contradictories is true not only in propositions of necessary and remote matter, but also in contingent matter. He speaks, moreover, not of the rarely contingent, such as that one digging should find a treasure; nor of the frequently contingent, such as that a man should lie down at night; but of the contingent ad utrumlibet, that is, toward either side, which can equally be and not be: as that Peter should sin, or live virtuously.

Et præsupponit tanquam certum. Primò, veram esse regulam in omnibus præsuppositionibus materiæ necessariæ, & remotæ, siue vniuersales sint, seu singulares: nam si determinatè

And he presupposes as certain, first, that the rule is true in all propositions of necessary and remote matter, whether they are universal or singular: for if it is determinately Mm

p. 546

verum est. Petrum esse hominem: determinatè est falsum, Petrum non esse hominem: & si determinatè verum est, omnem leonem non esse lapidem: determinatè est falsum, quòd aliquis leo sit lapis. Secundò præsupponit tanquam certum, veram quoque esse regulam in propositionibus contingentibus de subiecto vniuersali: nam si determinatè verum est hominem esse album: determinatè est falsum, nullum hominem esse album. Tertium quoque certum esse ait: nempe eandem regulam esse veram in propositionibus contingentibus, de subiecto singulari, si sint de præsenti, aut præterito: nam si determinatè verum est, Petrum studiosè viuere, aut vixisse: determinatè est falsum, Petrum non studiosè viuere, aut vixisse. Nulla enim in his propositionibus potest esse indeterminatio, sed sicut determinatè verum est, quod fuit, & est ita: determinatè falsum erit, non fuisse, aut non esse. Solùm ergo procedere quæstionem ait, de propositionibus singularibus, de futuro contingenti: An vna earum sit determinatè vera, & alia determinatè falsa. Et ratio dubitandi est manifesta: quia causa contingens aut libera, non est determinata ad effectum futurum, sed potest se determinare, & potest se non determinare: & ideo quamdiu determinatio eius futura enunciatur, per propositionem singularem de futuro, tamdiu quasi suspensa manet: & ideo veritas eiusdem popositionis indeterminata semper videtur.

true that Peter is a man, it is determinately false that Peter is not a man; and if it is determinately true that every lion is not a stone, it is determinately false that some lion is a stone. Second, he presupposes as certain that the rule is also true in contingent propositions with a universal subject: for if it is determinately true that every man is white, it is determinately false that no man is white. He says that a third thing is also certain: namely, that the same rule is true in contingent propositions with a singular subject, if they are about the present or the past: for if it is determinately true that Peter lives, or has lived, virtuously, it is determinately false that Peter does not live, or has not lived, virtuously. For in these propositions there can be no indetermination; but just as it is determinately true that what has been and is, is so, it will be determinately false that it has not been or is not. He says, therefore, that the question proceeds only about singular propositions about the contingent future: whether one of them is determinately true and the other determinately false. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because a contingent or free cause is not determined to a future effect, but can determine itself and can not determine itself; and therefore, as long as its future determination is enunciated by a singular proposition about the future, so long does it remain as it were suspended; and therefore the truth of that same proposition always seems indeterminate.

Respondet autem Arist. In his propositionibus, determinatè verum esse totum disiunctum, ex vtraque contradictoria constans. Vt Petrus peccabit, aut non peccabit: nam peccare, aut non peccare, ita necessarium est, sicut esse, vel non esse: ergo ita determinatè verum Sed vtramlibet contradictoriam per se sumptam, non esse determinatè veram, aut falsam, vt Petrus peccabit, atque etiam Petrus non peccabit. Quod probat duplici arg. ducente ad impossibile. Primò: Quia si determinatè essent veræ, nihil esset in rebus contingens, sed omnia euenirent necessariò: vt si determinatè verum esset, Petrus hoc efficiet, aut illud: studiosus, aut vitiosus erit: bellum erit futurum cras, vel non erit futurum, necessariò euenirent effectus isti: & ideo non possent non euenire: quare nihil esset in rebus contingens, quod est absurdum.

Aristotle replies, however, that in these propositions the whole disjunction made up of both contradictories is determinately true, as Peter will sin or will not sin: for to sin or not to sin is as necessary as to be or not to be; therefore it is likewise determinately true. But either contradictory taken by itself is not determinately true or false, as Peter will sin, and also Peter will not sin. This he proves by a twofold argument leading to the impossible. First: because if they were determinately true, nothing in things would be contingent, but all things would come about necessarily; as, if it were determinately true that Peter will do this or that, will be virtuous or vicious, that a battle will take place tomorrow or will not take place, those effects would come about necessarily, and therefore could not fail to come about; wherefore nothing in things would be contingent, which is absurd.

Secunda ratio: Quia si propositiones istæ singulares de futuro contingenti essent determinatè veræ, & omnes futuri effectus, necessariò euenirent, neque aliquis esset effectus contingens, non esset consultandum de rebus futuris, nec deliberandum: quare nec esset consilium, nec libertas: nam deliberatio

The second reason: because if these singular propositions about the contingent future were determinately true, and all future effects came about necessarily, and no effect were contingent, there would be no need to take counsel about future things, nor to deliberate; wherefore there would be neither counsel nor freedom: for delibe

p. 547

, & consultatio, solùm est de rebus contingentibus: quæ possunt esse, & non esse: de his enim quæ necessariò futura sunt, vt de ortu solis crastino, nullus vnquam suæ mentis consultandum esse dixit. Tollere autem contingentiam, consilium, deliberationem, imò, & libertatem nostram, absurdum est: ergo non est dicendum propositiones singulares de futuro contingenti esse determinatè veras, aut determinatè falsas.

ration and consultation concern only contingent things, which can be and not be; for about things that will necessarily come to be, such as tomorrow’s sunrise, no one in his right mind ever said that one must take counsel. But to take away contingency, counsel, deliberation, nay, even our freedom, is absurd; therefore it must not be said that singular propositions about the contingent future are determinately true or determinately false.

Explicat tandem duplicem distinctionem necessitatis rerum, & enunciationum. Prima talis est: Quædam res sunt necessariæ ex propria natura, vt cœlum: aliæ verò, non nisi ex conditione temporis, quo mensurantur: cùm tamen ex propria natura contingentes sint: vt Petrum ambulare, dum ambulat, necessarium est, non ex propria natura, sed ex conditione temporis, quo mensuratut ambulatio eius: & hoc modo verum esse vniuersaliter ait, quòd omnis res quando est, necessariò sit: & omnis propositio pro tempore, quo vera est, necessariò est vera, sed necessitatem primam simpliciter esse talem affirmat: secundam verò, non nisi secundùm quid: hoc est ab extrinseco, & ex suppositione temporis, in quo res est, vel in quo propositio vera est.

Finally he explains a twofold distinction of the necessity of things and of enunciations. The first is this: Some things are necessary from their own nature, as the heavens; others only from the condition of the time by which they are measured, although from their own nature they are contingent: as it is necessary that Peter walk while he walks, not from his own nature but from the condition of the time by which his walking is measured. And in this way he says it is universally true that every thing, when it is, necessarily is, and every proposition, for the time at which it is true, is necessarily true; but he affirms that the first necessity is such simply, while the second is such only in a qualified sense, that is, extrinsically and from the supposition of the time at which the thing is, or at which the proposition is true.

Secunda est distinctio necessarij: Quædam sunt necessaria absolutè, id est, sine comparatione ad aliud: vt hominem esse animal. Alia non nisi ex comparatione ad suum oppositum: ita, vt quod per se sumptum contingens est, sumptum cum suo opposito fit necessarium: vt contingens est hæc, Petrus ambulabit, at si sumatur cum sua opposita, necessarium facit totum, disiunctum, vt, Petrus ambulabit, aut non ambulabit. Et hunc etiam modum necessitatis extrinsecum esse ait, & secundùm quid talem: cùm tamen primus simpliciter sit talis, & ab intrinseco. Et hunc modum necessitatis, atque etiam secundum, primæ distinctionis, reperiri docet in enunciationibus singularibus contingentibus de præsenti, præterito, & futuro: nam dum Petrus ambulat, necessarium est ex suppositione, ambulare: & etiam quòd ambulauerit, supposito, quòd ambulauit: & etiam est necessaria hæc de futuro, Petrus ambulabit, ex suppositione, quòd ambulabit. Necessarium quoque est disiunctum hoc, Petrus ambulabit, vel non ambulabit: sed cum vtraque hac necessitate totius disiuncti, & etiam cuiuslibet partis per se sumptæ, ex suppositione temporis verum est, quamlibet per se sumptam esse contingentem, & indeterminatè veram.

The second is the distinction of the necessary: Some things are necessary absolutely, that is, without comparison to another, as that man is an animal. Others only from comparison to their opposite, so that what, taken by itself, is contingent, taken together with its opposite is necessary: as this is contingent, Peter will walk; but if it is taken with its opposite, it makes the whole disjunction necessary, as Peter will walk or will not walk. And he says that this mode of necessity too is extrinsic and such in a qualified sense, whereas the first is such simply and intrinsically. And he teaches that this mode of necessity, and also the second of the first distinction, is found in singular contingent enunciations about the present, the past, and the future: for while Peter walks it is necessary, on the supposition, that he walk; and also that he has walked, on the supposition that he did walk; and this one about the future is also necessary, Peter will walk, on the supposition that he will walk. This disjunction too is necessary, Peter will walk or will not walk; but with both of these necessities, of the whole disjunction and also of each part taken by itself from the supposition of time, it is true that each, taken by itself, is contingent and indeterminately true. MM ij

p. 548

Quæst. vnic. An singulares enunciationes de futuro contingenti habeant veritatem, aut falsitatem determinatam — SINGLE QUESTION. Whether singular enunciations about the contingent future have determinate truth or falsity.

QVÆSTIO VNICA.

[…]

An singulares enunciationes de futuro contingenti, habeant veritatem, aut falsitatem determinatam.

[…]

De solis singularibus, & contingentibus procedit quæstio: nam propositiones necessariæ, atque etiam ex materia remota constantes, necessariò veræ sunt, vel necessariò falsæ: siue sint vniuersales, siue singulares: & ideo determinata est earum veritas, aut falsitas: determinatè etiam veræ sunt contingentes de subiecto vniuersali, aut determinatè falsæ: vt omnis homo ambulabit: nullus homo ambulabit: &, homo ambulabit: homo non ambulabit. Quia licèt effectus futurus, atque contingens, in singulari possit esse, & non esse, vniuersaliter tamen verum est, quòd causa contingens determinabitur ad operandum: imò necessaria est determinatio eius in singulari vago, licèt sit omnino contingens in quolibet singulari determinato. Necessitate quidem morali: quia moraliter loquendo, hoc est, more humano, vel vt res humanæ solent euenire, necesse est, homines ambulare: & ideo determinatè vera hæc, homo ambulabit: & aliquis homo ambulabit: & determinatè falsa, omnis homo ambulabit: nullus homo ambulabit. In hoc enim sensu accipitur illud Christi apud Matthæum: Necesse est, vt veniant scandala. Certum quoque est, singulares propositiones contingentes de præsenti, & præterito, esse determinatè veras, vel falsas: imò necessarias, non quidem ab intrinseco, vel simpliciter, sed ab extrinseco, & ex suppositione temporis: vt iã fuit à nobis expositum. Solùm ergo de singularibus de futuro contingenti quæstio esse potest: An determinatam habeant veritatẽ, vel indeterminatam: quia determinatio causæ futuræ, à qua pendet veritas earum, quamdiu futura enunciatur, indeterminata est: & ideo non videtur posse tribuere veritatem determinatam eisdem propositionibus.

The question proceeds only about singular and contingent ones: for necessary propositions, and also those consisting of remote matter, are necessarily true or necessarily false, whether they are universal or singular; and therefore their truth or falsity is determinate. Contingent ones with a universal subject are also determinately true or determinately false: as every man will walk, no man will walk; and, man will walk, man will not walk. Because, although a future and contingent effect can, in the singular, be and not be, it is nevertheless universally true that the contingent cause will be determined to operate; nay, its determination is necessary in the vague singular, although it is wholly contingent in any determinate singular. By a moral necessity, that is: because, speaking morally, that is, in the human manner, or as human affairs are wont to turn out, it is necessary that men walk; and therefore this is determinately true, man will walk, and some man will walk; and determinately false, every man will walk, no man will walk. For in this sense is taken that saying of Christ in Matthew: It must needs be that scandals come. It is also certain that singular contingent propositions about the present and the past are determinately true or false; nay, necessary, not indeed intrinsically or simply, but extrinsically and from the supposition of time, as was expounded by us. The question, then, can be only about singular ones about the contingent future: whether they have determinate truth, or indeterminate; because the determination of the future cause, on which their truth depends, is indeterminate as long as it is enunciated as future; and therefore it does not seem able to confer determinate truth on those same propositions.

Ideò prima opinio asserit: Nullam prorsus habere veritatem, aut falsitatem tales propositiones, sed neutras esse: hoc est, nec veras, nec falsas. Ita Antonius Cordubensis, lib. 1. sui Quæstionarij, q. 55. dub. 2. Probatur: quia veritas, vel falsitas enunciationis sumitur, per conformitatem, aut difformitatem, ad rem significatam: sed res significata per hanc enunciationem: Petrus peccabit, non est in rerum natura, quamdiu enunciatur futura: ergo enunciatio ipsa non est ei conformis, nec deformis: quare non erit vera, neque falsa, sed neutra, & certè si vera, aut falsa

Therefore the first opinion asserts: that such propositions have no truth or falsity at all, but are neutral, that is, neither true nor false. So Antonio de Córdoba, bk. 1 of his Quaestionarium, q. 55, doubt 2. It is proved: because the truth or falsity of an enunciation is taken from its conformity or disconformity to the thing signified; but the thing signified by this enunciation, Peter will sin, is not in the nature of things as long as it is enunciated as future; therefore the enunciation itself is neither conformed nor disconformed to it; wherefore it will be neither true nor false, but neutral. And certainly, if true or false

p. 549

concedatur, sequitur simul esse veram, & falsam, quod repugnat. Probatur consequentia: quia cùm res significata indifferens sit ad essendum, & non essendum, & non magis ad vnum, quàm ad alterum determinata, non est maior ratio, ob quam enunciatio sit vera, potiùs quàm falsa: quare vel neutrum habebit, vel vtrumque: & hoc impossibile: ergo aliud necessarium, quod est esse neutram.

is granted, it follows that it is at once true and false, which is repugnant. The consequence is proved: because, since the thing signified is indifferent to being and not being, and not determined to the one more than to the other, there is no greater reason why the enunciation should be true rather than false; wherefore it will have either neither or both; and the latter is impossible; therefore the other is necessary, namely that it is neutral.

Secunda opinio: Aliquam veritatem tribuit his enunciationibus, non quidem determinatam, sed confusam, aut indeterminatam: ita vt totum disiunctum ex vtraque contradictoria cõpositum, sit determinatè verum, ac necessarium, vt Petrus disputabit, vel non disputabit: sed vtraque, earum per se sumpta indeterminatè, vera sit aut falsa, quod est dicere indifferentem esse ad veritatem, aut falsitatem: & ideo non esse actu veram, nec actu falsam, sed quasi in potentia, nondum determinata. Ita Alber. Mag. 1. lib. de interpretatione, tract. de oppositione, cap. 4. Catherinus in opus. de veritate enunciationum, Louanien. & Tolet. cap. præsenti. Et hæc videtur expressa sententia Aristotelis, qui eam probauit hac ratione: Quod determinatè verum est, necessarium existimatur: ergo si enunciatio singularis de futuro contingenti, determinatè vera est, erit necessaria. Ex quo sequitur, futura omnia necessariò euenire.
