the consequent false, so in the particular negative de necesse: That some animal is not a man is necessary; therefore that some man is not an animal is necessary.

In secunda parte cap. agit de conuersione propositionum de contingenti: quod duobus modis sumi posse ait, Primò, prout est idem, quod possibile: & hoc modo etiam conuenit rebus necessariis: quia si necesse est hominem esse animal: ergo etiam est possibile, & consequenter contingens, sumpto contingenti pro possibili. Sed hanc acceptionem contingentis, impropriam esse docet. Ideo secundo modo, sumitur propriè, pro eo, quod potest esse, & potest non esse.

In the second part of the chapter he treats of the conversion of propositions de contingenti, which he says can be taken in two ways. First, as it is the same as possible; and in this way it belongs even to necessary things: because if it is necessary that man be an animal, then it is also possible, and consequently contingent, taking contingent for possible. But he teaches that this acceptation of contingent is improper. Therefore, in the second way, it is taken properly for that which can be and can not be.

Hoc supposito, prima regula est: Quòd omnes propositiones de contingenti, Primo modo, eadem prorsus ratione conuertantur, ac propositiones de inesse, & de modo necesse. quam nec oportet probare, nec exemplis ostendere, cùm sit satis manifesta.

This supposed, the first rule is: That all propositions de contingenti in the first way are converted in altogether the same manner as propositions de inesse and of the mode de necesse. This needs neither to be proved nor shown by examples, since it is sufficiently manifest.

Secunda regula: Omnes propositiones affirmatiuæ de contingenti, Secundo modo accepto, conuertuntur, etiam eisdem modis: nempe, Vniuersalis affirmatiua in partem: vt contingit omnem hominem esse album: ergo contingit aliquod album esse hominem, & particularis affirmatiua simpliciter, vt contingit aliquem hominem esse album: ergo cõtingit aliquod album esse hominẽ. Quæ etiam regula non probatur ab Arist. quia manifesta est.

The second rule: All affirmative propositions de contingenti, taken in the second way, are converted also in the same modes: namely, the universal affirmative into part, as: It is contingent that every man is white; therefore it is contingent that something white is a man; and the particular affirmative simply, as: It is contingent that some man is white; therefore it is contingent that something white is a man. This rule too is not proved by Aristotle, because it is manifest.

Tertia: Vniuersalis negatiua, non conuertitur, particularis verò negatiua conuertitur simpliciter: & in hoc differunt propositiones de contingenti, ab omnibus aliis. Hanc regulam probat alia ratione, nisi quia negatiuæ de modo contingenti propriè sumpto, affirmatiuam habent figuram: quid autem hoc sit, statim explicabitur.

The third: The universal negative is not converted, but the particular negative is converted simply; and in this propositions de contingenti differ from all the others. He proves this rule by no other reason than that negatives of the contingent mode, properly taken, have an affirmative figure; but what this is will be explained presently.

Dubium primum circa conuersionem propositionum de necesse.

F I R S T D O U B T, C O N C E R N I N G T H E C O N V E R S I O N O F P RO P O S I T I O N S D E NECESSE

An vera sit secunda regula conuersionis, vniuersalis affirmatiuæ, & particularis affirmatiuæ, de necesse.

Whether the second rule of conversion, of the universal affirmative and the particular affirmative de necesse, is true.

14 Primò agendum est de cõuersione propositionum de necesse, vt ordinem Arist. sequamur. Deinde de conuersione propositionum de cõtingenti: & tandem dicemus, quid sentiendum sit, de propositionibus de possibili, & impossibili. Est ergo primũ dubium: Quia secundùm hanc regulam, propositio vniuersalis affirmatiua de necesse, conuertitur in particularem, & particularis affirmatiua simpliciter: sed probatur vtrumque falsum: quia in vtraque conuersione datur antecedens verum, & cõsequens falsum: ergo vtraq; est mala conuersio. Probatur

14 First we must treat of the conversion of propositions de necesse, so as to follow Aristotle’s order; then of the conversion of propositions de contingenti; and finally we shall say what is to be held concerning propositions de possibili and de impossibili. The first doubt, then, is this: According to this rule the universal affirmative proposition de necesse is converted into a particular, and the particular affirmative simply; but each is proved false, because in each conversion the antecedent is true and the consequent false; therefore each is a bad conversion. This is proved

p. 567

antecedens in his: Necesse est omnem grammaticum esse hominem: ergo necesse est aliquem hominem, esse grammaticum: & rursus, Necesse est aliquem grammaticum esse hominem: ergo necesse est aliquem hominem esse grammaticum. Aliqui respondent, has propositiones modales, duobus modis sumi posse. Primo in sensu composito: ita, vt significatio modi, cadat supra totum illud concretum, vt compositum ex homine, & grammatica: & sensus sit, Necesse est omne quod necessariò est grammaticum, esse hominem: & tunc antecedens est falsum, sicut & consequens: quare non probatur malam esse conuersionem. Si verò sumantur in sensu diuiso: ita vt modus non componat grammaticam cum homine, sed naturæ suæ relinquat: verbi gratia, si talis sensus sit, Omnem grammaticum, non posse nõ esse hominem, non possunt conuerti iuxta traditas regulas: quas solùm in sensu composito intellexit Arist. Hæc solutio non placuit Villalpandeo in Commentariis huius capitis: quia verè diminuta est. Nam cùm in vtroque sensu, possit sumi modus, & meliùs atque frequentiùs sumatur in sensu diuiso, vt per se est manifestum, satis diminutus esset Arist. si regulas conuersionis non assignaret iuxta communem, & magis proprium sensum propositionum. Propterea respondet ipse: Veram esse eandem regulam, etiam exemplo allato, si seruetur idem sensus vtriusque propositionis Quod in conuersione vniuersalis negatiuæ probat, Videlicet Necesse est nullum grammaticum esse hominem: ergo necesse est nullum hominem esse grammaticum, nam vtraque in eodem sensu accepta, est falsa.

the antecedent in these: It is necessary that every grammarian be a man; therefore it is necessary that some man be a grammarian; and again: It is necessary that some grammarian be a man; therefore it is necessary that some man be a grammarian. Some reply that these modal propositions can be taken in two ways. First, in the composite sense, so that the signification of the mode falls upon the whole of that concrete as composed of man and grammar, and the sense is: It is necessary that everything that is necessarily a grammarian be a man; and then the antecedent is false, as is the consequent, wherefore it is not proved that the conversion is bad. But if they are taken in the divided sense, so that the mode does not compound grammar with man but leaves it to its own nature (for example, if the sense is: That every grammarian cannot not be a man), they cannot be converted according to the rules handed down, which Aristotle understood only in the composite sense. This solution did not please Villalpando in his Commentaries on this chapter, because it is truly defective. For since the mode can be taken in either sense, and is better and more frequently taken in the divided sense, as is manifest of itself, Aristotle would be quite defective if he did not assign the rules of conversion according to the common and more proper sense of the propositions. Therefore he himself replies that the same rule is true even with the example adduced, if the same sense of each proposition is preserved. This he proves in the conversion of the universal negative, namely: It is necessary that no grammarian be a man; therefore it is necessary that no man be a grammarian: for each, taken in the same sense, is false.

Sed hæc solutio minùs satisfacit, quàm prima: nam regula non habet difficultatem in conuersione vniuersalis negatiuæ, sed in solis affirmatiuis: quæ etiam si in eodem sensu accipiantur, necesse est dari aliquando in earum conuersione, antecedens verum, & consequens falsum. Vt exemplum datum probat euidenter.

But this solution satisfies less than the first: for the rule has no difficulty in the conversion of the universal negative, but only in the affirmatives; and these, even if they are taken in the same sense, must sometimes have in their conversion a true antecedent and a false consequent, as the example given proves evidently.

Ideo respondemus: Propositiones de modo Necesse, vniuersaliter loquendo accipiendas esse, supposita existentia extremorum: vt in eis vera esse possit regula conuersionis tradita ab Aristo. Vt in exempli argumento, supposito, quòd homines, & grammatica sint in rerum natura, tunc verum est antecedens: Necesse est omnem grammaticum esse hominem: quia sensus est, existente homine, & grammatica, necesse est omnem grammaticam esse in homine. Et etiam verum est consequens, Necesse est aliquem hominem esse grammaticum; quia sensus est, homine, & grammatica existentibus

Therefore we reply: Propositions of the mode de necesse, speaking universally, are to be taken with the existence of the extremes supposed, so that in them the rule of conversion handed down by Aristotle may be true. As in the argument of the example: supposing that men and grammar exist in the nature of things, then the antecedent is true, It is necessary that every grammarian be a man, because the sense is: man and grammar existing, it is necessary that all grammar be in a man. And the consequent is also true, It is necessary that some man be a grammarian, because the sense is: man and grammar existing, Nn iiij

p. 568

in rerum natura, necesse est aliquem hominem esse grammaticum: quamuis non supposita existentia extremorum, sed absolutè accepta, sine tali suppositione, falsa esset propositio.

in the nature of things, it is necessary that some man be a grammarian; although, without the existence of the extremes being supposed, but taken absolutely, without such a supposition, the proposition would be false.

Dubium secundum.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

An bene probauerit Aristoteles regulas conuersionis propositionum de necesse.

Whether Aristotle proved well the rules for the conversion of propositions de necesse.

15 Videtur non bene id probasse, propter hoc arg. quia non bene probatur res aliqua per medium minùs notum, quàm ipsa sit: sed Arist. probauit regulas conuertendi propositiones de necesse, per conuersionem particularis de contingenti, de qua nihil adhuc dixerat: ergo minùs bene id probauit. Minor patet ex litera Aristotelis. Respondetur, quòd si bene intelligatur ratio Aristotelis, non vtitur conuersioné propositionis de modo contingenti, sed propositionis de inesse: ex qua postea colligit, propositionem particularem de contingenti hoc modo: Si non conuertitur simpliciter vniuersalis negatiua de necesse: ergo potest dari antecedens verum, & consequens falsum: sit ergo verum hoc antecedens, Necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: & consequens falsum, Necesse est nullum equum esse hominem. Et si hoc consequens falsum est, benè sequitur ex eo, veram esse hanc propositionem: Contingit aliquem equum esse hominem, quæ est eius contradictoria. Et quia contingens, sumptum pro possibili, significat id, quod potest esse: ex propositione particulari de contingenti, hoc modo sumpto, infert Aristotel. propositionem particularem de inesse, per illam regulam, Possibili posito in esse, nullum sequitur inconueniens hoc modo: Contingit aliquem equum esse hominem: ponatur ergo in esse: Quòd aliquis equus sit homo: & tunc propositio hæc de inesse, Aliquis equus est homo, conuertitur simpliciter in hanc: ergo aliquis homo est equus, per regulas conuertendi propositiones de inesse, iam traditas ca. præcedenti: ex qua colligit hanc modalem de contingenti pro possibili, Contingit aliquem hominem esse equum: quia ex propositione de inesse, euidenter colligitur propositio de possibili sicut ex actu, colligitur bene potentia. Et hæc vltima, est contradictoria illius antecedentis malę conuersionis, quod verum esse concedebatur videlicet, Necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: & ideo colligit duas contradictorias simul esse veras, sine vlla conuersione propositionis de contingenti, per

15 It seems that he did not prove it well, on account of this argument: because a thing is not well proved through a middle less known than the thing itself; but Aristotle proved the rules for converting propositions de necesse through the conversion of the particular de contingenti, of which he had as yet said nothing; therefore he proved it less well. The minor is plain from the letter of Aristotle. The reply is that, if Aristotle’s reasoning is well understood, he does not use the conversion of a proposition of the contingent mode but of a proposition de inesse, from which he afterwards gathers the particular proposition de contingenti, in this way: If the universal negative de necesse is not converted simply, then the antecedent can be true and the consequent false. Let, then, this antecedent be true, It is necessary that no man be a horse, and the consequent false, It is necessary that no horse be a man. And if this consequent is false, it follows well from it that this proposition is true: It is contingent that some horse is a man, which is its contradictory. And since contingent, taken for possible, signifies that which can be, from the particular proposition de contingenti taken in this way Aristotle infers the particular proposition de inesse by that rule, When the possible is posited as being, nothing impossible follows, in this way: It is contingent that some horse is a man; let it then be posited as being: That some horse is a man. And then this proposition de inesse, Some horse is a man, is converted simply into this: therefore some man is a horse, by the rules for converting propositions de inesse already handed down in the preceding chapter. From this he gathers this modal de contingenti taken for the possible: It is contingent that some man is a horse; because from a proposition de inesse a proposition de possibili is evidently gathered, just as potency is well gathered from act. And this last is the contradictory of that antecedent of the bad conversion which was granted to be true, namely, It is necessary that no man be a horse; and therefore he gathers that two contradictories are true at the same time, without any conversion of a proposition de contingenti, through

p. 569

solam conuersionem propositionis de inesse, & per regulam contradictoriæ oppositionis, traditam lib. 2. de interpretatione quòd si vna est falsa, altera debet esse vera: & quòd propositiones de necesse, habeant oppositionem cum propositionibus de contingenti, etiam sumpto pro possibili, modo, quo explicatur.

the sole conversion of a proposition de inesse, and through the rule of contradictory opposition handed down in bk. 1 of On Interpretation, that if one is false the other must be true; and that propositions de necesse have opposition with propositions de contingenti, even taken for the possible, in the way that is explained.

Circa conuersionem propositionum de modo contingenti — On the Conversion of Propositions of the Contingent Mode.

Primum notabile.

First Note.

Duobus modis docuit Arist. sumi contingens. Primo, Impropriè. Secundò, Propriè, Impropriè quidem pro possibili, & ita sumpto, eisdem modis conuerti propositiones eius, ac conuertuntur propositiones de necesse & eisdem argumentis probandæ sunt, atque etiam, vt regulæ veræ esse possint, intelligi debent propositiones, supposita existentia extremorum; vt dictum est in eisdem propositionibus de necesse. Et tandem in cõuersione omnium modalium, intelligendum est, solùm agere Arist. de propositionibus, de modo affirmato: sed variatis ex parte dicti, secundùm quantitatem, & qualitatem. Hoc est de vniuersalibus, & particularibus, affirmatiuis, & negatiuis.

Aristotle taught that contingent is taken in two ways: first, improperly; second, properly. Improperly, indeed, for the possible; and taken in this way, its propositions are converted in the same modes as propositions de necesse are converted, and are to be proved by the same arguments; and also, so that the rules may be true, the propositions must be understood with the existence of the extremes supposed, as was said in the case of those same propositions de necesse. And finally, in the conversion of all modals, it must be understood that Aristotle treats only of propositions of an affirmed mode, but varied on the part of the dictum according to quantity and quality; that is, of universals and particulars, affirmatives and negatives.

Secundum notabile.

Second Note.

Circa propositiones verò de contingenti, secundo modo sumpta, notandum est, Omnes propositiones eius efficere sensum copulatiuum, vt hæc propositio: Contingit hominem esse album, efficit hunc sensum, Possibile est hominem esse album, & hominem non esse album: sicque de reliquis: cuius ratio euidens est, significatio ipsius modi: quæ est, rem posse esse, & posse non esse: & propterea contingens hoc modo sumptum, vocatur ad vtrumlibet, quasi vtrumque partem possibilem significet. Vnde sequitur ex affirmatiua inferri negatiuam, & ex negatiua, affirmatiuam. Bene enim sequitur, Contingit hominem esse album: ergo contingit hominem non esse album: atque etiam, Contingit hominem non esse album: ergo contingit hominem esse album. Et ideo propositionibus de modo contingenti, opponũtur propositiones de modo necesse, & de modo impossibili: quia ex duobus potest prouenire, quòd aliquid non sit cõtingens: nempe, ex eo, quòd sit necessarium, & ex eo, quòd sit impossibile: vnde vtraque hæc est falsa, Contingit hominem esse animal: atq; etiam, Contingit hominẽ esse equum

Concerning propositions de contingenti taken in the second way, it should be noted that all its propositions produce a copulative sense: as this proposition, It is contingent that a man is white, produces this sense: It is possible that a man is white and that a man is not white; and so of the rest. The evident reason for this is the signification of the mode itself, which is that a thing can be and can not be; and for this reason contingent taken in this way is called ad utrumlibet, as if it signified each part as possible. Whence it follows that from the affirmative the negative is inferred, and from the negative the affirmative. For it follows well: It is contingent that a man is white; therefore it is contingent that a man is not white; and also: It is contingent that a man is not white; therefore it is contingent that a man is white. And therefore to propositions of the contingent mode are opposed propositions of the mode de necesse and of the mode de impossibili, because it can come about from two things that something is not contingent: namely, from its being necessary and from its being impossible. Whence each of these is false: It is contingent that a man is an animal; and also, It is contingent that a man is a horse

p. 570

Prima: quia necessaria. Secunda, quia impossibilis. Et ex hoc procedit, tam diuersum modum conuersionis habere propositiones de contingenti, ab aliis omnibus aliorum modorum. Nam cùm vniuersalis negatiua aliorum modorum, conuertatur simpliciter, de modo tamen contingenti, non conuertitur simpliciter. Et cùm particularis negatiua aliorum modorum, non conuertatur, si sit de modo contingenti, conuertitur simpliciter: & hæc est sententia Aristotelis.

the first because it is necessary, the second because it is impossible. And from this it comes about that propositions de contingenti have a mode of conversion so different from all the others of the other modes. For whereas the universal negative of the other modes is converted simply, in the contingent mode it is not converted simply. And whereas the particular negative of the other modes is not converted, if it is of the contingent mode it is converted simply; and this is the opinion of Aristotle.

Tertium notabile.

Third Note.

17 Sed vt eam intelligamus, notandum est Tertiò, quòd vt aliqua propositio conuertatur, necesse est, secundùm omnia quæ includit conuerti: nam si secundùm aliquid non conuertatur, non fiet conuersio secundùm integrum sensum eius: nec dicetur ipsa conuerti, sed aliquid eius: quare talis conuersio, fiet secundùm vocem tantùm, & non secundùm sensum, & veritatem: & ideo non erit vera, sed apparens tantùm. Ex quo præsupposito certissimo, non erit difficile intelligere, verum esse vtrumque assertum ab Aristo. Primum quidem, quòd vniuersalis negatiua de contingenti, non conuertatur simpliciter. Exempli gratia: Contingit nullum hominem esse album: non conuertitur in hanc, Contingit nullum album esse hominem: quia includit has duas propositiones, de possibili, Nullum hominem esse album, est possibile: & Possibile est omnem hominem esse album: sed hæc secunda non conuertitur simpliciter, vt per se est manifestum: ergo nec vniuersalis negatiua eam includens poterit simpliciter conuerti.

17 But in order that we may understand it, it should be noted, third, that for some proposition to be converted it is necessary that it be converted according to everything it includes: for if it is not converted according to something, the conversion will not take place according to its whole sense, nor will it itself be said to be converted, but something of it; wherefore such a conversion will take place according to the word only, and not according to the sense and truth, and therefore it will not be true but only apparent. From this most certain presupposition it will not be difficult to understand that both of Aristotle’s assertions are true. The first, indeed, that the universal negative de contingenti is not converted simply. For example: It is contingent that no man is white is not converted into this, It is contingent that nothing white is a man; because it includes these two propositions de possibili: That no man is white is possible, and It is possible that every man is white; but this second is not converted simply, as is manifest of itself; therefore neither can the universal negative that includes it be converted simply.

Quòd verò secunda regula, de conuersione particularis negatiuæ vera sit, hoc modo probatur: Propositio particularis negatiua, propter significationem modi, infert affirmatiuam: vt probauimus: ergo hæc est bona consequentia, Contingit aliquem hominem non esse album: ergo contingit aliquem hominem esse album: ex qua sequitur per conuersionem simplicem iam traditam: ergo contingit aliquod album esse hominem: & ex hac sequitur etiam, propter significationem modi, negatiua, nempe, Contingit aliquod album non esse hominem, quæ est conuertens negatiuæ particularis in principio sumptæ: ergo euidenter probatur, conuertendam esse simpliciter. Sed vt hæc regula vera sit, propositiones habent sumi supposita existentia extremorum: vt in propositionibus de possibili, & necesse diximus, alioqui dabitur antecedẽs verum,

That the second rule, on the conversion of the particular negative, is true is proved in this way: The particular negative proposition, on account of the signification of the mode, infers the affirmative, as we proved; therefore this is a good consequence: It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that some man is white. From this there follows, by the simple conversion already handed down: therefore it is contingent that something white is a man; and from this there follows also, on account of the signification of the mode, the negative, namely, It is contingent that something white is not a man, which is the converse of the particular negative taken at the beginning; therefore it is evidently proved that it is to be converted simply. But in order that this rule may be true, the propositions have to be taken with the existence of the extremes supposed, as we said in the case of propositions de possibili and de necesse; otherwise the antecedent will be true

p. 571

& consequens falsum: vt in hoc exemplo: Cõtingit hominem non esse ridentem: ergo contingit ridentem non esse hominem: atque etiam, Contingit hominem non esse grammaticum: ergo contingit grammaticum non esse hominem. Supposita autem existentia extremorum, nempe, risus, & hominis, aut Grammaticæ, & hominis, sicut consequens est falsum, ita & antecedens: nam homine, & Grammatica existentibus, non est contingens, quòd Grammaticum sit homo: sed necessarium ex suppositione: nam si Grammatica est in rerum natura, non potest esse nisi in homine, seu non esse in homine: ergo necesse est eam in homine esse: quare falsum erit, quòd contingat Grammaticum esse hominem.

and the consequent false, as in this example: It is contingent that a man is not laughing; therefore it is contingent that something laughing is not a man; and also: It is contingent that a man is not a grammarian; therefore it is contingent that a grammarian is not a man. But supposing the existence of the extremes, namely of laughter and of man, or of grammar and of man, just as the consequent is false, so is the antecedent; for when man and grammar exist, it is not contingent that a grammarian is a man, but necessary by supposition: for if grammar is in the nature of things, it cannot be except in a man, or cannot not be in a man; therefore it is necessary that it be in a man; wherefore it will be false that it is contingent that a grammarian is a man.

18 Sed aduersus hanc conuersionem particularis negatiuæ, est arg. satis difficile. Nam ideo dictum est ab Arist. particularem negatiuam de inesse non conuerti simpliciter: quia datur antecedens verum & consequens falsum: & hoc ideo, quia fit argumentum à termino non distributo, ad terminum distributum, ex parte subiecti propositionis conuertendæ: vt patet in hac, Aliquod animal non est homo: ergo aliquis homo non est animal, Animal enim non est distributum in antecedente: & tamen distribuitur in consequente, ratione negationis supra illud cadentis: sed idem defectus contingit in conuersione particularis negatiuæ de contingenti: ergo falsum erit, quòd conuertatur, Et hæc regula erit contraria illi, quæ negat particularem negatiuam de inesse conuerti. Probatur minor: quia dum sic procedimus, Contingit aliquem hominem non esse album: ergo contingit aliquod album non esse hominem, homo, qui est subiectum in antecedente, non distribuitur, sed solùm afficitur signo particulari: & tamen distribuitur in consequente, ratione negationis cadentis supra illum: ergo ex parte eius erit talis conuersio, argumenti à termino non distributo, ad terminum distributum, sicut conuersio particularis negatiuæ de inesse: & consequenter, erit vitiosa, & nulla, sicut est illa.

18 But against this conversion of the particular negative there is a rather difficult argument. For Aristotle said that the particular negative de inesse is not converted simply for this reason, that the antecedent is true and the consequent false; and this because the argument is made from a term not distributed to a term distributed, on the part of the subject of the proposition to be converted, as is plain in this: Some animal is not a man; therefore some man is not an animal. For animal is not distributed in the antecedent, and yet it is distributed in the consequent, by reason of the negation falling upon it. But the same defect occurs in the conversion of the particular negative de contingenti; therefore it will be false that it is converted. And this rule will be contrary to the one that denies that the particular negative de inesse is converted. The minor is proved: because when we proceed thus, It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that something white is not a man, man, which is the subject in the antecedent, is not distributed, but is only affected by a particular sign; and yet it is distributed in the consequent, by reason of the negation falling upon it; therefore on its part such a conversion will be an argument from a term not distributed to a term distributed, like the conversion of the particular negative de inesse; and consequently it will be faulty and null, as that one is.

Respondetur, Distinguendo minorem, quòd in conuersione negatiuæ de contingenti: fiat argumentum à non distributo ad distributum: quia diuerso modo fit, atque in propositione de inesse; nam in hac fit, ex parte totius, atque integri extremi, sed in modali de contingenti, tantùm ex parte extremi partialis, cùm tamen ex alia parte maneat extremum sine distributione, nam extremum propositionis modalis est dictum: & cùm propositio de modo contingente negatiua, contineat etiam affirmatiuam, duas habet partes dictum eius:

The reply is by distinguishing the minor: that in the conversion of the negative de contingenti an argument is made from the non-distributed to the distributed, because it is made in a different way than in the proposition de inesse; for in the latter it is made on the part of the whole and entire extreme, but in the modal de contingenti only on the part of a partial extreme, while on the other side the extreme nevertheless remains without distribution; for the extreme of a modal proposition is the dictum; and since a negative proposition of the contingent mode also contains the affirmative, its dictum has two parts;

p. 572

vnam negatam, & alteram affirmatam. Et ideo vnam distributam, & alteram sine distributione. Gratia exempli, dum sic procedimus, in eodem exempli loco allato arg. Cõtingit aliquem hominem non esse album: ergo contingit aliquod album, non esse hominem: hoc consequens negatiuum, continet etiam affirmatiuum, nempe, Contingit aliquod album esse hominem: in quo patet hominem non distribui, licèt distribuatur in alia parte eiusdem dicti negatiua: ex affirmatiua autem, sequitur iterum alia pars negatiua: nempe, Contingit aliquod album, non esse hominem: quæ est conuertens eiusdem particularis negatiuæ. Vnde sequitur, non impedire conuersionem, nec vitiosam eam reddere argumentationem, à non distributo ad distributum, ex parte extremi partialis, manentis sine distritione in alia parte affirmatiua eiusdem.

one negated and the other affirmed, and therefore one distributed and the other without distribution. For example, when we proceed thus, in the same argument adduced as an example: It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that something white is not a man: this negative consequent also contains the affirmative, namely, It is contingent that something white is a man, in which it is plain that man is not distributed, although it is distributed in the other, negative part of the same dictum; and from the affirmative there follows in turn the other, negative part, namely, It is contingent that something white is not a man, which is the converse of that same particular negative. Whence it follows that argumentation from the non-distributed to the distributed, on the part of a partial extreme that remains without distribution in the other, affirmative part of the same, does not impede conversion nor render it faulty.

Sed aduersus hanc solutionem, est argum. adhuc difficilius: Quia ex eo sequitur vniuersalem negatiuam eiusdem modi contingentis, conuerti simpliciter, contra aliam regulam negantem conuersionem eius. Probatur id sequi, quia ex eo tantùm non potest conuerti vniuersalis negatiua simpliciter, quia includit vniuersalem affirmatiuam, non conuertibilem simpliciter, sed vniuersalis affirmatiua, ex eo solùm non potest conuerti simpliciter: quia talis conuersio erit argumentum à non distributo ad distributum, ex parte prædicati eius: quod cùm non sit in ea distributum, distribuitur in conuertente, vt patet, dum sic procedimus: Contingit omnem hominem esse album: ergo contingit, omne album esse hominem. Constat verò vniuersalem affirmatiuam, solùm esse partem dicti vniuersalis negatiuæ, eam includentis: & ideo solùm esse extremum partiale eius: ergo si non reddit vitiosam conuersionem, quòd in ea fiat argumentum, à non distributo ad distributum, ex parte extremi partialis: vt dictum est in conuersione particularis negatiuæ, nec igitur efficietur vitiosa conuersio vniuersalis negatiuæ. Respondetur, Esse diuersam rationem in vniuersali negatiua, includente vniuersalem affirmatiuam, ac in particulari negatiua: nam in conuersione huius duo sunt: Primum, quòd idem terminus, qui non est distributus in subiecto antecedens, non distribuitur in vtraque parte consequentis, sed in altera tantùm: in alia verò, sine distributo manet, cùm sit particularis affirmatiua.

But against this solution there is a still more difficult argument: Because from it it follows that the universal negative of the same contingent mode is converted simply, against the other rule denying its conversion. That this follows is proved: because the universal negative cannot be converted simply only for this reason, that it includes the universal affirmative, which is not convertible simply; but the universal affirmative cannot be converted simply only for this reason, that such a conversion would be an argument from the non-distributed to the distributed on the part of its predicate, which, since it is not distributed in it, is distributed in the converse, as is plain when we proceed thus: It is contingent that every man is white; therefore it is contingent that everything white is a man. But it is certain that the universal affirmative is only part of the dictum of the universal negative that includes it, and therefore only its partial extreme; therefore, if it does not render the conversion faulty that an argument is made in it from the non-distributed to the distributed on the part of a partial extreme, as was said in the conversion of the particular negative, then neither is the conversion of the universal negative rendered faulty. The reply is that the reason is different in the universal negative, which includes the universal affirmative, and in the particular negative: for in the conversion of the latter there are two things. First, that the same term which is not distributed in the subject of the antecedent is not distributed in both parts of the consequent, but in one only, while in the other it remains without distribution, since it is a particular affirmative.

Secundum est, quòd eadem pars affirmatiua conuertitur simpliciter: & per talem conuersionem, colligitur euidenter ex ea particularis negatiua: quæ est conuertens particularis negatiuæ, in principio assumptæ ad conuersionem: & ideo à

The second is that the same affirmative part is converted simply, and through such a conversion the particular negative is evidently gathered from it, which is the converse of the particular negative assumed at the beginning for conversion; and therefore from

p. 573

primo ad vltimum, sequitur euidenter particulam negatiuam conuerti. In vniuersali verò affirmatiua, inclusa in negatiua vniuersali, neutrum horum reperitur. Non primum: quia sic argumentum à non distributo ad distributum, dum eam conuertimus: vt terminus qui non distribuitur in antecedenti, semper in consequenti distribuatur: hoc est, tam in conuertente affirmatiua, vt patet, cùm sit vniuersalis quàm in negatiua vniuersali, quam includit, cuius omnes terminos patet esse distributos. Ideo omni ex parte est argumentatio à non distributo ad distributum: & plus infertur in consequenti, quàm contineatur in antecedenti. Sed nec reperitur secundùm: quia vniuersalis affirmatiua, in quam conuertitur, non includit propositionem conuertibilem, ex qua possit deduci conuertens vniuersalis negatiuæ, sed solùm vniuersalem negatiuam non conuertibilem, vel de qua disputatio est, an conuertatur: quare non possumus vti conuersione eius in eadem argumentatione, sicut possumus vti conuersione particularis affirmatiuæ inclusæ in alia particulari negatiua, ideo nunquam possumus colligere ex conuersione vniuersalis affirmatiuæ, quam includit, vniuersalem negatiuam, quæ sit conuertens alterius vniuersalis negatiuæ: de cuius conuersione agitur. Ex his igitur duabus differentiis, tanquam à signo euidenti colligimus, propositionem particularem negatiuam, continere virtualiter suam conuertentem: cùm per euidentes consequentias ex ea deducatur: & ideo conuerti posse, vt docuit Arist. Vniuersalem verò negatiuam, non continere suam conuertentem vllo modo, cùm ex ea non possit deduci: sed solùm affirmatiuam vniuersalem, quæ impedimento est ei, ne possit simpliciter conuerti.

first to last it follows evidently that the particular negative is converted. But in the universal affirmative, included in the universal negative, neither of these is found. Not the first: because when we convert it, the argument is made from the non-distributed to the distributed in such a way that the term which is not distributed in the antecedent is always distributed in the consequent; that is, both in the converse affirmative, as is plain, since it is universal, and in the universal negative which it includes, all of whose terms are plainly distributed. Therefore the argumentation is in every respect from the non-distributed to the distributed, and more is inferred in the consequent than is contained in the antecedent. But neither is the second found: because the universal affirmative into which it is converted does not include a convertible proposition from which the converse of the universal negative could be deduced, but only the universal negative, which is not convertible, or about which the dispute is whether it is converted; wherefore we cannot use its conversion in the same argumentation, as we can use the conversion of the particular affirmative included in the other, particular negative; and therefore we can never gather, from the conversion of the universal affirmative which it includes, the universal negative that would be the converse of the other universal negative whose conversion is in question. From these two differences, then, as from an evident sign, we gather that the particular negative proposition virtually contains its converse, since it is deduced from it through evident consequences, and therefore that it can be converted, as Aristotle taught; but that the universal negative in no way contains its converse, since it cannot be deduced from it, but only the universal affirmative, which is an impediment to it, so that it cannot be converted simply.

Et si tandem dicatur, hinc sequi, quòd vniuersalis negatiua saltem possit conuerti in partem: cùm vniuersalis affirmatiua, quam includit, & propter quam solam non potest conuerti, in particularem conuertatur: quod tamen videtur esse contra regulam Arist. negantem vllo modo conuerti, Respondeo: Necessariò concedendum esse, quòd vniuersalis negatiua conuertatur in particularem: quia id conuincit argumentum: quia hoc nunquam Arist. negauit: quia nullum est fundamentum, propter quod negari possit, sed solùm negauit conuerti, vt petit propria natura: hoc est conuersione simplici, sicut conuertitur in aliis modis, atque in propositionibus de inesse. Et hæc de conuersione propositionum de modo contingenti.

And if, finally, it is said that it follows from this that the universal negative can at least be converted into part, since the universal affirmative which it includes, and on account of which alone it cannot be converted, is converted into a particular (which nevertheless seems to be against the rule of Aristotle denying that it is converted in any way), I reply: It must necessarily be granted that the universal negative is converted into a particular, because the argument convinces of it; because Aristotle never denied this; because there is no foundation on account of which it could be denied. He denied only that it is converted as its own nature demands, that is, by simple conversion, as it is converted in the other modes and in propositions de inesse. And this concerning the conversion of propositions of the contingent mode.

p. 574

Notabile vnicum.

Single Note.

Notabile vnicum circa conuersionem propositionum de possibili, & impossibili — On the Conversion of Propositions de Possibili and de Impossibili.

12 Vltimò notandum est, circa conuersionem propositionum de possibili: & impossibili: non esse locutum Arist. expressè, & non in particulari de illis: quia eisdem modis conuertuntur, secundùm sensum, & æquipollentiam, ac propositiones de necesse: licèt aliquando diuersæ appareant ab eis, præsertim propositiones de impossibili, Et de propositionibus de possibili, res est manifesta, cùm sint de contingenti in impropriè sumpto, de quibus suprà diximus, eodem modo conuerti posse, ac propositiones de necesse. Sed de propositionibus de impossibili, intelligetur facile, si consideremus propositiones de impossibili affirmato, æquipollere propositionibus de necesse, habentibus oppositum dictum, vt hæc propositio: Impossibile est aliquem hominem esse equum, æquipollet huic, necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: quare sicut illa conuertenda est: & sic de cæteris de impossibili, affirmato modo: nam de his solis loquitur Arist. in his conuersionibus: vt diximus. Solùm est repetendum in hac parte, quod intelligitur semper, supposita existentia extremorum.

12 Lastly, it should be noted that, concerning the conversion of propositions de possibili and de impossibili, Aristotle did not speak expressly and in particular of them, because they are converted in the same modes, according to sense and equipollence, as propositions de necesse, although they sometimes appear different from them, especially propositions de impossibili. And as for propositions de possibili, the matter is manifest, since they are of the contingent improperly taken, of which we said above that they can be converted in the same way as propositions de necesse. But as for propositions de impossibili, it will be easily understood if we consider that propositions of an affirmed de impossibili are equipollent to propositions de necesse having the opposite dictum: as this proposition, It is impossible that some man is a horse, is equipollent to this, It is necessary that no man be a horse; wherefore it is to be converted as that one is; and so of the others of the affirmed de impossibili mode, for of these alone Aristotle speaks in these conversions, as we said. It need only be repeated in this part that this is always understood with the existence of the extremes supposed.

CHAPTER IIII

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Determinatis verò his. Dicamus iam per quæ, & quando, & quomodo fiat omnis syllogismus, &c.

These things having been determined, let us now say through what things, and when, and how every syllogism comes about, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

22 Intentum Arist. cap. præsenti est, explicare naturam, & rationem primæ figuræ. Diuiditur autem in duas partes. In prima, Explicat modos vniuersales, quibus syllogismi fieri possunt: ex quibus alios omnes inutiles, qui videntur eis similes, reijcit. In secunda: Explicat duos alios modos particulares vtiles, & ex eis tanquam inutiles, omnes alios, qui in simili dispositione fieri possunt, etiam reiicit.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the na22 T ture and ratio of the first figure. And it is divided into two parts. In the first he explains the universal moods in which syllogisms can be made, and from them he rejects all the other, useless ones that seem similar to them. In the second he explains two other, particular useful moods, and from them he likewise rejects as useless all the others that can be made in a similar disposition.

Modos vniuersales explicat his verbis: Quando tres termini sic se habent, vt postremus sit in toto medio, & medius in toto primo, sic, vel non sit, extremorum fieri syllogismum necesse est, &c. Per medium terminum intelligit eum, qui bis sumitur in præmissis. Per postremum terminum, minorem extremitatem

He explains the universal moods in these words: When three terms are so related that the last is in the whole middle, and the middle is or is not in the whole first, there must be a syllogism of the extremes, etc. By the middle term he understands the one that is taken twice in the premises. By the last term, the minor extreme

p. 575

: & per primum, maiorem extremitatem. Sensus igitur verborum eius talis est: Quando tres termini, ita sunt dispositi, vt medium subiiciatur vniuersaliter maiori extremitati, in prima propositione: in secunda verò, minor extremitas subiiciatur vniuersaliter medio, affirmatiuè quidem fit syllogismus in primo modo, qui vocatur, Barbara: quia constat tribus propositionibus affirmatiuis, & est talis: Omne animal est substantia: omnis homo est animal: ergo omnis homo est substantia. Negatiuè verò, in secundo modo, qui vocatur Celarent: quia constat minori affirmatiua, & maiori, & conclusione negatiuis: & ita constituitur: Nullum animal est lapis: omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis. Quomodocunque autem aliter disponantur medium, & extremitates in propositionibus vniuersalibus, modos inutiles, ac vitiosos efficiunt: in quibus tam propositiones vniuersales affirmatiuæ, quàm negatiuæ, indifferenter sequuntur: vel, vt alij dicunt: dantur termini, in quibus Omni, & etiam termini, in quibus Nulli, & probatur vitiosas esse consequentias, v. g. dari duas contradictorias simul veras. Itaque, ex dispositione vniuersali terminorum solùm duo producti modi vtiles resultant, in quibus perfecti efficiuntur syllogismi. Quod probatur euidenter, quia in primo, dicitur de omni: hoc est prædicatum maioris quod vniuersaliter dicitur de subiecto in maiori, dicitur necessariò de aliquo contento, & sumpto sub eo in conclusione. In secundo verò, dicitur de nullo: nam prædicatum maioris negatur vniuersaliter de subiecto eiusdem: & ideo negatur etiam necessariò de subiecto minoris in conclusione.

and by the first, the major extreme. The sense of his words, then, is this: When three terms are so disposed that the middle is subjected universally to the major extreme in the first proposition, and in the second the minor extreme is subjected universally to the middle, there comes about, affirmatively, a syllogism in the first mood, which is called Barbara, because it consists of three affirmative propositions; and it is this: Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance. Negatively, in the second mood, which is called Celarent, because it consists of an affirmative minor and of a negative major and conclusion; and it is constructed thus: No animal is a stone; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone. But however else the middle and the extremes are disposed in universal propositions, they produce useless and faulty moods, in which universal propositions, affirmative as well as negative, follow indifferently; or, as others say, terms are given in which “all” follows and also terms in which “none” follows; and the consequences are proved to be faulty, for example by two contradictories being given true at the same time. And so from the universal disposition of the terms only the two moods produced result as useful, in which perfect syllogisms are made. This is proved evidently: because in the first, said of all holds, that is, the predicate of the major, which is said universally of the subject in the major, is necessarily said of something contained and taken under it in the conclusion. In the second, said of none holds: for the predicate of the major is denied universally of its subject, and therefore it is also necessarily denied of the subject of the minor in the conclusion.

In secunda part. cap. Explicat duos alios modos vtiles eiusdem figuræ, quos vocat particulares: quia altera præmissarum particularis est, & vniuersalis altera. Si ergo inquit vtraque præmissa sit particularis, inutiles fiunt omnes modi: Si verò particularis vna, & vniuersalis altera: vel maior est vniuersalis, in qua maior extremitas dicitur vniuersaliter de medio: & minor particularis, in qua medium dicitur de minori extremitate, modo particulari: fit tertius modus perfecti syllogismi, qui dicitur Darij, quia constat maiori vniuersali affirmatiua, & minori, & conclusione, particularibus etiam affirmatiuis. Et talis est modus is, Omne animal rationale, est risibile: Aliquis homo est animal rationale: ergo aliquis homo est risibilis. Si verò maior sit vniuersalis negatiua in qua maior extremitas negetur vniuersaliter de medio: & minor particularis affirmatiua, in qua medium dicatur de

In the second part of the chapter he explains two other useful moods of the same figure, which he calls particular, because one of the premises is particular and the other universal. If, then, he says, each premise is particular, all the moods become useless. But if one is particular and the other universal: either the major is universal, in which the major extreme is said universally of the middle, and the minor particular, in which the middle is said of the minor extreme in a particular mode, and there comes about the third mood of perfect syllogism, which is called Darij, because it consists of a universal affirmative major and of a minor and conclusion that are particular and also affirmative. And this mood is such: Every rational animal is risible; some man is a rational animal; therefore some man is risible. Or if the major is a universal negative, in which the major extreme is denied universally of the middle, and the minor a particular affirmative, in which the middle is said of

p. 576

minori extremitate, modo particulari, fit modus vtilis quartus primæ figuræ, qui vocatur Ferio, & est talis: Nullum animal est lapis: Aliquis homo est animal: ergo aliquis homo non est lapis. Quòd verò duo isti syllogismi perfecti sint, euidens est, ex duobus aliis prioribus: à quibus solùm differunt ex parte minoris propositionis, quæ in illis est vniuersalis, & in his particularis: & consequenter conclusiones eorum sunt particulares. Cùm ergo particulares propositiones eorum, contineantur sub vniuersalibus aliorum, si illi euidentes sunt, & in eis dicitur de omni, & de nullo, idem prorsus habebunt isti. Cæteri verò modi, quibus disponi possunt præmissæ vniuersalis, & particularis: inutiles sunt: & in quibus dantur termini, in quibus Omni, & in quibus Nulli. Hæc Arist.

the minor extreme in a particular mode, there comes about the fourth useful mood of the first figure, which is called Ferio; and it is this: No animal is a stone; some man is an animal; therefore some man is not a stone. That these two syllogisms are perfect is evident from the two other, prior ones, from which they differ only on the part of the minor proposition, which in those is universal and in these particular; and consequently their conclusions are particular. Since, then, their particular propositions are contained under the universals of the others, if those are evident and in them said of all and said of none hold, these will have altogether the same. But the other moods in which a universal and a particular premise can be disposed are useless, and in them terms are given in which “all” follows and in which “none” follows. Thus far Aristotle.

Quid sit figura, & quotuplex, & qui modus — What a figure is, and how many kinds, and what a mood is, is explained.

Figura syllogismorum, nihil aliud est quàm debita dispositio trium terminorum: hoc est, medij, & extremitatum, secundùm debitum modum prædicationis, & subiectionis. Dicitur autem per metaphoram, ex similitudine figuræ geometricæ: nam sicut hæc resultat ex lineis terminatis per puncta, ita dispositis, eodem modo figura syllogistica, ex propositionibus, quæ sunt quasi lineæ terminatæ extremis punctis, hoc est, subiecto, & prædicato: quæ vocantur termini propositionum, quia sunt extrema eius.

The figure of syllogisms is nothing other than the due disposition of three terms, that is, of the middle and the extremes, according to the due mode of predication and subjection. It is so called by metaphor, from its likeness to a geometrical figure: for just as the latter results from lines terminated by points and so disposed, in the same way the syllogistic figure results from propositions, which are as it were lines terminated by extreme points, that is, by the subject and the predicate, which are called the terms of propositions because they are their extremes.

Figura triplex est: quia tribus tantùm modis disponi possunt media, & extremitates. Nam vel medium in prima est subiectum, & in secunda prædicatum: & vocatur prima figura propter tria. Primò, Quia medium in hac dispositione, non solùm rationem habet medij, quod per id coniungantur extremitates: sed etiam proprium situm medio debitum, cùm sit inter extremitates collocatum: ita vt sit subiectum vnius, & prædicatum alterius. Secundò, Quia in hac figura, omne genus propositionis colligitur, nempe vniuersalis affirmatiua, vniuersalis negatiua, particularis affirmatiua, & particularis negatiua. Tertiò, Quia ex hac figura deriuantur aliæ: nam vel medium est prædicatum vtriusque præmissæ, & sic est secunda figura: vel est subiectum vtriusque, & sic est tertia. Cuius ratio satis congruens est: quia prædicatum est nobilius subiecto: & ideo nobiliorem rationem, & locum habet medium: & nobilior ex consequenti est dispositio ipsa, in qua semper est prædicatum ea, in qua semper est subiectum: &

The figure is threefold: because the middle and the extremes can be disposed in only three ways. For either the middle is the subject in the first and the predicate in the second, and this is called the first figure, for three reasons. First, because the middle in this disposition not only has the ratio of a middle, in that the extremes are conjoined through it, but also the proper position due to a middle, since it is placed between the extremes, so as to be the subject of one and the predicate of the other. Second, because in this figure every kind of proposition is concluded, namely the universal affirmative, the universal negative, the particular affirmative, and the particular negative. Third, because the others are derived from this figure: for either the middle is the predicate of both premises, and so it is the second figure; or it is the subject of both, and so it is the third. The reason for this order is quite fitting: because the predicate is nobler than the subject, and therefore the middle has a nobler ratio and place, and consequently the disposition itself in which it is always the predicate is nobler than that in which it is always the subject; and

p. 577

propterea dispositio illa, Secundam, hæc verò figuram Tertiam meritò constituit,

therefore that disposition rightly constitutes the Second figure, and this one the Third.

Modus est, debita dispositio præmissarum, secundùm debitam qualitatem, & quantitatem hoc est, secundùm rationem vniuersalis, & particularis: in qua consistit quantitas propositionis: & secundùm affirmationem, & negationem, in quibus consistit qualitas.

A mood is the due disposition of the premises according to due quality and quantity, that is, according to the ratio of universal and particular, in which the quantity of a proposition consists, and according to affirmation and negation, in which its quality consists.

25 Modi primæ igitur, quatuor tantùm enumerati sunt, nempe, duo vniuersales, & duo particulares. Quia his tantùm quatuor modis, debito modo disponi possunt præmissæ: vt ex eis euidenter inferatur conclusio: cæteri verò omnes modi, inutiles sunt vt dictum est.

25 Of the first, then, only four moods have been enumerated, namely two universal and two particular, because only in these four moods can the premises be disposed in the due manner so that the conclusion is evidently inferred from them; but all the other moods are useless, as has been said.

Dubium Secundum.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

An præter tres figuras enumeratas ab Arist. addenda sit quarta — Whether, besides the three figures enumerated by Aristotle, a fourth is to be added.

Prima opinio tenet, Addendam esse quartam: quam tribuunt Galeno medicorum principi. Et probatur hoc arg. Figura est debita dispositio medij, & extremitatum, secundùm debitam subiectionem, & prædicationem: sed præter tres modos: quibus disponuntur ab Arist. possunt quarto alio modo ab eis diuerso disponi: ergo ex tali dispositione efficietur diuersa figura, quæ sit quarta. Probatur minor: quia dispositio primæ figuræ est, in qua medium est subiectum maioris, & prædicatum minoris: dispositio secundæ, in qua medium est prædicatum vtriusque præmissæ: & dispositio tertiæ, in qua medium est vtriusque subiectum, sed possunt etiam quarto modo disponi, ita vt medium sit prædicatum maioris, & subiectum minoris: scilicet vt ex tali dispositione non minùs euidenter sequatur conclusio, quàm ex tribus prioribus: ergo resultabit ex tali dispositione quarta figura, distincta à tribus. Minor probatur hoc exemplo: Omne risibile est homo: omnis homo est animal rationale: ergo omne animal rationale, est risibile.

The first opinion holds that a fourth is to be added; they attribute it to Galen, the prince of physicians. And it is proved by this argument: A figure is the due disposition of the middle and the extremes according to due subjection and predication; but besides the three modes in which they are disposed by Aristotle, they can be disposed in a fourth mode different from them; therefore from such a disposition a different figure will be produced, which is the fourth. The minor is proved: because the disposition of the first figure is that in which the middle is the subject of the major and the predicate of the minor; the disposition of the second, that in which the middle is the predicate of each premise; and the disposition of the third, that in which the middle is the subject of each; but they can also be disposed in a fourth mode, so that the middle is the predicate of the major and the subject of the minor, namely in such a way that from such a disposition the conclusion follows no less evidently than from the three prior ones; therefore from such a disposition there will result a fourth figure, distinct from the three. The minor is proved by this example: Everything risible is a man; every man is a rational animal; therefore every rational animal is risible.

26 Communis tamen consensus totius scholæ, tres tantùm figuras ponit cum Arist. Et ita nobis sentiendum est. & probatur hac ratione: Quia figura propriè loquendo, est quasi forma syllogismi: in qua formaliter disponuntur propositiones: hoc est secundùm modum naturalem, ac debitum formæ earum. Debitus autem modus, in eo consistit, vt id quod se habet, vt forma, sit prædicatum, & quod se habet vt materia, sit subiectum: sed tribus tantùm modis ita possunt propositiones disponi

26 The common consensus of the whole school, however, posits only three figures with Aristotle. And so we must hold; and it is proved by this reason: Because a figure, properly speaking, is as it were the form of the syllogism, in which the propositions are formally disposed, that is, according to the natural mode and that due to their form. But the due mode consists in this, that what stands as form be the predicate, and what stands as matter be the subject; but only in three modes can propositions be disposed Oo

p. 578

, ergo tres tantùm erunt figuræ enumeratæ ab Aristot. Minorem sic probo: Non possunt disponi quarto illo modo, nisi in maiori prædicetur, id, quod verè se habet vt materia, & subiiciatur, quod se habet vt forma: atqui hæc dispositio præter naturam, & formam propositionis est, vt idem exemplum assignatum probat: ergo ex illa dispositione nõ potest propria aliqua figura resultare: quare rarò, vel nunquam in disputationibus tali dispositione syllogismorum vtimur. Talis ergo dispositio, si aliquid simile figuræ habere potest, imperfectum quiddam est, & dispositioni primæ figuræ, quodammodo affine, ad quam reduci debet. Ad argum. verò: Distinguenda est minor: quia disponi possunt, sed non modo debito ad efficiendam figuram, vt probatum est: & ideo talis dispositio, figuram distinctam non efficit, sed propter quandam similitudinem, reducitur ad primam.

in this way; therefore there will be only the three figures enumerated by Aristotle. The minor I prove thus: They cannot be disposed in that fourth mode unless in the major that which truly stands as matter is predicated, and that which stands as form is subjected; but this disposition is against the nature and form of the proposition, as the same example assigned proves; therefore no proper figure can result from that disposition; wherefore we rarely or never use such a disposition of syllogisms in disputations. Such a disposition, then, if it can have anything like a figure, is something imperfect, and in a certain way akin to the disposition of the first figure, to which it ought to be reduced. To the argument: the minor must be distinguished, because they can be disposed, but not in the due manner for producing a figure, as has been proved; and therefore such a disposition does not produce a distinct figure, but on account of a certain likeness it is reduced to the first.

27 Et si aliquis obiiciat ex opposito, primam solam sufficere, cùm per eam inferatur omne genus propositionis: & ideo, secundam, & tertiam non fuisse addendas. Respondeo, Necessarias esse secundam, & tertiam: quia licèt in prima colligi possit omne genus propositionis, non tamen semper ea vti possumus in disputationibus: quia non semper tam manifesta cõsequentia constitui potest, vt omnibus euidens appareat: sed necesse est, aliis minus euidentibus sæpe vti, vt per eas ad euidentiores primæ figuræ perueniamus. Necessariæ præterea sunt, vt copiam syllogismorum habeamus, ad instituendas disputationes: quam per solam primam figuram non haberemus.

27 And if someone objects from the opposite side that the first alone suffices, since every kind of proposition is inferred through it, and therefore that the second and third ought not to have been added, I reply that the second and third are necessary: because, although every kind of proposition can be concluded in the first, we cannot nevertheless always use it in disputations, because a consequence cannot always be constructed so manifest that it appears evident to all; but it is necessary often to use others, less evident, so that through them we may arrive at the more evident ones of the first figure. Moreover, they are necessary so that we may have an abundance of syllogisms for conducting disputations, which we should not have through the first figure alone.

CAPVT V.

C H A P T E R V.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Quando vero huic quidem omni, illi autem nulli insit, aut vtrique omni, aut nulli, figuram quidem talem voco secundam.

But when the same belongs to all of one and to none of the other, or to all of each, or to none, such a figure I call the second.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

28 Intentum Arist. cap. præsenti est, explicare naturam secundæ figuræ. Diuiditur autem in duas partes: In prima, Explicat dispositionem secundæ figuræ, In secunda: Modos omnes vtiles syllogizandi in ea, refutatis inutilibus, percenset.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the na28 T ture of the second figure. And it is divided into two parts. In the first he explains the disposition of the second figure; in the second he reviews all the useful moods of syllogizing in it, the useless ones having been refuted.

Secunda figura efficitur, (inquit Arist.) quando sic disponuntur

The second figure is produced (says Aristotle) when they are so disposed

p. 579

præmissæ: vt medium sit prædicatum vniuersale de extremitatibus, in vtraque: ita vt affirmetur in vna, & negetur in alia: indifferenter quidem, quia siue maior sit negatiua, siue minor, dum modo non sit vtraque affirmatiua, aut negatiua, bona est dispositio, vt his duobus exemplis ostenditur: Nullus lapis est animal: Omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis, & rursus: Omnis homo est viuens: Nullus lapis est viuens: ergo nullus lapis est homo. Ideo medium in hac figura, ait Aristot. esse, quod omni, vel nulli extremitati inest: Extremitates verò, quibus inest medium: & vt vtramque distinguat, asserit maiorem extremitatem esse eam, quæ iuxta medium posita est: esse autem iuxta medium positam dicit, quia sicut medium est prædicatum in præmissis, ita maior extremitas in conclusione. Ideo medio similis est. Minorem verò extremitatem, longiùs ait distare à medio: quia cùm medium semper sit prædicatum, minor extremitas, semper est subiectum. Vnde (inquit) sequitur, quòd medium quasi foris seu extrà ponatur respectu extremitatum: quia semper prædicatur, & nunquam subiicitur: atque etiam primum sit positione: quia cùm sit prædicatum semper, præcipuum locum in hac figura tenet: extremum porrò vtrumque in præmissis subiicitur. In hac figura nullum syllogismum perfectum fieri dicit: quia syllogismus perfectus ille est, qui nullo indiget, vt appareat necessarius: sed omnes syllogismi huius figuræ, indigent reductione ad syllogismos primæ: ergo nullus eorum perfectus est.

the premises, that the middle is a universal predicate of the extremes in each, so that it is affirmed in one and denied in the other; indifferently, indeed, because whether the major is negative or the minor, provided that both are not affirmative or negative, the disposition is good, as is shown by these two examples: No stone is an animal; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone; and again: Every man is a living thing; no stone is a living thing; therefore no stone is a man. Therefore the middle in this figure, says Aristotle, is that which belongs to all or to none of the extremes; and the extremes are those to which the middle belongs. And to distinguish the two, he asserts that the major extreme is the one placed next to the middle; and he says it is placed next to the middle because, just as the middle is the predicate in the premises, so is the major extreme in the conclusion; therefore it is similar to the middle. The minor extreme, however, he says stands farther from the middle, because, since the middle is always the predicate, the minor extreme is always the subject. Whence (he says) it follows that the middle is placed as it were outside, or beyond, in respect of the extremes, because it is always predicated and never subjected; and also that it is first in position, because, since it is always the predicate, it holds the principal place in this figure, while each extreme is subjected in the premises. He says that no perfect syllogism is made in this figure: because a perfect syllogism is that which needs nothing in order to appear necessary; but all the syllogisms of this figure need reduction to syllogisms of the first; therefore none of them is perfect.

29 In secunda parte capitis: Enumerat modos vtiles huius figuræ, inutilésque reiicit. Inquit ergo: Quando medium huic quidem omni, illi verò nulli inest, fit primus modus vtilis, qui vocatur Cesare, hoc modo: Nullus lapis est animal: Omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis. Reducitur autem ad secundum modum primæ figuræ, per solam conuersionem simplicem maioris, hac ratione: Nullum animal est lapis: Omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis.

29 In the second part of the chapter he enumerates the useful moods of this figure and rejects the useless ones. He says, then: When the middle belongs to all of the one and to none of the other, there comes about the first useful mood, which is called Cesare, in this way: No stone is an animal; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone. And it is reduced to the second mood of the first figure by the simple conversion of the major alone, in this way: No animal is a stone; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone.

Si verò è contrario medium huic quidem nulli, illi verò omni inest: id est, si in maiori negatur vniuersaliter de maiori extremitate, & in minori vniuersaliter affirmatur de extremitate minori, fit secundus modus, qui dicitur Camestres, vt ostenditur hoc exemplo: Omnis homo est animal: Nullus lapis est animal: ergo nullus lapis est homo, Qui reducitur ad secundum modum primæ figuræ: conuersa minori simpliciter, & transmutatis præmissis. Ita vt minor conuersa fiat maior, & maior sit minor, hoc modo: Nullum animal est lapis:

But if, on the contrary, the middle belongs to none of the one and to all of the other, that is, if in the major it is denied universally of the major extreme and in the minor is affirmed universally of the minor extreme, there comes about the second mood, which is called Camestres, as is shown by this example: Every man is an animal; no stone is an animal; therefore no stone is a man. It is reduced to the second mood of the first figure by converting the minor simply and transposing the premises, so that the converted minor becomes the major and the major becomes the minor, in this way: No animal is a stone; Oo ij

p. 580

Omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis.

Every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone.

Tertium modum fieri, ait, si medium, huic quidem nulli: id est in maiori vniuersaliter negetur de maiori extremitate: illi verò alicui insit, id est, in minori dicatur de aliqua extremitate minori, fit tertius modus: qui dicitur Festino. Fit autem vtrumque, si maior sit vniuersalis negatiua: & minor particularis affirmatiua, hac ratione: Nullus lapis est animal: Aliquis homo est animal: ergo aliquis homo non est lapis. Reducitur autem ad quartum modum primæ figuræ, per solam conuersionem simplicem maioris hoc modo: Nullum animal est lapis: Aliquis homo est animal: ergo aliquis homo non est lapis.

The third mood comes about, he says, if the middle belongs to none of the one, that is, is denied universally of the major extreme in the major, but belongs to some of the other, that is, is said of some of the minor extreme in the minor: there comes about the third mood, which is called Festino. And both of these come about if the major is a universal negative and the minor a particular affirmative, in this way: No stone is an animal; some man is an animal; therefore some man is not a stone. And it is reduced to the fourth mood of the first figure by the simple conversion of the major alone, in this way: No animal is a stone; some man is an animal; therefore some man is not a stone.

30 Quartum denique modum, fieri ait: quando medium, huic quidem omni, illi verò alicui non inest: hoc est, quando maior est vniuersalis affirmans, in qua vniuersaliter prædicatur de maiori extremitate: & minor particularis negans, in qua negatur de ea sumpta in particulari, resultat modus iste, qui vocatur, Baroco: & est talis, Omnis homo est animal: Aliquis lapis non est animal: ergo aliquis lapis non est homo. Modus autem iste non potest reduci ad primam figuram ostensiuè, vt per se est manifestum: ideò Aristoteles illum reducit per impossibile, ad primum modum: hac ratione: vt ex maiori, & contradictoria conclusionis, pro minori, inferatur contradictoria minoris, eiusdem syllogismi, simul vera cum ea: vt si ita dicamus: Syllogismus in Baroco, dicis: non est bona consequentia: ergo dari potest in ea, antecedens verum, & consequens falsum: sit ergo verum illud antecedens, pro maiori, & minori, & sit conclusio falsa: cuius contradictoria, vtique debet esse vera, nempe, Omnis lapis est homo: quam sic accipio pro minori: & cum maiori eiusdem syllogismi, hunc syllogismum efficio: Omnis homo est animal: Omnis lapis est homo, ergo omnis lapis est animal: quæ est contradictoria minoris illius syllogismi, nempe, Aliquis lapis non est animal: & vtraque est vera: hæc quidem, quia erat pars antecedentis malæ consequentiæ: altera verò, quia erat contradictoria consequentis falsi, eiusdem malæ consequentiæ. Vnde sequitur, vel bonum esse syllogismum, quarti modi huius figuræ, vel dari duas contradictorias simul veras. Cæteri autem modi huius dispositionis inutiles sunt: & tales probari possunt per terminos: in quibus omni, & in quibus nulli.

30 The fourth mood, finally, he says comes about when the middle belongs to all of the one but does not belong to some of the other; that is, when the major is a universal affirmative, in which it is predicated universally of the major extreme, and the minor a particular negative, in which it is denied of that extreme taken in particular, there results this mood, which is called Baroco; and it is this: Every man is an animal; some stone is not an animal; therefore some stone is not a man. But this mood cannot be reduced to the first figure ostensively, as is manifest of itself; therefore Aristotle reduces it through the impossible to the first mood, in this way: so that from the major and the contradictory of the conclusion, taken as minor, there is inferred the contradictory of the minor of the same syllogism, true at the same time with it. As if we say thus: The syllogism in Baroco, you say, is not a good consequence; therefore in it the antecedent can be true and the consequent false. Let, then, that antecedent be true, for the major and the minor, and let the conclusion be false; its contradictory must then certainly be true, namely, Every stone is a man. This I take thus as a minor, and with the major of the same syllogism I make this syllogism: Every man is an animal; every stone is a man; therefore every stone is an animal; which is the contradictory of the minor of that syllogism, namely, Some stone is not an animal; and both are true: the latter because it was part of the antecedent of the bad consequence, the former because it was the contradictory of the false consequent of the same bad consequence. Whence it follows either that the syllogism of the fourth mood of this figure is good, or that two contradictories are true at the same time. But the other moods of this disposition are useless, and such can be proved by terms in which “all” follows and in which “none” follows.

p. 581

CHAPTER VI

TEXTVS ARIST. Si autem eadem, hoc quidem omni, illud verò nulli inest, vel ambo omni, vel nulli figuram quidem huiusmodi voco tertiam.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE. But if the same term belongs to all of the one and to none of the other, or to all of both, or to none of either, such a figure I call the third.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

Intentum huius capitis est, explicare naturam tertiæ figuræ. Diuiditur autem in duas partes. In prima definit, & explicat tertiam figuram: medium atque extremitates, quomodo sint in ea dispositio. In secunda: Modos vtiles, qui in ea fieri possunt, enumerat, inutilibus exclusis.

he intent of this chapter is to explain the nature of the third fig‐ T ure. It is divided into two parts. In the first he defines and explains the third figure: the middle and the extremes, how they are disposed in it. In the second he enumerates the useful moods that can be made in it, the useless being excluded.

In prima parte. Tertia, inquit, figura fit, quando tres termini sic disponuntur, vt medium in vtraque præmissa subiectum sit: maior verò extremitas, prædicatum maioris, & minor prædicatum minoris: sed necesse est, vt maior propositio semper sit vniuersalis, & conclusio semper particularis: ideo medium sic definit: Medium autem in hac dico, de quo ambo prædicantur. Id est, de quo prædicantur ambæ extremitates. Extremitates verò esse ait, quæ prædicantur, tam in præmissis, quàm in conclusione. Medium verò semper subiicitur, ideo quasi dissimiles & oppositas rationes habent: ac propterea hanc extremitatem longiùs esse dicitur à medio. Minor verò extremitas (inquit) est, quæ propiùs, hoc est, quæ magis accedit ad medium, cùm saltem in conclusione sit subiectum, sicut medium in vtraque præmissa. Nullum autem syllogismum perfectum fieri in hac figura docet: quia omnes indigent reductione ad primam, vt appareant necessarij.

In the first part he says: The third figure is made when three terms are so disposed that the middle is the subject in each premise: but the major extreme is the predicate of the major, and the minor the predicate of the minor; but it is necessary that the major proposition always be universal, and the conclusion always particular. Therefore he defines the middle thus: But the middle in this figure I call that of which both are predicated. That is, that of which both extremes are predicated. The extremes, he says, are those which are predicated, both in the premises and in the conclusion; but the middle is always subjected, and so they have as it were dissimilar and opposite rationes; and for this reason this extreme is said to be farther from the middle. But the minor extreme (he says) is the one which is nearer, that is, which comes closer to the middle, since at least in the conclusion it is the subject, just as the middle is in each premise. He teaches that no perfect syllogism is made in this figure, because all need reduction to the first, in order that they may appear necessary.

31 In secunda parte capitis, enumerat modos vtiles, qui in hac figura effici possunt, inutilib. exclusis. Primus igitur modus efficitur: Quando vtraque præmissa est vniuersalis affirmatiua: vt si dicamus: Omnis homo est viuens: Omnis homo est animal: ergo Aliquod animal est viuens. Et vocatur modus iste Darapti. Reducitur autem ad tertium modum primæ figuræ per solam conuersionem minoris in partem, hoc modo: Omnis homo est viuens: Aliquod animal est homo; ergo Aliquod animal est viuens.

31 In the second part of the chapter he enumerates the useful moods that can be produced in this figure, the useless ones being excluded. The first mood, then, is produced when each premise is universal affirmative: as if we say, Every man is living; Every man is an animal; therefore Some animal is living. And this mood is called Darapti. It is reduced to the third mood of the first figure by the sole conversion of the minor in part, in this way: Every man is living; Some animal is a man; therefore Some animal is living.

Secundus modus fit: Quando maior est vniuersalis negatiua, & minor vniuersalis affirmatiua; & vocatur Felapton, atque est talis. Nullum animal est lapis; Omne animal est viuens; ergo

The second mood is made when the major is universal negative, and the minor universal affirmative; and it is called Felapton, and is as follows: No animal is a stone; Every animal is living; therefore Oo iij

p. 582

aliquod viuens non est lapis. Reducitur autem ad quartum modum primæ figuræ, per solam conuersionem minoris in partem: hoc modo, Nullum animal est lapis: Aliquod viuens est animal: ergo aliquod viuens non est lapis.

some living thing is not a stone. It is reduced to the fourth mood of the first figure by the sole conversion of the minor in part, in this way: No animal is a stone; Some living thing is an animal; therefore some living thing is not a stone.

Tertius modus fit, Quandò maior propositio est particularis affirmatiua, & minor vniuersalis negatiua: & dicitur Disamis. Vt si dicamus, Aliquod animal est corpus: Omne animal est viuens: ergo aliquod viuens est corpus. Reducitur autem ad tertium modum primæ figuræ, per conuersionem maioris, & transmutationem præmissarum. Ita, vt maior conuersa fiat minor, idque per conuersionem simplicem conclusionis, & ex minori, fiat maior, hoc modo: Omne animal est viuens, aliquod corpus est animal: ergo aliquod corpus est viuens. Quartus modus fit: Quando maior est vniuersalis affirmatiua, & minor particularis etiam affirmatiua: vt si dicamus: Omne animal est viuens, Aliquod animal est corpus: ergo aliquod corpus est viuens: & vocatur Datisi.
