Reducitur autem ad tertium modum primæ figuræ, per solam conuersionem simplicem minoris: hoc modo: Omne animal est viuens: Aliquod corpus est animal: ergo aliquod corpus est viuens. Quintus modus fit, Quando maior est particularis affirmatiua: & minor vniuersalis affirmatiua: vt si dicamus; Aliquod animal non est lapis; Omne animal est viuens; ergo aliquod viuens non est lapis. Et vocatur Bocardo, qui non potest deduci ad modos primæ figuræ ostensiuè, sicut alij, sed solùm per impossibile, secundùm regulas huius reductionis hoc modo: Omne viuens est lapis: Omne animal est viuens, ergo Omne animal est lapis.

The third mood is made when the major proposition is particular affirmative, and the minor universal affirmative; and it is called Disamis. As if we say, Some animal is a body; Every animal is living; therefore some living thing is a body. It is reduced to the third mood of the first figure by conversion of the major and transposition of the premises, so that the converted major becomes the minor, and this through simple conversion of the conclusion, and the minor becomes the major, in this way: Every animal is living; some body is an animal; therefore some body is living. The fourth mood is made when the major is universal affirmative, and the minor particular, also affirmative; as if we say: Every animal is living; Some animal is a body; therefore some body is living; and it is called Datisi. It is reduced to the third mood of the first figure by the sole simple conversion of the minor, in this way: Every animal is living; Some body is an animal; therefore some body is living. The fifth mood is made when the major is particular negative, and the minor universal affirmative; as if we say: Some animal is not a stone; Every animal is living; therefore some living thing is not a stone. And it is called Bocardo, which cannot be brought back to the moods of the first figure ostensively, as the others can, but only through the impossible, according to the rules of this reduction, in this way: Every living thing is a stone; Every animal is living; therefore Every animal is a stone.

Sextus modus fit. Quando maior est vniuersalis negans, & minor particularis affirmans, vt in hoc exemplo: Nullum animal est lapis; aliquod animal est viuens, ergo aliquod viuens non est lapis; & vocatur Ferison, qui reducitur ad quartum modum primæ figuræ, per solam conuersionem simplicem minoris, hoc modo: Nullum animal est lapis: aliquod viuens est animal, ergo aliquod animal non est lapis. Per has autem reductiones ad modos primæ figuræ, probatur euidenter, vtiles ad bonas esse omnes syllogismos secundæ ac tertiæ figuræ. Solùm autem vsi sumus reductione ostensiua: quia breuis est. Reductionem verò per impossibile, tanquam longiorem ad Summulas remittendam censemus, vbi iuuenes in ea frequenter exercentur: & propterea non est necessarium hac in parte eam repetere. Ex tribus figuris, resultant quatuordecim tantùm modi vtiles sequentibus dictionibus significati, quarum quælibet significat suum modum: & quatuor primę significant

The sixth mood is made when the major is universal negative and the minor particular affirmative, as in this example: No animal is a stone; some animal is living; therefore some living thing is not a stone; and it is called Ferison, which is reduced to the fourth mood of the first figure by the sole simple conversion of the minor, in this way: No animal is a stone; some living thing is an animal; therefore some living thing is not a stone. And through these reductions to the moods of the first figure it is evidently proved that all the syllogisms of the second and third figures are useful and good. We have, however, used only ostensive reduction, because it is brief. Reduction through the impossible, as being longer, we judge should be referred to the Summulae, where the young are frequently exercised in it; and for this reason it is not necessary to repeat it in this place. From the three figures there result only fourteen useful moods, signified by the following words, each of which signifies its own mood; and the first four signify

p. 583

quatuor modos primæ figuræ: quatuor sequentes, significant quatuor alios secundæ figuræ: sex verò vltimæ, sex alios tertiæ figuræ. Dictiones verò istæ sunt: Barbara, Celarent, Darij, Ferio, Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, Darapti, Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison. Quinque enim alij imperfecti primæ figuræ, non sunt constituti ab Aristot. sed post eum ab aliis additi.

the four moods of the first figure; the four following signify four others of the second figure; and the last six, six others of the third figure. The words are these: Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio, Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, Darapti, Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison. For the five other, imperfect moods of the first figure were not established by Aristotle, but were added after him by others.

Traditur ars inueniendi medium, ad conficiendos syllogismos, & probandum quodlibet genus propositionum — The art of finding the middle is delivered, for constructing syllogisms and proving any kind of proposition.

De hac arte agit Arist. cap. 29. huius primi lib. vbi quod ex se obscurum est, obscurius multò fecit, vtens elementis, aut literis, nihil significantibus, pro mediis inueniendis. Nos verò eam in terminis significantibus, nobísque familiaribus, atque etiam verbis minimè obscuris, breuiter explicabimus: tanquam fundamentum præsupponentes, proprium officium medij in syllogismo: quod non est aliud quàm vnire, aut disiungere extremitates, vnire quidem in syllogismo affirmatiuo, seu prædicatiuo: qui componitur ex propositionibus affirmatiuus, disiungere verò, in syllogismo negatiuo, hoc est, constante aliqua propositione negatiua. Et ratio huius distinctionis est manifesta: quia per syllogismum affirmatiuum probanda est propositio affirmatiua, in qua aliquod prædicatum vnitur alicui subiecto: medium autem ad vniendum terminos accedere debet. In syllogismo verò negatiuo, probanda est positio negatiua, in qua prædicatum negatur de subiecto: quod est separari ab eo: medium verò, ad aliqua separanda, tale debet esse: vt disiungat ea, non vt vniat. Vtrumque ergo officium conuenit medio, respectu diuersorum syllogismorum, & diuersarum propositionum probandarum.

Of this art Aristotle treats in ch. 29 of this first book, where what is obscure of itself he made much more obscure, using elements, or letters signifying nothing, for finding middles. We, however, shall explain it briefly in significant terms familiar to us, and also in words that are not at all obscure, presupposing as a foundation the proper office of the middle in a syllogism: which is nothing other than to unite or to disjoin the extremes; to unite them in an affirmative or predicative syllogism, which is composed of affirmative propositions, but to disjoin them in a negative syllogism, that is, one consisting of some negative proposition. And the reason for this distinction is manifest: because through an affirmative syllogism an affirmative proposition is to be proved, in which some predicate is united to some subject; and the middle must come in to unite the terms. But in a negative syllogism a negative proposition is to be proved, in which the predicate is denied of the subject, which is to be separated from it; and a middle for separating some things must be such that it disjoins them, not that it unites them. Both offices, therefore, belong to the middle, with respect to diverse syllogisms and diverse propositions to be proved.

Ex quibus sequuntur duę regulæ vniuersales. Prima, Ad probandam propositionem affirmatiuam quamcumque quærendum esse medium, quo extrema eius, hoc est prędicatum, & subiectum vniantur. Ad probandam verò quamlibet negatiuam, medium potius quærendum, quod ea disiungat. Sed vt particulares regulas, quas Arist. tradit intelligamus, aliud fundamentum debet præsupponi, nempe, medium comparatum ad extremitates: quas vnire, aut separare debet, triplex esse, Antecedens, Consequens, & Extraneum. Medium antecedens, illud dicitur: ex quo aliqua, vel vtraque extremitas sequitur: vt homo, respectu risibilis. Medium cõsequens, quòd ex vna, vel ex vtraque extremitate, sequitur. Medium deniq; extraneum, quod alteri, vel vtriq; extremitati repugnat: vt lapis respectu animalis atque etiam viuentis.

From which follow two universal rules. The first: To prove any affirmative proposition whatever, a middle must be sought by which its extremes, that is, the predicate and the subject, are united. But to prove any negative whatever, a middle must rather be sought that disjoins them. But in order that we may understand the particular rules which Aristotle delivers, another foundation must be presupposed: namely, that the middle, compared to the extremes which it must unite or separate, is threefold: Antecedent, Consequent, and Extraneous. The antecedent middle is said to be that from which one or both extremes follow: as man, with respect to risible. The consequent middle, that which follows from one or from both extremes. The extraneous middle, finally, that which is repugnant to one or both extremes: as stone with respect to animal and also to living. Oo iij

p. 584

Ex quo infertur, Primò, Quòd ad probãdam propositionem quamlibet affirmatiuam, quærendum sit medium antecedens, vel consequens respectu vnius, aut vtriusque extremitatis: ad probandam verò propositionem negatiuam, non est quærendum medium antecedens neque consequens, sed extraneum.

From which it is inferred, first, that to prove any affirmative proposition whatever, an antecedent or consequent middle must be sought, with respect to one or both extremes; but to prove a negative proposition, one must seek neither an antecedent nor a consequent middle, but an extraneous one.

Secundò sequitur, Ad probandam quamlibet propositionem oblatam, considerandum esse, quonam modo se habeant prædicatum & subiectum eius: nam si vnum conueniat alteri, per medium antecedens, vel consequens probanda est: si verò ei repugnet, per medium extraneum. Supponimus autem propositionem probandam, veram esse debere, aut probabilem, vel quòd talis existimetur: nam ad probandũ propositiones falsas vt tales nec mediũ dari potest, neque ars vlla illud inueniendi.

It follows, second, that to prove any proposition offered, one must consider in what way its predicate and subject are related: for if the one belongs to the other, it is to be proved through an antecedent or consequent middle; but if it is repugnant to it, through an extraneous middle. We suppose, moreover, that the proposition to be proved must be true, or probable, or thought to be such: for to prove false propositions as such, neither can a middle be given, nor any art of finding it.

His suppositis, quatuor regulas tradit Aristot. vbi suprà, ad concludenda quatuor genera propositionum sub quibus comprehenduntur omnes aliæ. Prima regula est, Ad inferendam vniuersalem affirmationem, tale medium quærendum est, quod sit consequens respectu subiecti, & antecedens respectu prædicati, v. g. ad inferendam hanc propositionem, Omnis homo est substantia, assumendum erit animal, quod est consequens ad hominem, & antecedens respectu substantiæ & syllogismus fiet hoc modo in Barbara: Omne animal est substantia; Omnis homo est animal: ergo Omnis homo est substantia.

These things supposed, Aristotle delivers four rules in the place cited above for concluding the four kinds of propositions under which all others are comprehended. The first rule is: To infer a universal affirmation, such a middle must be sought as is consequent with respect to the subject and antecedent with respect to the predicate. For example, to infer this proposition, Every man is a substance, animal will have to be assumed, which is consequent to man and antecedent with respect to substance; and the syllogism will be made in this way in Barbara: Every animal is a substance; Every man is an animal; therefore Every man is a substance.

Secunda regula: Ad inferendam particularem affirmatiuam, assumendum est medium, quòd sit antecedens respectu subiecti, & prædicati eius, quæ sunt extremitates: vt ad inferendum hanc, Aliquod animal est substantia, assumi debet homo, ex quo vtrumque sequitur: & fiet hoc modo in Darapti: Omnis homo est substantia: Omnis homo est animal: ergo Aliquod animal est substantia.

The second rule: To infer a particular affirmative, a middle must be assumed which is antecedent with respect to the subject and to the predicate, which are the extremes: as, to infer this, Some animal is a substance, man must be assumed, from which both follow; and it will be done in this way in Darapti: Every man is a substance; Every man is an animal; therefore Some animal is a substance.

Tertia regula: Ad inferendum vniuersalem negatiuam, assumendum est medium quòd sit consequens respectu subiecti, extraneum respectu prædicati: vt ad probandam hanc, Nullus homo est lapis assumendum est animal: & sic probabitur, in Cesare. Nullus lapis est animal. Omnis homo est animal: ergo Nullus homo est lapis.

The third rule: To infer a universal negative, a middle must be assumed which is consequent with respect to the subject and extraneous with respect to the predicate: as, to prove this, No man is a stone, animal must be assumed; and thus it will be proved in Cesare: No stone is an animal; Every man is an animal; therefore No man is a stone.

Quarta regula: Ad concludendam particularem negatiuam. assumendum est medium, quod sit antecedens ad subiectum & extraneum respectu prædicati, vt ad concludendam hanc, Aliquod animal non est lapis assumendum est Homo: & ita concludetur in Festino: Nullus homo est lapis: Aliquis homo est animal: ergo Aliquod animal, non est lapis.

The fourth rule: To conclude a particular negative, a middle must be assumed which is antecedent to the subject and extraneous with respect to the predicate: as, to conclude this, Some animal is not a stone, Man must be assumed; and so it will be concluded in Festino: No man is a stone; Some man is an animal; therefore Some animal is not a stone.

Finis huius operis.

End of this work.

p. 585

COMMENTARIES ON THE TWO BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE THE STAGIRITE, ON THE POSTERIOR

Analysi, seu resolutione, vnà cum dubiis & quæstionibus hac tempestate agitari solitis.

Analysis, or Resolution, together with the doubts and questions customarily debated in this age.

Proœmium totius operis — P RO E M O F T H E W H O L E WO R K .

CVM officium Dialecticæ sit dirigere operationis, hoc est disponere illa, atque ordinare, in diuisiones, definitiones, & propositiones & syllogismos. cæterásque argumentationes, iuxta triplicem operationem intellectus dirigendam, diuiditur hæc scientia ab omnibus, Ita vt prima pars eius, censeatur illa, quæ primam operationem nempe apprehensionem simplicem ordinat, naturam eius sic explicãs, vt sciamus ea apprehendere, vt oportet, ad efficiendam compositionem: quod pertinet ad secundam operationem intellectus, ita dirigendam, vt per illam sciamus ex simplicibus iam apprehensis, compositionem constituere, nempe diuisionem, definitionem, & argumentationem, per debitam namque constructionem horum instrumentorum directa, atque ordinata censetur operatio. Tertiam verò dirigit logica, dum ex eisdem compositionibus argumentationem constituit. Nam in argumentatione, iuxta regulas Dialecticæ constituta, ordinata censetur tertia operatio intellectus, cuius officium est, vnum ex alio colligere. Prima igitur pars Dialecticæ sunt prædicamenta, ex simplicibus ordinatis constituta. Prædicabilia verò, non tam primam partem constituere censentur: quàm præambulum quoddam esse, ad primam partem prædicamentorum.

ince the office of Dialectic is to direct the operations of reason, S that is, to dispose and order them into divisions, definitions, propositions, syllogisms, and the other argumentations, according to the threefold operation of the intellect to be directed, this science is divided by all in such a way that its first part is considered to be the one that orders the first operation, namely simple apprehension, explaining its nature so that we may know how to apprehend things as is fitting for effecting composition: which pertains to the second operation of the intellect, to be so directed that through it we may know how to construct a composition out of simples already apprehended, namely division, definition, and argumentation; for through the due construction of these instruments the operation is considered directed and ordered. The third, however, Logic directs when out of these same compositions it constructs argumentation. For in an argumentation constructed according to the rules of Dialectic the third operation of the intellect, whose office is to gather one thing from another, is considered ordered. The first part of Dialectic, therefore, is the categories, constituted out of ordered simples. The predicables, however, are considered not so much to constitute the first part as to be a certain preamble to the first part, that of the categories.

2 Secunda pars Dialecticæ, est opus de interpretatione, in quo traduntur regulæ constituendi propositionem, seu enunciationem. Ad tertiam verò partem pertinent, libri priorum, in quibus agitur de syllogismo in communi, libri posteriorum, topicorum, & elenchorum, in quibus de syllogismis in speciali agitur: nempe, demonstratiuo, topico, seu probabili, atque sophistico. Et hac ratione habemus totam hanc scientiam

2 The second part of Dialectic is the work On Interpretation, in which the rules are delivered for constructing a proposition or enunciation. To the third part belong the books of the Prior Analytics, in which the syllogism in general is treated; the books of the Posterior Analytics, the Topics, and the Sophistical Refutations, in which syllogisms in particular are treated, namely the demonstrative, the topical or probable, and the sophistical. And in this way we have this whole science

p. 586

in tres partes diuisam: per quam tres operationes intellectus diriguntur, ordinantur, perficiuntur. Ad cuius postremam partem pertinere, duos istos libros, de Posteriori analysi, aut resolutione, quos nunc interpretandos suscipimus, ex eadem diuisione efficitur manifestum: qua supposita, ad scopum huius operis, (quod subiectum, vel obiectum vocant) oculis subiiciendum veniamus.

divided into three parts, through which the three operations of the intellect are directed, ordered, and perfected. That these two books, on the Posterior Analysis or Resolution, which we now undertake to interpret, belong to its last part is made manifest from the same division. This supposed, let us come to set before our eyes the scope of this work (which they call its subject or object).

Quodnam sit subiectum, vel obiectum huius operis?

Which is the subject or object of this work?

PRo eodem iam accipiuntur, subiectum, cuius notitiam tradit scientia, demonstrando proprietates, aut passiones eius, & obiectum, circa quod, quasi circa scopum, versatur, consideratio eius. Quærimus ergo primò, Quodnam sit subiectum, vel obiectum huius Posterioristicæ partis. Præsupponendæ autem sunt conditiones obiecti, in 6. quæst. proœmiali à nobis traditæ.

By the subject, whose cognition a science delivers by demonstrating its properties or attributes, and by the object, about which its consideration is concerned as about a scope, the same thing is now understood. We ask, therefore, first: Which is the subject or object of this posterioristic part. The conditions of the object, delivered by us in Proemial Question 6, are to be presupposed.

3 Prima opinio tenet: Esse modum sciendi, vt comprehendit non solùm demonstrationem, sed etiam definitionem. Imò hanc principaliter, ita commentator, Alexander, & Theophrastus, in proœmio huius operis: quos sequuntur nonnulli ex modernis.

3 The first opinion holds: That it is the mode of knowing, as it comprehends not only demonstration but also definition; indeed, the latter principally. So the Commentator, Alexander, and Theophrastus, in the proem of this work; whom some of the moderns follow.

Et probatur hac ratione: Quia definitio est principale instrumentum scientiæ: ergo per se pertinet ad Dialecticam, docentem instrumenta omnia sciendi facere: sed in nulla alia parte docet Arist. modum efficiendi definitionem, nisi in his libris: ergo ad eos pertinet per se, de definitione agere, quare ad eius obiectum simul cum demonstratione pertinebit. Probatur minor, quia in libris Topicorum, & si quæ est alia pars Dialecticæ, in qua aliquid de definitione agatur, non de modo eam efficiendi agitur, sed supponendo eam iam constitutam in his libris, examinatur eadem.

And it is proved by this argument: Because definition is the principal instrument of science; therefore it pertains per se to Dialectic, which teaches how to make all the instruments of knowing. But in no other part does Aristotle teach the mode of producing a definition except in these books; therefore it pertains per se to them to treat of definition, wherefore it will pertain to their object together with demonstration. The minor is proved: because in the books of the Topics, and in any other part of Dialectic, if there is one, in which something is treated concerning definition, it is not the mode of producing it that is treated, but, supposing it already constituted in these books, it is examined.

4 Secunda opinio est communis, & vera, quòd sola demonstratio, & non modus sciendi, communis demonstrationi, ac definitioni, sit obiectum huius operis. Sic Thom. Albertus magnus, Caier. Sotus, Toletus, Mercatus, & omnes ferè moderni interpretes. Probatur testimonio Arist. qui statim in principio primi capitis, omnem doctrinam, omnemque disciplinam, ex præexistenti cognitione fieri docet, & probat: quod potissimum fundamentum est, totius artis demõstratiuæ. Ex quo cognoscimus, assensum conclusionis, ex notitia principiorum generi: quod est naturam demonstrationis intelligere.

4 The second opinion is the common and true one: that demonstration alone, and not the mode of knowing common to demonstration and to definition, is the object of this work. So St. Thomas, Albert the Great, Cajetan, Soto, Toledo, Mercado, and almost all the modern interpreters. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who at the very beginning of the first chapter teaches and proves that all doctrine and all discipline comes about from pre-existing cognition: which is the chief foundation of the whole demonstrative art. From this we know that the assent to the conclusion is generated from the cognition of the principles; which is to understand the nature of demonstration.

p. 587

Probatur deinde ratione: Quia illud est obiectum alicuius operis, cuius partes essentiales traduntur in eo, cuius natura explicatur, & cuius passiones probantur: sed hæc omnia præstantur in his libris, de sola demonstratione, & non de modo sciendi communi: vt in discursu eorum est manifestum: ergo. Nam si de definitione agitur (quod concedimus) non vt de alio modo sciendi, à demonstratione distincto, sed tanquam de parte eius essentiali agitur: quia potissimum principium eius est: ergo sola demonstratio est obiectum, & non aliquid aliud commune demonstrationi, & definitioni.

It is proved next by reason: Because that is the object of some work whose essential parts are delivered in it, whose nature is explained, and whose attributes are proved; but all these things are performed in these books concerning demonstration alone, and not concerning the common mode of knowing, as is manifest in the course of them: therefore. For if definition is treated (which we concede), it is treated not as another mode of knowing distinct from demonstration, but as an essential part of it, because it is its chief principle: therefore demonstration alone is the object, and not something else common to demonstration and definition.

Et ex hoc soluitur argum. contrariæ opinionis, cui omnia concedenda sunt, sed ex concessione eorum, solùm habetur: quòd per se in his libris agatur de definitione, tanquam de parte essentiali demonstrationis, non verò tanquam de alio modo sciendi distincto. Vnde qui asserit demonstrationem solam esse obiectum, non excludit definitionem, sed eam comprehendit: non tanquam sub aliquo prędicato communi, sed vt pars comprehenditur sub toto: & consequenter sub consideratione eius.

And from this the argument of the contrary opinion is solved; everything in it is to be conceded, but from conceding it one has only this: that in these books definition is treated per se as an essential part of demonstration, but not as another, distinct mode of knowing. Hence whoever asserts that demonstration alone is the object does not exclude definition, but comprehends it: not as under some common predicate, but as a part is comprehended under the whole, and consequently under its consideration.

Digniorem esse hanc partem dialecticæ cæteris omnibus ostenditur — This part of Dialectic is shown to be more worthy than all the others.

5 CVm notum sit, scientiam ex obiecto sumere dignitatem, colligitur opus hoc dignius, atque perfectius esse, cęteris partibus dialecticæ: quod sic probo: Notitia simplicium, de quibus agit prima pars dialecticæ, ordinatur ad compositionem, tanquam ad finem, de qua agitur in secunda parte: & compositio, ad syllogismum eodem ordinatur modo: ergo sicut erit perfectior compositione, & eisdem simplicibus, sed inter syllogismos perfectissima est demonstratio, ad quam ordinantur, quæcunque tractantur in hac scientia, tanquam ad potissimum instrumentum, per quod generatur scientia: ergo opus hoc quasi finis est aliarum partium dialecticæ: & ideo dignius erit cæteris omnibus.

5 Since it is known that a science takes its dignity from its object, it is gathered that this work is more worthy and more perfect than the other parts of Dialectic; which I prove thus: The cognition of simples, of which the first part of Dialectic treats, is ordered to composition, as to its end, which is treated in the second part; and composition is ordered in the same way to the syllogism: therefore, just so, the syllogism will be more perfect than composition and than these same simples. But among syllogisms the most perfect is demonstration, to which whatever is treated in this science is ordered as to the chief instrument through which science is generated: therefore this work is as it were the end of the other parts of Dialectic, and for this reason it will be more worthy than all the others.

6 Sed contra hoc, est arg. difficile: Quia libri de priori resolutione, agunt de forma syllogismi, hoc est, de figura, & modo, in quo debet constitui: cæteri verò libri, de materia eiusdem, nempe libri de posteriori resolutione, de materia necessaria, ex qua constat demonstratio, libri Topicorum de materia probabili: ex qua conficitur syllogismus Dialecticus, libri Elenchorum, de materia apparenti, ex qua conficitur syllogismus

6 But against this there is a difficult argument: Because the books on the Prior Resolution treat of the form of the syllogism, that is, of the figure and mood in which it must be constructed; but the other books, of its matter: namely, the books on the Posterior Resolution, of the necessary matter of which demonstration consists; the books of the Topics, of the probable matter out of which the Dialectical syllogism is made; the books of the Sophistical Refutations, of the apparent matter out of which is made the syllogism

p. 588

speudographus, aut deceptorius: sed forma cùm sit actus, est perfectior materia, quę est potentia: ergo libri Priorum, sunt pars nobilior Dialecticæ, quàm libri Posteriorum, Topicorum, & Elenchorum. Probatur consequentia, quia sicut scientia totalis, sumit suam dignitatem, ex dignitate obiecti totalis: ita quælibet pars scientiæ, ex obiecto partiali sibi proprio. Vnde sequitur, falsum esse quod dicimus, hos libros posteriorum, esse nobiliorem partem totius Dialecticæ.

that is pseudographic or deceptive. But form, since it is act, is more perfect than matter, which is potency: therefore the books of the Prior Analytics are a nobler part of Dialectic than the books of the Posterior Analytics, the Topics, and the Sophistical Refutations. The consequence is proved: because just as a total science takes its dignity from the dignity of its total object, so each part of a science takes it from the partial object proper to it. Hence it follows that what we say is false, that these books of the Posterior Analytics are the nobler part of the whole of Dialectic.

7 Hoc arg. concludit, aduersus plures, qui tenent hoc opus solùm agere de materia necessaria syllogismi: & per hanc distingui à libris Priorum, agentibus de forma syllogistica, & à libris Topicorum, & Elenchorum, agentibus de materia probabili & apparenti. Ideo dicendum est, hoc opus, non solùm de materia syllogismi agere: sed etiam de forma. Sed forma syllogismi duplex est, generica, & specifica. Forma generica est dispositio in modo & figura. Forma verò specifica, ex modo speciali concludendi vnum ex alio, sumitur. Quod sic probo: Forma generica syllogismi, sumitur ex modo inferendi conclusionem ex præmissis, dispositis in modo, & figura: ergo specialis modus inferendi conclusionem ex præmissis erit specialis forma syllogismi: sed demonstratio, de qua agitur in hoc opere, tanquam de proprio obiecto, continet non solùm dispositionem, in modo, & figura, sed etiam specialem modum inferendi conclusionem ex præmissis: nempe tanquam effectum ex causa per se, & propria aut tanquam causam ex effectu proprio, & per se: ergo continet formam specialem, & perfectissimam syllogismi.

7 This argument is conclusive against the many who hold that this work treats only of the necessary matter of the syllogism, and is distinguished by this from the books of the Prior Analytics, which treat of syllogistic form, and from the books of the Topics and the Sophistical Refutations, which treat of probable and apparent matter. Therefore it must be said that this work treats not only of the matter of the syllogism but also of its form. But the form of the syllogism is twofold, generic and specific. The generic form is the disposition in mood and figure. The specific form, however, is taken from the special mode of concluding one thing from another. Which I prove thus: The generic form of the syllogism is taken from the mode of inferring the conclusion from premises disposed in mood and figure: therefore the special mode of inferring the conclusion from the premises will be the special form of the syllogism. But demonstration, which is treated in this work as its proper object, contains not only the disposition in mood and figure, but also a special mode of inferring the conclusion from the premises: namely, as an effect from its per se and proper cause, or as a cause from its proper and per se effect: therefore it contains the special and most perfect form of the syllogism.

8 Secundò probatur: Quia demonstratio generat scientiam, syllogismus verò probabilis opinionẽ, at isti duo effectus, sunt specie distincti: ergo duo isti syllogismi nempe demonstratiuus, & probabilis, qui sunt causæ per se eorum effectuum, distinguuntur specie. Et distinctio specifica, non est per materiam, sed per formam: ergo distinguuntur per formam. Non per formam vtique communem, quæ est dispositio in modo, & figura: cùm hæc sit generica, & vtrique communis: ergo per formam specialem, & non solùm per materiam.

8 It is proved second: Because demonstration generates science, but the probable syllogism opinion; and these two effects are distinct in species: therefore these two syllogisms, namely the demonstrative and the probable, which are the per se causes of these effects, are distinguished in species. And specific distinction is not through matter, but through form: therefore they are distinguished through form. Not, surely, through the common form, which is the disposition in mood and figure, since this is generic and common to both: therefore through a special form, and not only through matter.

Itaque tenendum est, quòd præter communem formam, & genericam syllogismi, ex modo, & figura desumptam, datur duplex forma specialis, ex modo speciali concludendi desumpta, per quam distinguuntur specie demonstratio, & syllogismus Dialecticus, seu probabilis. Forma specialis demonstrationis est, modus concludendi euidenter, effectum per se ex causa, vel causam per se ex effectu: modus verò concludendi syllogismi probabilis, non est euidens

It must be held, therefore, that besides the common and generic form of the syllogism, taken from mood and figure, there is given a twofold special form, taken from the special mode of concluding, through which demonstration and the Dialectical or probable syllogism are distinguished in species. The special form of demonstration is the mode of concluding evidently an effect per se from its cause, or a cause per se from its effect; but the mode of concluding of the probable syllogism is not evident

p. 589

, sed probabilis. Itaque in modo, & figura conueniunt, sed in modo speciali inferendi conclusionem ex præmissis, dispositis in modo, & figura, distinguuntur: quia modus concludendi demonstrationis euidens, & necessarius est. Modus verò concludendi syllogismi Dialectici, non est euidens, aut necessarius, sed probabilis, & cùm ille modus sit perfectissimus, perfectissima species syllogismi erit demonstratio. Exemplo esse possunt duo isti syllogismi, Omne animal diligit sibi simile: sed Omnis homo est animal simile alteri homini: ergo omnis homo diligit alterum hominem: Et, Omne animal rationale est risibile: Omnis homo est animal rationale: ergo Omnis homo est risibilis. Nam cùm vterque sit constitutus in primo modo primæ figuræ, secundus concludit euidenter: quia conclusio eius sequitur ex præmissis, tanquam effectus proprius, & per se, ex sua causa. Nam risibilitas, proprius effectus, necessarius, & per se rationalitatis est, cum qua conuertitur. Nihilominus primus syllogismus non concludit euidenter, sed solùm probabiliter quia conclusio eius non sequitur ex præmissis, tanquam effectus necessarius, aut per se: sed tanquam effectus quasi contingens. Nam licèt similitudo inclinet ad dilectionem, tamen non tanquam ad effectum necessarium, sed liberum, & qui sæpe impeditur aliis rationibus. Syllogismus verò Sophisticus, distinguitur specie ab vtroque: quia peccat in forma: non enim habet debitam dispositionem in modo, & figura, licèt videatur habere: quare nec habet veram formam, sed solùm apparentem.

but probable. Thus they agree in mood and figure, but they are distinguished in the special mode of inferring the conclusion from the premises disposed in mood and figure: because the mode of concluding of demonstration is evident and necessary, whereas the mode of concluding of the Dialectical syllogism is not evident or necessary, but probable; and since the former mode is the most perfect, demonstration will be the most perfect species of syllogism. These two syllogisms can serve as an example: Every animal loves its like; but Every man is an animal like another man; therefore every man loves another man. And: Every rational animal is risible; Every man is a rational animal; therefore Every man is risible. For although each is constructed in the first mood of the first figure, the second concludes evidently, because its conclusion follows from the premises as a proper and per se effect from its cause. For risibility is a proper, necessary, and per se effect of rationality, with which it is convertible. Nevertheless the first syllogism does not conclude evidently, but only probably, because its conclusion does not follow from the premises as a necessary or per se effect, but as a quasi-contingent effect. For although likeness inclines to love, yet not as to a necessary effect, but to a free one, and one which is often impeded by other reasons. The Sophistical syllogism, however, is distinguished in species from both, because it sins in form: for it does not have the due disposition in mood and figure, although it seems to have it; wherefore it does not have a true form, but only an apparent one.

9 Ad arg. igitur. Negandum est antecedens, quòd opus hoc solùm agat de materia syllogismi: agit enim etiam de forma non communi, aut generica, de qua agunt libri Priorum, sed de specifica: & perfectissima quidem, vtpote ex perfectissimo modo euidenter concludendi desumpta, & ex hoc habet, quòd sit nobilissima pars totius Dialecticæ, ad quam ordinantur cæteræ omnes, tanquam ad finem, Sed deceptio eorum, qui falsò putant agere de sola materia: occasionem sumpsit ex hoc: quòd modus iste perfectissimus, euidenter inferendi conclusionem ex præmissis, non reperitur, nisi in propositionibus in materia necessaria constitutis: vnde verum est, opus hoc agere, de materia necessaria syllogismi: sed falsum, quod agat de sola materia: sed præcipuè, de forma speciali, & perfectissima.

9 To the argument, then: the antecedent must be denied, namely that this work treats only of the matter of the syllogism; for it treats also of form, not the common or generic form, of which the books of the Prior Analytics treat, but the specific form, and indeed the most perfect, inasmuch as it is taken from the most perfect mode of concluding evidently; and from this it has it that it is the noblest part of the whole of Dialectic, to which all the others are ordered as to their end. But the deception of those who falsely think that it treats of matter alone took its occasion from this: that this most perfect mode of evidently inferring the conclusion from the premises is not found except in propositions constituted in necessary matter. Hence it is true that this work treats of the necessary matter of the syllogism, but false that it treats of matter alone; rather it treats chiefly of the special and most perfect form.

Finis huius operis, & titulus, seu inscriptio eius explicatur — The end of this work, and its title or inscription, is explained.

10 FInis huius operis nihilominus est: quia naturale desideriũ hominis: vt est rationalis, perficit. Ab ipsa enim rationalis natura

10 The end of this work is most noble: because it perfects the natural desire of man as he is rational. For from rational nature

p. 590

hominis procedit, naturale desiderium sciendi, hoc est, cognoscendi effectus per causas, aut causas per effectus: vt docuit expresè Arist. 1. lib. Met. in principio dicens, omnes homines natura scire desiderant. & ad hoc desiderium adimplendum ordinatur opus hoc, de natura demonstrationis agens: quæ est potissimum instrumentum sciendi, vt patet ex eius definitione, tradita ab Arist. c. 2. huius 1. li. in hunc modum: Demonstratio est syllogismus faciens scire. Inscribitur verò, de posteriori resolutione.

of man there proceeds the natural desire of knowing, that is, of cognizing effects through causes or causes through effects, as Aristotle expressly taught at the beginning of Metaph. 1, saying: all men by nature desire to know. And to fulfill this desire this work is ordered, which treats of the nature of demonstration, which is the chief instrument of knowing, as is plain from its definition, delivered by Aristotle in ch. 2 of this first book in this way: Demonstration is a syllogism that makes one know. It is inscribed, however, On the Posterior Resolution.

11 Quem titulum vt intelligamus, vtraque particula eius explicanda est: nempe, Resolutio, & Posterior. Resolutio verò alicuius rei, duplex est, Physica, seu realis & Logica, aut rationalis. Physica resolutio, est dissolutio aut destructio realis rei: vt dum equus moritur, dicitur resolui in materiam: & dum domus destruitur, dissolui, aut resolui eam dicimus, in ligna, lapides & terram, ex quibus constructa fuit. Logica verò, seu rationalis resolutio, non est destructio, sed perfectio rei. Consistit enim, in quodam examine singularium partium, ex quibus res est constituta: quo examine ostenditur, singulas eius partes tales esse, quales esse debent, secundùm præcepta illius artis, per quam constructa est. Vt dum examinamus partes definitionis, iuxta regulas definiendi traditas à Dialectica, ostendentes proprio genere, & propria differentia constare, dicimur resoluere definitionem. Quod patet idem esse, ac ostendere perfectam esse. Resoluere igitur demonstrationem, non erit aliud, quàm partes, hoc est principia, seu præmissas eius examinare: dum scilicet ostenduntur non vtcunque veræ, sed etiam necessariæ esse, & per se, atque immediatæ: ita vt cognitis terminis, sine vllo argumento, quo probentur, eis assentiatur intellectus, vel certè, per euidentes demonstrationes reducantur, vsque ad prima principia, ex sola notitia terminorum euidentia: nisi enim vno, aut altero modo cognoscat quis, esse per se euidentia, nec veram demonstrationem habebit, nec scientiam conclusionis, sed syllogismum Dialecticum & opinionem. Vt Aristot. docet cap. 2. huius 1. lib. his verbis, Ex primis autem indemonstrabilibus, quoniam non sciet non habens demonstrationem ipsorum.

11 In order that we may understand this title, each of its particles must be explained: namely, Resolution and Posterior. Now the resolution of anything is twofold, Physical or real, and Logical or rational. Physical resolution is the real dissolution or destruction of a thing: as when a horse dies, it is said to be resolved into matter; and when a house is destroyed, we say it is dissolved or resolved into the wood, stones, and earth out of which it was constructed. Logical or rational resolution, however, is not the destruction but the perfection of a thing. For it consists in a certain examination of the single parts of which the thing is constituted, by which examination it is shown that its single parts are such as they ought to be according to the precepts of that art through which it was constructed. As when we examine the parts of a definition according to the rules of defining delivered by Dialectic, showing that it consists of its proper genus and proper difference, we are said to resolve the definition. Which is plainly the same as to show that it is perfect. To resolve a demonstration, therefore, will be nothing other than to examine its parts, that is, its principles or premises: namely, when they are shown to be not true in just any way, but also necessary, per se, and immediate, so that once the terms are known the intellect assents to them without any argument by which they are proved; or at least that they are reduced through evident demonstrations back to first principles evident from the sole cognition of the terms. For unless someone knows in one way or the other that they are per se evident, he will have neither a true demonstration nor science of the conclusion, but a Dialectical syllogism and opinion. As Aristotle teaches in ch. 2 of this first book in these words: But from first indemonstrable premises, since he who does not have a demonstration of them will not know.

12 Res fit manifesta hac demonstratione. Omne animal rationale est risibile: Omnis homo est animal rationale: ergo Omnis homo est risibilis: cuius minor est propositio, per se nota, aut immediata, cùm in ea prædicetur definitio de suo definito, sine vllo medio, vel argumento probante, sola per se immediatè conueniat definito: ita vt statim ac significationem terminorum cognoscit intellectus, iudicet esse veram. Hoc

12 Let the matter be made manifest by this demonstration: Every rational animal is risible; Every man is a rational animal; therefore Every man is risible. Its minor is a proposition known per se, or immediate, since in it the definition is predicated of its definitum without any middle or proving argument, and it belongs per se and immediately to the definitum alone, so that as soon as the intellect cognizes the signification of the terms it judges it to be true. This

p. 591

est enim esse principium immediatum, aut per se notum. Cæterùm maior non est per se nota: quia risibilitas non conuenit homini immediatè, sed media alia passione priori, nempe admiratione. Demonstranda igitur est, vt intellectus certò atque euidenter cognoscat esse veram. Demonstratur verò per admirationem, pro medio assumptam, hoc modo: Omne admiratiuum, est risibile: Omnis homo est admiratiuus: ergo Omnis homo est risibilis. Sed adhuc demonstratio hæc non sufficit: quia licèt maior præmissa sit immediata, in qua prædicatur vna passio immediata de alia, nempe risibilitas de admiratione, quæ sine vllo medio ex ea sequitur: minor tamen in qua prædicatur admiratio de homine, non est immediata: quia admiratio non sequitur ex rationalitate per se immediatè, sed media alia passione priori, nempe capacitate disciplinæ.

is what it is to be an immediate principle, or one known per se. But the major is not known per se, because risibility does not belong to man immediately, but by means of another, prior attribute, namely wonder. It must therefore be demonstrated, so that the intellect may know certainly and evidently that it is true. And it is demonstrated through wonder, assumed as the middle, in this way: Everything capable of wonder is risible; Every man is capable of wonder; therefore Every man is risible. But this demonstration still does not suffice: because although the major premise is immediate, in which one immediate attribute is predicated of another, namely risibility of wonder, which follows from it without any middle, yet the minor, in which wonder is predicated of man, is not immediate: because wonder does not follow from rationality per se immediately, but by means of another, prior attribute, namely capacity for learning.

Quare vt cognoscat intellectus esse certam, & euidentem, scire debet eam demonstrare, per capacitatem disciplinæ sumptam pro medio: hoc modo: Quidquid est capax disciplinæ, est admiratiuum: Omnis homo est capax disciplinę: ergo Omnis homo est admiratiuus. Porrò hæc demonstratio perfectissima est: quia constat præmissis immediatis aut per se euidentibus: atque indemonstrabilibus. talis est enim maior, in quo vna passio immediata prædicatur de alia, nempe admiratio de capacitate disciplinæ, qua mediante, sequitur ex rationalitate. Talis est etiam minor, in qua prima passio, quæ immediatè sequitur essentiam, prædicatur de definitione, explicante eandem essentiam: & ad hanc demonstrationem reducta est prima, quæ non esset vera demonstratio, nisi ad eam reduceretur per veras demonstrationes. Quòd si aliquis nesciat eam ita reducere, non erit in eius intellectu demonstratio vera, sed syllogismus probabilis: nec habebit per eam scientiam conclusionis, sed opinionem. Et hæc reductio, est resolutio logica, & rationalis, quia per eam examinantur partes demonstrationis, & probantur euidenter tales esse: quales esse debent secundùm regulas huius artis: hoc est secundùm definitionem eiusdem demonstrationis, tradendam in 2. cap. huius lib. quæ prima regula est totius artis, & scientiæ. Et tandem, quia in hoc opere, docetur modus iste resoluendi, demonstrationem, per reductionem præmissarum vsque ad prima principia per se nota, aut indemonstrabilia, ideo inscribitur de resolutione.

Wherefore, in order that the intellect may know that it is certain and evident, it must know how to demonstrate it through capacity for learning taken as the middle, in this way: Whatever is capable of learning is capable of wonder; Every man is capable of learning; therefore Every man is capable of wonder. Now this demonstration is most perfect, because it consists of premises that are immediate, or evident per se, and indemonstrable. For such is the major, in which one immediate attribute is predicated of another, namely wonder of capacity for learning, by means of which it follows from rationality. Such also is the minor, in which the first attribute, which immediately follows the essence, is predicated of the definition that explains that same essence. And to this demonstration the first is reduced, which would not be a true demonstration unless it were reduced to it through true demonstrations. But if someone does not know how to reduce it thus, there will not be a true demonstration in his intellect, but a probable syllogism; nor will he have through it science of the conclusion, but opinion. And this reduction is logical and rational resolution, because through it the parts of the demonstration are examined and are evidently proved to be such as they ought to be according to the rules of this art: that is, according to the definition of that same demonstration, to be delivered in ch. 2 of this book, which is the first rule of the whole art and science. And finally, because in this work this mode of resolving demonstration through the reduction of the premises back to first principles known per se, or indemonstrable, is taught, it is therefore inscribed On Resolution.

14 Sed qua demonstratio duplici forma constat (vt iam diximus) communi, aut generica ex modo, & figura desumpta, & speciali desumpta ex modo concludendi: duobus modis resoluitur

14 But since demonstration consists of a twofold form (as we have already said), the common or generic, taken from mood and figure, and the special, taken from the mode of concluding, it is resolved in two ways

p. 592

: nempe, secundùm formam communem, quæ examinatur, & probatur per illa principia, dici de omni, & dici de nullo: & etiam secundùm formam specialem, quam resolutionem modo ostendimus: & resoluto secundùm formam genericam, prior est resolutione secundùm formam specificam: quia vniuersaliora sunt priora: & genus est prius specie: ideo libri agentes de syllogismo in communi, appellantur de priori resolutione, hoc est de resoluere syllogismi, secundùm formam genericam, quæ prior est. Hoc verò opus, docens resoluere syllogismum secundùm formam specialem, quæ est posterior inscribitur de posteriori resolutione.

namely, according to the common form, which is examined and proved through those principles, said of all and said of none; and also according to the special form, which resolution we have just shown. And resolution according to the generic form is prior to resolution according to the specific form, because more universal things are prior, and the genus is prior to the species. Therefore the books that treat of the syllogism in general are called On the Prior Resolution, that is, on resolving the syllogism according to the generic form, which is prior. But this work, which teaches how to resolve the syllogism according to the special form, which is posterior, is inscribed On the Posterior Resolution.

Sed contra hoc est argum. Quia in his libris non solùm docet Arist. resoluere demonstrationem, vsque ad prima principia, sed etiam componere illam ex talibus præmissis, & partibus. & prius est demonstrationem componere, quàm eam resoluere: quia resolutio est quasi examen compositionis: ergo de compositione potiùs tanquam de prima, quàm de resolutione debent appellari.

But against this there is an argument: Because in these books Aristotle teaches not only how to resolve demonstration back to first principles, but also how to compose it out of such premises and parts; and it is prior to compose a demonstration than to resolve it, because resolution is as it were an examination of the composition: therefore they ought rather to be named from composition, as from what is first, than from resolution.

15 Respondeo, omissis aliis solutionibus: Concesso antecedente, sed negata consequentia: quia licèt de compositione per se tractetur, & prior sit, resolutio tamen est perfectior: quia est quasi forma, & anima compositionis, per quam constat euidenter, factam esse secundùm regulas artis, & ideo bonam esse: & demonstrationem compositam esse exactam, firmam & stabilem, atque generatiuam scientiæ.

15 I reply, other solutions being omitted: the antecedent is conceded, but the consequence denied. Because although composition is treated per se, and is prior, resolution is nevertheless more perfect: because it is as it were the form and soul of the composition, through which it is evidently established that it has been made according to the rules of the art, and is therefore good; and that the demonstration composed is exact, firm, and stable, and generative of science.

Ex quibus sequitur, non esse distinguendam resolutionem rationis in Logicam, & Mathematicam: vt distinguit Toletus, in proœmio huius operis, q. 2. quia si resolutio certa sit, per veras demonstrationes fieri debet. Omnis autem resolutio facta per demonstrationes, est logica: quia ad solam logicam pertinet eam docere. Quocirca solùm potest appellari Mathematica, in quantum ad hanc scientiam applicatur, sicut etiam potest appellari Physica aut Metaphysica, vt applicatur ad has scientias. Nam licèt omnis scientia resoluat suas conclusiones, & demonstrationes, vsque ad prima principia, tamen modum resoluendi per veras demonstrationes, à Dialectica accipit, cuius proprium est id docere.

From which it follows that the resolution of reason is not to be distinguished into Logical and Mathematical, as Toledo distinguishes it in the proem of this work, q. 2: because if the resolution is to be certain, it must be made through true demonstrations. But every resolution made through demonstrations is logical, because it pertains to Logic alone to teach it. Wherefore it can be called Mathematical only insofar as it is applied to that science, just as it can also be called Physical or Metaphysical as it is applied to those sciences. For although every science resolves its conclusions and demonstrations back to first principles, yet it receives the mode of resolving through true demonstrations from Dialectic, to which it properly belongs to teach it.

Explicatur quem locum obtinere debeat opus hoc inter cæteras partes Dialecticæ — It is explained what place this work ought to hold among the other parts of Dialectic.

QVidam (vt Villalpandeus) in proœmio lib. de priori resolutione, asserunt, vnum, & eundem, tractatum componi, ex libris priorum, & posteriorum: & ideo eundem locum esse concedendum

Some (as Villalpando, in the proem to the book on the Prior Resolution) assert that one and the same treatise is composed of the books of the Prior and the Posterior Analytics; and therefore that the same place must be granted

p. 593

his lib. & illis. Alij verò, vt Philoponus, & Auicenna, Distinctum tractatum esse dicunt, tamen libros Topicorum collocant immediatè, post lib. Priorum: hoc verò opus statim post lib. Topicorum.

to these books and to those. Others, however, as John Philoponus and Avicenna, say that it is a distinct treatise, yet they place the books of the Topics immediately after the books of the Prior Analytics, and this work immediately after the books of the Topics.

Verùm communis sententia, duo asserit. Primum: Opus hoc distinctum esse à lib. priorum. Quia in eo agitur de syllogismo, secundùm formam specialem, in lib. verò priorum, de eodem, secundùm formam communem tractatur, & considerationes istę diuersæ sunt, ideo ad distinctos pertinent tractatus. Secundum: Hos libros immediatè post libros priorum, & ante libros topicorum, & Elenchorum esse collocandos: ita D. Tho. in proœmio huius operis, Alber. Mag. 1. Posteriorum, tract. 1. Caiet, Sotus, Louanien. Tolet. Marc. & moderni omnes, in hoc proœmio: & ratio est manifesta: Quia in libris priorum, agitur de syllogismo in genere, sub qua consideratione prior est, quàm secundùm suas species de quibus agitur in cæteris libris: ergo libris priorum, debetur primus locus, respectu aliorum, in quibus agitur de syllogismo; sed inter species syllogismi, perfectissima est demonstratio (de qua agit hoc opus) & ex consequenti prima: ergo statim post lib. priorum collocari debet.

But the common opinion asserts two things. First: That this work is distinct from the books of the Prior Analytics. Because in it the syllogism is treated according to the special form, but in the books of the Prior Analytics the same is treated according to the common form; and these considerations are diverse, and therefore they belong to distinct treatises. Second: That these books are to be placed immediately after the books of the Prior Analytics, and before the books of the Topics and the Sophistical Refutations. So St. Thomas in the proem of this work; Albert the Great, Posterior Analytics 1, tract. 1; Cajetan, Soto, the Louvain commentators, Toledo, Marc., and all the moderns, in this proem. And the reason is manifest: Because in the books of the Prior Analytics the syllogism is treated in general, under which consideration it is prior to its being treated according to its species, which are treated in the other books: therefore the first place, with respect to the others in which the syllogism is treated, is owed to the books of the Prior Analytics. But among the species of syllogism the most perfect is demonstration (of which this work treats), and consequently the first: therefore it ought to be placed immediately after the books of the Prior Analytics.

Quare dicatur iudicatiua hæc pars posterioristica, pars verò topica inuentiua — Why this posterioristic part is called judicative, but the topical part inventive.

SEd quæri tandem solet in hoc proœmio, Quare hæc pars Dialecticæ dicatur Iudicatiua? Cui omissis aliis opinionibus, Respondeo, ex doctrina D. Tho. in hoc proœmio posita, rationem rei huius esse: quia iudicium intellectus factum de veritate rei, est quædam sententia: & perfectum iudicium, non quæcunque sententia ab intellectu prolata, sed firma, atque certa: firmam autem, & certam sententiam, non potest ferre intellectus, nisi firmiter, & certò adhæreat alteri parti contradictionis. Hoc autem consequitur per demonstrationem: cuius non solùm præmissæ, sed etiam conclusio ex eis deducta, certa atque euidens est: vt docuit Arist. lib. 2. ca. 1. dicens: Oportet scientem simpliciter à credulitate: impermutabilem esse. Meritò ergo dicicitur, hæc pars posterioristica iudicatiua: quia in ea docetur modus certum iudicium ferendi, de veritate propositionum: quod perfectissimum quid est. Pars verò Topica, non vocatur iudicatiua, quia per syllogismum Topicum, non fertur iudicium certum de conclusione, sed probabile tantùm. Inuentiua verò dicitur, quia ad inuentionem (vt bene D. Thom. inquit) non requiritur certitudo: quamuis loca ipsa inuenta, per certam

But finally it is customarily asked in this proem: Why this part of Dialectic is called Judicative? To which, other opinions being omitted, I reply, from the doctrine of St. Thomas set down in this proem, that the reason of the matter is this: because the judgment of the intellect made about the truth of a thing is a certain sentence; and a perfect judgment is not any sentence whatever pronounced by the intellect, but a firm and certain one. But the intellect cannot pass a firm and certain sentence unless it adheres firmly and certainly to one part of a contradiction. And this it attains through demonstration, of which not only the premises but also the conclusion deduced from them is certain and evident, as Aristotle taught in bk. 2, ch. 1, saying: He who knows simply must be immovable from belief. Rightly, therefore, is this posterioristic part called judicative: because in it is taught the mode of passing certain judgment on the truth of propositions, which is something most perfect. But the Topical part is not called judicative, because through the Topical syllogism certain judgment is not passed on the conclusion, but only probable judgment. It is called inventive, however, because for invention (as St. Thomas well says) certitude is not required: although the places themselves, once found, by certain Pp

p. 594

demonstrationem probentur in parte Topica in quantum pars est logicæ docentis. Per Topicam quoque eadem logica docet, in cæteris scientiis, loca adinuenire, ad eruenda argumenta probabilia. Itaque quælibet pars Dialecticæ, habet aliquid inuentionis, & aliquid etiam iudicij. Sed iudicare, quasi per ἀντωνομασίαν conuenit huic operi posterioristico, cæteris verò per participationem eius, & inuenire loca argumentorum probabilium, eodem modo conuenit parti Topicæ, & cæteris ex eius participatione. Ideo pars posterioristica, vocatur Iudicatiua, Topica verò Inuentiua: quia ab eo, quod participale est, vel principaliùs conuenit, finitur appellatio.

demonstration, are proved in the Topical part insofar as it is a part of logica docens. Through the Topics, too, the same Logic teaches how to find places in the other sciences for drawing out probable arguments. Thus each part of Dialectic has something of invention and also something of judgment. But to judge belongs as it were by antonomasia to this posterioristic work, and to the others by participation in it; and to find the places of probable arguments belongs in the same way to the Topical part, and to the others by participation in it. Therefore the posterioristic part is called Judicative, but the Topical Inventive: because the name is determined from that which is principal, or belongs more principally.

Modus procedendi, & diuisio totius operis — The mode of proceeding, and the division of the whole work.

19 CIrca modum procedendi: An definiendo ac diuidendo procedat Arist. vel etiam demonstrando, non omnes conueniunt. Sed Venetus ca. 1. huius operis, affirmat, diuisionibus, ac definitionibus, vti Arist. in discursu huius operis, non demonstrationibus: quod probari potest testimonio Arist. qui in 2. c. 1. lib. duplici definitione definit demonstrationem. Et etiam hoc arg. Arist. in hoc opere, agit de demonstratione: ergo non procedit demonstrando. Probatur consequentia, quia si per demonstrationes procederet, daretur processus in infinitum: & idem probaretur per seipsum. Probatur consequentia, quia si per demonstrationem probaretur natura demonstrationis: ergo natura illius demonstrationis: qua vteretur, esset probanda per aliam demonstrationem, & ita in infinitum. Et si per demonstrationem probatur natura demonstrationis, illa eadem demonstratio, per quam probaretur, seipsam probaret, cùm sit vera demonstratio: vel ignotum per ignotius: cùm ante demonstrationem, per quam probatur natura demonstrationis, non sit illa demonstratio cognita.

19 Concerning the mode of proceeding, whether Aristotle proceeds by defining and dividing, or also by demonstrating, not all agree. But Paul of Venice, in ch. 1 of this work, affirms that in the course of this work Aristotle uses divisions and definitions, not demonstrations; which can be proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who in ch. 2 of bk. 1 defines demonstration with a twofold definition. And also by this argument: Aristotle in this work treats of demonstration; therefore he does not proceed by demonstrating. The consequence is proved: because if he proceeded through demonstrations, there would be a process to infinity, and the same thing would be proved through itself. The consequence is proved: because if the nature of demonstration were proved through demonstration, then the nature of that demonstration which he would use would have to be proved through another demonstration, and so to infinity. And if the nature of demonstration is proved through demonstration, that same demonstration through which it would be proved would prove itself, since it is a true demonstration; or the unknown would be proved through the more unknown, since before the demonstration through which the nature of demonstration is proved, that demonstration is not known.

20 Duo tamen dicenda sunt in hac re. Primò: Omnem scientiam, aut omnem partem scientiæ, vt plurimùm procedere definiendo. Quia necesse est proprium obiectum in principio definire, vt definitio eius assumi possit, tanquam medium ad probandas passiones de illo: & ideo in hoc opere non sic procedit Aristot. demonstrando, quin etiam procedat definiendo. Secudò dicendum est. Proprium modum procedendi huius operis, esse per demonstrationem, vt in 2. & 10. cap. pluribusquę aliis ostenditur, in quibus demonstrationibus vtitur Aristo. ad ostendendam naturam demonstrationis, & proprietates eius, & de hoc

20 Two things, however, must be said on this matter. First: That every science, or every part of a science, for the most part proceeds by defining. Because it is necessary to define the proper object at the beginning, so that its definition can be assumed as the middle for proving attributes of it; and therefore in this work Aristotle does not so proceed by demonstrating that he does not also proceed by defining. Second, it must be said: That the proper mode of proceeding of this work is through demonstration, as is shown in chs. 2 and 10 and in many others, in which Aristotle uses demonstrations to show the nature of demonstration and its properties; and concerning this

p. 595

nemo potest dubitare. Ad argum. verò: negandum est inconuenientia illa sequi: nam assignata prius definitione demonstrationis, iam per illam cognoscitur natura cuiuscunque demonstrationis: etiam illius, quæ postea adducitur ad probandum aliquid de demonstratione. Nec tamen demonstratio, quæ adducitur: indiget alia, per quam probetur: sed seipsam probat, diuersa ratione: quia in quantum conuenit cum cæteris demonstrationibus, in natura communi demonstrationis, explicata per definitionem, est id, de quo aliquid probatur: & in quantum est medium, per quod probatur, est id, quo aliquid de natura eadem communi probatur: non verò de qua id probatur. Diuersa autem ratione esse id, de quo aliquid probatur, & id, quo illud idem probatur, non est inconueniens: quia definitio, per quam explicatur natura communis definitionis, seipsam explicat diuersa ratione, vt notum est.

no one can doubt. To the argument, however: it must be denied that those inconveniences follow. For once the definition of demonstration has first been assigned, the nature of any demonstration whatever is already known through it, even of that which is afterwards adduced to prove something about demonstration. Nor yet does the demonstration that is adduced need another through which it is proved; rather it proves itself under a diverse ratio: because insofar as it agrees with the other demonstrations in the common nature of demonstration, explained through the definition, it is that of which something is proved; and insofar as it is the middle through which something is proved, it is that by which something is proved of that same common nature, but not that of which it is proved. And to be, under a diverse ratio, that of which something is proved and that by which that same thing is proved is not inconvenient: because the definition through which the common nature of definition is explained explains itself under a diverse ratio, as is well known.

Generalis diuisio totius operis est in duos libros: In quorum Primo, de natura demonstrationis, & partibus eius agit Arist. In Secundo: De modo constituendi definitionem: quæ potissimum medium est eiusdem demonstrationis: particularis autem diuisio, cuiuscunque libri, suis locis designabitur.

The general division of the whole work is into two books. In the First of these Aristotle treats of the nature of demonstration and its parts. In the Second: Of the mode of constituting a definition, which is the chief middle of that same demonstration. The particular division of each book will be indicated in its own place.

CHAPTER I

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Omnis doctrina, omnisque disciplina intellectiua, ex præexistenti si cognitione, &c.

All doctrine and all intellective discipline comes about from pre-existing cognition, etc.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

PRimus hic liber, de posteriori resolutione, in tres partes diuiditur. In prima, docet Arist. Demonstrationem esse. In secunda: Quid sit demonstratio, & quibus partibus constet. In tertia: Qualis sit, hoc est, quas habeat passiones, aut proprietates.

his first book, on the Posterior Resolution, is divided into three T parts. In the first Aristotle teaches That demonstration exists. In the second: What demonstration is, and of what parts it consists. In the third: Of what sort it is, that is, what attributes or properties it has.

Intentum huius capitis, Quòd actualis rerum notitia, atque scientia, verè sit in nobis: & ex alia notitia priori generetur. Habet autem duas partes, in quarum prima, tradit Arist. vniuersalem quandam propositionem, prædictam veritatem continentem: eamque probat in omni genere intellectualis cognitionis. In secunda quot, & quæ sint præcognitiones, & de quibus habeantur.

The intent of this chapter is: That actual cognition of things, and science, truly exists in us, and is generated from another, prior cognition. It has two parts: in the first of which Aristotle delivers a certain universal proposition containing the aforesaid truth, and proves it in every kind of intellectual cognition. In the second, how many and which are the precognitions, and about what they are had. Pp ij

p. 596

Duo versabantur errores in scholis tempore Arist. circa acquisitionem scientiæ. Primus, Heracliti, & Cratylli antiquorum Philosophorum: qui non distinguentes notitiam intellectiuam à sensitiua, nec putantes aliquid esse in rebus vniuersale, sed solùm singularia sensibilia, quæ in continuo motu, & fluxu sunt consequenter asserebant, nec dari scientiam de rebus, nec dari posse: quia scientia si esset possibilis, de vniuersalibus, atque perpetuis deberet esse.

Two errors were current in the schools in Aristotle’s time concerning the acquisition of science. The first was that of Heraclitus and Cratylus, ancient Philosophers, who, not distinguishing intellective cognition from sensitive, and not thinking that anything universal exists in things, but only sensible singulars, which are in continual motion and flux, consequently asserted that there neither is science of things nor can there be, because science, if it were possible, would have to be of universal and perpetual things.

2 Secundus error, fuit Platonis, vt testatur idem Arist. 1. & 7. lib. Meta. concedentis quidem scientiam, non tamen de nouo acquisitam, sed à principio habitam, hoc modo: vt dum materia, ex qua generatur homo, disponitur ab agente naturali, statim per impressionem, atque virtutem ideæ hominis separatæ, infundatur anima, plena speciebus rerum omnium: per quas posset scire omnia: solùm quod non exeat in actum cognoscendi, propter impedimentum corporis, & quasi ligamentum sensuum, quousque tale impedimentum exercitatione tollatur: quo sublato cognoscere incipiat anima, non ea, quæ priùs ignorabat, sed quæ à principio cognouerat: impedita tamen fuerat ab actuali consideratione eorum: & ideo se habuit, ac si obliuioni tradidisset, quæ priùs cognouerat: Vnde inferebat Plato, Scire nostrum esse, quasi reminiscentiam quandam eorum, quæ prius cognouimus. Quod hoc argum. probabat, in quodam dialogo de scientia, & virtute qui vocatur Menon, à Menone persona quadam eiusdem appellationis in eo introducta. Dum homo vult aliquid scire: aut scire vult, id quod iam sciebat, vel quod nesciebat: primum est impossibile, quia nemo scire vult ea, quæ iam cognoscit. Nec minùs impossibile est secundum, quòd scire velit id quod ignorat: nam sicut frustra aliquis quęreret hominem, quem non nouit: quia etiam si illum inueniat, cognoscere non poterit: ita frustra quæreret aliquis scientiam eius, quod non cognouit, quia non poterit illud cognoscere, etiam si ei sese offerat. Necesse est ergo dicere, quòd ea velimus scire, quæ priùs cognoscebamus: sed quasi obliuioni tradidimus: & ideo non de nouo, sed quasi per quandam reminiscentiam illud modò cognoscimus.

2 The second error was that of Plato, as the same Aristotle testifies in Metaph. 1 and 7, who granted science, yet not newly acquired, but possessed from the beginning, in this way: that when the matter out of which a man is generated is disposed by the natural agent, immediately, through the impression and power of the separated idea of man, a soul is infused full of the species of all things, through which it could know all things; only that it does not go out into the act of cognizing, on account of the impediment of the body and as it were the binding of the senses, until such impediment is removed by exercise; and once this is removed, the soul begins to cognize, not the things of which it was previously ignorant, but those which it had cognized from the beginning, though it had been impeded from the actual consideration of them; and therefore it was as if it had consigned to oblivion what it had previously cognized. Hence Plato inferred that our knowing is as it were a certain reminiscence of the things which we previously cognized. Which he proved by this argument in a certain dialogue on science and virtue which is called Meno, from a certain person of the same name, Meno, introduced in it. When a man wishes to know something, either he wishes to know what he already knew, or what he did not know. The first is impossible, because no one wishes to know the things he already cognizes. Nor is the second less impossible, that he should wish to know what he is ignorant of: for just as someone would seek in vain a man whom he did not know, because even if he found him he could not recognize him, so someone would seek in vain the science of what he has not cognized, because he will not be able to cognize it even if it offers itself to him. It must be said, therefore, that we wish to know the things which we previously cognized but have as it were consigned to oblivion; and therefore we cognize it now not anew, but as it were through a certain reminiscence.

3 Aduersus hos duos errores, proponit Arist. hanc propositionem vniuersalem: Omnis doctrina, omnisque disciplina, intellectiua, ex præexistenti fit cognitione. Cuius sensus est: Omne iudicium intellectus, non ex sola notitia terminorum habitũ, sed aliquo medio, aut ratiocinatione acquisitum, siue propria industria, aut labore, ita vt doctrina appelletur: siue à magistro acceptum: & ideo disciplina vocatum, fit, hoc est, verè datur

3 Against these two errors Aristotle proposes this universal proposition: All doctrine and all intellective discipline comes about from pre-existing cognition. Whose sense is: Every judgment of the intellect that is had not from the sole cognition of the terms, but is acquired by some middle or reasoning, whether by one’s own industry or labor, so that it is called doctrine, or received from a master, and therefore called discipline, comes about, that is, is truly given

p. 597

aduersus Heraclitum, & fit de nouo: ita vt res per illud cognita, non fuerit cognita priùs, sed simpliciter ignorata, aduersus Platonem. Hanc veritatem vniuersalem, probat Arist. in triplici genere cognitionis. In scientifica quidem certissima qualis est ea quæ habetur, per Mathematicas disciplinas: in quibus euidens est, iudicium ac notitiam conclusionis fieri, ex notitia præmissarum priùs habita. Et eodem modo in cæteris Artibus non solùm liberalibus, sed etiam mechanicis: in quibus vnum semper cognoscitur, ex notitia alterius priùs habita, quousque perueniatur ad primum principium illius artis, non per aliud, sed per se notum, hoc est, ex sola notitia terminorum. Probat deinde in cognitione probabili, quę habetur per syllogismum Dialecticum, cuius conclusio cognoscitur ex notitia probabili præmissarum, vel euidenti, per consequentiam probabilem, aut per inductionem: in qua, ex notitia singularium, fit experimentum, quod est iudicium vniuersale. Probat tandem in Rhetoricis argumentationibus, quæ sunt Enthymema, & exemplum: nam Enthymema, est quasi syllogismus truncatus, cui deficit maior vel minor, subintellecta tamen ab arguente: & iudicium conclusionis, fit ex iudicio alterius præmissæ priùs habito. Exemplum verò procedit, ex vno singulari ad aliud, per similitudinem: & ideò notitia vnius habetur, ex notitia alterius prius habita.

(against Heraclitus) and comes about anew, so that the thing cognized through it was not cognized before but was simply unknown (against Plato). This universal truth Aristotle proves in a threefold kind of cognition. In scientific cognition, indeed the most certain, such as is that which is had through the Mathematical disciplines, in which it is evident that the judgment and cognition of the conclusion comes about from the cognition of the premises previously had. And in the same way in the other Arts, not only the liberal but also the mechanical, in which one thing is always cognized from the cognition of another previously had, until one arrives at the first principle of that art, known not through another but through itself, that is, from the sole cognition of the terms. He proves it next in probable cognition, which is had through the Dialectical syllogism, whose conclusion is cognized from the probable or evident cognition of the premises through a probable consequence, or through induction, in which from the cognition of singulars there comes about experience, which is a universal judgment. He proves it finally in the Rhetorical argumentations, which are the Enthymeme and the example: for the Enthymeme is as it were a truncated syllogism, which lacks the major or the minor, which is nevertheless understood by the one arguing; and the judgment of the conclusion comes about from the judgment of the other premise previously had. The example, however, proceeds from one singular to another through likeness, and therefore the cognition of the one is had from the cognition of the other previously had.

4 In secunda part. cap. agit Arist. de Præcognoscendis, & Præcognitis. Nam si notitia conclusionis debet fieri, ex præexistenti cognitione, necesse est explicare, quæ, & quot sint præcognoscenda, & de quibus: vt ex eis haberi possit notitia conclusionis: Duo ait esse præcognoscenda, aut duas esse præcognitiones ad notitiam conclusionis necessarias, An sit, & Quid sit. Tria autem esse de quibus habendæ sunt præcognitiones, nempe, Subiectum, Passio, & Principium, & hæc appellantur præcognita. Subiectum, est illud, de quo est scientia, vel scientifica conclusio. Principia, sunt pręmissæ demonstrationis. ex quibus infertur conclusio. Passio est, quæ demonstratur de subiecto in conclusione. Exempla ponit Arist. in Mathematicis disciplinis: sed nos ea afferemus in rebus nobis notioribus hoc modo: Vt habeamus euidentem notitiam huius conclusionis: Omnis homo est risibilis, necesse est, duo præcognoscamus, An sit, & quid sit: & de tribus quidem, nempe, de subiecto, circa quod versatur conclusio, quod est homo: de principiis, quæ sunt præmissæ istæ, per quas demonstratur, nempe, Omne animal rationale est risibile: & omnis homo est animal rationale: & de passione demonstrata de illo, quæ est risibilitas,

4 In the second part of the chapter Aristotle treats of the things to be precognized and the things precognized. For if the cognition of the conclusion must come about from pre-existing cognition, it is necessary to explain what and how many are the things to be precognized, and about what, so that from them the cognition of the conclusion can be had. He says that two things are to be precognized, or that two precognitions are necessary for the cognition of the conclusion: Whether it is, and What it is. But that there are three things about which precognitions are to be had, namely the Subject, the Attribute, and the Principle; and these are called the things precognized. The subject is that of which there is science, or the scientific conclusion. The principles are the premises of the demonstration, from which the conclusion is inferred. The attribute is what is demonstrated of the subject in the conclusion.
