Aristotle gives examples in the Mathematical disciplines, but we shall bring them forward in things better known to us, in this way: In order that we may have evident cognition of this conclusion, Every man is risible, it is necessary that we precognize two things, Whether it is and What it is; and about three things, namely about the subject concerning which the conclusion is occupied, which is man; about the principles, which are those premises through which it is demonstrated, namely, Every rational animal is risible, and every man is a rational animal; and about the attribute demonstrated of it, which is risibility, Pp iij

p. 598

Non est tamen habenda vtraque præcognitio de singulis: sed de subiecto tantùm: de principiis verò, prima, nempe, an sint, hoc est, an sint vera: de passione verò, secundum, nempe, quid sit, hoc est, quid nomen significet: nam quòd sit, probatur in conclusione: id est, quòd insit subiecto: quia cùm sit accidens, non habet aliud esse, quàm subiecto inesse.

Yet both precognitions are not to be had of each one, but only of the subject; of the principles, the first, namely whether they are, that is, whether they are true; of the attribute, the second, namely what it is, that is, what the name signifies: for that it is is proved in the conclusion, that is, that it inheres in the subject; because, since it is an accident, it has no other being than to inhere in the subject.

5 His explicatis, respondet Arist. in fine cap. ad arg. Platonis. Distinguendo maiorem: nam dum interrogatur: An qui vult scire aliquid, velit scire, quod sciebat priùs, vel quod ignorabat: Respondendum esse ait, non velle scire, quod simpliciter sciebat: nec quod omnino ignorabat: sed quod ignorabat formaliter, atque simpliciter, sciebat tamen virtualiter, & secundùm quid, hoc est: non in se, sed in alio priùs cognito: in quo virtualiter continetur. Gratia exempli, dum volo scire, An homo sit capax disciplinæ: volo scire, id quod non sciebam actu, & formaliter, sed solùm virtualiter, in illis duabus præmissis priùs cognitis: Omne animal rationale est capax disciplinæ, &, omnis homo est animal rationale: in quibus notitia eius virtualiter continetur: & ideo dum infertur in eis, cognosci potest: quia non prorsus ignorabatur, sed virtualiter saltem cognoscebatur: & per illationem, cognoscitur formaliter.

5 These things explained, Aristotle replies at the end of the chapter to the argument of Plato by distinguishing the major. For when it is asked whether he who wishes to know something wishes to know what he knew before or what he was ignorant of, he says it must be replied that he does not wish to know what he knew simply, nor what he was altogether ignorant of, but what he was ignorant of formally and simply, yet knew virtually and in a certain respect, that is, not in itself, but in another thing previously cognized, in which it is virtually contained. For example, when I wish to know whether man is capable of learning, I wish to know what I did not know actually and formally, but only virtually, in those two premises previously cognized: Every rational animal is capable of learning, and every man is a rational animal, in which its cognition is virtually contained; and therefore, when it is inferred in them, it can be cognized: because it was not altogether unknown, but was at least virtually cognized; and through the inference it is cognized formally.

QUESTION I

An de omni, & sola cognitione intellectiua, intelligatur vniuersalis propositio Aristotelis.

Whether Aristotle’s universal proposition is understood of all and only intellective cognition.

6 PRiùs quàm diuersas sententias proponamus, paucis explicanda est propositio Aristot. In qua per doctrinam, & disciplinam, idem assensus intellectus significatur: qui, vt propria industria acquiritur, vel, vt à magistro procedit, doctrina dicitur: vt verò à discipulo acceptus, disciplina. Deinde per cognitionem intellectiuam, non quodlibet iudicium intellectus significatur, sed illud solùm, quod per aliquod medium, vel ratiocinationem habetur: nam si ex sola cognitione terminorum habeatur, certum est non fieri ex alio iudicio intellectus: quamuis fiat ex notitia apprehensiua terminorum, & significationis eorum. Alioqui, si ex alio iudicio fieret, daretur processus in infinitum. Sensus igitur propositionis est, Omne iudicium intellectus, per aliquod medium, vel ratiocinationem habitum, fit ex alio, habito etiam

6 Before we propose the various opinions, Aristotle’s proposition must be explained in a few words. In it, by doctrine and discipline the same intellectual assent is signified, which, as it is acquired by one’s own industry or as it proceeds from a master, is called doctrine, but as received by the disciple, discipline. Next, by intellective cognition not just any judgment of the intellect is signified, but only that which is had through some middle or reasoning: for if it is had from the sole cognition of the terms, it is certain that it does not come about from another judgment of the intellect, although it comes about from the apprehensive cognition of the terms and of their signification. Otherwise, if it came about from another judgment, there would be a process to infinity. The sense of the proposition, therefore, is: Every judgment of the intellect had through some middle or reasoning comes about from another, also had

p. 599

per ratiocinationem, vel ex sola notitia terminorum: ita vt tandem ad aliud per se notum, aut sine medio habitum reducatur. Iste est sensus propositionis, de qua inquiritur, An de omni, & sola cognitione intellectiua accipiatur, & an vera sit.

through reasoning, or from the sole cognition of the terms, so that it is finally reduced to another known per se, or had without a middle. This is the sense of the proposition about which it is inquired whether it is to be taken of all and only intellective cognition, and whether it is true.

Et prima opinio tenet, Non solùm in scientiis, sed etiam in opinione, & fide humana verum esse, ac de eis intelligi, & ex consequenti, ex omni iudicio intellectus, per medium habito. Ita Sotus q. 1. huius ca. in solutione ad primam confirmationem 2. arg. probat id: Quia vtraque generatur ex aliquo principio euidenti, per probabilem, aut ineuidentem consequentiam: opinio quidem, dum sic argumentamur: Corpus sphęricum, aut perfectè rotundum, tãgit aliud corpus perfectè planum in puncto: ergo datur punctum indiuisibile. Fides etiam humana, dum dicimus, Homini fide digno credendum est: ergo vera sunt, quæ ab hoc homine, fide digno, dicuntur.

And the first opinion holds that it is true and is understood not only of the sciences, but also of opinion and human faith, and consequently of every judgment of the intellect had through a middle. So Soto, q. 1 of this chapter, in the solution to the first confirmation of the 2nd argument. He proves it: Because both are generated from some evident principle through a probable or inevident consequence: opinion, indeed, when we argue thus: A spherical, or perfectly round, body touches another perfectly plane body at a point; therefore there is an indivisible point. Human faith also, when we say: A man worthy of faith is to be believed; therefore the things said by this man, worthy of faith, are true.

Secunda opinio asserit, Non solùm ad scientias humanas, sed etiam ad scientiam angelorum se extendere, & in ea veram esse. Ita moderni quidam: qui hanc sententiam ita probant: Quia Angelus cognoscit effectum per causam: vt quòd homo sit risibilis: quia est rationalis: & cognitio causæ, est prior cognitione effectus, sicut causa est prior effectu: ergo cognitio effectus fit in eo, ex præexistenti cognitione causæ. Præterea Angeli inferiores illuminantur à superioribus: & illuminatio non videtur esse aliud quàm manifestatio veritatis, quam superior cognoscit, & ignorat inferior: ergo cognitio inferioris angeli, fit ex præexistenti cognitione superioris.

The second opinion asserts that it extends not only to the human sciences but also to the science of the angels, and that it is true in it. So certain moderns, who prove this view thus: Because an angel cognizes the effect through the cause, as that man is risible because he is rational; and the cognition of the cause is prior to the cognition of the effect, just as the cause is prior to the effect: therefore the cognition of the effect comes about in him from pre-existing cognition of the cause. Moreover, inferior angels are illuminated by superior ones; and illumination does not seem to be anything other than the manifestation of a truth which the superior cognizes and the inferior is ignorant of: therefore the cognition of the inferior angel comes about from the pre-existing cognition of the superior.

8 Nostra sententia, & communis omnium ferè expositorum Arist. in hoc capite, his conclusionibus explicatur. Prima: Non intelligitur propositio Arist. de scientia angelorum, nec in ea potest habere veritatem. Vt hanc explicemus, atque probemus simul, notandum est: Aliud esse cognoscere, quàm vnum sit ab alio, aut ex alio, vel propter aliud: & aliud habere cognitionem vnius, ex cognitione alterius: nam primum: non dicit distinctam cognitionem vtriusque, nec vllam imperfectionem ex parte cognoscentis, sed per vnam & eandem cognitionem, potest vtrumque cognosci, cum illo ordine, aut dependentia, quam secundùm se habent: & ita cognoscuntur à Deo, & ab angelis, causa, & effectus quicunque. Ita, vt per vnam simplicem cognitionem, vtrumque cognoscant: & quàm vnum habet esse ab alio: sic etiam cognoscũt essentiam quamcunque & omnes passiones ab ea procedẽtes. Habere autem cognitionem vnius ex cognitione alterius, dicit distinctionem cognitionum, & causalitatem, non solùm inter obiecta cognita,

8 Our view, and the common view of almost all the expositors of Aristotle on this chapter, is explained by these conclusions. First: Aristotle’s proposition is not understood of the science of the angels, nor can it have truth in it. In order to explain and at the same time prove this, it should be noted: That it is one thing to cognize how one thing is from another, or out of another, or on account of another; and another thing to have cognition of one thing from the cognition of another. For the first does not imply a distinct cognition of each, nor any imperfection on the part of the one cognizing, but through one and the same cognition both can be cognized, with that order or dependence which they have according to themselves: and thus any cause and effect whatever are cognized by God and by the angels, so that through one simple cognition they cognize both, and how the one has being from the other; so too they cognize any essence and all the attributes proceeding from it. But to have cognition of one thing from the cognition of another implies a distinction of cognitions, and causality, not only between the objects cognized, Pp iiij

p. 600

sed etiam inter cognitiones ipsas, ita vt vna sit causa alterius in aliquo genere: & hæc est maxima imperfectio: quæ solùm reperitur in cognitione nostra discursitiua, per quam successiuè plura cognoscimus: & cognitio vnius sequitur post aliam, & fit ex alia, & hoc est fieri: ex præexistenti cognitione, vt asserit propositio Arist.

but also between the cognitions themselves, so that the one is the cause of the other in some genus; and this is the greatest imperfection, which is found only in our discursive cognition, through which we cognize several things successively, and the cognition of one follows after another and comes about from another; and this is to come about from pre-existing cognition, as Aristotle’s proposition asserts.

9 Ex hac ergo verissima doctrina probaturam, Nullum iudicium intellectus diuini, aut angelici, fieri ex præexistenti cognitione. Quod sic probo: Iudicium intellectus fieri ex pręexistenti cognitione dicit distinctionem cognitionum: quia eadem cognitio non dicitur fieri ex seipsa: sed Deus, & Angeli, non cognoscunt effectum, & causam distinctis cognitionibus: ergo cognitio effectus in eis, non fit ex præexistenti cognitione causæ.

9 From this most true doctrine, then, it is proved that no judgment of the divine or angelic intellect comes about from pre-existing cognition. Which I prove thus: For a judgment of the intellect to come about from pre-existing cognition implies a distinction of cognitions, because the same cognition is not said to come about from itself; but God and the angels do not cognize the effect and the cause by distinct cognitions: therefore the cognition of the effect in them does not come about from pre-existing cognition of the cause.

Quod verò dicitur, Angelum cognoscere effectum per causam, Distinguendum est, nam ex parte rei cognitæ, verum est, quia verè cognoscit Angelus, effectum habere esse à causa, & propter eam esse: sed ex parte cognitionis, non est verum: quia cùm cognitio causæ, & effectus sit eadem, non est verum, quòd cognitio vnius fiat ex cognitione alterius: hoc enim distinctionem cognitionum dicit, quæ non reperitur in Deo, nec in angelis, respectu causæ, & effectus. Et quod de scientia Angelorum dicimus, eodem modo intelligendum est, de scientia infusa primi Parẽtis, quam habuit à principio, quo factus est à Deo.

As for what is said, that an angel cognizes the effect through the cause, a distinction must be made: for on the part of the thing cognized it is true, because the angel truly cognizes that the effect has being from the cause and is on account of it; but on the part of the cognition it is not true: because, since the cognition of the cause and of the effect is the same, it is not true that the cognition of the one comes about from the cognition of the other; for this implies a distinction of cognitions, which is not found in God, nor in the angels, with respect to cause and effect. And what we say of the science of the angels is to be understood in the same way of the infused science of our first Parent, which he had from the beginning, in which he was made by God.

10 De illuminatione verò, Concedimus, quòd cognitio inferioris angeli, fiat ex præexistenti cognitione superioris, propositio tamen Aristot. intelligitur in eodem intellectu, non in diuersis.

10 As to illumination, however, we concede that the cognition of the inferior angel comes about from the pre-existing cognition of the superior; yet Aristotle’s proposition is understood in the same intellect, not in diverse ones.

Secunda conclusio: In opinionibus non semper est verum, quòd vna cognitio fiat ex alia, vt asserit prima opinio: sed solùm ea quæ habetur per discursum. Probatur hæc Conclusio: Quia opinio nõ solùm habetur per discursum, ex propositione euidenti, sed dantur etiam opiniones per se notæ, hoc est, per se probabiles: sicut principia scientiarum per se euidentia: & in eis non habetur vna cognitio ex alia, sed ex sola notitia terminorum: vt hęc propositio, Mater diligit filium suum, per se est probabilis: & non quia colligitur ex alia, sed sola significatione terminorum habita, necessariò iudicat intellectus esse probabilẽ, ergo in his opinionibus, non fit cognitio ex præexistenti alia cognitione, verùm hoc ipsum ex professo explicabitur in ca. 26. huius lib.

Second conclusion: In opinions it is not always true that one cognition comes about from another, as the first opinion asserts, but only in those which are had through discursive reasoning. This conclusion is proved: Because opinion is not had only through discursive reasoning from an evident proposition, but there are also opinions known per se, that is, probable per se, just as the principles of the sciences are evident per se; and in them one cognition is not had from another, but from the sole cognition of the terms: as this proposition, A mother loves her son, is probable per se; and not because it is gathered from another, but, once the signification of the terms alone is had, the intellect necessarily judges it to be probable: therefore in these opinions cognition does not come about from another, pre-existing cognition. But this very point will be explained expressly in ch. 26 of this book.

11 Tertia conclusio: Assensus fidei humanæ, non fit ex præexistenti cognitione. Probatur hæc etiam, contra Sotum: Quia formalis, & proxima ratio assentiendi in fide, est testimonium fide digni

11 Third conclusion: The assent of human faith does not come about from pre-existing cognition. This too is proved, against Soto: Because the formal and proximate reason for assenting in faith is the testimony of one worthy of faith

p. 601

, per quam rationem distinguitur ab opinione. Huius enim assensus, vel habetur ex sola notitia terminorum, vel colligitur ex alio assensu euidenti, per consequentiam probabilem: ergo assensus fidei, non fit ex alio, nec per discursum, sed ex solo testimonio habetur sine discursu: quare non fit ex præexistenti cognitione. Et quod de fide humana dicimus, eodem modo intelligendum est, de fide diuina, & de reuelationibus Prophetarum.

by which ratio it is distinguished from opinion. For the assent of the latter is either had from the cognition of the terms alone, or gathered from another evident assent through a probable consequence; therefore the assent of faith does not come about from another, nor through discursive reasoning, but is had from testimony alone, without discourse: wherefore it does not come about from preexisting cognition. And what we say of human faith is to be understood in the same way of divine faith and of the revelations of the Prophets.

Ad arg. verò primæ opinionis: Respondeo, Assensum opinionis, habitum per illum discursum, fieri ex præexistenti cognitione, sed non omnem assensum opinionis, haberi discursum, vt probauimus: & ideo non semper fieri ex præexistenti cognitione. Quòd verò assensus fidei humanæ fiat per illum discursum negamus. Immediatè quippe habetur ex testimonio fide digni: alias si fieret per illum discursum, opinio esset, non fides humana.

But to the argument of the first opinion I reply that the assent of opinion had through that discursive reasoning comes about from preexisting cognition, but that not every assent of opinion is had by discursive reasoning, as we have proved; and therefore it does not always come about from preexisting cognition. But that the assent of human faith comes about through that discursive reasoning we deny. For it is had immediately from the testimony of one worthy of credence: otherwise, if it came about through that discursive reasoning, it would be opinion, not human faith.

Ex his tribus conclusionibus, sequitur, propositionem Aristotelis vniuersaliter esse veram, in omni scientia, humano more acquisita, & in opinione, quæ habetur per discursum tantùm. Et ideo sensum eius hunc esse, Omne iudicium intellectus, per discursum habitum, siue euidens sit, vel probabile fieri ex præexistenti aliquo iudicio intellectus, ex sola notitia terminorum habito: vel etiam per discursum, reducibili tamen ad iudicium aliud, ex sola notitia terminorum habendum.

From these three conclusions it follows that Aristotle’s proposition is universally true in every science acquired in the human manner, and in opinion which is had through discursive reasoning only. And therefore its sense is this: Every judgment of the intellect had through discursive reasoning, whether it be evident or probable, comes about from some preexisting judgment of the intellect had from the cognition of the terms alone; or also had through discursive reasoning, but reducible to another judgment to be had from the cognition of the terms alone.

QUESTION II

Quæst. 2. An de subiecto sit præsupponenda actualis existentia — Whether actual existence is to be presupposed of the subject.

An de subiecto sit præsupponenda actualis existentia.

[…]

12 DVas præcognitiones assignauit Arist. nempe, An res sit, & Quid sit, & vtraque habendam esse docuit de subiecto vel obiecto, circa quod versatur scientia, & huius ratio est manifesta: quia si subiectum non habet esse, neque habebit essentiam, aut quidditatem: & ideo nec proprias passiones: quæ de illo probentur in scientia. Nec denique habebit definitionem quidditatiuam, per quam probentur: quare si non sit, non poterit esse subiectum scientię. Esse autem, vt modò loquimur, non est aliud, quàm existentia in rerum natura. Sed hæc duobus modis habetur, Actu quidem, dum res existit extra suas causas: vel Potentia, dum non est extra illas, sed in virtute earum, à quibus produci potest. De existentia autem subiecti possibili, nemo dubitat, quin sit necessariò præsupponenda: quia si non possit vllo modo eam habere, reputabitur ens impossibile, sicut Chimæra: quare non poterit de illo haberi scientiam. Ideo solùm

11 Two precognitions were assigned by Aristotle, namely Whether the thing is and What it is, and he taught that both are to be had of the subject or object with which the science is concerned; and the reason for this is manifest: because if the subject does not have being, neither will it have an essence or quiddity, and therefore not proper attributes either, to be proved of it in the science. Nor, finally, will it have a quidditative definition through which they might be proved: wherefore, if it is not, it will not be able to be the subject of a science. Now being, as we are speaking now, is nothing other than existence in the nature of things. But this is had in two ways: In act, while the thing exists outside its causes; or In potency, while it is not outside them but in the power of those by which it can be produced. Concerning the possible existence of the subject, no one doubts that it must necessarily be presupposed: because if it could not have it in any way, it would be reputed an impossible being, like a Chimera; wherefore there could not be science of it. Therefore we inquire only

p. 602

quærimus de existentia actuali: An necesse sit de subiecto præcognoscere, quòd actu sit in rerum natura, vt de illo habeatur scientia, vel sufficiat præsupponere, quòd eam possit habere.

about actual existence: Whether it is necessary to know beforehand of the subject that it is in act in the nature of things, in order that science may be had of it, or whether it suffices to presuppose that it can have it.

13 Et prima opinio affirmat, Necessarium esse, quòd de subiecto præsupponatur actualis existentia: non quam semper habeat, sed saltem temporibus à natura statutis: vt de rosa, actu non existente, habetur scientia in hyeme: quia præcognoscimus illam habituram tempore veris. Si verò eam suo tempore non esset habitura, non posset de ea haberi scientia. Ita Caiet. c. præsenti, & Toletus, quæst. vnica ad 5.

13 And the first opinion affirms that it is necessary that actual existence be presupposed of the subject: not that it always have it, but at least at the times established by nature; as of the rose, though it does not actually exist, science is had in winter, because we know beforehand that it will have it in the time of spring. But if it were not going to have it in its own time, science could not be had of it. So Cajetan on the present chapter, and Toledo, the single question, ad 5.

Et probatur testimonio Aristo. id expressè asserentis, lib. 2. huius operis, textu. 8. his verbis: Quærere autem Quid est, non habentis Quod est, nihil est quærere. Quasi dicat, non esse quęrendam definitionem eius, quod non habet existentiam: quia non poterit conueniri: & ideo nec poterit esse obiectum scientiæ.

And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who expressly asserts it in bk. 1 of this work, text 8, in these words: But to ask What it is when one does not have That it is, is to ask nothing. As if to say that the definition of that which does not have existence is not to be sought, because it cannot be found; and therefore neither will it be able to be the object of a science.

Probatur etiam ratione: Quia ab eo quòd res est, vel non est, propositio dicitur vera, vel falsa: id est, ab eo, quòd actu existit: vel non existit: ergo actualis existentia subiecti temporibus saltem, quibus eam accipere potest à causis naturalibus, fundamentum est omnium veritatum, quæ de illo possunt cognosci in scientia: quare necessariò erit de illo præcognoscenda.

It is proved also by reason: because a proposition is said to be true or false from the fact that the thing is or is not, that is, from the fact that it actually exists or does not exist; therefore the actual existence of the subject, at least at the times at which it can receive it from natural causes, is the foundation of all the truths that can be known of it in a science: wherefore it will necessarily have to be known beforehand of it.

14 Secunda opinio est opposita, Quòd non sit necessariò præcognoscenda actualis existentia subiecti, temporibus etiam à natura statutis: sed licèt eam nunquam habeat, nec habiturum sit, posse haberi scientiam de illo, si præcognoscatur, quòd eam habere possit. Ita Sot. q. 1. de præcognitis, vbi docet, quod dum Arist. ait de subiecto præcognoscendum esse, An sit, hunc sensum tenet, id est, An sit verum ens, habens saltem esse possibile in suis causis.

14 The second opinion is the opposite: That the actual existence of the subject need not necessarily be known beforehand, even at the times established by nature; but that, although it never has it nor ever will have it, science can be had of it if it is known beforehand that it can have it. So Soto, q. 1 on the precognitions, where he teaches that when Aristotle says that it must be known beforehand of the subject Whether it is, this has the sense, that is, Whether it is a true being, having at least possible being in its causes.

Ratio huius sententiæ est: quia sufficit subiectum habere esse possibile in suis causis: vt veram habeat definitionem, verásque passiones: quæ de illo possint probari in scientia: ergo sufficit hoc de illo præcognoscere.

The reason for this opinion is: because it suffices for the subject to have possible being in its causes in order that it may have a true definition and true attributes which can be proved of it in a science; therefore it suffices to know this of it beforehand.

Nostra sententia duabus conclusionibus explicatur. Prima est: Intrinseca ratio scientiæ, non petit actualem existentiam subiecti, ideo non est necessariò præcognoscenda de illo, sed sufficit præcognoscere existentiam possibilem. Probatur hoc argum. Scientia ex propria natura est perpetua, & circa obiectum necessarium, & perpetuum debet versari: sed actualis existentia, nec semper cõuenit subiecto, nec necessariò, sed modo quodam contingenti, cùm passim res eam amittant, dum corrumpuntur: ergo non habetur scientia de subiecto, vt actu existente etiam statutis temporibus

Our view is explained by two conclusions. The first is: The intrinsic ratio of science does not require the actual existence of the subject; therefore it need not necessarily be known beforehand of it, but it suffices to know beforehand its possible existence. This is proved by an argument. Science by its own nature is perpetual, and must be concerned with a necessary and perpetual object; but actual existence belongs to the subject neither always nor necessarily, but in a certain contingent manner, since things everywhere lose it when they are corrupted: therefore science is not had of the subject as actually existing, even at the established times

p. 603

. Nec erit necessariò præcognoscenda actualis eius existentia, sed sufficiet præcognoscere possibilem. Hæc est contra Caiet.

Nor will its actual existence necessarily have to be known beforehand, but it will suffice to know beforehand its possible existence. This is against Cajetan.

15 Secunda conclusio, Vt habeatur scientia de aliquo subiecto à nobis, imperfectè cognoscentibus necesse est quòd habuerit aliquando actualem existentiam, non quocunque tempore à natura statuto, sed vel semel. Hæc ex parte est contra vtramque opinionem. Et probatur hac ratione: Imperfecta nostra cognitio habetur per sensus: ergo non possumus habere scientiam de aliquo obiecto, nisi per aliquem sensum illud percipiamus: sed sensus non percipiunt, nisi res actu existentes: ergo necesse est obiectum aliquando habuisse actualem existentem, vt notitia eius scientifica ad intellectum perueniat mediis sensibus. Quòd verò in temporibus à natura statutis, eam habeat, necessarium non est, cùm possit per eam, quam semel habuit, modo scientifico à nobis cognosci. Vtramque conclusionem nostram, tenet Ferrar. 1. lib. contra gentes, cap. 66.

15 The second conclusion: In order that science may be had of some subject by us who know imperfectly, it is necessary that it have had actual existence at some time; not at every time established by nature, but at least once. This is in part against both opinions. And it is proved by this reason: our imperfect cognition is had through the senses; therefore we cannot have science of any object unless we perceive it through some sense; but the senses perceive only things actually existing; therefore it is necessary that the object have at some time had actual existence, in order that the scientific cognition of it may reach the intellect by means of the senses. But that it should have it at the times established by nature is not necessary, since it can be known by us in a scientific manner through that existence which it once had. Both our conclusions are held by Ferrara, bk. 1 Contra Gentiles, ch. 66.

16 Testimonium verò Arist. pro sententia Caiet. adductum, de esse possibili intelligendum est: quod sufficit, vt quidditas eius inueniatur. Vel, si de actuali intelligitur, de modo quo à nobis acquiritur scientia, loquitur in eo Arist. non de scientia secundùm rationem intrinsecam.

16 But the testimony of Aristotle adduced for Cajetan’s opinion is to be understood of possible being, which suffices in order that its quiddity may be found. Or, if it is understood of actual being, Aristotle speaks in that passage of the mode in which science is acquired by us, not of science according to its intrinsic ratio.

Ad arg. verò eiusdem sententiæ, Distinguendum est antecedens: Nam ab eo, quòd res est, vel non est, id est ab eius existentia possibili accipitur veritas propositionis scientificæ: non ab actuali: & illa est fundamentum sufficiens veritatum totius scientiæ.

To the argument of the same opinion, the antecedent must be distinguished. For it is from the fact that the thing is or is not, that is, from its possible existence, that the truth of a scientific proposition is taken, not from its actual existence; and that possible existence is a sufficient foundation for the truths of the whole science.

Argu. verò pro sententia Soti, Concedendum est: quia solùm probat sufficere existentiam possibilem subiecti præcognoscere, ad intrinsecam rationem scientiæ: vt asserit prima conclusio nostra: sed ad imperfectum modum: quo eam nos communiter acquirimus, necessarium est, vt eam habuerit aliquando, & aliquando de illo fuisse præcognitam: vt probat conclusio secunda.

But the argument for Soto’s opinion is to be granted: because it proves only that it suffices to know beforehand the possible existence of the subject for the intrinsic ratio of science, as our first conclusion asserts; but for the imperfect mode in which we commonly acquire it, it is necessary that it have had existence at some time, and that it have at some time been known beforehand of it, as the second conclusion proves.

QUESTION III

An de subiecto præcognoscendum sit quid rei, vel solùm quid nominis.

Whether what the thing is, or only what the name is, must be known beforehand of the subject. 17

17 DVplex est definitio. Vna per quam explicatur essentia rei: & hæc vocatur definitio rei, vel quid rei: vt animal rationale. Alia est definitio, seu potiùs explicatio vocis: vt

Definition is twofold. One is that through which the essence of a thing is explained; and this is called the definition of the thing, or what the thing is, as rational animal. The other is the definition, or rather the explanation, of the word, as

p. 604

dum dicimus: magnanimum esse, magnum habentem animum: vel infinitum, quod non habet finem. Et hęc dicitur definitio nominis, vel quid nominis: quia quidditas nominis, videtur esse significatio eius, per eam explicata. Et hæc, non est dubium, quin sit necessariò præcognoscenda de subiecto scientiæ: nam si ignoremus, quid significet hæc vox, homo, non poterimus habere de illo veram aliquam notitiam, nec scientiam. Sed quæstio procedit de definitione, quid rei, aut quidditatiua subiecti: An sit necessariò præcognoscenda.

when we say: magnanimous is having a great soul; or infinite, that which has no end. And this is called the definition of the name, or what the name is, because the quiddity of a name seems to be its signification explained through it. And there is no doubt that this must necessarily be known beforehand of the subject of a science: for if we do not know what this word man signifies, we shall not be able to have any true cognition of him, nor science. But the question proceeds concerning the definition of what the thing is, or the quidditative definition of the subject: whether it must necessarily be known beforehand.

Et prima opinio asserit: Non esse necessariò præcognoscendam, sed sine eius notitia, posse haberi de re scientiam. Ita Tolet. vbi suprà probat hoc modo: Quia ad demonstrandum effectum per causam: non requiritur præcognoscere quid sit Causa, & quid effectus, sed solùm quòd effectus procedit per se à causa: ergo non requiritur præcognitio, quòd quid est. Vnde Astrologi demonstrant lunam eclipsari, per suam causam, ignorantes definitionem lunæ & cœlorum: Mathematici multa demonstrant de figuris, & numeris, ignorantes definitiones eorum.

And the first opinion asserts that it need not necessarily be known beforehand, but that without cognition of it science can be had of the thing. So Toledo in the place cited above, who proves it in this way: because in order to demonstrate an effect through its cause it is not required to know beforehand what the Cause is and what the effect is, but only that the effect proceeds per se from the cause; therefore the precognition of what it is is not required. Hence Astrologers demonstrate that the moon is eclipsed through its cause, though they are ignorant of the definition of the moon and of the heavens; Mathematicians demonstrate many things about figures and numbers, though ignorant of their definitions.

18 Vt autem quid sit tenendum in hac quæst. decernamus: Notandum est: Duplicem esse demonstrationem, Quia, & Propter quid. Demonstratio propter quid: est illa, per quam demonstramus effectum per suam causam: & talis est hæc: Omne animal rationale est risibile: Omnis homo est animal rationale: ergo Omnis homo est risibilis. Demonstratio Quia, est, per quam ex opposito demonstramus causam per effectum, vt si dicas: Omne risibile est admiratiuum: Omnis homo est risibilis: ergo Omnis homo est admiratiuus. Præterea demonstratio propter quid, adhuc est duplex: Vna, per quam demonstratur propria passio de subiecto: & talis est prima, quam adduximus, tales etiam sunt plures in scientiis particularibus, demonstrantibus passiones de subiecto: vt Metaphysica, & vtraque Philosophia Naturali, & Morali. Alia est, in qua demonstratur effectus per causam, cuius non est propria passio: & talis est secunda demonstratio adducta: tales etiam sunt ferè omnes demonstrationes Mathematicæ. Nam istæ scientiæ non tam demonstrant passiones de subiecto, quàm rationes quasdam figurarum, & proportiones numerorum, posteriorum per priores.

18 But in order that we may decide what is to be held in this question, it should be noted that demonstration is twofold, Quia and Propter quid. Demonstration propter quid is that through which we demonstrate an effect through its cause; such is this: Every rational animal is risible; every man is a rational animal; therefore every man is risible. Demonstration quia is that through which, conversely, we demonstrate the cause through the effect, as if you say: Everything risible is capable of wonder; every man is risible; therefore every man is capable of wonder. Moreover, demonstration propter quid is in turn twofold: One, through which a proper attribute is demonstrated of the subject; and such is the first that we adduced; such also are many in the particular sciences, which demonstrate attributes of the subject, as Metaphysics and both Philosophies, Natural and Moral. The other is that in which an effect is demonstrated through a cause of which it is not the proper attribute; and such is the second demonstration adduced; such also are almost all the Mathematical demonstrations. For these sciences do not so much demonstrate attributes of the subject as certain rationes of figures and proportions of numbers, the posterior through the prior.

19 His suppositis, tribus conclusionibus explicatur nostra sententia. Prima est: Præcognitiones, & ordo quo habenda sunt de subiecto, passione, & principiis, quæ vocantur præcognita, non habent locum in demonstratione Quia sed solùm in demonstratione propter quid. Probatur testimonio Arist. cap. 2. huius 1. lib. asserit, de

19 These things supposed, our view is explained by three conclusions. The first is: The precognitions, and the order in which those things called precognita are to be had of the subject, the attribute, and the principles, have no place in demonstration Quia, but only in demonstration propter quid. It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in ch. 2 of this bk. 1, who asserts of

p. 605

modo sciendi à posteriori, hoc est per demonstrationem Quia, nondum se fuisse locutum, sed nec locuturum vsque ad decimum cap. vbi vtramque demonstrationem distinguit. Ergo regulæ in hoc capite secundæ, de præcognitionibus, & præcognitis, solùm intelliguntur in processu demonstrationis Propter quid, vt etiam ostendunt exempla omnia ab Arist. adducta.

the mode of knowing a posteriori, that is, through demonstration Quia, that he had not yet spoken, and would not speak of it until the tenth chapter, where he distinguishes the two demonstrations. Therefore the rules of the second chapter on precognitions and precognita are understood only of the process of demonstration Propter quid, as all the examples adduced by Aristotle also show.

Probatur etiam ratione: Quoniam per demonstrationem Quia, sæpe demonstratur definitio, vel essentia rei, per propriam passionem: vt ostendit hæc demonstratio: Omne risibile est animal rationale: Omnis homo est risibilis: ergo Omnis homo est animal rationale. Aliquando etiam probari solet, quòd subiectum sit, quando non est adeò manifestum. Sed id quod demonstratur, non potest præsupponi, aut præcognosci: ergo in demonstratione Quia, non est præcognoscendum de subiecto, an sit neque quid sit, sed sufficiet præcognoscere quid nominis.

It is proved also by reason: because through demonstration Quia the definition or essence of a thing is often demonstrated through its proper attribute, as this demonstration shows: Everything risible is a rational animal; every man is risible; therefore every man is a rational animal. Sometimes, too, it is customarily proved that the subject is, when this is not so manifest. But that which is demonstrated cannot be presupposed or known beforehand; therefore in demonstration Quia it need not be known beforehand of the subject whether it is, nor what it is, but it will suffice to know beforehand what the name is.

Secunda conclusio: In demonstrationibus etiam Propter quid, in quibus non demonstratur propria passio de subiecto, sed effectus de sua causa, non est necessariò præcognoscendum quid rei de subiecto: sed sufficit præcognoscere proprium conceptum causæ, ac dependentiæ effectus ab ea, seu rationis, per quam demonstratur effectus. Probatur: Quia in his definitionibus, non sumitur pro medio demonstrandi definitio subiecti, sed solùm dependentia per se effectus à causa: ergo non requiritur præcognitio illius: sed huius sufficiet.

The second conclusion: Also in demonstrations Propter quid in which a proper attribute is not demonstrated of the subject, but an effect from its cause, it is not necessary to know beforehand what the thing is of the subject; but it suffices to know beforehand the proper concept of the cause, and the dependence of the effect on it, or the ratio through which the effect is demonstrated. It is proved: because in these definitions the definition of the subject is not taken as the middle of demonstrating, but only the per se dependence of the effect on the cause; therefore the precognition of the former is not required, but that of the latter will suffice.

Tertia conclusio: In demonstrationibus probantibus passionem, de subiecto, necessariò præcognoscenda est definitio quid rei: Hæc est etiam manifesta: Quia in his demonstrationibus, definitio quid rei assumitur pro medio: ergo est altera præmissarum: sed præmissæ pręcognoscuntur ad inferendam conclusionem: ergo necesse est quid rei de subiecto præcognoscere. Et in his demonstrationibus intelligitur præceptum Aristot. de præcognoscendo quid rei, de subiecto: vt docet expressè D. Th. 1. p. q. 1. art. 7. ad primum: ex quo desumptæ sunt omnes tres conclusiones nostræ, quas tenet etiam Caiet. cap. præsenti. Ex quibus intelligitur, regulas Arist. de præcognitionibus, & præcognitis, secundùm proportionem intelligendas esse, in diuersis demonstrationibus. Ita vt de subiecto præcognoscendum sit, quid rei, atque etiam, quid nominis in his demonstrationibus, quæ probant passionem de subiecto in aliis verò, in quibus ratio posterior, vt effectus per rationem priorem, vel causam probatur, solùm conceptus causæ, & dependentia eius ab effectu

The third conclusion: In demonstrations that prove an attribute of the subject, the definition of what the thing is must necessarily be known beforehand. This too is manifest: because in these demonstrations the definition of what the thing is is assumed as the middle; therefore it is one of the premises; but the premises are known beforehand in order to infer the conclusion; therefore it is necessary to know beforehand what the subject is. And it is in these demonstrations that Aristotle’s precept about knowing beforehand what the subject is is understood, as St. Thomas expressly teaches, 1 p., q. 1, a. 7, ad 1; from which all three of our conclusions are taken, which Cajetan also holds on the present chapter. From these it is understood that Aristotle’s rules on precognitions and precognita are to be understood proportionally in the different demonstrations; so that of the subject what the thing is, and also what the name is, must be known beforehand in those demonstrations which prove an attribute of the subject; but in the others, in which a posterior ratio, as an effect, is proved through a prior ratio or cause, only the concept of the cause and its dependence on the effect

p. 606

est præcognoscenda, verùm quid nominis in omnibus.

is to be known beforehand; but what the name is, in all.

Argum. verò Tolet. solùm probat non esse necessariò præcognoscendum, quid rei, de subiecto, in demonstrationibus probantibus effectus per causas, vel rationes posteriores per priores: quod concedit secunda conclusio nostra: ideo nihil efficit contra tertiam.

But Toledo’s argument proves only that it is not necessary to know beforehand what the subject is in demonstrations that prove effects through causes, or posterior rationes through prior ones: which our second conclusion grants; therefore it achieves nothing against the third.

QUESTION IIII

An præcognitiones de subiecto, passione, & principio, haberi debeant ante demonstrationem, vel etiam in demonstratione ipsa.

Whether the precognitions of the subject, the attribute, and the principle must be had before the demonstration, or also in the demonstration itself.

21 VT intelligatur titulus quæstionis, Explicandum est, Quid sit aliquid præcognoscere de aliquo: & qua necessitate haberi debeant præcognitiones istæ, de tribus præcognitis, Præcognoscere aliquid de aliquo, est, priusquam de illo disputetur, vel probetur vnum aliquid, aliud distinctum cognoscere, vel præsupponere: quod non probatur, sed tanquam certum præsupponitur. Gratia exempli: Si demonstrare velimus de homine, quòd sit admiratiuus, aut risibilis priusquam intellectus assentiatur conclusioni, oportet, vt intelligat hominem esse: & etiam quid sit, quid nomen risibile significet. Nisi enim hęc cognoscantur, non poterit intellectus præmissis assentiri, nec ex eis inferre conclusionem. Et hęc est necessitas præcognoscendi. An verò hęc pręcognoscenda sint, antequam formetur demonstratio: vel satis sit, dum pręmissę disponuntur, & eis assentitur intellectus, ea præcognoscere, de hoc est, quæst.

n order that the title of the question may be understood, it must be ex21 I plained what it is to know something beforehand of something, and with what necessity these precognitions of the three precognita must be had. To know something beforehand of something is, before one thing is disputed or proved of it, to know or presuppose another distinct thing, which is not proved but is presupposed as certain. For example: if we wish to demonstrate of man that he is capable of wonder, or risible, before the intellect assents to the conclusion it must understand that man is, and also what he is, and what the name risible signifies. For unless these are known, the intellect will not be able to assent to the premises, nor infer the conclusion from them. And this is the necessity of knowing beforehand. But whether these things are to be known beforehand before the demonstration is formed, or whether it is enough to know them beforehand while the premises are being disposed and the intellect assents to them, this is the question.

22 Circa quam prima opinio tenet, Ante totam demonstrationem, necessariò esse præcognoscenda: & non sufficere in demonstratione ipsa. Ita Tolet. quod probat testimonio Aristot. qui exempla posuit in illo principio vniuersalissimo: Quodlibet est, vel non est: & in vnitate, quæ est principium numeri, pro subiecto. In triangulo verò, pro passione: de quibus euidens est cognosci ante totam demonstrationem: ergo intellexit Arist. pręcognitiones ante demonstrationem habendas esse, & non in demonstratione ipsa.

22 On this the first opinion holds that they must necessarily be known beforehand before the whole demonstration, and that it does not suffice in the demonstration itself. So Toledo, who proves it by the testimony of Aristotle, who gave as examples that most universal principle, Anything whatever either is or is not; and unity, which is the principle of number, for the subject; and the triangle for the attribute: of which it is evident that they are known before the whole demonstration; therefore Aristotle meant that the precognitions are to be had before the demonstration, and not in the demonstration itself.

Probat etiam ratione: Quia præcognitiones, & præcognita, præsupponuntur scientiæ acquirendæ: sed ad acquisitionem scientiæ pertinet tota demonstratio, cùm scientia acquiratur per eam: ergo ante demonstrationem

He proves it also by reason: because the precognitions and precognita are presupposed to the science to be acquired; but the whole demonstration pertains to the acquisition of science, since science is acquired through it; therefore before

p. 607

necessariò habendæ sunt præcognitiones. Pro solutione quæst. notandum est, Præcognitiones, & præcognita, duobus modis considerari posse. In communi, & in particulari. vel in exercitio, aut in apprehensione vniuersali. vt si dicamus, Principium esse, Totum est maius sua parte: Subiectum verò, vnitatem: & Communem passionem, triangulum figuræ. Hæc enim vix, aut nunquam ingrediuntur demonstrationem, sed tanquam communissima exempla, & quasi speculatiua afferuntur. Subiectum verò, Passio, & principium accipiuntur in particulari, pro his, quæ ingrediuntur demonstrationem, & pertinent ad particulares scientias: vt Subiectum in scientia de homine, est homo. Passiones, quæ de illo probantur, sunt admiratio, & risibilitas. Principium, per quod probantur, est eius definitio.

the precognitions must necessarily be had. For the solution of the question it should be noted that the precognitions and precognita can be considered in two ways: In common, and in particular; or in exercise, or in universal apprehension. As if we say that the principle is The whole is greater than its part; the subject, unity; and the common attribute, the triangle of a figure. For these hardly ever, or never, enter a demonstration, but are brought forward as most common examples and as it were speculative ones. But the subject, the attribute, and the principle are taken in particular for those things which enter a demonstration and pertain to the particular sciences: as the subject in the science of man is man; the attributes which are proved of him are wonder and risibility; the principle through which they are proved is his definition.

23 Quo supposito, duo asserit nostra sententia. Primum est, Præcognitiones, & præcognita, sub vniuersali ratione considerata: ante demonstrationem haberi. Secundum, Si considerentur in particulari, hoc est, ea quæ pertinent ad particulares scientias, possunt quidem ante demonstrationem haberi, & communiter ante illam habentur: hoc tamen non est necessarium ad assensum conclusionis, nec ad acquisitionem scientiæ sed in demonstratione ipsa haberi possunt, simul ac intellectus disponit præmissas, & eis assentitur. Hæc est communis sententia, quam tenent Themistius, in sua Paraphrasi, super 1. lib. Posterior. cap. 1. & 2. D. Thom. Caiet. Venetus, Sotus, & cæteri cap. præs. Et primum non oportet probare, cùm illud concedat opposita sententia: sed probatur secundum hac ratione: Præcognosci dicitur illud, quod non probatur per demonstrationem sed præsupponitur ante assensum conclusionis. Sed ea quæ cognoscuntur in præmissis demonstrationis, & non ante demonstrationẽ integram, non probantur per demonstrationem, sed præsupponuntur ante assensum conclusionis: ergo verè, & propriè dicuntur præcognosci: & sufficit ad assensum conclusionis, & acquisitionem scientiæ, quòd intra demonstrationem præcognoscantur. Quòd verò communiter præsupponantur demonstrationi, manifestum est: quia experientia constat, ferè semper nos ea cognoscere, antequam formemus syllogismum demonstratiuum: sed contingere posset vnum vel alterum eorum non esse nobis cognitum: & tunc sufficere inter disponendas præmissas, illud percipere.

23 This supposed, our view asserts two things. The first is that the precognitions and precognita, considered under a universal ratio, are had before the demonstration. The second, that if they are considered in particular, that is, those which pertain to the particular sciences, they can indeed be had before the demonstration, and commonly are had before it; yet this is not necessary for the assent of the conclusion, nor for the acquisition of science, but they can be had in the demonstration itself, at the same time as the intellect disposes the premises and assents to them. This is the common opinion, which is held by Themistius in his Paraphrase on Posterior Analytics 1, chs. 1 and 2; St. Thomas, Cajetan, Paul of Venice, Soto, and the others on the present chapter. And there is no need to prove the first, since the opposite opinion grants it; but the second is proved by this reason: that is said to be known beforehand which is not proved through the demonstration but is presupposed before the assent of the conclusion. But the things that are known in the premises of the demonstration, and not before the integral demonstration, are not proved through the demonstration, but are presupposed before the assent of the conclusion; therefore they are truly and properly said to be known beforehand; and it suffices for the assent of the conclusion and the acquisition of science that they be known beforehand within the demonstration. But that they are commonly presupposed to the demonstration is manifest: because it is established by experience that we almost always know them before we form the demonstrative syllogism; but it could happen that one or another of them is not known to us, and then it suffices to perceive it while disposing the premises.

24 Testimonium Arist. pro prima opinione nihil probat contra nostram: Quia Aristo. in communissimis præcognitis,

24 The testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion proves nothing against ours: because Aristotle, in the most common precognita,

p. 608

exempla posuit, quæ cùm demonstrationem vix, aut nunquam ingrediantur, ante illam habendæ sunt eorum præcognitiones. Ad arg. verò, Distinguendum est antecedens: nam per acquisitionem scientiæ possumus intelligere, constitutionem totius demonstrationis: & tunc negandum est: quòd ante acquisitionem scientiæ necessariò debeant haberi præcognitiones. Vel solùm assensum conclusionis intelligimus, in quo magis propriè consistit acquisitio scientiæ: nam præmissæ potiùs sunt principia acquisitionis, quàm acquisitio: & in hoc sensu magis proprio, concedendum est antecedens: quod ante acquisitionem scientiæ haberi debeant, sed ex hoc non sequitur, quòd ante demonstrationem, vt per se est manifestum.

gave examples which, since they hardly ever or never enter a demonstration, have to be precognized before it. But to the argument, the antecedent must be distinguished: for by the acquisition of science we can understand the constitution of the whole demonstration, and then it must be denied that the precognitions must necessarily be had before the acquisition of science. Or we understand only the assent of the conclusion, in which the acquisition of science more properly consists (for the premises are rather the principles of the acquisition than the acquisition); and in this more proper sense the antecedent is to be granted, that they must be had before the acquisition of science; but from this it does not follow that they must be had before the demonstration, as is manifest of itself.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

Quæst. 5. An assensus conclusionis fiat ex assensu præmissarum, aut principiorum in genere causæ efficientis, vel solum materialis — Whether the assent of the conclusion comes about from the assent of the premises or principles in the genus of efficient cause, or only of material cause.

An assensus conclusionis fiat, ex assensu præmissarum, aut principiorum, in genere causæ efficientis, vel solùm materialis.

[…]

25 QVæstio hæc fundamentum habet in propositione vniuersali Arist. asserentis, Doctrinam, vel disciplinam, quæ est iudicium conclusionis, fieri ex præexistenti iudicio præmissarum, vel principiorum. Vnum autem fieri ex alio, aliquod genus causæ denotat. Et potest denotare materialem, vt dum dicimus, domum fieri, ex lignis, & lapidibus: vel cognitionẽ intellectiuam, fieri ex sensitiua: hoc enim materialem quoque causalitatem denotat. Quia cognitio sensitiua concurrit ad intellectiuam, determinando materiam, vel obiectum circa quod versari debeat. Et potest etiam denotare causam efficientem: vt dum dicimus calorem fieri ex igne, aut ab igne: ideo quærimus, An assensus conclusionis fiat ex assensu principiorum in genere causæ efficientis, vel materialis tantùm. Et quod materialiter ex eo fiat certissimum est: quia conclusio componitur ex terminis præmissarum, nempe ex maiori, & minori extremitate: & præterea determinatur per assensum principiorum: quia ex talibus principiis, tales conclusiones deducere potest intellectus, & non alias diuersas. Hæc autem ad genus causæ materialis pertinere manifestum est. Sed, An præter genus causæ materialis, efficiens quoque reperiatur in eis: ita vt assensus præmissarum sint causæ efficientes assensus conclusionis, de hoc est quæstio.

his question has its foundation in the universal proposition of 25 T Aristotle, who asserts that Doctrine or discipline, which is the judgment of the conclusion, comes about from a preexisting judgment of the premises or principles. Now that one thing comes about from another denotes some genus of cause. And it can denote the material cause, as when we say that a house comes about from wood and stones; or that intellective cognition comes about from sensitive cognition: for this too denotes material causality, because sensitive cognition concurs toward intellective cognition by determining the matter, or the object, with which it must be concerned. And it can also denote the efficient cause, as when we say that heat comes about from fire, or by fire. Therefore we ask whether the assent of the conclusion comes about from the assent of the principles in the genus of efficient cause, or of material cause only. And that it comes about from it materially is most certain: because the conclusion is composed of the terms of the premises, namely of the major and minor extreme; and moreover it is determined by the assent of the principles, because from such principles the intellect can deduce such conclusions, and not other, different ones. And it is manifest that these things pertain to the genus of material cause. But whether beyond the genus of material cause the efficient is also found in them, so that the assents of the premises are efficient causes of the assent of the conclusion, this is the question.

Circa quam est prima opinio Durandi, negantis eis efficientiam, in 2. d. 2. q. 2. ad quartum: propter hæc duo argumenta. Primò: Quia causa efficiens agit, in quantum est actu in rerum natura: nam quod non est, nihil potest efficere: sed

On this there is the first opinion, of Durandus, who denies them efficiency, in 2, d. 2, q. 2, ad 4, on account of these two arguments. First: because an efficient cause acts insofar as it is in act in the nature of things; for what is not can effect nothing; but

p. 609

dum intellectus assentitur conclusioni, iam non sunt assensus principiorum: ergo non possunt esse causa efficiens eius. Probat minorem: quia intellectus non potest simul habere plures actus, vel assensus: sed vnum post alterum: ergo dum habet assensum conclusionis, iam transiuit assensus præmissarum: quare non poterit esse efficiens causa eius. Et vniuersaliter loquendo vnus actus non potest habere virtutem effectiuam alterius.

when the intellect assents to the conclusion, the assents of the principles no longer exist; therefore they cannot be its efficient cause. He proves the minor: because the intellect cannot have several acts or assents at the same time, but one after another; therefore when it has the assent of the conclusion, the assent of the premises has already passed: wherefore it will not be able to be its efficient cause. And, speaking universally, one act cannot have effective power over another.

Secundò: Assensus principiorum, cùm per solam notitiam terminorum habeatur, specie distinguitur ab assensu conclusionis, qui habetur per medium demonstrationis: ergo si ille sit causa efficiens huius, erit causa æquiuoca specie distincta, ab effectu: sed non potest esse causa æquiuoca: ergo nec erit efficiens. Probatur minor: quia causa æquiuoca est vniuersalis, & remota, vt cœlum, vel Sol: assensus autem principiorum, est causa particularis, & proxima conclusionis: vt per se est manifestum: ergo non est æquiuoca.

Second: the assent of the principles, since it is had through the cognition of the terms alone, is distinguished in species from the assent of the conclusion, which is had through the middle of the demonstration; therefore if the former is the efficient cause of the latter, it will be an equivocal cause, distinct in species from its effect; but it cannot be an equivocal cause; therefore neither will it be efficient. The minor is proved: because an equivocal cause is universal and remote, as the heavens or the Sun; but the assent of the principles is the particular and proximate cause of the conclusion, as is manifest of itself; therefore it is not equivocal.

27 Secunda opinio est opposita: Quòd assensus principiorum, non solùm sint causa materialis conclusionis: sed etiam efficiens: hanc tenet expressè D. Th. cap. præsenti, lect. 3. vbi asserit, esse sententiam Arist. 2. lib. Physic. & 1. lib. contra gentes. cap. 57. ratione 4. vbi eum exponit, & sequitur Ferra. atque etiam Gabriel q. 8. prologi dub. 2. Sotus q. 1. huius capitis, ad 2. Toletus in expositione primi textus, notab. 3. Et hæc est vera, & tenenda.

27 The second opinion is the opposite: That the assents of the principles are not only the material cause of the conclusion, but also the efficient cause. This is expressly held by St. Thomas on the present chapter, lect. 3, where he asserts that it is the opinion of Aristotle, Phys. 2; and Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 57, reason 4, where Ferrara expounds and follows him; and also by Gabriel, q. 8 of the prologue, doubt 2; Soto, q. 1 on this chapter, ad 2; Toledo in the exposition of the first text, note 3. And this is true and to be held.

Probatur duplici argu. Primò: Quia illud quod constituit potentiam in actu primo, cõcurrit cum ea efficienter ad actum secundum: vt species coloris, tanquam virtus eiusdem coloris, qui est obiectum visus, constituit potentiam visiuam in actu primo ad videndum: & ideo concurrit efficienter cum ea ad visionem, quę est actus secundus: sed per species principiorum, & assensum eorum constituitur intellectus in actu primo ad assentiendum conclusioni: ergo assensus eorum concurrit efficienter ad assensum conclusionis. Minorem probo: Quia intellectus nudus, non est sufficiens, neque completa causa assensus conclusionis, nisi informetur per assensum principiorum: ergo assensus iste concurrit, per modum formæ determinantis intellectum, & constituentis ipsum in actu primo ad assensum conclusionis: sed forma determinans, atque constituens in actu primo, est causa efficiens operationis: ergo assensus principiorum concurrit effectiuè ad assensum conclusionis.

It is proved by a twofold argument. First: because that which constitutes a power in first act concurs efficiently with it toward second act: as the species of a color, as the power of that same color, which is the object of sight, constitutes the visive power in first act for seeing, and therefore concurs efficiently with it toward the vision, which is second act; but through the species of the principles and the assent to them the intellect is constituted in first act for assenting to the conclusion; therefore the assent to them concurs efficiently toward the assent of the conclusion. I prove the minor: because the bare intellect is not a sufficient nor a complete cause of the assent of the conclusion unless it is informed by the assent of the principles; therefore this assent concurs by way of a form determining the intellect and constituting it in first act for the assent of the conclusion; but a form determining and constituting in first act is an efficient cause of the operation; therefore the assent of the principles concurs effectively toward the assent of the conclusion.

28 Secundò: Ratio formalis obiectiua est causa efficiens actus, vt patet, in actu videndi: cuius ratio formalis obiectiua

28 Second: the formal objective ratio is an efficient cause of the act, as is plain in the act of seeing, whose formal objective ratio Qq

p. 610

est visibilitas eiusdem coloris, & ideo efficiens causa. Item in fide humana, cuius ratio formalis obiectiua, est testimonium fide digni: & ideo efficiens actus credendi: sed ratio formalis obiectiua, propter quam assentitur intellectus conclusioni, est assensus principiorum, vt docet expressè Arist. cap. sequenti. Et probat euidens ratio: quia propter principia assentitur intellectus conclusioni: ergo erit causa efficiens assensus conclusionis.

is the visibility of that same color, and therefore it is an efficient cause. Likewise in human faith, whose formal objective ratio is the testimony of one worthy of credence, and therefore it is efficient of the act of believing; but the formal objective ratio on account of which the intellect assents to the conclusion is the assent of the principles, as Aristotle expressly teaches in the following chapter. And an evident reason proves it: because it is on account of the principles that the intellect assents to the conclusion; therefore it will be the efficient cause of the assent of the conclusion.

Ad primum arg. Durandi: Neganda est minor: quòd dum intellectus assentitur conclusioni, non permaneant assensus principiorum. Et cùm dicitur, intellectum non posse simul habere plures assensus: distinguendum est: quia duobus modis possunt se habere plures assensus, vel per modum plurium, quando non sunt inter sese ordinati, vel per modum vnius, quando sunt ordinati. Intellectus ergo non potest habere plures assensus per modum pluriũ, bene tamen per modum vnius & ita se habent assensus principiorum & conclusionis, qui ordinati sunt, cùm ille sit ratio formalis assentiendi huius. Dum ergo intellectus assentitur conclusioni, perseuerare potest, & perseuerat in assensibus principiorum, quasi continuans eos: & ideo possunt esse causa efficiens assensus conclusionis. Quòd verò vnus actus intellectus, non possit esse causa alterius, negandum est: nam saltem potest esse causa, Qua, licèt non sit causa, Quæ: hoc est, ratio formalis causandi, licèt non sit id quod causat: & ita assensus principiorum, est ratio formalis assentiendi, licèt non sit causa, quæ efficiat assensum conclusionis: sed hoc solus intellectus habet, ratione eiusdem assensus principiorum: & ideo assensus iste est efficiens, Quo assensus conclusionis, non efficiens, Quod: sicus veritas rei, est causa efficiens intellectionis eius, tanquam Quo, non tanquam Quod.

To the first argument of Durandus: the minor must be denied, namely that while the intellect assents to the conclusion the assents of the principles do not remain. And when it is said that the intellect cannot have several assents at the same time, a distinction must be made: because several assents can be related in two ways, either by way of many, when they are not ordered among themselves, or by way of one, when they are ordered. The intellect, then, cannot have several assents by way of many, but it can indeed by way of one; and so are related the assents of the principles and of the conclusion, which are ordered, since the former is the formal ratio of assenting to the latter. While, then, the intellect assents to the conclusion, it can persevere, and does persevere, in the assents of the principles, as it were continuing them; and therefore they can be the efficient cause of the assent of the conclusion. But that one act of the intellect cannot be the cause of another must be denied: for at least it can be a cause Quo [by which], although it is not a cause Quod [which], that is, the formal ratio of causing, although it is not that which causes. And so the assent of the principles is the formal ratio of assenting, although it is not the cause which effects the assent of the conclusion; but the intellect alone has this, by reason of that same assent of the principles; and therefore this assent is efficient Quo of the assent of the conclusion, not efficient Quod: as the truth of a thing is the efficient cause of the understanding of it as a cause Quo, not as a cause Quod.

29 Ad secundùm: Concedenda est prima cõsequentia, quòd assensus principiorum sit causa æquiuoca assensus conclusionis: quia specie distinctus ab eo, sed minor neganda, quòd sola causa vniuersalis, & remota sit æquiuoca: nam omnis causa, siue vniuersalis, siue particularis: proxima, vel remota, verè est æquiuoca: quia ratio causæ æquiuocæ, non consistit in eo quòd particularis sit, vel vniuersalis, proxima, vel remota, sed solùm in eo, quòd sit distincta specie à suo effectu: quod patet: quia eo ipso, quòd est eiusdem speciei, est vniuoca

29 To the second: the first consequence is to be granted, namely that the assent of the principles is an equivocal cause of the assent of the conclusion, because it is distinct in species from it; but the minor is to be denied, namely that only a universal and remote cause is equivocal: for every cause, whether universal or particular, proximate or remote, is truly equivocal, because the ratio of an equivocal cause does not consist in its being particular or universal, proximate or remote, but only in its being distinct in species from its effect: which is plain, because by the very fact that it is of the same species, it is univocal.

p. 611

QUESTION VI

An assensus principiorum includatur formaliter in assensu conclusionis.

Whether the assent of the principles is formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

30 CErtum est, quòd intellectus diuerso actu, atque priori assentitur præmissis, deinde conclusioni: & diuerso quidem numero, atque specie: quia principiis assentitur propter se: hoc est, sine aliquo medio: sed habita solùm significatione terminorum. Conclusioni verò non propter se: sed propter principia, quorum accedit, præsupponitur assensui conclusionis: Quæstio igitur est, An postquam intellectus habuit assensum principiorum, & accedit ad assentiendum conclusioni, sic ei assentiatur propter principia, vt assensum eorum iterum repetat: vel satis sit, vt dicatur assentire conclusioni propter principia, quòd assensum eorum immediatè habuerit absque eius repetitione: nam si primo modo fiat, includetur formaliter assensus principiorum in assensu conclusionis: si verò secundo modo, non includetur formaliter, sed solùm præsuppositiuè: quod est verè non includi formaliter, sed præsupponi.

30 It is certain that the intellect assents by a different and prior act to the premises, and then to the conclusion; and by one different indeed in number and in species: because it assents to the principles on account of themselves, that is, without any middle, but having only the signification of the terms; but to the conclusion not on account of itself, but on account of the principles, the assent to which is presupposed to the assent of the conclusion. The question, then, is whether, after the intellect has had the assent of the principles and comes to assent to the conclusion, it assents to it on account of the principles in such a way that it repeats the assent to them again; or whether it is enough, for it to be said to assent to the conclusion on account of the principles, that it has had the assent to them immediately before, without its repetition: for if it comes about in the first way, the assent of the principles will be formally included in the assent of the conclusion; but if in the second way, it will not be included formally, but only presuppositively: which is truly not to be included formally, but to be presupposed.

Et prima opinio, quam sequuntur moderni quidam, tenet, necessariò quidem præsupponi, sed cùm sit prior, realiter atque specie distinctus ab assensu conclusionis, non posse in eo includi formaliter. Probat testimonio Aristo. Et duplici argum. Aristo. enim in libris priorum, agens de forma syllogistica, asserit, Medium bis sumendum esse in præmissis: & ideò non esse repetendum in conclusione, sed in ea vnam extremitatem prædicari de altera. Peccaret igitur syllogismus in forma: si medium ingrederetur conclusionem: sed hoc est necessariò concedendum, si assensus principiorum includatur formaliter in conclusione: ergo non potest includi. Minorem sic probo: Præmissæ componuntur ex medio, & extremitatibus: ergo si repetantur in assensu conclusionis, medium erit necessariò in conclusione repetendum: sed non potest includi formaliter, nisi repetatur, vt per se est manifestum: ergo falsum est, quòd formaliter includatur. Asserit etiam Aristoteles cap. præsenti, agens de modo demonstrandi, notitiam conclusionis fieri ex præexistenti notitia principiorum: si ergo assensus principiorum præexistens, est respectu assensus conclusionis, erit præsuppositus: & consequenter, non inclusus formaliter in eo: nam si formaliter includeretur, simul haberetur, & non prius.

And the first opinion, which certain moderns follow, holds that it is indeed necessarily presupposed, but that, since it is prior, and really and in species distinct from the assent of the conclusion, it cannot be formally included in it. It proves this by the testimony of Aristotle and by a twofold argument. For Aristotle, in the books of the Prior Analytics, treating of the form of the syllogism, asserts that the middle is to be taken twice in the premises, and therefore is not to be repeated in the conclusion, but in it one extreme is to be predicated of the other. The syllogism would therefore sin in form if the middle entered the conclusion; but this must necessarily be granted if the assent of the principles is formally included in the conclusion; therefore it cannot be included. I prove the minor thus: the premises are composed of the middle and the extremes; therefore if they are repeated in the assent of the conclusion, the middle will necessarily have to be repeated in the conclusion; but it cannot be included formally unless it is repeated, as is manifest of itself; therefore it is false that it is formally included. Aristotle also asserts in the present chapter, treating of the mode of demonstrating, that the cognition of the conclusion comes about from the preexisting cognition of the principles: if, then, the assent of the principles is preexisting with respect to the assent of the conclusion, it will be presupposed, and consequently not formally included in it: for if it were formally included, it would be had at the same time, and not before. Q q ij

p. 612

31 Primum arg. eiusdem sententiæ est: quia si principia includuntur formaliter in conclusione, ergo eodem actu, quo assentitur intellectus conclusioni, assentitur etiam principiis: sed assensus conclusionis, est scientificus, procedens ab habitu scientiæ: ergo per actum & habitum scientiæ assentiremus principiis: consequens autem est falsum: quia assensus conclusionis est notitia discursiua, assensus verò principiorum intuitiua, & sine discursu: ergo non potest iste formaliter in illo includi. Quod etiam probatur impossibile: quia assensus principiorum, numero, & specie distinctus est, ab assensu conclusionis: ergo non potest includi in eo formaliter. Probatur consequentia, quia quæ sic distincta sunt: non possunt formaliter se includere.

31 The first argument of the same opinion is: because if the principles are formally included in the conclusion, then by the same act by which the intellect assents to the conclusion it assents also to the principles; but the assent of the conclusion is scientific, proceeding from the habit of science; therefore we would assent to the principles through an act and habit of science; but the consequent is false, because the assent of the conclusion is a discursive cognition, whereas the assent of the principles is intuitive and without discursive reasoning; therefore the latter cannot be formally included in the former. This is also proved to be impossible: because the assent of the principles is distinct in number and in species from the assent of the conclusion; therefore it cannot be formally included in it. The consequence is proved: because things that are thus distinct cannot formally include one another.

Probatur secundò: Quia in syllogismo euidenti infertur aliquando conclusio vera, ex pręmissis falsis. Vt patet in hoc: Omnis arbor est animal: Omnis homo est arbor: ergo, Omnis homo est animal: Si ergo præmissæ includuntur in conclusione formaliter, falsum includetur formaliter in vero: quod repugnat. Confirmari etiam potest experientia: quia in conclusione solùm coniungitur vna extremitas cum altera, nulla ibi facta mentione medij: coniungitur ergo propter medium pręsuppositum, non formaliter inclusum, sed ad summum virtualiter. Probatur consequentia: quia formalis inclusio impossibilis est, sine formali mentione, aut repetitione.

It is proved second: because in an evident syllogism a true conclusion is sometimes inferred from false premises, as is plain in this one: Every tree is an animal; every man is a tree; therefore every man is an animal. If, then, the premises are formally included in the conclusion, the false will be formally included in the true: which is repugnant. It can also be confirmed by experience: because in the conclusion only one extreme is joined with the other, no mention being made there of the middle; it is joined, therefore, on account of the middle as presupposed, not as formally included, but at most virtually. The consequence is proved: because formal inclusion is impossible without formal mention or repetition.

Secunda opinio, Affirmat assensum principiorum, non solùm præsupponi assensui conclusionis, sed formaliter includi in eo. Ita D. Tho. 1. 2. qu. 8. art. 3. his verbis: Primò aliquis intelligit, ipsa principia secundùm se: postmodum autem intelligit ea in ipsis conclusionibus, secundùm quod assentit conclusionibus, propter principia. Idem etiam tenet, q. 12. art. 4. D. Tho. sequuntur Capr. in 1. d. 2. q. 1. in solutione ad arg. contra 4. conclus. Ferra. 1. lib. contra gentes, ca. 57. Soncin. 6. Meta. q. 10. Duran. in 2. d. 38. q. 3. ad 3. qui omnes docent, intellectum eodem actu ferri in conclusionem, & principia, cùm ei propter principia assentiatur: quod aliter fieri repugnat, nisi assensus principiorum includatur formaliter in assensu concl.

The second opinion affirms that the assent of the principles is not only presupposed to the assent of the conclusion, but formally included in it. So St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 8, a. 3, in these words: First someone understands the principles themselves according to themselves; but afterwards he understands them in the conclusions themselves, inasmuch as he assents to the conclusions on account of the principles. He holds the same also in q. 12, a. 4. St. Thomas is followed by Capreolus in 1, d. 2, q. 1, in the solution to the arguments against the 4th conclusion; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 57; Soncinas, Metaph. 6, q. 10; Durandus in 2, d. 38, q. 3, ad 3; who all teach that the intellect is borne by the same act to the conclusion and to the principles, since it assents to it on account of the principles: which cannot come about otherwise unless the assent of the principles is formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

32 Deinde probatur hoc arg. satis efficaci: Eodem actu fertur potentia quælibet in obiectum, & in rationem formalem eius, vt visus eodem actu fertur in colorem, & in rationem visibilitatis: aut in colorem, & lucem, si lux se teneat ex parte obiecti in visione coloris. Et ratio huius euidens est: quia ex obiecto, quod percipitur, & ex ratione formali illud percipiendi, constituitur vnum obiectum totale, atque completum, tanquam

32 Next, this is proved by a quite efficacious argument: any power is borne by the same act to its object and to its formal ratio, as sight is borne by the same act to color and to the ratio of visibility; or to color and light, if light stands on the side of the object in the vision of color. And the reason for this is evident: because from the object which is perceived and from the formal ratio of perceiving it there is constituted one total and complete object, as

p. 613

ex Quo, & Quod, sed assensus principiorum, est ratio formalis obiectiua assentiendi conclusioni: ergo eodem actu fertur intellectus in conclusionem, quæ est obiectum, cui assentitur, & in principia, quæ sunt rationes essentiendi: sed non potest ferri in principia eodem actu, nisi in obiecto eiusdem actus includantur formaliter: ergo necessarium est formaliter includi præsertim cùm assensus conclusionis distinguatur specie, à fide humana, & opinione, solùm propter diuersam rationem formalẽ assentiendi: quæ in opinione est, ratio probabilis, in fide humana, testimonium fide digni, in assensu scientifico, principia per se euidentia.
