11 From which definition he gathers that the proposition in which the first attribute is predicated of the definition, as A rational animal is capable of learning, is distinct from that in which it is predicated of the definitum, as Man is capable of learning; which he proves by many arguments, thinking perhaps that the contrary of this is the view of St. Thomas. But these arguments are to be omitted, because St. Thomas does not deny it, as we shall see. Scotus is followed by Auriol and Gregory (of Rimini), whom Capreolus cites, In 1, d. 2, q. 2, a. 2, who argue thus against the definition of St. Thomas.

Primò: Multæ sunt propositiones per se notæ in Mathematicis scientiis, in quibus prædicatum non est de intrinseca ratione subiecti: vt totum est maius sua parte: &, à quolibet puncto in quodlibet punctum, possumus lineam ducere. Et in Philosophia naturali, Motum esse, atque etiam Naturam esse: imò, & hæc per se nota est: Animal rationale est capax disciplinæ: Nix est alba: Coruus est niger. Et ex opposito, aliæ sunt, in quibus prædicatum est de intrinseca ratione subiecti: vt homo est substantia. Animal est corpus: & tamen non sunt immediatæ, quia inter prædicatum & subiectum dantur alia prædicata media vt patet. Ergo definitio D. Th. ex vtraque parte probatur insufficiens.

First: There are many propositions known per se in the Mathematical sciences in which the predicate is not of the intrinsic ratio of the subject: as The whole is greater than its part; and From any point to any point we can draw a line. And in natural Philosophy, That motion exists, and also That nature exists; indeed, this too is known per se: A rational animal is capable of learning; Snow is white; The raven is black. And on the other side, there are others in which the predicate is of the intrinsic ratio of the subject, as Man is a substance, An animal is a body; and yet they are not immediate, because between the predicate and the subject other middle predicates are given, as is plain. Therefore the definition of St. Thomas is proved insufficient on both sides.

12 Secundò arguunt: Contra diuisionem: quia propositionem esse per se notam, non consistit in eo, quòd termini eius à nobis cognoscantur, sed solùm in eo, quòd ex se habeat euidentem veritatem: & multò minùs consistit in eo, quòd à solis sapientibus, vel ab omnibus cognoscantur eius termini: sed solùm in eo, quòd per se sint cognoscibiles. Ergo diuisiones in per se notam ex natura sua: & quoad nos: & in per se totum sapientibus, vel insipientibus, extra rationem propositionis per se notæ sunt: & ideo admitti non debent.

12 Second, they argue against the division: because for a proposition to be known per se does not consist in its terms being cognized by us, but only in its having evident truth of itself; and much less does it consist in its terms being cognized by the wise alone or by all, but only in their being cognizable per se. Therefore the divisions into known per se by its nature and as regards us, and into known per se to the wise or to the unwise, are outside the ratio of a proposition known per se, and therefore ought not to be admitted.

Tertiò: Quia propositio per se nota est illa, quæ ex propriis conceptibus, à quocunque intellectu formatis, talis est: ergo omnis propositio per se nota, nobis etiam erit per se nota: & ideò malè diuiditur, in per se notam ex natura sua, & quoad nos. Antecedens probant, quia vel formamus proprios conceptus eius vel alios diuersos: si proprios, nobis erit per se nota: si diuersos, non erit eadem propositio, sed alia diuersa: ergo propositio per se nota, ex se cuilibet intellectu erit per se nota: nulla

Third: Because a proposition known per se is that which is such from its proper concepts, formed by any intellect whatever; therefore every proposition known per se will also be known per se to us; and therefore it is badly divided into known per se by its nature and as regards us. They prove the antecedent: because either we form its proper concepts or other, different ones; if its proper ones, it will be known per se to us; if different ones, it will not be the same proposition, but another, different one; therefore a proposition known per se of itself will be known per se to any intellect whatever: none

p. 629

ergo dabitur per se nota, ex natura sua, quæ non sit etiam per se nota, quoad nos.

therefore will be given known per se by its nature which is not also known per se as regards us.

In hac re, nostra sententia est, Propositionem per se notam, definiendam esse, ac diuidendam, vt Arist. c. præsenti definiuit ac diuisit: eius autem definitioni, ac diuisionibus magis esse conformem sententiam D. Th. & commune, quàm sententiam Scoti.

On this matter our view is that a proposition known per se is to be defined and divided as Aristotle defined and divided it in the present chapter; and that the view of St. Thomas, which is the common one, is more conformable to his definition and divisions than the view of Scotus.

13 Verba Arist. sic habent: Principium demonstrationis, est propositio immediata: immediata verò, quæ non est alia prior: Quibus per principium demonstrationis, intelligit propositionem per se notam: hæc enim sola principium vocari potest: nam quæ mediata est, non principium, sed conclusio vocatur. Sic ergo definienda est propositio per se nota apud Arist. vt breuis, clara, & vniuersalis sit definitio: Propositio per se nota est, inter cuius prædicatum & subiectum nullum datur medium, per quod à priori possit demonstrari. In qua definitione, solùm definitur propositio per se nota demonstrationis, aut demonstratiua: hoc est, necessaria, quod Arist. apertè significauit, dicens: Principium demonstrationis esse propositionem immediatam, quod dicimus, ad excludendas aliquas propositiones, quæ cùm verè accidentales sint, & ex contingente, & non demonstratiuæ, ab aliquibus dicuntur per se notæ, atque immediatæ: vt nix est alba, superficies est colorata, & similes.

13 Aristotle’s words run thus: A principle of demonstration is an immediate proposition; and an immediate one is that to which there is no other prior. By which, by a principle of demonstration he understands a proposition known per se: for this alone can be called a principle; for that which is mediate is called not a principle but a conclusion. Thus, therefore, the proposition known per se is to be defined according to Aristotle, so that the definition may be brief, clear, and universal: A proposition known per se is one between whose predicate and subject no middle is given through which it could be demonstrated a priori. In which definition only the proposition known per se of demonstration, or demonstrative, that is, necessary, is defined, which Aristotle openly signified, saying: A principle of demonstration is an immediate proposition; which we say in order to exclude certain propositions which, since they are truly accidental and contingent and not demonstrative, are called by some known per se and immediate: as Snow is white, The surface is colored, and the like.

14 Ex definitione autem sic intellecta, Colligitur primò: Omnino conuerti propositionem per se notam, & immediatam, atque indemonstrabilem: quia de vtraque verum est, nullum eam habere medium, per quod à priori possit demõstrari. A priori autem dicimus: quia nil impedit, quominus propositio sit per se nota, & per effectũ demonstretur: vt homo est animal rationale, demonstratur per illam: homo est risibilis: & nihilominus est per se nota: quia non demonstratur à priori, sed à posteriori: & hæc de definitione propositionis per se notæ.

14 But from the definition so understood it is gathered, first, that a proposition known per se and an immediate and indemonstrable one are altogether convertible: because of each it is true that it has no middle through which it could be demonstrated a priori. And we say a priori because nothing prevents a proposition from being known per se and being demonstrated through an effect: as Man is a rational animal is demonstrated through this, Man is risible, and nevertheless it is known per se, because it is not demonstrated a priori but a posteriori. And so much for the definition of a proposition known per se.

Hanc Arist. diuisit, quatuor diuisionibus, ex quibus tres posuit c. præsenti, quartam verò cap. sequenti. Prima in Dignitatem, & Positionem. Dignitatem vocauit vniuersalissimam, quæ vix ingreditur scientiam, vel demonstrationem, sed quasi fundamentum est plurium, vel omnium scientiarum, & demonstrationum, vt quodlibet est, vel non est: totum est maius sua parte: quæ ideo dixit necessariò debere cognosci ab his, qui aliquam scientiam addiscere incipiunt. Positionem verò, quæ est propositio per se nota non tamen vniuersalis, nec etiam, quam cognoscere debet, qui aliquã scientiam addiscere vult: sed particularis, & propria alicuius scientiæ, ex qua fiunt demonstrationes in ea, & quæ in ipsamet scientia traditur: & tales

Aristotle divided it by four divisions, of which he posited three in the present chapter, but the fourth in the following chapter. The first is into dignity and position. He called a dignity the most universal one, which scarcely enters a science or demonstration, but is as it were the foundation of many or of all sciences and demonstrations: as Anything whatever is or is not; The whole is greater than its part; which he therefore said must necessarily be cognized by those who begin to learn some science. But a position is a proposition known per se, yet not universal, nor even one that he who wishes to learn some science ought to cognize, but particular and proper to some science, from which demonstrations are made in it, and which is handed down in that very science. And such R r iij

p. 630

sunt omnes definitiones, & omnia principia propria particularium scientiarum. Hæc autem diuisio, eadem est cum secunda, quam tradit D. Thom. dicens, Propositionem per se notam vnam esse, cuius termini omnibus patent: quales sunt vniuersalissimæ, quas appellauit Arist. dignitates. Et in aliam, cuius termini non omnibus, sed sapientibus tantùm sunt manifesti: & istæ sunt, quas vocat Arist. positiones.

are all definitions and all the proper principles of the particular sciences. And this division is the same as the second, which St. Thomas hands down, saying that one proposition known per se is that whose terms are plain to all: such are the most universal ones, which Aristotle called dignities. And another, whose terms are manifest not to all but only to the wise; and these are the ones which Aristotle calls positions.

Secunda diuisione: eam diuisit in Positionem, & suppositionem: circa quam versabitur quæstio sequens.

By the second division he divided it into position and supposition, about which the following question will be concerned.

51 Tertiam verò diuisionem, satis apertè insinuauit, dum notiora diuisit in ea, Quæ sunt notiora natura, & quoad nos. Ex hac enim diuisione sequitur, per se notum, aliud esse ex natura sua, & non quoad nos, aliud verò ex natura sua, & quoad nos: & ex consequenti propositionem per se notam, eiusdem modis diuidi ab Arist. Et probatur hoc arg. Omnis definitio constituit propositionem per se notam, cum definito: sed plures sunt definitiones nobis incognitæ: ergo propositiones, quas constituere possunt cum suis definitis, erunt ex natura sua per se notæ, non tamen quoad nos: imò quæ demonstrari, quoad nos, poterunt, à posteriori, per aliquem effectum.

51 The third division he insinuated clearly enough when he divided things better known into those which are better known by nature and as regards us. For from this division it follows that one thing known per se is so by its nature and not as regards us, and another by its nature and as regards us; and consequently that the proposition known per se is divided by Aristotle in the same ways. And this is proved by this argument: Every definition constitutes a proposition known per se with its definitum; but many definitions are unknown to us; therefore the propositions which they can constitute with their definita will be known per se by their nature, yet not as regards us; indeed, they could be demonstrated, as regards us, a posteriori, through some effect.

Quartam denique diuisionem, posuit c. seq. In per se notam positiuè, cuius prædicatum positiuum, sine medio demonstratiuo conuenit subiecto, & In per se notam negatiuè, cuius prædicatum negatiuum, sine medio conuenit subiecto: tales sunt propositiones, in quibus vnum prædicatum negatur de altero: vt Substantia non est Quantitas. Non tamen illæ, in quibus particulare genus vnius prædicamenti, aut vna species negatur de alia, vel de supremo genere alterius prædicamenti: vt Albedo non est Quantitas: Linea non est color, Habitus non est Numerus: quia istæ possunt demonstrari per supremum genus, alterius prædicamenti, negatum: vt Albedo non est quantitas: quia est qualitas: & qualitas non est quantitas: & linea non est color: quia non est qualitas. Et vna species, vel vnum genus negatur de altero: vt substantia non est quantitas: & homo non est equus. Negationes enim istæ essentiales sunt: & ideo propositiones necessarias, atque demonstratiuas, & per se notas constituunt Verba Aristot. sunt: Sicut quædam principia sunt indemonstrabilia Quòd sit hoc illud, & quòd sit hoc in illo: sic & quòd non erit hoc illud, nec quòd sit hoc in illo: quare, hæc quidem esse aliquid, alia autem non esse aliquid, erunt principia.

Finally, he posited the fourth division in the following chapter: into known per se positively, whose positive predicate belongs to the subject without a demonstrative middle, and into known per se negatively, whose negative predicate belongs to the subject without a middle. Such are propositions in which one predicate is denied of another: as Substance is not quantity. Not, however, those in which a particular genus of one category, or one species, is denied of another, or of the supreme genus of another category: as Whiteness is not quantity, A line is not color, A habit is not number; because these can be demonstrated through the supreme genus of the other category, denied: as Whiteness is not quantity, because it is quality, and quality is not quantity; and A line is not color, because it is not quality. And one species or one genus is denied of another: as Substance is not quantity and Man is not a horse. For these negations are essential, and therefore constitute necessary, demonstrative, and per se known propositions. Aristotle’s words are: Just as certain principles are indemonstrable, that this is that, and that this is in that, so also that this will not be that, nor that this is in that; wherefore some will be principles that something is, and others that something is not.

Quòd verò duæ diuisiones à D. Thom. assignatæ, sint conformes primæ, ac tertiæ diuisioni, designatis ab Aristot. vel

But that the two divisions assigned by St. Thomas are consonant with the first and third divisions designated by Aristotle, or

p. 631

potiùs, quòd sint eadem, probauimus iam. Restat igitur ostẽdere, quòd eius definitio conformis sit definitioni Aristo. à nobis ex verbis eius desumptæ.

rather, that they are the same, we have already proved. It remains, therefore, to show that his definition is conformable to the definition of Aristotle, taken by us from his words.

Quod sic probari potest: Definitio D. Thom. est, Propositio per se nota est ea, cuius prædicatum includitur in ratione intrinseca subiecti. Sed propositio talis non habet medium, per quod possit à priori demonstrari: vt probabitur ex solutionibus argumentorum Scoti, & aliorum: ergo consona est definitioni Aristot. Definitionem verò Scoti, non reiicimus ex eo, quòd non possit reduci ad eandem: sed quia prolixa satis est, atque obscura: vt verba eius ostendunt.

Which can be proved thus: The definition of St. Thomas is: A proposition known per se is that whose predicate is included in the intrinsic ratio of the subject. But such a proposition does not have a middle through which it could be demonstrated a priori, as will be proved from the solutions of the arguments of Scotus and the others; therefore it is consonant with the definition of Aristotle. But the definition of Scotus we do not reject on the ground that it cannot be reduced to the same, but because it is prolix enough and obscure, as its words show.

Pro solutione primi arg. Duplici distinctione distinguendum est prædicatum intrinsecum. Primò quidem, in Recto, aut in Obliquo. Deinde, Secundùm esse, aut secundùm causalitatem. & in Recto, nulla pars est prædicatũ intrinsecum, respectu totius: quamuis secũdùm esse sit ei intrinseca: sed in obliquo intrinsecum est: & hoc modo est propositio per se nota: Totum est maius sua parte. Præterea, effectus per se, atque immediatus, non est intrinsecus causæ: sed intrinsecus est ordo causalitatis, inter causam proximam, & per se, atque eius effectum & ex consequenti, effectus ipse quodam modo est prædicatum intrinsecum, respectu causæ, ratione eiusdem ordinis intrinseci. Dum autem definit D. Thom. propositionem per se notam, cuius prædicatum est intrinsecum subiecto: quæcumque ratione intrinsecũ esse debere intelligit. Hoc est, aut secundùm esse, aut secundũ ordinem intrinsecum proximæ causalitatis.

For the solution of the first argument: The intrinsic predicate is to be distinguished by a twofold distinction. First, indeed, in recto or in obliquo. Next, according to being or according to causality. And in recto no part is an intrinsic predicate with respect to the whole, although according to being it is intrinsic to it; but in obliquo it is intrinsic; and in this way this proposition is known per se: The whole is greater than its part. Moreover, a per se and immediate effect is not intrinsic to its cause; but the order of causality between the proximate and per se cause and its effect is intrinsic; and consequently the effect itself is in a certain way an intrinsic predicate with respect to the cause, by reason of the same intrinsic order. And when St. Thomas defines a proposition known per se as one whose predicate is intrinsic to the subject, he understands that it ought to be intrinsic by any ratio whatever: that is, either according to being or according to the intrinsic order of proximate causality.

18 Ex his respondetur ad arg. Negando antecedens, quòd aliqua sit propositio per se nota, cuius prædicatum non sit intrinsecum subiecto, aut secundùm esse, aut secundùm intrinsecum ordinem proximæ causalitatis: in recto aut in obliquo: secundùm se, aut secundùm ordinem intrinsecum vnius ad alterum. Et cùm intrinsecus sit ordo causalitatis, inter effectum & causam proximam, & per se, propositionem per se notam constituit, dum de causa prædicatur: cùm sit intrinsecum prædicatum causæ: si non ratione sui: bene tamen ratione ordinis intrinseci. Et si non in recto, bene tamen in obliquo. Aliæ autem prædicationes accidentales, si aliquo modo sint per se notæ, non sunt propositiones demonstratiuæ: quia non sunt necessariæ. D. Thom. autem solùm definit propositionem per se notam demonstratiuam: vt de Aristot. etiam notum est, hanc tantùm eum diffinisse.

18 From these things the reply is made to the argument, by denying the antecedent, namely that there is any proposition known per se whose predicate is not intrinsic to the subject either according to being or according to the intrinsic order of proximate causality; in recto or in obliquo; according to itself or according to the intrinsic order of one to the other. And since the order of causality between the effect and the proximate and per se cause is intrinsic, it constitutes a proposition known per se when it is predicated of the cause, since it is a predicate intrinsic to the cause: if not by reason of itself, yet well by reason of the intrinsic order. And if not in recto, yet well in obliquo. But other, accidental predications, if in some way they are known per se, are not demonstrative propositions, because they are not necessary. St. Thomas, however, defines only the demonstrative proposition known per se; as of Aristotle too it is known that he defined this alone.

Pro aliis denique propositionibus essẽtialibus, & mediatis, quas adducit idem argum. alia distinctione vtendum est,

Finally, for the other essential and mediate propositions which the same argument adduces, another distinction is to be used, R r iiij

p. 632

nempe, Medium esse duplex, Reale vel rationis, aut formale, & virtuale. Medium reale, dicitur illud quod est re distincta à prædicato, & subiecto, inter quæ ponitur medium: vt admiratiuum, est medium reale, inter hominem, & risibile: & hoc etiam dicitur medium formale. Medium verò rationis est, quod solùm ratione nostra distinguitur à subiecto, & prædicato, & dicitur medium virtuale: quia secundùm rem, aut formam, non est distinctum ab extremis, sed secundùm nostrum intellectum plures conceptus eiusdem rei concipientem: virtute tamen, & quasi fundamentaliter contentos in re ipsa. Et quantum pertinet ad propositiones demonstratiuas, vtrumque medium constituit propositionem simpliciter mediatam, & simpliciter demonstrabilem. Probatur ex Aristot. qui concedit definitionem esse medium demonstrationis: atqui Definitio solùm potest esse medium rationis, & virtuale.

namely that the middle is twofold, real or of reason, or formal and virtual. A real middle is said to be that which is distinct in reality from the predicate and the subject between which the middle is posited: as capable of wonder is a real middle between man and risible; and this is also called a formal middle. But a middle of reason is that which is distinguished from the subject and the predicate only by our reason; and it is called a virtual middle, because according to the thing or form it is not distinct from the extremes, but according to our intellect, which conceives several concepts of the same thing, contained, however, virtually and as it were fundamentally in the thing itself. And as far as pertains to demonstrative propositions, each middle constitutes a proposition simply mediate and simply demonstrable. This is proved from Aristotle, who grants that a definition is a middle of demonstration; but a definition can only be a middle of reason, and virtual.

Vnde sequitur, Omnes propositiones, quæ possunt demonstrari per definitionem prædicati aut subiecti, esse simpliciter mediatas: vt sunt illæ, in quibus prima passio, prædicatur de definito, atque etiam de definitione: quia illa potest demonstrari per definitionem subiecti, hæc verò per definitionem passionis, & etiam illa, in qua vna passio prædicatur de alia: vt admiratiuum est risibile, & etiam illæ: quæ assumuntur in arg. Sed communiter dicuntur immediatæ, quia secundùm rem tales sunt,

Whence it follows that all propositions which can be demonstrated through the definition of the predicate or of the subject are simply mediate: such as are those in which the first attribute is predicated of the definitum, and also of the definition; because the former can be demonstrated through the definition of the subject, but the latter through the definition of the attribute; and also that in which one attribute is predicated of another, as What is capable of wonder is risible; and also those which are assumed in the argument. But they are commonly called immediate, because according to the thing they are such.

19 Ad secundum: Distinguendum est antecedens. Nam sicut notiora, vel minùs nota dicuntur talia, & ex natura sua, & etiam in ordine ad intellectum imperfectè cognoscentem: sic etiam propositio per se nota, & licèt per accidens sit ad rationem propositionis per se notæ secundùm de sumptę, quòd non sit per se nota quoad nos: nihilominus sumpta in communi, quasi analogicè diuiditur, in propositionem per se notam natura sua, & quoad nos.

19 To the second: The antecedent is to be distinguished. For just as things are called better known or less known both by their nature and also in order to an intellect that cognizes imperfectly, so too is a proposition known per se; and although it is per accidens to the ratio of a proposition known per se, taken according to itself, that it is not known per se as regards us, nevertheless, taken in common, it is divided, as it were analogically, into a proposition known per se by its nature and as regards us.

Ad tertium, negandum est antecedens, quòd propositio per se nota sit, quæ ex propriis conceptibus, & quocunque intellectu formatis talis est: sed illa est, inter cuius prædicatum, & subiectum non datur medium, per quod à priori sit demonstrabilis, & quia hoc non est semper nobis notum, de quacunque propositione, ideo non quæcunque per se nota ex natura sua, est per se nota quoad nos. Talis autem propositionis non formamus proprios conceptus distinctos, sed confusos: & ideo non est alia, sed eadem: non tamen per se nota nobis quia immediationem prædicati & subiecti non cognoscimus.

To the third: The antecedent is to be denied, namely that a proposition known per se is that which is such from its proper concepts formed by any intellect whatever; rather it is that between whose predicate and subject no middle is given through which it is demonstrable a priori. And because this is not always known to us of any proposition whatever, therefore not every proposition known per se by its nature is known per se as regards us. Of such a proposition, however, we do not form proper distinct concepts, but confused ones; and therefore it is not another but the same; yet not known per se to us, because we do not cognize the immediacy of the predicate and the subject.

p. 633

QUESTION III

QVÆSTIO III.

[…]

An nuda definitio sit principium, quod vocatur positio.

Whether a bare definition is a principle which is called a position.

20 DEfinitio duobus modis considerari potest: Primo, Secundùm rationem definitionis præcisam, vt explicat naturam definiti: vt animal rationale. Secundo, vt simul definitio coniungitur in propositione: vt cùm dicimus, homo est animal rationale. Et primo modo nuda sumitur, hoc est, sine definito: & de ea sic accepta quærimus, An sit principium demonstrationis, quòd vocatur positio. Et rationem dubitandi ex vna parte præbuit Arist. qui positionem diuisit in eam, quæ est propositio, verum aut falsum continens. Et in aliam, quę non continet verum, aut falsum: qualis est definitio, nudè quidam accepta, & non cum definito: quia dum definito coniungitur, iam continet verum aut falsum, cùm efficiat cum eo propositionem. Ex quo euidenter infertur pars affirmatiua, quòd nudè definitio sit principium, quòd vocatur positio.

20 A definition can be considered in two ways. First, according to the precise ratio of definition, as it explains the nature of the definitum: as rational animal. Second, as the definition is at the same time joined in a proposition: as when we say, Man is a rational animal. And in the first way it is taken bare, that is, without the definitum; and of it so taken we ask whether it is a principle of demonstration which is called a position. And on the one side Aristotle supplied the reason for doubting, who divided position into that which is a proposition containing the true or the false, and into another which does not contain the true or the false; such as is the definition, taken barely, that is, and not with the definitum: because when it is joined to the definitum it already contains the true or the false, since it makes a proposition with it. From which the affirmative part is evidently inferred, namely that a bare definition is a principle which is called a position.

21 Sed opposita pars, quòd non possit esse positio, videtur probari euidenter hoc argu. à superiori ad inferius negatiuè: Quia principium diuisir Aristo. in Dignitatem, & Positionem, & rursus positionem, in eam, quæ continet verum, aut falsum: & in eam quæ nihil horum dicit: qualis est definitio. Ex hoc ergo desumitur tale arg. Principium est quid superius, ratione dignitatis, & positionis, cùm in hæc principia specialia diuidatur: ergo euidens est talis consequentia, à superiori ad inferius negatiuè. Definitio non est principium: ergo non est positio. Antecedens probatur, ex definitione principij tradita ab eodem Arist. Principium, inquit, est propositio immediata: sed nuda definitio, non est propositio: ergo nec propositio immediata, & ex consequenti, nec est principium.

21 But the opposite part, that it cannot be a position, seems to be proved evidently by this argument from the superior to the inferior negatively: Because Aristotle divided principle into dignity and position, and again position into that which contains the true or the false, and into that which says neither of these, such as is the definition. From this, therefore, such an argument is taken: Principle is something superior in ratio to dignity and position, since it is divided into these special principles; therefore such a consequence from the superior to the inferior negatively is evident: A definition is not a principle; therefore it is not a position. The antecedent is proved from the definition of principle handed down by the same Aristotle: A principle, he says, is an immediate proposition; but a bare definition is not a proposition; therefore neither an immediate proposition; and consequently it is not a principle.

Plures solutiones adhibentur huic difficultati, quas consultò prætermitto: quia iam nemo eas curat. Solùm afferam solutionem D. Tho. in Comment. huius ca. quam sequuntur ferè omnes moderni: & videtur mihi necessariò admittenda. Positionem duplicem esse, Formalem, & Virtualem Formalis, est propositio. Virtualis verò, est definitio: quia ex ea proximè potest effici propositio, quæ sit formalis suppositio, Arist. ergo vocauit definitionem positionem: non quòd formalis sit positio, sed quòd sit virtualis. Et hoc etiam modo est principium, & immediata propositio.

Many solutions are applied to this difficulty, which I deliberately pass over, because no one now cares for them. I shall bring forward only the solution of St. Thomas in the Commentary on this chapter, which almost all the moderns follow, and which seems to me necessarily to be admitted: that position is twofold, formal and virtual. The formal is a proposition. But the virtual is the definition, because from it can proximately be made a proposition which is a formal supposition. Aristotle therefore called the definition a position, not because it is a formal position, but because it is a virtual one. And in this way also it is a principle and an immediate proposition.

22 Sed cõtra hanc solutionem est arg. Quia si hoc sufficit, vt

22 But against this solution there is an argument: Because, if this suffices in order that

p. 634

definitio dicatur positio, etiam definitum poterit vocari positio. Probatur consequentia: quia sicut ex definitione adiuncta definitio, potest proximè effici propositio, quæ sit formalis positio: eodem modo ex definito adiuncto definitioni: sed definitum non potest vllo modo vocari positio alioqui, cuilibet parti poterit attribui denominatio totius: ergo nec definitio vocari potest positio, propter illam rationem virtualem. Respondetur, negando consequentiam: quia specialis est ratio in definitione: vt dicatur positio virtualis, quę non est in definito, nec in aliis. Nam definitio ex propria natura, est medium ordinatum, per quod passiones demonstrantur de subiecto in scientia: vnde per se & proximè ordinatur, ad constituendam propositionem necessariam, & per se notam: quam non potest constituere, nisi cum definito. Per se etiam ponitur in scientia, tanquam fundamentum omnium veritatum eius, & hæc est etiam specialis ratio, propter quam vocari debet positio. Et has speciales rationes considerans Arist. meritò eam vocauit principium, & positionem, quæ non reperiuntur in definito. Nam cùm non sit medium ordinatum ad demonstrandas passiones, nec per se ordinatur ad propositionem per se notam constituendam, potiùs quàm ad constituendam quamlibet aliam, non ponitur, tanquam fundamentum proximum omnium veritatum eiusdem scientiæ, sed ad summum remotum. Ideo non potest vllo modo vocari positio.

the definition be called a position, the definitum too could be called a position. The consequence is proved: because, just as from the definition joined to the definitum a proposition can proximately be made which is a formal position, so in the same way from the definitum joined to the definition. But the definitum cannot in any way be called a position; otherwise the denomination of the whole could be attributed to any part whatever; therefore neither can the definition be called a position on account of that virtual ratio. The reply is made by denying the consequence: because there is a special ratio in the definition, so that it is called a virtual position, which is not in the definitum, nor in the others. For the definition, of its proper nature, is the ordered middle through which attributes are demonstrated of the subject in a science; whence it is per se and proximately ordered to constituting a necessary and per se known proposition, which it cannot constitute except with the definitum. It is also posited per se in a science as the foundation of all its truths; and this too is a special ratio on account of which it ought to be called a position. And considering these special rationes, which are not found in the definitum, Aristotle deservedly called it a principle and a position. For since the definitum is not a middle ordered to demonstrating attributes, nor is it per se ordered to constituting a proposition known per se rather than to constituting any other whatever, it is not posited as the proximate foundation of all the truths of the same science, but at most as a remote one. Therefore it cannot in any way be called a position.

QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

Quæst. 4. An principia demonstrationis sint magis vera, quàm conclusio: & vniuersaliter, vna propositio an possit esse verior altera — Whether the principles of demonstration are more true than the conclusion, and universally, whether one proposition can be truer than another.

An principia demonstrationis sint magis vera, quàm conclusio, & vniuersaliter, vna propositio, an possit esse verior altera.

[…]

23 PRæsupponenda est definitio veritatis quam omnes recipiũt: Veritas est, adæquatio intellectus cum re, vel ad rem. Adæquatio intellectus vocatur: quia veritas, saltem cõplexa (quam formalem vocare solent) primò, & formaliter reperitur in intellectu, & propositione mentali, per quam enunciat vnum de altero. In propositione verò vocali, & scripta, solùm reperitur tanquam in signo. Dum ergo intellectus ita enunciat per propositionem mentalem, sicut res se habet in se, dicitur verus: dum verò enunciat aliter, ac res se habet in se, dicitur falsus. Nam, vt sæpè Aristot. repetit, ab eo quod res est, vel non est, enunciatio dicitur vera, vel falsa: vt si de Petro sedente enunciet, quòd sedet: verus est, si verò quòd stet, vel non sedeat,

23 The definition of truth which all accept is to be presupposed: Truth is the adequation of the intellect with the thing, or to the thing. It is called an adequation of the intellect because truth, at least complex truth (which they are accustomed to call formal), is found primarily and formally in the intellect and in the mental proposition through which it enunciates one thing of another; but in the vocal and written proposition it is found only as in a sign. When, therefore, the intellect enunciates through a mental proposition as the thing is in itself, it is called true; but when it enunciates otherwise than the thing is in itself, it is called false. For, as Aristotle often repeats, from the fact that the thing is or is not, an enunciation is called true or false: as, if of Peter sitting it enunciates that he sits, it is true; but if that he stands, or does not sit,

p. 635

erit falsus. Veritas igitur consistit, in adæquatione conceptus cum re ipsa: vel in adæquatione rei, vt repræsentatæ per conceptum, cum seipsa, vt est in se. Quærimus ergo: An complexa hæc veritas, suscipiat magis & minus, in ordine ad præmissas, & conclusionem: ita vt intellectus dum assentitur præmissis, magis verus sit, quàm dum assentitur conclusioni: & ex consequenti, præmissæ in intellectu, quæ sunt propositiones mentales, sint magis veræ, quàm conclusio, etiam in mente: quæ est propositio mentalis ex eis deducta: & consequenter, eadem principia, vt sunt propositiones vocales, aut scriptæ, sint veriora conclusione vocali, aut scripta. Et vniuersaliter, intellectus per vnam propositionem mentalem, an magis verus sit quàm per alteram: & propositio ipsa mentalis, sit verior: atque ex consequenti, vocalis & scripta.

it will be false. Truth therefore consists in the adequation of the concept with the thing itself, or in the adequation of the thing, as represented through the concept, with itself as it is in itself. We ask, therefore, whether this complex truth admits of more and less in order to the premises and the conclusion: so that the intellect, when it assents to the premises, is more true than when it assents to the conclusion; and consequently the premises in the intellect, which are mental propositions, are more true than the conclusion, also in the mind, which is a mental proposition deduced from them; and consequently the same principles, as they are vocal or written propositions, are truer than the vocal or written conclusion. And universally, whether the intellect is more true through one mental proposition than through another, and the mental proposition itself is truer, and consequently the vocal and written one.

24 Prima opinio: Negat præmissas esse veriores conclusione: & vniuersaliter vnam propositionem esse veriorem altera. Ita tenent ex modernis nonnulli. Probant ex intrinseca ratione veritatis. Nam veritas consistit in adæquatione conceptus cum re ipsa repræsentata. Ita vt tunc verus sit, quando repræsentat rem, sicut se habet in se: falsus verò, cùm eam alio modo repræsentat: sed adæquato consistit in diuisibili: ita vt non possit intelligi maior, aut minor: ergo veritas propositionis etiam consistit in indiuisibili: ita, vt non possit maior, aut minor intelligi in diuersis propositionibus. Probatur minor: quia adæquatio est quædam æqualitas conceptus repræsentantis, cum re repræsentata: sed æqualitas consistit in indiuisibili: ita vt non possit esse maior vel minor. Quia si duo corpora habent æqualem magnitudinem, ita vt neutrum excedat alterum: tunc dicuntur æqualia: si verò vnum excedat alterum, quantumuis minimo excessu, non erunt æqualia, sed simpliciter inæqualia: ergo eodem modo: vel conceptus repræsentat rem, sicut est in se, vel excedit, aut deficit, quantumlibet minimo excessu. Si primo modo se habeat, verus erit: si secundo, falsus: & consequenter, si propositio enunciat rem sicuti est, erit vera, si verò excedat, vel deficiat, quantumlibet parum, erit falsa: non potest igitur intelligi, quòd sit vna magis vera, quàm alia: sed eo ipso, quòd minùs vera excogitatur, erit falsa. Gratia exempli: Non minùs verum erit Petrum esse album, si ei albedo inhæret, quàm esse hominem: quia non minùs adæquatur vna propositio rei significatæ, quàm altera: sicut si duo corpora sint æqualia, non erit possibile excogitare alia magis æqualia.

24 The first opinion denies that the premises are truer than the conclusion, and universally that one proposition is truer than another. So hold some among the moderns. They prove it from the intrinsic ratio of truth. For truth consists in the adequation of the concept with the thing itself represented, so that it is true when it represents the thing as it is in itself, but false when it represents it in another way. But adequation consists in an indivisible, so that a greater or lesser cannot be understood; therefore the truth of a proposition also consists in an indivisible, so that a greater or lesser cannot be understood in different propositions. The minor is proved: because adequation is a certain equality of the representing concept with the thing represented; but equality consists in an indivisible, so that it cannot be greater or lesser. Because if two bodies have equal magnitude, so that neither exceeds the other, then they are called equal; but if one exceeds the other by however small an excess, they will not be equal, but simply unequal. Therefore in the same way: either the concept represents the thing as it is in itself, or it exceeds or falls short by however small an excess. If it is in the first way, it will be true; if in the second, false. And consequently, if a proposition enunciates the thing as it is, it will be true; but if it exceeds or falls short, however little, it will be false. It cannot, therefore, be understood that one is more true than another; but by the very fact that it is thought of as less true, it will be false. For example: it will be no less true that Peter is white, if whiteness inheres in him, than that he is a man: because the one proposition is no less adequated to the thing signified than the other; just as, if two bodies are equal, it will not be possible to think of others more equal.

Secundam opinionem tenent ex modernis alij. Affirmantes,

Others among the moderns hold the second opinion, affirming

p. 636

principia esse veriora conclusione: & vniuersaliter, vnam propositionem veriorem altera. Probatur testimonio Arist. 4. Met. tex 18. vbi docet aliquid esse magis verum, quàm aliud, & pariter magis falsum. quod sic probat: Quia non æquè mentitur, qui dicit quatuor esse quinque, ac ille, qui dicit, quatuor esse millia: ergo magis falsum est, quod iste asserit, quàm quod ille: sed falsum, est contrarium veritati: ergo eodem modo erit vna propositio magis vera quàm alia. Probatur consequentia: quia contrariorum eadem est ratio. Præterea cap. præsenti, docet expresè, conclusionem esse veram propter præmissas: ergo pręmissę erunt magis veræ: quia propter quod vnumquodque tale, & illud magis.

that the principles are truer than the conclusion, and universally that one proposition is truer than another. This is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 18, where he teaches that something is more true than something else, and likewise more false; which he proves thus: Because he who says that four are five does not lie equally with him who says that four are a thousand; therefore what the latter asserts is more false than what the former asserts; but the false is contrary to truth; therefore in the same way one proposition will be more true than another. The consequence is proved: because the ratio of contraries is the same. Moreover, in the present chapter he teaches expressly that the conclusion is true on account of the premises; therefore the premises will be more true, because that on account of which each thing is such is itself more so.

Probant deinde ratione: Quia à nemine negatur principia esse certiora, euidentiora, & magis necessaria, quàm conclusionem, cùm sint per se certa, per se euidentia, per se necessaria, hoc est, sine vllo medio, sed quibus intellectus, cognita tantùm significatione terminorum assentitur: conclusio verò non sit certa, euidens, aut necessaria per se, sed per aliud: hoc est, per principia, quibus mediis ei assentitur intellectus sed magis certum, magis euidens, & magis necessarium, est magis verum: ergo erit eodem modo magis vera. Et certè, si vna propositio non esset verior altera, non esset fides diuina magis vera, quàm scientia, aut quàm quælibet alia cognitio humana. Vnde, nec magis verum esset, quòd Deus est trinus & vnus, quàm quòd paries est albus, cui inhæret albedo: quod tamen falsum est, & contra D. Tho. 2. 2. q. 4. art. 8. vbi docet: fidem diuinam ex propria natura certiorem esse quacunque scientia nostra.

They prove it next by reason: Because it is denied by no one that the principles are more certain, more evident, and more necessary than the conclusion, since they are certain per se, evident per se, necessary per se, that is, without any middle, but such that the intellect assents to them once the signification of the terms alone is cognized; whereas the conclusion is not certain, evident, or necessary per se, but through another, that is, through the principles, by means of which the intellect assents to it. But what is more certain, more evident, and more necessary is more true; therefore in the same way it will be more true. And certainly, if one proposition were not truer than another, divine faith would not be more true than science, or than any other human cognition whatever. Whence neither would it be more true that God is three and one than that the wall in which whiteness inheres is white; which, however, is false, and against St. Thomas, 2.2, q. 4, a. 8, where he teaches that divine faith, of its proper nature, is more certain than any science of ours.

26 Nostra sententia, medium tenet inter hæc extrema, & explicatur hac distinctione: Veritas duobus modis potest considerari. Primo, Formaliter, ex parte essentiæ: quæ consistit in adæquatione intellectus per conceptum, vel iudicium cum re, extra existente, per eundem conceptum repræsentata. Secundo, ex parte fundamenti, & causarum eius. Fundamentum, est entitas & perfectio ipsarum rerum, circa quas versatur. Nam cùm verum, sit passio entis, quæ perfectiora sunt secundùm entitatem, censentur etiam perfectiora secundùm veritatem. Causæ autem veritatis esse possunt, necessitas, infallibilitas, certitudo, atque euidentia: pondus etiam, siue momentum rationum, quibus probatur.

26 Our view holds the middle between these extremes, and is explained by this distinction: Truth can be considered in two ways. First, formally, on the part of its essence, which consists in the adequation of the intellect, through a concept or judgment, with the thing existing outside, represented through the same concept. Second, on the part of its foundation and its causes. The foundation is the entity and perfection of the things themselves with which it is concerned. For since the true is an attribute of being, the things that are more perfect according to entity are judged also more perfect according to truth. And the causes of truth can be necessity, infallibility, certitude, and evidence; also the weight, or moment, of the reasons by which it is proved.

27 Duplici ergo conclusione respondemus. Prima, Veritas ex parte rationis formalis, & essentialis ipsius adæquationis, in qua consistit, non potest esse maior in vna propositione, quàm in alia. Secunda, ex parte fundamenti, & causarum eius, maior esse potest: &

27 We reply, therefore, with a twofold conclusion. The first: Truth, on the part of the formal and essential ratio of the adequation itself in which it consists, cannot be greater in one proposition than in another. The second: On the part of its foundation and its causes it can be greater; and

p. 637

ideo vna propositio ex hac parte magis vera, quàm altera. Vtraque conclusio cum distinctione adducta, continetur expresè in doctrina D. Th. q. 2. de virtutibus, art. 9. vbi ita ait: Cùm veritas consistat in adæquatione intellectus, & rei: si consideretur veritas secundùm rationem æqualitatis, quæ non recipit magis & minus, sic non contingit esse aliquid magis, & minus verum. Sed si consideretur ipsum esse rei, quæ est ratio veritatis, sicut dicitur in 2. Meta. eadem est dispositio rerum in esse, & veritate: vnde quæ sunt magis entia, sunt magis vera: & propter hæc etiam in scientiis demonstratiuis, magis creduntur principia, quàm conclusiones. Et primam conclusionem nostram probat arg. primæ opinionis. Secundam verò, probant arg. opinionis secundæ. & ideo non est necessarium illi, aut his respondere.

therefore one proposition, on this side, is more true than another. Each conclusion, with the distinction adduced, is expressly contained in the doctrine of St. Thomas, On the Virtues q. 2, a. 9, where he says thus: Since truth consists in the adequation of the intellect and the thing, if truth is considered according to the ratio of equality, which does not admit of more and less, then it does not happen that something is more and less true. But if the very being of the thing is considered, which is the ratio of truth, as is said in Metaph. 2, the disposition of things in being and in truth is the same; whence the things that are more beings are more true; and on account of this also in the demonstrative sciences the principles are believed more than the conclusions. And the argument of the first opinion proves our first conclusion; but the arguments of the second opinion prove the second; and therefore it is not necessary to reply to the former or to the latter.

29 Solùm restat explicandum, quomodo sit loquendum absolutè in hac re: An dicendum sit absolutè, Præmissas esse veriores conclusione: & vnam propositionem veriorem alia: vel absolutè negandum. Respondeo: Eodem modo loquendum esse, vt loquimur in substantia. Quia sicut substantia non habet latitudinem gradualem, sed consistit in indiuisibili ratio eius, ita veritas non habet latitudinem gradualem, sed ratio eius consistit in indiuisibili adęquationis. In substantiis autem, non dicimus vnam esse magis substantiam, quàm aliam, sed id negamus absolutè cum Arist. dicimus autem, vnam substantiam esse meliorem aut perfectiorem alia: aut secundùm maiorem perfectionem specificam, aut indiuidualem: pari ratione de veritatibus seu propositionibus veris loquendum est. Ita vt absolutè negandum sit, vnam propositionem esse veriorem altera. Concedendum tamen, habere perfectiorem veritatem: aut essentialiter, aut indiuidualiter. Et ideo dicendum est: Præmissas perfectiorem veritatem specificam continere, quàm conclusionem, & vnam conclusionem, perfectiorem veritatem indiuidualem, quàm alteram: quia proximior est principiis, à quibus ambæ deriuantur. Et eodem modo loquendum est de falsitate. Quamuis perfectio, non bene ad falsitatem applicetur, quæ nihil est, sed loquẽdum est de illa, iuxta naturam eius, eodem modo, ac loquimur de veritate: quamuis distinctis terminis, aut modis loquendi. Hæc tamen ratio reperitur particularis in falsitate, quòd hæc, cùm sit quasi recessus à veritate, præter causas illas, propter quas vna veritas dicitur perfectior alia: & vna propositio perfectiorem veritatem continere quàm alia: vna falsitas dicitur etiam maior, aut ingentior alia: & vna propositio continere maiorem falsitatem, quàm alia: quia magis à veritate recedit. In quo sensu dixit Aristot. vbi supra,

29 It only remains to explain how one is to speak absolutely on this matter: whether it is to be said absolutely that the premises are truer than the conclusion, and one proposition truer than another, or it is to be denied absolutely. I reply: one is to speak in the same way as we speak of substance. Because just as substance does not have a gradual latitude, but its ratio consists in an indivisible, so truth does not have a gradual latitude, but its ratio consists in the indivisible of adequation. But in substances we do not say that one is more a substance than another; rather, we deny this absolutely with Aristotle; but we do say that one substance is better or more perfect than another, either according to a greater specific perfection or a greater individual one. In like manner one is to speak of truths, or true propositions; so that it is to be denied absolutely that one proposition is truer than another; but it is to be granted that it has a more perfect truth, either essentially or individually. And therefore it is to be said that the premises contain a more perfect specific truth than the conclusion, and one conclusion a more perfect individual truth than another, because it is nearer to the principles from which both are derived. And in the same way one is to speak of falsity. Although perfection is not well applied to falsity, which is nothing, yet one is to speak of it according to its nature in the same way as we speak of truth, though in distinct terms or modes of speaking. This particular ratio, however, is found in falsity: that, since it is as it were a recession from truth, besides those causes on account of which one truth is said to be more perfect than another, and one proposition to contain a more perfect truth than another, one falsity is also said to be greater or more enormous than another, and one proposition to contain a greater falsity than another, because it recedes more from truth. In which sense Aristotle said, in the place cited above,

p. 638

magis mentiri eum, qui dicit quatuor esse mille, quàm alium qui diceret quatuor esse quinque: cuius sensus est, ingentius proferre mendacium.

that he lies more who says that four are a thousand than another who should say that four are five: whose sense is that he utters a more enormous lie.

QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

An semper sit necessarium, vtramque præmissam demonstrationis, certiorem esse conclusione.

Whether it is always necessary that each premise of a demonstration be more certain than the conclusion.

30 PRæmissæ demonstrationis, in duplici differentia possunt esse. Nam vel sunt propositiones Immediatæ, atque indemonstrabiles: vel Demonstrari possunt. Quod vt intelligatur, sciendum est, quòd omnes conclusiones totius scientiæ, continentur virtualiter in principiis eiusdem scientiæ, à quibus suo ordine procedunt, ita vt quædam proximiores sint principiis, quã aliæ: Vnde quædam demonstratur per alias priores, mediatas tamen, & adhuc demonstrabiles, quousque perueniatur ad aliquam immediatè deriuatam ex principiis. Et hinc est, quòd non omnes demonstrationes habent præmissas immediatas, vel indemonstrabiles: sed plures, vnam saltem, vel alteram, quæ demonstrari potest. Gratia exempli: Ab essentia hominis procedunt plures passiones, vt capacitas disciplinæ, admiratio, & risibilitas: tali ordine, vt capacitas disciplinæ procedat immediatè. & hac media, admiratio: media verò admiratione, risibilitas: & iuxta hunc ordinem demonstrantur in scientia de illo: prima per essentiam: secunda per primam: & tertia per secundam: & ideo demonstratio illa, per quam demonstratur prima passio de essentia, habet vtramque præmissam immediatam, atque indemonstrabilem: alia verò in quibus demonstrantur reliquæ, vnam quidem præmissam indemonstrabilem, & aliam quæ demonstrari potest. Prima passio demonstratur sic: Omne animal rationale est capax disciplinæ: Omnis homo est animal rationale: ergo Omnis homo est capax disciplinæ. Cuius demonstrationis vtraque præmissa est immediata, maior quidem, in qua prædicatur prima passio de essentia: & minor, in qua prædicatur definitio de definito. Sed in sequente demonstratione per primam demonstratur passio secunda: Quidquid est capax disciplinæ: est admiratiuum: Omnis homo est capax disciplinæ: ergo Omnis homo est admiratiuus. Cuius maior, est propositio immediata, in qua vna passio immediata prædicatur de altera: minor verò demonstrari potest.

30 The premises of a demonstration can be of a twofold kind. For either they are immediate and indemonstrable propositions, or they can be demonstrated. In order that this may be understood, it must be known that all the conclusions of a whole science are contained virtually in the principles of the same science, from which they proceed in their order, so that some are nearer to the principles than others. Whence some are demonstrated through other, prior ones, which are, however, mediate and still demonstrable, until one arrives at some one derived immediately from the principles. And hence it is that not all demonstrations have immediate or indemonstrable premises, but many have at least one or the other which can be demonstrated. For example: from the essence of man proceed many attributes, such as capacity for learning, wonder, and risibility, in such an order that capacity for learning proceeds immediately, and by means of this, wonder, and by means of wonder, risibility; and according to this order they are demonstrated in the science of man: the first through the essence, the second through the first, and the third through the second. And therefore that demonstration through which the first attribute is demonstrated of the essence has each premise immediate and indemonstrable; but the others, in which the remaining ones are demonstrated, have one premise indeed indemonstrable, and another which can be demonstrated. The first attribute is demonstrated thus: Every rational animal is capable of learning; every man is a rational animal; therefore every man is capable of learning. Each premise of this demonstration is immediate: the major, in which the first attribute is predicated of the essence; the minor, in which the definition is predicated of the definitum. But in the following demonstration the second attribute is demonstrated through the first: Whatever is capable of learning is capable of wonder; every man is capable of learning; therefore every man is capable of wonder. Whose major is an immediate proposition, in which one immediate attribute is predicated of another; but the minor can be demonstrated.

31 His expositis, vnum pręsupponit quæstio & alterum quærit

31 These things set out, the question presupposes one thing and asks

p. 639

. Præsupponit quidem, Præmissas esse certiores conclusione sic in communi. Quod non solùm est assertum ab Aristotele, sed expresè probatum: quia certitudo conclusionis deriuatur à præmissis: & ideo certiores esse oportet. Quod præsertim verum est, ac necessarium, dum præmissæ sunt propositiones immediatæ: nam illæ ex se, & à se habent certitudinem: conclusio verò, non ex se, neque à se, sed deriuatam ab eis: at magis certum est, quod à se habet certitudinem, quàm quod habet ab alio: ergo præmissæ immediatæ certiores sunt conclusione. Quæstio igitur solùm potest esse, de præmissis demonstrabilibus, An istæ etiam debeant esse certiores conclusione? ita vt dum demonstratio habet vnam immediatam, & alteram demonstrabilem, sufficiat conclusionem esse minùs certam, quàm illam: & possit esse æqualis in certitudine cum altera: vel necesse sit, etiam esse minùs certam, quàm præmissam demonstrabilem.

another. It presupposes, indeed, that the premises are more certain than the conclusion, taken thus in common. Which has been not only asserted by Aristotle but expressly proved: because the certitude of the conclusion is derived from the premises, and therefore they must be more certain. Which is especially true and necessary when the premises are immediate propositions: for they have certitude of themselves and from themselves, but the conclusion not of itself nor from itself, but derived from them; but what has certitude from itself is more certain than what has it from another; therefore immediate premises are more certain than the conclusion. The question, therefore, can only be about demonstrable premises: whether these too ought to be more certain than the conclusion; so that, when a demonstration has one immediate premise and another demonstrable one, it suffices that the conclusion be less certain than the former, and it can be equal in certitude with the other; or whether it is necessary that it also be less certain than the demonstrable premise.

32 Et prima opinio tenet, Hoc non esse necessarium, sed posse esse conclusionem æqualiter certam cum præmissa demonstrabili. Ita tenent moderni quidam. Et probant, testimonio Aristo. in fine huius cap. vbi non dixit necessarium esse magis credere omnibus principiis, quàm conclusioni, sed aut omnibus, aut aliquibus: Sentit ergo habere conclusionem æqualem certitudinem, cum aliquo eorum.

32 And the first opinion holds that this is not necessary, but the conclusion can be equally certain with the demonstrable premise. So hold certain moderns. And they prove it by the testimony of Aristotle at the end of this chapter, where he did not say that it is necessary to believe all the principles more than the conclusion, but either all or some; he thinks, therefore, that the conclusion has equal certitude with some one of them.

Probant deinde ratione: Quia si præmissæ debent semper esse certiores conclusione, maximè propter rationem Aristot. nempe propter quod vnumquodque tale, & illud magis: sed hæc non probat, nisi in causis æquiuocis, non in vniuocis: ergo non probat de omnibus præmissis, sed solùm de immediatis. Probatur consequentia: quia solùm præmissæ immediatæ sunt causæ æquiuocæ conclusionis, quia differunt specie ab illa: pręmissa verò demonstrabilis, cùm sit assensus scientificus, eiusdem speciei est cum conclusione: & ideo non potest esse causa æquiuoca eius, sed vniuoca semper erit. Vnde non erit necessarium, quòd sit certior conclusione. Minorem verò probant: quia effectus causæ vniuocæ, æqualis perfectionis est cum ea, vt patet in homine generante, & genito.

They prove it next by reason: Because, if the premises ought always to be more certain than the conclusion, it is most of all on account of Aristotle’s reason, namely, that on account of which each thing is such is itself more so; but this does not prove except in equivocal causes, not in univocal ones; therefore it does not prove of all premises, but only of the immediate ones. The consequence is proved: because only the immediate premises are equivocal causes of the conclusion, because they differ in species from it; but the demonstrable premise, since it is a scientific assent, is of the same species as the conclusion, and therefore cannot be its equivocal cause, but will always be a univocal one. Whence it will not be necessary that it be more certain than the conclusion. And they prove the minor: because the effect of a univocal cause is of equal perfection with it, as is plain in the man generating and the one generated.

Secundò potest probari: Quia conclusiones eiusdem scientiæ deriuantur ab eisdem principiis: ergo æqualem habent certitudinem ab eis deriuatam: sed sæpè contingit conclusionem, & præmissam demonstrabilem, pertinere ad eandem scientiam, vt ostendit secunda demonstratio à nobis adducta, in principio huius quæstionis: ergo habebit æqualem certitudinem cum ea. Quod firmiùs probari potest in

Second, it can be proved: Because the conclusions of the same science are derived from the same principles; therefore they have equal certitude derived from them; but it often happens that the conclusion and the demonstrable premise pertain to the same science, as the second demonstration adduced by us at the beginning of this question shows; therefore it will have equal certitude with it. Which can be proved more firmly in

p. 640

demonstrationibus Theologicis, in quibus conclusio procedit, ex vna præmissa pertinente ad fidem diuinam, & ex altera pertinente ad Philosophiam naturalem: vt ostenditur in hac: Omnis homo est risibilis: Christus est homo: ergo Christus est risibilis. Tunc ergo vel conclusio pertinet ad fidem diuinã, vel ad habitũ scientiæ Theologicæ: & vtroque modo est certior præmissa euidenti: Quia fides diuina certior est scientia. Igitur id etiam, quod à fide diuina deriuatur, certius erit: illa ergo conclusio, Christus est risibilis, certior est, quocunque modo accipiatur, maiore præmissa, nempe Omnis homo est risibilis, quare non solùm conclusio æqualem potest habere certitudinem, cũ altera præmissarũ, sed aliquando maiorem.

Theological demonstrations, in which the conclusion proceeds from one premise pertaining to divine faith and from another pertaining to natural Philosophy, as is shown in this one: Every man is risible; Christ is a man; therefore Christ is risible. Then, therefore, the conclusion pertains either to divine faith or to the habit of Theological science; and in either way it is more certain than the evident premise. Because divine faith is more certain than science; therefore that too which is derived from divine faith will be more certain. That conclusion, therefore, Christ is risible, in whatever way it is taken, is more certain than the major premise, namely Every man is risible. Wherefore the conclusion can have not only equal certitude with one of the premises, but sometimes greater.

Nostra sententia est: Vtramque præmissam semper, & necessariò esse certiorem conclusione: ita, vt nullo casu possit habere æqualem certitudinem cum aliqua earum. Et hæc est magis communis inter modernos.

Our view is: Each premise is always and necessarily more certain than the conclusion, so that in no case can it have equal certitude with either of them. And this is the more common view among the moderns.

Probatur duplici arg. Primo: Quia in demonstratione propter quid (de qua loquimur) præmissa demonstrabilis agit in virtute principiorum, à quibus proximiùs deriuatur, quàm conclusio: cùm hæc deriuetur mediante illa: ergo maiorem habebit certitudinem. Probatur euidenter consequentia: quia quo effectus proximus deriuatur à causa, eò perfectiùs participat virtutem eius: pręsertim comparatione alterius effectus: à quo non nisi vllo mediante participatur.

It is proved by a twofold argument. First: Because in a demonstration propter quid (of which we are speaking) the demonstrable premise acts in virtue of the principles, from which it is derived more proximately than the conclusion, since the latter is derived by means of it; therefore it will have greater certitude. The consequence is evidently proved: because the more proximately an effect is derived from a cause, the more perfectly it participates its virtue, especially in comparison with another effect, by which it is participated only through some medium.

Secundo. Quia præmissæ, quæcunque illæ sint, continent vnionem extremitatum cum medio: conclusio verò continet vnionem earundem extremitatum inter sese, media vnione earum cum medio, tãquam ratione formali, ac totali: propter quàm vniuntur inter se: ergo prior vnio, à quo totaliter dependet secunda fortior est, cùm sit immediatior: sed fortioré esse vnionem extremitatum cum medio, est certiores esse præmissas, ergo maior certitudo prouenit eis, ex natura demonstrationis. Quare repugnat conclusionem, habere æqualem certitudinem, cum aliqua earum.

Second: Because the premises, whatever they may be, contain the union of the extremes with the middle; but the conclusion contains the union of the same extremes with each other, by means of their union with the middle, as the formal and total ratio on account of which they are united with each other; therefore the prior union, on which the second totally depends, is stronger, since it is more immediate. But for the union of the extremes with the middle to be stronger is for the premises to be more certain; therefore greater certitude comes to them from the nature of demonstration. Wherefore it is repugnant that the conclusion should have equal certitude with either of them.

Ad testimonium Arist. Respondet D. Thom in Commentariis illius, non dixisse, omnia principia certiora esse conclusione sed saltem aliqua: quia licet ex virtute demonstrationis semper sit vtraque pręmissa certior, contingit tamen aliquando conclusionem habere aliam certitudinem experientiæ, præter eã, quam à præmissis participat, ratione cuius habebit æqualem certitudinem cum aliqua præmissarum: vt dum quòd luna nunc eclipsetur, experientia sensuum cognoscimus: & ideo non est minus nobis certa, quã quòd terra interponatur inter

To the testimony of Aristotle, St. Thomas replies, in his Commentary on that passage, that he did not say that all the principles are more certain than the conclusion, but at least some: because, although by the force of the demonstration each premise is always more certain, it nevertheless happens sometimes that the conclusion has another certitude, of experience, besides that which it participates from the premises, by reason of which it will have equal certitude with one of the premises: as when we cognize by the experience of the senses that the moon is now eclipsed; and therefore it is not less certain to us than that the earth is interposed between

p. 641

eam, & solem, per quam demonstratur à priori: tamen per accidens contingit hoc: & ideo non tollit, quin per se, & ex virtute demonstrationis semper sit vtraque præmissa certior conclusione.

it and the sun, through which it is demonstrated a priori. Yet this happens per accidens, and therefore it does not prevent each premise from always being, per se and by the force of the demonstration, more certain than the conclusion.

35 Primum arg. petit expositionem illius vniuersalis axiomatis: Propter quod vnumquodque tale, & illud magis. Vt constet in quo sensu verum sit: & cur ab Arist. adductum, ad probandum pręmissas debere esse certiores conclusione. Et an ex illo efficaciter probetur. Plures ac variæ expositiones eius adducuntur à diuersis interpretibus. Plures etiam, & diuersas conditiones requirunt, ad veritatem eius quas molestum esset referre. Nos igitur tres conditiones requisitas esse dicimus, vt verum sit: quarum duas posuit ipsemet Arist. 4. lib. Meta. tex. 4. idemmet axioma referens his verbis: Vnumquodque autem maximè tale est, præ cæteris, cuius causa nomine & ratione idem conuenit: sic ignis est calidissimus, quòd cæteris caloris causa sit. Quibus, Primò, asserit, prædicatum debere conuenire pluribus formaliter: & vni eorum per se primò, aliis verò per participationem eius, & non aliundo. Secundò: Eidem primo & cæteris nomine, & ratione, hoc est vniuocè: & ideo essentialiter. Tertiam conditionem posuit D. Th. 1. part. q. 87 art. 2. ad 3. quòd in eodem ordine causarum contineantur, hoc est, in eodem genere causæ efficientis, vel finalis, aut quouis alio. Ita, vt si illud cui per se primò prædicatum conuenit, sit finis, cætera sint media ad ipsum ordinata: & si illud sit efficiens, cætera sint quasi effectus ab ipso procedentes. His igitur tribus conditionibus concurrentibus verum est, ac necessarium illud axioma. Propter quod vnumquodque tale, & illud magis tale. Cuius sensus est: Si aliquid conuenit multis, & vni eorum per se primò: quòd ideo dicitur maximè, tale, aliis verò propter ipsum, necesse est magis conuenire primo, quàm cæteris. Nec potest dari aliquis casus, in quo oppositum contingat.

35 The first argument asks for an exposition of that universal axiom, That on account of which each thing is such, is itself more so: so that it may be clear in what sense it is true, and why it was adduced by Aristotle to prove that the premises must be more certain than the conclusion, and whether it is proved efficaciously from it. Many and various expositions of it are brought forward by different interpreters. They also require many and diverse conditions for its truth, which it would be tedious to report. We, then, say that three conditions are required for it to be true. Two of them Aristotle himself laid down in Metaph. 4, text 4, reporting this same axiom in these words: Each thing is most of all such, in preference to the others, to which, as cause, the same thing belongs in name and in ratio: thus fire is hottest, because it is the cause of heat to the others. By which he asserts, first, that the predicate must belong to several formally, and to one of them per se primarily, but to the others through participation in it, and not from elsewhere. Second, that it belongs to the same one first and to the others in name and in ratio, that is, univocally, and therefore essentially. The third condition St. Thomas laid down in 1 p., q. 87, a. 2, ad 3: that they be contained in the same order of causes, that is, in the same genus of efficient or final cause, or any other whatever; so that, if that to which the predicate belongs per se primarily is the end, the others are means ordered to it; and if it is the efficient, the others are as it were effects proceeding from it. When these three conditions concur, then, that axiom is true and necessary: That on account of which each thing is such, is itself more such. Its sense is: If something belongs to many, and to one of them per se primarily (which is therefore said to be most of all such), but to the others on account of it, it must belong more to the first than to the others. Nor can any case be given in which the opposite happens.

Ex eodem axiomate, efficax deduxit arg. Arist. ad probandum, certiores, euidentiores, magis necessarias esse, perfectiorémque veritatem continere præmissas, quàm conclusionem: quia tam illis, quàm huic conuenit formaliter certitudo, euidentia, necessitas, atque veritas: & omnes continentur in eodem ordine causæ efficientis: præmissis etiam conueniunt hęc, per se primò: conclusioni verò, vt conclusio demonstrationis est solùm propter pręmissas, & non aliunde: ideo euidenter infertur, quòd magis aut perfectiùs eis conueniant.

From this axiom Aristotle drew an efficacious argument to prove that the premises are more certain, more evident, more necessary, and contain a more perfect truth than the conclusion: because certitude, evidence, necessity, and truth belong formally both to them and to it, and all are contained in the same order of efficient cause; and these belong to the premises per se primarily, but to the conclusion, as the conclusion of a demonstration, only on account of the premises and not from elsewhere. Therefore it is evidently inferred that they belong to the premises more, or more perfectly.

Ad formam etiam arg. Neganda est consequentia, quòd solùm teneat verum, prædictum axioma in causis æquiuocis:

To the form of the argument, too: the consequence is to be denied, namely that the aforesaid axiom holds true only in equivocal causes; Ss

p. 642

negandum est, quòd solùm probet de præmissis immediatis, & non de demonstrabilibus. Nam licèt primò probet de illis, consequenter tamen etiam probat de his: quia præmissæ demonstrabiles, non sunt causa conclusionis ex propria virtute, aut secundùm se, sed virtute principiorum, à quibus deriuantur, & vt ab eis deriuantur: cuius euidens signum est, quòd si is qui demonstrationem constituit, nesciat eas reducere ad prima principia, per euidentes demonstrationes: non efficiet demonstrationem, nec habebit scientiam conclusionis: sed efficiet argumentum probabile, generans opinionem. Vnde sequitur, prima principia: virtualiter, & vt talia, esse causam conclusionis. Et ideo per se primò, secundùm eandem rationem virtualem, conuenire eis veritatem, necessitatem, certitudinem, & euidentiam, conclusioni verò solùm propter illa: & propterea illis perfectiùs.

it is to be denied that it proves only of immediate premises and not of demonstrable ones. For although it proves first of the former, it consequently proves of the latter as well: because demonstrable premises are not the cause of the conclusion by their own power, or according to themselves, but by the power of the principles from which they are derived, and as derived from them. Of this there is an evident sign: if the one who constructs a demonstration does not know how to reduce them to the first principles through evident demonstrations, he will not produce a demonstration, nor will he have science of the conclusion, but he will produce a probable argument, generating opinion. Whence it follows that the first principles, virtually and as such, are the cause of the conclusion. And therefore truth, necessity, certitude, and evidence belong to them per se primarily, according to the same virtual ratio, but to the conclusion only on account of them; and for this reason more perfectly to them.

Ad secundum: neganda est consequentia, quòd æqualem habeat certitudinem conclusio, cum præmissis demonstrabilibus, quia omnes deriuantur ab eisdem principiis, nam non deriuantur æquè proximè: ideo non æqualiter non participant certitudinem principiorum, sed perfectiùs illæ: quia magis propriè deriuantur

To the second: the consequence is to be denied, namely that the conclusion has equal certitude with the demonstrable premises because all are derived from the same principles; for they are not derived equally proximately. Therefore they do not participate equally in the certitude of the principles, but the premises more perfectly, because they are derived more properly.

37 Vltimum quod additur in eo secundo arg tangit demonstrationes scientiæ Theologicæ, quæ procedunt ex vna præmissa diuinæ fidei, & ex altera euidenti: & aliquando ex vtraque de fide, per consequentiam euidentem. In quibus dicimus conuincere rationem Aristot. quòd ambæ præmissæ sint certiores conclusione. Quod pręterea probatur, ex cõmuni alio axiomate in scholis recepto: Cõclusio sequitur debiliorem partem præmissarum: ergo si vna, vel ambę sint fidei diuinę, cùm diuina fides sit obscura, non poterit esse euidens conclusio: imò neque habere eandem certitudinem fidei, sed obscura quoque erit. Et si vtraque pręmissa sit diuinę fidei, conclusio obscura erit, & minùs certa vtraque pręmissa. Cuius ratio est: quia pręmissæ fidei non concurrunt in demonstratione Theologica ad inferendã conclusionem, nisi media demonstratione: ergo certitudo earum modificatur per certitudinem consequentiæ quę non potest esse, nisi naturalis: vnde nec poterunt producere conclusionem perfectiorem in certitudine quàm sit perfectio certitudinis naturalis. Sed hęc est minor certitudine diuinæ fidei: ergo minorem habebit certitudinem conclusio, quàm pręmissæ. Et si altera pręmissarum sit certa, certitudine Philosophica minorem habebit certitudinem conclusio. Et si contingeret, quòd altera præmissarum esset solùm probabilis, non posset

37 The last point added in that second argument touches the demonstrations of the science of Theology, which proceed from one premise of divine faith and from another that is evident, and sometimes from both of faith, through an evident consequence. In these we say that Aristotle’s reasoning holds conclusively, namely that both premises are more certain than the conclusion. This is further proved from another common axiom received in the schools: The conclusion follows the weaker part of the premises. Therefore, if one or both are of divine faith, since divine faith is obscure, the conclusion cannot be evident; indeed, it cannot even have the same certitude as faith, but will be obscure as well. And if both premises are of divine faith, the conclusion will be obscure, and less certain than either premise. The reason for this is that the premises of faith do not concur in a Theological demonstration to infer the conclusion except by means of the demonstration; therefore their certitude is modified by the certitude of the consequence, which can be no other than natural. Whence they cannot produce a conclusion more perfect in certitude than is the perfection of natural certitude. But this is less than the certitude of divine faith; therefore the conclusion will have less certitude than the premises. And if one of the premises is certain with philosophical certitude, the conclusion will have less certitude. And if it should happen that one of the premises were only probable, the conclusion could not

p. 643

esse certa conclusio, sed probabilis tantùm. Probantur hæc omnia, duabus illis rationibus: quibus probatum est, præmissas perfectiores esse debere conclusione, in veritate, in certitudine, necessitate, atque euidentia, & in cæteris omnibus. Ex quo deductum est hoc idem axioma: Conclusio sequitur debiliorem partem præmissarum cuius sensus est, nullam posse habere perfectionem æqualem, cum præmissis, sed quicquid imperfectionis est in eis, manifestari debet in conclusione.

be certain, but only probable. All these things are proved by those two reasons by which it was proved that the premises must be more perfect than the conclusion in truth, in certitude, necessity, and evidence, and in all other respects. From which this same axiom was deduced: The conclusion follows the weaker part of the premises; whose sense is that it can have no perfection equal to the premises, but whatever imperfection is in them must be manifested in the conclusion.
