For example, what belongs to man as he is such, namely as he is man, belongs to him as he is such an animal, and not as he has the sensitive nature common to the other animals; but as he is an animal, he is not such an animal; therefore animal does not belong to him as such, nor according as he is himself, or universally. Thus our view asserts two things. The first is that, in order that a predicate belong to a subject universally, it is not required, nor does it suffice, that it belong to it essentially, or in the first mode per se, or even immediately. For it can well belong in these modes and not belong universally; and conversely, it can well belong in the second mode, and not essentially, nor immediately, and belong universally. Thus substance belongs to man essentially and in the first mode per se, and animal even immediately; and yet neither belongs to him universally. And capacity for learning, or wonder, does not belong to man in these modes; nevertheless they belong to him universally. Second, it asserts: That predicate belongs to the subject universally which belongs to it primarily, and according as it is itself, or as it is such; and to belong in this way is to be its adequate ratio, or to belong to it according to its adequate ratio, and by reason of it to whatever others it is attributed. For example: sensible does not belong to man by reason of himself, because it does not belong to him as he is man, but as he is an animal; nor does it belong to him according to his adequate ratio, but according to an inadequate one. Nor does animal belong to man as he is man, since it is common to him with the other animals; nor is it his adequate ratio. And, to explain this in a word: only that predicate belongs to the subject universally which belongs to it per se and is convertible with it. Such are the propositions in which the whole definition is predicated of the thing defined, or also the difference; such too those in which a proper attribute is predicated of its species or genus, from which it proceeds proximately and adequately. And whenever something belongs to something with a reduplication, it is said to belong to it universally, or according as it is itself.

Ad testimonium Arist. Respondetur primò, Quòd dum dicit vniuersaliter idem esse, quod per se: nõ est sensus, quòd cum eo conuertatur, sed quòd sit idem, cum eo, secundùm rem: sicut prędicatum inferius cum superiori. Vel secundò, idem esse vniuersaliter asserit, quod per se conuertibiliter: quòd enim non

To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is, first, that when he says that universally is the same as per se, the sense is not that it is convertible with it, but that it is the same with it in reality, as an inferior predicate with a superior. Or, second, he asserts that universally is the same as per se convertibly; for what is not

p. 659

intelligat esse idem simpliciter, patet ex eo, quod statim docet: nempe, addere supra vtrumque terminum, de omni & per se, quòd sit secundùm quod ipsum.

the same simply, is plain from what he teaches immediately afterward: namely, that what it adds over both terms, of every and per se, is that it be according as it is itself.

Ad arg. Concessa maiori, & minori, negatur consequentia: quòd quælibet pars definitionis, per se sumpta, prædicetur vniuersaliter de definito: quia non conuenit ei vtraque vt tale est: sed sola differentia.

To the argument: granting the major and the minor, the consequence is denied, namely that any part of the definition, taken by itself, is predicated universally of the thing defined; because not both belong to it as it is such, but the difference alone.

CHAPTER X

CAPVT X.

[…]

TEX. ARISTOTELIS.

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE.

Quia verò differt, & propter quid scire, primùm quidem in eadem scientia, & in hac dupliciter.

But knowing that and knowing why differ, first indeed in the same science, and in this in two ways.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

Intentum Arist. in hoc decimo c. est distinguere demonstrationem, Quia, & demonstrationem, Propter quid, & rationem vtriusque explicare. Diuiditur caput in duas partes. In prima, docet differre demonstrationem, Quia, à demonstratione Propter quid, in eadem scientia. In secundis, differre in diuersis scientiis.

ristotle’s intent in this tenth chapter is to distinguish demonstration A quia and demonstration propter quid, and to explain the ratio of each. The chapter is divided into two parts. In the first he teaches that demonstration quia differs from demonstration propter quid in the same science. In the second, that they differ in different sciences.

Differunt, inquit, scire, Quia, & scire, propter quid: & cõsequenter demonstrationes ipsæ, in eadem scientia, duobus modis.

Knowing quia and knowing propter quid, he says, and consequently the demonstrations themselves, differ in the same science in two ways.

1 Nam demonstratio Propter quid, procedit à causa proxima & adæquata: Demonstratio: Quia, à causa remota, & inadæquata: quia non infert positiuè effectum, sed solùm per modum negationis. Et ponit duplex exemplum. Primum, in hac demonstratione, Quidquid respirat, est animal: Paries non est animal: ergo Paries non respirat, in qua patet, esse animal, non esse causam proximam respirandi, sed habere pulmonem: nec etiam esse adæquatam: quia multa sunt animalia, quæ non respirant: quia pulmone carent. Exemplum secundum adducit, ex dicto cuiusdam Philosophi: qui cùm Scytha esset, & Athenis videret mulieres saltantes: rogatus, an in Scythia essent similes saltatrices, respondit, non esse vites. Causam remotam, & inadæquatam reddens: ex qua talis demonstratio constitui potest: Vbi non sunt vites, non sunt saltatrices: sed in Scythia non sunt vites: ergo non sunt saltatrices. Proxima verò causa esset, negatio vini: quod cùm sit causa lætitiæ, ex qua saltatio prouenit: negatio eius, causa esset negationis saltandi. Et quia demonstrationes istæ, procedunt per negationẽ, asserit Arist. fieri semper in secunda figura

1 For demonstration propter quid proceeds from the proximate and adequate cause; demonstration quia from a remote and inadequate cause, because it does not infer the effect positively, but only by way of negation. And he gives a twofold example. The first, in this demonstration: Whatever breathes is an animal; a wall is not an animal; therefore a wall does not breathe; in which it is plain that to be an animal is not the proximate cause of breathing, but to have lungs; nor is it the adequate cause either, because there are many animals which do not breathe, because they lack lungs. The second example he adduces from the saying of a certain Philosopher, who, being a Scythian and seeing women dancing at Athens, when asked whether there were similar dancing-girls in Scythia, replied that there were no vines, giving the remote and inadequate cause; from which such a demonstration can be constructed: Where there are no vines, there are no dancing-girls; but in Scythia there are no vines; therefore there are no dancing-girls. But the proximate cause would be the absence of wine: for since wine is the cause of merriment, from which dancing comes, its absence would be the cause of the absence of dancing. And because these demonstrations proceed by negation, Aristotle asserts that they are always made in the second figure Tt ij

p. 660

quia medium quoque eis, debet esse prędicatum. Secundò differunt: Quia in eadem scientia demonstratio, propter quid, semper procedit à causa: & cùm causa sit prior effectu, dicitur demonstratio à priori: sed demonstratio, quia, procedit ab effectu, quia cùm sit posterior, dicitur demonstratio à posteriori. Duo alia exempla demonstrationis, quia, adducit Arist. Primum in stellis, quæ sunt in duplici differentia: nam aliæ sunt fixæ, vt illæ quæ sunt in octauo cœlo: quod firmamentum appellatur, aliæ verò, quæ sunt in corporibus cœlestibus inferioribus. Et istæ dicuntur Planetæ. Illæ igitur quia longè distant à nobis, videntur habere motum quendam tremoris. & ideo videntur micare vel scintillare, cùm tamen nullum talem motum habeant: sed propter imperfectionem visus, putamus stellas illum habere. Planetæ verò, non apparent cum tali motu, quia minùs distant à nobis. Ex hoc igitur effectu, talis demonstratio, Quia, constitui potest. Stellæ non scintillantes sunt prope nos: Planetæ non scintillant: ergo sunt prope nos. Aliud exemplum adducit in Luna: de qua probare possumus, quòd sit circularis, aut rotunda, ex hoc effectu: quia augmentum lucis modo circulari suscipit. Erit autem talis probatio: Quidquid circulariter illuminatur, rotundum est: sed Luna illuminatur circulariter à Sole: ergo est rotunda.

because their middle too must be predicated. Second, they differ because in the same science demonstration propter quid always proceeds from the cause; and since the cause is prior to the effect, it is called demonstration a priori. But demonstration quia proceeds from the effect, which, because it is posterior, is called demonstration a posteriori. Aristotle adduces two other examples of demonstration quia. The first in the stars, which are of two different kinds: for some are fixed, like those which are in the eighth heaven, which is called the firmament; but others are those which are in the lower heavenly bodies, and these are called Planets. The former, then, because they are far distant from us, seem to have a certain trembling motion, and therefore they seem to twinkle or scintillate, although they have no such motion; but on account of the imperfection of our sight we think the stars have it. But the Planets do not appear with such motion, because they are less distant from us. From this effect, then, such a demonstration quia can be constructed: Stars that do not twinkle are near us; the Planets do not twinkle; therefore they are near us. He adduces another example in the Moon, of which we can prove that it is circular, or round, from this effect: that it receives the increase of its light in a circular manner. And the proof will be this: Whatever is illuminated circularly is round; but the Moon is illuminated circularly by the Sun; therefore it is round.

Sed distinguit duplicem effectum: Adæquatum, quia conuertitur cum causa: & Inadæquatum, qui non conuertitur cum ea: & inquit, quòd si effectus sit adæquatus, ex demonstratione, quia, procedente ab eo, potest fieri demõstratio, propter quid: & ex opposito, ex demonstratione, propter quid, demonstratio quia, vt patet in rationalitate, & risibilitate. Nam illam possumus probare, per hanc, & erit demonstratio, quia: & rursus hanc per illam, & erit demonstratio, propter quid. Si verò effectus sit inadæquatus, poterit ex eo fieri demonstratio, quia per quam probemus causam: non tamen demonstratio, propter quid, per quam ex causa probemus effectum. Et ratio huius differentiæ est, quia effectus adæquatus, conuertitur cum sua causa: sed inadæquatus non conuertitur, & ideo in illo potest vtraque demonstratio fieri: in hoc verò, solùm demonstratio, quia. Nam causa inadæquata, non necessariò infert effectum. Vt si dicamus, quidquid mouetur motu progressiuo, est animal: homo mouetur motu progressiuo: ergo est animal. non licebit demonstrationem, propter quid, à causa procedentem constituere: quia non est verum dicere, quidquid est animal, mouetur motu progressiuo: nam quædam sunt animalia: quibus talis motus non conuenit.

But he distinguishes a twofold effect: adequate, because it is convertible with the cause; and inadequate, which is not convertible with it. And he says that, if the effect is adequate, from a demonstration quia proceeding from it a demonstration propter quid can be made; and conversely, from a demonstration propter quid a demonstration quia: as is plain in rationality and risibility. For we can prove the former through the latter, and it will be a demonstration quia; and again the latter through the former, and it will be a demonstration propter quid. But if the effect is inadequate, a demonstration quia can be made from it, by which we prove the cause, but not a demonstration propter quid, by which we prove the effect from the cause. And the reason for this difference is that the adequate effect is convertible with its cause, but the inadequate one is not convertible; and therefore in the former both demonstrations can be made, but in the latter only demonstration quia. For an inadequate cause does not necessarily infer the effect. Thus, if we say, Whatever moves with progressive motion is an animal; man moves with progressive motion; therefore he is an animal, it will not be possible to construct a demonstration propter quid proceeding from the cause, because it is not true to say that whatever is an animal moves with progressive motion: for there are certain animals to which such motion does not belong.

p. 661

2 In secunda parte docet Arist Differre demonstrationem, propter quid, à demonstratione, quia, in diuersis scientiis: sed diuersas esse scientias, duobus modis contingit, vel subordinatas, ita vt vna collocetur sub altera: & tales sunt Geometria, & Perspectiua: illa agit de linea, & hæc, de linea visuali: & ideo illa vocatur subalternans, hæc verò subalternata. Et eodem modo Arithmetica, agens de Numero, dicitur subalternans: Musica verò, agens de numero sonoro, ei subalternata. Aliæ sunt diuersæ scientiæ non subalternatæ, vt Geometria, & Medicina. Asserit ergo Arist. differre demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, in scientiis subalternatis: quia demonstratio propter quid, pertinet ad scientiam subalternantem: quæ cùm sit superior, reddit causam principiorum scientiæ subalternatæ, & ea probat à priori: demonstratio verò, quia, pertinet ad scientiam subalternatam, procedentem ab effectu.

2 In the second part Aristotle teaches that demonstration propter quid differs from demonstration quia in diverse sciences. But that sciences are diverse happens in two ways: either they are subordinated, so that one is placed under the other; and such are Geometry and Perspective: the former deals with the line, and the latter with the visual line; and therefore the former is called subalternating, the latter subalternated. And in the same way Arithmetic, dealing with Number, is called subalternating, while Music, dealing with sonorous number, is subalternated to it. Other sciences are diverse but not subalternated, as Geometry and Medicine. Aristotle asserts, then, that demonstration quia and propter quid differ in subalternated sciences: because demonstration propter quid pertains to the subalternating science, which, since it is superior, gives the cause of the principles of the subalternated science and proves them a priori; but demonstration quia pertains to the subalternated science, proceeding from the effect.

Differunt etiam in diuersis scientiis non subalternatis: Quia aliquando contingit, quòd aliqua propositio in vna scientia sit euidens: quæ tamen non reddit causam eius, sed ad aliam scientiam pertinet reddere talem causam, per demonstrationem, Propter quid: & ideo ad illam scientiam pertinet, demonstrare talem propositionem per demonstrationem, Quia, ad hanc verò, per demonstrationem, Propter quid. Vt, in Medicina, aut Chirurgia, euidens est hæc propositio: Vulnus circulare difficiliùs sanatur, quàm oblongum. Eius tamen causam, non reddit hæc scientia, sed Geometria: quia latera circuli magis distant: & ideò difficiliùs coniunguntur. Distinguuntur ergo in his scientiis diuersis, demonstratio, quia, & propter quid.

They also differ in diverse sciences that are not subalternated: because it sometimes happens that some proposition is evident in one science which nevertheless does not give its cause, but it pertains to another science to give such a cause through demonstration propter quid; and therefore it pertains to the former science to demonstrate such a proposition through demonstration quia, but to the latter through demonstration propter quid. As in Medicine or Surgery this proposition is evident: A circular wound heals with more difficulty than an oblong one. Yet this science does not give its cause, but Geometry does: because the sides of a circle are farther apart, and therefore are joined with more difficulty. In these diverse sciences, then, demonstration quia and propter quid are distinguished.

QUESTION I

Quæst. 1. An demonstratio procedens à causa remota sit quia, vel propter quid — Whether demonstration proceeding from a remote cause is quia or propter quid.

QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

An demonstratio procedens à causa remota sit, quia, vel propter quid.

[…]

3 Circa remota duplex est, Adæquata, & Inadæquata. Adæquata quæ conuertitur cum effectu: vt rationalitas, est causa remota risibilitatis, conuertibilis cum ea. Causa remota inadæquata, est, quæ non conuertitur cum effectu: vt natura sensitiua, est causa remota respirationis: quæ non conuertitur cum effectu, cùm constet non omne animal respirare. Et de causa remota adæquata certum est, non constituere demonstrationem, quia: sed propter quid. Quæstio igitur procedit, de causa remota inadæquata: An demonstratio ab eo procedens, sit demonstratio, quia, vel propter quid.

3 A remote cause is twofold, Adequate and Inadequate. Adequate is that which is convertible with the effect: as rationality is the remote cause of risibility, convertible with it. An inadequate remote cause is one that is not convertible with the effect: as sensitive nature is the remote cause of respiration, which is not convertible with the effect, since it is established that not every animal breathes. And concerning the adequate remote cause it is certain that it does not constitute demonstration quia, but propter quid. The question therefore proceeds concerning the inadequate remote cause: whether demonstration proceeding from it is demonstration quia or propter quid. T t iij

p. 662

4 Et quòd non sit demonstratio, quia, sed propter quid, probatur testimonio Arist. ca. 2. huius lib. vbi agens de demonstratione, propter quid, asserit, procedere ex primis, vel ex his quæ reducuntur ad prima: & cùm principia sint causa conclusionis, idem est, ac si dicat, procedere ex causa proxima, aut remota, quæ ad proximam reduci possit: sed causa remota, etiam inadæquata, potest reduci ad proximam, cùm respectu illius dicatur remota: ergo demonstratio ex ea procedens erit, propter quid.

4 And that it is not demonstration quia but propter quid is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, ch. 2 of this book, where, treating of demonstration propter quid, he asserts that it proceeds from first things, or from things that are reduced to first things; and since principles are the cause of the conclusion, it is the same as if he said that it proceeds from a proximate cause, or from a remote one that can be reduced to the proximate; but a remote cause, even an inadequate one, can be reduced to the proximate, since it is called remote with respect to it; therefore demonstration proceeding from it will be propter quid.

Probatur etiam ratione. Primò: Quia demonstratio propter quid, est demonstratio à priori: demonstratio verò, quia, à posteriori, non alia ratione, nisi, quia illa procedit à causa, quæ prior est effectu, & hæc ab effectu, qui posterior est causa: sed causa remota vera causa est, & prior effectu: ergo demonstratio ab ea procedens, à priori est, & causam conclusionis reddit: ideo est demonstratio, propter quid.

It is proved also by reason. First: because demonstration propter quid is demonstration a priori, and demonstration quia a posteriori, for no other reason than that the former proceeds from the cause, which is prior to the effect, and the latter from the effect, which is posterior to the cause; but a remote cause is a true cause, and prior to the effect; therefore demonstration proceeding from it is a priori and gives the cause of the conclusion; therefore it is demonstration propter quid.

Secundò: Omnis demonstratio procedens ab effectu proximo, vel remoto, adæquato, vel inadæquato, est demonstratio quia: ergo omnis demonstratio procedens à causa proxima, vel remota, adæquata, vel inadæquata, erit demonstratio propter quid. Probatur consequentia, quia sicut se habet effectus ad demonstrationem, quia, ita se habet causa ad demonstrationem, propter quid.

Second: Every demonstration proceeding from an effect, proximate or remote, adequate or inadequate, is demonstration quia; therefore every demonstration proceeding from a cause, proximate or remote, adequate or inadequate, will be demonstration propter quid. The consequence is proved: because as the effect stands to demonstration quia, so the cause stands to demonstration propter quid.

Pro solutione huius quæst. notandum est, Causam remotam, & inadæquatam: de qua quæritur, duplicem esse Superiorem, & inferiorem. Superior est, ex qua quidem procedit effectus, mediante proxima: non tamen ab omni ea procedit: sed ab aliqua. Vt esse animal, est causa remota, & inadæquata respirationis, quia ab ea procedit respiratio, media proxima: quæ est habere pulmonem, & sanguinem calidum: sed non ab omni animali procedit, cùm sint multa, quæ his carent: & ideo natura sensitiua in eis, non est causa respirationis. Alia est causa remota & inadæquata inferior, à qua quidem semper procedit effectus, & ab omni ea, sed non à sola: cùm possit etiam ab alia procedere: vt patet in exemplo saltationis, adducto ab Arist. cuius causa remota, & inadæquata, sunt vites & vinum: non tamen ab his solùm procedit, sed ab aliis etiam causis lætitiæ: quæ proxima causa saltationis est.

For the solution of this question it should be noted that the remote and inadequate cause about which the question is asked is twofold, Superior and inferior. The superior is that from which the effect indeed proceeds by means of the proximate cause, yet it does not proceed from every instance of it, but from some. As being an animal is the remote and inadequate cause of respiration, because respiration proceeds from it by means of the proximate cause, which is having lungs and warm blood; but it does not proceed from every animal, since there are many that lack these; and therefore sensitive nature in them is not the cause of respiration. The other is the remote and inadequate inferior cause, from which the effect indeed always proceeds, and from every instance of it, but not from it alone, since it can also proceed from another: as is plain in the example of dancing adduced by Aristotle, whose remote and inadequate cause is vines and wine; yet it does not proceed from these alone, but also from other causes of gladness, which is the proximate cause of dancing.

Hæc est autem differentia inter duas causas: Quod inferior infert effectum. Bene enim sequitur, ex vitibus, & vino, saltatio aliqua, sed non infertur ab illo: cùm non sequatur, si saltatio aliqua est, vinum esse, & vites: nam ex causa alia prouenire potest saltus, etiam si neutrum horum sit. Negatio tamen effectus, bene infert negationem causæ. Vnde bene

Now this is the difference between the two causes: that the inferior infers the effect. For it follows well: from vines and wine, some dancing; but it is not inferred from the effect, since it does not follow: if there is some dancing, there are wine and vines; for dancing can come from another cause, even if neither of these exists. The negation of the effect, however, does infer the negation of the cause. Whence it

p. 663

respondit Anacharasis Philosophus ille Scytha, dum rogatus, cur in Scythia non essent saltatrices, & tibicines: Respondit ideo non esse, quia non sunt vites: causam reddens inadæquatam, per modum negationis.

is that Anacharsis, the famous Scythian Philosopher, replied, when he was asked why there were no dancing-girls and flute-players in Scythia: he replied that there are none because there are no vines, giving an inadequate cause by way of negation.

5 Secundò, notandum est, Quòd dum Arist. asserit, demonstrationem procedentem à causa remota: non solùm de adæquata non loquitur, sed nec de inaæquata inferiori: & ideo de sola inadæquata superiori, quod colligitur euidenter, ex verbis eius: non postquam propriam sententiam proposuit, & eam exemplis comprobauit: hæc verba subiunxit: Assimilantur autem tales causæ his, quæ secundùm excessum dicuntur. Id est, prædicatis superioribus, quæ inferiora dicuntur excedere: ergo de solis causis superioribus loquitur. Ex quibus solùm potest inferri effectus per modum negationis.

5 Second, it should be noted that when Aristotle asserts that demonstration proceeding from a remote cause [is quia], he is speaking not only not of the adequate cause, but not of the inadequate inferior one either, and therefore only of the inadequate superior one. This is gathered evidently from his words: for after he had proposed his own view and confirmed it with examples, he added these words: Such causes are like those that are said according to excess; that is, superior predicates, which are said to exceed the inferiors; therefore he speaks only of superior causes. From these alone the effect can be inferred by way of negation.

6 Notandum item est tertiò, quòd adhuc non infertur effectus ex his per modum negationis, tanquam ex causis formaliter: sed sicut, ex negatione prædicati superioris, infertur negatio inferioris: & ex negatione generis, negatio differentiæ: atque ex opposito, ex negatione differentiæ, negatio generis, absque vlla causalitate propria. Quod probari potest efficaciter, his exemplis: Quidquid est homo, est viuens: sed Paries non est viuens: ergo Paries non est homo. Quidquid est rationale, est animal: Lapis non est animal: ergo non est rationalis. Sed in his non infertur, tanquam ex causis, sed tanquam ex puris negationibus superioris prædicati: ergo nec in illis causis remotis infertur ratione alicuius causalitatis, sed solùm ratione negationis superioris prædicati. Probatur consequentia, quia sicut probamus de pariete, quòd non respiret: quia non est animal, probare æquè possumus, non esse rationalem: quia non est animal: hoc modo, Quidquid est rationale, est animal: Paries non est animal: ergo non est rationalis. Imò quod non respiret, ex sola negatione risibilitatis, dicentes, Quidquid est risibile, respiret: Paries non est risibilis: ergo non respirat. Vbi nulla interuenit ratio causalitatis: sed ex sola negatione generis, sequitur negatio differentiæ. Aut ex negatione proprietatis, negatio eiusdem respirationis. Vnde sequitur, quòd sicut per demonstrationes procedentes ab effectibus, non redditur causa conclusionis, nec propter quid eius, sed solùm probatur, quòd hoc, vel illud sit: vt quòd homo sit rationalis, per risibilitatem: & ideo appellantur ab Aristo. demonstrationes, Quòd hoc est. Ita per negationem causæ remotæ superioris, solùm probatur, quòd in aliquo non sit effectus eius: non posito propter quid talis negationis,

6 It should likewise be noted, third, that even so the effect is not inferred from these by way of negation as from causes formally, but just as from the negation of a superior predicate the negation of the inferior is inferred, and from the negation of the genus the negation of the difference, and conversely, from the negation of the difference the negation of the genus, without any proper causality. This can be proved effectively by these examples: Whatever is a man is living; but a wall is not living; therefore a wall is not a man. Whatever is rational is an animal; a stone is not an animal; therefore it is not rational. But in these it is not inferred as from causes, but as from pure negations of the superior predicate; therefore neither in the case of those remote causes is it inferred by reason of any causality, but only by reason of the negation of the superior predicate. The consequence is proved: because just as we prove of a wall that it does not breathe because it is not an animal, we can equally prove that it is not rational because it is not an animal, in this way: Whatever is rational is an animal; a wall is not an animal; therefore it is not rational. Indeed, [we can prove] that it does not breathe from the negation of risibility alone, saying: Whatever is risible breathes; a wall is not risible; therefore it does not breathe. Where no ratio of causality intervenes, but from the negation of the genus alone the negation of the difference follows, or from the negation of the property the negation of that same respiration. From which it follows that, just as through demonstrations proceeding from effects the cause of the conclusion is not given, nor its propter quid, but it is only proved that this or that is so (as that man is rational, through risibility), and therefore they are called by Aristotle demonstrations That this is, so through the negation of a remote superior cause it is only proved that its effect is not in something, without the propter quid of such a negation being posited, T t iiij

p. 664

& absque vlla causalitate. Sicut ex negatione vnius prædicati, probatur negatio alterius, etiam absque causalitate. Quare ratio causæ, in his solùm reperitur materialiter: & ideo valde similes sunt demonstrationes istæ, procedentes à causa remota, & inadæquata, per negationem, demonstrationibus, Quia: vel, Quòd hoc est. Et propterea Arist. eas reduxit potiùs ad demonstrationes, quia, quàm ad demonstrationes, propter quid.

and without any causality; just as from the negation of one predicate the negation of another is proved, even without causality. Wherefore the ratio of cause is found in these only materially; and therefore these demonstrations, proceeding from a remote and inadequate cause by way of negation, are very similar to demonstrations Quia, or That this is. And for this reason Aristotle reduced them to demonstrations quia rather than to demonstrations propter quid.

Duo igitur asserit nostra sententia. Primum, Omnem demonstrationem procedentem à causa, vt causa est, siue sit proxima, vel remota, siue sit adæquata, vel inadæquata, esse propter quid, seu διότι. Quod euidenter probat testimonium Arist. & rationes adductæ pro hac parte.

Our view, then, asserts two things. First, that every demonstration proceeding from a cause as it is a cause, whether it be proximate or remote, whether adequate or inadequate, is propter quid, or διότι. This is evidently proved by the testimony of Aristotle and the reasons adduced for this side.

7 Secundum, Demonstrationes procedentes à causa remota inadæquata, & superiori per negationem, de quibus solùm loquitur Arist. ca. præsenti, meritò fuisse ab eo connumeratas inter demonstrationes, Quia, siue ὅτι, potiùs quàm inter demonstrationes, Propter quid. Cuius est ratio: quia non procedunt ex negatione talis causę per modum causalitatis, sed solùm per modum negationis superioris prædicati, sicut in simili forma, probantur negationes quorundam prædicatorum, per negationes aliorum: imò etiam negatio eiusdem effectus causæ remotæ, per negationem alterius, absque vlla causalitate: ergo negatio causæ, solùm concurrit materialiter. Quare per tales demonstrationes, non dicitur, propter quid, sed solùm probatur, quòd negatio effectus talis causæ conueniat alicui: sicut probatur ex effectu, & per demonstrationem, quia, quòd homo sit animal, vel rationale. Quare argumenta non sunt soluenda, cùm efficaciter probent, quòd intendunt.

7 Second: Demonstrations proceeding from a remote, inadequate and superior cause by way of negation, of which alone Aristotle speaks in the present chapter, were deservedly numbered by him among demonstrations Quia, or ὅτι, rather than among demonstrations Propter quid. The reason for this is that they do not proceed from the negation of such a cause by way of causality, but only by way of the negation of a superior predicate, just as in a similar form the negations of certain predicates are proved through the negations of others; indeed even the negation of the same effect of a remote cause [is proved] through the negation of another, without any causality; therefore the negation of the cause concurs only materially. Wherefore through such demonstrations the propter quid is not stated, but it is only proved that the negation of the effect of such a cause belongs to something, just as it is proved from the effect, and through demonstration quia, that man is an animal, or rational. Wherefore the arguments need not be answered, since they effectively prove what they intend.

QUESTION II

QVÆSTIO II.

[…]

An diuisio demonstrationis in demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, sit generis in species, vel analogi in analogata.

Whether the division of demonstration into demonstration quia and propter quid is a division of a genus into species, or of an analogous term into its analogates.

8 Præsupponit titulus quæstionis tanquam certum, hanc diuisionem esse sufficientem, quod admittunt omnes: Et potest probari hac ratione: Illa diuisio est sufficiẽs, cuius membra continent omnia, quæ sub diuiso comprehenduntur: Sed membra huius diuisionis, comprehendunt quamcunque demonstrationem: ergo continent, quidquid continetur sub demonstratione in communi, quæ est diuisum eiusdem diuisionis. Probatur minor, nam præter demonstrationem procedentem à causa, & ab effectu, enumeratur ab Arist. in sequentibus demonstratio ad impossibile: per quam probatur, vnum esse alterum

he title of the question presupposes as certain that this division is 8 T sufficient, which all admit. And it can be proved by this reason: that division is sufficient whose members contain everything that is comprised under the thing divided; but the members of this division comprise any demonstration whatever; therefore they contain whatever is contained under demonstration in general, which is the thing divided of this same division. The minor is proved: for besides demonstration proceeding from the cause and from the effect, Aristotle in what follows enumerates demonstration to the impossible, through which it is proved that one is the other

p. 665

, vel non esse, deducendo ad impossibile. Ab aliis etiam additur demõstratio à signo: per quem ex signo nobis euidenter noto, probamus rem ita se habere: vt Lunam eclipsari: quia videmus lumen amittere: sed vtraque hæc demonstratio comprehenditur, sub demonstratione: ὅτι vel διότι, atque etiam alia quæcunque excogitabilis: vt bene docet Sotus, & Toletus, ca. præsenti: ergo hæc diuisio, comprehendit omnes demonstrationes. Probo iterum minorem: Quia demonstrationes ad impossibile semper procedunt per viam causę, aut effectus: & ideo reducuntur ad demonstrationem, quia, vel propter quid: vt ostendunt duæ sequentes. Si homo non esset risibilis, non esset rationalis: sed consequens est impossibile: ergo & antecedens. Cuius sensus est: si homo non esset risibilis, non esset rationalis: sed verum est esse rationalem: ergo verum est esse risibilem. Et hæc alia: Si homo non esset rationalis, non esset admiratiuus: sed consequens est impossibile: ergo antecedens. Illa enim procedit à causa, hæc verò ab effectu, vt patet.

or is not, by leading to the impossible. Others also add demonstration from a sign, through which, from a sign evidently known to us, we prove that a thing is so: as that the Moon is eclipsed, because we see it lose its light. But both of these demonstrations are comprised under demonstration ὅτι or διότι, and also any other that can be thought up, as Soto and Toledo rightly teach in the present chapter; therefore this division comprises all demonstrations. I prove the minor again: because demonstrations to the impossible always proceed by way of the cause or of the effect, and therefore are reduced to demonstration quia or propter quid, as the two following show. If man were not risible, he would not be rational; but the consequent is impossible; therefore the antecedent also. Whose sense is: if man were not risible, he would not be rational; but it is true that he is rational; therefore it is true that he is risible. And this other: If man were not rational, he would not be capable of wonder; but the consequent is impossible; therefore the antecedent. For the former proceeds from the cause, but the latter from the effect, as is plain.

9 Demonstratio verò à signo, semper procedit ab effectu: quia signum nobis notum per experientiam, semper est effectus: vt exemplum eclipsis lunæ adductum manifestat: Duo autem membra huius diuisionis, nempe demonstratio, quia, & propter quid, communia sunt: sub quibus comprehenduntur diuersæ demonstrationes procedentes à causis, vel ab effectibus. Vnde malè Caiet. dixit: aliud membrum demonstrationis, propter quid, esse distinguendum: nam quodcunque illud sit, comprehenditur sub vno membro huius diuisionis, tanquam species sub genere. Supposito, quòd diuisio sufficiens sit, quęrimus, An sit vniuoca, ita vt demonstratio diuidatur, in hæc duo membra, tanquam genus in suas species. Vel, an sit analoga? ita vt tanquam analogum potiùs, in sua analogata.

9 Demonstration from a sign, however, always proceeds from the effect, because a sign known to us through experience is always an effect, as the example of the eclipse of the moon adduced above shows. But the two members of this division, namely demonstration quia and propter quid, are common, and under them are comprised the diverse demonstrations proceeding from causes or from effects. Whence Cajetan wrongly said that another member of demonstration propter quid must be distinguished; for whatever it may be, it is comprised under one member of this division, as a species under a genus. Supposing that the division is sufficient, we ask whether it is univocal, so that demonstration is divided into these two members as a genus into its species; or whether it is analogous, so that [it is divided] rather as an analogous term into its analogates.

Et prima opinio asserit, Analogam esse diuisionem, & non vniuocam. Ita Themistius, in sua paraphrasi super 1. lib. posteriorum, c. Venetus ca. præsenti. Et probatur testimonio Arist. qui definiens demonstrationem c. 2. huius libri solam demonstrationem propter quid duplici definitione explicauit: quæ definitio non potest vllo modo conuenire demonstrationi, quia. Imò ipsemet Arist. eodem ca. quasi cum conditione asseruit de demonstratione, quia, loquens. Si autem alius modus sciendi, dicemus postea. Ad hoc nimirum decimum c. se referens secundùm communem sententiam expositorum.

And the first opinion asserts that the division is analogous, and not univocal. So Themistius in his paraphrase on bk. 1 of the Posterior Analytics, ch., and Paul of Venice in the present chapter. And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who, defining demonstration in ch. 2 of this book, explained only demonstration propter quid by a twofold definition, which definition cannot in any way belong to demonstration quia. Indeed, Aristotle himself in the same chapter asserted as it were with a condition, speaking of demonstration quia: If there is another mode of knowing, we shall say later; referring, no doubt, to this tenth chapter, according to the common view of the expositors.

10 Ex quo infertur, demonstrationem non esse vniuocam, nec genus ad vtramque. Nam si vniuoca esset, vt communis vtrique definienda esset, & non pro vna eius specie tantùm:

10 From which it is inferred that demonstration is not univocal, nor a genus to both. For if it were univocal, it would have to be defined as common to both, and not for one of its species only;

p. 666

cùm ergo sola demonstratio propter quid definita sit: hanc solam demonstrationem simpliciter sentit Arist. Demonstrationem verò, quia, non nisi secundùm quid, & per attributionem ad illam, tanquam ad principale analogatum. Cuius signum est etiam, quòd Arist. nunquam eam definiuit, satis esse putans definisse præcipuam, ex cuius similitudine, & attributione, facilè intelligitur alia.

since, then, only demonstration propter quid was defined, Aristotle regards this alone as demonstration simply; but demonstration quia only in a certain respect, and by attribution to the former as to the principal analogate. A sign of this is also that Aristotle never defined it, thinking it enough to have defined the chief one, from whose likeness and attribution the other is easily understood.

Tandem ratione probatur. Primò: Quia demonstratio est instrumentum acquirendi scientiam: sed scientia acquisita per demonstrationem, quia, non potest esse talis simpliciter, sed solùm secundùm quid: ergo nec demonstratio, quia, erit demonstratio simpliciter, sed secundùm quid. Probatur minor ex duobus. Ex primo quidem: Quia non scimus simpliciter aliquid, cuius naturam, & essentiam ignoramus: sed habita demonstratione, quia, ignoramus naturam, & essentiam rei: & solùm cognoscimus eam esse talem, ex aliquo effectu extrinseco, ex quo procedit demonstratio, quia: vt dum demonstramus hominem esse rationalem, ex effectu ridendi, quem experimur: ergo non potest esse demonstratio simpliciter. Ex secundo verò: Quia de primis principiis, non habetur scientia simpliciter, cùm ex terminis sint nota: sed nullum est principium, quantumuis immediatum, quòd non possit probari aliquo modo, per demonstrationem, quia: ergo hæc non generat scientiam simpliciter sed quandam aliam notitiam conclusionis, scientia inferiorem: & ideo non erit simpliciter demonstratio, sed secundùm quid.

Finally it is proved by reason. First: because demonstration is the instrument for acquiring science; but science acquired through demonstration quia cannot be such simply, but only in a certain respect; therefore neither will demonstration quia be demonstration simply, but in a certain respect. The minor is proved from two things. From the first indeed: because we do not know simply something whose nature and essence we are ignorant of; but when demonstration quia has been had, we are ignorant of the nature and essence of the thing, and only know that it is such from some extrinsic effect, from which demonstration quia proceeds: as when we demonstrate that man is rational from the effect of laughing, which we experience; therefore it cannot be demonstration simply. From the second: because of first principles there is no science simply, since they are known from their terms; but there is no principle, however immediate, that cannot be proved in some way through demonstration quia; therefore this does not generate science simply, but a certain other cognition of the conclusion, inferior to science; and therefore it will not be demonstration simply, but in a certain respect.

11 Secundò: Si demonstratio genus est ad demõstrationem, quia, & propter quid: ergo scientia erit etiam genus, ad eam, quæ generatur per vtramque: distinguenturque specie, tã scientia actualis, quia, & propter quid: quæ sunt assensus vtriusque demonstrationis, quàm habitualis, genita per vtrumque assensum. Sed consequens est falsum: ergo etiam antecedens. Probatur minor: quia vtraque demonstratio habetur sæpe de eodem obiecto, vt de homine, aut quouis alio: sed scientię distinguuntur specie, per obiecta: ergo nec scientiæ actuales, nec habituales genitæ per has demonstrationes possunt distingui specie: Atque adeò nec demonstrationes ipsæ, sed solùm vt quædam analogata demonstrationis in communi quæ in eas diuiditur.

11 Second: If demonstration is a genus to demonstration quia and propter quid, then science also will be a genus to that which is generated through each; and both actual science quia and propter quid, which are the assents of each demonstration, and habitual science, generated through each assent, will be distinguished in species. But the consequent is false; therefore also the antecedent. The minor is proved: because both demonstrations are often had concerning the same object, as concerning man or any other; but sciences are distinguished in species by their objects; therefore neither the actual nor the habitual sciences generated through these demonstrations can be distinguished in species; and so neither can the demonstrations themselves, but only as certain analogates of demonstration in general, which is divided into them.

Secunda opinio, tenet, Demonstrationem diuisam esse ab Arist in demonstrationem quia, & propter quid, tanquam vniuocum quid, & verum genus in suas species Ita videntur sentire Ammonius super 1. libr. de Anima, textu 21. & 34. & Flandria ibid. quæst. 29. artic. 3. Sed expressè Sotus, & Toletus

The second opinion holds that demonstration was divided by Aristotle into demonstration quia and propter quid as a univocal term, and as a true genus into its species. So Ammonius seems to hold, on On the Soul bk. 1, texts 21 and 34, and Dominic of Flanders, ibid., q. 29, a. 3. But expressly Soto and Toledo

p. 667

, cap. præsenti, & omnes moderni interpretes: & videtur mihi vera, & tenenda. Prob. primò: Quia demonstratio, quia, procedit ex principiis certis, & euidentibus, & per consequentiam euidentem in modo & figura constitutam: ergo est syllogismus necessarius, & euidens, specie distinctus à probabili, & sophistico. Quod est, esse speciem syllogismi demonstratiui, distinctam ab ea quam constituit demõstratio, propter quid, vtraque ergo specie syllogismi demonstratiui, abstrahi potest ratio communis syllogismi demõstratiui vniuoca, atque generica, sub qua distinguentur specie.

in the present chapter, and all the modern interpreters; and it seems to me true and to be held. It is proved, first: because demonstration quia proceeds from certain and evident principles, and through an evident consequence constituted in mood and figure; therefore it is a necessary and evident syllogism, distinct in species from the probable and the sophistical. That is, it is a species of demonstrative syllogism distinct from that which demonstration propter quid constitutes. From both species of demonstrative syllogism, therefore, a common ratio of demonstrative syllogism, univocal and generic, can be abstracted, under which they will be distinguished in species.

12 Quod probatur secũdò: Ex principiis vtriusque, & assensibus conclusionum, per vtramque genitis. Nam demonstrationes, distinguuntur per principia, ex quibus procedunt, & per assensus conclusionum, quos generant: cùm principia sint rationes formales assentiendi conclusionibus: & conclusiones, effectus proprij principiorum, ac demonstrationum: sed principia demonstrationis, quia, & propter quid, distinguuntur essentialiter: Quia hæc continent causam conclusionis, & reddunt propter quid eius: illa verò effectum: & ideo solùm probant conclusionem à posteriori. Et etiam assensus conclusionum distinguuntur essentialiter, per eadem principia diuersa, tanquam diuersas rationes assentiendi, quæ sunt quasi obiecta formalia earum: ergo vtraque parte distinguuntur speciei demonstratio, quia, & propter quid: ideoque demonstratio in communi diuidetur in eas, tanquam genus.

12 This is proved, second, from the principles of each, and from the assents to the conclusions generated through each. For demonstrations are distinguished by the principles from which they proceed and by the assents to the conclusions which they generate, since principles are the formal rationes of assenting to the conclusions, and conclusions are the proper effects of principles and demonstrations; but the principles of demonstration quia and propter quid are distinguished essentially, because the latter contain the cause of the conclusion and give its propter quid, but the former the effect, and therefore they only prove the conclusion a posteriori. And also the assents to the conclusions are distinguished essentially through these same diverse principles, as through diverse rationes of assenting, which are as it were their formal objects; therefore on both sides demonstration quia and propter quid are distinguished in species, and therefore demonstration in general will be divided into them as a genus.

13 Vt autem explicetur testimonium Arist. & soluatur primum argumentum. Notandum est, Quòd licèt genus ex parte sua æqualiter participetur ab speciebus, nihilominus ex parte differentiarum inæqualis perfectionis, per quas descendit ad illas, constituit easdem species inæquales in perfectione: vt constat in genere animalis. Ita ergo demonstratio in communi, abstracta ab vtraque æqualiter participatur ab eis ex parte sua, sed differentia vtriusque diuersæ sunt perfectionis: quia longè perfectiùs est reddere causam conclusionis: & ideò propter quid eius, quàm solùm eam probare ex effectu. Ideo demonstratio, propter quid, longè perfectior species demonstrationis est, quàm demonstratio, quia: non ratione generis, sed ratione differentiæ perfectissimæ: sicut homo inter species animalis. Et sicut hæc maior perfectio speciei humanæ, non tollit rationem vniuocam animalis: eodem modo, nec maior perfectio demonstrationis, propter quid, tollit rationem vniuocam, aut genericam respectu vtriusque demonstrationis.

13 Now, in order that the testimony of Aristotle may be explained and the first argument answered, it should be noted that although a genus on its own part is participated equally by its species, nevertheless, on the part of the differences of unequal perfection through which it descends to them, it constitutes those same species unequal in perfection, as is established in the genus animal. In this way, then, demonstration in general, abstracted from both, is participated equally by them on its own part, but the differences of the two are of diverse perfection: because it is far more perfect to give the cause of the conclusion, and therefore its propter quid, than only to prove it from the effect. Therefore demonstration propter quid is a far more perfect species of demonstration than demonstration quia, not by reason of the genus, but by reason of its most perfect difference, as man among the species of animal. And just as this greater perfection of the human species does not take away the univocal ratio of animal, in the same way neither does the greater perfection of demonstration propter quid take away the univocal or generic ratio with respect to each demonstration.

p. 668

Arist. ergo, solùm definiuit præcipuam speciem demonstrationis in secundo capite: quia illa est potissimum instrumentum artis demonstratoriæ, ad generandam scientiam, explicaturus aliam speciem imperfectam, cap. præsenti: quod & fecit, dicens talem esse, vt procedebat ab effectu: non reddens propter quid conclusionis, sed ostendens ita esse. Negamus igitur Arist. sentire, quòd sola demonstratio, propter quid, sit demonstratio simpliciter: demonstratio verò, quia, tantùm secundùm quid: quamuis sentiat, perfectissimam speciem demonstrationis esse illam, hanc verò imperfectissimam ratione differentiarum.

Aristotle, then, defined only the chief species of demonstration in the second chapter, because it is the foremost instrument of the demonstrative art for generating science, intending to explain the other, imperfect species in the present chapter; which he also did, saying that it is such as proceeds from the effect, not giving the propter quid of the conclusion but showing that it is so. We deny, therefore, that Aristotle holds that only demonstration propter quid is demonstration simply, and demonstration quia only in a certain respect; although he holds that the former is the most perfect species of demonstration and the latter the most imperfect, by reason of the differences.

Ad primum arg. neganda est minor, quòd assensus demonstrationis, Quia, non sit scientia simpliciter. Et dum primò dicitur, per illam nos non cognoscere naturam, & essentiam rei. Respondeo, essentiam rei, non cognosci per demonstrationem etiam propter quid, sed cognitam præsupponi, per habitum principiorum, cùm definitio sit princium ex se indemonstrabile, & non cognoscibile, per scientiam propter quid, in suo genere: sed ex sola notitia terminorum. Vnde nec est defectus demõstrationis, quia, quòd per eam cognoscatur essentia rei: sed officium vtriusque demonstrationis est, tradere cognitionem obiecti, ex aliqua eius proprietate: quod facit demonstratio propter quid, probans à priori, & ex causa proprietates subiecti. Officium verò demonstrationis, quia ex proprietate ipsa, per experientiam cognita tradit cognitionem eiusdem subiecti: nullam causam reddens, sed solùm probans, quòd talis sit naturæ ex illa proprietate. Negandum igitur est, quòd scientia genita per demonstrationem, quia, non sit simpliciter talis: quamuis concedamus esse valde imperfectam. Quòd verò secundò dicitur, de principiis non haberi scientiam. Distinguendum est, quia perfecta scientia, & à priori, non potest de illis haberi: quia per se nota sunt, & à priori indemonstrabilia. Esse autem per se nota non tollit, quin à posteriori possint demonstrari, per demonstrationem, quia, per quam habebitur scientia de illis. Imperfecta quidem, tamen vniuocè talis, cum scientia à priori, & propter quid, quare & demonstrationes ipsæ, vniuocam, atque genericam habebunt conuenientiam.

To the first argument, the minor must be denied, namely that the assent of demonstration Quia is not science simply. And when it is said, first, that through it we do not know the nature and essence of the thing, I reply that the essence of the thing is not known even through demonstration propter quid, but is presupposed as known through the habit of principles, since the definition is a principle indemonstrable of itself and not knowable through science propter quid in its own genus, but from the cognition of the terms alone. Whence it is not a defect of demonstration quia that the essence of the thing is not known through it; but the office of each demonstration is to deliver the cognition of the object from some property of it. This demonstration propter quid does by proving the properties of the subject a priori and from the cause. But the office of demonstration quia is to deliver the cognition of the same subject from the property itself, known through experience, giving no cause, but only proving from that property that it is of such a nature. It must be denied, then, that science generated through demonstration quia is not such simply, although we grant that it is very imperfect. As to what is said second, that of principles science is not had, a distinction must be made: because perfect science, and a priori, cannot be had of them, since they are known per se and indemonstrable a priori. But being known per se does not prevent their being demonstrable a posteriori through demonstration quia, through which science of them will be had: imperfect indeed, yet univocally such with science a priori and propter quid; wherefore the demonstrations themselves also will have a univocal and generic agreement.

Secundum arg. duo petit. Primum: An assensus demonstrationis, quia, & propter quid, qui dicuntur scientiæ actuales, distinguantur, specie. Secundum: An per assensus generentur habitus scientiæ, specie distincti. Circa primum, est prima sententia Soti, q. 1. huius cap. qui licèt teneat demonstrationes ipsas distingui

The second argument asks two things. First: whether the assents of demonstration quia and propter quid, which are called actual sciences, are distinguished in species. Second: whether through these assents habitual sciences distinct in species are generated. On the first, there is the first view of Soto, q. 1 of this chapter, who, although he holds that the demonstrations themselves are distinguished

p. 669

specie, negat tamen assensus specie distingui, sed vult esse eiusdem speciei. Quod probat hoc arg. Principia demonstrationis, sunt causa æquiuoca conclusionis, cùm distinguantur specie ab ea: sicut sol est causa æquiuoca caloris, sed idem effectus secundùm speciem, potest procedere à causis æquiuocis diuersæ speciei, vt idem calor à sole, & igne: ergo idem assensus conclusionis procedere, à diuersis principiis diuersisque demonstrationibus secundùm speciem. Licèt ergo demonstrationes sint specie distinctæ, non sequitur, quòd assensus conclusionis vtriusque specie distinguantur. Quod videtur sibi necessariò concedendum, de eclipsi lunæ, demonstrata per demonstrationem, propter quid, ex causa, & per demonstrationem, quia, ex effectu: non enim habemus ex eo assensus specie diuersos, sed eundem secundùm speciem: & solùm accidentali quadam, atque extrinseca ratione distinctum, vt per vnam & aliam demonstrationem procedit.

in species, nevertheless denies that the assents are distinguished in species, and holds that they are of the same species. This he proves by this argument: The principles of a demonstration are an equivocal cause of the conclusion, since they are distinguished in species from it, as the sun is an equivocal cause of heat; but the same effect according to species can proceed from equivocal causes of diverse species, as the same heat from the sun and from fire; therefore the same assent to the conclusion [can] proceed from principles and demonstrations diverse according to species. Although, then, the demonstrations are distinct in species, it does not follow that the assents to the conclusion of each are distinguished in species. This he thinks must necessarily be granted of the eclipse of the moon demonstrated through demonstration propter quid from the cause, and through demonstration quia from the effect: for we do not have from this assents diverse in species, but the same according to species, and distinguished only by a certain accidental and extrinsic ratio, as it proceeds through one demonstration and the other.

15 Hæc tamen sententia falsa est. Quod ita probo: Assensus conclusionis sumit suam speciem ex principiis, à quibus procedit, tanquam ex medio formali assentiendi, vt concedunt omnes, & probat euidens ratio. Nam assensus huius conclusionis, terra est rotunda, genitus ex principiis philosophicis, hoc est, motus physici, & ex principiis mathematicis, distinguitur specie: etiam si sit eiusdem propositionis, & ab eodem intellectu habeatur: sed media assentiendi conclusioni demonstrationis, quia, & propter quid, (quæ sunt principia continentia causam ejus, vel ab effectu eam probantia) constat distingui specie: sicut de demonstrationibus, quia, & propter quid probatum est: ergo assensus conclusionum vtriusque demonstrationis, etiam si de eadem re habeatur specie, distinctus erit: quia per diuersa media formalia habetur.

15 This view, however, is false, which I prove thus: The assent to a conclusion takes its species from the principles from which it proceeds as from the formal medium of assenting, as all grant and evident reason proves. For the assent to this conclusion, The earth is round, generated from philosophical principles, that is, from those of motion and the physical, and from mathematical principles, is distinguished in species, even if it is of the same proposition and is had by the same intellect; but the media of assenting to the conclusion of demonstration quia and propter quid (which are the principles containing its cause, or proving it from the effect) are established to be distinguished in species, as was proved of demonstrations quia and propter quid; therefore the assent to the conclusions of each demonstration, even if it is had concerning the same thing, will be distinct in species, because it is had through diverse formal media.

16 Nostra igitur sententia est, Assensus vtriusque demonstrationis, specie distingui. Quod euidenter probatur, supposita distinctione specifica demonstrationum, quam admittit Sotus. Nam repugnat per diuersa media assentiendi, quæ sunt obiecta formalia eorundem assensuum, non generari diuersos assensus secundùm speciem.

16 Our view, therefore, is that the assents of each demonstration are distinguished in species. This is evidently proved, supposing the specific distinction of the demonstrations, which Soto admits. For it is repugnant that through diverse media of assenting, which are the formal objects of those same assents, diverse assents according to species should not be generated.

Nec arg. Soti probat oppositum. Sed minor distinguenda est, nempe, quòd à causis æquiuocis specie diuersis, possit procedere idem effectus, secundùm speciem: nam si inadæquatę sint, potest: si verò sint adæquatæ, repugnat. Et ratio huius distinctionis est: quia à causis inadæquatis indifferenter procedit idem effectus: à causis verò adæquatis, determinatè & necessariò. Quia causa inadæquata, conuertitur cum suo effectu: ideo

Nor does Soto’s argument prove the opposite. But the minor must be distinguished, namely that from equivocal causes diverse in species the same effect according to species can proceed: for if they are inadequate, it can; but if they are adequate, it is repugnant. And the reason for this distinction is that from inadequate causes the same effect proceeds indifferently, but from adequate causes determinately and necessarily. Because the adequate cause is convertible with its effect; therefore

p. 670

repugnat, eundem effectum secundùm speciem procedere à causis adæquatis, diuersæ speciei. Ignis verò & sol, causæ sunt æquiuocæ caloris, diuersæ speciei, sed inadæquatæ: & ideo potest calor, ab vtralibet indifferenter procedere, & ab vtraque calor idem secundùm speciem: at assensus conclusionis, procedit à demonstratione, & principiis eius tanquam à causæ adæquata: & ideo repugnat, quòd idem assensus secundùm speciem procedat ab vtraque, supposita distinctione specifica earum à nobis probata, & ab eodem Soto concessa.

it is repugnant that the same effect according to species should proceed from adequate causes of diverse species. But fire and the sun are equivocal causes of heat, of diverse species, but inadequate; and therefore heat can proceed indifferently from either, and from both the same heat according to species. But the assent to a conclusion proceeds from the demonstration and its principles as from an adequate cause; and therefore it is repugnant that the same assent according to species should proceed from both, supposing their specific distinction, proved by us and granted by the same Soto.

Secundum: quod petebat idem arg. est, An per has demonstrationes, non solùm generentur assensus diuersi, qui vocantur diuersæ scientiæ actuales: sed etiam diuersi habitus, qui vocantur absolutè diuersæ scientiæ. Circa quod est prima opinio multorum, ex his qui nobiscum tenent, diuersos esse assensus vtriusque demonstrationis, asserentium non generare diuersum habitum scientiæ secundùm speciem: si tales demonstrationes circa eandem rem versentur: vt circa hominem, vel circa ens naturale, quod est obiectũ naturalis Philosophiæ. Sed assensum vtriusque demonstrationis, esse inadæquatum, respectu eiusdem habitus: & solùm differre ab alio, quasi specie partiali, & inadæquata, ideo posse procedere ab eodem habitu scientiæ, secundùm speciem. Quia habitus solùm distinguuntur specie, per actus adæquatos, sicut etiam per adæquata obiecta: & non per inadæquatos.

The second thing which the same argument asked is whether through these demonstrations there are generated not only diverse assents, which are called diverse actual sciences, but also diverse habits, which are called absolutely diverse sciences. On which there is the first opinion of many of those who hold with us that the assents of each demonstration are diverse, asserting that they do not generate a habit of science diverse according to species, if such demonstrations are concerned with the same thing, as with man, or with natural being, which is the object of natural Philosophy; but that the assent of each demonstration is inadequate with respect to the same habit, and differs from the other only by a partial and as it were inadequate species, and therefore can proceed from the same habit of science according to species. Because habits are distinguished in species only by adequate acts, just as also by adequate objects, and not by inadequate ones.

17 Probatur testimonio Arist. qui cap. præsenti docet, demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, differre, in eadem scientia atque in diuersis. Quod non potest esse verum, nisi pertineant aliquando ad eandem scientiam: sed eadem scientia est, idem habitus: ergo nec verum esse potest, nisi pertineant ad eundem habitum. Quare non potest defendi in doctrina. Arist. quòd per demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, circa eandem rem, generentur diuersi habitus scientiæ: alioqui de eodem homine habebit quia plures scientias: & de eodem ente naturali, plures philosophias, si per demonstrationes, quia, & propter quid, naturam & proprietates eorum cognoscat: quod inauditum est in scholis.

17 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who in the present chapter teaches that demonstration quia and propter quid differ in the same science and in diverse ones. Which cannot be true unless they sometimes pertain to the same science; but the same science is the same habit; therefore neither can it be true unless they pertain to the same habit. Wherefore it cannot be defended in the doctrine of Aristotle that through demonstration quia and propter quid concerning the same thing diverse habits of science are generated; otherwise one will have several sciences of the same man, and several philosophies of the same natural being, if he knows their nature and properties through demonstrations quia and propter quid: which is unheard of in the schools.

Probant deinde ratione: quia sicut potentia habet maiorem extensionem, quàm habitus, & ideo potest eadem secundùm speciem, intra latitudinem sui obiecti, habere plures habitus, specie distinctos, qui sint quasi inadæquati respectu illius: eodem modo habitus, habet maiorem extensionem, quàm actus, cùm videamus eundem habitum scientiæ, plures atque diuersas habere demonstrationes: & ideo plures

They prove it next by reason: because just as a power has a greater extension than a habit, and therefore one and the same according to species can, within the latitude of its object, have several habits distinct in species, which are as it were inadequate with respect to it, in the same way a habit has a greater extension than an act, since we see the same habit of science have many and diverse demonstrations; and therefore several

p. 671

assensus diuersos, qui sunt plures actus: etiam si solùm procedat à causa, vel solùm ab effectu: ergo poterit habere plures actus, vel assensus, quorum quidam procedant à causa, per demonstrationem, propter quid, alii verò ab effectu, per demonstrationem, quia.

diverse assents, which are several acts, even if they proceed only from the cause or only from the effect; therefore it will be able to have several acts or assents, of which some proceed from the cause through demonstration propter quid, and others from the effect through demonstration quia.

18 Et sicut demonstrationes, ita assensus erunt inadæquati, respectu eiusdem habitus. Non est ergo necessarium, plures multiplicare habitus, circa idem obiectum, propter demonstrationes, quia, & propter quid, & assensus earum specie distinctos: sed idem habitus poterit se extendere ad illos, tanquam ad diuersos, sed inadæquatos.

18 And just as the demonstrations, so the assents will be inadequate with respect to the same habit. It is not necessary, then, to multiply several habits concerning the same object on account of demonstrations quia and propter quid and their assents distinct in species; but the same habit will be able to extend itself to them as to diverse but inadequate ones.

Nostra sententia est, Per has demonstrationes, non solùm generari diuersos assensus secundùm speciem, sed etiam diuersos habitus scientiæ. Quod est distinctione specifica assensuum vel actuum (quam amittit opposita scientia) sic probo: Habitus generantur ex actibus, & ab eisdem sumunt vnitatem, & distinctionem specificam: sed assensus conclusionum vtriusque demonstrationis, qui sunt proprij actus, ex quibus generantur habitus, distinguuntur specie: ergo generant habitus distiuctos. Et si dicas, Esse partiales actus, & inadæquatos. Ex hoc inprimis sequitur euidenter, generare habitus distinctos specie partiali: vnde iam teneris concedere, circa idem obiectum plures habitus, & plures scientias partiales: quod falsum probauimus in quæst. proœmialibus. Idem præterea probo, Quòd non solùm assensus distinguantur specie partiali, sed etiam totali.

Our view is that through these demonstrations not only diverse assents according to species are generated, but also diverse habits of science. This, given the specific distinction of the assents or acts (which the opposing view admits), I prove thus: Habits are generated from acts, and take their specific unity and distinction from them; but the assents to the conclusions of each demonstration, which are the proper acts from which the habits are generated, are distinguished in species; therefore they generate distinct habits. And if you say that they are partial and inadequate acts: from this, first of all, it evidently follows that they generate habits distinct by a partial species; whence you are now bound to grant several habits and several partial sciences concerning the same object, which we proved false in the proemial questions. I prove besides that the assents are distinguished not only by a partial species, but also by a total one.

Quia ea quæ distinguuntur partialiter, debent esse partes alicuius totius: ergo si assensus distinguuntur partialiter, & inadæquatè, cùm distingui debeant per rationem formalem obiectiuam, dabitur aliqua ratio obiectiua totalis, atque communis, cuius sint partes: sed hæc est impossibilis: ergo impossibile est, quòd distinguantur specie partiali. Probatur minor: quia principia sunt ratio obiectiua assensuum, sicut sunt ratio assentiendi conclusionibus: sed principia quæ continent causam, & quæ continent effectum, sunt quasi opposita, & omnino diuersa nec dantur alia superiora, vel inferiora, quorum sint partes: ergo non possunt distingui specie partiali, sed totali debent distingui: & ex consequenti non possunt generare habitus specie partiali distinctos, sed totali.

Because things that are distinguished partially must be parts of some whole; therefore if the assents are distinguished partially and inadequately, since they must be distinguished by the objective formal ratio, there will be some total and common objective ratio of which they are parts; but this is impossible; therefore it is impossible that they be distinguished by a partial species. The minor is proved: because the principles are the objective ratio of the assents, as they are the ratio of assenting to the conclusions; but the principles that contain the cause and those that contain the effect are as it were opposed and altogether diverse, nor are there any other superior or inferior ones of which they are parts; therefore they cannot be distinguished by a partial species, but must be distinguished by a total one; and consequently they cannot generate habits distinct by a partial species, but by a total one.

Sed vt testimonium Arist. explicemus & argu. soluere possimus, notandum est, Vtrumque genus demonstrationis, quia, & propter quid, versari aliquando circa eandem rem, aliquando circa

But in order that we may explain the testimony of Aristotle and be able to answer the argument, it should be noted that each kind of demonstration, quia and propter quid, is sometimes concerned with the same thing, sometimes with

p. 672

diuersas. Res autem circa quam versatur scientia, solùm est obiectum materiale: formale verò sunt principia, per quæ demonstrantur passiones de illo: vnde licèt versantur aliquando circa idem obiectum materiale, semper habent diuersa obiecta formalia. Neque hoc vllam continet repugnantiam, cùm circa idem obiectum materiale, versari etiam possint scientia, & opinio, per diuersa media, aut principia: quæ sunt rationes assentiendi, & quasi obiecta formalia. Non est ergo nouum, circa eandem rem ponere diuersos habitus scientiæ, cùm plus differant scientia, & opinio: & tamen sint aliquando etiam de eadem re. Isti autem diuersi habitus, geniti per demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, circa eandem rem, sub nomine eiusdem scientiæ comprehenduntur propter identitatem obiecti materialis, & abstractionis à materia. Et hoc est, quod voluit Arist. significare, dum dixit, Scire, quia, & propter quid, & ex consequenti, demonstrationes differre in eadem scientia, & in diuersis: per eandem scientiam vtrumque habitum intelligens, qui intra latitudinem eiusdem obiecti materialis, & eodem modo abstrahentis à materia, continentur: per scientias verò diuersas, eas etiam intelligens, quæ versantur circa res diuersas, & diuerso modo, abstrahentes à materia, vt exempla eius ostendunt. Itaque non est sensus eius, quòd scire quia, & propter quid, differant intra eundem habitum, sed intra cognitionem scientificam eiusdem rei, circa quam versari solent, & quam nomine eiusdem scientiæ intelligit. Et eadem ratione, sub nomine eiusdem Philosophiæ, intelligitur vterque habitus: quia Philosophiam naturalem vocamus, in communi modo loquendi, cognitionem scientificam entis naturalis: siue per plures assensus, vel habitus distinguatur scire quia, & scire propter quid, siue non.

diverse ones. Now the thing with which a science is concerned is only the material object; the formal object is the principles through which the attributes are demonstrated of it. Whence, although they are sometimes concerned with the same material object, they always have diverse formal objects. Nor does this contain any repugnance, since science and opinion too can be concerned with the same material object through diverse media or principles, which are the rationes of assenting and as it were the formal objects. It is nothing new, then, to posit diverse habits of science concerning the same thing, since science and opinion differ more, and yet are sometimes also of the same thing. These diverse habits, then, generated through demonstration quia and propter quid concerning the same thing, are comprised under the name of the same science, on account of the identity of the material object and of the abstraction from matter. And this is what Aristotle meant to signify when he said that knowing quia and propter quid, and consequently the demonstrations, differ in the same science and in diverse ones: by the same science understanding both habits, which are contained within the latitude of the same material object, abstracting from matter in the same way; but by diverse sciences understanding those also which are concerned with diverse things, and abstract from matter in a diverse way, as his examples show. And so his sense is not that knowing quia and propter quid differ within the same habit, but within the scientific cognition of the same thing, with which they are wont to be concerned, and which he understands by the name of the same science. And by the same reasoning both habits are understood under the name of the same Philosophy: for in the common way of speaking we call natural Philosophy the scientific cognition of natural being, whether knowing quia and knowing propter quid are distinguished through several assents or habits or not.

20 Ad argu. verò, Concedimus primum, quod in antecedenti assumitur: nempe maiorem habere extensionem potentiam, quàm habitum: sed negamus secundum: quòd habitus maiorem habeat extensionem, quàm actus, vel assensus. Et huius ratio est, quia habitus proximè specificatur ab actu, secundùm rationem formalem, quia per illum attingit obiectum: & cùm hæc sit limitata, non habet maiorem extensionem habitus, quàm actus. Potentia verò vniuersalior est: & sub vniuersaliori ratione attingit obiectum: & ideo per actus & habitus diuersæ speciei id fit. Vnde sequitur non esse superfluum multiplicare habitus, vbi actus distinguuntur specie, sed omnino necessarium, vt iam probauimus.

20 To the argument, then: we grant the first thing that is assumed in the antecedent, namely that a power has a greater extension than a habit; but we deny the second, that a habit has a greater extension than an act or assent. And the reason for this is that the habit is proximately specified by the act according to the formal ratio, because through it it attains the object; and since this is limited, the habit does not have a greater extension than the act. But the power is more universal, and attains the object under a more universal ratio; and therefore it happens through acts and habits of diverse species. Whence it follows that it is not superfluous to multiply habits where the acts are distinguished in species, but altogether necessary, as we have already proved. Treatise

p. 673

TRACT. De subalternatione scientiarum — T R E AT I S E O N T H E S U B A L -ternation of Sciences.

TRACTATVS DE SVBALternatione scientiarum.

[…]

Quid nomine scientiæ subalternantis, & subalternatæ intelligatur — What is understood by the name of subalternating and subalternated science.

Quid nomine scientiæ subalternantis, & subalternatæ intelligatur.

[…]

21 In secunda part. cap. docuit Arist Scire quia, & propter quid: & consequenter, demonstrationes differre in diuersis scientiis, non subordinatis, sed totaliter diuersis, & quasi disparatis. Atque etiam idem fieri in diuersis scientiis subordinatis tamen, quas vocat subalternatas, in eodem sensu, quo propositiones docuit, 2. lib. de interpretatione, quandam habere oppositionem: quasi Subalternam: quando fiunt ex eodem prædicato, & subiecto, sed vna collocatur sub altera, vna est vniuersalis, & particularis altera. Tales igitur asserit esse quasdam scientias, quarum vna versatur circa rem aliquam vniuersalem, alia verò circa rem particularem, sub ea contentam, vt Geometria, quæ versatur circa lineam, & perspectiua, circa lineam visualem, sic Arithmetica circa numerum, Musica verò circa numerũ sonorum. Et vniuersalem vocat Subalternantem: particularem verò Subalternatam: aut illam continẽtem, & hanc contentam. De natura igitur, & ratione harum scientiarum, nobis est, de qua agunt oẽs interpretes Arist. c. præsenti, agendum, differentiam demonstrationis, quia, & propter quid, in eis designatam intelligamus. Nam quæ sint scientiæ totaliter diuersæ, & quomodo in eis differant, satis notum est.

n the second part of the chapter Aristotle taught that knowing 21 I quia and propter quid, and consequently demonstrations, differ in diverse sciences that are not subordinated, but totally diverse, and as it were disparate; and also that the same happens in diverse sciences that are, however, subordinated, which he calls subalternated, in the same sense in which, in bk. 1 of On Interpretation, he taught that propositions have a certain opposition, as it were Subaltern, when they are made of the same predicate and subject, but one is placed under the other, one being universal and the other particular. He asserts, then, that there are certain sciences of which one is concerned with some universal thing, and another with a particular thing contained under it: as Geometry, which is concerned with the line, and Perspective, with the visual line; so Arithmetic with number, but Music with sonorous number. And the universal he calls Subalternating, but the particular Subalternated; or the former containing and the latter contained. Of the nature and ratio of these sciences, then, we must treat (which all the interpreters of Aristotle treat in the present chapter), in order that we may understand the difference of demonstration quia and propter quid designated in them. For what sciences are totally diverse, and how they differ in them, is well enough known.

Expositis nominibus Subalternantis & subalternatæ scientiæ, quatuor de illis explicanda sunt. Primum, Quidnam sit, vnam scientiam esse subalternatam alteri? Secundum, An talis subalternatio sit possibilis? Tertium, Quonam modo dependeat scientia subalternata à subalternante, & an sine illa esse possit, & veram habere rationem scientiæ? Quartum, An subalternata intra proprios limites, demonstret, propter quid, suarum conclusionum.
