Having expounded the names of subalternating and subalternated science, four things must be explained about them. First, what it is for one science to be subalternated to another. Second, whether such subalternation is possible. Third, in what way the subalternated science depends on the subalternating, and whether it can exist without it and have the true ratio of science. Fourth, whether the subalternated science, within its own limits, demonstrates the propter quid of its conclusions.

Quidnam sit subalternatio scientiarum — What the subalternation of sciences is.

Quidnam sit subalternatio scientiarum.

[…]

22 Circa conditiones requisitas, & sufficientes ab subalternationem scientiarum, diuerso modo loquuntur authores: nam quidam plures: alij verò pauciores assignant: quidam easdem, alij diuersas. Inter omnes verò, optimè eas videtur enumerasse Caie. in tract. de subalternatione scientiarum, vbi ad 4. aut 5. præcipuas reduxit omnes. Prima est, Quòd subiectum vnius, contineatur sub subiecto alterius: cuius defectu Medicina

22 Concerning the conditions required and sufficient for the subalternation of sciences, authors speak in diverse ways: for some assign more, others fewer; some the same, others diverse ones. But among all, Cajetan seems to have enumerated them best, in his treatise On the Subalternation of Sciences, where he reduced them all to four or five chief ones. The first is that the subject of one be contained under the subject of the other; for lack of which Medicine Vu

p. 674

nõ subalternatur geometriæ: nam corpus sanabile, non continetur sub linea, sed disparata sunt. Secunda, Quòd subiectũ inferioris, includat subiectum superioris: & addat supra illud aliquam differentiam accidentalem. Cuius defectu scientia de specie, non subalternatur scientię de genere. Nam licèt species sub genere, non addit tamen supra genus conditionem accidentalem: sed essentialem differentialem: vnde ferè semper eadem est scientia de vtroque. Tertia conditio est, Quòd differentia, quam addit, nõ sit propria passio eiusdem subiecti: Quia licèt passio sit differẽtia quodammodo accidentalis: non est tamen purè accidentalis: & ideo non pertinet ad distinctam scientiam, ac subiectum: sed ad eandem, in qua demonstratur de illo. Quarta conditio est, Quòd principia scientiæ inferioris, probentur à priori, & per causam à scientia superiori. Principia autem, quæ assumit scientia subalternata ad probandum suas conclusiones, sunt in duplici differentia: quædam enim sumit ex subiecto scientiæ subalternantis: alia verò ex materia alterius scientiæ, ad quam per se pertinet conditio accidentalis, quam addit obiectum eius supra obiectum scientiæ subalternantis.

is not subalternated to geometry: for curable body is not contained under line, but they are disparate. The second, that the subject of the inferior include the subject of the superior, and add over and above it some accidental difference; for lack of which the science of the species is not subalternated to the science of the genus. For although the species is under the genus, it does not add over and above the genus an accidental condition, but an essential differential one; whence the science of both is nearly always the same. The third condition is that the difference which it adds be not a proper attribute of the same subject: because, although an attribute is in a certain way an accidental difference, it is not purely accidental; and therefore it does not pertain to a distinct and subalternated science, but to the same one in which it is demonstrated of that subject. The fourth condition is that the principles of the inferior science be proved a priori and through the cause by the superior science. Now the principles which the subalternated science assumes for proving its conclusions are of two kinds: for some it takes from the subject of the subalternating science, and others from the matter of another science, to which the accidental condition belongs per se which its object adds over and above the object of the subalternating science.

23 Et illa omnia, & sola, debet probare à priori scientia subalternans, non alia. Quia cùm ad materiam alterius scientiæ pertineant, non possunt ab illa probari. Exempli gratia: Perspectiua, assumit vnum principium, quasi geometricum ex materia lineæ, quæ obiectum geometriæ est, & aliud philosophicum, ex materia visualis: nam visuale ad philosophiam naturalem pertinet. Geometria igitur, cui subalternatur: solùm probare debet illa, quæ ex eius materia, aut obiecto deriuantur: non, quæ pertinent ad philosophiam naturalem. Ex his conditionibus vna, vel altera reperietur aliquo modo in diuersis scientiis, non subalternatis, sed omnes simul in solis subalternatis reperiri possunt, & ideo omnes simul sunt requisitæ, & sufficienter, ad veram, & propriam subalternationem. Ita, vt solùm illæ scientiæ, & omnes in quibus reperiuntur, veræ, & propriæ sint subalternatæ. Et sic est explicatum, quid sit subalternatio scientiarum.

23 And all of the former, and they alone, the subalternating science must prove a priori, and not the others: because, since they pertain to the matter of another science, they cannot be proved by it. For example, Perspective assumes one principle that is as it were geometrical, from the matter of the line, which is the object of geometry, and another that is philosophical, from the matter of the visual: for the visual pertains to natural philosophy. Geometry, then, to which it is subalternated, must prove only those that are derived from its own matter or object, not those that pertain to natural philosophy. Of these conditions one or another will be found in some way in diverse sciences that are not subalternated, but all together can be found only in subalternated sciences; and therefore all together are required, and sufficient, for true and proper subalternation, so that only those sciences, and all those in which they are found, are truly and properly subalternated. And thus it has been explained what the subalternation of sciences is.

An subalternatio scientiarum explicata sit possibilis, vel sola imaginatione excogitata — Whether the subalternation of sciences explained above is possible, or devised by the imagination alone.

24 Tria arg. proponemus, quę videtur probare subalternationem scientiarum nõ esse possibilẽ, & est primũ tale: Quia si obiectũ scientiæ subalternatæ, addit conditionẽ accidentalẽ, supra obiectũ sciẽtiæ subalternãtis, sequitur subalternatã non esse vnã scientiã per se. Probatur consequentia: quia scientia sumit suam

24 We shall propose three arguments which seem to prove that the subalternation of sciences is not possible; and the first is this: Because if the object of the subalternated science adds an accidental condition over and above the object of the subalternating science, it follows that the subalternated science is not one science per se. The consequence is proved: because a science takes its

p. 675

vnitatem per se ab obiecto: sed obiectum eius non est vnũ per se, sed per accidens, cũ constet ex duplici ente in actu, vt ostendit linea visualis, aut numerus sonorus: ergo nec ipsa erit vna scientia per se, sed per accidens. Secundum: Scientia subalternans, & subalternata, debent esse distinctæ specie: sed nõ possunt distingui specie, si vera est eadem conditio: ergo nec erit possibilis subalternatio. Probatur minor: quia scientiæ distinguuntur specie per obiecta: sed obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, solùm distinguitur accidentaliter, ab obiecto scientiæ subalternantis: cùm solùm addit supra ipsum differentiam accidentalem, vt linea visualis, solũ distinguitur accidentaliter à linea, ergo scientia ipsa subalternata, solummodo distinguetur accidentaliter à scientia subalternante. Quod etiam videtur probari, ex vltima conditione subalternationis, quòd subalternans debeat probare à priori principia scientiæ subalternatæ: nam si hoc verum est: principia subalternatæ erunt conclusiones subalternantis: sed conclusiones pertinent ad eandem scientiam, in qua probantur à priori: ergo eandem scientiã efficiet subalternata cum subalternante. Tertium: Si subalternata addit in suo subiecto conditionem accidentalem supra obiectum subalternantis, sequitur obiectum eius habere duplicem partem: vna erit obiectum subalternantis, alia verò accidentalis conditio, addita supra illud, & pertinens quidem ad aliam scientiam, quo supposito, non erit maior ratio, quare dicatur magis subalternata vni, quàm alteri: & ideo nec vni, nec alteri subalternata erit, sed subalternatio ipsa impossibilis reputabitur. Gratia exempli: Obiectum perspectiuæ, quod est linea visualis, includit, duplicem partem: nempe lineam, pertinentem ad Geometriam, & conditionem accidentalem visualis, pertinentem ad Philosophiam naturalem: ideo non erit maior ratio, ob quam vni earum quàm alteri subalternetur, & ita non erit alicui earum subalternata.

unity per se from its object; but its object is not one per se but per accidens, since it consists of a twofold being in act, as visual line or sonorous number shows; therefore neither will it be one science per se, but per accidens. Second: The subalternating and the subalternated science must be distinct in species; but they cannot be distinguished in species if the same condition is true; therefore neither will subalternation be possible. The minor is proved: because sciences are distinguished in species by their objects; but the object of the subalternated science is distinguished only accidentally from the object of the subalternating science, since it adds over and above it only an accidental difference, as visual line is distinguished only accidentally from line; therefore the subalternated science itself will be distinguished only accidentally from the subalternating science. This also seems to be proved from the last condition of subalternation, that the subalternating science must prove a priori the principles of the subalternated science: for if this is true, the principles of the subalternated science will be conclusions of the subalternating; but conclusions pertain to the same science in which they are proved a priori; therefore the subalternated science will make one and the same science with the subalternating. Third: If the subalternated science adds in its subject an accidental condition over and above the object of the subalternating, it follows that its object has a twofold part: one will be the object of the subalternating science, but the other the accidental condition added over and above it, and pertaining indeed to another science; which supposed, there will be no greater reason why it should be called subalternated to one rather than to the other; and therefore it will be subalternated neither to one nor to the other, but subalternation itself will be reckoned impossible. For example: the object of perspective, which is the visual line, includes a twofold part, namely line, pertaining to Geometry, and the accidental condition of visual, pertaining to natural Philosophy; therefore there will be no greater reason for which it should be subalternated to one of them rather than to the other, and so it will not be subalternated to either of them.

25 His tamen non obstantibus, omnes tenent cum Arist. possibilem esse subalternationem scientiarũ, & quasdam esse scientias subalternatas aliis. in quibus quatuor illæ conditiones concurrunt, vt perspectiua subalternatur geometriæ, & musica arithmeticæ.

25 Notwithstanding these things, however, all hold with Aristotle that the subalternation of sciences is possible, and that there are some sciences subalternated to others, in which those four conditions concur, as perspective is subalternated to geometry, and music to arithmetic.

Sed circa solutionẽ primi arg. est prima opinio Sonc. 4. Met. q. 9. asserentis, Scientiam subalternatam, esse vnam per se, atque distinctam à subalternante: quia differentia, quam obiectũ eius addit, supra obiectum subalternantis, non est accidens commune, sed propria passio eiusdem obiecti subalternantis: vt visuale, inquit, non est accidens commune lineæ, sed propria passio eius: quia linea est quantitatis: & quantitas est per se sensibilis, vt docet Aristot. 2. lib. de anima: ergo linea est per se visibilis,

But concerning the solution of the first argument there is the first opinion, of Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 9, who asserts that the subalternated science is one per se and distinct from the subalternating: because the difference which its object adds over and above the object of the subalternating is not a common accident, but a proper attribute of that same object of the subalternating: as visual, he says, is not a common accident of line, but a proper attribute of it; because line belongs to quantity, and quantity is per se sensible, as Aristotle teaches in On the Soul 2; therefore line is per se visible, V v ij

p. 676

ita vt visibilitas sit propria eius passio, ex subiecto autem, & propria passione, fit vnum per se, & non per accidens: sicut fit ex subiecto, & accidenti communi, vt ex corpore, & albedine.

so that visibility is its proper attribute; and from a subject and a proper attribute there comes about something one per se and not per accidens, as there does from a subject and a common accident, as from body and whiteness.

26 Hæc tamen sententia falsa est: & vt talis refutatur à Caie. c. præsenti. Probatur euidenter, quia duo quæ asserit, sunt apertè falsa. Primum: quòd visuale sit propria passio lineæ, vt est obiectum geometriæ. Nam geometria est scientia mathematica, abstrahens à materia sensibili: ergo agit de linea, vt abstrahit à materia sensibili: sed visuale est conditio per se sensibilis, cùm dicat respectum ad visum: ergo euidens est non conuenire lineæ, vt est obiectum geometriæ: quare falsum erit, quòd conditio, quam addit perspectiua supra geometriam, sit propria passio obiecti geometriæ Imò etiamsi concederemus, esse propriam passionem eius, falsum est. Secundum, quod asserit, efficere vnum per se cum linea: quia propria passio verum accidens est, & extra essentiam subiecti: ergo si accidens commune non potest facere vnum per se cum subiecto, nec poterit accidens proprium efficere vnum per se cum eo. Quia non minùs risibile, constabit duplici ente in actu, nempe subiecto, & accidente, quàm album. Et tandem: Si conditio addita obiecto scientiæ subalternatæ, sit propria passio obiecti subalternantis, ad eandem scientiam pertinebit cum eo. Probatur consequentia: quia propria passio obiecti alicuius scientiæ, probatur de illo in eadem scientia cuius est obiectum.

26 This view, however, is false, and is refuted as such by Cajetan in the present chapter. It is proved evidently, because the two things it asserts are openly false. The first: that visual is a proper attribute of line as it is the object of geometry. For geometry is a mathematical science, abstracting from sensible matter; therefore it deals with line as it abstracts from sensible matter; but visual is a per se sensible condition, since it implies a relation to sight; therefore it is evident that it does not belong to line as it is the object of geometry. Wherefore it will be false that the condition which perspective adds over and above geometry is a proper attribute of the object of geometry. Indeed, even if we granted that it is its proper attribute, the second thing it asserts is false, that it makes something one per se with line: because a proper attribute is a true accident, and outside the essence of the subject; therefore if a common accident cannot make something one per se with its subject, neither will a proper accident be able to make something one per se with it. For risible no less than white is composed of a twofold being in act, namely of subject and accident. And finally: if the condition added to the object of the subalternated science is a proper attribute of the object of the subalternating, it will pertain to the same science with it. The consequence is proved: because the proper attribute of the object of any science is proved of it in the science whose object it is.

27 Nostra igitur sententia in primis asserit: Conditionem, quam addit obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, non esse propriam passionem obiecti subalternantis, sed accidens commune. Obiectum tamen includens talem conditionem, vt lineam visualem, dupliciter sumi posse. Vnum modum, prout includit vtrumque, per modum aggregationis. Et hoc modo euidens est, quòd sit vnum per accidens: & non possit esse obiectum scientiæ. Quia vt sit sumptum, non habet vnam naturam, vel essentiam, sed duplicem essentiam: nec vnam definitionem, nec determinatas passiones, quæ de eo probari possint. Alio modo sumitur prout includit vnum cum ordine ad aliud: vel vt determinatum per illud, aliud verò vt determinans. Et ita est vnum per se, non entitate, sed ordine, quæ vnitas sufficit vt definiri possit, & per se considerari ab vna scientia, & vt determinatæ passiones de eo probari possint in ea Et hoc modo consideratur obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ ab eadem: quare vt vnum per se, ex quo habebit illa, quòd sit vna scientia per se. Et ideo ex hac parte, non erit impossibilis subalternatio scientiarum.

27 Our view, therefore, asserts first of all that the condition which the object of the subalternated science adds is not a proper attribute of the object of the subalternating, but a common accident. The object, however, that includes such a condition, as visual line, can be taken in two ways. One way, as it includes both by way of aggregation. And in this way it is evident that it is one per accidens and cannot be the object of a science: because, as so taken, it does not have one nature or essence, but a twofold essence; nor one definition, nor determinate attributes that could be proved of it. In another way it is taken as it includes one with order to the other, or the one as determined by the other, and the other as determining. And so it is one per se, not in entity but in order; which unity suffices for it to be able to be defined and considered per se by one science, and for determinate attributes to be able to be proved of it in that science. And in this way the object of the subalternated science is considered by it: wherefore as one per se, from which that science will have it that it is one science per se. And therefore on this side the subalternation of sciences will not be impossible.

Secundum argumentum soluitur alia distinctione: Nam

The second argument is answered by another distinction: for

p. 677

conditio, quam addit obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, duobus modis sumi potest: vel, vt est accidens obiecti subalternantis, ei inhærens, vel, vt per se consideratur, à tali scientia, & primo modo, solùm accidentaliter illud determinat, vel contrahit, sicut quodlibet aliud accidens subiectum, cui inhæret. Secundo verò modo, contrahit illud per se, ad considerationem talis scientiæ: quia linea per se consideratur à perspectiua, vt visualis est. Itaque, licèt visuale sit accidens lineæ, vt sumitur secundùm propriam entitatem, vel essentiam: tamen vt ad obiectum perspectiuæ pertinet, per se coniungitur cum visuali: quia per se consideratur à scientia, in ordine ad visuale: vel vt per talem conditionem determinatur. Vnde quamuis linea, quæ est obiectum geometriæ secundùm entitatem, solùm distinguatur à linea visuali quæ est obiectum perspectiuæ, etiam secundum, entitatem sumptæ, accidentaliter: nihilominus si vtraque sumatur, vt per se consideratur à sua scientia, per se, & essentialiter distinguuntur: vel vt vno verbo dicatur, solùm distinguuntur accidentaliter in esse rei: in esse verò obiecti essentialiter, & per: & ideo possunt distinguere scientias specie.

the condition which the object of the subalternated science adds can be taken in two ways: either as it is an accident of the object of the subalternating science, inhering in it, or as it is considered per se by such a science. And in the first way it determines or contracts that object only accidentally, as any other accident [determines] the subject in which it inheres. But in the second way it contracts it per se to the consideration of such a science: because line is considered per se by perspective as it is visual. And so, although visual is an accident of line as line is taken according to its own entity or essence, nevertheless, as it pertains to the object of perspective, it is joined per se with visual: because it is considered per se by the science in order to the visual, or as determined by such a condition. Whence, although line, which is the object of geometry according to entity, is distinguished only accidentally from visual line, which is the object of perspective, also taken according to entity, nevertheless, if each is taken as it is considered per se by its own science, they are distinguished per se and essentially; or, to put it in one word, they are distinguished only accidentally in the being of a thing, but in the being of an object essentially and per se; and therefore they can distinguish sciences in species.

29 Ad formam ergo secundi arg. distinguenda est minor secundi syllogismi, quòd obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, solùm distinguatur accidentaliter ab obiecto subalternantis: nam in esse rei accidentaliter solùm distinguitur, sed in esse obiecti scibilis, per talem scientiam, essentialiter. Et ideo scientia subalternata non accidentaliter: sed essentialiter distinguitur à subalternante.

29 To the form of the second argument, then, the minor of the second syllogism must be distinguished, namely that the object of the subalternated science is distinguished only accidentally from the object of the subalternating: for in the being of a thing it is distinguished only accidentally, but in the being of an object knowable through such a science, essentially. And therefore the subalternated science is distinguished from the subalternating not accidentally but essentially.

Pro solutione tertij notandum est: Quòd ex duobus, quæ includit obiectum subalternatæ scientiæ, nempe, obiectum subalternantis, & accidentalem conditionem superadditam, primum ac præcipuum est obiectum: conditio verò quasi limitatio eius est, per quam determinatur: & imperfectior quidem, quia materialis, atque sensibilis: obiectum verò subalternantis, vt magis à materia abstractum, perfectius est. Et ex hoc sequitur ratione eius: eandem scientiam esse subordinatam superiori, & vocari subalternatam, & non ratione conditionis: quod ex alia conditione colligitur euidenter: quia principia subalternatæ scientiæ, superior probat à priori potius, quàm illa scientia, ad quem conditio pertinet. Et ideo potiùs illi subalternatur, quàm huic. Gratia exempli: Obiectum perspectiuæ includit lineam & conditionem visualis: ex quibus linea est primum, & principale, ratione cuius subordinatur geometriæ: est etiam magis abstracta à materia, & quia demonstrare, propter quid, conclusionum, potiùs pertinet ad illam scientiam,

For the solution of the third it should be noted that of the two things which the object of the subalternated science includes, namely the object of the subalternating and the accidental condition superadded, the first and chief is the object, while the condition is as it were its limitation, by which it is determined; and it is more imperfect, because material and sensible, whereas the object of the subalternating, as more abstracted from matter, is more perfect. And from this it follows that it is by reason of the former that the same science is subordinated to the superior and called subalternated, and not by reason of the condition: which is evidently gathered from another condition, because the superior science proves the principles of the subalternated science a priori rather than does that science to which the condition pertains. And therefore it is subalternated to the former rather than to the latter. For example: the object of perspective includes line and the condition of visual; of which line is the first and principal, by reason of which it is subordinated to geometry; it is also more abstracted from matter, and because demonstrating the propter quid of the conclusions pertains rather to that science, V v iij

p. 678

quæ magis abstrahit à materia sensibili: cùm scientiæ respicientes materiam sensibilem, ab effectu potiùs demonstrare soleant: hinc est, quòd perspectiua potiùs subalternatur geometriæ, quàm philosophiæ naturali.

which abstracts more from sensible matter: since the sciences that regard sensible matter are wont rather to demonstrate from the effect, hence it is that perspective is subalternated to geometry rather than to natural philosophy.

30 Hoc est enim principium perspectiuæ, Visio facta secundùm lineam rectam, est perfectissima: quod licèt præsupponat aliud, per se notum in philosophia, nempe agens naturale fortiùs agit in proximum, quàm in remotum: tamen à priori demonstratur à geometria: quia linea recta est perfectissima, & breuissima.

30 For this is a principle of perspective: Vision effected along a straight line is most perfect; which, although it presupposes something known per se in philosophy, namely that a natural agent acts more strongly on what is near than on what is remote, is nevertheless demonstrated a priori by geometry, because the straight line is the most perfect and the shortest.

Ad formam igitur arg. neganda est consequentia, quòd non sit maior ratio, propter quam scientia inferior magis dicatur subalternata vni, quam alteri scientiæ: quia cùm obiectum superioris scientiæ sit primum, quod includit, & ratione cuius subordinatur scientiæ superiori, agenti de illo, ad quam etiam pertinet probare à priori principia eiusdem scientiæ inferioris: potiùs quàm ad aliam scientiam, ad quam conditio pertinet: ideo potiùs illi, quàm huic subalternatur.

To the form of the argument, then, the consequence must be denied, namely that there is no greater reason why the inferior science should be said to be subalternated to one science rather than to the other: because, since the object of the superior science is the first thing it includes, and that by reason of which it is subordinated to the superior science which deals with that object, to which it also pertains to prove a priori the principles of that same inferior science, rather than to the other science to which the condition pertains, therefore it is subalternated to the former rather than to the latter.

An subalternata scientia, existens sine subalternante, sit vera scientia: vel potiùs opinio — Whether a subalternated science, existing without the subalternating, is true science, or rather opinion.

PRæsupponit titulus quæstionis tanquam certum, quòd scientia subalternata, possit esse separata à scientia subalternante, & omnino sine ea esse: quod constat experientia, cùm plures cognoscamus musicos, ignorantes Arithmeticam. Quærit autem hoc supposito, An musica in his sit vera scientia, vel solùm opinio.

The title of the question presupposes as certain that the subalternated science can be separated from the subalternating science, and exist altogether without it: which is established by experience, since we know many musicians ignorant of Arithmetic. But, this supposed, it asks whether music in them is true science, or only opinion.

31 Et prima sententia tenet. Non esse scientiam, sed opinionem: ita Soncinas 4. Meta. quæst. 9. quem sequuntur plures moderni: quorum hæc est ratio: Quia vt docuit Arist. 2. cap. huius libri, aliquis habeat scientiam alicuius conclusionis, necesse est, quòd principia sint ei certa, ita, vt ex terminis ea cognoscat vel si demonstrabilia sint, sciat ea reducere ad prima indemonstrabilia: & qui hoc non scit, (inquit Aristot.) non habet demonstrationem, nec scientiam conclusionis: atqui principia scientiæ subalternatæ non sunt immediata, sed demonstrabilia, per scientiam subalternantem, quam cùm non habeat musicus, nescit ea reducere ad immediata, sed solùm ea credit propter testimonium Arithmeticorum: ergo non habet scientiam conclusionum eius, sed opinionem.

31 And the first view holds that it is not science but opinion: so Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 9, whom many moderns follow; whose reason is this: because, as Aristotle taught in ch. 2 of this book, for someone to have science of some conclusion it is necessary that the principles be certain to him, so that he knows them from the terms, or, if they are demonstrable, that he know how to reduce them to the first indemonstrable ones; and he who does not know this (says Aristotle) does not have demonstration, nor science of the conclusion; but the principles of the subalternated science are not immediate, but demonstrable through the subalternating science, which, since the musician does not have it, he does not know how to reduce them to the immediate ones, but only believes them on account of the testimony of the Arithmeticians; therefore he does not have science of its conclusions, but opinion.

Secunda opinio est aliorum, Quòd vera sit scientia, quamuis imperfecta. Et ratio horum est opposita: quia si non esset scientia

The second opinion is that of others, that it is true science, although imperfect. And their reason is the opposite: because if it were not science

p. 679

sed opinio, maximè hoc esset propterea, quia is qui eam habet sine subalternante, non habet certitudinem principiorum, sed fides humana potest esse certa, propter frequentia testimonia: vt patet in hac propositione, Roma est: cui, licèt multi assentiantur, solùm propter testimonium eorum, qui eam viderunt, tot tamen testimonia multiplicantur: vt certum efficiant assensum eorum: cuius signum est: quia nemo est qui dubitet de veritate eius.

but opinion, this would be chiefly because he who has it without the subalternating science does not have certitude of the principles; but human faith can be certain on account of the frequency of testimonies, as is plain in this proposition, Rome exists: to which, although many assent only on account of the testimony of those who have seen it, yet the testimonies are so multiplied as to make their assent certain; a sign of which is that there is no one who doubts its truth.

32 Pro explicatione nostræ sententię, notandum est Duobus modis posse cõtingere, quòd scientia subalternata sit sine subalternãte. Primò, Ita, vt principia eius solùm sint accepta, per testimoniũ habentium scientiam subalternantem. Secundò: Ita vt etiam ab eo, qui habet eam sine subalternante nota, per experientiam euidentem multorum singularium: ex quibus colligitur euidenter, experimentum vniuersale principiorum.

32 For the explanation of our view it should be noted that it can happen in two ways that the subalternated science exists without the subalternating. First, so that its principles are only accepted through the testimony of those who have the subalternating science. Second, so that they are known also by him who has it without the subalternating, through evident experience of many singulars, from which the universal experiential knowledge of the principles is evidently gathered.

Hoc supposito: Tria asserit nostra sententia. Primum est: Siue subalternata scientia, sine subalternante existens, sit vera scientia siue non, certum est, non esse actu, & formaliter scientiam subalternatam: prout sic habetur, sed solùm materialiter. Quod sic probo: Scientia dicitur subalternata, quia subordinatur subalternanti, à qua principia eius accipiunt certitudinem, & euidentiam requisitam ad veram scientiam: sed scientia inferior existens, sine superiori, vt sic existens, non subordinatur actu superiori scientiæ, nec ab ea participat euidentiam suorum principiorum: ergo non est actu, & formaliter scientia subalternata: sed solùm materialiter, & quasi in potentia: in quantum cum ea coniungi potest, in eo, qui vtramque habeat.

This supposed, our view asserts three things. The first is: Whether the subalternated science existing without the subalternating is true science or not, it is certain that it is not actually and formally a subalternated science as it is so had, but only materially. This I prove thus: A science is called subalternated because it is subordinated to the subalternating science, from which its principles receive the certitude and evidence required for true science; but an inferior science existing without the superior, as so existing, is not actually subordinated to the superior science, nor does it participate from it the evidence of its principles; therefore it is not actually and formally a subalternated science, but only materially and as it were in potency, inasmuch as it can be joined with it in one who has both.

33 Secundum, quod asserit, Quòd scientia subalternata, sine subalternante, erit vera scientia (licèt imperfecta,) si ei, qui eam habuerit, nota sint principia per experientiam. Probatur hoc: Quia tunc erunt certa, atque euidentia principia: ex quibus per demõstrationem à posteriori, colligitur euidenter conclusio: quæ ex sequenti erit certa, & euidens, & per consequens, verè sciẽtifica.

33 The second thing it asserts is that a subalternated science without the subalternating will be true science (although imperfect) if the principles are known through experience to him who has it. This is proved: because then the principles will be certain and evident, from which through demonstration a posteriori the conclusion is evidently gathered; which consequently will be certain and evident, and consequently truly scientific.

Tertiò dicimus: Quòd si principia eius solùm cognoscantur per testimonium eorum, qui habent subalternantem scientiam, non erit vera scientia, sed opinio. Et hoc probat efficaciter argum. primæ opinionis, quam in hoc sensu veram esse existimamus. Argu. verò secundæ opinionis nihil probat: Quia testimonium humanum, per se loquendo, nõ potest generare assensum certum cùm non repugnet ei subesse falsum. Quòd verò per frequentiam testimoniorum, sublatum sit actuale dubium, per accidẽs est: quia hoc non obstante, assensus illius propositionis, Roma est, ab intrinseco est incertus: & cui potest subesse falsum.

Third, we say that if its principles are known only through the testimony of those who have the subalternating science, it will not be true science, but opinion. And this the argument of the first opinion proves effectively, which we judge to be true in this sense. But the argument of the second opinion proves nothing: because human testimony, speaking per se, cannot generate certain assent, since it is not repugnant that falsity underlie it. And that through the frequency of testimonies actual doubt is removed is per accidens: because, notwithstanding this, the assent to that proposition, Rome exists, is intrinsically uncertain, and falsity can underlie it. V u iiij

p. 680

Et eo igitur non potest per se colligi certa conclusio, nisi ratione quadam materiali, & accidẽtali. Per se autem, est incerta: quod repugnat scientiæ. Quemadmodum dicimus, Conclusionem nõ esse per se, & formaliter certam nec scientificam, quæ colligitur per aliquam consequentiam, solùm necessariam in his, aut illis terminis: quod est, esse necessariam solùm materialiter, formaliter verò, & per se incertam: cùm in simili forma, possit dari antecedens verum, & consequens falsum.

From it, therefore, a certain conclusion cannot be gathered per se, except by a certain material and accidental reason. Per se, however, it is uncertain: which is repugnant to science. Just as we say that a conclusion is not per se and formally certain, nor scientific, which is gathered through some consequence that is necessary only in these or those terms; that is, necessary only materially, but formally and per se uncertain, since in a similar form there can be given a true antecedent and a false consequent.

An subalternata scientia, inter proprios limites, demonstret propter quid, vel solùm quia — Whether a subalternated science, within its own limits, demonstrates propter quid, or only quia.

IAm hoc intelligitur de scientia subalternata, non sine subalternãte: sed illi actu coniuncta in eo, qui habet vtramque: & tunc habet statum scientiæ subalternatæ, de qua quærimus, An intra proprios limites, hoc est, in quantum solùm se extendit, vsque ad principia à se indemonstrabilia: sed quæ possunt demonstrari à priori, & verè demonstrantur, à subalternante: cui quasi continuantur: an, inquam, intra hos limites, veras habeat demonstrationes, propter quid, per quas demonstret à priori suas conclusiones, ex propriis principiis: vel solùm dicatur demonstrare ea, quasi per demonstrationes, quia. Exempli gratia: Hęc est conclusio perspectiuæ scientiæ, Res ad maiorem distantiã visa minor apparet, quam ipsamet existat in se. Perspectiua eam demõstrat per hanc, Res à longè visa, minori, aut acutiori angulo mouet potentiam: & ideo apparet minor. Sed illius secundæ propositionis, per quã probat primam, nescit reddere causam: eam verò reddit geometria: quia angulus eo est acutior, quo magis protrahitur: esse verò acutiorem est esse minorem.

This is now understood of the subalternated science not without the subalternating, but actually joined to it in one who has both; and then it has the status of a subalternated science, about which we ask whether within its own limits, that is, inasmuch as it extends only as far as the principles that are indemonstrable by itself, but can be demonstrated a priori, and are in fact demonstrated, by the subalternating science, to which it is as it were continued: whether, I say, within these limits it has true demonstrations propter quid, through which it demonstrates its conclusions a priori from its own principles; or whether it is said to demonstrate them only as it were through demonstrations quia. For example: this is a conclusion of the science of perspective: A thing seen at a greater distance appears smaller than it exists in itself. Perspective demonstrates it through this: A thing seen from afar moves the power at a smaller or more acute angle, and therefore appears smaller. But it does not know how to give the cause of that second proposition, through which it proves the first; geometry, however, gives it: because the angle is the more acute the more it is drawn out; and to be more acute is to be smaller.

35 Et ideo res visa ad maiorem distãtiam, minori angulo mouet potentiam. Quærimus ergo, An demonstratio illa, per quam perspectiua probat, quòd res à longè visa minor apparet: quia minori angulo mouet potentiam, (hoc est enim intra proprios limites demonstrare suas conclusiones sit demonstratio propter quid, & à priori: vel solùm demonstratio, quia.

35 And therefore a thing seen at a greater distance moves the power at a smaller angle. We ask, then, whether that demonstration through which perspective proves that a thing seen from afar appears smaller because it moves the power at a smaller angle (for this is to demonstrate its conclusions within its own limits) is demonstration propter quid and a priori, or only demonstration quia.

Prima opinio est Soti, & Veneti cap. præsenti, asserentium, verè demonstrare, propter quid, intra latitudinem propriam: quam tamen sine limitatione, videtur tenuisse Albertus Mag. tract. 2. de vsu principiorum, c. 7. vbi negare omnino videtur quòd propria principia subalternatæ scientię, demonstrentur à scientia subalternante. Quia cùm subalternans abstrahat à materia sensibili, & principia subalternatæ respiciant materiam sensibilem, non potest se extendere, aut descendere ad illa demon-

The first opinion is that of Soto and Paul of Venice in the present chapter, who assert that it truly demonstrates propter quid within its own latitude; which, however, Albert the Great seems to have held without limitation, tract. 2 On the Use of Principles, ch. 7, where he seems altogether to deny that the proper principles of the subalternated science are demonstrated by the subalternating science: because, since the subalternating science abstracts from sensible matter, and the principles of the subalternated regard sensible matter, it cannot extend itself or descend to demonstrating them

p. 681

stranda. Quod verum est non solùm intra proprios limites demonstrabit, propter quid, suarum conclusionum, scientia subalternata, sed omnino. Nam si principia eius non demonstrantur à subalternante, neque ab alia, erunt prorsus indemonstrabilia: ex quibus perinde demonstrabit subalternata proprias conclusiones, atque quælibet alia scientia etiam subalternans.

Which is true: the subalternate science will demonstrate its conclusions propter quid not only within its own limits, but absolutely. For if its principles are not demonstrated by the subalternating science, nor by another, they will be altogether indemonstrable; and from them the subalternate science will demonstrate its own conclusions just as any other science does, even a subalternating one.

Probatur hæc sententia. Primò: Quia scientia subalternata, licèt non reddat causam primam suę conclusionis: nec demonstret illam: vsque ad principium primum, reddit tamen causam proximam eius: ergo eam demonstrat à priori, per causam proximam: vt patet in exemplo designato.

This opinion is proved. First, because the subalternate science, although it does not render the first cause of its conclusion, nor demonstrate it up to the first principle, nevertheless renders its proximate cause: therefore it demonstrates it a priori through the proximate cause, as is plain in the example indicated.

36 Et certè si sola scientia subalternans demonstraret à priori, conclusiones scientiæ subalternatæ, solus Arithm. diceretur Musicus: & solus Geometra, perspectiuus, Quod patet esse falsum. Probatur consequentia: quia sciens, & scientia, denominationem accipiunt à conclusionibus, quas demonstrant: cùm in eis consistat, vera, & propria ratio scientiæ: ergo sicut dicitur philosophus, qui scit demonstrare conclusiones philosophiæ: ita dicitur perspectiuus, qui scit demonstrare conclusiones perspectiuæ: præsertim si à nullo alio demonstrentur, sed ab eo solo.

36 And certainly, if the subalternating science alone demonstrated a priori the conclusions of the subalternate science, the Arithmetician alone would be called a Musician, and the Geometer alone a Perspectivist; which is plainly false. The consequence is proved: because the knower and the science receive their denomination from the conclusions which they demonstrate, since the true and proper ratio of science consists in them: therefore, just as he is called a philosopher who knows how to demonstrate the conclusions of philosophy, so he is called a perspectivist who knows how to demonstrate the conclusions of perspective; especially if they are demonstrated by no other science, but by it alone.

Secundò: Quia si scientia subalternata non demonstrat à priori suas conclusiones, maximè id facit, quia non reddit causam earum, vsque ad primam, sed solùm reddit proximam, relinquens primam reddendam à subalternante: sed hoc est impossibile: ergo non est negandum, quòd demonstret à priori suas conclusiones. Probatur minor: quia si hoc ita esset, sequeretur subalternantem demonstrare à priori principia subalternatæ: & ideo principia subalternatę esse conclusiones subalternantis. Quod repugnat fieri propter duo. Primum, Quia subalternans abstrahit à materia sensibili: principia verò subalternatæ, respiciunt materiam sensibilem: ergo repugnat: quòd hæc illis coniungantur, in eadem demonstratione coniungi autem necessarium est, si sunt conclusiones per illa demonstratæ.

Second, because if the subalternate science does not demonstrate its conclusions a priori, it is chiefly because it does not render their cause up to the first, but renders only the proximate cause, leaving the first to be rendered by the subalternating science; but this is impossible: therefore it must not be denied that it demonstrates its conclusions a priori. The minor is proved: because if this were so, it would follow that the subalternating science demonstrates a priori the principles of the subalternate, and therefore that the principles of the subalternate are conclusions of the subalternating science. Which cannot be the case, for two reasons. First, because the subalternating science abstracts from sensible matter, whereas the principles of the subalternate regard sensible matter: therefore it is repugnant that the latter be joined with the former in the same demonstration; yet it is necessary that they be joined, if they are conclusions demonstrated through them.

Secundum: Quia principia inferioris essent conclusiones superioris, non essent distinctæ scientiæ, superior & inferior, sed eandem efficerent. Probatur consequentia: Nam conclusiones ad eam sententiam pertinent, in qua demonstrantur: sed principia inferioris, sunt conclusiones demonstratæ à superiori: ergo ad hanc pertinebunt, & non efficient scientiam subalternatam distinctam.

Second, because if the principles of the inferior were conclusions of the superior, the superior and the inferior would not be distinct sciences, but would make up one and the same. The consequence is proved: for conclusions pertain to that science in which they are demonstrated; but the principles of the inferior are conclusions demonstrated by the superior: therefore they will pertain to it, and will not make up a distinct subalternate science.

Secunda opinio: Negat subalternatam, aut simpliciter demonstrare proprias conclusiones priori, aut etiam intra proprios limites:

The second opinion denies that the subalternate science demonstrates its own conclusions a priori, either absolutely or even within its own limits:

p. 682

sed solùm auxilio superioris, & vt continuatur cum illa, veras demonstrationes efficere posse. Hæc est communis, quam tenent D. Th. in Comment. huius cap Soncinas 4. Meta. qu. 9. Caiet. tract. de subalternatione scientiarum circa finem, Louanienses, & Tolet. in expositione huius cap. Et videtur nobis in doctrina Arist. necessaria, & in ratione vera.

but holds that it can produce true demonstrations only with the help of the superior science, and as it is continued with it. This is the common opinion, which is held by St. Thomas in his Commentary on this chapter; Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 9; Cajetan, in his treatise on the subalternation of sciences, toward the end; the Louvain commentators; and Toledo in his exposition of this chapter. And it seems to us necessary in the doctrine of Aristotle, and true in reason.

Probatur primum: Quia Arist cap. pręsenti in principio, docet expressè, differre demonstrationem quia, & propter quid, in diuersis scientiis subalternatis: quia demõstratio, propter quid, pertinet ad scientiam subalternantem: demonstratio verò, quia, ad subalternatam. Quæ differentia, non potest esse vera, si scientia subalternata demõstrat proprias conclusiones demõstratione, propet quid, etiam intra proprios limites: vel etiam reddens causam proximam earum, licèt non primam. Nam si hoc verum est, ad eam pertinebit demonstratio propter quid, & non quia. Præterea loquens Arist. de vtraque scientia in particulari, & vocans subalternantem Mathematicam, & subalternatam sensibilem, quia illa abstrahit à materia sensibili, hæc verò respicit illam, expressè docet: subalternatam solùm demonstrare, quia: ad subalternantem verò pertinere demonstrationem, propter quid, his verbis: Hic enim, ipsum quidem sensitiuorum est scire, ipsum vero, propter quid, Mathematicorum.

The first is proved: because Aristotle, at the beginning of the present chapter, teaches expressly that demonstration quia and propter quid differ in diverse subalternate sciences: because demonstration propter quid pertains to the subalternating science, but demonstration quia to the subalternate. Which difference cannot be true if the subalternate science demonstrates its own conclusions by demonstration propter quid, even within its own limits, or even by rendering their proximate cause, though not the first. For if this is true, demonstration propter quid will pertain to it, and not demonstration quia. Moreover, Aristotle, speaking of each science in particular, and calling the subalternating science Mathematical and the subalternate sensible, because the former abstracts from sensible matter while the latter regards it, teaches expressly that the subalternate science only demonstrates quia, but that demonstration propter quid pertains to the subalternating science, in these words: For here to know the that belongs to those who deal with sensibles, but to know the propter quid belongs to the Mathematicians.

Secundum verò, quòd vera sit nostra sententia, probatur hoc arg. Vt aliquis habeat scientiam alicuius conclusionis, & veram demonstrationem eius, necesse est, quòd præmissis assentiatur ex sola notitia terminorum: vel si demonstrabiles sint, eas sciat reducere vsque ad principia omnino indemonstrabilia: alioqui si sic eas reducere nesciat, non habebit veram demonstrationem conclusionis, nec veram scientiam eius. Sed principia propria scientiæ subalternatæ, per quæ demonstrat suas conclusiones, non sunt immediata, sed demonstrabilia: cùm possint demonstrari à scientia subalternante: ergo non fiet vera demonstratio alicuius conclusionis ex eis, nisi ab eo, qui sciat ea reducere vsque ad prima omnino indemonstrabilia, per veras demonstrationes. Atqui subalternata scientia, intra proprios limites, nescit ea sic reducere, vt patet, à solaque subalternante reduci possunt: ergo subalternata intra proprios limites, non potest veram demonstrationem, propter quid, suarum conclusionum efficere, nisi auxilio scientiæ subalternantis aut in quantum cum ea continuatur.

That the second part, namely that our view is true, is proved by this argument. For someone to have science of some conclusion, and a true demonstration of it, it is necessary that he assent to the premises from the sole cognition of the terms; or, if they are demonstrable, that he know how to reduce them up to altogether indemonstrable principles: otherwise, if he does not know how to reduce them in this way, he will not have a true demonstration of the conclusion, nor true science of it. But the proper principles of the subalternate science, through which it demonstrates its conclusions, are not immediate but demonstrable, since they can be demonstrated by the subalternating science: therefore there will be no true demonstration of any conclusion from them, except by one who knows how to reduce them up to the first, altogether indemonstrable, principles through true demonstrations. But the subalternate science within its own limits does not know how to reduce them in this way, as is plain, and they can be reduced by the subalternating science alone: therefore the subalternate science within its own limits cannot produce a true demonstration propter quid of its conclusions, except with the help of the subalternating science, or inasmuch as it is continued with it.

39 Sed vt explicemus, quonã modo fiat cõtinuatio hæc, quo etiam modo demonstrentur à subalternante: notandum est, Quòd in quacunque demonstratione, necessarium est medium con-

39 But in order to explain in what way this continuation takes place, and in what way also they are demonstrated by the subalternating science, it should be noted that in any demonstration whatever it is necessary that the middle

p. 683

iungi cum extremitatibus in præmissis, vt ratione talis coniunctionis extremitates ipsæ coniungantur in conclusione: & hoc est fundamentum totius artis demonstratiuæ. Vt ostenditur in hac demonstratione: Omne animal rationale est risibile: Omnis homo est animal rationale, ergo Omnis homo est risibilis. In qua animal rationale, quod est medium, coniungitur in præmissis cum homine, qui est maior extremitas, & cum risibilitate, quæ est minor: & virtute huius coniunctionis, coniunguntur homo, & risibile in conclusione.

be joined with the extremities in the premises, so that by reason of such a conjunction the extremities themselves are joined in the conclusion: and this is the foundation of the whole demonstrative art. As is shown in this demonstration: Every rational animal is risible; Every man is a rational animal; therefore Every man is risible. In which rational animal, which is the middle, is joined in the premises with man, which is the major extremity, and with risibility, which is the minor; and by virtue of this conjunction man and risible are joined in the conclusion.

Secundò notandũ, Medium in demonstratione propter quid continere causam conclusionis. Vnde sequitur non posse scientiam subalternantem demonstrare à priori principium scientiæ subalternatæ, per medium sibi proprium nudè acceptum: hoc est, in propria abstractione à materia sensibili consideratum, sed necesse est, vt tale medium coniungatur extremitatibus, ex quibus constat principium eiusdem subalternatæ scientiæ demonstrandum, tanquam conclusio, alioqui non erit medium.

It should be noted, second, that the middle in a demonstration propter quid contains the cause of the conclusion. Whence it follows that the subalternating science cannot demonstrate a priori a principle of the subalternate science through a middle proper to itself taken barely, that is, considered in its own abstraction from sensible matter; but it is necessary that such a middle be joined with the extremities of which the principle of that same subalternate science, to be demonstrated as a conclusion, is composed; otherwise it will not be a middle.

40 Sed extremitates eius respiciunt materiam sensibilem: ergo necesse est medium scientiæ subalternantis quasi descendere ad materiam sensibilem, ad eamque determinari, vt per talem coniunctionem cum extremitatibus in præmissis, efficiat, vt coniungantur extremitates ipsæ in conclusione: & ita conclusio ipsa, quæ principium est subalternatæ scientiæ, à priori demonstretur. Et talis coniunctio medii cum extremitatibus, ex quibus constat principium scientiæ subalternatæ demonstrandum, est continuatio inferioris scientiæ cum superiori: in qua cõtinuatione cõsistit formalis ratio subalternationis. Quæ omnia hoc exemplo fiunt manifesta. Principium sciẽtię subalternatæ, nempe perspectiuæ: quod ipsa nec scit, nec potest demonstrare intra proprios limites, est hoc: Res à longè videtur sub minori, vel acutiori angulo. Demõstratur autem sic, à sciẽtia subalternante, nempe à geometria: Res quæ videtur sub angulo magis protracto, videtur sub angulo minori, (nam angulus magis protractus acutior est, & ideo minor: ) sed res visa à longè videtur per angulum magis protractum, aut longiorem vt est manifestum, ergo videtur sub angulo minori. Ecce medium geometricũ, nempe angulum magis protractum, esse minorem, quod nõ posset demõstrare principium illud perspectiuæ nisi coniungeretur cum extremitatibus, ex quibus componitur, videlicet cum re à longè visa, & cum minori angulo: & nisi ita coniunctum efficeret cum eis vtraque pręmissam eiusdem demonstrationis per quam demonstraretur idem principium, tanquam conclusio composita ex eisdem extremitatibus,

40 But its extremities regard sensible matter: therefore it is necessary that the middle of the subalternating science descend, as it were, to sensible matter and be determined to it, so that through such a conjunction with the extremities in the premises it may bring it about that the extremities themselves are joined in the conclusion; and thus the conclusion itself, which is a principle of the subalternate science, is demonstrated a priori. And such a conjunction of the middle with the extremities of which the principle of the subalternate science to be demonstrated is composed is the continuation of the inferior science with the superior; and in this continuation consists the formal ratio of subalternation. All of which is made manifest by this example. A principle of the subalternate science (namely of perspective), which it neither knows nor can demonstrate within its own limits, is this: A thing far off is seen under a smaller, or more acute, angle. And it is demonstrated thus by the subalternating science, namely by geometry: A thing which is seen under a more protracted angle is seen under a smaller angle (for a more protracted angle is more acute, and therefore smaller); but a thing seen from far off is seen through a more protracted, or longer, angle, as is manifest; therefore it is seen under a smaller angle. Behold the geometrical middle, namely that a more protracted angle is smaller, which could not demonstrate that principle of perspective unless it were joined with the extremities of which it is composed, namely with the thing seen from far off and with the smaller angle; and unless, so joined with them, it produced each premise of the same demonstration through which that same principle would be demonstrated, as a conclusion composed of the same extremities,

p. 684

Et ecce continuatam scientiam subalternatam, cum subalternante, in eadem demonstratione, per tales coniunctiones. Continuatiuum autem, est medium scientiæ subalternantis, vt coniunctum in præmissis cum extremitatibus, ex quibus componitur, principium scientiæ subalternatæ, per illud demonstratum.

And behold the subalternate science continued with the subalternating science in the same demonstration, through such conjunctions. And that which effects the continuation is the middle of the subalternating science, as joined in the premises with the extremities of which the principle of the subalternate science, demonstrated through it, is composed.

Et continuatio hæc, non tollit distinctionem vtriusque scientiæ, vt statim probabitur.

And this continuation does not take away the distinction of the two sciences, as will be proved presently.

42 Ex his intelligitur, primò quomodo sit possibile, quòd scientia subalternans probet per demonstrationẽ à priori, principia scientiæ subalternatæ, etiam si abstrahat à materia sensibili, & principia probanda eam respiciant, id enim facit, per vnionem proprij medij, cum extremitatibus principij probandi, cum quibus coniungitur in pręmissis & per coniunctionem, quasi descendit, & contrahitur per eas, ad materiam sensibilem: & per talem contractionem continuatur cum ea.

42 From these things it is understood, first, how it is possible that the subalternating science should prove the principles of the subalternate science by demonstration a priori, even though it abstracts from sensible matter and the principles to be proved regard that matter: for it does this through the union of its own middle with the extremities of the principle to be proved, with which it is joined in the premises; and through that conjunction it descends, as it were, and is contracted through them to sensible matter; and through such contraction it is continued with it.

43 Iam ergo soluuntur facilè arg. oppositæ opinionis. Nam ad primum, Concedimus antecedens, quòd subalternata scientia reddat causam proximam suæ conclusionis: sed negamus consequentiam, quòd demonstret eas intra proprios limites. Nam ad veram demonstrationem, non sufficit reddere causam, sed requiritur reddere omnes causas, vsque ad primam: alioqui nõ habebit certum assensum præmissarum, cùm nesciat eas reducere vsque ad principia per se nota, & indemonstrabilia: & ideo nec habebit veram scientiam conclusionis, nec veram demonstrationem eius.

43 Now, therefore, the arguments of the opposite opinion are easily solved. To the first: we grant the antecedent, that the subalternate science renders the proximate cause of its conclusion; but we deny the consequence, that it demonstrates them within its own limits. For to a true demonstration it is not enough to render the cause; rather it is required to render all the causes up to the first: otherwise it will not have a certain assent to the premises, since it does not know how to reduce them up to principles known per se and indemonstrable; and therefore it will have neither true science of the conclusion nor a true demonstration of it.

Ad aliud verò, quod additur in eodem arg nempe, solum Arithmeticum esse musicum, & solum geometram, perspectiuum: si hi soli demonstrare dicuntur à priori conclusiones musicæ, perspectiuæ, negandum est, quia principia alicuius scientiæ, per quæ demonstrantur conclusiones eius, non pertinent ad habitum talis scientiæ, sed ad alium distinctum, qui dicitur habitus principiorum: & ideo nec suscipiunt denominationem sciẽtiæ: nec ea habent denominationem à scientiis. Principia autem scientiæ subalternatæ, quæ demonstrantur à scientia subalternante, comparantur ad principia eius, per quæ demonstrantur, tanquam conclusiones eorum: & ideo non pertinent ad eam, sed ad alium habitum inferiorem, qui est scientia subalternata.

But to the other point which is added in the same argument, namely that the Arithmetician alone would be a musician, and the geometer alone a perspectivist, if these alone are said to demonstrate a priori the conclusions of music and of perspective, it must be denied: because the principles of any science, through which its conclusions are demonstrated, do not pertain to the habit of such a science, but to another distinct habit, which is called the habit of principles; and therefore they do not receive the denomination of the science, nor do they have a denomination from the sciences. But the principles of the subalternate science, which are demonstrated by the subalternating science, are related to its principles, through which they are demonstrated, as their conclusions; and therefore they do not pertain to it, but to another, inferior habit, which is the subalternate science.

44 Quare nec Geometra denominatur perspectiuus, nec Arithmeticus denominatur musicus, sicut nec conclusiones musicæ, dicuntur geometria, quamuis verum sit, non denominari musicum verè scientem, nisi simul sit Arithmeticus: nec scientem perspectiuum, nisi simul sit geometra,

44 Wherefore neither is the Geometer denominated a perspectivist, nor the Arithmetician denominated a musician; just as neither are the conclusions of music called geometry; although it is true that one is not denominated a musician truly knowing unless he is at the same time an Arithmetician, nor a perspectivist knowing unless he is at the same time a geometer,

p. 685

Ad secundum, Concedimus primam & secundam consequentiam: quòd principia subalternatæ, sunt conclusiones subalternantis, negamus tamen, quòd non possint eis coniungi in eadem demonstratione. Nam licèt principia subalternantis, abstrahant à materia sensibili, determinari tamen possunt, & quasi contrahi, per principia subalternatæ, ad conficiendam eandem demonstrationem: vt explicatum est. Per hanc autem vnionem principiorum vnius, cum principiis alterius, vt conclusionibus eorum, non tollitur distinctio vtriusque scientiæ: sicut per vnionem principiorum cuiuslibet scientiæ, cum conclusionibus eiusdem, in eisdem demonstrationibus, non tollitur distinctio habitus scientiæ, ab habitu principiorum. Præsertim cùm semper scientia subalternata, & subalternans, habeant diuersa obiecta, & diuerso modo à materia abstrahentia, ex quibus distinctio habituum apertè colligitur. Et si aliquis quęrat, Quid ergo, aut quomodo dicendum est, demonstrare scientiam subalternatam, intra proprios limites, aut quomodo loquendum. Respõdeo, Si intra proprios limites, accipiatur præcisè, nullam demonstrationem propter quid, habere posse, neque etiam, quia, neque aliquam posse demonstrare conclusionem. Vnde neque esse scientiam, hoc modo sumptam: quia sub hac præcisione accepta, nescit demonstrare propria principia, verè demonstrabilia: ergo non habebit certum assensum eorum: & ideò, non poterit certam cõclusionem, aut scientificam colligere. De demonstratione verò, quia certum est, eam non habere, sub ratione formali scientiæ subalternatæ, quia vt talis est, non procedit ab effectu, sed à causa: Solùm igitur demonstrat suas conclusiones: demonstratione propter quid, auxilio subalternantis, vt continuatur cum ea, quare solùm hoc modo est vera scientia subalternata.

To the second, we grant the first and the second consequence, namely that the principles of the subalternate science are conclusions of the subalternating science; we deny, however, that they cannot be joined to them in the same demonstration. For although the principles of the subalternating science abstract from sensible matter, they can nevertheless be determined, and as it were contracted, through the principles of the subalternate science, so as to construct the same demonstration, as has been explained. And through this union of the principles of the one with the principles of the other, as their conclusions, the distinction of the two sciences is not taken away; just as, through the union of the principles of any science with its conclusions in the same demonstrations, the distinction of the habit of science from the habit of principles is not taken away. Especially since the subalternate and the subalternating science always have diverse objects, abstracting from matter in a diverse manner, from which the distinction of the habits is plainly gathered. And if anyone should ask what, then, or in what manner it must be said that the subalternate science demonstrates within its own limits, or how one must speak of it, I reply: if within its own limits is taken precisely, it can have no demonstration propter quid, nor even quia, nor can it demonstrate any conclusion. Whence, taken in this way, it is not a science either: because, taken under this precision, it does not know how to demonstrate its own principles, which are truly demonstrable; therefore it will not have a certain assent to them; and therefore it will not be able to infer a certain or scientific conclusion. As for demonstration quia, it is certain that it does not have it under the formal ratio of subalternate science, because as such it does not proceed from the effect but from the cause. It demonstrates its conclusions, therefore, only by demonstration propter quid, with the help of the subalternating science, as it is continued with it; wherefore only in this manner is it a true subalternate science.

CHAPTER XXVI

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

Scibile autem, & scientia differunt ab opinabili, & opinione, quoniam scientia quidem vniuersalis.

But the knowable and science differ from the opinable and opinion, since science is universal.

Breuis expositio textus.

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

INtentum Arist. in hoc cap. est, distinguere scientiam ab opinione, postquam scientias distinxit inter sese, in his capitibus intermediis, à decimo vsque ad hoc vigesimum sextum. Diuiditur autem in duas partes. In prima, Asserit, & probat scientiam, & scibile, distingui ab opinio-

he intention of Aristotle in this chapter is to distinguish science from T opinion, after he has distinguished the sciences from one another in these intermediate chapters, from the tenth up to this twenty-sixth. And it is divided into two parts. In the first, he asserts and proves that science and the knowable are distinguished from opinion

p. 686

ne & opinabili. In secunda, Duo proponit dubia in contrarium solui.

and the opinable. In the second, he proposes two doubts to be solved in the contrary sense.

Conclusio, Arist. est hæc: Scientia, & scibile, ex vna parte, differunt ab opinione, & opinabili, ex altera. Quam probat hac ratione: Scientia versatur circa vniuersale, & necessarium: ergo scibile est vniuersale, & necessarium: opinio verò circa contingens, & sæpe particulare, aut etiam singulare: ergo opinabile est contingens, & particulare: ergo diuersa est scientia ab opinione: & scibile ab opinabili. Antecedens probat, ex parte scientiæ, quia vt cap. 2. dictum est, Scientia est de his, quæ non possunt aliter se habere: ergo de necessariis, quia necessarium est, quod non potest aliter se habere. Præterea: Scientia est de his, quæ sunt de omni, per se, & vniuersaliter, aut secundùm quod ipsum: ergo est de vniuersalibus. Probat deinde idem antecedens, de opinione, & opinabili. Nam quædam ait vera sunt in existimatione, quæ in re possunt esse vera, aut falsa: de quibus non est scientia, neque intellectus, qui est notitia principiorum: ergo de his erit opinio, & cùm possint aliter se habere, quod est esse contingentia: erit de contingenti: & ideo opinabile erit contingens.

Aristotle’s conclusion is this: Science and the knowable, on the one side, differ from opinion and the opinable, on the other. Which he proves by this argument: Science is concerned with the universal and necessary: therefore the knowable is universal and necessary; but opinion is concerned with the contingent, and often with the particular, or even the singular: therefore the opinable is contingent and particular: therefore science is diverse from opinion, and the knowable from the opinable. He proves the antecedent, on the side of science, because, as was said in ch. 2, science is of things which cannot be otherwise: therefore it is of necessary things, because the necessary is that which cannot be otherwise. Moreover, science is of things which are said of all, per se, and universally, or according as it is itself: therefore it is of universals. Next he proves the same antecedent on the side of opinion and the opinable. For certain things, he says, are true in estimation which in reality can be true or false: of these there is no science, nor understanding, which is the cognition of principles: therefore of these there will be opinion; and since they can be otherwise, which is to be contingent, it will be of the contingent; and therefore the opinable will be contingent.

2 Probatur antecedens, Quòd de his, quæ possunt aliter se habere, non sit scientia, neque intellectus, quia scientia, est de his, quæ non possunt aliter se habere: intellectus verò, quasi scientia quædam immediata est: & sic definiri potest, Intellectus est certa cognitio immediatæ propositionis quod est, esse certam cognitionem, ex sola significatione terminorum habita, sed certa cognitio ex terminis habita, non potest esse de re contingenti, nisi tantùm de necessaria: ergo repugnat, quòd intellectus, & scientia sint de re contingenti. Consequentiam verò, quod de re contingenti sit opinio, probat, quia si certa cognitio dari non potest, de re contingenti, dabitur incerta, & fallibilis. Hoc est talis, quæ licèt vera esse existimetur, tamen non repugnet ei subesse falsum.

2 The antecedent is proved, namely that of things which can be otherwise there is neither science nor understanding: because science is of things which cannot be otherwise; and understanding is as it were a certain immediate science, and can be defined thus: Understanding is the certain cognition of an immediate proposition; that is, it is a certain cognition had from the sole signification of the terms. But a certain cognition had from the terms cannot be of a contingent thing, but only of necessary things: therefore it is repugnant that understanding and science be of a contingent thing. And the consequence, namely that opinion is of a contingent thing, he proves because, if a certain cognition cannot be had of a contingent thing, there will be an uncertain and fallible one. This is such that, although it is thought to be true, nevertheless it is not repugnant to it that falsity underlie it.

Vnde infert, sic esse definiendam opinionem: Opinio est acceptio, vel existimatio, seu assensus immediatæ propositionis, & non necessariæ. Et per primam particulam, Immediatæ propositionis, distinguitur opinio à scientia, quæ est cognitio propositionis mediatæ: & conuenit cum intellectu. Per secundam verò, nempè, Non necessariæ, distinguitur ab vtroque, videlicet intellectu, & scientia: quia vtrumque est de necessariis, vt probatum est.

Whence he infers that opinion should be defined thus: Opinion is the acceptance, or estimation, or assent of an immediate and non-necessary proposition. And by the first particle, of an immediate proposition, opinion is distinguished from science, which is the cognition of a mediate proposition, and it agrees with understanding. But by the second, namely non-necessary, it is distinguished from both, that is, from understanding and from science, because both are of necessary things, as has been proved.

3 Sed hæc definitio opinionis, non traditur ab Arist. de omni opinione, sed solùm de immediata. Datur enim mediata

3 But this definition of opinion is not delivered by Aristotle of every opinion, but only of the immediate one. For there is also a mediate

p. 687

opinio, quæ ex immediata colligitur, per euidentem, aut probabilem consequentiam: vel ex propositione euidenti, per consequentiam non necessariam, vt Arist. docet in hoc eodem cap. Sed solùm voluit immediatam definire, vt cùm notum sit dari opinionem mediatam, definitione ipsa ostenderet, dari etiam opiniones immediatas, quibus assentitur intellectus probabiliter, ex sola notitia terminorum: sicut dantur propositiones necessariæ, quibus ex sola notitia terminorum assentitur, assensu certo, ac necessario.

opinion, which is inferred from an immediate opinion through an evident or probable consequence, or from an evident proposition through a non-necessary consequence, as Aristotle teaches in this same chapter. But he wished to define only the immediate one, so that, since it is known that a mediate opinion is given, he might show by the definition itself that immediate opinions are also given, to which the intellect assents probably from the sole cognition of the terms; just as there are necessary propositions to which it assents from the sole cognition of the terms with a certain and necessary assent.

Sed contra differentiam probatam, inter scibile, & scientiam, & opinabile, & opinionem, proponit duo dubia in secunda parte capitis. Primum est, ad probandum: quod non differant scibile, & opinabile: quia sæpe contingit, vt quod vnus scit, alter opinetur: ergo idem erit scibile, & opinabile. Respondet, quòd de eadem re simplici, aut incomplexa, possunt esse scientia, & opinio, vt de homine. Non tamen de eadem re complexa: vt de propositione. Nam de homine, potest esse scientia, & opinio, sed non de propositione: vt de hac, Quod diameter sit commensurabilis, aut æqualis costæ: opinio fortè esse poterit, non scientia.

But against the difference proved between the knowable and science, and the opinable and opinion, he proposes two doubts in the second part of the chapter. The first is for proving that the knowable and the opinable do not differ: because it often happens that what one man knows, another opines: therefore the same thing will be knowable and opinable. He replies that of the same simple or incomplex thing there can be science and opinion, as of man; not, however, of the same complex thing, as of a proposition. For of man there can be science and opinion, but not of a proposition: as of this one, That the diagonal is commensurable, or equal to the side, there could perhaps be opinion, not science.

4 Secundum dubium est: Quia sicut scientia procedit ex immediatis principiis, ad mediatam conclusionem, ita opinio potest procedere, ex propositione immediata probabili, ad mediatam, quam de ea colligit. Præterea: Sicut demonstratio, si procedat à causa, erit propter quid: & si ab effectu, erit quia: eadem ratione opinio, si procedat ab immediata, continente causam conclusionis, dicitur, propter quid: si verò ab ea, quæ continet effectum, dicitur, quia: ergo conueniunt in his duobus, scientia, & opinio: quare non distinguentur. Respondet, Verum esse antecedens, sed negandum esse consequentiam. quia diuersus est modus procedendi vtriusque. Nam scientia procedit per medium necessarium, hoc est, ex necessariis principiis, & per necessariam consequentiam: opinio verò, per medium contingens, hoc est, vel ex principiis non necessariis, vel per consequentiam non necessariam, sed probabilem: & hoc est, distingui essentialiter, per diuersa media assentiendi. Vnde sequitur, scientiæ non posse subesse falsum, opinionem verò falsam esse posse.

4 The second doubt is: because just as science proceeds from immediate principles to a mediate conclusion, so opinion can proceed from an immediate probable proposition to a mediate one, which it infers from it. Moreover, just as demonstration, if it proceeds from the cause, will be propter quid, and if from the effect, will be quia, by the same reasoning opinion, if it proceeds from an immediate proposition containing the cause of the conclusion, is called propter quid; but if from one which contains the effect, it is called quia: therefore science and opinion agree in these two things; wherefore they will not be distinguished. He replies that the antecedent is true, but that the consequence must be denied, because the mode of proceeding of each is diverse. For science proceeds through a necessary middle, that is, from necessary principles and through a necessary consequence; but opinion through a contingent middle, that is, either from non-necessary principles, or through a consequence that is not necessary but probable: and this is to be distinguished essentially, through diverse middles of assenting. Whence it follows that falsity cannot underlie science, but that opinion can be false.

TRACTATVS I.

T R E AT I S E I .

De habitu principiorum.

On the Habit of Principles.

5 DE tribus agit Arist. cap. præsenti, De Intellectu, qui est notitia principiorum. De Scientia, quæ est notitia

Of three things Aristotle treats in the present chapter: of Understanding, which is the cognition of principles; of Science, which is the cognition

p. 688

conclusionum: quæ demonstrantur ex principiis. Et de Opinione: quam ab his differre docet. De quibus eodem ordine agendum nobis est, & de singulis singulos tractatus instituimus: in quibus ea, quæ necessaria sunt ad intelligendam eorum naturam, & rationem, breuissimè explicamus. Vt sic meliùs possimus intelligere, differentiam, quam inter ea posuit Aristot. Et primò de habitu principiorũ quatuor explicabuntur. Primum, An sit, hoc est, an pręter potentiam intellectiuam, & species intelligibiles, per quas principia, hoc est, propositiones immediatas apprehendimus, ponendus sit habitus, per quem facilè possit intellectus iudicare de veritate eorum, eisdemque assensum præstare. Secundum, Quid sit habitus iste. Tertium, An sit naturalis: Ita, vt illum receperit anima, simul cùm potentia intellectiua, dum creata fuit à Deo: vel an acquisitus per proprios actus. Quartum, An sit vnus secundùm speciem, pro principiis omnium scientiarum, vel diuersus pro diuersis principiis.

of conclusions, which are demonstrated from principles; and of Opinion, which he teaches differs from these. Of which we must treat in the same order, and we institute a separate treatise on each: in which we explain very briefly the things that are necessary for understanding their nature and ratio, so that in this way we may better understand the difference which Aristotle posited among them. And first, concerning the habit of principles four things will be explained. First, whether it exists: that is, whether, besides the intellective power and the intelligible species through which we apprehend principles, that is, immediate propositions, a habit must be posited through which the intellect may easily judge of their truth and give them its assent. Second, what this habit is. Third, whether it is natural, so that the soul received it together with the intellective power when it was created by God; or whether it is acquired through its own acts. Fourth, whether it is one in species for the principles of all the sciences, or diverse for diverse principles.

An præter intellectum, & species intelligibiles detur habitus principiorum — Whether, besides the intellect and the intelligible species, there is a habit of principles.

6 PRimò præsupponendum est, tanquam certum in doctrina Arist. & in schola Peripatetica, Quòd in intellectu, & voluntate, dantur habitus virtutum moralium, & intellectualium.
