6 First, it must be presupposed, as certain in the doctrine of Aristotle and in the Peripatetic school, that in the intellect and the will there are habits of the moral and of the intellectual virtues.

Secundò præsupponendum est, Hos habitus ponendos esse in intellectu, distinctos à speciebus intelligibilibus. Quod eorum, & illarum officium efficaciter probat. Nam officium speciei intelligibilis, solũ est vnire obiectum intelligendũ, cum potentia intellectiua, ex qua vnione sequitur apprehensio eius, quæ est prima operatio (Intellectus) vel vnio ipsa est apprehensio. Vnde sequitur, species intelligibiles, solùm ad apprehendendum obiecta proximè deseruire. Sed cùm post apprehensionem, sequatur iudiciũ de veritate, aut falsitate propositionum: in qua principaliter consistit secunda operatio intellectus: & in quo potest esse aliqua indifferentia, aut etiam difficultas, ad iudicandum, additur alius habitus ab Arist. & omnibus (solis exceptis nominalibus) qui species ipsas intelligibiles, dicũt esse habitus: & ideo, nihil aliud præter illas ad iudicandum ponunt.

Second, it must be presupposed that these habits are to be posited in the intellect as distinct from the intelligible species. Which the office of the former and of the latter effectively proves. For the office of the intelligible species is only to unite the object to be understood with the intellective power, from which union follows the apprehension of it, which is the first operation of the intellect; or the union itself is the apprehension. Whence it follows that intelligible species serve proximately only for apprehending objects. But since after apprehension there follows the judgment of the truth or falsity of propositions, in which the second operation of the intellect principally consists, and in which there can be some indifference, or even difficulty, in judging, another habit is added by Aristotle and by all (the Nominalists alone excepted), who say that the intelligible species themselves are habits, and therefore posit nothing besides them for judging.

His suppositis, Primum dubium est: An præter species intelligibiles, per quas principia apprehendimus, necessarius sit habitus principiorum, ad iudicandum de veritate eorum: quod est eis assentire. Et est prima opinio Duran. in 3. d. 33. q. 1 ad finem. & Soti 1. li. de Iustitia, & iure, q. 4. art. 2. qui licèt habitus scientiarum, in intellectu ponant, præter species intelligibiles, ad assensum

These things supposed, the first doubt is: whether, besides the intelligible species through which we apprehend principles, a habit of principles is necessary for judging of their truth, which is to assent to them. And the first opinion is that of Durandus, in 3, d. 33, q. 1, toward the end, and of Soto, On Justice and Right bk. 1, q. 4, a. 2, who, although they posit habits of the sciences in the intellect, besides the intelligible species, for assent to

p. 689

cõclusionum: nihilominus ad assentiendum principiis, nullum habitum esse ponendum asserunt: sed sufficere aiunt lumen naturale, quod est potentia ipsa intellectiua.

conclusions, nevertheless assert that no habit is to be posited for assenting to principles; rather, they say, the natural light suffices, which is the intellective power itself.

7 Probant hoc arg. Ad operationes naturales, in quibus nulla est indifferentia, vel libertas, non ponuntur habitus, vt in potentia visiua: imò nec in volũtate, respectu vltimi finis, in quem naturaliter tendit, per amorem, sed intellectus, naturaliter assentitur principiis, cùm sint veritates immediatæ ac necessariæ: ita vt eis propositis, non possit non assentire: ita enim se habet ad illa: sicut voluntas ad vltimum finem, vel visus ad colores: ergo nullo indiget habitu, ad eis assentiendem.

7 They prove it by this argument. For natural operations, in which there is no indifference or liberty, habits are not posited: as in the visual power; nay, not even in the will with respect to the ultimate end, to which it tends naturally through love. But the intellect assents naturally to principles, since they are immediate and necessary truths, so that, once they are proposed, it cannot fail to assent to them; for it is related to them as the will is to the ultimate end, or sight to colors: therefore it needs no habit in order to assent to them.

Opposita sententia tenet, præter intellectum, & species intelligibiles, ponendum esse habitum, ad assentiendum primis principiis indemonstrabilibus. Hæc est expressa apud Arist. 6. lib. Ethic. cap. vbi inter virtutes intellectuales, quæ sunt habitus superadditi potentiis, enumerat intellectum, qui est habitus principiorum. Et D. Tho. in Commentariis eiusdem loci, declarat non de intellectu pro potentia, sed pro habitu superaddito potentiæ, loqui Arist. his verbis: Accipitur autem hic intellectus, non pro ipsa intellectiua potentia, seu pro habitu quodam quo homo ex virtute luminis intellectus agentis, naturaliter cognoscit principia indemonstrabilia. Et 1. 2. q. 94. art. 1. inquit, Principia indemonstrabilia in speculatiuis, non sunt ipse habitus principiorum, sed sunt principia, quorum est habitus: quam sententiam sequuntur, Henricus quodlib. 5. 28. Caiet. 1. 2. q. 51. art. 1. & ibidem Conradus Ferr. 1. li. contra gentes, ca. 94. Medina 1. 2. q. 49. & moderni omnes. Et videtur nobis vera, & tenenda.

The opposite opinion holds that, besides the intellect and the species intelligible, a habit is to be posited for assenting to the first indemonstrable principles. This is express in Aristotle, Ethics bk. 6, ch., where among the intellectual virtues, which are habits superadded to the powers, he enumerates understanding, which is the habit of principles. And St. Thomas, in his Commentary on the same passage, declaring that Aristotle speaks of understanding not as a power but as a habit superadded to the power, in these words: But understanding is taken here not for the intellective power itself, but for a certain habit by which man, by virtue of the light of the agent intellect, naturally knows indemonstrable principles. And in 1-2, q. 94, a. 1, he says: Indemonstrable principles in speculative matters are not the habit of principles itself, but are the principles of which there is the habit. This opinion is followed by Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 5, 28; Cajetan, 1-2, q. 51, a. 1, and Conrad in the same place; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 94; Medina, 1-2, q. 49; and all the moderns. And it seems to us true and to be held.

8 Probatur primò: Necessitas ponendi habitum in potentia: circa aliquod obiectum, est indifferentia eius, ad bene, vel malè operandum, circa illud: vt cùm vtroque modo possit operari, determinetur ad bene operandum, per habitum: Nam habitus, vt vidimus apud Arist. in prædicamento qualitatis, est dispositio subiecti, per quam bene vel malè se habet in ordine ad propriam naturam, vel operationem: sed intellectus circa prima principia, potest bene vel malè operari, cùm possit errare circa illa: ergo indiget habitu ad bene operandum: & ideo necesse est eum ponere.

8 It is proved, first: the necessity of positing a habit in a power with respect to some object is its indifference to operating well or badly with respect to it, so that, since it can operate in either way, it may be determined to operating well through the habit. For a habit, as we saw in Aristotle in the category of quality, is a disposition of the subject by which it is well or badly disposed in order to its proper nature or operation. But the intellect can operate well or badly with respect to the first principles, since it can err about them: therefore it needs a habit for operating well; and therefore it is necessary to posit it.

Secundò: Quia si intellectus non indiget habitu ad assentiendum principiis: quia sicut euidentia, & naturaliter eum mouent: sequitur nec indigere habitu, ad assentiendum cõclusionibus. Probatur consequentia: quia habito assensu principiorum, euidentem veritatem continet conclusio in eis contenta, & etiam naturaliter mouet intellectum: sed opposita

Second: because if the intellect does not need a habit for assenting to principles, because they are evident and move it naturally, it follows that neither does it need a habit for assenting to conclusions. The consequence is proved: because, once assent to the principles is had, the conclusion contained in them contains evident truth, and also moves the intellect naturally; but the opposite Xx

p. 690

opinio ponit habitum pro conclusionibus: ergo necessariò debet eum ponere circa principia.

opinion posits a habit for conclusions: therefore it must necessarily posit one with respect to principles.

9 Et ad arg. eius: Distinguenda est minor, quòd intellectus naturaliter assentiatur primis principiis. Nam quantum ad specificationem, verum est: quia supposita debita apprehensione eorum: si iudicium ferat circa illa, non potest esse iudicium dissensus, sed assensus debet esse: quantum verò attinet ad exercitium, libertatem habet circa illa, dependenter à voluntate: & ideo potest assensum suspendere, vt superiùs probauimus, quam libertatem non habent sensus, nec voluntas circa bonum in communi: ideo non sunt capaces habitus.

9 And to its argument: the minor must be distinguished, namely that the intellect assents naturally to the first principles. For as regards specification, it is true: because, given the due apprehension of them, if it passes judgment on them, it cannot be a judgment of dissent, but must be one of assent. But as regards exercise, it has liberty with respect to them, dependently on the will; and therefore it can suspend its assent, as we proved above. Which liberty the senses do not have, nor the will with respect to the good in general: therefore they are not capable of a habit.

Quidnam sit habitus principiorum — What the habit of principles is.

10 NAtura & essentia habitus, ex proprio actu, & obiecto, circa quod natus est, operari intelligenda est. Nam ab his sumunt speciem potentiæ, & habitus, vt docet Arist. lib. 2. de Anima, c. 4. Explicare igitur oportet: Quodnam sit proprium obiectum huius habitus, & quem habeat actum circa illud. Obiectum, proprium habitus, est euidens, & immediata veritas: siue vniuersalis sit illa, siue particularis. Proprius modus tendendi in obiectum, à quo formalis, & vltima ratio habitus desumitur, est per immediatam comparationem ad ipsam veritatem euidentem, quam sine vllo medio respicit. Vnde, sicut alij habitus intellectus, constituuntur, & distinguuntur specie, per tale, vel tale medium assentiendi: vt scientia, per medium demonstratiuum: opinio, per medium probabile, & fides per testimonium: ita habitus principiorum, qui dicitur intellectus, talis est in propria specie, & à cæteris habitibus distinguitur, quia per se immediatè comparatur ad euidentiam veritatis. Vnde proprius actus eius est, sine vllo medio ei assentire, sicut actus scientiæ, assentire per medium demonstratiuum, Definitio igitur eius talis erit: Habitus principiorum, est virtus intellectualis, per quam potentia intellectiua, determinatur ad assensum principiorum per se euidentem, & facile eundem eliciendum. In quo autem consistat hæc facilitas, dicemus inferiùs.

10 The nature and essence of a habit are to be understood from its proper act and from the object with respect to which it is apt to operate. For from these powers and habits take their species, as Aristotle teaches in On the Soul bk. 2, ch. 4. It is necessary, therefore, to explain what the proper object of this habit is, and what act it has with respect to it. The proper object of the habit is evident and immediate truth, whether it be universal or particular. Its proper mode of tending to its object, from which the formal and ultimate ratio of the habit is taken, is through an immediate comparison to the evident truth itself, which it regards without any middle. Whence, just as the other habits of the intellect are constituted and distinguished in species through this or that middle of assenting (as science through a demonstrative middle, opinion through a probable middle, and faith through testimony), so the habit of principles, which is called understanding, is such in its proper species, and is distinguished from the other habits, because it is compared per se and immediately to the evidence of truth. Whence its proper act is to assent to it without any middle, just as the act of science is to assent through a demonstrative middle. Its definition, therefore, will be this: The habit of principles is an intellectual virtue through which the intellective power is determined to the assent to principles evident per se, and to eliciting that assent easily. And in what this facility consists we shall say below.

An habitus principiorum sit naturalis, vel acquisitus ab intellectu, per proprios actus — Whether the habit of principles is natural, or acquired by the intellect through its own acts.

11 HAbito iam quòd habitus intellectus sit, & quid sit: sequitur tertium explicandum: Quoniam modo generetur, aut fiat in nobis. Videlicet, an eum accipiat anima simul cum propria natura, & intellectu, dum creatur à Deo: vel sicut

11 Having now explained that the habit of understanding exists, and what it is, there follows the third thing to be explained: in what manner it is generated, or comes to be in us; namely, whether the soul receives it together with its own nature and intellect when it is created by God, or whether, just as

p. 691

in ipsa creatione, accipit intellectum sine vlla specie intelligibili, sed tanquam tabulam rasam: in qua nihil depictum est, vt asseruit Arist. eodem modo eum accipiat, sine vllo habitu principiorum. Nam de cæteris habitibus scientiarum, & virtutum, certum est, nullum habere intellectum à principio tales tum, certum est, nullum habere intellectum à principio tales habitus: & ita sicut eos acquirit successu temporis, per proprios actus pari ratione acquirat habitum principiorum. Nam si cum intellectu eum accipiat anima, naturalis dicetur: hoc est à natura inditus, si verò per actus eum acquirat: non naturalis, sed acquisitus dicetur, sicut cæteri.

in its very creation it receives the intellect without any intelligible species, but as a blank tablet in which nothing is painted, as Aristotle asserted, it receives it in the same manner, without any habit of principles. For concerning the other habits, of the sciences and of the virtues, it is certain that the intellect has no such habits from the beginning; and thus, just as it acquires these in the course of time through its own acts, by parity of reasoning it would acquire the habit of principles. For if the soul receives it together with the intellect, it will be called natural, that is, implanted by nature; but if it acquires it through acts, it will be called not natural but acquired, like the others.

Prima opinio affirmat, Esse naturalem, & non acquisitum, Ita Cõradus 1. 2. q. 94. art. 1. & Bãnes 1. par. q. 1. art. 6. notabili 3. & videtur expressa apud D. Th. 1. 2. q. 49. art. 1. ad 3. vbi sic ait: 12 Puer non potest vti habitu intellectus principiorum, vel etiam lege naturali, quæ ei habitualiter inest propter defectum ætatis. Quibus verbis, habitum principiorum ponit in puero, nondum habente vsum rationis, & addit, non posse eo vti, propter defectum ætatis: ergo sentit inesse ei à natura, & non esse acquisitum per actus, & in 2. d. 24. q. 2. art 3. ad 3. Vocat eum naturalem, his verbis: Habitus naturalis nunquam amittitur, sicut patet de habitu principiorum.

The first opinion affirms that it is natural and not acquired. So Conrad, 1-2, q. 94, a. 1, and Báñez, 1 p., q. 1, a. 6, notable 3, etc.; and it seems to be express in St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 49, a. 1, ad 3, where he says: 12 A child cannot use the habit of the understanding of principles, or even the natural law, which is in him habitually, on account of the defect of age. In which words he posits the habit of principles in a child who does not yet have the use of reason, and adds that he cannot use it on account of the defect of age: therefore he thinks that it is in him from nature, and is not acquired through acts. And in 2, d. 24, q. 2, a. 3, ad 3, he calls it natural, in these words: A natural habit is never lost, as is plain of the habit of principles.

Et ratione probatur: Quia habitus acquisiti, sunt facilitates quædam: & ideo ponuntur, ad vincendam difficultatem: quam habet potentia ad operandum, circa tale obiectum, sed intellectus nullam habet difficultatem, in assentiendo primis principiis, pręsertim vniuersalissimis, vt his, Quodlibet est, vel non est. Totum est maius sua parte: ergo neque aliquam acquirit facultatem in assensu frequenti eorum: imò neque ea indiget. Probatur consequentia: Quia facilitas difficultati opponitur, & ad eam superandam ordinatur, vnde sequitur: vel non esse ponendum talem habitum, vel esse naturalem, & non acquisitum. Et talem eum appellat communis modus loquendi, fundatus fortè in nomine ipso: quia intellectus vocatur: sicut potentia ipsa, in qua recipitur: quia naturalis est ei.

And it is proved by reason: because acquired habits are certain facilities, and therefore they are posited for overcoming the difficulty which the power has in operating with respect to such an object. But the intellect has no difficulty in assenting to the first principles, especially the most universal ones, such as these: Anything whatever either is or is not; The whole is greater than its part: therefore it does not acquire any facility in the frequent assent to them; nay, it does not even need one. The consequence is proved: because facility is opposed to difficulty, and is ordered to overcoming it; whence it follows either that such a habit is not to be posited, or that it is natural and not acquired. And the common manner of speaking calls it such, founded perhaps on the very name: because it is called understanding, like the power itself in which it is received, because it is natural to it.

13 Secunda opinio est, Caiet. 1. 2. qu. 51. art. 1. d. 1. Vbi negat esse acquisitum: sic autem esse naturalem docet, vt eum non accipiat anima à principio, cum ipso intellectu: sed sicut intellectus nullam accipit speciem intelligibilem, dum creatur anima & infunditur corpori: ita nullum accipit habitum: sed acquisitis speciebus primorum principiorum, per abstractionem intellectus agentis, statim ait, profluere naturaliter habitum principiorum ac ipsa natura intellectus passibilis: cui tribui-

13 The second opinion is that of Cajetan, 1-2, q. 51, a. 1, d. 1, where he denies that it is acquired; but he teaches that it is natural in such a way that the soul does not receive it from the beginning together with the intellect itself; rather, just as the intellect receives no intelligible species when the soul is created and infused into the body, so it receives no habit; but once the species of the first principles have been acquired through the abstraction of the agent intellect, the habit of principles, he says, immediately flows forth naturally from the very nature of the passive intellect, to which it is attributed X x ij

p. 692

tur, vt statim per ipsum assentiatur eiusdem principiis, apprehensis per species. Et hoc modo, ait, vocandum esse naturalem.

so that through it the intellect immediately assents to the same principles, once they are apprehended through the species. And in this way, he says, it is to be called natural.

Tertia sententia, asserit: Habitum principiorum cum natura, neque ab eadem natura intellectus fluere, eo ipso, quòd habet species principiorum, per quas ea apprehendit: sed esse acquisitum per actus ipsos: quibus intellectus assentitur principiis. Sicut habitus scientiæ, & virtutum, acquiruntur per proprios actus: ita Ferrar. 2. contra gentes, c. 78. Et est communis modernorum: & videtur nobis vera, & tenenda. Probatur primò, expresso testimonio Arist. cap. vlt. huius 1. lib. vbi explicans modum, quo habitus iste generatur in nobis, ita ait, Neque itaque insunt determinati habitus, neque ab aliis habitibus fiunt notioribus, sed assensu. Quibus verbis, docet non inesse nobis à natura: neque ex aliis notioribus notitiis fieri, sicut habitus scientiæ, sed per assensum immediatum veritatis per se notæ. Quod est acquiri per proprios actus.

The third opinion asserts that the habit of principles neither comes with nature, nor flows from that same nature of the intellect by the very fact that it has the species of the principles through which it apprehends them; but that it is acquired through the very acts by which the intellect assents to the principles, just as the habits of the sciences and of the virtues are acquired through their own acts. So Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 78; and it is the common opinion of the moderns, and seems to us true and to be held. It is proved, first, by the express testimony of Aristotle in the last chapter of this book 1, where, explaining the manner in which this habit is generated in us, he speaks thus: Therefore the determinate habits are neither innate in us, nor do they come to be from other, better-known habits, but from assent. In which words he teaches that it is not in us from nature, nor does it come to be from other, better-known cognitions, as the habit of science does, but through the immediate assent to truth known per se. Which is to be acquired through its own acts.

Probatur deinde ratione: Quia natura non concedit rebus, nisi ea quæ necessaria sunt ad essendum, & operandum simpliciter: quæ verò ad meliùs vel faciliùs operandum seruiunt, acquirenda eis relinquit propria industria, & labore tribuens principia, quibus possint operari, & operando ea acquirere: & hac de causa non concessit hominibus habitus virtutum: quia non requiruntur ad operandum simpliciter bona opera, sed ad meliùs, hoc est, cum facilitate & promptitudine operandum. At habitus principiorum, non est necessarius ad assentiendum simpliciter, primis principiis: sed solùm ad assentiendum cum facilitate: ergo non est nobis à natura datus: sed propria industria, & labore acquisitus. Probatur minor: quia assensus principiorum, non excedit facultatem intellectus: sed is informatus per species intelligibiles, per quas apprehendit terminos, ex quibus principia fiunt, dum cognoscit significationem eorum: potest ipse propria virtute iudicare de veritate eorum, quòd est eis assentire: ergo ad assentiendum simpliciter, non indiget habitu. Probatur antecedens: quia principia sunt veritates quædam naturales, per se euidentes: ergo sunt proportionatæ lumini naturali, eiusdem intellectus: quare per propriam virtutem potest circa eas operari, per assensum.

It is proved next by reason: because nature does not grant to things anything but what is necessary for being and for operating simply; but the things which serve for operating better or more easily it leaves to be acquired by their own industry and labor, granting them principles by which they can operate and, by operating, acquire them. And for this reason it did not grant to men the habits of the virtues: because they are not required for doing good works simply, but for doing them better, that is, for operating with facility and promptness. But the habit of principles is not necessary for assenting to the first principles simply, but only for assenting with facility: therefore it is not given to us by nature, but acquired by our own industry and labor. The minor is proved: because the assent to principles does not exceed the faculty of the intellect; rather, informed by the intelligible species through which it apprehends the terms of which the principles are made, while it knows their signification, it can by its own power judge of their truth, which is to assent to them: therefore for assenting simply it does not need a habit. The antecedent is proved: because principles are certain natural truths, evident per se: therefore they are proportioned to the natural light of the same intellect; wherefore by its own power it can operate with respect to them through assent.

15 Sed vt hæc nostra sententia meliùs intelligatur, & vt testimonia D. Th. iuxta mentem eius explicentur: notandum est: Quòd licet habitus principiorum, non sit nobis à natura datus, maximum tamen habet principium in natura ipsa, ratione cuius naturalis etiam aliquo modo dici potest. Quod non habent alij habitus. Vt enim superiùs dicebamus, propria ratio huius

15 But in order that this view of ours may be better understood, and that the testimonies of St. Thomas may be explained according to his mind, it should be noted that, although the habit of principles is not given to us by nature, it nevertheless has its greatest principle in nature itself, by reason of which it can also in some manner be called natural. Which the other habits do not have. For, as we were saying above, the proper ratio of this

p. 693

habitus sumitur, per immediatam comparationem, ad ipsam veritatem per se euidentem: quam nec respicit, neque attingit per aliquod medium, sed solùm indiget notitia terminorum: quam item habet per species terminorum, ex quibus principia ipsa componuntur. Istæ autem species, producuntur ab intellectu agente, & imprimuntur intellectui passibili, mediis speciebus sensibilibus obiectorum: quæ vocantur phanthasmata. Operatio porrò sensuum, & eiusdem intellectus agentis: per quam efficiuntur species, naturalis est, & sine habitu efficitur. Informatus autem intellectus patiens per has species principiorum, & intellecta per eas significatione terminorum, sine vlla arte, vel industria, sine vllo medio, vel discursu, assentitur principiis: & per talem assensum, generatur habitus principiorum: qui postea intenditur, & perficitur, per frequentem repetitionem eiusdem assensus. Et ideo, tam ex parte specierum, naturaliter productarum: quàm ex parte assensus principiorum, dicitur habitus iste naturalis: quamuis liber assensus, & ex consequenti, liberè producatur habitus per eum. Et tandem, quia assensus principiorum, & habitus ipse, producuntur sine medio, sine discursu, sine arte, solùm per naturale lumen eiusdem intellectus: ideo non est nomen aliud ei inditum, sed nomine eiusdem intellectus significatur: dum dicimus, esse intellectum principiorum.

habit is taken from its immediate comparison to truth itself evident per se, which it neither regards nor attains through any middle, but needs only the cognition of the terms; which, again, it has through the species of the terms of which the principles themselves are composed. And these species are produced by the agent intellect and impressed on the passive intellect, by means of the sensible species of the objects, which are called phantasms. Now the operation of the senses, and of the same agent intellect, through which the species are produced, is natural, and is performed without a habit. And the patient intellect, informed through these species of the principles, and having understood through them the signification of the terms, assents to the principles without any art or industry, without any middle or discursive reasoning; and through such assent the habit of principles is generated, which is afterwards intensified and perfected through frequent repetition of the same assent. And therefore, both on the side of the species, which are produced naturally, and on the side of the assent to the principles, this habit is called natural; although the assent is free, and consequently the habit is freely produced through it. And finally, because the assent to principles and the habit itself are produced without a middle, without discursive reasoning, without art, solely through the natural light of the same intellect, therefore no other name has been given to it, but it is signified by the name of the same intellect, when we say that it is the understanding of principles.

16 Hæc autem non habent alij habitus intellectuales, vt habitus scientię. Is enim præter operationem intellectus agentis, præter species conclusionis, quas imprimit intellectui patienti, prærequirit artem, per quam disponantur principia: prærequirit assensum eorum, tanquam medium formale, quo intellectus assentitur conclusioni: & per talem assensum generatur. Et ideo neque habitus scientiæ, neque alij similes dicuntur naturales.

16 But the other intellectual habits do not have these features, as the habit of science. For besides the operation of the agent intellect, and besides the species of the conclusion, which it impresses on the patient intellect, it prerequires art, through which the principles are disposed; it prerequires the assent to them, as the formal middle by which the intellect assents to the conclusion; and through such assent it is generated. And therefore neither the habit of science nor other similar habits are called natural.

Ex quibus intelligitur: Vtrumque habere habitum principiorum: & quòd naturalis sit, & quòd sit acquisitus per proprios actus: non tamen sicut acquiruntur cæteri habitus: sed sine vllo medio, sine vlla arte, vel industria, per solam virtutem naturalem vtriusque intellectus, agentis, & patientis, ac sensuum, quorum naturales operationes præsupponuntur. Et in hoc sensu loquitur D. Tho. dum vocat naturalem hunc habitum: vel dum dicit à natura haberi: non negans per hos modos loquendi, quòd sit acquisitus per proprios actus: quia vterque sensus verus est, & neuter contradicit alteri. Hunc autem esse sensum eius, colligitur euidenter ex proprio loco, vbi ex professo agit D. Th. de hoc habitu inquirens, An sit naturalis,

From which it is understood that the habit of principles has both features: both that it is natural and that it is acquired through its own acts; not, however, as the other habits are acquired, but without any middle, without any art or industry, solely through the natural power of both intellects, the agent and the patient, and of the senses, whose natural operations are presupposed. And it is in this sense that St. Thomas speaks when he calls this habit natural, or when he says that it is had from nature; not denying, by these ways of speaking, that it is acquired through its own acts, because each sense is true and neither contradicts the other. And that this is his sense is evidently gathered from the proper place where St. Thomas treats expressly of this habit, inquiring whether it is natural, X x iij

p. 694

nempe 1. 2. q. 1. art. 1. asseritque esse naturalem secundùm inchoationem, quod non habent cæteri habitus: & nihilominus esse acquisitum, per operationem intellectus agentis, & sensuum, præsuppositam assensui intellectus passibilis, per quem proximè acquiritur. In quo etiam sensu, dixit Arist. ex sensibus, & non à natura haberi hunc habitum.

namely in 1-2, q. 1, a. 1; and he asserts that it is natural according to its inchoation, which the other habits do not have; and nevertheless that it is acquired, through the operation of the agent intellect and of the senses, presupposed to the assent of the passive intellect, through which it is proximately acquired. In which sense also Aristotle said that this habit is had from the senses and not from nature.

17 In eodem etiam sensu, intelligitur ad testimonium D. Th. de puero; quem dicit habere hunc habitum: sed non vti eo propter defectum ætatis. Intelligit autem eum habere secundùm inchoationem: quia hoc modo est naturalis: quem tamen non habet formaliter: quousque per primum assensum principiorum in eo generetur, & per sequentes perficiatur.

17 In the same sense, too, is understood the testimony of St. Thomas about the child, whom he says has this habit but does not use it on account of the defect of age. For he understands that he has it according to its inchoation, because in this manner it is natural; yet he does not have it formally, until it is generated in him through the first assent to principles and perfected through the subsequent ones.

Circa solutionem primi argu. Asserunt moderni quidam: Non esse ponendum habitum: pro assensu principiorum vniuersalissimorum, quæ vocantur dignitates: quia cùm sint nobis notissima, absque vlla difficultate eis assentimus: & ideò per frequentem assensum eorum, non acquirimus habitum. Sed solùm esse ponendum: pro principiis particularibus scientiarum, quibus non facilè assentitur intellectus, cùm non sint adeò nobis nota: ideo facilitate acquisita pro iis indigemus: quæ vocatur habitus. Et hæc sententia videtur mihi satis probabilis: quamuis etiam sit probabile: quòd in assentiendo his principiis, nõnihil difficultatis habeat intellectus: licèt minùs longè, quàm in assentiendo principiis particularibus, & hoc satis est, vt indigeat habitu ad assentiendum, & vt nouam acquirat facilitatem per frequentem repetitionem assensuum.

Concerning the solution of the first argument, certain moderns assert that a habit is not to be posited for the assent to the most universal principles, which are called axioms: because, since they are most known to us, we assent to them without any difficulty; and therefore through frequent assent to them we do not acquire a habit. But they say it is to be posited only for the particular principles of the sciences, to which the intellect does not easily assent, since they are not so known to us; therefore we need for them an acquired facility, which is called a habit. And this opinion seems to me sufficiently probable; although it is also probable that in assenting to these principles the intellect has some difficulty, though far less than in assenting to particular principles; and this is enough for it to need a habit for assenting, and to acquire a new facility through frequent repetition of the assents.

18 Et ex hac doctrina respondetur ad arg. Concessa maiore, sed minori negata, quòd intellectus nullam habeat difficultatem in assensu primorum principiorum, & ideò nec vllam acquirat facilitatem, per repetitionem assensus. Nam experientia, docet oppositum: & quòd aliquam habeat intellectus difficultatem, quem per exercitationem vincit: & ex consequenti, quòd nouam acquirat facilitatem.

18 And from this doctrine the reply is given to the argument: the major being granted, the minor is denied, namely that the intellect has no difficulty in the assent to the first principles, and therefore acquires no facility through repetition of the assent. For experience teaches the opposite: both that the intellect has some difficulty, which it overcomes by exercise, and consequently that it acquires a new facility.

Quid autem sit hæc facilitas: aut in quo consistat, diuersis modis explicatur ab auctoribus. Quibus omissis, dicendum est, Facilitatem, non esse aliud, quàm modum quendam, per quem potentia efficitur expedita, atque prompta ad operandum, aptaque, vt cum delectatione operetur, quod non habet ex se, vel à natura: & hunc modum tribuit ei habitus, tanto perfectiorem, quanto magis intenditur, atque perficitur, per repetitionem actuum.

But what this facility is, or in what it consists, is explained in diverse ways by the authors. Leaving these aside, it must be said that facility is nothing else than a certain mode by which the power is rendered ready and prompt for operating, and apt to operate with delight, which it does not have of itself or from nature; and the habit gives it this mode, the more perfect the more it is intensified and perfected through the repetition of acts.

p. 695

An habitus principiorum sit idem secundum speciem pro omnibus principiis: vel diuersus pro diuersis — Whether the habit of principles is the same in species for all principles, or diverse for diverse ones.

An habitus principiorum sit idem secundùm speciem, pro omnibus principiis, vel diuersus pro diuersis.

[…]

DE distinctione specifica huius habitus nihil inuenitur apud auctores. Ideo sola ratione agendum nobis est. Videtur autem vnum esse ponendum pro omnibus, quod sic probo: Habitus distinguuntur per diuersos actus, vt sæpè diximus: sed habitus principiorum habet actum eiusdem speciei, circa omnia principia: ergo est idem secundùm speciem pro omnibus.

Concerning the specific distinction of this habit nothing is found in the authors; therefore we must proceed by reason alone. And it seems that one habit is to be posited for all, which I prove thus: Habits are distinguished through diverse acts, as we have often said; but the habit of principles has an act of the same species with respect to all principles: therefore it is the same in species for all.

19 Probatur minor, quia actus huius habitus, est assensus principiorum: & assensus sunt eiusdem, vel diuersæ speciei, per eandem, vel diuersam rationem assentiendi: quæ est quasi formale obiectum eorum: sed eadem est ratio formalis assentiendi semper primis principiis: ergo omnes assensus sunt eiusdem speciei, & ideo idem quoque erit habitus, secundùm speciem. Probatur minor: quia semper assentitur intellectus primis principiis, sine medio, habita solùm significatione terminorum: ergo semper eodem modo.

19 The minor is proved: because the act of this habit is the assent to principles; and assents are of the same or of diverse species through the same or a diverse ratio of assenting, which is as it were their formal object; but the formal ratio of assenting to the first principles is always the same: therefore all the assents are of the same species, and therefore the habit too will be the same in species. The minor is proved: because the intellect always assents to the first principles without a middle, having only the signification of the terms: therefore always in the same manner.

Nostra tamen sententia duabus conclusionibus explicatur, hoc modo. Prima est, Habitus principiorum practicorum, & speculatiuorum, specie distinguuntur: quam tenet D. Tho 1. p. quęst. 79. art. 12. Et probat euidens ratio: Quia actus, & habitus distinguuntur specie, per diuersa obiecta: sed veritas practica, quam continent principia practica, & circa quam versatur habitus, tanquam circa proprium obiectum, est diuersa specie à veritate speculatiua: cùm illa ex propria natura ordinetur ad operandum, hæc verò non: ergo distinguuntur habitus isti specie. Principia practica sunt hæc, & similia: Bonum est prosequendum, & Malum fugiendum. Virtus est amplectenda, & Vitium est repudiandum. Quæ per se patet ordinari ad operandum. Speculatiua sunt: Totum est maius sua parte. Homo est animal rationale: & similia, de quibus manifestum est nullum ordinem dicere ad operandum.

Our view, however, is explained by two conclusions, in this manner. The first is: The habits of practical and of speculative principles are distinguished in species. Which St. Thomas holds, 1 p., q. 79, a. 12. And an evident reason proves it: because acts and habits are distinguished in species through diverse objects; but practical truth, which practical principles contain, and with which the habit is concerned as with its proper object, is diverse in species from speculative truth, since the former by its own nature is ordered to operating, but the latter is not: therefore these habits are distinguished in species. Practical principles are these and the like: Good is to be pursued, and Evil is to be fled; Virtue is to be embraced, and Vice is to be rejected; which, it is plain per se, are ordered to operating. Speculative ones are: The whole is greater than its part; Man is a rational animal; and the like, of which it is manifest that they say no order to operating.

20 Secunda conclusio: Habitus etiam principiorum speculatiuorum, distinguuntur specie, secundùm quòd in diuersis materiis inueniuntur: hoc modo, vt habitus principiorum vnius scientiæ, distinguatur specie ab habitu principiorum alterius. Et si pro principiis vniuersalissimis, ponendus est habitus, pro diuersis etiam ponendus est habitus distinctus specie. Ita, vt alius sit habitus, per quem assentimus huic principio, Quodlibet est, vel non est, ab eo per quem assentimur illi, Totum est maius sua parte. Hanc conclusionem sic probo: Habitus distinguuntur per diuersos actus, & actus sunt

20 The second conclusion: The habits of speculative principles, too, are distinguished in species, according as they are found in diverse matters; in this manner, that the habit of the principles of one science is distinguished in species from the habit of the principles of another. And if a habit is to be posited for the most universal principles, for diverse ones too a habit distinct in species is to be posited; so that the habit through which we assent to this principle, Anything whatever either is or is not, is another from that through which we assent to that one, The whole is greater than its part. This conclusion I prove thus: habits are distinguished through diverse acts, and acts are XX iiij

p. 696

diuersi per diuersa obiecta: sed assensus principiorum vnius scientiæ, specie distinguitur ab assensu principiorum alterius: & assensus vnius principij vniuersalissimi, distinguitur etiam specie, ab assensu alterius: ergo habitus etiam erunt distincti specie. Probatur minor: quia diuersa principia, continent diuersam veritatem, quam respiciunt assensus, tanquam proprium obiectum: vt diuersam veritatem specie continet, hoc principium, Homo est animal rationale, ab illo, Natura est principium motus, & quietis, eius in quo est: ergo efficiunt assensus specie distinctos, in intellectu, & diuersi assensus, efficient habitus etiam diuersos. Et idem exemplum adduci potest, in diuersis principiis vniuersalissimis.

diverse through diverse objects; but the assent to the principles of one science is distinguished in species from the assent to the principles of another; and the assent to one most universal principle is also distinguished in species from the assent to another: therefore the habits too will be distinct in species. The minor is proved: because diverse principles contain diverse truth, which the assents regard as their proper object; as this principle, Man is a rational animal, contains a truth diverse in species from that one, Nature is the principle of motion and of rest of that in which it is: therefore they produce assents distinct in species in the intellect, and diverse assents will produce diverse habits too. And the same example can be adduced in diverse most universal principles.

21 Et si dicas, Distingui specie assensus: sed tamen pertinere ad eundem habitum: quia sunt actus inadęquati respectu illius, ad omnia principia, & ad omnes assensus eorum se extendentis. In contrarium est, quòd si distinguuntur specie: licèt inadæquata, necesse est eos generare habitus partiales specie distinctos. Quia quælibet causa, producit effectum secundùm suam speciem, (licèt inadæquatum) ergo à causis specie distinctis, (licèt inadæquatis) necesse est effectus specie diuersos (licèt inadæquatos) procedere. Quare iam dabuntur diuersi habitus, saltem partiales, specie distincti. Verùm probatur, debere distingui specie totali: quia habitus principiorum, non habet tantam extensionem, ac intellectus: vt possit idem se extendere ad omnes veritates, nec habet maiorem extensionem: quàm habitus scientiæ, cui proportionatur, ac necessariò præsupponitur: sed habitus scientiæ, distinguuntur specie per diuersa obiecta formalia: ergo habitus principiorum, qui eis correspõdent, debent etiam distingui specie, per diuersas veritates principiorum, circa quas versantur, tanquam circa propria obiecta.

21 And if you say that the assents are distinguished in species, but nevertheless pertain to the same habit, because they are inadequate acts with respect to it, since it extends itself to all principles and to all the assents to them: against this is the fact that, if they are distinguished in species, though inadequate, they must necessarily generate partial habits distinct in species. Because any cause whatever produces an effect according to its own species (though an inadequate one): therefore from causes distinct in species (though inadequate) effects diverse in species (though inadequate) must proceed. Wherefore there will now be diverse habits, at least partial ones, distinct in species. But that they must be distinguished by a total species is proved: because the habit of principles does not have so great an extension as the intellect, so that one and the same habit can extend itself to all truths; nor does it have a greater extension than the habit of science, to which it is proportioned and by which it is necessarily presupposed. But the habits of science are distinguished in species through diverse formal objects: therefore the habits of principles, which correspond to them, must also be distinguished in species through the diverse truths of the principles with which they are concerned as with their proper objects.

Ad arg. oppositę opinionis, neganda est minor; quòd habitus principiorum habeat assensum eiusdem speciei, circa omnia principia: nam licèt omnibus assentiatur, intellecta significatione terminorum sine medio, modus tamen iste assentiendi, & ratio formalis generica est: sicut etiam est generica in scientiis, assentire conclusionibus, per medium demonstratiuum. Sicut ergo in scientiis, specie distincta est ratio assentiendi, secundùm distinctam rationem principiorum per quæ assentitur intellectus conclusionibus, huius, aut illius scientiæ: & sicut per hanc distinctam rationem specificam: distinguuntur habitus scientiæ specie, ita in assensu principiorum distincta est ratio assentiendi specifica, secundùm distinctionem specificam diuersarum veritatum, quas diuersa principia continenti. Nam ratio

To the argument of the opposite opinion: the minor must be denied, namely that the habit of principles has an assent of the same species with respect to all principles. For although the intellect assents to all of them without a middle, once the signification of the terms is understood, this mode of assenting and formal ratio is generic; just as in the sciences, too, to assent to conclusions through a demonstrative middle is generic. Just as, therefore, in the sciences the ratio of assenting is distinct in species according to the distinct ratio of the principles through which the intellect assents to the conclusions of this or that science, and just as the habits of science are distinguished in species through this distinct specific ratio, so in the assent to principles the specific ratio of assenting is distinct according to the specific distinction of the diverse truths which the diverse principles contain. For the ratio

p. 697

assentiendi principiis, ipsamet veritas principiorum per semetipsam est, & non per aliud medium: diuersa igitur veritas immediata cùm sit, diuersa etiam ratio assentiendi erit, & diuersum assensum secundùm speciem efficiet: & diuersi assensus secundùm speciem, diuersos habitus principiorum generabunt.

of assenting to a principle is the very truth of the principles, through itself and not through another middle; since, therefore, the immediate truth is diverse, the ratio of assenting will also be diverse, and will produce an assent diverse in species; and assents diverse in species will generate diverse habits of principles.

TRACTATVS II.

T R E AT I S E I I .

De habitu scientiæ,

On the Habit of Science.

CIrca habitum scientiæ explicanda sunt, An sit, & Qui sit, & An sit de singularibus, & contingentibus, atque entibus per accidens.

oncerning the habit of science, these things are to be explained: C whether it exists, and what it is, and whether it is of singulars and contingents, and of beings per accidens.

An præter habitum principiorum, ponendus sit pro conclusionibus alter habitus distinctus, qui appellatur scientia — Whether, besides the habit of principles, another, distinct habit, which is called science, is to be posited for conclusions.

An præter habitum principiorum, ponendus sit pro conclusionibus alter habitus distinctus, qui appelletur scientia.

[…]

23 PRima opinio est, quorundam modernorum, qui cùm pro vniuersalissimis principiis non ponant habitum principiorum: sed solùm pro particularibus huius aut illius scientiæ: asserunt nihilominus, talem habitum principiorum, postquam assensum eorum habet, habita notitia terminorum extendere se ad assensus omnium conclusionum eiusdem scientiæ: & ita præter habitum principiorum, non esse ponendum habitum scientiæ, ab eo distinctum.

23 The first opinion is that of certain moderns, who, although they do not posit a habit of principles for the most universal principles, but only for the particular principles of this or that science, nevertheless assert that such a habit of principles, after it has the assent to them, the cognition of the terms being had, extends itself to the assents to all the conclusions of the same science; and thus that, besides the habit of principles, no habit of science distinct from it is to be posited.

Probant testimonio Aristot. 6. lib. Ethic. cap. 3. vbi enumerans habitus intellectuales, de sapientia, quæ est habitus vnus Intellectus, asserit, esse scientiam, & intellectum, simul eorum, quæ honorabilissima sunt: ergo sentit eundem habitum, sufficere pro principiis, & conclusionibus; quare non est necessarium multiplicare alterum.

They prove it by the testimony of Aristotle, Ethics bk. 6, ch. 3, where, enumerating the intellectual habits, he asserts of wisdom, which is one habit of the intellect, that it is science and understanding together, of the things that are most honorable: therefore he thinks that the same habit suffices for principles and conclusions; wherefore it is not necessary to multiply another.

22 Probant deinde ratione: Quia assensus, quorum vnus dependet ab altero non possunt generare distinctos habitus: quia diuersi habitus independentes esse debent, sed assensus conclusionum, præsupponit assensum principiorum, à quo intrinsecam habet dependentiam, vt ex se patet: ergo non generat distinctum habitum ab eo, sed idemmet habitus, qui principiorum est, se extendit ad conclusiones. Maiorem probant, exemplo vniuersaliorum scientiarum, vt Dialecticæ, atque Philosophiæ, quæ licèt diuersas habeant conclusiones: non ideo tamen ponuntur in eis, pro singulis singuli, ac diuersi habitus, sed vnus qui se extendat ad omnes, propter intrinsecam dependentiam

22 They prove it next by reason: because assents of which one depends on the other cannot generate distinct habits, because diverse habits must be independent; but the assent to conclusions presupposes the assent to principles, on which it has an intrinsic dependence, as is plain of itself: therefore it does not generate a habit distinct from it, but the very same habit which is of the principles extends itself to the conclusions. They prove the major by the example of the more universal sciences, such as Dialectic and Philosophy, which, although they have diverse conclusions, nevertheless do not on that account have posited in them a single and diverse habit for each conclusion, but one which extends itself to all, on account of the intrinsic dependence

p. 698

vnius conclusionis ab alia: cui præsupponitur necessariò, vel quam præsupponit: quod nos asseruimus, atque probauimus q. 3. Proœmiali: ergo cùm magis intrinsecam dependentiam habeant: conclusiones eiusdem scientiæ, à principiis eiusdem, quàm possint habere inter sese conclusiones ipsæ, sequitur non esse ponendum habitum distinctum pro conclusionibus, ab habitu principiorum: sed hunc se extendere ad omnes.

of one conclusion on another, by which it is necessarily presupposed, or which it presupposes, as we asserted and proved in Proemial q. 3: therefore, since the conclusions of the same science have a more intrinsic dependence on the principles of the same science than the conclusions themselves can have among themselves, it follows that no habit distinct from the habit of principles is to be posited for the conclusions, but that this one extends itself to all.

Hæc tamen sententia manifestè contraria est eidem Arist. in eodem loco: cap. 6. vbi expressè docet: Non solùm habitum principiorum: quid dicitur intellectus, esse distinctũ ab habitu scientię, & aliis: sed neque posse cum aliquo eorum coincidere, his verbis: Intellectus neque est scientia, nec ars, nec prudentia. Scientia: quia ipsum scibile demonstrabile est: ars, & prudentia: quia in his versantur, quæ sese aliter habere possunt. At nec sapientia est: est enim sapientis de quibusdam demonstrationem habere. Quod si ea quibus verum dicimus, & nunquam falsum, in his quæ possunt, aut non possunt aliter se habere, (& hæc sunt, scientia, prudentia, sapientia, intellectus: horum autem trium habituum, nullus esse potest, atque tres dico, prudentiam, scientiam, sapientiam) restat intellectum esse principiorum.

This opinion, however, is manifestly contrary to the same Aristotle in the same place, ch. 6, where he teaches expressly that not only is the habit of principles, which is called understanding, distinct from the habit of science and from the others, but that it cannot coincide with any of them, in these words: Understanding is neither science, nor art, nor prudence. Not science, because the knowable itself is demonstrable; not art and prudence, because they are concerned with things that can be otherwise. But neither is it wisdom: for it belongs to the wise man to have demonstration of certain things. If, then, the things by which we speak the truth, and never falsehood, about things which either can or cannot be otherwise (and these are science, prudence, wisdom, understanding), and of these three habits none can be it (and I call the three prudence, science, wisdom), it remains that understanding is of principles.

25 Est etiam contra rationem. Quod sic probo: Habitus distinguuntur per actus: qui in intellectualibus, sunt ipsi assensus: sed assensus principiorum eiusdem scientiæ, & conclusionum eius distinguũtur specie: ergo ad habitus specie distinctos: quos generabũt, pertinere debent. Probatur minor: quia assensus distinguuntur specie, per diuersas rationes formales assentiendi: sed assensus conclusionum, habet diuersam rationẽ, ab assensu principiorum: vt ex se est manifestum, cùm assentiatur intellectus principiis sine medio, propter ipsam veritatem per se euidentem: conclusionibus verò, propter principia in demonstratione disposita: ergo assensus ipsi distinguentur specie. Et si dicas, distingui specie, tanquam actus inadæquatos eiusdẽ habitus: Contra hoc est: quòd si inadæquati sunt assensus, dabitur aliqua ratio assentiendi vniuersalior vtroque, sub qua comprehendantur: & quæ adęquata sit habitui, qui ponitur pro vtroque. Sed talis ratio est impossibilis: ergo impossibile est eundem esse habitum. Probo iterum minorem: quia talis ratio cõmunis vtrique assensui, esset assensus necessarij, aut euidentis, abstrahentis ab vtroque: quæ non potest esse vna, nisi vnitate generica, comprehendente sub se diuersos assensus secundùm speciem. Præterea: Etiam si inadæquatos esse daremus assensus principiorum, & conclusionum: cùm sint specie distincti necesse est, distinctos habitus, saltem partiales, & inadæquatos

25 It is also contrary to reason, which I prove thus. Habits are distinguished through acts, which in intellectual matters are the assents themselves; but the assents to the principles of the same science and to its conclusions are distinguished in species: therefore they must pertain to habits distinct in species, which they generate. The minor is proved: because assents are distinguished in species through diverse formal ratios of assenting; but the assent to conclusions has a ratio diverse from the assent to principles, as is manifest of itself, since the intellect assents to principles without a middle, on account of the truth itself, evident per se, but to conclusions on account of the principles disposed in a demonstration: therefore the assents themselves will be distinguished in species. And if you say that they are distinguished in species as inadequate acts of the same habit: against this is the fact that, if the assents are inadequate, there will be given some ratio of assenting more universal than both, under which they are comprehended, and which is adequate to the habit that is posited for both. But such a ratio is impossible: therefore it is impossible that it be the same habit. I prove the minor again: because such a ratio, common to both assents, would be that of a necessary or evident assent, abstracting from both; which cannot be one except by a generic unity, comprehending under itself assents diverse in species. Moreover, even if we granted that the assents to principles and to conclusions are inadequate, since they are distinct in species it is necessary that distinct habits, at least partial and inadequate

p. 699

generare: & ita distinctus iam erit ponendus habitus pro conclusionibus, specie saltem partiali.

generate; and thus a distinct habit, at least by a partial species, will now have to be posited for the conclusions.

Testimonium Arist. pro opposita sententia exposuit egregiè D. Th. non solùm in Commentariis eiusdem, sed etiam 1. 2. q. 57. art. 1. ad 2. vbi ait: Sapientiam propriè sumptam, de qua ibi loquitur Arist. esse quendam habitum, verè quidem scientificum, sed vniuersalissimum, qui circa conclusiones etiam vniuersalissimas, sibi proprias versatur: & simul de principiis, & conclusionibus scientiarum particularium, quodammodo iudicat, tanquam de inferioribus: Quia considerat altissimas causas, ad quas reducuntur inferiores, & à quibus dependent: atq; etiam vniuersalissimas rationes entis, vt essentiam, totum, partem, ac similes: à quibus particulares conclusiones, omnium scientiarum dependent; & quas aliquando demonstrat, per rationes vniuersales extrinsecas, vel ducentes ad impossibile.

The testimony of Aristotle for the opposite opinion St. Thomas explained excellently, not only in his Commentaries on the same passage, but also in 1- 2, q. 57, a. 1, ad 2, where he says that wisdom properly taken, of which Aristotle speaks there, is a certain habit, truly a scientific one, but the most universal, which is concerned with conclusions, also the most universal ones, proper to itself; and at the same time judges in a certain manner of the principles and conclusions of the particular sciences, as of inferiors: because it considers the highest causes, to which the inferior ones are reduced and on which they depend; and also the most universal rationes of being, such as essence, whole, part, and the like, on which the particular conclusions of all the sciences depend, and which it sometimes demonstrates through universal extrinsic reasons, or reasons leading to the impossible.

26 Et propter has excellentias, quodam modo se habet ad alias scientias, tanquam intellectus, qui est habitus principiorum, & simul est etiam habitus scientiæ, respectu suarum conclusionum, non tamen est idem habitus, cum eo, qui ponitur pro principiis eius: sed diuersus. Et eiusmodi vniuersalis scientia, non est alia, præter Metaphysicam, cui prædictæ excellentiæ conueniunt.

26 And on account of these excellences it is related in a certain manner to the other sciences as understanding, which is the habit of principles; and at the same time it is also the habit of science with respect to its own conclusions; yet it is not the same habit as that which is posited for its principles, but a diverse one. And a universal science of this kind is none other than Metaphysics, to which the aforesaid excellences belong.

Ad arg. eiusdem sententiæ, Respondetur, Maiorem esse falsam, absolutè: quod probant scientia subalternans, & subalternata. Nam obiectum huius, continetur sub obiecto alterius: & conclusiones eius habent intrinsecam dependentiam, à conclusionibus alterius, per quas probantur, quasi per principia, & nihilominus, sunt habitus, & scientiæ specie distincti, apud Ar. & omnes. Et multò meliùs distinguentur, habitus scientiæ, & principiorum, licèt assensus conclusionum, habeat intrinsecam dependentiam, ab assensu principiorum: cùm habeant rationes formales diuersas: vt probatum est. In scientiis verò vniuersalioribus, alia est ratio: quia conclusiones, non solùm se præsupponunt, & intrinsecam habent dependentiam à principiis, eodem modo se præsupponentibus, ac dependentibus: sed omnes etiam conclusiones, habent eandem rationem formalem assentiendi, per medium demonstratiuum, & nihilominus etiam in his scientiis; distinctus ponitur habitus, pro principiis, & conclusionibus, apud Arist. & omnes.

To the argument of the same opinion the reply is that the major is false absolutely: which the subalternating and the subalternate science prove. For the object of the latter is contained under the object of the former, and its conclusions have an intrinsic dependence on the conclusions of the other, through which they are proved, as through principles; and nevertheless they are habits and sciences distinct in species, according to Aristotle and all. And much better will the habits of science and of principles be distinguished, although the assent to conclusions has an intrinsic dependence on the assent to principles, since they have diverse formal ratios, as has been proved. But in the more universal sciences the reasoning is different: because the conclusions not only presuppose one another and have an intrinsic dependence on the principles, which presuppose and depend in the same manner, but all the conclusions also have the same formal ratio of assenting, through a demonstrative middle; and nevertheless even in these sciences a distinct habit is posited for principles and for conclusions, according to Aristotle and all.

An euidentia pertineat ad essentiam scientiæ — Whether evidence pertains to the essence of science.

An euidentia pertineat ad essentiam scientiæ.

[…]

27 HOc est secundum explicandum de scientia, pertinens ad essentiã eius, An videlicet euidentia sit ei essentialis. Et

27 This is the second thing to be explained concerning science, pertaining to its essence: namely, whether evidence is essential to it. And

p. 700

quia prædicata essentialia cuiuscunque rei, & ex eius definitione: constat, necesse est definitionem scientiæ afferre, eamque explicare: vt ex eius explicatione, constare possit, an inter prædicata essentialia eius numerari debeat euidentia: quia si numeranda non sit, nec essentialis ei censebitur.

because the essential predicates of anything whatever are established from its definition, it is necessary to bring forward the definition of science and to explain it, so that from its explanation it may be established whether evidence ought to be numbered among its essential predicates: because if it is not to be numbered among them, it will not be judged essential to it either.

Arist. 2. cap. huius libri definiuit scientiam in concreto, dicens: Scire, est rem per causam cognoscere, & quod illius est causa: & quod impossibile est, aliter se habere: quam definitionẽ, si ad scientiam in abstracto applicemus, sub forma quidditatiuæ definitionis, hoc modo assignari potest: Scientia, est cognitio vera & certa rei necessariæ, per propriam causam. In qua Cognitio, habet rationem generis, quia in ea conuenit scientia cum cæteris actibus intellectus. Potest autem cognitio sumi, pro actuali, vel habituali, vel pro vtraque: & sic definietur vtraque scientia, actualis, & habitualis. Actualis, est assensus conclusionis. Habitualis verò, habitus per eam genitus. In communi autem modo loquendi, pro habituali potiùs sumitur. Reliquæ verò particulæ ponuntur pro differentia, vt per eas distinguatur à cæteris habitibus intellectus. Nam Vera, dicitur, cognitio vt distinguatur ab errore. Certa, vt distinguatur ab opinione, & cæteris cognitionibus, quibus nõ repugnat subesse falsum: per Rem necessariam, separatur à prudentia, & arte, quæ versantur circa contingentia. Particula denique per causam distinguit scientiã ab habitu principiorũ, qui non procedit per medium, sed immediatè assentitur veritati, habita notitia terminorum.

Aristotle, in ch. 2 of this book, defined science in the concrete, saying: To know is to know a thing through its cause, and that it is the cause of that thing, and that it is impossible for it to be otherwise. Which definition, if we apply it to science in the abstract, can be assigned under the form of a quidditative definition in this manner: Science is the true and certain cognition of a necessary thing through its proper cause. In which cognition has the ratio of genus, because in it science agrees with the other acts of the intellect. Now cognition can be taken for actual or habitual cognition, or for both; and in this way both sciences, actual and habitual, are defined. Actual science is the assent to the conclusion; habitual science the habit generated through it. But in the common manner of speaking it is taken rather for habitual science. The remaining particles are posited in place of the difference, so that through them it may be distinguished from the other habits of the intellect. For a cognition is called true so that it may be distinguished from error; certain, so that it may be distinguished from opinion and the other cognitions to which it is not repugnant that falsity underlie them; by of a necessary thing it is separated from prudence and art, which are concerned with contingent things. Finally, the particle through its cause distinguishes science from the habit of principles, which does not proceed through a middle, but assents immediately to the truth, once the cognition of the terms is had.

28 Distinguitur etiam à scientia, quæ habetur à posteriori, & per effectum: quam non comprehendit Arist. sub hac definitione: sed solam scientiam perfectam, quæ vocatur propter quid. Possumus autem definitionem vtrique communem, & quasi genericam designare, comprehendentem vtramque, mutata solùm vltima particula: per causam, & posita huius loco, particula, per demonstrationem: & erit hæc: Scientia est cognitio vera, rei necessariæ, per demonstrationem.

28 It is distinguished also from the science which is had a posteriori and through the effect, which Aristotle does not comprehend under this definition, but only perfect science, which is called propter quid. But we can designate a definition common to both, and as it were generic, comprehending both, by changing only the last particle, through its cause, and putting in its place the particle through demonstration; and it will be this: Science is the true cognition of a necessary thing through demonstration.

Sed an completæ sint istæ definitiones, vel desit eis particula, euidens, saltem intelligenda: de hoc est præsens quæstio. Quæ vt meliùs intelligatur, explicandi, ac distinguendi sunt isti tres termini, Certitudo, Necessitas, & Euidentia. Certitudo, est firma adhæsio intellectus alicui obiecto, absque dubitatione, vel formidine. Ita eam definiunt Scholastici Doctores, in 3 d. 26. præsertim D. Th. quæst. 2. art. 4 Bonau. q. 4. Durand. in 4. d. 37. q. 8. Cæterùm firma adhæsio intellectus duplex est, Apparens, & Vera. Apparens est, quando intellectus, ex aliqua ratione probabili, atque ex efficaci applicatione voluntatis, tenaciter

But whether these definitions are complete, or whether they lack the particle evident, which must at least be understood: of this is the present question. For its better understanding, these three terms must be explained and distinguished: Certitude, Necessity, and Evidence. Certitude is the firm adhesion of the intellect to some object, without doubt or fear. So the Scholastic Doctors define it, in 3, d. 26, especially St. Thomas, q. 2, a. 4; Bonaventure, q. 4; Durandus, in 4, d. 37, q. 8. But the firm adhesion of the intellect is twofold, Apparent and True. It is apparent when the intellect, from some probable reason and from an efficacious application of the will, tenaciously

p. 701

inhæret alicui obiecto: & de hac apparenti adhæsione, intelligitur illud axioma, positum ab Arist 7. lib. Ethi. c. 3. Ita firmiter adhærent nonnulli suis opinionibus falsis, aut erroribus, sicut alij adhærent scientiis. De hac verò firma adhæsione, non intelligitur definitio: sed de Vera, qua intellectus propter veritatem ipsam rei, aut solidam, ac firmam rationem, seu infallibililem auctoritatem, adhæret alicui obiecto. Certitudo autem sic explicata, habet illos tres gradus, quos superiùs explicuimus.

adheres to some object; and it is of this apparent adhesion that the axiom laid down by Aristotle, Ethics bk. 7, ch. 3, is understood: Some adhere as firmly to their false opinions or errors as others adhere to the sciences. But the definition is not understood of this firm adhesion, but of the True one, by which the intellect, on account of the truth of the thing itself, or of a solid and firm reason, or of an infallible authority, adheres to some object. Certitude, then, explained in this way, has those three degrees which we explained above.

Necessitas verò, in ordine ad propositionem sumpta, de qua non loquimur, est determinatio intellectus ad veritatem: & propositio necessaria erit, quæ ita est vera: vt repugnet esse falsam. quod explicuit Arist, illo verbo, impossibile aliter se habere. Habet autem necessitas eosdem gradus quos certitudo.

But Necessity, taken in order to a proposition (of which we are not speaking), is the determination of the intellect to truth; and a proposition will be necessary which is true in such a way that it is repugnant for it to be false; which Aristotle expressed by that phrase, impossible to be otherwise. And necessity has the same degrees as certitude.

Euidentia denique, addit supra firmam adhæsionem manifestationem veritatis, sub claritate alicuius luminis: ita vt euidens dicatur obiectum, quasi clarum, ac perspicuum, seu manifestum. Hanc euidentiam seu claritatem habent principia ex se, scientia veró participatam à principiis. Et de certitudine, ac necessitate, nemo potest dubitare, quin sint essentiales sciẽtiæ, cùm vtraque sit expressè posita in definitione Arist. De sola igitur euidentia, cùm non sit expressa, quæstio esse potest: An sit ei essentialis? & ideo in definitione subintelligenda, aut declaranda.

Finally, Evidence adds over firm adhesion the manifestation of the truth under the clarity of some light, so that an object is called evident as being clear and perspicuous, or manifest. This evidence or clarity principles have of themselves, but science has it as participated from the principles. And of certitude and necessity no one can doubt that they are essential to science, since both are expressly set down in Aristotle’s definition. Concerning evidence alone, therefore, since it is not expressed, there can be a question: Whether it is essential to it? and therefore whether it must be understood, or declared, in the definition.

Et prima opinio negat essentialem esse, ita Massius cap præsenti, q. 3. conclusione 1. & 2. Probat, primò: Quia scientia subalternata, est vera scientia, & tamen non est euidens: ergo euidentia, non est de ratione scientiæ. Minorem probat: quia potest contingere, quòd sit sine subalternante, & solùm habeat principia accepta, per testimonium eius, qui habet subalternantem: & tunc patet non esse euidentem. Et, etiamsi cum subalternante sit, intra tamen proprios limites, nescit reducere sua principia vsque ad prima & indemonstrabilia: ergo non habet euidentiam eorum, & ex consequenti neque conclusionum, quæ ex eis deducit. Nihilominus vtroque modo vera scientia est, cùm sit de re necessaria, per euidentem consequentiam.

And the first opinion denies that it is essential. So Diego Mas, on the present chapter, q. 3, conclusions 1 and 2. He proves it, first: Because subalternate science is true science, and yet it is not evident; therefore evidence is not of the ratio of science. He proves the minor: because it can happen that it exists without the subalternating science and has only principles accepted through the testimony of him who has the subalternating science; and then it is plain that it is not evident. And even if it is together with the subalternating science, still within its own limits it does not know how to reduce its principles all the way to the first and indemonstrable ones; therefore it does not have evidence of them, and consequently neither of the conclusions which it deduces from them. Nevertheless in both ways it is true science, since it is of a necessary thing through an evident consequence.

Secundò probat: Quia Theologia, quæ deducitur ex principiis diuinæ fidei, per veras demonstrationes, non est euidens cùm ex principiis obscuris fidei, non possit colligi euidens cõclusio: & tamen est vera scientia, vt est manifestum: ergo euidentia non pertinet ad essentiam scientiæ.

Second, he proves it: Because Theology, which is deduced from the principles of divine faith through true demonstrations, is not evident, since from the obscure principles of faith an evident conclusion cannot be gathered; and yet it is true science, as is manifest; therefore evidence does not pertain to the essence of science.

Hæc tamen sententia duo asserit falsa, Primum, Quòd scientia subalternata, existens sine subalternante, & habens principia

This opinion, however, asserts two false things. First, that subalternate science, existing without the subalternating science, and having principles

p. 702

solùm accepta per testimonium eius, qui habet subalternantem, sit vera scientia. Nam si principia solùm habentur, per testimonium illius, assensus eorum solùm erit fides humana, cui potest subesse falsum: ergo non possunt esse causa conclusionis certæ, aut scientificæ: alioqui effectus esset perfectior, quàm propria causa.

accepted only through the testimony of him who has the subalternating science, is true science. For if the principles are held only through the testimony of that man, the assent to them will be only human faith, under which falsehood can lie; therefore they cannot be the cause of a certain or scientific conclusion; otherwise the effect would be more perfect than its proper cause.

31 Secundum quod asserit, est, Scientiam subalternatam, etiam dum cum subalternante existit, in eodem homine, esse scientiã, intra proprios limites: sed non esse euidentem: quia nescit reducere suas conclusiones, vsque ad principia indemonstrabilia. Hæc autem duo, manifestam continent repugnantiam: quia si nescit reducere principia: ergo non erit scientia. Probatur euidenter consequentia ex his verbis Aristotelis, quæ habentur cap. 2. huius libri: Non scit, qui demonstrationem horum non habet, &c. Hoc est, præmissarum, ex quibus constat demonstratio: quas si non scit reducere, non erunt sibi certæ: ergo nec certam cõclusionem ex eis deducere vllo modo poterit.

31 The second thing it asserts is that subalternate science, even when it exists together with the subalternating science in the same man, is science within its own limits, but is not evident, because it does not know how to reduce its conclusions all the way to the indemonstrable principles. But these two things contain a manifest repugnance: because if it does not know how to reduce its principles, then it will not be science. The consequence is evidently proved from these words of Aristotle, which are found in ch. 2 of this book: He does not know who does not have the demonstration of these, etc., that is, of the premises of which the demonstration consists; and if he does not know how to reduce them, they will not be certain to him; therefore neither will he be able in any way to deduce a certain conclusion from them.

Sulalterna igitur scientia, simul cum subalternante existens duobus modis consideratur. Primo: Intra proprios limites præcise: hoc est, non considerando continuationem, aut vnionẽ, quam habet cum subalternante: & hoc modo, nec est scientia, vt probauimus capite 10. nec est euidens. Sed erit opinio quædam. Secundo consideratur, vt continuata, vel vnita cum subalternante in qua continuatione consistit formaliter subalternatio: & ideo solùm, vt sic sumpta, est formaliter subalternata: & hoc modo vera scientia est, & euidens: quia per talem continuationem auxilio subalternantis, reducit sua principia, vsque ad prima indemonstrabilia.

Subalternate science, then, existing together with the subalternating science, is considered in two ways. First, precisely within its own limits: that is, without considering the continuation or union which it has with the subalternating science; and in this way it is neither science, as we proved in chapter 10, nor is it evident, but it will be a kind of opinion. Second, it is considered as continued or united with the subalternating science, in which continuation subalternation formally consists; and therefore only as taken in this way is it formally subalternate; and in this way it is true science, and evident, because through such a continuation, by the help of the subalternating science, it reduces its principles all the way to the first indemonstrable ones.

32 Et, si dicas. Ipsam non reducere sua principa: sed subalternantem. Respondeo, Subalternantem reducere, vt sibi continuantur subalternata: & non alio modo: & hoc idem est, ac subalternatam reducere, vt continuatur cum subalternante. Ita enim fit, qui habet vtramque, habeat euidentiam principiorum subalternatæ, ratione continuationis: & ideo subalternata sit in eo vera scientia, & euidens.

32 And if you say: It is not it that reduces its principles, but the subalternating science; I reply: the subalternating science reduces them as the subalternate science is continued with it, and in no other way; and this is the same as the subalternate science reducing them as it is continued with the subalternating science. For thus it comes about that he who has both has evidence of the principles of the subalternate science by reason of the continuation; and therefore the subalternate science is in him true science, and evident.

Vt igitur nostram sententiam explicemus, notandum est, Scientiam duobus modis sumi posse. Primo, In quantum per lumen naturale intellectus haberi potest: & hanc tantùm definiuit Aristoteles quia hanc tantùm potuit cognoscere. Secundo modo, potest considerari vniuersalius, prout solùm dicit assensum conclusionis, habitum per demonstrationem ex præmissis, siue per lumen naturale, siue per aliud quodcunque cognitis: quarum tamen certum habeat assensum

In order, then, to explain our view, it should be noted that Science can be taken in two ways. First, insofar as it can be had through the natural light of the intellect; and Aristotle defined only this, because only this could he know. In the second way it can be considered more universally, as it says only the assent to a conclusion had through demonstration from premises known whether by natural light or by any other whatever, of which, however, it has a certain assent,

p. 703

, siue per reductionem ad prima indemonstrabilia, siue alio modo.

whether by reduction to the first indemonstrable principles, or in another way.

33 Quia distinctione supposita, duabus conclusionibus continetur nostra sententia. Prima est, Ad essentiã scientiæ primo modo consideratæ, pertinet euidentia. Probatur: Quia si quis demonstrat conclusionem, per causam, vel effectum, cognitum per lumen naturale intellectus, necesse est, habeat euidentiam præmissarum: cùm sibi sint manifestæ sub claritate luminis naturalis: & consequentia, etiam eodem modo est sibi euidens: ergo conclusio, ex eis deducta, etiam est euidens. Probatur consequentia: quia ex causa per se omni ex parte euidenti, euidens quoque effectus debet sequi: sed ex tali assensu conclusionis euidenti generatur habitus scientiæ: ergo erit etiam euidens essentialiter. Quamuis autem euidentia, sit prædicatum essentiale scientiæ, eam tamen non expressit Aristot. in definitione quia satis manifestum erat, in verbis eiusdem definitionis hanc contineri. Si autem quis velit eam exprimere, sic dicet: Scientia est, cognitio vera, certa, & euidens, rei necessariæ per causam. Et si velit definire omnem scientiam, quia, & propter quid, sic dicet: Scientia est cognitio vera, certa, & euidens, rei necessariæ, per demonstrationem.
