On the one hand the Dialectical predicates seem to be five, on account of this argument: Because a predicate is distinguished from a predicable as act from potency; but act and potency must be numbered in the same way, because potency takes its unity and distinction from act; therefore there will be as many predicates as predicables. But it is established from Porphyry that the predicables are five; therefore the predicates too must be five.

Ex alia verò parte videntur esse decem, propter secundum argum. Quia prædicamentum non est aliud, quàm prædicatorum series, & ordinatio: ergo idem erit numerus prædicatorum & prædicamentorum. Constat autem decem esse prædicamenta

But on the other hand they seem to be ten, on account of a second argument: Because a category is nothing other than a series and ordering of predicates; therefore the number of predicates and of categories will be the same. But it is established that there are ten categories

p. 719

, ex Arist. ergo ponenda sunt decem prædicata.

from Aristotle; therefore ten predicates must be posited.

5 His tamen non obstantibus: Nostra sententia est, Quatuor tantum esse prædicata Topica. Vt Arist. expressè docet, 1. lib. c. 4. quæ sunt: Definitio, Genus, Proprium, & Accidens, ita, vt nec plura addenda sint, neque aliquod ex his auferendum. Tota autem difficultas huius rei, consistit in assignanda ratione, propter quam Arist. quatuor hæc prædicata posuit. Pro cuius explicatione, notandum est, Finem huius artis topicæ, vt diximus, esse methodum tradere, probabiliter disputandi de quacunque re proposita. Disputatio autem tribus partibus constat, ita ordinatis. Primò, Quæstione, seu interrogatione, quam titulum disputationis solemus vocare, sic dicentis: Vtrùm cœlum sit incorruptibile, vel non? aut quid simile. Deinde Locis, ex quibus eruenda sunt argumenta probabilia, quibus mediis dubiam reddamus quæstionem: & tertio loco, Argumentis ipsis, quæ sunt syllogismi Dialectici, ex propositionibus Dialecticis compositi. Propositio autem Dialectica, (vt postmodum dicetur) est altera pars problematis. Problemata verò, & ex consequenti propositiones Dialecticæ, ex prædicatis fiunt: quia non est aliud problema, quàm quæstio, vel interrogatio, An aliquod prædicatum conueniat tali subiecto: vt dum dicimus, An cœlum sit incorruptibile, vel non? idem est, ac si quæramus, An hoc prædicatum incorruptibile, conueniat cœlo, vel non. Vnde sequitur: prædicatum topicum non esse aliud, quàm id quod de re aliqua quæri potest. Tot igitur erunt prædicata, quot quæstiones possunt de re aliqua fieri: & tot etiam quæstiones, quot prædicata. Et cùm quæstio idem sit, ac problema: idem erit numerus prædicatorum, ac problematum. Et tandem cùm propositio, & problema, forma tantùm interrogationis differant, quia problema est interrogatio vtriusque partis contradictionis: vt si dicas, Vtrùm cœlum sit incorruptibile, vel non, problema efficis. Propositio verò, interrogatio alterius partis, vt putásne cœlum est incorruptibile: tot sunt propositiones Dialecticæ, quot problemata. Et ita intelligitur, prædicatum Dialecticum esse primum, ex quo numerus problematum desumi debet. Deinde ex numero problematum, numerus propositionum Dialecticarum. Et ita, ex ordine ad problemata, & propositiones constituendas, desumitur numerus prædicatorum. Et discursus iste deducitur ex 4. cap. 1. lib.

5 These things notwithstanding, our view is that there are only four Topical predicates, as Aristotle expressly teaches, bk. 1, ch. 4, which are: Definition, Genus, Property, and Accident, so that neither are more to be added nor any of these to be taken away. But the whole difficulty of this matter consists in assigning the reason on account of which Aristotle posited these four predicates. For whose explanation it should be noted that the end of this topical art, as we said, is to hand down a method of disputing probably on any thing proposed. But a disputation consists of three parts, ordered thus. First, of the Question, or interrogation, which we usually call the title of the disputation, saying thus: Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? or something similar. Next, of the Places from which probable arguments are to be drawn, by which means we may render the question doubtful; and in the third place, of the Arguments themselves, which are Dialectical syllogisms composed of Dialectical propositions. Now the Dialectical proposition (as will be said afterward) is one part of the problem. And problems, and consequently Dialectical propositions, are made of predicates: because a problem is nothing other than a question or interrogation whether some predicate belongs to such a subject: as when we say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? it is the same as if we asked whether this predicate, incorruptible, belongs to the heavens, or not. Whence it follows that a topical predicate is nothing other than that which can be asked about some thing. There will therefore be as many predicates as there can be questions made about some thing, and as many questions as predicates. And since a question is the same as a problem, the number of predicates and of problems will be the same. And finally, since a proposition and a problem differ only in the form of the interrogation (because a problem is an interrogation of both parts of a contradiction: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible or not, you make a problem; whereas a proposition is an interrogation of one of the two parts, as Do you think the heavens are incorruptible?), there are as many Dialectical propositions as problems. And thus it is understood that the Dialectical predicate is the first thing from which the number of problems must be taken; then from the number of problems, the number of Dialectical propositions. And thus the number of predicates is taken from the order to the problems and propositions to be constituted. And this discourse is drawn from ch. 4 of bk. 1.

6 Quo supposito, hac ratione probatur ab Arist. quatuor tantum esse prædicata. Prædicatum est id, quod de re aliqua quæri potest, ad disputationem Dialecticam instituendã: sed quatuor

6 This supposed, it is proved by Aristotle by this argument that there are only four predicates. A predicate is that which can be asked about some thing for setting up a Dialectical disputation; but four

p. 720

tantùm quæri possunt: ergo quatuor tantùm sunt prædicata? Minorem probat: Nam vel quærimus de aliquo definitionem vt intelligamus naturam eius, vel genus: vt intelligamus, in quonam prædicamento sit: vel proprietates, aut communia accidentia: Et nihil aliud quæri potest, quod ad hæc non reducatur: ergo quatuor sunt prædicata: ita, vt nec plura, nec pauciora. Et hæc sunt, definitio, genus, proprium, & accidens, quæ suis definitionibus sic explicat cap. 4. 1. lib. Definitio, est oratio, quid erat esse significans. Orationem esse dicit: quia non est propositio, cùm nec verum contineat, nec falsum, vt animal rationale. Vocat etiam defintionem terminum, sumpta metaphora ex terminis agrorum. Nam ad quemlibet, solùm, & totum pertinet illud, quod intra terminos eius clauditur: ita vt nihil eius extrà sit, sed totum, quod habet, intra terminos comprehendatur. Sic definitio continet, quidquid pertinet ad essentiam rei: ita vt nihil eius sit extrà, nec aliquid sit eius, quod intra illam non comprehendatur: & ideo vocatur ab Arist. terminus. Genus verò, inquit, est, quod prædicatur pluribus differentibus specie in quid: Vt animal: Proprium, quod non indicat, quid est esse rei, soli autem inest, & conuersim prædicatur: Vt risibile, respectu hominis. Accidens est, quod nec est definitio, nec genus, nec proprium, inest autem rei. aut etiam, Accidens est, quod inesse eidem potest: vt albedo, respectu parietis.

only can be asked; therefore there are only four predicates. He proves the minor: For either we ask about something its definition, in order that we may understand its nature; or its genus, in order that we may understand in which category it is; or its properties, or its common accidents. And nothing else can be asked which is not reduced to these; therefore there are four predicates, so that there are neither more nor fewer. And these are definition, genus, property, and accident, which he explains by their definitions thus in ch. 4 of bk. 1. Definition is an expression signifying what it was to be. He says it is an expression because it is not a proposition, since it contains neither truth nor falsehood, as rational animal. He also calls the definition a term, taking the metaphor from the boundaries of fields. For to any field there belongs alone and wholly that which is enclosed within its boundaries, so that nothing of it is outside, but the whole that it has is comprehended within its boundaries. So the definition contains whatever pertains to the essence of the thing, so that nothing of it is outside, nor is there anything of it that is not comprehended within it; and therefore it is called a term by Aristotle. Genus, he says, is that which is predicated of many things differing in species, in quid, as animal. Property, that which does not indicate what the being of the thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly, as risible in respect of man. Accident is that which is neither definition, nor genus, nor property, but belongs to the thing; or also: Accident is that which can belong to the same thing, as whiteness in respect of a wall.

7 Si autem dixeris: Vltra has quatuor quæst. aut interrogationes, seu problemata, quæ generalia esse videntur, plura possunt specialia quæri de re: vt, an sit homo: an sit leo: an sit substantia & innumera alia: ergo plura quàm quatuor, imò innumera prędicata debent concedi. Et præterea, generalia prædicata adhuc sunt plura: quia sicut quærimus de genere alicuius rei, vt, vtrùm Animal sit genus hominis, nec ne: ita possumus quærere de eius differentia, nempe, an Rationale sit differentia hominis: atque etiam de specie, vt an Homo sit species Petri, aut Ioannis: vel etiam an sit species animalis: ergo duo alia prædicata generalia sunt addenda, nempe, Species, & Differentia.

7 But if you say: Beyond these four questions, or interrogations, or problems, which seem to be general, many special ones can be asked about a thing: as whether it is a man, whether it is a lion, whether it is a substance, and innumerable others; therefore more than four, indeed innumerable predicates must be granted. And besides, the general predicates are still more: because just as we ask about the genus of some thing, as whether Animal is the genus of man or not, so we can ask about its difference, namely whether Rational is the difference of man; and also about the species, as whether Man is the species of Peter or John, or even whether it is a species of animal; therefore two other general predicates must be added, namely Species and Difference.

8 Circa primam partem arg. de interrogationibus specialibus asserit Rodolphus Agricola, lib. 1. de Inuentione Dialectica, cap. 3. errasse Arist. in assignando numero prędicatorum: quia sicut plura sunt genera problematum particularium, ita plura debent constitui prędicata, quàm quatuor. Sed plus mihi videtur errasse hic author reprehendendo Aristotelem: quia vera solutio ex doctrina eiusdem Arist. 1. lib. Topicorum, cap. 4. & lib. 5. cap. vltimo, sub finem, colligenda est. Quibus locis

8 Concerning the first part of the argument, about the special interrogations, Rudolph Agricola, On Dialectical Invention bk. 1, ch. 3, asserts that Aristotle erred in assigning the number of predicates: because, just as there are many kinds of particular problems, so more predicates than four must be established. But this author seems to me to have erred more in reproving Aristotle, because the true solution is to be gathered from the doctrine of the same Aristotle, Topics bk. 1, ch. 4, and bk. 5, last chapter, toward the end. In which places two

p. 721

duo asserit. Primum, Quòd cùm problemata ordinentur ad disputationem dialecticam, cuius finis est determinatio eiusdem problematis circa quod disputatur: ita vt præiactis probabilibus argumentis pro vtraque parte, tandem decernatur: vtra earum sit probabilior: hinc sequitur, omnia problemata, quæ eisdem argumentis, & eodem modo determinantur, ad idem genus problematis pertinere: & omnia prædicata eorundem sub aliquo ex quatuor designatis comprehendi. Et ideo in hoc primo loco asserit, differentiam, si generalis sit, hoc est, si de pluribus speciebus prædicetur sicut genus, cum genere esse connumerandam, & non esse addendum pro ea aliud prædicatum. Secundum est, quod secundo loco docet, Quæstionem accidentis finiri, aut determinari, ex eo solùm, quod quis probet conuenire subiecto. Ex qua doctrina deducimus nos, omnia problemata specialia, quæcumque illa sint, reduci ad problema accidentis. Et omnia prædicata eorundem, ad prædicatum accidentis, Et ratio huius deductionis est: quia in omni problemate speciali quæritur: An hoc prædicatum conueniat tali subiecto, vel ei insit, necne, quod patet habere modum interrogationis, aut problematis accidentis, quo solùm quærimus, An accidens conueniat, vel insit subiecto. Et eisdem prorsus argumentis finiuntur, aut determinantur: quia si inquiras, an animal conueniat homini, necne, vel an homo conueniat Petro, necne, sufficienter determinatur, & disputatio eius finita erit: si probemus vtcumque ei inesse: quamuis nec probetur esse de essentia eius aut cum eo conuerti: nec alio modo speciali ei conuenire. Ergo ad formam problematis accidentalis reducuntur: & prædicata eorum sub prædicato accidentis comprehenduntur, nec opus est alia multiplicare.

he asserts two things. The first: Since problems are ordered to dialectical disputation, whose end is the determination of the same problem about which the dispute is held, so that, after probable arguments have been set out for each side, it may finally be decided which of them is the more probable, it follows that all problems which are determined by the same arguments and in the same way belong to the same genus of problem; and that all their predicates are comprised under one of the four designated. And therefore in this first place he asserts that difference, if it is general, that is, if it is predicated of several species as a genus is, must be counted together with genus, and that no other predicate is to be added for it. The second is what he teaches in the second place: that a question of accident is settled, or determined, solely from someone’s proving that it belongs to the subject. From this doctrine we deduce that all special problems, whatever they may be, are reduced to the problem of accident, and all their predicates to the predicate of accident. And the reason for this deduction is that in every special problem it is asked: Does this predicate belong to such a subject, or is it in it, or not? which plainly has the mode of interrogation, or of problem, of accident, in which we ask only whether an accident belongs to, or is in, the subject. And they are settled, or determined, by exactly the same arguments: because if you ask whether animal belongs to man or not, or whether man belongs to Peter or not, it is sufficiently determined, and the disputation about it will be finished, if we prove that it is in it in any way whatever, even though it is not proved to be of its essence, or to be convertible with it, or to belong to it in any other special way. Therefore they are reduced to the form of an accidental problem, and their predicates are comprised under the predicate of accident, and there is no need to multiply others.

Ex eadem doctrina: Respondere possumus ad aliam partem eiusdem argumenti de specie, & differentia. Quòd si differentia sit subalterna, ad prædicatum generis reducitur: si verò infima, ad prædicatum definitionis. Species verò, ad prædicatum generis. Et ratio omnium est: quia iisdem argumentis definitur quæstio generis, & differentiæ subalternæ, cùm vtrumque prædicetur, de pluribus differentibus specie, in quid. Eisdem namque argumentis probamus animal esse genus hominis, & sensibile, differentiam subalternam eius: atque etiam, hominem esse speciem Petri, & Ioannis. Quia sicut genus prædicatur, in quid de speciebus, ita species, de indiuiduis. Iisdem etiam probamus: Animal rationale esse definitionem hominis, & rationale, esse differentiam atomam eius. Quod verò ad speciem attinet, satis etiam probabiliter respondent, Albertus

From the same doctrine we can reply to the other part of the same argument, concerning species and difference: that if the difference is subaltern, it is reduced to the predicate of genus; but if it is lowest, to the predicate of definition. Species, however, is reduced to the predicate of genus. And the reason for all of these is that a question of genus and of subaltern difference is settled by the same arguments, since each is predicated of several things differing in species, in quid. For by the same arguments we prove that animal is the genus of man, and that sensible is its subaltern difference; and also that man is the species of Peter and John, because just as genus is predicated in quid of species, so species is predicated of individuals. By the same arguments we also prove that rational animal is the definition of man, and that rational is its atomic difference. As to what concerns species, a quite probable reply is also given by Albert Zz

p. 722

Magnus, tract. 2. Topicorum ca. 8. in fine, & Sotus quæst. 5. vniuersalium ad primum: Non esse inter prædicata enumerandam: quia prædicata sumuntur per respectum ad subiectum commune, quòd non respicit species, sed singularia. Et ratio huius est: quia prædicata, vt dicebamus, ex propria ratione ordinantur ad constituenda problemata, & propositiones dialecticas: & vtrumque horum ad constituendum syllogismum dialecticum: qui non constituitur per se ex propositionibus singularibus, sed constantibus subiecto communi: in quibus solis reperiri potest forma syllogistica, ex modo, & figura constans, vt per se est manifestum.

the Great, Topics tract. 2, ch. 8, at the end, and Soto, q. 5 on universals, ad 1: that it is not to be enumerated among the predicates: because predicates are taken by relation to a common subject, which species does not regard, but singulars. And the reason for this is that predicates, as we were saying, are ordered by their proper ratio to constituting problems and dialectical propositions, and each of these to constituting the dialectical syllogism, which is not constituted per se out of singular propositions, but out of those consisting of a common subject, in which alone the syllogistic form, consisting of mood and figure, can be found, as is manifest per se.

11 Ad primum argu. de prædicabilibus: Distinguendum est antecedens. Nam prædicatum vniuersaliter sumptum, distinguitur à prædicabili, sicut actus à potentia: & ideo eodem modo numeratur, ac prædicabile. Verùm prædicatum sumptam specialiter, pro Topico, non respicit prædicabile vt potentiam, sed solùm pro actuali sumitur: & modo quidem speciali, à generali prædicato distincto, hoc est, in ordine ad quæstionem, seu problema instituendum. Vnde alio etiam modo diuerso prædicata numerantur, diuersumque sortiuntur numerum à prædicabilibus, atque etiam à prædicamentis: quæ sunt ordinationis prædicatorum, vt sub ratione generali considerantur: non vt speciali, & Topica, ad specialem etiam finem iam explicatum ordinata. Quare non sequitur ex eo, quòd prędicamenta sint decem tot debere esse prædicata Topica. Et hæc est solutio secundi argumenti.

11 To the first argument, concerning the predicables: the antecedent must be distinguished. For predicate taken universally is distinguished from predicable as act from potency, and therefore it is numbered in the same way as predicable. But predicate taken specially, for the Topical one, does not regard the predicable as a potency, but is taken only for the actual one, and indeed in a special mode, distinct from the general predicate, that is, in order to setting up a question, or problem. Hence predicates are also numbered in another, different way, and are allotted a number different from the predicables, and also from the categories, which belong to the ordering of predicates as they are considered under a general ratio, not under a special and Topical one, ordered also to the special end already explained. Wherefore it does not follow from the fact that the categories are ten that the Topical predicates must be as many. And this is the solution of the second argument.

Quid sit, & quotuplex problema Dialecticum — What a dialectical problem is, and how many kinds there are.

Quid sit, & quotuplex problema dialecticum.

[…]

12 ARistoteles 1. libro, cap. 3. definit problema dialecticum, dicens: Esse interrogationem, seu quæstionem vtriusque partis contradictionis: vt si dicas: Vtrùm animal gressibile bipes, sit definitio hominis, necne? Quatuor autem sunt genera problematum: vt cap. 3. & 4. asserit idem Aristoteles: sicut quatuor sunt prædicata, Vt Problema definitionis: quale est illud, ex definitione hominis assignatum. Problema Generis: vt si dicas, Vtrùm animal sit genus hominis, necne? Problema proprij, vt dum dicimus, Vtrùm risibile sit proprium hominis, necne, & tandem, Problema accidentis, Vtrùm albedo sit accidens parietis, necne, cap. etiam 9. eiusdem lib. diuidit problema dialecticum vniuersaliter Aristot. dicens: Aliud esse Practicum: Quod pertinet ad electionem, vel fugam, vel aliquid de prosequendo

12 Aristotle, bk. 1, ch. 3, defines the dialectical problem, saying that it is an interrogation, or question, of either part of a contradiction: as if you say, Whether walking two-footed animal is the definition of man, or not? And there are four genera of problems, as the same Aristotle asserts in ch. 3 and 4, just as there are four predicates. Thus the Problem of definition, such as the one assigned from the definition of man. The Problem of genus, as if you say, Whether animal is the genus of man, or not? The Problem of property, as when we say, Whether risible is a property of man, or not? And finally the Problem of accident: Whether whiteness is an accident of the wall, or not? In ch. 9 of the same book, too, Aristotle divides the dialectical problem universally, saying that one is Practical: that which pertains to choice or avoidance, or to something to be pursued

p. 723

, aut fugiendo. Hoc enim, inquit, ad praxim, aut operationem ordinatur: & ideo dicitur practicum. Tale est hoc: Vtrùm voluptas sit eligenda, vel non. Aliud verò est Speculatiuum: Quod nihil de prosequendo, aut fugiendo continet, nec ad operationem ordinatur: sed solùm ad cognitionem veritatis: vt si dicas: Vtrùm cœlum sit incorruptibile: vel non? Alia etiam diuisione, potest diuidi problema, secundùm materias diuersarum scientiarum, in quibus reperitur: qua ratione dicimus: Aliud esse problema Physicum, vt, An principium motus, & quietis, eius, in quo est, sit definitio naturæ, necne? Aliud Metaphysicum, vt si dixeris: Vtrùm ens sit vniuocum respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, necne? Veruntamen formalis consideratio omnium problematum secundùm quam reducuntur ad quatuor illa, ex diuersis prędicatis desumpta, dialectici propria est: quia ad solum dialecticum pertinet, docere omnes, quonam modo disputatio sit instituenda, & quibus instrumentis in ea vtendum, ad consequendam notitiam veritatis, de qua disputatur.

or avoided. For this, he says, is ordered to practice, or operation, and therefore it is called practical. Such is this: Whether pleasure is to be chosen, or not. Another, however, is Speculative: that which contains nothing about something to be pursued or avoided, nor is ordered to operation, but only to the cognition of truth: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? The problem can also be divided by another division, according to the matters of the diverse sciences in which it is found; for which reason we say that one is a Physical problem, as, Whether the principle of motion and rest of that in which it is, is the definition of nature, or not? Another Metaphysical, as if you should say, Whether being is univocal with respect to substance and accident, or not? Nevertheless, the formal consideration of all problems, according to which they are reduced to those four, taken from the diverse predicates, is proper to the dialectician: because it pertains to the dialectician alone to teach all how a disputation is to be set up, and what instruments are to be used in it for attaining cognition of the truth about which the dispute is held.

Quidnam sit propositio Dialectica, & quotuplex, & quomodo distinguatur à problemate — What a dialectical proposition is, and how many kinds there are; and how it is distinguished from a problem.

Quidnam sit propositio dialectica, & quotuplex: & quomodo distinguatur à problemate.

[…]

14 TRia hæc tradit Arist. li. 1. c. 3 in fine: sic in primis definiens propositionem dialecticam, quòd sit, quasi propositio alterius partis contradictionis: vt si dicas: Putásne animal rationale, esse definitionem hominis? Differre autem à problemate ait: non re, sed modo: quia propositio, vt vocabuli etymologia ostendit, proponit alteri aliquid: vt eidem rei propositæ respondeat, explicans, quidnam de illa iudicet, vel sentiat. Problema verò: Modum habet quæstio. & vtramque partem, per modum quæstionis agitandæ proponit: vt si dicas: Vtrùm animal rationale sit definitio hominis, necne? Itaque propositio dialectica, interrogat per modum simplicis propositionis: non per modum quæstionis: & assumit vnam tantùm partem: cùm problema vtramque, & per modum quæstionis interroget. Id duobus modis solet præferri, vel formaliter vtramque partem interrogando: vt in assignato fit exemplo: vel formaliter vnam, & virtualiter alteram: vt si solùm dixeris: Vtrùm animal rationale, sit definitio hominis? Et hoc modo proferuntur problemata in communi vsu scholarum, quoties quæstio aliqua disputanda proponitur: quod breuitatis studio, absque dubio fit, eo quòd iam ab omnibus intelligitur altera etiam pars interrogata, ex modo ipso problematicæ interrogationis.

14 Three things Aristotle delivers in bk. 1, ch. 3, at the end. In the first place he defines the dialectical proposition as being, as it were, the proposition of the other part of a contradiction: as if you say, Do you think that rational animal is the definition of man? And he says that it differs from the problem not in reality but in mode: because the Proposition, as the etymology of the word shows, proposes something to another, so that he may reply to the thing proposed, explaining what he judges or thinks about it. The Problem, however, has the mode of a question, and proposes both parts to be debated by way of a question: as if you say, Whether rational animal is the definition of man, or not? Thus the dialectical proposition interrogates by way of a simple proposition, not by way of a question, and takes up only one part; whereas the problem takes up both, and interrogates by way of a question. This is customarily put forward in two ways: either by interrogating both parts formally, as in the example assigned; or one formally and the other virtually, as if you should say only, Whether rational animal is the definition of man? And in this way problems are put forward in the common usage of the schools whenever some question to be disputed is proposed: which is done, no doubt, for the sake of brevity, because the other part too is now understood by all to be interrogated, from the very mode of the problematic interrogation. Z z ij

p. 724

15 Vbi aduertere debemus, quòd Arist. 1. lib. priorum, c. 1. non distinxit propositionem dialecticam à problemate: imò neque à propositione probabili: cùm dixerit esse interrogationem contradictionis: quod problemati proprium est, & rursus, propositionem dialecticam, per contanti esse interrogationem contradictionis: ratiocinanti verò, esse sumptionem apparentis, & probabilis. Ideo remisit distinctionem horum trium, ad cap. 3. lib. 1. Topic. quem citauit dicens: vt in Topicis dictum est. Ibi siquidem proprius erat locus distinguendi hæc: eo modo, quo à nobis distincta sunt. Propositio dialectica quadruplex est, sicut de problemate diximus: Definitionis est hæc: Putásne animal rationale est definitio hominis? Proprij, Putásne risibile est propria passio hominis? Generis, Putásne animal est genus hominis! Accidentis, Putásne albedo est accidens hominis?

15 Here we must notice that Aristotle, Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1, did not distinguish the dialectical proposition from the problem, nor indeed from the probable proposition: since he said that it is an interrogation of a contradiction, which is proper to the problem; and again, that the dialectical proposition is, for the one who questions, an interrogation of a contradiction, but for the one who reasons, the taking of something apparent and probable. Therefore he referred the distinction of these three to ch. 3 of Topics 1, which he cited, saying: as was said in the Topics. For there was the proper place to distinguish these things, in the way in which they have been distinguished by us. The dialectical proposition is fourfold, as we said of the problem. Of Definition is this: Do you think rational animal is the definition of man? Of Property: Do you think risible is a proper attribute of man? Of Genus: Do you think animal is the genus of man? Of Accident: Do you think whiteness is an accident of man?

16 Sed valde notandum est in hac parte, Propositionem sub hac generali ratione sumptam: solùm significare enunciationem, vt proponitur in syllogismo ad inferendam conclusionem. Quæ si proponatur primo loco, dicitur Propositio simpliciter, aut Propositio, seu præmissa maior, vel Prima pars antecedentis. Si secundo loco, dicitur Assumptio: quia sub propositione maiori: sub qua continetur, assumitur: dicitur etiam, Minor propositio, aut Præmissa minor, ac Secunda, vel posterior pars antecedentis. Et si in syllogismo demonstratiuo proponatur, dicitur Principium: si in syllogismo dialectico, Propositio probabilis: & Propositio apparens: si in syllogismo sophistico. Propositio verò dialectica præter enunciationem, addit modum propositionis, quasi per modum dubitantis: & problema, modum interrogantis, vt explicatum est.

16 But it should be carefully noted in this matter that Proposition, taken under this general ratio, signifies only an enunciation as it is proposed in a syllogism for inferring the conclusion. If it is proposed in the first place, it is called Proposition simply, or Proposition, or major premise, or the First part of the antecedent. If in the second place, it is called Assumption, because it is assumed under the major proposition, under which it is contained; it is also called Minor proposition, or Minor premise, and the Second, or posterior, part of the antecedent. And if it is proposed in a demonstrative syllogism, it is called a Principle; if in a dialectical syllogism, a Probable proposition; and an Apparent proposition, if in a sophistical syllogism. But the dialectical Proposition adds to the enunciation the mode of a proposition, as it were by way of one who doubts; and the problem the mode of one who interrogates, as has been explained.

Ex quibus intelligitur, tam propositionem Dialecticam, quàm problema, atque etiam propositionem probabilem, deseruire ad disputationem instituendam: sed diuersa ratione: nam problema dialecticum deseruit per modum quæstionis propositæ ad disputandum: & ideo primum locum tenet, & quasi caput totius disputationis vocatur.

From which it is understood that the Dialectical proposition, as well as the problem, and also the probable proposition, serve for setting up a disputation, but in a different ratio: for the dialectical problem serves by way of a question proposed for disputing, and therefore it holds the first place and is called, as it were, the head of the whole disputation.

17 Propositio verò dialectica, deseruit, quasi pro interrogatione ad respondentem facta, vt per eam respondens proferat aliam: qua media, quid de re proposita sentiat, explicet: & ex data responsione, possit interrogans occasionem sumere, disputandi in vnam per alteram partem propositæ quæstionis. Propositio verò probabilis, deseruit iam ad constituendum syllogismum, quo possit intentum probari, & quæstio terminari, aut definiri. Itaque problema & propositio dialectica, sub

17 The dialectical Proposition, however, serves as it were for an interrogation made to the respondent, so that by means of it the respondent may put forward another, through which he explains what he thinks of the thing proposed; and from the reply given the interrogator may take occasion to dispute for one or the other part of the proposed question. The probable proposition, in turn, serves now for constituting the syllogism by which what is intended may be proved, and the question terminated or settled. Thus the problem and the dialectical proposition, under

p. 725

propriis rationibus formalibus, ad instituendam disputationem pertinent, non tamen ad syllogismum dialecticum: nisi solùm antecedenter, & quasi præsuppositiuè. Sola autem propositio probabilis, pertinet ad eandem disputationem, tanquam pars syllogismi dialectici. Vbi aduertere debemus, quòd Arist. hoc loco distinguit propositionem à problemate, dicens problema partem interrogare.

their proper formal ratios, pertain to setting up a disputation, yet not to the dialectical syllogism, except only antecedently and as it were presuppositively. The probable proposition alone pertains to the same disputation as a part of the dialectical syllogism. Here we must notice that Aristotle in this place distinguishes the proposition from the problem, saying that the problem interrogates both parts.

Quid sit, & quotuplex propositio probabilis — What a probable proposition is, and how many kinds there are.

Quid sit, & quotuplex propositio probabilis.

[…]

18 PRobabile definit Arist. lib. 1. c. 1 his verbis: Probabilia autẽ sunt, quæ videntur omnibus aut plurimis, aut sapientibus: & his vel omnibus, vel plurimis, vel maximè familiaribus, & probatis. Quod intelligitur: aut propter rem ipsam, quæ ex se apparet vera: vel propter verisimilem aliquam rationem. Itaque probabile, non est idem, quod verum: nec etiam, quod necessarium, aut certum: sed quod apparet verum omnibus, aut pluribus, aut sapientibus. Sunt enim propositiones in triplici differentia. Nam quædam sunt euidenter veræ, & quarum veritas euidenter est cognita. Aliæ euidenter falsæ, & quarum etiam falsitas euidenter cognoscitur. Aliæ verò medium tenent: quia veræ sunt, aut falsæ, sed veritas, vel falsitas earum non est euidenter nota: quia causa earum, aut ignoratur, aut non plenè cognoscitur: & ideo pluribus apparent veræ, aliis verò etiam contingit apparere falsas, qui verisimilis ratio, pro vtraque parte esse solet. Et istæ dicuntur probabiles. Patet igitur, quo pacto probabilis propositio distinguatur à propositione, Vera, Certa, Necessaria, & falsa. Qui fieri potest, vt secundùm rem sit necessaria, veritatem habens necessariam: vel in re sit necessariò falsa, habens necessariam causam suæ falsitatis: & tamen probabilis videtur, propter verisimilitudinem, apparentiam veritatis, quam habet: vel propter verisimilem rationem, qua probari potest. Vt intelligatur, formalem rationem probabilis propositionis, nõ tam in re ipsa consistere, quàm in apparentia, vel apparenti ratione, respectu plurium, vel sapientum, vt docuit Arist.

18 Aristotle, bk. 1, ch. 1, defines the probable in these words: Probable things are those which seem so to all, or to most, or to the wise; and to these, either to all, or to most, or to the most familiar and approved. Which is understood either on account of the thing itself, which of itself appears true, or on account of some verisimilar reason. Thus the probable is not the same as the true, nor yet as the necessary or certain, but is that which appears true to all, or to most, or to the wise. For propositions are of three different kinds. For some are evidently true, and their truth is evidently known. Others evidently false, and their falsity too is evidently known. Others, however, hold the middle: because they are true or false, but their truth or falsity is not evidently known, because their cause is either unknown or not fully known; and therefore they appear true to many, while to others it happens that they appear false, since there is usually a verisimilar reason for each side. And these are called probable. It is plain, then, how the probable proposition is distinguished from the proposition that is True, Certain, Necessary, and false. For it can happen that in reality it is necessary, having necessary truth, or that in reality it is necessarily false, having a necessary cause of its falsity, and yet it seems probable on account of the verisimilitude, the appearance of truth, which it has, or on account of a verisimilar reason by which it can be proved. So that it may be understood that the formal ratio of the probable proposition consists not so much in the thing itself as in the appearance, or in an apparent reason, with respect to many, or to the wise, as Aristotle taught.

Vnde sequitur, quòd quamuis repugnet, duas contradictorias esse simul veras, non tamen repugnat esse simul probabiles: quia sæpe contingit, vt vtraque habeat pro se viros doctos, quibus vera appareat, & etiam verisimiles rationes: quibus probetur. Verùm in ipsa re, necesse est alteram earum esse falsam. Non tamen est necessarium (vt aliqui decepti existimant) quòd si vna propositio est probabilis: eo ipso probabilis etiam sit eius contradictoria: cùm manifestum sit, posse contingere:

From which it follows that, although it is repugnant that two contradictories be true at the same time, it is nevertheless not repugnant that they be probable at the same time: because it often happens that each has on its side learned men, to whom it appears true, and also verisimilar reasons by which it is proved. But in the thing itself one of them must be false. It is not, however, necessary (as some mistakenly think) that if one proposition is probable, by that very fact its contradictory is also probable, since it is manifest that it can happen Z z iij

p. 726

quòd illa appareat viris doctis vera, & verisimiles rationes pro se habeat: hæc verò, nulli appareat vera, nec aliqua verisimilis ratio inuenta sit, per quam probetur.

that the one appears true to learned men and has verisimilar reasons on its side, while the other appears true to no one, nor has any verisimilar reason been found by which it may be proved.

Propositio probabilis duplex est: Quædam per se: Alia verò, propter aliam: ex qua deducitur. Per se probabilis, illa dicitur, cuius probabilitas ex sola notitia terminorum, absque alia ratiocinatione, per quam probetur, euidens est: ita vt intellectus non possit non iudicare, esse probabilem. Talis est hæc: Omnis mater diligit filium: aut omnis amicus diligendus est: & hanc propositionem per se probabilem, definiuit Arist. 1. lib. Posteriorum, dicens: Opinio, est acceptio immediatæ propositionis, & non necessariæ: Opinionis nomine, assensum talis propositionis immediatæ intelligens: hoc est, quæ sine medio iudicatur probabilis, ex sola notitia terminorum. Et assensus huius propositionis, per se probabilis, vocari potest intellectus, intra genus probabilis propositionis: sicut intra genus euidentis, vocatur intellectus assensus propositionis necessariæ, qui sine medio habetur, sola significatione terminorum cognita. Alia est Propositio, non per se probabilis, sed quæ ex alia per se probabili colligitur, per euidentem, aut probabilem consequentiam: aut ex euidenti alia, per consequentiam solùm probabilem. Et hęc est similis conclusioni scientificæ, quam ex euidentibus præmissis, & per euidentem syllogismum colligimus. Nihilominus ex vtraque propositione probabili, potest fieri syllogismus dialecticus, vt per se est manifestum.

The probable proposition is twofold: one per se, the other on account of another, from which it is deduced. That is called per se probable whose probability is evident from the cognition of the terms alone, without any other reasoning by which it is proved, so that the intellect cannot but judge that it is probable. Such is this: Every mother loves her son; or, Every friend is to be loved. And this per se probable proposition Aristotle defined in Posterior Analytics 1, saying: Opinion is the acceptance of an immediate and non-necessary proposition, understanding by the name of opinion the assent of such an immediate proposition, that is, of one which is judged probable without a middle, from the cognition of the terms alone. And the assent of this per se probable proposition can be called understanding within the genus of the probable proposition, just as within the genus of the evident the assent of a necessary proposition which is had without a middle, once the signification of the terms alone is known, is called understanding. The other is the Proposition not per se probable, but which is gathered from another that is per se probable through an evident or probable consequence, or from another evident one through a consequence that is only probable. And this is similar to a scientific conclusion, which we gather from evident premises and through an evident syllogism. Nevertheless, from either probable proposition a dialectical syllogism can be made, as is manifest per se.

Quidnam sit syllogismus topicus, aut dialecticus — What a Topical or dialectical syllogism is.

Quidnam sit syllogismus Topicus, aut dialecticus.

[…]

EXplicatis singulis partibus, syllogismi dialectici: non erit difficile definitionem eius intelligere: quam assignauit Arist. c. 1. lib. 1. Topic. his verbis: Dialecticus autem syllogismus est, qui ex probabilibus est collectus: id est, qui ex propositionibus probabilibus procedens, probabilem etiam conclusionem colligit. Quæ sic intelligenda est, vt ex vtraque præmissa probabili, vel saltem ex altera, procedere debeat, nam sæpe contingit, vt ex vna euidenti, & altera probabili efficiatur. Talis est enim iste, Omne animal diligit sibi simile: Omnis homo est animal: ergo, Omnis homo diligit sibi simile. Conuenit autem cum syllogismo demõstratiuo, in communi: & generica ratione dispositionis, in Modo, & figura: distinguitur autem ab eo, specie, per modum concludendi: nam demonstratio concludit per medium necessarium: hoc est, per causam, vel effectum necessarium: probabilis verò: per medium probabile: quia nec reddit

Once the single parts of the dialectical syllogism have been explained, it will not be difficult to understand its definition, which Aristotle assigned in Topics 1, ch. 1, in these words: But the dialectical syllogism is one which is gathered from probable things; that is, one which, proceeding from probable propositions, gathers a conclusion that is also probable. This is to be understood thus: that it must proceed from both premises probable, or at least from one of them; for it often happens that it is made from one evident and the other probable. For such is this one: Every animal loves its like; Every man is an animal; therefore Every man loves his like. And it agrees with the demonstrative syllogism in the common and generic ratio of disposition in Mood and figure; but it is distinguished from it in species by the mode of concluding: for demonstration concludes through a necessary middle, that is, through a necessary cause or effect; whereas the probable syllogism concludes through a probable middle, because it neither renders

p. 727

causam nec effectum conclusionis necessarium, sed solùm probabilem: hoc est, quæ talia apparent pluribus, aut sapientibus, vt explicatum est. Itaque non distinguuntur per solam materiam, vt probauimus in posterioribus, sed etiam per formam specialem, ex modo speciali concludendi desumptam: cùm in forma generica dispositionis syllogisticæ, conueniant. A syllogismo verò sophistico, distinguitur per formam veram, aut apparentem: atque etiam per probabiles, aut apparentes propositiones. Nam ex illis procedit dialecticus, sophisticus verò ex his. Sed diuersum quid est procedere, ex probabilibus, aut ex apparentibus: nam licèt probabilis propositio sit illa: quę apparet vera quamuis fortè vera non sit, non tamen cuicumque id apparet, sed tantùm sapientibus, idque propter fundamentum verisimilis rationis: vel propter verisimilitudinem eiusdem veritatis. Apparentia verò, ex quibus procedit syllogismus sophisticus, nec respectu sapientum dicuntur talia: nec etiam vera apparent, cum fundamento rationis probabilis, aut cum verisimilitudine eiusdem veritatis, sed cuicunque, & sine his fundamentis. Vnde solam, & nudam habent apparentiam veritatis, & ideo deceptoriæ propriè dicuntur: & syllogismus ipse, ex sic apparentibus procedens, vocatur etiam deceptorius.

a necessary cause nor a necessary effect of the conclusion, but only a probable one, that is, such as appear so to many or to the wise, as has been explained. Thus they are not distinguished by matter alone, as we proved in the Posterior Analytics, but also by a special form, taken from the special mode of concluding, since they agree in the generic form of syllogistic disposition. From the sophistical syllogism, however, it is distinguished by true or apparent form, and also by probable or apparent propositions. For the dialectical proceeds from the former, but the sophistical from the latter. But to proceed from probable things and from apparent ones is something different: for although a probable proposition is one which appears true, even though perhaps it is not true, yet it does not appear so to anyone whatever, but only to the wise, and this on account of the foundation of a verisimilar reason, or on account of the verisimilitude of that same truth. But the apparent things from which the sophistical syllogism proceeds are not called such with respect to the wise, nor do they appear true with the foundation of a probable reason, or with the verisimilitude of that same truth, but to anyone whatever, and without these foundations. Hence they have only the bare appearance of truth, and are therefore properly called deceptive; and the syllogism itself, proceeding from things so apparent, is also called deceptive.

Enumeratio, atque explicatio locorum, ex quibus deducuntur argumenta probabilia, pro disputatione ineunda — Enumeration and explanation of the places from which probable arguments are deduced for entering upon a disputation.

Enumeratio, atque explicatio locorum, ex quibus deducuntur arg. probabilia, pro disputatione ineunda.

[…]

22 HOc solùm restabat explicandum ex his, quæ pertinen ad disputationem dialecticam instituendam: nempe Locus, ex quo desumenda sint probabilia arg. vel syllogismi. Explicatis namque & cognitis huiusmodi locis, facile erit cuique argumenta probabilia inuenire, quibus in disputationibus vti possit. Et licèt vsus locorum, ad quamcumque scientiam pertineat, secundùm applicationem ad propriam materiam: eorum tamen explicatio, ad solam spectat dialecticam, cuius proprium munus est, methodum præbere omnibus scientiis, ac disciplinis, disputationem instituendam.

22 This alone remained to be explained among the things that pertain to setting up a dialectical disputation: namely the Places from which probable arguments, or syllogisms, are to be taken. For once places of this kind have been explained and known, it will be easy for anyone to find probable arguments which he can use in disputations. And although the use of the places pertains to any science whatever, according to their application to its proper matter, their explanation nevertheless belongs to Dialectic alone, whose proper office is to furnish all the sciences and disciplines with a method for setting up a disputation.

23 Locus autem, ex quo eruuntur argumenta, diuiditur in Intrinsecum, & Extrinsecum. Locus Intrinsecus, vocatur ille, qui ad substantiam rei pertinet, vel substantiam eius comitatur. Quæ ad substantiam pertinent, sunt hæc, Definitio, Genus, Differentia, aut Pars aliqua rei, vt Materia, & Forma: vel Partes integrantes, vt Caput, Manus, aut Brachium. Quod verò comitatur substantiam, aut est Totum: (quod ideo comitari dicitur substantiam rei: quia includit partes:)

23 The Place, then, from which arguments are drawn out, is divided into the Intrinsic and the Extrinsic. The Intrinsic place is called that which pertains to the substance of the thing, or accompanies its substance. Those that pertain to the substance are these: Definition, Genus, Difference, or some Part of the thing, such as Matter and Form; or the integral Parts, such as the Head, the Hand, or the Arm. That which accompanies the substance, on the other hand, is either the Whole (which is said to accompany the substance of the thing because it includes the parts), Z z iiij

p. 728

aut Descriptio ipsius rei, aut Proprium rei: aut Accidens: aut subiectum illius. Vnde loci intrinseci, tantùm sunt nouem, Definitio, Genus, Differentia, Partes, Totum, Descriptio, Proprium, Accidens, & Subiectum,

or the Description of the thing itself, or the Property of the thing, or an Accident, or its subject. Hence there are only nine intrinsic places: Definition, Genus, Difference, Parts, Whole, Description, Property, Accident, and

Locus extrinsecus, dicitur ille, qui non est in ipsa re, nec ab ea procedit, sed ex aliquo extrinseco desumitur. Locus autem extrinsecus diuiditur, in Eum, qui habet aliquam affinitatem cum ipsa re, & in Eum, qui habet aliquam repugnantiam cum ea. Loci extrinseci habentes affinitatem, sunt Coniugata, Similia, Causæ extrinsecæ, nempe Efficiens, & Finalis: Effectus extrinseci, Maius, Minus, Auctoritas Diuina, vel humana. Loci verò extrinseci repugnantes, sunt, Contraria, Disparata, & Dissimilia. Vnde loci extrinseci, vndecim sunt: quos si cum nouem extrinsecis coniungamus, inueniemus locos omnes, tam intrinsecos quàm extrinsecos, viginti tantùm esse: quos singillatim, breuissimè tamen explicabimus: Vt ratio singulorum intelligatur, & vsus eorum reddatur facilis.

Subject. The extrinsic place is said to be that which is not in the thing itself, nor proceeds from it, but is taken from something extrinsic. And the extrinsic place is divided into That which has some affinity with the thing itself, and That which has some repugnance to it. The extrinsic places having affinity are Conjugates, Similars, extrinsic Causes, namely the Efficient and the Final, extrinsic Effects, the Greater, the Lesser, Authority Divine or human. The repugnant extrinsic places, on the other hand, are Contraries, Disparates, and Dissimilars. Hence the extrinsic places are eleven; and if we join them with the nine intrinsic ones, we shall find that all the places, intrinsic as well as extrinsic, are only twenty. These we shall explain one by one, though very briefly, so that the ratio of each may be understood and their use made easy.

Locus primus à Definitione.

The first place, from Definition. 24

24 Frequens vsus est huius loci à Definitione, in disputationibus, ex eo, quòd essentiam definiti continet, & cum eo conuertitur. Vnde fit: vt plures propositiones vniuersales deduci possint ex ea, quæ vocantur Maximæ, & quasi capita sub quibus plures particulares desumuntur, ad instituendos syllogismos dialecticos. Et si quæstio proposita, circa quam disputatur, sit Absoluta, possumus assumere in argumentatione, definitionem subiecti, aut prędicati, aut vtriusque: ex quibus deducuntur Maximæ, Affirmatiuæ, & Negatiuæ. Affirmatiuæ sunt, Quidquid conuenit definitioni, conuenit definito: & Quidquid potest conuenire definitioni potest conuenire definito, & aliæ similes. Negatiuæ, Quod non conuenit definitioni, non conuenire definito: & Quod non potest conuenire definitioni: non potest conuenire definito. Gratia exempli: Si proposita q. disputanda sit. An dialectica sit necessaria ad alias scientias comparandas, Subiectum huius quæstionis est Dialectica, Prædicatum verò necessarium: Possumus ergo vti definitione Dialecticæ, sic arguentes: Scientia docens argumenta conficere, necessaria est ad alias scientias comparandas: sed dialectica est scientia, docens argumenta conficere: ergo necessaria ad alias scientias comparandas. Et secundùm eandem proportionem, possumus vti definitione necessarij, quod est prædicatum quæstionis, atque etiam definitione, simul subiecti, & prædicati.

Frequent is the use of this place from Definition in disputations, because the definition contains the essence and is convertible with it. Hence it happens that several universal propositions can be deduced from it, which are called Maxims, and as it were heads under which several particular ones are taken for setting up dialectical syllogisms. And if the proposed question about which the dispute is held is Absolute, we can take up in the argumentation the definition of the subject, or of the predicate, or of both; from which are deduced Maxims, Affirmative and Negative. The affirmative are: Whatever belongs to the definition belongs to the defined; and Whatever can belong to the definition can belong to the defined; and others like them. The negative: What does not belong to the definition does not belong to the defined; and What cannot belong to the definition cannot belong to the defined. For example: if the proposed q. to be disputed is, Whether dialectic is necessary for acquiring the other sciences, the Subject of this question is Dialectic, and the Predicate is necessary. We can therefore use the definition of Dialectic, arguing thus: A science teaching how to construct arguments is necessary for acquiring the other sciences; but dialectic is a science teaching how to construct arguments; therefore it is necessary for acquiring the other sciences. And according to the same proportion we can use the definition of necessary, which is the predicate of the question, and also the definition of subject and predicate together.

p. 729

Si verò quæstio sit Comparatiua, nempe, An necessitas ad alias scientias, magis conueniat dialectica, quàm cæteris artibus, vti possumus definitione subiecti, atque etiam prædicati, vel vtriusque deducendo ex eis Maximas quasdam, similes superioribus, cum his aduerbiis magis, & minus. Vt si dicamus, Cui magis conuenit definitio, magis conuenit definitum: & Cui minùs conuenit definitio: minùs conuenit definitum, & sic de cæteris.

But if the question is Comparative, namely, Whether necessity for acquiring the other sciences belongs more to dialectic than to the other arts, we can use the definition of the subject, and also of the predicate, or of both, deducing from them certain Maxims similar to the ones above, with these adverbs more and less. As if we say: To that to which the definition belongs more, the defined belongs more; and To that to which the definition belongs less, the defined belongs less; and so of the rest.

Secundus locus à Genere.

The second place, from Genus. 25

25 Eisdem ferè modis vti possumus, loco à genere. Nam propter necessariam connexionem: quam habet cum speciebus, deducuntur ab hoc loco plures Maximæ. ex quibus instituere possumus argumenta: vt sunt istæ, Quicquid essentialiter conuenit generi, etiam conuenit essentialiter speciebus: &, Quod repugnat generi, repugnat etiam speciebus, sicque ad aliis, iuxta modos arguendi à definitione explicatos. Et ad hunc locum generis, reducitur locus Speciei: quia similem habet connexionem cum indiuiduis: & ideo non additur alter locus à specie, sed eædem ferè Maximæ deduci possunt, atque à genere: & eodem modo debent applicari, ad formanda argumenta à specie.

In almost the same ways we can use the place from genus. For on account of the necessary connection which it has with the species, several Maxims are deduced from this place, from which we can set up arguments: such as these, Whatever belongs essentially to the genus also belongs essentially to the species; and, What is repugnant to the genus is also repugnant to the species; and so of the others, according to the modes of arguing explained for definition. And to this place of genus is reduced the place of Species, because it has a similar connection with the individuals; and therefore no other place from species is added, but almost the same Maxims can be deduced as from genus, and they must be applied in the same way to forming arguments from species.

Tertius locus à Differenti,.

The third place, from Difference.

Valde similis est locus à Differentia, duobus præcedentibus à definitione & à genere. Nam duplex est differentia Subalterna, & Atoma. Et si subalterna sit, de eisdem speciebus prædicatur ac genus: & eandem habet connexionem intrinsecam cum eis. Quare eædem Maximæ, ex ea deduci possunt, ac ex genere, Si verò sit Atoma, cum definitione conuenit in duobus. Primò, In eo, quod intrinseca est speciei. Secũdò: Quia cum ea conuertitur. Vnde similes etiam Maximæ ex ea deduci possunt: ac deducuntur ex definitione, & eisdem modis applicari debent ad syllogismos dialecticos conficiendos.

Very similar to the two preceding places, from definition and from genus, is the place from Difference. For difference is twofold, Subaltern and Atomic. And if it is subaltern, it is predicated of the same species as the genus is, and has the same intrinsic connection with them. Wherefore the same Maxims can be deduced from it as from genus. But if it is Atomic, it agrees with definition in two things. First, in that it is intrinsic to the species. Second, because it is convertible with it. Hence similar Maxims too can be deduced from it as are deduced from definition, and they must be applied in the same ways to constructing dialectical syllogisms.

Quartus locus à partibus.

The fourth place, from the parts.

Partes sunt in triplici differentia, Subiectiuæ, vt species respectu generis, Essentiales, vt materia, & forma: aut genus, & differentia: & Integrantes, vt caput, manus, & brachium. Et ex his: Quædam sunt necessariæ ad consistentiam totius, sine quibus esse non potest: vt caput, cor, & similes. Aliæ non sunt necessariæ, sed sine illis esse potest: vt manus, digitus, pes, Et à primis potest deduci argum, à secundis deduci non potest: quia neque

Parts are of three different kinds: Subjective, as species with respect to genus; Essential, as matter and form, or genus and difference; and Integral, as head, hand, and arm. And of these, some are necessary for the consistence of the whole, without which it cannot be, such as the head, the heart, and the like. Others are not necessary, but it can be without them, such as the hand, the finger, the foot. And from the first an argument can be deduced; from the second it cannot be deduced, because neither

p. 730

inferunt consistentiam totius, nec eam tollunt. A partibus plures Maximę deduci possunt, propter necessariam cõnexionem, quam habent cum toto, & cum eis totum: vt sunt ista: Quod necessariò comitatur partem, necessariò etiam debet comitari totum, &, Quod repugnat parti, etiam repugnat toti. Et hæc accipiuntur ex parte subiecti propositæ q. Aliæ verò possunt sumi, ex parte prædicati secundum proportionem.

do they infer the consistence of the whole, nor do they remove it. From the parts several Maxims can be deduced, on account of the necessary connection which they have with the whole, and the whole with them: such as these, What necessarily accompanies the part must necessarily also accompany the whole; and, What is repugnant to the part is also repugnant to the whole. And these are taken on the side of the subject of the proposed q. Others, however, can be taken on the side of the predicate, according to proportion.

Quintus locus à Toto.

The fifth place, from the Whole. 27

27 Totum duplex est. Aliud vniuersale, quod est vniuersale prædicatum respectu inferiorum, quæ sunt partes eius subiectiuæ: vt genus respectu specierum: & terminus distributus signo vniuersali: vt omnis homo, respectu particularium, quæ sub eo continentur, Et ab hoc toto, ad eius partes, sumuntur omnia argumenta quæ fiunt à superiori ad inferius negatiuè: & in summulis sunt manifesta. Aliud est totum Essentiale, aut integrale, vt homo, equus, domus. Et ab hoc toto deduci possunt plures Maximæ, & ex eis confici plures syllogismi: vt, Posito toto necesse est poni omnes pates necessarias. Vnde valet arg. à positione totius, ad positionem cuiuscunque partis necessariæ, & etiam Ablato toto, necesse est auferri aliquam partem necessariam. Vnde valet argum. à negatione totius ad negationem alicuius partis necessariæ, sub distinctione: vt si deficit domus, aut non est fundamentum, aut non est tectum, aut non ex aliqua alia pars necessaria.

The Whole is twofold. One is universal, which is a universal predicate with respect to its inferiors, which are its subjective parts: as genus with respect to the species, and a term distributed by a universal sign, as every man, with respect to the particulars which are contained under it. And from this whole to its parts are taken all the arguments that are made from superior to inferior negatively; and these are manifest in the Summulae. The other is the Essential or integral whole, as man, horse, house. And from this whole several Maxims can be deduced, and from them several syllogisms constructed: as, When the whole is posited, all the necessary parts must be posited. Hence the argument holds from the positing of the whole to the positing of any necessary part whatever. And also, When the whole is taken away, some necessary part must be taken away. Hence the argument holds from the negation of the whole to the negation of some necessary part, under a disjunction: as, if the house is lacking, either the foundation does not exist, or the roof does not exist, or some other necessary part does not exist.

Locus sextus à Descriptione.

The sixth place, from Description. 28

28 Descriptio est definitio, quam appellare solent descriptiuam: quia non explicat essentiam rei, nec per genus, & differentiam traditur, sed per propriam passionem, conuertibilem tamen cum re descripta: vt animal, aptum ad ridendum cũ homine: & ideo omnes Maximæ, quæ ex definitione deducuntur, ex descriptione deduci possunt, & eodem modo applicari ad syllogismos constituendos. Et quod de descriptione dicitur, de definitione, quid nominis intelligi debet: cùm conuertatur etiam cum re, non tamen de etymologia nominis: quia sæpe contingit, diuersa esse, id à quo nomen imponitur, & illud quod significat: quare non potest argumentum firmum duci ab etymologia ad rem significatam.

Description is a definition which they usually call descriptive, because it does not explain the essence of the thing, nor is it delivered through genus and difference, but through a proper attribute, which is nevertheless convertible with the thing described: as animal apt to laugh with man. And therefore all the Maxims which are deduced from definition can be deduced from description, and applied in the same way to constituting syllogisms. And what is said of description ought to be understood of the definition of what the name means, since it too is convertible with the thing; but not of the etymology of the name: because it often happens that that from which the name is imposed and that which it signifies are different; wherefore a firm argument cannot be drawn from the etymology to the thing signified.

Locus septimus à Proprio.

The seventh place, from Property.

Proprium est, quod non indicat, quid est esse rei, soli autem inest, & conuersim prædicatur: vt definit Aristot. cap. 4. 1. lib. quasi

Property is that which does not indicate what it is to be for the thing, but is in it alone, and is predicated convertibly, as Aristotle defines it, ch. 4, bk. 1: as if

p. 731

dicat propriam passionem, non pertinere ad quod quid est, seu rei essentiam, conuerti tamen cum ea, sicut definitio conuertitur cum definito. Et ideo iisdem ferè modis, eadem ferè argu. deduci possunt à proprio, atque à definitione: quia, Cui conuenit definitio, conuenit propria passio: &, Cui non conuenit propria passio, nec definitio conuenit. Et sicut bene colligitur, Rem esse perfectiorem, quo perfectiorem definitionem habet: Ita quò perfectiorem habet passionem; cùm hæc procedat ab essentia, tanquam à propria causa.

to say that a proper attribute does not pertain to what the thing is, or to its essence, yet is convertible with it, just as the definition is convertible with the defined. And therefore in almost the same ways almost the same arguments can be deduced from property as from definition: because, To whatever the definition belongs, the proper attribute belongs; and, To whatever the proper attribute does not belong, neither does the definition belong. And just as it is rightly gathered that a thing is more perfect the more perfect the definition it has, so also the more perfect the attribute it has, since the latter proceeds from the essence as from its proper cause.

Locus 8. ab Accidente.

The 8th place, from Accident. 29

29 Accidens est, quod adest, & abest subiecto, præter corruptionẽ eius. vt definit ibidem Arist. Sed hæc definitio, solùm videtur conuenire accidentibus verè inhærentibus, quæ ideo vocantur intrinseca: nihilominus etiam alia quæ solùm videtur extrinsecam denominationem significare, sub nomine accidentis hoc loco debet intelligi: vt dextrum esse, vel sinistrũ parietem: aut visum vel intellectum esse: quia in modo denominandi, similia sunt accidentibus intrinsecis. Ab accidente, deduci possunt plures Maximæ, & ab his plura arg. Vt, Si accidentia prædicati, non conueniunt subiecto, non cohærebit prædicatum subiecto: quo arg. vsus videtur beatus Petrus, Actor. 2. probans discipulos non fuisse ebrios: quia tempus illud tertiæ horæ diei, non erat conueniens ebrietati, & ideo, nec discipulis, cùm eadem hora eis imponeretur ebrietas. Et bene probatur, aliquem non occidisse alterum, si probatur eo tempore, quo occisus est, in eodem loco occisionis non fuisse, sed alibi.

An accident is that which is present to and absent from the subject without its corruption, as Aristotle defines it in the same place. But this definition seems to belong only to truly inhering accidents, which are therefore called intrinsic; nevertheless, the others too, which seem to signify only an extrinsic denomination, ought in this place to be understood under the name of accident: as for a wall to be right or left, or to be seen or understood; because in the mode of denominating they are similar to intrinsic accidents. From accident several Maxims can be deduced, and from these several arguments. As, If the accidents of the predicate do not belong to the subject, the predicate will not cohere with the subject: which argument blessed Peter seems to have used, Acts 2, proving that the disciples were not drunk because that time, the third hour of the day, was not suited to drunkenness, and therefore not to the disciples either, since drunkenness was imputed to them at that same hour. And it is well proved that someone did not kill another if it is proved that at the time when he was killed he was not in the same place as the killing, but elsewhere.

Locus 9. à Subiecto.

Place 9, from the Subject.

De subiecto inhæsionis, intelligitur locus iste, cui inhærent accidentia, non de subiecto prędicationis, cui potest prędicatum essentialiter conuenire: & ideo meritò numeratur inter locos intrinsecos. A subiecto possunt deduci Maximæ istæ & similes: Cui repugnant accidentia, etiam repugnat subiectum: vt si alicui repugnat intellectus, etiam anima, & si repugnant corporea accidentia, etiam repugnabit corpus. Vbi subiectum est, ibi debent esse accidentia: & Vbi non sunt accidentia, nec est subiectum: & Motis nobis mouentur omnia, quæ sunt in nobis: id est accidentia. Et ex his, & aliis Maximis, multa possunt effici arg. à loco subiecti: & isti sunt omnes loci intrinseci. Sequuntur extrinseci.

This place is understood of the subject of inherence, in which accidents inhere, not of the subject of predication, to which a predicate can belong essentially; and therefore it is rightly numbered among the intrinsic places. From the subject these Maxims and the like can be deduced: To whatever the accidents are repugnant, the subject too is repugnant: as, if intellect is repugnant to something, so also is the soul; and if corporeal accidents are repugnant to it, the body too will be repugnant to it. Where the subject is, there the accidents must be; and Where the accidents are not, neither is the subject; and All things move with our motion that are in us, that is, the accidents. And from these and other Maxims many arguments can be made from the place of the subject. And these are all the intrinsic places. The extrinsic ones follow.

p. 732

Locus decimus, & primus inter Extrinsecos, à Coniugatis.

The tenth place, and the first among the Extrinsic ones, from Conjugates.

30 Coniugata dicuntur voces, quæ sub diuersa terminatione, eandem formam significant, atque participant: & propterea quasi idem iugum ducere videntur, vt Iustus, Iustitia, & Iustè; & omnes casus per quos variatur idem nomen: & verbum. Ad hæc reducuntur alia, quæ eandem formam significant, licèt diuersæ omnino sint voces: vt Iustus, & Studiosus: quæ ita se habent, quantùm ad rem significatam, sicut iustitia, & iustus. Ex his deducuntur istæ maximæ, & similes: Quæ dicuntur de vno coniugatorum, suo etiam modo, & cum debita variatione, dicuntur de alio: vt si Philosophus est sciens, Philosophia erit scientia: &, de quo dicitur vnum coniugatorum, dicitur etiam suo modo alterum. Et ex his, ac similibus propositionibus possunt fieri multa argumenta à coniugatis.

30 Conjugates are said to be words which under different endings signify and participate in the same form; and for this reason they seem as it were to draw the same yoke, as just, justice, and justly; and all the cases by which the same noun and verb are varied. To these are reduced others which signify the same form, although they are altogether different words: as just and virtuous, which are related, as regards the thing signified, as justice and just are. From these are deduced these maxims and the like: What is said of one of the conjugates is said also of the other in its own way, and with due variation: as, if the Philosopher is knowing, Philosophy will be knowledge; and, Of whatever one of the conjugates is said, the other too is said in its own way. And from these and similar propositions many arguments can be made from conjugates.

Locus 11. à Simili.

Place 11, from the Similar.

Similia sunt, quæ participant eandem formam: vt omnia alba. Ad quæ reducuntur, quæ habent eandem proportionem: vt auriga, & dux, quia similem curam ei, quam habet auriga in suo curru, debet habere dux in exercitu. Ad similia etiam reducuntur æqualia, & ab eis deducuntur Maximæ plures, pro argumentis instituendis, similes huic: Cygnus disgregat visum: ergo etiam paries albus. Sed semper debet fieri in his argumentum à ratione formali similitudinis, & non ab aliis materialibus, quæ habere possunt similia: non est enim bonum argu. si dicamus, Cygnus est auis, ergo etiam paries albus est auis.

Similar things are those which participate in the same form: as all white things. To these are reduced those which have the same proportion: as the charioteer and the general, because the general ought to have in the army a care similar to that which the charioteer has in his chariot. To similars are also reduced equals; and from them several Maxims are deduced for setting up arguments, similar to this: The swan disperses the sight; therefore the white wall does too. But in these the argument must always be made from the formal ratio of similitude, and not from other material features which similar things can have: for it is not a good argument if we say, The swan is a bird; therefore the white wall too is a bird.

Locus 12. à Causa.

Place 12, from Cause. 31

31 Quadruplex est causa, Finalis, Efficiens, Materialis, & Formalis. Verùm locus iste, cùm sit extrinsecus, solam Finalem, & Efficientem complectitur: non Materialem, & Formalem, quæ cùm sint partes rei Intrinsecæ, potiùs ad locum partium pertinebunt. Causa finalis est, cuius gratia operatur efficiens & producit effectum: Causa efficiens, à qua effectus procedit Maximæ, quæ ex eis deduci possunt, similes sunt his: Posita causa, necessariò ponitur effectus: quæ intelligitur de causa actuali, & sufficienti, & Non posito effectu, non ponitur causa: quæ proprietatem harum causarum pertinent, in secundo lib. Phys. à nobis explicantur.

Cause is fourfold: Final, Efficient, Material, and Formal. But this place, since it is extrinsic, embraces only the Final and the Efficient, not the Material and the Formal, which, since they are intrinsic parts of the thing, will rather pertain to the place of the parts. The final cause is that for the sake of which the efficient operates and produces the effect; the efficient cause, that from which the effect proceeds. The Maxims which can be deduced from them are similar to these: When the cause is posited, the effect is necessarily posited, which is understood of an actual and sufficient cause; and When the effect is not posited, the cause is not posited. The things which pertain to the property of these causes are explained by us in Phys. bk. 2.

p. 733

Locus 13, ab Effectu.

Place 13, from the Effect.

Valde similis est locus iste præcedenti: quia eædem Maximæ, à causa, & effectu deducuntur: idem est modus arguendi in eis, vt à Positione effectus, ad positionem causæ: v.g. Si dies est, sol est in nostro hemisphærio. Ablato effectu, aufertur causa: vt, non est dies, ergo nec sol est in nostro hemisphærio. Sed intelliguntur istæ & aliæ similes, de causis necessariis, & sufficientibus.

Very similar to the preceding is this place, because the same Maxims are deduced from cause and from effect: the mode of arguing in them is the same, as from the positing of the effect to the positing of the cause: e.g., If it is day, the sun is in our hemisphere. When the effect is taken away, the cause is taken away: as, It is not day; therefore neither is the sun in our hemisphere. But these and others like them are understood of necessary and sufficient causes.

Locus 14. à Maiori, & 15. à Minori.

Place 14, from the Greater, and 15, from the Lesser. 32

32 Similiores sunt duo isti loci, à maiori, & minori. & ideo de illis simul loquendum est. A maiori, sumitur hæc Maxima: Quod potest efficere maius, potest efficere minus. & à minori hæc, Quod non potest efficere minus, nec potest efficere maius. Sed vtraque debet intelligi, de maiori & minori, eiusdem conditionis. Nam si diuersæ rationis sint, non valebit argumentum. v.g. Angelus potest intelligere, quod est maius: ergo potest ambulare, quod est minus. Quia diuersæ conditionis sunt, intelligere, & ambulare. Item non potest ambulare, ergo nec intelligere.

Very similar are these two places, from the greater and the lesser, and therefore we must speak of them together. From the greater this Maxim is taken: What can effect the greater can effect the lesser; and from the lesser this one: What cannot effect the lesser cannot effect the greater either. But each must be understood of a greater and a lesser of the same condition. For if they are of a different ratio, the argument will not hold: e.g., An angel can understand, which is greater; therefore he can walk, which is lesser; because understanding and walking are of different conditions. Likewise, He cannot walk; therefore neither can he understand.

Locus 16. & 17. ab Authoritate Diuina, & humana.

Place 16 and 17, from Authority, Divine and human.

Testimonium fide digni, cui fides innititur, valde extrinsecum est rebus testificatis vel creditis: vt ex se est manifestũ. Vnde locus ab authoritate fide digni, maximè extrinsecus est. Sed si sit ab authoritate Diuina, infallibilem veritatem tribuit rei: quia cùm Deus sit summa, & prima veritas, non potest falli: & cùm sit summa bonitas, fallere non potest. Vnde quæ DEVS testificatur, ea infallibilem veritatem habent: & tales sunt res nostræ fidei, quas propter Diuinam authoritatem credimus, & argumenta Theologica, ab hoc præcipuè loco deducuntur.

The testimony of one worthy of belief, on which faith rests, is very extrinsic to the things testified or believed, as is manifest of itself. Hence the place from the authority of one worthy of belief is supremely extrinsic. But if it is from Divine authority, it attributes infallible truth to the thing: because, since God is the highest and first truth, he cannot be deceived; and since he is the highest goodness, he cannot deceive. Hence the things which G o d testifies have infallible truth; and such are the things of our faith, which we believe on account of the Divine authority; and Theological arguments are deduced chiefly from this place.

33 Ab humana verò authoritate aut testimonio, non adeo firmum argum. deduci potest. Sed valet plurimùm, ad explicandas res diuinæ fidei. Nam licèt sacri Doctores, homines fuerint, tamen expositio sacræ Scripturæ, quam omnes, vel plures eorum adferunt (etiam si dissentiat vnus, vel aliter) maximam facit fidem: quia non est credendum, permisisse Deum eos in hac re decipi, ad quos pertinet Scripturam exponere, & expositam aliis tradere. Valet etiam multùm in rebus, quæ dependent ex libera hominum voluntate: vt ad impositionem, & significationem nominum: quia nominibus vtendum est, vt plures

33 From human authority or testimony, however, so firm an argument cannot be deduced. But it is of very great value for explaining the things of divine faith. For although the sacred Doctors were men, nevertheless an exposition of sacred Scripture which all, or most of them, put forward (even if one, or another, dissents) produces the greatest belief: because it is not to be believed that God has permitted those to be deceived in this matter to whom it pertains to expound Scripture and to hand it on, expounded, to others. It is also of great value in matters which depend on the free will of men, as for the imposition and signification of names: because names are to be used as most

p. 734

vtuntur. Præterea in rebus quæ per sensus euidenter cognoscuntur: atque etiam in his, quæ ad historiam pertinent: quæ inniti debent euidentiæ alicuius, vt plurimùm, per assensus habita, ex qua ita contigisse, credunt alij. Sed non valet in his, quæ cognoscuntur per discursum, in quibus præcipuum locum ratio tenet, quanquam adhuc in his multùm valeat communis consensus omnium. Semper ergo ducitur arg. probabile, ab authoritate humana: & quo plures sunt, qui aliquid testificantur, eo efficacius arg. deducitur. Negatiuè tamen, non est ab authoritate humana arguendum, quasi probetur, rem non ita esse, quia à nemine narratur: quia non est necessarium scripta fuisse omnia.

use them. Moreover, in things which are evidently known through the senses, and also in those which pertain to history, which must rest on some evidence, had for the most part through assents, from which others believe that things happened thus. But it is not of value in those things which are known through discursive reasoning, in which reason holds the chief place, although even in these the common consent of all is still of much value. A probable argument, therefore, is always drawn from human authority; and the more there are who testify to something, the more efficacious the argument that is deduced. Negatively, however, one must not argue from human authority, as if it were proved that a thing is not so because it is related by no one: because it is not necessary that all things have been written.

Locus 18. & 19. ab Oppositis, & Repugnantibus seu Disparatis.

Place 18 and 19, from Opposites, and from Repugnants or Disparates.
