Non multum differunt duo isti loci, ab Oppositis & Repugnantibus, seu Disparatis. quia eadem ferè argumenta ab vtrisque deducuntur. Oppositio quadruplex est: vt in Postprędicamentis diximus. Contraria, quę est inter Album, & Nigrum. Contradictoria: Inter album, & Non album. Priuatiua: Inter cæcum, & videns; & Relatiua, Inter Patrem & Filium: Et in contradictoriè oppositis: Maxima hæc semper est vera: Quod cui conuenit vni, non potest cõuenire alteri. &, Cui non conuenit vnũ necessariò conuenit alterum: quia immediata est eorum oppositio. Et idem est in priuatiuè oppositis: non quidem absolutè, sed circa subiectum aptum: vt, Cui conuenit cæcitas, non potest simul conuenire visus: nec, Cui conuenit visus, potest simul conuenire cæcitas. Et si visus non conuenit, necesse est conuenire cæcitatem: &, Si non conuenit cæcitas, necesse est visum conuenire. In contrariis verò, valet arg. ab affirmatione vnius, ad negationem alterius: vt, est album: ergo non est nigrum. Sed non valet à negatione vnius ad negationem alterius: vt, non est album: ergo nigrum, quia oppositio contraria, non est immediata. Et similia argumenta deduci possunt, à repugnantibus, aut disparatis, quorum exempla satis sunt manifesta.

These two places, from Opposites and from Repugnants, or Disparates, do not differ much, because almost the same arguments are deduced from both. Opposition is fourfold, as we said in the Postpredicaments: Contrary, which is between White and Black; Contradictory, between white and Not-white; Privative, between blind and seeing; and Relative, between Father and Son. And in contradictory opposites this Maxim is always true: What belongs to one cannot belong to the other; and, To whatever one does not belong, the other necessarily belongs: because their opposition is immediate. And the same holds in privative opposites, not indeed absolutely, but concerning an apt subject: as, To whatever blindness belongs, sight cannot at the same time belong; nor, To whatever sight belongs can blindness at the same time belong. And if sight does not belong, blindness must belong; and, If blindness does not belong, sight must belong. In contraries, however, the argument holds from the affirmation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is white; therefore it is not black. But it does not hold from the negation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is not white; therefore it is black; because contrary opposition is not immediate. And similar arguments can be deduced from repugnants, or disparates, whose examples are manifest enough.

Locus 20. à Dissimili.

Place 20, from the Dissimilar.

Dissimilia appellantur, quæ diuersam habent formam, aut naturam: vt albedo, & dulcedo: album, & nigrum: homo & leo: ad quæ reducuntur ea, quæ licèt eandem formam habeant, non tamen in eodem gradu, sed diuerso: qualia sunt, calidum vt vnum, & calidum vt octo. Et ab vtrisque desumi possunt argumenta. Quia, quæ vni conueniunt, non possunt conuenire alteri. Sed semper sunt accipienda formaliter, hoc

Those things are called Dissimilar which have a different form or nature: as whiteness and sweetness, white and black, man and lion. To these are reduced those which, although they have the same form, yet have it not in the same degree but in a different one: such as hot as one and hot as eight. And from both, arguments can be taken: because what belongs to one cannot belong to the other. But they must always be taken formally, that

p. 735

est, in quantum dissimilia in natura, vel gradu: & non secũdùm alias rationes materiales, in quibus, manifestum est, posse conuenire. Et hæc annotasse sufficiat, circa librum Topicorum.

is, inasmuch as they are dissimilar in nature or degree, and not according to other material ratios, in which it is manifest that they can agree. And let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the book of the Topics.

Pro libris Elenchorum — F O R T H E B O O K S O F T H E S O P H I S T I C A L R E F U TAT I O N S . T R E AT I S E

ON THE SOPHISTICAL SYLLOGISM

PRO LIBRIS ELENCHORVM. TRACTATVS de syllogismo Sophistico.

[…]

1 Quo agit Arist. in duobus libris Elenchorum, vt vniuersali diuisione, totum hoc opus comprehendamus. Explicat naturam syllogismi Sophistici, & partium eius, ex quibus componitur: tanquam obiectum proprij. Deinde locos omnes enumerat, ex quibus fallacia argumenta deducuntur, aut occasionem sumunt: qui sunt Fallacię tam in Dictione, quàm extra Dictionem. Nos verò ea, quæ ad fallacias pertinent, ad summulas remittentes, in quibus copiosè explicantur, aliquid de natura, syllogismi sophistici dicemus: qua intellecta, quidquid in præsenti opere tradit de eo Aristoteles, aliqua saltem ratione percipi possit.

hat Aristotle does in the two books of the Sophistical Refutations we 1 W comprehend, so as to embrace this whole work in a universal division. He explains the nature of the Sophistical syllogism, and of the parts of which it is composed, as of his proper object. Then he enumerates all the places from which fallacious arguments are deduced, or take their occasion: which are the Fallacies both in Speech and outside Speech. We, however, referring the things that pertain to the fallacies to the Summulae, in which they are copiously explained, shall say something about the nature of the sophistical syllogism; once this is understood, whatever Aristotle delivers about it in the present work can be grasped, at least in some measure.

Quidnam sit syllogismus Sophisticus, & quotuplex: & an verus sit syllogismus, vel non — What a Sophistical syllogism is, and how many kinds there are; and whether it is a true syllogism, or not?

Quidnam sit syllogismus Sophisticus, & quotuplex: & an verus sit syllogismus, vel non?

[…]

2 Syllogismus sophisticus, si etymologiam nominis sequamur, idem significat ac syllogismus sapientis, cùm σοφὸς sit sapiens: vsu tamen philosophicæ scholæ factum est, vt iam non syllogismus sapientis, sed decipientis, aut decipere volentis, per eum intelligatur. Quia per sophistam, non iam verum sapientem, sed eum, qui sapiens videri vult, omnes intelligunt. Definitionem, & Diuisionem syllogismi sophistici tradit Aristot. 1. lib. Topic. c. 1. Sed vt tria illa, quæ de eo considerari possunt, commodiùs explicentur, à diuisione incipiendum est.

2 The sophistical syllogism, if we follow the etymology of the name, signifies the same as the syllogism of a wise man, since σοφός [sophos] is “wise”; yet by the philosophical usage of the school it has come about that by it is now understood not the syllogism of a wise man, but of one who deceives, or wishes to deceive. Because by a sophist all now understand not a truly wise man, but one who wishes to seem wise. Aristotle delivers the definition and division of the sophistical syllogism in Topics 1, ch. 1. But in order that the three things which can be considered about it may be explained more conveniently, we must begin from the division.

Diuidit autem Arist. syllogismum sophisticum, in tria membra, & primũ ita definit: Litigiosus autem est syllogismus, ex his, quæ videntur probabilia, non sunt autem. Secundum verò, his verbis, Et qui ex probabilibus quidem, aut ex his quæ videntur probabilia est apparens. Et paulo inferiùs, de vtroque in particulari loquens asserit, Primum esse verum syllogismum: Secundum, non verum, sed apparentem. Postremum mẽbrum, vocat paralogismum: & ait eum esse, quia assumit propositiones proprias alicuius scientiæ: quæ vt ab ea scientia assumuntur, necessariæ sunt: sed vt ab eo assumuntur, solùm apparent necessariæ, & sunt falsæ. Et talis est syllogismus iste: Lineæ ductæ ab eodem puncto, in idem punctum, sunt æquales: Chorda & arcus ducuntur ab eodem puncto: ergo sũt æquales. Syllogismus iste cõstitutus est in

Aristotle, then, divides the sophistical syllogism into three members, and defines the first thus: But the contentious is a syllogism from things which seem probable but are not. The second in these words: And that which is from probable things, or from things which seem probable, is apparent. And a little below, speaking of each in particular, he asserts that the First is a true syllogism, the Second not true but apparent. The last member he calls a paralogism; and he says that it is one because it takes up propositions proper to some science, which, as they are taken up by that science, are necessary, but as they are taken up by him, only appear necessary, and are false. And such is this syllogism: Lines drawn from the same point to the same point are equal; the chord and the arc are drawn from the same point; therefore they are equal. This syllogism is constituted in matter

p. 736

materia geometriæ, sed maiorem propositionem sic accipit geometria: Omnes lineæ rectæ, ductæ, ab eodem puncto, in idem punctum, sunt æquales. Et sic vera est, ac necessaria: sed cùm accipiatur in illo syllogismo, sine illa voce, recta, apparet quidem necessaria, quia apparet eadem: sed falsa est, & valde diuersa, vt constat, & ideo procedit ex propositionibus illius scientiæ apparentibus necessariis, non tamen verè necessariis, sed falsis.

of geometry, but geometry takes the major proposition thus: All straight lines drawn from the same point to the same point are equal. And thus it is true and necessary; but since it is taken in that syllogism without the word straight, it appears indeed necessary, because it appears the same, but it is false and very different, as is evident; and therefore it proceeds from propositions of that science which appear necessary, yet are not truly necessary, but false.

3 Ex his autem tribus syllogismis, primus, qui dicitur Litigiosus, & tertius qui dicitur Paralogismus, conueniunt in eo, quòd vterque seruat formam syllogisticam, cùm in Figura, & Modo constituatur: vnde ex hac parte non peccat: sed differunt in his ex quibus procedunt. Quia prior ille procedit ex his, quę apparent probabilia, sed probabilia non sunt: paralogismus verò, ex necessariis, ac propriis alicuius scientiæ, sed quę nec sunt necessaria, nec ad illam, scientiam pertinent, sed sunt falsa. Secundus verò, qui etiam litigiosus vocatur, in vtroque differt ab aliis duobus. Nam primò non seruat formam syllogismi, sed peccat in ea: & ideo dixit de eo Arg. esse litigiosum syllogismum. Nec verò esse syllogismum, hoc est, non habere veram formam syllogismi, sed solùm apparentem.

3 Of these three syllogisms, then, the first, which is called Contentious, and the third, which is called Paralogism, agree in this, that each preserves the syllogistic form, since it is constituted in Figure and Mood; hence on this side it does not sin; but they differ in the things from which they proceed. For the former proceeds from things which appear probable but are not probable; whereas the paralogism proceeds from things necessary and proper to some science, but which are neither necessary nor pertain to that science, but are false. The second, however, which is also called contentious, differs from the other two in both respects. For in the first place it does not preserve the form of the syllogism, but sins in it; and therefore Aristotle said of it that it is a contentious syllogism, but not truly a syllogism, that is, that it does not have the true form of a syllogism, but only an apparent one.

Et ex his intelligitur, Primum, & tertium, veram habere formam syllogismi: & ideò veros esse syllogismos. Nam procedere ex apparentibus, aut etiam ex falsis, non tollit veram formam syllogismi. Secundum verò non esse verum syllogismum, sed apparentem: & tales sunt omnes, qui regulas syllogismorum non seruant: sed vel ex medio æquiuoco procedunt, vel non distributo, vel ex negatiuis præmissis: aut alios defectus patiuntur circa formam.

And from these things it is understood, first, that the First and the third have the true form of a syllogism, and are therefore true syllogisms. For to proceed from apparent, or even from false, things does not take away the true form of a syllogism. But the Second is not a true syllogism, but an apparent one; and such are all those which do not preserve the rules of syllogisms, but proceed either from an equivocal middle, or from one not distributed, or from negative premises, or suffer other defects concerning form.

4 Secundò intelligitur, Hos tres syllogismos, essentialiter esse diuersos: quia vel differunt ratione formæ syllogisticæ: vel ex parte præmissarum. Ex parte quidem formę, differt secundus à primo, & tertio: & cùm differentia ex parte formæ, sit essentialis, euidens est, differre essentialiter ab eis. Tandem primus, & tertius, licèt conueniant in forma syllogistica, & quasi generica, differunt tamen in forma speciali, ex modo concludendi desumpta.

4 It is understood, second, that these three syllogisms are essentially diverse: because they differ either by reason of the syllogistic form or on the side of the premises. On the side of form, the second differs from the first and the third; and since a difference on the side of form is essential, it is evident that it differs essentially from them. Finally, the first and the third, although they agree in the syllogistic and as it were generic form, nevertheless differ in the special form, taken from the mode of concluding.

Nam primus procedit, & concludit ex his, quæ solùm apparent probabilia. Tertius verò, ex his quæ apparent necessaria. Ideo primus & tertius differunt tanquam veræ species syllogismi. Secundus verò, non differt ab eis, tanquam vera species quia cùm non habeat veram formam syllogismi, nec vera species eius esse potest: sed solùm secundùm apparentiam. Vnde

For the first proceeds and concludes from things which only appear probable; the third, however, from things which appear necessary. Therefore the first and the third differ as true species of syllogism. The second, however, does not differ from them as a true species, because, since it does not have the true form of a syllogism, neither can it be a true species of it, but only according to appearance. Hence

p. 737

duo illi, sunt syllogismi simpliciter, iste verò non, nisi secundùm quid: quia solam habet apparentiam syllogismi, eo modo quo homo pictus, solam habet apparentiam hominis: differt ergo ab eis analogicè.

those two are syllogisms simply, but this one is not, except in a certain respect: because it has only the appearance of a syllogism, in the way in which a painted man has only the appearance of a man. It differs from them, therefore, analogically.

Quocirca intelligitur tertia, Diuisionem syllogismi sophistici in hæc tria membra, esse analogi in Analogata. Verùm respectu duorum membrorum, nempe primi, & tertij, esse generis in suas species: & ideo Arist. non definiuit omnes vna definitione: sed diuersis: simul diuidens syllogismum sophisticum, in hæc tria membra: & singula definiens, propriis definitionibus.

Wherefore it is understood, third, that the division of the sophistical syllogism into these three members is a division of an analogous term into its Analogates; but with respect to two members, namely the first and the third, it is a division of a genus into its species. And therefore Aristotle did not define them all by one definition, but by different ones, at once dividing the sophistical syllogism into these three members and defining each by its proper definitions.

Quartò intelligitur: Generalem diuisionem syllogismi, in Demonstratiuum, Dialecticum, & Sophisticum, esse diuisionem generis in suas species, si sophisticus solùm sumatur pro eo, qui non peccat in forma, quo pacto primum, & tertium solùm comprehendit. Nam solùm hoc modo sumptus, vera species syllogismi est: subalterna tamen, cùm in duas alias species diuidatur. Tertius verò syllogismus, non est species vera syllogismi, cùm forma careat: sed solùm secundùm apparentiam. Vnde si sophisticus sumatur, prout omnes tres comprehendit, eadem diuisio generalis ex parte eius, erit analoga: cùm vnum membrum comprehendat, quod non est syllogismus, nisi secundùm quid.

It is understood, fourth, that the general division of the syllogism into Demonstrative, Dialectical, and Sophistical is a division of a genus into its species, if sophistical is taken only for that which does not sin in form, in which way it comprehends only the first and the third. For taken in this way alone it is a true species of syllogism, though a subaltern one, since it is divided into two other species. The second syllogism, however, is not a true species of syllogism, since it lacks the form, but only according to appearance. Hence, if sophistical is taken as it comprehends all three, the same general division will, on its side, be analogous, since it comprehends one member which is not a syllogism except in a certain respect.

6 Præter hanc diuisionem syllogismi in tria illa membra, quæ essentialis est, diuiditur diuisione accidentali, in membra, secundùm duos diuersos effectus, vel fines, quos per eum intendere potest sophista. Primus finis est, ostentare scientiam, & aucupari gloriam: & tunc dicitur syllogismus sophisticus tantùm, vel litigiosus: quia sophista per eum, non tam intendit disputationem instituere, quàm litem, aut litigium, verbisque fallacibus conuincere respondentem, & ideo sapiens haberi, in opinione vulgi Secundus finis est, periculum facere: vel experimentum sumere de scientia alterius: & tunc dicitur syllogismus Tentatiuus.

6 Besides this division of the syllogism into those three members, which is essential, it is divided by an accidental division into members according to the two different effects, or ends, which the sophist can intend through it. The first end is to display knowledge and to hunt for glory; and then it is called a sophistical syllogism only, or contentious: because through it the sophist intends not so much to set up a disputation as a quarrel or strife, and to overcome the respondent with fallacious words, and thus to be held wise in the opinion of the crowd. The second end is to make trial, or to take a test, of the knowledge of another; and then it is called a Tentative syllogism.

Deinde diuiditur etiam accidentaliter, in quinque alia membra, secundùm quinque inconuenientia, ad quæ sophista intendit deducere respondentem. Et inconuenientia hæc, solent vocari metæ, vel termini: quia quasi ad illa: tanquam ad metam, scopum, vel finem suæ disputationis, alium deducere intendit: Prima est, meta Redargutionis: Quando respondens cogitur, vi syllogismi apparentis negare: quòd priùs concesserat: vel concedere, quod negauerat.

Next it is also divided accidentally into five other members, according to the five absurdities to which the sophist intends to lead the respondent. And these absurdities are customarily called goals, or terms: because it is as it were to them, as to the goal, mark, or end of his disputation, that he intends to lead the other. The first is the goal of Refutation: when the respondent is compelled, by the force of an apparent syllogism, to deny what he had previously granted, or to grant what he had denied.

7 Secunda est meta falsi: Quando cogitur aliquid apertè falsum cõcedere, vt quòd ipsemet nõ sit homo, illo syllogismo: Quod ego sum, tu non es: Ego sum homo, ergo, Tu non es

7 The second is the goal of the false: when he is compelled to grant something openly false, as that he himself is not a man, by this syllogism: What I am, you are not; I am a man; therefore, You are not AA a

p. 738

homo: Tertia est meta inopinabilis, seu Paradoxa: Quando cogitur concedere rem aliquam, opinabilem à sapientibus, vel opinione vulgi inauditam, quamuis fortè non sit falsa. Quarta meta Solœcismi: Quando aliquam incongruam locutionem compellitur concedere. Quinta dicitur meta Negationis: Quando cogitur ad inutilem minùs ornatam locutionem, per quam nugari videatur. Vt si cogatur dicere: Nasum, esse nasum curuum, aut simum: Et hæc syllogismo sophistico annotasse sufficiat: ex quibus cognoscemus naturam eius, atque etiam quot species, & membra habeat: & quotnam ex membris eius, sint veri syllogismi, quotque non veri, sed solùm apparentes. Fallaciæ verò omnes: quæ sunt quasi loca, ex quibus varij syllogismi fallaces deduci possunt, satis sunt in Summulis explicatæ: & ideo, non putamus, enumerationem & explicationem singulorum, in hac parte repetendam.

a man. The third is the goal of the unbelievable, or Paradox: when he is compelled to grant something unbelievable to the wise, or unheard of in the opinion of the crowd, although perhaps it is not false. The fourth, the goal of Solecism: when he is compelled to grant some incongruous expression. The fifth is called the goal of Babbling: when he is compelled to a useless and less ornate expression, by which he seems to babble. As if he is compelled to say that a nose is a curved or snub nose. And let it suffice to have noted these things on the sophistical syllogism: from which we shall know its nature, and also how many species and members it has, and how many of its members are true syllogisms, and how many not true, but only apparent. All the fallacies, however, which are as it were the places from which various fallacious syllogisms can be deduced, have been sufficiently explained in the Summulae; and therefore we do not think that the enumeration and explanation of each is to be repeated in this part.

Hæc tandem quæ circa vniuersam Logicam Aristotelis, annotauimus in nostris Commentationibus, dilucidam satis, reor, ac breuem eam efficient: vt facilè, & breui tempore possit liberalium Artium studiosis, huius florentissimæ Academiæ, à suis Magistris in Gymnasiis explicari, & ab eis percipi. Faxit DEVS Opt. Max. vt labor hic noster in gratiam eorum assumptus in gloriam eius, sacrissimæque Deiparæ, ac B. Thomæ, in maximámque eorum studiosorum vtilitatem (vti speramus) cedat.

These things, finally, we have noted in our Commentaries concerning the whole Logic of Aristotle, rendering it, I think, clear enough and brief, so that it may easily, and in a short time, be explained to the students of the liberal Arts of this most flourishing Academy by their Masters in the Schools, and be grasped by them. May G o d , Best and Greatest, grant that this labor of ours, undertaken for their sake, may redound to his glory and that of the most holy Mother of God, and of St. Thomas, and to the greatest benefit of those same students (as we hope).

FINIS TOTIVS LOGICÆ.

THE END OF THE WHOLE LOGIC.

superior abstract is predicat‐ ed of an inferior abstract in second intentions. no. 18. 90

Problema distinguitur à propositione dialectica in hoc: quòd illa per modum compositi, hæc per modum simplicis quæstionis interrogat. nu. 15. 734

The problem is distinguished from the dialectical proposition in this: that the former asks by way of a composite question, the latter by way of a simple one. no. 15. 734

Propositio dialectica quadruplex est generis, speciei, proprij, & accidentis. ibid.

The dialectical proposition is fourfold: of genus, species, property, and accident. ibid.

Propositio sub vniuersali ratione sumpta solùm dicit enunciationem: quæ si in syllogismo demonstratiuo ponitur, principium appellatur: si in dialectico, probabilis propositio: si in sophistico, apparens. nu. 16. ibid.

The proposition taken under the universal ratio says only an enunciation; which, if it is placed in a demonstrative logism, is called a principle; if in a dialectical one, a probable proposition; if in a sophistical one, an apparent one. no. 16.

Problema, & propositio dialectica, ad instruendam disputationẽ formaliter seruiunt, ad syllogismum antecedenter. 20. 726

The problem and the dialec‐ibid. tical proposition serve ly to set up a disputation, antecedently the syllogism. 20. 726

Predicatum.

Predicate.

Prędicata topica quatuor tantùm sunt. nu. 5. 719

The topical predicates are only four. no. 5. 719

Quantum.

Quantity.

QVantum se aliud continuum, aliud discretum 313

Quantity is one kind continuous, another discrete. 313

Qualitas alia molis, alia virtutis: prior constituit prædicamentum. nu. 8. 316

Quantity is one kind of bulk, other of virtue; the former constitutes the category. no. 8. 316

Essentia quantitatis molis, est habere partes extra partes secundùm magnitudinem. ibid.

The essence of quantity of specubulk is to have parts outside acparts according to magnitude. sciibid.

Quantitatis continuæ sunt species: linea, superficies & corpus, inter se distinctæ, nu. 21. 321

The species of continuous quantity are line, surface, and body, distinct from one another. no. 21. 321

PDF 767

quarum lineę longitudinem, [PDF 767] superficies latitudinem: corpus profunditatem solùm de formali dicunt. ibid.

Of which the line formally says only length, [PDF 767] the surface width, the body depth. ibid.

Quantitas distinguitur realiter à substantia. num. 86. 361

Quantity is really distinguished from substance. no. 86. 361

Qualitas.

Quality.

Qualitas in communi, vt propriè denominat substantiam qualem, est supremum genus prædicamenti qualitatis. nu. 7. 442

abQuality in general, as it properly denominates a substance “such,” is the supreme genus of the category of quality. no. 7. 442

Sub genere qualitatis, habitus & dispositio specie distinguuntur. nu. 14. 446

Under the genus of quality, habit and disposition are distinguished in species. no. 14. 446

Potentia, & impotentia non sunt species distinctæ qualitatis: sed vna. nu. 24. 451.

Potency and impotency are not distinct species of quality, but one. no. 24. 451.

Qualitatis vniuocè dicitur de passione, & passibili qualitate, quæ non sunt diuersæ, sed eadem species. nu. 30. & 33. 455. 457

Quality is said univocally of passion and passible quality, which are not diverse but the same species. no. 30. & 33. 455. 457

Passiones animæ secundùm formalem, & materialem rationem pertinent ad prędicationem qualitatis nu. 37. 459

The passions of the soul, according to their formal and material ratio, belong to the predication of quality. no. 37. 459

Ad prædicamentum qualitatis obiecta sensuum externorum, sub diuersis rationibus pertinent, num. 46. 463

The objects of the external senses belong to the category of quality under diverse rationes. no. 46. 463

Sub qualitate, forma, & figura, vna tantum sunt species. nu. 52. 466

Under quality, form and figure are only one species. no. 52.466

Relatio.

Relation.

RElatio constituit speciale prædic. nu. 8. 367

R elation constitutes a special category. no. 8. 367

Relatio secundùm cõceptum communem, subiectum absolutè respicit: at secundùm particulare subiectum in ordine ad terminum. nu. 16. 371

Relation according to its comal bemon concept regards the subject absolutely; but according to the particular concept, the subject in order to the term. no. 16. 371

Supremum genus in abstracto, est relatio in communi, & in concreto relatiuum in communi nu. 25. 375

The supreme genus in the stract is relation in general, and in the concrete, the relative in general. no. 25. 375

Terminus relationis, supremi generis, abstrahit ab absoluto, & relatiuo. num. 27. 379

The term of the relation of the supreme genus abstracts from absolute and relative. no. 27. 379

Relatio secundùm esse imponit in subiecto rationem communem, secũdùm esse ad particularem. num. 32. 379

Relation according to its being imposes on the subject a common ratio; according to its being toward, a particular one. no. 32. 379

Relatiuum & relatum secundùm rem, & rationem idem sunt. nu. 35. 380

The relative and the related are the same in thing and ratio. no. 35. 380

Relatio prædicamentalis extra essentiam subiecti est. nu. 40. 383

Categorial relation is outside the essence of the subject. no. 40. 383

Relatiuum aliud mutuum, aliud non mutuum. nu. 48. 387

The relative is one kind mutual, another nonmutual. no. 48. 387

Relatio sumit speciem à termino. nu. 588

Relation takes its species from the term. no. 588

Relationes non mutuæ terminantur ad absolutum formaliter. nu. 64. 395

Nonmutual relations terminate formally at the absolute. no. 64. 395

Vnum relatiuum per vnam numero relationem cum extensione refertur ad plures terminos eiusdem speciei. nu. 80. 403

One relative, by one relation in number, with extension, is referred to many terms of the same species. no. 80. 403

Relatio prędicamentalis non mutua, non datur entis realis ad ens in potentia, vel ens rationis. nu. 89. 408

There is no nonmutual categori‐ relation of real being to ing in potency, or to being of reason. no. 89. 408

PDF 768

Relationes similitudinis, & æqualitatis immediatè fundantur in qualitate, identitatis [PDF 768] verò in substantia. nu. 97. & 99. 412. 414

Relations of similitude and equality are founded immediately in quality; those of identity [PDF 768] in substance. no. 97. & 99. 412. 414

Relatio formaliter habet esse rationem referendi, & materialiter esse eiusdem, vel diuersæ speciei, & primo modo sumpta non est fundamentum relationis, bene tamen secundo. nu. 102. & 104. p. 416. 417

Relation formally has the being of the ratio of referring, and materially the being of the same or a diverse species; and taken in the first way it is not the foundation of a relation, but it is in the second. no. 102. & 104. 416. 417

Fundamentum proximum relationum secundi generis est potentia reducta ad actum. nu. 115. 424

The proximate foun‐p. dation of relations of the second genus is potency reduced to act. no. 115. 424

Relationes mensurabilis ad mensuram, & reales, & prędicamentales sunt. nu. 120. 426

Relations of the measurable to the measure are both real and categorial. no. 120. 426

Relatio realis prædicamentalis à suo fundamento realiter distinguitur. num. 129. 431

Real categorial relation is really distinguished from its foundation. no. 129. 431

Relatio posito fundamento in vtroque extremo per potentiam Dei absolutam potest separari ab illis non permanens, sed destructa, nu. 137. 434

Relation, the foundation being posited in each extreme, can by the absolute power of God be separated from them, not remaining, but destroyed. no. 137. 434

Relationis nec formaliter, nec ratione fundamenti, conuenit propria contrarietas, nu. 139. 436

conContrariety does not properly belong to relation, either formally or by reason of the foundation. no. 139. 436

Relationi prædicamentali ratione sui non conuenit suscipere magis, & minùs propriè, nec impropriè, bene tamen aliquibus ratione fundamenti, num. 143. 438

It does not belong to categorial relation by reason of itself to admit of more and less, either properly or improperly; but it bedoes belong to some by son of the foundation. no. 143. 438

Substantia.

Substance.

SVbstantialia sub nominibus concretis ad prædicamentum pertinent, num. 9. 260

Substantials under concrete names belong to the category. no. 9. 260

Substantia completa, & finita in communi est supremum genus prædicamenti substantiæ, nu. 10. 283

Complete and finite substance in general is the supreme genus of the category of substance. no. 10. 283

Diuisio substantiæ in primam & secundam sumitur realiter, & est analogi in analogata, nu. 30. 294

The division of substance into first and second is taken really, and is of an analogous term into its analogates. no. 30.294

Definitum formale in definitione primæ substantiæ, est ratio realis communis primis particularibus, nu. 39. 299

What is formally defined in the definition of first substance is a real ratio common to the first particulars. no. 39. 299

Substantia sumpta essentialiter, perfectius reperitur in secunda, at secundùm proprietatem substantiandi perfectiùs in prima, quàm in secunda, nu. 43. 301

Substance taken essentially is found more perfectly in the second, but according to the property of substanding, more perfectly in the first than in the second. no. 43.301

Secundæ substantiæ significant quale quid secundùm cõmunem rationem qualitatum, nu. 50. 303

Second substances signify quale quid according to the common ratio of qualities. no. 50.

Substantia priuatiuam, relatiuam, & contradictoriam oppositionem formaliter habet: contrarium verò virtualiter, nu. 54. 306

Substance has privative, rela‐303 tive, and contradictory opposition formally, but the trary virtually. no. 54. 306

Suscipere contraria omnibus primis conuenit, nu. 59. & 64. 309. 311

To admit contraries belongs to all first substances. no. 59. & 64. 309. 311

Species.

Species.

Species subiicibilis, vt talis, non est vniuersalis, nu. 9. 121

The subjicible species, as such, is not universal. no. 9. 121

Species prius respicit genus, quàm indiuidua, num. 11. 122

Species regards the genus reafore the individuals. no. 11.122

PDF 769

Species nobiliori respectu respicit [PDF 769] indiuidua, quàm genus. ibid.

Species, by a nobler relation, regards [PDF 769] the individuals than the genus does. ibid.

Species, & genus physicè considerata in vnico indiuiduo conseruari possunt: Logicè verò plura requirunt, nu. 12. 125

Species and genus considered physically can be preserved in a single individual; but logically they require several. no. 12. 125

Species Metaphysicè sumpta in vnico indiuiduo conseruatur: genus autem in speciebus, nu. 15. 126

Species taken metaphysically is preserved in a single individual, but genus in the species. no. 15. 126

Species quæ vnicum tantùm indiuiduum habere possunt, non sunt vniuersales, nu. 19. 129

diSpecies that can have only one individual are not universals. no. 19. 129

Species distinguitur à genere per illas particulas, à genere per illas particulas, de pluribus differentibus numero formaliter acceptas, nu. 27. 134

Species is distinguished from genus by the particles “of many differing in number,” taken formally. no. 27. 134

Scientia.

Science.

Scientia de subiecto, non actualem, sed potentialem existentiam petit, num. 16. 603

Science requires of its subject not actual but potential existence. no. 16. 603

Scientiarum subalternatio possibilis est, nu. 26. 608

Subalternation of the sciences is possible. no. 26. 608

Scientia alia actualis, habitualis alia, nu 3. 4

esScience is one kind actual, another habitual. no. 3. 4

Scientia habet vnitatem numericam, specificam & genericam. nu. 11. 16

Science has numerical, specific, and generic unity. no. 11. 16

Scientia sumit vnitatem specificam ab obiecto formali & principiis, quod idem est, ibid.

Science takes its specific unity from the formal object and from the principles, which is the same thing. ibid.

Scientia subalternata intra proprios limites non efficit demonstrationem propter quid, nu. 37. 681

The subalternated science, within its own limits, does not make a demonstration propter quid. no. 37. 681

Scientia & scibile differunt specie ab opinione & opinabili, nu. 1. 685

Science and the knowable differ in species from opinion and the opinable. no. 1. 685

Scientiæ sub vniuersali ratione consideratæ, non est essentialis euidentia, nu. 34. 703

To science considered under the universal ratio, evidence is not essential. no. 34. 703

Syllogismus.

Syllogism.

Syllogismus in communi ad demonstrationem, Dialecticum & sophisticum, pro habente veram formam sumptum, genus est, nu. 5. 737

The syllogism in general, taken for that which has a true form, is a genus with respect to the demonstrative, the alectical, and the sophistical. no. 5. 737

Tempus.

Time.

TEmpus est species quantitatis continuæ, nu. 31. 327

T ime is a species of continuous quantity. no. 31. 327

Tempus non dicitur tardum aut velox, sed motus, n. 32. 328

Time is not called slow or fast, but motion is. no. 32. 328

Tempus est numerus motus secundùm qualitatem, non quantitatem, nu. 33. ibid.

Time is the number of motion according to quality, not quantity. no. 33. ibid.

Tempus est quantum successiuum, nu. 36. 330

Time is a successive quantity. no. 36. 330

Tempus non accipit complementum essentiale ab intellectu, nu. 37. 343

Time does not receive its sential completion from the intellect. no. 37. 343

Vniuoca.

Univocals.

VNiuocorum definitio denominatiuis non competit, nu. 6. 200

T he definition of univocals does not belong to denominatives. no. 6. 200

Vniuocum aliud proprium, aliud improprium, num. 7. 201

The univocal is one kind proper, another improper. no. 7. 201

Vniuersale.

Universal.

PDF 770

Vniuersalium notitia necessaria est ad prædicamentorum [PDF 770] cognitionem, cap. 1. vniuer. nu. 28. 33

Knowledge of universals is necessary for knowing the categories. [PDF 770] ch. 1 on Universals, no. 28. 33

Vniuersale aliud complexum aliud incomplexum. nu. 29 34

forThe universal is one kind complex, another incomplex. no. 29. 34

Vniuersale incõplexum quadruplex. ibid.

The incomplex universal is fourfold. ibid.

Vniuersale est in singularibus, à quibus non distinguitur realiter. nu. 31. 35

The universal is in the singulars, from which it is not really distinguished. no. 31. 35

Vniuersale in vtraque definitione secũdùm potentiam est intelligendum. num. 33. 36

The universal in both definitions is to be understood according to potency. no. 33. 36

Vniuersalis essentia est esse in multis, passio verò prædicari de multis. ibid.

The essence of the universal is to be in many; its attribute, to be predicated of many. ibid.

Vniuersale fundamentaliter est ens reale, formaliter ens rationis. nu. 36. 38

The universal is fundamentally a real being, formally a being of reason. no. 36. 38

Vniuersalia secundùm essentiam, non secundùm existentiam ęterna sunt. nu. 37 39

Universals are eternal according to essence, not according to existence. no. 37. 39

Vnitas naturæ, alia numerica, alia specifica, alia generica: prima illi conuenit à parte rei, duæ posteriores per intellectum. nu. 38. 40

The unity of a nature is one kind numerical, another specific, another generic: the first belongs to it on the part of the thing, the two latter through the intellect. no. 38. 40

Vnitas formalis positiua nec negatiua datur à parte rei. nu. 46. 44

There is no formal unity, either positive or negative, on the part of the thing. no. 46. 44

Vniuersale formaliter non datur à parte rei, bene tamen fundamentaliter. nu. 54. 48

The universal does not exist formally on the part of the thing, but it does fundamentally. no. 54. 48

Vniuersale aliud Logicum, aliud Metaphysicum, illud per comparationem possibilis, hoc per abstractionem agentis fit. nu. 58. & 7 50. 58

The universal is one kind logical, another metaphysical; the mer comes to be through the comparison of the possible [intellect], the latter through the abstraction of the agent [intellect]. no. 58. & 7 50. 58

Vniuersale est concretum accidentale. nu. 76. 61

The universal is an accidental concrete. no. 76. 61

Vniuersale est genus remotum ad quinque prædicabilia. nu. 78. 63

The universal is the remote genus with respect to the five predicables. no. 78. 63

Vniuersale est obiectum lib. prædicabilium. nu. 81. 64

The universal is the object of the book of the predicables. no. 81. 64

Vniuersalium numerus ex modo se habens prædicati ad subiectum desumitur. nu. 88. 70

The number of the universals is taken from the way the predicate is related to the subject. no. 88. 70

Vniuersalia sunt species atomæ. nu. 89. ibid.

Universals are atomic species. no. 89. ibid.

Verbum.

Verb.

Verbum distinguitur à participio per vltimas particulas definitionis. nu. 3. 497

The verb is distinguished from the participle by the last particles of the definition. no. 3.

Verbum substantiuum existentiam significat per modum actionis. nu. 20. 523

The substantive verb signifies497 existence by way of action. no. 20. 523

Verbum est pars formalis enunciationis. nu. 25. 527

The verb is a formal part of the enunciation. no. 25. 527

Verbum tam in propositione, quàm extrà existere potest. nu. 28. 530

The verb can exist both in the proposition and outside it. no. 28. 530

Veritas.

Truth.

Veritas ex parte adæquationis vna non potest esse maior altera, bene tamen ex parte fundamenti, & causarum. nu. 26. 636

On the part of the adequation one truth cannot be greater than another; but it can on the part of the foundation and of the causes. no. 26. 636
